## Volume front matter

### Series title page

# Complete Course of the Fathers

## Or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

Of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which places of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others, if one takes into account the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the low price; above all, this collection is one, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works formerly scattered here and there, from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, under the direction of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrologia has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The 120 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the 130 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## Letter One. Anselm to the monks of Bec

### Concerning his election as archbishop of Canterbury, despite his utmost resistance, and his urging them to consent to that election

[Note: Collated, like the following letters, with one manuscript copy belonging to the Victorines, bound in Codex Ef. 20.]

### 362

To his most beloved and most desired lords, brothers and sons, the servants of God residing at Bec: Brother Anselm, their own in heart after God: may they rejoice always under the direction and consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Whatever you send, whether written or spoken collectively or individually, out of the affection of your hearts, to your most beloved and most desired brother, and whatever neither tongue can express nor pen write, has all been openly and clearly written in my heart. Moreover, many other things arising from my affection and understanding—would that they were similarly written and expressed in your hearts. There, namely, in my inmost being, there I read and reread them, turn them over and over, frequently before God. He himself sees within and without with what affection I do this. My tears, my voices, and the groans issuing from the sighing of my heart bear witness—such as I do not remember ever having come from me in that sorrow before the day on which that grievous lot of the archbishopric of Canterbury seemed to have fallen upon me.

I think that these voices and groans were not feigned by any contrivance, but that swords of sorrow, piercing my soul, forced them out and still force out my anguished cries. Those who looked upon my face that day could not have failed to know this, when bishops, abbots, and other prelates dragged me, protesting and objecting, to the church; so that it might have seemed doubtful whether the sane were dragging the insane or the insane the sane—except that they were singing, while I, more like a dead man than a living one in color, grew pale with stupor and grief.

And those who later that same day heard me mourning in an unusual manner, with grief surpassing reason, when I was at last able to think intently both of your affection and of the burden imposed upon my weakness, came running from afar. Seeing me, they feared that I was about to lose either my life or my senses. Because of this fear they sprinkled me with holy water and offered it to me to drink.

Perhaps I ought to be ashamed that the wounds of sorrow overcame—and still overcome—my soul, wholly intent on being torn away from your souls and on its own grave danger, to such a degree that it often bears deep groans amid streaming tears. But certainly I am not ashamed to confess that the fear of God and the love of human beings, especially your love, wounded it and continue to wound it in this way.

All these things bear witness to my conscience: with what desire and with what eagerness I awaited the dignity and burden of the archbishopric, and with what joy I receive it. If some suspect otherwise of me than my conscience judges concerning itself before God, I am comforted because it ought to matter little to me to be judged by them or by the human day. We shall pass through this life amid evil report and good report, as deceivers and truthful, as unknown and known; provided only that my conscience does not accuse me before God.

Until now I resisted this election—or rather this violence—concerning me, insofar as I could, while preserving the truth. But now, whether I wish it or not, I am compelled to confess that each day the judgments of God resist my effort more and more, so that I now see no way at all to escape them—not without grave bodily and spiritual harm on both sides, and not without God’s anger—nor to hinder, either for myself or anyone else, the intention that has been formed.

Therefore, overcome now not so much by human as by divine violence—for against God there is neither prudence nor strength—I understand that I ought to use this counsel alone: after I have prayed and striven as much as I could that, if possible, this cup might pass from me and that I might not drink it, and after seeing my prayer rejected and my effort broken, I shall now say to God: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

For since I fear God on both sides, and love nothing except God and human beings for God’s sake, I think nothing safer for me in so dangerous a matter than to set aside my own judgment and will and commit myself wholly to God’s judgment and will.

Although in this matter it is exceedingly difficult for me to give, and for you to accept, counsel that is contrary to my affection and yours, nevertheless, because both you and I belong more to God than I belong to you or you to me—for whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s (Romans 14:8)—I do not dare, in God’s cause and in so great a necessity, whatever people may suspect, to withhold my counsel from those entrusted to me for consultation before God.

I therefore counsel my most beloved friends that no consideration should make you stubbornly oppose God’s ordinance, because “to refuse to acquiesce is like the sin of divination” (1 Samuel 15:23), and “it is exceedingly hard to kick against the goad of God” (Acts 9:5). For this matter has unmistakably been brought to this point by God’s judgment, so that it is necessary either that I serve and benefit you and many others, if God deigns to work some good through me, or that I benefit no one at all—not myself, not you, and not others—not because the will is lacking, but because the power is lacking.

If, because of your stubbornness, this should happen, you will cause my old age to be spent and to fail in inconsolable sadness, because of the great and manifold evils that will follow from it. These will rightly seem attributable both to me and to you, even to those who do not now foresee them.

For if you knew how many evils this delay alone has already inflicted upon bodies and souls, and how execrable that delay is, together with those through whom it occurs, to the better and wiser people and likewise to the people of England, I think that you too—if you are not inhuman—would execrate the same delay.

Perhaps what I say seems strange to you. Many who do not see me inwardly, and who are rash in judging the consciences of others, which they do not know, will judge something perverse about me because I speak to you in this way about the matter. But I speak before God, to whom I reveal my way, and I hope in him that he himself will act (Psalm 36:5), because my conscience does not accuse me before him of being drawn to these words by desire for earthly riches or exalted rank.

If anyone henceforth thinks otherwise about me, I believe he will be against the truth, and God will be my witness against him.

Farewell; and may the Lord, who directs the meek in judgment and teaches his ways not to the rigid but to the gentle (Psalm 24:9), direct your thoughts and wills in judging this matter.

# Letter Two. Osbern to Anselm

### He advises him humbly to undertake the burden of the archbishopric of Canterbury

To the most holy lord, the most beloved elect archbishop of the English, Anselm: his servant, as he has always been and always desires to be, and his son and brother, Osbern; may he be guided by right counsels, so that he may merit the favor of God, who gives right counsels.

Since I know you, most beloved lord, to be exceedingly learned in every knowledge of truth, it is very strange that in this one matter all knowledge of discerning the truth should have fled from you, so that you are able to remain ignorant of what pleases God in the judgment that the whole holy Church has pronounced concerning you.

Or if your mind inclines especially to the opinion that you alone should strive to displease God in what the universal election—or that of all, or certainly of the very great majority, and of the wisest among them—proclaims to be pleasing to God, then, most precious lord, it must be feared that you may appear to wish to seem better and holier than all other people, while attempting to defend as more rightly understood by you what they understand most rightly.

To speak, then, with the love I bear you, which I cannot offend, either you will confess yourself better than everyone—which we do not believe—since to you alone has been revealed what it was not lawful to reveal to the whole Church of the English; or you must do what the universal Church of the English advises: namely, that you not refuse to accept the primacy of the pontifical mitre among the blessed apostles.

But perhaps you are waiting for God to prove what he has begun through greater delays. I would not dare to say this, because I know you to be most wise; but I fear that someone seeking such things may be answered indirectly: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4:7).

For what more remarkable sign could God have shown for choosing you than this: that, for your promotion, a king renowned for his victories and feared by all for his severity should have taken to his bed and fallen ill to the point of death, while, once you had been advanced, he immediately breathed again, recovered, and was transformed from savage and brutal into exceedingly gentle and mild?

What, I ask, could be sweeter in its effect or more outstanding as a sign of innocence than this: that you were violently dragged before the sick man’s bed; that the right hand of others was shamelessly pulled from your bosom, while your left hand—lest it help your sister—was held fast; that, with the other fingers stubbornly closed, a staff was cruelly thrust between your thumb and index finger; and that afterward, with your whole body lifted from the ground, you were carried to the church in episcopal arms, where, while you were still protesting and resisting with the utmost persistence, the *Te Deum laudamus* was sung?

What, I ask, could be more magnificent for divine praise or more gratifying for human spectacle than that, at your election, with all the afflictions of the past season excluded, everything hastened toward the recovery of its rightful possession as though toward a jubilee’s completion, while those bound for military service returned to the open, prisoners to the light, captives to freedom, and those oppressed by the harshest violence of the tax collectors returned to uprightness?

All these things speak of you, serve you, and are ascribed to your merits.

If all these divine caresses have not stirred you to consent, know assuredly that the supremely just Judge will deal with you in strict retribution and will set before you on the day of the final judgment:

“O man, nourished at my breasts, enriched by my virtues, enlightened by my teachings, exalted by my honors, what burden did I impose upon you, that you fled from me as your teacher, despised me as your adviser, and cast off with your head held high the yoke I imposed? Was it not better to have contributed nothing of yours to me than cruelly to have taken away what was mine? Was it not clear that through your negligence what had not been brought to me through your diligence was taken away? Why did you not consider that you had killed countless thousands of people while wishing to care for the salvation of a few?

“Behold my bride, the holy Church of Canterbury, sanctified from the beginning by the blessing of my apostle Peter, nobly founded through the devoted labor of the most devoted Gregory, and always endowed with the singular privilege of the holy Boniface, Honoratus, Vitalian, Agatho, and the other orthodox Fathers. To her, without prejudice to the authority of the Roman and apostolic See, the churches of all the surrounding regions were accustomed, in their oppressions, to flee and to seek and receive from her the means of defending their liberty.

“Behold her, reduced to such utter refuse in everyone’s eyes and trampled under the feet of all who pass by, unable not only to restore to others the rights of their lost liberty but even to preserve her own rights inviolate for any length of time.

“The men whom I appointed to guard her, from whom I received the assurance that her integrity would be preserved, not only prepared no defense for her against others eager for corruption, but themselves plotted the most disgraceful business of corruption.

“When she protested and cried out, mindful of how dearly she had been acquired, how she had been bound by laws, and finally how she had been endowed with gifts, they seized the garments of her ornaments and left her naked, for sale, and full of shame.

“Then the great throng of her sons cried out—the sons whom she herself had borne to me in the washing of a second birth and had tenderly nourished within the bosom of holy love—desiring to remedy their mother’s shame and cover her nakedness with an outspread veil.

“Behold, those who had afflicted their mother rage against her sons with even greater torments: one is torn away from her breasts and mangled by a pitiable slaughter; another is oppressed by a rusting, shrill clangor; another inhabits dark hiding places; another laments long exiles.

“And what was the chief crime of all: while adulterous men, by criminal cunning, wished to denounce the innocent as guilty, they brought the mother and her offspring into such hatred among earthly powers that anyone who killed them would think he had rendered service to God.

“But the final and, as it were, crowning outrage of the whole evil was this: had its root been brought into the light of this sun, not only would a Christian shudder at it, but every pagan, Jew, and heretic would also execrate it.

“Unable any longer to endure such calamity of my bride, I chose you, Anselm, from the whole fullness of humanity, and presented you as a friend of the bridegroom to show zeal on my behalf. I gave you teaching and bestowed virtue upon you. I foretold it through oracles and confirmed it through miracles. Yet you preferred to me the count of Normandy—a worm before God, a mortal before the living one, a narrow solitary nest before the breadth of the English.

“Did it escape your mind that the apostle Peter was enthroned at Antioch and yet did not yield to the sobbing of anyone, lest he encounter the Romans?”

[Editorial note: Saint Anselm, in Letter 7 below, expressly says that Saint Peter migrated to Rome. This, however, is still unknown to our German and English Gnostics. It is certainly lamentable that men more sharp-eyed than Argus and yet blinder in this matter than moles have not yet seen it in Irenaeus, Book VIII, chapters 1 and 3; Tertullian, *On Baptism* and *On the Prescription of Heretics*; Ignatius, *To Mary*; Cassiodorus; Eusebius of Caesarea, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, in Rufinus’s translation, chapters 14, 15, and 25; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 27; Ambrose, Book III of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*; Optatus of Milevis, Book II; Augustine, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, heresy 1; *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book II, chapter 51; and many others, whom I willingly pass over in silence lest their blindness become still more manifest.

Who, then, would not laugh with more than Democritean laughter at that ridiculous thesis debated by the Germans—and by those Lutherans—in the year 1520: whether Peter had been in Rome? It is noted in the marginal scholion to Abbot Usperg, where he speaks of Peter. The negative side of that proposition is shamelessly and, as usual, falsely defended by John Bale, an Englishman, Sudolvogius, a stranger among the Germans—as he boasts, and for this reason joined by me to the German theologasters—in the profession of Christ (thus falsely disguising Antichrist under the beautiful name of Christ).

These are his very words, in the first century of the *British Scriptures*, page 16, Basel edition, 1557:

“Since Peter, by the command and instruction of Christ the Lord, was an apostle of the circumcision (Galatians 2), it was certainly not fitting that, abandoning the flock of the Jews, he should sit for twenty-five years—as the papists dream—among the uncircumcised Gentiles at Rome, or rule them after the manner of Gentile kings. Therefore he remained in Judaea and the neighboring regions, bound by Christ’s command, preaching in the coastal cities the gospel of the kingdom of God; and the miracles that God performed through him themselves bear witness to this. For at Lydda he restored Aeneas the paralytic to health; at Joppa he raised Tabitha from the dead. At Caesarea he baptized Cornelius the centurion and did many other things. All these things show that he neither sat nor died at Rome. Hence Baptista Mantuanus, in Book VI of the *Fasti*:

> After the death of Christ, after his return  
> to heaven, he is said to have spent twice seven years  
> among the Assyrian cities, troubling their evil gods  
> with grievous war.  
>   
> Then, entering the seas and carried around  
> by the long winding of the roads, he turned his journey  
> toward the Bithynian shores, traversing Cappadocia,  
> Galatia, and Pontus;  
>   
> he taught Christ to all the kingdoms that were there,  
> whose inhabitants were Jewish by origin,  
> and drew them back from their ancient practice.

“Jerome and Lyra, too, commenting on Christ’s words, ‘Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men,’ and so forth, assert that Peter was crucified by the Jews at Jerusalem; and this agrees most aptly with those words.”

Thus Bale. But let us see whether these things are so.

First of all, Christ did not confine the gospel entrusted to Peter within the walls of the Jewish Church in such a way that it could not reach the ears of the Gentiles. On the contrary, in Acts 10, through a square vessel brought down from heaven and filled with impure animals, Peter was commanded to preach the gospel even to the Gentiles. Later, in their hearing, he declared that God is not a respecter of persons, but that in every nation whoever is righteous is pleasing to him, as the one who rules over all. Therefore Luke says there, near the end of chapter 10:

“Those of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations.”

But Mantuanus, whom Bale cites, does not contain even a syllable about Peter’s death or papacy, much less deny it. Moreover, you do not find any of the cities he lists in Palestine; this is a most weighty argument that Peter left Judaea in order to teach the uncircumcised Gentiles, contrary to Bale’s opinion and judgment. For just as by divine command he taught the Jews for a time, so afterward, by the same command, he taught the Gentiles.

That Mantuanus understood and wrote that Saint Peter was killed at Rome is clear from Book I of *On the Contest of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite*. Describing Dionysius as having come to Rome with great effort in order to see his teacher Saint Paul, he says:

> But that labor was cut short by an adverse event,  
> for only a few days, alas, was it permitted  
> to enjoy the teacher and his holy speech,  
> because fate suddenly buried  
> the two greatest lights of the world, newly arisen.  
>   
> He saw Peter drawing his final sighs  
> from the lofty wood—  
> alas, a deed horrible to behold!

And again, in Book X of the *Fasti*, he sings of the same Dionysius:

> He came to Rome across the seas after Peter’s death,  
> after Paul’s passing, at the time when  
> Roman Clement held Peter’s little boat, and so forth.

But let us defeat Bale with his own weapons. For in the cited Book VI of the *Fasti*—observe a man more deceitful than deceit itself—Mantuanus says, speaking of Peter:

> Having suffered many dangers by sea and land, he came  
> to the Romulean city, mistress of the world  
> and mighty in its affairs,  
> where the beginnings of the eternal kingdom lay.

The passage of Jerome that was indicated, and that I have copied out in full and faithfully, will once more expose Bale as more mendacious even than the Cretans.

Jerome, in Book IV of his *Commentary on Matthew*, commenting on chapter 23 and explaining the Evangelist’s words, “And some of them you will kill, and crucify, and scourge,” adds that the disciples of Christ received various gifts:

“Some,” he says, “were prophets, who foretold what was to come; others were wise men, who knew how they ought to deliver their speech; others were scribes, most learned in the law. Of these, Stephen was stoned, Paul was killed, Peter was crucified, the disciples were scourged in the Acts of the Apostles, and they persecuted them, driving them from city to city, expelling them from Judaea so that they might migrate to the people of the Gentiles.”

Thus Jerome, who did not write even a word about Peter being crucified in Judaea. Rather, if we examine his words exactly, we find that Peter was expelled from Judaea and thus migrated to the Gentiles.

If anyone, more brazen in the name of Bale, denies this, I shall rightly prove that Saint Paul also was killed in Judaea—despite the protests of the most ancient and reliable historians. The Acts of the Apostles relates that Stephen was buried beneath a hailstorm of stones. But let judgment be deferred not to me or to Bale, but to Jerome himself, who seems to have provoked this dispute.

In *On Illustrious Men* he says:

“Simon Peter, chief of the apostles, after the episcopate of the Church of Antioch, and in the second year of Claudius, went to Rome to overthrow Simon Magus, and there held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero.”

Again, to Pope Damasus:

“I judged that I ought to consult the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth.”

And shortly afterward:

“I speak with the successor of the fisherman and the disciple of the cross. Following no one first except Christ, I am joined in communion to your blessedness—that is, to the chair of Peter. I know that the Church was built upon that rock.”

In his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, on the very chapter from which Bale establishes Peter’s permanent residence in Judaea, Saint Jerome observes that many things are lacking in the history of the Acts of the Apostles and adds the final point, saying:

“Finally, we have received that Peter was the first bishop of the Church of Antioch and was thereafter transferred to Rome, a fact that Luke entirely omitted.”

It is enough for me to cite from the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers a testimony not to be rejected, where Jerome says: “Clement, the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter,” and so forth.

I pass over Lyra, because he says the same things as Jerome, content to have exposed the shameless malice of Bale.]

Why, then, did it escape you that Paul’s head was drenched with the tears of the Milesians and Ephesians, and yet he was not prevented from plowing the sea that was to carry him to foreign nations? I ask you, wisest of men: if a judge were to attack you with such arguments, would you not, pressed by the weight of reason, cry out, “Spare me, judge!”?

Now, if you should say that the Church to which you have recently been appointed is not so highly esteemed by God, although you acknowledge its great merit, we know that Archbishop Laurence was scourged with many blows by the aforesaid apostle because, terrified by fear of the pagans, he had fled and attempted to abandon that same Church while it was still inexperienced in receiving the faith.

The same apostle appeared in splendor to the blessed confessor of Christ, Dunstan, together with his fellow apostles Paul and Andrew. Handing him a sword inscribed with the word of God, he prefigured that he would become, as later happened, the pontiff of that same Church.

If, then, such great favor from Christ and the apostles is said to have existed toward that same Church from the beginning, you must take great care, possessing the most holy knowledge, lest you refuse to share in that favor, since you have not been presented as one favored by private grace, nor as a hireling, nor as a disciple of Simon, but as one whom divine election has called and apostolic instruction has formed.

Moreover, although you have no need of an adviser, I shall nevertheless dare, out of affection, to advise you to do nothing rashly, and not to act too much on the counsel of those who are foreign to us, whether the matter concerns your consecration or the granting or changing of the Church’s affairs. For we know that your most holy predecessor ordered many things at the beginning of his arrival which afterward displeased him throughout the whole of his tenure.

There are many who have always labored for the destruction of the Church and who now think they will reign above all, saying that you will always be dealing with God and will not care for the Church’s affairs—as though caring for the Church’s affairs were not dealing with God. But, with God’s help, when they have come to know you as I do, I think they will speak and think otherwise.

Now I repeat with all the marrow of my being what I promised when I sent greetings: I pray God that you may be so guided by right counsels that you may merit the favor of God, who gives right counsels, most holy and most wise lord, and in spirit most gentle beyond all others.

# Letter Three. Bishop Gundulf to the monks of Bec

### That they should not grieve over having Anselm taken from them as abbot

Gundulf, by the grace of God bishop of Rochester, sends greetings and faithful prayers to his most beloved lords and friends, the servants of God residing at Bec.

Most beloved, your affection knows how long the English Church has been deprived and bereft of its own shepherd, and desolated by every paternal consolation. But God, hearing with compassion the weeping of orphans, the groans and sighs of widows that have lasted so long, and also the prayers of his faithful, has at last deigned to visit and console it by his grace.

For through his inexpressible power at work, our Lord the king of the English, at the counsel and request of his princes and at the petition and election of the clergy and people, has given Lord Abbot Anselm the governance of the Church of Canterbury. There is no doubt that this was done through God’s most loving operation and ordinance.

Therefore we humbly command and earnestly beg you, dearest brothers, that, laying aside all sadness or indignation of heart, if any exists, you in no way resist the divine will, operation, and election of good men, but, giving thanks to God for what has happened, grant it with joy and good will.

There is also another matter that ought not to remain hidden from you. This affair may perhaps be hindered for a time, but it cannot in any way remain unresolved altogether. For I tell you truly: knowledge and counsel concerning this matter have advanced greatly, and without doubt have already reached the apostolic See. Therefore use wise counsel and, out of charity, do without delay what you will eventually do without hesitation.

Farewell.

[Column 0018A]

# Letter Four. Anselm to the monks of Bec

### That they should write to Anselm himself and to the king that they willingly consent to his election as archbishop of Canterbury

To his most beloved lords, brothers, and sons, the monks of Bec: their most beloved brother Anselm, their abbot: may they rejoice in the continual protection and consolation of God.

Textual notes and variant readings:

- [Col. 0009C] The preceding letter, like those following, was collated with manuscript copy 1 of the Victorines, bound in Codex Ef. 20.
- [Col. 0009C] “Grievous archbishopric”: the manuscript reads “more grievous archbishopric.”
- [Col. 0009C] “My soul”: the manuscript reads *anima mea* (“my soul,” nominative).
- [Col. 0009C] “Piercing”: the manuscript reads *penetrantis* (“of one piercing”).
- [Col. 0009C] “Protesting and objecting”: the manuscript reads “protesting and contradicting.”
- [Col. 0009C] “As deceivers”: the manuscript reads “and deceivers.”
- [Col. 0009C] “Does not accuse”: the manuscript reads “excuses.”
- [Col. 0011D] “On both sides”: the manuscript has the defective form *utrmque*.
- [Col. 0011D] “For you to accept”: the manuscript reads “and for you to accept.”
- [Col. 0011D] “Contrary to my”: the manuscript reads “concerning my.”
- [Col. 0011D] “God deigns”: the manuscript reads “deigns.”
- [Col. 0011D] “Would execrate”: the manuscript reads “you execrate.”
- [Col. 0011D] “Not to the rigid”: the manuscript reads “not to the rigid [feminine].”
- [Col. 0011D] “Universal Church of the English”: the manuscript reads “universal Church.”
- [Col. 0011D] “Hastened”: the manuscript reads “ran together.”
- [Col. 0013C] “On the day of the final judgment”: the manuscript reads “on the day of judgment.”
- [Col. 0011D] “The right hand of others was shamelessly pulled from your bosom, while your left hand … was held fast; that, with the other fingers stubbornly closed, a staff was cruelly thrust”: the manuscript reads, “pulled out; the left hand, lest it help the sister, was firmly held; the staff …,” preserving a different punctuation and arrangement.
- [Col. 0013C] “Did you not consider”: the manuscript reads “will you not consider.”
- [Col. 0013C] “Boniface, Honoratus, Vitalian, Agatho”: the manuscript reads “Boniface, Honorarius, Agatho.”
- [Col. 0013C] “Defending”: the manuscript reads “holding.”
- [Col. 0013C] “Rights”: the manuscript reads “care.”
- [Col. 0013C] “Bound by laws”: the manuscript reads “joined by laws.”
- [Col. 0013C] “And finally”: the manuscript reads “and how finally.”
- [Col. 0013C] “From the whole fullness”: the manuscript reads “from the whole.”
- [Col. 0015A] “Spare me, judge!”: the manuscript reads “Equal things, judge, you would protest.”
- [Col. 0015A] “Acknowledge”: the manuscript reads “forgive.”
- [Col. 0015A] “The blessed confessor of Christ, Dunstan”: the manuscript reads “the confessor Dunstan.”

What you have humbly requested through Lord Baldwin and Lord Teson—and, had I been present, would have asked of me with suppliant devotion—I grant, with paternal and pious affection, to all who ask it, insofar as it depends on me; [Note: Col. 0017D: the manuscript reads “and for affection” (*et pro affectu*) for “and with pious affection.”] and I pray God mercifully to grant what depends on Him. When I speak with you about the lot of the archbishopric, which by divine disposition has fallen upon me, it seems very alien both to me and to you—if our mutual affection is taken into account—for me to advise you concerning it and for you to accept counsel from me. [Note: The manuscript reads “your affection” instead of “our mutual affection.”] If anyone considers that we owe more to God than to ourselves, it will not seem strange to him that, in God’s cause, I advise those entrusted to me, whom I do not at all wish to deviate from the right path—those same persons being witnesses—against both my own affection and theirs, according to God’s will. [Note: The manuscript reads “concerning my own” instead of “against my own.”]

You did well to send me, through Lord Teson, your consent, since the matter cannot be changed by me for you. But you will do better if, by letters, you send one message to the king and another to me: namely, that whatever God deigns to ordain concerning me, the king himself and all those who belong to the Church of God, according to the fear of God, have ordered; and that our archbishop, acting with religious and ecclesiastical judgment, has commanded it; and that, as it seems to you, you grant it with humble devotion out of the fear of God, and entrust me to God and to His Church. Retain only this: that, insofar as it is possible for you, you may always enjoy my counsel for as long as I live.

This is my advice; this is my exhortation. For it must be done in this way, so that you may show yourselves more subject to God’s will than to your own; so that you do not lose the king’s favor, which is necessary for you, without any advantage—in fact, with very great loss; and so that you do not make my mind, already burdened with many troubles, still more burdened by your disagreement.

Serve the Countess of Lermend, who, as I have heard, has come to you, with generous and kindly willingness, honorably in every way you can, according to her wishes. [Note: Col. 0017D: the manuscript reads “has come to us” instead of “has come to you.”] For your honor is great, and I hope that this will greatly benefit our Church. Greet her sweetly on our behalf. [Note: The manuscript reads simply “Greet her.”] Farewell.

### 365. LETTER V. OSBERN TO ANSELM

*That he should hasten his inauguration.*

To the most holy lord, his sweetest father, now—though I say it not without despair—archbishop of the English, ANSELM, his servant and son OSBERN sends greetings full of mourning and tears.

[Col. 0019A]

How long, sweetest lord, will you suspend our desires? How long will you take away our lives? If you are the one who is to come, show it by coming to us; and do not wish to delay any longer the good which, proceeding from an eternal design, Christ has deigned to bestow upon the human race. Otherwise, my sweetest lord, you have shaken the earth and disturbed it; and it would have been better to have endured the losses of death than ever to have received anything concerning your name.

For what do you suppose—the mourning, the tears that are poured out against you today? [Note: Col. 0019D: the manuscript reads, “What greater [mourning, tears] are poured out, which before this time were poured out in the sight of God?”] What greater misery can there be than for men who, like harmful humors, weighed upon the body of the Church, to have recently been seen excluded, and now to see those same men not only excluded but incorporated into the body of the Church? Think, sweetest of all, that these complaints are directed against you.

Is this the man over whom we rejoiced so greatly, about whom we heard such great things? See how he has deceived us, how he has destroyed our lives. [Note: Col. 0019D: the manuscript reads “We hope” instead of “We hoped.”] We hoped for peace, and there is no good; for a time of healing, and behold, a cry. Is this the man whom Osbern for these thirteen years praised so highly before the people, whom in every speech he proclaimed a master, most holy and most wise? See how he has made our latter state worse than the former.

Believe me, these things will never cease to be said unless you cease to remain far away. Come, then; let your name alone be invoked over us; take away our reproach. [Note: Col. 0019D: the manuscript reads “your garment” (*vestimentum tibi*) instead of “you must hasten” (*festinandum tibi*).] You must hasten. Be our prince. This will be praise for God, a reward for you, and life for us.

Let us recover in you what, in the death of our most holy Father Lanfranc, we lost with the whole world—him whom we shall always mourn as dead until we see him in you. May almighty God’s anathema fall among men upon whoever has hindered Anselm from what he began. Believe me: I have written this amid the greatest flood of tears, and I am concerned for you unto death. The Mother and all her sons greet you.

### LETTER VI. THE MONKS OF BEC TO ANSELM

*The monks of Bec grant Anselm to the Church of Canterbury.*

To their sweetest lord and father, formerly given to them by God, Abbot ANSELM, the humble servants and sons of the Church of Bec: may they always be guided and fortified by God’s continual protection in all His ways.

Having heard of the concession made concerning you by our lord, the prince of Normandy, and by our archbishop of Rouen, at the request of the king of the English and of nearly all the princes of that people—that you should be advanced, namely, to the dignity of the archbishopric—and having also taken into account the concession concerning you that pertained to us and was requested from us, [Note: The manuscript reads “the confession that was expected” instead of “the concession that was requested.”] we all assembled together. Each of us was questioned individually by name concerning his opinion by the one presiding over us.

Many different thoughts and statements were expressed by us on this matter, but there is no need now to repeat and explain them to you. We shall briefly inform you only of the outcome of the matter for which we assembled.

One part of us, although deeply grieved and saddened by its sweet and singular affection for you, nevertheless, out of fear of God—for it is believed that this is being done by His will and counsel—gladly grants what is requested of you, for the honor and advantage of the Church of God, in accordance with the counsel you also give. But the other part of us, relying and trusting in its own counsel rather than in yours, and, as it seems to itself, acting from a more ardent and more righteous zeal of love for you, grants it not at all, nor in any way yields to the persuasion of any of its superiors or inferiors so as to grant it. [Note: The manuscript reads “of a more righteous” instead of “more righteous.”]

But which party outweighed the other, whether in number or in reason, Lord Lanfranc, who was present and both saw and heard everything done or said here among us, will tell you fully and sufficiently in person. We are dictating this very briefly and hurriedly because the bearer of this letter is pressing us by his haste to proceed in this way. May almighty God rightly order your life according to His good pleasure and, for the common benefit and joy of His faithful, preserve it for a long time in the present life. Amen.

### LETTER VII. ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF BEC

[Note: Compared with two copies in one manuscript, Vict. Ef. 20.]

*He explains that he suffers greatly from being separated from the monks of Bec and that, contrary to the slanders of certain ill-wishers, he did not refuse the archbishopric through feigned humility.*

To his beloved Lord Prior BALDRIC and the other servants of God residing in the monastery of Bec, their servant and fellow servant, Brother ANSELM: may he always be ruled by the divine counsel and protected by its aid.

Although divine providence separates me bodily from you, not without great and pious grief of my heart, I nevertheless pray God that the love by which, through His gift, my soul embraces you within itself may continue indissolubly. Through that love, with God’s favor, I shall always be your servant; for, insofar as God grants me the ability, I shall always be devoted to your interests. [Note: One manuscript reads “with providence ... for your wishes” instead of “with God’s favor ... to your interests.”]

For although that love itself is so great that, whenever I think intently of your friends concerning this separation, so inseparable and contrary to our will, my heart immediately swells and is troubled by a kind of storm, like the sea by the winds, and my eyes rain tears, it is nevertheless sweeter for me to endure this from that love than to separate it from me.

God knows—for before His sight I speak according to my conscience—that I loved you more for God and for your own sakes, and myself for your sake, than I loved you for my own sake, or precedence, lordship, or earthly possession, which I held for your sake. Therefore your sadness over whatever need of me may exist among you weighs upon me more heavily than any earthly exaltation or abundance can console me.

Behold, even now, in this very address by which I speak to you from afar while dictating, my tears bear witness: my eyes cannot contain them, and the sobs rising from the groaning of my heart force themselves upon me, obstructing, interrupting, and delaying the words of my mouth for the scribe.

Although there are some, as I hear—who they are, God knows—who either invent maliciously, suspect in error, or are compelled to say in undiscriminating grief that I am drawn to the archbishopric by vicious desire rather than compelled by religious necessity, I do not know how I could persuade them of what my conscience is in this matter if my life and conduct do not satisfy them. [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscript reads “than I am compelled” instead of “than I may be compelled.”] [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscript reads “does not satisfy” instead of “do not satisfy.”] Thus I have lived for thirty-three years in the monastic habit: three years without a position of authority, fifteen in the priory, and as many years in the abbacy. [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscript reads “in the habit of a monk” instead of “in the monastic habit.”] All good people who knew me loved me—not because of my own efforts, but through God’s grace—and especially those who knew me more inwardly and familiarly. No one could see in me any deed by which he might recognize that I delighted in ecclesiastical authority. [Note: The manuscripts read “some saw in me ... might recognize” instead of “no one could see in me ... might recognize.”]

What, then, shall I do? How shall I drive away and extinguish this false and hateful suspicion, lest it harm the souls of those who loved me for God’s sake by diminishing their charity toward me; or lest it persuade those to whom some sort of counsel or example of my littleness might have been useful that I am worse than I am; or lest it offer a bad example to these and to others who do not know me but will hear this? [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscripts read “or of others” instead of “and of others,” and “that example” instead of “an example to them.”]

O God, You who know all things, I do not justify myself according to the examination of Your strict judgment. For that great Apostle of Yours who could say, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4), after saying this added, “But I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who judges me.” And that simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil, to whom—as You Yourself bear witness—there was none like him on earth, said, “I fear all my works” (Job 9:28). But according as my soul understands its own conscience, I speak of it before You, so that all who read or hear this letter of mine may know and believe it under Your testimony.

You, Lord, see; and You be my witness that, as my conscience tells me, I do not know whether love of anything which Your servant, a despiser of the world, ought to despise seizes me or binds me to consent to the archbishopric to which I am suddenly snatched and drawn. [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscripts read “that seizes me” instead of “what seizes me.”] And if, while preserving the obedience and charity that I wish to keep for Your sake insofar as You have granted them to me, I were free to choose, I would rather serve and obey under a superior as a monk, and receive from him counsel for my soul and the necessities of my body, than rule or preside over other men, whether for the governance of souls or for their bodily support, or possess earthly riches.

You see, and You be my witness that, as my conscience tells me, I do not know how I can extricate myself without sin from the intention of those who choose me; and that Your fear, charity, and obedience—which I owe to You and to Your Church—compel and bind me, so that I do not dare obstinately to contradict their religious prayers and the great desire which, as they show me, they possess.

Lord, if my conscience deceives me, show me myself, correct me, and direct my way in Your sight (Ps. 5:9). Whether it pleases me that what men have begun concerning my election should be carried out, or rather that it should not be carried out, [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscripts read “what all men have begun concerning this” instead of “what men have begun concerning my election.”] “Lead me in Your way, and I shall walk in Your truth” (Ps. 85:11). Lord, You see my conscience, as I have said; be my witness before those who receive a different impression of me, and show it to them, lest by judging it wrongly they injure their own souls or those of others.

Behold, my beloved brothers, you have heard the truth of my conscience concerning desire for, or contempt of, the archbishopric. For if I knowingly lie to God, I do not know to whom I can speak the truth. If anyone henceforth, contrary to what I have said about this matter while invoking God’s testimony, openly or craftily wishes to malign me to anyone, I think that God will be with me against him and will answer him on my behalf; [Note: Col. 0021D: one manuscript reads “does not wish openly or craftily to malign me to anyone”; another, “wishes openly or craftily, [to speak] ill to anyone”; another, “wishes, openly or craftily, to malign me to anyone.”] and I shall console myself under God’s testimony.

I am certain, however, that if this false suspicion harms any soul, those who have originated it will take that sin upon themselves, if there are several of them; and whether there is one or more than one, it will rest especially upon the one who is chiefly responsible for it.

As for the arguments by which some of you think that I could reasonably have resisted the aforesaid election, I shall answer briefly. They say: “When he was compelled to become our abbot, he gave himself to us as a servant in the name of the Lord.” Good: I did this in the name of the Lord. What do they understand by this? Do they think that I swore servitude to you by the name of the Lord? Certainly I did not do that.

Or is what the Lord says—“If you ask anything in my name” (John 16:24)—to be understood as though He had said, “If he swears to the Father while asking something through my name”? Or when we say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 123:8), or whenever we do or say anything in the name of the Lord, do we swear each time by the name of the Lord? [Note: Col. 0021D: the manuscripts read “whenever we do or say anything” instead of “whenever we do anything or say [anything].”] Certainly not. How those words are to be understood is irrelevant to me now. But what I myself said then, “in the name of the Lord,” I understood and understand as “in the Lord,” that is, in God. [Note: Col. 0023D: the manuscripts read “what I said then” instead of “what I myself said then.”] What is done in God is done according to God, that is, rightly.

Therefore, when I gave myself to you as a servant in the name of the Lord, I gave myself to you as a servant, insofar as I could, according to God. Judge now whether in this way I denied myself; or whether I could, according to God, deny God’s disposition concerning me, to which, whether I wished it or not, I was rightly subject; or deny the obedience to which I had wholly surrendered myself.

For when I professed to be a monk, I denied myself to myself, so that henceforth I would not belong to myself—that is, so that I would not live according to my own will, but according to obedience. True obedience is owed either to God, or to the Church of God, and after God especially to superiors. This obedience, therefore, I did not abjure or deny; rather, I preserved it when I said, “In the name of the Lord.”

Learn, then, what I gave you at that time. I gave you this: that I could not, by my own will, withdraw myself from your service, nor seek to be withdrawn, unless compelled by that disposition and obedience of which I had first become a servant according to God.

But if I had acted otherwise than I said, then certainly you would not be monks if you demanded from me what I had promised you contrary to God. Before you consented to my being advanced to the archbishopric, I never explained this surrender of myself to anyone; rather, I put it forward as an utterly firm obstacle, so that I would not be advanced, until I understood that those wishing to advance me persisted with such constancy in their intention that they understood even this to be no obstacle, and asserted that they neither wished nor ought in any way to desist from what they had begun. [Note: Col. 0023D: one manuscript reads “so that this too, etc.” instead of “so that even for this purpose, etc.”; the manuscripts read “from what they had begun, in no way” instead of “from what they had begun they in no way.”]

Some also say that I had been given to you according to God, and that, since I had rightly been set over you, I could not rightly be taken away from you, nor ought I to consent to it. [Note: The manuscripts read “that I consent” instead of “that I ought to consent.”]

Blessed Martin was an abbot according to God, yet he was taken away from monks and set over clerics, monks and laymen, men and women. [Note: Col. 0023D: the manuscripts read “Blessed Mark” instead of “Blessed Martin.”] The apostle Peter, I suppose, held the episcopal chair at Antioch according to God; yet no one says that he sinned when, leaving it and pursuing greater fruitfulness, he migrated to Rome.

Does this mean that he did not love his former disciples, or that he loved them less afterward? Or that God despised and abandoned them because he abandoned them bodily? It certainly does not mean that, brothers. I do not compare myself with their greatness; nevertheless, I am not to be condemned if God does something with me resembling what He did with them.

Perhaps someone says: “You are not a man to whom so great a responsibility is appropriate.” [Note: Col. 0023D: the manuscripts read “responsibilities are appropriate” instead of “a responsibility is appropriate.”] I judge this very thing concerning myself in heart and speech. But they say to me: “Whatever you may be, we want you; we will not let you go.”

Some remember that I used to say that I did not wish to live except for you and that I would never hold any position of authority other than that of Bec. But I said this according to the inclination of my will and according to what I trusted in my defense and reply, if I should be called to another position of authority. But what if God ordains that I should live and serve others as well? Should I resist arrogantly?

Both I and you belong more to God than I belong to you and you to me. The prince of the apostles said to the Lord, “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8). Such was his will. But what did the Lord say? “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me” (ibid.). And what did Peter say? “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (ibid., 9). Yet God did not condemn him because he changed his opinion in accordance with the divine will; rather, he humbled himself at His feet.

I had relied on my strength and ingenuity to defend myself; [Note: Col. 0023D: the manuscripts read “I rely” instead of “I had relied.”] but God was stronger and more ingenious than I, and therefore my presumption came to nothing. Perhaps someone will say that I spoke foolishly, as though justifying myself and proving myself worthy of the archbishopric. But my false accusers compelled me to speak, lest they infect you or anyone else with the poison of their falsehood. I am not striving to prove myself worthy of the archbishopric, but to clear myself of a false charge. [Note: The manuscripts read “I cleared myself” instead of “to clear myself.”]

But concerning these matters, of which I have spoken thus far, let this now suffice. I shall add a few words for your consolation.

I therefore beg you, my most beloved brothers, not to grieve beyond measure because of my absence. Certainly, your sadness is my sadness, and your consolation is my consolation. Let your hope not be in man, but in God; for if I benefited you in any way, it was not from me but from Him.

Many of you—and almost all of you—came to Bec because of me, but no one became a monk because of me; nor did you vow yourselves to God in hope of any reward from me. From Him to whom you gave everything you possessed, expect everything you need. Cast your care upon the Lord, and He Himself will nourish you. Turn all your concern toward serving Him, and He Himself will take up the whole care of nourishing you.

Concerning me, I beg you not to love me less if God is accomplishing His will in me; and do not let me lose you because I once wished to do your will, since I neither dare, nor ought, nor can resist God. Nor do I yet see how I can withdraw myself from the Church of the English except by resisting God.

Let it become clear that you loved me not only for yourselves, but also for God and for me. Pray for me, so that whatever happens to me may be brought to a good conclusion by God’s grace.

From this hour, do not expect me to be your abbot; but know that, for as long as I live, I shall be your lover and one concerned for you, if God preserves the will He has given me concerning you.

Nevertheless, I shall never relinquish the power of binding and loosing, nor of giving you counsel, which I possessed among you, for as long as the abbot who succeeds me and you who will be under him permit me to retain it. I say this through tears and with difficulty.

I commend you, my most beloved brothers, to our Lord Jesus Christ; to His devout mother Mary; to blessed Peter, to whom He entrusted His sheep; to blessed Benedict, according to whose rule you have professed obedience; [Note: One manuscript reads “you have professed the Rule” instead of “you have professed obedience according to the Rule”;] and to the other saints of God. Through their merits and intercessions, may He who redeemed you be your abbot and your guardian; [Note: Col. 0025B: the manuscripts read, “May He who redeemed you with His blood, through their merits and intercessions, thus be your [abbot],” instead of “and through their merits and intercessions, may He who redeemed you be your [abbot].”] may He Himself grant you, after this life, to live blessedly in His kingdom. There, in His mercy, may He grant me to see you and rejoice with you without end—He who is blessed forever. Amen.

Many of you wonder—those whom I embraced with such sweet and familiar affection that each one could think I had loved no one else equally—why I do not write to each of them individually some remembrance of our affection. But let them know that this is not caused by my forgetfulness, but by their multitude. Perhaps I shall do so when it is more opportune; and if not for all, at least for some.

For the present I say this to them alone: let them remember that I loved them in this way for no other reason than that they might love God and their own souls. They themselves are my witnesses that I have always desired this of them and of all of you; this I pray, this I urge, this I advise. Let them do this, and so they will always preserve my unbroken love toward them.

Hasten to accept an abbot over you; it is advantageous for you. Farewell.

Show this letter of ours, to as many people as you can, as a defence against the false suspicion concerning me; [Note: Col. 0025B: the manuscripts read “of the false suspicion” instead of “of the false suspicion concerning me.”] especially show it to my reverend lords and fathers, the bishops and abbots who, for God’s sake, loved me through His grace. I am more troubled if they are deceived by suspecting something perverse about me. [Note: The manuscripts read “if they are to suspect” instead of “if they suspect.”] For I do not wish in any way to lose their affection; rather, by venerating and loving them, I wish always to merit and preserve it.

### LETTER VIII. ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF BEC

[Note: Collated with the copies containing the same text.]

*That they should elect William, formerly prior at Pexium, as abbot; he commands William to undertake this responsibility, while forbidding Baldric to resign the priory.*

To his sweetest and most beloved, Lord Prior BALDRIC and the other monks of Bec, Brother ANSELM, who until now has served them under the name of abbot, [Note: The manuscripts read “who until now serve under the name of abbot” instead of “who until now has served them under the name of abbot,”] may he always be guarded and protected by God.

With God disposing concerning me, His creature, as He wills, whether I wish it or not; with our reverend lord Robert, prince of the Normans, giving his consent; with our archbishop William commanding it; and with you, compelled by God and giving your support, I have been released from your care and enveloped in a greater one.

If God grants you the favor of our aforesaid lord prince, so that he wishes to give you an abbot for our Church and deigns to hear your counsel concerning it, I say to him and to you that—

[Col. 0025C]

No one seems better to me than Lord William, and so forth. From this it is absolutely certain that Anselm knew this William inwardly and thoroughly, since he not only advises that he be elected in his place, but also makes a vow concerning him. These things are indeed the clearest proof of William’s integrity and holiness. Come, then, let us look at that little boy, and gradually at the young man; let us look at the novice, while here we see one who will become—not, I say, a veteran soldier, but a commander. The anonymous author of Bec, in the prologue to his History of the same man, promises to leave to posterity the Life of him and of his successor. Hence we have all the more reason to trust his account as he begins to weave it into the fabric of these words.

> “The venerable abbot of Bec, William, descended from a noble Northman lineage and was born to distinguished parents in the old castle above the Risle, which is called Montfort. His father was named Turstin, and his mother Albereda, niece through her sister of Roger of Beaumont, father of Count Robert. While still a child lying in his cradle, he was struck by a severe illness and almost lost his sight. His terrified mother, mourning for her son, ran to a certain church of Saint Germanus situated in that same castle, placed him upon the altar of that church, and vowed to God, to Mary, the most blessed Mother of God, and to Saint Germanus that, if through their aid the boy escaped that affliction of the eyes, she would raise him for the service of God and hand him over to be instructed in letters. At the same time she begged God that, if He did not wish to heal the boy otherwise, He would transfer that illness to herself—that is, to the mother. What more is there to say? The grace of our Savior, the piety of His most holy Mother, and likewise that of the most blessed confessor Germanus granted the good mother’s petition and vow; the child was restored to complete health, but illness seized his mother and soon afterward killed her.

> “The boy grew, and when he reached a suitable age, he was handed over to be instructed in literary studies. He therefore began to show a good disposition: he burned with love of God, associated with honorable people, and withdrew his mind from dishonorable ones. Already he despised the luxury of the world; already, in speech, conduct, and dress, he displayed himself in such a way that even then everyone regarded him as practically a monk, insofar as this concerned the formation of his life and character. Whenever his relatives and friends sent him some money for his schooling, he avoided accepting it as though it were an evil thing; as his fellow students regularly reported, he so detested avarice.

> “When he was twenty-five years old, desiring to fulfill the Lord’s word, which says, ‘Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple; and if anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,’ he renounced the world and became a monk at Bec under the most holy abbot Anselm. After entering the monastery, he devoted himself most earnestly to the monastic life; assiduous in reading and silence, he took the greatest care to guard his life honorably. Thus, desiring to please God, dear to human beings, and following the Lord’s standards in the camp of the Lord of Hosts, he served for fifteen years in the office of a vigorous soldier. Under blessed Anselm as his commander, he served in this warfare so energetically that everyone loved him and no one complained about him. The reputation of his goodness carried from place to place the good fragrance of Christ concerning him.

> “Accordingly, after blessed Anselm had been transferred to England and made archbishop—whose dignity the aforesaid William had previously honored—he afterward deserved to receive it.”

Thus far the Bec Chronicle concerning William’s origins, childhood, and monastic life. Since what follows was taken from Anselm’s fourth book, I pass over the eulogy for the moment, amazed that this biographer omitted the fact that William had been prior at Brixiensis [place-name uncertain], as Anselm specifically indicated. But, to join together what has been separated, at last the votes of everyone were united in William’s election.

After this, the Chronicle says:

> “He was summoned and came, and took his place in the proper order. Then the prior told him that they were electing him to govern the Church of Bec and, on God’s behalf and on behalf of Saint Mary and all the saints, as well as on behalf of the most reverend Father Anselm, commanded him to undertake the office of abbot and the care of souls. But he, prostrating himself on the ground, said: ‘I beg you, either release me altogether from what you command, or teach me how I can fulfill it.’

> “To this the prior replied: ‘There is no need to labor in order to have yourself released. Rather, undertake this care in the name of the Lord, and we shall obey you wholeheartedly.’

> “Immediately, on that same day, Abbot Roger [he had been made abbot of the monastery from a monk of Bec], the prior, and certain other brothers with them, taking their chosen candidate, hurried to the court and presented him to Robert, Duke of the Northmen. Receiving him eagerly and with great honor, Robert bestowed the abbey upon him according to the custom of his predecessors. The princes were present: Count Robert of Meulan and Robert, son of Anschitil, William’s cousins, who rejoiced greatly at the promotion of the man elected at Bec.

> “Then the count of Meulan instructed Robert, son of Anschitil, to escort the newly elected abbot of Bec to the monastery, ordering all his officials and commanding them not to presume to cause the abbot or his men any annoyance in any matter. At that time the count of Meulan granted Robert that the goods purchased for the brothers’ sustenance should be free from every customary levy. Until then, on goods relating to the monks’ food, wherever they were purchased—even in the kitchen at Bec—the officials of the castle of Brionne had exacted such payments.

> “As time went on, the same count of Meulan granted, throughout all his territory, wherever he had the right to exact or remit such a levy, that the goods of the monks of Bec, belonging to their food or clothing, wherever the monks might be and for whose use they were purchased—whether in the cloister or outside the cloister on the monastery’s business—would be free from every customary charge, whether called toll, transit duty, or by any other name. He did this for the love of God and of William, the abbot of Bec, his kinsman. He also conferred many other benefits on the monastery of Bec during his lifetime, for the sake of that same abbot.

> “And so the newly elected man, having received, as stated, the gift of the abbey from Duke Robert and the care of souls from William, archbishop of Rouen, returned from the court with his companions, with the prince’s favor. He came to Bec late in the evening after Compline, on the day before the feast of the Dedication. This feast falls on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, and in that year occurred on a Sunday.

> “Rising for Matins, the newly elected abbot came into the choir and stood in the place beside the abbot’s seat; and he fittingly completed the entire office of the feast, both nocturnal and diurnal, as abbot. These events took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093. On that very day William, the elected abbot, first sat as abbot in the chapter, from that day onward managing all the monastery’s internal and external affairs suitably. Everyone rejoiced that God had given Anselm so worthy a successor and had given them such a pastor.

> “Nevertheless, before his blessing he neither entered the abbot’s seat nor carried the pastoral staff. Nor did he seem to take any care to hasten the blessing; this blessing was postponed until the month of August of the following year. But Anselm, not forgetting what he had begun, asked William, archbishop of Rouen, about the blessing of the abbot of Bec, and notified Prior Baldric and the convent of this by letter.

> “When the month of August began, Prior Baldric and certain other brothers with him went to Rouen to speak with the archbishop about the abbot’s blessing. The archbishop appointed the day of the blessing for the next feast of Saint Lawrence. When the prior returned, he told the convent what he had received from the archbishop.

> “On the feast day of Saint Lawrence, while the archbishop stood at the altar wearing his mitre, and the elected abbot of Bec was dressed in sacred vestments, and the hour was approaching for him to be presented for blessing, he heard from those reporting to him that the archbishop would not bless him unless he made a profession; but he replied that he would do so in no way.

> “Then Baldric, prior of Bec, went with several monks to Robert, count of Normandy, informing him that the archbishop was demanding from the abbot of Bec a profession which his predecessors had not made. Immediately the duke sent William of Bretteville and William, son of Richard of Bardeville, together with his chancellor Ernulf, ordering and commanding William the archbishop to bless the abbot of Bec without delay and to demand nothing from him except what it was established that his predecessors, the abbots of Bec, had done.

> “When the archbishop heard this, he was extremely angry; nevertheless, he completed what had been begun and blessed the abbot without a profession, because the prince’s command compelled him to do so. Afterward the abbot spoke with the archbishop, and the prelate received him into such favor that he had no abbot in Normandy dearer or more familiar to him.

> “The following day the abbot returned to the monastery. The archbishop, however, ordered Abbot William of Cormeilles to go with him and, in the archbishop’s place, introduce him into the abbot’s seat. He came with the greatest humility he could show, barefoot, and was received by the brothers with great honor and joy and led into the church. Then Abbot Cormery, as he had been ordered, installed him in the seat; and, beginning the *Te Deum laudamus*, he kissed the entire convent.”

Thus far the Bec manuscript concerning William’s election. I have set this down so that posterity may know that it found in William a successor most worthy of Anselm, and a fitting lid for the worthy pot, without, I hope, wearying the devout reader. For discourse about worthy men itself stifles even nascent nausea, so far is it from arousing it.

I shall append a few shorter and more substantial outlines of his virtues from the same Bec record:

> “This good man of whom we are speaking, namely Abbot William, was a man of great wisdom, adorned with good morals, related to great men, and esteemed by the king and the leading men of the kingdom. He conducted himself so modestly, humbly, and gently that at times he appeared to some people ignorant and almost an idiot. Yet if one came closer and, as though examining him, questioned his judgment concerning doubtful matters, one would discover deep prudence, profound counsel, and the evidence of the greatest integrity.

> “He was also devoted to God, submissive to his superiors, kind to his subjects, good to the gentle, and severe toward the undisciplined. He claimed nothing beyond his proper measure; he showed all reverence toward divine matters; he feared God and avoided sin, hating it as though it were deadly poison. If anyone asked him for a blessing, he blessed more with words than with his hand, saying that it was not his to bless with the hand, but the bishops’.

> “Those who adhered to him more familiarly know that no abbot was more concerned for his convent. He was so well-disciplined a man that he never uttered obscene speech, abhorred every kind of buffoonery, and knew no impurity of mind or body, as a virgin knows none from her mother’s womb. Temperate in food and drink, honorably modest, and dignified in religious character, he understood matters with a sound intelligence, pleased people with gentle speech, and was useful through teaching and example,” and so forth.

I had almost overlooked a passage in Book VIII, chapter 6, of the *History of Jumièges*, where he calls our William “of Beaumont” through his maternal lineage, as may be seen at the beginning of this account.

> “I can think of no one better than Lord William, who was prior at Pexeium. And if the command of our glorious lord prince should be directed to this end—which may God grant—then I too, brother William, in the name of the Lord, by holy obedience command you to undertake this care humbly, in hope of God’s assistance, setting aside your repose for the benefit of your brothers. I wish these letters to be presented at the appropriate time to our lord, to the congregation, and to whoever else it may be necessary to approach.

> “To you also, Prior Baldric, by holy obedience I command that, whoever the abbot may be, you do not leave the priory without his consent and mine, as long as I live.

> “Farewell.”

## Letter IX

*[Compared with the two aforementioned manuscripts.]*

### Anselm to Roger, Abbot

**Commendation of the monks of Bec**

To the reverend lord Father, Abbot Roger, Brother Anselm: prosperity in holiness in this life, and happiness in eternity in the life to come.

You and I are so mutually conscious of our shared love in God that I do not think I need prayers to ensure that this love may always live within us, as long as you live; nor do you need persuasion, because, with God’s consent, it will not fail in me as long as I live.

Concerning the Church of Bec—for I have loved and do love nothing purer in this world—if your Holiness needed supplication, I would certainly entreat you with heart and letters, since I cannot do so in person by word, as much as I could, so that your consolation, counsel, and assistance might not be lacking to it, and so that you might cherish its sons, as their firstborn and elder brother, with a father’s solicitude and a mother’s gentleness.

But since your prudence and the sincerity of your charity are sufficient to persuade you of this without my exhortation, and since, because of the abundance of my heart, I cannot remain entirely silent, I think this brief admonition from me will suffice.

Remember the Lord’s word to the chief of the apostles, as to the firstborn of his brothers: “And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22).

Greet our lords and brothers, your sons, and persuade them by our prayers and by your admonition, so that it may not fail, as He does not fail for whose sake they began it.

Believe without hesitation concerning my conscience with regard to the archbishopric, and confidently assert to others that no desire—which ought not to exist in the heart of a servant of God who despises the world—draws or binds me, but rather the fear, charity, and obedience owed to God and His Church.

Have these letters, or a copy of them, read at Bec.

Farewell.

Textual variants: At “for I have loved … nothing purer,” the manuscripts read *qua nihil* (“in which [I have loved] nothing”) for *quia nihil* (“because I have loved nothing”). At “for whose sake they began it,” the manuscript readings are *quem inceperam* (“whom I began”) and *quem illam inceperunt* (“for whom they began it”). At “fear, charity, and obedience,” one manuscript reads *timor, aut charitas, aut obedientia* (“fear, or charity, or obedience”).

## Letter X

*[Compared with one copy of the two aforementioned manuscripts in the same codex.]*

### Anselm to Gislebert, Bishop of York

**That he did not undertake the burden of the archbishopric out of desire for honor or any earthly thing**

To his most beloved Father, the reverend lord Gislebert, bishop of York, Brother Anselm: that a faithful servant and son may prosper.

At the beginning of my letter I wish to excuse myself before your reverend Fatherhood because I have written to you late, after the heavy lot of the archbishopric fell upon me. This was not caused by negligence or forgetfulness, but by the very great uncertainty of my troubled heart.

For the fear of God and fear of the burden which I was compelled to undertake struggled within me, as did love for those from whom I could not separate without great sorrow. I did not dare obstinately to resist God’s ordinance, yet I greatly dreaded the heavy burden and the rending of my soul from the souls of those whom I loved as myself and for whom alone I wished to live. Since I did not wish to offend God on either side, I was entirely uncertain what I ought rather to choose or for what I should preferably seek the help of my friends.

In this matter I chose what seemed to me the one and safest counsel: that, as it is written, “Cast your care upon the Lord” (Psalm 54:23), I should entrust myself wholly to divine governance and counsel. Yet I would do whatever I could without sin so that what those who elected me wished to do with me would not happen; and I would do nothing that I could leave undone without sin, so that it might happen.

With what feeling and what simplicity I wished to do this, and toward which side my heart leaned more heavily, God Himself knows. According to His rule, I wished, as far as my understanding and ability allowed, to direct my intention in this matter.

I shall come to what immediately causes no little sorrow, if it is true. Your prudence knows, my dearest Father, that the more sincerely someone loves and is loved by the beloved, the more grievously he suffers if that love for him is in any way diminished.

I cannot doubt that your Excellency sincerely loved my insignificance, because I can prove this by the clearest evidence: the benefits which you have bestowed upon me and upon the Church of Bec, which until now I governed under the name of abbot, in words and deeds, with great kindness and tender piety.

Since I consider that I had not previously deserved you through any service or benefit, nor afterward repaid you, I judge myself very blameworthy if I do not faithfully love your fatherly holiness. The more sincerely, therefore, I love you, the more bitter it is for me if your affection toward me is in any way clouded.

I say this, my reverend Father and Lord, because I have heard that your fatherly Holiness suspects that I have been ensnared, at least in part, by desire for the archbishopric, toward which I am being dragged in sorrow and fear, as many tears bear witness. I greatly fear that the kindness of your mind toward my humility—although I in no way deserve it—may thereby be discolored.

I call God as my witness; before Him I must not lie, and I know that it is wicked to call Him as witness to a lie. So far as I understand my conscience before Him, I would rather, if I could preserve the charity and obedience that I owe to God and to the Church of God, serve in monastic poverty and regularly obey an abbot than rule over one, many, or all human beings in earthly eminence and the wealth of earthly possessions.

I speak equally before God, my reverend Father: no desire for any earthly thing that a servant of God who despises the world ought to despise draws or binds my mind to the archbishopric. Rather, the necessity of fearing God compels me—a necessity which I do not yet see how I can break without sin.

As for what I communicated to our lord Robert, count of the Northmen, to our reverend Father William, archbishop, and to our brothers at Bec—that I could no longer resist without sin, that I could in no way withstand the will of God, and that therefore the same archbishop should, on the advice of spiritual men who feared God more than human beings, act so as to command me, as a monk who wished to live only through obedience, what I ought rather to do; and as for what I wrote to the aforesaid brothers, namely, that matters had inevitably been brought to the point where I would either benefit them and others if they consented to God’s ordinance, or benefit neither them nor others but live thereafter in sorrow if they acted obstinately, and that I therefore advised them, as one entrusted to advise those committed to me, to do nothing concerning the concession of me that was being demanded from them except on the counsel of spiritual men—some people, not understanding what compelled me, thought when they read these things that I had been overcome by desire for the archbishopric.

But that was not and is not the case.
