I saw that from the mere delay—because it had not been determined what would happen to me—many present and serious evils harmful to the bodies and souls of many were already arising, and that many more and worse evils would arise if they delayed longer. There is no need now to describe them.

Among these evils was the destruction of the Church of Bec, as I understood it, irreparable as well as inevitable. If I saw that, I would thereafter live in such great sorrow that I would be of no use either to myself or to anyone.

I also knew that, whether our brothers granted or opposed the matter, what had been begun would happen neither more nor less. Therefore I wanted them to be free from blame and from every occasion of the impending danger, whatever might happen.

When I indicated that what was happening was happening by God’s will, against which I could not resist, I did not mean that I was certain that it pleased God, but that it would happen by the will of God—whether merciful or angry—a will that cannot be resisted. For we are accustomed to say, even when we are certain that God does something in anger, that no one can resist His will.

Finally, whatever anyone may understand in my letters concerning the archbishopric, I am certain that I spoke in the simplicity of my heart, insofar as I was able to preserve it before God.

I therefore beg your beloved Fatherhood that, in my sorrow and fear, I may feel the consolation of your compassion rather than your indignation, which would increase my sadness. I desire to obtain this not only from your piety but also from all those who have hitherto loved me for God’s sake, so that, unjustly suspecting something perverse in me, they may not prefer to cast away that same love rather than preserve it.

But whatever they may do, I pray to God and hope in God that I shall always love them.

I ask your Fatherhood, as I ask concerning your counsel and affection, that whenever necessary you confidently defend me before others against the suspicion of the aforesaid desire.

I commend to your piety and counsel the Church of Bec, which I have loved and love more than my bodily life, and which, grieving over my loss so far as concerns my bodily presence, I do not doubt is itself grieving. I commend it to you as my own soul, with my whole heart’s affection and flowing tears, so that you may sustain it—not only through yourself but also through whoever you can move, by turning them through your pious compassion toward compassion for that Church.

May almighty God long preserve your Fatherhood in this life under the continual protection of His grace and lead you to eternal life.

This letter has no seal, because I am no longer an abbot and am not yet an archbishop; nor do I take pleasure in being portrayed as what I am not.

Textual variants: At “love for those,” one manuscript has *dilectio earum* (“love of them”) for *dilectio eorum* (“love for them”); at “on either side,” it has *in mentis parte* (“in the part of the mind”) for *in neutra parte* (“on neither side”). One manuscript reads *mihi pater* for “my Father”; another has “fear, or charity, or obedience” for “fear and charity and obedience”; and one reads *venire vult* (“wishes to come”) for *vivere vult* (“wishes to live”). At “destruction of the Church of Bec,” one manuscript has *distinctio Beccensis* (“distinction of Bec”). For the transition after “your compassion,” one manuscript reads: “consolation, rather than your indignation, which would increase my sadness. Which …” At “all,” one manuscript reads *ab hominibus* (“from human beings”); at “something perverse,” *parvum* (“something small”) for *pravum* (“something wicked”); at “against the aforesaid suspicion,” *a praedicta* for *a praedictae*; and at “through your pious compassion,” *persuasione* (“persuasion”) for *miseratione* (“compassion”).

## Letter XI

*[Compared with the two aforementioned manuscripts in Codex Ef. 20, with manuscript Bd. 18 of the same Victorine Library, and with the editions of Goth and Cologne 1573.]*

### Anselm to Fulk, Bishop of Beauvais

**It has the same subject as the preceding letter**

To his sweetest and most beloved friend, Fulk, bishop of Beauvais, Brother Anselm: may he rejoice in the eternal protection and consolation of God.

I know, my sweet friend, how much your affection would be saddened by the unexpected bodily absence of the one whom you love above all human beings, unless you wisely consoled yourself by considering the divine dispensation.

For just as, in the hearts of those who love one another, hope and the opportunity to enjoy one another nourish a certain delightful sweetness, so despair of that same thing introduces a painful bitterness. In this matter your Prudence can recognize my conscience.

I know the sincerity of your affection toward me so well that I am certain you do not fail to understand the truth of my affection toward you and toward those to whom I displayed it, and especially toward the monks of Bec. For no one knows the conscience of a true heart so well as the person who bears true friendship.

Consider, then, what complete joy could exist in my heart when the irreversible loss, in this present life, of the bodily presence of so many friends who desired me and whom I desired grieves me. Each of them mourns only the bodily loss of me; my soul mourns for all of them, because against my will it is so unexpectedly torn away from their presence.

And although the greater number of people showing me similar affection in England may seem to make me happy, it cannot in any way eradicate from my heart the earlier affection, rooted and nourished over so long a time.

True charity does not love earlier friends less inwardly, even when, as it extends to more people, it cannot act equally toward them outwardly. Nor does it fear being loved less by earlier friends, if they are true friends, when it is loved by more people.

Indeed, if I have any consolation from the multitude of present friends for the anguish I bear over the absence of the former, it cannot bring about that I should not grieve over the sorrow of those who, the more they love me, the more they are saddened by the absence of their beloved and loving friend.

It delights me, when I write to my sweet friend, to discuss for a long time the sincerity of charity and its efficacy. But since the brevity proper to a letter does not permit this, and since I also wish to say something else, I must now change the subject.

Some people, as I have heard, suspect that I am being held by desire for the archbishopric, toward which I am dragged in sorrow and fear. Whether they do this through their own error or through someone else’s persuasion, may God pardon them, for He sees that they are deceived and sin.

I do not excuse myself before your fraternity, which is most dear to me and which, from the time it came to know me through intimate and prolonged association, unquestionably learned and believed my conscience concerning ambition for secular honor. You knew it all the more truly because you entrusted yourself and your entire life more securely to my judgment and discernment.

But I excuse myself before all who will read this letter, so that they may know what my conscience says to me before God, and, when necessary, may answer on my behalf to those who do not know—if not for my sake, then for God’s sake.

For the opinion of some vice in a particular person, whether true or false, greatly harms the weak in the Church of God, especially when it concerns someone placed in the Catholic Church in such a way that he ought and is able to benefit others both by word and by the example of his life.

Let everyone know, as my conscience tells me before God—and I know that it is wicked to call Him as a witness to a lie—that it is not desire for any thing which a servant of God who despises the world ought to despise that snatches or binds me to the archbishopric of the English. Rather, the fear of God compels me to endure being dragged, though sorrowful and fearful, from the Church of God.

For if I were permitted, while preserving the obedience and charity that I owe to God and to His Church, my mother, for His sake, I would prefer and more willingly choose to be under an abbot, in monastic poverty and humility under regular discipline, to obey and serve, rather than to reign secularly in this world, to rule, to possess an archbishopric or bishopric, or an abbey, or to preside over any people for the governance of souls or the support of bodies, amid great possession and wealth of lands and earthly goods.

I do not count this confession about myself so much as a virtue as for this reason: I know myself to be so little useful, so little strong, so little energetic, so little prudent, and so little just, that it is more fitting and advantageous for me to choose to be subject to a prelate rather than to preside over others, to obey rather than command, to serve rather than rule, and to minister rather than be ministered to.

I am compelled to confess these things about myself. But, in my simplicity, as I think, and without any duplicity, I prefer to say them about myself rather than allow other people to sin against me or, through ignorance and their own error, to take a bad example from me.

Whoever believes these things about me when I confess them should be certain that, in believing, he is not deceived—provided that my conscience does not deceive me before God. Whoever does not believe them should know that he himself is deceived by judging falsely and rashly concerning me.

May the almighty Lord grant you joy in this life and in the life to come through His unfailing protection and consolation. Amen.

Textual variants: At “whom you love above all human beings,” the manuscripts and edition read *omnem diligit hominem* (“he loves every human being”). One manuscript and the edition read *se invicem* for *sese invicem* (“one another”); the manuscripts and edition read *de qua vestra* (“in which your”) for “in this matter your”; and manuscript Bd. 18 omits “and toward those.” It reads *monachos hic existentes* (“the monks present here”) for “the monks of Bec.” The manuscripts read *dilecti dilectoris* (“beloved loving friend”) for “beloved and loving friend,” and one manuscript reads *delectat cum* for “it delights me when.” At “witness to a lie,” one manuscript reads *testem monachis* (“witness to monks”). The manuscripts and edition read *trahat* (“may drag”) for *trahar* (“I am dragged”), and *mihi licebit* (“it will be permitted me”) for *mihi liceret* (“it were permitted me”). Manuscript Bd. 18 reads *quibusdam praeesse* (“to preside over some people”) for “any people”; the manuscripts and edition omit *eligere* (“to choose”) in “it is advantageous to choose to be subject”; and manuscript Bd. 18 adds *suam et* (“their own and”) after “through ignorance.” The manuscripts and edition read *confiteri credit* for “believes me when I confess”; manuscript Bd. 18 and the edition read *mea me conscientia* (“my conscience [does not deceive] me”) for “my conscience”; and manuscript Bd. 18 reads *verum est quia* (“it is true that”) for “it is true, and that.” Manuscript Bd. 18 adds “Amen.”

## Letter XII

*[Compared with the three aforementioned manuscript copies, and with the editions of Goth and Cologne 1573.]*

### Anselm to Godefroy, Bishop of Paris

**That he should release freely the cantor of the Church of Paris who had undertaken to receive the monastic habit at the monastery of Saint Martin in the Fields, but had been forcibly removed from it by him; and that he should not bind in the world one who had chosen Christ**

To the lord and reverend Father, Godefroy, bishop of Paris [the name appears elsewhere as Gaufrey and Gauffrey; the readings of the manuscripts and printed volumes vary greatly. Paulus Aemilius, Book III of his *Annals*, has “Gotofredus”; he asserted that this man was the brother of Count Eustace of Boulogne, chancellor of France, and a man of great power not only in sacred affairs but also in secular matters. There is, indeed, an ancient testimony to his dignity as chancellor in a charter of Philip, king of the Franks, issued at Orléans in the year 1075, in which he is called the king’s chancellor and bishop of Paris. It is therefore clear that he governed the Church of Paris for many years. But let this suffice for the present, since we shall say more in the *History of the Bishops of Paris*, which we are planning. May God bring that work also to completion], [the name is written “Joiffrido” in two manuscripts and in the edition; manuscript Bd. 18 merely records it as “G.”], Brother Anselm, elected archbishop of Canterbury by the dispensation of God, who disposes all things: holiness pleasing to God in the present life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

Although divine providence places my insignificance very far from Your Reverence, no distance ought to diminish the fidelity that your kindness, deserved in so many ways, has elicited from me. Therefore, if I hear anything about Your Highness that should make me rejoice with you, I always wish to rejoice; and if I learn of anything that indicates your dignity ought to be changed [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “that it is fitting to change”; the other reading is “that it ought to be imitated.”], I ought, with familiar confidence, charitably and humbly to admonish you. [Note: The manuscript Bd. 18 reads “with charity and in this matter humbly.”]

I have learned that the lord Walerannus, our dearest friend, cantor of your church, earnestly and most ardently seeking, by God’s inspiration, the habit of holy conduct, was received into the monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields [Note: The manuscripts and edition read “of Campia” and “of the Fields,” respectively;] with the joy with which he ought to have been received [Note: The manuscripts and edition read “with which they ought to have received him”;]—and that from there he was violently withdrawn by you, and in a manner that was not necessary [Note: The manuscript Bd. 18 and the edition read “by you, in a manner that was not necessary.”] Concerning this matter, although your prudence has no need of my advice, fidelity and affection nevertheless compel my mind—fidelity and affection that I owe both to you and to him [Note: The manuscript Bd. 18 reads “which I owe to you”;]—to offer something to Your Reverence. I am not speaking to one wiser than I as though teaching him, but briefly recalling matters that he knows better than I do. [Note: The manuscript Bd. 18 reads “matters that you know better than I do.”]

My Father, if everything must be done with counsel, whose counsel is more appropriate than that of him who is called “Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God”? He himself counsels those striving toward perfection to leave everything and follow him. He promises those who leave everything and follow him that they will sit with him in judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. [Note: The words “and follow him” are absent from manuscript Bd. 18 and from the edition.] He is the one who invites those laboring and burdened by love of and concern for worldly affairs to come to him and find rest. The holy Fathers understood that this counsel is fulfilled more in the monastic way of life than in any other purpose of living. [Note: “To be fulfilled” is absent from manuscript Bd. 18.]

Indeed, blessed Gregory, in Book XIV of the Register [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “Book IX of the Register”;]—you know what he commands Bishop Desiderius concerning a certain man who, pierced by divine inspiration, had desired the grace of monastic conduct [Note: The Picard edition reads “conversion” rather than “conduct”;]—explains how he exhorts that same bishop in no way to impede his resolve, but rather, insofar as he is able, to inflame him by pastoral admonition, lest the fervor conceived in him grow cold; nor ought the man who has sought the harbor of a monastery to be entangled again in the disturbances of ecclesiastical cares.

In the Fourth Council of Toledo you read that clerics seeking the purpose of monks, because they desire to follow a better life, ought to be free from bishops for entering monasteries. [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “the holy Fathers’ sayings” rather than “the sayings of so many holy Fathers.”]

I have said little about many things. If, then, to speak against the Lord and against the words of so many holy Fathers who truly understand the Lord’s words is a sin, what is it to act against them—not how I know, I will not say, but how you know? [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “the holy sayings” rather than “so many holy Fathers’ sayings”; and “how, I will not say, but how you know.”] If the one who separates what is precious from what is worthless—that is, the soul from the world—will be, as it is written, “like the mouth of God,” what will become of the man whose mouth and hands draw back the soul, which clings to the Lord’s counsel, toward the world? [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “draw back the soul clinging after God to the world” and “draw back the soul clinging to the Lord’s counsel toward the world.”]

God forbid, my lord; may God prevent what God says from falling upon a bishop: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters,” and “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). It is dreadful even to hear that those whom Christ chose from the world, a bishop should bind again to the world; that those whom Christ draws to the harbor from the world’s storms and tempests, a bishop should pull back from the harbor into shipwreck amid the world’s whirlwinds; and that those whom Christ hides in the fold from the multitude of lurking wolves, a bishop should snatch from the fold and expose to the multitude of wolves. [Note: The manuscripts and edition read “that which Christ hides” rather than “those whom Christ hides.” Manuscript Bd. 18 reads “pull back into the shipwrecked,” while two others and the edition read “pull back from the harbor into the perilous whirlwinds.”]

My revered Father, may it not trouble Your Prudence that I speak in this way. I do not do this because I wish to show that you are such a man, but because I desire that you not be such a man. Let Your Prudence consider and reconsider what you did concerning your aforementioned canon; and if it recognizes that you did something that ought to be changed, let it not be ashamed to do what is more fitting. It is not so very surprising if, in a sudden impulse over the loss of so energetic a cleric, you did something without prior deliberation; but it is highly praiseworthy if you change what you recognize ought to be changed.

I greet our lords and friends, your canons. Although I have not known each of them individually, I love them all nevertheless, and I have wished to serve them all. [Note: The manuscripts and edition read “to love and serve”; manuscript Bd. 18 reads “to love and to serve all.”] I humbly beg all of them, together with you, that they forestall by their prayers—not through my merits but through their charity—the fulfillment, with God’s assent, of my consecration, which has been appointed for the Sunday on which “People of Zion” is sung. [Note: The consecration was arranged for the Sunday on which “Populus Sion” is sung, and so on. This is the Second Sunday of Advent. Since in that year it fell on 4 December, that is, the day before the Nones of December, as Anselm indicates in the following Letter 15, the First Sunday of Advent necessarily fell on 27 November. Advent has no earlier beginning than that date, nor a later one than 3 December. Therefore, on the day before the Nones of December, Anselm—called a saint, and deservedly so—born in the border region of Burgundy, a monk of Bec and its second abbot, was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury by Wakelin, bishop of Winchester, and Maurice, bishop of London. The Canterbury tables, a manuscript in the Library of Saint Victor in Paris, recount Anselm’s inauguration in these words; it took place in that same year, namely 1093, after his election, according to the witnesses Eadmer in Book II of his Life of Anselm, Malmesbury, Roger Hoveden, Thomas Walsingham, and Matthew Paris. Therefore Matthew Palmer is not to be heeded when, in additions to the Chronicle of Eusebius, he writes under the year 1090: “Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, shines in England through the goodness of his life and the keenness of his intellect.” Nor is George Lilius to be heeded, who reports this under the year 1095; still less Sigibert, who says that after Lanfranc’s death in 1097 Anselm succeeded him in the archiepiscopate of Canterbury. I say that they are not to be heeded, especially Palmer; for Anselm was so far from shining in England at that time that he was not even living there. For according to Lilius’s reckoning, that is the year of Lanfranc’s death; indeed, during Lanfranc’s final illness, Anselm was at Bec in Normandy, as is clear from Letter 53 of Book II, addressed to that same man lying ill with dysentery. To expose and overcome the error of Sigibert and Lilius is to prevail through the testimony of others who followed Eadmer, Anselm’s companion.] May Almighty Lord direct and guard you in this life until its end [Note: Manuscript Bd. 18 and the edition read “until the end of life”;] so that after this life he may repay you with eternal blessedness.

This letter bears no seal, because I am no longer an abbot and am not yet an archbishop; nor do I take pleasure in being painted as what I am not.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: Compared with two manuscripts of Saint Victor bound together in one codex.]

### ANSELM TO WALERANNUS, CANTOR OF THE CHURCH OF PARIS

That he should vigorously pursue the monastic way of life he has undertaken.

To the lord Walerannus, dearest friend, formerly cantor of the Church of Paris, brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: always to advance toward better things and never to fail.

I have heard, dearest friend, that, choosing the purpose of holy conduct, you entered the monastery of Saint Martin under my most illustrious friend, lord prior Ursus, and I rejoiced greatly at so great a good having come to my friend. But afterward I learned that our lord, your bishop, had forcibly drawn you away from there, and I became sad. And since I have loved and do love your uprightness—with whose affection I am certain, without pretense—my conscience reproves me if I do not strive to visit you by my letters and, insofar as I can, offer you charitable counsel in so great a danger. For I fear that the devil’s cunning may deceive your soul, which is dear to me, and persuade you that, since you were forcibly and unwillingly withdrawn from your holy purpose, you can lawfully and without guilt remain in the clerical state, as before.

Be certain, dearest friend, that your soul cannot in any way accept this without rejecting itself, even if it wishes to defend the matter by the authority of its bishop. For Christ says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:64). Your mind looks back from Christ’s plow if, by growing cold, it withdraws from the purpose to which Christ called you and which you began. Just as bishops retain their authority so long as they agree with Christ, so they themselves deprive themselves of it when they disagree with Christ.

Every bishop who has Christ’s voice is Christ, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice. Read in the Gospel what follows these words: “They do not follow a stranger, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John 10:6). [Note: After these words, the manuscripts read: “The sheep do not follow him, and they flee from him because they do not know the voice of strangers,” or, “whose voice they do not know.”]

If persecution of the body is to be fled from one city to another, how much more the persecution of the soul? Is not the persecution of the soul to be fled—that is, preventing the soul from following Christ’s counsel?

Dearest friend, if you had not read much and did not possess a rational intellect, I would say many things to you to show how good is what you began and how evil it is if you abandon what you began. I say briefly: you could have begun nothing more salutary, and you can abandon nothing more dangerous. Therefore let nothing separate your soul from the monastic purpose that you began.

Read in the Fourth Council of Toledo concerning clerics seeking the monastic life, and in Book XIV of the Register the letter to Bishop Desiderius concerning a cleric made a monk.

May Almighty Lord direct, strengthen, and console your heart. Amen.

## 371 LETTER XIV

[Note: Compared with one of the two aforementioned exemplars bound together in manuscript codex Ef. 20.]

### ANSELM TO FUDO

He indicates that he has already replied concerning placing lord William over the Church of Bec, and commends the Church of Bec to Fudo’s care.

To the lord Fudo, dearest friend, brother Anselm: greetings and faithful prayers.

It is long since I replied to your letters concerning the election of an abbot for the Church of Bec; but, as I hear, the bearer of my letters was captured at sea and prevented from coming to you. Having learned this only late, I again send to our lord the count and to you our counsel concerning the matter, according to his command.

Of none of the brethren of that Church do I wish or advise so strongly that he be made abbot there as I do of lord William, formerly prior at Pexeium, although, by God’s grace, there are several others among them who are not unworthy of this office. [Note: The manuscript reads “although there are several others.”]

I give you as much thanks as I can, as to a most faithful friend, for your almsgiving and for the personal care you have for the Church of Bec, which I commend to you as my own soul, because I love it more than my present life. For I commend no matter so dear to my heart more confidently to anyone than to my truly beloved and loving friend.

I beg and beseech you not only to assist and support it through your own counsel and aid, but also, by turning others toward compassion, support, and love for it insofar as you can, to sustain it. And if it should happen that at some time or in some way it is otherwise than it ought to be—which God forbid—confidently correct and rebuke it as a true friend, and charitably persist until it is corrected.

Know that my love and fidelity toward you, which I have possessed since I came to know you and which have grown in my heart all the more as I have found your love toward me to be more genuine, will, with God’s assent, endure as long as I live.

May Almighty Lord guard you under his continual protection in this life and lead you to eternal life. Amen.

## LETTER XV

[Note: Compared with the aforementioned manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF BEC

Concerning the very sweet letter sent to him by Robert, duke of the Normans, and that his consecration was to take place on the day before the Nones of December.

To his dearest lord prior Baldric and the other monks of Bec, brother Anselm: always to will and do what pleases God and what is beneficial to them. [Note: The manuscript reads “what is beneficial.”]

By God’s grace, our lord, the prince of the Normans, sent me a letter full of great kindness and an apology for himself, if, compelled by his love for me and grief at my loss on account of my election to the archbishopric, he had believed or said anything about me otherwise than he ought. In that letter he kindly asked my advice concerning appointing an abbot for you; and he promised that he would gladly accept it not only in this matter but in other matters as well. I send him my counsel concerning this matter, and send it again to you, as I sent it through our brother, lord Girard.

The king of the English sends you greetings, his assistance, and protection for your possessions that are under his authority, as long as you act and live according to my counsel. If you despise it, however, you will gain no advantage from him. When a letter is sent to me from your side, intended to be read privately and by me alone, let the writing not be too fine [Note: The manuscript reads “not too small.”] For after what you grieve has begun concerning me came to pass, many tears, by day and by night, have harmed my sight too greatly. The dignity or wealth of the archbishopric has not been able to restrain those tears by its consolation [Note: The manuscript reads “wealth” instead of “consolation.”] as much as fear and weariness of it have been able to draw them forth through their disturbance.

My friends, have compassion on me, for I have compassion on you. Pray for me, because I, if I can, pray for you.

My consecration has been arranged to take place on the first Sunday after the feast of Saint Andrew, namely on the day before the Nones of December. Anticipate it with your prayers, and communicate this to the monks and nuns enclosed throughout Normandy, to the members of the cloister, and to our friends in France.

Farewell.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF BEC

He congratulates the abbot whom the men of Bec have appointed in his place, instructing him to be a father to the monks and instructing the monks themselves to obey him as sons.

Anselm, servant of the servants of God, called archbishop, to his dearest sons in Christ, William, abbot, and the other monks of the Church of Bec, greetings.

Glory to God in the highest, and peace in the Church of Bec to brethren of good will. Immense thanks are due to the clemency of God, which, just as it wished to grant the grace of its visitation to you, deprived of pastoral consolation, so it did not wish to prolong that same grace through a long waiting for what was to come. Again I give thanks to his clemency, because, although not altogether as I wished, it has nevertheless deigned in some manner to satisfy my friend’s desire by appointing another abbot over the aforesaid Church, according to my constant desire, while I am still alive.

Yet, since I continually desired that, after having made provision for you before my death, I might await the end of my life with joy and, separated from every appearance of worldly affairs, live a quiet life among you, heavenly Providence did not wish to fulfill my desire in this respect, but, to the great detriment of my soul, as I greatly fear, wished to involve me in greater tumults of affairs than before. Therefore, just as I rejoice in one matter—that I have been heard by God—so I grieve in another—that he did not wish to hear me.

Nevertheless, now as always, maintaining fatherly concern for you, I admonish you as my dearest sons and as those whom I have always loved, and wish to love, with the most tender affection in the depths of Christ, to think alike among yourselves, in the words of the blessed Apostle, and to direct your purpose of mind toward better things each day. [Col. 0041A] Show humble obedience in all things to him whom divine mercy has wished to preside over you, remembering that command by which the same Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Obey your leaders and submit yourselves to them” (Hebrews 13:17). [Note: The manuscript reads “be subject to them.”]

To you, dearest brother William, approved in my mind for every observance of holy religion, whom God’s grace has appointed to become rector after me of so holy a flock of monks, I make this recommendation: be so concerned for the souls of the brethren under your rule that, with God’s protection, the snares of the cunning enemy may not be able to harm them by any device; rather, surrounded by the guard of your concern, may they rejoice that they have found the protections of a good shepherd.

Hasten to show yourself so moderate in all that you do that neither justice may ever exclude grace through any private encroachment, nor grace justice. Always join one to the other in such a way that the order of the monastery may be preserved with inviolate rectitude in both.

Never let slip from your mind what the Lord says through Solomon to a negligent shepherd: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have struck hands with a stranger; you have been ensnared by the words of your mouth, and captured by the words of your lips” (Proverbs 6:1).

I would be pleased to say more, if either the brevity proper to a letter permitted it or your holiness did not know better how to act than I know how to speak. Nevertheless, I appeal to all of you in this final supplication: do not allow the love of your proven sweetness toward me to grow cold, since, although I cannot be with you in bodily presence, I never cease to remain with you in the love of my heart.

Remember also the manner in which I have always been accustomed to acquire friends for the Church of Bec, and hasten to acquire friends for yourselves everywhere by following the good of hospitality, extending kindness to everyone, and, where the ability to perform a deed is lacking, offering the grace of agreeable speech. Never believe that you have enough friends; but whether rich or poor, join them all to yourselves in the love of brotherhood, so that this may advance the welfare of your Church and reach the salvation of those whom you love.

I have written to the count and to the archbishop concerning your blessing, and I have asked that everything be done becomingly. I did not reply to the letters that you sent through lord Gislebert and lord Goffridus because these letters had been written earlier, and the bearer of them was in great haste.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF BEC

Replying to their letter, he consoles them concerning his absence and absolves them from their sins, as they had asked.

Anselm, called archbishop, to his sweetest and dearly beloved sons, the young men and adolescents of Bec, who sent him their letters to England: God’s blessing, and his own blessing insofar as it has value, if it has any value.

In your letters I read your most dear and sweetest affection toward your beloved lover. I read them often, and often, in considering your love, they piously stirred the depths of my heart and covered my face with flowing tears. Although the love of only one of you would have been enough for this, they did so all the more fully and powerfully because, in your words, I imagined the similar mind and affection of the others who did not send letters.

Your Love has thus been cemented to my soul that it cannot think intently without a great wound to itself of the violent removal and separation of its beloved sons. As for your indication that you wish always to be with me [Note: One manuscript reads “you indicated”;], certainly I too desire this. But since God disposes otherwise than we desire, and I do not see that it is advantageous for your souls, which I love as my own, as your conscience bears witness, that you should live with me, I beg, admonish, and advise you to endure patiently with me the heavenly disposition; and, by enduring and mitigating your sadness, to mitigate mine also. For your sadness is mine, and your consolation is mine.

I say this not only to you, sweetest sons [Note: The manuscript reads “sweetest brothers”;], but also to all who bear with you the same distress over the absence of their most beloved beloved one. I know that if you hoped to live with me for some further time in this life, it would be a great consolation to you. How much greater consolation, then, ought we to have if we hope that in the future life we shall live and rejoice together forever?

Therefore, be consoled, my sons, be consoled, and submit yourselves to the will of God, who knows better than you yourselves what is beneficial to you, so that God may repay you more for this patience than could come to you from my presence. Be certain that no distance of place and no length of time will be able, as I hope in God, to separate the sweetness of your love from my heart.

To those who indicated in their letters that they wished my absolution, and also to those who, although they did not request it by letter, nevertheless desire it, I send before God my absolution and blessing; and I pray that Almighty God may absolve them from all sins and bless them into eternal life. Amen.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO COUNTESS IDA

He exhorts the countess to persevere in holiness.

Anselm, servant of the servants of God, called archbishop, to Ida, countess, deserving of reverence and love for her manner of life: so serve God in this life that in the future she may deserve to reign with God.

I know, and I am certain, most beloved lady in God, dearest sister, sweetest daughter, that your holy love—by which you reverently and joyfully embrace me in your heart as though I were your spiritual father—incessantly desires to know what concerns me and what has happened to me, and to hear or read something from my side [Note: The manuscript reads “to hear or read.”], so that according to the rule of true charity it may rejoice or suffer with me. To this love of yours [Note: The manuscript reads “to this love”;] my heart certainly responds with a like affection.

Since, then, it is not fitting to recount in a letter what has happened to me this year or how my heart bears it—and since our beloved friend lord Rainerius, your cleric, saw much himself and learned more from my account—I asked him, as he acknowledges that he was sent by Your Reverence for this very purpose, to make known orally, with a living voice, what he learned concerning me inwardly and outwardly.

And since I have long since learned with complete certainty, daughter most beloved by me in God, that my admonitions are joyfully received by your heart, and since I remember that you have wholly entrusted your soul to my care, it is necessary to add something pertinent to your exhortation.

Dearest friend in God, the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20:16). Therefore, never be confident that you ought to be counted among the chosen until you live in such a way that there are few with whom your life ought to be compared. And when you know that you are among the few, still be afraid; for it will still be uncertain whether you are among those few chosen ones until you see yourself among that small number concerning whose election no doubt remains.

For he who said, “Few are chosen,” certainly did not say how few. Thus, however much progress we may seem to have made, we must always judge that we have reached no more than the beginning of making progress.

Therefore I exhort and advise my daughter, who has entrusted herself to my counsel, that the zeal for living well which she began long ago should in no way grow weak; rather, as though beginning each day, let it grow fervent day by day.

May Almighty God mercifully absolve you from all sins and bless you forever; and, insofar as divine grace grants it to me, may you always have my absolution and blessing. Amen.

## 373 LETTER XIX

[Note: Compared with the aforementioned manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO WULSTAN, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

He asks his advice against the bishop of London, who wished to dedicate the village churches of the archbishop of Canterbury within his own diocese.

Anselm, servant of the servants of Christ, called archbishop, to the beloved and revered bishop Wulstan of Worcester. [Note: “Wulstan.” The name is read with considerable variation: at times Wulstanus, elsewhere Wolstanus and Ulstanus; but most frequently Wulstanus, as here and in the manuscript lists of the bishops of Worcester in our library. Thus: “Aldred, bishop of Worcester, built a church from its foundations in the city of Gloucester and constructed it in honor of the chief of the apostles, Peter; afterward, with the king’s permission, he appointed Wulstan, a Worcester monk ordained by him, as abbot.” In the same place, in 1062, Saint Wulstan became bishop through Aldred, previously archbishop of York, while Stigand was prohibited from acting as archbishop of Canterbury. The deeds of this Saint Wulstan are preserved. His feast is on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. That is enough concerning him. William of Malmesbury, Book IV of On the Deeds of the English Bishops, and incidentally Book III on the archbishops of York, gives more; Roger Hoveden, in the first part of his Annals under the year 1062, records the particular events at considerable length; and in 1095 Bravonius, a Worcester monk, compiled an epitome of his deeds, found in Surius, volume I. Polydore Vergil repeatedly and honorably mentions the most holy bishop in Books VIII, IX, and X of his English History; likewise Matthew Paris, in his Greater History under the years 1088 and 1095, composed a more extended account of his life and character. Although Thomas Walsingham narrated only a few things about him, he is nevertheless said to have left delirious tales and fabrications in his histories—not in my judgment, but in that of Matthew Parker, the pseudo-archbishop of Canterbury, and an English Calvinist, who joins Matthew Paris to Walsingham in the preface to the Histories of Walsingham, published at London in 1574 under his care and direction. And lest anyone think that I am too boldly attributing this to an opponent, let him read his very words on this subject: “Who today,” he says, “would think that either Archbishop Dunstan held the devil, lying in wait for his work, suspended by the nose, or that Wulstan of Worcester fixed his staff beside the tomb of Saint Edward so firmly in the marble that it could be removed by neither Lanfranc nor anyone else except Wulstan alone? It is salutary for young men to recognize all these delirious tales of antiquity.” A little later, warning the reader, he says: “Nor should you wholly reject these very ancient histories of your country, since false miracles are reported in them.”]

O man of keen discernment and lynx-like vision, who knows well how to distinguish purple beside purple and separate false miracles from true ones! Would that he had also explained to the young men, for whose salvation he fears, the difference between false and genuine miracles, lest they embrace a cloud in place of the sun! For what he means, I confess that I do not grasp, unless by “false miracles” he signifies those matters which we have just described in his own words; and if any falsehood lurks in them, he alone has exposed it. For if the best possible judge of these matters—and, as the saying goes, the proverbial “Herculean argument” [Greek, as printed: *ἡραχλέα λόγος*]—be applied to Holy Scripture (which we know is not sufficient for him and the other Calvinists or Protestants, though it is sufficient for us), nevertheless nothing therein will be accused of fraud or falsehood.

For, to begin with the most holy Dunstan, no one is unaware that, just as the devil used the serpent’s instrument and malice to deceive our first parents, so, in order to beguile anyone, and especially men devoted to holiness and chastity, he may assume the deceptive appearance of a woman. Now, if contraries produce contrary consequences, as they do, who will deny that, since Abraham received good angels appearing as men as guests, washed them, and conversed with them (Genesis XVIII); since Lot also compelled them to enter his house as guests (Genesis X); indeed, since Jacob wrestled with an angel (Genesis XXXII); and since sacred Scripture records many other occasions on which human beings dealt with good angels displaying a male appearance, Saint Dunstan could have held the devil fast by his compressed nose, bound and subdued, if Jacob was able to grasp a good angel so tightly?

I hasten to Vulstan, whose splendid deed, although it needs neither my praise nor my defense, I shall at least briefly turn against the slander brought against it—a slander which I could not prevent a heretic’s sacrilegious hand from bringing. What delirium or trickery, then, was discovered in this divine and heavenly work? Perhaps the fact that the marble was almost at the same time both soft and hard. But who, unless ignorant of the divine Scriptures, does not see that this is very similar to what occurs in sacred history?

In Exodus IX several plagues are enumerated with which the God of vengeance struck Egypt; yet the land of Goshen in Egypt was immune to them. In IV Kings VI, the same iron was at almost the same moment heavy, so that it sank to the bottom of the water, and light, so that it rose upward while floating. In Daniel III, the same fire, at the same time, burned Nebuchadnezzar’s torturers, while it touched the holy boys thrown into the furnace only very lightly—indeed, it lightly drenched them as though with morning dew. Matthew XIV tells of the same sea as stable for Christ but unstable for Peter.

What, then, prevents the sepulchral marble from having been both soft and hard at once—soft when the episcopal staff was driven into it, hard when someone other than Vulstan attempted to pull it out? To make it easier for the reader to accept these brief rebuttals, I shall give a short account of each matter.

Blessed Dunstan was once forging some artifact when he suddenly saw the devil in the form of a girl. The devil attacked the man of God with feminine laughter and shameless words. But his more wanton speech revealed the enemy. Therefore Dunstan suddenly seized his nose, which was wrinkled in laughter, with red-hot tongs, and gripped it so firmly that the devil gave a terrible howl as witness to the pain inflicted.

But if Parker regards the deed as ridiculous because of its novelty, at least a very similar story, made venerable by its great antiquity, has gained widespread acceptance. The same thing is related of Appelles, a blacksmith and inhabitant of the Nitrian desert, in Palladius’s *Historia Lausiaca*, chapter 60; the *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1; and Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28.

Saint Vulstan was present in 1078 at the synod held in London, at which, with King William acting and Lanfranc ordering him because of his ignorance—although Bravonius, Malmesbury, and Matthew Paris speak otherwise—he was compelled to lay aside his episcopal insignia. And indeed he did so, saying: “I declare myself unworthy of the honor and the burden; but from him from whom I received them, I return them.” Scarcely had he spoken these words when he removed his episcopal garments and went to Saint Edward’s tomb. There he drove his staff so deeply into the stone that it could be pulled out by no one’s strength except that of the man who had driven it in.

Terrified by this miracle, both the king and Lanfranc ordered him to take up the staff again, put on the episcopal robe (*poderis*) again, and enjoy the priesthood conferred upon him by Edward. Here is a summary of both matters; let the reader judge what delirium they contain.

I should certainly like to demonstrate more plainly the delirium of that writer, who raves so wildly that he considers every other excellent deed a delirium as well; but I am not permitted to do so. For I should then have to dance outside the choir. Besides, in that same work he recounts many other dreams, as he calls them, whose explanation would require both many pages and many nights of labor.

Since Dunstan was mentioned above and has now been mentioned together with Vulstan, it seemed worthwhile—or rather necessary—to examine these matters briefly. Moreover, since Anselm, already archbishop, wrote to Vulstan, the grossest error that crept into the life of Vulstan inserted in Surius’s first volume is easily detected and, once detected, more easily corrected: namely, the claim that he died in the year 1067. This is contradicted by Thomas Walsingham in the *Hypodigma Neustriae*, Matthew Paris, Florence of Worcester’s *Chronicle* (p. 462, although he writes about him more fully earlier, on p. 421), and Roger of Hoveden, all of whom state that he died in 1095.

This correction is certainly necessary, since elsewhere we have shown that Anselm was consecrated archbishop toward the end of 1093. Even without that evidence, however, many other facts reported in the histories of the English would prove that this was not the year of Vulstan’s death. From these facts it is clear when Anselm sent this letter to Vulstan: namely, in 1094, since we have shown above that Anselm was consecrated toward the end of 1093 and that Vulstan died at the beginning of 1095.

Thus may he persevere in the purpose of holiness he has undertaken, so that he may deserve to reign without end in eternal blessedness. [Column 0045A]

Your holiness and wisdom, which by God’s grace have greatly increased in you over your long life, and the certainty of your affection, which I have unquestionably recognized toward me, urge me, whenever circumstances require, to have recourse to your reverence’s counsel in our affairs. Therefore I seek your advice concerning a certain accusation which one of our fellow bishops—namely, the bishop of London—is bringing against me, contrary to the ancient custom that our Church has freely and peacefully possessed in former and ancient times down to the present.

For, as every kind of person in the diocese of Canterbury and in the other bishoprics surrounding that same diocese bears witness, the archbishop of Canterbury has always possessed this power and custom: that, within the diocese of any bishop, the Church of Canterbury might have a village or church belonging by proper right to that archbishop, with everything concerning that village or church that pertained to episcopal office—whether dedication or anything else.

There are still countless men alive who [Note: “who saw my predecessor, Lanfranc, of venerable memory.” Anselm stated and asserted this generally, on the basis of popular report: that Lanfranc exercised in the villages of the Church of Canterbury everything pertaining to episcopal duties. Lanfranc, however, in his letter to Stigand, bishop of Winchester, seems to discuss the matter somewhat more precisely, saying:

“The clergy of our villages who are situated in your diocese have complained to us that your archdeacons, whenever opportunities arose, demanded money and have already received it from some. Your Fraternity ought to remember that, contrary to the custom of our predecessors and yours, we have granted them permission and ordered them to attend your synods, and to hear from you, without any interruption or investigation, whatever may contribute to knowledge of the Christian religion. If any faults should be found in them, they were to be reserved for our judgment while punishment was suspended, and they were to remain subject to us either for mercy or for vengeance.

“We therefore command you to order that whatever was wrongly taken be returned without delay, and, in the interest of preserving charity, to prohibit your ministers from presuming to do such things again. As for our priests who are established outside Kent, we categorically order them no longer to attend your synod or that of any bishop, nor to answer either you or any of your ministers for any fault. For when we come to our villages, we must investigate by pastoral authority what sort of men they are, both in conduct and in knowledge of their order.

“They are to receive chrism from you alone and pay what has been established from ancient times for receiving chrism. For just as we carefully wish to preserve intact whatever our predecessors possessed from ancient times down to our own day, so we do not wish—God forbid—to deny through any usurpation what is owed to others.”]

who saw my predecessor, Lanfranc, archbishop of venerable memory, dedicate the churches of his villages within the dioceses of other bishops, with those bishops’ knowledge and without opposition. Saint Dunstan and my other predecessors are also proven to have done this, and the churches they dedicated still stand.

The aforesaid bishop—namely, a suffragan of his archbishop and primate—is now attempting to take away and abolish this dignity and power, which the Church of Canterbury has possessed undisturbed for so long, from his mother. [Note: “of his mother” (*matris suae*), manuscript reading “from his mother” (*matri suae*).]

For this reason I ask your counsel and assistance in this matter, so that, as a faithful son, you may come to the aid of your mother against her son—not, I shall not say, an unfaithful son, but one who wishes to disinherit her—and, if you know anything that may aid our defense [Note: manuscript reading: “may avail for us,” rather than “may avail for our defense”], may diligently inform us by letter. Farewell.

## Letter XX

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

Anselm to Osbern, Bishop of Exeter.

That the Exeter clergy should not trouble the monks, and that the bishop should allow them to distinguish the divine offices by the sound of bells.

Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury by God’s disposition, to the reverend bishop Osbern of Exeter, greetings.

It is fitting for episcopal dignity to invite everyone it can to the service of God and to strengthen those who wish to serve God, insofar as it is able, by advising and helping them. Therefore, trusting in this, I beg your reverence, for God’s sake and for the sake of our affection—if that can avail anything in this matter—to assist with fatherly and episcopal kindness the monks residing in your city from the monastery commonly called Battle, and, as far as you are able, to defend them against all adversaries, as befits you. Thus, if God deigns to work some good through them, you may receive a reward from God together with them.

For I have heard that some of your clergy have done certain things to them that ought not to have been done. I therefore ask you to order that such satisfaction be made to the aforesaid monks that thereafter they cannot justly complain of the indiscretion of your clergy.

I also admonish those same clergy, with brotherly charity and fatherly confidence, by entreating them to conduct themselves toward those same brothers in such a way that, by this very display of charity and kindly familiarity, they may prove that they are pleased with the monks’ progress and zeal in serving God.

But your prohibition against their ringing their bells according to their custom is nowhere properly observed except where monks serve in the mother church of the city. [Note: manuscript reading: “in the greater church,” rather than “in the mother church.”] For where canons are established in the principal church to serve God, each order—the canons and the monks—rings its bells earlier or later according to the requirements of the service assigned to it, without any legitimate prohibition.

Therefore, having been admonished by reason itself, do not wish henceforth to prohibit them from ringing their bells according to their order. The brothers themselves ask this, and I with them and on their behalf also ask that, whenever they wish at some public gathering to seek the people’s assistance for the construction of their church, they should in no way be forbidden. Farewell.

## Letter XXI

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

Anselm to William, abbot, and the monks of Bec.

What may be learned from the mouths of messengers.

To his most beloved lords and brothers, Lord Abbot William and the servants of God residing at Bec, brother Anselm, called archbishop, may be led along the way of God and enter into his truth.

I know, my dearest ones, that you have always wished to know what concerns me, and I do not think that anyone in this life sympathizes with me or rejoices with me more faithfully than you. But since through our brother Lord William and through Ansfrid, our servant [Note: manuscript reading: “Lord William and Austrid,” rather than “our brother Lord William, through Ansfrid”], you can learn more fully what my situation is than through a brief letter—and since I think you have already heard much of it through Lord Farman and others who recently came from me to you—I do not think it necessary in this letter to extend the matter further.

But I hope that you will pray for me, your beloved friend, in what I believe is a greater need than I have ever experienced; I do not think that you need any further urging to do so. It seems enough for me that you know how greatly I need your prayers.

I especially admonish, beg, and entreat my sweetest sons, weaned before their time—I mean my young men—who, because of the tenderness and natural restlessness of their age, often stir my heart affectionately when I remember them, to remember throughout their lives both me and the affection [Note: manuscript *quem erga* (“whom toward”), rather than *quam erga* (“the affection toward”)] they have experienced from me toward them, and never by any perversity to grieve my heart.

Let them know for certain that, if they live according to my desire and according to the admonitions [Note: manuscript *admonitionem quas* (“the admonition which”), rather than *admonitiones quas* (“the admonitions which”)] they have received from me, they will greatly console my soul in every tribulation; but if they act otherwise, they will sin greatly by grieving it. For I hope, with God’s help, that their life will not be hidden from me, since I shall always be anxious to inquire into their conduct.

May almighty God lead you in such a way that he brings you into the sight of his glory.

## 374. Letter XXII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

That it should not be attributed to negligence that he did not write to him.

Anselm, called archbishop, to his most beloved brother and son Boso, God’s and his own blessing.

[Note: “Boso.” Concerning this Boso I shall say what I have found, though more briefly, in order to avoid most of what his biographer records that is of no or very little importance and would create tiresome delays for the reader. How worthy Boso is of a longer and fuller remembrance is shown by the mutual, indeed more than fraternal, love with which Anselm loved him and he loved Anselm in return. Even if we did not learn this from Anselm’s letters, his honorable eulogy, preserved in Gemmeticensis, Book VIII of the *History of the Dukes of Normandy*, chapter 24, would indicate it even to a blind man.

Let us therefore begin with the words of his biographer:

“In the days of King William, who subdued the English by arms, in the region of Rouen, at a place commonly called Montivilliers in the Pays de Caux, Boso was born in a village estate of the monastery to Haimeric and Lezelina. Through their care he was imbued with good arts and piety, so that amid the waves of the world he contracted no impurity at all. To avoid contracting any, he withdrew to Bec and remained there chiefly for the reason which Eadmer explains in Book I of the *Life of Saint Anselm*, its final chapter. We shall not repeat here what is there explained and again clarified in the *Chronicle of Bec*. Nor shall we pause over the fact that Anselm’s praises of him, transferred from that work, are also included there; instead, we shall continue with the supplementary material of the *Chronicle of Bec*, which begins as follows:

“‘Meanwhile, when Prior Baldric died, William the abbot ordered Boso to succeed him in the priory. He was a man of honorable life and great prudence, distinguished by humility, endowed with the spirit of counsel, and steadfast in courage. He consoled the desolate, becoming all things to all people. As far as he could, he helped everyone; he was kind in exhortation, restrained in correction, generous to the poor, courteous to guests, firm in faith, confident in God through hope, and abounding in charity. When he had nothing to give, he urged people to place their hope in God and asserted that God’s help would soon arrive, that the end of the world had not yet come. He said such things in jest, but in his heart he humbly begged God, who very often helped him according to his faith.

“‘Not only his subjects but also the rulers of the earth, bishops and abbots alike, and many religious and secular persons, having discovered his wisdom, counsel, and goodness of heart, admired them as a precious treasure and as a divine oracle. So great was the grace of God in him, and so vigorously did the spirit of counsel operate in him, that he answered those who came to him for advice subtly and adequately according to what they asked.

“‘During this period King Henry ordered William the abbot to give Boso, the prior of Bec, to his nephew Count Theobald, so that he might make him abbot in his own land. Whether the king requested this out of affection or resentment, without providing any estate, in order to drive Boso from the region, we do not know. When the abbot heard this, he was greatly saddened and sent to the king, ordering and earnestly begging him to spare the Church and himself, to withdraw his mind from such an order, and not to take away his prior. For the abbot, exhausted by old age and illness, was already without bodily strength.

“‘The king, appeased by this entreaty, released the prior. But when Abbot William, worn down by a long illness, seemed close to death, two monks of Bec approached King Henry, who was then staying at Bec and around Bec because of the incursions of certain men who had rebelled against him. They said that if Boso succeeded Abbot William, as the community desired, he would in no way perform homage or swear an oath of fidelity to the king, and that therefore the king ought to substitute for him another man whom they named and praised. They did this because they did not want the prior as abbot. We do not know why they were hostile to him.

“‘When the king heard this, he became exceedingly angry in spirit, though at that time he concealed his anger. They, however, acting cunningly and without the community’s knowledge, wished, contrary to the rule of Saint Benedict, to impose upon it without its consent a man whom it is clear they were setting above it, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, who said that no one should be ordained against his will, but that the community of the Church should choose its pastor for itself according to the fear of God.

“‘Although the cunning of these malicious men disturbed the community somewhat, it could not accomplish what it plotted. For when Abbot William died, the entire community elected Boso. All the bishops and abbots, clergy and people, neighbors and those from farther away who knew him, praised this election and declared him worthy of the highest honor. Accordingly, the community earnestly begged him to accept their choice.

“‘He set forth many reasons arising from his weakness. They prostrated themselves on the ground and begged him; he resisted with all his strength by refusing. The matter was reported to the king, but he remembered what he had heard from the two monks concerning homage, as we related above, and was exceedingly angry about it.

“‘Meanwhile, Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, a prudent and honorable man, and John, bishop of Lisieux, who had come to the king’s court—at that time the king was besieging Bridou Castle, which the men of the count of Meulan held against him—came to Bec and spoke with the brothers about choosing an abbot. Then all of them, prostrated on the ground—for they were sitting in the chapter house—begged the prior to consent to the oft-mentioned election and asked the archbishop to compel him by command.

“‘The archbishop, admiring the brothers’ unanimity, praised their religious intention and their great love for their prior. Then, turning to him, he admonished and begged him, and finally commanded him under obedience to comply with the will of the brothers. But he replied that he could not do so because of his great bodily weakness and raised certain other serious matters, almost as though they were sins, by which he claimed that he was unworthy of this office.

“‘“Are you a monk?” [the archbishop asked.] He replied that he wished to be one.

“‘Then the archbishop said: “Indeed, if you had killed twenty men, I would not release you, since I see such great and such intense affection for you.”

“‘“I have never killed a man,” he replied.

“‘Then he was compelled to reveal what he had kept hidden. Taking the archbishop aside with the bishops, he said that the pope had forbidden him ever to perform homage to a lay person; for that reason he did not dare to accept this obedience, lest he be forced either to become a transgressor of the apostolic prohibition or to offend the king.

“‘When the archbishop heard this, he received it wisely. The bishop of Lisieux, however, took it badly, because the prior of Bec disdained to do what he and all the prelates of Normandy did according to the ancient custom of the country.

“‘Moreover, the archbishop helped the men of Bec with the king as much as he could, speaking with them, on their behalf, and without them. One day, when he was discussing this matter with the king, the king said to him: “He will perform homage neither to me nor profession to you.”

“‘A little later, however, the king became more lenient and, when two men of Bec happened to meet him, advised them to commend the matter to God with some general supplication. Nor was the king’s advice fruitless. For afterward he ordered the prior to come to Rouen, where he gave him the government by word alone. He also pleaded on behalf of the two monks whom we said had opposed his election, asking that Boso not harm them because they had held an opinion against him.

“‘It was not a difficult labor for him to pardon an offender.

“‘When the archbishop saw that the king had freely done what was requested, he wished, as he had promised, honorably to do what pertained to him in this matter. He therefore came for the feast of Pentecost, and at Terce, when the cantor began “Come, Creator Spirit,” the archbishop entered the choir and, with due honor, placed Boso in the abbot’s seat.

“‘Then, on the octave of Pentecost, Boso was ordered to proceed to receive the blessing. Before Mass, however, he spoke with the archbishop and asked him not to compel him to make the profession, which he absolutely did not wish to make, because if he did so he would create a great scandal in the monastery.

“‘The archbishop replied: “Let it be; all will be well.”

“‘When the time for Mass arrived, Boso was brought forward to be blessed. The archbishop stood at the holy altars and questioned him according to custom until they came to the question: “Do you wish to be obedient to this Church, to me, and to my successors?”

“‘He replied: “I do.”

“‘Then some of the clergy standing around began to urge him to say: “I profess.”

“‘Again he said: “I do.”

“‘When they persisted that he should answer “I profess,” he said a third time: “I do, and I do so from the heart.”

“‘Then John, legate of the Holy Roman Church, who happened to be present, said: “You have heard what he says. What more do you want?”

“‘And so the archbishop blessed him.

“‘The next day the abbot returned to Bec. The community, dressed in sacred vestments and proceeding in an ordered procession, went out to meet him as he arrived. He, though weak, came humbly to meet them barefoot, and was received with joy.’”

The *Chronicle of Bec* weaves together certain other matters in more polished language. Among them, it seemed wrong to omit this: when someone reported that the commands he had issued were not being carried out, he replied: “We often disregard God’s commands, and he endures it; how much more ought we to endure it if our commands are disregarded?”

At length, after long-standing pains in his feet, head, and internal organs; blindness endured with equanimity for several years; and the sharp, sudden torments of repeated attacks of paralysis, he came to the threshold of death. Strengthened beforehand by the sacraments of the Church, while the brothers took turns singing penitential psalms about that city in whose streets, according to Tobit’s prophecy, alleluia is sung (Tobit XIII, 22), he departed this life on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of Christ 1136, at the age of seventy-one, after twelve years and twenty-two days of rule.

His body was buried to the left of Herluin in the chapter-house courtyard, with this rather unpolished epitaph:

> Adorned in character, this shepherd lies buried here;  
> Distinguished in intellect, sober and devout.  
> He was gentle, prudent, and strong amid sorrows;  
> For as long as he lived, he endured many scourges.  
> Powerful in counsel, he was a support to many,  
> A comfort to the afflicted and a help to the devout.  
> This fourth abbot ruled for twice six years  
> The monastery of Bec, the glory and form of the flock.  
> Despising the world and loving true virtue,  
> He rendered devoted service to Christ.  
> This father had passed seventy years  
> When he suffered death and became the ashes now lying here.  
> While, beneath Cancer, the sun was making for its eighth rising,  
> The final lot tore him from us in sorrow.  
> The birth of the Baptist is celebrated as this man dies;  
> His name was Boso: may God be gracious to him!

After his death, Boso left an heir to his teaching in a letter to some physician who was babbling about the monastic profession, as is clear from the text of the letter itself. I found it in the manuscript of Bec and transferred it here so that it would not be consumed by time; it begins with these words: “Boso, etc.”]

God’s and his own blessing.

Perhaps someone may wonder—someone whose conscience I know so well that he loves no human being above me, and whom I love so greatly that I do not know whom I love more—why, during so long an absence, I have not consoled him, distressed by my absence, with some written visit. But be assured that it was not through negligence or forgetfulness of you.

For just as I am certain that you would always wish to be with me, so do not doubt that I would always wish to be with you. If God deigns to grant me peace and opportunity, so that I may enjoy the presence of your affection, know that I shall gladly do whatever is necessary to make this happen—and, if not always, at least as much as reason permits.

Whatever happens, preserve my affection, dearest one, because I desire to preserve yours. Greet my sweetest son, your brother Rainald. Frequently encourage as many of your brothers as you can, especially the young men and novices. May almighty God always guard you from every evil.

## Letter XXIII

Anselm to Rodulf, abbot, and his monks.

That a monk who was ordained by a bishop under interdict is himself subjected to perpetual interdict. And that a man who sought herbs from a woman with which to kill her husband must never be ordained if the husband was killed by means of them.

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

To his beloved lords and brothers, the reverend Rodulf, abbot of Séez, and the other servants of God residing under him, brother Anselm, called archbishop: may you always advance to higher virtues and in the monastic purpose, and never fail.

[Note: “Rodulf.” All printed copies have “Radulfum,” as do two lists of the archbishops of Canterbury in manuscript in our library. One of these, while including Radulf, adds the following apart from the name:

“In the year of the Lord from the Incarnation 1089, Robert I, first abbot of the monastery of Séez, a good and simple man, fell ill in January and, having received the Lord’s sacraments, departed from this world on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. He was succeeded in the government by Radulf, son of Seisfred of Scurris, a monk of the same monastery. He was very learned, eloquent, and pleasant, and therefore beloved by all. In his youth he came from a distinguished family to the monastic life and for ten years humbly served in the monastery through various stages of office. Finally, in the eleventh year, at the command and under the consecration of Girard, bishop of Séez, he assumed responsibility for the abbacy. For sixteen years he governed it energetically amid the savage storms of war, and, relying on God’s help, carefully increased the Church’s possessions as circumstances allowed. Later, when the cruelty of Robert of Bellême became too oppressive, he fled to England. King Henry kept him honorably at his side and, after Bishop Gundulf, placed him over the bishopric of Rochester. Some years later he was promoted and succeeded the venerable Anselm as archbishop, ruling the metropolitan see of Canterbury for nine years.

“This Radulf, in the time of Pope Paschal, came to the king in Normandy and from there began to travel to Rome, although he was already suffering from swelling of the feet. When he heard rumors of the pope’s death, he sent legates to Rome. He himself returned to Rouen and spent nearly three years in Normandy. Once, while staying there, after Mass had ended on the translation of Saint Benedict, he was suddenly struck by a sharp attack while he was removing his vestments. He became speechless and after several days began to speak, but not fully. He suffered from paralysis for two years and, carried in a vehicle to his own seat, died among his people.

“In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, Archbishop Radulf died at Canterbury on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. After several years William of Corbeil, a regular canon, succeeded him.”

Thus far the account of Radulf in the Victorian manuscript. I have observed one point in it which I should mention to the reader: namely, the year of his death, which Malmesbury, Hoveden, and Matthew Paris unanimously give as 1122. I suspect that the third numeral was added through the carelessness of a copyist: just as he had read “the thirteenth day before the Kalends,” so, writing hastily, he may have written the year 1123, perhaps so as to obtain the pallium more easily and quickly. There is also Ivo of Chartres, Letter 252, to Pope Paschal.

The monastery of Séez over which Radulf presided, I think, was the one which Gemmeticensis, Book VII, chapter 22, states was founded for Saint Martin in the suburbs of Séez by Roger of Montgomery, the father of Robert of Bellême, mentioned above, in the time of William the Bastard, duke of Normandy. Following his example—for he had arranged for the construction of a monastery at Caen in honor of Saint Stephen—all the lords of Normandy modeled themselves upon him and, in a holy rivalry, established very many churches, which Gemmeticensis, still abbot of Séez, describes briefly. Eadmer also mentions him in Book I of the *Life of Anselm*.]

Concerning the brother whom you say was ordained by a certain bishop who is under interdict from us, I answer that, if he was ordained by the bishop of Wales named Hereward, he shall never use, with our permission, the orders he received from him, nor should he be reordained by any bishop.

Concerning the other brother, who sought herbs for a woman with which she might kill her husband: although you have near you in Normandy sufficient counsel concerning this matter, nevertheless, since you ask my opinion, I ought not to withhold it. If he were our monk, and if the man for whose death he sought the herbs had been killed by means of them, he would never, through me, ascend to the diaconate or the priesthood.

If I followed the affection of my heart, I would write much to your affection. But since, as I think, I am speaking to those who know me from their own conscience, I shall say briefly that, just as we have loved one another for God’s sake, so I desire and pray to God, and ask you, that we may persevere in the same affection for God’s sake. Thus, just as the cause for which charity itself began will never cease, so may that charity remain inviolate.

I know that you wish, as friends, to learn about the state of our life. I do not know what God will do with me in the future; but since I took the name of archbishop, I have not yet felt anything over which my heart might dare to rejoice. Therefore I humbly pray and earnestly entreat you to assist me in my need with your prayers, until you learn for what purpose God has separated me from you and from our other friends who are in Normandy—a separation that still continues and causes me no slight sorrow.

May the almighty Lord always gladden you by his grace and blessing, and multiply virtues in your souls.

## Letter XXIV

[Note: Collated with the aforementioned manuscript.]

Anselm to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon.

He consults the primate of Lyon about what should be done amid his many adversities. Concerning the schism between Urban, whom he supported, and Guibert. He promises the king a large sum of money, which, through God’s mercy, he does not pay; hence the king becomes angry.

To his most beloved lord and friend, the reverend Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, brother Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, whether by God’s command or by his permission: may you shine long in this life and rejoice forever in the life to come.

If everything is to be done with counsel, those things above all must be done with careful counsel in which nothing is to be sought except what obeys the will of God. I therefore beg your Holiness to ask God, for His sake and for the sake of the charity which I know he has toward me, for counsel that He may give me. To speak briefly, you have heard, I think, how I was suddenly seized and carried off to the archbishopric. Before I gave my consent, I openly declared that I supported Lord Pope Urban and opposed Guibert; and for six months I did and said whatever I could without sin in order to be released. At last, compelled by fear of God and for many reasons, I submitted, grieving, to the command of my archbishop and to the election of all England, and I was consecrated. Perhaps there I trembled where there was no fear; but I did not know—God knows—and I still do not know.

Shortly afterward our king, intending to go to Normandy, needed a great deal of money. Before he asked me for anything, on the advice of friends I promised him a considerable sum—God knows with what intention. He despised it as too little, so that I would give more; but I refused. Thanks be to God, by whose mercy this happened through the simplicity of my heart, lest, if I had promised nothing or little, he should seem to have a just cause for anger, or, if he had accepted it, it should become a burden to me and give rise to suspicion of an abominable purchase. From that hour he appeared to seek opportunities against me.

I spoke about the pallium. He did not want me to request it so long as he himself received no apostolic one, or at least to inform the lord pope of the excuse for this delay. Until now I have endured this, on the advice of the bishops, in order to avoid an unfruitful disagreement, in case God might meanwhile accomplish something by which he could be persuaded to accept that lord pope.

I asked that a council be summoned, something that had not been done in England for many years, so that certain matters in that kingdom which plainly seemed wholly intolerable might be corrected. I also admonished him to correct certain things which seemed to me to be done otherwise than they ought to be. In consequence of these words he openly showed himself angry and declared that he had lost his love for me. I replied that I would rather he be angry with me than that God be angry with him, and so I withdrew from his presence.
