The next day, returning to him, I said that I would willingly make amends to him if any fault on my part toward him were found—although I myself knew of none—and I asked him to restore his affection to me. He replied that he would then accept neither amends nor restore his affection, unless I said why he ought to restore it to me. He seemed to me to want the money which I had refused to give, lest I should appear to confess a fault that did not exist.

He became so angry that he said things he ought not to have said, and would partly give and partly arrange to give to knights certain lands—not inconsiderable—which Archbishop Lanfranc had held peacefully in his father’s time and in his own until the day of his death. This was to be done under the pretext of a certain voluntary form of justice, according to which he wants me to plead concerning those lands, although I say that he ought not to force me to plead concerning lands which my predecessor the archbishop held peacefully for so long, and which he himself gave to me just as that predecessor held them.

This, then, is the voluntary justice I mentioned. Since the same lands are said to have been held from the archbishop of Canterbury by English knights before the Normans invaded England, and those knights died without heirs, he wishes to assert that he can justly appoint as their heirs whomever he chooses.

Let your prudence therefore attend and consider what I think about the matters described above, so that in your letters you may either approve my judgment or weaken it by setting forth your reasons, and confirm me in what ought more properly to be maintained.

This is my present thought: the king gave me the archbishopric just as Archbishop Lanfranc held it until the end of his life; and now he is taking from the Church and from me what the Church and that same archbishop held peacefully for so long, and what he himself gave to me. I am certain, moreover, that this archbishopric will be given after me to no one except in the condition in which I hold it on the day of my death; and even if another king comes while I am alive, he will grant me only what he finds me holding.

If, therefore, I hold the archbishopric in a diminished state until my death, the Church will lose it through me. For if someone else, to whom the guardianship of the Church did not belong, were to inflict this violence upon it, or patiently endure it once inflicted, it would be plain that in the future nothing could be said why the Church’s possessions ought not to return to it. But now, since the king himself is its advocate and I am its guardian, what will be said in the future except that the king did it and the archbishop, by enduring it, confirmed that it ought to be considered valid?

It is therefore better for me before God not to hold the Church’s lands in this way, and to make the office of bishop poor, in the manner of the apostles, as a testimony to the violence inflicted, than, by holding it diminished, to make its diminution irreparable.

There is another matter on which I think similarly. If I, a metropolitan and consecrated bishop, do not seek a living pope or the pallium throughout the whole first year, when I am able to do so, I ought justly to be removed from that office. But if I cannot do this without losing the archbishopric, it is better for it to be violently taken from me; indeed, it is better for me to reject the archbishopric than to deny the Apostolic See. This is what I think, and this is what I intend to do, unless you write to me why I ought not to do it.

May Almighty Lord preserve your Holiness in this life by His grace in such a way that in the life to come He may grant you eternal happiness. Amen.

[Col. 0056A]

## LETTER XXV

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO BOSO

That he does not write more frequently because of the king’s anger and hostility. And concerning the book *Why God Became Man*, which Eadmer was transcribing.

What a father writes to his son, a brother to his brother, the most beloved to the most beloved: A. to B., what he is to him.

I give thanks to you, just as I do on your behalf, for your epistolary visit, for your counsel, for your consolation, and for your longing. Although you desire me above all worldly things, your heart is nevertheless more inclined toward the consolation of my tribulation, of which you know, than toward the satisfaction of your own desire, which is the greatest among the things you possess in this world.

The sweetness of your love for me knows the sweetness of my love for you, and my affection for you knows your affection for me. Each of us knows the other’s inmost feelings from his own inmost feelings, because true sincerity understands true sincerity, and certain experience allows no doubt to arise in either of us. Thus our true and God-given mutual love had its beginning; and I do not merely pray that it may continue as it has continued until now, but confidently declare in the hope of God that it will continue.

I cannot often send you letters as both you and I desire, because even if I had the opportunity, I would nevertheless fear that some scandal might arise from the king, who hates everything that comes from me and everyone who loves me, whether against our Church or against the bearer of the letter, if this were somehow discovered.

The book I composed, entitled *Why God Became Man*, is being gladly transcribed for the Church of Bec by Lord Eadmer, my dearest son and the staff of my old age, a monk of Bec, to whom my friends owe as much as they love me.

Because I do not wish to write to the lord abbot of our Church on account of the matter mentioned above, I commend the memory of me to you, so that among the hearts of those whom I have loved as my own soul—as they themselves testify—and whom, while I live, God willing, I shall continue to love, your frequent reminder may not allow that memory to grow old and fade away.

I have heard that Lord Folcherad, our cousin, is with you. If he is, I beg all of you on his behalf as you would on behalf of my own flesh. For he is an exile for God’s sake, and long ago became a monk of Bec. Greet him, and be there for him in my place.

May Almighty God bless your soul and body. Greet those whom you know and wish to greet.

[Col. 0056D]

## LETTER XXVI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO WILLIAM THE ABBOT AND THE BROTHERS OF BEC

That they should pray for him without ceasing and persevere steadfastly in their holy purpose, especially that they should not wander outside the cloister. That he should not allow almsgiving to be diminished.

To his most beloved and most greatly longed-for sons, Lord Abbot William and the other servants of God residing in the monastery of Bec, Brother Anselm, a man of Bec in profession and in heart, called by God’s disposition archbishop of Canterbury: continual prosperity in the present life and eternal happiness in the life to come.

Since it is neither new nor unexpected nor unfamiliar that your fraternal charity, kindled by pious compassion, continually implores divine help for me through its prayers amid my continual necessities, and since you do not fail to know that your love fills and possesses my heart completely, I do not think it necessary to set forth in a letter the thanks which you know I always keep in the treasury of my heart. For where there is such unity of heart and soul, the consciences themselves are more fully known to one another than tongue or pen could express.

And so that you may persevere in what you continually do, I have no greater prayers than to repeat what you already know: namely, that you should have no doubt that my soul, wherever my body may be, is always yours, longs for you as far as it can, and wastes away because of your absence. If consideration of the divine disposition did not temper its grief, it could not endure the vastness of that grief without the gravest injury.

Nothing, therefore, pleases me more to write to your love at present than that you should strive to advance in the holy purpose for which you have assembled, and that you should not allow the snares of the ancient enemy to break in upon you, secretly or openly, from any direction. To enable you to do this more effectively, guard one another charitably, admonish one another, correct one another, and kindly endure these things when they are offered to you by one another as great benefits.

Let those in authority support the diligent among their subjects with kindness and kindle the lukewarm by exhortation; if there are any obstinate ones, let them restrain them by discipline. Let subjects submit to those in authority with sincere obedience, and especially to the abbot; and show yourselves not burdensome but easy to bear. For subjects greatly sin before God if they are not afraid to burden by their conduct those in authority who, solely through fear of God and fraternal charity, have undertaken to bear them.

Let the cloister brothers not seek opportunities for riding outside the cloister unless obedience requires it, and not even accept such opportunities when they arise. Those who gladly leave the monastery cloister are harmful not only to themselves but also to others by their example, since they become causes of murmuring or wandering for them. Nor should the lord abbot permit this in any way if he wishes to preserve the strictness of the order.

Receive guests joyfully and serve them with every cheerfulness according to your means. Do not in any way allow our constitution and yours concerning alms for the poor to be diminished; rather, if you can discern how it may reasonably be increased, increase it.

May Almighty God direct your wills and actions according to His good pleasure, and make you see one another in His kingdom. Amen.

[Col. 0058A]

## LETTER XXVII

### TO BALDRIC THE PRIOR

He praises him for his good reputation and earnestly forbids subjects to judge the actions of those in authority.

Anselm, called archbishop, to his most beloved brother, Lord Prior Baldric: greetings and the blessing of God, and his own blessing, if it is of any value.

I give thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes, and to your most sweet love, for all the good things reported to me about you by everyone who comes to me from you. Although your good will and good purpose have already been tested and confirmed by long practice, so that they require no frequent admonition, it is nevertheless sweet for me to beg you with all my heart to persevere in an intention pleasing to God, so that in the life to come you may rejoice in a blessed recompense.

Although I rejoice in all your good studies and works, my heart rejoices especially in this: that you agree with the lord abbot through kindly obedience, lighten his laborious burden and burdensome labor by your consolation, and cannot endure anyone’s speaking against or resisting his ordinances. For it is certain, and often known by experience, that a monastery in which subjects judge the actions of those in authority is not ordered by the kindly disposition of God; rather, it is dissolved through the precipices of vices and destroyed by discord as it tears it apart.

But where the actions and ordinances of those in authority are commonly accepted by all as inspired by God, there God dwells and orders and governs the place as His own house, whose entire care is cast upon Him.

This, therefore, I ask and admonish you above all to preserve, and to persevere earnestly in this effort. May Almighty God direct all your actions, dearest brother, and lead you to eternal life. Amen.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: Compared with the two aforementioned manuscript copies bound together in one codex, Ef. 20.]

### TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS

He urges him to pursue justice more and more.

To the most beloved lord and revered prince of Flanders, Robert, Anselm, servant of the servants of Christ Jesus, called archbishop of Canterbury: faithful prayers.

[Col. 0058D]

Since your Excellence’s kindness is dear to me, which you have deigned to show me whenever I have spoken with you, I ought at some time to signify by letter that its memory never grows old within me, and that I pray God to deign by His kindness to defend you from every evil.

And since it has been entrusted to me that, in the exile of this life, I should never cease exhorting those whom I can toward the heavenly homeland, I certainly ought not to withhold this service from those whom I know myself to be joined to by the debt of love.

My humility therefore suggests to your loftiness—not by rebuking you, but by inviting you from good things to better things—that you should constantly consider what sacred authority commands: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom I, 5).

For the greater the power of those to whom the earth has been entrusted for governing, the more, if they depart from justice, they do not govern or help the human race but disturb and oppress it by their violence. Against such men that terrible threat is directed: “The mighty shall be mightily tormented, and a stronger punishment awaits the strong” (Wisdom V, 7, 9).

Let your prudence therefore always preserve justice in its actions, and in the offenses committed against it let its mercy show indulgence. For justice also commands that whoever wishes mercy to be shown to him should extend mercy to others.

I have briefly offered the admonition that my heart constantly desires, but I pray Almighty God to grant you to govern your earthly principality in such a way that in the life to come He may repay you with a heavenly kingdom.

The brothers of our Church greet you as faithful servants greet their lord. On behalf of their needs we are sending the bearers of this letter to Flanders; together with me they earnestly ask your piety that, just as they desire you to be their brothers in those things which please God in them, if there are any such things, so you may deign, when need and opportunity arise, to receive them under your protection.

Together we also greet your wife as our most beloved lady. We ask that, when circumstances require it, she be our helper together with you, just as we embrace her, together with you, in love and prayers. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: Compared with one of the aforementioned manuscript copies.]

### TO HENRY THE PRIOR, ANTONY THE SUBPRIOR, ERNULF, OSBERN, AND THE OTHER MONKS OF CANTERBURY

That the monks of Canterbury should obey the prior and subprior and one another in this way.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop, to his most beloved lords and sons, Lord Prior Henry, Subprior Antony, Lord Ernulf, Lord Osbern, and the other servants of God residing in the Church of Christ: may they always rejoice in the Lord and be protected by His perpetual blessing.

I hear that there are scandals and murmurings among you, because certain people among you refuse to submit to the lord prior and openly do things which are to be done with his permission while he is entirely unaware and without his permission; and when they are reproved by him or by someone else in chapter, they disdain to submit with the humble obedience of the Rule to his judgment. Moreover, they assert that they do all this entirely by our authority.

Hence, as though there were different sects and quarrels among divided parties, disputes and dissensions arise among you. Concerning this I want your love to know that it has never been my will, nor, with God’s protection, will it ever be, that such great and reprehensible disorder should arise in the Church entrusted to my governance; or, if it should arise by some circumstance, that it should be nourished or permitted.

I therefore command that all of you, just as you are subject to me while my precedence is preserved, should also be subject to the lord prior, and after him to the subprior, with humble kindness and kindly gentleness, both in seeking permissions and in carrying out commands and in judging negligences.

Since certain people place the cause and burden of the aforesaid murmuring especially upon Lord William, I state expressly concerning him that I have never wished, nor do I wish, him to resist the prior disobediently in any way. Nor do I establish anything else concerning him than what I entreated and advised, in your hearing, about him in chapter—both because of the memory of our lord and father, Archbishop Lanfranc, and because of his infirmity. Yet I in no way permit this to be done without discretion and humble obedience.

May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds (Philippians 4:7). Amen.

## LETTER XXX

### TO MATILDA, ABBESS, AND THE NUNS OF WINCHESTER

He begs that the prayers begun in his name be continued perpetually, and that the nuns devote themselves constantly to piety.

Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, to his most beloved sisters and daughters, the reverend abbess of Winchester, Matilda, and the other maidservants living under her, may they always please Christ, their chosen Bridegroom.

I give thanks to your Holiness because, as I hear, you do not cease praying continually for me. I humbly beg you to continue steadfastly what you have begun charitably, until it becomes clear what the divine disposition intends concerning me, so that God, entreated by your prayers, may be more merciful to me in my tribulations and, for the charity you have shown, more favorable to you.

Moreover, the office entrusted to me, the love which I perceive you have for me, and the charity with which I love you all urge and persuade me that, in accordance with your zeal and purpose, my admonition should always encourage you to advance toward better things, and that through your negligence you should never fall away from those things to which, with the help of God’s grace, you attain.

You will certainly be able to fulfill this effectively if, considering what is written, “He who despises small things shall gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1), you do not neglect even the smallest matters of your order. For we ought to guard against minor transgressions all the more vigilantly the more frequently we recognize them forcing themselves upon us, and the more cunningly our deceiver strives to persuade us that there is no fault in them, or that, if there is one, it is to be despised.

You must preserve this discipline not only in external works but also in your innermost thoughts, and you must judge an unbecoming thought to be no less displeasing to God than an action deserving human reproach.

Finally, just as the brides of earthly husbands, detesting the outward ugliness of carnal vices, strive to please them by the beauty of their flesh and the fittingness of their clothing, so spiritual brides of the King of kings, the Son of God, detesting inward ugliness, must always strive to please Him through beauty of mind and the adornments of virtues.

Certainly, the beauty of the mind and the nourishment of virtues is purity of heart, to which the vision of God is spiritually promised; no one is brought to this purity except through great vigilance over the heart. Hence it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23).

For this guardianship, after the grace of God, the following is the particular and most effective counsel as far as human effort is concerned: let your heart always and everywhere, as long as you are awake, be occupied either with reading, prayer, psalms, or some useful thought or intention.

You, Lady Abbess, I beg as a mother, admonish as a sister, exhort as a friend, and command as a most beloved daughter, to show to Bishop Osmund every kind and holy obedience pleasing to God, as is fitting; to strive to receive from him love, familiar friendship, counsel, and assistance in bodily and spiritual matters; and to offer him, as far as depends on you, the same in the charity of Christ.

May Almighty God, your Bridegroom, always be your guardian. Amen.

[Note: Concerning Osmund, bishop of Salisbury. Before him the bishops were called Sherborne bishops, after Sherborne in England, in the West Saxon region—a lowly and unattractive village. It is therefore remarkable that bishops remained there for so long. Finally, in 1075, a synod was held at London on the initiative of Lanfranc. At that synod, as the acts of the same synod, together with letters of Lanfranc and decrees of the supreme pontiffs—namely Damasus and Leo—as well as the decrees of the Councils of Sardica and Laodicea, attest, in which it is forbidden for episcopal sees to exist in villages, the king’s generosity and synodal authority permitted the three bishops in question to transfer from villages to cities: Herman from Sherborne to Salisbury, and so forth.

The common reading of the printed codices has *Sarisberiam* and *Schereburniam*; the lists of the bishops of Salisbury in the library of Saint Victor at Paris likewise preserve these forms. Thus, as soon as Herman transferred his see to Salisbury, he began the principal church, but death intervened and delayed its completion. His successor Osmund placed the crowning stone upon the work already begun, as William of Malmesbury noted in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*.

Moreover, near Salisbury lies the Wiltonian nunnery (*Parthenon*), by the River Wylye, in a village of no small size named Wiltuna, from which it derived both its site and its name. Its origin, however, goes back to King Edgar, who, after introducing Benedictine nuns there, placed his daughter Edith, by name, over them as abbess in the year 974, as Lilio thinks.

Late, but not inopportunely—for the memory of holy men is customarily useful at every time—it occurred to me to record what Dominicus Antoninus wrote in Part III, history 24, chapter 12: namely, that this Osmund, whom he calls Osimund, was enrolled among the saints by Pope Callixtus III in 1457 because of his reputation for holiness and the frequency of his miracles, and that an office was prescribed to be celebrated in his memory under the title of a confessor-bishop.

This canonization of Osmund had indeed been attempted by Gregory IX, but, when various storms arose against the Church, it was postponed until a calmer day dawned on which so holy a work of inscription could be undertaken more religiously and prudently.

Antoninus had it in mind to append there an epitome of the miracles accomplished through Saint Osmund’s prayers and merits, but he refrained both to avoid tedium and because he had ordered a book containing material of that kind to be kept in the archives of the Church of Salisbury; to it he sends the reader eager for ecclesiastical history.

Besides Antoninus, the following also remember this canonization: Polydore Vergil, Book XXIII of his *History of the English*; and before him Matthew Palmer, the Pisan; Peter of Natalibus, Book XII, chapter 22; Schedel, in the sixth age of his register; the *Bergomian Chronicle*, Book XV, supplement; Sabellicus, Book VI; Eadmer, Book X; and Platina in his account of Callixtus III.

In these five later writers, however, the spelling varies greatly, so that instead of Osmund one reads Hosimund, Edimund, Eadimund, or Edmund. Nor is there reason for anyone to think that Sabellicus, Platina, the Bergomian, and Schedel mean Saint Edmund the king or the archbishop: the former had been enrolled among the saints much earlier, while the latter was enrolled among the saints in 1246, according to Walsingham in *Neustria* and Matthew Paris, or in 1248, as Molanus notes in his additions to Usuard, on the day before the Nones of December.

William of Malmesbury reports more about these matters in his account of the bishops of Salisbury, and Polydore again in Book IX—little, but excellent and distinguished. The most holy bishop finally went to heaven in the year 1099, in the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate, and was buried at Salisbury, according to the agreement of Henry of Huntingdon, Book VII, and Matthew Paris, on the day before the Nones of December, as Baronius notes after Molanus.

These details, which had escaped those writers, we have gathered and placed here.]

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO LANFRID, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT WLMAR

That he should not abandon his flock because of various troubles.

[Col. 0062B]

Anselm, called archbishop, to his dearest brother, Lord Lanfrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Wlmar: may he be directed by divine counsel and assisted by divine aid.

Concerning your request, by which you persistently urge me to try, through the counsel and prayers of your bishop, to obtain permission for you to leave the abbey in which divine providence has established you, I have often and at length reflected with myself and have spoken with others in whom I hoped to find spiritual counsel.

I have understood that, although, because of the compassion with which I sympathize deeply with your fraternal sorrow, I would greatly rejoice with you if, by God’s mercy and with the counsel and permission of your archbishop and your bishop, you were to attain your desire, it would nevertheless be dangerous for me to request and advise such an unusual course.

For I fear that I would sin considerably if, through my insistence, the place entrusted to you were deprived of every ruler and destroyed by a greater—or rather, complete—devastation both of its goods, its morals, and its order.

For if your presence there were of no other benefit except that, because evil cannot reign there or be freely exercised without some rebuke, it is not as bad there as it would be if it were without a ruler, whether in the destruction of its order or of its possessions, you nevertheless could not complain as though you were living there uselessly, since you are restraining such great bodily and spiritual evil lest it destroy the aforesaid place.

How much more, then, can your prudence be consoled when there are some under its authority who desire to use its counsel and governance and obey it through voluntary submission.

There is also another reason why you ought to rejoice amid your tribulation: there is no doubt that you possess that office through a good zeal for God, and that through fear of God—because of which consideration you do not dare flee from it—you endure it.

Certainly, where there are so many reasons for consolation and spiritual joy, the bitterness of sorrow ought not to have great weight. For God considers not only how much someone’s effort benefits others, but also—or perhaps even more—how much labor he bears in the intention of advancing, and how much pain he endures because he does not advance according to his intention.

It is our task to labor and sow; it is God’s to give growth and effect. What is ours, although it is accomplished with His help, He repays to us; but what is His, He attributes to Himself.

If your mind does not wish or is not able to accept these things, I do not forbid you, provided that through your bishop and those to whom this matter belongs you can, by God’s disposition, reach your desire in an orderly way.

Farewell.

[Col. 0064A]

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

### TO GERVIN, BISHOP OF AMIENS

That a monk cannot be ordained abbot who has secretly departed without the knowledge of his superior.

Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, to the reverend Gervin, bishop of Amiens: greetings.

That Northman brother, professed in our Church, whom you informed me had been elected abbot and whose ordination you urge me to approve, crossed the sea without my knowledge or that of the brothers of our Church, so that we knew neither his journey nor the reason for it.

Therefore, just as you state in your letters, you ought not to ordain him without our consent; nor do I give my consent in this matter, nor ought I to give it, insofar as I am able to understand. If he comes to me and to his own Church, as a monk who has departed from his Church in such a manner ought to come, and afterward someone speaks to me concerning him in the matter mentioned above, I shall answer accordingly, as I understand that I ought to answer.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript and with the Gothic Edition and the edition of 1573.]

### TO RICHARD THE MONK

That a professed monk is not bound by a vow of pilgrimage made by him in the world.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop, to Brother and Son Richard the monk: greetings and blessing.

[Source column anchors for the foregoing portion: Cols. 0053C–0055D; 0056A–0059D; 0060A–0064D.]

- Col. 0059D, on Ecclesiasticus 19:1: For *despicit* (“despises”), the printed Bible and six of our manuscripts read *spernit* (“spurns”); since the word is synonymous, it does not alter the meaning. The saying signifies that, for the whole cycle of virtues, flight from small errors and most careful observance of lighter precepts are absolutely necessary, as Anselm repeatedly and frequently teaches, as do the other Fathers: St John Chrysostom, Homily 27 on Matthew and his address to the people of Antioch; Jerome, to the monk Rusticus and to Eustochium on the guarding of virginity; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 1 against Julian; St Ephrem, vol. II, tract *On Intemperance*, beginning, “Woe to those who [neglect] the smallest and lightest things,” and in the *Paraenesis*, vol. XXIX; and St Caesarius of Arles, Sermon 8. Our Anselm, again, in Eadmer, Book I, uses the comparison of a wine-vessel whose cracks, however slight, if not stopped, immediately let out all its water, resulting in the death of the fish.

Leonius, our canon and a poet not to be despised, was preparing four hundred years ago a heroic poem on the whole Bible; but death forestalled him and numbed and checked the hand that was just beginning to write. For that reason he left only twelve books completed, on the history of Ruth. Besides these and other poems, I found the following relevant piece, entitled “That Venial Sins Must Not Be Neglected.” Its poem is as follows:

> You who rightly flee every crime of grievous harm,
> 
> Take care not to fall through a lighter fault.
> 
> Contempt for light sins is always counted a grave fault,
> 
> And makes great the crimes that had been small.
> 
> What profit is it to have avoided mud, only to sink in sand?
> 
> Perhaps mud stinks; the sand kills no less.
> 
> Thus in vain does the fearful man flee the sea’s deep perils
> 
> Whom a river-wave kills in a safe ford.
> 
> Nor is it enough to avoid open pits in one’s path:
> 
> Even a level road trips the unwary feet.
> 
> That you may rightly avoid the harms that show themselves,
> 
> Many noxious things lie hidden beneath the appearance of usefulness.

Thus far the ten-line poem, which had not previously been published, like its author’s other poems. Among those other works I saw letters, one to Adrian IV and another to Alexander III, supreme pontiffs. The final two chapters of Plutarch’s treatise entitled *How One May See Whether One Is Making Progress in Virtue* also concern this subject.

- Cols. 0062C–0064D, on Osmund: R. [the reverend] Bishop Osmund of Salisbury, or Sarum. Before him the other bishops were called bishops of Sherborne, from Sherborne in the West Saxon region of England, an insignificant and unpleasant village; hence it is remarkable that bishops had sat there for so long. At last, in 1075, a synod was held in London through Lanfranc’s initiative. As its acts, together with Lanfranc’s appended letters and the decrees of the supreme pontiffs Damasus and Leo, as well as the Councils of Sardica and Laodicea—which forbid episcopal sees to exist in villages—attest, royal generosity and synodal authority allowed the aforesaid three bishops to move from villages to cities: Herman from Sherborne to Salisbury, and so forth. As soon as Herman transferred his see to Salisbury, he began the cathedral church; death, intervening, delayed the work. His successor Osmund put the finishing touch to the work begun, as William of Malmesbury records in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*. Wilton Abbey, near Salisbury on the River Wylye, derived its site and name from the sizeable village of Wiltuna. King Edgar founded it, according to Lilius, when he installed Benedictine nuns there and placed his daughter Edith over them as abbess in 974. Antoninus, Part III, History 24, chapter 12, records that Osmund—whom he calls Osimund—was enrolled among the saints by Pope Callixtus III in 1457 because of his holiness and frequent miracles, and that an office in memory of him was prescribed under the title of a confessor-bishop. Gregory IX had attempted this canonization, but ecclesiastical disturbances delayed it until calmer times permitted this holy act of enrolment to be completed more devoutly and prudently. Antoninus wished to append an epitome of the miracles wrought through St Osmund’s prayers and merits, but refrained both to avoid tedium and because a booklet on that subject was ordered to be kept in the archives of Salisbury Church. Besides Antoninus, the canonization is mentioned by Polydore Vergil, Book XXIII of the *History of England*; Matthew Palmer the Pisan; Peter of Natalibus, Book XII, chapter 22; Schedel, the sixth age of his register; the *Bergomian Chronicle*, Book XV, supplement; Sabellicus, Book VI; Eadmer, Book X; and Platina, under Callixtus III. In the latter five the spelling varies remarkably: for Osmund one finds Hosimund, Edimund, Eadimund, or Edmund. Sabellicus, Platina, Bergomensis, and Schedel are not to be understood as referring to St Edmund the king or the archbishop: the former was enrolled among the saints much earlier; the latter in 1246, according to Walsingham in *Neustria* and Matthew Paris, or in 1248, as Molanus notes in his additions to Usuard on the day before the Nones of December. Malmesbury gives fuller information in his account of the bishops of Salisbury, and Polydore again in Book IX, brief but excellent and distinguished information. The most holy bishop died in 1099, the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate, and was buried at Salisbury, on the day before the Nones of December, according to Henry of Huntingdon, Book VII, Matthew Paris, and Baronius after Molanus.

- Col. 0063C: The manuscript reads *episcopi* (“of the bishop”) for *episcopi vestri* (“of your bishop”).

- Col. 0063C, Letter XXXII: Compared with the same manuscript.
- Col. 0063C: The manuscript reads *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”) for *Ecclesiae nostrae* (“of our Church”).

- Col. 0063C, Letter XXXIII: Compared with the same manuscript and with the Gothic edition and the Cologne edition of 1573.]

I have heard, my brother, that before you became a monk, while ill, you vowed that you would go to Saint Giles; and for that reason you are now fearful and excessively anxious about fulfilling that vow, so that your heart cannot rest unless you have gone to Saint Giles. Concerning this matter, you ought not to trust yourself as much as your abbot, to whose counsel and direction you have entrusted your soul, and those others who know better than you what is more pleasing to God [Note: Edition: “what is pleasing,” for “what is more pleasing”] and more beneficial for your soul. Therefore I advise and command you to abandon entirely the intention of the aforesaid journey and anxiety about that vow, and to remain quiet and steadfast in the undertaking you have assumed; and, calmly [Note: Edition: “in calm”], to devote yourself to what you have resolved upon—namely, obedience and penance for your sins, and other good practices. You must be certain that, when through your monastic profession you vowed and surrendered yourself wholly to God, you fulfilled all the lesser vows concerning whatever actions you had previously promised without an oath or binding of faith [Note: Edition: *illegatione*, for *alligatione*, “binding”]. Therefore be quiet and confident: by the authority which, through God’s grace, I possess over you, I release you from that vow. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO WILLIAM, A MONK OF CHESTER

He professes that he is not as virtuous as the monk had portrayed him in his poems.

Anselm, archbishop by the grace of God, sends greetings to his dearest brother and son, William, a monk of Chester.

Although I do not know myself to be such as your affection praises me as being in your poems, I ought nevertheless not to be ungrateful, since this is the result of an abundance of love. For a lover often either fails to perceive the faults of the beloved or judges them slight; he praises good qualities that are not present and exaggerates those that are. When charity alone does this, neither should the error be accepted because of the affection’s good intention, nor should the love be despised because of the error’s fault. Love must be nourished in such a way that error is corrected, and error must be driven out in such a way that love is retained.

I thank you for loving me as being such as you praise me to be; and I urge you not to think me such, but rather to pray that God may make me such as you love and believe me to be. Since it is written, “Do not praise a man during his lifetime” (Ecclus. 11:30), and elsewhere, “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16), a person ought not, in this life, to praise another with great effort, but rather to pray with devout affection that he may become praiseworthy; praise, however, should be entrusted to God, whose proper function it is to judge merits.

I do not say that the virtues of good men ought not to be shown to others as examples of good living, but that they ought not to be exaggerated to those same men. Since, however, a work of charity ought not to be without recompense, I return prose for your poems, and exhortation for your praise.

Certainly, my son, when you love and praise in me the good qualities which you think to be present, you testify by that very action that everyone who strives to be good is lovable and praiseworthy. Since, therefore, we all wish—not merely to be praised, but to be lovable and praiseworthy—we ought to strive for nothing so much as to be judged good in the sight of him who is not deceived.

Every faithful person, however, is judged good by him who strives to attain perfection in his own order. For although we cannot all reach the summit of perfection equally, we shall nevertheless not be outside the number of the good, if we wish to strive constantly and courageously toward that perfection, as it is written: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 138:16).

Let laymen, therefore, strive courageously to advance always in their own order, clerics in theirs, and monks in theirs, so that those who belong to the higher calling may surpass those of the lower in humility [Note: Edition Picard: “are in humility,” for “surpass in humility”], in which [Note: Manuscript: “in which, insofar as”; printed text: “in which, the more”] the more a person advances, the more he is exalted and excels in the other virtues. Therefore, dearest son, always remember the degree of the calling which you have ascended, and never let the holiness of your life be sufficient for you unless by it you surpass those who are of lower degrees [Note: Manuscript: “unless by it you surpass him”; printed text: “unless by it you surpass those”].

For just as those who belong to a lower calling praiseworthily ascend to the virtues of a higher one, so those who have resolved to pursue greater things are blameworthy if they descend to the level of those who have chosen lesser things. Since, therefore, by your habit you profess to be a monk, I urge, beg, and advise you always to strive inwardly before God to be what outwardly, before men, you appear to be. I do not speak as though you did not do this, but so that, continually kindled by paternal exhortation, you may advance toward better things. Farewell.

## 379. LETTER XXXV

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO WALTER, CARDINAL

He says that he cannot act with him concerning the needs of the Church, or provide for them, without his assent and the counsel of the other bishops, especially at a time when enemies were invading England.

To the lord and reverend legate and cardinal bishop of the Roman Church, Walter, Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, sends faithful prayers and faithful service.

What your prudent concern commands me—that we meet somewhere [Note: Manuscript: “in some place”] to deal with the affairs [Note: Manuscript: “the affair”] of the Churches of God through fraternal and charitable counsel, and to correct what needs correcting—is certainly, according to your intention, highly praiseworthy [Note: Manuscript: “praiseworthy indeed”] and, as circumstances require, would be very useful, if it could be done at a suitable time.

But your prudence does not fail to understand that the two of us would accomplish nothing [Note: Manuscript: “will accomplish nothing”] unless the king were approached, so that what we decided might be brought to completion with his assent and assistance [Note: The manuscript reads “and with his … it might be brought forward”; the edition has “so that … it might be brought to completion”].

There is also this: I do not dare to leave Canterbury at all, since every day we expect enemies from overseas to invade England through those ports which are near Canterbury. For this reason my lord the king ordered me personally, before I left him at Nottingham, and after I returned to Canterbury he instructed me by letters bearing his own seal, to guard Canterbury and always to be ready, so that at whatever hour I should hear the message of those who are guarding the seacoasts for this very purpose, I might order horsemen and foot soldiers to be summoned from every direction, so that, hurrying to the spot, they might resist the violence of the enemy.

And for that reason I do not dare to leave Canterbury except toward the region from which we expect the enemy’s arrival. I therefore ask your holiness’ discretion to receive with an even and peaceful mind these reasonable excuses of ours, which cannot be weakened because they are true. Let your reverence know for certain that I have the same desire as you have: that what needs correcting should be corrected. But I await the return of my lord the king and of the bishops and princes who are with him, so that we may suggest to them at a suitable time and in a reasonable manner what must be done. Thus, with God’s help, by his assent and assistance, we may more effectively accomplish what we desire.

If, however, it pleases you to send me your advice through our most beloved brother, the reverend Abbot II [Note: Manuscript: “Abbot N.”; manuscript H: “Abbot H.”], concerning what matters and in what manner I ought to speak with the king, I gladly accept this. And if it should please your prudence to advise the king through that same abbot and the reverend bishop of Winchester concerning such matters, I approve and request it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO THE SAME

He refutes the calumnies brought against him and indicates that he neither favors schism nor was then able to provide for the affairs of the Church.

To the lord and reverend bishop of Albano and cardinal, Walter, Anselm, by divine disposition archbishop of Canterbury [Note: Manuscript: “archbishop of Canterbury,” in the dative], sends fidelity in prayer together with service.

If I were permitted, I would answer the letters directed to me by your holiness more fully than the brevity appropriate to a letter allows. Nevertheless, as the time permits, I shall briefly answer, in summary, what concerns me.

You say that we ought to have spoken together about the vineyard of the Lord, which is being destroyed in this kingdom, so that it might not be utterly ruined until Saint Peter the Apostle, through his vicar Urban, the supreme pontiff [Note: The manuscript reads “the supreme”; the edition has “the supreme pontiff”], should visit it. I myself would certainly have wished this, if it had been done at a suitable time—that is, when my lord the king, and the bishops and princes of this kingdom, were present with you or near you.

But after you had received permission from the king to return to Rome, and the king had gone on his expedition with the archbishop of York and certain other bishops and princes, and you had departed from them and I from you, as though we were not [Note: Edition Picard: “you were not”] to see one another again in this land; and after the king had ordered me carefully to guard that part of his kingdom in which we daily fear an invasion by the enemy most of all, and to be ready every day to resist the enemy if they invaded, since the land was in danger of being devastated or lost—when I could in no way dare to go far from the city in which I was, except toward the enemy whom we feared—then, when I was urged to meet you so that we might discuss what needed correcting in this kingdom, I gave a reasonable and acceptable explanation: because of the danger mentioned above and the king’s command, I could not come, and the two of us would accomplish nothing in the king’s absence and without the others by whose assent, counsel, and action our discussion could be brought to completion.

I myself see what needs correcting, and I have a will to correct it, which no person can increase, with God’s help, through the assent and assistance of my lord the king and of the others to whom the matter belongs, when there is a suitable place and opportunity.

As for your complaint that you have been kept waiting, like a fruitless tree and a stranger without help or counsel, you know about the others; concerning me, however, I know that I did not prevent you from bearing fruit, nor, in proportion to my reason and ability, did I deny you my help or counsel at the time of fruitfulness.

But when you ask me [Note: Manuscript: “when you ask why”] why, and by what justice, the other bishops, having rejected me, departed from me and did not return after performing fitting penance, this ought rather to have been asked of them than of me. For I do not know that I did anything for which they ought to have done this. Nevertheless, they have returned to the extent of acknowledging that they will observe toward me the obedience which they had promised to the see of Canterbury.

You say that some of them told you that they had not offended me for this reason [Note: Manuscript: “that they had therefore offended you”]: that I had allowed myself to be transferred from the Catholic Church to the schismatics and to be consecrated by them, if this could be done, as you add, and had received investiture from a schismatic king, and had given him fealty and homage, although I knew that all of them were schismatics and separated from the Church of Christ and from my head, Pope Urban, whom they themselves, in my hearing, denied.

Certainly, I did not know, nor do I know, that they were schismatics or so separated from the Church as they say. And if any one of those who tell you this were to say it in my presence, I would show reasonably that it was not so. For they did not deny the canonical Roman pontiff, whoever he might be, nor did they deny that Urban was pontiff; but because of the dissension which had recently arisen [Note: Manuscript: “which had arisen in the world”], and because of their uncertainty, they postponed accepting him as certain. No judgment [Note: Manuscript: “sign”] had separated them from the Church, and they openly professed that they held to the obedience of the Roman see; and under a profession of obedience to the Roman pontiff they consecrated me.

Finally, the lord pope knew that I had been consecrated, by whom, and for which king I had done what I did. And nevertheless—

[Note: The archbishop of Canterbury’s pallium was sent to me through your charity, etc. He mentions again the pallium sent to him in the following letter and gives thanks to Urban for it. Urban sent it most honorably—for it was enclosed in a small silver case—and Anselm received it with the greatest devotion and splendor. When the legate Walter carried it, Anselm went out to meet him wearing pontifical vestments and barefoot. He received the sacred insignia upon the altar and placed it upon his shoulders; thus adorned with that stole, he performed the sacred rite on Sunday, the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the year 1095. Florence of Worcester and Hoveden recorded this event, and also that the others present kissed it out of reverence for Saint Peter. Since I considered it worthwhile to know this ceremony, I wished to record it.

On the form of the archiepiscopal pallium and other matters not unworthy of notice, Onuphrius writes in his *Explanation of Ecclesiastical Terms*, as does John Durandus in Book II of *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 9, numbers 41, 42, and following. Jarland of Chrysopolis, in Book V of his work, which he called *The Candle*, explains what mystery it contains, drawing upon a letter of Pope Leo to this effect:

“Honor is granted to an archbishop through the pallium, so that, by the sign of the same cross depicted on the back and breast of the purple garment, he may show the people the sign of our redemption and piously reflect in his mind upon the Passion of the Redeemer, saying: ‘But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Gal. 6:13).”

Amalarius had joined Leo in this interpretation. Our Hugh, however, also imitated him in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, at the final chapter, where, by way of an appendix, he interprets the little thorns of that pallium which was sent; apart from the fact that he treats it again in Book II, chapter 16, part four, of *On the Sacraments*.

Paschal II, writing to Guido, archbishop of Vienne in Gaul, points out a particular mystery which had escaped earlier writers:

“Let your fraternity remember to use the pallium only for the solemn celebrations of Mass, and only on those days which were granted to your predecessors by the authority of the Roman Church, whose bosom we wish you to preserve in every respect. For the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your fraternity hasten with all your heart to show yourself humble in prosperity and, in adversity, should it ever arise, to be found upright with justice; friendly to the good and opposed to the perverse; never trembling before anyone’s face when speaking the truth; devoting yourself to works of mercy in accordance with the power of your resources, yet desiring to go beyond that power; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with those who are well; exulting in others’ joys as though they were your own; raging piously when correcting vices; soothing the minds of your hearers when fostering virtues; exercising judgment without anger in anger; and, in tranquillity, not abandoning the discipline of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium. If you carefully preserve it, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.”

Thus Paschal wrote in the letter which the library of Fleury displays in full to the reader.

Since the matter is especially relevant here, we shall note that two pallia were conferred upon Lanfranc, as Alexander III himself records in Letter 3:

“Nothing,” he says, “will ever be able, on any occasion, to cast from the ark of my breast that unheard-of kindness which you showed me at Rome, the least of men and unworthy of such honors, and by which, to demonstrate your benevolence toward me, you bestowed upon me two pallia—one from the altar according to custom, and another with which your holiness was accustomed to celebrate Mass.”

After Lanfranc, this was reported by the manuscript *Chronicle of Bec* in its account of his deeds, and by William of Malmesbury in Book III of *On the Bishops of the English*.

As for the honor, petition, and use of the pallium, the entire hundredth distinction of Gratian is devoted to the subject. Since its first canon commands a metropolitan to profess his faith within three months of consecration and to request the pallium from the Roman Church, Roger of Hoveden seems, with good reason, suspect of having recorded the year in which Anselm received the pallium inaccurately. For Anselm himself testified that he had been elected and inaugurated as pontiff in the year 1093, and it certainly does not seem likely to me that, being no stranger to ecclesiastical law, he received the pallium a year and a half after his consecration. Hence, in a way condemning himself and grieving that, through the wicked obstinacy of the English king, he had not been given or allowed the opportunity to go to Rome, he said above, at the end of Letter 24: “If a metropolitan bishop does not seek either the living pope or the pallium throughout the entire first year, he ought justly to be removed from that very honor.” For this reason Matthew Paris calculated this reception more precisely as having occurred in 1094 in his *Greater History*.]

—the pallium which the archbishop of Canterbury customarily possesses he sent to me through your charity, not as to a schismatic but as to one accepted, not as to one rejected but as to one approved; and in this way he confirmed what had been done concerning me. He himself was the author of this confirmation, and the lord Walter, bishop of Albano and cardinal, who knew all these things, was his minister and executor.

If you think this calumny deserved attention, why did you keep silent about it before the granting of the pallium? If you think it should be disregarded, judge for yourselves how diligently it ought to be pressed by you. I could say more to weaken the malicious statement of those who offer you what you report as an excuse for their sins, but I know that your wisdom does not need a lengthy demonstration of what is clear.

Let your prudent simplicity and simple prudence therefore see how it ought to receive and enlarge upon the fabricated calumnies and calumnious fabrications against me which those who acted against me have made as an excuse for themselves, lest you appear to wish to weaken what was knowingly confirmed by the authority of the lord pope and through your execution [Note: The manuscript reads “confirm”; the edition has “weaken”]. Certainly, as the kingdom of England bears witness, I did not so take the name of the lord Pope Urban in vain that I should recognize myself to have deserved this from him or from his faithful servants.

You say that, with God as your witness, you defended my cause as far as you could, and that on this account the business for which you came has been obstructed until now. I thank you for your good intention in defending it; but I do not know that the obstruction was caused for you by this reason [Note: The manuscript reads “certainly”; the edition has “I do not know that it was caused for you”]. If the heart of the matter is carefully considered as it can be, and if your prudence defends me as far as it can, I am certain that your conscience cannot accuse me concerning the matters stated above.

As for your reverence’s saying that you were unable to speak with me or with others as you wished because you lacked obedience to the Roman Church, let it know why it was unable to do so. I know, however, that I long and greatly desired and awaited speaking with you before I was able to do so; and when at last I could, I was not able to do as much as I wished.

You ask me to let our brothers of the Church of Canterbury possess their property quietly and peacefully. I answer that no one desires their quiet and peace more than I do, nor is anyone more concerned for the welfare of that Church. Therefore it is my intention, with God’s favor, to dispose of its property for its present and future benefit, as well as I know and can. May your blessedness prosper, and may you deign to pray that God direct me and all my actions.

## LETTER XXXVII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO POPE URBAN

Why he has not yet approached the pope, and he humbly asks him to advise what ought to be done.

To the reverend and reverently received supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church, Urban, Anselm, called metropolitan bishop of Canterbury not by his own merits but by the divine will, sends due submission with devoted service.

I give thanks to your holy munificence because you have sent worthy legates of the Apostolic See to us, and because you ordered the benefit of the pallium to be delivered to me solely through the generosity of your grace.

It was indeed the duty of our order and office both to visit your presence according to custom and to honor it with fitting reverence, as is proper. From the time when I received the episcopal rank, I have ardently desired to do this—both because reason required it and because I wished to enjoy your counsel and conversation, so that, when I asked you about matters both public and private which required attention, your prudence might instruct me and your authority strengthen me.

I beg your holy eminence not to attribute my failure to do so to negligence or arrogance. My conscience bears witness that, after I learned that you had been raised to the summit of the holy Church, I rejoiced, and reverently loved and still love you; I wished and still wish for your daily advancement, and I rejoice when I hear that it has occurred.

But because we are shaken by wars on every side, and constantly fear hostile attacks and the ambushes of our adversaries, our lord the king has so far not permitted me to leave the kingdom, nor has he in any way yet agreed that I can do so. Moreover, even if no other causes intervened to prevent me from seeing your face at this time—which I deeply regret—my age, illness, and bodily weakness would be enough to make me incapable of a long journey and the immense hardships of the roads.

Yet under these circumstances, burdened by what labor and anxiety, how could I attempt the journey if Almighty God were to calm the wars in the kingdom of the English and grant such peace in the kingdoms and provinces through which one must travel to reach you that I might be allowed to complete the journey as necessity and expediency required? But as long as this cannot be done, so long does impossibility hold me back [Note: The manuscript reverses the wording: “But for as long as this cannot be done, for so long …”].

With the help of divine clemency, wherever I may be [Note: Manuscript: “wherever I may rush”], I shall be ready to obey and serve you and to honor your eminence. And because, as I desire, I am not permitted to pour out the daily complaints of my miseries before your presence, I presume to disturb the holy ears of your serenity with a few complaints in writing [Note: Manuscript: “I humbly supplicate,” for “I supplicate”].

Holy Father, I grieve that I am what I am; I grieve that I am not what I was. I grieve that I am a bishop, because, owing to my sins, I do not perform the office of a bishop. In a humble position I seemed able to accomplish something; placed in a lofty one, I am weighed down by a great burden and bring fruit neither to myself nor to anyone else.

I succumb to the burden because I suffer, beyond what may seem credible, from a lack of the strength, virtues, industry, and knowledge appropriate to so great an office. I desire to flee the unbearable care and abandon the burden; on the other hand, I fear offending God. Fear of God compelled me to undertake it, and the same fear compels me to retain the same burden.

If amid these circumstances I recognized the will of God, I would undoubtedly direct my will and actions toward it as far as possible. But now, because God’s will is hidden from me and I do not know what I should do, I sigh like one wandering astray and do not know what conclusion I ought to bring to the matter.

I therefore ask your holy clemency and kindly holiness, for God’s sake and for that charity by which you strive to assist the Church of God, to nourish the poverty of our counsel through the hand of your holy prayers, lest, tossed by the waves of such thoughts, I either fall altogether or grasp nothing.

I also ask and humbly supplicate, with submissive groans of the heart, your exalted and devout fatherhood: since I am situated in a shipwreck, if ever, when storms burst upon me, I flee to the bosom of Mother Church in need of your assistance, may I find in you, for the sake of him who gave his blood for us, compassionate and ready help and consolation.

I humbly pray your clemency concerning the lord Fulk, bishop of Beauvais, according as your prudence shall judge. In our little gift, I beg your greatness to weigh not only its size but also the good will with which it was sent.

May Almighty God preserve your fatherhood for a long time in his grace and peace. Amen.

## 381. LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO LAMBERT, THE ABBOT

That he should receive a fugitive monk who is penitent.

Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury by God’s disposition, offers temporal mercy to the lord and brother beloved in God, Abbot Lambert, that he may merit eternal mercy.

This brother, having eaten from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, has learned by experience how great is the difference between the delights of the cloistered paradise and the exile of secular life. Therefore, penitent and grieving, as his tears testify, he confesses that he has sinned greatly; and promising that henceforth he will correct his ways and live obediently according to your direction, he asks with all the feeling he can muster that he be admitted within the fold from which he wretchedly fled of his own accord.

And because he does not think his petition sufficient in view of the magnitude of his guilt, he asks that his request be aided by our prayers before your clemency. Although I have deserved nothing from your holiness, nevertheless, since we are commanded to have compassion for one another and to pray for one another, I presume to beg that your fatherhood [Note: An added *non* (“not”) is indicated] not close the door of the fold against the sheep which Christ, having sought and found it, carries back to the fold upon his shoulders [Note: The manuscript reads “to the sheep”; the edition has “to the fold”]. Otherwise Christ himself might appear to have labored in vain in seeking the lost sheep and carrying it back once found, and might complain before the friends and neighbors whom he ought to have summoned to rejoice with him, not so much that the sheep as that he himself—and, what must be especially noted, burdened [Note: The manuscript reads “bereaved”; the edition has “burdened”]—had been excluded from his fold.

Therefore, “I will sing mercy and judgment to the Lord,” and let mercy so exalt judgment [Note: The manuscript reads “let mercy exalt judgment”; the edition has “let mercy exult in judgment”]. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### TO THE MONKS OF BEC

He praises the monks of Bec for their steadfastness in observing the order [Note: The heading continues: “And he urges them not to judge the deeds of their superiors more than others.”].

To the lords and dearest brothers residing in the monastery of Bec, Brother Anselm, by will a monk of Bec, by necessity called archbishop of Canterbury, sends continual holiness in the present life and eternal happiness in the future.

Although you rarely see a letter from me, I know nevertheless that you do not doubt that your affection burns in the innermost part of my heart [Note: Manuscript: “in the innermost part”; printed text: “in the innermost part of my heart”]. You ought to be all the more certain of this affection the more you know it from the past, and because you strive to do what I loved in you and for which I loved you.

For I hear that, with the grace of God inspiring and cooperating, you are fervent in the pursuit of good living, and that under the pressure of poverty you hold inflexibly to the rigor of your order. This is fitting for servants of God: the more the tribulations of the present life constrict them, the more ardently they should strive toward the rest of eternal life and extend themselves toward progress in virtue.

Although you labor willingly and diligently in holy conduct and religious works, I know the sincerity of your affection, and I know that you will gratefully accept my exhortation that you persevere in what you have undertaken. To enable you to fulfill this more effectively, it is necessary that, bound together in holy unanimity, you obey your superior in heart and will. Do not judge his deeds and words, but, without any questioning, preserve them with a reverent and kindly mind as though divinely inspired.

For when subjects become judges of their superior [Note: Manuscript: “when superiors become judges”; printed text: “when subjects become judges of their superior”], they openly disparage and contradict God’s ordinance, by whose disposition he has been placed over them. God then withdraws from them the assistance of his governance and permits them to be precipitated into the counsel of their own error. But where the superior is received with reverence as Christ, there the whole household of Christ is governed by counsel, protected, and sustained by assistance.

The more securely subjects submit themselves to his vicar, the more benignly he provides all things for the superior and the subjects.

May Almighty God bless you with his blessing and make you eternally blessed, dearest brothers and friends. Amen.

[Col. 0074A]

## LETTER XL. TO POPE PASCHAL

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

He excuses himself for having sent greetings to him only belatedly by letter and, after setting out his calamities, gives the reasons why he left England; he earnestly begs that he not return to England unless all the affairs of the Church have been restored. Meanwhile, he declares that he is being sustained at Lyon by the archbishop. 

To the reverend lord and father, Paschal, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends heartfelt due submission and, if they have any value, the devotion of his prayers.

As for the reason why I delayed so long in sending a messenger to Your Eminence after we had learned with certainty of your elevation and had given thanks to God and rejoiced, [Note: [Col. 0073D] “Vestra Deo” in the manuscript, instead of “vestrae sublimationis Deo.”] it was this: a messenger of the King of the English came to the venerable Archbishop of Lyon concerning our case, but he did not bring anything that ought to be accepted. After hearing the archbishop’s reply, he returned to the king, promising that he would return to Lyon shortly. [Note: [Col. 0073D] The manuscript reads “rediturum”; the printed text has “Lugdunum rediturum.”] I waited for him so that I might know what I could report to you concerning the king’s will, but he did not come.

I shall therefore briefly explain our case, because when I was staying at Rome I often related it to the lord Pope Urban and to many others, as Your Holiness, I think, knows. I saw many evils in England whose correction belonged to me, but which I could neither correct nor tolerate without sinning. For the king demanded that I give my assent, under the name of rightfulness, to his wishes, which were contrary to the law and [Col. 0074C] will of God. Without his command he did not want an apostolic letter to be received or even mentioned in England; nor did he want me to send him a letter, receive one sent by him, or obey his decrees. He has not permitted a council to be held in his kingdom since he became king—now thirteen years. He gave the lands of the Church to his own men. In all these matters and others like them, whenever I sought advice, everyone in his kingdom, including my fellow bishops, refused to give counsel except according to the king’s will.

Seeing these and many other things contrary to the will and law of God, I asked him for permission to visit the apostolic see, so that I might receive counsel there concerning my soul and the office entrusted to me. The king replied that I had sinned against him merely by requesting this permission, and he proposed that I either make satisfaction concerning this matter as though it were a fault and assure him that I would never again ask for such permission or appeal to the Apostolic See, or else leave his land immediately. I chose to leave rather than consent to so wicked a thing.

I came to Rome, as you know, [Note: [Col. 0073D] The manuscript reads “veni; scitis”; the printed text has “veni, ut scitis.”] and laid the whole matter before the lord pope. As soon as I left England, the king, after simply assessing the food and clothing of our monks, invaded the entire archbishopric and [Col. 0075A] converted it to his own uses. Though warned and requested by the lord pope to correct this, he despised the admonition and persists in it still.

It is now the third year since I left England in this way. I have spent the little that I brought with me, as well as much that I borrowed, and I remain in debt for it. Thus, owing more than I possess, [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads “debilis quam habilis”; the printed text has “debens quam habens.”] I have been detained by our venerable father, the Archbishop of Lyon, and am sustained by his generous benevolence and benevolent generosity. [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads “Lugdunensem ejus”; the printed text has “Lugdunensem detentus ejus.”]

I do not say this as though I desired to return to England; but I fear that Your Eminence may be angry with me if I do not inform you that I am his. I therefore beg and implore you with all the feeling I can command: do not in any way order me to return to England unless I may there prefer the law and will of God, and the apostolic decrees, to the will of a man; and unless the king restores to me the lands of the Church and whatever he seized from the archbishopric because I sought the Apostolic See—or at least something that may benefit the Church as a worthy compensation for these things. [Col. 0075B] Otherwise I would show that I ought to place a man before God, and that I was justly stripped of my possessions because I wished to seek the Apostolic See.

It is sufficiently clear how harmful and detestable an example this would be for posterity. [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads “requirere. Quaerunt etc.” instead of the printed “requirere. Quod satis patet quam noxium exemplum sit posteris et execrabile. Quaerunt etc.”] Some less discerning people ask why I do not excommunicate the king. But wiser men, who possess sound judgment, advise me not to do so, because it does not belong to me both to make the complaint and to exact vengeance. Finally, our friends who are under the same king have sent me word that, if it were imposed, my excommunication would be despised by him [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript adds “et in derisum converteretur,” “and would be turned into ridicule.”] and turned into ridicule. [Col. 0075C]

Your authority and prudence need no counsel from us concerning all these matters. [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads “authoritatis vestrae prudentiae”; the printed text has “authoritas vestrae prudentiae.”] We pray that almighty God may cause all your actions to please him, and may long allow his Church to rejoice in the prosperity of your governance. [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads simply “Ecclesiam”; the printed text has “Ecclesiam suam,” “his Church.”] Amen.

[Col. 0075C]

## LETTER XLI. OF HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM.

[Note: [Col. 0075D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He excuses himself for having been inaugurated by other bishops because of the invading enemies, and begs Anselm to return to England as quickly as possible.

Henry, by the grace of God king of the English, to his most devout spiritual father Anselm, bishop of Canterbury: greetings and every expression of friendship.

Know, dearest Father, that my brother, King William, has died; and I, by God’s will, elected by the clergy and people of England, though unwilling, have now been consecrated king because of your absence. I therefore appeal to you as a father, together with all the people of England, to come as soon as you can to give counsel to me, your son, and to that same people whose souls have been entrusted to your care.

I commit myself and the whole people of the kingdom of England to your counsel and to that of those who ought to counsel me together with you. I beg you not to be displeased that I received the royal blessing without you; for, if it had been possible, I would more gladly have received it from you than from anyone else. But the necessity was such that enemies were intending to rise against me and against the people entrusted to my government. Therefore my barons and that same people would not allow it to be delayed any longer; and on this account I received it from your vicars.

Indeed, I would have sent several men from my side to you, through whom I would also have sent you money, but because of my brother’s death [Note: [Col. 0075D] The manuscript reads “per mortem”; the printed text has “pro morte.”] the whole world has been so shaken around the kingdom of England that they could in no way have reached you safely.

I therefore command and instruct you not to come through Normandy, but through Wissant. I shall have my barons meet you at Dover, together with money for receiving you; and, with God’s help, you will find enough to repay properly whatever you have borrowed.

Hasten, therefore, Father, to come, lest our mother, the Church of Canterbury, long tossed about and desolate on your account, suffer further loss of souls. Witnesses are Bishop Girard; William, elect bishop of Winchester; William of Wareham; Count Henry; Robert son of Haimon; Haimon the steward; and other bishops and barons of mine. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. OF POPE PASCHAL TO ANSELM.

That, now restored to the Church of Canterbury, he should devote himself to restoring the English Church and reconcile the King of the English with the Count of Normandy.

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“As we have sympathized with your injuries and exile,” etc. See below, in Paschal II, under the year 1118.

## LETTER XLIII. OF ANSELM TO BURGUNDIO AND HIS WIFE RICEZA.

[Note: [Col. 0075D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He congratulates them that their nephew has been devoted to God’s service, and that God has taken away their younger children so that they might now serve God more freely with their whole minds.

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest lord and friend Burgundio and to his most beloved wife, his sister Riceza: greetings and God’s blessing.

Know that your son Anselm, our dearest nephew, is well and happy with me at Lyon; and, by God’s grace, I am in good health. [Col. 0076D] I tell you this about your son so that you may rejoice greatly that you offered him to God. For he loves God and what he ought to love. Therefore you ought to give thanks to and love those who nurtured him in the love of God, in the love of his order, and in good morals.

Indeed, I believe that, because of the merit of having given your firstborn to God with devoted minds, God did not wish to lose any of your offspring. Nor did he permit those whom you had begotten to reach the age at which they would be stained by the sins and wickedness of this world and lose eternal life; instead, he caused all of them to pass from this life to himself with a good end. [Col. 0077A]

Moreover, if you are wise and consider the matter wisely, you will understand that God has shown great mercy to you yourselves, because he has taken away from you the opportunity to love this world and desire things that pass away. In taking away your heirs in this life, he made your children his heirs and his children in eternal life.

Now give thanks to God because you have been relieved of burdens and set free, so that you may run freely toward God with all your heart, all your purpose, and all your strength, and concern yourselves solely with the salvation of your souls. May you reach by willing choice the place to which God mercifully drew your children who died, against your wishes, and to which we hope, with God’s help, this one whom you gave to God will come: there father and mother, sons and daughters, you may rejoice together before God in eternal glory, and each person may glory in the others as much as in himself or herself.

Therefore, dearest and most loving friends, dearest brother and dearest sister, I beg, implore, admonish, and counsel you not to despise the mercy God has shown you without your having planned it, and not to lose the glory God has prepared for you, if the fault is not yours. Understand, understand that God’s making you, now left alone in this life, bereft of all your children, is not God’s anger but God’s grace. Since you alone remain, having nothing to love, run without any impediment toward him and return yourselves and all that is yours to him. [Col. 0077C]

May almighty God kindle you with his love so that he makes you despise every pleasure of this life and strive toward him with your whole heart, and attain to him. Amen.

## LETTER XLIV. OF POPE PASCHAL TO ANSELM.

That he should conduct himself steadfastly in defending the liberty of the English Church.

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Anselm of Canterbury: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You are not unaware of the purpose of the divine will, etc. See in Paschal II under the year 1118.

[Col. 0077D]

## LETTER XLV. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

Anselm consults him about several doubts, and he replies.

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Anselm: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Those matters which you consulted us about through your venerable messengers Baldwin and Alexander,” etc. See in Paschal II.

384 ## LETTER XLVI. OF BENEDICT TO ANSELM.

It is a consolatory letter, composed with sentiments of affection for his friends.

To the lord and venerable father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury by the grace of God, Benedict sends greetings in the Lord.

Love compels me to write, and the grief of my heart compels me to open my sorrow to Your Charity. Since I am speaking to wise men, who know how to prepare many dishes from a small quantity of material, I shall therefore tell Your Holiness briefly and concisely that Satan appears to have been released. For the king of pride is near; and, what it is wicked to say, an army of priests is being prepared for him, because those appointed to provide examples of humility are fighting with raised necks. Thus Daniel’s prophecy seems to have been fulfilled.

Therefore, “let him who is in Judea flee to the mountains, and let him who is on the housetop not come down to take anything from his house” (Matthew 24:17), etc. Accordingly, you who have been a solitary sparrow on the Lord’s housetop and have manfully cut through God’s field with the plow of your tongue ought neither to flee to the mountains nor to take anything from the level ground.
