Although Gregory is not now at Rome, there is nevertheless an Augustine of England; and he who gave him power to perform signs and wonders will give you power to fight manfully for the faith of Christ to the end. “For God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

I received your blessing with the disposition of mind I owed it, for it was full of good sense and good fragrance. We give thanks to God that what you do, say, and give is savory and fragrant. Concerning your life, let us say together—let us all say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

I ask you to pray for me, that Simon may not corrupt me in any respect, and that God may lead me from this sea to the gate of salvation.

## LETTER XLVII. OF ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

After hearing the decrees of the Roman council, which Anselm had attended, the king asks the supreme pontiff about them; Anselm asks that the pope’s judgment be made known to him.

To the revered lord and beloved father Paschal, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers the submission he owes and constant prayers.

After I had been recalled and returned to England to my bishopric, I made known the apostolic decrees which I had heard in person at the Roman council. Concerning this matter my lord king sought Your Holiness through his legate, and I sought your counsel by my letter, according to your knowledge of the matter. You replied to the king by letter, but not at all to me. Since you did not give him an answer sufficient for him, [Note: [Col. 0077D] The manuscript reads “vestras responsum quod illi sufficeret”; the printed text has “vestras respondistis, mihi vero minime: sed quoniam illi responsum quod illi sufficeret.”] several bishops are still coming to your presence concerning the same matter; and I am sending our legates, who will report your answer to me, lest I should appear to do anything according to my own judgment or personal will alone.

Therefore, while preserving in me reverence for the Apostolic See, I beg you to decide concerning the petition which the aforesaid bishops will present to you whatever Your Wisdom, according to God, judges to be better and more useful; and whatever it may be, make me certain of it through our legates. For just as it does not belong to me to absolve those whom you bind, so it is not mine to bind those whom you absolve.

## LETTER XLVIII. OF ANSELM TO THE SAME.

He awaits counsel concerning the adversities he has suffered for nine years, and asks him to grant the pallium to the elected archbishop of York.

To the revered lord and father Paschal, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers the submission he owes.

The many and very serious tribulations of my heart, known only to God and me, testify how earnestly my mind, according to its ability, embraces reverence and obedience toward the Apostolic See. From the beginning of my episcopate I have continually suffered them for nine years now, both in exile and in my episcopate, because I adhered inseparably to the submission and obedience owed to that See. I hope in God that nothing can draw me back from this purpose.

Since I have received no answer concerning the matters about which I formerly consulted Your Eminence through William, our king’s legate, I must repeat them. Concerning what lies between the king and me, I think it is enough for Your Wisdom that I indicate it in other letters and that you will learn it through our legates. On this matter it is not for my humility to give counsel to Your Wisdom, but to await counsel from it.

I pray almighty God to direct your heart toward the praise and glory of his name and the benefit of his Church, so that your judgment may proceed from his countenance and his eyes may see equity in all your actions.

Concerning the elected archbishop of York, as you will be able to learn through the bishops who are with him, I humbly beg you to send him back to us confirmed and honored by your favor, for the sake of the pallium over which he approaches Your Eminence. I believe that there is no one in England who could be of such great benefit in ecclesiastical affairs; and I hope in God that, just as he has received ability from God, so he also possesses the will.

I ask you to deign to hear and answer certain other matters which our legates will present to Your Paternity on our behalf. We pray that almighty God may preserve Your Holiness for us for a long time.

## LETTER XLIX. OF ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF CHESTER.

[Note: [Col. 0079D] Collated with the same manuscript, with the Gothic edition, and with the edition of Cologne, 1573.]

He rejoices in the progress of his monks and exhorts them to careful observance even in the smallest matters.

Anselm, archbishop, sends greetings and God’s blessing, as well as his own, to his dearest brothers and sons, the monks residing in the monastery of Saint Werburga at Chester.

Blessed is God in his gifts and holy in all his works, who causes you both to increase in number and to advance in the growth of your religious life. Although I rejoice in the progress of all God’s servants, I nevertheless have a particular reason in you to rejoice in your progress, because through me God saw fit to establish the beginning of your community, namely our dearest son, Lord Richard, as abbot.

I therefore give thanks to God for the grace he has shown in you, and I pray that, just as he has deigned to go before you with this grace, so he may follow you unceasingly, so that he never allow you to fall away from that to which he has advanced you, but always grant you progress toward better things. He will certainly do this if you are not negligent in preserving the good things to which you have already attained.

Since it belongs to God by his grace always to go before us, it belongs to us diligently to guard, with his help, what we receive. For although we can neither possess nor preserve anything except through him, it is nevertheless only through our negligence that we lose or fall away; and this negligence very often begins with the smallest matters, in which our crafty enemy is accustomed to deceive us by persuading us not to value them highly. From this follows that execrable harm of which we read: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1).

It is absolutely certain, as we have learned by experience in many churches, that in a monastery where small matters are strictly guarded, the rigor of the monks’ order remains inviolate; there peace among the brothers prevails, and complaints in the chapter cease. But where the smallest transgressions are neglected, the whole order is gradually scattered and destroyed.

If, therefore, you wish to ascend from virtue to virtue and from progress to progress, always fear offending God in each of the smallest matters. You should not consider how small the matter is in which you act against a prohibition, but how great an evil is the disobedience into which you fall for the sake of a small matter.

Only obedience could have kept a human being in paradise, from which he was expelled through disobedience; nor is anyone brought to the kingdom of heaven except through obedience. [Note: [Col. 0079D] The manuscript and edition continue: “Consider that if a human being, through a single act of disobedience, was cast into the great misery which we suffer in this world, how greatly we ought to abhor it and strive for the good of obedience. In obedience the whole strength of right living is built; through its neglect it is destroyed. To your abbot,” etc.] Consider, then, that if a human being was cast by a single act of disobedience into the great misery we suffer in this world, how greatly we ought to abhor it and strive for the good of obedience. In obedience the whole strength of right living is built; through its neglect it is destroyed.

Therefore show obedience to your abbot in everything, not only in action but also in will, [Note: [Col. 0079D] The manuscript and edition read “voluntate exhibere”; the printed text has “voluntate per omnia exhibete.”] and maintain peace and harmony among yourselves through mutual love. You will be able to nourish and preserve this love if each person strives not to do his own will as another’s, but to do the other person’s will as his own.

Also exclude idleness from yourselves as an enemy of souls, and let each person consider that we shall have to render an account to God for every moment of our lives. Therefore, whatever grace God gives anyone for any useful purpose, let that person use it whenever he has the opportunity. For whoever does not use the power of doing good that he possesses will be judged on the day of judgment as though he did not possess it; and from him will be taken even that which he seems to have, because he will both be deprived of the reward he could have deserved and thereafter, in punishment, have no power to perform any good work.

It will be as though what is taken from him were given to another, when the reward of the person who acts well according to what he has received will be increased, because, beside one who lived negligently, he did not cease from good works by that person’s example. [Note: [Col. 0081C] The manuscript and edition read “secundum donum quod,” “according to the gift which.”]

I thank you because you pray for me, and I pray that you may not cease from this charity.

386 ## LETTER L. OF ANSELM TO BERNARD THE MONK.

[Note: [Col. 0081C] Collated with the same manuscript.]

That a single scourging received through obedience is worth more than countless ones undertaken according to one’s own judgment.

Anselm, archbishop, to Bernard, monk of the monastery of Saint Werburga: greetings and prayer.

I have heard from your abbot that you judge a monk to possess greater merit when he scourges himself or asks to be scourged by another than when, in the chapter, he undergoes scourging at the command of his superior and not according to his own will. [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Vapulat” is absent from the manuscript.] This is not as you think. The punishment which someone imposes on himself voluntarily is royal; but that which he endures through obedience in the chapter is monastic. [Note: [Col. 0081C] The manuscript reads “regale est: illud” instead of the printed “regale. Illud.”] The one proceeds from his own will, the other from obedience and not from his own will. What I call royal is often ordered by kings and proud rich men for themselves; what I call monastic is received not by those who command, but by those who obey. The royal punishment is lighter in proportion as it agrees with the will of the person enduring it. [Note: [Col. 0081C] The manuscript reads “lenius est”; the printed text has “levius est.”] The monastic punishment, however, is heavier in proportion as it conflicts with the will of the person suffering it.

In the royal punishment it is shown that the person enduring it belongs to himself; in the monastic punishment it is proved that he does not belong to himself. For although a king or rich man, when he voluntarily scourges himself, humbly shows himself to be a sinner, he would not submit himself to this humility at the command of another person, but would resist the one commanding with all his strength.

When a monk, however, at the sentence of his superior, humbly submits himself to blows in the chapter, truth judges that he possesses the greater merit, inasmuch as he humbles himself more fully and more truly than the other. The one humbles himself before God alone because of consciousness of his sins; the other humbles himself before a human being as well, because of obedience. The person who humbles himself before both God and a human being for God’s sake is more humble than the person who humbles himself before God alone and not before a human command.

Therefore, if “the one who humbles himself will be exalted,” the one who humbles himself more will be exalted more. [Col. 0082B] What I said about a monk’s scourging—that it conflicts with his own will—must not be understood as though he were unwilling to endure it patiently with an obedient will, but because, by the natural appetite of the flesh, he would be unwilling to tolerate the pain.

If you say, “I do not avoid public scourging so much because of the pains, which I also feel in private, as because of the shame,” know that the stronger person is the one who gladly endures this as well for the sake of obedience. Be certain, therefore, that one scourging of a monk endured through obedience has greater merit than countless scourgings accepted according to his own judgment.

But when a monk is such that he always has a heart prepared to undergo scourging through obedience without murmuring, then whether he is scourged privately or publicly, we ought to judge him to possess great merit.

## LETTER LI. OF ANSELM TO STEPHEN THE ARCHDEACON.

[Note: [Col. 0081C] Collated with the same manuscript.]

That he should prohibit the abbess and nuns of Ramsey from the superstitious worship of a dead man whom they regarded as a saint.

Anselm, archbishop, to Stephen the archdeacon: greetings and blessing. [Note: [Col. 0081C] The manuscript reads “diacono” instead of “archidiacono.”]

I command you to go to Ramsey and say—and by saying it command the lady abbess [Note: [Col. 0081C] The manuscript reads “Dominae Abbatissae”; the printed text has “Domnae Abbatissae.”] and the nuns, on our behalf and on behalf of the bishop of Winchester and yourself [Note: [Col. 0083B] The manuscript reads “episcopi et vestra”; the printed text has “episcopi Wintoniensis et vestra”]—that, if they do not wish to prevent me from celebrating the divine office for them, they must then entirely prohibit the display, by themselves or anyone else, of any honor which ought to be shown to a saint to the dead man whom some wish to be regarded as a saint. [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Go to Ramsey and say,” etc. I confess that this passage caused me no slight difficulty. While reading the Anglo-Saxon writers, I repeatedly encountered Rameseia, Ramesiensis, and the monks living there, but I remained uncertain because the abbess’s name is expressly given in this letter. The manuscript tables of the Church of Lincoln, preserved in our library, removed the difficulty in a few respects. Aluvinus, the counsellor, founded the abbey of Remeseta within the marshes at that time. I understand the attribution of the foundation of Ramsey monastery to Aluvinus as meaning that he contributed a very large amount of his labor and resources to the work. For the remaining writers—Malmesbury, Book IV of *On the Bishops of England*; Hoveden; Polydore; and Lilius in the *Chronicle* under the year 971—proclaim Saint Oswald, bishop of York, to have been the monastery’s principal and chief founder. Malmesbury and Hoveden, however, in Part I of the *Annals*, under the year 971, admit that the church was founded through the common labor and resources of both men. In Hoveden, the Aluvinus whom the written Lincoln tables call Etheluvius is named Egeluvinus in Malmesbury. The Ramsey of which Anselm speaks here is a nunnery in the diocese of Winchester, established by King Edward, as Hoveden testifies in these words: “In the year 967 the peaceful king of the English, Edgar, placed nuns in the monastery of Ramsey—not Rameseia, as the corrupted printed books have it—which King Edward the Elder, his grandfather, had built; and he appointed Saint Merewenna abbess over them.” Malmesbury too, when listing the monasteries of the diocese of Winchester in Book II of *On the Bishops of England*, mentions it and calls it Ramsey, differing from Hoveden in asserting that Edgar, not Edward, was its founder. Thus the diversity of places, times, and founders clearly distinguishes these two monasteries, although, with the letter *u* changed into *a*, their names are precisely the same. As for the man whom Anselm here orders the virgins of Ramsey to refrain from worshipping and honoring, though some regarded him as a saint, he was Valdeosus, Valtheofus, Valdefus, or Veldeofus, a most noble count whom William the Conqueror condemned to death for the slightest suspicion of conspiracy. Many splendid miracles testified to his innocence, as reported by Malmesbury, Book IV of *On the Bishops of England*, and Walsingham in the *Hypodigma Neustriae* under the year 1075. The abbess of Ramsey, moved either by a rumor of some miracle or by the unjust death of the count, was therefore offering public prayers and making vows to one whom the Church had not yet enrolled among the saints. Anselm rightly orders her to cease; for public honors to saints do not depend upon the fervent zeal of just anyone, but upon the judgment of the Apostolic See and the Catholic Church. Nevertheless, at the Synod of Pontoise, held in 1102, he promulgated an edict on this matter, which Malmesbury reports in Book I of *On the Bishops of England* in these terms: “Let no one, through rash novelty, show the bodies of the dead—or springs or other things, which we know have been affected in this way—reverence as holy without episcopal authority.” By this prohibition Anselm wished to restrain certain sudden superstitions of the common people, born of immature piety, not to reject the praiseworthy and ancient custom of the Roman Church ordinarily observed in the glorification of saints.]

Furthermore, drive the son of that dead man from the village, and do not allow him to live there any longer.

## LETTER LII. OF ANSELM TO GERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.

[Note: [Col. 0083B] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He explains that, with his consent, a respite was granted to the sacrilegious man who had dared to take a veiled woman as his wife.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to Gerard, archbishop of York: greetings.

I inform Your Reverence, my dear friend, that the respite which the bishop of London granted, at your insistence and with my support, in the case of the man who presumed to take a veiled woman as his wife has been turned into such great disgrace for me, for you, and for all those with whose consent it was granted—among the Londoners and all who hear of it—that no one could tolerate it, unless, lacking religious shame, he were able to flee from it. [Note: [Col. 0083B] The manuscript reads “ut nullus hoc”; “nullius hoc” is printed, but incorrectly.] They also despair that any good will ever come to the Church of God through those bishops who were able to consent to the prolongation of so execrable a crime.

Therefore it is fitting—indeed, it is necessary—for all of us who consented to this, if we do not wish to remain subject to such an indecent reproach, that a day be appointed as soon as possible for deciding this case. On that day we wish you and I to be present, or, if this cannot be done, some reasonable person from our side and likewise from yours. Although it is too distant for us because of the aforementioned matter, we appoint the eighth day after the Nativity of Saint Mary, Mother of God, since I know that you wish to attend.

Indeed, neither would the bishop to whom the case belongs wish to delay it further if I wished to proceed, nor would I wish to delay it if he wished to proceed, provided God protects us from every impediment. [Col. 0084B] For after our conversation we learned so much about the truth of the matter that, if we hasten what we had proposed to defer, this cannot be marked as levity in such a case. [Note: [Col. 0083B] The manuscript reads “nullus hoc”; the printed text has “nulla notandum hoc.”]

## LETTER LIII. OF HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, TO ANSELM.

[Note: [Col. 0083B] Collated with the same manuscript and with the manuscript of Saint-Ouen of Rouen.]

He gives thanks for the treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, written against the Greeks and sent to him.

To the venerable archbishop of Canterbury, most worthy of glory and honor, Anselm, Hildebertus [Note: [Col. 0083D]

Hildebertus. Robert Cenalis, in book I of *On Gallic Affairs*, section 6, writes *Gildebertus*; Guillelmus Gemmetensis, in book VI of the *History of the Norman Dukes*, chapter 10, has *Idebertus*, and others *Ildeberdus*. The manuscripts have the latter form, as well as the inscription of this letter, indiscriminately; the printed editions, however, have *Hildebertus*. In his *Deeds* also—which I obtained from the venerable prior Tufferus, a monk of Saint Vincent of Le Mans—I found both forms used alternately. But so that these *Deeds* may no longer remain hidden from posterity, we shall add them here:

“Venerable Hildebertus was born at the castle of Lavardin to parents of modest but respectable standing. He was made master of the schools by Hoel [elsewhere Boel], bishop of Le Mans, then archdeacon, and after the death of Lord Hoel was appointed in his place. Thus, gentle and modest in character, at the very beginning of his episcopate he diligently set about restoring whatever through the negligence of his predecessors had either been destroyed or lost. He immediately began to build the chapter house from its foundations, adorned it on every side with windows, and arranged for it to be covered with vaulted masonry.

“At that same time a very serious war arose between Henry I, king of the English, and Helias, count of Maine, because the king was laying claim to the bishopric and therefore sought to obstruct the bishop’s appointment. When he heard that the bishop had been appointed, he made his hostility known through open military attacks. Count Helias began to resist his undertakings. When Fulk, count of Anjou, learned of this, he came into the city, placed a guard in the city’s fortifications with the consent of its citizens, and, leaving his son there, hastened elsewhere.

“Meanwhile, the king of the English, seeing that the city was deprived of the protection of its own ruler, approached it. He came to Colonia, settled before the city with a large army, and afterward burned Colonia. But when the king saw that he had been mocked, he withdrew with his army. The citizens, who had prepared themselves for battle, learned of the king’s flight and returned to the city.

“When Count Helias heard this, fearing that Fulk, count of Anjou, might seek his proscription, he summoned Bishop Hildebertus and certain leading citizens to him. With them he began to consider by what means they might surrender the city to the king and free him from his bonds. For Count Helias himself was being held in the king of England’s chains: he feared that Count Fulk, deceived by royal gifts, might make peace with the king and, after the city had been handed over, condemn him forever. The bishop, taking pity on his distress, conferred with him about his release. Shortly afterward the king permitted him to depart free and untroubled. The king, having taken the city and placed garrisons in its fortifications, crossed over to England.

“Some clerics, however, envious of the bishop’s advancement and plotting deceit against him, accused him before the king of England, saying that he had been privy to the treachery when Count Helias seized the city with everyone’s consent. Consequently, suspecting Hildebertus, the king insistently demanded that he order the church towers to be demolished—for he claimed that harm had been done to him through them—before he crossed over to England. To induce the bishop to demolish the towers, he offered him, as he said, a very large quantity of gold and silver for the construction of Saint Julian’s tomb.

“Seeing that this was intended as a disgrace, the bishop, after taking counsel, returned to his church. First he brought out two precious cymbals, an excellent cope of fine cloth, and two silver basins, together with many other ornaments. Meanwhile the bishop, deeply distressed by the king’s command, by the burning of the city, the destruction of his houses, the expulsion of the citizens, and the scattering of the clergy, continually entreated the clemency of almighty God, asking that He deign to turn away the wrath of His indignation from the Church and the people.

“Taking pity on his affliction, the Lord mitigated His indignation beyond what could have been hoped, and filled the faces of his enemies with confusion and disgrace, so that their song was turned into mourning and their music into the voice of those who weep. For one day, while the king had gone into the forest to hunt, he was struck by an arrow from one of his own soldiers who were with him and died.

“When the city had been pacified and the enemies put to flight, Hildebertus set out for Rome, where Pope Paschal II received him with particular attention. Thereafter, as he proceeded through Sicily and Apulia, everyone honored him as though he were an angel of God.

“Roger, duke of Sicily, having heard of the bishop’s reputation and learning, received him with the greatest honor and reverence. Roger gave him one hundred ounces of gold for the work of Saint Julian and ten pounds of coin for the sustenance of the canons. Afterward the same bishop returned to the province of Le Mans. At that time Count Helias, in his generosity, adorned with gold and silver the bed in which the blessed relics of Saint Julian rested.

“Then, in the year of the Lord 1120, hastening to the dedication of the church and supplying there many necessities, Hildebertus consecrated it on the eighth day of Easter in honor and under the name of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, and of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and of the most devout Julian. Later he made at his own expense two reliquary chests beautifully covered with gold and silver, in which he solemnly deposited the relics of the saints Tutilius, Victor, and Innocent, and of Saint Tenestina, Saint Oda, and Saint Hilary the priest.

“After some time Guillebertus, archbishop of Tours, died, and Hildebertus, bishop of Le Mans, received the highest office in his place and see, with the consent of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks. This occurred in the year of the Lord 1129.

“Finally, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, 18 December—in the year of the Lord 1136, he fell asleep in the Lord in a good old age and was buried at Tours in the church of Saint Maurice. He governed the Church of Tours for seven years and six months, and the Church of Le Mans for twenty-two years; and his life lasted about eighty years.”

Thus far the memorandum sent to me.

The love of historical truth compels me to make one or two observations concerning it. Arnoldus Wion, in book II of his *Lignum vitae*, chapter 39, reports from a manuscript of the *Chronicle of Cluny* that Hildebertus had been a Cluniac monk. Yet this brief narrative, recalling Hildebertus’s beginnings, says that he afterward served as master of the schools and archdeacon, and that he had previously heard Berengar as his teacher. I do not see to what period of Hildebertus’s life Guillelmus of Malmesbury and the other historians could assign his monastic profession.

Moreover, a monk—as Jacobus de Graflis, a Cassinese monk, notes in part II of the *Golden Decisions*, book III, chapter 20—cannot be promoted to dignities of churches that differ in profession and habit. It is clear from the foregoing that the Church of Le Mans then had, and still has, clerical canons. Indeed, it is evident from chapter 3 of the *Life of Saint Panacius*, also bishop of Le Mans, that from the beginning clerics lived there according to a rule and after the example of the apostles; John a Bosco also noted this in the same place.

The election of Hildebertus to the bishopric of Le Mans in the year 1106, according to the *Chronicle of Cluny*, is plainly contradicted by the murder of William Rufus, king of the English, previously mentioned and committed in 1100, as is shown by Sigebert and the others cited above in connection with Letter 40. In the same book, chapter 22, the author also most carelessly said that Hildebertus was created archbishop of Tours in 1106. If you attribute this slip to a slipping typesetter, I do so too. Let us examine the matter more carefully.

The manuscript memorandum states that Hildebertus bore the archiepiscopal mitre of Tours in the year 1129. The tables of Le Mans, in Demochare and Wion, state that he sat at Le Mans for twenty-nine years, while the manuscript memorandum says that he occupied the see of Tours for seven years and six months.

The earlier part of this chronology is weakened by a letter of Pope Honorius II—who was created in 1124—to Hildebertus, already archbishop of Tours, and by Hildebertus’s reply to Honorius; these are found as Hildebertus’s Letters 67 and 68. On the other hand, Letter 124 of Saint Bernard occurs, urging him in 1130 to support the cause of Innocent II, who had been proclaimed pope.

If, finally, we say that Hildebertus presided over the Church of Le Mans for twenty-nine years, he must have been consecrated at least in 1099, and from then until 1100 must have overseen the construction of the chapter house, as we read at the beginning of the narrative; he must then have been transferred to Tours in 1123 and died in 1136, with the additional months counted as though they were complete years. If one prefers the view that he governed Le Mans for only twenty-two years, one is forced to make him bishop in 1100, archbishop in 1123, and finally deceased in 1130, shortly after Innocent II, elected in 1130 on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.

But this calculation conflicts with the statement that Hildebertus died on 18 December; besides, it appears more forced and more violent. I therefore more willingly embrace the former chronology. The manifestly conflicting dates above compelled me to investigate and record these matters—conflicts which even the blind would have noticed.

, humble [Col. 0085A] priest of Le Mans, greetings and prayers in the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: The manuscript reads “greetings and prayers in the Lord Jesus Christ.”]

A joyful day and solemn faces came to me together with your treatise, most holy Father.

[Note: The Saint Andrew manuscript reads “most holy Father” and “together”; another manuscript reads “your servant, I”; the present text has “your servant, I, your servant.”]

Previously I, your servant, had received your blessing, and a devoted affection gave thanks to the Lord God and to you.

[Note: The manuscript reads “Thanks to the Lord God and to you”; the Saint-Ouen manuscript reads “thanks to God and to you.”]

It was human to assist one’s neighbor through compassionate affection.

[Note: The Saint Andrew manuscript reads “through an affection of charity”; the printed Picardy edition reads “through compassionate affection.”]

But it was divine to defend the Catholic faith through the Holy Spirit dwelling in you. The one and the same Spirit accomplished both, willing to make the grace of virtues overflow in you, and reserving you as the defender of His procession from the Son.

[Note: The Saint Andrew manuscript omits *ille*, “that one,” in “the one and the same.”]

For wisdom could not enter a malicious soul or dwell in a body subject to sins. Therefore it was fitting that the advocate of truth should offer an example of religious devotion.

[Note: The manuscripts read “left an example.”]

Such a man was consequently suited to pastoral watchfulness, lacking nothing for the fullness of righteousness and nothing for the integrity of doctrine.

[Note: The Saint Andrew manuscript reads “nothing is lacking”; other manuscripts read “fullness, nothing”; the present text has “fullness of righteousness, nothing.”]

Blessed indeed is the heart which the assembly of virtues consecrated as its venerable inner sanctuary. From its inner chambers, as it were, divine oracles proceed, and the sacred lips profess nothing other than the interpreter of the heavenly will.

[Note: The manuscript reads “sacred words.”]

When I recall them frequently, amazement overwhelms me; and as I contemplate each one carefully, I acknowledge that all must be ascribed to the Spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “This is the Lord’s doing; it is marvelous in our eyes” (Psalm 117:23).

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Amazement overwhelms me, and, marveling that a man of our time can accomplish such things, I acknowledge that all must be ascribed to the Spirit, as the swift-writing scribe.” The Saint-Ouen and Victor manuscripts, in a more recent hand, read: “Amazement overwhelms me; and as I contemplate each thing carefully, I acknowledge that all must be ascribed to the Holy Spirit.”]

Farewell, most holy Father, knowing that my soul longs intensely to see you and will not find the winds or the sea burdensome, provided that I may receive from you counsel for salvation, which I believe exists nowhere unless it is with you.

[Note: The Victor manuscript reads “provided that I may receive counsel for salvation.” The Saint Andrew manuscript adds: “Holy Father, knowing that my soul longs intensely to see you, will not find the winds or the sea burdensome, provided that I may receive counsel for salvation from you. Farewell.”]

## LETTER LIV. TO THE MONKS OF ST ALBANS

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

He urges the monks to continual observance of their rule. (See Letter 160 below.)

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest brothers and sons, the lord prior and the other servants of God residing in the monastery of Saint Alban, greetings and blessing.

I give thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes, and to you, who preserve His gift, because I hear every good thing about you. You show that you remember that you must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations, and that temptation tests and tries the righteous, whether they love God, since no adversity can prevent you from guarding your order. Thus you can securely await the reward of which it is said: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:22).

The more diligently I recognize that you apply yourselves to preserving the monastic order, the more confidently I exhort you with paternal admonition to persevere in your good purpose and in that to which God has advanced you; and always to strive, in hope of divine assistance, to progress toward better things and never to fail. You will be able to accomplish this effectively if you refuse to despise any of the smallest matters of your order, for “whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1).

God sees what is expedient for you. If He delays in consoling you, wait for Him, because He will not delay; for He is the helper in times of need and in tribulation. May almighty God deign to strengthen and console your hearts in His service. I ask you: pray for me.

## LETTER LV. MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

[Compared with the same Victor manuscript.]

That he should relax his daily fast somewhat.

To the lord and reverend father Anselm, archbishop of the primatial see, primate of all the Irish and of all the northern islands called the Orkneys, Mathilda, by the grace of God queen of the English, his most humble handmaid, wishing to complete happily the course of the present life and reach its end, which is Christ.

It is scarcely doubtful to anyone that you have now turned your daily fast into a natural habit, and it is no less known to me. What I find still more astonishing I have learned from the frequent reports of many good men: after long fasts, you habitually take food not because nature demands it, but at the prompting of someone from your household.

[Note: The manuscript reads “from your household.”]

I also know that you take even these foods with such frugality that you seem rather to have done violence to nature by diminishing its proper right than to have violated a rule. Therefore, with many others—and with me above all—we must fear that the body of so great a father, to whom I am bound by such benefits, so strong an athlete of God and victor over human nature, whose unfailing vigor has strengthened and defended the peace of the kingdom and the dignity of the priesthood, so faithful and prudent a steward of God, by whose blessing I was consecrated in a lawful marriage, by whose ordination I was raised to the dignity of an earthly kingdom, and by whose prayers, with God’s assent, I hope to be crowned in heavenly glory, may waste away; that the windows of sight, hearing, and the other senses may be blocked; that the voice which builds up spiritual things may grow hoarse; and that the voice which was accustomed to dispense the beautiful and sweet word of God in measured, calm, and gentle speech may in the future perform its task so much more feebly that those who are somewhat more distant from you, deprived of hearing that very voice, may also be left without its fruit.

Therefore, good and holy Father, do not deprive yourself so untimely of bodily strength through starvation, lest you cease to be an orator. For, as Tully says in the book he wrote *On Old Age*: “The orator’s task belongs not only to intelligence but also to the sides and the strength of the body.”

Whither is so much brilliance of mind hastening to perish—such great memory of past things and foresight of things to come, so many arts, so many sciences, so many discoveries, such extensive knowledge of human affairs, and prudence in divine matters joined with simplicity? Consider the multitude of talents that your rich Lord has given you, what He has entrusted to you, and what He demands. Bring the good into the common benefit, so that, when brought forth, it may shine more beautifully and be returned to the Lord with manifold interest.

Do not defraud one another. Just as spiritual drink and food are necessary for the soul, so bodily nourishment is necessary for the body. You must therefore eat and drink, since, by God’s will, a long road of this life remains before you, a great harvest to sow, hoe, and reap, and to store in the Lord’s granary, where no thief can approach. You see that the laborers are very few in so great a harvest. You have entered into the labors of many in order to bring back the gains of many.

Remember that you hold the place of John the apostle and evangelist, dear to the Lord, whom the Lord Himself wished to survive, so that he, the beloved virgin, might care for the Virgin Mother. You have undertaken the care of Mother Church, for the brothers and sisters of Christ, whom He Himself entrusted to you after redeeming them at the price of His own blood, will be in peril every day unless you come to their aid with great care. Feed, shepherd of so great a Lord, His flock, lest the needy flock fail on the way.

Let the holy priest Martin, an ineffable man, be an example to you. Although he foresaw the heavenly rest prepared for him, he nevertheless said that he did not refuse labor for the needs of the people. I know that you are invited and strengthened to fast by the examples of many and by many testimonies of Scripture. Constant reading frequently reminds you how, after fasting, the raven fed Elijah, the widow fed Elisha, and the angel through Habakkuk fed Daniel; and how Moses deserved, through fasting, to receive the tablets written by God’s finger, and through that same fasting recovered them after they had been broken.

The examples of the gentiles also invite you to moderation. No one can be unaware that you have read of the frugality of Pythagoras, Socrates, Antisthenes, and the other philosophers—whose enumeration would be lengthy and unnecessary in the present little work.

We must therefore come to the grace of the new law. Christ Jesus, who consecrated fasting, also consecrated eating. He went to the wedding feast, where He changed water into wine; He went to Simon’s banquet, where Mary, after seven demons had been cast out, was first nourished by Him with spiritual foods; and He did not refuse the meal of Zacchaeus, whom He recalled from the power of worldly military service and called to the heavenly warfare.

Listen, Father; listen to Paul, who advises Timothy to drink wine because of his stomach ailment, saying: “Do not continue to drink only water, but use a little wine.” Behold, the Apostle dissuades his disciple from his purpose of fasting. By saying, “Do not continue to drink only water,” he plainly declares that Timothy had previously drunk nothing but water.

Imitate Gregory, who relieved the weariness and weakness of his stomach by the strengthening of food and drink, and applied himself manfully and indefatigably to teaching and preaching. Do, then, what he did, so that you may reach the one whom he reached—that is, Jesus Christ, the fountain of life and the lofty mountain—with whom he has long rejoiced in everlasting glory, and rejoices and will rejoice forever and ever.

May your holiness fare well in the Lord. Do not cease to assist me, your faithful handmaid, who loves you with all the affection of her heart, by your prayers; and may you deign to receive, read, hear, and heed this letter, which I have sent you not feignedly, but with faithful and steadfast charity.

[Col. 0090C]

## LETTER LVI. ANSELM TO COUNTESS IDA

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

Concerning the son whom he admonished, and concerning the prebend of his chaplain Lambert.

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury,

[Note: The manuscript reads “Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

to the lady, mother, and dearest daughter, the reverend Countess Ida, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as he can give it.

My dearest, my letter greets you; but my memory beholds you every day, and I hope in God that you will never be erased from my heart. I spoke with your son and entreated him on your behalf, as I understood was fitting; and he replied to me that he would do nothing more willingly than fulfill your wishes.

Lord Lambert, your chaplain, who remains in England in your service, asks—and I ask together with him—that, until he returns to you, he lose nothing through any circumstance of the benefit of his prebend. We also ask that you admonish his fellow canons by entreating them to do this. We both greet them in this letter and earnestly ask them to accept your petition.

May almighty God guard you from every adversity and continually direct, kindle, and bring your desire to fulfillment. Amen.

## LETTER LVII. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

He gives thanks for gifts and for a friendly admonition.

To Mathilda, glorious queen of the English, reverend lady and dearest daughter, Anselm, archbishop, offers due honor, service, prayers, and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as he can give it.

I give great thanks for your generosity, but much greater thanks for the holy affection from which your gifts proceed. With pious concern it also urges me to indulge the body more generously in taking nourishment, lest voice and strength fail me for the care entrusted to me. For when you hear that, even if it were done daily, I do not feel hunger from fasting for an entire day, you fear that hoarseness and bodily weakness may come upon me.

[Note: The manuscript reads “even if it were done.”]

Would that the wisdom and power appropriate to me were available in as great a measure as the voice and strength I possess are sufficient for the work entrusted to me. Although I can fast in this way without the discomfort of hunger, I have nevertheless suffered enough, and when I ought to, I wish to restore the body with as much food as is expedient.

Your gracious dignity recalls in its letter that your highness was betrothed through me in lawful marriage and crowned to the height of the kingdom by my consecration. But when you recall so kindly and with such grace that I was, insofar as I could be, merely the faithful minister of this event, it is possible to estimate how many thanks you render in your heart to Christ, who is the author and giver of this gift.

If you wish to repay those thanks rightly, well, and effectively through action itself, consider that queen whom He chose from this world as His bride. This is the one whom in Scripture He calls beautiful, His beloved, and His dove, and of whom it is said to Him: “The queen stands at your right hand” (Psalm 44:10). This is the one to whom the same Bridegroom, Christ, says: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (ibid., 11).

The more she forgets by despising worldly conduct and the dwelling place of her father—that is, of this world—the more beautiful and more lovable she is recognized to be in the sight of her Bridegroom. He proved how greatly He loved her when He did not hesitate to hand Himself over willingly to death for her love.

Consider, I say, how she dwells in exile as a pilgrim and, like a widow, groans and sighs for her husband with her true children, waiting until he comes from the distant region to which he has gone to receive a kingdom for himself, and, transferring her to his kingdom, repays all who have done good or evil to that beloved according to each person’s deeds.

Those who honor her will be honored with her; those who trample her will be trampled outside her; those who exalt her will be exalted with the angels; those who abase her will be abased with the demons. Exalt her, honor her, defend her, so that with her and in her, as the bride of God, you may please Him and live reigning with her in eternal blessedness. Amen. Let it be so.

[Col. 0092A]

389

## LETTER LVIII. ANSELM TO COUNTESS IDA

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

He gives thanks for the generosity shown to his envoys; praises her fear in matters concerning salvation; absolves her from sins and imposes a penance.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop, to the lady, mother, and dearest daughter, Countess Ida, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as it has value.

I give thanks to your highness for the kindness and generosity that you recently showed to our envoys returning from Rome, as you habitually do for me and all our people. As for what you sent me word through Lord John, I can perceive no fault of yours.

[Note: The manuscript reads “through Lord N.”]

But since it is always safer in such matters to fear more than to trust, I praise your fear, because “blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14). Blessed Job also said: “I feared all my words” (Job 9:28).

Therefore, solely from this love and from the grief you felt over the evil that occurred through wicked men, I believe that, insofar as it concerns you, you have made satisfaction to God. Nevertheless, since I know what you desire, I pray God to absolve you from this and from all your sins and to lead you to the contemplation of His glory. Amen. Say one psalter for all your sins, according to your opportunity.

## LETTER LIX. ANSELM TO COUNTESS CLEMENTIA

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

He praises the count because he granted no investiture, celebrates this as having been done by the countess’s counsel and prudence, and Anselm urges her herself always to advise her husband.

[Col. 0092C]

Anselm, although unworthy, called archbishop of Canterbury,

[Note: The manuscript reads “Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury.”]

to the lady and dearest daughter, the reverend Countess Clementia, wishing her, through the lasting prosperity of this life, to merit the eternal happiness of the life to come.

It has been reported to me that certain abbots in Flanders were appointed in such a way that your husband, the count, granted none of them investiture with his own hand. Just as I judge that this was not done without his prudent clemency, so I judge that it was not done without your gracious prudence.

[Note: The manuscript reads “I do not consider it.”]

Therefore I rejoice in this good work of yours all the more because I love you both more truly in God. For when you act by harmonious agreement in matters belonging to the Christian religion, you show yourselves to be true children of the Church, the bride of God, and faithful defenders.

Princes, if they are Christians, ought not to regard God’s bride, their mother, as given to them for hereditary domination, but as entrusted to them by God, so that they may deserve to be coheirs with her for her reverence and defense.

For David was a king, and he understood what pertains to princes, when he cursed princes who wished to possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance: “My God, make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Psalm 82:14), and the words that immediately follow. It is not David who speaks these things, but the Spirit of God, the Son of David, who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:15).

It belongs to you, reverend lady and dearest daughter, frequently and opportunely—inopportunely if necessary—to suggest these things and similar ones to your husband, and to counsel him to prove himself not a lord but a defender, not a stepson but a son of the Church.

[Note: The manuscript reads “and to prove himself not only a lord but”; the present text has “not a lord but.”]

Certainly, in this way his power will be pleasing to God, all his acts will be directed by Him, and He will be with him against all his adversaries. Warn him never to oppose the law of God, because Scripture, which does not lie, declares that those who are subject to it are without doubt enemies of God.

Let him not trust counsel against the counsel of God, because “the Lord rejects the counsels of princes, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 32:10), and “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). The counsel of the Lord is sacred Scripture, the teaching of those to whom He said, “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16), and the institutions established for the Christian religion.

Let these things, I beg you, Countess Clementia, be brought to his attention and be the subject of your counsel, so that divine clemency may raise both him and you to the kingdom of heaven. So may it be. Amen.

## LETTER LX. ANSELM TO GERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

That he did not write the letters for which the bishops of England accused him.

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to Gerard, reverend archbishop of York, greetings.

Although my conscience does not know me to be such a man as your prudence portrays me, nevertheless I ought not to be ungrateful, because the good qualities you attribute to me are persuaded to you by the goodwill you bear toward me. I gladly accept your affection’s exhortation that I should neither endure nor wish for an insult to you and your companions, nor do I recall ever having sought or desired such a thing.

For I neither copied those letters, whose publication you think caused this affair, nor showed them to anyone for copying, nor did anyone do so through me. Finally, when I speak with you, I trust in God that you will recognize me as entirely free of blame in this matter. Farewell.

[Col. 0093D]

## LETTER LXI. ANSELM TO THE MONKS OF SAINT EDMUND

He praises the monks’ unbroken constancy in adversity.

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest brothers and sons, the monks of the monastery of Saint Edmund, greetings and the consolation of God’s mercy in tribulation.

I praise you and rejoice because you did not resist with violence those who inflicted violence upon you, but entrusted yourselves solely to God’s protection and disposition. In this matter they were violent against God rather than against you, while you cried out more to God that He might look upon and judge what they had unjustly done to you against Him.

Do not be surprised, and do not let your hearts be troubled beyond measure, if you suffer tribulations in this life, because it is written: “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (Acts 14:21). We ought also to rejoice with the Apostle in tribulation, knowing that “tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5:6).

You must hope in God, because He is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear. Thanks be to God, insofar as human judgment is concerned, you do not suffer because of any crime but because of righteousness; whereas those who attack you do so because of their own desire.

When you stand together before the tribunal of Christ, where each person will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, it is clear that justice is with you in this matter, while wickedness is with them. If God distinguishes these things in the action, He will certainly distinguish them in the recompense.

I also advise you as a father advises his sons: attribute what you suffer to your sins according to God’s judgment, so that each of you may examine his conscience and make satisfaction to God through the fruit of repentance and confession. God is accustomed to scourge the multitude because of the guilt of the few. Therefore let each person attribute to himself what you suffer together, and, insofar as he can, invoke God’s clemency upon himself and the others through satisfaction.

For God says: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7). May almighty God visit you with His protection and defense and make you joyful with merciful consolation. Amen.

## LETTER LXII. ANSELM TO WILLIAM THE ARCHDEACON

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

Concerning the nonpublication of the Acts of the Council of London until he has first communicated them again to the bishops. Meanwhile, he suggests some of the council’s decisions.

Anselm, archbishop, to William, his beloved archdeacon, greetings and blessing.

### Canonical textual apparatus and editorial notes

Each entry below is translated from the supplied source in source order.  A
Latin form is retained only where the variant is one of spelling, inflection,
word order, or exact scope; its English force follows it. `ms` means the
unnamed manuscript; `mss` means manuscripts; S. And. = Saint Andrew; S. Aud.
= Saint-Ouen; Vict. = Victor; Mary. = the Victor manuscript at Mary; Edit.
Pic. = the Picardy edition.

#### Closing fragment before Letter LIV — [Col. 0085A–0087B]

- `salutem` (“greetings”): the manuscript instead has `salutem, et orationes in Domino Jesu Christo` (“greetings and prayers in the Lord Jesus Christ”); the additional words govern the salutation.
- `Sanctissime Pater` (“most holy Father”): S. And. has `Sanctissime Pater … pariter` (“most holy Father … together”), the source's variant at the arrival of the treatise.
- `servus ego, servus tuus` (“I, a servant, your servant”): the manuscript has `ego servus tuus` (“I, your servant”), at the opening of the blessing sentence.
- `gratias Domino Deo, et tibi` (“thanks to the Lord God and to you”): S. Aud. has `gratias Deo et tibi` (“thanks to God and to you”).
- `devotus affectus` (“devoted affection”): the manuscript has the same words; S. Aud. has `devotus affectus meus` (“my devoted affection”); Edit. Pic. has the difficult `devotus effectus est affectus` (“a devoted effect became affection”), retained as printed rather than normalized.
- `compassionis affectum` (“an affection of compassion”): S. Aud. and Edit. Pic. instead have `charitatis affectum` (“an affection of charity”).
- `unus atque idem Spiritus` (“one and the same Spirit”): S. Aud. omits `ille` (“that one”) from the alternate `unus ille atque … idem Spiritus`; the omission belongs to `ille` alone.
- `exemplum praetenderet` (“should set forth an example”): the manuscripts read `exemplum relinquerat` (“had left an example”).
- `talis propterea` (“such therefore”): S. Aud. has `talis etiam` (“such also”); the variant modifies the opening of the pastoral-watchfulness clause.
- `nihil deesset ad` (“nothing might be lacking for”): S. Aud. has `nihil deest ad` (“nothing is lacking for”).
- `plenitudinem justitiae, nihil` (“the fullness of righteousness, nothing”): the manuscripts have `plenitudinem, nihil` (“fullness, nothing”); `justitiae` (“of righteousness”) is absent from their reading.
- `quod virtutum conventus reverendum` (“which the assembly of virtues [consecrated] as venerable”): the manuscripts have `quod reverendus virtutum conventus reverendum` (“which the venerable assembly of virtues [consecrated] as venerable”); the first `reverendus` qualifies the assembly.
- `sacra labia` (“sacred lips”): S. Aud. has `sacra verba` (“sacred words”).
- At `stupor opprimit` (“amazement overwhelms me”), S. Aud. and Vict. in Mary., in a later hand, have the full alternative: `opprimit; et dum singula diligenter intueor, omnia Spiritui sancto fateor ascribenda` (“amazement overwhelms me; and while I consider each thing carefully, I acknowledge that all must be ascribed to the Holy Spirit”).  Their contrasting difficult printed reading is `opprimit et mutatus nostri temporis hominem talia posse, calamo scribae velociter scribentis omnia fateor ascribenda` (“amazement overwhelms me, and [I acknowledge] that a changed man of our time can do such things; I ascribe everything to the pen of a swiftly writing scribe”); its syntax is corrupt or uncertain in the supplied printing, so no smoother expansion is asserted.
- At the farewell, S. Aud. and Vict. in Mary., in a later hand, have `vicem mihi, Pater sancte, rependes, si tuarum me participem feceris orationum. Vale` (“Holy Father, you will repay me in return if you make me a sharer in your prayers. Farewell”).
- `sciens` (“knowing”) after `Pater` (“Father”): S. Aud. omits it; the omission has this one-word scope.
- `consilium salutis accipere` (“to receive counsel of salvation”): Vict. has `consilium accipere` (“to receive counsel”); `salutis` (“of salvation”) is absent.

#### Letter LIV — [Col. 0087B]

- `Collata cum eodem ms` means “compared with the same manuscript.”
- `Anselmus gratia Dei archiepiscopus, fratribus` (“Anselm, by God's grace archbishop, to the brothers”): the manuscript has `Anselmus vocatus archiepiscopus Cantuariensis fratribus` (“Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, to the brothers”).

#### Letter LV — [Col. 0087B–0090C]

- `Cum eodem ms Victorino collata` means “compared with the same Victor manuscript.”
- `Domino et Patri reverendo Anselmo` (“to the lord and reverend Father Anselm”): the manuscript has `Venerando Patri Anselmo` (“to the venerable Father Anselm”).
- `vertitis in naturam, ut nulli` (“you turn [it] into a habit, so that to no one …”): the manuscript has `verteritis ut nulli` (“you have made [it such] that to no one …”); the difference is tense and construction, not a newly supplied meaning.
- `e famulitio` (“from the household/retinue”): the manuscript has `famulitie`, an inflected form with the same force; the source does not warrant a more specific expansion.
- `corporis viribus` (“with powers of the body”): the manuscript has `corporalibus viribus` (“with bodily powers”).

#### Letter LVI — [Col. 0089D–0090C]

- `Cum eodem ms collata` means “compared with the same manuscript.”
- `Anselmus servus Ecclesiae Cantuariensis` (“Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury”): the manuscript has `Anselmus archiepiscopus Cantuariensis` (“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury”).

#### Letter LVII — [Col. 0089D–0092A]

- `Cum eodem ms collata` means “compared with the same manuscript.”
- `etiam si quotidie fieret` (“even if it happened daily”): the manuscript has `etiam si fieret` (“even if it happened”); `quotidie` (“daily”) is absent.

#### Letter LVIII — [Col. 0091D–0092C]

- `Cum eodem ms collata` means “compared with the same manuscript.”
- `domnum Joannem` (“Lord John”): the manuscript has `Dominum N.` (“Lord N.”); the initial is preserved because the supplied source does not resolve it.
- `tutius est in` (“it is safer in”): the manuscript has `tutius in` (“safer in”); `est` (“is”) is omitted.

#### Letter LIX — [Col. 0091D–0093D]

- `Cum eodem ms collata` means “compared with the same manuscript.”
- `Anselmus quamvis indignus archiepiscopus dictus Cantuariae` (“Anselm, although unworthy, called archbishop of Canterbury”): the manuscript has `Anselmus volutus archiepiscopus Cantuariae` (“Anselm, voluted/rolled? archbishop of Canterbury”); `volutus` is the supplied difficult form and is not silently emended.
- `non esse aestimo` (“I judge that [it] was not”): the manuscript has `non aestimo` (“I do not judge [it]”), shifting the placement of negation.
- `sibi datam` (“given to them”): the manuscript has `sibi dare` (“to give to them”); the forms differ in inflection and construction.
- `ut non Dominum sed advocatum` (“that [he prove himself] not a lord but an advocate/defender”): the manuscript has `ut non solum Dominum sed` (“that [he prove himself] not only a lord but …”); `solum` (“only”) changes the scope of the contrast.
- `religionem. Haec` (“religion. Let these things”): the manuscript has `religionem instituta. Haec` (“institutions established for religion. Let these things”); `instituta` (“institutions”) is the additional word.

#### Letter LXII — [Col. 0093D]

- `Cum eodem ms collata` means “compared with the same manuscript.”

I do not wish at present to send you, or anyone else, the statements of the council’s canons as expounded, because, when they were expounded at the council itself, they could not be recited fully and perfectly, since they were issued suddenly, without the forethought and appropriate discussion that ought to have preceded them [Note: The manuscript reads *prolata* (“issued”) rather than *prolatae* (“were issued”)]. Hence some things appear to require addition, and perhaps some alteration; and I do not wish to do this except with the common agreement of our fellow bishops. I therefore wish to dictate them and first show them to those same bishops when we meet together, before they are sent throughout the churches of England in dictated and expounded form. Nevertheless, we are sending you the names of the matters about which we spoke there, so that, insofar as you are able to remember, you may know what we decreed concerning them [Note: The manuscript reads *decrevisse faciatis* (“so that you may make us decree”) rather than *decrevisse sciatis* (“so that you may know what we decreed”)].

Concerning those who, whether before or after excommunication, committed the sin of sodomy without knowing that excommunication had been imposed, the sentence will be equal and the same if, after confessing, they ask for penance [Note: The manuscript reads “and the sentence will likewise be” rather than “and the sentence will be the same”]. You will impose it according to your judgment, taking into consideration their age, the duration of the sin, and whether or not they have wives; and according to how you see them repent and promise thereafter complete correction. It must also be considered that until now this sin was so public that scarcely anyone felt shame on account of it; and therefore many, not knowing its enormity, rushed into it. Those, however, who contaminated themselves with the sin after they had learned of their excommunication must be punished with a more severe penance. We likewise leave this to your judgment, according to the considerations mentioned above.

Concerning those who refuse to have their hair cut, it was said that they should not enter a church; it was not, however, ordered that, if they did enter, the priests should cease their service, but only that they should announce to them that they were entering against God and to their own damnation. We decreed nothing concerning the footwear of laymen, but only concerning that of clerics.

Concerning archdeacons and canons who place their abandoned wives outside their own houses, in their manors: for the present, until something else is decreed, I think this may be tolerated if they have made a definite promise that they will have no relations with them and will not speak with them without legitimate witnesses.

[Note: What was decreed in the council concerning priests will be observed. The council intended is the one recently mentioned, held at London, over which Anselm presided, with the archbishop of York and the other bishops of England, as well as the abbots, sitting in attendance. It enacted many matters of the greatest necessity, especially this:

“That, so long as a priest has an illicit relationship, he shall not be in lawful standing; nor shall he celebrate Mass; and, if he celebrates it, his Mass shall not be attended. That no one shall be ordained to the subdiaconate or above without a profession of chastity. That no archdeacon, priest, deacon, or canon shall marry a wife or retain one whom he has married; but that any subdeacon who is not a canon, if he marries after his profession of chastity, shall be bound by the same rule.”

These matters are contained in the London synod as Willelm of Malmesbury gives them in full, book I of *De pontificibus Anglorum*, p. 120, London edition, 1596.

Henry of Huntingdon, archdeacon, published in the same year and by the same printers, folio 217, page 1, book VII of his *Histories*, writes of this council as follows:

“In the same year, at the feast of Saint Michael, Archbishop Anselm held a council at London, in which he prohibited the wives of English priests, who had not previously been prohibited.”

In these words, who would not see both the man’s arrogant presumption—since he dared to criticize a council lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit for imprudence because of a new constitution, as he judged it—and, in the historian, a profound ignorance or forgetfulness of the truth and of domestic affairs? Against him I shall proceed above all with a single sealed tablet.

For in book IV of his *Histories*, at the beginning, after Bede, he recounts the acts of the council held at Hatfield under Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, in the year 680. After many matters had been discussed there for the confirmation of the purity of orthodox faith, the holy synod added the following in its letter:

“We accept the holy and universal five synods of the blessed and God-pleasing Fathers, that is, those who were assembled at Nicaea, numbering 318.”

Yet in this synod clerics were plainly forbidden wives, by canon 3, which Gelasius of Cyzicus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, records in precisely these words, in part IX of the Acts of that council, chapter 32:

*Ἀγηγθρευσε ξαθόλου ἡ μεγάλη σύνοδος, μὴ ἐπισχόπω, πρεσβυθέρῳ, διαχόνῳ μηθ` ὅλως τῶν ὲν τῳ χλήρῳ πεὶ, ἐξεῖναι συνείσαχτον ἔγειν, εἰ μὴ ἄρα μητέρα, καὶ θείαν, καὶ ἂ μονα πρόσωπα διαπέφευγε πᾶσαν ὑποψίαν; Ὁ δὲ παρὰ ταῦτα ποιῶν κινδυνεῦσει περὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίαν.*

“The great synod altogether forbids that it be permitted to a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all among the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she be his mother, sister, paternal aunt, or some other person who entirely escapes suspicion. Whoever acts contrary to this will endanger his dignity.”

Balfour translated this canon as follows:

“The great synod most fully forbids a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric to have a woman brought in to live with him, unless perhaps his mother, sister, paternal aunt, or finally those persons alone who customarily remain free from every suspicion. Whoever acts otherwise will endanger his dignity.”

Photius in the *Nomocanon*; Burchard of Worms, book II, chapter 109; Ivo of Chartres, part IX, chapter 186; Jatland of Chrysopolis, near the end of book VI of his *Candle*; and Gratian, under “Interdixit,” have reported this sanction, and indeed somewhat more elaborately than Rufinus, book I, continuation of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6.

Therefore, since the Nicene synod was accepted so unanimously by the primate of all England, as well as by the bishops and the five kings seated there, whatever the Nicene Fathers sanctioned was also approved by the English bishops, including that decree concerning the celibacy of priests. This shines forth even more clearly than the midday sun when we see that, after examining matters relating to the faith, they praised the Nicene decrees with one voice as an addition and confirmation.

Although this reasoning derives strengthened authority from the common agreement of both ecclesiastical synods, so that the sharpest intellects grow dull before the edge of laws promulgated under the prompting of the divine Spirit, I shall nevertheless set down whatever comes to mind concerning this matter from English history.

That priestly celibacy endured for a longer period in England is demonstrated, after the matters mentioned above, by the letter of Fulco, archbishop of Reims in Belgic Gaul, sent to Alfred, king of the West Saxons in England. In it Alfred is commended for having placed over the Church of Canterbury an exceptionally upright archbishop and for having cut off with the sword of the divine word a most pestilential license, drawn from the troubled source of the pagan Danes. Through this license most bishops and priests not only kept wives in their households, but even kept female relatives; and, as the summit of their crimes, wickedly violated virgins consecrated to God and brought a concubine in addition to a wife, so that nothing might be lacking for the satisfaction of lust—if lust can in fact be satisfied.

Fulco taught at length that all these practices were opposed both to the divine commands and to the purity of the Catholic religion, as Floard testifies in chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History of Reims*. There the French translator renders Alfred, or Aelfred and Alvred, as “Albrado.” In chapter 6 of the same history, Peigmund, bishop of Canterbury, is also praised with full voice for his most holy efforts to cleanse away the filth of lust, fornication, incest, and sexual immorality.

Anyone who reads Malmesbury, book II, chapter 4 of *De regibus Anglorum*, will know that Fulco was very well known to King Alfred. This restoration of the English Church occurred approximately in the year 890, the eighteenth year of Alfred’s reign and the second year of Peigmund’s episcopate, whom the French translator calls “Peonicus.”

For it is known and attested from the letter of Saint Boniface, martyr and archbishop of Mainz, which appears in Malmesbury, book I of *De regibus Anglorum*, folio 14, page 2, that unrestrained lust had invaded the kingdom and Church of England long before this. Roger of Hoveden, under the year 975, censures Alfer, prince of the Mercians, and several English magnates who, attracted by the gifts of married clerics, expelled worthy monks from churches from which incontinent clerics had previously been removed.

Ethelwine, the most honorable and upright duke of the East Angles, together with his brother Elfwold and Earl Brithnoth, courageously resisted the raging avarice and impiety of those nobles. Hoveden, briefly turning in the year 957 to praise King Edgar, or Eadgar, says:

“He restored and enriched ruined churches, having also cast out from the monasteries the poisons of scholarly clerics,” and so forth.

What were these poisons, unless they were fornication, adultery, and sexual immorality, which gradually creep into the innermost recesses of the heart and, after banishing all the warmth of divine grace, suffocate the soul? In his *History*, folio 302, page 2, Ingulf calls these same poisons “the dirges of clerics.”

Edgar himself professes and asserts this in his charter, which appears in Malmesbury, book II, chapter 8, folio 32, where, among other things, he recalls:

“After ignorant clerics, subject to no discipline of regular religion, had been expelled, in very many places I appointed pastors of a holier order, namely, of the monastic habit.”

These words, worthy of the king’s royal mouth and of my purpose, are confirmed by the deeds of Athelwold, or Ethelwold. Under that most holy king, and himself a most holy bishop, he expelled from his Winchester Church clerics who kept women, as Malmesbury above and Osbern of Canterbury, precentor, testify in chapter 39 of the *Life of Saint Dunstan* in Surius, volume III.

When some of these expelled clerics complained to the king about their expulsion, Saint Dunstan was asked to pardon them once more. He remained silent at these requests, turning over in his mind what he should do, placed between an anvil and a hammer, when suddenly an image of the crucified Christ forbade it in a clear voice, saying: “It shall not be; it shall not be.” Osbern testifies to this in the place cited; so also Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum historiale*, book XV, chapter 80; Dominic of Antoninus, part II of his *History*, chapter 6, title 16, section 1; and Peter de Natalibus, book VIII of his *Catalogue of the Saints*, chapter 49.

Moreover, this is so openly acknowledged even by our Anglo-Calvinist opponents—if one excepts the unfrocked Bale with his Dorothea and Polydore Virgil, the more shameless slanderers of this event—that it requires no longer proof.

After some time, the sons of the expelled clerics revived and rekindled the matter, which had been settled and extinguished, at the assembly of Talne, or Calne, attended by King Edward and the nobles of all England. All those who opposed Saint Dunstan and assented to the disgraceful petition of the clerics fell so violently from their seats to the ground that some died, while others scarcely escaped the hands of imminent death. This is reported by Osbern, Vincent, Antoninus, and Hoveden under the year 977. Hoveden indeed describes the fall, but not its cause: the cause was both well known and unnecessary to state, since the assembly had not been convened for that reason alone.

Moreover, what Ethelwold accomplished at Winchester was accomplished by Saint Oswald and Dunstan in their own churches. But in order that my opponent may be judged by his own words and overcome by his own weapons, consider what he writes about Ethelwold in book V, folio 204:

“In the second year of his episcopate he expelled certain canons living in the old monastery at Winchester, who observed their order sluggishly and negligently, and he installed monks in their place.”

Thus far Huntidoniensis. Although he did not explain this sluggishness and negligence more explicitly, it is nevertheless clear from what has been said above.

Let us approach the year 1000: it will produce for us Lanfranc, the most vigorous enemy and persecutor of married clerics. In his second letter to Pope Alexander II, concerning the bishop of Chester, whom he calls the bishop of Lichfield, he writes as follows:

“The bishop of Lichfield, who, although accused before your legates of carnal incontinence—to which the public keeping of a wife and the children begotten by him bore witness—and of other crimes, nevertheless refused to come to their synod. Therefore your aforesaid legates excommunicated him and, as is said, obtained leave from the king to appoint a successor in his place. At Easter he came to court, but refused to undertake a defense against the charges brought against him; in the assembly of bishops and laymen he restored the bishopric to the king; and by oath, freely and willingly, he affirmed that he would neither hold it any longer nor inflict accusation or harm upon his successor. Thereafter he returned to the monastery in which he had been raised as a monk from childhood.”

Again, in a letter to John, bishop of Rouen, before whom certain malicious and hostile persons had accused Lanfranc as a detractor of John, Lanfranc rejected the charge and the falsehood as untrue, saying:

“You have reported to me that many people have told you that I criticize certain things you have done. Above all, that I reproach you for having misunderstood the institutions of the holy Fathers concerning the chastity to be preserved by clerics.”

After a short interval he adds, dissolving the substance of the accusation:

“Indeed, encouraged by your example and that of other venerable Fathers, I have by pastoral authority prohibited throughout the whole English land that anyone of any order who is a canon should take a wife; nor may anyone who has previously taken one, if he is a priest or deacon, retain her any longer, unless he wishes to lose his prebend.”

Having seen these words of Lanfranc and the institutions requiring clerical celibacy to be observed exactly, let us consider the strict guardianship of the same decree in his letter to Herfast, bishop of Thetford, in these words:

“Lanfranc, by the grace of God, not by his own merits, to his fellow bishop Herfast, greetings.

“This cleric recently came to me and told me the cause of his misfortune; he asserted that what he had said was true, as was confirmed by the testimony of your letters. He testified that he had been ordained irregularly: namely, that, although he belonged to no order, he had been made a deacon by your fraternity. When I asked him whether he had a wife, he replied that he had one and did not wish to leave her. Therefore, supported by divine authority, I decree that he must be dealt with by the following arrangement.

“Remove the diaconate from him. At suitable times promote him to the other minor orders. But he must never again receive the order of the diaconate unless he lives chastely, unless he promises by canonical testimony that he will henceforth live chastely. If, however, he has lived a celibate life and wishes to promise that he will do so for all time, you shall not indeed ordain him again to the order of the diaconate; but you shall restore the office to him through the text of the holy Gospel, either in a synod or in an assembly of many clerics.”

Thus far Lanfranc, whose testimonies make it clear that priests had been forbidden marriage even before the canon of the London synod.

Let Huntidoniensis’ ignorance and slander therefore have no weight. As for what he advances in defense of his own opinion and that of others—namely, that Anselm’s decree appeared extremely dangerous, lest, while people sought forms of purity greater than their strength permitted, they should fall into dreadful uncleanness, to the supreme disgrace of the Christian name—I make no account of it. For if this little argument had even the slightest force, it would necessarily prove that God had wrongly forbidden the same things: “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal.” For murders occur every day, and those of the most disgraceful and grievous kind; likewise adulteries, fornications, sacrileges, incest, and other horrifying crimes that surpass all these in impiety.

In short, as Jerome teaches the monk Rusticus: “It is not a fault of the Christian name if a pretender to religion is in sin.” Indeed, it is a disgrace to the pagans—and I add, to the wicked and the heretics—when they see the Churches displeased by what does not please all good people.

Moreover, so that later generations may know with how great a multitude of consenting minds the statutes of the London synod were received, Roger of Hoveden testifies that Anselm, with the archbishop of York and the whole company of the other English bishops sitting in attendance, renewed these statutes while King Henry I, the counts, and the barons—as he calls them—stood by and listened, all consenting with one mind and voice, in the year 1108. In the same century they were repeated in the council convened at York in 1195, whose acts Hoveden reported in that same year, 1235.
