Matthew Paris, in the *Greater History*, folio 436 of the Zurich edition, relates that the prohibition was again issued in another London synod. Under the year 1225 he likewise records the most severe punishment imposed by Stephen of Langton, archbishop of Canterbury, upon the concubines of clerics, decreed in these words:

“Let the concubines of priests and clerics who are in holy orders and hold benefices be deprived of ecclesiastical burial, unless they correct themselves properly; and, since it is written, ‘The living, the living, he shall confess you,’ unless they correct themselves and, while alive, confess—as it is written, ‘The living, the living, he shall confess you’—or unless such great repentance appears in their final moments that they may not unjustly be granted a dispensation.”

Likewise:

“They shall not be received to the kiss of peace, nor shall they receive blessed bread in church, so long as their concubiners retain them in their houses or publicly outside their houses.”

Likewise:

“If they give birth, they shall not be purified unless they have first given sufficient security to the archdeacon or his official that they will make satisfaction at the next chapter, after their purification.”

Likewise:

“Priests in whose parishes the concubines of such men reside, if they do not disclose this to the archdeacon or his official, shall be suspended. And before they are released, they shall undergo severe penance.”

Likewise:

“She who can be convicted of having been carnally known by a priest shall perform public and solemn penance; and, as though she had been convicted of adultery, she shall be punished as for a double adultery, lest impunity for so great a crime become for others an occasion of wrongdoing.”

These punishments against clerical concubiners and clerical concubines—for the concubines are struck and the concubiners struck back—were established by Stephen of Langton, an educated man of holy memory, formerly cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, who held office for twenty-one years and twenty-three days. He transferred the body of Blessed Thomas into a most precious casket.

Thus the manuscript records of the archbishops of Canterbury in our library speak of the archbishop justly punishing clerics who kept women.

Let it therefore remain established for all ages that English clerics had appropriated wives to themselves, so that what was accepted by some contrary to the reason of law—indeed, I add, of ecclesiastical law, borrowing the words of the jurist Paul in book CLXXXIV—must not be carried forward as a precedent for what follows.

After I had collected these materials, I came upon the same passage in book VIII, chapter 19, of Bertrand d’Argentré’s *History of Brittany*: the passage concerning wives first prohibited to priests by Anselm. The historian took it from the *Chronology* of Robert, monk of Bec.

Argentré reported this after mentioning that Victorius, bishop of Rennes, had a daughter named Demnola and after writing at some length about her. He adds that it had been observed that bishops and priests not only of Victorius’ time but also in the age of Saint Jerome and Augustine could freely and with impunity be married, because the Catholic Church had not yet forbidden it; but that, on account of countless serious causes, it later forbade it, and that this prohibition was finally received in the English Church through Saint Anselm, archbishop.

How absurdly this learned man spoke, silently producing Saint Jerome and Augustine as witnesses to his statement, apart from the Nicene decree cited above, is clear from the writings of Bellarmine, Gregory, Valentine, and other defenders of clerical continence. The mind of Saint Jerome and Augustine is evident: Jerome’s from his own confession, printed at Paris by Nivellius; Augustine’s likewise from his own confession, pages 467, 468, and 469, where it is said that the apostles taught celibacy and that the ancients observed it.

I therefore acknowledge that formerly many married men were consecrated bishops, but that after consecration they abstained from their wives. Thus, in our Gaul, Saint Germanus of Auxerre, after being consecrated, changed his wife into a sister, as Constantius the contemporary presbyter testifies in book I, chapter 7, of his life.

Saint Hilary of Poitiers did likewise. Although Fortunatus did not report this, the man’s outstanding holiness, his steadfast observance of the ecclesiastical canons, and his splendid letter to his daughter Abra concerning the preservation of virginity testify to it most fully.

Saint Genebaldus, the first bishop of Laon, and Urbicius, formerly a senator and bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, conducted themselves in this way for some time. But when they returned to their wives, they suffered the bitter punishment of incest. The former repented, shut up in a prison for seven years, as Hincmar testifies in the *Life of Saint Remigius*. “The latter expiated his crime with tears,” according to Gregory of Tours, book I of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 44.]

As for priests who, through fear, do not dare to leave their wives, what was decreed in the council will be observed: so long as they retain them for any reason, they will neither celebrate Mass nor be in lawful standing. But until the beginning of Lent, if they have people who serve chastely in their place in the churches, they will not be deprived of the church’s benefices. Those, however, who prevent priests from leaving their female relatives, rebuke as people acting against God and against Christianity. Show them that the entire sin of the priests’ fornication must be imputed to them, and promise them our excommunication and that of all our fellow bishops [Note: The manuscript reads “our excommunication and that of all” rather than “our and all”].

[Col. 0098A]

## LETTER LXIII. ANSELM TO BURGUNDIUS AND HIS WIFE RICHERA

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript, and with the Gothic edition and the 1573 edition.]

That they should remember the life to come and kindle one another’s love for it.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his dearest Burgundius and his wife Richera: greetings and God’s blessing.

Your messenger will be able to explain better in words than I can write how I am. Nothing, however, gives me greater pleasure to commend to you than that you take care for yourselves. God has relieved you of everything that might give occasion for loving this world, and has given you every opportunity to love your salvation.

Set your end before your eyes every day. Think with the greatest concentration whose they will be and what benefit they will bring you—the things that will remain after you. Consider where you will go, what you will carry with you, and what you will find there that has been sent on ahead by you [Note: The edition reads “who will find what is there” rather than “what you will find there”]. Certainly you will neither carry with you nor find there anything other than your merits, whether good or evil.

See what merits you have sent on ahead. If the good are more numerous than the evil, you may rejoice. If the evil are more numerous than the good—which I do not think—then you ought to fear greatly [Note: The manuscript and edition read “You may rejoice. If—something I do not think—the good are more numerous, you must fear greatly,” with a differing arrangement], especially since it is very necessary for a person who wishes to be saved to have many more good merits than evil ones [Note: The manuscript and edition read simply “to have more good merits,” rather than “to have many more good merits”].

Think about these things; discuss them with one another day and night, in private and in public. Let these be your conversations with each other:

“My lord, my beloved, what are we doing? Why are we delaying? Our last day is near. How are we spending our life? How are we making satisfaction to God for our sins? Let us prepare ourselves as though we saw the day of our calling close at hand, and let us arrange our lives so that we may go confidently to judgment, since without doubt we shall receive according to what we do in this life, whether good or evil.”

God joined us together in this life; let us act so that he may join us together in eternal life, and let us see there our child, whom God has already taken to himself. These are to be your pursuits, your concern, your sighs.

I command you through this messenger not to come to me unless an order has been given by me through my seal [Note: The manuscript reads “through my commands,” while the edition reads “through an order.”] I say this to you, my most dear lord and brother Burgundius: if you love me, receive it in good spirit.

May almighty God rule your hearts and direct them toward eternal joys. Amen.

[Col. 0101B]

## 391. LETTER LXIV. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, TO ANSELM

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

Concerning his safe return from Jerusalem.

To his most desired father, Anselm, venerable archbishop of the people of Canterbury: Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyons, sends greetings.

We wish your Holiness to know that, through the favor of your merits and intercessions, we have returned safely from Jerusalem. We have thought it worthy to inform you of this because we believe that it will not be displeasing to you [Note: The manuscript reads “because we thought it worth informing you” rather than “because we believe that it will not be displeasing to you”].

We have heard from the king of the English that you are being greatly harassed and that he is acting rashly in many matters against God and his Church. We must therefore implore the divine clemency, so that he may convert your enemies—or rather, the disturbers of God’s holy Church—and subject them to your holy obedience [Note: The manuscript reads “your enemies, the holy disturbers” rather than “your enemies, or rather, the disturbers of the holy Church”].

But if, because our sins demand it, this cannot be accomplished for the present, and if, persecution pressing upon you, it should become necessary for you to withdraw or even to change your residence, we humbly beg your Holiness not to disdain to turn to your child, and to come to your house, which was yours, which is now yours, and which from day to day will always be more truly yours.

This is humbly implored not only by us, but also by the Church entrusted to us. In the most devout manner she commends herself with us to your holy prayers; she is most ready to serve you and longs to see your face.

We commend to you the bearer of this letter, named Elvred [Note: The manuscript reads “Haered,” while the name “Elvred” is written in a more recent hand in the same manuscript; another reading is “Lelvred”]. He came with us from Apulia to Lyons and served us faithfully.

[Col. 0102A]

## LETTER LXV. ANSELM TO HUMBERTO, COUNT AND MARQUIS

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

He rejoices at receiving his letters and briefly touches upon the benefits conferred upon him by Humberto. He urges him to protect the Church, not to rule over her.

To his reverend and dearest lord Humberto [Note: The manuscript reads “Guiberto” rather than “Humberto”], count and marquis, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends faithful service with prayers.

I received with great joy the letter directed to me by your graciousness, because I found it full of honor, affection, and the riches of good will. How great an honor it is to me when your highness—whose people rejoice to be regarded as my relatives—deigns to say that I am joined to you by kinship [Note: The manuscript reads “joined to you and by kinship” rather than “joined to you by kinship”]. How great an affection is revealed when, from so far away, you take the trouble to write that you greatly rejoice at the good things you hear about me!

How fervently your good will burns before God in matters belonging to God is clearly shown by the fact that, from a distant kingdom, you are stirred to great joy and gladness by good things that you hear through mere reputation. Indeed, although the good things reported about me or about my actions ought, insofar as I am concerned, to be judged as nothing or almost nothing, nevertheless your benevolence merits reward from the just Judge no less than if those things were true.

I do not know that I have earned such great favor from you by any service, unless it is because, to speak truthfully, I know that I have always loved your prosperity and your successes with a sincere heart, even before I had seen you. Remembering that by nature I owe myself to my forefathers and to you as to a lord, I have never allowed the love of you to be absent from my heart.

Nor have I forgotten that, when I was traveling toward Rome, your kindly generosity was ready at Lyons to provide me with transportation and everything necessary. This affection grew greatly after many people made known to me your life and integrity, because you employ the power of your principate with piety for the preservation of peace and justice.

I understand that I ought henceforth to hold this affection in still greater esteem, because your love toward me deigns to merit it. Although your good intention does not need our admonition, it is nevertheless my responsibility that my letter to you not be without some exhortation. Just as we see a fire stirred by the wind blaze up, so good will is accustomed through exhortation to kindle itself toward better things.

You see, my dearest lord, how our mother, the Church of God—which God calls his beautiful, friendly, and beloved bride—is trampled by wicked rulers; how she is afflicted to the eternal damnation of those to whom God entrusted her, as advocates, for her protection; with what presumption they have seized her possessions for their own use; with what cruelty they reduce her freedom to servitude; with what impiety they despise and scatter her law and religion.

When they disdain to obey the decrees of the Apostolic, which contribute to the strengthening of the Christian religion, they show themselves disobedient to the apostle Peter, whose place he occupies—indeed, to Christ, who entrusted his Church to Peter.

[Note: “Apostolic” means “of the pope.” I find many writers using this word to designate the Roman pope; indeed, Pope Nicholas II uses it in distinction 79, canons “Apostol” and “Si quis,” where, with a clever play on words, he says that someone who has not ascended the apostolic see by the unanimous vote of the cardinals and clergy should not be called “apostolic” but “apostatic.” The abbot of Ursperg under the year 1106, and the librarian Malmesbury in book IV of *De regibus Anglorum*, seem to have had this passage in mind when speaking of Anselm:

“By his voice, beloved of God, he pronounced Urban the apostolic, and the other the apostate”—namely, Guibert, the antipope.

He does not use this expression only once. For in book II, chapter 12, he writes: “Certainly this Leo”—that is, the one mentioned in the epitaph—“had been the apostolic at Rome,” and so forth. He uses it also in the preceding book, chapter 3, writing about Leo V; in book I, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, very frequently in the *Life of Anselm*; and elsewhere throughout.

Henry of Huntingdon, book IV, uses the same word when counting the Roman popes who sat during the reign of Adelard, king of the West Saxons:

“In his time the apostolics were Pope Sergius, John,” and so forth.

Our Anselm likewise uses it again in letter 24 of this book, and also in letters 87 and 92 below.

Theodore the Studite, writing to Paschal I, says:

“To Paschal, pope of Rome, endowed in all things with the highest virtue, a great light, the first among priests, our lord, the apostolic pope Paschal,” and so forth, in Baronius, volume IX, under the year 817.

To these may be added the letters of Gabriel, patriarch of Alexandria, and John Conius, chorepiscopus of Alexandria, sent in the year 1395 to Our Most Holy Lord Clement VIII, in Baronius, in the appendix to volume VI. In these letters Clement VIII is called “the thirteenth of the apostles of the world.”

This passage brings to mind the expression customary among our ancestors, by which they called the pope in the vernacular “the apostle.” I first noticed this in an old form of the capitular prayers customarily said among us, in these exact words and letters:

“Prion por nostre segnor Lapotoire: por tote la cort de Rome,” that is, “Let us pray for our lord the Pope, and for all the court of Rome,” and so forth.

In a Victorine manuscript containing the lives of the saints written in the vernacular, in the *Life of Saint Sylvester*:

“une bonne fame pris apostoile” (“a good woman took the apostle”).

Again, on the feast of Saint Peter’s Chair:

“Explicit la chaiere seint Pere l’Apostre comment fu Evesques d’Antioche et puis Apostoles de Rome” (“Here ends the chair of Saint Peter the Apostle: how he was bishop of Antioch and then Apostle of Rome”).

Helinand, a monk of Frigidmont, likewise calls the pope “apostle” in the tenth *Apostrophe* of his poem *On Death*, written more than four hundred years ago:

“de Cardonal ou d’Apostoile” (“of Cardinal or Pope”).

Villardouin does the same in his *History and Chronicle of France*, in the third volume, dedicated to Charles VIII, king of France.

From this arose many other expressions, namely “see,” “chair,” “letters,” and “apostolic decrees,” that is, papal decrees. The reason was certainly not otherwise than this: although all bishops are successors of the apostles, as Saint Jerome writes to Evagrius, volume II, nevertheless the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished in the Roman Church. Saint Augustine, letter 162—or, as Rupert of Deutz prefers, book I *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 27—says that the successors of the other apostles are called patriarchs, while Peter’s successor, out of reverence for the chief of the apostles, is called “apostolic.”]

Let those who, as vicars of Peter—and in him, of Christ—despise Christian decrees seek other gates of the kingdom of heaven, because they certainly will not enter through those whose keys the apostle Peter carries [Note: The manuscript reads “the decrees of Christ, Christian” rather than “the Christian decrees”]. For all who refuse to be subject to the law of God are undoubtedly counted as enemies of God.

Therefore, my lord, do not think that the Church located within your principate has been given to you for hereditary domination, but for hereditary reverence and protection. Love her as your mother; honor her as the bride and friend of God. Those who trample her will be trampled outside her together with the demons; those who glorify her will be glorified in her and with her among the angels.

I greet my revered lady, your wife, together with your children. To them, together with you, I grant the prayers of our Church in true charity [Note: The manuscript reads simply “in charity” rather than “in true charity”].

May almighty God direct and protect you in this life, so that in the life to come he may raise you to eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0104A]

## LETTER LXVI. ANSELM TO BURGUNDIUS AND RICHEZA, HIS WIFE

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

He advises him, as he is about to depart for Jerusalem, what he should do: that he should first make a general confession of all his sins from childhood, and arrange his affairs so that he does not leave his wife without help and counsel.

**ANSELM**, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to his brother and beloved friend **BURGUNDIUS**, and to his wife, his sister **RICHEZA**, greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as he can give it.

You informed me, my lord and dearest friend Burgundius, that you wished to go to Jerusalem for the service of God and the salvation of your soul, and that you wished to do this with my permission and that of your son, my nephew, Anselm. I rejoice in your good intention, and I advise and [Col. 0104B] beg you that, if you undertake this journey, you should neither carry with you the sins you have committed nor leave sin behind at home; and that henceforth you should possess the will to live well, as a true Christian of your rank.

Make a confession, naming all your sins from your childhood, as far as you can remember. See that you have no sin concerning your wife, whose goodness you know better [392] than I do [Note: The manuscript reads “you will know” (*cognoscetis*) instead of “you know” (*cognoscitis*)]. Let matters remain so that she is not without [Note: The manuscript reads *non sit sine* (“that she not be without”) instead of *sit non sine* (“that she be not without”).] help and counsel, whatever God may do with you; and let her not be driven from your house and honor against her will for as long as she lives, so that she may be able to serve God for the salvation of your body and soul, and for her own soul and those of your children.

Arrange your entire household as you would if you knew that you were about to die at this moment and render an account to God for your whole life. You seek our permission. I pray God that you may always and everywhere have his permission, counsel, help, and protection.

To you I say, my dearest sister: turn your entire purpose and your whole life toward serving God; and believe that God has taken away from you every delight of this life for this reason, so that you may delight in him alone. Love him, desire him, think of him, serve him at every hour and in every place.

May almighty God always bless you both.

**LETTER LXVII. ANSELM TO RICHERA.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That he cannot return to England with a clear conscience, nor live there peacefully; and that her son, his nephew, has recovered his health.

[Col. 0105B]

**ANSELM**, archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest sister **RICHERA**, greeting and God’s consolation in all her tribulations.

I know, dearest sister, that, apart from your husband, there is no person in the world whose safety and prosperity you desire to know and hear about as much as mine and that of your son Anselm, who is with me; for I am your only brother, and he is your only son. Our messengers will be able to tell you by word of mouth more fully than I can by letter about what concerns us.

Nevertheless, know that your son, my dearest nephew, after leaving you, suffered a long and serious illness, but at last, by God’s mercy, recovered his complete health. As for me, I say that I am physically well, but my heart is involved in great tribulations. Thus I dare neither flee England because of the fear of God, nor can I live there in any peace, tranquility, or quiet. Every day my heart is so suspended, as though I were about to depart immediately.

But whatever may happen to me, I rejoice concerning you, because your messengers have reported to me your safety and prosperity. Since both the prosperity and adversity of this life are brief and passing, let us despise them, strive to flee eternal adversity, and earn everlasting prosperity by living well [Note: The manuscript reads “by living truly” instead of “by living well”].

Therefore, dearest sister, since in this life you have nothing in which your heart can delight, turn it wholly toward God, so that in the life to come it may rejoice in him.

Farewell. If your husband returns and wishes to come to me, I order him not to come under any circumstances.

[Col. 0106A]

**LETTER LXVIII. ANSELM TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That he should recall the abbot of Saint Edmund’s, who was intruded by the abbot of Saint-Evroul, and that the property and men from which that church was unjustly dispossessed should be restored to it.

To the reverend lord and father, **WILLIAM**, archbishop of Rouen, **ANSELM**, servant of the Church of Canterbury, faithful service with prayers.

We have cried out, and cried out again, and still cry out to God [Note: The manuscript reads “still to God” instead of “still cry out to God”], and to you and to the whole Church of Normandy—especially to the bishops and abbots and all religious persons—concerning the abbot of the monastery of Saint-Evroul, who, as we have already written to you, irregularly and irreligiously installed in the church of Saint [Note: The manuscript reads “Saint N.” instead of “Saint Edmund”] Edmund as abbot one of his utterly foolish young men, a monk by profession.

Take care that it does not become necessary for us, as I speak familiarly to my reverend father, to cry out to God against you if you refuse to correct this matter, which falls within your responsibility.

It is said, as has been reported to me, that the same abbot claims that the man is not his monk but belongs to Saint-Sever. Yet, according to what he himself confessed in England, as I learned from one who heard it, he professed himself to his own church. Therefore it is untrue [Note: The manuscript reads “It is not true” instead of “Therefore it is untrue”] that he denies him to be his monk.

In any event, whatever the truth about his profession may be, he himself—I repeat, he himself—has obstructed the Church. Compel him, insofar as this lies within your responsibility and power, to set it free. He sold us his wolf-cub far too dearly: by force, against their will and without the consent of those whose consent was required, he stripped the church of its property and its men, and installed in that same church such a monk as I have often shown you; and, to God’s injury and the disgrace of the monastic order, he left him there.

I beg you, see that he returns to the church those whom he took away and receives those whom he brought in.

Farewell.

**LETTER LXIX. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL II.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He declares that Abbot Gualo is worthy of the episcopate.

To the reverend lord and father, **PASCHAL**, supreme pontiff, **ANSELM**, servant of the Church of Canterbury, due submission and faithful prayers.

The Church of Beauvais [Note: The manuscript reads “Beccensis” instead of “Belvacensis”], directed by your counsel and strengthened by your authority, [Col. 0106D] has chosen Lord Gualo, abbot of the Church of Saint-Quentin, and wishes the chosen man to be constituted its bishop.

[Note: “Lord Gualo.” Thus in Ivo of Chartres, letters 41, 220, and 245; but in letters 49, 50, 169, and 171 one reads *Galonem*. Likewise, in a letter of Pope Paschal sent to Adam, abbot of the Dionysian monastery at Paris, preserved in the Victorine manuscript, the form is *Galonem*. Again, in Ivo’s letters 120 and 193 one finds *Gallonem*, but in letter 269, in the continuation of Aimoinus, book V, chapter 50, and in Andrew’s *History of the Franks*, book III, and Eadmer’s book II of the *Life of Our Anselm*, the form written is *Vualo*, not *Gualo* or *Gallo*. Thus scribes were remarkably inconsistent in the same name. I thought it appropriate to alert the reader to this variation, so that he would not be held up while reading or left at a crossroads. Nevertheless, I think the latter form is the more genuine, because it is closer to the Picard dialect. What the Celtic peoples and Gauls pronounce with *g*, the Belgians and especially the Picards pronounce with a doubled *w*. Even today a family of this name, *les Vualons*, survives among the people of Beauvais.

Vualo was from Beauvais. As a boy he served under Ivo, then provost of the Church of Saint-Quentin, and under the same leader joined the community of regular canons. Later, when Ivo became bishop of Chartres, Vualo was appointed in his place. Finally, after Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, died, Vualo had been chosen for the episcopate by the better clergy; but the worse men, corrupted by the gifts of Stephen Garland, a thoroughly wicked man, resisted the election, although the elected man’s opponents had nothing to bring against him. At last, after various disputes between the elected bishop and the wicked clergy had continued for two full years, he was appointed successor to Fulco, bishop of Paris, for several reasons that, God willing, we shall relate in the bishops of Paris.

While he was bishop of Paris, he sent to the abbot of Saint-Denis the letter of Paschal that I recently mentioned, in these words: “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the abbot and the monks of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing. And from the report of our brother Galon, bishop of Paris, we have learned, and so forth.” See below, in the section on Paschal II.

Since I had never happened to see this letter of Paschal anywhere, and since it supported Galon’s claim, I thought it should be added here. Gualo died in the year 1114, on 23 February. I found this date in the necrology of the Church of Saint-Quentin, whose monastery he had governed, in the following terms:

“On this day died the lord Galo, of holy memory, second abbot of this church, afterward bishop of Paris.”]

For, as far as human judgment can determine, he is so suitable and useful for this in every respect that must be considered in choosing a bishop, that no better or more suitable man could be found in that Church. But because a person who desires something is satisfied with nothing until he obtains what he desires, the Church is not content with its own prayers; it earnestly seeks the assistance also of others whom it believes can support its desire before your eminence.

For it has learned from past times and from a similar affair that there are many whose custom is to call evil good and good evil, to seek what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ, and to sharpen their tongues like serpents. It fears that such men may attempt, under a pretended dove-like simplicity, to infect and destroy with their poison a good undertaking already begun.

Although I am now far away from that Church, both because of the personal affection we have for one another and because of my familiarity with the matter [Note: The manuscript reads “affection” instead of “familiarity”], they persist in asking me faithfully to inform your holiness what I think of this man’s character; and, insofar as I can, to secure through my prayers that what they desire may not be destroyed by any circumstance.

I therefore speak about the person whom they have chosen according to my conscience. I understand that in the aforesaid Church no better or equal man can be found for the episcopate, nor have I ever detected in him anything, either in reputation or in experience, that could obstruct his election. Rather, I have learned by experience and reputation many things that commend his election.

Therefore, although we do not doubt your authority, insofar as it depends on you, we nevertheless presume, prostrate in mind at your feet, to implore you with whatever prayers we can offer, so that after the many tribulations which you know that Church has suffered, your mercy may come to its aid and bring to completion without delay what has been well begun.

May almighty God preserve your fatherhood for a long time in prosperity. Amen.

**LETTER LXX. ANSELM TO ATHELIZ, ABBESS OF WINCHESTER.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

That she should not grieve over the bishop of Winchester, who was expelled for the sake of justice.

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend mother and dearest daughter **ATHELIZ**, abbess of Winchester [Note: The manuscript reads “Atheltz” instead of “Atheliz”], greeting and blessing.

There is no need to write here how and why Lord William, the elected bishop, is leaving England, because you can learn this from many others. But your religious devotion and prudence will understand how great your joy should be, and with how great thanksgiving you should receive the honor God is bestowing upon him, if you consider the matter attentively [Note: “His glory is greater because he is expelled for justice. So that the reader, on reading this, will not fail to understand it, let him remember that in the year 1103 a great fire of discord broke out between Anselm and Henry I, king of the English. Henry wished, at his pleasure, to appoint and invest bishops and abbots with ring and pastoral staff, to use the terminology of that time. Anselm steadfastly resisted, declaring that not only could the king not bestow ecclesiastical dignity on anyone, but that such a person was not even to be consecrated or associated with him.

During this dispute Henry gave the bishopric of Winchester to William Giffard, who strongly disagreed and resisted, and who also assailed the electors with insults. Thus, preferring to obey God rather than Henry, William incurred such anger from him that, stripped of all his possessions, he left England and did not return until Anselm—who had kindled the fire in zeal for ecclesiastical liberty—had extinguished it, Henry himself being the first to pour water upon it.

For this reason Anselm consoles the bishop of Winchester, who was mourning over his expulsion from the pastoral office, reminding him that one should rejoice especially when one suffers on account of justice.”]

For his glory and praise before God and good people are greater because he is stripped and expelled for justice than if he were enriched with all riches and every worldly possession while justice was violated [Note: The manuscript reads “than if he were enriched as though with everything” instead of “than if he were enriched with everything”].

Let his friends therefore rejoice and exult, because no violence and no fear could overcome him, nor could any desire separate him from the truth. Let this be your consolation concerning his expulsion, and let your daily prayer be that God strengthen and console him in it.

I greet and bless your daughters—and mine—as far as I can.

Farewell.

[Col. 0108C]

**LETTER LXXI.**

[Note: Or rather, a charter of Anselm, compared with the same manuscript.]

A charter by which Anselm returned to the monks of Canterbury the oratory and suburban estate.

I, **ANSELM**, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury [Col. 0109A], return to the monks of the same Church one-half of the altar of Christ, which I held in my possession after the death of my predecessor, Archbishop Lanfranc, who during his lifetime had returned to them the other half once it had been established that it belonged to them.

Likewise, I return to the same monks the manor called Sistede, since it is known to belong, and to have belonged, to their property.

Witnesses: William, archdeacon of the Church of Christ; Haimo, sheriff; Haimo, son of Vitalis [Note: The manuscript reads “Hanno, son of N.” instead of “Haimo, son of Vitalis”]; Robert, son of Watson [Note: The manuscript reads “son of N.” instead of “son of Watson”]; Wimund, the sheriff’s man; Ralph, nephew of Bishop Gundulf; and many others.

[Col. 0109B]

**LETTER LXXII. ANSELM TO SAMUEL, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF DUBLIN.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He reproves him for giving away the property of his Church to outsiders at his pleasure, and advises him to restore it.

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his venerable brother [Note: “To Samuel, bishop of the city of Dublin.” Dublin—also *Dublina* or *Dublinia* (for this is the form I consistently and repeatedly find in Silvester Giraldus, in his *Topography of Ireland* and *Conquest of Ireland*)—is commonly called *Dyuclin* in the latter part of Roger of Hoveden’s *Annals*. It is the capital of the kingdom of Ireland, as Giraldus says in *The Conquest of Ireland*, chapter 28.

As is especially clear from Anselm’s heading, this Church bore merely the title of a bishopric. Had Anselm, who elsewhere shows himself extremely knowledgeable about Christian discipline and honorably greeted each person according to his station, considered Samuel an archbishop, he would certainly not have omitted that title. Therefore Parker must be corrected in his *Antiquity of the British Church*, where he reports that Anselm appointed this Samuel archbishop of Dublin.

For, according to Hoveden above and Giraldus Silvester, chapter 17 of the *Topography of Ireland*, John—called Papyrio, or Paparo, or Papirus—who was sent as legate to Ireland by Eugenius III, brought four pallia: one for the Church of Armagh, another for Dublin, a third for Cashel, and a fourth for Connacht.

A later statement of Giraldus seems to conflict with the notes on letter 149 below, where we show that the bishops of Ireland and Scotland were to be inaugurated by the archbishop of York and by two bishops whom the archbishop of Canterbury ought to send. The first archbishop of Dublin was named Gregory, as Giraldus specifically observed, adding that this increase in honor occurred in the year 1152, or, if one prefers, 1151. Hoveden assigns it to that year.

I do not know how the testimony of these writers and of the English historians—who flourished in the same period, approximately from 1130 to 1200 and beyond—can be reconciled with St Bernard, who, although he sometimes calls St Malachy a bishop in letters 315, 316, and 317, calls him an archbishop in his *Life*, and says that he died in 1148, two years before the pallia were brought to Ireland by the apostolic legate. Unless one should say—as I recall Bale writing when speaking of Malachy—that he had gone to Rome in order to obtain the pallium. But let the author bear responsibility for his own credibility.]

greeting.

I have heard that the books, vestments, and other ornaments of the Church which Lord Archbishop Lanfranc gave to your uncle, Lord Bishop Donatus, for the use of the Church over which your fraternity presides, you dispose of according to your own will and give to outsiders. If this is true, I am astonished that you do so, since those ornaments were given not to him but to the Church, as the brothers of the Church of Canterbury testify.

Therefore I advise you, and in advising beg you, that if any of the aforesaid property has been given outside the Church, you promptly have it restored.

I have also heard that you expel and disperse the monks who had gathered in that Church to serve God [Note: The manuscript reads “gathered to serve” instead of “gathered to serve God”], and that you are entirely unwilling to receive those who wish to return. If this is so, it is not fitting for you; for it is known to be your duty rather to gather what has been dispersed than to disperse what has been gathered.

Therefore I order you that, if any have been cast out and wish to return and keep themselves in God’s service under obedience, you receive them and diligently attend to their salvation with fatherly affection [Col. 0110A], unless—God forbid—there is some obstacle in them of such a kind as wholly to forbid this.

Moreover, I have heard that you have a cross carried before you on the road. If this is true, I order you not to do so any longer, because this belongs only to an archbishop confirmed by the Roman pontiff with the pallium. Nor is it fitting for you, by any presumption in an unusual matter, to make yourself conspicuous and blameworthy before people.

Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIII. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

He earnestly begs to be informed of the rule governing ecclesiastical investitures.

To the lord and reverend **PASCHAL**, supreme pontiff, **ANSELM**, servant of the Church of Canterbury, due submission and faithful service.

First of all, my humility gives your eminence as many thanks as it can, because you received and treated our messengers so kindly and honorably that I recognize that in this matter I can trust your goodness beyond what I deserve.

I received with the reverence due to it the letter which they brought me from your majesty. But the king of England neither wished to see it nor to show me the one which you sent to him. For the archbishop of York and the other two bishops [Note: The manuscript reads “and the other bishops” instead of “and the other two bishops”] who presented themselves with our messengers before your presence, on their return reported orally something different from what the letter’s written text commanded me.

For they publicly asserted, in that truth which bishops are bound to preserve, that you had secretly instructed the king through them that, if he acted rightly in other matters, you would neither prohibit his investitures of Churches nor subject him to excommunication if he made them; but that you did not wish to commit this to writing, lest other princes, to whom the same thing was forbidden, should thereby obtain an occasion for complaint.

They also told me, on your behalf and with the same episcopal insistence on truth, that I should believe them about this matter and entrust myself to their counsel. If I refused to comply, they said, the king, even against my opposition, would unhesitatingly accomplish by your authority whatever he pleased, since you did not prohibit it; and if I wished to persist in what your letter commanded me, he would certainly expel me from his kingdom.

Thus, since I neither wished to disbelieve your letters nor dared disregard the assertion of the bishops who put forward your authority, because on both sides the sword of disobedience was being brandished against me, I asked for a delay, until I could receive certainty about this matter from your eminence. I nevertheless gave no assent to anything being done contrary to the decree of the Roman council; I merely tolerated it, and in the meantime condemned no one as disobedient if it should occur.

Thus the king, with what he believes to be your authority, gives bishoprics and abbeys. Prostrate in mind at your feet, therefore, and placed in great anguish, I beg you with all the affection I can summon to let me experience in you the apostolic compassion toward my soul; and, in order to obtain this, I humbly invoke the charity of the whole Roman Church.

I fear neither exile, poverty, tortures, nor death, because, with God strengthening me, my heart is ready for all these things in obedience to the apostolic see and for the liberty of my mother, the Church of Christ. I seek only certainty, so that without any ambiguity I may know what I ought to uphold by your authority.

I heard in the Roman council from the lord Urban, of venerable memory, that kings and all laymen who give or receive investitures and the property of Churches are excommunicated, as are those who become their men on account of this, and those who consecrate those who receive them [Note: The manuscript reads “those who receive consecrate” instead of “those who consecrate those who receive them”].

Therefore either, if it pleases your holiness, absolve this excommunication in England, so that I may remain there without danger to my soul; or inform me by your letter that you wish to preserve it, whatever may happen to me as a result; or, if your discernment wishes to make any exception, tell me with the same certainty exactly what it is.

I also desire to be instructed by your command about what I should do concerning those who, during the aforesaid delay, receive the prohibited investitures and those who consecrate them. In the matters which, through the bearers of this letter, I bring to your fatherhood’s attention outside this document, I humbly and earnestly ask that you deign not to reject our prayers.

**LETTER LXXIV. POPE PASCHAL TO ANSELM.**

A reply to the preceding letter.

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable brother and fellow bishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received your most pleasing letter of affection, and so forth. See under Paschal II, at the year 1118.

[Col. 0112A]

**LETTER LXXV. ANSELM TO HIS FRIEND CONNIUS.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript and with the Gothic Edition and the edition of 1573.]

He explains and subdivides the three forms of pride.

**ANSELM**, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved friend, Lord **CONNIUS** [Note: The edition reads “Cuno” instead of “Connio”], greeting.

Your affection requires me to recall in this letter the two forms of pride which have slipped from your memory, among the three about which I spoke to you.

I said that there are three. The first is in estimation: when someone thinks more highly of himself than he ought. Against this it is said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20). And he denies that this was present in himself who says: “Lord, my heart is not exalted” (Psalm 130:1), and what follows.

The second is in the will: when someone wishes to be treated in some way more highly than he ought. Against this it is said: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” (John 5:44). And: “I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jeremiah 17:16).

The third is in action. Against this the Lord says: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place” (Luke 14:8). This occurs when a person treats himself more highly than he ought.

Many other statements are found in sacred Scripture against each of these forms, if one searches for them. Against all of them it is said: “He who exalts himself will be humbled” (ibid., verse 11). And: “God resists the proud” (James 4:6), along with many other passages.

Of these three, when each exists alone, the lighter is the one found only in action [Note: The manuscript and the edition read “which is in action” instead of “which is found only in action”], because it occurs only through ignorance; nevertheless, since it is a vice, it must be corrected.

Of the other two, the one found only in the will is more damnable, because it sins knowingly. But the one found in estimation alone is the most incurable, because it does not reveal itself and appears just to the person who possesses it.

If these three kinds of pride are considered individually, they may be called three simple forms of pride. If they are understood in pairs, three double forms are found. If all three are joined together, there will be one triple form; and if there are seven, there are three simple forms, three double forms, and one triple form. [Note: The manuscript and the edition repeat the sequence “and if there are seven, three simple forms, three double forms, one triple form.”]

Against these forms of pride stand the members of humility: that a person think humbly of himself; that, in his dealings and conduct toward others, he humbly wish to be regarded; and that he himself treat himself humbly.

For each individual form of pride a person is called proud; but for each individual member of humility, or for two of them, a person is not called humble unless all the members are present together. Thus, when one bodily member is diseased, a person is called sick; but he is not called healthy unless all his members are healthy.

I have recalled these matters briefly for your affection. If your prudence considers them repeatedly, it will understand more fully what has been said here.

Farewell, and pray for me, that just as God has given me understanding of pride and humility, so he may give me the ability to avoid the former and acquire the latter. Greet on my behalf our revered lord and friend, the bishop of Arras.

**LETTER LXXVI. ANSELM TO ERNULF, PRIOR, AND THE MONKS OF CANTERBURY.**

At Chartres, where he was received by the countess and the bishop, he writes about the success of his journey and urges the men of Canterbury to remain faithful to their religious discipline.

**ANSELM**, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest sons and brothers, Lord **ERNULF**, prior, and the others serving God in the Church of Christ at Canterbury, greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as he can give it.

I inform your affection how I am and what I am doing. Since I began our journey, with your prayers accompanying me, the grace of God has protected me from every adversity up to the present day. [Col. 0113B]

[Note: He was traveling toward Rome with the same intention with which he had left England. Those to whom he was writing knew this, but not everyone who reads this passage will understand it unless we unravel the interrupted thread of the narrative.

After receiving Paschal’s penultimate letter, which exposed the shameless lie of the royal envoys, Anselm defended more firmly the liberty and authority of the Church against investiture. The king and the nobles of the kingdom, seeing that the man of God possessed such an exalted and steadfast spirit that neither flattery softened him nor threats shook him, advised him to go to Rome, confident and even believing that through his efforts the whole matter would reach a very favorable conclusion.

Anselm obeyed their advice, determined to leave nothing undone for the sake of peace, and departed England on 27 April 1104, as Lilius writes in his *Chronicle*. I prefer to agree with him rather than with Matthew Paris, Hoveden, and the Worcester historian, who place the event in 1103.

For, as we have said elsewhere, Anselm was recalled from Lyon to England by Henry I in August 1100, and it is probable that he arrived in England toward the end of that same month. Indeed, if we follow Hoveden, Henry invited Anselm to England on 7 September. The precise month or day does not matter to me, since all the English historians agree that in November of that year Anselm joined King Henry in the sacred marriage with Matilda, daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots.

But Eadmer, Anselm’s inseparable companion during his travels, in book II of his *Life*, and Walsingham in his *History of Normandy*, observe that the hostility between Henry and Anselm began only after a year and a half, in the second year after Anselm’s return. That period is missing from Paris’s and Hoveden’s calculations. Eadmer’s chronology is therefore more reliable—indeed, no chronology is more reliable—for he alone saw Anselm, accompanied him when he went and returned, and remained with him to the final breath of his life; I therefore more readily place my trust in him than in anyone else.]

Traveling to Rome with the intention with which I had left England, I reached Chartres, where I was received with joy and honor by the countess, the sister of our king, by the bishop, and by many others. But they were greatly astonished that I had begun my journey at such a time.

They said that, because of the excessive heat and because no pilgrim travels at this season, I would reach neither Rome nor return again, since I would be unable either to escape the hands of the enemies of God’s Church or, because of my bodily weakness, to avoid death while traveling at such a time.

Thus, on the strength of their advice, they did not permit me to go farther for the present, but compelled me to wait for a suitable time, when pilgrims travel. For I knew that divine Scripture says: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24). I feared that if I did not accept such reasonable and friendly advice, repentance would follow.

For this reason, although the aforesaid countess most willingly wished to keep me in her land and provide everything necessary, I returned to Normandy and am waiting to complete at a suitable time what I have begun, if God so wills.

You know, dearest sons, my desire concerning you; you have often heard what in you consoles me in my tribulations. If your hearts strive to remain free for God alone; if you labor vigorously at the purpose which you have firmly undertaken, like good workers in Christ’s vineyard; if your life testifies that the world is crucified to you and you to the world; if you live not for yourselves but for God—that is, not according to your own will but according to God’s will; if you fear God greatly even in the smallest matters; if you love the strictness of your order—for anyone who hates it demonstrates by the clearest sign that he is vicious and loves laxity; if you preserve peace among yourselves and obedience toward the lord prior—this is my desire concerning you, this is my consolation and rest in you.

Think about these things, reconsider them, and practice them, if you wish to make me joyful—or rather, if you wish to please God. May the Holy Spirit persuade you of these things and grant you the blessed vision of his glory on their account. Amen.

**LETTER LXXVII. ANSELM TO THE SAME PERSONS.**

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

On the same subject as the preceding letter.

**ANSELM**, archbishop, to his dearest lords and brothers, Lord **ERNULF**, prior, and the other servants of God dwelling in the Church of Christ at Canterbury, greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as he can give it.

With the grace of God favoring us through your prayers and those of our other friends, ever since I departed from your presence everything concerning me and my companions has prospered up to the present day. I ask, however, that, just as I trust you, you not cease praying for us, so that divine mercy may so protect and order us and our affairs that, when we return to you, your charity may be able to rejoice with us over our complete prosperity. [Col. 0114C]

As far as we are concerned, as I said, everything is prosperous for us; but if you are living in peace and, as I hope, devoting yourselves to living well and saving your souls, according to my desire, then my joy is increased much more and more truly. I therefore ask you with all the affection I can muster [Col. 0115A] to be always solicitous to advance toward better things and in no way to fall away from those to which the grace of God has raised you.

Preserve among yourselves, according to God, the sweetness of love and concord; love without pretence the strictness of your order; raise your hearts continually to the fellowship of the angels [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “of the English” (*Anglorum*) instead of “of the angels” (*angelorum*)], for whose sake you live well. In every difficulty and temporal adversity, should such things occur, so that your good zeal may not in any way be disturbed [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “in adversity” instead of “in temporal adversity”], hope through prayer for God’s consolation [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “your zeal” instead of “your good zeal”]. Wherever you are, whether in the sight of human beings or only in the sight of God, from whom you are never absent, carry your souls always in your hands in all your actions, great or small, even in your thoughts, together with the Psalmist.

May Almighty God so protect you in all things [Col. 0115B] and direct you that through temporal prosperity he may lead you to eternal blessedness. Amen.

I commend my nephew Anselm to your charity, as my own flesh, so that he may both be able to learn and guard his life. I instruct Lord Robert, who oversees our household, to give you all the wine that I left at Canterbury and to spend it for your use according to the will of the lord prior.

## 396. LETTER LXXVIII. ANSELM TO GONDULF, ARCHBISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

That a king ought not to demand money from monks or from the Church.

ANSELM, archbishop, to the reverend bishop GONDULF, greetings.

[Col. 0115C]

I have heard that our lord the king is asking money from the prior and monks of our Church [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “your king” instead of “our king”], which they neither have nor can have, since, as I have been informed, they owe a considerable sum to creditors and, because of their lack of means in what is necessary for them [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “lack of means that is necessary for them” (*indigentiam quae sibi*) instead of “lack of means in those things that are necessary for them” (*indigentiam in his quae sibi*)]., are suffering great hardship [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “are suffering hardship” instead of “are suffering great hardship”].

They cannot even obtain half of what I had arranged to be available for the work of the church that has been begun; and even if they had it, it is not fitting for the king to demand anything from them [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “anything pertaining to them” instead of “anything from them”], since they have nothing—not even themselves—as monks, nor is it their responsibility to give or lend what does not belong to them.

Therefore I instruct and beg you to persuade the king by your prayers to order that all our possessions remain undisturbed and in peace until I return, as he promised. [Col. 0115D] For if God grants me a prosperous return, as I have resolved, I shall serve him as I ought, as my lord and king. If he does this, I shall give thanks to God and to him; but if he does not hear our prayers and wishes to do something that will grieve me [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “something else” instead of “something”], he will act, as lord, according to what pleases him [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “what pleases” without “him”], but it will not seem to me that he is doing what he ought [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “what is fitting” instead of “what he ought”].

For the monks and I are not divided, but everything established for their benefit [Col. 0116A] is mine and subject to my authority; and if they were in need, whatever I possessed I ought to spend for their necessity. Therefore, since every worldly adversity touches my spirit according to its own measure and character, that adversity which grieves them [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “that adversity touches my spirit” instead of “that adversity which grieves them”] wounds my heart more deeply. And you know that I ought not to give my assent to such an unheard-of and unprecedented matter; and because I ought not, I do not dare allow money to be demanded from monks [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “from the monks” instead of “from monks”] without their prelate. Therefore it is neither advantageous to me nor to anyone else that this practice be introduced into the Church of God with anyone’s consent.

[Col. 0116B]

## LETTER LXXIX. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He exhorts the king to obey the heavenly King.

[Col. 0116B]

To HENRY, reverend lord and glorious king of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, faithful service with prayers.

I give thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “from whom every good thing” without “comes”], for your safety and cheerfulness, and because he advances your successes toward greater and better things [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “better” instead of “greater and better”], to the joy of yourself and your faithful people. I also give thanks to your highness because you have deigned to inform me of these matters, as one informs a faithful servant in whom one trusts, who rejoices with him in all his prosperity and gives thanks to the one by whose ordering these things come about.

For in truth, this is what I pray and desire every day: that God may so rule and protect you and your affairs in the glory of your temporal kingdom over the English that he may cause you to reign in eternal happiness among the angels. [Col. 0116C] This is precisely the service I most wish to render you. Therefore, since this concerns me—for I have been placed here for this purpose—I advise, beg, and, as Scripture says, exhort you in season and out of season: just as God increases your prosperity and exalts your power, so may you love him above all things [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “may you always love” instead of “may you love him above all things”] and preserve his will in all your works.

May God grant you to do this for a long time in prosperity during this life, so that after this life he may make you rejoice with him in eternity [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “into eternity” instead of “in eternity”].

By the grace of God, everything concerning me is prosperous. Before the Assumption of holy Mary I shall depart from Bec, so that, with God’s approval, I may pursue the purpose for which I left England. Although I trust in your good will concerning our affairs [Note: [Col. 0115D] The manuscript reads “your will” instead of “your good will”], I nevertheless ask you to order that they remain undisturbed [Col. 0116D] until I return.

## LETTER LXXX. ANSELM TO ERNULF AND THE MONKS OF CANTERBURY

Concerning the reception of clerics as monks.

ANSELM, archbishop, to the lord prior ERNULF and the other brothers of Christ Church at Canterbury, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as he can give it.

[Col. 0117A]

Concerning the matter about which you wrote to me, I reply as follows. If any clerics who can be useful to the Church and to themselves ask to be received into the order, and you judge that this is so, I approve your receiving them; nor do I want you to doubt my wishes in this matter, since you know that I am displeased when such men do not come to you as I would wish. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, THE QUEEN

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

Concerning his safety and the appointed time of his Roman journey.

To his most beloved lady MATHILDA, queen of the English, ANSELM, archbishop, faithful service and the continual protection of heavenly grace.

[Col. 0117B]

I am not unaware that the kindness of your graciousness is pleased to know how I am and how I fare. Therefore, rejoicing and giving thanks for your very good will, I inform you that ever since I left England, by God’s mercy he has kept me and everything belonging to me in complete prosperity [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads “God’s mercy and what belongs to me” instead of “by God’s mercy he has kept me and everything belonging to me”].

Until now I have remained at Bec, awaiting a suitable time for undertaking the journey; but shortly, before the Assumption of holy Mary, I shall depart from there, intending, with God’s approval, to complete what I have begun. I recently learned that it pleases God to exalt the dignity of the kingdom of my lord the king and of yourself, and, according to your will, to restore to your honor and advantage those things that were not pleasing to him, to you, or to your faithful people [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads “I recently learned that it pleases God” without “recently”]. Therefore, as a faithful servant and as one who desires your good in the present [Col. 0117C] and future life, I rejoice and give thanks as I ought to the heavenly King from whom these blessings come to you; and I pray and desire that, always preserving unharmed the good things he has given, he may advance you under his grace to greater and better things.

Since it is therefore my office to exhort you to desire the heavenly kingdom, I exhort, beg, and advise you with all the affection I can muster not to take greater delight in rejoicing over the passing glory of an earthly kingdom than in yearning for the eternal happiness of the heavenly kingdom. You will certainly be able to do this sincerely and effectively if you order the things subject to your authority more according to God’s counsel than according to human counsel. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God (1 Corinthians 3:19), [Col. 0117D] as true Scripture says; and, “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God” (Romans 8:7).

Advise your lord the king about these matters; make them known to him privately and publicly; repeat them often; and, insofar as it concerns you, consider them carefully and diligently. For, as you are accustomed to say, the glory of the world passes away. May God grant that after passing glory he may lead you both to eternal glory. Amen.

[Col. 0118A]

## 397. LETTER LXXXII. ANSELM TO ERNULF AND THE MONKS OF CANTERBURY

That the monks of Canterbury should not be disturbed but serve God quietly, whatever the king may do.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his most beloved lords, brothers, and sons, the lord prior ERNULF and the other monks serving God under him, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as he can give it.

You will learn from the present messenger about our health and prosperity and where I am. For the present, however, I cannot return to England until I know what the king replies to the letters I am sending him through the bishop of Rochester. What those letters contain you will learn from the same bishop after they have been shown to the king.

Whatever the king replies, and whatever may happen concerning me, remember that “whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14:8). Therefore live in such a way that you may live for him and, when you die, pass to him. Let not the tribulations of this life disturb you, for “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will not allow the righteous to be tossed about forever. Pray to God by living well and by not disturbing your minds, so that he may always make you rejoice in his consolation.

As dearly beloved sons, I exhort and admonish the boys and young men, with all the affection I can muster, not to forget the admonition and instruction with which I used to teach them to guard their hearts and thoughts. Rather, by frequently reconsidering our counsel, which I used diligently to magnify and commend to them, let them strive by God’s grace to preserve it.

“May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds” (Philippians 4:7). I thank you for the charity you have shown to our nephew, and I instruct him to remain with you and devote himself to learning and letters until I command him to come to me.

## LETTER LXXXIII. ANSELM TO EUSTACHIUS

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

After his wife had been enclosed as a religious woman with his consent, he had taken another woman for himself; Anselm reproves him for this sin.

ANSELM, called archbishop of the Church [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads “Anselm, archbishop, servant of the Church” (*Anselmus archiepiscopus servus Ecclesiae*)], servant of the Church of Canterbury, to EUSTACHIUS [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads “Eustachicus” instead of “Eustachius”], father of Gaufridus, the monk of Bec, greetings.

Lord Gaufridus, your son, concerned for the salvation [Col. 0118D] of your soul and fearing your damnation, asks me to show you in how great a danger you remain. For he says that you gave your wife, his mother [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads “his mother” instead of “your wife, his mother”], permission to abandon the world and become a religious woman, and that you vowed the chastity of your body to God, but afterward took another woman, by whom you fathered a son.

If this is so, know without any doubt that if your soul leaves this life in this sin, it will be completely lost [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “your soul, completely” instead of “your soul will be completely lost”], and there will be no hope of its salvation, either before or after the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “before judgment” instead of “before the day of judgment”]. Let your prudence therefore consider how grave an evil it is to lose eternal life and the fellowship [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “eternal glory and fellowship” instead of “eternal life and the fellowship”] of the angels, and to suffer eternal torment in the fellowship of demons.

Consider also how dangerous and how foolish it is to delay correction in such a matter [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “to delay in such a matter”], without which you may expect certain destruction. For as long as you remain in this sin, God’s anger remains over you; and just as sin grows the longer it remains, so God’s anger burns increasingly against you day by day.

I therefore advise and beg you, as a Christian addressing a Christian and as a friend addressing a friend, not to delay escaping from so grave a sin and so great a danger, lest your soul pass from this life into death and eternal torment at an hour when you do not expect it.

I also advise you to seek the counsel of your son, Lord Gaufridus, concerning this matter, if you ever wish to receive from God the help of salvation. For even if you did not promise the chastity of your body when you gave your wife permission to become a religious woman, nevertheless you could in no way violate that same chastity without the sin and danger I have mentioned, so long as that wife continued to live [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “so long as the wife lived”].

## LETTER LXXXIV. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, ABBESS OF CAEN

[Note: [Col. 0119C] Collated with the same manuscript.]

Feeling herself weaker, she consults Anselm about whether she ought to lay down her burden. He replies that she may commend it honorably with the consent of the count, the archbishop of Rouen, and the nuns; otherwise, she should divide her burdens and entrust to wiser sisters those tasks that she herself is not sufficient to perform. [Col. 0119C]

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to the lady and reverend mother MATHILDA, abbess of Caen, may she always be ruled by the counsel of divine grace.

Your holiness asks through Lord Robert, the brother of Eustachius, our counsel concerning your abbey, which you would wish to leave, if you were permitted to entrust it to another, because through illness and weakness of age you cannot govern it as you ought.

Since this cannot be done except through the count, the archbishop of Rouen, your bishop, and the consent of the nuns entrusted to you [Col. 0120A], I can offer you no help in that matter. But since you ask this of me [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “since you ask” instead of “since you ask this of me”], I send such counsel as I can.

Try to bring about your desire, insofar as it seems advantageous to you, through those to whom the matter belongs. If you cannot do so, assign to the sisters who are your members—especially those in whom you recognize greater prudence and religious fervor—the care of those matters in which your strength fails, doing so by commanding, asking, and exhorting them.

For even if it should happen that you did not have such persons in whom you could trust according to your desire [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads *desiderium possitis* (“you might [according to] desire be able”) instead of *desiderium vestrum possitis* (“your desire you might be able”)], which I do not hope is the case in your Church, [Note: [Col. 0119C] The manuscript reads “For thus” (*nam sic*) instead of “For if” (*nam si*)]. your reverence would nevertheless be excusable before God if you chose those whom you recognized as better and more suitable for this purpose, since, as I believe, you could not do better [Col. 0120B].

## LETTER LXXXV. ANSELM TO GONDULF, BISHOP OF ROCHESTER

[Note: [Col. 0119C] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He praises him for being concerned about the affairs of the Church of Canterbury. He does not wish the bishop of York to be condemned unheard and in his absence.

ANSELM, archbishop, to the reverend and beloved bishop of Rochester, GONDULF, may he always will and perform what is pleasing to God.

First I give thanks to God because, as you informed me, all our affairs and yours are everywhere proceeding prosperously; [Col. 0120C] then I thank you, whose prudence and care govern them. By God’s grace, ever since I left England, everything concerning me and what belongs to me has been ordered according to my wishes.

As for the debts you have paid, if the debts from Romescot are among them, I rejoice; and I await, with thanks, your promise concerning our revenues. You acted well in informing me about the words exchanged between the king and you concerning me and my journey, concerning the letters that I said had been sent to him and to me by the pope, and concerning the messages to the emperor.

But know that since I departed from you I have received neither letters nor any embassy from the pope, except what he sent me through Tiberius, in words and in writing [Note: [Col. 0119D], to help him concerning Romescot.

### Note on Romescot

[Col. 0119D]

“To help him concerning Romescot.” *Romescot*, *Romischeot*—in French, *la taille de Rome* (“Rome’s levy”), according to Cujas on *Auditis*, *De praescriptionibus*, book II—is also called *Romscot* or *Romescot*. It is an English expression, as appears in the laws of William the Bastard, king of the English, recorded by Roger Hoveden in the latter part of his *Annals*, p. 344. One of those laws bears this title and statute:

“Concerning Saint Peter’s penny, which in English is called *Ramescot*. Everyone who has thirty pence-worth of live property in his house shall, according to the law of the English, give Saint Peter’s penny from his own property, and according to Danish law half a mark. That penny must be demanded on the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul, before the feast called the Chains of Saint Peter, so that it is not withheld beyond another day. If anyone withholds it, a complaint shall be brought to the king’s custody, because this penny is the king’s alms; justice shall ensure that the penny is returned, together with the forfeiture owed to the bishop and the king. And if anyone has several houses, he shall pay it at the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul from the house in which he resides.” [Col. 0120D]

Thus William called the Conqueror ordered that what belongs to God should be rendered to God, and observed exactly what he had ordered, as is witnessed by the letter he sent to Gregory VII in these words:

“To the most excellent shepherd of Holy Church, Gregory, William, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of Normandy, greetings with friendship. [Col. 0121B]

“Your legate Hubert, religious Father, came to me on your behalf and admonished me that I should render fidelity to you and your successors, and should give more careful consideration to the money which my predecessors were accustomed to send to the Roman Church. I accepted one matter and did not accept the other. I did not wish, nor do I wish, to render fidelity, because I neither promised it nor find that my predecessors rendered it to your predecessors.

“The money was collected negligently for nearly three years while I was in Gaul. But now, by divine mercy, since I have returned to my kingdom, what has been collected is being sent through the aforesaid legate; and what remains will be sent through the envoys of Lanfranc, our faithful archbishop, when the opportunity arises. Pray for us and for the condition of our kingdom, because we have loved your predecessors and desire to love and obey you sincerely above all others.”

Thus far William’s letter, which I found among Lanfranc’s letters.

[Col. 0121C]

But William also wrote that Gregory, in a letter to a kinsman, had admonished him in the following terms in the year 1073, on the eleventh day before the Nones of April, in the twelfth indiction:

“Concerning Saint Peter’s possessions, which are collected in England, we admonish you to watch over them as you watch over your own affairs, and we entrust them to your generosity as to your own, so that you may find Peter a devout and favorable debtor and admonish him to assist you from what he owes, since he will not be unaware that you have contributed much to him.”

Hubert, the pope’s legate to England for collecting Saint Peter’s tribute, is mentioned in Letter 32 of Book II and Letter 42 of Book III.

As for William’s ordering that half a mark be paid according to Danish law, this seems to be understood of the Danish kings who held the reins of the English kingdom for several years. One of them, namely Cnut, first king of Denmark, Norway, and England, returning from Rome, which he had visited on account of a vow, gave a letter to the English in the year 1030, ordering that all debts be paid before his return. He says: “The pennies which you owe to Rome, to Saint Peter, whether from cities or from villages.” [Col. 0121D]

Ingulf, abbot of Crowland, recorded that this letter was written in 1032 in his *History*, where he copied out a complete transcript of it and also narrated Cnut’s devout pilgrimage; the matter is likewise recorded by William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of the English*, book II, chapter 11; Hoveden, first part of the *Annals*, under the year 1031; Polydore Vergil, book VII of the *English History*; Lilius in his *Chronicle*; and Henry of Huntingdon, book VI: “King Cnut,” he says, “went splendidly to Rome, and permanently assigned to Saint Peter the alms called *Romescot*, which his predecessors had given to the Roman Church.”

[Col. 0122B]

Thus *Ramoscot*, or *Romscot*, is the annual tribute that the kings of England paid each year to the Roman pontiffs. For this reason the English vernacular called it *Pitrepence* or *Petrepence*, as though it were Peter’s payment or penny, as above in Letters 32 of Book II and 42 of Book III; in Peter of Blois, Letter 136, Paris edition of 1515—for the Mainz edition separated it from the letters and entitled it a separate invective; and in the chapters *Auditis*, *De praescriptionibus*, book II, and *Ea quae*, *De censibus*, book III.

This penny was paid by kings even when the kingdom of England was governed by the heptarchy. In particular, it was paid by Ine, king of the West Saxons, around the year of salvation 740; and by Æthelwulf, or Adulf, as it is written in book III, chapter 4 of Æthelweard’s *Chronicle*, king of the West Saxons, or Western English, in the year 855, as Asser of Sherborne—now called Salisbury—bishop, recorded in his *History of Alfred, king of the Anglo-Saxons*, in these words: [Col. 0122C]

“He also ordered that every year a large sum of money, namely three hundred mancuses, be carried to Rome for the sake of his soul, to be divided there in this way: namely, one hundred mancuses especially in honor of Saint Peter, to purchase oil with which all the lamps of that church might be filled on Easter Eve; and one hundred mancuses in honor of Saint Paul, under the same condition, to provide oil in the church of Saint Paul the Apostle, to fill the lamps on Easter Eve and at cockcrow; and one hundred mancuses to the venerable apostolic pope.”

Florence of Worcester transcribed nearly every word of Asser in his *Chronicle*, p. 300. William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of the English*, book II, chapter 2, concludes the whole matter more briefly and specifically: “He went to Rome after establishing his kingdom, and there, in the presence of Pope Leo IV, offered Saint Peter the tribute which England pays to this day.”

[Col. 0122D]

Roger of Hoveden calls the mancuses mentioned above *manclae*, and Malmesbury, in the passage just cited, calls them marks. William Lambard, however, in his notes on the ancient laws of the Saxons, asserts that a *mancla* and a mark are the same thing, namely a coin worth thirty pence.

But enough of this, since these matters are more familiar to students of English history than would require me to explain them more fully. I have nevertheless examined them at greater length because I heard certain people refer this payment of the Roman penny to the period of the English king commonly called John Lackland, although the two payments are diametrically opposed: the one was imposed, the other voluntary, as Matthew Paris recounts at length in his *Greater History.*

Ut eum de Romascot adjuvarem: “to help him concerning Romescot.”
