De litteris autem papae ad regem nihil scio, nisi quod vos mihi mandastis. Si autem alicubi mansurus sum et per legatum meum sim facturus quod incoepi, nondum sum certus.

I know nothing about the pope’s letters to the king except what you reported to me. I am not yet certain whether I shall remain somewhere and accomplish through my legate what I have begun.

[Col. 0121A]

Concerning Gerard, archbishop of York, I ought not in such a matter to decide anything in the absence of an absent and unheard man, especially since he himself denies the charge brought against him; therefore I do not dare give advice, lest someone accept my advice as a judgment.

Accordingly, if it seems right to you, speak about this to the king entirely on my behalf—unless he himself asks you—according to what I command you, if you cannot do better.

Regarding the dispute between our people and the men of Robert of Montfort, I ask you to arrange through the king that either complete peace or a truce [Note: [Col. 0121A] The manuscript reads “truce” (*tremae*) instead of “truces” (*treviae*)] be established between them until I return.

Take care of all our affairs, within and outside the house, as you have done until now, and I beg you to do so, since you know that I trust you.

Concerning the property and household of Robert, your foster-son, who is with me, I give you thanks, because you are defending them against his adversaries as he instructed you [Col. 0122A]. I earnestly beg you to ensure that everything belonging to him remains entirely undisturbed, and to give the same command, on my behalf and yours, to William of Maidstone.

For I tell you that I would rather suffer some injury in my own possessions than in his affairs.

With God’s approval, I wish to depart from Bec before the Assumption of holy Mary and be at Chartres for the feast; afterward, as God shall arrange, and with your prayers accompanying us, I shall complete our journey.

As for the fact that some people reproach me for my familiarity with those whom the king does not love, know that I do nothing against his honor or for which I ought justly to be reproached.

Because of the disputes concerning the church of Hergas, order Ralph [Note: [Col. 0121A] The manuscript reads *Rudolpho* instead of *Rodulpho*; both are forms of “Ralph”] the provost to hold it in my hand until I return, and in the meantime to find someone to serve there. [Col. 0123A]

May Almighty Lord preserve you and yours under his grace and always [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads “now and always” instead of “always”] direct you in the way of salvation. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript omits “Amen.”]

## LETTER LXXXVI. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

He congratulates the king on his concern for him.

To his most beloved lord HENRY, glorious king of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, faithful service with prayers.

I give great thanks to your highness for the great love that you have shown you bear toward me and for the personal concern you have for me as for your faithful servant—namely, lest I fail on the journey I have begun because of the excessive burden of labor, given the weakness and illness of my body. [Col. 0123B]

But I had already advanced as far as the valley of Maurienne [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads “Moriana” instead of “Morianna”] when I received your letter. I was therefore afraid that the lord pope might be displeased if, after completing so great a part of the journey, I stopped and he sent me no response through his envoys unless I myself reached him, as I had begun to do [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads “unless I reached him myself” instead of “unless I myself reached him, as I had begun to do”].

For I learned from letters that he sent me through Tiberius that, if it were possible, he would gladly speak with me [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads *mihi loquerer* (“I would speak to me”) instead of *mecum loqueretur* (“he would speak with me”)]. Trusting in God, therefore, and relying on what I felt within myself and had learned from the journey already completed—that I would be able to endure the labor of the journey—I judged it good to complete personally, as I had resolved, the purpose for which I left England, unless something should occur that I could not reasonably resist.

May Almighty God so rule and strengthen your earthly kingdom in your joy for a long time over the English that after [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads “and after” instead of “that after”] this life he may make you reign among the angels. Amen.

## LETTER LXXXVII. ANSELM TO GERONTIUS, ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

A cleric bound by an oath of religious profession to two churches: in which should he remain? For many reasons it is more advantageous for him to remain at Chartres than to return to Gerontius.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his reverend abbot and friend GERONTIUS [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads “Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury … to Gerontinus” (*Gerontino*) instead of “Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury … to Gerontanus” (*Gerontani*)], greetings.

A certain monk, as I learned from him, is bound to your Church by a profession that he made to you while wearing clerical dress, and likewise to the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Chartres, where he assumed the monastic habit through another profession. He says that he can obtain release neither from you nor from the abbot of Chartres, so as to save his soul either in the monastery at Chartres or in yours; and he cannot do so unless he is absolved either by you or by the abbot of Chartres. [Col. 0124A]

Let your prudence therefore consider that it is neither fitting nor advantageous for you abbots to tear his soul apart, each drawing him to himself. Rather, show that maternal compassion exists in you and that you love the soul of your neighbor more than your own will.

The one who says to the other, “Keep the living child for yourself alone; let us not both kill him,” shows himself more truly a mother, so that when the true Solomon comes he may say, “Give the living child to this woman, for she is its mother.” For the true mother prefers her son to live in another’s embrace rather than to cherish him dead in her own.

Know that, as far as I have been able to determine, for many reasons it is more advantageous for him to remain at Chartres than to return to you. [Col. 0124B] Therefore, if I dared, I would suggest to your religious conscience, in offering counsel, that you prove yourself not a false but a true mother. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Collated with the same manuscript and with the published *History of New Affairs* by Eadmer.]

What the pope replied to his consultation concerning the conferral of ecclesiastical benefices; and that Anselm will obey the pope.

To his reverend lord HENRY, king of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, faithful service with prayers.

Although you may learn through William of Warelwast [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript and Eadmer read “William of Warelimast” instead of “William of Warelwast”] what we did at Rome, I shall nevertheless briefly explain what concerns me.

I came to Rome and explained to the lord pope the reason for which I had come. He replied that he was in no way willing to dissent from the statutes of his predecessors [Col. 0124C]. In addition, he ordered me to have no fellowship with those who, after learning of this prohibition, had received investitures of churches from your hand [Note: [Col. 0123D] Eadmer reads *manu vestra* (“from your hand”) instead of *manu tua* (“from thy hand”)], unless they did penance and abandoned what they had received without hope of recovering it; nor was I to have fellowship with bishops who had consecrated such men, unless they presented themselves for judgment before the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0123D] Eadmer reads *repraesentarent* (“should present themselves”) instead of *praesentarent* (“should be presented”)].

The aforesaid William can testify to all this, if he wishes.

When William and I parted, he recalled on your behalf the love and kindness that you had always shown me. He urged me, as your archbishop, to make myself such that I might enter England in a condition in which I could be with you as my predecessor had been with your father, and that you might treat me with the same honor and freedom with which your father had treated my predecessor.

From these words I understood that, unless I made myself such a person, you would not wish me to return to England. I give thanks for your love and kindness. [Col. 0123D]

But to be with you in the way my predecessor was with your father, I cannot do so. Girgilius would be needed to disentangle these words. For when, toward the end of the eleventh century, the granting by a lay prince of power over a priesthood, a pastoral staff, or a bishop’s ring came to be called simony—and likewise the homage (to use the common expression) rendered to him, or any service of the same kind—Lanfranc will appear free of this stain, and indeed William the Bastard himself, the father of this Henry to whom Anselm’s present letters are addressed. For we have seen him praised in Baronius on the testimony of Pope Alexander, because he had extinguished the plague of simony.

William of Malmesbury, however, if we believe what he says in Book III of *The History of the Kings of England*, makes Gregory VII the inventor and first person to hurl anathema against lay investitures and those invested by laymen. I observe nothing in these words that touches Lanfranc. Indeed, Lanfranc’s inauguration was accomplished more through royal insistence and the command of the supreme pontiff than through such questionable favors, as he himself testified in a letter addressed to that same pontiff and reproduced in Letter 23 of Book I.

Moreover, at the command of that same Alexander, he restored Thomas, archbishop of York, and Remigius, bishop of Lincoln, as men unworthy of their sees—Thomas because he was the son of a priest, and Remigius because he had acquired his bishopric by supplying assistance to William the Bastard when he came to England.

But according to William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The English Bishops*:

> “The pope, shifting responsibility for what he had done away from himself, transferred the consideration of the matter to Lanfranc, saying that he should judge whether it was rightly or wrongly done; if he wished, he could restore the investitures; if not, he should do what he knew to be advantageous. Thus, receiving staffs and rings from Lanfranc’s hand, they plotted with him a joyful return to their homeland. Nor did Gregory, Alexander’s successor, take less care to flatter him with the diligence of affection, transacting many matters by his counsel and entrusting to his conscience many things unknown even to his household.”

From these words of Malmesbury it is apparent that these two pontiffs regarded Lanfranc in England as a kind of substitute for a most sacred sanctuary, from which matters necessarily to be made known to the public were brought forth according to the circumstances of places, persons, and times, while other matters were either to be entirely concealed or to be made less manifest, as Lanfranc’s prudence judged appropriate, since he enjoyed the confidence of the popes.

Therefore, if Lanfranc performed something that Anselm declines to perform, no one should rashly attribute it as a fault to that most excellent prelate. The pupil does not criticize his teacher; rather, Anselm declares that he does not dare to do what was permitted to his teacher, if circumstances should at some time require it, because of the prohibition promulgated by Urban II and Paschal II in his hearing.

Yet at this point one cannot help thinking that Malmesbury had forgotten himself in Book III of *The History of the Kings of England*, where, speaking of Pope Gregory VII, he writes:

> “What others had been unaccustomed to do, he brought openly into prominence, excommunicating those elected who received investitures from a layman’s hand by ring and staff.”

Malmesbury, I say, suffered a serious lapse of memory in writing this. For nearly two hundred years before Gregory, Pope Nicholas I—and before Nicholas, Leo IV—had plainly decreed the same thing under penalty of anathema, as can be read in Volume II of the councils, in these words:

> “That no cleric or priest may in any way obtain a church through laymen, neither freely nor for a price.”

Indeed, Alexander II, Gregory VII’s predecessor, approved this decree of Nicholas and ordered that it, together with Nicholas’s other constitutions, be observed. Gratian included it under Alexander’s name in Chapter 6, Question 7, canon *Per laicos* (“Through laymen”).

Where, however, he renewed these statutes, Alexander himself makes clear, writing as follows:

> “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Catholic bishops, and to the entire clergy and people, the dearest of all, greeting and apostolic blessing. Since, as those responsible for the continual care demanded by the vigilance of universal government, we owe constant concern to everyone, we have resolved to notify you of what was canonically established in the Constantinopolitan synod recently held in the presence of more than one hundred bishops, although we were unworthy to be present; for we desire you to be its executors for our salvation, and by apostolic authority we command and enjoin it. First, with God as witness, we decree that, as was previously established by blessed Pope Leo and Nicholas of blessed memory, no mercy is to be shown to simoniacs with respect to the retention of their dignity.”

A little later the holy synod established the following under threat of excommunication, saying:

> “Any priest, deacon, or subdeacon who, after the constitution of our predecessor of blessed memory, the most holy Pope Leo or Nicholas, concerning the chastity of clerics, has taken a concubine, or has failed to abandon one already taken, we command, on the part of almighty God and by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, and we altogether forbid, to sing Mass, or to read either the Gospel or the Epistle at Mass.”

These points are excerpted from the Lateran synod.

It is moreover clear from the fact that we observed the circumstances that these letters of Anselm were written from Lyons in the year 1105: in Letter 76 we noted that Anselm, on his way to Rome, left England in 1104 and remained in Gaul for more than three months because of excessive heat and the weakness of his similarly frail body, so that he set out on his journey around the Nones of August; Letters 81 and 85 indicate this date. Besides, it is contrary to the truth that a man worn out by old age should have gone and returned so quickly that he came back in the same year in which he had departed, especially during the winter season.

Eadmer, Malmesbury, and others testify that this separation of Anselm and the royal legate William of Warelwast took place not far from Lyons. Anselm therefore, after going to Lyons, wrote many of the following letters to the king, the queen, bishops, abbots, and monks, while others were written to him.

> But in order to be with you in such a way as my predecessor was with your father, I cannot do so, because I neither dare to render you homage nor, on account of the prohibition mentioned above, made in my hearing, dare to associate with those who receive the investitures of churches from your hand. I therefore ask you, if it pleases you, to communicate your will to me: whether, in the manner I have described, I may return to England in your peace and in possession of my office. For I am ready, according to my strength and knowledge, faithfully to render service both to you and to the people divinely entrusted to me, while preserving regular obedience.  
>   
> [Note: The manuscript and Edmund read *servati*; the printed text has *servata*.]  
>   
> But if this does not please you, I think that, if any harm to souls should result from it, the fault will not be mine. May almighty God so reign in your heart that you may in all things reign by his grace. [Col. 0125B] Amen.  
>   
> [Note: The manuscript and Edmund omit “Amen.”]

## LETTER LXXXIX

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO THE BROTHERS OF CANTERBURY

On the return to England greatly desired by the monks of Canterbury.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his most dear lords, brothers, and sons dwelling in the Church of Christ at Canterbury: greeting and the blessing of God—and his own, insofar as he can bestow it.

I gratefully receive, love, and approve your sweet longing for our return, since it proceeds from the sweetness of affection, even if God should wish to arrange matters otherwise than I desire to be with you. For God often orders the life of his servants contrary to what the human mind, however good its intention, desires. As gold is tested in the furnace, so he examines the minds of his elect in the fire of tribulation.

If this should happen to you through his fatherly correction or testing, do not lose heart; rather, as sons, strive to advance through the tribulation itself. It is not unusual for God’s servants in this pilgrimage to be shaken by adversities of many kinds, since they are not of this world. The more they are troubled here, the more they come to know the world and desire to pass from this world into rest.

Therefore I warn and beseech you, as most dear sons, that, if circumstances require it, the more intently the enemy of mankind attempts to scatter you from the state of your religious life, the more earnestly you should gather yourselves together for the service of God. In this way you will fight the enemy more vigorously and obtain God’s help more effectively.

It is not necessary for me to write much to you about these matters, because by God’s grace you know them, and the testimonies of Scripture are present to you. If you are willing to trust him, the wisdom of our lord prior can advise and encourage you.

What you ask me to entrust to the lord prior—the entire care of your souls, privately and publicly, until I return to you—I have done and am doing, as I would for myself. Let him, according to the wisdom God has given him and according to the zeal for God’s house that he carries in his heart, judge and arrange matters, punish and spare, so that souls may be nourished in innocence and, with God’s help, vices may be rooted out and excluded from God’s house as far as possible.

I know that each of you desires absolution from me; but since I cannot now do this for each one individually, I wish, pray, and command for all of you, insofar as I can, the absolution and blessing of God and of myself.

Always love the discipline of your order. Preserve peace among yourselves and obedience to the prior inviolate. May the Lord always be with you. Amen.

## LETTER XC

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO ERNULF

On the same subject.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his reverend and most dear brother, the lord prior ERNULF: greeting and the grace of God.

[Col. 0127B]

The fact that you and our friends are grieved because, on returning from Rome, I did not come to England is the result of affection. But that I seem to be abandoning pastoral care without any reason is not the judgment of religious and wise men to whom I explain the matter, nor do I myself understand it so. For, insofar as it depends on me, I am not abandoning it; but I cannot be present in the place where I ought to exercise it, as you can understand if you pay careful attention.

You have heard with whom, by the Apostle’s command, I cannot communicate without danger to my soul. Since the king shares their communion by communicating with them, I cannot avoid that communion.

Let someone consider what I could do when I come to crown the king, celebrate Mass, and they are present around me. Certainly I cannot expel them; I do not dare to pray with them; I ought not to deprive the king of his customary service, since the lord pope both grants him permission to perform it and commands me to do so if I am present.

If he told me to remain at home and not come to court, and thus, while performing the other good duties of my office, to abstain from communion with evil men, the king would complain, together with all his bishops and princes:

[Note: “Because I do not wish to crown him.” I do not see in what sense Anselm says this, since, before Henry had first recalled him to England, Henry had already assumed the royal insignia, as Anselm himself testifies above in Letter 40. Moreover, as we have shown in the note to Letter 88, these letters were written at Lyons within the year 1105; Henry, however, was anointed king of England in the year 1100, on the day after the Kalends of August, as unanimously attested by Huntingdon, Book VII; Malmesbury, Book V of *The History of the Kings of England*; Florence of Worcester in his *Chronicle*; Hoveden in Part I of his *Annals*; Newburgh, Book I, chapter 3.]

because, by refusing to crown him, I would take away the honor of his crown, which the primate of his kingdom owes him by custom. It will therefore seem just to them, and they will carry it out in practice, that the dignity of our Church be transferred to another church. If this happens while I am alive, in the kingdom, and I am unable to prevent it either personally or through someone else, the intolerable diminishment of our Church will be confirmed.

As for what they say—that one ought not to flee because of a single word when one ought to shed one’s blood for one’s sheep and for the Church of God—I say that the word in question must not be regarded as insignificant, since it contains the grave evils I have already described, into which I cannot in any way involve myself without danger to my soul and detriment to the Church entrusted to me.

In the end, I do not fear the shedding of blood, or any destruction of my body, or the loss of my possessions. If such things happened to me personally, I would gladly endure them for the assertion of truth. But none of these things will fall upon me; rather, if I contended with the king in England, severe oppression would uselessly crush our Church and the people belonging to it, and the multitude of those afflicted would, by cursing me, turn their sufferings into my fault.

It therefore seems better to me that, in my absence, whatever tribulation cannot be avoided should rage in England, than that, through my presence and endurance, some evil custom should be confirmed for the future, or that a multitude of people should lament, as they watched me, that they were suffering tribulation on my account.

If it is objected that the loss of souls resulting from my absence would be greater than the temporal evil that would result from my presence, and that therefore the latter should be disregarded for the sake of the former, I have already said that, if it came upon me, I would preserve steadfast patience.

But since we must not do evil so that good may come, I ought not to draw every kind of evil upon innocent people so that good may come to the souls of others.

Last year, when they threatened to expel me, I said that I would not leave because of the care and obedience imposed upon me. But I said this for the sake of those who made the threat, so that I would not leave merely because of their words, not because I had any confidence that it would be useful to remain. As soon as discord and contention appeared between the king and me, bodily evils would likewise flare up, while spiritual goods would grow completely cold.

The charge brought against me—that I had cunningly defamed the king and his kingdom, and the bishop of Lincoln, not openly myself but secretly through our monks—is certainly false, because no one was instructed by me to do this.

Nor do our own brothers Eadmer and Alexander, who are especially accused of this, know it to be as it is alleged.

[Note: The manuscript reads *Dinerus*; the printed text has *Edmerus*, Eadmer.]

You know that informers, adding great things to small ones, are usually liars. Indeed, before we came to Rome, many things were being said about England both inside and outside Rome.

In all these matters, neither by myself nor through wiser men can I follow a better course than to await God’s ordering and entrust the matter to his judgment.

Know this, however: my intention is, with God’s help, never to become the man of any mortal, nor to promise faith to anyone by oath.

You ask our advice about what you should do among, and with, those whose communion the lord pope has forbidden me. The matter is so uncertain that it is less difficult not to associate with those with whom the king associates, especially since the pope imposed this prohibition of communion upon me alone at Rome.

I do not dare to command you to associate with those with whom I do not associate. But if you remain as I left you, I do not blame you at all. You cannot quarrel with the entire kingdom, nor are you participants in the malice of those who may ask you to do something unsuitable to your honesty and religious profession.

Prepare yourselves in advance, lest threats, flattery, or any cunning persuade you to do something of which you will later repent.

Do not abandon the counsel and care of the brothers, whatever may happen, for God’s sake and for the sake of love of neighbor, unless violence expels you from the Church. If adversities and tribulations arise, then be stronger, and do not fail your brothers in temptation.

If anyone demands from one of the monks of our Church an oath, a bond of faith, or any agreement contrary to the order for the sake of retaining some authority—which we call obedience—consider the matter and, as far as you can and as far as you know, turn away the evil.

[Note: The manuscript reads “to turn away the evil”; the printed text has “turn away the evil.”]

Whatever the future may bring, I commend you and all our brothers, together with everything belonging to our Church, to God’s protection.

## LETTER XCI

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO ANTONY, SUBPRIOR

He praises and admonishes him.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his most dear brother and son ANTONY, subprior: greeting and blessing.

I rejoice and give thanks to God and to you for the good zeal you possess, because you willingly observe your order and earnestly strive that others may observe it. I pray, as I have often prayed, that you persevere in this good purpose, because it is pleasing to God and you will receive a good reward from him.

There is something about which I once heard certain people complain. They say that sometimes, when a complaint is made in your presence about certain negligences that can be understood without evil intention and attributed merely to the fault of frivolity, your affection interprets them before the audience as evidence of an evil suspicion. Such things include gestures, looks, and similar matters, in which no certainty of malice can be detected.

I therefore warn you, my beloved one whom I love, and advise you, as a most dear son, not to do this unless the matter is so clear that it cannot be excused from malice. For it causes great harm.

You can sharply punish a fault merely as a violation of the order, while turning away every evil suspicion when it cannot be proven. In this way they will love you and correct themselves without shame. Farewell.

## LETTER XCII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO GONDULF

He gives thanks to the bishop for his good services.

ANSELM, by God’s ordering archbishop, to his reverend and most dear fellow bishop GONDULF: greeting and whatever is best and possible.

I give you great thanks for your good deeds, but much greater thanks for your good will, which always desires to do more than it can. I love and praise your good desire for our return and your counsel proceeding from true affection; but I do not dare to promise anything certain about the fulfillment of that same desire. I commend myself and everything concerning me to God’s ordering, to which all things are subject.

I pray to him, and ask all my friends to pray, that he may dispose me according to his good pleasure and never permit me to seek my own will apart from his will.

Know this: I hope in God, and it is my intention never knowingly to do anything contrary to episcopal integrity for the sake of returning to England. I would rather disagree with human beings than, by agreeing with them, disagree with God.

I briefly indicated in my letter to the prior what you ask—what you should do if my lord the king and I do not agree. For the present I say only this: let no threat, promise, or cunning extort from your religious profession either homage, an oath, or a bond of faith.

If anyone demands any of these things, let this be your response:

> “I am a Christian, I am a monk, I am a bishop; therefore I wish to keep faith with everyone according to what I owe to each person.”

Whatever else may be said to you, add nothing to these words and subtract nothing from them that departs from this meaning.

I say the same about myself, and, with God’s help, I do not wish either to add anything beyond this or to take anything away from it.

Greet your sons and ours, as you know how, and pray that they may remember us.

## LETTER XCIII

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

Worthy of a royal heart and full of holy affections.

To the truly supreme lord and father ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury by the grace of God, MATHILDA, queen of the English, his humble servant, offers the service of supreme devotion and servitude.

Turn, holy lord, merciful Father, my mourning into joy, and surround me with gladness. Behold, lord, your humble servant, prostrate on the knees of your mercy, stretching out imploring hands toward you, asking for the affection of your customary kindness.

Come, lord, come and visit your servant. Come, I say, Father, and soothe my sighs, wipe away my tears, lessen my sorrows, remove my mourning. Fulfill my desire; favor my prayers.

But, you will say, “I am forbidden by the law, and, bound by the constraints of certain decrees of my elders, I do not presume to transgress them.” What then, Father? Did that teacher of the nations, the vessel of election, while he labored wholly to abolish the law, not offer sacrifices in the Temple, lest those who had believed from the circumcision should take offence? Did he who condemned circumcision not himself circumcise Timothy, so that he might become all things to all people? What then will the son of mercy do—your disciple, who, in order to redeem servants, offered himself to death?

Do you not see—behold, do you not see—your brothers, your fellow servants, the people of your Lord, already enduring shipwreck, already collapsing at the very end? Yet you neither come to their aid, nor extend your right hand, nor expose yourself to the danger.

Did not the Apostle wish to be anathema from Christ for the sake of his brothers? Bend, therefore, good lord and pious Father, this severity; and, if I may say so in your peace, soften this iron breast.

Come and visit your people, and among them your servant, who longs for you with all the inward parts of her being. Find a way by which neither you, the shepherd who leads, may give offense, nor the rights of royal majesty be dissolved.

But if these things cannot stand together, at least let the Father come—let him come—to his daughter, the lord to his servant, and teach her what she ought to do. Let him enter to her before she departs from the world.

For if it should happen that I do not see you before I die, I fear—I speak impudently—that even in that land of the living and joyful every opportunity for rejoicing will be cut off from me.

You are my joy, my hope, and my refuge. My soul is like dry land without water before you. Therefore I have stretched out my hands toward you, so that you may flood its dryness with the oil of exultation and moisten it with the dew of your innate sweetness.

But if neither my tears nor the public prayers move you, then, setting aside my royal dignity, abandoning my insignia, I will lay down my fasces, despise my diadem, trample underfoot purple and linen, and go to you overcome with grief.

[Note: “I will embrace your footprints and kiss your feet.” I ask the reader not to suppose that these are merely words and utterances. For what that most modest queen promised Anselm, she fulfilled in the same year, and, as is credible, in other cases as well. I have Matthew Paris as a witness, reporting it in the year 1105 of his *Greater History*:

> “At that same time David, brother of Mathilda, queen of the English, came to England to visit his sister. When, one night, he had been summoned by her into her bedchamber, he found the house full of lepers. The queen, standing in their midst, laid aside her cloak, girded herself with a linen cloth using both hands, and, after water had been brought, began to wash their feet and wipe them with the cloth; then, holding their feet with both hands, she began most devoutly to kiss them. Her brother said to her: ‘What are you doing, my lady? Surely, if the king knew of this, he would never deem your mouth worthy to kiss with his lips, polluted as it was by the filth of lepers’ feet.’ She smiled and replied: ‘Who does not know that the feet of the eternal King are to be preferred by the lips to those of a mortal king? Behold, my dearest brother, I summoned you for this reason: that by my example you might learn to do such things. Please do what you see me doing.’”

Thus far Matthew Paris. We would have added some further details if the book written about her life had come into our hands; William of Jumièges mentions it in Book VIII, chapter 10, of his *History of the Norman Dukes*. The Victor manuscript has the following reading:

> “How great was the holiness and knowledge, both secular and spiritual, of the two queens, namely Margaret and Mathilda, the book written about their lives describes in full discourse.”

This passage of Jumièges provides an opportunity to remind the reader of the knowledge of divine and human matters in which Mathilda excelled, and which these and other letters of hers to Anselm sufficiently testify to, lest anyone suppose that they were written merely in her name. William of Malmesbury agrees with Jumièges, Book I of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, in the following sense: “She exercised a woman’s heart in letters also.”]

I will embrace your footprints and kiss your feet, and I will not be turned away, even if Gehazi comes, except when the fullness of my desire has been fulfilled. May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and your understanding, and make you abound in the inward mercies of compassion.

[Col. 0133A]

## LETTER XCIV

### HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

He grieves that Anselm stubbornly resists him. He indicates that he has sent to the apostolic see and meanwhile consents that Anselm should have suitable provision from the benefice of the Church of Canterbury.

HENRY, king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and friendship.

You informed me that you could not come to me or be with me as your predecessor Lanfranc was with my father for many years. I am therefore very grieved that you are unwilling to do so, because, if you had wished to do it, I would gladly have received you, and I would have granted you all the honors, dignities, and friendships that my father granted your predecessor.

The apostolic lord has sent me letters containing requests and admonitions concerning certain matters. Therefore I intend to send my legates to Rome, to respond to the lord pope there according to the counsel of God and of my barons, and to seek what I must seek. After I receive the pope’s response, I will inform you of what God grants me.

Meanwhile I will consent that you should have suitable provision from the benefice of the Church of Canterbury, although I do this unwillingly, because I would have wished to have no mortal man in my kingdom more willingly with me than you—unless this disposition had remained in you, as Bishop Robert of Lincoln and William testify.

[Col. 0133C]

## LETTER XCV

[Note: Collated with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO HENRY

A reply to the preceding letter.

To HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English and his lord, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service and prayers.

In the letter of your highness that I recently received, your dignity conveyed to me your friendship and that you would wish to have no mortal man in your kingdom more willingly than me, if I were willing to be with you in the way Archbishop Lanfranc was with your father.

I give thanks for your friendship and good will.

To what you say about your father and Archbishop Lanfranc I reply that neither at my baptism nor in any ordination of mine did I promise that I would observe the law or custom of your father or of Archbishop Lanfranc, but rather the law of God and of all the orders I have received.

Therefore, if you wish me to be with you in such a way that I may live according to the law of God and my order, and if you restore to me, according to that same law of God, everything you have taken from my archbishopric after I departed from you—things which, if I were present, you ought not to take against my will—and if you promise this to me, I am ready to return to you in England and to serve God, you, and all those entrusted to me, according to the office imposed upon me by God, with his help.

Indeed, I do not wish to be with or serve any other mortal king or prince so willingly. But if you are unwilling to accept this, you will do what pleases you; I, for my part, with God’s consent, will not deny his king.

Nor do I dare to do so, since I ought not to keep silent before you about the fact that God will require from you not only what royal power owes him, but also everything belonging to the ministry of the primate of England.

That burden is too heavy for you to bear, and you ought not to be displeased by what I say. No one has more to gain than a king by submitting himself to the law of God, and no one withdraws himself from his law more dangerously.

For sacred Scripture says—not I:

> “The mighty will suffer mighty torments, and a severe judgment awaits the powerful” (Wisdom 6:7).

May God avert this from you!

In the answer you have now given me twice, I understand nothing except, if I may say so, a certain delay that benefits neither your soul nor the Church of God.

Therefore, if you continue to delay giving a definite answer to these matters, I, because the cause is not mine but God’s, entrusted to me by him, fear that I may delay too long in raising my cry to God.

I therefore pray and beseech you not to force me, grieving and unwilling, to cry out:

> “Rise up, O God; judge your cause” (Psalm 73:22).

May almighty God quickly turn your heart toward his will, so that after this life he may bring you into his glory.

## LETTER XCVI

### MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

She explains how greatly Anselm’s letter rejoiced her.

To the piously remembered Father and deservedly revered lord, ANSELM, archbishop, MATHILDA, queen of the English by the grace of God, the least of his holy servants, perpetual salvation in Christ.

I offer countless thanks to your unceasing goodness, which, not forgetting me, has deigned through the letter you presented to make your absent presence present.

When the clouds of sadness with which I was enveloped had been driven away, a stream of your words passed over me like a ray of new light. I embrace the little letter sent by you in place of the Father, cherish it in my breast, draw it as near as I can to my heart, read aloud the words flowing from the sweet fountain of your goodness, reconsider them in my mind, reflect upon them in my heart, and store what I have reflected upon in the innermost sanctuary of my heart.

Among all the matters which you commend worthily, I marvel only at what your excellent discernment inserted concerning your nephew.

For I do not judge that I act differently toward your own people and toward mine—that is, differently toward mine than toward mine. For they are yours by birth and mine by adoption and affection.

The consolation of your writing strengthens my patience, creates and preserves my hope; it raises me when I fall, supports me when I slip, gladdens me when I grieve, calms me when I am angry, and pacifies me when I weep.

For, frequently and secretly advising me, it promises me the daughter’s return to the Father, the servant’s return to the lord, and the sheep’s return to the shepherd.

The confidence I possess in the prayers of good men likewise promises this, as does the goodwill that I carefully investigate and weigh from the heart of my lord.

His disposition toward you is more composed than most people think. With God’s consent, and with whatever suggestions I can offer, it will become more favorable and harmonious toward you.

What he presently permits to be done for you from your revenues, he will permit to be done in the future in the same way, and better and more fully, when circumstances and time demand it.

Although he holds for himself more than I judge equitable—[a gloss added in the margin: “more than is fitting”—] I nevertheless ask the abundance of your piety not to turn the sweetness of your affection away from him because of the bitterness of human resentment, which is not ordinarily present in you; indeed—

[Apparatus and editorial notes omitted above, translated: At [Col. 0125B], the manuscript and Edmund read *servati* (“having preserved”) for printed *servata* (“preserving”); Edmund reads *votis* (“prayers/wishes”) for *vobis* (“to you”); and the manuscript and Edmund omit “Amen.” Letter LXXXIX is “collated with the same manuscript.” In its address, the manuscript reads “Anselm, called archbishop of Canterbury, to the lords,” for “Anselm, archbishop, to the lords”; it reads “dwelling … and blessing” for “dwelling … greeting and blessing.” It reads *dilectionis vestrae procedit* (“proceeds from your affection”) for *dilectionis procedit*; “the mind, although” for “the human mind, although”; “grace, and you” for “by God’s grace you”; and *Sico quia* for *Scio quia*.

At [Col. 0127C], the manuscript reads *possum, cum* (“I can, when”) for *possim, cum* (“I could, when”), and *praecipit, si mihi praecipit* (“commands, if he commands me”) for *praecipit, si mihi dixit* (“commands, if he told me”). The note on “because I do not wish to crown him” adds that the editor cannot see in what sense Anselm says this: before Henry first recalled him to England he had already assumed the royal insignia, according to Anselm himself in Letter 40; these letters were written at Lyons within 1105, whereas Henry was anointed king of England in 1100, the day after the Kalends of August, as Huntingdon, Book VII; Malmesbury, Book V of *The History of the Kings of England*; Florence of Worcester’s *Chronicle*; Hoveden, Part I of the *Annals*; and Newburgh, Book I, chapter 3, unanimously attest. The manuscript reads “because I have already said” for “which I have already said”; “into England” for “in England”; “which is known” for “which will occur”; and “upon me, every kind” for “upon every innocent person, every kind.”

At [Col. 0129D], the editorial note on Eadmer and Alexander states: “And Alexander, who especially, etc.” This Alexander, also repeatedly mentioned by William of Malmesbury among the archbishops of Canterbury, especially where he writes about Anselm, was a monk of Canterbury; he dedicated to Anselm, nephew of our Anselm, Book I, compiled from the sayings of Archbishop Anselm and divided into nineteen chapters, as listed in century 10 of the catalogue of British writers. The manuscript reads *Dinerus* for *Edmerus*; “religious profession not” for “your religious profession not”; “your Church” for “our Church”; and “to turn away evil” for “turn away evil.”

Letter XCI is collated with the same manuscript; its manuscript reads “can be imputed to the fault” for “imputed to the fault.” Letter XCII is likewise collated with that manuscript; its manuscript reads *de affectu* (“concerning the feeling”) for *de effectu* (“concerning the outcome”). Letter XCIII is collated with the same manuscript. Its manuscript reads “soothe my sighs” for “soothe my sighs [with ‘my’ expressed]”; *nexibus tentus seniorum* (“bound by the bonds of certain elders”) for *vinculis tentus servorum* (“bound by the chains of certain servants”); *circumcidit* (“did he circumcise?”) for *non circumcidit* (“did he not circumcise?”); *labentem* (“falling”) for *labantem* (“tottering”); and *rigeas* (“may you moisten”) for *riges* (“you moisten”).

At [Col. 0133D], the manuscript reads “from you, which” for “after I departed from you, which”; *minus est* (“is less”) for *nimis est* (“is too much”); *subtrahet* (“will withdraw”) for *subtrahit* (“withdraws”); and “and after” for “so that after.” In Letter XCVI, the manuscript reads “forgetting me indeed” for “not forgetting me,” and *expulsus* for *expulsis*. The text has a doubtful added *Deo* (“with God’s consent”) before “and with whatever suggestions I can offer,” and a doubtful added *decet* (“is fitting”) after “more than I judge equitable.”]
before God, for him, for me, for our common offspring, etc. That common offspring was Matilda, daughter of this same-named Matilda, queen of the English, born from the legitimate and chaste bed of Henry I—not from incestuous intercourse, as Matthew Paris and Polydore assert, and as Arnold Vuion, following them most imprudently, asserts in Book IV, chapter 19 of *The Tree of Life*, on the basis of an uncertain and popular rumor. For they have no more certain testimony than such words as “some say,” “it is reported,” and so forth. Thus they say:

> “They report that Matilda, having been raised among the nuns of Wilton and Romsey and already dedicated to virginity, was compelled—both by the entreaties of her kinsmen and by the importunate love of the new king—to marry; and that she then devoted any offspring she might bear to dreadful curses. It is said that, in accordance with the mother’s imprecation, the sea swallowed her son William when he was crossing to England, and that the disastrous outcomes of the wars deprived Matilda, the daughter, of the kingdom of England which Henry had left to her.”

Truly, these are remarkable predictions—or rather, the products of minds wandering from the truth.

But to return to the matter. Who could believe that Saint Anselm, a man judged by Matthew Paris, Polydore, and Vuion to have been utterly upright, had brought about such an abominable marriage? I therefore do not value them even a hair’s breadth in this matter: partly because, as we have said, they speak from popular report—which is often false—and partly because Polydore wrote four hundred years after Anselm, while Paris wrote one hundred and twenty years later, under King Henry III. It is therefore preferable to listen to contemporary historians of these events.

First, let us hear the librarian of Malmesbury speaking in Book V of *The Kings of the English*:

> “Not long afterward, when his friends, and especially the bishops, advised him that, putting aside the pleasure of mistresses, he should embrace a legitimate marriage, on Saint Martin’s Day he took Matilda, daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots, toward whose love he had long since inclined his heart, placing little value on her dowry, provided only that he might enjoy the embraces he had long desired.”

And again, on pages 92, verso 2, and 93:

> “In order that she might reject an ignoble marriage—namely, Matilda, who had been offered one by her father more than once—she wore the veil that indicated a holy profession. Consequently, when the king took her into his bedchamber, the matter became subject to dispute, and the archbishop could not be induced to consent unless legitimate witnesses were produced who would swear that she had worn the veil at the urging of her nobles, without having made a profession.”

So speaks Malmesbury. He says not a word about a vow violated by Matilda—not even about a vow made—nor about accursed offspring. On the contrary, he calls the marriage legitimate and, in explaining the reason for the temporary wearing of the virginal veil, gives a serious account rather than repeating popular rumor.

Florence of Worcester, William of Jumièges, and Henry of Huntingdon, contemporaries of Malmesbury, do not recall even in a dream any part of this tale, although elsewhere they speak briefly and admirably of Matilda. I must not, moreover, pass over the testimony of Matilda herself, in order to vindicate her own injury; for she may be heard not as an accuser but as a witness. Thus she says above, in Letter 55:

> “By whose [namely, Anselm’s] blessing I have been consecrated to a legitimate marriage; by whose prayers, with God’s approval, I am to be crowned in heavenly glory.”

And Anselm, not forgetting these words, writes back to her:

> “Your gracious dignity remembers in its letter that through me your highness was betrothed in a legitimate marriage and, with me as your consecrating minister, crowned to the exaltation of the kingdom.”

Thus Anselm speaks. If anyone does not believe his words, one might rightly call that person shameless.

Nor can I bring myself to believe that a most holy virgin of singular chastity, had she been bound by a vow, would have consented to so abominable a marriage. And who, moreover, could believe that she had uttered an evil imprecation against her offspring, when Anselm’s prayers in these letters earnestly beseech her salvation?

As for what Paris and Polydore finally suppose—that the unhappy death of William, Matilda’s son, served their purpose, and that England’s being taken away from Matilda, her daughter, did so as well—I attach no importance to it, since I have overturned the arguments on which their case chiefly depends. I am content to have defended Matilda’s innocence in passing.]

before God, for him, for me, for our common offspring, and for the condition of our kingdom, show yourself a devout intercessor. May your holiness always prosper.

## LETTER XCVII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO MATILDA, QUEEN

He replies to her preceding letter.

To the reverend lady, his dearest daughter, MATILDA, by the grace of God queen of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service, prayers, and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as it has any value.

I give immense thanks to your highness, loving you and praying for you, because of the immense holiness of your love for my lowliness, which I have understood from your letter. In it you sufficiently show how great is the affection with which you love me, since you receive and treat my little letter just as you have written.

There also your graciousness so exalts me that what nature denies me, your grace grants, when it declares that those who are mine by birth are yours by adoption and affection. In striving, through your desire for my return, to soften my lord the king’s heart toward me, you are doing what befits you and what I understand to be useful to him.

For if he has any bitterness of heart toward me, I do not know that I have ever deserved it in any way, insofar as it depended on me. And if I have ever served him, he himself knows it, and I think he will not consign it to oblivion. If, then, he hates me to some extent without cause, it is advantageous for him to drive this rancor from himself, lest he sin before God.

You promise me that, concerning our revenues, of which he permits me to retain a certain portion, he will permit me to retain more and better in the future. I should therefore not be ungrateful for this goodwill, because, insofar as it lies within your power, you do this out of good will. But there should have been no need for this promise to be made to me, because against my will no prohibition or diminution of those revenues ought to be imposed upon me. And whoever advises him to take anything from them is advising him to commit no minor sin—nor one that ought ever to be tolerated.

For whoever strips a bishop in this way of his possessions cannot in any manner be reconciled to God unless he restores all that belongs to him in full. And know that, as far as I am concerned, the loss of any small part is equivalent to being stripped of the whole. I do not say this out of love of money, but out of love of the justice of God.

Your goodness asks me not to turn my love away from the king, but to intercede for him, for you, for your offspring, and for the condition of your kingdom. This I have indeed done until now; as for the future, I entrust myself to God’s disposition, before whom a son does not bear the iniquity of his father, nor a wife that of her husband.

And I hope in God that I harbor no bitterness of heart against anyone on account of which I would not have God with me. May Almighty God always preserve you and your offspring in his grace.

## 403. LETTER XCVIII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

That he cannot injure his adversary, the count, on account of the wrongs inflicted upon him by that same count.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to WILLIAM, his beloved and loving friend, elect bishop of Winchester: greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as it has any value—and may you always be guided by divine counsel and protected by divine assistance.

Your messenger reported your case, for which he was sent to us, to our reverend lord and father, Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and to me together, just as you instructed; and I showed that same father the letter you sent me. Therefore, at his command, I reply in this letter on behalf of him and myself.

We certainly rejoice and give thanks to God for your steadfastness in the truth, and because you seek no counsel except what may please God and befit your honor and the order to which you have been elected. We examined the entire matter as carefully as we could, with the assistance of other prudent and religious men, and, invoking God to direct us, reached a unanimous judgment concerning the advice you request.

As far as we understand, the substance of that counsel is this: whether, on account of the injustices which the count inflicts upon you, as you have reported, you may serve his brother, King Henry, against Count Robert with the castle that you hold from Count Robert. We understand that this can in no way lawfully be done before God and just men.

For even if the king absolved you from what you owed Count Robert by homage, by a pledged oath, or by some common agreement, he could not absolve you from what, through Christian religion, you owe to God and to your neighbor for God’s sake. Therefore we understand that you ought not to dispossess the aforesaid count of what you hold from him and hand his inheritance over to his enemy.

You must also pay close attention to the fact that your affection has not yet received episcopal consecration. If you were to do what the king demands of you, no one could extinguish the detestable reputation that this action had been undertaken as a purchase of the bishopric, because you feared losing it. Since we are concerned to provide for what is good not only before God but also before human beings, may God turn this away from you and never permit so wicked an example to emerge from you under any pretext.

As for your having received the aforesaid castle from the king, since you were his man, we do not at all understand that this binds you to allow him to use that same castle against the count, provided that you performed homage to him only with the rights and order of your ecclesiastical position safeguarded. Finally, just as no one ought to promise anything against God, so no one ought in any way to fulfill a promise made against God, nor can anyone rightly demand this.

We have ordered certain other matters to be conveyed to you orally through this messenger. The aforesaid lord and father of ours greets you as a friend greets a friend. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX

### MATILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, TO POPE PASCHAL II

She gives thanks for the exhortatory letter sent to her husband.

To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, PASCHAL, MATILDA, by the grace of God queen of the English: may he so administer temporally the rights of apostolic dignity that, together with the sheaves of justice, he may deserve to be enrolled forever in the apostolic senate amid the joys of everlasting peace.

As for the elevation of your holiness, O apostolic man, etc. See under Paschal II, for the year 1118.

[Col. 0138D]

## 404. LETTER C

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO ORDUVIN

He congratulates a monk devoted to his reputation and suggests what he should answer his detractors.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest brother and son ORDUVIN: greeting and blessing.

I give thanks to your affection because you are concerned for my reputation and ask what answer you should give my false slanderers, who seek occasions against me. As you have written to me, they say that I prohibit the king from granting investitures; and, what is worse, that I allow evil and perverse clerics to invade and devastate churches, without opposing them.

They also say that I give churches to laymen. Tell them that they are lying. For I do not personally prohibit the king from granting the investitures of churches; rather, because I heard the apostolic authority excommunicate in a great council laymen who give those investitures and receive them, and those who consecrate persons receiving them, I do not wish to associate with the excommunicated or to become excommunicated myself.

As for the clerics, I tolerate them oppressing churches not willingly but sorrowfully, and I oppose them so strongly that for this reason I am in exile and stripped of the possessions of my bishopric. The thing they allege about the clerics would not happen if the investitures against which I oppose myself were not taking place.

I do not give churches to laymen when I lease my manors to them; rather, I entrust them to guard the churches, not to install or introduce a cleric in them except through me, our archdeacon, or the prior in the manors of our church.

They therefore reproach me most wickedly for caring about what belongs to others while neglecting my own, because they do not say this out of love of truth but to close the mouth of one who speaks for the truth. Farewell.

## LETTER CI

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO THE BROTHERS OF CANTERBURY

What disposition the monks of Canterbury should have amid the calamities they endure in his absence.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his dearest brothers and sons serving God in the Church of Canterbury in Christ: greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as it can avail.

[Col. 0139C]

I know your longing and the tribulation you are presently enduring, as well as the greater tribulation you fear in the future. In this matter no better counsel can be given you than that you devote yourselves wholly to the service of God.

For whether God is testing you through tribulation, correcting you, or exercising you, your perseverance in living well must always answer these things. Through it you show how strong you are and how truly you love him; through it you appease him; through it you advance by being trained for greater things, so that, once purified, you may deserve higher gifts.

Let idle talk therefore cease among you; let all detraction be rooted out; let murmuring be stifled; let impatience be extinguished; let curiosity about useless things vanish; let idleness be driven away; let muttering be destroyed; let indignation be emptied out; and, for every offense, let agitation of mind be quieted, negligence be removed, and envy be eradicated.

Let whatever disagrees with your way of life be regarded as accursed; let whatever accords with monastic discipline be loved. Let obedience burn brightly, together with zeal and diligence for all the virtues that oppose the vices mentioned above and the others.

Let each one carefully examine his hidden and public life. If he finds anything requiring it, let him hasten to make fitting satisfaction, lest perhaps God scourge the entire congregation on account of his fault. Divine judgments often act in this way, so that a great multitude is disturbed because of one person’s fault. If it were not too lengthy, many examples could be given.

I shall bring this address of ours to an end, because many of you understand the Scriptures, and because you have our most beloved brother, Lord Prior Ernulf, who knows these things and others and can explain them to you.

May Almighty God deign to correct you from all evils, make you abound in every good thing, and cause you to rejoice in his kingdom after this life. May God’s blessing be upon you, and may he grant you forgiveness of all your sins. Amen.

For the present I do not know when our return to you will take place, but I hope in God that your prayer will not be in vain.

[Col. 0140B]

## LETTER CII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO CERTAIN APOSTATE MONKS

He advises monks who have returned to the cloister not to reject penance out of shame.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his dearest brothers and sons WULFRIC, PHILIP, and WILLIAM: greeting and the blessing of God and his own.

I heard that, through the persuasion of the ancient serpent, whose cunning expelled our first parents from paradise, you abandoned the cloistered paradise and religious way of life, insofar as it concerned you, and I grieved greatly. But I was consoled and rejoiced because God did not close the door of paradise to you so that you could no longer enter it; rather, in his mercy he compelled you to return to the rest that had been left behind.

If, for this mercy that he showed you against your will, you give him thanks, and if you promise correction not only with your mouths before everyone but also in your hearts before God, I shall give thanks to God with you and drive from my heart all the rancor that I conceived on account of your fault.

I therefore admonish you as my sons to drive entirely from your hearts, through repentance before God, that depraved and diabolical will which you had. After God has called you back to himself, do not, on account of any shame, confuse your minds without discretion. Rather, trusting that God kindly receives the penitent, rest in good will and love for your order.

It commonly happens that, when the devil—through God’s mercy and while God defends his servant—cannot complete what he began, he turns to another stratagem. The person whom he cannot overthrow in the manner in which he began, he overthrows through the impatience of excessive shame.

Before God alone, marvel at how you could have been willing to do this and be ashamed; but before human beings, strengthen and encourage yourselves through a good conscience. By a good way of life show that every depraved will is foreign to you. In this way you will ensure that others retain no memory of what you did and no evil suspicion of you.

[Col. 0141A]

May Almighty God absolve you from your past faults and preserve you forever from every sin in the future. Amen.

## 405. LETTER CIII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO WARNER

That he should not despise the holy purpose he began through fear of death, but should advance in it through holy love; he entrusts him to Prior Ernulf’s care and counsel and advises him to read his letter to Lanzon.

ANSELM, archbishop, to WARNER: greeting and God’s blessing—and his own—and may the best completion follow a good beginning.

Blessed is God in his gifts and holy in all his works. By his grace he visited you, dearest son, when your soul and body were in danger of death, and in his mercy recalled you to life in both respects.

Consider and reflect on how great a sign of his love God gave you when, although you were not merely fleeing from him but also despising him and opposing him toward your own death, he compelled you with paternal care to return to him and desire to serve him.

Never think that what you have begun is of less value because you were compelled by fear of death and drawn not by spontaneous will. For God does not weigh so much by what beginning or occasion a person starts something good as by the will and devotion with which he preserves the grace of God bestowed upon him.

The apostle Paul was compelled to convert to the Christian faith; but because he preserved the faith with his whole heart and completed his course in it, he showed us in his words, with joy, that the crown of righteousness had been laid up for him.

You have with you my dearest brother, Lord Prior Ernulf, who is present and can advise you no less than I can, both in knowledge and in willingness, and can absolve you with my authority. I entrust you to God and to him; after God, entrust yourself to him, in accordance with our counsel and command.

By God’s grace you are educated. Turn the knowledge that God allowed you to acquire through love of the world toward love of God, from whom you have whatever you possess, so that in place of the earthly glory toward which your studies made you yearn, you may attain eternal glory, which you either despised or desired only lukewarmly.

Diligently observe the customs of the order you have entered, as though they had been established by God, because none is useless and none superfluous.

I advise you to seek the letter I wrote to Lord Lanzon when he was a novice (Book I, Letter 29). There you will find how you should conduct yourself at the beginning of your conversion and how to answer the temptations assailing a novice.

As far as I can, I pray that God may grant you absolution and remission of all your sins, and may nourish you in the purpose you have begun so that he may lead you to eternal glory. Amen.

## LETTER CIV

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO RAYNALD

He consoles a devout man who, after being unwillingly forced into a bishopric, rejected it for the sake of truth.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to RAYNALD [Raynalmus in the Picard edition; Reinaldus], who wisely places truth before vanity, courageously despises transient glory for the sake of integrity, and manfully overcomes poverty: greeting, and may he always be protected and strengthened by God’s salvation and grace.

Your affection asks me to send you some consolation. I gladly do so, insofar as I understand it to be more fitting for you and more beneficial to you before God.

May your conscience, your virtue, and your perseverance be the consolation of your heart in God’s sight. You acted courageously when you rejected for the sake of truth the bishopric into which you had been unwillingly forced, not according to God’s will.

Do not let your heart expect God to repay you with this reward of virtue because you despised the bishopric for the sake of truth. The virtue you preserved is far more precious than what you rejected for its sake.

You therefore greatly discolor your beauty before God if you expect from him as a reward and consolation something that is worthless and transient. I am not saying that you ought not to have a bishopric or that you did not deserve one; rather, I advise you to rejoice in your conscience over the grace in which God has caused you to stand, and to entrust both your tribulation and your consolation to God’s disposition alone.

Remember what the Holy Spirit says: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26:14).

When you feel necessities and poverty seething around you, then be certain that God is increasing his grace toward you in many ways. I desire this to be your consolation; in this I desire you to strengthen your hope.

“Then the Lord will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday” (Psalm 36:6).

Because I do not know what God intends to do with me, I dare promise nothing from myself for your consolation; but I can show you the will that God has given me and that you have deserved from me. Certainly, if God grants me the opportunity, I shall at some time desire to benefit you both in body and in soul.

May Almighty God cause you, my dearest brother, to rejoice continually in his protection and consolation. Amen.

## LETTER CV

### TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

He exhorts him to persevere with the firmness of spirit with which he began in observing ecclesiastical sanctions.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his beloved and loving brother WILLIAM, bishop of Winchester: greeting, and may the grace of God preserve you in all things.

Although by God’s grace I trust in your steadfastness, nevertheless, because I continually desire that you never be bent away from uprightness but always advance toward better things, the abundance of my heart delights in exhorting your affection.

All who offer counsel against the sincerity of integrity and justice are poisonous serpents, children of the ancient serpent. I therefore ask you as a beloved friend, and advise you as a dearest son, that if anyone wishes to counsel you in such a way against God’s counsel, you never allow him so to hiss into your ears—by promising, threatening, flattering, or pleading—that he poisons your mind by persuasion.

You know that the Lord rejects the counsels of princes, whereas the Lord’s counsel remains forever. I say this because I do not doubt that the ancient enemy, whom you have confounded by persevering courageously in uprightness, is seeking by many kinds of cunning how he might overturn the state and reputation of your integrity and turn the praise you have attained, with God’s help, into ridicule—which God forbid.

I do not specify anything in particular against which you should beware, because I consider nothing that in any way discolors integrity to be negligible before God.

May Almighty God always and everywhere so protect and fortify your life in all things that none of your enemies may in any way laugh at any blemish in your beauty. Amen.

[Col. 0143B]

## 406. LETTER CVI

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO GUNTER, CANON OF SAINT-QUENTIN

Although he is most devoted to quiet, if he has been elected he ought nevertheless to serve the brothers in true obedience and undertake the burden of the abbacy.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved brother and friend GUNTER, canon of Saint-Quentin: greeting, and may he always be guided by God’s counsel.

As I hear, your brothers, the canons of Beauvais of the Church of Saint-Quentin, do not wish rashly but for many reasons to remove Lord Odo, now called your abbot, from this prelacy and substitute your fraternity in his place. But they fear that your religious devotion, because of your love of the quiet which you now enjoy, may be unwilling readily to consent to their intention.

Since they know that you love my humility and hope that you will trust my counsel more than that of certain others, they ask me to reveal to your affection what I think about the matter.

Certainly, if in the body of Christ we are mutually members of one another, especially in one church of religious persons, whoever does not permit or wish the other members and the whole body to use him as one of its members, I do not see how he can prove himself a member of that body; and if that body is the body of Christ, how can he show himself to be a member of Christ?

There is also this consideration: no one, if he conducts himself rightly, wishes to live for himself alone. Rather, just as he desires and believes that, if he is a member of God, all the advantages of the other members will be his in the future life, so he ought to wish that whatever good exists in him should belong to the other members in the present life.

Therefore, insofar as I can, I advise and beseech you, dearest brother and friend, that if your entire congregation, or the better part of it, after taking the advice of the reverend bishops Ivo of Chartres and Galon of Paris—who were your fathers and raised you—has earnestly elected you to the position I mentioned above, you should not entirely refuse or prove impervious to persuasion.

For I consider it more beneficial for you to preserve the quiet of contemplation through love in your mind and the obedience of fraternal charity in action than to choose contemplation alone while despising the prayers and usefulness of others. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII

### ANSELM TO MATILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

Concerning the queen’s goodwill toward him.

To the lady and daughter beloved in God, MATILDA, queen of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and God’s blessing—and his own, insofar as it can avail—and faithful prayers together with service.

In her letter your highness made me as joyful as she gave me good hope concerning herself. For a sure hope of correction is ordinarily found in the humble acceptance of correction and admonition.

I therefore give thanks to God, who gives you the good will that you expressed to me in your reply; and I give you thanks because you preserve it with a loving affection. I therefore ask God to preserve and increase what he mercifully inspires in you, so that when your soul leaves your body and is presented before his sight, it may receive from him the reward of eternal happiness.

If your prudence needed instruction about how you ought to live in order to please God, I would strive, according to my ability, to show you. But since, by God’s grace, I know that you are not ignorant in your understanding of how to distinguish good from evil, I ask, beseech, and admonish you that this be the unfailing purpose of your heart: in all your actions, great and small, choose rather what you judge to please God more.

In the same letter you expressed with sufficiently devout and gentle affection your desire for my return to England. Yet I do not see that the person in whose power my return chiefly lies, as far as human beings are concerned, is in this matter in harmony with God’s will; nor is it beneficial for my soul to be at odds with God’s will.

I fear that he may understand only late that he has strayed from the right path by despising God’s counsel and following the counsels of princes, which the Lord rejects. Nevertheless, I am certain that someday he will understand.

May Almighty God, according to his will, someday gladden your excellence and my lowliness through our mutual sight, and multiply in you the gifts of his grace.

## LETTER CVIII

[Compared with the same manuscript.]

### ANSELM TO FARMAN, ORDUVIN, AND BENJAMIN

[Col. 0144D]

Why he cannot grant them permission to come to him; he answers each of their difficulties.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his dearest sons FARMAN, ORDUVIN, and BENJAMIN: greeting and God’s blessing—and his own.

I know, dearest sons, that the abundance of your affection makes you desire my presence, so that you may open to me what you carry in your hearts, as sons do to a father, and receive counsel concerning each of your anxieties.

But although it is good and praiseworthy to have good zeal, if it is not according to knowledge it is not acceptable to God. You wish to obtain my permission to come to me, but it is certainly true that this is more difficult—indeed, more impossible—than you realize: the road is too long, the people foreign, and the journey dangerous. Monks from the same land are captured and badly treated; their horses, and whatever they possess, are taken away. A great deal of money is necessary, the labor is severe, and there are many disturbances. The advantage is not so great that others would not judge me blameworthy if I readily gave my consent to this.

If you wish to inform me about the evils that are taking place in England and in the Church, which you see and hear, I know enough of them and cannot correct them. Tell God about them, and pray while awaiting him to correct them.

If you wish to seek counsel about your souls, you have with you our venerable brother and son, Lord Prior Ernulf, a spiritual man in whom, by God’s grace, both good will and wisdom abound. I left him to you in my place, as though he were another me. Have recourse to him as to me; entrust yourselves to him as to me; receive him as you would receive me.

I grant the same concerning Lord Bishop Gundulf, if anyone wishes to do so.

To you, son Farman, who ask permission to live elsewhere because, as you say, you cannot save your soul amid so many disturbances, I say that, as long as I cannot govern or gather you, it is not fitting for me to begin dispersing you. Therefore it is not advisable either that you request this or that I do it.

Finally, if I grant permission to one or two either to leave the Church to live elsewhere or to leave the kingdom to come to me, there are so many others with the same reason that it could not be done without great scandal or great dissolution.

Let whoever wishes this therefore have the discretion and patience that the others have, so that together, through your patience, you may possess your souls. [p. 407]

To you also, son Benjamin, who terribly adjure me and plead the destruction of your soul, I point out—since I ought and wish to advise him whose soul is concerned—that you ought not to have done so indiscreet a thing, nor to have exposed my soul and your soul to so grave a danger.

For when, insofar as it depends on you, you drive a soul into such danger, be certain that this is not healthy counsel for your soul. What you ask cannot be done for any rational reason. It might perhaps be done through indiscreet and disorderly rashness.

For it is not reasonable to follow wherever an impulse of the mind drives us, even when our intention is good, without discretion. I cannot understand how your soul could be in danger of destruction merely because you cannot speak with me. For even if I were somewhere in this world—or in the next life—where you could in no way approach me, you would still have no reason to despair of your soul’s salvation.

I therefore beseech and advise you, dearest son, to endure God’s disposition without scandal to your soul; and, insofar as you see him ordering us and what pertains to us, strive to save yourself as a prudent man who places his hope in God.

As for what you, brother and son Orduvin, allege against me—that I do not return to England—know that I do not flee death, the cutting off of limbs, or any kind of torture, but rather sin and disgrace to the Church of God, especially the Church of Canterbury.

For if I were to return in such a way that it was not clear that the king ought not to strip me and invade the possessions of the Church entrusted to me, as he has done, I would confirm, by my example, a wicked—indeed servile and most evil—custom for myself and my successors. May God turn this away from me.
