Unless, therefore, he wishes to acknowledge his sin and make satisfaction to God for what he has sinned and continues to sin against me, so that neither he nor his successor can say to me or to my successors, on the basis of my example, that he is doing this by custom, I do not at all understand how I could agree with him or return to him for the honor of God and of our Church, and the salvation of my soul.

If what ought to be done to me is done, I shall do what I ought for the honor of God.

May the peace of the Lord, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds (Philippians 4:7).

## LETTER CIX

### ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH
He rebukes the king because he was unjustly exacting money from the priests of England who had violated the council held by Anselm at London, although the punishment of this offense belongs only to the bishops.

**To Henry, his dearest lord, by the grace of God king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful prayers with faithful service.**

It is my duty, if I hear that you are doing something which is not good for your soul, not to keep silent about it before you, lest—God forbid—God become angry both with you, if you do what does not please him, and with me because of my silence. I hear that your excellence is exercising vengeance [Col. 0146D] upon the priests of England and exacting a penalty from them [Note: [Col. 0145D] “He exacts a penalty.” *Forisfactura*, *forisfactio*, and *forisfactum* are commonly synonymous. Here, however, *forisfactura* signifies a monetary fine imposed by a prince or judge upon an offender: “a fine in punishment for an offense.” Thus some advise that Anselm’s words here be understood as follows: “For I tell you that you ought to fear greatly, because money received in this way—to say nothing of how much it harms the soul—will not, when spent, help earthly affairs as much as it will disturb them.” [Col. 0146D] The same word is used again in the laws of William the Conqueror, in Roger of Hoveden, page 342, column 2: “But if he does otherwise, let him pay the satisfaction-fine.” On the following page: “Let it be paid from the property of that man who brought the accusation, which is called *scapus*, and in addition the king’s penalty.” On folio 345, page 2: “*Sacca* is this: if anyone has accused a particular person by name of anything, and that person has denied it, the penalty for the proof or denial, if it arises, shall belong to him.” [Col. 0147C] In the title “Concerning those who have the king’s peace by writ,” and in the immediately following title: “Of these eight pounds the king shall have one hundred shillings, and the count of the county, who has the third penny of the penalty, fifty [Col. 0147D] shillings.” Again, in the title “Concerning thieves killed for theft”: “From that very day, within fifteen days, let the killer return three penalties to the bishop.” The passage in chapter 18, distinction 2, of the manuscript *Course of Normandy* in our library seems to have the same meaning: “All movable penalties belong to the duke. Movable penalties are the goods, or movable property, of those who have been condemned by judgment.” Thus the Normans in their *Course*.

“Moreover, *forisfactura* is sometimes used for the crime itself, or for a sin or violence committed against another, as in the title “Concerning the times and days of the peace of the lord king” in the same laws of William: “The king shall compel the wrongdoer to make amends to the person against whom he committed the offense.”

“In the same place *forisfactum* is also used synonymously beside the latter meaning of *forisfactura*, in these words: “If anyone who has incurred the king’s penalty should ask the king’s mercy for his offense.”

“John Gerson, in his treatise against the exceedingly obscene poem of John of Meung, commonly called the *Romance of the Rose*, also uses this word, introducing Chastity as supplicating in the following manner: “Let a remedy be provided, and a brief provision made against the countless offenses which he has inflicted upon me and still does not cease to inflict.” [Col. 0148C]

“To this may also be added the verb *forisfacere* (“to do wrong”) and the participle *forisfactus* (“having done wrong”), derived from our vernacular words *forfaict*, *forfaire*, and *forfaicture*, meaning “sin,” “to sin,” and “a sin.” The word seems to be derived from the adverb *foris* (“outside”), so that *forisfacere* would be, as it were, “to do outside,” since sin makes or casts people outside justice and what is right. We might also refer its formation to the monosyllable *for*, which often means “badly,” so that *forisfacere* would mean “to do evil.”

“Malmesbury mentions these words and the monetary fine imposed by Henry upon the clerics who violated the council of London in his account of Anselm.

“Furthermore, it may be inferred from Florence of Worcester and Matthew Paris that this letter was sent from Normandy in 1107, since they record that in that year a conference was held between the king and the archbishop at Eagle Castle, as Anselm indicates in the following letter, 112. Compare Letters 111, 112, and 115.”]

because they did not observe the decree [Col. 0147A] of the council which, with your favor, I held at London with the other bishops and religious persons. This is something hitherto unheard-of and unprecedented in the Church of God, whether on the part of any king or of any prince. For according to the law of God, the punishment of such an offense belongs only to the individual bishops within their dioceses; or, if the bishops themselves have been negligent in this matter, to the archbishop and primate.

I therefore beg you, as my dearest lord, whose soul I love more than the present life of my body, and I counsel you, as one truly faithful to your body and soul, not to commit so grave a sin against ecclesiastical custom; and, if you have already begun, to desist from it altogether. For I tell you that you ought to fear greatly, because money [Col. 0147B] received in this way—to say nothing of how much it harms the soul—will not, when spent, help your earthly affairs as much as it will afterward disturb them.

Indeed, you know that in Normandy you received me into your peace and restored me to my archbishopric; and since the care and punishment of such an offense especially belong to the archbishopric, because I am a bishop more for spiritual care than for earthly possession, may almighty God direct your heart in this and in your other actions according to his will, so that after this life he may lead you to his glory.

## Letter CX

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0147C]]

**Anselm to Ernulf, prior, and the brothers of Canterbury**

He excuses himself for having informed them only belatedly about the agreement between himself and the king, by which the king restored him to his archbishopric and returned all the property of the Church of Canterbury. Nevertheless, Anselm does not wish to enter England until the king’s envoy has returned from Rome. Meanwhile, having recovered the use of his authority, he deprives of every ecclesiastical benefice all priests who kept women. [Col. 0148A] He permits the count of Meulan, who had promised his support to the Church, to enter the Church.

**Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest brothers and sons, the lord prior Ernulf and the others serving God under him in the Church of Christ at Canterbury: greeting and God’s blessing, and his own, insofar as he can give it.**

The reason I delayed so long in writing to you about what was agreed between the king and me on the eve of the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene was not negligence, but the absence of the opportunity which it is unnecessary to explain.

[Note: “Not through negligence, but through the absence of the opportunity which you show; there is no need to explain it.” The manuscript reads: “not through negligence, but through the absence of the opportunity which there is no need to explain.” [Col. 0147C]]

Know that the king has restored me to our archbishopric and promises that he will return what he has hitherto taken from our revenues. He has shown himself willing to do this with great joy and goodwill, and all who are with him declare that they rejoice in it. [Col. 0148B]

For the king hopes that such agreement will come about between the lord pope and himself before Christmas that I shall be able to be in agreement with both of them in England without offense. For this reason he intends to send his envoy to Rome, so that before the appointed time he may learn the certainty of the matter.

But since the matter has not yet been established with such certainty of peace and concord between them that, if I now entered England, I could confidently expect to remain there in peace, I have preferred to remain outside England for a time, until the aforesaid envoy returns from Rome—so that meanwhile both the affairs of the archbishopric may be in my power and our people may be at peace—rather than at present to thrust myself into uncertainty [Note: The manuscript reads *ad ambiguitatem* (“into uncertainty”) for *in ambiguitatem*.], lest perhaps, because of renewed and irreconcilable discord, I should again have to leave England.

I certainly think that this delay in my return will in no way harm the perfect concord which we hope will come about.

Concerning the priests whom the king commands to possess both churches and women, as they possessed them in the time of his father and of Archbishop Lanfranc: since the king has restored the whole archbishopric to me, and since in the time of his father and of that same archbishop such an execrable union was prohibited by the council, I confidently command, by the authority which I possess from the archbishopric, not only in the archbishopric but throughout all England, that all priests who have kept women be deprived of their churches and of every ecclesiastical benefice.

The lord pope recently sent his greeting and blessing to the count of Meulan, on this condition: that he should be willing to favor the liberty of the Church, which until now he has appeared to resist. Otherwise, he was to be barred from entering the Church, just as had previously been done with him and with his other associates, the king’s counselors, in the letter whose copy I sent you. [Col. 0149A]

But since the same count promised me that he would strive to make the king obey the pope’s commands, I permitted him to enter the Church, from which he had been kept away. As for the others, none is named in the aforesaid letter, nor can I certainly name anyone; and, as I hear, they are all striving for concord between the pope and the king. [Col. 0149B]

With regard to those who have received investitures, and to those who consecrated them, no sentence has been changed.

We give thanks to God because you, lord prior, are recovering from your illness, as you reported, and we pray God to restore you to complete health. May almighty God always protect you by his grace and always cause you to advance toward better things, dearest brothers and sons.

## Letter CXI [Col. 0149C]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0149D]]

**Anselm to Henry, king of the English**

He says that he is not displeased by the king’s envoy’s longer-than-appointed stay in Rome, but by his own longer absence from his flock, especially since the king sets no definite term.

**To his dearest lord Henry, glorious king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.**

Because your greatness greets me in your letters with such honor and with so great an affection of goodwill, I give you great thanks, as I ought.

But although you so earnestly ask me not to be displeased that the envoy whom you are sending to Rome has delayed so long, I certainly ought not, insofar as it lies within me, to disregard your request. Yet the matter concerns God more than me; therefore, with a faithful heart and kindly spirit, I tell you what I ought not to keep silent about. [Col. 0149D]

For me, to be displeased by something—unless I am displeased because of God—is not a great matter. But to be displeasing to God in anything must in no way be taken lightly. Certainly, it is not a small thing in God’s sight that a bishop should be stripped of his property, which, through God’s inspiration, you have now corrected. But God judges it exceedingly serious that a bishop should be separated from his office, and the Church from its bishop, without a cause approved by God.

It is therefore advantageous to your soul that you take care that I, whatever kind of bishop I may be, of the Church which God entrusted to your royal power and to your kingdom to protect, [Col. 0150A] may be restored more quickly, in your peace, and that the opportunity to exercise, according to my ability, the office for which I was placed there may no longer be obstructed.

[Note: Manuscript readings: *aliud displicere* (“to be displeased by something else”) for *aliquid displicere*; *satagitis* for *satagatis*; *qua icunque* for *qualiscunque*; and *quod Deus* for *quam Deus*.]

I must also fear greatly that this displeases God and that the lord pope may justly rebuke me, because, after you and I met together at the castle called Eagle, during so long a period I have not sent him our envoy, through whom he might learn what has been done between us concerning so great a matter and what must be done, and through whom I might receive his counsel and command.

It is therefore dangerous for me to wait a long time for your envoy, whom I understood from your words to be returning from Rome before the coming Christmas, especially since, I do not know by what counsel or for what reason, [Col. 0150B] you now set no term.

Since, then, my concern that I cannot be present to the Church entrusted to me ought to matter more to me than any earthly possession, I beg you to name for me, in your letters, some nearby term at which I may expect your envoy to go to Rome. For I dare not delay—however mildly I put it—beyond the coming Christmas without sending my own envoy.

Farewell.

## Letter CXII

**Anselm to Gundulf, bishop; Ernulf, prior; and others**

He confirms the excommunication, justly pronounced by his archdeacon, against priests who keep women.

**Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend Gundulf, bishop; Ernulf, prior; William, archdeacon of Canterbury; and all those in his diocese who, for the love of God, observe the religious discipline of their order: greeting.**

A proud presumption—execrable to God and hateful to all Christians—of certain men who call themselves priests has recently been reported to me.

Our archdeacon William wrote to me that certain priests under his authority, returning again in their uncleanness to the forbidden women from whom they had been withdrawn by salutary counsel and command, have reverted to them. When the same archdeacon wished to correct them, they utterly despised his admonition and the command which he had the authority to impose.

After summoning several religious and obedient priests, he struck the proud and disobedient with the sword of deserved excommunication. In their bestial madness they despise this excommunication and, insofar as lies within them, do not fear polluting the sacred ministry. [Col. 0150D]

Therefore I, Anselm, although a sinner, archbishop, by the authority which God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit has given me through the archbishopric, confirm the same excommunication imposed by that archdeacon, until satisfaction has been accepted according to his judgment.

## Letter CXIII [Col. 0151A]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0151D]]

**Anselm to Warner**

He praises him for his holy desire for his father’s return and at the same time urges him to be most observant of his order.

**Anselm, archbishop, to Warner, his dearest brother and son: greeting and God’s blessing, and his own.**

For the love which I perceived toward me in your letters, and for your desire for my return, I thank you as a beloved brother and son.

I shall not, with God’s consent, delay my return when, by his arrangement, I understand that I can reasonably make it.

But I earnestly admonish you, and the one whose soul God has entrusted to my care, not to be negligent in learning and observing the order which you have received [Note: The manuscript has *quae accepistis* (“which you [plural] have received”) for *quem accepisti* (“which you [singular] have received”).], but to be attentive with your whole heart to advancing in those things which belong to the perfection of a monk. [Col. 0151B]

For it is true that if a novice monk is lukewarm in his purpose, he will be fervent in the monastic life either only with difficulty or never at all.

Therefore, desire to be found at the time of your death such as you strive daily to show yourself; and, as though you were going to die tomorrow, prepare yourself today to render an account of your life. In this way you will advance from virtue to virtue.

May the Lord direct and protect you.

## Letter CXIV [Col. 0151D]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

**Anselm to Henry, king of the English**

He sends Gislebert of Bec to the king, so that the king may safely trust what must be reported to him. He declares Paschal canonically elected and the other man to be an invader of the apostolic see.

**To Henry, his dearest lord, by the grace of God king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.**

Your highness instructed me in your letters to send you someone from among our familiars to whom you could familiarly entrust whatever you wished to command me.

I therefore send Brother Gislebert, a monk of Bec and my familiar, to whom you may entrust whatever you are pleased to command me, just as you would to me.

He will also inform you how Baldwin and William had already begun their journey to Rome when I received your letter, and what we have heard about the apostolic lord Paschal and about the man who is said to have seized his see by robbery.

I say only this: the apostolic lord Paschal has been canonically elected according to God’s will, and has already been received and confirmed throughout the whole Catholic Church. The other man, the invader of whom there is report, has no election or recognition except from the sons of the devil, enemies of the Church of God.

Therefore we await the falling upon him—if it has not yet fallen—which the Lord spoke: “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15:13).

No Christian ought to be disturbed if the Church of Christ suffers persecution, since Christ himself suffered it and foretold that the same Church would suffer it: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33); and he strengthens it by adding: “But take courage: I have overcome the world” (ibid.). [Col. 0152A]

May almighty God cause you to reign over the English in this life, so that in the life to come you may reign among the angels.

[Note: Manuscript readings: *Domino regi* (“to his lord the king”) for *domino suo*; *cui sic* (“to whom thus”) for *cui sicut* (“just as to me”); *Baldeninus* for *Balduvinus*; *non cecidit* (“has not fallen”) for *nondum cecidit* (“has not yet fallen”); and *vicinandum* [uncertain reading] for *vici mundum* (“I have overcome the world”).]

## Letter CXV [Col. 0152B]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

**Anselm to G., the abbot**

He advises the man elected bishop that, while preserving obedience, he should have his mind shun so great a burden. But to those who elected him he advises that, because he is more worthy, they should compel him to undertake the burden.

**To the dearest lord and father, the reverend abbot G., Brother Anselm: always to will and do what pleases God.**

Your prudence deigns to know the counsel of my littleness concerning the matter under discussion. I therefore first ask the gracious mercy of almighty God to arrange the entire matter according to his good pleasure.

As for our counsel—which I pray may proceed from the face of God—this is what I can best understand.

I advise him, insofar as he can, while nevertheless preserving obedience and pious gentleness, to have his mind shun so great a burden.

But to you and to the others to whom this matter belongs I give this advice: I see no one more suitable; therefore, by asking and commanding him, compel him to undertake it. Thus his conscience will be more secure in God’s sight, since he will see that he has advanced only through the fear of God and holy obedience; and God, as though under an obligation, will bring to a good end what he understands to have been begun for God’s sake alone. [Col. 0152C]

You also will receive a reward from the Judge above, because with pious solicitude you strive to sustain the Church of God through its members.

[Note: The manuscript reads “from you,” rather than “to you.”]

Farewell.

## Letter CXVI [Col. 0152D]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

**Anselm to Odo**

He further inflames him, already kindled, to pursue a purer way of life. His vows to go to Rome or Jerusalem are fulfilled in the monastic profession.

**To the beloved lord and brother in Christ, Odo, Brother Anselm: greeting.**

If your affection, still weighed down by love of the world, were laboring under the thorny anxieties of its riches, it would be necessary to bring back to your mind the words of the Lord: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”

But since you already perceive that the world will pass away, together with its desire; since you no longer love the world or the things that are in the world, but seek the things above and not those upon the earth, I see nothing more appropriate to say to you than what is written: “Son, do not delay turning from day to day”; and: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly.” [Col. 0153A]

Let this brief letter be a certain sign to you that our fraternal service is ready for this purpose.

Those who, while in the world, vowed that they would go to Rome or Jerusalem, if they come to our order and conduct themselves devoutly and obediently, have fulfilled all the vows which they made.

For those who had handed themselves over by vows into God’s portion, after they have handed themselves over wholly to God, must not afterward reclaim any part of themselves for their own portion—unless they wish to steal back into private ownership what they offered to God, and thus become not merely undevout but guilty both of their own renunciation and profession and of their own condemnation.

[Note: The manuscript reads “of your renunciation,” rather than “of their own.” [Col. 0153B]]

## Letter CXVII [Col. 0153B]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript.]

**Anselm to Ernulf, prior, and William, archdeacon**

He instructs them to receive Robert, who has abandoned Judaism and embraced Christianity, with great kindness and to assist him.

**Anselm, archbishop, to the lord prior Ernulf and the archdeacon William: greeting and the blessing of God.**

[Note: Ernulf—that is, the prior of the Church of Canterbury—succeeded Henry, a monk of Bec, to whom Letters 49, 54, 58, and 64 of Book I, as well as several letters of Books II and III, are addressed.

Although he is written *Ernulfus* in Letters 80, 82, 90, 101, and 110 of this book, and in Book II of William of Malmesbury’s *De gestis Anglorum pontificum*, in our manuscript lists, in Roger of Hoveden’s *Annals*, in Florence of Worcester’s *Chronicle*, [Col. 0153C] and in Letter 31 of Ivo of Chartres, he is written *Arnulfus*. The relevant passage reads:

“Arnulf of Beauvais, a monk of the monastery of Saint Symphorian, a prudent and religious man, for a similar reason having left the monastery—for that is how it should be read there, not ‘Canterbury,’ as is clear from the passages above—governs the monastery.”

The monastery of Saint Symphorian was founded to the south by Drogo, forty-third bishop of Beauvais, on a hill opposite the city gate called Saint John’s Gate.

Ivo, whose homeland was Beauvais but who was called of Chartres because he held the bishopric there, and Arnulf’s contemporary, removes certain doubts raised by the two English writers, especially by Malmesbury, who says that Arnulf had first been a monk at the monastery of Saint Lucian, about thirty miles north of Beauvais, in sight of the river Tara flowing past it.

This can easily be excused in the librarian, who, having learned that Arnulf had formerly been a monk at Beauvais, perhaps suspected that it was at Saint Lucian’s, which was much older and more famous than Saint Symphorian’s. Bale, in the second century of his work, in order to adorn his *England* with stolen feathers, categorically denies that Arnulf was at Beauvais, despite Ivo and William of Malmesbury, Arnulf’s contemporaries, and despite our Anselm, who concludes Letter 65 of Book I with the words: “Greet Lord Arnulf of Beauvais.” [Col. 0153D]

After administering the priory, or deanery, of Canterbury honorably and splendidly, Arnulf proved worthy to be placed over the monastery of Saint Peter at Burgh (Peterborough) in England, and finally, after the death of Gundulf—whose episcopate is discussed in our note on a letter of Book I—over the Church of Rochester.

Malmesbury describes how elegantly he fulfilled the duties of an excellent bishop in his account of the bishops of Rochester, where, calculating the years of his episcopate, he says: “He lived in the episcopate for a few days more than nine years; and he died at the age of eighty-four, leaving many monuments of his goodness.”

Malmesbury is supported by the Continuator of Florence of Worcester, Matthew Paris in the *Greater History*, and Roger of Hoveden in his *Annals*. Arnulf finally died in 1124, and indeed at Rome, if Bale—who frequently *ἐμβαλλάων* (“throws things in”)—deserves belief, although the English writers cited above, who were older than Bale, do not say a word about it. [Col. 0154B]

Bale’s account of Arnulf, as woven among the historians, is so various and changeable that, after reading everything, one does not know what one is about to read.

Martin of Poland, in Book IV of *On the Roman Pontiffs*, speaks under Paschal II of a certain heresiarch Arnulf—thus it is read in our manuscript, although the Antwerp edition of 1574 has *Arnulphum*—but assigns him no dignity or status.

Schedel, in his register of chronicles, says that he was made archbishop of Lyon after having been abbot of Saint Medard at Soissons. The *Supplement to the Chronicle*, Book XII, says that he was an abbot—though of an unnamed monastery—and afterward archbishop of Lyon, a magnificent promoter of the canons regular and an eminent preacher of the divine word, so much so that when at Rome he attacked the licentiousness of the clergy too severely, he was killed by them.

Platina reports the latter story under Honorius II, but does not say whether he was a monk, hermit, or priest. Bale’s mere use of the same name made him bold and mendacious. For whom have we ever seen more fraudulent in assigning a man’s homeland, and therefore less trustworthy in recounting his death?

Nor should we regard Bale as trustworthy, truthful, and consistent with the approved English writers, when he has been exposed as wavering and cast down from the rank of a witness to truth. [Col. 0154C]

This alone will expose the story: regarding the archbishopric of Lyon attributed to Arnulf by Jacob Bergomensis and Schedel, in the two lists of the archbishops of Lyon described by Demochares, you will find not even one bishop of this name; nor does Bale care about the matter. It was only hatred—indeed, more than Vatinian hatred—with which he attacked the Roman Church, that dipped his pen in this ink.

But lest anyone think that religion alone flourished in Arnulf, the following monuments of his learning may be mentioned: *Solutions of the Questions Proposed by Lambert, Abbot of Bertin, to the Venerable Man in the Bosom of Charity*; *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, Book I; *Do Not Hide Your Face*; *On the Six Words of the Lord*, concerning Christ’s final words on the cross; *On the Works of the Six Days*, Book I; and *Homilies and Sermons*, Book I. [Col. 0154D]]

With heartfelt affection I command and beg you, in your religious devotion, to care for this Robert, who is fleeing from Judaism to Christianity, with that cheerful piety and pious cheerfulness with which all Christians ought to meet and assist such a person, so that no poverty or circumstance which we could avert may compel him to regret having abandoned his parents and their law for Christ. [Col. 0154A]

For it is exceedingly shameful for Christians, and especially for religious persons, to allow such a thing to happen through their negligence and hardness while they are present.

Therefore, lord prior, arrange for alms to be given—not through servants, who seek more what is their own than what is God’s, but through a monk responsible for almsgiving.

And you, lord William, provide from what you ought to preserve for me from the revenues of the archdeaconry enough that he and his little household may suffer no harsh deprivation, but may rejoice that he has passed from unbelief to the true faith and may learn from our very kindness that our faith is nearer to God than the Jewish one. [Col. 0154B]

For if necessary, I would rather spend everything that comes to me from the revenues of the archdeaconry on this matter, and much more besides, than allow this man, who has fled from the hands of the devil to us as to servants of God and true Christians, to live miserably among us.

Again I beg and implore you to show them that you possess Christian piety and love of Christianity. His poverty, whether in food or in clothing, deeply wounds my heart. [Col. 0155A]

Therefore act so that my heart may rest from this wound, if you do not love this wound.

[Note: The manuscript has *illum* (“him”) for *illam* (“it” or “this wound”).]

Farewell.

## Letter CXVIII [Col. 0155B]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0155D]]

**Anselm to Alfer, prior, and the monks of Saint Edmund**

He praises their unconquered spirit amid adversity and exhorts them to confess their sins to the prior and to guard their hearts with every care.

**Anselm, archbishop, to his beloved sons and brothers, the lord prior Alfer and the other servants of God living under him in the monastery of Saint Edmund: greeting and God’s blessing, and his own, insofar as it avails.**

I give thanks to God and to you for your steadfastness and patience in your tribulations [Note: The manuscript has *tribulationibus vestris; hortans* (“in your tribulations; exhorting”) for *tribulationibus, hortans*; another reading gives *tributionibus: hortans* [the first word uncertain/OCR-corrupt].], exhorting and beseeching you, as dearest sons, not to lose heart, but patiently, as you have begun, to await God’s consolation.

Let no adversity delay you from God’s service; let nothing remove you from carrying out his will. Remember that all who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer tribulations.

Therefore, the more tribulations rise up, the more each of you should exercise himself through the work of holy conduct and bind himself more firmly to the observance of his order. [Col. 0155C]

If you do this, know that you will obtain God’s consolation sooner, perhaps, than you expect.

Let none of you love or wish to conceal his sins, but let him confess them with a pure and simple heart to the lord prior, or to whomever the prior permits, and let him amend them according to the prior’s judgment. Afterward let him strive by every means to guard himself.

Those who have confessed or shall confess their sins in this manner and with this intention I absolve [Note: The manuscript reads *ego autem* (“but I”) for *eos autem* (“but those”).], insofar as I can, by the authority which God has granted me, in the place of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; and I humbly pray that almighty God may forgive them [Note: The manuscript has *et ut omnipotens* (“and that almighty”) for *et ut eis omnipotens* (“and that almighty [God] may forgive them”).]. [Col. 0155D]

Farewell, and pray for me.

## Letter CXIX [Col. 0156A]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0155D]]

**Queen Matilda of the English to Anselm**

She expresses how highly she values Anselm’s letters and reports that she has granted the abbey of Malmesbury to Edulf, while preserving all the rights of the archbishop.

[Note: Malmesbury Abbey is called *Maildulfesburch* in the West Saxon language and commonly Malmesbury or Malmesberia. It is situated in Wiltshire, in the diocese of Salisbury, England. It was first begun by Meidulf, a Scottish monk, but in 657 was greatly enlarged and endowed by Leutherius, bishop of the West Saxons and nephew of Agilbert, bishop of Paris.

It was much richer in learned men, among whom William, named Malmesbury after his monastery—though properly a man of Somerset—was not the least. He was an exceedingly learned and diligent historian, whom I have cited more than once and who died in 1142.

After English Calvinists demolished this monastery and handed it over to their ministers to teach youth there, no one could live in it; or if anyone did occupy it, he was either insane or impious. [Col. 0155D]]

**To her lord and reverend father, equally beloved and honored, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, Matilda, the devoted servant of his holiness, with her Christ, sends greeting.**

Whenever, through the gift of a letter, you grant me some token of your holiness, you brighten the dark gloom of my soul with the light of renewed joy.

For your letter is in a certain way a kind of visitation from you, though absent; the handling of the little document and the reading and rereading of your letter, so delightful and so often repeated, bring me great pleasure.

For what, my lord, is more adorned in your writings than their style, or richer than their meaning? They lack neither the gravity of Fronto, nor the force of Cicero, Fabius, or Quintilian [Note: The manuscript reads “the acumen of Cicero, Demosthenes, or Quintilian,” rather than “the gravity of Fronto, nor the force of Cicero, Fabius, or Quintilian.”].

In them, indeed, there is an abundance of Paul’s learning, Jerome’s diligence, Gregory’s labor, Augustine’s exposition; and, greater than these, the sweetness of evangelical eloquence drips from them. [Col. 0156B]

Therefore, because this grace has been poured from your lips, my heart and my flesh have rejoiced in affection for your love and in the fulfillment of your fatherly admonition.

For the memory of your exhortation and most kindly entreaty, returning again and again, strikes upon the door of my heart and adjudges it to obedient compliance. [Note: The manuscript reads “judges obedience,” rather than “assigns me to the judgment of obedience.”]

Trusting, therefore, in the favor of your holiness, I have entrusted the abbey of Malmesbury, insofar as it belonged to me, to Lord Edulf, a monk of Winchester and formerly its sacristan, whom I believe is known to you. [Col. 0156C]

I have wholly reserved for your gift and disposition whatever belongs to it, so that both the rod and the pastoral care may be entrusted to the judgment of your discretion.

May the divine power of heavenly grace repay with a worthy gift this favor of your goodwill, which toward me does not grow cold.

For the rest, may Christ preserve your dignity; and may he who blesses you on earth soon gladden me with your return.

Amen.

## Letter CXX [Col. 0156D]

[Note: Compared with the same manuscript. [Col. 0155D]]

**Anselm to Matilda**

He did not wish to confirm Edulf as abbot because Edulf had sent him a cup through envoys together with his letters.

**To his dearest lady and daughter, the glorious queen Matilda, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.**

Let your excellence know, dearest lady, that concerning the abbey of Malmesbury [Note: The manuscript reads *quia de abbatia* (“because concerning the abbey”) for *de abbatia* (“concerning the abbey”).] and the brother about whom you wrote to me, I would willingly confirm your wish if I could. [Col. 0157A]

You, for your part, acted well and according to God in what you did concerning him. But he himself acted very foolishly in this matter, doing what he ought not to have done.

For through the same envoys who brought me your letters and those of others concerning his affair, he sent me a cup. I absolutely refused to keep the cup, and I was saddened by it, because I do not see how he can be excused from fault in this matter.

May almighty God direct all your actions according to his good pleasure and defend you from every evil.

Amen. [Col. 0157B]

## LETTER CXXI [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. OF GERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK; ROBERT, BISHOP OF CHESTER; HEREBERT, BISHOP OF NORWICH; RALPH, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER; SAMSON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER; AND WILLIAM, ELECT OF WINCHESTER, TO ANSELM

They invite Anselm to England, promising him their assistance.

To their most beloved father, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0157C],

Gerard, archbishop of York, etc. There are letters addressed to Gerard above, Letters 53 and 60. He, formerly bishop of Hereford after Thomas Bayeux, obtained the insignia of the archbishopric of York. York—called *Iortz* in English and *York* in French—is a most famous city of the English island, toward the north, between the rivers Usk and Foffa, which flow past the city and, joining together there, flow into the Humber. Although the see became archiepiscopal after the year of salvation 182, it was nevertheless transferred by some to Hexham, a town of that same archbishopric, as the Malmesbury author carefully observed in his account of the archbishops of York.

Robert of Chester was surnamed de Limesey and held the see for more than thirty years, as I have read in the manuscript Lists of the Bishops of Chester in our library.

Herebert was the first among the bishops of the East Angles to be called “of Norwich,” after the village of Norwich, famous for its commerce and the multitude of its people, to which Herebert transferred his cathedra. The earlier bishops had been of Dommoc and Elmham; eventually the two priestly sees were made one at the village of Elmham. From there Agelmar, or Ethelmer, withdrew to Thetford, as the manuscript lists of the bishops of Elmham in our library attest. Yet in Book II of *On the Bishops of England*, I see this attributed by the Malmesbury author to Herfast, who is placed before Agelmar in our manuscript.

“Finally, Herebert, a magnanimous and highly learned man, a devout monk and prior of Fécamp, then abbot of Ramsey, and from being abbot of Ramsey made bishop of the Church of Thetford after purchasing the episcopate, went to Rome in repentance and, having received absolution, returned and transferred the see to Norwich. There, after founding a church, he piously established a community of monks.” Thus far our manuscript codex concerning Herebert.

[Col. 0158C]

Ralph of Chichester. We have restored the name in this form from the manuscript stories of the bishops of Chichester, printed in Florence of Worcester and in the other printed histories of Britain. For the handwritten exemplar of these letters read Robert—perhaps through the copyist’s inadvertence, as he was turning over in his mind the name of another Robert.

Samson of Worcester, not Satiso, as it is read in Ivo of Chartres, Letter 76. His scholion nevertheless notes that other manuscripts have Sanson; and we have read it in this form from numerous English writers and manuscript lists of the bishops of Worcester, as follows: “In the year 1096, Samson of Bayeux was consecrated by Archbishop Anselm in the church of Saint Paul in London, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June]. He was the brother of Thomas of York, whom Odo, bishop of Bayeux, promoted.”

Anselm mentions William of Winchester in Letters 70, 95, and 105. These British prelates send this letter to Anselm for the following reason. Although he had received from King Henry, at the Council of Eagle, all the possessions and rights of his archbishopric, as appears from Letters 110 and 111 above, he nevertheless delayed returning to England because he did not wish to associate with bishops invested by the king. For this reason William Warelwast, the king’s envoy, and Baldwin, Anselm’s envoy, went once more, and finally, to Rome. At length, after a lawsuit which had been contested for a very long time and so unjustly, they brought back this judgment from the mouth of Paschal: namely, that the elected prelates were to receive the episcopal ring and staff from Anselm, but were to render fealty to the king. Meanwhile, while the journey to Rome was being undertaken, frequent complaints and letters were brought from England, asking him to return as quickly as possible. All the bishops saw that everything was rushing toward ruin and that what had fallen backward was being dragged still farther behind; they wished to remedy the situation, but could not do so except in Anselm’s presence.]

—GERARD, archbishop of York; ROBERT, of Chester; HEREBERT, of Norwich; RALPH, of Chichester; SAMSON, of Worcester; and WILLIAM, elect of Winchester—send greetings.

[Col. 0158A] We endured peace, and peace withdrew ever farther; we sought good things, and turmoil grew strong. The roads of Zion mourn because the uncircumcised trample them. The Temple grieves because laymen have burst into the Holy of Holies and even upon the altar itself. Rise up, as once did that old man Mattathias; have strength in your sons [Note: [Col. 0157B] The manuscript reads “have in your sons”]; behold the courage of Jonathan and the prudence of Simon. These men will fight the Lord’s battle with you; and if you should be gathered to your fathers before us, we shall receive from your hand the inheritance of your labor. But now you must no longer delay. Why are you wandering abroad while your sheep perish without a shepherd? You have no excuse remaining before God. We are ready not only to follow you but even to perish, if you command it. Come, then, to us; come quickly—or command us, or some among us, to come to you [Note: [Col. 0157B] The manuscript reads “to us, come quickly, or”] [Col. 0158B], lest, while we are separated from you, the counsels of those who seek their own interests incline you toward the left. For in this matter we now seek not what is ours, but what belongs to God [Note: [Col. 0157B] The manuscript reads “what is ours, but”].

## 411. LETTER CXXII. ANSELM TO HIS BISHOPS

He grieves over the misery of the English Church and of the bishops, and rejoices in the assistance they have promised him.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friends and fellow bishops, whose letter he received by the bearer of this one, sends greetings.

[Col. 0159A] I grieve with you and sympathize in my heart with the tribulations that you and the Churches of England are enduring. For the present, however, I cannot help according to either my own or your wishes, because I am not yet certain what I can do or how much I can do, until I learn from our envoys, whom I expect to return from Rome shortly, what they have accomplished with the lord pope. Nevertheless, it is good and pleasing to me that at last you recognize what your patience has brought you to—if I may put it mildly—and that you promise me your assistance not in my cause but in God’s cause, and invite me not to delay coming to you. Although I cannot do this in the present circumstances, because the king does not yet wish me to be in England except as one who disagrees with the pope’s command and agrees with the king’s will, and although, as I have said, I am not yet certain what I can do, I nevertheless rejoice in your good and episcopal will and steadfastness, which you promise, and in the encouragement you give me.

As for bringing some of you to me, as you request, lest, while we are separated from one another, those who presently seek their own interests pervert my counsel, I do not think it advisable. For I trust in God that no one will be able to turn my heart away from the truth, insofar as I know it; and because I hope that shortly God will show me what I can do, I shall inform you of it as soon as I can. What you ought to do in the meantime, your prudence understands well enough. Nevertheless, I say this: insofar as, by hoping in God, I perceive my conscience, I would not give my consent to redeem my life, nor make myself the agent or executor of the evil which, I hear, has recently been promulgated against the Churches of England [Col. 0159C]. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

He asks to be strengthened by the archbishop’s prudent responses.

To his own lord and father, HUGH, reverend archbishop of Lyons, sincerely beloved by the mother Church, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends whatever he can understand more deeply and express more worthily.

What I have done since departing from your fatherly and beloved presence, and what has taken place between the king of England and me, need not be set out in a long account in this letter, because the bearers of this letter [Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads “because the bearers,” rather than “because the bearers of this letter”] can report it more fully and better by word of mouth. Since, however, I would wish, if it were possible, to use your counsel in all my actions above that of all the people I know—especially in this matter for which I am sending these same envoys to Rome—I humbly ask that they be instructed and fortified by your prudence. I also venture to ask that, if it seems appropriate to your holiness, you suggest something to the lord pope, insofar as you understand what would be useful to this matter.

You know that when the disposition of some matter depends upon the counsel of different people, just as not everyone has the same understanding, so they do not all give the same assent. Since, therefore, I am certain that your mind is firmly established in the truth, I would wish your judgment to be present wherever the liberty and true welfare of the Church of God are being discussed.

The chief difficulty in the case between the king and me now seems to consist especially in this: although I hope the king will allow himself to be defeated by the apostolic decrees concerning the investiture of churches, he still does not wish, he says, to relinquish the homage of prelates [Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads “he does not wish,” rather than “he still does not wish”]. On this matter he asks the apostolic see, through his embassy, to obtain permission for his will. If he obtains it, I am uncertain what I ought to do if some religiously minded elected person should refuse to become the king’s man for an episcopate or abbey. For it seems harsh to me to command this of him under obedience; yet if I do not do so, I shall seem to those inclined to do it irreligiously to be loosening the restraint on an unworthy rush toward dignities.

As for those who have already accepted the prohibited investitures, and those who consecrated them, I think that the king will demand that they remain in what they presumptuously undertook unlawfully. Therefore, concerning these matters, and concerning those about which I seek your wisdom through our envoys, I ask you to make your judgment known to me. May almighty God preserve your holiness unharmed for a long time, with every prosperity. Amen.

## LETTER CXXIV [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, TO ANSELM

He replies to the preceding letter.

To his desirable and wholeheartedly beloved father and lord, ANSELM, venerable bishop of the English, HUGH, servant of the Church of Lyons, sends continual consolation through divine protection.

[Col. 0160C] Your holiness, reverend Father, remembers that we have always desired—and, if it could be done according to God’s will, advised you—that you receive again the care of the English Church entrusted to you, and that, for the common salvation of the flock committed to you, you not refuse to submit your neck in obedience to so heavy a yoke.

Now, therefore, from the report of Lord Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads “Baldivini,” rather than “Balduvini”], I learn that what you have labored so greatly to attain, and for which you exposed not only your possessions but also yourself, you have at last, by God’s grace, attained in large part. So that you may be encouraged to hope for what remains, we ask by advising, and advise by asking, that you not evade obedience to the apostolic command, lest, by valuing your own judgment more highly than apostolic authority, you be judged to resist not only the world and the kingdom but also the Church and the priesthood.

For although in the field of the English Church one seed falls upon rock, another beside the road, and another among thorns, good soil is also found there, which will produce fruit with patience after receiving the seed of your preaching. But wretched me! I myself become the author and kindler of my own desolation, as I strive to remove from the sight of these eyes—which I now seem to bear in vain [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “which I bear humanly,” rather than “which I now seem to bear in vain”]—the one consolation and joy of my life, and, after God, the life of my soul: the presence of my sweetest Father, which they were accustomed most gratefully to enjoy, and which they are permitted not only not to see [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “useful,” rather than “to see”], but even not to hope that they will see again. But far be it from me to begrudge the general salvation of so many and such great people for the sake of my temporal advantage. Rather, may I seek not what is mine but what belongs to Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “what belongs to Christ I shall seek,” rather than “may I seek not what is mine but what belongs to Jesus Christ”].

Therefore, most blessed Father, hold me in the embrace of your memory, since I am not granted the sight of your present face. We always wish you good health and ask you to care for our salvation.

## 412. LETTER CXXV [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO EULALIA, ABBESS

He gratefully receives the prayers of the abbess and her daughters, and exhorts them to be obedient and faithful in the smallest matters.

[Col. 0161B] ANSELM, archbishop, sends greetings to the reverend abbess EULALIA and her daughters.

I give thanks to your religious devotion because you prayed for me as long as I was outside England in exile, desiring my return. Now I ask you still more earnestly to pray that my return may be fruitful. I wish you to know this: my love for you, from the time I came to know you, lives and endures, and, while I live, with God’s help it will endure. Therefore, although you have no need of it, I shall nevertheless write something to you out of that same love, so that you may know that I love you and care for you.

You, beloved sisters and my daughters, I exhort and admonish to be subject and obedient to your mother, not merely in the sight of human beings but also in the sight of God, for whom nothing is hidden. Obedience is true when the will of the subject obeys the will of the superior, so that, wherever the subject may be, she wills what she understands the superior to will, provided it is not contrary to the will of God.

Your community ought to be the temple of God, and the temple of God is holy. Therefore, if you live holily, as I hope, you are the temple of God. You live holily if you carefully keep your order and your way of life; and you do this carefully if you do not despise the smallest matters. For your way of life ought always to strive toward perfection, and with your whole heart to shudder at failure. For it is written: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). Whoever falls does not advance.

Therefore, if you wish to advance and dread falling short, do not despise small things [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “falls. Therefore,” rather than “falls; whoever falls does not advance. Therefore”]. Just as it is true that “whoever despises small things will gradually fall,” so it is true that whoever does not despise small things gradually advances [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “falls: so,” rather than “fails: so”]. Do not think that any sin is small, although one may be greater than another. Nothing done through disobedience—which alone cast the human being out of paradise—ought to be called small.

For what sin will be small if, as Truth testifies, “whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment, and whoever says, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council, and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna”? Therefore I ask you, dearest daughters, to neglect nothing, but always strive to guard your works and your hearts as in the sight of God [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “your [works and hearts] as in,” rather than “your works and your hearts as in”]. Keep peace among yourselves, because God’s dwelling was made in peace, and “great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them” [Note: [Col. 0161C] The manuscript reads “there is no stumbling block for him,” rather than “for them”]. With heart and mouth I ask God’s blessing and absolution for you; and, insofar as mine has any value, I give and bestow my own as much as I can. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVI [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

That the translation of a bishop ought not to take place without the consent of the archbishop and bishops of the province, and only after great deliberation and with apostolic authority.

To his most beloved lord, HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of the Normans, ANSELM, archbishop, sends faithful service with prayers.

Your dignity commanded me through the elected bishop of Winchester to write whether Lord [Note: [Col. 0161C] Hervaeus. Polydore, in Book XI of his *History of England*, has Henry; but Malmesbury, Huntingdon, Matthew Paris, and the manuscript lists of the bishops of Ely establish the more reliable reading, which calls him Hervaeus. He was first bishop of Bangor, successor to David—that famous champion of Emperor Henry V on account of the unjust and disgraceful captivity of Pope Paschal II. Bangor (whence the forms *Bancoriensis*, *Bangoriensis*, and *Bancorensis*) was, in Brito’s time, a city and, under King Arthur, an episcopal see in Wales, the third part of the island of Britain, at the navel of Gaul (a place in Arfon, the land of the Venedoti), not far from the crossing to the island of Mona; in the British tongue it was called Banchor, but is now Bangor or Bancora. There, according to Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 2, flourished a monastery of two thousand monks, governed in seven divisions. Saint Bernard, in the *Life of St Malachy*, suggests that the flock was more numerous, adding that, because of the holiness of its elder and foremost inhabitants, an oratory was founded there by Malachy himself and inhabited. But when, under King Henry I, the site of the bishopric had been levelled with the ground, so that there was nowhere for the bishop to set his foot, he asked the king to grant him the Church of Lisieux. I write *Lexoviensis*, not *Luxoviensis*, as do Letters 174, 178, 179, and 181 of Ivo of Chartres. Otherwise one would see no distinction between the episcopal Church of Lisieux, of Second Lyons in Neustria, and the monastery of Luxeuil, famous through its foundation in Burgundy by Columbanus, the first monastic founder—not in Germany, as Robert Cenalis, bishop of Avranches, supposed in Book II, ninth summary, of *On French Affairs*. For Guillaume Paradin shows, in chapter 10 of his book *On the Ancient State of Burgundy*, that Burgundy always belonged to French jurisdiction: “Accordingly, since Hervaeus could not obtain the see of Lisieux for the reasons given by Anselm (for thus I understand Ivo of Chartres to have described Walo’s transfer from the Church of Beauvais, to which he had been consecrated, to that of Paris, Letter 169 near the end, and Letter 171), and since the diocese of Lincoln extended too far, a council was held, and, to lessen the bishop’s care and labour, a new bishop was installed in the monastery of Ely in the year of Christ 1109, Anselm’s last year and King Henry’s ninth. Ely (from which the monastery of Ely takes its name) is an island in the south of England, surrounded by fresh waters within the bounds of Cambridgeshire; Hervaeus obtained it, for himself and his successors, as an ample means of living honourably in accordance with their rank.”] Hervaeus, bishop of Bangor, could [Col. 0163A] be appointed bishop in the Church of Luxovium [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads “of Lisieux” (*Lexoviensi*) for “of Luxovium” (*Luxoviensi*)].

I do not understand how this can easily be done. For just as no bishop ought to be consecrated for any Church without the consent and counsel of the archbishop and the other bishops of the whole province, so one who has been consecrated a bishop cannot canonically be appointed bishop in another province without the counsel and consent of the archbishop and bishops of that province, with apostolic authority, nor without the absolution of the archbishop and bishops of the province in which he was consecrated. Such absolution cannot be granted without the great and common deliberation and counsel of those without whom, as I have said, he could not have been consecrated—even if his episcopate appears to have been so destroyed that he cannot remain in it.

May almighty God direct you in this and in your other actions. Amen.

[Col. 0163B]

## LETTER CXXVII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO MABILIA, A RELIGIOUS WOMAN

That one consecrated to God should abstain from worldly association.

ANSELM, archbishop, sends his dearest daughter, the religious woman MABILIA, greetings and God’s blessing and his own.

I love you, and in the manner in which I love my own soul, I also love yours. I love my soul so that in this life it may deserve to enjoy God and in the future life may enjoy him; this is what I love and desire for you. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, as my dearest daughter, not to take delight in worldly things, because no one can love worldly and eternal goods at the same time [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads “to love and,” rather than “to love worldly and eternal goods at the same time”]. I do not want you to love the company of worldly people, but the cloister. Let there be nothing between you and this world [Col. 0163C].

If you wish to be a nun and the bride of God, say with blessed Paul the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). With the same Apostle, regard all the passing things of this world as dung.

My daughter, what need have you to visit any of your relatives? Since they in no way need your counsel or assistance, you will receive from them no counsel or assistance for your way of life and profession that you cannot find in the cloister. Your way of life has been separated from their manner of living. They will not become monks for your sake, nor will you return to secular life for theirs. What, then, beloved daughter, is there for you or them in God, if you do not benefit them in the life they pursue, nor they you in what you ought most to love?

If they wish to see you, or need your counsel or assistance in some way, let them come to you. They are permitted to wander and travel through various places; you should not go to them, because you are not permitted to leave the cloister except in a necessity attested by God.

Do not, my daughter—do not love the world, because “whoever is a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4). Do not love familiarity with worldly people, because the more familiar you willingly become with them, the less familiar you will be with God and his familiar angels. Do not be anxious to make yourself known in the world, because then God will say to you all the more: “I do not know you” [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads “to make yourself known in the world, because,” rather than “to make yourself known, because”]. Desire to please God alone; desire to know only God and those things that help you toward this [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads “those things that help him,” rather than “those things that help you”]. Commend yourself to him daily. I commend you to him, insofar as it lies with me. May he always rule, direct, and guard you. Amen.

## 413. LETTER CXXVIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

He refuses to give testimony concerning a man unknown to him, although asked by the queen.

To his lady and dearest daughter, MATHILDA, by God’s grace glorious queen of the English, ANSELM, archbishop [Col. 0164B], sends faithful service, faithful prayers, and the wish that by God’s grace she may always rejoice in this life and in the future.

The bearer of this letter brought me your seal together with a letter from you, which informed me that you wished his disgrace to be driven away by the testimony of my letters, on account of a certain purgation he had undergone, and that through my intercession he might recover from my lord the king what he had lost by the king’s command.

I neither ought nor wish to disregard your will; but I am certain of your highness’s kindness, because you do not wish me to do anything other than what is proper. Your prudence certainly knows that it is not my role to testify concerning things I have neither seen nor heard, but the role of those who saw them [Col. 0164C]. Nor is it my place to intercede for someone whose life and conduct I do not know, so that he may recover what he lost by royal command.

I therefore ask that it not displease your gracious highness that I hesitate to do what I understand does not belong to me [Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads “what I understand belongs to me,” rather than “what I understand does not belong to me”]. May almighty God continually protect and direct you with his blessing. Amen.

## LETTER CXXIX. ANSELM TO HELGOT, ABBOT OF SAINT OUEN

He explains to his friend, most eager to know, how matters stand after his return to England.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his truly beloved lover, the venerable HELGOT, abbot of the monastery of Saint Ouen, sends whatever can best be desired for a friend.

[Col. 0164D]

A true friend is always concerned about his true friend as about another self, so that he may know what concerns him, in order either to rejoice with him or to sympathize with him according to the circumstances. Although no one loves sorrow, nevertheless, if there is something over which one ought to grieve, one desires in a remarkable way to know it so as to grieve with the other rather than remain ignorant and feel no pain.

Your beloved and sweet affection desires to know my circumstances and whatever concerns me, so that, just as my heart is disposed toward me, your heart too may be disposed toward me. By God’s gracious ordering, and with the support of the prayers of you and the other servants of God, our friends, I recently returned to England. I was received by high and low, by prelates and subjects, with great joy and honor, insofar as this depended on human beings.

What you heard—that my lord the king commended his kingdom and all his possessions to me, so that my will might prevail in everything that belongs to him—is true. In this he showed the kindness of his will and his great affection toward me. But since it is written, “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial” (1 Corinthians 6:12), and elsewhere, “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything builds up” (2 Corinthians 10:23), I do not think it advisable for me to begin attempting anything great through myself at present. But when God by his grace restores the king to us with that good will which I perceive in him, I hope that God by his grace will work through him many things among us for his honor, so that we may rejoice.

So far as the changes of this age permit, everything concerning me—in my body and in other matters—is prosperous, God willing, except for the weakness of my body, which I feel increasing daily. May all those blessings that you pray for me in your letters also come upon your head. I greet our brothers, your dearest sons, and ask that they remember me.

[Col. 0165C]

## LETTER CXXX [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO P., MONK OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES

He disapproves the desire of a monk planning to go to Jerusalem, in accordance with the judgment of the pope which he himself had heard from him.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greetings to his beloved brother P., monk of the monastery of Saint Martin of Sées, and the wish that he may always be directed and consoled by God’s grace.

I hear, my dearest friend [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “I heard, my friend,” rather than “I hear, my dearest friend”], that you desire to go to Jerusalem. First of all, therefore, I tell you that this desire of yours does not arise from a good source, nor does it tend toward the salvation of your soul. It is contrary to your profession, by which you promised stability before God in the monastery where you received the monastic habit [Col. 0165D]. It is also contrary to the pope’s command, issued with great authority, that monks should not presume to undertake this journey, unless the person in question were a religious man useful for governing the Church of God and teaching the people—and then only with the counsel and obedience of his superior.

I was present when the pope promulgated this judgment. It is also contrary to the obedience owed to your abbot, whose will hates and abhors this as a danger to your soul.

[Col. 0166A]

## LETTER CXXXI. POPE PASCHAL II TO GERARD, BISHOP OF YORK

That he should render fealty to Anselm according to ancient custom.

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his venerable brother GERARD, bishop of York.

“Although wickedly against us,” etc. See the account of Paschal II under the year 1118.

## 414. LETTER CXXXII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO ALEXANDER, KING OF THE SCOTS

He congratulates the king on being raised to his father’s throne.

To ALEXANDER, by the grace of God king of the Scots, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greetings, faithful prayers, and God’s blessing and his own, insofar as it has worth.

We give thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “I give thanks to God,” rather than “We give thanks to God”], and I and the whole congregation of the Church of Christ at Canterbury rejoice because God has raised you to your hereditary kingdom after your brother, and because he has adorned you with conduct worthy of the kingdom.

For your brother, who by living holily deserved to pass from this life by a good end through the mercy of God, we pray and shall pray, at your request, as for our beloved friend and lover, that God may grant his soul eternal joy in his glory with his elect and bestow eternal blessedness.

I know that your highness loves and desires my counsel. First, therefore, I pray God that he may direct you by the grace of his Holy Spirit and grant you counsel in all your actions, so that after this life he may lead you to the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “may lead you to the kingdom,” rather than “may lead you to the heavenly kingdom after this life”].

Our counsel is that, with the help of him from whom you received them, you strive to retain the fear of God and the good and religious conduct which you began to possess in your youth and from childhood [Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads the singular “you began to possess,” rather than the plural “you began to possess”]. Kings then rule well when they live according to the will of God and serve him in fear, and when they rule over themselves, refusing to subject themselves to vices and overcoming their importunity with steadfast courage.

For steadfastness in virtue and royal courage are not incompatible in a king. Certain kings, such as David, both lived holily and ruled the people entrusted to them with the strictness of justice and the gentleness of piety, according as circumstances required.

So conduct yourself that the wicked may fear you and the good love you; and so that your life may always please God, let your mind always retain the memory of the punishment of the wicked and the reward of the good after this life. May almighty God entrust you and all your actions to no one but his own gracious providence.

Concerning our brothers whom, according to the will of your brother—who, as we believe, passed from the labor of this life to rest—we sent to Scotland, we have not thought it necessary to ask your graciousness for anything, because we are not unaware of your good will.

[Col. 0167A]

## LETTER CXXXIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO ROBERT AND HIS SISTERS AND DAUGHTERS

He sends the requested exhortation to set them aflame for right living. That they should have a good will in all things, and should strive to overcome troublesome thoughts and involuntary impulses by despising them, lest they be disturbed by them.

ANSELM, archbishop, sends greetings to his dearest friend and son ROBERT, and to his most beloved sisters and daughters SEIT, EDIT, HYDIT, LUVERIM [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads “Lunerim,” rather than “Luverim”], VIRGIT, and GODIT, together with God’s blessing and his own, insofar as it has worth.

I rejoice and give thanks to God for the holy purpose and holy manner of life that you maintain toward one another in the love of God and holiness of life, as I have learned through our brother and son Guillelmus. Your affection, dear to me, most beloved daughters, asks that I write you some admonition to teach and stir you to live well; although you have with you our beloved son Robert, whom God has inspired to care for you according to God, and to teach you daily, by word and example, how you ought to live. Nevertheless, since I ought, if I am able, to favor your holy request, I shall try to write you a few things suited to your desire.

Most beloved daughters, every praiseworthy or blameworthy action derives its praise or blame from the will. For the will is the root and beginning of actions that lie within our power; and even if we cannot do what we will, each person is nevertheless judged before God according to his or her own will. Therefore, do not consider only what you do, but what you will; not only what your works are, but what your will is. For every action that is done with a right—that is, a just—will is right; and an action done with a will that is not right is not right [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads “right, and which” for “and an action ...”]. A person is called just because of a just will, and unjust because of an unjust will.

If, then, you wish to live well, guard your will unceasingly [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads *custodire* (“to guard”) for *custodite* (“guard”)], in great matters and small, in things subject to your power and in things beyond your power, so that it may not in any respect depart from uprightness. If you wish to know whether your will is right, that will certainly is right which is subject to the will of God. Therefore, whenever you either plan or think of doing something important, say in your hearts: “Does God will that I should will this, or does he not?” If your conscience answers you, “Truly God wills that I should will this, and such a will pleases him” [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads *tali voluntas* for *talis voluntas*], then, whether or not you are able to do what you will, love the will nevertheless. But if your conscience testifies to you that God does not want you to have that will, then with all your effort [Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads *ut toto nisu* (“that with all effort”) for *in toto nisu* (“with all effort”)] turn your heart away from it; and if you truly wish to drive it from you, exclude its thought and memory from your heart as far as you can.

But how you should exclude a depraved will or thought from yourselves, understand and hold fast this little counsel that I give you. Do not quarrel with perverse thoughts or a perverse will; rather, when they trouble you, occupy your mind forcefully with some useful thought and will until they vanish. For a thought or will is never driven from the heart except by another thought and another will that does not agree with it. Thus conduct yourselves toward useless thoughts and desires so that, by applying yourselves wholly to useful ones, your mind may disdain even to remember or look upon them.

When you wish to pray or devote yourselves to some good meditation, if at that moment importunate thoughts that you ought not to accept trouble you, never, because of their importunity, be willing to abandon the good thing you have begun, lest the devil, their instigator, rejoice that he has made you fail in the good you began. Instead, overcome them by despising them in the manner I have described. Nor should you grieve or become saddened by their assault, so long as, as I have said, you despise them and give them no assent, lest they return to your memory by occasion of your sadness and revive their importunity. For the human mind has this habit: whatever it takes pleasure or sorrow in returns more often to its memory than what it regards or thinks should be neglected.

Likewise, a person devoted to a holy purpose ought to conduct herself with respect to every indecent movement, whether in body or soul, such as the stimulus of the flesh, anger, envy, or empty glory. Such movements are most easily extinguished when we disdain to feel that we wish to experience them, to think about them, or to do anything at their persuasion. Do not fear that movements or thoughts of this kind will be counted against you as sin if your will in no way joins itself to them, since “there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh.” For to walk according to the flesh is to agree with the flesh by one’s will. The Apostle calls every vicious movement in soul or body “flesh” when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.”

We easily extinguish suggestions of this kind if, following the counsel given above, we crush their beginning; but it is difficult after we have admitted their head within the mind.

To you, my friend and most beloved son Robert, I give as much thanks as I can for the care and love that, for God’s sake, you show toward these same handmaids of God; and I entreat you with all affection to persevere in this holy and pious will. You may be certain that a great reward from God awaits you for this holy devotion. May almighty God always guard your whole life. Amen.

May almighty and merciful Lord grant you absolution and remission of all your sins, and may he always cause you to advance humbly toward better things and never to fail. Amen.

[Note: The manuscript omits “Amen ... Amen.”]

[Col. 0169A]

## LETTER CXXXIV. ANSELM TO VALERANNUS

It is found above, in Part I of the *Patrologia*, vol. CLVIII, col. 511.

## LETTER CXXXV. VALERANNUS TO ANSELM

Col. 547.

## LETTER CXXXVI. ANSELM TO VALERANNUS

It is found in the same Part I, col. 551.

## LETTER CXXXVII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO TUROLD, MONK OF BEC

He rejoices greatly that Turold has renounced the world.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his most dear brother and friend TUROLD [Note: The manuscript reads “to his friend Turold” rather than “to his most dear friend Turold”] [Note: The Chronicle of Bec contains a lengthy account of him, which is here abridged so that nothing relevant to history is omitted. Turold, brother of Hugh of Évreux, a man of no mean nobility and power, was raised to the governance of the Church of Bayeux. Soon afterwards he so burned with divine love that he regarded all worldly distinction as dung and assumed the habit of a monk at Bec. Nor was this without great fruit. He eventually attained such humility, modesty, gravity, prudence, and observance of the monastic life that he was an object of admiration even to the nobles of Bec. But, that he might shine ever more brightly, divine wisdom saw fit to refine him longer in the furnace of pain—what we call a rupture—tormenting him so that no small portion of his intestines descended into the scrotum and almost deprived him of life; when it ascended again, it exacted, with usury upon usury, whatever torment had seemed lacking in its descent. Meanwhile the servant of God, struggling bravely with his inward enemy, always concealed its violence, hoping that it would at last be repressed by divine aid, so that he would not be compelled to disclose to anyone what he earnestly wished to remain hidden, and this from a concern for virginal modesty. He yielded, however, when on one occasion the intestines became so relaxed and swollen that, despairing of their returning inwardly, he sent for Abbot William, who promptly came running with the brothers. Seeing Turold almost killed by illness, the abbot invoked the hand of the heavenly physician. The sick man too, sound and very vigorous in mind, quickly had recourse to the aid of Saint Faith the virgin. Not in vain: he began to improve somewhat and fell asleep. In his sleep he heard a voice saying: “Rise healed, and understand that through the prayers of blessed Faith you have been restored whole to health; and, having summoned the abbot to you, you shall report this to him. You shall also ask him to send Brother Gerard, surnamed Giffard, to Longueville, to give thanks to your Savior for the health granted you and most reverently to offer candles upon the altar of the church.” These are the Chronicle of Bec’s very words. Turold, awakened from sleep, put his hand to his private parts and by touch discovered the truth of the heavenly warning and the restoration of this wholly unexpected health. He therefore poured out doxologies and thanks due to the supreme physician and also to his most holy handmaid Faith. Hearing this, the abbot exulted with incredible joy and sent Turold together with Giffard to Longueville to fulfil the vow. This Saint Faith, through whose intercessions Turold recovered, appears to be the very one mentioned in the Martyrology on the day before the Nones of October.], by the grace of God a monk of Bec, greetings and perseverance in his good purpose [Col. 0169B] to the end.

Blessed is God in his gifts and holy in all his works, who has turned your heart from vanity to truth. For all who desire the heights, honors, and riches of this world pursue vanity [Note: The manuscript reads “pursue vanity, which in no way can satisfy the mind, just as ...”], since these things cannot satisfy the mind as they promise; rather, the more they abound, the more they make the hungry soul hunger, and they lead it to no good end.
