But those who despise earthly and transitory things with all their heart and strive with all their strength to ascend to true humility hold the truth. For those who humble themselves do not seem to descend to spiritual eyes; rather, they ascend to the highest mountain, from which one rises to the kingdom of heaven.

Divine mercy has directed you into the way of paradise—indeed, it has introduced you into a kind of paradise in this life—by introducing you into the cloistered life of the monastic vocation. [Col. 0170A] Let your prudence therefore beware lest your heart look backward. A monk looks backward when he frequently recalls the things he has abandoned. When he does this often, the love of heaven grows cold in him, the love of the world comes back to life, and weariness and disgust with his vocation arise. Therefore, just as your body has been separated from the life of secular people, so let your heart be separated from worldly thought and always occupied with some useful and spiritual meditation. May the Holy Spirit always make you rejoice and give thanks to God for the good beginning. Amen.

## LETTER CXXXVIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO BASILIA

He writes a very pious letter to this most devout woman: that a person is always either ascending to heaven or descending into hell, and that this must be considered above all.

ANSELM, archbishop, to BASILIA, friend and most beloved daughter in the Lord, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, if it is worth anything.

I have learned through your messengers that you greatly desire a letter from me; in this I recognize your good will and Christian intention. For I see no reason why you would desire one unless you might receive from it some wholesome counsel for your soul. Although all of Holy Scripture teaches you how you ought to live, if you have it explained to you, I nevertheless ought not to be stingy or unyielding toward your devout request.

I shall therefore tell you something, dearest daughter, which, if you frequently consider it with your whole attention, can greatly kindle your heart toward the fear of God and the love of living well. Let it always be before the eyes of your mind [Col. 0171A] that the present life has an end; and no one knows when the final day will arrive, the day toward which he draws unceasingly, day and night.

The present life is a road. For as long as a person lives, he does nothing but travel. He is always either ascending into heaven or descending into hell. [The printed text reads “ascending into hell”; the heading and the following contrast show that this is an obvious contextual error.] When he does some good work, he takes one step upward; but when he sins in any way, he takes one step downward. Each soul recognizes this ascent or descent when it leaves the body. Whoever diligently strives, while living here, to ascend through good character and good works will be placed in heaven with the holy angels; and whoever descends through evil character will be buried in hell with the fallen angels.

This must certainly be noted: one descends much more quickly and easily than one ascends. Therefore, in each of his or her wills and actions, every Christian man and woman ought carefully to consider whether he or she is ascending or descending. With all their heart, they should embrace those things in which they see themselves ascending and flee from and abhor those things in which they recognize a descent into hell [Note: The manuscript reads “in which descent into hell takes place”].

I therefore warn and advise you, friend in God and most beloved daughter [Note: The manuscript reads “sweetest” rather than “most beloved”], to withdraw yourselves, as far as you can with God’s help, from every sin, great or small, and to exercise yourselves in holy actions. I pray almighty God that he himself may always and everywhere protect, direct, and guard you. Amen.

416

## LETTER CXXXIX [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. TO LAMBERT, ABBOT OF SAINT-BERTIN

He advises him to accept the office that has been offered.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his dearest friend, the reverend abbot of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, LAMBERT, greetings, love, and prayers.

Because the Church of Reims desires and requests your reverence [Note: The manuscript reads “your reverence, as ...” rather than “your reverence”] for the governance of the archbishopric, as you have written to me, your prudence asks my insignificance for counsel about what should be done in so great, burdensome, and dangerous a matter. First of all, I pray God that he permit nothing to happen to you except what pleases him and is beneficial to you.

As for the counsel you request, insofar as I can understand it, this seems to me the healthier course: that, as far as it lies with you, your will should give no assent to the matter; that you should say or do nothing that might help draw you by any occasion toward the burden to which you are being called. Let no necessity compel you, except sole and pure obedience. But accept obedience from no one except the lord abbot of Cluny, to whom you have subjected yourself.

As for your saying that you would rather incur the guilt of disobedience than accept so burdensome an undertaking and so laborious a burden, that is not my advice. Disobedience that is not followed by repentance is more dangerous than obedience which, in the hope of God’s mercy, undertakes even what appears impossible. For the virtue and merit of obedience, when it alone drives a person into dangers, either protects him from sin or, if he should happen to sin, the sin is very venial [Note: The manuscript reads “venial indeed”], provided repentance always accompanies it. But whoever lives in disobedience performs no good thing without stain.

[Note: Arnulf of Lisieux, in a letter to Daniel, prior of Saint-Barbara, rightly says that just as one ought not thrust oneself forward into a priorship, so, when called, one ought not refuse it: “For,” he says, “the swelling of disobedience brings no less guilt than the zeal of ambition. But if you withdraw not from pride but rather from humility, as you suppose, and from fear, this humility seems to me to savor of faintheartedness. Come, therefore, since divine grace will grow together with the burden itself.” Thus he.]

## LETTER CXL. POPE PASCHAL TO ANSELM

He greatly rejoices that Henry has obeyed ecclesiastical commands. He absolves Anselm from the excommunication he feared he had incurred because of the king’s investitures and gives him authority to absolve others who have been invested by the king, and the king himself, except the abbot of Ely.

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and blessing.

“As for the heart of the English king toward obedience to the Apostolic See ...” It is found in the *Register of Paschal II*, below, under the year 1118.

## LETTER CXLI [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO ARNULF, ABBOT OF TROARN

He sympathizes with him in his illness and gives the requested counsel concerning relinquishing his office: that he should resign it if the archbishop and the brothers consent.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved friend ARNULF, reverend abbot of Troarn [Note: The manuscript reads “Droarn” rather than “Troarn”], greetings and the continual protection and consolation of God’s grace.

The letter that you sent to the lord abbot Rodulf [Note: The manuscript reads “to Lord Rodulf” rather than “to the lord abbot Rodulf”] concerning your illness and distress struck our heart deeply with charitable compassion. In it your holiness also asks my insignificance for advice concerning the administration of your Church, since, because of the severity of your illness, you despair of being able to govern and administer it as you have hitherto done and as is necessary.

With regard to your illness, your mind ought to gather great consolation from it, because God chastises every son whom he receives. The examples of holy men who suffered many and very serious illnesses—such as Job, and as is read of a certain holy man [Note: “And as is read of a certain holy man,” etc. This was, unless I am mistaken, Paul, abbot of the desert of Panephysis, who was afflicted by such weakness of his limbs for four years that he was entirely unable to use them and could not be treated by men. For this reason he was entrusted to holy virgins, among whom he also died. See Cassian, *Collations* VII, chapter 26, where one finds that oil flowing from the anointed limbs of the holy man was so beneficial that it restored health to the sick] who was paralyzed throughout his body and, because the brothers could not move him, was entrusted to women—ought greatly to strengthen you.

For nowhere do we read that the illnesses of the saints were to their detriment; rather, we always read that through tribulations they advanced toward better things [Note: The manuscript reads “through tribulation”]. For even if good works are sometimes hindered by illness, thanks be to God, grace is not diminished but increased if good will does not decrease in tribulation; nor does God demand more from his servants than they are able to do.

As for the advice you request concerning the administration of your Church, we pray God that he himself may counsel you and protect and govern both you and your Church with its sons. Nevertheless, I must not remain silent about what seems to me, insofar as I can understand it. You ought not reject solely by your own will the care of the Church that you accepted through the obedience and charity of those to whom this responsibility belonged; rather, you should preserve obedience unto death.

But if, with the assent and counsel of the archbishop—since you do not have a bishop—and of the brothers and of those who understand the necessity of the matter, a person is chosen who can worthily assume the burden that you have hitherto carried, then, if you despair of returning to health, you may lawfully relinquish what you accepted through obedience.

I exhort and advise your sons that, the less they are presently able to make use of your help and counsel, the more earnestly they should themselves take care that the religious life which flourished in them while you were well does not decline. Rather, exhorting one another charitably, let them preserve their purpose inviolate.

[Col. 0173C]

## LETTER CXLII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO MURIARDACH, KING OF IRELAND

He praises this king for the peace of his kingdom and admonishes him to correct what needs correction, especially the marriages of kinsmen and the irregular ordinations of bishops.

To MURIARDACH, glorious king of Ireland by the grace of God, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, greetings with prayers, and may God’s mercy always be with and protect the king [Note: The manuscript reads “with and protect the king”].

I give thanks to God for the many good things that I hear about your highness. Among them is this: you cause the people of your kingdom to live in such peace that all good people who hear of it give thanks to God and desire the prolongation of your life. For where there is peace, all who have good will are able to accomplish what they desire without disturbance from evil people. Therefore your highness, through whom God brings these things about, ought certainly to expect a great reward from him.

Upon this foundation of peace it is easy to build the other things that ecclesiastical religion requires. I therefore ask for the constancy of your good will, so that you may consider whether there are things in your kingdom that need correction, both for the reward of eternal life and so that God’s grace may increase in you more and more, and may diligently strive, with God’s help, to amend them.

Nothing that can be corrected should be despised, because God demands from everyone not only what they do wrongly but also what they fail to correct when they are able to correct it. And the more powerful people are to correct something, the more strictly God demands from them that, according to the power mercifully entrusted to them, they should will and do what is good. This seems especially to concern kings, since they are known to possess greater power among human beings and to meet with less opposition.

If you cannot do everything at once, you ought not for that reason cease striving to advance from better things to better things, because God customarily brings good intentions and good efforts graciously to completion and rewards them with blessed fullness.

It is heard among us that marriages in your kingdom are dissolved and exchanged without any reason, because kinsmen, whether under the name of marriage or in some other way, do not fear to mingle openly and without reproach, contrary to canonical prohibition. Bishops also, who ought to be a pattern and example of canonical religion to others, are, as we have heard, consecrated irregularly, either by bishops alone or in places where they ought not to be ordained.

These matters, and whatever else your greatness’s prudence recognizes as needing correction in Ireland, I ask, entreat, and advise you—as one whom I greatly love and whose progress I desire in every respect—to strive to correct with the counsel of the good and wise men of your kingdom. And I pray God that you may pass from an earthly kingdom to the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## LETTER CXLIII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO GISLEBERT, BISHOP OF LUNICENSIS

He thanks the bishop, who rejoices that ecclesiastical affairs have gone well under his auspices.

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to GISLEBERT, bishop of Lunicensis [Note: The manuscript reads *Ludinensis* rather than *Lunnicensis*], greetings.

I give thanks to your reverence because your letter indicates that you rejoice that God deigns to accomplish something through me in his Church for the advancement of religion. Since we formerly became acquainted with one another at Rouen and were joined in affection, and since I now know that by God’s grace you have advanced to the dignity of the episcopate, I confidently dare to entreat you and, insofar as I understand the need, to offer you counsel.

God has raised your prudence in Ireland to so great a dignity and has placed you there so that you might labor for the strength of religion and the benefit of souls. Therefore, as it is written concerning one who presides, “with diligence,” strive carefully, insofar as it lies with you, to correct and uproot what must be corrected in that people, and to plant and sow good morals.

Insofar as you can, draw your king, the other bishops, and everyone whom you are able to persuade to this by showing them the joys prepared for the good and the evils awaiting the wicked, so that you may deserve to receive from God a reward for your good works and those of others [Note: The manuscript reads “and for your good works” rather than “for your good works and those of others”].

I give thanks for your gift, which you kindly sent me. Pray for me.

## LETTER CXLIV [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. TO AN APOSTATE MONK

By commands, counsels, and threats, he recalls two wandering sheep to the flock.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury by the grace of God, to ADRIAN, who was a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, and, persuaded by the devil, abandoned his habit, greetings and true love—if he wishes to return to his monastery and [Note: The manuscript reads “to his monastery and”] to the monastic vocation.

I ought not to call you brother and son until I know that you are doing penance for your sin and error; and I shall know this through your return. If, by God’s inspiring grace [Note: The manuscript reads “by God’s grace”], I see this according to my desire, be certain that, with God’s assent, you will find in me paternal piety and fraternal charity without deceit.

I therefore advise and, in advising, entreat you—as a man whose soul’s salvation I desire from the affection of my heart—and I command you, by the authority given to me by God and by the Church of God, before all the living who have professed obedience and stability in the monastery mentioned above. I adjure you by that same profession and stability, which you promised before God that you would keep in that place, and by both advents of our Lord Jesus Christ—as you wish the first to be for your salvation and the second not to be for your condemnation—that you come to your senses and return to the Church in which you were a monk as far as the habit is concerned, and in which you ought to be one according to the truth; and return to me and to the brothers who, for the salvation of your soul, desire you, if you do not wish to die in excommunication and anathema.

For no person living in the present life can absolve you from these bonds of excommunication and anathema unless you do what, with true love, I entreat and advise you to do.

I command you, if any trace of obedience still lives in you, to show this letter of mine, if you have the opportunity, to Airard, who departed from Christ Church with you; and whatever I write to you, I command him with the same charity and authority.

Although you do not yet deserve that I should pray for you [Note: The manuscript reads “that you still deserve” rather than “that you do not yet deserve”], nevertheless I pray almighty God that he himself may convert you to himself and to the salvation of your souls, and gladden me with your desired return. Amen.

[Col. 0176A]

## LETTER CXLV [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. WALTER TO ANSELM

He rejoices at Anselm’s successful return to England and at the same time asks him for some pious consolation.

To the desirable lord ANSELM, whom the Catholic mother Church should cherish with all the marrow of her inmost bowels, brother WALTER, the least and outermost part of his devoted followers, offers a sufficient draught of desired richness and deepest sweetness.

My tongue is stuck, my understanding is stuck, my hand falters as I reflect on the sweetness of your greeting, by which your highness deigned to bend down to so insignificant a little man. At the sound of your voice my bones have been strengthened and my inmost heart gladdened, because I have now truly learned that I did not love your glory in vain, [Col. 0176B] since you did not disdain to recognize my humility. Indeed, the more I see that nothing in me is ready or strong, the more highly I value your care for my weakness.

Therefore, together with me, all your friends offer a sacrifice of praise to almighty God, who has gladdened our age—deprived of the light of your presence—by the happier return of your blessedness. In whatever way he wished, he removed whatever opposed the peaceful repose of your will; and in a single moment he brought to completion, with the fullest effect, what had seemed to us exceedingly long.

Your entrance was peaceful both for us and for you, because, when you brought prolonged complaints to an end and the churches had been canonically conferred, you too found rest. Therefore all your friends rejoice with you in your rest and in the common good, and, since they cannot visit you joined to you in body, they do not cease to visit you on the footsteps of their desires.

I speak especially of our monks, whom you have bound to yourself all the more readily by the greater gift of your familiarity and by your assistance in their past need. But since I began on account of myself, I must return to myself.

It would be most desirable to me, if it could happen, to enjoy your presence before my end and to complain to you face to face about my misfortunes. My time has passed away, and I do not know whether I have gathered any fruit from the length of my life. But since the weakness of old age resists my desire, behold, here where I am, sighing toward you, I present the miseries and illnesses of soul that I have contracted. Above all, I entreat you to deign to shape me, by a written reply of your gentleness, in the manner in which you would console me in person, had that been possible, just as you have become all things to all people. This will be a great protection for my need and a welcome memorial of your sweetness.

This is truly the aim of my prayer: since I cannot enjoy you wholly according to my desire, at least grant me some small portion of yourself—not one in whose place I may delight, but one by looking upon which I may breathe again through your consolation [Note: The manuscript reads “through the regard” rather than “by looking upon which”]. This is not because the nourishment of Scripture sufficient for my illness is lacking, but because it is always better for a sick person if what he desires is given to him. Often the touch of one person soothes someone to whom the medicines of many do not cling.

May almighty God preserve your mind and tongue longer for the consolation of his little ones, and may he subject the efforts of your adversaries to your peaceful will by the right hand of his power [Note: The manuscript reads “May he subject” rather than “and may he subject”]. Amen.

## LETTER CXLVI [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO WALTER

This is a reply to the letter placed above.

ANSELM, archbishop, to his brother and beloved WALTER, greetings and the blessing of God and his own, insofar as it is worth anything.

[Col. 0177B]

I received the letter of your devout sweetness like a rich honeycomb, overflowing and dripping thick, sweet drops of your inexplicable love toward me. In it, your soul, beloved and dear to my soul and filled with holy fervor, shows itself to burn with so great a desire for conversation with me that, because it despairs this can happen, it longs at least for a letter containing my greeting and edifying admonition. Thus my soul wonders from where yours conceived so great an affection of love toward me, unless it is because “the Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8).

Certainly my merits cannot obtain from human beings that I should be loved in this way by a human being; but the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into the hearts of God’s servants, has himself made your soul fruitful with an affection so noble and so great. I hear his voice in your letter, but I do not know from where he inspires this, because I find no reason why he should do this in me. I ask him never to depart from you, but always to remain in you and unceasingly to make your whole spirit burn with love of God and neighbor.

I give thanks to God, who has granted that I be loved by you in this way; but he has given you a far greater gift when he has filled your heart with love of neighbor. For it is much more pleasing to God to love one’s neighbor than to be loved by one’s neighbor. Therefore we ought always to strive more to love than to be loved, and to rejoice more and regard it as a greater gain when we love than when we are loved.

We should also grieve more and consider it a greater loss when we lose the love with which we love [Note: The manuscript reads “when we lose the one whom we love”] than when we lose the person by whom we are loved; for reward is owed to the lover, not to the beloved.

I pray to God, for whose love you love me, that he himself may love you, that he himself may instruct you to live well, as you ask of me, that he himself may absolve you from all sins, and that he himself may lead you to eternal life. Amen.

419

## LETTER CXLVII [Note: Compared with the same manuscript]. ANSELM TO MURIARDACH, KING OF IRELAND

He again and again asks him to remedy, or arrange for the remedy of, the pestilential customs of his kingdom: that men should no longer exchange their wives for the wives of other men, and that a bishop should be established only in one definite place and ordained only by several bishops.

To MURIARDACH, glorious king of Ireland, ANSELM, archbishop and servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers faithful service with prayers, and wishes that through the earthly kingdom he may merit the heavenly one.

Since many things are reported about Your Excellence that befit royal dignity, we rejoice greatly; and we therefore render devoted thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes. We trust that he who has bestowed his grace upon you in doing the good things you do [Note: [Col. 0177C] *Quae fecistis* (“which you did”) in the manuscript instead of *quae facitis* (“which you do”)] will also bestow the desire to complete those things which you recognize him to will beyond what you are doing. Therefore, glorious son and most beloved in God, I beg you to correct with every diligence and care whatever you recognize as needing correction in your kingdom according to the Christian religion. For God established you in royal eminence so that you might govern subject peoples with the rod of equity, and with that same rod strike down and remove whatever in them is opposed to justice.

Indeed, something is said to occur among the very people whom you have undertaken to govern which urgently requires correction, because it is altogether contrary to the Christian religion. For it is said that men so freely and publicly exchange their wives for the wives of others [Note: [Col. 0177D] It is said that men so freely and publicly exchange their wives for the wives of others. In Epistle 141 above he had given the same warning; but because, as is clear, it had been disregarded, he repeats it here. Even before Anselm, Pope Gregory VII had heard something similar and therefore warned Lanfranc by letter—most of which we have reproduced in Epistle 31 of Book II—to confront this spreading disease in these words:

“Although your fraternity needs no admonisher, nevertheless, impelled by our concern, we admonish you to strive everywhere to cut away the more serious vices, and above all, among everything else, to prohibit in every way the abomination we have heard about the Scots: namely, that many not only abandon their wives, but even sell them. For this purpose we wish you to be supported by apostolic authority, so that not only among the Scots, but also among others—if you discover any such people in the island of the English—you may punish them with severe correction, and not delay to root out entirely the origin of so great an evil with the prudent hoe of correction.”

Thus Gregory wrote to Lanfranc, who immediately complied with the pontiff’s admonitions. For directly after Gregory’s letter there follow other letters of Lanfranc himself to Gothric, king of Ireland, in which, after winning his goodwill at the outset, he writes:

“It is reported that in your kingdom men take wives either from their own family or from the family of deceased wives. Others abandon those lawfully joined to them according to their own discretion and will; some give their own wives to others and receive the wives of others in an unspeakable exchange. For God’s sake and for the sake of your soul, command that these things, and any other crimes there may be, be corrected in the land under your authority, and show yourself to your subjects, with God’s help, in such a way that lovers of good may love good things more ardently and seekers of evil may not dare to practice wicked deeds.”

Thus Lanfranc admonished the king. Yet I do not know whether he passed these words by with deaf ears, or whether invading death forestalled his holy desires. At least it is clear from another letter of Lanfranc to Terdelvacus, Gothric’s successor, that no remedy had been applied to so pestilential a disease. Complaining, he writes shortly before the middle:

“Among many things that please us, certain things have been reported to us that displease us: namely, that in your kingdom each person, according to his own will, abandons a wife lawfully joined to him, without any canonical cause intervening, and joins himself with another woman—whether related by blood to himself or to the wife he has abandoned, or one whom another has abandoned with similar wickedness—in an act of rashness punishable under marital or fornication law.”

Thus far Lanfranc. If it is permissible to confirm Anselm’s present statements by Lanfranc’s earlier admonitions, I would dare say that this lethal gangrene arose not from the long-corrupted customs of the Scots or Irish, but from those of the English, and gradually acquired strength and increase. For Gildas, in *The Ruin of Britain*, said more than a thousand years ago: “Britain has very many kings who have several wives, but live in fornication.” The blessed martyr and archbishop Boniface brings the same charge against Ethelbal[d], king of the English, in William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Kings of England*, chapter 4: “We have heard that almost all the nobles of the Mercian people, following your example, abandon their lawful wives and violate adulteresses and nuns,” and so forth.

That this lust was almost hereditary among the Scots is argued by St Jerome, Book II, *Against Jovinianus*: “The nation of the Scots has no wives of its own; and as though it had read Plato’s *Republic* and followed Cato’s example, no wife is regarded as belonging to anyone in particular among them, but, like cattle, they indulge themselves promiscuously according to each person’s pleasure.” I pass over the shameful and closely similar practices that Sylvester Giraldus recorded about the Irish a hundred years after Anselm, *Topography of Ireland*, distinction 3, chapter 19.

How deep a root this disease had struck, so that it could not be uprooted even by the remedies advised in this letter, is shown by the council held at Cashel, an archiepiscopal city of Ireland, in the year 1171 and approved by Alexander III. Among the council’s decrees, the chief injunction was that all laymen who wished to have wives should have them according to ecclesiastical law. Roger Hoveden reported this in the second part of his *Annals*. Yet this decree too, as is clear from the testimony cited by Sylvester Giraldus, proved unable to uproot it: so deeply black is the evil of impious Venus.] as one exchanges any horse for another horse, or one thing for another thing; or they abandon them according to their pleasure and without reason. Everyone who knows Christian law understands how evil this is.

Therefore, if Your Excellence cannot personally read the judgments of the divine Scriptures that oppose this infamous practice, command the bishops and religious clerics who are in your kingdom to declare them to you, so that, once you know them, you may recognize with what zeal you must watch over the correction of this evil.

It is also said that bishops are elected indiscriminately in your land, established without a definite episcopal see, and that one bishop ordains another bishop as though he were an ordinary priest. This is plainly altogether contrary to the sacred canons; and they command that those who have been appointed or ordained in this manner, together with their ordainers, be removed from the episcopal office. For a bishop cannot be established according to God unless he has a definite parish and a people over whom he is to preside, since even in secular affairs a man cannot bear the name or office of shepherd if he has no flock to feed. The episcopal dignity is also greatly diminished when someone is raised to the pontificate who does not know where he is to reside or over whom he is to preside with episcopal ministry.

Nor should anyone be ordained by fewer than three bishops: both for many other reasonable causes that the brevity of a letter does not permit me to set out, and so that the faith, life, and diligence of the man who must keep watch may be attested by suitable and legitimate witnesses.

I therefore beg, exhort, and admonish Your Excellence to take care that these matters be corrected in your kingdom, so that the reward which you seek from God for other good works [Note: [Col. 0179C] *Expeditis* (“you accomplish”) in the manuscript instead of *expetitis* (“you seek”)] may be increased for you on their account. Moreover, if you perceive anything in yourself or in those whom you have undertaken to govern that could in any way oppose God’s will, strive diligently to correct it, so that when you have passed from the earthly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0179C] *Transibitis* (“you will pass”) in the manuscript instead of *transieritis* (“you have passed”)] you may come to the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

Concerning our brother Cornelius, whom Your Highness requested to be sent to you, I say that he is so occupied with serving his father that he cannot be separated from him without danger to the latter’s life, nor can he in any way take with him the man who is already worn out by old age.

## EPISTLE CXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0179C] Collated with the same manuscript.]

**ANSELM TO ODO, A MONK**

That he should not abandon the office entrusted to him because of advancing age.

**ANSELM**, archbishop, to his most beloved brother **ODO**, monk and cellarer [Note: [Col. 0179C] *Cellario* in the manuscript instead of *cellerario*], greetings and the blessing of God and of Anselm.

It is said that, because you feel your end approaching through age and illness [Col. 0180B], you therefore wish to abandon your obedience, in which until now you have served God and the community of the church where you live. Yet I wish your affection to know that this counsel does not come from a good source [Note: [Col. 0179C] *De bona* (“from a good source”) in the manuscript instead of *ex bona*]. We must indeed repent of evil works and abandon them before death, lest the final day find us in them. But in good works we must persevere to the end, so that our soul may be taken from this life while engaged in them.

For it is said of those who do good perseveringly: “He who perseveres to the end, he [Note: [Col. 0179C] *Sic salvus* (“thus saved”) in the manuscript instead of *hic salvus* (“this one saved”)] will be saved” (Matthew 10:12), not of those who fail in good works before the end. It is therefore beneficial for your soul, dearest brother and son, that you persevere in the obedience which, according to your ability, you have maintained for the pleasure of God, insofar as we can know it, and for the pleasure of your abbot and brothers, for as long as life remains in you and your abbot commands you to do so—with a good and joyful spirit, without any resentment or complaint—so that, even while speaking and arranging something concerning that obedience, you may breathe out your spirit.

Thus the promise that is made to those who persevere to the end will be fulfilled for you. Nor should it frighten you that, because of bodily weakness, you are now unable to perform and manage what must be done in this obedience as effectively as you once did in health and youth. For God does not demand from you more than your ability. Nor should any adversities disturb you, from whatever source they come, by which the enemy of your soul wishes to trouble and weary you, so that you may fail before the end and lose the reward of perseverance.

I therefore exhort and beg you to establish and fix this in your heart: that you should never abandon, while you live, the good work which until now you have faithfully maintained with God’s help, unless your abbot and brothers command you to do so—not because of your importunity, but of their own free will. Be certain that the greater the difficulty with which you perform the obedience imposed upon you—both because of your weakness and because of whatever adversities—the greater reward you will receive from God [Note: [Col. 0181C] *Facias* (“you may do”) in the manuscript instead of *facies* (“you will do”)].

I pray almighty God that he himself direct your heart; and, insofar as it lies with me, I send you, dearest brother, God’s blessing and absolution.

420 ## EPISTLE CXLIX

**ANSELM TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK**

A church ought not to be without a pastor for more than three months; he therefore commands Thomas to present himself at Canterbury on 6 September to be consecrated by Anselm, and forbids him, before his own consecration, to consecrate the elected bishop of St Andrews in Scotland.

**ANSELM**, archbishop of Canterbury, to **THOMAS**, elected archbishop of the church of York, greetings.

[Col. 0182A]

Canonical authority commands that a church of a bishopric not remain without a pastor for more than three months. Since, however, the king, with the counsel of his barons and our consent, was pleased that your person should be elected to the archbishopric of York, the salutary time-limit established ought not to be delayed further by you. I therefore wonder why, after your election, you did not request to be consecrated for the office to which you were elected.

I therefore command you to be at our mother church of Canterbury on 6 September, to do what you ought to do and to receive your consecration. If you do not do this, it belongs to me to take care of and perform whatever pertains to episcopal office in the archbishopric of York.

Furthermore, I have heard that before you are consecrated [Col. 0182B], you wish to arrange for the elected bishop of St Andrews in Scotland to be consecrated at York.

[Note: [Col. 0181C] You wish to arrange for the elected bishop of St Andrews in Scotland to be consecrated at York. Since the consecration of all bishops destined for the churches of the Orkney Islands—that is, of Ireland and Scotland—belonged to the archbishop of York, Thomas wished, although he had not yet received episcopal ordination (*χειροτονία*), to confer or arrange for the conferring of ordination upon another. Anselm rightly forbade this, saying that a man cannot entrust the care of souls which he himself has not received. The bishop being initiated was named Turgodus, prior of the church of Durham.

Moreover, that the initiation of the Scottish and Irish bishops belonged to the archbishop of York, and that the man under discussion was his cousin, is shown by a letter of Lanfranc—but not by a letter from Lanfranc to him—which I reproduce here in full. The earlier letter reads:

“To the most pious [Father], etc. Behold, most holy Father, your son cries out to you—or rather your daughter, the church of York, cries out to the church over which you preside by divine appointment—; like one returning to a mother’s lap, she piously asks that, from the abundance of maternal delights, the poverty of those who have abandoned her—or rather of those powers situated far away among barbarous nations—may be relieved. For a certain cleric has come to us, sent by Count Paul with sealed letters stating that he has granted this cleric the episcopate of his land. Following the order of his predecessors, he asks us to consecrate him bishop; and although he asks justly, we cannot justly deny his request.

“We therefore beg Your Paternity to send us two bishops, supported by whose prayers and assistance we may canonically complete the sacrament of so great a matter. Let the suspicion also be kept far away which our brother Remigius recently insinuated to us and our fellow bishops: namely, that for this reason I might later seek the submission of the bishop of Dorchester or Worcester. For I declare before God that I will never do this.

“If it pleases Your Holiness to grant our request, we have fixed and notify you of the place—York—and the date—5 March—without alteration. Therefore may you live and prosper, and advance in every way in spiritual growth.”

Thus far Thomas. His words make it clear that he had once raised his head more proudly against Lanfranc for the same reason as his cousin Thomas here, but had now bowed it much lower, so much so that he feared to call himself archbishop of York except with Lanfranc’s silent permission. But let us join to this Lanfranc’s reply, by which he more forcefully confirms the right belonging to the see of York.

[Col. 0182D]

“Lanfranc, etc. Our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of York, has informed you that a certain cleric has come to him from the Orkney Islands, whom, at the command and notification of Count Paul, he testifies to have been elected to the bishopric of that land. Since by ancient custom it is his right to consecrate the bishops of the aforesaid islands, he has asked me to send him two of our suffragans who may celebrate with him the sacrament of so great a matter.

“Therefore, while asking, we command; and while commanding, we ask that, setting aside every excuse, you go there and, by our command, complete with him what is just in the mystery of so great a matter. For it is not fitting that one who has come to this land to be consecrated, and who with all humility requests consecration, should depart from so great a kingdom unconsecrated for lack of assistants. The bearer of this letter will indicate to you the date of this consecration.

“And lest you should perhaps be anxious, supposing that either he or his successors might on this occasion at some time attempt to seize a right of precedence over your churches, he has taken care, out of concern for the future, to send your fraternity the letters he transmitted to me. I also command that these letters, as well as those which I am sending you, be preserved in the archives of your churches, for the memory of future generations.”

Thus Lanfranc, who also declares that the bishops of the Orkneys are to be anointed by the archbishop of York, but in such a way that the primate of Canterbury sends him two bishops of his province to assist him in carrying out the sacred inauguration; and that York may not on this account claim any right over them. Hence this Thomas, to whom Anselm is writing, could not initiate the designated bishop of the Scottish church.]

You ought neither to do this, nor do I permit it; I altogether forbid it, whether in his case or in that of any person who ought to be advanced to the governance of souls by the archbishop of York, because it does not belong to you to give or grant to anyone the care of souls which you have not yet received. Farewell.

## EPISTLE CL

**ANSELM TO GOFFRIDUS**

He praises a good man for the integrity of his life and warns him to beware of something, especially lest, judging the deeds of others, he despise them.

**ANSELM**, archbishop, to **GOFFRIDUS**, greetings and the blessing of God and of Anselm.

[Col. 0182C] Juhel, your nephew, told me about your life [Col. 0183A] and asked me on your behalf to advise you how you ought to live. But when I had heard about your life, I could not think of anything I might add to you concerning psalms, prayers, abstinences, or bodily affliction beyond what, by God’s grace, you have begun and are doing.

Therefore, as long as you can do what you are doing without harm to your bodily health, continue it. But if you perceive that it is turning into illness for you, then I advise you to moderate yourself as you recognize to be beneficial. For it is better to do something with a joyful spirit while preserving bodily health than, through illness, to regard as worthless the things you do well with joy. Nor should you in any way despise those who do not do these things, or think that they are of lesser merit before God than you are.

Bodily exercise is good, but God loves much more a heart full of piety, love, humility, and the desire to reach the place where it can and delights to see God himself. May almighty God teach, strengthen, and console you. I send you God’s absolution and mine, if it has any force, from all your sins. I ask you to pray for me.

## EPISTLE CLI

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Collated with the same manuscript.]

**ANSELM TO JOHN, PRIOR, AND THE COMMUNITY OF BATH**

That they will become God’s house and temple if they preserve mutual concord and observe discipline in small matters.

**ANSELM**, archbishop, to **JOHN**, prior, and the entire community at Bath, servants of God, God’s blessing and Anselm’s, if it has any force.

[Col. 0183C] Lord John, the bearer of this letter, asked me to write to your fraternity some admonition that might be a sign of fatherly love. I could briefly include everything that ought to be avoided and sought by saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27). But I think it more appropriate to admonish your religious community specifically concerning some virtue.

I therefore exhort you to strive with all your heart to preserve peace among yourselves, because it is said of God: “His dwelling has been established in peace” (Psalm 75:5). You will truly be God’s house and temple if you constantly maintain peace among yourselves.

You will be able to obtain and preserve it in this way: if each person does not focus on making another do his own will, but, while preserving righteousness and God’s will, always gives preference to the will of the other [Col. 0183D]. Among secular people there is contention over each person’s own will, so that each one says, “Not as you will, but as I will” [Note: [Col. 0183D] *Voluntate ut unusquisque* (“over the will, so that each person”) in the manuscript instead of *voluntate, unusquisque* (“over the will: each person”)]. But the contention of monks is: “Let it not be according to my will, but according to yours” [Note: [Col. 0183D] *Contentio volo* (“contention, I will”) in the manuscript instead of *contentio vero* (“but the contention”)].

Nor should each person wait for another to repay him by doing the same when he himself does the other’s will. Rather, he should strive in this: whatever the other may do, he himself should never depart from his own good purpose.

There is also something else that greatly fosters peace and love among brothers: no one should ever say to his brother something about another by which his friend might in any way be offended. Instead, whenever possible, a brother should speak about a brother in such a way that his heart is drawn toward love.

Observe these things, my dearest brothers and sons. You must also be so attentive to the discipline of your order that you violate it nowhere and never—not even in the smallest matter, whether secretly or in the presence of others. For it is written: “He who despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). Therefore, if you wish to make progress before God, never despise the least commandments.

Just as he who despises small things gradually falls, so he who does not despise small things does not merely progress gradually, but makes vigorous progress. Brothers, act so that you may say with the Prophet: “My soul is always in my hands” (Psalm 113:15). In all your works you must consider that your soul is always in your hands, because whatever each person does, that is what his soul will receive.

May almighty God guard you from every evil and, having absolved you from all sins, make you persevere in good works. Amen. I beg you to pray for me.

421 ## EPISTLE CLII

**ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL II**

That he should not send the pallium to the archbishop of York before his consecration, nor to the bishop of London, who has never had it, lest the primacy of the church of Canterbury fall from its dignity, something Anselm absolutely cannot endure. He also asks whether the pope permits the king of the Germans to grant investitures, as the king of England had heard.

To the lord and beloved and revered Father **PASCHAL**, supreme pontiff, **ANSELM**, servant of the church of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0183D] The manuscript reads “Anselm of the church of Canterbury” instead of “Anselm, servant of the church of Canterbury”], sends due obedience with faithful prayers.

Since, after God, the strength and direction of God’s churches depend chiefly upon the authority of Your Paternity [Col. 0184D–0185A], whenever reason requires it we gladly have recourse to your help and counsel.

Gerard, archbishop of York, has departed this life, and another, named Thomas, has been elected in his place. There is a report that the pallium is being sought for him before he has been consecrated and before he has made his profession to me according to the ancient custom of my predecessors and his.

This, then, is the substance of all my requests in this matter: before he is consecrated and professes to me the obedience due, as I have said, and before you learn from our letters that this has been done, let him not receive the pallium from Your Excellence. I do not say this because I begrudge him the pallium, but because some people assert—and are even working to bring it about—that, if this is granted by you, they may confidently deny me the profession that is due.

If this happens, know that the church of England would be divided; and, according to the Lord’s saying, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste,” the rigor of apostolic discipline in it would be considerably weakened. I too would not remain in England. For I ought not, and could not, endure that, while I was alive in it, the primacy of our church should be destroyed.

I make the same suggestion to Your Reverence with the same feeling concerning the bishop of London, for whom the pallium is being requested although he has never had it: namely, that you should give no assent whatever to this. Some people are contriving, under the appearance of good, to humble the dignity of Canterbury’s primacy in a manner that ought not to be permitted.

This year, after Pentecost, I sent Your Holiness a letter through Bernard, servant of Lord Peter, your chamberlain, saying that the king of England complains that you tolerate the German king’s granting investitures of churches without excommunication, and that he therefore threatens without doubt to resume his own investitures, since the other king retains his in peace.

Let Your Prudence therefore see without delay what you ought to do about this, lest what you have built so well be irreparably destroyed. For our king is diligently asking what action you are taking concerning that king.

We pray God to gladden us through your long prosperity.

## EPISTLE CLIII

[Note: [Col. 0185B] Collated with the same manuscript.]

**A LETTER OF POPE PASCHAL TO ANSELM**

In reply to the preceding letter, he says that he will in no way detract from the dignity of Anselm’s church, nor has he ever tolerated investitures being granted by the German king.

**PASCHAL**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother **ANSELM**, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letter of your affection, etc. See Paschal II under the year 1118.

## EPISTLE CLIV

**ANSELM TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF BEC**

Vows made before monastic profession remain at the disposition of the superior.

**ANSELM of Bec**, now minister of the church of Canterbury, to his beloved and revered abbot **WILLIAM**, his beloved friend [Note: [Col. 0185C–0188C] This was that same William, third abbot of Bec, concerning whose election the account is given in Epistle 8 above. There we recorded William’s birth, childhood, and monastic life, using a manuscript of Bec which will also provide material for a brief and clear account of his death. Since we described there his holy and happy beginnings, here we shall relate his happier end, though it was mournful for the monks of Bec.

In the twentieth year of his office, in September, he fell ill. The illness slowly consumed his aged limbs and prolonged his death until March of the following year. Then, becoming more severe and powerful than usual, it bound him more tightly to his bed than Prometheus was bound to Caucasus.

During this illness Richard, abbot of the monastery of Préaux—which Roger of Beaumont, son of Humphrey, founded on his own estate; William of Jumièges carefully observed this in Book VII, chapter 22 of his *History of the Norman Dukes*—visited William and soon afterward the brothers of Bec. William was then strengthened both by their entreaties and by ecclesiastical chrism.

Boso, prior of Bec—for Baldwin, to whom Epistles 7 and 8 above are addressed, had already departed this life—admonished William, as he lay dying, to leave his sons some heavenly blessing. William therefore raised his hand, blessed them, and said:

“Love the cloistered life, because it is the restoration of our order; and do not seek to hold obediences in the world, for many lose their souls in them. Choose an abbot as soon as possible, because it is not good to delay such a work.”

After saying this, he earnestly asked them to pour out prayers in his name. It was customary for him, whenever he knew a man of wholly blameless life, eagerly to seek a share in that man’s prayers.

At that time, because several sudden disturbances had arisen in Normandy, Henry, son of Noth and king, had hurried over from England. Around the feast of Easter he came to Bec, where some of the monks of Bec begged him to appoint someone in the place of the dying man. When this reached William’s ears, he took care that no one should solicit his position.

Henry, having learned of William’s illness, visited him with great courtesy and, speaking with him, sat on the ground in observance of the man’s dignity. William, for his part, looking ahead to the future state of his monastery, begged Henry to place over Bec a monk of mature age and more blameless life.

“Whom?” Henry asked.

William replied: “The ecclesiastical sanctions forbid all superiors to elect their own successor.”

He had said this, and the king brought his right hand to the speaker’s mouth and eyes. The brothers therefore began to recite the penitential psalms and the litany of the saints, during which William breathed out his soul.

As customary, the body was soon clothed in sacred vestments and carried into the basilica, where it was placed before the high altar. Monks, laypeople, and neighboring villagers came there to offer mournful prayers. The king too, who had seen him breathing his last and devoid of every breath, honored him with a final visit.

Besides the king, nine abbots and an innumerable crowd of clergy and monks came; among them the distinguished John, bishop of Lisieux, who also performed the final rites for the dead. A multitude of beggars was likewise present. For their benefit and in aid of the deceased, alms were distributed so generously for two days that no one returned empty-handed.

Meanwhile William’s body remained unburied in the chapter house, to the right of Herluin, its founder. William professed as a monk of Bec in the twenty-fifth year of his age, lived there for fifteen years as a private monk, governed it for thirty and a half years, and thus died at the age of seventy in the year 1124, on the Kalends of May. He was honored with this epitaph:

> Abbot William, born of illustrious stock,  
> In the first season of his life became a lover of religion.  
> When five lustrums of his age had duly passed,  
> Sighing for God, he began to despise the world.  
> He divided his earthly goods, but clung wholly to Christ,  
> So that, naked, the servant might follow the naked Lord.  
> At once he took upon himself at Bec the easy yoke of Christ,  
> Which he steadfastly bore for fifteen years.  
> When Anselm had become prelate of the English,  
> This man began to govern the place and rule the brothers.  
> The gravity of his character, the excellence of his life, and the honor of his parents  
> Made him distinguished and venerable to very many.  
> He was learned and pleased people by his gentle speech;  
> By deeds and words he instructed those subject to him.  
> From childhood he had been a guardian of an honorable life,  
> Preserving purity of heart and perpetual chastity of flesh.  
> For thirty years he enlarged and ruled Bec:  
> Gentle to his subjects, harsh to the proud.  
> Such a great man, enriched with abundant merits and virtues,  
> Was nevertheless unable to escape the bonds of death.  
> On the sixteenth day of April, as the day was rising,  
> He completed the course and task of this present life,  
> Commending his soul to heaven and his body to the grave.  
> He awaits the time when Christ will judge all things.  
> Behold, beneath this tomb lie members buried as dust;  
> Let us ask that the Lord grant him pardon and life.

I did not see this epitaph, which was inserted in the manuscript of Bec, in the aforementioned chapter-house location. I would suppose—and not wrongly—that when it was restored—for the very appearance of the place, new and somewhat childish, bears witness to a more recent restoration—it had either been covered over by dirt or obscured by rust, and for that reason neglected.]

Greetings.

[Col. 0187A]

Concerning the monk’s vow about which you wish to hear our advice: before coming to our order he vowed that he would never again drink wine. It seems to me that what is done by the elders of our order, especially at Cluny, ought to be done in this case—namely, that vows of this kind, made without a pledge of faith and an oath, should be regarded as fulfilled in the vow of the monastic order, in which a man offers to God everything belonging to him and his entire self. It should therefore remain at the superior’s discretion either reasonably to preserve such vows or to alter them.

As for the monk of whom we are speaking, you may, if you wish, allow him for a time to continue what he has begun. But if you should at some point understand that this is not beneficial, command him confidently to do what the brothers generally do.

## EPISTLE CLV

**ANSELM TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK**

He forbids the archbishop to exercise any of his functions before he has made the customary pledge of fidelity.

**ANSELM**, servant of the church of Canterbury, to **THOMAS**, archbishop.

To you, Thomas, in the presence [Note: [Col. 0188C–0189D] “To you, Thomas, in the presence…” Anselm wrote this letter with not a single stone of charity omitted. According to the librarian of Malmesbury, when Thomas was first summoned by Anselm to come to Canterbury to be inaugurated by him and to confirm his obedience to him by oath according to custom, he expressed kind thanks for the invitation and asked for time to prepare for so solemn an undertaking.

When summoned a second time, he replied that he was constrained by the arguments of his clerics. Finally, through the bishops of London and Rochester, he openly refused to come. Therefore Anselm, unable to draw him over by private admonitions, at last publicly proclaimed him contumacious in this dreadful proclamation, which William of Malmesbury also reported in his account of the archbishops of York.

After this, while Thomas was being admonished by Henry and the leading men of England, Anselm died, leaving Thomas deprived of his blessing—which Thomas had arrogantly rejected and later regretted having rejected. Finally compelled, he promised obedience to Richard Belmeis, bishop of London, and was consecrated.

After five years, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, he ceased to live, all the more conspicuously because he had lived obscurely under the shameful darkness of his obstinacy. When he had taken to his bed, the physicians consulted replied that he would never recover except through intercourse with a woman. Rejecting this foul and detestable remedy, he groaned in lamentation:

“Woe to the illness for which such a medicine is appropriate!”

And thus, says Roger Hoveden in his *Annals*, he died a temporal virgin, chosen by the Lord. Hence the following words, which Angelus Politianus wrote about Michael Verinus, may rightly be sung of him:

> Only Venus could help the lingering disease.  
> Rather than pollute himself, he preferred to die.

Indeed, it is permissible to express Thomas’s manly and praiseworthy reply through the couplets of Verinus, who was suffering in the same way. One of them he addressed to a certain Peter:

> Why, Peter, do you urge me to lay down the virgin flower?  
> I will not do it—not even if certain health must be won by this.

And again, to his teacher:

> The physicians promise me health through intercourse, Paul:]

Let the certain safety of my life not be of such great value to me. By the authority of almighty God, I, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, speak on behalf of that same God. The priestly office which, at my command, you undertook in my parish through my suffragan, I prohibit you from exercising and command you not to presume to involve yourself in any pastoral care whatsoever until you withdraw from the rebellion which you began against the Church of Canterbury and profess toward it the submission which your predecessors—namely, the archbishops Thomas and Gerard—professed in accordance with the ancient custom of their predecessors. But if you choose to persevere in what you have begun rather than desist from it, I prohibit all the bishops of all Britain, under perpetual anathema, from laying hands upon you for promotion to the episcopate; or, if you have been promoted by outsiders, from receiving you as a bishop or into any Christian communion.

To you also, Thomas, under the same anathema, I prohibit, on behalf of God, from ever receiving the episcopal blessing of York unless you first make the profession which your predecessors Thomas and Gerard made to the Church of Canterbury. But if you entirely relinquish the bishopric of York, I grant you permission to use the priestly office which you have already undertaken.

[Col. 0188B]

## LETTER 156

### Anselm to William, abbot, and the congregation of Bec

[Textual note: Compared with the same manuscript. The manuscript reads *parochia* for *paroecia* (“parish”) in the preceding letter; *totius Britanniae* (“of all Britain”) for *Britanniae*; and, for “if you have been promoted by outsiders, that they not receive you as a bishop or in any Christian communion,” it reads “if you have been promoted, that the same persons not receive you as a bishop in any Christian communion.” It reads *suscepisti* (“you have undertaken”) for *incoepisti* (“you have begun”).]

He has nothing dearer to him than them, and will not forget them until he ceases to exist.

To his dearest and most longed-for lords and brothers, Lord William, abbot, and the holy congregation serving God at Bec under him, Brother Anselm, called archbishop: may they always be directed toward good by heavenly grace and blessing, and defended from evil.

[Textual notes: The manuscript reads *charissimis et desideratissimis domno* (“to the dearest and most longed-for lord”) for the heading’s *charissimis domino*, etc.; *quantumque* for *quantumcunque* (“however greatly”); and singular *frater uterinus* (“a brother by the same mother”) for plural *fratres uterinos*.]

If I wish to set out fully for you what my heart feels toward your love, a large book would not suffice; and if I propose to speak briefly, it cannot satisfy my affection. Yet amid this uncertainty your own conscience consoles me, since you know how constantly and truly I have loved you, how many things I have desired from you and how greatly, and how, for as long as I lived among you, I strove to advance you in some measure. If not all of you know this by experience—for God has increased your number since I departed from you—learn it from those who know and have experienced it.

Let there therefore be no doubt whatever in your love that, just as I loved the root, so I love the branches, however greatly they may multiply; and all the children of my mother, both those born first and those born after me, I embrace and love in my heart as uterine brothers—that is, brothers by the same mother.

[Textual notes: The manuscript reads *semper vos, et* (“always yourselves, and”) for *semper vos extendatis, et*; this is the reading supplied in the text.]

I therefore beg and beseech all of you that memory of and love for me not grow cold in the hearts of those who knew me, and that it be kindled and endure in the minds of those who did not know me. Although I am absent from you in body, I nevertheless always carry my nest—by which I mean the church of Bec—with all its young, in my heart; and in my prayers and in every good desire of mine, if these amount to anything, I present it to God.

Therefore, let the sincerity of your love pray for me, and let heavenly piety inspire you so that your constant prayers for me do not fail. Although your souls burn with good desire, nevertheless, since those who love are not wearied of hearing what they love, I beg, beseech, admonish, and advise you always to extend yourselves toward better things, and never to fall away from those things to which God has advanced you.

Let mutual love according to God always burn among you; let peace and concord, with truth preserved, continually remain in your minds; let humble obedience in all your actions please God; and let zeal for religion and for excluding vice from yourselves blaze up. Admonish one another about these things; hold fast to them without ceasing.

This is what I ask, what I desire, what I long for from you; may he from whom all good comes grant you this, with his full and perpetual blessing. Amen.

## LETTER 157

### Anselm to a certain woman

Anselm, by God’s ordinance archbishop of Canterbury, to a certain woman: to despise the world, not Christ, and to love Christ more than the world.

[Textual notes: The edition entitles this “An exhortation to a fallen virgin.” It reads *soror mihi* for *soror vere mihi* (“sister truly beloved by me”); *ut te fraterno* for *te fraterno*; *nobis evenit* for *in nobis non evenit* (“the opportunity has arisen for us”); *Dei ad* for *Dei, et ad*; *et congaudeant* for *ut gaudeat Deus et congaudeant*; *decet esse* (“it is fitting that there be”) for *debet esse*; *salutem spero* for *salutem tuam spero*; *objectum* for *abjectum*; *iste nunc* for *ista nunc*; and *ut sit legitima* for *ut sis legitima*.]

I would gladly speak with you, if I could, sister truly beloved by me in God, because the love by which I wish every human being to be saved, and the office entrusted to me, require me to love you with brotherly and fatherly affection and, through that same love, to be concerned for the salvation of your soul. But since the opportunity for conversation has not arisen for us, I am compelled to write what disposition I have toward you and what I desire for you.

I therefore beg you not to despise the love with which, for God’s sake, for the honor of God, and for your salvation, I love you, nor to reject my counsel. For if you are willing to heed me, be certain that in the end it will please you greatly, and that there will be great joy over you among the angels of God. But if you are unwilling, know that it will displease you exceedingly, and that you will be without excuse at God’s strict judgment.

I have heard, my sister, that you long bore the habit of holy conduct. How you abandoned it, what you suffered, and what you did is not hidden, but is entirely exposed.

Consider now, therefore, dearest daughter, how far the embraces of men and carnal pleasure differ from the embraces of Christ and from the pleasure of chastity and purity of heart. By Christ’s embraces I mean not bodily embraces, but those which the soul, as his intimate companion, creates through love and desire for him within a good conscience.

Consider, I say, what difference there is between these two pleasures. I am not now speaking of lawful marriage. Consider, I say, how great is the purity in spiritual pleasure and how great the impurity in carnal pleasure; what the spiritual promises and what the carnal threatens; how great is the hope in the spiritual life and how delightful the expectation of Christ; how great also are security and consolation in the present life, and how great is the fear of God’s judgment in the carnal life, as well as the shame that exists in the present life.

Think what it is to despise Christ as bridegroom, when he promises the dowry of the heavenly kingdom, and to prefer a mortal man, who gives and promises nothing but corruption and contemptible things, to the Son of God, the King of kings. Certainly that King of kings desired your beauty, as the beauty of a lawful bride.

But how that man whom you know desired the beauty of your flesh, my sister—how shall I say it? Noble woman, how shall I say it? You had been chosen as God’s bride, a virgin, and assigned to God by your habit and conduct. What shall I now say that you are, my daughter? God knows.

I do not speak in this way because I rejoice in your shame, but so that God may rejoice and the angels may rejoice with him over your conversion and saving repentance. What, then, shall I say? If I do not speak, perhaps you will not notice; if I speak, perhaps you will become angry. From being chosen, marked, and betrothed to God, what have you become? Let your nobility blush at what you blush to hear, and I, because of your nobility and because of my love, blush to say it.

Behold, dearest daughter: if you set these things before your eyes, how great a grief ought there to be in your heart over so great and so grievous a fall! For if you grieve intensely, I rejoice greatly in sympathy with you; but if you do not grieve, there is no reason for me to rejoice, and I grieve all the more. For if you grieve, I still hope for your salvation; but if you do not grieve, what can I expect except your damnation?

For it is impossible for you to be saved in any way unless you return to the abandoned habit and purpose. Although you were not consecrated by a bishop and did not read your profession before him, this alone is nevertheless clear and cannot be denied:

[Editorial note, [Col. 0191C–0192D]: Anselm appears here to speak in accordance with Pope Leo’s view, expressed in chapter 13 of Letter 90 to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne: “Girls who have undertaken the purpose and habit of virginity not under compulsion from parental authority but by spontaneous judgment, if they later choose marriage, violate their undertaking, even if consecration has not been added; certainly they would not be deprived of its gift if they remained in their purpose.” Before Leo, Innocent I appears to have held the same view. Gregory the Great produced Innocent’s decree on this subject in his letter to Boniface, cited by Ivo of Chartres in Part III of his *Pannonia* and by Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 38: “Those who, though not yet covered with the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed to remain in the virginal purpose, even if not veiled, must do penance if they marry at any time, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract of good faith is customarily dissolved on no ground, how much more can the promise they made with God be dissolved without punishment?” Likewise: “If un-veiled virgins are punished in this way by public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction,” etc. Lombard adds: “From these things it is clear that virgins or widows bound by a vow of continence, whether veiled or not, can in no way enter marriage.” Thus far Innocent. Since such severe punishment was imposed upon un-veiled virgins, the woman to whom Anselm writes would rightly have had to undergo the same penalty. Hence Lombard, weighing Innocent’s words exactly, concludes: “It must therefore not be omitted what Pope Innocent decreed concerning widows and girls who marry Christ spiritually: if they later marry publicly, they are not to be admitted to penance unless the men to whom they joined themselves have departed from the world. For if this rule is observed in all cases, so that any woman who marries another while her husband lives is judged an adulteress, and is not allowed to do penance unless one of the two has died, how much more must it be observed in the case of one who had first joined herself to an immortal Bridegroom and afterwards passed over to human marriage?” Thus far the Master. I would willingly have added canon 17 of the Council of Gangra, cited above by Ivo, had I not seen that it was enacted against Eustathian women, as Johannes Quintinus of Autun rightly observes there, as in other matters. More properly should be added decree 27 of the Council of Chalcedon, under *Si qua virgo*; canons 13 and 14 of Elvira; the Fourth Council of Toledo, cited there by Gratian, I, *Devotam peccantem*; chapter 108, Book VI, of Charlemagne’s *Capitularies*, and chapter 257, Book VII. In the former both man and woman are commanded, once separated, to be banished in perpetual exile: “They are to be excluded from the assembly of Christians until,” says the most Christian emperor, “they amend what they have unlawfully done. But if they neglect amendment, let them be separated forever from communion and from the fellowship of all Christians.”] you made a profession, because you publicly and privately wore the habit of a holy purpose, by which you affirmed to all who saw you that you were dedicated to God, no less than by reading the profession.

Before the profession and consecration of the monastic purpose now customary had come into use, many thousands of men and women attained exaltation and the crown by professing themselves members of that purpose through the habit alone. Those who then rejected the assumption of the habit without the profession and consecration were judged apostates.

You are therefore without excuse if you abandon the holy purpose which you professed for a long time by habit and conduct, even though you have not read the profession now customary and have not been consecrated by a bishop. Certainly, dearest daughter, the Lord, your creator and redeemer, still awaits you. The King who desired your beauty, so that he might be your lawful bridegroom, still awaits and calls you back, so that you may be his lawful bride—even if not a virgin, at least chaste.

For we know many holy women who, after losing their virginity, pleased God more and became more intimate with him through repentance in chastity than many others, although holy, did in virginity.

Return, therefore, Christian woman; return to your heart, and consider whom you ought rather to love and to whom you ought rather to cling: him who chose you for such great honor, called you by choosing you, and, by calling you, assigned you to himself with a bridal habit, and who still awaits and calls you back, although despised and rejected; or the one through whom, to put it mildly, you fell from such great height into the condition in which you see yourself cast down—especially since he himself, as I think, already despises you, or will certainly despise and abandon you.

Would that you might despise one another in such a way that God does not despise you; abandon one another in such a way that God does not abandon you; reject one another in such a way that God does not cast you from his presence; turn away from one another in such a way that you turn toward God.

Certainly it is better and far more honorable for both him and you that you be despised by him rather than retained, because as long as you are retained by him, beyond doubt—leaving him aside for the moment—you will be despised by God. But if, despised by him, you despise him for God’s sake, you will certainly not be despised but received and loved by God, as one redeemed by his own blood.

Pay attention, daughter, whose salvation I desire; pay attention to the kindness of him who, although despised by you, calls back the one who despises him, so that he may introduce you into his royal chamber—not an earthly one but a heavenly one. Pay attention and shake your heart; grieve intensely over your fall.

Reject and trample underfoot the worldly habit which you assumed, and take up again the habit of Christ’s bride which you cast away. For Christ will in no way acknowledge or receive you unless you are in that habit by which he marked you as his own and by which you publicly and privately testified that you were his bride.

In that habit return to his kindness. Present yourself opportunely before him. Accuse your own conscience; wash away your guilt with tears. Pray to him without fatigue; cling to him inseparably. He is merciful and will not reject you; rather, rejoicing in your return, he will kindly receive you.

If you do this, there will be joy over you in heaven and on earth among all the holy angels and human beings who know of it. But if you despise doing this, all will be opposed to you, and I and the Church of God will do what we understand must be done in such a matter.

May almighty God visit your heart and pour his love into you, dearest daughter.
