## LETTER 159

### Anselm to William, abbot

On consecrating an altar again after it has been moved.

[Textual note, [Col. 0193C–0195A]: The editor observes that Anselm had apparently treated this issue earlier, perhaps before his first departure from England in 1097; the manuscript wording is *epicopis* for *episcopis*, “bishops”; *tuntum* for *tantum*, “only”; and *conconcordant* for *concordant*, “agree.”]

To his dearest lord and friend, the revered abbot William, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, greetings.

When I replied to what you asked concerning the altar and the church, my heart was so burdened by a certain anxiety that I could not attend to what I was saying, and your messenger was in such haste that I could not defer the matter to another time.

I do not remember having read anything about this either in decretals or in canons. But I heard from a certain bishop that the decretals of Pope Eugenius state that a moved altar must be consecrated again. I discussed these matters with Lord Pope Urban in the presence of certain bishops. The pope, however, said that an altar table which had been moved was neither to be reconciled nor consecrated again, nor any longer regarded as an altar.

Others said that it was merely to be reconciled, but they produced no authority. In this, however, all agree: if the principal altar has been violated, the whole church together with the altar must be consecrated again, and the church must not be consecrated without the consecration of an altar, whether the principal altar or some other altar in the same church.

In these matters all with whom I have spoken agree, except concerning the altar table. Likewise, if some part of the church is destroyed and rebuilt, or if a new part is added while the altar remains unmoved, they say that it need only be sprinkled with water blessed by a bishop.

The reason which you asked me for seems to me to be this: the altar is not made for the sake of the church, but the church for the sake of the altar. Therefore, when the principal altar has been violated, it no longer seems to be a church, because it no longer possesses that for the sake of which a church is built and consecrated. Consequently, when that altar is made new, it seems right that the church should be consecrated again with it, since through it the church receives what makes it a church.

I also have this reason for consecrating an altar again after it has been moved. The altar stands for the Christian faith: just as we offer our sacrifice only on an altar, so we offer the sacrifices of good works only in right faith, if we wish to please God. Therefore, just as faith moved from its foundation, which is Christ, and from its stability is no longer faith, so an altar moved from its foundation is no longer an altar. Whether the new altar is made entirely from the same material or from different material, and is thus a new and different altar from what it was, it seems for this reason to require consecration.

For this reason I think care must be taken that a portable altar not be consecrated without a foundation. Many people observe this, and it is observed almost everywhere, although when I was in Normandy you did not observe it there; instead, bare stones, fixed nowhere, were consecrated. I do not condemn this, but neither do I wish to do it.

It follows from what I have said that if the whole church is made new while the altar remains unviolated, since nothing is to be consecrated without the consecration of some altar, either some altar there must be renewed so that it may be consecrated together with the church, or the inside and outside must simply be sprinkled with water blessed by the bishop for this purpose.

What I have said should be done in these matters I learned from the words and practice of others. I do not deny that others may have the same reasoning, but I received it from no one. Therefore, what I think either by myself or through others I simply make known to your holiness, as you have requested, until something more certain or better becomes clear to you.

Farewell.

### Editorial notes

The phrase “When I replied,” and so forth, makes it especially clear that Anselm had treated this subject elsewhere, perhaps shortly before his first departure from England—namely, in 1097, as we have observed elsewhere. This is shown by Anselm’s subsequent words, in which he says that he had been so burdened by anxiety that he could scarcely attend to himself, unquestionably because of the various serious and public troubles and misfortunes narrated by Eadmer in Book II, chapters 12, 14, 15, and 19 of his *Life*. Since these could not be remedied because of the obstinate perversity of William Rufus, king of the English, Anselm was grievously harassed.

I had previously failed to notice the reply appended at the beginning of the letter, although it is clear that Bale had seen it from this title and its opening words, “On the moving of the altar: What gives occasion concerning the altar,” and so forth. I also encountered the letter under discussion among the letters of Ivo of Chartres in the library of Bec, attached to the very letter in which he explains the same subject.

Since Anselm says that he discussed the central point of this matter in the hearing of Pope Urban and certain bishops, it is clear that he answered William after returning to England, namely toward the end of the year 1100.

The words “In the decretals of Pope Eugenius it is read that a moved altar,” and so forth: the name of the pope appears to be spurious. First, the few things transmitted to us concerning Eugenius I and Eugenius II have nothing to do with this matter. Second, Burchard in Book II of the *Decretals*, chapter 11; Jarlandus Chrysopolitanus in Book XII of his *Candle*; Ivo of Chartres in Part III and again in Part II of his *Pannormia*; and Gratian in *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “If the altar has been moved,” attribute these words expressly to Pope Hyginus:

“If the altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated again; if the walls are changed but not the altar, they are merely to be exorcised with salt.”

Nevertheless, Ivo, who cites this statement from the sanctions of Pope Hyginus in the places just mentioned, produces it in Letter 32 from the Council of Meaux, as transmitted by Burchard. The canon under consideration here is preceded by two decrees of the Synod of Meaux. Perhaps the copy of Burchard which Ivo used was that same fuller and richer copy about which Johannes Molinaeus of Ghent testifies in his dedicatory letter concerning Ivo’s *Decree*: namely, that the collection of Burchard printed at Cologne in 1548 scarcely reaches a sixth of the archetype, although it exceeds it in the number of booklets.

I say that perhaps this was the fuller codex in which the Council of Meaux was cited in place of Pope Hyginus, or in which Hyginus’s edict was attributed to the acts of the Synod of Meaux. In any case, by the altar of which Hyginus speaks above, the principal altar is understood—the main altar, as Anselm calls it; the church’s titular altar, as John of Faenza calls it in the cited chapter “If the altar has been moved.” When this altar has been moved, the church must be consecrated again. So say the gloss in the same place, Anselm in this letter, and Ivo in Letter 32, who extends the rule to any altar.

The words “The altar table having been moved, neither to be reconciled nor consecrated again, nor,” and so forth, are contrary to Alexander III, Book III of the *Decretals*, title 40, chapter 1:

“If an altar has been moved, or if only that stone placed upon it which contains the seal has been broken or even diminished, it must be consecrated again.”

John Andreae in his gloss on this title, John de Turrecremata and the Archdeacon on the chapter “If the altar has been moved” in *On Consecration*, distinction 1; Astesanus in Book VI of his *Summa*, title 29; and others agree with this. They consistently assert that when the upper slab of the altar, or table on which consecration is performed, has been moved or altered in its form, or when one of the stones supporting and touching it—or the stone in which the relics are contained and the consecration has been impressed—has been moved, the altar must again be consecrated.

Bernard, provost of Pavia, reports Alexander’s view somewhat differently and more clearly in Book III of his *Breviary*:

“An altar on which there is a slab to which the blessing of consecration has been applied through pontifical ministry, if it has been moved or excessively broken, ought rightly to be consecrated again; nor do we deny that unconsecrated oil may be mixed with consecrated oil.”

## LETTER 160

### Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to Anselm

Hildebert, bishop, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Textual apparatus: alternative readings are *scientiam* (“knowledge”) for *inscientiam* (“ignorance”); *timui* (“I feared”) for *timeo* (“I fear”); *eum* (“him”) for *eam* (“it”); *dementiam* (“madness”) for *clementiam* (“gentleness”); *si quidem* for *si quem*; *nobis* (“us”) for *vobis* (“you”); *definitur* (“is defined”) for *desinitur* (“ceases”); *poterunt* (“will be able”) for *potuerunt* (“were able”); and *Appulsorum* for *Apulorum* (“of the Apulians”).]

It is characteristic of the wise to tolerate one who does not know. For this reason I do not fear to disclose my ignorance, since I am conversing with a wise man. Unless I am mistaken, your knowledge will instruct it and your charity will support it.

Happy should I be, I say, if I had deserved either to be instructed in person or, as one familiar to you, to receive a letter addressed to me. But distance begrudges me this, and has granted me no other service of greeting unless I first consult half the world; for one must test the gentleness—or, as another reading has it, the madness—of the sea and of the air if one judges that someone in England should be greeted.

For the rest, the inconveniences of separation are supplied by the bond of charity, which allows no one to be absent from you and no one to be unfamiliar. Nothing is more extensive than it; the breadth of charity and of the world is equal. Charity embraces whatever the Ocean contains. In the sanctuary of love, charity gathers both friend in God and enemy for God. It does not cease to love when it ceases to be loved—or, according to another reading, when it ceases to be defined. It keeps all present and all related; those whom it cannot assist by service, it helps by affection.

Therefore, let it be far from me that the public benefit of charity should be taken away from me by the waves of the sea, since it is written: “Many waters could not—or, according to another reading, will not—extinguish charity.” It is easy for charity to unite people who dwell on different shores, since it made earth and heaven one commonwealth.

With this confidence, I have presumed to inquire and request something whose expenditure will not diminish the one who gives it. If you ask what the sum of my requests is, the following page will disclose it.

From the reports of those who have arrived—or, according to another reading, of those who have been driven ashore—I learned that at the Council of Bari you delivered a discourse on the Holy Spirit, whom the slanderous cunning of the Greeks falsely claims does not proceed from the Son. I therefore beg that what you promulgated against their madness at that council be recorded in a concise treatise, together with the testimonies of the Latin Fathers which they themselves do not accept.

[Textual apparatus: *promulgastis* (“you promulgated”) for *promulgasti*; and *quia* (“because”) for *quae* (“which”).]

It will not weary you to strengthen the requested work with these authorities, which Greek cleverness may acknowledge as both its own and ours. I ask for something great, blessed Father, but something that will benefit equally the one who receives and the one who gives. For knowledge is a noble possession: when distributed, it receives increase; but, disdaining a miserly possessor, it slips away unless it is made public.

May the Lord preserve your holiness for us, and may my eyes see you before I die.

## LETTER 161

### The same to Anselm

Hildebert, bishop, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Textual apparatus: *egit* (“gave thanks”) for *egi* (“I gave thanks”); *effectus* (“effect”) for *affectus* (“affection”); and *verba* (“words”) for *labia* (“lips”).]

Both a joyful day and a solemn countenance came to me together with your treatise. I, your servant, had previously received your blessing, and my devoted affection—or, according to another reading, my devoted response—gave thanks to God and to you.

It was human to assist one’s neighbor through compassionate affection; but it was divine to defend the Catholic faith through the Holy Spirit dwelling in you. Yet one and the same Spirit accomplished both, willing to make the grace of the virtues abound in you, whom he had reserved as a defender of his procession from the Son.

For wisdom could not enter a malevolent soul or dwell in a body enslaved to sins. It was therefore fitting that the advocate of truth should display an example of religious devotion. Such a person was suited to pastoral watchfulness, lacking nothing for the fullness of justice and nothing for the integrity of doctrine.

Truly blessed is the breast which the assembly of virtues consecrated as a revered inner sanctuary. From there, as from holy shrines, divine oracles proceed, and your sacred lips—or, according to another reading, your sacred words—proclaim nothing other than the interpreter of the heavenly will.

As I recall these things again and again, amazement overwhelms me; and while I contemplate each one carefully, I confess that all must be attributed to the Holy Spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Psalm 117:23).

You will repay me, holy Father, if you make me a participant in your prayers.

Farewell.

## LETTER 162

### The same to Anselm

Hildebert, bishop, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

I have sent you a fan, plainly an instrument suitable for driving away flies. There is also something which you ought to interpret in our little gift. Pay attention, then, to what kinds of flies more grievously infest priests sacrificing to the Lord, and by what things the salutary offices of the altar are frequently impeded.

[Textual apparatus: *inopinato* (“unexpected”) for *inopino* (“unforeseen”).]

There are a thousand phantoms of approaching thoughts, a thousand suggestions of the devil, a thousand temptations of mortal minds. When these intrude upon the minds of those offering sacrifice by an unforeseen—or, according to another reading, unexpected—incursion; when they draw them away to think of one thing after another; when they attempt to introduce heretical depravity, what else do they do but infest and impede the ministers sacrificing at the altar like so many flies?

Our patriarch Abraham prefigured the driving away of such monstrous flies when he drove away the birds that descended upon the sacrifices. For it is written: “The birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away.”

Therefore, when with the fan intended for you, you have driven away the flies descending upon the sacrifices, the incursions of temptations that come upon the mind of the one offering sacrifice must be driven out with the winnowing-fan of the Catholic faith. Thus what was received for practical use will offer you a mystical meaning.

And since the birds mentioned above are read to have descended upon the sacrifices but not to have interrupted the service that had begun, Christ’s priests are thereby taught to drive away the temptations they endure in such a way that such a lapse does not compel them to abstain from the sacraments of the altar. For this failing is an infirmity which perfects virtue, not one which nullifies the works of virtue.

[Col. 0198A]

## LETTER 163

### Anselm to Gelduin, abbot of Aquicinctum

This letter exists in the manuscript of the library of Aquicinctum and in the manuscript of the library of Saint Martin of Tournai.

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to Gelduin, revered abbot of the monastery of Aquicinctum, greetings.

[Textual apparatus: *illis* (“those”) for *aliis* (“others”); *de hoc quoque quaeritis* (“you also ask concerning this”) for *de hoc quod quaeritis*; *quis* (“anyone”) for *quivis* (“any person whatever”); *super hoc* (“concerning this”) for *hoc*; *denuntiato* (“reported”) for *nominato* (“specified”).]

I shall answer briefly concerning what your reverence has consulted me about. You ask whether you may buy from laymen the tithes belonging to your church which they hold. Certainly you may, in accordance with the concession of the apostolic authority, redeem from others whatever ecclesiastical properties have come into the jurisdiction of your church through episcopal grant.

Nor ought you, insofar as it lies within your power, allow any layman to hold tithes, churches, or altars from you as a fief. Concerning what you also ask—whether it is to be rejected or accepted if any person, with your knowledge but without your having initiated the matter either by word or gift, wishes to redeem some ecclesiastical property for the use of your church—it seems to me that, with the counsel and grant of the bishop, you may lawfully accept it.

Concerning those who have been deposed on account of the crime of simony, about whom you consulted me, it seems to me that no abbot can restore them on his own authority, even if they have converted to the monastic order.

As for your question whether clerics converted from the priesthood because of any other crime besides homicide ought to be barred from it, I do not presume now to determine easily for which crimes they ought to be barred. I fear that my judgment might obstruct the mercy which, for many reasons, is extended to some in the same offense but denied to others, or might cause it to be extended to someone to whom it ought not to be extended.

A more certain judgment is possible when the matter concerns a named crime, whether public or secret, and a known person.

As for what you ask to have answered in the brevity of a letter concerning ecclesiastical matters, I have neither the time nor the opportunity to satisfy your request, nor do I think it can be done briefly.

I do not advise you to make excommunicated persons monks unless the absolution of their bishop has first been granted.

Farewell.

# BOOK FOUR, CONTAINING LETTERS THAT HAVE HITHERTO REMAINED UNPUBLISHED

(From a manuscript of the Cottonian Library in England.)

427 ## LETTER I

### LANFRANC TO LANFRANC AND GUIDO, BROTHERS

To his most beloved brothers LANFRANC and GUIDO, Brother LANFRANC: perpetual blessing from God.

Since, by divine providence, etc. This letter exists as the forty-seventh among Lanfranc’s letters, in *Patrologia*, volume CL, column 511.

[Col. 0201A]

## LETTER II. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To the reverend lord and beloved father, PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission and the constancy of his prayers.

Since the directions and counsels of the sons of the Church depend upon the authority of the Apostolic See, I therefore have recourse to the command and counsel of your paternity. Why, however, I delayed so long to write anything to your highness after I returned to England, your lordship will, if you please, be able to learn from the bearer of this letter. After King William died—the violence of whom had kept me exiled from England for three years—I was recalled with great eagerness by my lord King Henry, by his princes, and by the Church [Col. 0201B] of England, and was received with great joy. After they learned of the decree which I heard being issued in the Roman council by your predecessor, Pope Urban, of blessed memory—namely, that no one should receive the investiture of a church from the hand of a layman, and that no bishop or abbot should become his man—I perceived and heard that neither the king nor his princes would in any way accept it. For this reason I await the counsel of your highness, which is necessary to me.

When I was in Rome, I explained to the aforesaid lord pope the Roman legation over the kingdom of England, which the people of that kingdom assert that the Church of Canterbury has held from ancient times down to our own day, and which must necessarily be so, since it could not otherwise be done except to the detriment of the Roman Church and of England. We have instructed the bearer of this letter to report to you some of the reasons for this matter. The legation which, according to the testimony mentioned above, the Church had held down to our own time, my lord pope did not take away from me. Yet I heard that, while I was in exile for my fidelity to the Apostolic See, your authority entrusted that very legation to the archbishop of Vienne.

How full of difficulty, indeed impossibility, this is will be understood by those who know the long and perilous distance of sea and kingdoms—namely, France and Burgundy—between England and Vienne, so that the archbishop of Vienne might frequently travel to England, or the English to Vienne, for their affairs. Therefore I, your paternity’s suppliant servant and son, beg that in my time the Church which, out of compassion for me, endured many adversities while I was living in poverty in exile for my fidelity to the Roman Church, not be deprived of that dignity which it declares, through your see, that it possessed before me in my predecessors.

When I left England, there was there a priest by profession, but not merely a publican: he was the most infamous prince of publicans, named Ranulf, on account of his cruelty, like a consuming flame, surnamed Flambard. The nature of his flame has become widely known, not only in England but far and wide in foreign kingdoms. The recently deceased king, contrary to the will of all religious men and against all justice, dared, while I was in exile, to elevate him to the episcopate without any correction of his conduct. What sort of man he was before and after becoming bishop, in simony and in other crimes, the bearer of this letter will be able to explain.

Such a prelate, however, just as he had been irregularly consecrated where he ought not to have been, so did not hesitate to defile churches and persons outside his own diocese by his consecration. When I returned to England, I found him imprisoned by the king for money which, like a publican, he owed because he had fraudulently retained it from his offices—as the entire royal court fully attests—while the people rejoiced as though a lion ravaging everything around them had been subdued.

When he was captured, his archbishop, who later died, confessed in the hearing of the royal court that he did not regard him as either a brother or a bishop, and that he had lied to him about everything he had promised when he was to be consecrated. When he heard [Col. 0202B] of my return, he asked that he be assisted through my help as a bishop. I therefore sent him four bishops with the bearer of this letter, saying that if he wished to demonstrate that he had approached the episcopate in such a way that he ought to be treated as a bishop, I would ensure that he had the freedom to do so. I confess, however, that I feared being overwhelmed by the curses and stones of the people if I led into liberty the man whose cruelty had been restrained.

But the bishops reported that, since I had sought him through them, he had rejected them. Later he secretly fled from captivity into Normandy and, joining the enemies of his lord the king, made himself, as is reliably said, leader of the pirates whom he sent out upon the sea. Since the Church entrusted to him, exposed to many dangers among barbarians, cannot remain long without a pastor, and since we seek your counsel and command concerning the churches and persons whom he consecrated, [Col. 0202C] we ask your direction.

After the archbishop of York died, following my return, the bishop of Hereford was elected in his place—a very learned man, instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines. In this election we bishops gave our consent, together with the clergy and people of that Church. He greatly desires to present himself before your presence, so that your benevolence might honor him, according to custom, by granting him the pallium. The king, however, has detained him for certain reasons on the advice of his princes; and he desires to obtain from your highness, by petition, that you send him the pallium. We humbly beg that your generosity favor his petition, if you are pleased to accept our prayers.

[Col. 0202D]

## LETTER III. OF WULFSTAN, BISHOP OF WORCESTER, TO ANSELM

[Note: This letter responds to Anselm’s Letter 19 of Book III.]

To the most reverend and most blessed ANSELM in the holiness of his life and the dignity of the highest see, archbishop, WULFSTAN, least of the servants of God and, deservedly, an unworthy bishop of the Church of Worcester, offers the services of prayer and faithful offices of charity.

Concerning the matters about which your dignity has deigned to write to us and to seek the counsel of our lowliness, we shall not omit to say as much as we can remember. We have never heard that the case about which he consulted us was brought into dispute, since no one has ever appeared who wished to take away from the archbishop of Canterbury the power [Col. 0203A] to do this, or who would defend his not publicly dedicating his own churches alone.

Indeed, in our diocese there are altars, and also certain churches in those villages which Stigand, your predecessor, possessed—not by right of ecclesiastical inheritance, but by a grant from secular authority—during the time of both my predecessor and myself. This happened without our advice, and neither before nor afterward did we make any accusation about it, since we knew that this was a special power of that metropolitan bishop.

We have never heard, however, that a judgment was brought concerning this, or that he claimed this right for himself. But since we freely acknowledge that he exercised it in our diocese, we believe that he can also exercise it in the dioceses of others. Behold, we have made known to your prudence as much as we could remember or know about the matter. Let your own judgment now consider what ought to be done. May your paternity prosper, and pray for us.

## LETTER IV. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

[Note: The distinguished Henry Wharton published this letter in volume II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 178, with the following heading: “A letter of Anselm corrupted in the edition of Anselm’s works prepared at Paris in 1675 by Gabriel Gerberon, restored from an old manuscript of the Lambeth Library.” When I read this inscription, I could not help being astonished at the learned man’s extreme carelessness—for the title of his own book itself prevents the suspicion of bad faith, since by it he openly admits that England had been sacred down to the year 1540, that is, for as long as it adhered to the Roman pontiff as its true and legitimate head. Indeed, if he had examined Gerberon’s edition neither superficially nor, perhaps, with hurried eyes, he would have found that very letter which he thought he was restoring, pure and unaltered, exactly as he himself printed it, published by Gerberon in Book IV, Letter 4, p. 428. Thus Anselm wrote two letters to Paschal on the same subject: one appears in Book III, no. 47; the other among the new letters, Book IV, Letter 4. Had Wharton read it, he would undoubtedly not have reprinted it, still less accused Gerberon of bad faith. MARTENE.]

To the reverend lord and beloved father, PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission and constancy of prayer.

After I was recalled and returned to England for the episcopate, I displayed the apostolic decrees which I had heard in person at the Roman council: namely, that no one should receive the investitures of churches from the hand of the king or any layman, so as thereby to become his man, and that no one should presume to consecrate anyone who transgressed these provisions. When the king and his princes heard this, and the bishops and others of lower rank as well, they took it so seriously that they declared that they would in no way give their assent to this matter, that they would expel me from the kingdom rather than observe it, and that they would withdraw from the Roman Church.

Therefore, reverend Father, I sought your counsel by a letter, which I sent to your highness through William, the king’s legate. But since I have not received a letter containing your reply, I now humbly seek once again, through the legates whom I am sending with my beloved brothers and fellow bishops, who are approaching your holiness concerning this same matter, a definite decision from your highness in writing. We pray our Lord Jesus Christ to preserve you for the praise and glory of his name and for the benefit of his Church.

## LETTER V. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

[Col. 0203D]

To his glorious lord, HENRY, by the grace of God king [Col. 0204A] of the English, ANSELM, archbishop, offers faithful service and faithful prayers.

I beg you, my most beloved lord, as lord, king, and guardian of the Church of God entrusted to you, to listen attentively to the lament of this monk from Micelei, and, according to what you understand to be fitting for you and beneficial to the Church, to let him experience your royal and paternal assistance and consolation.

I, for my part, as one utterly faithful to your soul, your body, and your true honor, advise and beseech you not to bring upon yourselves—God forbid!—the anger of God by proposing to the Churches of God persons whom you ought not to propose, and in a manner you ought not, or by following the counsel of those whose counsel you ought not to follow. For it is certain that some wicked and faithless counselors have already advised you, so far as concerns your soul, [Col. 0204B] otherwise than they should have. May almighty God grant that you govern what he has entrusted to you in such a way that he himself may govern you and protect you from every evil.

## LETTER VI. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To the reverend lord and beloved father, PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission and constancy of prayer.

How earnestly my mind, according to its ability, embraces reverence and obedience toward the Apostolic See is testified by the many and most grievous tribulations of my heart, known only to God and me, which I have suffered from the beginning of my episcopate for four years in England and [Col. 0204C] for two years in exile, because I refused to deny submission to that See. From this resolve, I hope in God, nothing can draw me back.

Therefore, insofar as it is possible for me, I wish to entrust all my actions to the direction of that authority, so that they may be corrected wherever necessary. I shall therefore briefly write how I presently stand in England, leaving it to the bearers of this letter to explain the matter more fully in person.

After I was recalled by the present king of England and returned to the episcopate, I set forth the apostolic decrees which I had heard in person at the Roman council: namely, that a layman should not give the investitures of churches, that no one should receive them from his hand or thereby become his man, and that no one should consecrate anyone who presumed to do these things; whoever transgressed them was to be subject to the excommunication of the holy council.

When the king and his princes heard this, and the bishops as well, they exclaimed what evils would result from it and what they would do instead of accepting these decrees—what they said I hesitate to repeat; let the legates who were present and heard them speak. Finally, turning to me, they all declared with one accord that I could extinguish every evil which might proceed from these decrees. They asserted that, if I were willing to join my prayers to those of the bishops, I might persuade your highness to mitigate the aforesaid judgment. But if I refused to do so, they would judge that every evil which resulted from it must be attributed to me, without any excuse on my part.

Therefore, so that I may not appear to despise anything, or to act according to my own judgment or private will alone, I dare neither refuse to hear them nor in any way depart from the disposition of your holiness. Maintaining, therefore, my reverence and obedience toward the Apostolic See, I beg that, insofar as your dignity permits according to God, you accommodate yourself, in your wisdom, to the petition which the legates will explain to you; and whatever you command me to do in this matter, whatever may happen, make me certain of it through the legates who are present. We pray almighty God to preserve your paternity long, safe, and in complete prosperity, for the strength and consolation of his Church.

## LETTER VII. ANSELM TO WILLIAM, ELECTED BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

ANSELM, archbishop, sends greetings to his beloved friend WILLIAM, elected bishop of Winchester.

Tell me whether you will come to me in the approaching Ember Days for priestly ordination, and whether, on the day following your reception of the priesthood, you wish to receive episcopal consecration. I must know this beforehand, for if you are then to receive episcopal consecration, I shall come to Canterbury at that time and invite the bishops to be with me, so that the ceremony may be performed as is fitting.

But if you wish to receive only the priesthood at the aforesaid time, I shall not come to Canterbury then, since I shall be able to perform that ordination wherever I am. I shall first notify your charity where I shall be at that time.

## LETTER VIII. ANSELM TO JOHN, THE PRIOR

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greetings to his friend JOHN, prior of the canons of Mount Saint Eligius, [Col. 0205D] and to the congregation serving God under him.

This cleric, an Englishman by nation, named Northmannus, comes to you from a certain church in which clerics have recently gathered who wish to live according to regular discipline in your manner. He desires to remain with you for as long as you please, so that he may be instructed in your order and customs for the service of God, for his own benefit and that of others.

Since he is a familiar of ours, he asks that, by the testimony of our letter, it be made known that he is not traveling abroad for any other reason, and that through our recommendation and request he be assisted by you in what he desires. Although we have received nothing from your religious community except affection, nevertheless, because I trust your conduct [Col. 0206A] and benevolence—and because it is characteristic of religious men, when opportunity presents itself, willingly to instruct those who wish to advance in religion—I ask you to grant him, insofar as it is convenient for you, permission to remain among you, as he requests.

## LETTER IX. ANSELM TO BALDWIN, KING OF JERUSALEM

To BALDWIN, by the grace of God king of Jerusalem, his most beloved lord, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury: may he be raised through an earthly kingdom to the heavenly one.

Blessed is God in his gifts, and holy in all his works (Psalm XLIV, 13), who by his grace has exalted you to royal dignity in that land in which our Lord Jesus Christ himself, personally sowing the beginnings of Christianity, planted a new Church so that it might spread from there throughout the world. After it had long been oppressed there by unbelievers through God’s judgment on account of human sins, his mercy has wondrously restored it in our own times.

I therefore, remembering the great affection and benefits which I experienced from your father and mother and their children toward me, cannot express in writing how greatly I rejoice in the grace of God which he has displayed in your brother and in you by choosing you for that dignity, nor with what affection I desire that you, who succeeded your brother, strive to reign not so much for yourselves as for God.

Therefore, my most beloved lord, even if you do not need my exhortation, nevertheless, out of the abundance of my heart, as a most faithful friend I beg, admonish, and beseech you, and pray to God that, living under God’s law, you submit your will to God’s will in all things. For then you truly reign for your own benefit, if you reign according to God’s will.

Do not think, as many wicked kings do, that the Church of God has been given to you as a lord for service, but understand that she has been entrusted to you as her advocate and defender. God loves nothing more in this world than the freedom of his Church. Those who wish not so much to benefit her as to dominate her are, without doubt, shown to be adversaries of God.

God wishes his bride to be free, not a servant. Those who treat and honor her as sons treat their mother truly prove themselves to be her sons and sons of God. Those who dominate her as though she were subject to them make themselves not sons but strangers, and therefore are justly disinherited from the inheritance and dowry promised to her.

Whatever condition you establish for her in your kingdom in this new restoration, such will people long uphold and preserve for her in the coming generation. As for what I desire to persuade you of, I pray almighty God himself to persuade you of it, to lead you in the way of his commandments, and to bring you to the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

I commend to your highness Remerius, the bearer of this letter, who knows himself to be of your household. Since he has long lived with me in our household, where he made himself greatly lovable through his diligence and good conduct, and now goes to you, I ask, beloved lord, that, for our love, it may go better with you for him. Farewell.

[Col. 0207A]

## LETTER X. ANSELM TO ANHELIT, ABBESS, AND HER NUNS

ANSELM, archbishop, sends greetings and blessing to his most beloved daughter, the lady ANHELIT, abbess, and to the nuns serving Christ under her.

If I did not love you greatly, I would rebuke you greatly, because after you yourselves sent your messenger to me and asked our advice about what you ought to do concerning that dead man whom some wish to be regarded as a saint, you did not abide by our counsel; indeed, you proved disobedient to our command.

Therefore, by this letter I command you that, if you do not wish to be suspended from the divine office, you henceforth remove from that dead man every honor due to any saint, and neither make an offering to him nor accept for your own use any offering that has been made. Drive his son, who lies at his tomb and remains there, out of the village, and do not leave him any further means of staying there. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. ANSELM TO HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS

[Note: This is a response to Letters 161 and 162 of Book III.]

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends temporal and eternal greetings to HILDEBERT, lord and reverend fellow bishop of Le Mans.

The letters of your holiness make me greatly indebted to you—not because they exalt me above myself, but because they display the immense sincerity of your affection toward me. For if, in order to please God, we ought to love our enemies, how much more ought we to love our friends so as not to displease him?

Therefore, if I show you either no affection or less affection, I judge myself unjust in my conscience. Just as I wish to avoid this injustice, so I desire to embrace your friendship. I confess also that, if it were possible for me, I ought to love you twice as much as you love me, because you anticipated me in love, as you have proved by your gift. Since you have loved one who did not deserve it, I ought no less to return your love; and just as you give me an example, so I ought freely to give an equal return.

Since you have indicated that you were pleased with what you saw of our little works, we presume to send you certain things which, I think, you have not yet seen.

[Col. 0207D]

## LETTER XII. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

To his most beloved lady and daughter MATHILDA, queen of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, offers faithful prayers, faithful service, and the blessing of God and of himself.

I give thanks to God and to your highness for the goodwill which you have toward me and toward the Church of God. I pray almighty God to increase your devotion in his love, and to make you persevere in it in such a way that you may receive eternal recompense from him.

I also pray that he may make your good intention prosper, so that through you he may turn the heart of our lord the king away from the counsels which he rejects, and make him adhere to his own counsel, which endures forever. I gladly receive your consolation and exhortation as coming from a lady and a friend according to God, because I understand that they proceed from the love of God.

If your affection wishes to entrust anything to me, you may safely communicate it to the bearer of this letter, as though speaking to me in person. May almighty God direct all your actions and guard you from every evil.

## LETTER XIII. ANSELM TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS

To ROBERT, lord and beloved in God, count of Flanders, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers faithful prayers together with service.

[Col. 0208B]

I have heard that you have permitted certain of your abbots to be appointed by canonical election, so that they would not receive investiture from your hand. I therefore give thanks to God, whose grace has directed your heart toward what pleases him, and I rejoice for you because you favor without opposition ecclesiastical institutions that contribute to the advancement of Christian religion.

For when you do this, you obey not man but God; you show yourself to be a true and faithful son of the Church of God and a true Christian; and you show that you belong to the sheep commended to the blessed apostle Peter, to whom God gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven. It is certain that whoever does not obey the ordinances of the Roman pontiff, which are made for the preservation of Christian religion, is disobedient to the apostle Peter, whose vicar he is, and does not belong to that flock which God entrusted to him.

Let such a person seek other gates of the kingdom of heaven, for he will not enter through those whose keys the apostle Peter carries. Therefore, rejoicing, I give you thanks and pray that God may reward you, because you give other princes a good example, invite all the servants of God to pray for you in this way, and call upon God to love and help you in your affairs.

I beg, beseech, admonish, and advise you, as one faithful to your soul, my lord, and as one truly beloved in God: never suppose that the dignity of your highness is diminished if you love and defend the freedom of God’s bride and your mother, the Church. Do not think that you are humbled if you exalt her, nor believe that you are weakened if you strengthen her.

Look around you and consider: examples are readily available. Consider the princes who attack and trample her. What do they accomplish? What do they become? It is sufficiently evident and needs no explanation. Certainly, those who glorify her will be glorified with her and in her. May God number you, your wife, and your offspring among them, in the present life and in the life to come. Amen.

431 ## LETTER XIV. ANSELM TO ROGER, ROBERT, AND OTHER ABBOTS

ANSELM, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to ROGER the abbot, ROBERT son of Count Hugh, and the other monks of the monastery of Saint-Evroul.

[Col. 0209A]

It is altogether obvious, and cannot in any way be concealed, how you entered the monastery of Saint Edmund and with what violence you are attempting to extort an election from the brothers of that Church and impose the consent of your disorderly will.

God himself, who distinguishes between a shepherd and a ravenous wolf, sees how irreligiously you act, how contrary to the monastic purpose, to the rule of Saint Benedict which you have professed, and to Sacred Scripture, which says: “No one takes the honor for himself, but only the one who is called by God” (Hebrews V, 4); and he sees how you act against God himself.

Indeed, I cannot prevent my lord the king from placing you over earthly matters, but over souls—for whose sake a man is both called and appointed abbot—no one can appoint anyone except those to whom God has given the power of binding and loosing.

That Church lies within my primacy and archbishopric, and its consecrations properly belong to the archbishop of Canterbury, whom you know to be me. Therefore, I have never granted, nor do I grant, to any of you anything that belongs to me. Rather, I pray to God and will strive, insofar as I can with God’s help, that he turn my lord the king’s heart toward what pleases God more and benefits his soul; and he will make the king correct whatever he does against God’s will, according to that will.

You are Christians under Christian law, and you profess that you live under monastic profession. If you act against this, you openly confess by your deeds that you are neither Christians nor monks. It is absolutely certain that, if you persist in this, you act against the profession mentioned above.

I therefore admonish you, as Christians and monks, to show that you fear God more than man and firmly desist from the perversity you have begun. But if you prefer to oppose God rather than human beings, I announce to you that God will oppose your souls.

May God, to whom it is said, “To you the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm X, 14), himself see and observe whether you henceforth cause any tribulations to the brothers of that Church.

## LETTER XV. ANSELM TO GERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greetings to the reverend archbishop GERARD of York.

Let your charity know that, concerning those letters which you complain were read and copied, I neither showed, gave, nor sent them to anyone, nor did anyone do so through me. I do not know how it happened that someone obtained them for transcription; and when I read in your letters that this had occurred, it displeased me.

Although your prudence suspects nothing unbecoming of me, it is nevertheless my duty to confess and affirm that I do not desire an insult to you or to any of my fellow bishops, and, whatever the truth may be concerning those letters, I do not think that you ought to be accused of falsehood.

When I speak with you—or, if anything I write back is insufficient, when I speak to you in person—I hope to satisfy you, because I am not guilty in this matter, nor has any falsehood been introduced by our legates. I am sending only the chapters of the council, because I do not wish anyone to transcribe their explanations until they have been approved by the judgment of you and the other bishops who were present at the council.

## LETTER XVI. ANSELM TO THE SAME

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greetings to the reverend archbishop GERARD of York.

I rejoice in your good and religious zeal concerning the integrity of your clergy. Regarding the matters about which your prudence seeks our advice, I reply that I advise relaxing nothing of what was established at our council by the common agreement of our fellow bishops.

As for matters which we did not discuss at that council—for we were not able to deal with everything necessary—such as the removal of prebends sold before that council, and [Col. 0210B] similar matters, since they concern not only my person, yours, and our churches but also many churches and persons, and since many people disagree about them, it seems appropriate to me that at the next Nativity of the Lord we establish a definite judgment, God directing us, by the common counsel of ourselves and our fellow bishops.

## LETTER XVII. HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO ANSELM

To the sweetest and venerable, deservedly beloved and revered father, the lord ANSELM, supreme pontiff of the holy Church of Canterbury, Brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, with his little flock, which God has prepared for those who love him in truth.

Since, most holy man, it is difficult for us to satisfy our desire for one another’s presence, or to delight our hearts by mutual and frequent conversation, we think it good if, at least through a written visit, we nourish our spirits for the time being.

For who, having in Christ a friend so glorious and spiritual as divine grace has granted us in you, would not desire by every means to be refreshed and relieved by the most wholesome remembrance of him and by a holy communication? Before we had seen your face, that most sweet fragrance of your good reputation, striking our ears, was already fattening our inner man with its sweetness.

But after, by God’s will, we were granted the sight of your cheerful presence, it is not easy to say how completely we clung to you and united ourselves to your heart as though it were a part of us. Yet these things are not ours, but belong to him who breathes where he wills (John III, 8). To him we give thanks, and we beseech him that those whom he has so joined in this life he may not permit to be separated in heavenly glory.

We understand well that, after you departed from us, you endured many and serious anxieties. And if it had been the will of the supreme disposer, we know that you would have desired much more to sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet (Luke X, 39) and contemplate his face than to labor in serving with Martha (ibid., 40).

Nevertheless, since a person’s power is not in his own hand, give your hand to the will of him who cares for you and who, more clearly than light, knows what is more beneficial for you. Place all your hope in him; seek from him, as far as possible, strength and perseverance, patient in all things. May he be with you who has never failed anyone who hopes in him.

But why do we, inexperienced as we are, carry water to the sea while presuming to teach your holiness? We do not teach you; we wish to console our heartfelt friend. We add only this with confidence: the house of Cluny, your handmaid, will not fail in your service during your life or at your death.

We do not consider it necessary to commend to your paternity our son, Lord Gofridus the sacristan, whom we are sending to those regions, as you will hear more fully from him, since he frequently tells us how much charitable counsel and assistance you gave him in the past year.

Nor does he alone, but all our brothers who pass through your presence, loudly proclaim the great charity of your holiness. For these things, offering you as many thanks as we can, we humbly ask you to deign, through this man returning to us, to make known to us your condition and your wishes, so that we may rejoice with the one who rejoices and, with the one who grieves—something may almighty God avert from you—grieve as sons. May the grace and peace of God be with you, glorious father. Remember us in your holy prayers.

## LETTER XVIII. ANSELM TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

[Note: This is a response to Letter 64 of Book III.]

To the reverend lord and beloved father, HUGH, venerable primate of Lyons, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury—his servant, his son, wholly his own.

We thank God with rejoicing, and with thanksgiving we rejoice, because divine mercy has fulfilled your desire to visit the place where our salvation was accomplished, and has gladdened us by your return and by the restoration of your health. I also give thanks to your fatherly goodness, not only for the many benefits you have bestowed upon me, but also for your unfailing goodwill, which does not cease to visit me with fatherly concern and through your letters, nor, when necessary, to urge the renewal of those same benefits. Since I can think of nothing by which I might repay such goodness, I pray Almighty God, for whose love you do these things, with all the devotion of which I am capable, that he himself may deign to reward you.

Your charity desired to learn by letter what our situation is like in England, but your legate will be able to show you more fully in person than I can by writing. I say only this: whenever I hope that my adversities are becoming milder, I then feel them burning more fiercely. For the whole power of England, since I am alone there, is striving to overthrow me because it cannot turn me away from obedience to the Apostolic See; and the bishops themselves, together with the king, are so inflamed in this matter that they do not hesitate to presume even to perform consecrations which belong exclusively to me, if there is anyone willing to receive them.

May the Almighty Lord preserve your fatherly goodness safe and unharmed in his grace for a long time, for us. Amen.

[Col. 0212A]

## LETTER XIX. ANSELM TO DIACO, BISHOP OF SAINT-JAMES

To Diaco, reverend bishop of Saint-James, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: the aid and consolation of heavenly grace.

Since we Christians ought always to rejoice with one another and grieve with one another, and especially when we recognize that the prosperity and exaltation of Christendom, or its adversity and humiliation, are involved, having learned from your letters the cause of your fear and grief, we fear what you fear and grieve what you grieve.

Since you desire that our soldiers be summoned to your aid against the Saracens, we shall willingly, as our circumstances permit, exhort them and stir them to the assistance of Christians. But let your holiness know that the kingdom of the English is disturbed by almost daily reports of wars arising everywhere against it. I therefore greatly fear that we may prove less useful to you, because we fear that our enemies may harm us. For while each person is concerned to protect his own interests, he is less able to care for what is common.

Nevertheless, with God’s favor, we shall strive to accomplish by the devotion of our prayers what we cannot accomplish by gathering soldiers. We hope in the mercy of God, for he will not allow “the rod of sinners to rest upon the lot of the righteous” (Psalm 124:3), nor “deliver the souls confessing him to the beasts” (Psalm 73:9). May Almighty God, “a helper in times of trouble” (Psalm 9:10), come to your aid according to the need of your tribulation. Amen.

[Col. 0212C]

## LETTER XX. ANSELM TO GUILLELMUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

To Lord and Father Guillelmus, reverend archbishop of Rouen, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: greetings.

I cry out and appeal to you—to you, to all the bishops and abbots, and to the whole Church of Normandy—for myself and for the community of the Church of Saint Edmund in England, against the abbot of the monastery of Saint-Evroul in Normandy, and I ask for your justice. The wrong which he has inflicted upon us in England, most outrageously and contrary to the opinion we had held of him, is this.

He forcibly introduced into the Church of Saint Edmund, with royal authority, a certain young man, the son of Count Hugh of Chester, utterly lacking in the prudence, usefulness, and virtues appropriate to the person of an abbot. He did so with arms and with monks, insofar as they were able, refusing and protesting, and entirely without our consent, although all consecrations of that church belong to us. This man is attempting to extort from the monks obedience and election, and to make them entrust their souls to him for safekeeping. How unfit he is for this is plainly evident, since he never goes anywhere without a lantern and a guard—and before he was appointed to this position, he was believed to be a danger even to himself.

I therefore beg you to compel that abbot, by your authority, to recall his monk, and to free the church which he is wickedly oppressing, like a ravenous wolf scattering the sheep, lest, while your authority is inactive, we be compelled to exercise some measure of our authority over your monk. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. ANSELM TO ELFER AND THE OTHER MONKS

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest brothers and sons, Prior Elfer and the other monks of the monastery of Saint Edmund: greetings and God’s blessing.

I pity and sympathize with your charity as it struggles under a long and excessive tribulation. I do so with all the greater affection because I see that you are suffering not from desire for earthly possessions but for the sake of justice. It is indeed justice: you do not wish to accept an abbot contrary to your order, contrary to the rule of Saint Benedict, contrary to the authority of the other holy Fathers, or without the counsel of those from whom you ought to expect the governance and counsel of your religious life.

Therefore, if you suffer disturbances and troubles on this account, God will see—he who either corrects or punishes every evil and nourishes and strengthens what is good—and at the proper time he will give you his consolation. He is “a helper in times of trouble” (Psalm 9:10), provided that you are willing humbly to endure the Father’s scourges and do not fail in hope of his mercy.

Cry out to him not only in prayer, but also by preserving with all your heart and all your strength, in every place and at every time, your life according to his commandments and your order’s observance. Consolation through words without any other assistance is sometimes burdensome and unwelcome to those suffering in tribulation. But this ought not to be so for God’s servants, who have a sure hope in God, since the greater the tribulation, the greater the recompense of patience that follows.

May Almighty God gladden you with his consolation, and in prosperity and adversity always protect you with his blessing.

433

## LETTER XXII. ANSELM TO GUILLELMUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

To Lord and reverend Father Guillelmus, archbishop of Rouen, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: faithful service with constant prayers.

For the wrong, oppression, and burdens inflicted upon us, and for the destruction of the Church of Saint Edmund, I cried out to your fatherly goodness. Yet you have not listened to our cry; I complained, yet I have not felt your compassion. You promised that you would do what I had asked concerning the monks of the monastery of Saint-Evroul who burden, despoil, and destroy the aforesaid church. But the fulfillment of your promise is delayed too long.

I still cry out, compelled by the intimate pain of my heart, for myself, to whose particular care that church belongs, and for the brothers who dwell in it. For God’s sake—if you have zeal for God, if you possess episcopal compassion—I beg and implore you, prostrate in mind at your feet: come to our aid and take pity on the orphans and widow of the Church. In her place there is imposed a stepson; in place of a shepherd, a wolf; in place of a guide, a blind man; in place of a teacher, an ignorant man; in place of an abbot, a thief and robber, because he does not enter through the door.

Recall your monks and free us from their oppression. See to it that the abbot of Saint-Evroul recalls his monks, whom he introduced into the aforesaid church contrary to God’s law and their own order, and that he justly restore the property of that church which he removed from it by sacrilegious robbery. Farewell, and come to our aid, I beg you; hasten.

## LETTER XXIII. ANSELM TO ROBERT, ERNULF, RADULF, PHILIP, BERNARD, AND THE OTHERS

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to Robert, count; his brother Ernulf, count; Radulf de Mortuo Mari; Philip de Brajosa; Bernard de Novo Mercato; and the others residing in the bishopric who hold lands belonging to Bishop Wilfrid: his dearest friends and sons in God, greetings and God’s blessing.

Although you yourselves ought to be concerned for your salvation, it nevertheless belongs to me to stir you, by friendly exhortation, toward what is fitting before God and beneficial for your souls, and to invite you, by fatherly admonition, to what is your duty. I therefore beg you as friends, and counsel and admonish you as beloved sons, to show the beloved Wilfrid, bishop of Saint David’s, for your honor and for the sake of the Christian religion, all the reverence and obedience owed to a bishop in his episcopate, and to carry out according to his counsel whatever ought to be done by episcopal disposition.

For you will exalt yourselves before God if, with religious humility, you submit yourselves to your bishop as God has ordained. And if he should need your counsel in anything, let him find you ready as good Christians, so that God may repay you by coming to your aid in all your needs.

I especially admonish and counsel you on this point because it is very necessary for you, if you do not wish to offend God: if you hold lands, tithes, churches, or anything belonging to his Church according to ecclesiastical right, take diligent care to return it for fear of God. For it is certain that whoever disinherits God, or his churches, in this life, if he dies without repentance and amendment, will be disinherited from the kingdom of God in the life to come.

May Almighty God grant that you perform these and other good works in this age, so that he may make you rejoice forever in blessed recompense.

## LETTER XXIV. ANSELM TO ROBERT, PRINCE OF NORMANDY

To his lord and the prince of all Normandy, Robert, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.

There is no need to explain in writing how Lord Guillelmus, the elected bishop of Winchester, left England, since through him and through others who know the matter you will be able to learn it. But since it is especially my duty to sympathize with him and, through myself and others, to assist him as far as I can and ought, I beg your highness that, if there is anything I can obtain from you that would be fitting to ask, he may find in you, as your man and as you know to be expedient for him, aid and counsel offered with affection.

## LETTER XXV. ANSELM TO GUILLELMUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

To Lord and Father Guillelmus, reverend archbishop of Rouen, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: faithful prayers with service.

Since we ought always to rejoice and give thanks to God whenever we see God’s servants despise worldly glory for the love of Christ and refuse to be separated from righteousness by either violence or persuasion, we ought to do this especially when we see it at work in our sons and household members.

Your son Lord Guille lmus—your son, and by your favor ours—whom you charitably granted to us as the canonically elected bishop of the Church of Winchester, although he had been elected canonically as a canon and dean of your church, refused with great courage and steadfastness to receive consecration from those from whom, as it was being offered, he ought not to receive it. How, on that account, he was stripped of his possessions and expelled from England, your fatherly goodness will be able to learn better from his living voice and from the testimony of those who were with him when these things occurred than from anyone’s writing.

This action, insofar as it depended upon him, was carried out with such courage and displays itself with such evident honor that no one’s report could add to his praise. Therefore, although your prudence has no need of our petition, I nevertheless beg from the abundance of my heart that you receive him kindly, as your son and mine, exiled for justice, and offer him, with love and honor, your help and counsel wherever circumstances require. Also, whatever you hear from him concerning this matter, confidently testify to others as truth, and exhort them to love and honor him as he deserves. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI. ANSELM TO HIS FRIEND ROGER

Anselm, archbishop, to his friend Roger: greetings and God’s blessing.

It is commonly said that a friend, like a physician, is tested in time of need. I say this because, if the friendship you showed Lord Guille lmus, the elected bishop, in prosperity was genuine, it will now become evident, and your love will be more steadfast in his greater need.

If our prayers and admonition can add anything to your goodwill, I beg you, for the sake of your honor and your affection, not to fail in the things you have hitherto done well and faithfully in assisting him. Rather, the more you see him in need, the more diligently offer him the aid of your vigor.

434

If you do this, you will make me, your friend, still more your friend, and you will show everyone that your friendship is genuine. Farewell. May Almighty God grant you absolution and remission of all your sins, and, if they have any value, a share in my prayers in true charity.

## LETTER XXVII. ANSELM TO MALCHUS, BISHOP OF WATERFORD

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friend and fellow bishop Malchus of Waterford: greetings and God’s blessing.

I have heard that Lord Samuel, bishop of Dublin, expels the monks of the Church of Dublin for no reason or only a slight one, and refuses to receive them for any satisfaction; that, contrary to custom, he has a cross carried before him when traveling; and that he distributes as his own the property of that church given by Archbishop Lanfranc.

Concerning all these matters I am sending him a letter of ours, and I am instructing the people of that city to prohibit the distribution of the aforesaid property. Since I cannot find anyone through whom I can more suitably send our letter to him, I beg your fraternity to present it to him in person. Kindly admonish him, by asking and advising him in person, to give his assent to the admonition we are sending him. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII. ANSELM TO GUILLELMUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

To Lord and reverend Father Guille lmus, archbishop of Rouen, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: what a son owes his father.

Although Lord Guido, the bearer of this letter, once adhered to us, as he says, with familiar acquaintance as to a lord and father, nevertheless, because he knows how great the mutual affection is between you and me, he has asked to be commended to your holiness by our letter.

Let your fatherly goodness therefore know that, with our friendship and permission, he is returning from England to Normandy and to his own church. I beg you to have your authority testify to this wherever necessary. I also beg that, wherever he needs your counsel and assistance, he may find you ready to help him, as befits your reverence, for the salvation of his soul. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX. ANSELM TO BISHOP GONDULF

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend bishop Gondulf: greetings.

Let your affection know that, by God’s grace and with your prayers assisting me, I am well, and traveled without disturbance as far as Carrotum on my way to Rome. When I arrived there and had been honorably received by the Lady Countess and the bishop, they were astonished that I had undertaken such a dangerous journey at such a time. They declared that, if I continued on the journey I had begun, I would neither see Rome nor be able to return any farther, because of the extreme unhealthiness of the place and the oppressive heat. For me to travel at such a time, they said, was as though I deliberately wished to bring death upon myself.

Therefore, following their counsel and that of all my friends, I postponed the journey until a suitable time and returned to Normandy to await my opportunity at Bec. I beg you—indeed, I earnestly beg you—to pay what I owe in England, and to send me as soon as possible through Ansfred, the present messenger, whatever remains of my revenues that you are able to obtain. You may defer the payment of Romescot until the feast of Saint Michael.

As for the alms, let your prudence take care that they suffer no want. Tell Godefrid of Mellinges to give twenty shillings in silver pennies to his son Guille lmus. Give twenty marks of silver to Guille lmus, son of Hion, and two to Albrito at the feast of Saint Michael. Pray for me, that God may direct me and my actions, and order them according to his good pleasure for my salvation and that of all entrusted to me. Greet the sons and brothers of both our communities.

## LETTER XXX. ANSELM TO QUEEN MATHILDA

To his reverend lady, the glorious Queen Mathilda, Anselm, archbishop: faithful prayers with faithful service, and God’s blessing and his own, insofar as he can give it.

I offer great thanks for your generosity toward me, but much greater thanks for the holy love which I have experienced from you. Since I cannot repay it through bodily action, I desire continually to repay it through the affection of my heart, for however great your bodily absence may be, your prudent and faithful love cannot be removed from my mind.

Therefore I pray with longing, and long in prayer, that God himself may repay you on my behalf for what I cannot do myself, and that, insofar as he knows it to be expedient, he may perfect both his love toward you and your love toward him.

With all the affection I can command, and insofar as I dare to presume upon what I hear concerning your highness, I beg, implore, entreat, and faithfully counsel you to labor for the peace and tranquility of the churches of England, and especially to assist their weaker and less powerful sons in their tribulations and desolations, like Christ’s orphans. In the likeness of the Gospel hen, teach them, comfort them, and cherish them beneath the wings of your protection.

May the anointing of the Holy Spirit teach you in all things, persuade you of what pleases him most and is most expedient for you, and lead you from your temporal kingdom to the eternal one.

## LETTER XXXI. ANSELM TO HIS NEPHEW ANSELM

Anselm, archbishop, to Anselm, his nephew by blood and dearest son in affection: greetings, God’s blessing, and his own.

Because I love you uniquely among all my relatives, I desire that you may progress before God and before everyone. Therefore I admonish and command you, as my dearest son, diligently to complete the task for which I left you in England, and not to let any time pass in idleness.

Devote yourself especially to learning the declension and the power of grammar; practice composition, and more in prose than in verse. Above all, guard your conduct and actions before men, and your heart before God, so that, when I see you, God willing, I may rejoice in your progress, and you may rejoice in my happiness. Farewell. Commend your body and soul to God.

435

## LETTER XXXII. ANSELM TO PRIOR ERNULF AND THE OTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

Anselm, archbishop, to his lords, brothers, and dearest sons, Lord Prior Ernulf and the others serving God under him in the Church of Christ at Canterbury: may they always be governed and consoled by the counsel of divine grace and blessing.

I gladly received the earlier letter sent by your fraternity, because from the letter of the bishop of Rochester and from its bearer I learned that, in every respect, you remain prosperous under God’s protection. Although the following letter did not greatly disturb that joy, it nevertheless clouded it somewhat.

I was not a little astonished by the king’s request, which you reported. But I rejoiced that you wished to do nothing without our counsel, as it is fitting for you to do, and that you remembered our command. God is able to turn the royal will away from all the indignation which you fear may arise against us on this occasion, when he sees you acting rightly and properly. Or, if it should not please him to do so, and something should happen to you against your will as a result—God forbid!—you must be certain that it is better to suffer something for the sake of justice under God’s consolation than to do something improperly and thereby offend him.

I shall therefore await God’s disposition, to whom I commend myself, you, and all that belongs to us. As you advised the king, through our reverend friend the bishop of Rochester, to allow our entire bishopric to remain in peace and quiet, as he promised me, so I shall instruct him. If God, by his grace, orders matters according to both your desire and mine, praise God’s mercy. If things turn out otherwise, whatever it may be, report it to me through whatever messenger you can, wherever I may be.

Arm yourselves against this and against every adversity with the weapons of justice, on the right and on the left. Fear God; always think of him as present, publicly and privately, and think of yourselves as present before him. By correcting your order, preserve your thoughts and actions in complete innocence. Thus God will work all things together for your good (Romans 8:28), and he will be with you, whether in peace or in tribulation, throughout all the days of your life.

Concerning my return to England, before I complete what I have begun, about which you wrote to me, our lord the king has sent me no instruction. He merely communicated by letter his prosperity and cheerfulness toward me, as toward his faithful servant and one who rejoices with him.

May Almighty God pour out his blessing upon you and within you, in prosperity and adversity alike, and never allow his consolation to be absent from you. I thank the lord prior and all of you for the affection and benefits you show my nephew for love of me. Although I do not doubt this, he himself nevertheless conveyed it to me in his letter with great feeling.

## LETTER XXXIII. ANSELM TO BISHOP GONDULF OF ROCHESTER

Anselm, archbishop, to his reverend friend, Gondulf, bishop of Rochester: greetings.

Through the bearers of this letter you can learn of our health and prosperity. Since I left England, I am trying, with God’s help, to accomplish it myself as far as I can, because I see that I cannot do otherwise.

I thank your goodwill and concern, because you recently came to my aid in my need. Of the 330 marks of silver which I brought from England, I had only 24 when I received what you recently sent; for I have had to spend much more than I expected.

Concerning our affairs, since I trust you no less than myself and know your goodwill, I am sure that you need no request from me to guard and manage them as you ought. Nevertheless, thanking you for what you have done and are doing, I ask that, just as you recently assisted me, so you may assist me in the future as soon as possible, sending whatever you have from our revenues from the past year, and collecting whatever you can obtain from our stewards for the future by entreating, admonishing, and making my need known.

I earnestly beg you to ensure that the poor whom I must feed at Canterbury suffer no want. I gladly receive what you wrote to me concerning our land at Roginges, and I have no other desire than the one you asked me to have. I have heard that Hugh, son of Mabilia, wishes to sell the land which I have hitherto allowed him to hold without any grant. Therefore prohibit him, or anyone else, from selling anything belonging to our land or hindering it in any way; let everything remain as I left it until I return.

Greet our sons and daughters, and I beg you to ask them to pray for me. Give one hundred shillings to Radulf, son of Herengod, who was with me.

## LETTER XXXIV. ANSELM TO THE SAME

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend bishop of Rochester, Gondulf: greetings.

You will learn from the bearer of this letter where and how I am; why I am not presently returning to England, you will be able to learn from the letters which I am sending back. I instruct you to greet him faithfully on our behalf, and to give him our seal, which our messengers are delivering to you and which I am sending to him. If he wishes to reply to me by letter, send it to me through the present envoy. If he does not, report to me in your own letter whatever answer he gives.

Do not show our seal to the king before Guille lmus de Warelwast comes to England. Privately show that same Guille lmus a copy of the letter I am sending to the king. Take care that no one except him and our prior alone knows of the letter before it is given to the king. After the king has learned its contents, inform the bishops and others of it. Greet the queen most warmly on our behalf. [Note: See Letter 83, Book III.] I am sending you a copy of the letter I am sending to the king.

## LETTER XXXV. ANSELM TO THE SAME

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend bishop Gondulf: greetings.

I have received a letter from our lord the king in which, as you know, he promised me that he would answer me after the court. I therefore instruct your charity to go to him on my behalf and say the following:

“Lord, the archbishop of Canterbury sends you faithful service as his lord and king, and he instructed me to remind you to answer him, as you commanded me. If he wishes to send me his answer under his seal, that is acceptable. But if he does not wish to answer by letter, report to me by your own letter whatever answer he gives.

“If he still wishes to postpone his answer to another date, I shall accept the delay and another date for answering, provided that in the meantime he allows me to remain in possession, as I was when I left England, so that you can send me revenues from our property, as I instruct you now and shall continue to instruct you.

“But if he dispossesses me, so that our property is not in my control, tell him that I accept no adjournment, but shall conduct myself as a dispossessed bishop, without the judgment by which a bishop ought to be dispossessed.

436

“If he wishes both to answer and yet not to leave me in possession, do not conceal his answer. Nevertheless, do not fail to repeat this very point: that I shall conduct myself as a dispossessed bishop without the judgment by which a bishop ought to be dispossessed.”

Greet the queen gently, as my dearest lady and daughter.

## LETTER XXXVI. ANSELM TO BALDWIN, KING OF JERUSALEM

To Baldwin, by the grace of God king of Jerusalem, his dearest lord, Anselm, though unworthy, archbishop of Canterbury: may you so reign over the earthly Jerusalem in this life that you may reign in the heavenly Jerusalem in the life to come.

Although by God’s gift you possess knowledge which, with God’s help, can suffice you for living well, and although I know that there is good will in you, yet the abundance of the affection I have for you compels me to write something from so great a distance to your highness. For as a burning fire is kindled more intensely by the wind, so good will is stirred by a friendly admonition to burn more fervently.

You know, my dearest lord, that God chose the city of Jerusalem, both before the Lord’s coming and at his very coming, as though it were his own and familiar city out of all the world. From it came the first kings whom the Lord loved; from it came the prophets; in it were God’s own house and his sanctuaries; there our redemption was accomplished; there the King of kings dwelt; from there the salvation of humankind was spread throughout the whole world.

Let your highness therefore consider what an eminent grace of God it is that he has willed you to be king in this city, and with what affection and zeal a king whom he has placed there ought to submit himself to God’s will and service.
