I therefore beg, implore, and admonish you, as lord and as beloved, that you strive so to govern both your own person and all those subject to you according to God’s law and will that in your life you may offer a shining example to all the kings of the earth. May our Lord Jesus Christ so reign in your heart and works that you may reign without end in heaven with King David, your forefather. Amen. Know that I pray for you daily, although my prayers are insignificant.

## LETTER XXXVII. ANSELM TO COUNTESS MATHILDA

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his lady and mother in God, Countess Mathilda: continual and lasting joy in the prosperity of this life, and enduring delight in the happiness of the life to come.

I wish to give thanks to your highness, but I cannot write thanks worthy of its merits. I recognize as a very great benefit that God has delivered me through you, not only once but on several occasions, from the power of my enemies, who were waiting for me to fall into their hands. But when I consider with how kind, how devout, how maternal an affection this was done, I understand it far more deeply than I can express it.

For I cannot forget how anxiously you instructed me, through our brother and son Alexander, by prayer and entreaty not in any way to expose my body to danger; nor with what zeal you commanded your people to receive me with no less—indeed, if possible, greater—care than your own person, and to conduct me by the safer, not the shorter, road as far as safety. They faithfully carried this out, as they understood your will. The affection of my heart does not fail in giving thanks, but mouth and pen are unequal to expressing what the heart feels. Therefore I pray God to repay you for what I cannot do, and, defending you from every enemy of body and soul, to lead you to blessed and eternal safety.

I always preserve in my heart the memory of your holy desire, by which your heart yearns for contempt of the world, but which the holy and necessary love that you devoutly bear toward mother Church restrains. In this it is understood that your reverence is pleasing to God on both counts; and therefore you ought patiently, in an even spirit and with good hope, to bear the burden which you carry under compulsion while awaiting God’s sure counsel. Yet I venture to advise this: if in the meantime you should perceive certain danger of death to be imminent—may God avert it!—give yourself wholly to God before departing this life, and always keep this veil ready secretly beside you. Whatever I may say, this I pray and desire: that God commit you to no disposition or counsel other than his own.

Your highness instructed me through our aforesaid son Alexander that you did not possess the prayers or meditations which I dictated and thought you had; and therefore I send them to you. May Almighty God always govern and protect you with his blessing.

## LETTER XXXVIII. POPE PASCHAL II TO GERARD, BISHOP OF YORK

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gerard, bishop of York.

“The kindness of the Apostolic See,” etc. See Paschal II under the year 1118.

## LETTER XXXIX. GIRARD TO ANSELM

To his beloved father Anselm, from his son Girard: service and obedience.

A mind friendly to truth ought to beware lest it readily yield to the opinion of those whom either hatred, love, or a certain empty and idle willingness to lie impels to falsehood. Such are those whose indolence, since it rises to nothing honorable, kindles in them the fire of envy against those who live honorably. I know that men of this sort strive to make the sweetness of your spirit bitter to me. Added to this is the fact that our labor has sometimes been more sluggish than was fitting in the cause of God and yours.

437

But far be it from me, far be it from the love by which I cling to you, that from this point onward you should not have me as a helper in the word of God in which you labor, even unto exile. For if you know how to restore to me that sweetness of affection which I have often experienced in you in many great matters, you will have me as faithful servant, fellow servant in Christ, and fellow laborer in his word. Yet I had been made more negligent than I ought in this cause because I heard that you had sympathized with me in my tribulation more negligently than was fitting. Nevertheless, that great love which I have for you shows itself everywhere among my household and yours, and often in the hearing of the king and the magnates of the realm. Do not be reluctant to write to me, likewise without naming our names, what your disposition toward me is.

## LETTER XL. ANSELM TO PRIOR ERNULF

Anselm, archbishop, to Lord Prior Ernulf: greetings and God’s blessing.

You did well to write to me in your letter what you felt [Col. 0222D]. We too feel the same and see it clearly; at present I do not see how our desire, and that of our brothers, can be fulfilled through me. Nevertheless, I am sending our letters to the king, a copy of which I am sending you. I want this to remain secret until you learn what the king replies to me, or how he receives the same letter. Once you know this, however, I think it would be good for the copy I am sending to be shown publicly.

Concerning me and our cause, I can now give you no other instructions than those you already know. Be our letter to our brothers: greet, exhort, and encourage them according to the prudence God has given you. Through you I commend to them the blessing and absolution which, insofar as I can obtain them from God, I send them. Regarding the complaint that the brothers have written to me [Col. 0223A] about the poverty they suffer because of the negligence—as they believe—of Lord Roger, I have written to him and ordered him to conduct all matters belonging to him according to your counsel and prudence.

I ask you to greet the younger men and boys individually, privately and affectionately, on our behalf, and to impress upon their hearts, as you know how, that they should remember our admonition. Before I went to Rome, after I had left you, while I was still staying at Bec, you asked me what I thought if a certain cleric, considered both learned and energetic, wished to come to our church to become a monk. I replied at that time in a letter—I do not know whether it reached you—that if you saw a person whom your discretion judged suitable to receive, I too would consider it good and pleasing that he be received [Col. 0223B].

I am sending you the privilege that the lord pope gave me, for you to copy and carefully preserve. Everard told me that you wished to have the council we held at London. I am sending it to you with the instruction that you neither present it publicly nor have it copied until you and I have reconsidered it with the advice of the bishops.

## LETTER XLI. ANSELM TO THE SAME

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend prior, Lord Ernulf: greetings and the blessing of God, and his own, if it is of any worth.

I have received the letters of your reverend affection, full of prudent counsel, charitable concern for my cause [Col. 0223C], sincere affection, and a complaint about the tribulations weighing upon your heart and our Church. I could not follow your counsel in part, because Lord Everard did not come to me in such a way that he could conveniently return to England by the feast of Saint Michael. In other matters, however, with God’s help, I shall attempt what you advise, if I can bring it about.

For the concern I have mentioned, and for your affection, I give thanks to God and to you. As for tribulations, you have no need of our consolation except in those matters that can be mitigated by our counsel or power. You know that we must pass through many tribulations, and through water and fire, to reach refreshment. There are many other things, too, that are not hidden from your prudence and that urge us to rejoice in tribulation [Col. 0223D]. I do not doubt that, with God’s consolation, you do so and will continue to do so until the end.

Regarding the matters on which you ask our reply, I say first that the settlement arranged by the archbishop of York and the bishop of London neither could nor should have been established or carried out without the archbishop of Canterbury. Even if the Church of Canterbury had not had a living bishop, it ought to have been awaited. If anything was done through that settlement, it ought not to stand, and I declare it null.

Concerning the damage you suffered either from the provosts or from the cellarer, since it is past, I do not know what advice to give; nevertheless, if you can recover anything by any means, I shall be glad. For the future, I approve your counsel concerning associates of the provosts.

Regarding Geoffrey, I advise you—and I instruct the lord bishop of Rochester—that he be dealt with according to justice, so that he does not complain, blaspheming, that he has been treated unjustly either before the king or before others. Let him either satisfy you, as is just, concerning what he owes, or return to you the village for which he is indebted [Col. 0224A].

Concerning Lord Joseph, I instruct the aforesaid bishop that, if necessary, he should assist you, so that you may deal with him concerning the debts and lands he holds according to your decision; and I entrust this to your arrangement.

Concerning the reception of boys and young men, for many reasonable causes I support your counsel until, with God’s arranging, I return, and then we shall conduct this and other matters by common counsel. I do wish and ask this, however: wherever I may be, if persons of this age are to be received, let those be received first to whom permission has been granted.

As for the matter over which certain people criticize both me and you—namely, the persons of our Church—you know the necessity that brings this about. Scarcely anyone comes to us except those whom we willingly accept [Col. 0224B].

Concerning the layman whom you mercifully received, God has arranged matters well: you showed charity to him and to his friends, and he himself rested in a good end. May God absolve him from all his sins.

Regarding the cleric of Beauvais whom God mercifully drew to you, I rejoice. I advise you—although I think you already do this—to edify him frequently through your conversation concerning contempt for worldly glory, the uncertainty of human life, and the danger faced by souls passing from this world while loving the age.

Regarding the London cleric whom you received, I approve what you did.

Concerning Robert, servant of the poor, do what you consulted me about. If he comes in good health, I believe he will be useful for the salvation of his soul in some service of the Church; and if he comes in death, he will be saved.

Regarding Robert of Leminges, this is my judgment: if he becomes a monk at this time, I grant his wife, for as long as she lives, the lands that she holds from me. If anyone should receive them from another—not from the archbishop of Canterbury, whether myself or my canonical successor—let that person be subject to the excommunication I can impose upon him and to the wrath of God that I can call down upon him. Whenever Robert comes to conversion, or ends his life without conversion, what I have said concerning the lands shall remain valid [Col. 0224C].

Concerning the brothers who left the monastery disorderly and were brought back to God in an orderly manner, I praise in every respect what you did. Regarding those who remained, if they are of good will, I give thanks to God. But the man who is known to be incorrigible in so many ways I consider, through his wickedness, to have been handed over to Satan, and I do not think he should ever again be received into your fellowship.

As for the disgrace over which the foolish people cry out against you, your wisdom ought to console you. It is not blasphemy but praise of the monastery when some flee from it, for they are not seeking a better life; rather, they are utterly unable to tolerate the good conduct demanded of them [Col. 0224D].

Concerning his father, Lord Cornelius asks me—he to whom, as you know, both you and I gave hope of acceptance. If it seems good to you that he be received, I think it would be good, since he has come from far away solely out of love for holy religious life and has already reached the dignity of old age.

Regarding the priests who returned to dismissed women [Col. 0225A], I sought counsel from our revered father, the archbishop of Lyon. He absolutely refused to advise that they be admitted again to the churches; rather, he advised that infants be baptized by any clerics or laypeople. Nor does he approve their being received for any other necessity that customarily occurs in the absence of priests. Nevertheless, consider what I say and the necessity you see; and, having accepted the bishop’s counsel, do what you would advise me if I were present.

I entrust to your arrangement the celebration of the feasts about which you wrote to me. Whatever you arrange concerning them, I confirm, and let it stand. Likewise, concerning the octaves of the Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, which several of our brothers ask to have celebrated in our Church [Col. 0225B] because they are celebrated in many churches, do whatever seems best to you.

Tell Lord Robert, a monk and our beloved son, who usually guards our possessions, on our behalf that, if he has the authority, he should cause Robert the cleric who is with me to retain the house they have at Canterbury as peacefully as Roger Puntel held it.

You ask me to share in your tribulations and pray for you; I certainly do so, and I know that you do the same for us. May almighty God always grant you his consolation.

The king’s response was not given to the bishop on the appointed day. I instructed him to seek it as far as he could and to send it to me by Vulgar of Limminges with a companion, or by two other foot-messengers, since this cannot be done so quickly through Lord Everard [Col. 0225C].

## LETTER XLII. ANSELM TO THEODORIC

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest son Theodoric: greetings and the blessing of God.

I thank you for the visit expressed in your letter, which overflows with the gentle sweetness of your affection. Even when you are silent, I do not doubt that this affection always burns in your heart. Concerning my affection for you, since you know it, I need not say much.

In the statement of the fourth chapter, *On the Virginal Conception*, insert the Apostle’s words in full, as you will find them here. For the same apostle says that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh (Romans 8:1).

Farewell, my son.

## LETTER XLIII. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

To Mathilda, reverend lady, dearest daughter, queen of the English, Anselm, archbishop: greetings and the blessing of God, and his own service and prayers in affection, if they are of any worth.

My heart gives thanks for your great benevolence, which bears fruit as much as it can and does not cease to desire what it cannot accomplish. May he who inspires this repay you. For you show most clearly, as you write, how pious and sweet an affection, inspired by God, you bear toward me amid the bitterness, sadness, and anxiety that you experience because of my absence.

As I and those who carefully consider the matter understand, this absence of mine has been prolonged for so long through no fault of mine [Col. 0226A]. Your Excellence piously laments that my intemperance has disturbed the peace of mind of my lord the king and his nobles, and has hindered the good beginning of your desire from being brought to its conclusion.

Yet, in our letters, in which that intemperance is said to exist, nothing indiscreet and nothing absurd is found, although this has been charged against me in royal letters, if what was said there—and the prohibition I heard and everyone knows—is examined with right understanding and a tranquil mind. I said nothing against the king’s father or against Archbishop Lanfranc, men of great and religious reputation. I demonstrated that at my baptism and ordinations I had not promised to observe their law and customs, and I declared that I would not deny the law of God [Col. 0226B].

For what is now demanded of me, merely because they did it, I cannot do, on account of what I heard with my own ears at Rome, without the gravest offense. If I were to disregard that offense, I would certainly act against the law of God.

Therefore, to show how reasonably I refuse to do what is demanded of me according to their custom, I demonstrated how much more I am bound to observe the apostolic and ecclesiastical constitution known to all. In it the law of God is undoubtedly understood, since it was promulgated for the strengthening of the Christian religion. I shall say nothing now about the danger with which it is disregarded, since Christians who have ears to hear can learn this daily from the divine words [Col. 0226C].

I do not attribute the perverse interpretation of my statements, according to which I am said to have spoken absurdly, either to the royal judgment or to yours. The king, as I have heard, initially received our charter graciously; afterward, I do not know who, with a malicious and insincere mind, stirred him up against me through a perverse interpretation. Who that person is, I do not know; but I do not doubt that he either does not love his lord or does not know how to love him.

May almighty God foster you and your offspring in the prosperity of this life in such a way that he may raise you to the happiness of the life to come. Amen.

## LETTER XLIV. ANSELM TO GONDULF, BISHOP

[Col. 0226D]

Anselm, archbishop, to the ancient yet ever-new and true friend, and beloved in God, the reverend bishop Gondulf: greetings.

Although your steadfastness in the good works you have begun has no need of words of thanks, it nevertheless ought frequently to be sustained, lest others think that I do not recognize your benevolence and concern, which I am certain you maintain through great labors for my benefit, or that I do not value them as I ought. I therefore give thanks to your Reverence with heart, mouth, and writing.

In everything concerning me and our affairs, I understand that, insofar as you can, you speak and act prudently and courageously, with entirely sincere affection, as is fitting. I am also certain that, with God’s help, as long as you live, your good will toward me will neither have failed, as it has not failed since it began, nor will it fail [Col. 0227A].

Your Charity complains that I did not return to England because of the contemptible words of one cleric, but that is not so. Read the letter that I sent previously to Lord Prior Ernulf concerning this matter; I thought you had seen it. There, I believe, you will read the reasonable causes why I neither ought nor ought now, given the present circumstances, to return to England. Do not, however, make those causes public.

I am certain that Lord Everard, or one of our messengers, cannot receive on that day the reply that the king postponed giving me on the feast of Saint Michael, because he did not come to me in such a way that he could hurry to that day.

If, therefore, you do not receive that reply on that day, I ask you to seek another as quickly and urgently as you can, and to send me whatever it may be [Col. 0227B] that is written in the king’s letter. Even if he wishes to give no answer or to delay it longer, communicate that very fact to me without delay by your letters.

Since this cannot be done so quickly and conveniently through Lord Everard, do it through Vulgar, our servant from Limminges, with a companion, or through some other foot-messengers. I do not wish any longer either to give or to receive delays before beginning, with the counsel of God and his Church, what ought to be done in such a matter.

For I trust in God, whose cause is at issue here, that the matter will eventually be concluded to his honor, and that his Church will not always be troubled as it is now.

I do not know which malicious people, out of the wickedness of their hearts, have interpreted the letters I sent to the king as though I were boasting that I had always observed the law of God and accusing his father and Archbishop Lanfranc of having lived outside God’s law [Col. 0227C]. But surely those who say this have either an exceedingly perverse or an exceedingly limited understanding. At their time, the king’s father and Archbishop Lanfranc—men of great and religious reputation—did certain things that at this time I cannot do according to God, nor without the condemnation of my soul.

You did well, and I am grateful, because in your letters you clearly explained the whole matter as it had occurred.

I have often commended Robert, who is with me, and his affairs and household to you, but that is not enough. Because of the great good will I bear toward him, I commend him again and ask you to keep those affairs at peace as far as you can [Col. 0227D].

I greet your sons and daughters, and ours, and especially Lord Ernulf, your chaplain.

May almighty God always guard you everywhere by *contemnendo* [“despising,” with the object unexpressed in the supplied text]. Amen.

## LETTER XLV. ANSELM TO ADRUIN, HIS DEAREST

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest brother and son Adruin: greetings and the blessing of God.

May the Lord be concerned for you, since you are concerned about my reputation; for this I thank you. Previously I replied to you concerning certain people who chatter against me—people who prefer to lie about me by speaking evil rather than tell the truth by speaking of whatever good may be in me.

But you still ask, with charitable concern, that I reply to those who say they have often seen, in churches properly under my care, laypeople standing at the altar after priests had been expelled, collecting alms, and audaciously usurping burials and certain other matters belonging to the rights of priests [Col. 0228A]. When you investigated these things, you found them worse, as you say, than you had heard, with our archdeacon as witness.

You also heard the clerics of the churches say that they had repeatedly complained to me, privately and publicly, in synod, about those injuries, but had received no help. Therefore I tell you that none of these things was ever done at my command, by my will, or with my consent. And if I ever heard a complaint about them—which I do not know—I never left it without a rebuke that I believed sufficient.

In short, I certainly do not think that this happens in our churches. If it ever happened, or is happening, in the churches of others, I am completely unaware of it; and insofar as it depends on me, I have never desired it and do not desire it now.

Therefore it matters little to me if I am judged by those who devise such things without any love of truth, but at the prompting of malice.

As for your statement that you have heard that I do not greatly care to return to you, I reply that, ever since I left England, I have never understood how I could reasonably return. Certainly I neither wish nor ought to despise the care entrusted to me by God or forget the affection of the brothers and sons committed to me.

Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To Lord and Father Paschal, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: due submission with prayers.

[Col. 0228C] I think your Majesty remembers how I prayed to you on behalf of our beloved brother, the archbishop of Bourges, and how graciously he replied. Now, too, as he presents himself to you, I presume to pray with all the affection I can, so that he may rejoice to find apostolic kindness in you.

After I departed from your presence, William, the king of England’s legate, who caught up with me before I came to Lyon, told me on the king’s behalf to arrange matters so that I could be in England as my predecessor Lanfranc had been with his father. From this I understood that he did not want my return to England unless I became his man, swore fealty to him, and consecrated those to whom he gave the investitures of churches.

I therefore informed the king that I could not do these things, and that you had ordered me not to associate with those who had received investitures from him. But if it were permitted me, while preserving my order and my obedience to you, I would be ready to be in England and to serve God, him, and the people entrusted to me according to my office. I asked him to give me his reply concerning this matter, but he has not yet done so.

Since William returned to England, I have been able to receive nothing from the revenues of our bishopric.

As for the letters [Col. 0228D] that you ordered me to send to the king and queen on your behalf: since it was said at Rome to William that they had been composed at my direction, and since, as I have heard, that same William later received other letters from Your Holiness, I did not think it appropriate for them to be directed through me. I am certain that, if they were sent through me, they would not be seen at all [Col. 0229A], or would be held in contempt and derision; for, as I hear, the king has said that I alone am his adversary.

Concerning all these matters I await the counsel of your authority, ready, with God’s granting, to suffer for the truth whatever is not unfitting for a Christian.

May God long preserve your fatherhood safe and sound for us. Amen.

## LETTER XLVII. ANSELM TO THE SAME

To Paschal, lord and father, supreme pontiff, revered with love and loved with reverence, Anselm, called bishop of the Church of Canterbury: due submission with prayers.

Since the cause between the king of the English and me, for which I once sought your presence, is known for the most part to your Highness, and since what still needs to be made known can be explained by the bearer of this letter, your most faithful servant and our dearest brother Baldwin, I do not need to linger over writing it down.

I send this same brother—an adviser in my affairs and a lover of the liberty of God’s Church—to your feet as though he were myself, and I entrust to him my role in hearing and speaking.

I write only this: because of the obedience owed to you and to your predecessors, and because of the liberty of the Church, which I do not wish to deny, I am an exile from my bishopric and have been stripped of all its possessions [Col. 0229B]. In this matter your wisdom needs neither our plea nor our counsel.

May almighty God long preserve Your Holiness safe and sound for us in prosperity. Amen.

## LETTER XLVIII. ANSELM TO JOHN OF TUSCULUM AND CARDINAL JOHN

To the reverend lords and dearest friends, John, bishop of Tusculum, and John, cardinal, Anselm, called bishop of Canterbury, as a faithful friend to friends in whom he trusts.

I am sending Lord Baldwin, our dearest brother and son, who truly loves you, to the feet of the lord pope, concerning the cause between the king of the English and me—or rather, between him and the liberty of God’s Church, for which I am an exile from the bishopric and have been stripped of all its possessions [Col. 0229D].

I therefore ask Your Holiness to assist him in every way before the lord pope in this cause, as lovers of truth and of the liberty mentioned above, and to defend me so that the steadfastness of ecclesiastical religion and apostolic authority may never be weakened in any way through me or on my account.

For I would rather die and, as long as I live, be burdened by every poverty in exile than see the honor of God’s Church violated in any way because of me or by my example.

Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To Paschal, supreme pontiff, to be loved with reverence and revered with affection, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury: faithful prayers with due submission.

Regarding the matter between the Church of Chartres and the countess of Chartres, about which I spoke to Your Highness at Rome, your prudence does not need our counsel. But the necessity of the matter demands, as I understand it, our prayer and that of all who love the peace and welfare of that Church, so that what is known to have been done by the clerics as a grave scandal may, through the discretion of apostolic wisdom, be restored to peace [Col. 0230A].

You will be able to learn how intolerable an evil will arise from this, unless it is corrected, from what you will hear from the bearers of this letter, who know the matter itself.

As for the fact that the same countess honors your legates above the princes of Gaul, I think it is so well known to Your Holiness that it needs no information from us.

Therefore, if the prayers of my humility can rise to the ears of so great a Highness, I ask as earnestly as I can [Col. 0230B] that it please you to impose a harmonious end upon so harmful a discord, as the matter requires and as befits you.

For it is recognized as belonging to you both to confirm what is usefully established in God’s Church and, insofar as possible, to amend what disperses peace and charity.

May almighty God long preserve your fatherhood safe and sound for us in his grace. Amen.

## LETTER L. KING PHILIP OF THE FRENCH TO ANSELM

Philip, by the grace of God king of the French, to Anselm, venerable archbishop of Canterbury: greetings.

Since, reverend pastor, I have heard that you are being unjustly oppressed, I do not wish to conceal from you that I am deeply saddened. And if your oppression could be restrained by any assistance of ours [Col. 0230C], we would not delay in applying ourselves to this.

But since you are exiled in a place contrary to bodily health, we ask you to deign to visit our France by your arrival. There you will experience the affection of my heart and will provide for your health.

Farewell.

## LETTER LI. KING LOUIS OF THE FRENCH TO ANSELM

To the venerable Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, Louis, king-designate of the French, sends greetings.

Most holy father, I sympathize with your affliction. If you could in any way be relieved of it through my service, I would strive with greater care to restore your former tranquility.

Nevertheless, our heart is pierced by a deeper pain because the wisdom that is in you wanders so far away from our regions [Col. 0230D]. To the accumulation of your exile is added the fact that you have chosen for habitation places more conducive to illness than to health, and that you value so little preserving your life for the whole world.

We therefore ask you to deign to come to our regions; and if it should please you to dwell here, you will suffer a gentler exile.

Farewell.

## LETTER LII. ANSELM TO HIS NEPHEW

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest nephew: greetings and blessing.

I do not need to commend my affection and concern for you to you, since nature itself persuades you on my behalf [Col. 0231A]. I exhort you, admonish you, and command you to devote yourself to good conduct and knowledge, and, after God’s grace, to advance toward better things as far as lies within you. Remain where you are until, with God’s arranging, I make another disposition concerning you.

Greet kindly on our behalf your teacher, Lord Walter, concerning whom I asked the lord prior in the letter I am sending him, and also your companion Lord Theodore.

“The Lord guard you from every evil; the Lord guard your soul” (Psalm 120:7).

Lord Eadmer greets you warmly; as far as I understand, he truly loves you with sincere affection.

Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. ANSELM TO G., CANON OF SAINT-QUENTIN

[Col. 0231B]

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved brother and friend G., canon of Saint-Quentin: greetings, and may God’s counsel always rule you.

As I hear, your fellow canons of Beauvais, canons of the church of Saint-Quentin, wish to remove Lord O., who is now called your abbot, from this office—not rashly, but for many reasons—and to substitute your fraternity in his place. But they fear that, because of your love for the peace you now enjoy, your religious devotion may not readily wish to consent to their intention.

Since, therefore, they know that you love my humanity and hope that you will trust my counsel more than that of certain others, they ask me to disclose to your Charity what I think about the matter.

If we are members of one another in the body of Christ, and especially in the Church of religious persons, then I do not see how someone who does not allow or wish the other members and the whole body to use him as its member can prove himself a member of that body—or how he can show himself to be a member of Christ, if that body is the body of Christ [Col. 0231C].

There is also this consideration: no one, if he orders his life rightly, wishes to live for himself alone. Just as he desires and believes that, if he is a member of God, all the advantages of the other members will be his in the life to come, so he ought to wish that, if there is any good in him, it should belong to others in the present life.

Therefore, insofar as I can, I advise and ask you, dearest brother and friend, that if your entire congregation—or the better part of it—should earnestly elect you to the office mentioned above, with the counsel of the reverend bishops of Chartres and Paris, who were your fathers and nurtured you, you should not altogether shrink from it or prove impossible to persuade [Col. 0231D].

For I think it would be more useful for you to preserve the peace of contemplation through love in your mind, and the obedience of fraternal charity in action, than to choose contemplation alone while despising the prayers and usefulness of others.

Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. ANSELM TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

To Mathilda, glorious queen of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: God’s blessing and faithful service with prayers.

I shall speak briefly but from the heart, as to one whom I desire to be raised from an earthly kingdom to a heavenly one [Col. 0232A]. When I hear something about you that does not please God and is not beneficial to you, if I neglect to admonish you, I neither fear God nor love you as I ought.

After I left England, I learned that you treat the churches in your power differently from what is beneficial to them and to your soul. I do not now wish to say how you do this, according to what has been reported to me, since no one knows it better than you.

Therefore, I ask you as a lady, advise you as a queen, and admonish you as a daughter—as I did formerly—that the churches of God under your authority may know you as a mother, a nurturer, and a kind lady and queen. I say this not only concerning those churches, but concerning all the churches of England to which your assistance can extend [Col. 0232B].

For he who says that each person will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10), excepts no person.

Again I ask, advise, and admonish you, lady and dearest daughter, not to consider these matters negligently in your mind. If your conscience testifies that anything in them needs correction, hasten to correct it, so that in the future you may not offend God, insofar as this is possible for you through his grace; and if you recognize that you have sinned in the past, make him favorable toward you.

For it is not enough for anyone simply to cease from evil, unless he takes care, if he can, to make satisfaction for the things committed.

May almighty God always direct you in such a way that he may repay you with eternal life.

## LETTER LV. ANSELM TO THE PRIOR AND BROTHERS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

Anselm, archbishop, to the lord prior and the brothers living under him in the Church of Christ at Canterbury: greetings, and blessing from God and absolution from sins.

Your fraternity asks my advice concerning its tribulation, and specifically concerning the exaction of money imposed upon you by the king. You know how he stripped me of the possessions of the archbishopric. Therefore he shall in no way obtain through me anything from the entire income of the whole archbishopric, unless he first canonically restores me to office and returns to me what he took. Nor ought you willingly to give him money without my order.

But if he forces you to give it, either through fear that he may treat you worse or through some necessity, I shall cry out to God and invoke his judgment alike concerning what he has taken and what he will take from me or from you, since what is yours is mine [Col. 0232D].

Do not let present tribulations frighten or disturb you excessively, because God is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13).

“Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his power” (Ephesians 6:10).

God, who does not abandon those who hope in him, will put an end to these evils.

Lord Baldwin, returning from Rome, reported this from the lord pope: at the council he is to celebrate in the coming Lent, he will act concerning our affair according to the counsel he receives from that council. He has communicated this same thing to the king.

I ask you to have the book *Why God Became Man* and *On the Virginal Conception* copied for me in one volume, because I wish to send them to the lord pope. I ask you to have them copied by someone who writes clearly and distinctly [Col. 0233A].

Farewell. Do this as soon as you can conveniently, and send them to me.

## LETTER LVI. MATHILDA, MARQUISA, TO POPE PASCHAL II

To the most holy and venerable father and lord in Christ, Paschal, prelate of the First See, Mathilda, marchioness, by the grace of God, if she is anything, offers the service of all submission, both dutiful and faithful.

Among the matters concerning which we presume to ask your fatherhood, etc. See among the letters of Paschal II, under the year 1118.

[Col. 0233B]

## LETTER LVII. ANSELM TO HAIMON, VISCOUNT

Anselm, archbishop, to Haimon, his friend, viscount: greetings and blessing.

Previously I instructed and asked you, as my faithful friend and that of our Church, to restore the market that you changed from our land to the condition it was in when I left England; and to return to me the toll that you collected at Fordwick from our possessions, because nowhere in all England ought our lordly possessions to be subject to such exactions, and especially not within the proper parish of our archbishopric. Yet, as I hear, you have done neither.

Moreover, after our possessions ought, by the king’s order, to have remained undisturbed until my return, your men broke into our house at Sandwich and violently took away our fish. In the city of Canterbury they broke into another house of ours, on our land, and carried away what was inside [Col. 0233C].

I therefore ask you, as a friend in whom I ought to trust, both to restore to me what was taken from us, as I have said, and not to force me to make a complaint to someone else. For not only ought injuries from your side not to befall me and our Church; as you know, you ought also, when you can, to repel those coming from elsewhere.

Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. ANSELM TO PRIOR ERNULF

Anselm, archbishop, to the reverend brother, and lord prior Ernulf, whom I love above all in affection [Col. 0233D]: greetings and the blessing of God, and his own, insofar as he can.

It is mine, in accordance with the present divine dispensation, only to sympathize with your sufferings and tribulations—and not only with yours, but also with those of all England, which I learn in many ways through flying report; it belongs to God alone to come to your aid. Concerning what is being done against me, I can presently write you nothing other than what I commissioned Odo of London to tell you, and what I left the bearer of this letter to report to you orally. I am certain that the wrong William is doing at Eynsford would have been done by someone else, and perhaps more severely, if he himself had not done it. I am sending you copies of the letters I sent—you informed me by letter about four of them. Greet our brothers [Col. 0234A], whom God has entrusted to your care through me, with the pious and kindly affection that you know to be fitting and incumbent upon me; and, according to the wisdom given you by God, console and strengthen them. Since they are neither the first servants of God, nor the only ones, nor the last whom the world’s tribulation oppresses, frequently urge them by the example of others to embrace patience. Commend to each of the young men and boys the affection of my love, which I used to show them and still retain for them; gently entreat them, begging that they remember my admonition. You will do well for the bearer of this letter, because he has often and greatly labored on our missions, if you alleviate his poverty at least somewhat with old clothing, or in some other way. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. ANSELM TO WILLIAM CALVELLUS

ANSELM, archbishop, to WILLIAM CALVELLUS, greeting and blessing.

I still greet you as a friend and son, until I learn whether your friendship is pure and sincere or not. Until now you have conducted yourself toward our Church and me in such a way that you seemed thereby to deserve God’s favor and to possess our friendship. But now I hear that you have transferred our market from our land and taken it away from me and from the Church of Christ, your mother. Everything belonging to that Church is hers; and what belongs to the Church belongs to me. I therefore admonish and beg you, as a friend a friend and as a bishop a Christian [Col. 0234C] son, to restore to our land its market, as it was when I left England, if you do not wish to incur God’s anger, lose my friendship and that of the whole Church, which you have hitherto possessed, and become subject, together with those by whose counsel and assistance you are doing this, to the gravest excommunication. Farewell. And I advise you to do amicably and without excommunication what I command you affectionately.

443 ## LETTER LX. ANSELM TO WILLIAM THE ARCHDEACON

ANSELM, archbishop, to WILLIAM the archdeacon, greeting and blessing.

I love and praise the good things you do; but if I hear that you are doing something unbecoming to you, I must not remain silent about it. I think you remember how serious and strict a case the familiarity and association of Peter and Solomon, which they maintained with you, once established between you and me, after they had tried, so far as lay in them, to inflict insult and disgrace upon me and our Church—an injury equal to which we have never suffered from any man. Now, indeed, I hear that they associate familiarly with you in your house and are sustained by your benefits; as though exulting in the effectiveness of their will and insulting that same Church, they thrust themselves daily from your house into its presence, recalling the injury inflicted. Your prudence can judge not only by itself what this is and how it ought to be weighed, but also from the aforesaid case that existed between you and me and is still kept in writing among your papers. [Col. 0235A] As for what you should do about it, consult your faithful wisdom. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. ANSELM TO BISHOP GUNDULF

ANSELM, archbishop, to the reverend bishop GUNDULF, a true friend, greeting.

Concerning what is being done against me, I can presently write nothing other than what I commissioned Odo of London to tell Your Reverence, and what I expressly left the bearer of this letter to report to you orally. I hear that William son of Ralph is demanding from Prior Ernulf money which priests customarily give at the time when they receive chrism, because the money already spent has been expended on the monastery’s building work, and [he demands] the money that is still to be given unless he learns that I have granted it for this work. [Col. 0235B] Let Your Holiness know this, therefore, and tell William that, so far as lies in me, I grant both these sums; and if I could grant more, I would. It has been reported to me that William Calvellus has transferred the market from our land, where it is customarily held, and has taken it away from me and from our Church. I therefore admonished him by letter to correct without delay what he has done wrongly; ask him to show you the letter. Concerning this matter, I instruct you to meet the sheriff on our behalf, greeting him and his wife, our daughter, and admonish him by your entreaties not to allow this injury to be done to us, as we ought to trust him. Although at present violent injustice is being done to me, my justice does not therefore perish in God’s judgment; he will one day require it. Also admonish him to listen to the letter I sent Calvellus concerning this matter. [Col. 0235C] Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. POPE PASCHAL TO ROBERT, COUNT OF MEULAN

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, count of Meulan, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have admitted you into our intimacy, etc. See under Paschal II.

## LETTER LXIII. KING HENRY OF THE ENGLISH TO ANSELM

HENRY, king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury and most beloved Father, greeting.

I inform you that, since the feast of Saint Michael, I sent William of Warelwast [Col. 0235D] to you, and from there to Rome on our business, about which you and I spoke together concerning the Roman See—unless the stormy sea, the swell, and contrary wind had detained him. Witness: Walric the chancellor, at Winchcombe.

## LETTER LXIV. TO THE SAME

HENRY, king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and friendship.

I command you, as my most beloved Father, to instruct the monk Baldwin to go with William of Warelwast to Rome on the matter, so that through both of them firm affection and peace may be established between us. Witnesses: [Col. 0236A] Walric the chancellor, Robert count of Meulan, and Eudo the steward, at Pontefract.

## LETTER LXV. ANSELM TO GERARD OF YORK

ANSELM, archbishop, to the reverend archbishop GERARD of York, greeting.

For the tribulations you have suffered since I left England, although I cannot presently offer consolation by deed, I bear in my heart the compassion that is owed. I understand, both from the words of many and from your letters, that your will has been kindled by zeal for God against the evils that blaze and multiply in God’s Church. As I grieve with you in adversity, so I rejoice with you in your courage. I therefore beg and admonish you not to let constancy be lacking from your good purpose, nor perseverance, which reaches onward to perfection. Why, after all, have we been appointed bishops [Col. 0236B] over God’s people if, like dogs unable to bark, we remain mute? I hope in God that our lord the king, just as he promises me under God’s inspiration, will become a good helper to us in every good work; and if God deigns to perfect the concord begun between him and me, he will not in any way withdraw from our counsel in matters belonging to our Order. Therefore, for the present I shall do nothing further concerning our business, until I learn the apostolic decision in the near future. Farewell.

444 ## LETTER LXVI. ANSELM TO PRIOR ERNULF AND THE SONS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

ANSELM, archbishop, to lord Prior ERNULF and his most beloved brothers, sons of Christ Church, Canterbury, greeting and blessing.

Because of the case between the lord king and me, the king has now sent his envoys to Rome, and I have sent mine. I therefore command and beg you earnestly to pray to God, so that he may establish such concord between the lord pope and the king that, while preserving due reverence for his will, I may agree with both. If this is already happening among you, I rejoice, and I greatly desire that it may be so. As soon, therefore, as you conveniently can, I command you to inform me by letter what your condition is. May almighty God guard you, make you steadfast in your holy purpose, and, propitiated, absolve you from all sins. Amen.

## LETTER LXVII. KING HENRY OF THE ENGLISH TO ANSELM

HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, his beloved Father, greeting and affection.

We have learned from the report of several people, especially from Robert, my chancellor’s clerk, rumors concerning the apostolic matter, and, if the situation is as rumor spreads it, I grieve. Since the rumor grows more frequent as the days pass, I fear that it may be true. For they say that at Rome—God forbid!—there are two apostolic claimants, and that they are maintaining a warlike dominion against one another. I therefore seek your counsel, so that you may provide both for me and for yourself, since the greater part of this business concerns you, as to what should be done with [Col. 0237A] our envoys in this stormy time. If it seems useful to you to retain them until a suitable time, then retain William and send me as quickly as possible Baldwin of Tournai, your monk, through whom I may communicate more privately to you our secrets; and through him tell me what in this matter I should hold to and do. If, however, it pleases you that they should go, and that is your counsel, let them go; and if they have gone, send me as quickly as possible one of your familiar associates, through whom we may communicate our counsels and affairs to one another with mutual confidence. Witnesses: Robert, bishop of Lincoln, and Robert, count of Meulan.

## LETTER LXVIII. WILLIAM TO ANSELM

To the lord and most excellent of all his friends, [Col. 0237B] ANSELM, one of his servants—and may he be the least of God’s servants—WILLIAM, joy in the desired salvation.

It is not ours to exalt the merits of holy men, nor to diminish their praises; but God, who glories in his saints and to whom every heart is open, knows how great is the devotion of our humility toward God and with what affection of heart I love your welfare. Nor is this without reason. It is not unknown to me that, if there were even the smallest good in me, you would embrace my welfare with excessive zeal. But since I distrust the quality of my merits—for the prayer of an unclean man is unclean—I beg you, prostrate as it were at your knees and feet, as earnestly as I can: if you ever wish to rejoice over me, pray more intently for my brother Geoffrey. For I know that, through God’s mercy, he will at some time obtain remission of his sins if you cry out to the Lord for him with your whole heart. I do not say this without cause; but for the present let what has been said suffice for you, until we meet together. I refrain from saying more about this and about other things that I would wish to tell you, because all things have their proper times. But since you see me miserably shipwrecked in the shipwreck of my brother, support the endangered man with the plank of your prayers, so that we who for a long time, because our sins demanded it, have endured shipwreck may at last, through your prayers, deserve to hold our course into the harbor of salvation.

## LETTER LXIX. ANSELM TO BISHOP ODO

To the reverend and most beloved lord, Bishop ODO, Brother ANSELM: so to pass through temporal goods that he may dwell in eternal ones.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] The abbot wrote this.]

The letter which Your Paternal Highness sent me and our brothers on behalf of your faithful deceased Osbern we received with humble obedience and obedient humility. For we have resolved to deny nothing to your request; rather, in whatever must be obeyed by our most beloved lord and most beloved Father, we have determined to comply with your command. Since we recognize that you have earned this by the price of affection and benefits, we would show ourselves greatly deserving of blame if we refused [Col. 0238A] obediently to submit ourselves to your will. In that letter I received one thing especially gratefully: I read there a certainty concerning the mutual affection between Your Greatness and my smallness. For although my own conscience and experience have already taught me that I cannot doubt this, it is nevertheless a sweet honor and an honorable sweetness to me when so great a man deigns to send this command to one so small.

## LETTER LXX. ANSELM TO THEODORIC

ANSELM, archbishop, to his most beloved son THEODORIC, greeting and God’s blessing.

The words of your letter are sweet to me, because sweet to me is the affection of your beloved soul. There is no need to linger in demonstrating this, since [Col. 0238B] your conscience knows how my heart feels toward you. I am not sending you the letters you seek from the king to the pope, because I do not understand it to be useful for them to be preserved. If, with God’s help, I write anything else, it will be shown at the proper time. As for the fact that you correct the books you have written, see that whatever copies have been made from them are corrected in those copies as well. You desire my presence; may God show you his presence, and meanwhile may he dwell in you through his grace. Amen.

## LETTER LXXI. ANSELM TO BISHOP GUNDULF

ANSELM, archbishop, to the reverend bishop GUNDULF, greeting.

I have begged the lord prior and our archdeacon, with all the affection I can, to care for this Robert, so that he may suffer no severe deprivation of food or clothing, since he has been converted from perfidy to the mercy and piety of the true [Col. 0238C] faith. I therefore ask you to read to them the letter I sent; and if at any time they neglect to do what I command them—which I do not believe—then, from our resources and with pious generosity, supply this man with whatever they fail to provide.

## LETTER LXXII. ANSELM TO GUIDO

ANSELM, archbishop, to his beloved son GUIDO, greeting and God’s blessing.

I hear that you are living in peace and tranquility in the cloister, concerned with the service of God and the salvation of your soul, and I rejoice greatly because of it. [Col. 0238D] I therefore admonish you, dearest son, although there is no need, to cast the world and the things of the world far from your heart, and not to bend yourself toward love of it in any way. Love God and serve him diligently, because through his grace you have never had as great an opportunity to serve him as you now have. You ask for my absolution; I send it to you.

## LETTER LXXIII. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To the lord and Father to be loved with reverence and revered with love, PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission, with faithful service and prayers.

[Col. 0239A]

I briefly write Your Highness about what has recently happened in the case between the king of England and me, leaving its fuller exposition to his envoy and ours. After Your Authority, by forbidding the count of Meulan and the others who were obstructing your command before the king to enter the Church, had brought this about, I approached Normandy. Through the countess of Chartres, the king’s most faithful sister, a daughter of God’s Church and obedient to your commands, it came about that the king and I met for a conference with some hope of a favorable outcome. There he reinstated me in the archbishopric from which he had stripped me. Concerning the matters on which we disagreed—namely, the investitures of churches and the homage of prelates, regarding which I heard a prohibition both together and in similar terms at the Roman council—he determined to consult the apostolic [Col. 0239B] see through his envoy before the coming Nativity of the Lord. I did not understand that I ought either to prohibit his embassy or reject my reinstatement. What he himself grants concerning the matters mentioned, or what he requests, Your Holiness will learn through the same envoy. Since the conclusion of the whole case depends upon your judgment, I sent our envoy at the same time, so that I might learn what agreement there is between you and the king and what your command directs me to do. By the authority of the charter you sent the count of Meulan, in which I read that, if he obeyed you, he would obtain your favor, I admitted him to the Church’s communion, since he promised that he would try to make the king obey your commands for the flourishing of the Church. Concerning the other matters about which I seek Your [Col. 0239C] Authority through envoys, I ask, if it pleases you, that his response be solicited through those same men. For my reverend Father, the archbishop of Rouen, I humbly prostrate myself in mind at your feet, asking that, in accordance with what you will learn through his envoys, you extend to him the kindness of apostolic mercy in response to his supplication and humility and to the need of his Church. May almighty God preserve Your Reverence’s safety in his Church for a long time and in every prosperity. Amen.

## LETTER LXXIV. MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

To her most beloved lord and Father, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, MATHILDA, queen of the English, sends continual greeting with affection and faithful service.

[Col. 0239D] Let your consoling affection know, dearest Father, that my soul is gravely troubled by your holiness’s very long and wearisome absence. For the more often and the more quickly several people promise me the desired end of your return, the more ardently I, who long to enjoy your presence and conversation, desire it. Therefore, most reverend lord, my soul will be gladdened by no perfect joy and cheered by no true affection until I can rejoice in seeing again your presence, which I desire with all the powers of my mind. [Col. 0240A] I therefore beg the honeyed sweetness of your kindness to deign, meanwhile, to console and gladden me in my absence with the pleasantness of your correction and the sweetness of your letters. May the almighty and merciful Lord preserve you everywhere and presently gladden me with news of your return. Amen.

## LETTER LXXV. KING HENRY OF THE ENGLISH TO ANSELM

HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, his most beloved Father, greeting and friendship.

Let your kindly fatherhood know that I ought to grieve, and that I grieve exceedingly within myself, because of the pain and illness of your body. And know that, unless I were waiting for you, I would already have been in Normandy. [Col. 0240B] I would have rejoiced if I had found you before I departed from my realm; but now I beg you, as a son begs a father, to indulge your bodily nature a little longer and not afflict your body so severely. I wish and command you to exercise authority everywhere throughout all my possessions in Normandy as over your own lordships, and my heart will rejoice if you do so. But now wait for me in Normandy, for I shall cross over shortly. Witness: Walric, at Windleshores.

## LETTER LXXVI. QUEEN MATHILDA TO ANSELM

To her lord and most beloved Father, ANSELM, archbishop, MATHILDA, queen of the English, sends the health of good well-being.

The joyful delight of expected happiness, which recently promised me the arrival of Your Holiness, would have brought me as much greater joy and consolation as the illness that intervened has brought me a greater misfortune of desolate grief. I therefore come to implore, with pitiable tears, the affection of your fatherhood known to me beforehand: if your concern for me has not entirely grown cold, make me as soon as possible secure, through whatever messenger, concerning the anxiety of my solicitude for your health. Either I shall immediately rejoice in your health—which is indeed also mine—or, as God’s mercy avert it, I shall bear without distinction the blow of our common misfortune. May the most merciful omnipotence of God restore you to health. Amen.

446 ## LETTER LXXVII. KING HENRY OF THE ENGLISH TO ANSELM

HENRY, king of the English, to his beloved Father ANSELM, [Col. 0240D] archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and a son’s affection.

Let Your Reverence know that my brother Count Robert came to me in England and departed graciously. Know also that on the day of the Lord’s Ascension I shall be ready at the sea to cross over. Once I have crossed, I shall do what must be done through you and your counsel. Meanwhile, if William of Warelwast and our other envoys have returned from Rome, let it be left to your discretion whether they should cross over to me in England before I cross, or remain with you until they speak with you and with me. Witness: W., the chancellor, at Northampton.

## LETTER LXXVIII. ANSELM TO PRIOR ELFER AND THE MONKS OF SAINT EDMUND

ANSELM, archbishop, to his beloved sons and brothers, Prior ELFER and the others serving God in the monastery of Saint Edmund, greeting and the blessing of God and of the archbishop.

That until now I withdrew from communion with Lord Robert, I did because of the command and obedience owed to the lord pope. Now, at the command of that same lord pope, and for the reason by which he precedes me, I have received him into peace and communion. I therefore command and instruct you henceforth to be obedient to him in all things and to render him confession and the other things that monks owe to an abbot; do not cease doing so [Col. 0241B] unless I should command otherwise in the future. I ask and exhort and admonish you, in every way I can, to be diligent concerning the observance of your order, so that nothing may be heard about you except what ought to be heard about good monks and true servants of God. Amen.

## LETTER LXXIX. HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO ANSELM

To the most reverend Father and sweetest friend, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, and to all his people, Brother HUGH, sinner and abbot of Cluny, sends greeting and joy without end.

Since we knew how great a familiarity, God willing, had existed between you and Lord Hugh, [Col. 0241C] archbishop of Lyons, we considered it fitting to inform you of his death—a death grievous and irreparably mourned by us and by all good men—so that through you and your people you may strive to repay him, now dead, for the true affection he showed while alive. He died in peace on the Nones of October at Susa, while he was going to the council summoned by the apostolic see, and was buried there quite honorably in the abbey of Saint Justus. We desire to learn more fully how Your Reverence is, and to be more abundantly gladdened by news of your prosperity, whenever a suitable time and place arise. May Christ Jesus, the supreme Pontiff, work with you in all things.

[Col. 0241D]

## LETTER LXXX. HUGH TO THE SAME

To the most loving and glorious Father, Lord ANSELM, venerable archbishop of the people of Canterbury, Brother HUGH, sinner and abbot of Cluny, sends greeting of mind and body in Christ and joy without end.

After you departed from us, man beloved by God, we were unable to learn what had happened to Your Holiness. Nevertheless, we hope this concerning God’s mercy: wherever your religious devotion may be, divine assistance will be at hand. Who could ever be so inhuman that, after experiencing the sweetness of your conversation, he would not receive and venerate you as an angel of God? Therefore we, although quite unworthy, implore divine clemency, so that he who granted you such grace on earth may deign to grant you eternal glory in heaven. And now, Father, [Col. 0242A] we have sent our sons—your servants and faithful friends—to those regions on the common business of our monastery. We commend them to Your Holiness and wish them to carry out there what they are to do according to your counsel and to be fortified by your assistance. Concerning the case of our son, Lord Theardus, we ask especially that, since the lord pope placed the whole disposition of his office at your discretion, and since, as we learned from him, while he was still in clerical dress you granted him the full authority of his office, now that by God’s mercy you have been restored to your principal dignity, you will not disdain to write us whatever we are to command him. May Your Holiness, remembering us, rejoice for a long time.

[Col. 0242B]

## LETTER LXXXI. ANSELM TO HUGH, COUNT

ANSELM, archbishop, to his lord and most beloved friend HUGH, count, greeting and the blessing of God and of the archbishop.

The bearer of this letter complains that you seized and are holding in captivity a certain Cluniac monk, and another man who had recently become a monk and had died, whom your men carried off and buried wherever they wished. If these things are so, I grieve greatly because of them on your account, since they have been done in a way very unlike what is fitting for you. I therefore command, beg, and advise you as a friend not to delay returning the monk whom you hold; and, since you seized him, offer yourself to [Col. 0242C] do justice in the matter. It is to your honor to do this. Afterwards, if you have any claim against this monk, make your complaint concerning it, and what ought justly to be done will be done for you. Concerning the dead man also, I advise you similarly to offer yourself for judgment, and to do so wherever justice more properly requires. I say to you familiarly, as to a man whose honor and welfare I greatly love, that if you do not do what I say, you will be blasphemed for it; and I too, if I do not do what ecclesiastical discipline commands should be done in the matter, will be blasphemed by many. I greet your wife, my dearest daughter.

[Col. 0242D]

447 ## LETTER LXXXII. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

To HENRY, by God’s grace glorious king of the English and duke of the Normans, ANSELM, archbishop, offers faithful service with faithful prayers, and the wish that he may always increase toward greater and better things and never decrease.

I rejoice and give thanks to God, from whom all good things proceed, with all the feeling I can, for your prosperity and your successes. I also rejoice and give thanks from my inmost heart because, together with earthly prosperity, he illuminates your heart by his grace so that you attribute nothing in his benefits or in your advancement to yourself or to human powers, but everything to his mercy. Since you promise, so far as lies in you, peace and liberty to the Church, I earnestly beg and advise you, as your faithful servant, to persevere in this, [Col. 0243A] because in it will lie the strength of your highness. With mouth and heart, as far as my mind can, I pray—and through me and others I ask almighty God—that he may unceasingly continue the mercy of his grace which he has begun to bestow upon you, so that after your earthly exaltation in this life he may lead you to the heavenly kingdom and eternal glory. Amen.

## LETTER LXXXIII. POPE PASCHAL II TO ANSELM

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God because, after darkness had been driven away by your many labors in the English Church, the ancient light has shone again. Yet one must be [Col. 0243B] watchful lest the enemy cast darnel among the good seed in the Lord’s field, and a corrupt root produce a corrupt shoot. Finally, we have heard that a certain Count Robert, who is held captive by the English king, took a wife under a prohibition of consanguinity, and that her relatives restored her to the aforesaid count. We therefore command Your Affection to meet with that count; and if you find these things to be true, after employing suitable witnesses, arrange the matter wisely so that, once both have been freed from sins, they may serve God freely. May Your Affection pray for us.

## LETTER LXXXIV. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

To his most beloved lord HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, ANSELM, archbishop, offers faithful service [Col. 0243C] with prayers.

I give thanks to God for the good will he has given you, and to you for striving to preserve it. Your Highness asks for advice about what should be done in this matter: you have promised to give your daughter to William of Warenne, although he and your daughter are related on one side in the fourth degree and on the other in the sixth. Know without doubt that no agreement may be kept against the law of Christianity. If they are so closely related, they cannot lawfully be joined in any way, either without the damnation of their souls or without great sin on the part of those who arrange that it should happen. I therefore beg and advise you, on God’s behalf and as my most beloved lord, not to involve yourself in this sin in any way, nor to give your daughter to that same William [Col. 0243D] against the law and will of God. May almighty God direct you and all your actions according to his good pleasure.

## LETTER LXXXV. MURIARDACH, KING OF IRELAND, TO ANSELM

MURIARDACH, king of Ireland, to ANSELM, archbishop of the English, greeting and faithful service.

How great are the thanks I owe you, lord, because, as I have been told, you remember me, a sinner, continually in your prayers; and you have also assisted my son-in-law Ernulf with your help and intercession, insofar as was permitted by your dignity. Know also that I shall serve you in whatever you command. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. GISLEBERT OF LUNI TO ANSELM

To ANSELM, by the grace of God archbishop of the English, GISLEBERT, by God’s mercy likewise bishop of Luni, offers faithful service and prayers.

Hearing, Father, of the labor of your struggle and of the victory of your labor—namely, that the untamed minds of the Normans have been subjected to the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers, so that the election and consecration of abbots and prelates may take place according to rule—I give immense thanks to divine clemency and pour out to God such prayers as I can, asking that he grant you perseverance and the reward of so great a labor. I am sending a small gift of my poverty and devotion: twenty-five little pearls, some among the best and some of lesser value; and I ask that you not forget [Col. 0244B] me in your prayers, in which, after God’s generosity, I place my confidence. Amen.

## LETTER LXXXVII. ANSELM TO JOTSERAN, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

To JOTSERAN, lord archbishop of Lyons, to be revered with affection and loved with reverence, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greeting with prayers and service.

Because your true charity rejoices with us, since God, who does not abandon those who hope in him, has gladdened us with his consolation after the days in which he humbled us, we give thanks; and because we feel that you rejoice with us, we rejoice more greatly. Since, however, your reverence is assailed by many and immense tribulations from those from whom you expected help and [Col. 0244C] consolation in your necessities, we sympathize and grieve with you. But this consoles us: we trust in God that by the force of no rivers and no winds will your constancy be shaken, and that God, who “resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5), will break the pride of the wicked and cast it beneath the feet of Your Authority; and when your virtue has been tested, you will receive the promised crown of life. As for our condition, which your kindness desires to know, you will be able to learn it better through your envoys than through a letter.

448 ## LETTER LXXXVIII. ANSELM TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friend THOMAS, elected archbishop of York, greeting.

You wrote to me that, on the date I set for you, you would be at Canterbury, with God’s help, if you could come conveniently, to receive and do what you ought; you also asked that, if you were unable to accomplish this, I should allow you to notify me of that fact ten days beforehand. But your messenger, William the cleric, begged me on your behalf to extend the date of your arrival somewhat, so that you might come to us more conveniently. I willingly do this for love of you and for your convenience. So that you need not notify me beforehand of anything concerning your arrival, I urge [Col. 0245A] you to be at Canterbury on Sunday, which will be the fifth day before the Kalends of October, to do what you ought to do and to receive your consecration. Moreover, you say in your letter that you are seeking money to send to Rome for the pallium of your Church; I do not approve this. I think you would do so in vain, since no one ought to have the pallium before he has been consecrated. The letters you request as testimony to your person and election I shall gladly prepare for you, as I ought to do for a friend, once you have spoken with me and shown me to whom I should address them.

## LETTER LXXXIX. ANSELM TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

To the reverend lord and Father, WILLIAM, archbishop of Rouen, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends greeting and faithful prayers [Col. 0245C] with service.

You wrote to me that William the chamberlain and his wife say that I told them they could redeem their sin by almsgiving—namely, the sin that William has as his wife the woman who had been his kinsman’s [wife]. Let Your Holiness know that I never told them this; rather, I say that neither of them, if he or she dies in this sin, will see the glory of God. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. ANSELM TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to the reverend archbishop of the Church of Lund in Denmark, though late, greeting and true friendship in Christ.

[The supplied source ends here.]

What you asked me concerning Lord Alberic, cardinal of the Roman Church, I gladly did, both out of regard for the honor of the Roman Church and out of regard for your own, for whom I gladly wish to do anything that I understand would please your holiness. We give thanks to God, who has raised your religious prudence and prudent religion in the kingdom of the Danes to the archiepiscopate. For we trust that, with the grace of God cooperating, you will correct what ought to be corrected, build what ought to be built, and nourish what ought to be nourished. Indeed, we have heard many good things about you from the aforesaid cardinal; hence we have this confidence, and we pray that God, who has begun this work in you, may always bring your will to a good result. I ask your holiness to cleanse that kingdom by your holy zeal of apostates, so that no foreigner may there receive any ecclesiastical order, since those who are rejected by their bishops go there and are disastrously ordained to various orders. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XCI. ANSELM TO COUNTESS ADA

To the lady and mother most beloved in God, ADA, venerable countess, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends what is best, sweetest, and most affectionate that he can offer according to God.

Whenever I wish to write to your highness, I cannot find words with which I might express the affection that my heart always preserves before God for you—unless perhaps I express it better by confessing that I cannot express it. Indeed, when I consider in my mind the affectionate love that, because of God, I have experienced from you toward me in so many ways, I can think of nothing in myself that, according to my desire, could suffice either as its repayment or as an act of thanksgiving. Since, therefore, I neither know nor am able to do anything better, I turn to God and pray that he may repay your love with his own love for me, which surpasses all human merits. This I do every day, and, as long as I live, with God’s consent I shall not cease to do it. You know my desire concerning you; would that, by the grace of God, I might hear before I die that it has been fulfilled. Truly I tell you that my soul would leave the body more joyfully. The bearer of this letter will be able to tell you sufficiently what is happening with us, which you wish to know. May the Holy Spirit always be the guardian and director of your heart and your life. Amen.

## LETTER XCII. ANSELM TO COUNT HACON

ANSELM, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to HACON, count of the Orkneys, greetings and God’s blessing.

I hear that, because of a lack of teachers, the people under your authority know and practice the Christian religion less than is fitting. But I rejoice because, from the report of the bishop whom by God’s grace you now have, I have learned that your prudence willingly receives the word of God and counsel pertaining to salvation. With this confidence, therefore, I send your vigor this letter of admonition, asking that you devote yourself diligently to the preaching and teaching of that same bishop; and, as far as lies within you, strive to ensure that your people do the same. For you can do nothing by which you may more surely obtain the remission of sins and the glory of eternal life than by urging your people toward the worship of the Christian religion and, by whatever means you can, drawing them to it. You will be able effectively to fulfill this, God granting it, if, as I said above, you submit yourselves to your bishop with devotion, holy humility, and a pure will. If, with God inspiring you, you wish to heed our counsel and exhortation, I pray almighty God that he himself may direct and protect you and your whole people by his grace, and I commend to you from my heart his blessing and absolution, together with the prayers of my humility. May almighty God cause you to live in this world in such a way that in the world to come you may be joined to the blessed company of the angels. Amen.

## LETTER XCIII. HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH, TO ANSELM

HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, his dearest father, greetings and affection.

Know, my father, that by the grace of God I am healthy and unharmed, and that all my affairs are proceeding safely and prosperously. As for what I have learned about you and your health through Aufridus, your cleric, and through others, and likewise that the matters around you are being conducted with the good fortune of health and prosperity, know that I rejoice no little. Nor, in the assurance of your goodwill, should you be unaware of how matters turned out for us concerning the conference between King Louis of France and me. Know that I, with a considerable number of my knights, and he, with his strength gathered from every quarter, held a conference. I, striving for reason and equity with measured humility, while nevertheless maintaining royal severity, assented to everything equitable and just until he, with presumptuous arrogance, made excessive and proud demands upon me. Thus, by the ordering of the grace of the Holy Spirit, I ended our discussion, so that, with the counts accompanying me, I withdrew on the side of reason and justice. Indeed, those whom Louis himself placed with me as hostages on his behalf in our agreement now assent to my case, defend my cause, and weaken and reject Louis’s cause. Therefore know that the business being negotiated between the emperor of the Romans and me, by God’s grace, has been brought to completion for the honor of God and of ourselves, and of the holy Church and the Christian people. For the rest, concerning the affairs in England and the matters being conducted there, I wish them to obey your will and be arranged according to your counsel. I have also made this known to our justices. I entrust my son and daughter to you, that you may cherish them with fatherly affection and care for them with parental love. Witnessed by Ranulf the chancellor at Rouen.

## LETTER XCIV. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

To his dearest lord HENRY, by the grace of God glorious king of the English, ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, sends faithful service with prayers, and God’s blessing and his own, insofar as he is able.
