I give thanks to almighty God from the innermost affection of my heart for all the prosperity and success that God, by his grace, graciously deigns to bring about for you, and I pray that he may always cause your highness to advance toward greater and better things and, through continual prosperity in your earthly kingdom, lead you to the happiness of the heavenly kingdom. I also give thanks for your graciousness, which, as though I were your faithful and true beloved, kindly informed me by letter about the matters concerning you and filled my heart with joy at your happiness and prosperity. As for the fact that you so carefully commend your son and daughter to my care and affection, and entrust your kingdom and the affairs of your kingdom to my will, although I do not possess sufficient wisdom for this, nevertheless, because I understand your immense goodwill and favor toward me, I gratefully accept, insofar as I can, what you entrust to me, and I commend it to the disposition and help of God, through whom all things are well ordered. Concerning the archbishop-elect of the Church of York, I am informing your highness by word of mouth through Lord Baldwin, your faithful and beloved servant, of how the matter stands. In this matter I beg your help and strength with all my heart, so that you will not permit the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, preserved by your predecessors, which God has entrusted to your protection and whose honor is your own, to be diminished. I tell you plainly of myself that I am more ready to die so that its dignity may be preserved intact than to allow it to be violated in any way through my negligence. May almighty God always direct and protect you and yours. Amen.

## LETTER XCV. ANSELM TO POPE PASCHAL

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, reverend with affection and beloved with reverence, ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, sends due submission with constant prayers.

Although not because of my merits, certain people, seeing that I always have your graciousness present in my affairs, think that I can accomplish something with your highness in matters appropriate to you, as though I were a faithful servant. Therefore, compelled by the requests of others, I venture to petition your majesty to deign to hear the case of the bearer of this letter and to issue concerning it whatever your wisdom shall approve. May almighty God preserve your holiness for us in enduring prosperity. Amen.

## LETTER XCVI. ANSELM TO SAMSON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to SAMSON, bishop of Worcester, greetings.

You know what the Church of York owes to the Church of Canterbury, and how it ought to be subject to it. After Thomas was elected archbishop of York, he ought to have sought his consecration and to have professed the obedience that the archbishop of York owes to the archbishop and Church of Canterbury. He scorned to do what he ought to have done. Nevertheless, out of an abundance of charity, I invited him twice through our clerics, and a third time through two bishops, to come to his mother, the Church of Canterbury, and to me, to whom his ministry has been entrusted, and to do and receive what he ought. He neglected what he ought to have done and replied that he had sent his messengers to Rome and to Normandy; when they returned, he would do what he received as the counsel of his own advisers. We understand that this answer cannot be accepted in this matter.

I therefore command you, as a friend and one who has professed himself a member of our Church, to stand by me in opposing this injury—which is directed not only against me but against all the bishops and churches of our archiepiscopate and primacy, and even against the kingdom of England—in order to suppress so intolerable a presumption. Let your reverence be certain that I shall omit nothing I can do, either before God or before men, so that this disordered presumption of his may be destroyed. He ought to remember that he received the higher orders that he holds in my archiepiscopate and the priesthood at my command, and that his election was made with my favor. Therefore, if he considered the matter rightly, he ought not to raise himself so disorderly against me—or rather above me. I demand your counsel concerning this matter.

And since, with the counsel of the other bishops to whom this injury pertains, I shall shortly send the bishops of Rochester and Thetford to our lord the king, on my behalf and theirs, to seek his help in doing what canonically I ought and wish to do in this matter, instruct those same bishops to carry out their embassy on your behalf as well as that of the other bishops. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII. SAMSON, PRIEST OF THE CHURCH OF WORCESTER, TO ANSELM

To his lord and dearest father ANSELM, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, SAMSON, priest of the Church of Worcester, sends greetings, service, and faithful prayers.

You commanded me, lord, and, as one who has professed himself a member of your Church and your servant, admonished me to stand by you and your Church—that is, the Church of Canterbury—in the matter between you and Thomas, the elect of the Church of York. Therefore I beg your excellence not to doubt that I wish in any way, or for anyone’s sake, to betray the profession that I have made and continue to make, and which I wish to preserve in every respect. For I think that you will have no one more faithful in your cause, nor a more devoted helper according to my ability.

As for the counsel you have sought from me, if I truly knew what would be more advantageous for you and for us, I would not delay in stating it. I say only this: it seems to me unworthy that you should become excessively angry over this matter. Since we have so many bishops, so many abbots, and so many distinguished men as witnesses, it seems easy to me to refute clerics of such little or no authority. For the controversy belongs to those who, in my view, should have no difficulty destroying such presumptuous audacity.

As for the elect himself, I affirm truthfully—as I have believed and do believe, and as he ought to be believed—that he bears no disposition toward you except a good one, and that, for as long as you live, he will be entirely devoted and subject to you and your Church. It pleases me, however, that you did what you ought to have done: persuading him out of goodwill and commanding him by due authority, because, if there is sin in delaying the consecration, it belongs to someone other than you.

## LETTER XCVIII. ANSELM TO COUNT ELIAS

ANSELM, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his lord and friend, and most beloved in God, COUNT ELIAS, sends greetings and prays that he may always be directed and protected by God’s grace.

I rejoice and give thanks to almighty God, from whom every good thing comes, because he has so filled your heart with good will and holy intention that you diligently seek counsel concerning by what path and in what manner you may reach the kingdom of heaven and the blessed fellowship of the angels more securely and effectively. Since you seek this from me, I send it to you through the beloved brother Hardus, your friend and familiar associate, as well as I am able to understand it; you will be able to learn it clearly from his spoken account. The absolution that, as that same brother reported to me, you request from me, I send to your love through him in heart, word, and writing, and I pray for you every day. May almighty God kindle your holy desire more and more and bring it to a blessed fulfillment. Amen.

## LETTER XCIX. ANSELM TO COUNT ROBERT

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his dearest lord and friend ROBERT, count of Meulan, sends greetings and God’s blessing and his own, insofar as he can.

Concerning the case between me and Thomas, the elect of York, I command and beg you, as a true friend and son of the mother Church of Canterbury, and I counsel you, as a faithful Christian and one who faithfully loves the honor and dignity of the king and of the whole kingdom of England, to consider with the utmost care and diligence the gravity of the great evil that Thomas himself is attempting, and with all your strength to suppress his intention as an injury and disgrace to the king, to the whole kingdom of England, to your mother Church, and to the archbishops of Canterbury.

As for myself, trusting in God’s help, I affirm that it will never be through me; and if I knew that I would die tomorrow before his calumny had been extinguished, I would impose upon him as severe a sentence as I understood myself able to impose. Let your love be certain of this: no one can in any way support this presumption of his without great sin on his own part and without incurring God’s anger. May the Holy Spirit direct your heart in truth. Amen.

## LETTER C. ANSELM TO RODULF, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to RODULF, bishop of Chichester, greetings.

I have heard that your archdeacon seized my men as though for an offense involving the violation of a feast, and took sureties from them, refusing to release them before he had obtained those sureties. Neither he nor anyone else has permission to do this to my men. Therefore I command you to declare those same sureties discharged and to do me justice concerning the archdeacon, who has dared to commit such acts against my men.

As for your instruction that I should discipline our men, lest others receive a bad example from them, I give thanks, and, as for what I ought to do about it, with God’s consent I shall do so. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. ANSELM TO BISHOP R.

ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, to his beloved friend, the reverend Bishop R., greetings.

I command and instruct you, by the holy obedience that you owe to the Church of Canterbury and to me, to conduct yourself henceforth toward Thomas, the elect of the Church of York, in accordance with what is written in the accompanying letter intended for him.

## LETTER CII. BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR TO ANSELM

[Note: From the manuscript of the monastery of Pratellis.—This is Richard, abbot of Pratellis, dedicating his Commentary on Genesis to Saint Anselm.]

To ANSELM, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, a certain servant of the Lord’s cross and minister of the monastery of Pratellum, wishing that, like a soldier of the supreme King, he may happily complete with tireless course the course of his pilgrimage to the fatherland.

Although, as a lover and cultivator of truth, and therefore one greatly beloved among the members of Christ, I often endure inwardly the frequent hostilities and attacks of wicked men, as well as the goads of evil spirits, nevertheless I consider the burden of the obedience that you impose upon me extremely light, both in action and in the sincere devotion with which I love you. Indeed, nothing difficult is found that does not seem easy to anyone inflamed by the fire of love.

Therefore, having already expounded the mysteries in the book of Genesis, and now about to undertake, at your command, and explain the four that remain, with the hand of my Lord Jesus Christ guiding my pen, I greatly need your prayers, so that he who shuts and no one opens, who opens and no one shuts (Rev. 3:7), may open for me the sealed book. I leave untouched its history, which blessed Augustine pursued in many ways according to the literal sense up to the departure of our first parent from paradise. For it could be counted intolerable arrogance if I dared to lay my hand upon the hand of that same man.

But when we come to the place where, through a sixfold arrangement, the forms of visible things are brought to completion, I shall attempt, insofar as divine wisdom assists me, at some point to treat the literal sense of this book according to its threefold meaning. The Lord, however, knows the poverty of my knowledge; my conscience and intention bear truthful testimony to him, for I do not presume upon my own strength, nor do I devote this work to the applause of mortals or to the fruit of a passing reward, in order to explain the perplexing mysteries of the Mosaic law.

I have withdrawn myself wholly into the beloved fellowship and companionable love of that law, in which nearly twenty-eight years have now passed. While I labor in pursuing its commandments, I find profound rest. And whenever I am frequently torn from its embraces by the overwhelming force of worldly business, I incur no small labor. Nor is this surprising, since in it are found the bread of life and understanding, and drink: bread by which the lost powers of a feeble mind are restored to their former vigor; drink by which the thirst of worldly desires is extinguished, and afterward the one who drinks from it is kindled by a most pleasing fervor to search eagerly into its secrets.

Now, at last, with the grace of God going before us, let us come to the words of the book, and, with the power of obedience supplying what is needed, let us diligently strive to investigate what mysteries they contain, insofar as the Lord grants us understanding.

## LETTER CIII. ANSELM TO LANFRANC

[Note: From the Vatican manuscript, folio 100, and from the manuscript of the monastery of Sées.]

He sends him his work, entitled *Monologion*, for correction or approval.

To the reverend and beloved lord, father, and teacher, LANFRANC, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of the English, greatly to be cherished by the mother Catholic Church on account of his deserts in faith and usefulness, brother ANSELM of Bec, a sinner in life and a monk in habit.

Since everything ought to be done with counsel, though not with every counsel, as it is written, “Do everything with counsel” (Ecclus. 32:24), and “Let your counselor be one among a thousand” (Ecclus. 6:6), I have chosen one whom you know—not from among a thousand, but from among all mortals—as the person whom above all others I would have as my counselor in doubts, teacher in ignorance [variant: “in what you do not know”], corrector in excesses, and approver of right actions. Although I cannot use him according to my desire, I have nevertheless resolved to use him as much as I can.

For although there are very many people besides your prudence from whose expertise an unlearned man such as I could benefit greatly [variant: “from whose presence”], and whose judgment my own ignorance compels me to submit to, I know none of them to whose teaching or judgment I would submit with such confidence and willingness as to yours, and none who would offer himself to me with such fatherly affection when circumstances require, or rejoice with me when the matter demands it.

Therefore, since whatever proceeds from your fatherly heart toward me is refined by wisdom, strengthened by authority, and seasoned with affection, whenever I draw anything from it, it delights me by its sweetness and satisfies me by its security. But since I am speaking to one who already knows these things, I shall pass over them and explain why I have remembered them.

Certain brothers, your servants and my fellow servants, repeatedly and insistently begged me and finally compelled me to agree to write something for them, as you will be able to see in the preface to that same work. Concerning this little work, something occurred beyond expectation: not only those at whose urging it was published, but also many others, now wish not merely to read it but even to copy it.

Thus, doubting whether I ought to refuse it to those who desire it or grant it, lest they hate me as they thought me envious or laugh at me when they recognized me as foolish, I turn to my one counselor and send the writing itself to your judgment for examination, so that by your authority it may either be kept from view as inept or, once corrected, be offered to those who desire it.

## LETTER CIV. ANSELM TO BERNARD AND HIS MONKS

ANSELM, archbishop by the grace of God, to the prior BERNARD and the other brothers living in the monastery of Saint Alban, greetings and blessing.

The brothers sent to me from your community reported that a certain doubt had arisen among you, together with some disagreement, because in the writings of the Catholic Fathers you sometimes find that God and man in Christ come together in one substance, and at other times that two substances—the divine and the human—are one person in Christ. For it seems contradictory both that there is one human and divine substance and that there are one person and two substances in the same person. But if it is properly understood how they say that several natures in Christ are one substance, or several substances one person, it will be recognized that there is no contradiction.

We believe and confess that there is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When, therefore, we say “God,” we say and understand only one. But when we say “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” we speak of and believe in several. Concerning God we have authoritative testimony, because we ought to say that God is one, singularly, and not several, as it is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4).

But concerning those three—namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we do not find in a prophet, apostle, or evangelist that they name them plurally by a single name, in order to signify the plurality that we understand in them. For nowhere do they say that they are three persons, or three substances, or three almighty beings, or anything of this kind.

Because of this necessity, when the Catholic Fathers spoke of those three, they chose terms by which they could name the three plurally. The Greeks chose the word “substance,” while the Latins chose the word “person,” but in such a way that what we understand there by “person,” they themselves understand by “substance,” and nothing else.

Thus, just as we say that in God there is one substance and three persons, so they say that there is one person and three substances, understanding and believing nothing different from us. Since, as I have said, they did not have names by which they could properly signify those three, so that the Greeks might say “three substances” and we “three persons,” they assigned, in speaking of God, to two terms the signification of the plurality they understood in those three but could not express by its proper name.

Therefore, just as we say that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another—and, in the sense that the Son of God is another from the Father, he is not another from the Son of the Virgin, but is the very same person, a person distinct from the Father and not distinct from the Son of the Virgin, but the same person—so the Greeks say that the Word, that is, the Son of God, is one substance distinct from the Father, but not another substance distinct from the assumed man.

When, therefore, we find in the writings of the Catholic Fathers that there are several natures but one substance in Christ, and when we find that there are several substances but one person, we do not take the word “substance” in the same sense. When we say “one substance,” we understand by it the very thing that is meant by the word “person.” But when we say that there are several substances in him and one person, by the word “substance” we signify what is meant by the word “nature.”

Accordingly, in view of this consideration, by which the faith of the Greeks and Latins is one, they sometimes call the person “substance,” although the Latins rarely do so. That the Greeks say of the Lord “one person, three substances” is attested by blessed Augustine in his book *On the Trinity*.

This, brothers, in response to your request, I think is a sufficient answer to the question being discussed among you, although more could be said about the Trinity and plurality: how the Word is one with the Father but not one person, and how he is one with the assumed man but not one substance. Farewell.

## LETTER CV. ANSELM TO ABBESS F. AND HER COMMUNITY

ANSELM, called archbishop by God’s providence, to the reverend lady and mother, Abbess F., and to the holy community entrusted to her, sends the wish that they may always advance in holiness and reach blessedness [variant: “always reach blessedness”].

Although your holy zeal has no need of my admonition, both [variant: “nevertheless”] the love I bear toward you and my office compel me to write to you by way of exhortation [variant: “something”]. Consider continually, my most beloved daughters and sisters, that you have set out and have already begun to ascend toward heaven, so that you may reign there and, in reigning, rejoice with your Lord and friend Jesus Christ, who awaits you there and, by awaiting you, constantly invites you.

For as long as a person lives, he either ascends to heaven by living well or descends into hell by living badly. If, therefore, you have set out to reach that place and wish to arrive there, you must advance toward it by holy actions [variant: “accusations”], as though by certain steps.

Examine carefully, then, the course of your life, so that [variant omits “so that”] not only in your works but also in your words, and not only in these but in all your thoughts, you may avoid finding that, although in all things you ought always to be striving upward [variant: “ascending”], something else is present that leads more toward descent. If you wish to guard this properly, it is useful always to see [variant omits “see”] and consider [variant: “that”] what is most truly written: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. 19:1). Whoever gradually falls does not advance but declines; and whoever declines does not ascend but descends.

Take care of this, therefore, with diligence: let nothing be so small that you are willing to neglect it within the order in which God has placed you. Thus, by holy steps, you will ascend to heaven—which, God assisting, may indeed come to pass. For this I ask that you pray [text: “through me”; variant: “for me”], and pray all the more attentively because you know that I trust in your affection, since I have never known myself to need prayers more than I do now.

## LETTER CVI. TO GISLEBERT

### On the Sacrament of the Altar

[Note: From the manuscript of the monastery of Chisleman.]

To Lord G. [Gislebert], once my dearest son, now, by God’s favor, venerable Father, brother A. [Anselm].

[Note: This letter does not belong to Saint Anselm. What misled the editor was that the author’s name is designated only by an A. From this he conjectured that it meant Anselm, and likewise conjectured that G signified Gilbert, as he marked in the margin, evidently implying that the person in question was Gilbert Crispin, abbot of Westminster, who had been a monk at Bec under Saint Anselm. The second conjecture would be quite natural if the first were true. But both are false, and this letter must be restored to Saint Anastasius, monk and hermit, who is its true author. (*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 439.)]

You commanded, venerable one, concerning the body and blood of the Lord, etc. It is extant under the name of Anastasius the hermit, reprinted in *Patrologia*, volume CXLIX, column 433.

## LETTER CVII. (G)*

Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*

[Note: The title borne by this letter would lead one to judge that it is not different from the work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, announced under Saint Anselm’s name in various manuscripts in the libraries of England, and which Dom Mabillon states that he saw, though in an imperfect form, in the library of the Friars Minor of Santa Croce in Florence. The editor took it from a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, in which it bears the same title and the name of Saint Anselm, described as archbishop of Canterbury, which removes all ambiguity.

In it the saint touches upon three or four points concerning the Eucharist. First, he establishes the correspondence between its institution in bread and wine and the needs of corrupt humanity, corrupted in soul and body since the Fall. He then shows that each species, taken separately, contains the whole of Jesus Christ, and explains why water is mixed with the wine before consecration, and why the species remain even though the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Jesus Christ. Finally, he copies a passage selected from Saint Augustine to prove that the wicked as well as the good receive the body of Jesus Christ, although they derive a very different benefit from it, and that wicked priests consecrate like the others because it is Jesus Christ himself who consecrates through their ministry. (*Literary History*, cited above.)]

Note that since the whole of human nature was corrupted in soul and body, it was necessary that God, who was coming to liberate both, unite himself to both, so that the soul might fittingly be redeemed through Christ’s soul, and the body through Christ’s body. Therefore, also, we place bread and wine upon the altar to represent both, so that through the bread, which has become the body and is worthily received by us, we may believe that our body will eventually be conformed to Christ’s body in immortality and impassibility; and likewise, through the wine changed into blood and received by us, we may believe that our souls will be conformed to Christ’s soul—in some manner already in the present, insofar as we abstain from sins as far as we can, and especially at the separation of soul and body, when our souls will be established in the blessedness in which Christ’s soul itself exists.

And since Christ’s soul had to be represented by something corporeal, nothing among all bodily things was found by which it could be represented more closely than by blood, which is the seat of the soul. Nevertheless, it must not be understood that, in receiving the blood, we receive the soul alone and not also the body, or that, in receiving the body, we receive the body alone and not also the soul. Rather, in receiving the blood we receive the whole Christ, God and human being; and in receiving the body we likewise receive the whole Christ.

Although we receive the body and the blood separately, we do not receive Christ twice, but once: immortal and impassible. This custom of receiving them separately became established in the Church because Christ, at the supper with his disciples, gave them separately, so that by this they might understand that they ought to be conformed to Christ’s soul and body.

Water is added to the wine in the sacrament so that the water which flowed from Christ’s side together with the blood might be represented. This water signifies baptism, in which the people are renewed through the pouring out of blood.

But since Christ’s body is inviolable and incorruptible, how can it be that it is worn down by teeth and even gnawed by mice? According to the definitions of the holy Fathers, it must be understood that the bread placed upon the altar is changed into Christ’s body through those solemn words, and that the substance of the bread and wine does not remain. Nevertheless, the appearance remains—that is, the form, color, and taste. According to the remaining appearance, certain things happen there which could in no way happen according to what it is: namely, that it is worn down, confined to one place, gnawed by mice, and swallowed into the stomach.

The reason why what is not there appears, while what is there is concealed, is that if what is there were seen, the human mind would recoil. According to the appearance, however, it can be received equally by a believer and an unbeliever. Believers nevertheless receive it in another, unique manner: because, being conformed to Christ through innocence and made like God through the reception of his body and blood, their virtues are increased in the present, free choice is strengthened, and in the future they will be conformed to him, especially when they put on immortality and impassibility as he himself did. The Lord’s body is received many times in order to receive this conformity.

Unbelievers altogether lack this manner of receiving. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that the wicked themselves receive the true substance of Christ’s body. Some shrink from this because of their uncleanness and the dignity of Christ’s body. But that reality is so worthy in itself that it is neither made worthier or cleaner by a worthy place, nor does it draw any uncleanness from an unclean vessel, as Augustine testifies in Book Four of *On Baptism*:

Concerning the Lord’s body received unworthily: just as Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel of bread, provided a place in himself for the devil—not by receiving something evil, but by receiving it evilly—so anyone who receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make the sacrament evil because he himself, receiving it, is evil; nor does he receive nothing because he does not receive salvation. For the Lord’s body and blood were nonetheless present in those of whom the Apostle said: “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

We must not ask what happens to the body, for God accomplishes it as he knows. Nor should anyone doubt how the bread is changed into Christ’s true body, so that the substance of the bread does not remain, when we see many other miracles no less remarkable: that a human being was substantially changed into stone, as Lot’s wife was, or even that, through a small human craft, hay was changed into glass. Again, if human beings, by the artifice of their own transformation, can conceal something so that it appears other than what it is, much more can God bring this about, so that, although his body is bread, this offering of the body may appear.

As Augustine testifies, this offering is changed daily, although Christ suffered once, because we sin daily, and mortal weakness cannot live without those sins. Therefore, because we fall daily, Christ is mystically offered for us daily.

Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of Christ’s body, the wicked receive nothing less, nor does a good priest confer anything greater, because it is effected not through the merit of the one who consecrates, but through the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it depended upon the priest’s merit, it would in no way belong to Christ. But now, just as he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself is the one who, through the Holy Spirit, causes this bread to be changed into his flesh and the wine to be transferred into his blood.

## LETTER CVIII. OF GISELBERT, ABBOT, TO ANSELM

To the reverend Father and lord Anselm, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, his servant and son, Brother Giselbert, administrator and servant of the monastery of Westminster: prosperity and long life in this life, and blessed eternity in the life to come.

To your Paternity, etc. This serves as a kind of prologue to the *Dialogue against the Jews* of Giselbert, abbot of Westminster. See below, under Giselbert, for the year 1117.

The following letters are reproduced here from the appendices to the edition of the year 1721.

## LETTER CIX. ANSELM TO RICHARD, A MONK

He exhorts Richard, a monk of Bec, to place obedience before indiscriminate mortifications of his body.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop, to his dearest brother and son Richard, monk of Bec: greeting and God’s blessing.

Since you know that I love you greatly, you ought not so often to disregard the advice and command I have given you, and by disregarding me and the abbot to whom I entrusted you, to grieve us. So often I have warned, advised, and commanded you to moderate your immoderate abstinences and bodily mortifications according to the direction of the aforesaid abbot; so often you have promised that in this matter you would obey my will and his completely; and yet you obstinately cling to your own will.

I fear that, while you wish to possess a reward—or rather the reputation or empty glory within your heart—of one who fasts, you may instead incur the punishment of disobedience. Certainly, just as simple obedience merits a greater crown than abstinence from foods beyond the common practice, so the one who despises obedience is punished more severely than the one who abandons such abstinence. Without this kind of abstinence, obedience can save a person; but without obedience, such abstinence can do nothing except condemn.

Therefore, submit—submit—and entrust your whole self to the disposition of your superior: if you wish to obey me, if you wish to please me, if you wish to preserve my love for you, if you wish to prove your love for me, if you do not henceforth wish to grieve me, and to burden the abbot under whom you live and the brothers among whom you live through your indiscretion.

For it is entirely evident that your body and your nature cannot tolerate what your indiscretion presumes. May the almighty Lord lead you in his way and in his truth. Amen.

## LETTER CX. ANSELM TO ROBERT, SEYT, AND EDIT

He exhorts them to observe even the smallest matters, and to keep in mind that angels are always standing beside them, imitating their way of life.

Anselm, archbishop, to Robert, Seyt, and Edit, his dearest sons: greeting and God’s blessing, insofar as he is able.

Would that you knew with what joy my beloved son Willelmus has filled my heart by reporting to me your mutual holy love, your religious way of life, your heavenly purpose, and your spiritual intention. Although I feel myself growing lukewarm in spiritual fervor under the pressure of many cares and tribulations, great joy is nevertheless born in my heart when I hear that others are fervent in the love of God.

Since it belongs to the office entrusted to me and to the care committed to me—and since, as I understand, you desire it—I admonish and entreat you with all the feeling I can muster to persevere, and indeed to bring to completion, that which not you but God has begun in you. You will certainly be able to accomplish this, with God’s help, if you refuse to neglect even the smallest matters. For one who is diligent in small things does not easily admit negligence in greater ones.

Nor does our enemy openly display greater sins to those whom he sees to be committed to a holy purpose. Rather, in small matters—as though they were things to be disregarded—he secretly strives to deceive them. For he knows that “whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. 19:1). Therefore, dearest ones, if you ever feel yourselves deviating, even slightly or only once, from your good custom, judge that you have incurred a serious fall, and lament it.

Let your conversations always be pure and about God. Take the example of life from the angels in heaven, except for those things which the frailty of human nature requires for its support. So that your way of life may always be in heaven (Phil. 3:20), consider and imitate the angelic way of life in all things. Let this contemplation be your teacher; let this consideration be your rule. Pursue the things that agree with angelic life; detest those that conflict with it.

Think of your angels—as the Lord says, “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10)—as always present to you and observing your deeds and thoughts. Therefore take care always to live as though you were looking upon them visibly. May almighty God never permit you to fall away from the state you have attained, but always cause you to advance toward better things. I pray; pray for me.

## LETTER CXI. ANSELM TO HUGH

He exhorts Hugh, a monk whom he had heard loved him greatly, neither to conceal nor defend his faults, to keep his heart always open to his abbot, and to subordinate his own judgments to obedience.

Anselm, archbishop, to his dearest brother and son Hugh: greeting and God’s blessing.

From the report of the lord abbot I have learned that you have such great love for me that you rejoice greatly when you hear of my prosperity, and are deeply saddened when you learn of adversity; that your heart is stirred against those from whom you perceive any adversity to have come upon me; and that you do not cease to pray for me as far as you are able.

Since, then, your love for me is so great, if I do not love you, I judge myself unjust. And because true love always desires the progress of the one whom it loves, I therefore exhort and admonish you to strive always to extend your mind toward better things.

If you ask how you can do this, love the monastic commitment above all else. You will then be able to keep it well if you never wish either to conceal or to defend your fault. Just as foxes have dens where they secretly give birth to and raise their cubs, and birds have open nests in which they brood over their young, so the devils make dens and multiply sins in the heart of one who conceals them; and they openly build nests in which they likewise gather sins in the heart of one who defends them.

Consider, therefore, whether you wish to be a den or nest of the devil, and never conceal or defend your fault. Let your heart always be open to your abbot; wherever you are, consider not only your body but also your thoughts to be in his sight. Do and think only what you would not be ashamed to do and think in his presence.

If you do this, the devil will flee the dwelling of your breast just as a thief avoids the house of one who is unwilling either to conceal or defend him. For a thief brings his thefts into the house of the one from whom he trusts he can be hidden or defended.

If you make what I say your practice, then the Holy Spirit will establish his dwelling in you. He will neither be rebuked nor expelled by an iniquity that comes upon you; rather, through him, your good practice will repel iniquity from itself. This will be transformed for you into such great delight that you will be able to consider nothing sweeter or more pleasing. Yet you will not be able to understand what I am saying unless you are willing to experience it through actual practice.

The lord abbot reported many good things to me about your youth, but he added one thing that could not please me: you judge that what your own judgment chooses is better than what obedience requires. Since you have the skill of writing, something else seems greater to you than writing through obedience. Be certain, therefore, that one prayer of an obedient person is better than ten thousand prayers of one who despises obedience.

Therefore I admonish you, as my dearest son and beloved, to place obedience before all your actions, to keep what I have said above in perpetual memory, and to strive earnestly to fulfill it in practice. May almighty God always guide you in all things through the blessing of his grace and guard you from every evil. Amen.

## LETTER CXII. ANSELM TO WILLERMUS

He advises his friend Willermus always to be present to God, and to preserve his love for Anselm by striving with every effort to avoid offending God.

Anselm, archbishop, to his beloved son Willermus: greeting, and God’s blessing and his own.

I have experienced that you love me with great and intimate affection, and therefore I cannot fail to return your love. You love me as a father in God, to whom you have entrusted your whole self without pretense; and I love you as a son, whom I have received with sincere affection. You received from God the capacity to love me, and I have from God the capacity to love you in this way.

Since, then, our mutual love is from God, it cannot and ought not to be destroyed unless some offense against God brings this about. Therefore, just as you wish to preserve my love, so strive with every effort to avoid offending God.

Love, that you may love me; but I desire still more that you love yourself. Love yourself, and, as far as love is concerned, regard me as yourself. Remember my admonition, and you will always belong to the love of God, and beneath that, to mine. I cannot always be present to you; may God, who is present everywhere, protect you. I admonish you always to be present to him.

## LETTER CXIII. ANSELM TO HERBERT, BISHOP OF THIOFORD

He exhorts Herbert, bishop of Thioford, to prohibit from sacred functions those priests who disobeyed the council and refused to dismiss women, and to substitute other clerics or monks for them in ecclesiastical duties.

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to Herbert, bishop of Thioford: greeting.

Concerning the priests about whom your prudence asks my advice, I reply that nothing should be relaxed concerning what has been established in the council. Since they prefer to relinquish whatever belongs to the office of a priest rather than dismiss the women, if any chaste men are found, let them serve in their place. But if none, or very few, of such men are found, order the monks, for the time being, to say Mass for the people wherever they are, and to make the Lord’s body, which the clerics are to carry to the sick.

At your command, let those clerics in turn hear confessions, pronounce absolution, and bury the bodies of the dead. You may also assign these duties to monks of more advanced age, until this hardness of the priests is softened by God’s visitation. It will not last long, with God’s favor, if we persevere in what we have begun.

Concerning baptism, you know that whoever baptizes, Christ baptizes. In God’s name and in the name of all of us who established this in the council, earnestly command all laypeople, great and small, that, if they profess themselves Christians, they assist you in expelling from the churches and their property the priests who disobey the council, and in appointing worthy men in their place.

And if those who have been expelled rise against those who wish to serve the churches chastely, or in any other way break out into some presumptuous act of pride, let all Christians oppose them. Let them exclude them, together with their women, not only from their fellowship but also from the lands they hold from them, until they repent.

[Note: Held at London in the year 1102, with Saint Anselm presiding.]

## LETTER CXIV. ANSELM TO HIS NEPHEW

Anselm commends good morals, diligence, and the continual use of the Latin language to his nephew. Concerning his sister, the nephew’s mother, he reports that she was admitted by the nuns at Marcigny, but that when he asked for her back, she was refused to him.

Anselm, archbishop, to his beloved nephew Anselm: greeting and blessing.

I too bear the concern and sadness that you have concerning your mother. Therefore I asked the lord abbot of Cluny to receive her into the monastery of the servants of God at Marcigny. He readily agreed to this through his favor, because of our affection, and the servants of God themselves were willing.

Accordingly, through a letter and through our messenger, I asked the abbot of Cluny and his monks, as humbly and earnestly as I could, to grant me our sister for this purpose. But they were entirely unwilling to give their consent. Rather, they were angered against me and considered that I had inflicted great dishonor upon them.

I shall not yet cease striving to find some way by which I may complete what I have begun. But if I cannot, you and I ought not therefore to take upon ourselves a fruitless and inconsolable sadness. We must patiently entrust ourselves and her to God’s disposition.

For I hope in God that he will not allow her to be tested by whatever hardships in such a way that she cannot endure them. Rather, through the many tribulations she has suffered from childhood and will suffer to the end, if God has so ordained, he will lead her and cause her to enter his rest. For my part, insofar as I can, I shall not cease to help her in every way for as long as I live.

As for you, I command and instruct you not to be idle in any way, but to determine each day to make progress in the purpose for which I left you in England. Study to learn the power of grammar; accustom yourself to dictating daily, especially in prose; and do not take great pleasure in difficult composition, but write plainly and rationally.

Always speak Latin unless necessity compels you otherwise. Above all, attend to good morals and dignity. Avoid loquacity; a person profits more by being silent, listening, and considering what he can learn from the words and life of others than by displaying his knowledge through excessive talk when no necessity compels him.

Greet your teacher courteously on our behalf. If God grants me the opportunity, I truly wish to be of benefit both to you and to the other brothers whom he teaches, as well as to him in his good morals. In the meantime, however, I have placed the matter before the lord prior and have earnestly asked him to treat him so well that you will not regret having joined yourselves to him. Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. ANSELM TO WALTER, CARDINAL

He asks Walter, cardinal bishop of Albano and papal legate in England, to seek help and support from the Roman pontiff to sustain the burden of his archbishopric.

To the lord Walter, cardinal bishop and legate of the Roman Church, Anselm, called metropolitan bishop of Canterbury, offers the devotion of faithful prayers together with service.

Because I trust in the love of your holiness, I ask you kindly to show our lord the pope, with reverence, our fidelity and affection, which I preserve in my heart for his eminence, as I have shown you; and to make known to him, with compassionate kindness, the distress of my mind under the burden of the archbishopric, as I confessed to you in my complaint.

Thus may his fatherly goodness, pitying the groans of his son and servant, deign to remember me sometime in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ and the blessed Apostle Peter; and, whenever I flee to him in my anxieties, may the bowels of his compassion not be closed to me.

I ask that you commend the small gift we have sent him according to our ability in such a way, through your kindness, that it may please him more through your recommendation than through its own value.

May your holiness be well, and may almighty God send you his good angel to accompany you and direct your journey well. I ask you: pray for me.

## LETTER CXVI. ANSELM TO DONNALD, DONATUS, AND THE OTHER BISHOPS

He asks the bishops of Ireland to intercede with God for him, pressed as he is by many hardships, while also admonishing each of them to fulfill the duties of his office and, if any dispute should arise among them, to refer the entire matter to him.

Anselm, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Canterbury, to his reverend fellow bishops Donnald, Donatus, and the others who, in the island of Ireland, hold pontifical dignity from God the Father and Jesus Christ, his only Son: greeting and the blessing of perpetual inheritance.

Recognizing the fragrance of your religion through many indications, I have decided above all to disclose to you the calamities I suffer, so that, the closer you stand to the Creator, the more familiarly you may be able to make known my troubles in his presence; and, by making them known, obtain his mercy for me through the groans of compassion.

After my predecessor of blessed memory, Archbishop Lanfranc, had died, when I had been abbot of the monastery of Bec in Normandy—for the aforesaid predecessor had gone before me from there to govern the Church over which, by God’s authority, I preside—I came to England by the hidden judgment of God for the interests of the churches.

When I arrived, both the king and the pontiff and the nobles of the kingdom dragged me to the episcopal chair—not by calling me, as is customary, but by violently seizing and compelling me—with clergy and people alike acclaiming the same thing, so that no one who might have disapproved of what was being done appeared to be present.

Finally, while I was still protesting that I did not wish or ought not to consent to this, saying that I had been taken away without the knowledge of those from whose power I had been striving to escape—namely, the duke of Normandy and the archbishop of Rouen—and from whose jurisdiction I was trying to flee, I was compelled by the command of those same men, the aforementioned duke and archbishop, to accept the burden of the office, obediently.

In this way I was raised to the episcopal rank, and I consented because I could not resist. Once invested with the episcopal insignia, I began diligently to consider what I owed to Christ and to his Church according to my position and office. I wished, through pastoral governance, to cut away vices, restrain presumptuous people, and restore everything disordered to its proper order.

For this reason, I suffer those whom I ought to have had as helpers in God’s cause to be terribly offended, and the cause of God, which ought to have grown through me, is wasting away in my presence. Therefore, reverend Fathers, speaking to you with groans, I confess that bitter tribulations have overtaken me: I remember having lost a fruitful peace, and I see that I have incurred an unfruitful danger.

For this has happened through the effect of my sins: those who had voluntarily subjected themselves to our authority now voluntarily withdraw from that authority, and I, who had been beloved by them, am hateful to almost everyone. Therefore, venerable brothers and children of your charity, I beseech you in the name of him who redeemed his enemies with his blood: pray that God may grant us all peace, convert our enemies to friendship, and cause us to live according to his will.

Furthermore, although your fraternity lives and thinks rightly, pastoral concern compels me to admonish you to act courageously and with greater vigilance in God’s teaching, restraining with canonical severity anything found in your provinces contrary to ecclesiastical doctrine, and arranging all things according to God’s will.

If at any time, whether in the consecration of bishops, in matters concerning ecclesiastical affairs, or for any other reason, something pertaining to holy religion should arise among you which you cannot settle canonically yourselves, we remind you, as a duty of charity, to bring it to our attention, so that you may receive counsel and consolation from us rather than be denounced as transgressors of God’s commands at his judgment.

Again, dearest ones, we ask you: pray for us. Raise us up from our tribulations by the hand of your prayer, striking the ears of God’s mercy with devout petitions. May the Lord, who commanded light to shine out of darkness (2 Cor. 4:6), pour the light of his wisdom into your minds, so that you may understand what he commands and, understanding it, fulfill it in practice.

## LETTER CXVII. ANSELM TO HUGH, ARCHDEACON

[Note: From manuscript 464 of the Royal Library.]

He indicates with how much honor and generosity he was received by everyone during his exile.

Anselm, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, although an exile, to his true and beloved friend Hugh, archdeacon: greeting and God’s blessing, and his own, if it has any worth.

Faithful love neither sleeps nor slumbers; no disturbance of the world and no misfortune exhausts it, and it always desires the presence of the one whom it loves. Since I am certain of your love, and, being absent, cannot communicate with you in person, I shall at least indicate through a letter, to some extent, how things stand with me.

By God’s gracious ordering, and through the prayers of God’s servants who, in many places far and wide, love me for God’s sake by his grace, ever since I left England—as God knows, and does not forget [variant: “or you do not forget”]—I have felt no lack of the temporal things necessary for me. Nor has the violence [variant: “ill will”] of anyone been able to harm me as much as God’s benevolence has wished to help me.

For through his goodness God grants me such great favor among many bishops, abbots, princes, and wealthy men of this world, as well as among people of lower rank—their number I do not presently know—from the Barensean Sea to the Bonojan Sea [variant: Bonian Sea]—that I fear offending many by staying away more than by visiting them.

Among these, the venerable archbishop of Lyon is presently delighted to show me his generosity abundantly and honorably, and he desires me to remain with him always, for as long as I am an exile from our Church. God brings this about not so much because of my merits as through the abundance of his goodness.

I cannot write to you with any certainty what will become of me or what I shall do, but I entrust myself entirely to the disposition of divine goodness. For the present, I cannot offer you better advice concerning me than that, where you now are, you should strive to serve God there, until God, under his grace, wishes otherwise to order you and your life.

Greet the lord archdeacon Guillelmus as our beloved friend. Greet our most beloved daughters, the abbesses with their servants who live with them, from Shaftesbury, Winchester, and Wintuna. I send them, insofar as I can, God’s blessing and ours, and ask you to request that they pray for me.

Know this: I hope in God, and this is my will [variant: “our will”], that just as I left England because of fear and love of God and for the honor of God and his Church, so I shall never enter it again except for that same reason and in accordance with it, insofar as I am able to understand it.

I ask that this poor man be better treated on your part for love of us, since he carries our message through many dangers and much labor. Farewell.

I, Brother Eadmerus, fellow exile of our lord and father the archbishop, greet you, giving thanks to God and to him because I have been deemed worthy to share this exile. I also ask that you greet on our behalf those whom the lord archbishop greets on his.

## LETTER CXVIII. ANSELM TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his reverend friend Lambert, bishop of Arras: greeting.

I ask your holiness, for love of the lord pope and of us, to arrange for this cleric of his to be escorted through your bishopric, as far as you are willing. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIX. ANSELM TO THE SAME

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to the venerable bishop of Arras and dearest friend Lambert: greeting and faithful prayers.

I give thanks to your reverend affection for the concern you show for me in wishing so earnestly to know about my health. I therefore tell you that, by God’s grace, I am physically well, but I suffer from continual weakness.

As for your request that I remember you in our prayers, know for certain that, although my prayers are poor, nevertheless—farewell, reverend Father and lord, together with all who love you truly, and pray for us.

## LETTER CXX. ANSELM TO HERNOSTUS

To the lord and dearest brother Hernostus, Brother Anselm offers as much bodily health as is expedient and as much health of soul as is sufficient.

I learned of the excessively aggravated distress of your illness, my beloved and equally beloved friend, first through the report of certain people and then through reading your letters. To say nothing of how much compassion I have taken into my soul, my conscience bears witness that I would gladly transfer the whole suffering itself into my body.

But since it is certain that God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6), the same love moves me in a wondrous way both toward compassion, because you are worn down by scourges, and toward rejoicing with you, because you are being educated for the inheritance.

We must consider, dearest one, how much consolation those pains carry with them which, while cleansing our sins outwardly through the external sufferings imposed upon us, transfer us into the lot of the children of God, to whom the joys of the heavenly kingdom are promised. Thus, while our outward person, which must daily decay, sighs under the weight of scourges, our inward person, which must be renewed from day to day, breathes again in exultation, relieved of the burden of sins.

This will certainly come to pass if the inward person, in the affliction of the outward person, does not recoil through impatience, but consents through thanksgiving to the hand that strikes. For we always please almighty God whenever we disagree in nothing with his arrangements; but we especially appease the merciful Lord if, while being beaten, we willingly agree with the one who beats us.

Since anger always expresses itself only against one who resists it, if the guilty person unites himself with the offended party through an agreement in judgment against himself, the movement of the angry one must subside, because he no longer finds an adversary whom he can strike.

Therefore, dearest one, since it is written that “we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (Acts 14:21), when we are scourged, let us maintain before God the saying of blessed Job, who, surrounded by excessive pains, said: “Let this be my consolation, that he who afflicts me with pains does not spare” (Job 6:10).

## LETTER CXXI. ANSELM TO ADELAIDE

To the venerable lady Adelaide, endowed with royal nobility but more nobly distinguished by the integrity of her character: Brother Anselm wishes that, adorned with the ornaments of virtue together with temporal nobility, you may deserve to be joined to the King of kings in eternal happiness.

The command concerning the flowers of the Psalms, which your sublimity, beloved by me in God, deigned to give, could not have been carried out sooner or better by our humility, devoted to you. Our obedience followed your command with greater devotion because the command itself proceeded from holy devotion.

I desire and pray that almighty God may preserve and nourish this devotion in us in such a way that he may refresh your mind on earth with his sweetest affection and in heaven with his blessed vision.

I ask that your wealthy nobility not despise the small and humble gift sent to you by our poor littleness. For although it is not encrusted with gold and gems, it is certainly made wholly through charitable fidelity and given with faithful charity.

After the flowers of the Psalms, seven prayers have been added. The first should be called not so much a prayer as a meditation: through it, the soul of the sinner should briefly examine itself; by examining itself, despise itself; by despising itself, humble itself; by humbling itself, be shaken by fear of the final judgment; and, once shaken, burst forth into groans and tears.

In the prayers of Saint Stephen and Saint Mary Magdalene there are certain passages which, if they are spoken from the depths of the heart when time permits, aim especially at kindling love. In all seven prayers I, the servant and friend of your soul, exhort you to deign to attend to the humility and the disposition of fear and love with which the sacrifice of prayer ought to be offered—even if you practice this better than I do.

Farewell, and farewell in God now and forever. May you have the little book sent to you as a pledge of our fidelity according to God and of our prayers, whatever they may be.

At the end of the letter I state what I desire to persuade you throughout the entire letter: hold in contempt, with an elevated mind, everything that must necessarily be lost, even while you possess it; and strive with a humble mind, as long as you do not possess it, toward that alone which can be possessed blessedly and eternally.

I wish to persuade you of this, and I pray that the Holy Spirit may persuade you of it. In him, farewell for the third time.

## LETTER CXXII. ANSELM TO LANFRANC

To the lord and Father, the archbishop Lanfranc, reverently loved by Catholics and affectionately revered, Brother Anselm, his because he is his.

Since one must either be silent or speak briefly when one knows, and since I do not wish to remain silent lest I fail to say what—and to whom—I gladly say, I shall briefly explain how our spirit is inwardly disposed toward the fidelity owed to your fatherly sublimity. Just as I daily desire that the affection of your love may continually increase in my heart, so no absence of ours from one another can cause it in any way to diminish. [Col. 0267A]

You commissioned me to write on the moral interpretation of Job, but the lord abbot William of Caen and the lord Hernostus, your faithful servants, found a copyist who, already possessing our book, has begun yours, as I suppose. I have labored and am laboring to obtain the books of the blessed Ambrose and Jerome, as you ordered. But I have not yet been able to obtain them. As soon as I can, I shall complete what I know you wish concerning this.

As for your Girard of Flanders, whom through your pious generosity and our intervention you redeemed from the world for God—so that, if I were not yours, I would confess myself your servant purchased by you—let your holiness know that on the day appointed by you he could not have been released from his creditors without serious loss. [Col. 0267B] Nevertheless, he came on the first Sunday of Lent, proclaiming your magnificent mercy toward him and explaining how your graciousness had supported, and had always indicated that it wished to support, not so much our petition as our slight expression of desire in his case. He said that he wished, and insofar as he had the ability, to repay what he owed in such a way that he would have something to offer along with himself, but that because of certain impediments he had not been able to do so at the appointed time as he ought.

He therefore returned, promising that, God willing, he would come to Bec at Easter and remain there—if not in the manner he wished, then at least in the manner he could. If, then, he has sinned because he has not fully carried out the promise made to you, since he does not seem to have committed this through malice, I confidently ask, as is my custom, of your kindness, [Col. 0267C] that, in place of a father, you permit your son to absolve him from this offense when he begins to live with us. In this matter I shall presume this concession to be certain, unless I read some prohibition.

## LETTER CXXIII. ANSELM TO HENRY

To the lord and brother Henry, brother Anselm sends greetings.

When, on your journey to Rome, you passed near us, we were surprised and saddened that you did not come through us—until we heard that this had been forbidden you on your outward journey but permitted on your return. The lord abbot, I, and your other brothers and friends therefore awaited your arrival, rejoicing in a false hope, until we learned that you had passed through into English territory, and then grieved in genuine despair. [Col. 0267D]

Although, if I know your affection well, I shall not believe that this happened without some reasonable cause, nevertheless, lest—God forbid—any suspicion remain concerning you, either of contempt or of slight love toward the monastery and your brothers, instruct me what I should answer others as to why your affection passed us by without visiting us either on the outward or on the return journey. For just as I desire you to do nothing that is not expedient for you, so I do not wish anyone to think of you anything except what becomes you.

Let your friend also know whether you have accomplished anything concerning the matter about which, both through the words of others and through your letters, you made your mind very anxious, so that you might visit your parents; then I shall know whether I ought to sympathize with you or rejoice with you.

## LETTER CXXIV. ANSELM TO BISHOP G.

To the reverend lord and father, Bishop G., brother Anselm, called abbot of Bec, sends temporal prosperity and eternal happiness.

We give thanks to your holiness, who, by asking for the prayers of us and our brothers, have graciously granted them to us through our beloved brother, the lord Riculfus, and have promised the assistance of your goodwill wherever opportunity presents itself. Since we possess so little with which we can worthily repay this, we must all the more devote whatever we can to the service of your highness, both in action and in intention, and pray to God—on whose account you make these promises to us—that he may repay you according to his abundant generosity what, on account of our smallness, we are unable to repay. [Col. 0268B]

Concerning your son and our brother, the lord Ricoardus: although it would be more honorable for us, and we would prefer, to serve before asking anything, nevertheless, since circumstances require it, we ask your kindness to grant him, for love of us, whatever he may request concerning himself or his prebend, provided that it does not compromise your honor.

## LETTER CXXV. ANSELM TO ABBOT MAINERIUS

To the beloved and reverend father, Abbot Mainerius, brother Anselm sends greetings.

Know that I shall not go to the place about which I had again sent you word before the octave of the Epiphany of the Lord. After that I do not know when I shall go, or whether I shall go at all. Meanwhile, if it pleased you, when it was convenient for you, that the lord Serlo should come to us and remain for as long as you ordered, it would please me, and I think it would not displease him. [Col. 0268C]

I ask your holiness that, if it is not burdensome to you, you make it known through yourself to our lords and friends at the monastery of Sées what I am sending concerning our journey. For I know that, like you, they are earnestly praying for me and for the success of that journey. Nor should your charity regret having prayed for our journey, because I am not going now. For God is able to preserve your prayers for me until an appropriate day. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVI. ANSELM TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

To his dearest lord Henry, by the grace of God king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, sends faithful service and faithful prayers. [Col. 0268D]

I have heard that you are ordering William, the elected bishop of Winchester, to leave the bishopric and England because he did not accept the consecration that the archbishop of York and the other bishops wished to perform for him. Therefore I beg and advise you—as a faithful archbishop to his lord and king—not to follow the counsel of those who advise you to do this, because in my judgment I do not understand how it serves your honor.

For it is sufficiently well known that his consecration belongs to me, and no one else ought to perform it except through me. If necessary, I am prepared to demonstrate this reasonably, as such a matter ought to be demonstrated. Therefore, if you expel him from your land so that I cannot canonically perform that same consecration, it seems to me that you are dispossessing me of my office without judgment. [Col. 0269A] I therefore beg you to permit him to remain peacefully in the bishopric, at least until the end of our appointed period, so that meanwhile I may be permitted to perform for him the consecration that I owe.

## LETTER CXXVII. ANSELM TO ATSER, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

[Note: Year 1094. From an old manuscript of the Colbert Library. Col. 0269D]

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, sends greetings and true friendship in Christ to the reverend Atser, archbishop of Lund, worthy of the Church’s praise.

What you asked me concerning Lord Albricus, cardinal of the Roman Church, I gladly did, both because of the honor of the Roman Church and because of my love for you; for your sake I gladly wish to do whatever I understand would please your holiness. [Col. 0269B]

We give thanks to God, who in the kingdom of the Danes has raised your religious character [alternative reading: your religiosity] to the archiepiscopate. For we trust that, with the grace of God cooperating, you will correct what must be corrected, build what must be built, and nourish what must be nourished. Indeed, we have heard many good things about you from the aforesaid cardinal. Hence we have this confidence, and we pray that God, who has begun this work in you, may always bring your will to a good result.

I ask your holiness to cleanse that kingdom by your holy zeal of apostates, so that no foreigner may there receive any ecclesiastical order; for those who are rejected by their own bishops go there and are execrably ordained into various orders. Farewell [Col. 0269C] and pray for me.

## LETTER CXXVIII. ANSELM TO EULALIA AND HER NUNS

[Note: From a manuscript of the Church of Tours and of the monastery of Pruliac. Col. 0269D]

Having sent the letters she had desired from him, he urges her to demonstrate sincere affection toward him by fervor in the love of God and in other pious works.

Anselm, archbishop, sends greetings and God’s blessing, and his own insofar as he is able, to his sisters most beloved in Christ, the lady abbess Eulalia and all her daughters.

Through a servant of the king, who brought me the king’s seal, your affection requested, as he himself said, that I greet you by letter. I preferred to do this through my messenger, whom I knew I was about to send to England. [Col. 0269D]

I know that the abundance of your religious affection causes you to wish to see my letters gladly, so that, when you cannot have my presence, which you desire with religious affection, according to your wish, you may at least receive something of it through my letter—perhaps so that you might stir up in me the remembrance of you, lest it should ever fall asleep [alternative reading: awaken it]. [Col. 0270A]

Finally, just as I know that your good will and sincere affection toward me do not grow cold, so know that mine toward you does not grow lukewarm.

Above all, I wish you to remember us and love me, as you do, so that, just as you know my desire, you may all strive unceasingly to burn with love of God; and you who are subject to your mother, take care to show obedience not merely for appearance’s sake, but from your inmost heart.

I know that you endure adversities and tribulations from various quarters, but then you must devote yourselves all the more to the true observance of your order and life, because by living well you obtain God’s consolation more abundantly than if, on account of some impediments alone, you cease in any degree from the fervor of your purpose.

Whatever solitude you are in, be certain, and do not doubt in any way, that each one of you has her own angel, who sees and records all her thoughts and actions and reports them in turn to God. Therefore I admonish you, dearest daughters, that in secret and in public each one of you guard the movements of her heart and body as though she saw that very guardian angel present before her bodily eyes. [Col. 0270B]

May almighty God protect you with his blessing and lead you to the sight of his glory. Amen.

Concerning our return, I know that you wish to learn something, but at present I can write nothing certain to you. Pray that I may act according to the good pleasure of God’s will.

## LETTER CXXIX. ANSELM TO THE SAME WOMEN

[Note: From a manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Pruliac. Col. 0270D]

He urges them toward perfection and not to despise what is least.

Anselm, called archbishop by God’s appointment, sends to the reverend lady and mother, Abbess Eulalia, and to the holy congregation entrusted to her, wishes for continual progress in holiness and attainment of blessedness. [Col. 0270C]

Although your holy zeal has no need of my admonition, the love I have for you and my office nevertheless compel me to write something to you by way of exhortation. Consider continually, my most beloved daughters and sisters, that you have resolved to ascend into heaven, so that there you may reign and rejoice in the kingdom with your Lord and friend Jesus Christ, who awaits you there and by awaiting you continually invites you. For as long as a person lives, he either ascends into heaven by living well or descends into hell by living badly.

If, then, you wish to reach what you have resolved upon, you must advance there by holy actions, as though by certain steps. Carefully examine the course of your life—not only in deeds but also in words, and not only in these but even in your smallest thoughts—lest, although you must always direct your course toward this in all things, something should be found there that is rather a descent. [Col. 0270D]

If you wish to guard this well, it is useful always to consider what is written most truly: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). For whoever gradually falls does not advance but declines; and whoever declines does not ascend but descends.

Take care, therefore, with vigilance, that nothing be so small that you violate the order in which you are able to live; and thus you will ascend by holy steps into heaven—which, may God assist, may indeed happen. I ask you to pray for me, and to do so all the more attentively because you know that I rely upon your affection, since I have never known myself to need prayers more than I do now. [Col. 0271A] For I am in such a bad situation in the archbishopric that, if I may say so without guilt, I would rather depart from this life than live in this way. [Col. 0272A]

# APPENDIX OF SPURIOUS WORKS

## DIALOGUE OF THE BLESSED MARY AND ANSELM ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0271A]

[Note: Collated with MS Thuano 519, MS *The Lament of the Blessed Virgin Mary to Anselm concerning the Passion of the Lord*. Col. 0271C]

The holy Anselm had for a long time implored the glorious Virgin with fasts, tears, and prayers to reveal to him how her son had suffered. At last the blessed Virgin appeared to him and said:

“My beloved Son suffered such things and so many things that no one can describe them without shedding tears.” [Col. 0271B]

[Note: The blessed Bishop Anselm had for a long time entreated the glorious Virgin with fasts, tears, and prayers to deign to reveal more fully to him the passion of her beloved Son. At last the blessed Virgin appeared to him and said: “My most beloved Son suffered such and so great things that no faithful person can express them without shedding tears.” Another manuscript reads: “The holy Anselm asked the holy Virgin Mary for a long time, with tears, prayers, and fasts, to reveal to him how her Son had suffered. At last the blessed Virgin appeared to him and said: ‘My beloved Son suffered such and so great things that no one can describe them without shedding tears.’” Col. 0271C]

“Nevertheless, because I have been glorified, I cannot weep. Therefore I shall explain to you in order the passion of my Son.” [Col. 0271C]

[Note: Another manuscript reads: “Nevertheless, because I have been glorified, I can no longer weep; and at your prayers, and for the salvation of many, I shall explain to you in order the passion of my Son.” Another reads: “Nevertheless, because I have been glorified, I cannot weep; therefore I shall explain in order the passion of my Son.”]

The blessed Anselm therefore asked about each detail, and blessed Mary answered each question.

[Note: The Blessed Virgin answered each question. Another manuscript reads: “Blessed Mary answered each question.” Col. 0271C]

### CHAPTER I. Christ’s Betrayal and His Prayer in the Garden

[Note: The manuscript has no division into chapters and no titles. Col. 0271C]

**ANSELM.** Tell me, dearest lady, what was the beginning of your Son’s passion?

**MARY.** When my Son rose from the supper held with his disciples, Judas Iscariot went to the chief priests and, betraying my Son, sold him for thirty denarii. [Col. 0271C]

[Note: Another version introduces this answer: “Anselm therefore first asked and said: ‘Dearest Lady, tell me how your Son’s passion began.’ Mary replied: ‘When, etc.’” A manuscript reads: “He first asked and said: ‘Dearest Lady, tell me how the passion of your Son began.’ Mary replied: ‘When, etc.’”]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Betraying him ... for silver”; the printed text reads: “he betrayed him ... for denarii.”]

**A.** What kind of denarii were they?

**M.** Ismaelite denarii, with which Joseph too had been sold four thousand years earlier; and by hereditary succession they had come down to those Jews who bought my Son. Each denarius was worth ten ordinary coins. [Col. 0272B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Maria replied: Ismaelite.” It also reads: “Joseph too,” rather than “Joseph also.” It reads: “After many years, and by hereditary succession,” rather than “four thousand years, by hereditary succession.” It reads: “They came down,” rather than “they had come down.” It reads: “Each denarius was worth thirty ordinary coins,” rather than “ten ordinary coins.” Col. 0271C]

Judas, however, was so greedy that, when he saw the denarii, he sold Christ for them. Although Christ had often foretold this to him, Judas had not been corrected by it.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “He was so greedy ... he betrayed him,” rather than “he was so greedy ... he sold him.” It also reads: “But he had not corrected himself by this,” rather than “that Judas had not been corrected by this.”]

**A.** Were you then with your Son and his disciples?

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Were you then with your Son and his disciples?” Another reads: “Were you then in council with the disciples?” Col. 0271C]

**M.** No. But know that, when my Son had eaten the supper, washed the disciples’ feet, given his body and blood to the disciples, and preached sweetly, while Judas had gone to the chief priests, my Son went from Mount Zion with his disciples through the gate to the pool of Siloam, where there was a garden. He entered it and, while the disciples slept, went up to the foot of the Mount of Olives, about a stone’s throw from the disciples, and prayed to the Father as follows:

“Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your mercies, look upon me. Do not turn your face away from me, for I am troubled; hasten to hear me. Attend to my soul and deliver it; because of my enemies, rescue me” (Psalm 68:17, 19). [Col. 0272C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “He prayed to the Father, saying: ‘Hear me, Lord ...’” It also reads “from me” rather than “from your servant.” It omits “his” after “disciples”; reads “and when he had washed the disciples’ feet” rather than “and washed the disciples’ feet”; reads “had given his body and his blood to the disciples” rather than “had given his body and blood to the disciples”; and reads “to the pool of Siloam” rather than “to the pool [feminine] of Siloam.” Col. 0271C]

**A.** Why did he pray?

**M.** For three reasons. First, because he had been delicately brought up, being the son of a Virgin and born of royal stock; for noble people suffer more when they are injured than peasants. [Col. 0273A]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “They suffer more, when injured, than peasants,” rather than “than ignoble people.” Col. 0273C]

Second, because such anguish overwhelmed him that he sweated drops of blood from his whole body; and because he was God, he foresaw everything he was going to suffer: spitting, blasphemies, scourging, crucifixion, and the like. [Col. 0273C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Because he was God, and therefore he foresaw everything he was to suffer—namely, spitting ...” Another reads: “And because he was God, he knew everything he was going to suffer. He foresaw, namely, spitting ...”]

For although a thief knows that he must die, he does not know what death tastes like until the rope tightens around his neck; but my Son foresaw everything as God and man.

Third, because he foresaw that the Jews would not have mercy on him.
