[Note: The manuscript reads: “That they would not have mercy on him,” rather than “that the Jews would not have mercy on him.” A manuscript gives the preceding passage, from “and the like” through “Third, etc.,” in the following expanded form: “and the like. For although a thief knows that he must die, he does not know what death tastes like until the rope tightens around his neck. But my Son foresaw everything as God and man. Third, etc.” Col. 0273C]

And when he prayed in this way, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matthew 26:39), an angel of the Lord appeared to him, strengthening him and saying:

“Be steadfast, Lord; now you are about to redeem the human race.” [Col. 0273B]

[Note: The manuscript omits “of the Lord.” It reads “and saying” rather than merely “saying.” It also reads “You must redeem” rather than “you are about to redeem.” Col. 0273C]

### CHAPTER II. Christ’s Arrest

After this my Son returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. He said to them: “Could you not watch with me for one hour?” (Matthew 26:40.) He added: “Behold, the one who will betray me is approaching” (Mark 13:42). [Col. 0273B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “To them he said,” rather than “to them and said.” It reads: “Saying also: ‘Behold ...’” rather than “he added: ‘Behold ...’” Col. 0273C]

And behold, Judas came with a great crowd and said to the Jews: “There are two who resemble one another, namely James and Jesus. Therefore I give you a sign: the one whom I kiss is he; seize him” (Matthew 26:48). [Col. 0273C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “A great crowd of Jews; and he said to the Jews: ‘There are two alike, namely James and ...’” Another reads: “A great crowd; and he said to the Jews: ‘There are two who resemble one another, namely James ...’”]

When Judas approached with the crowd, Jesus went out toward them, saying: “Whom do you seek?” They answered him: “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them: “I am he.” When he had said, “I am he,” they all fell backward.

Again Jesus said: “If you seek me, let these men go”—so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18:4–9). [Col. 0273C]

[Note: The manuscript reads “so that the Scripture may be fulfilled,” rather than “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.”]

Then Judas approached and kissed him.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Then Judas was kissing him,” rather than “Then Judas approached and kissed him.”]

Jesus said to him: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48.) Then they laid hands on Jesus and seized him (Matthew 26:50).

Peter then drew his sword and struck the servant of the chief priest, whose name was Malchus (John 18:10). [Col. 0273C]

[Note: The manuscript omits “of the chief priest.” It reads “Marchus” rather than “Malchus.”]

**A.** Did any miracle occur there? [Col. 0274A]

**M.** My Son brought the servant to himself and healed his ear (Luke 22:31), and he said to Peter:

“Put your sword into its sheath. For everyone who takes up the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:32, 33.) [Col. 0274A]

[Note: The manuscript reads “Put your sword into ...” rather than “Put the sword into ...” It reads “My Father, and ...” rather than “My Father, and he will provide ...” Col. 0273C]

Then all the disciples abandoned him and fled.

**A.** Tell me, most pious lady— [Col. 0274A]

[Note: The manuscript reads “Most pious Lady,” rather than “sweet Mary.” Col. 0273C]

—were you then with him?

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Were you then there?” Col. 0273C]

**M.** No.

**A.** Why, since you loved him so greatly?

[Note: The manuscript omits this question. Col. 0273C]

**M.** Night was approaching, and it was not suitable for young women to be found outside at that time.

[Note: The manuscript reads “women” rather than “young women.” Col. 0273C]

**A.** Where, then, most sweet lady, were you? [Col. 0274B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Were you then there, most sweet lady?” Col. 0273C]

**M.** I was in the house of my sister, the mother of John the Evangelist.

**A.** How, then—or who—told you what had happened? [Col. 0274B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Or by whom were you told that such a thing had happened?” rather than “or who told you what had happened?” Col. 0273C]

**M.** Hear now, Anselm, what is most lamentable. The disciples came running and crying out tearfully:

“O dearest lady, your beloved Son, our Lord and teacher, has been seized, and we do not know where he is being taken now that he is bound, or what is being done to him, or whether he has been killed.” [Col. 0274B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “The apostate disciples came running to me in tears and crying, ‘Good Lady.’” It also reads: “Your Son, our teacher,” rather than “Your Son, our Lord and teacher.” Another reading has: “We do not know where he is being taken, or what has happened to him, or whether he has been killed.” Col. 0273C]

**A.** Did you weep then, lady?

**M.** Although I knew that he was going to redeem the human race, nevertheless, because of maternal affection, the sword of sorrow of which Simeon had foretold (Luke 2:35) pierced my soul.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Although he was going to redeem the human race,” rather than “although I knew that he was going to redeem the human race.” It reads: “The sword of which Simeon had foretold pierced my soul,” rather than “the sword of sorrow ... pierced my soul.” Col. 0273C]

### CHAPTER III. Christ’s Removal to Annas and Peter’s Denial

**ANSELM.** Where was your beloved Son then taken?

**MARY.** From the aforesaid garden he was led through the valley of Jehoshaphat by the Golden Gate and was taken into the palace of the scribes, priests, and Pharisees beside the Temple, into the house of Annas. Annas questioned him about his teaching and his disciples. [Col. 0274B]

[Note: A manuscript reads “from the garden through,” rather than “from the aforesaid garden through”; another reads “through Jehoshaphat into the city, and he was led into,” rather than “through the valley of Jehoshaphat by the Golden Gate and was taken into”; and a manuscript omits “into the house of Annas.” Col. 0273C]

But he replied:

“I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in the synagogue and in the Temple, where all the Jews gather; I have said nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Ask those who heard me what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said to them.” [Col. 0275A]

Then one of the attendants standing there gave him a slap of unprecedented cruelty, saying:

“Is that how you answer the high priest?”

But my Son, like a gentle lamb, replied to him:

“If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:20–23.) [Col. 0275C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “He gave Jesus a slap, saying,” rather than “he gave him a slap of unprecedented cruelty, saying.” It also reads: “He struck him with a slap of unprecedented cruelty,” rather than “he gave him a slap ...”]

Then they covered his eyes like those of a thief—which, however, is done to no one unless he has first been condemned. They mocked him throughout the night, spitting in his face and striking him, saying:

“Prophesy to us; who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26:68.) [Col. 0275C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “They bound his eyes as those of a thief,” rather than “they covered his eyes like those of a thief.” It also reads: “They mocked him, saying: ‘Prophesy; who is he?’” rather than “they mocked him throughout the night ...”]

Now John, being inside because he was known to the high priest, brought Peter in.

[Note: A manuscript reads “who was known” rather than “because he was known.” Col. 0275C]

The doorkeeper, seeing him, said:

“Are you one of this man’s disciples?” (John 18:17.) [Col. 0275B]

Peter denied three times with an oath that he had ever seen or known him. Immediately the cock crowed. Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord that he had said to him:

“Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

And Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

[Note: The manuscript reads: “The word that my Son had said to him: ‘Before ...’” rather than “the word of the Lord that he had said to him.” It also reads: “The word that my Son Jesus had said: ‘Before ...’” Col. 0275C]

**A.** Where were you, dearest lady, when these things happened? [Col. 0275B]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “When these things had happened?” rather than “when these things happened?” Col. 0275C]

**M.** As soon as the disciples had told me what had happened, all my bones trembled. I rose and ran with Mary Magdalene toward the Temple. Hearing the tumult in Annas’s house, I wished to enter, but I was not permitted.

[Note: One manuscript reads: “When they had reported to me what had happened, all my bones trembled. Rising, I ran”; another: “When they told me what had happened, all my bones trembled. Rising, I ran.” A manuscript reads “Hearing the tumult, I wished to enter, but I was not permitted,” rather than “Hearing the tumult in Annas’s house ...” Col. 0275C]

Therefore I stood outside, weeping and crying:

“Alas! My beloved son, light of my eyes, who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes” (Jeremiah 9:1), so that I may mourn the killing of my only son? [Col. 0275C]

[Note: The manuscript reads “the killing of my only Son,” rather than “the killing of my son.”]

Mary Magdalene went all around and, looking in through the windows, heard Peter’s denial. All her inward parts were stirred because of the desolation of my only Son, since the chief of the disciples had denied him, and she said:

“O good Jesus, what kind of end have you met, or what will become of you, now that this chief of the disciples has denied you? O sweet Jesus, I shall never deny you.” [Col. 0275C]

[Note: The manuscript reads “O sweet Jesus,” rather than “O good Jesus.” It also reads: “The chief of them all, as it is evident, has denied you. Sweet Jesus,” rather than “this chief of the disciples has denied you. O sweet Jesus.” Another manuscript reads: “And hearing Peter’s denial, she was stirred in all her inward parts because of the desolation of ...,” rather than “and, looking in through the windows, heard Peter’s denial. All her inward parts were stirred because of the desolation of ...” Col. 0275C]

I stood there, full of sorrow, hearing all the mockery and insults they inflicted on my beloved Son, hearing Peter denying him and everything that took place there throughout the night.

When Peter had denied him a third time, my Son looked at him, and because he had denied him, Peter wept bitterly.

[Note: A manuscript reads: “When therefore Peter had denied him a third time, and my Son had looked at him, and had wept bitterly because he had denied him ...,” rather than the printed wording. Col. 0275C]

He went outside and found us standing outside. Touched inwardly by the pain in my heart, I said to him:

“Peter, Peter, what is being done with Jesus, or where is Jesus?” [Col. 0276A]

He cried out and answered in a tearful voice:

“Alas, dearest lady, he is being treated without mercy and is being tortured even unto death.”

[Note: The manuscript reads “Alas, good Lady.” It also reads “He is being tortured and killed even unto ...” rather than “he is being treated without mercy and tortured even unto ...” Col. 0275C]

Then, running away, he hid himself for fear in the stone called Gallicantus, and did not appear until Jesus had died on the cross. [Col. 0276B]

**A.** Tell me, dearest lady, what did you do when you heard this?

**M.** Simeon’s sword pierced my soul.

### CHAPTER IV. Christ’s Removal to Caiaphas

**ANSELM.** Tell me, what happened after this?

[Note: The manuscript reads: “What happened?” rather than “Tell me what happened?” Col. 0275C]

**MARY.** When morning came, they led him out of Annas’s house and took him to Caiaphas, the chief priest.

[Note: The manuscript reads “the high priest” rather than “the chief priest.” Col. 0275C]

Then, for the first time after he had been seized, I saw him.

[Note: A manuscript reads: “There I then saw him, after he had been seized, and ...,” rather than “Then, for the first time after he had been seized, I saw him, and ...” Col. 0275C]

I ran toward him like a lioness whose cubs have been snatched away. I saw that desirable face stained with the Jews’ spittle, and I said while weeping:

“Alas, dearest Son, how wretchedly I now see you, when so often I rejoiced in your sweetest appearance!” [Col. 0276C]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Tearing her hair, wailing and weeping, and crying out loudly: ‘Alas, sweetest ...’” rather than the printed wording. It also reads “How wretchedly I see you” rather than “How wretchedly do I now see you.” It reads “your most beloved appearance” rather than “your sweetest appearance.” Col. 0275C]

When I wished to embrace him, I was not permitted to approach. The Jews thrust me here and there, drove me away insultingly, and the crowd gathered from every side, as when thieves and robbers are condemned.

**A.** Did you have any hope that he could be freed?

[Note: The manuscript omits “then.” Col. 0275C]

**M.** Yes. I knew that he was clever and eloquent, and I hoped that he would excuse himself if he came to judgment. Then he stood like the gentlest lamb and did not open his mouth. [Col. 0277A]

[Note: The manuscript reads “as a gentle lamb,” rather than “as the gentlest lamb.” Col. 0277D]

He was also so amiable that I hoped they would take pity on him.

[Note: A manuscript omits the introductory “Likewise” before “he was also.” Col. 0277D]

After a short time had passed, he had been spat upon so much that he appeared almost like a leper.

For these men found many false witnesses against him, saying that he was a destroyer of the Law and a subverter of the people.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “They found many false witnesses against him, saying ...” It reads “a perverter” rather than “a subverter.” Col. 0277D]

At last two false witnesses came forward, saying:

“This man said: ‘I can destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matthew 26:60–61).

[Note: A manuscript reads “and rebuild it within three days” rather than “and rebuild it after three days.” Col. 0277D]

And Caiaphas said:

“Tell us whether you are the Christ” (ibid., 63).

Jesus answered:

“If I tell you, you do not believe me. But if I question you, you will not answer me, nor release me” (Luke 22:67–68). [Col. 0277B]

[Note: The manuscript reads “you will not answer me, nor ...” rather than “you will not answer, or release me.” Col. 0277D]

“Amen, I say to you: from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven.”

Then the chief priest tore his garments and said:

“Why do we still need witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy. What is your judgment?”

Then they all cried out:

“He is liable to death” (Matthew 26:64–66).

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Tearing his garments, he said,” rather than “tore his garments and said.” Col. 0277D]

When this sentence had been pronounced, Simeon’s sword pierced my soul.

[Note: The manuscript adds “and my heart” after “my soul.”]

### CHAPTER V. Christ’s Removal to Pilate

**ANSELM.** Where was he then taken?

**MARY.** To the judge Pilate.

**A.** Did you hope for anything there, dearest lady?

M. I had hoped greatly, when the crowd had gathered—the crowd to whom he had often preached so sweetly, whose sick he had healed, and whom he had fed in the wilderness—that they would free him from the hands of the Jews. Then they all cried out together before Pilate: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Luke 23:21). And they charged him with having said that he was the Son of God (Matt. 27:43), [Note: The manuscript reads “the crowd charged him with,” rather than “they charged him with.”] and with having forbidden tribute to be paid to Caesar (Luke 23:2). Then Pilate asked him about his kingdom, [Note: The manuscript reads “asked,” omitting “him.”] saying: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus answered: “Do you say this on your own, or have others told you about me?” Pilate replied: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and your chief priests have handed you over to me. [Note: The manuscript reads “the chief priests handed [you] over,” omitting “your.”] What have you done?” Jesus answered: “My kingdom is not of this world. [Note: The manuscript omits: “But now my kingdom is not of this world.”] If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews.” Pilate therefore said: “So you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” (John 18:33–38.) Christ did not resolve this question for him, because if he had resolved it, Pilate would certainly have set him free; and therefore the human race would not have been redeemed. [Note: The edition reads “and therefore the human race”; the manuscript reads “and then the human race.”] Then Judas, seeing that Jesus had been condemned, was moved to repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders of the people, and said: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” [Note: The manuscript reads “by betraying the innocent man.”] But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it.” And throwing the silver pieces into the Temple, he withdrew from them, and went away and hanged himself (Matt. 27:3–5).

But Pilate, having summoned the chief priests, the officials, and the people, said to them: “I find no cause of death in this man among the charges with which you accuse him.” [Note: The manuscript reads “I find no cause in this man.”] (Luke 23:4, 14.) But they grew more insistent, saying: “He has stirred up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place.” [Note: The manuscript omits “teaching.”] (ibid.,

## CHAPTER VI. The taking of Christ to Herod and his return to Pilate

Then Pilate, hearing the word “Galilee” and learning that he was a Galilean, sent him to Herod, who was also then in Jerusalem. [Note: The manuscript reads: “Hearing that he was a Galilean, he sent Jesus to Herod, who himself was also in Jerusalem in those days.”] When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly; for he had long wished to see him, because he had heard many things about him and hoped that he would perform some sign. Therefore he questioned Jesus at length (Luke 23:6–9), asking, in particular, whether he was that child whom his father had wanted to kill [Note: The manuscript reads “that one whom he had wanted to kill,” omitting “child”], and on whose account he had killed many children. [Note: The manuscript reads “had killed the children.”] He also asked whether he was the one who had given sight to the blind man [Note: The manuscript reads “to the blind,” in the plural], who had raised Lazarus, and who had raised the widow’s young son at the gate of the city of Nain; and whether he had performed many other miracles. [Note: The manuscript reads: “and many others.”] He begged him to perform some sign, promising that he would rescue him from the hands of the Jews. [Note: The manuscript reads “that he would rescue him from the hand,” rather than “from the hands.”] But Jesus gave him no answer (ibid., 9).

Herod then placed a crown upon his head, promising that if he performed a sign for him, he would make him a participant in his kingdom and likewise his co-heir. [Note: The manuscript omits this entire clause.] This is the crown with which the Romans crown their emperors. [Note: The manuscript reads: “With this crown all emperors are crowned.”] But Jesus did not answer him. Meanwhile the chief priests and scribes stood there, persistently accusing him (ibid., 10).

ANSELMUS. O sweetest lady, what did you hope for then?

MARIA. I knew that Herod was a king of natural elegance, and therefore I hoped that he ought to spare my most excellent kingly Son. [Note: The manuscript reads: “I hoped as a mother, O Anselm; for I knew that Herod was an elegant king, and therefore …”] But he despised my Son and sent him back to Pilate dressed in a white garment. And Herod and Pilate became friends, for previously they had been enemies. [Note: The manuscript reads: “They were not friends with one another”; elsewhere: “They were enemies.”] But Pilate, knowing with what savagery and cruelty the Jews had conspired in the death of my Son, sent some men ahead to escort Jesus from Herod, lest they kill him on the way. [Note: The manuscript reads “he provided some men.”]

After my Son had been sent back, Pilate summoned all the Jews and said: “You brought me this man as one who was turning the people away; and behold, I, questioning him before you, find no cause of death in him among the charges with which you accuse him. Nor did Herod either.” [Note: The manuscript omits this clause.] “For I sent you to him.” [Note: The manuscript reads: “I sent him back to you; and behold …”] “Behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him. Therefore, after having him chastised, I shall release him.” (ibid., 14–16.)

But they asked for Barabbas, who had been thrown into prison because of sedition and murder. [Note: The manuscript reads “because of murder.”] Pilate said a second time: [Note: The manuscript reads simply “Pilate said.”] “What evil, then, has he done? I find no cause of death in him. Therefore I shall chastise him and release him.” But they persisted with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified and crying: “Crucify, crucify him!” [Note: The manuscript reads: “with loud voices: ‘Crucify.’”] (ibid., 21–23.)

When Pilate was seated upon the tribunal, his wife sent word to him: “Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things in a dream this night because of him” (Matt. 27:19).

## CHAPTER VII. The scourging, the crown of thorns, and the outcries of the Jews

Pilate, hoping to satisfy the cruelty of the Jews, took Jesus and had him scourged while bound to a column, so that from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him (Isa. 1:6). [Note: The manuscript reads: “Hoping that he ought to satisfy the cruelty of the Jews, he had Jesus, bound to a column, scourged, so that from …”] This column was so thick that a hand could not touch the other hand around it across a distance of approximately two spans. [Note: The manuscript reads “the hand could not touch the large hand.”] Therefore they took leather thongs and bound his hands.

ANSELMUS. Did you hope for anything there, dearest lady? [Note: The manuscript reads “Did you hope for anything from this?”]

MARIA. I had hoped greatly for the reason that I shall disclose to you. For his delicacy, natural nobility, and beautiful structure of his principal limbs—known only to me, his mother—gave me hope. [Note: The manuscript reads: “I had hoped greatly for this reason, which I shall disclose to you. I was also speaking as a mother, Anselm. For his delicacy and natural nobility …”] I thought that, when his body was stripped and they saw the beautiful proportions of his limbs, they would be overcome and spare him. But alas! In an instant the entire surface of his body was so drenched with blood that, as though surrounded by purple, he appeared to everyone transformed into horror and deformity, as if he had been struck with leprosy. [Note: The manuscript reads: “The beautiful structure of his principal limbs was known to me alone through maternal familiarity, and had been observed by no one else; therefore I thought that, when his body was stripped, they would be moved to compassion by the noble proportion of his limbs. But alas! The entire surface of his body was so drenched with blood that, as though surrounded by purple, he was transformed into horror.”]

The soldiers braided a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, wrapped him in a purple garment, came up to him, and said: “Hail, King of the Jews!” And they struck him with blows (John 19:2–3). The king of France possesses this crown. This crown was not made of thorns but of sea reeds, which have sharper spikes than real thorns. [Note: The manuscript reads: “Of the Franks, which is not …”] Braiding this crown, they pressed it onto his head so that blood ran down over his face. [Note: The manuscript reads: “Striking with a lance, they tried to press it onto his head, so that …”] Thus Pilate led him out, adorned in this way, and said: “Behold your king.” But they cried out: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (ibid., 13–15).

Pilate answered them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him.” They replied: “We have a law, and according to this law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” When Pilate heard these words, he was even more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. [Note: The manuscript reads “he did not answer him.”] Therefore Pilate said to him: “You do not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no authority against me at all unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” From that point Pilate sought to release him. But the Jews cried out, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend.” (ibid., 6–12.) [Note: The manuscript reads “you are not a friend,” rather than “you will not be a friend.”]

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that rather a tumult was arising, he took water, washed his hands before all the people, and said: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you will see to it.” And the whole people answered: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:24–25). Therefore they persisted with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified, and their cries prevailed. Pilate adjudged that their petition should be carried out. He released to them the man who had been thrown into prison because of murder, whom they had requested (Luke 23:23–25).

[Col. 0281A]

## CHAPTER VIII. Christ’s condemnation and the carrying of the cross

Thus, because of the excessive persistence of the people, Pilate pronounced this sentence of death against my Son, saying: “I remove Jesus the Nazarene from life and adjudge him to the ignominious death of the cross.” [Note: The manuscript reads: “Because of the excessive persistence of the people, Pilate pronounced this sentence of death against my Son, saying: ‘I adjudge Jesus the Nazarene to the ignominious death …’”]

ANSELMUS. What did you do, sweetest lady, when you heard this? [Note: The manuscript reads “O sweetest Lady, what did you do when …”]

MARIA. When this sentence had been pronounced, Simeon’s sword pierced my heart and my soul.

A. O sweet Mary! What happened after this? [Note: The manuscript reads “O sweet Mary, what happened …”]

M. They took my beloved Son Jesus and led him out. As John writes, carrying his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, [Col. 0281B] where they crucified him (John 19:16–18). The cross was so large that it was fifteen feet long. [Note: The manuscript reads “And the cross,” rather than “But the cross”; it also reads “which had been fifteen feet long.”] My Son had been so weakened by the preceding night and that day [Note: The manuscript reads “by the whole night”] that he could not carry it. Therefore Luke also writes: “They seized a certain Simon of Cyrene and laid the cross upon him, to carry it behind Jesus, my only Son” (Luke 23:26). They did this not out of compassion, but because, owing to his weakness, he could not do it. [Note: The manuscript omits “because they felt compassion for him.”]

A. Did some people follow him as he was being led out? [Note: The manuscript reads “Did some women follow him?”]

M. The entire crowd rushed together, just as when thieves are led to punishment. Therefore Luke writes: “A great multitude of the people followed him, and women who were mourning and lamenting him” (ibid., 27). Children also followed, throwing mud and stones at him. But my Son Jesus turned toward the women and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children, who throw mud and stones at me without knowing what they are doing. For behold, the days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us’; and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’ For if they do this in the green wood—that is, in youth—what will happen in the dry—that is, in old age?” (ibid., 28–31). Or: “In the green wood,” that is, in me; “in the dry,” that is, in my other saints—what will happen? [Note: The manuscript reads “in the saints—what will happen?”] Two other evildoers were also led with him to be crucified (ibid., 22). They did this to increase their own confusion. [Note: The manuscript omits “their own.”]

## CHAPTER IX. The meeting of Christ and his mother

When my principal Son was being led outside the city gate with two criminals, amid the immense pressure of the crowd rushing forward and insulting him, I wanted to follow and see him, but I could not because of the enormous crowd that had gathered to heap disgrace upon my Son. But at last, together with Mary Magdalene, I decided that we would go around by the street lying alongside, near a certain fountain, so that we might meet him.

[Col. 0282B] When we had come near the fountain, we encountered my deformed Son, oppressed by every sorrow. He gently inclined himself toward me, as if he were saying: [Note: The manuscript reads “Inclining himself toward me, he said, ‘Hail, Mother,’ as if he were saying …”] “I give you thanks, my chosen mother, for the many benefits you bestowed upon me, and for the great labor by which, in the utmost poverty and humiliation, you nurtured the temple of my body; and now, when it has been brought to destruction amid insults and reproaches, you do not disdain or fear to follow me, although we are held in contempt by everyone.” [Note: The manuscript reads: “for the many benefits you bestowed upon me, and …”; also “to follow me, and you do not fear,” and “although we are contemptible.”]

## CHAPTER X. The crucifixion and erection of the cross

After they had come to the place of Calvary, they crucified him there, and the thieves with him, one on his right and the other on his left (Mark 15:27).

ANSELMUS. What did they do to him?

MARIA. Listen, Anselm: what I am about to tell you is exceedingly lamentable, and none of the evangelists records it. When they had come to the most ignominious place of Calvary, where dogs and other carrion were thrown, [Note: The manuscript reads “where carcasses were flayed.”] they stripped Jesus, my only Son, completely of his garments, and I became as one dead. Nevertheless, taking the veil from my head, I tied it around his loins.

After this they laid the cross upon the ground, stretched him out upon it, and first drove in one nail, so thick that the blood could not flow out, since the wound was filled by the nail. [Note: The manuscript omits “then completely”; the wording “the blood” is otherwise preserved.] Afterwards they took ropes and pulled the other arm of my Son Jesus, and drove a second nail into it. [Note: The manuscript reads “they drove in a similar nail.”] Then they pulled his feet with ropes and drove in an exceedingly sharp nail. He was stretched so tightly that all his bones and limbs became visible, so that the Psalm might be fulfilled: “They counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:18). [Note: The manuscript reads “they appeared, in accordance with …”]

Then the prophecy of David himself—that is, of Christ himself—was fulfilled, when he says in the Psalm: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11). [Note: The manuscript reads simply “The prophecy of David: ‘Hear …’”] It was as though my Son were saying: “Hear, my dearest mother, the sound of the hammers, and see how they have fastened my hands and my feet; and no one pities me except you alone, my chosen mother. Hear, O daughter, and have compassion on me.” Hearing and seeing this, Simeon’s sword pierced my heart and my soul.

Afterward they raised him with great effort, and he was suspended so high that I could nowhere reach his feet. When he had been raised up, then, because of the weight of his body, all the wounds were torn open and lacerated, and only then did blood flow more abundantly from his hands and feet. I was wearing a certain garment customary among the women of that region, which covered the head and the whole body and was like a linen cloth; this garment was entirely sprinkled with blood.

## CHAPTER XI. The insults directed at Christ on the cross

ANSELMUS. What happened after this?

MARIA. After they had crucified my Son, they divided his garments among themselves and cast lots for the seamless garment, so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” And sitting down, they kept watch over him (Matt. 27:33, 36).

Pilate also wrote above his head in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” Then the Jews asked Pilate not to write “King of the Jews.” But because he had written “King of the Jews,” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22).

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days, save yourself; if you are the Son of God, come down now from the cross.” [Note: The manuscript reads “who destroys … rebuilds,” rather than the second-person forms.]

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants him, for he said: ‘I am the Son of God’” (Matt. 27:39–43).

## CHAPTER XII. Christ’s words on the cross

ANSELMUS. What did your Son answer to such insults? [Note: The manuscript reads “Your Son replied.”]

MARIA. My beloved prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). [Note: The manuscript omits this entire clause.] The people stood waiting and mocked him. Then he could say to his mother: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11). [Note: The manuscript reads “say that saying of the Psalm: ‘Hear …,’” rather than simply “say: ‘Hear …’”]:  “Hear the voices of those who blaspheme your Son, and see my suffering. For you know that you conceived me of the Holy Spirit, that you gave birth to me as a virgin, and how you nourished me.” [Note: The manuscript reads “washed me,” rather than “nourished me.”] “Therefore, since these people do not believe in me, you nevertheless believe in me and have compassion.” [Note: The manuscript reads: “Believe that I am the Son of God; you nevertheless have compassion.”] Then once again Simeon’s sword pierced my soul.

When the thief hanging on the left heard this, he insulted him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” But the other, who was hanging on the right, answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And indeed we justly are, because we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.” And he said to Jesus: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” And Jesus said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:39–43). [Note: The manuscript reads: “But the other answered and said, rebuking him: ‘Do you not …’”]

A. What did you do then, dearest lady?

M. I stood beside the cross, so filled with grief that I could bear no consolation. My sisters and Mary Magdalene stood with me. When my Son saw me and John, his disciple whom he loved, he said: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:25–26). O how pitiable a permission! Then he said to the disciple: [Note: The manuscript reads “he says to the disciple”] “Behold your mother” (ibid., 27).

It was about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour. And Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lama sabbacthani,” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” But some were saying: “This man is also calling Elijah. Let us see whether Elijah will come to free him” (Matt. 27:43–49).

Afterward, knowing that all things had been completed, [Note: The manuscript reads “when he had completed all things”] Jesus said: “I thirst” (John 19:28). “What do you thirst for, Lord?” “The salvation of sinners.”

There was a vessel placed there, full of vinegar (ibid., 29), and one man ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it around a spear, [Note: The manuscript reads “around a reed”] and gave him a drink (Mark 15:39), so that he might die more quickly. When he had tasted it, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). [Note: The manuscript reads “when he had received the vinegar.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. Christ’s death and the wonders that followed it

After this he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). In this commending, with the offering of blood, [Note: The manuscript omits “with the offering of blood”] Christ commended to God the Father his sweetest mother, who is the treasury and purest dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, together with all who are to live from the Holy Spirit until the end of the age. [Note: The manuscript reads “his most beloved mother, a vigorous, serene, and pure receptacle of the Holy Spirit.”] And after this, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). [Note: The manuscript reads “and after these things.”]

Then the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split. Especially the rock upon which the cross stood was cleft, so that a hand could be placed in it. [Note: The manuscript reads “so that hands could be placed in it.”] The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose. Coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.

The centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were very much afraid (Matt. 27:51–54); and the centurion himself glorified God, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.” [Note: The manuscript reads “This man was just.”] (Luke 23:47.) Behold how all the elements sympathized with Christ, while the Jews alone remained hardened.

All who were present together at this spectacle, seeing what was happening, returned beating their breasts. [Note: The manuscript reads “seeing what was happening to him.”] All his acquaintances stood at a distance, as did the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things (ibid., 48–49). [Note: The manuscript reads “who were with him.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. The mother’s mourning for the death of her Son

ANSELMUS. Dearest lady, did your sorrow finally come to an end?

MARIA. No, Anselm, because Simeon’s prophecy had not yet been completely fulfilled, and “a sword will pierce your own soul” (Luke 2:35). [Note: The manuscript reads “had been fulfilled, namely: and …,” rather than “had been completely fulfilled, and ….”] Listen, then, to what is more lamentable than anything else.

Since it was the day of Preparation, the Jews asked that the bodies not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath. For that Sabbath was a great day; they asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away. Therefore the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man and of the other who had been crucified with him. [Note: The manuscript reads “They came, therefore,” rather than “But the soldiers came.”]

When they came to Jesus and found him already dead, they did not break his legs. [Note: The manuscript reads “saw him,” rather than “found him.”] Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out (John 19:31–34). When I saw that they were inflicting such cruelty upon one who was already dead, I became as one lifeless. [Note: The manuscript reads “I had already become almost lifeless.”] Then indeed Simeon’s prophecy was fulfilled, which says: “And your own soul …”

Then I began to cry out and lament; but by then my tears had entirely failed me. I had wept so much during the preceding night and that day. And I said: “Alas, my sweetest Son, where is now the consolation that I have always had in you? Who would grant me to die for you, my Son Jesus?” With these words and others like them, I mourned the death of my sweetest and only Son.

[Col. 0286B]

## CHAPTER XV. The descent of Christ’s soul into Limbo

Then great joy arose in Limbo when Christ’s soul descended into it, freed the fathers from there, destroyed Limbo, and shut up Hell, so that no Christian will be able to go there except by his own free choice, nor will any of those who are inside be able to leave before the Day of Judgment. He shut Hell with three bars.

The reason is this: before his death, no one could possess contrition, confession, or satisfaction. [Note: The manuscript reads: “He shut Hell by nights [noctibus]. For before the Passion no one could possess, namely, contrition, confession, and satisfaction,” rather than “He shut Hell with three bars [tribus vectibus]. And the reason is that before his death no one could possess contrition, confession, or satisfaction.”]

[Col. 0286C]

## CHAPTER XVI. The taking of Christ’s body down from the cross and his burial

ANSELMUS. What happened after this?

MARIA. After this, Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus (John 19:38), saying among other things: “Lord, unless you hand over the body quickly, an honorable woman, the mother of this young man, will die of grief.” Then Pilate [Note: “An honorable woman, the mother of this young man, is dying of grief. Pilate, etc.” The manuscript reads: “We shall lose the most beautiful Lady, the mother of the young man who has been killed; she showed such great grief that we sympathize with her as much as if he were the only son of us all. Then Pilate, etc.”] asked whether he was already dead, and, having learned from the centurion [Note: “Having learned from the Centurion” — the manuscript reads “having been dispatched by”] everything that had happened there, ordered the body of Jesus to be given over (Mark 15:47). And Joseph came and took the body of Jesus [Note: The manuscript omits “And Joseph came and took the body of Jesus”]. Note this, Anselm: it is greatly [Note: The manuscript reads “exceedingly”] lamentable.

While Joseph was taking down the body, I stood beside the cross, looking upward. I waited for the arm to be loosened, so that I might touch and kiss it, as indeed I did; and when he had been taken down from the cross, they placed [Note: “I stood looking upward, waiting for the arm to be loosened, so that I might touch and kiss him, as indeed I did; and when he had been taken down from the cross, they placed him upon the ground.” The manuscript reads: “I stood beside the Cross, looking upward. And when he had been taken down from the Cross, they placed him upon the ground. I waited for the arm to be loosened, so that I might touch and kiss him, as indeed I did. And when he had been taken down, they placed him.”] him upon the ground, a good three paces from the place of the cross. And taking his head into my lap, I began to weep most bitterly, saying: “Alas, my sweetest Son, what consolation do I have [Note: The manuscript omits “I have consolation from you”] when I see my dead Son [Note: “Whom I now see dead before me” in the manuscript] before me.”

Then John the Evangelist ran up, fell upon the breast of Jesus, and, weeping, said: “Alas, alas! Yesterday I drank sweet words from this breast; today, words of sorrow and lamentation [Note: The manuscript reads “sweet words, today”].”

Then Peter arrived; and he who had denied him [Note: The manuscript reads “he who denied him”] began to weep most bitterly. Then Mary Magdalene began to weep over her Lord more than all the others, saying: “Who will forgive my sins now? Who will now defend me before Simon and before my sister?”

James also came, who was called the brother of my Son [Note: The manuscript reads “is called my Son’s brother”], and who was very like him [Note: The manuscript reads “was like himself”]. With many tears [Col. 0287B] he said this: “Alas, Lord and Master [Note: The manuscript reads “Alas, Lord”], yesterday this most beloved face was very like mine [Note: The manuscript reads: “Alas, Lord and Master, yesterday you bestowed such grace upon me, unworthy as I was, above the others, because your sweetest face was very like mine”]. Alas, now it appears altogether unlike [Note: The manuscript reads “Alas, now your countenance appears unlike mine”]. Your hands and your feet have been fastened with nails [Note: The manuscript reads “your feet with nails”]; but your body appears wounded everywhere, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, whereas mine appears entirely unharmed [Note: The manuscript reads: “Wounded: but my body, on the contrary, appears entirely unharmed”].”

He swore that he would take neither food [Note: The manuscript reads “And he swore that he would never…”] nor drink until he had been conformed to his likeness. Then all the other disciples [Note: The printed text omits “all”] ran up and mourned over him [Note: The manuscript reads “mourning over him”]. And my Son [Note: The manuscript reads “Then my Son”] was glorified there before his own [Note: The manuscript reads “before us”] for my consolation and that of the disciples, so that no wound or bruise appeared on his body except the scars of the five wounds, which he will retain until the day of judgment. He appeared so healthy [Note: The manuscript reads “healthy and radiant”] in body as though he had never suffered. From this the disciples and I received immense consolation.

And when they wished to bury him [Note: The manuscript reads “when I wished to bury him”], I held the body with great sorrow and scarcely permitted it to be buried, saying: “Dearest John, leave me my dead Son, whom I could not have while he was alive. But if it is necessary for you to do this, I beg you to bury me with him.”

John replied: “You know, most beloved Lady, that it could not have been otherwise, and that the human race had to be redeemed in this way.”

At last, unwillingly, I allowed him to be buried. And when he had been placed in the tomb, I wished to enter it, threw myself upon the tomb, and behaved so miserably [Note: The manuscript reads “I walked about so miserably”] that everyone wept.

And when John wished to lead me into the city and remove me from the tomb [Col. 0288A], weeping, I begged him: “Dearest John [Note: The manuscript reads “Dear John”], do not do me this wrong [Note: The manuscript reads “this wrong to me”], to separate me [Note: The manuscript reads “to separate myself”] from my sweetest Son Jesus, for here I shall wait until I die [Note: The manuscript reads “I would wish to wait until…”].” And again everyone wept.

But John finally took me and, as it were, led me away by force into the city [Note: The manuscript reads “finally took me and, as it were, led me away by force into the city”]. When the people saw me wearing a garment sprinkled with blood, just as I had stood before Jesus and his blood had dripped upon me, they all cried out together in lamentation: “Oh, what a great wrong has today been done in Jerusalem to this most beautiful Lady and to her Son [Note: The manuscript reads “to this Lady and her Son”]!” And they sympathized with me.

But the Jews, out of envy, shut Joseph alive inside a wall because he had buried Christ. His wife later showed the place to his son Joseph [Col. 0288B] [Note: The manuscript reads “She showed it to Joseph’s sons”]. At last, after forty years, Titus and Vespasian came, destroying Jerusalem [Note: The manuscript reads “they destroyed Jerusalem”], and found Joseph alive within the wall [Note: The manuscript reads “they removed him from the wall”]. And just as the Jews bought Christ for thirty denarii, so they sold thirty Jews for one denarius [Note: “They sold.” The printed editions end here; but in manuscript Thu. 519 the following material continues immediately, without any intervening space.]

# BOOK ON THE MEASUREMENT OF THE CROSS

On Christ’s saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

[Col. 0289B]

Since your Son Christ commanded: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), and the Apostle exhorted us to advance toward perfection, we ought by every means to strive toward perfection of life. Yet, while striving without a guide, we can go astray. Your goodness, my God, gives us excellent counsel in this: you have deigned to give us that same only-begotten Son as our guide, so that by his deeds and words he might show and teach us the way of truth.

For you gave testimony that we should follow him confidently on the path to perfection, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). Therefore, in order to do your will, he showed us a kind of epitome of the way of perfection in brief words of immense weight, saying: [Col. 0289C] “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

In these words he shows how few are those who, by the freedom of their will, wish to follow him in perfection. Yet he wishes to be our guide: the beginning, middle, and end of the way of perfection, and he shows with what intention one must walk. Each point will become clear in its proper place.

[Col. 0290B]

# CHAPTER ONE  
## An examination of the first words, “If anyone,” concerning the roots and remedies of faintheartedness

You indicate, Lord, the small number of the perfect by saying: “If anyone,” as though one person among many wished to come after me. And why is this, my God, except because of a certain lethargy and excessive faintheartedness? Most people do not wish to force their minds to strive upward, and they do not dare to attempt the perfect way.

Faintheartedness also arises from excessive fear, especially because of past sins; from looking too little to one’s own merits for the sake of usefulness; from fearing obstacles too greatly; from not immediately feeling that one is making progress amid daily falls; and from considering your goodness too little. These things often deter many from daring to attempt the perfect way; indeed, they frequently cast down even beginners so far that they despair of being able to proceed.

But the first of these—that is, excessive fear because of past sins—ought not to hinder us. If we use it well, everything is counted to our advantage: for proclaiming your excessive goodness, for knowing you, and for loving and praising you. It must be noted, however, that sins principally involve three losses: in them we merit eternal punishment; we lose eternal blessedness; and—and this is the worst—we spend time without love and praise of our Creator. The first two concern human beings; the third, my God, seems to concern your loss.

Since, therefore, by your undeserved and excessive mercy you deign to recall us, already destined for death, to your life, we ought to turn to you so faithfully that we disregard our losses and strive by every means to make up, at least in some measure through the remainder of our time, the praise of you that we neglected.

How great a thing it is, Lord, to disregard fear of punishment because of love for you! But why, because of our desire for blessedness, should we diminish the renown of your praise, when we deserved to endure it eternally even because of your wrath? First, let us seek to praise you, who are the kingdom of God, as you say in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21); and, “This will be added to you in abundance” (Luke 12:31).

Grant us, Lord, charity that does not seek its own interests (1 Corinthians 13:5), but yours, so that fear of punishment may not compel us to serve you for our sins, nor love of our blessedness to serve you for a reward. For our time and strength are insufficient to praise you, whose goodness surpasses all understanding; and thus fear will not instill faintheartedness in us because of our sins.

The smallness of our merits also sometimes frightens us, so that we do not dare to strive toward perfection of life, because they are insufficient to merit it. But this is answered by the fact that you, Lord, commanded us to buy, and added that we must buy freely. For you said: “All you who are thirsty, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1).

What is it, Lord, that we must buy—wine of fervor in your praise and milk of a pure conscience—without any exchange, except that whatever we have to give you, however little it may be, is enough for you; indeed, even what we give is itself yours?

Faintheartedness is also induced by our seeing ourselves unworthy because we ask. Both are true: even if a person served God for a thousand years with the greatest fervor, he would not merit, by strict desert, half a day in the kingdom of heaven. But, Lord, we must not consider only our own advantage, but your praise, whose goodness surpasses all understanding.

Our excessive awareness of obstacles also makes us fainthearted. But, Lord, if we boldly propose to follow you, we must be certain that you remove whatever delays us from praising you. Whatever you do not remove according to your will, we ought willingly to bear. Our folly often thinks that the things your hidden wisdom has ordered for our progress are obstacles.

Fifth, we are frightened because we do not immediately feel that we are making progress. But, Lord, you often delay what is requested in order to stir up desire more strongly. You do not delay because you do not wish to give; rather, you delay so that, once desire has increased, you may give more abundantly.

Sixth, what draws us back is our daily failings. The remedy against this is always to set aside some hour of the day to examine how we are conducting ourselves inwardly and outwardly. Whatever we find useful for our progress, we should firmly resolve to pursue, and we should strive to reject every failing.

We should not be frightened if perhaps on some day we occasionally act contrary to our resolve, provided that we resolve no less firmly afterward. For the person who, through weakness, acts against his resolve returns to you much more easily than the person who, concealing his condition, made no resolve to amend. Indeed, sometimes the former’s punishment is greater than his fault; and your goodness knows how to use our evils well, often making our failings contribute to an increase in humility, so that it may be true that “the righteous falls seven times and rises again stronger” (Proverbs 24:16).

Seventh, we are made fainthearted because we do not appreciate your goodness. When we speak to you in prayer, we ought not to think of you as difficult to persuade, but as the most kind Father, who knows what we need even before we pray and who, by your natural goodness, are infinitely more inclined to hear us, as far as you are concerned, than we are eager to ask.

Grant, sweetest Lord, that we may not be fainthearted, but may be courageous in our weaknesses. Applying the medicine of your graces to those of us who strive to bring ourselves down, let us resolve firmly to follow you—not fainthearted, but courageous—especially if we do not possess strength enough to run after you, the giant who rejoiced to run his course (Psalm 18:6). Yet we have this remedy: we can cry out after you, “Draw us after you” (Song of Songs 1:2), and may your ear hear and answer our cry.

# CHAPTER TWO  
## Concerning freedom and its allurements toward perfection; an exposition of the word “wishes” in Christ’s sentence

Second, you indicate the freedom of the will of those who wish to follow on the way of perfection when you say: “If anyone wishes,” because you leave this to human will—but not to human power. No. You reserved power for yourself, Lord, since all power is from God (Romans 13).

Why, then, will a person complain against you if he wishes to follow you but cannot? Certainly, because he does not follow you: although he cannot do so by himself, he can do so through you. You did not reserve to yourself the power of our progress so that we would be unable to progress—for you perform all our works—but so that we might all the more admire and praise the abyss of your goodness: the very things you do in us are pleasing and acceptable to you, and you judge them worthy of reward, so that you do not even leave a cup of cold water without reward (Matthew 10:42). In this way you have made our will free, because of its likeness to you, so that it cannot be compelled.

You have also sought to draw us toward the way of truth and perfection in many other ways. What had we done to deserve this, Lord—that you should descend to us, unite our humanity to yourself so wondrously, and live among human beings in it with such humility—except that you wished to summon us to perfection of your love, so that, while we know God visibly, through him we might be carried away into love of invisible things?

What human being, then, was worthy that the Son of God should suffer death for him? Or who ever merited being refreshed by your body and blood, except that you, my God, thereby showed the eagerness of your love toward us, so that at least through the number and greatness of such wondrous benefits you might kindle our heart to mutual love and bring it into captivity to your love?

Your benefits, Lord, by which you stir our will to wish to follow you perfectly and ardently, are exceedingly innumerable; above all, however, the consideration of your goodness—from which all created goods proceed—would stir, indeed, if it were permissible to say so, compel our will.

Because, however, the person who wishes to think spiritually about you, who are Spirit, has had little experience and is not yet practiced in doing so, he can begin meditating on you in this manner. First, let him bring to mind a soul perfect in virtues, and think of it in such a particular way as though it were joined to no body. Let him imagine in it every perfection of virtue that could ever be conceived in any soul: how good, how sweet, how patient, how merciful, how wise, how charitable, how faithful, how devout, how just, how truthful, how humble, and so forth.

When he has considered such things in the soul, let him think that this soul is like its Creator in the virtues, since the Creator made it in his likeness. Then let him turn to the Creator and think that every perfection that can be found in the soul is infinite and immeasurable in the Creator; let him think of these very qualities as constituting the Creator’s nature. In this way, to some degree, he may behold and understand the invisible things of God through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20).

This is indeed an initial way of thinking about you, Lord. Whoever diligently follows it by meditating on you will enter the living fountain and sweetness of your nature. The greater this is than all your benefits, the more it affects our will, so that we may ardently follow Jesus, your Son, who forms us for the praise of your goodness.

# CHAPTER THREE  
## Concerning the following words, “come after me”

Third, he gave himself as our guide and instructor when he added: “Come after me.” However fervently we may run in following you, no one precedes you and no one walks beside you. We must all go after you, because you are the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

First you say to the disciples, Lord: “Come and see” (John 1:39). Later you say: “Come after me,” so that they may imitate what they have seen in you. Then you say: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28), and so forth, so that those who gladly take up your easy yoke and your light burden (ibid., 30) may bear them to the glory of your Father.

Finally you say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34). Thus, Lord, this is your most faithful ambassador: first he sets himself before us as an example when he says, “Come and see,” and afterward he invites us to come after him. He calls those who come to him [Col. 0294A] so that he may refresh them and keep them from failing. At last he will take them up into rest, although there we shall have no rest from saying day and night: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3).

There, Lord, you will wipe away every tear from the eyes of your beloved, for “there will be no more death, nor mourning” (Revelation 21:4), and so forth. But, Lord, my soul cannot fully comprehend how this can be: it has in some measure experienced how great an affliction it is to know you and be unable to praise you. Indeed, gratitude itself generates affliction, because the soul is permitted to be afflicted by its inability to praise you; everything it can ever think, say, or do for your praise causes it affliction, because it considers itself unworthy of these things and because it will be able to respond to you in nothing.

If, therefore, the soul imprisoned and placed in shadows is afflicted so insatiably for your praise, how will it be satisfied when your goodness appears to it at midday, since it will surely see that it cannot praise it fully? Perhaps you will say to me, Lord, that this will be its greatest joy: that it will know your goodness perfectly, and will know it to be so immeasurable that no creature can praise it fully.

I believe that it will rejoice in the immensity of your goodness. Nevertheless, it will still grieve that it cannot praise it perfectly—unless somehow its wounds were bound up and the bruises of its blows healed, because only then would oil first be added to the furnace.

Therefore, if it pleases you, Lord, I believe that there also the punishment and affliction for your praise that the soul has here will be satisfied and bound to the stake of praise, when you, who fill our desire with good things (Psalm 102:5), give us as much ability to praise you as we desire—indeed, far more than we desired.

For you said: “You will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice. Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Once the punishment it has suffered here is healed and what it desired here is fulfilled, it cannot have another punishment in itself there for greater praise, just as it cannot have such a punishment here. Nor will you give it one, since you arrange all things “by number, weight, and measure” (Wisdom 11:20). For then it will not be a time for weeping but for laughter, when your only-begotten Son appears to us, if we wish to come after him.

# CHAPTER FOUR  
## That we are not our own but God’s, concerning the words “let him deny himself”

Fourth, therefore, he shows us the beginning of the way by which we must come after Christ when he says: “Let him deny himself.” Whoever, then, wishes to follow Christ Jesus on the way of perfection must first labor to deny himself.

We rightly ought to deny ourselves, since we have no right of ownership over ourselves. There are seven reasons, each of which would be sufficient to compel a person to confess that he has no right of ownership in himself.

The first is that you, Lord, created us. Therefore, just as there is nothing good in us that you did not create, so it is fitting that all our goods should be yours. They may in no way be taken away from you, the Holy of holies, lest we commit sacrilege.

Why, then, should we not deny ourselves, since we are not our own? Whenever we deny anything of ourselves but do not offer that denied thing to you, even if we give it elsewhere for however brief a period, we immediately seize what belongs to another.

The second reason is that, when we were devoted to eternal death, you redeemed us through your most precious death. You died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all, as your chosen Vessel says (2 Corinthians 5:15). Therefore, just as you redeemed us all and wholly, so let us all and wholly be yours. Whoever wishes to be saved must return to you that most precious blood which you poured out for him.

The third is that, when we were ungrateful for all your goods and turned away from you because of our sins, you defended us from the devil after we had shamefully and wickedly departed from you, our Lord. We did not deserve to remain under your protection. Thus, with the enemy holding us captive without defense and according to his will, he ought to have plunged us into eternal punishments, unless you, through your superabundant goodness, had defended us from him and preserved us for repentance. For this reason we are especially your servants, as having been saved from the enemy.

Likewise, all who through your grace have escaped the devil’s snares are yours. Therefore nothing should be taken away from you on account of what either did not fall because you granted it, or, if it had fallen, was raised up again.

The fourth reason is that, although we had deserved eternal death because of our sins, you restored us to life by pardoning it. Why, then, should we not live for you, denying ourselves entirely, from whom we have received the fact that we are not eternally dead?

The fifth reason is that, by the same goodness with which you created us, you also preserve us, lest we be reduced to nothing. For how could we continue to exist in any way unless you preserved us? If, therefore, you are our life, we ought to live for no one else, just as we cannot subsist through anyone else.

The sixth reason is security. Whoever denies himself entirely in order to possess God—who is lost to himself so that he may avail for you, who is nothing to himself so that he may be something for you—if he has nothing in himself, fears losing nothing of his own. He is always secure that you will preserve what belongs to you.

If the punishments of hell or purgatorial fire are threatened against him, he is little affected by fear of them, because the traveler, empty-handed before the robber, will sing. The person who denies himself does not fear losing himself. For even if you wished to send him, who is yours, to punishments, he would still think of you in your goodness and be ready to endure whatever you wished; nor would he say: “Why are you doing this?” The preceding sentence is displeasing to anyone who does not understand that he must deny himself before you, Lord.

The seventh reason ought to press us most strongly: namely, that we should return or repay you, because “a child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6); you give yourself to us daily as food, and at last you will give yourself to us as a prize and as an exceedingly great reward.

Lord, what could be worthy of such great benefits of yours? What could we worthily give in return? Is it not necessary that, apart from this, we utterly deny ourselves and give ourselves to you, sweetest Lord?

If one human being were as great as all the creatures you have ever made, how great would he be if he gave himself wholly to you, who have given yourself wholly to us, whose goodness infinitely outweighs all else? Let the person who thinks himself better than you reserve as much of himself for you as he thinks himself better than you.

For this reason you say: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24)! Indeed, Lord, I am compelled to say—without violating your word—that no one can deny himself. For how will he deny himself who has never possessed any right of ownership in himself?

But, Lord, in this word you show your greatest gratitude: you esteem this so highly that whoever had usurped some right of ownership in himself should no longer dare to seize himself away from you. Grant me, Lord, to deny myself—or rather, to return what I violently seized.

According to the law, what has been taken must be returned fourfold (2 Samuel 12:6), so that we return not only ourselves but also what is ours: namely, natural, accidental, and gratuitous goods.

Natural goods are those that nature commonly provides to all human beings. Some belong to the soul alone, such as intellect and affection; others belong to the body through the soul, including the five interior senses.

Let us therefore return our intellect, while abandoning its own private judgment, which greatly hinders us from knowing the truth. For as long as a person relies so heavily upon his own opinion that he is unwilling to depart from it, he scarcely grasps the opinion of another, however rational that person may be.

We must therefore act according to the Apostle: “Whoever among you wishes to be wise, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18). If he humbly considered himself a fool for a time, then he could apprehend true wisdom from you or from those who belong to you, because “where there is humility, there is wisdom” (Proverbs 2:2). Paul is believed to have learned the Gospel during those three days when he was blind (Acts 9:9).

Let us also return our affection to God, always placing our will after the divine will, especially in our prayer. In every prayer we must place his will before our own advantage; indeed, if we use it rightly, his will is always our advantage.

It often arises from our own judgment that we do not believe the Lord’s will to be whatever happens around us. Thus we misuse it by receiving events with insufficient gratitude, as Augustine says (*Confessions* X.6.26): “That servant of yours is best who does not desire to hear from you what he himself wished, but wishes what he will hear from you.”

Together with these two—intellect and affection—let us return the five exterior senses as well, mortifying them with respect to all vanities and turning them toward your service. Then we shall possess, to some small degree, the first part of what we must deny along with ourselves: natural goods.

The second part consists of accidental goods, which we may call temporal possessions and friends. All these must be trampled underfoot lest they impede your love. “For he loves you less who loves anything with you that he does not love for your sake,” as Augustine says.

A person ought to be greatly indignant at loving something small when you have made him worthy of such dignity that he may love you. Excessive love of friends harms more secretly than love of temporal things, because it conceals itself beneath the veil of charity. Thus a person often thinks that a love is charity when it is carnal affection, which so sweetly and pleasantly holds the mind captive that he does not know with what hard bonds he has been bound until he has been released.

Must we not give our whole heart to your love, so that whatever we give of it to another we take away from you? It is therefore necessary that we deny, for your sake, all the things that fortune offers us to love, whether temporal goods or friends.

The third part of restitution consists of gratuitous goods, namely virtues. We must pour these back entirely into their source, attributing none of them to ourselves but to you, from whom every perfect gift comes (James 1:17), and giving you thanks for them.

If we deny everything found among these three kinds of goods—natural, accidental, and gratuitous—we restore fourfold to you what we defrauded you of. Let this, then, be the beginning of our perfect life: to deny ourselves entirely.

[Col. 0297B]

# CHAPTER FIVE  
## An examination of the words “let him take up his cross”

Source preparation: Embedded foreign-language text and all apparatus were retained from the supplied local archive and translated here.

Fifth, it has been considered what means of perfection is proposed to us, namely, that we should walk by it: that is, that we should take up our cross. The cross, moreover, is so called from *cruciatus*, “torment.” Lord, if I were to call our cross your service, according to their opinion I would understand this as those do who do not know that your yoke is easy and your burden light (Matt. 11:30), nor perceive how good and how sweet your Spirit is within us. I say, rather, that the cross is the torment of the heart which we ought to have because we are not as faithful and fervent in all your service and praise as we ought to be.

This cross has length, breadth, height, and depth. [Col. 0297C] We ought, therefore, to have torment because we are not humbled as much as we ought to be; and this is the depth of the cross. We do not love and praise you as much as your goodness demands; and this is its height. We are not as faithful as we ought to be; and this is its breadth. We do not always persevere, nor do we extol your praise abundantly, nor do we desist from unfaithfulness with all our strength; and this is its length.

Our own knowledge first compels us toward the depth of humility. For it is enough for a person, for humility, to know himself—especially if we remember our former iniquities, since we have acted wickedly in your sight, my God; for truly you are so faithful to us that, even when we remain in sins, you are ready both to forgive our sins and to bestow your grace upon us as abundantly as we might wish. [Col. 0297D] The greater the things a person presumes concerning you, the more necessary it is that he be humbled, because he has acted more wickedly against you by sinning, to the degree that you meanwhile intended to benefit him more generously. Hence Bernard says: “The more benignly I am compelled to think of him, the more unworthily I must think of myself.”

Likewise, daily failings humble us, since we are so unstable in your praise—indeed, we never remain in the same condition. The more ready you are each day to forgive, the more it humbles us to offend against your goodness. Likewise, the weight of grace humbles and depresses us when we consider that we are unworthy of it, since we deserved more to be in hell. Likewise, we are humbled by the fact that you, my Lord God, humbled yourself so greatly for us. Likewise, [Col. 0298A] by the fact that in the nature of your divinity you surpass all humility; and if we wish to be like you, we must humble ourselves. Likewise, by the fact that we are so cold that we cannot respond to your goodness either in love, in praise, or in anything else.

These things, and many others that are more generally applicable, suffice for our humility; indeed, they leave no place for pride. The depth of humility is greatly necessary for us in relation to your height, because the more unworthy a person considers himself, the more grateful he is for benefits; and the more grateful he is, the more praiseworthy he is; and the one who is most grateful will praise you most.

Grant us, therefore, Lord, true humility—that is, to be so tormented because in this life we cannot be humbled fully, that we may thereby possess the depth of the cross.

The height of the cross is to be tormented [Col. 0298B] because we cannot praise and love you fully. What we possess as a cause for loving you—what tongue could express it, or what understanding suffice to grasp it—I do not know. If we wish to love something freely, where could we place our love better than in you? If we love in return for gifts, who gives more than you? Yet the more you promise, the more deserving you are of being loved freely. If we wish to love those who love us, how much more justly should we love you? And if we expect and desire someone to compel love from us, are you not my God, who so often knock and beg at our door, saying, “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23:26)—indeed, even when often rejected, you thrust yourself upon us again with shameless persistence?

If, however, we wish to love something because it is good, why should we not rather love you, the immeasurable Good, [Col. 0298C] who claim our whole affection for yourself, so that we may love and praise your goodness? If we judge something worthy of our love because it has done so much for us, why should we not judge the same of you, who have done so many and such great things for us? If we consider your sufferings, you most worthily gave your soul for us, so that you might possess our whole soul.

There are infinite things, Lord, that compel us to love you, because everything you created proclaims your goodness. Those who do not perceive it in everything should attribute this not to you but to their own blindness. But since “the proof of love is the exhibition of works” (Gregory), the soul must conform itself so completely to your love that, just as you are toward it, so it may always strive to be toward you.

Especially in these matters. First, just as you always love, [Col. 0298D] so may it always love, and may it strive to show this to you by bringing all its affection into harmony with your will. There are four affections to which the others can be reduced: joy, sorrow, hope, and fear. The first two concern present or past things, and the other two future things. We ought therefore to order our affections toward you in such a way that we fear and grieve over everything opposed to you, and hope for and rejoice in whatever is honorable to you, driving all other affections from our hearts.

What benefit there would be in this, if only we avoided false and useless affections! Indeed, if a person truly examined himself according to these four affections whenever he felt some movement within him, [Col. 0299A] how would you deliver him, Lord? You alone know. For if we carefully observed the origin of our movements, we would often find that what we thought was virtue was vice, and that we are often hindered by what we believe advances us.

Second, just as you always keep us before your eyes, so we ought always to think of you as present. This compels us to keep all our thoughts, words, deeds, and conduct under the governance of discipline, since a bride would not dare to behave dishonorably in the presence of her bridegroom; rather, she would strive in everything to please him and seek counsel and help from him, so that in all things she might act according to his will. When we intend to please you in everything, we shall always have a secure conscience, even if something less useful [Col. 0299B] than you should incidentally intrude upon our intention.

Third, just as you always and continually serve us, performing or enduring all things so that we may not cease to exist—whether through others or in whatever manner—so no part of a good day ought ever to pass us by without our spending it in your service.

Fourth, just as you always protect us and guard us from every evil, whether through yourself or through your servants, so we ought carefully to withdraw ourselves from everything that could impede us in your service.

Fifth, just as your generosity never grows weary of giving, so we ought never voluntarily to fail in prayer.
