Sixth, just as you are always kind in forgiving, so we ought never to be so frightened by our failings that we do not immediately ask forgiveness after the fault. For when the human heart is distorted and in some way [Col. 0299C] alienated from you, it is much more prone to frivolities and to seeking false consolations outside than it was while it remained with you. Therefore the acquisition of forgiveness should not be delayed, lest a longer withdrawal make the return more difficult.

This is how we ought to be toward you, and we ought always to be tormented because we do not love you as much as we ought. How we ought to praise you, and for what we ought to give thanks, has been said above at the beginning. Grant us, Lord, to aspire with our whole desire to love and praise you, and to be tormented because we cannot do so worthily; and may this be for us the height of the cross we must take up.

The breadth of the cross is faithfulness, always tormenting and enlarging the spirit, so that it may subject every person to [Col. 0299D] your praise and service. This especially makes a person universal in prayer, compelling him, whatever he desires for himself or for certain persons dear to him—for he sees them as humble in a certain sense—to desire nothing human, but everything for the praise of your goodness.

Since faithfulness consists especially in prayer, we must consider how one who wishes to be heard ought to pray. He ought to pray wisely, ardently, humbly, faithfully, perseveringly, and confidently.

Wisely: so that he may pray for what is beneficial to your praise and to the salvation of his neighbors. If in certain matters we doubt whether they are beneficial—such as bodily health and similar things, which can sometimes harm and sometimes benefit—we should always pray for them conditionally, namely, if it is pleasing and honorable to you.

[Col. 0300A] Ardently—that is, devoutly, or at least earnestly—so that, when we clearly see what should be asked of you, we may ask it attentively from our heart, not in another’s words but in the proper words of our heart or mouth, since you understand and hear both equally.

Humbly: so that we trust not in our own merit but only in your grace. Although you have forgiven our sins and sometimes permit us to serve you, we must always consider ourselves as we have made ourselves by sinning, since by ourselves we can do nothing but evil.

Faithfully: so that in prayer we may offer ourselves to the lack of every joy and the endurance of every punishment that, through your help, may be turned to our benefit, so that when our desire is granted, our action may exalt your praise. But, Lord, will I deserve to offer myself to you in this way, when, [Col. 0300B] as wholly yours, I am bound to do so even if you should never wish to hear me?

Perseveringly: so that we never intend to cease desiring all that is praiseworthy and honorable to you. If some necessity should arise in us or in those dear to us, although we cannot always pray for it with constant intention, nevertheless we shall pray for it at times, with all the faithfulness of which we are capable, and thereafter entrust our desire to your will, always retaining our first faithfulness—not, perhaps, in act, but in disposition.

Confidently: so that at the end we may ask without hesitation.

There are seven reasons that compel us to trust in your goodness. First, because you give every just desire; and why would you give it unless you also wished to grant it? Second, because we wish to be heard not for our own benefit [Col. 0300C] but for your glory. Third, because the greater things you have done for us encourage us to trust you even concerning lesser things. For everything we can ask is far less than the fact that you graciously became incarnate and suffered for us. Fourth, because it is as easy for you to hear us in great matters as in small ones. Fifth, because consideration of your goodness urges us to this. Sixth, because we have you, Jesus Christ, as intercessor, and all the saints. Seventh, because you possess infinite goodness toward us.

For if the small love we have for you compels us to wish willingly to obey your will in everything, why should we not presume the same concerning your immeasurable love? Otherwise we would wish to appear [Col. 0300D] more faithful than you, if we were to present ourselves to you as such that we did not believe you to be toward us in return.

Thus, Lord, we shall pray, and for this reason we shall have confidence in prayer. Nevertheless, we shall be tormented because, by carrying this out worthily, we cannot draw and embrace every person in practice toward your praise; and this is the breadth of our spiritual cross.

## CHAPTER VI. On Perseverance in the Cross: “Daily”

The length of your cross ought to correspond to the whole of our life. Although we consider it pleasant to be with you, to praise you in your house, and to be absorbed in the abyss of your sweetness, may we nevertheless not grow weary of bearing your cross—that is, of being tormented [Col. 0301A] in this miserable life for the increase of your praise.

What is great, Lord, if I am with you in my homeland, where I am secure from every evil and have whatever I wish? Grant me, Lord, that the nails of the fear and misery of this life may never pierce me so deeply that I would prefer to descend, or at least to be taken down, from the cross before you, Lord, have commanded it. Nor would I desire you to have me taken down quickly from this cross; rather, may I always prefer to hang on the cross for your sake than to have you bury me secretly in these miseries. For you, Lord, neither descended from the cross nor asked to be taken down from it.

The will always to suffer for the increase of your praise will therefore be the length of the cross. “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23), and thus let him run through the middle of the way of perfection. If we take it up, Lord, [Col. 0301B] you yourself will carry it.

You indicate the end of the way of perfection—that is, perseverance in the will always to suffer for you—in the word “daily.” For if we wish to lay down the cross on a single day before you have commanded it, we do not take it up daily. But whoever perseveres until you take it down enters the tomb of eternal peace amid the abundance of your praise.

In this word we can also understand that, just as the torment endured for your praise falls away [Col. 0302A] through daily failing, so we ought to take up the cross daily by renewing our desire for your praise.

## CHAPTER VII. Explanation of the Final Words: “And Follow Me”

By what intention we should walk on this way, you indicate lastly when you say, “Follow me.” This can be understood both of bodily movement and of the mind. For many have followed you not only while bearing the cross but also while hanging upon the cross. Let us therefore follow you not only by the movement of good works but also by the intention of our hearts, so that we may consider not only by what works you went before us, but also with what intention you acted, and strive to follow you in this.

We find that in all your thoughts, [Col. 0302B] words, and deeds you principally sought the glory of your Father. Therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, direct our intention, so that in everything we may seek his glory and yours, denying ourselves, bearing the depth, height, breadth, and length of the cross, and persevering in it for your praise and glory. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0301B]

## TREATISE ON THE CONCEPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0301C]

*[Note: It has been collated with the Cluniac and Corbie manuscripts. The Cluniac manuscript begins: “Treatise of Blessed Anselm on the Conception of Blessed Mary the Virgin.”]* (G)

### Textual apparatus for the Treatise on the Conception

All notes below translate the supplied apparatus. Latin forms are retained where English cannot represent the textual distinction.

- **[Col. 0301C]** Cluniac: *Tractatus B. Anselmi De conceptione B. Mariae Virginis*, “Treatise of Blessed Anselm on the Conception of Blessed Mary the Virgin.” Corbie and Ray: *quae de conceptione … locis recolitur*, “which is commemorated in many places concerning the conception …”; Corbie: *a quibusdam praesentibus temporibus … celebratur*, “is celebrated by certain persons in the present times.”
- **[Col. 0301C]** Corbie has *Atque*, “And,” for *At*, “But”; *tandem*, “finally,” for *eamdem*, “the same”; *carentem*, “lacking,” for *vacantem*, “lacking/empty”; *vinculum*, “bond,” for the printed *ratione*, “reason”; and *quantum*, “how much,” for *quatenus*, “so that.”
- **[Col. 0301C]** Corbie: *non sine ratione*, “not without reason”; *in*, “in,” for *ex*, “from”; and *in peccatis concepta*, “conceived in sins,” for *concepta*, “conceived.”
- **[Col. 0303D]** Corbie: *latitudinem*, “expanse,” for *in huius mundi latitudine*, “in the expanse of this world”; *communicatur*, “is shared,” for *coleretur*, “would be venerated”; and the corrupt printed note *Domina rerum leg. puro Dominam nostram*: “Lady of things,” apparently read for *dominam nostram*, “our Lady.” The source calls that reading corrupt; no expansion is invented.
- **[Col. 0303D]** Corbie: *proficisci*, “to proceed,” for *proficientium*, “of those advancing”; omission of *gementium*, “mourning”; *enim*, “indeed,” for *tamen*, “nevertheless”; omission of *illorum*, “of those.” The edition: *nec magni ponderis est*, “nor is it of great importance,” for *non magni ponderis … videri*, “not to seem of great importance.”
- **[Col. 0303D]** Corbie: *videtur autem movere omnem*, “it seems moreover to move every,” for *videtur admonere*, “seems to admonish”; *testamenti*, “of the Testament,” for *Veteris instrumenti*, “of the Old Testament”; omission of *ita*, “so/directly”; *ipse*, “himself,” for *Dominus*, “the Lord”; omission of the second *ejus*, “his”; *tanti*, “of so great a thing,” for *ipsius*, “of it”; and addition of *et*, “and.”
- **[Col. 0303D]** Edition: *sacrarium*, “sanctuary,” for *seminarium*, “seedbed”; Corbie adds *et trinus*, “and triune.” Corbie: *testatur*, “testifies,” for *refert*, “reports,” and *emicuisse*, “to have shone forth,” for *enituisse*, “to have been conspicuous.”
- **[Col. 0303D]** Corbie and edition add *Virgo*, “Virgin”; both read *Deitatem illius*, “his Godhead,” for *divinitatis illius*, “his divinity.” Edition: *ita non*, “not thus,” for *non*, “not.” Corbie: *ita*, “thus,” for *hoc*, “this”; Corbie and edition: *ideo*, “therefore,” for *idcirco*, “therefore.” Edition: *multis fidelibus merito celebratur*, “is deservedly celebrated by many faithful.”
- **[Col. 0304C]** Corbie: *celebretur*, “may be celebrated,” for *ante ortum*, “before [her] birth.” Edition omits *vel conceptum*, “or conception.” Corbie and edition omit *haec*, “this,” before Isaiah; edition omits *Virgo*, “Virgin.”
- **[Col. 0304D]** Corbie and edition: *profundissima*, “most deeply,” for *perfudisse*, “to have flooded/poured over.” Edition: *praevidebat, perillustrasse*, “it foresaw, and illuminated throughout,” for *praevidebant, perlustrasse*, “they foresaw, and passed through/illuminated.” Corbie: *conceptio habitaculi fuerit*, “the conception was the foundation of the dwelling.”
- **[Col. 0305A–C]** Edition: *contraxit*, “contracted,” for *traxit*, “drew/bore,” and omits the Jeremiah quotation; Corbie and edition: *qui*, “who,” for *quia*, “because.” Edition: *olim*, “formerly,” for *omnium*, “of all,” and *magnitudinem*, “greatness,” for *magnificentiam*, “magnificence.”
- **[Col. 0305D–0306C]** Edition: *recipiatur*, “is received,” for *concipiatur*, “is conceived”; *creatis*, “you are created,” for *creabaris*, “you were being created”; *in tanta futura gloria*, “in such great future glory,” for *tanta futura*, “destined for such greatness”; *Dominium*, “dominion,” for *Dominum*, “lord”; and *talis tolleretur*, “such a one would be taken,” for *talis crearetur*, “such a one would be created.”
- **[Col. 0306C]** Corbie ends: *Explicit Anselmus de Conceptione B. Mariae Virginis*, “Anselm’s exposition on the Conception of Blessed Mary the Virgin ends.”

The beginning from which the salvation of the world proceeded comes before me as I wish to consider it: today’s solemnity, which in many places is made festive by the conception of blessed Mary, Mother of God. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript and Ray’s edition read: “which is commemorated in many places concerning the conception … .”]*

In former times it was indeed celebrated with more frequent observance, especially by those among whom pure simplicity and humbler devotion toward God flourished. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “by certain people of the present times … is celebrated.”]* But when greater learning and an exceptionally forceful examination of things filled and elevated the minds of certain persons, they removed the same solemnity from the midst, scorning the simplicity of the poor, and reduced it to nothing, as though it lacked rational basis. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “as though it lacked a bond.” It reads “And” for “But,” and “finally” for “the same.”]*

Their opinion grew especially strong because those who advanced it excelled in secular and ecclesiastical authority and in abundance of wealth. But while I was turning over in my mind both the simplicity of the ancients and the loftiness of the modern intellect, it occurred to me to place certain words of divine Scripture before us and, according to my understanding, to weigh with pious consideration what judgment they form concerning each matter, so that their authority might more clearly establish what should be attributed to what, and [Col. 0302C] what people like me ought to follow with more certain reasoning. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “how much” instead of “so that.”]*

Concerning the simple, it is found in the very words of Scripture that God speaks with them. But those whom much learning passes through without charity are said to be inflated by that learning rather than solidified by the integrity of true goodness. Since, then, God’s speech instructs the former, while their own learning distends the latter with a kind of windy vanity, those who do not fear to discern rightly which side should prevail—tell me, I beg you: should one yield more to the person clinging to conversation with God, or to the one swelling beyond measure with confidence in his own heart’s insight?

These men assert that it does not seem reasonable that any memory of the conception of the Virgin Mother should be made in the Church of her Son, since the beginning of her conception is sufficiently remembered in the nativity of her, which is celebrated festively everywhere; for, they say, she would not have been born if she had not been conceived. When she came into the light from the hidden place of her mother’s womb, it was clear that she had been conceived in her parent’s womb and formed into human shape. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “conceived in sins.”]* Since, therefore, the specifically formed composition of her body and [Col. 0303A] its manifestation in the expanse of this world are venerated by everyone, it would be superfluous to honor still that formless material which in many cases perishes and is destroyed before it fully passes into human form. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “which is shared.”]*

Having exercised this acumen of mind, they did not fear to abolish the feast of the conception of that most sacred Lady, which the simplicity of the ancients and their perfect charity toward our Lady had established, by the reasoning of the authority in which they took pride. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “which proceeds.”]*

Having seen, then, the reasoning of the eminent men who advanced the abolition of the feast of the Mother of God, let us also consider the charity of the simple who mourn the loss of so great a joy. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript omits “mourning.”]*

[Col. 0303B] They are simple, and perhaps they do not know how to give the answers they seek to the profound arguments of philosophers. Yet they say that, being founded upon devoted charity toward the Mother of the Lord, it does not seem to them a matter of great importance that everything bestowed upon her dignity or honor by human praise should be compared with her merits and distinctions. *[Note: The printed edition reads: “nor is everything bestowed upon her dignity or honor of great importance.”]*

Nevertheless, while the world everywhere venerates her distinctions with the devotion they deserve, they are somewhat astonished that it does not look with a pious eye upon the supreme origin of those distinctions. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript omits “of those.”]*

For the completion of such great benefits as have come through the Mother of the Lord to the whole creation seems to admonish every human mind, in an attitude of piety, to consider their beginning. The whole sequence of the Old Testament indeed reveals that she would come and become the Mother of the Lord. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “of the covenant” instead of “of the Old Testament.”]* But whether her imminent birth [Col. 0303C] was announced by some oracle or angel as directly as that of the Lord Christ, her Son, or of blessed John, the forerunner and baptizer of that same Son, or of those persons of whom, as is clear to nearly everyone, sacred history gives the fullest accounts, is not found in the divine page or in canonical Scripture. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “the Lord himself” instead of “the Lord Christ”; it omits the second “his Son.”]*

I confess that I cannot adequately consider what pleased the Holy Spirit, the dispenser of all things, in this matter. Nevertheless, I do not think it absurd or contrary to faith if the beginning of her conception is judged by the simple sons and daughters of the Church to have been so sublime, so divine, and so ineffable that no human mind, however perceptive, could rise to it. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “of so great a thing.”]*

[Col. 0303D] Nor is this surprising. For the foundation and, as it were, the seedbed of the city and dwelling of the highest Good was being laid in it; and the dwelling of eternal light, and the temple which the incorporeal, uncircumscribed, and created Spirit, who gives life to all things, would bodily inhabit, was being prepared. *[Note: The printed edition reads “sanctuary” instead of “seedbed”; the Corbie manuscript adds “and triune.”]*

Someone may perhaps say: Why should the conception of the future Mother of God be considered greater and more excellent [Col. 0304A] than the conception of the Son of God coming in the flesh? For, as the Gospel reports, the conception of the Son of God who was to become incarnate was foretold from heaven by an angel and understood by a human being. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “testifies” instead of “reports.”]* If, therefore, Mary’s conception is to be regarded as indicating something more excellent and surpassing human understanding, it seems reasonable that a more excellent glory and greater dignity shone forth divinely in her conception than in the conception of Christ the Lord. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “shone forth” instead of “was conspicuous.”]*

I do not say this. Rather, the Son of God, brightness of eternal light and himself inaccessible light, was about to receive the form of a servant and emptied himself, adapting his coming to human minds so that he could be received and understood; for if he had appeared coming in the essence of his divinity, no one could have received or endured him.

[Col. 0304B] Blessed Mary, however, who was to become the Mother of God, was to bear in an ineffable manner from her own substance him who is incomprehensible above all things and truly human; and thus she was to pass into union with his divinity. Therefore it may not unreasonably be believed that the beginnings of her conception were marked by such sublimity of divinity that the conception of human minds could not fully penetrate it. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript and the printed edition read “his Godhead” rather than “his divinity.”]*

Thus pure simplicity and humble purity of love toward God and toward his most beloved Mother do not hesitate to judge concerning the conception of that Mother of God. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “thus” instead of “this.”]*

And therefore, according to their judgment, the day of that conception deservedly ought to be celebrated by all the faithful with festive praises. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript and the printed edition read “therefore”; the printed edition has “is deservedly celebrated by many faithful.”]*

For it is certain that Isaiah, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke of her [Col. 0304C] many centuries before her birth or conception:

“A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse,  
and a flower shall rise from his root;  
and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him,  
the spirit of wisdom and understanding,  
the spirit of counsel and fortitude,  
the spirit of knowledge and piety,  
and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1–3).

*[Note: The Corbie manuscript and the printed edition omit *Haec* (“This”).]*

This shoot which produced such a flower from itself was, without dissent, the Virgin Mary; and the flower that rose from her root was the blessed Son, upon whom and in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwelt essentially.

This Virgin, therefore, the most worthy parent of so great a Son, when she was conceived in the womb of her parent according to the natural law, who would not grant that the Wisdom of God, reaching from end to end, [Col. 0304D] filling all things and ruling all things, poured a new and ineffable joy over heaven, earth, and all that is in them, and passed through them with ineffable exultation at their restoration—which they foresaw, through divine and hidden inspiration, would come to them through her? *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “Lady of things”; it also has “our Lady” where the text reads “that Lady.”]* *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “spread” instead of “passed through.”]* *[Note: The printed edition reads “which it foresaw, and made shine throughout” instead of “which they foresaw … would come to them.”]*

But since that conception, as we have said, was the foundation of the dwelling of the highest Good, what shall we say if it bore the stain of [Col. 0305A] some sin from the origin of the first transgression? *[Note: The printed edition reads “contracted” instead of “bore.”]*

The divine voice says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5). *[Note: The printed edition omits these words.]*

Concerning John also, the angel who foretold that he would be born asserted that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb (Luke 1:15). If, then, Jeremiah, because he was to be a prophet among the nations, was sanctified in the womb, and John, who was to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (ibid., 17), was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, who would dare to say that the unique propitiatory of the whole world, and the sweetest resting-place of the almighty Son of God, was deprived, at the very beginning of her conception, [Col. 0305B] of the illumination of the grace of the Holy Spirit?

Scripture bears witness: “Where the Spirit is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). She, therefore, was free from the slavery of every sin, she who was being built by the presence and operation of the Holy Spirit as the hall of propitiation for all sins, in which and from which he would personally become human. *[Note: The printed edition reads “formerly” instead of “every.”]*

But if someone declares that she was not entirely free from the sin of her first origin, since it is most certainly established that she was conceived from a lawful union of man and woman, this is the Catholic position. I do not wish in any way to dissent from the truth of the Catholic and universal Church. Nevertheless, while considering as best I can the magnificence of the works of divine power, as though through a kind of dimness of mind, I seem to see that if any original sin and common fault existed in her propagation, it belonged to those who propagated her, [Col. 0305C] not to the offspring propagated. *[Note: The printed edition reads “greatness” instead of “magnificence.”]*

Consider a chestnut by analogy. When it comes forth to be born from the tree of its own kind, its whole outer covering appears rough and surrounded on every side by dense, sharp spines. Inside, the chestnut is conceived: at first, a kernel of milky substance, containing nothing rough, nothing harsh, and nothing harmful through any spines. If it remains there for a time, it is nourished, fostered, and fed in complete gentleness; and when it has matured into its own form and condition, it emerges from the broken covering by nature entirely free from every prick and burden of the thorns. I call this to mind.

If God grants to a chestnut that it be conceived, nourished, and formed amid thorns without being pricked, could he not grant this to the human being whom he himself was preparing as his temple, [Col. 0305D] in which he would bodily dwell and from which, in the unity of his person, he would become perfect man, so that, although she was conceived amid the thorns of sins, she might nevertheless be made wholly free from the prick of those thorns? Certainly he could, and he wished to do so; therefore, if he wished it, he did it. *[Note: The printed edition reads “received” instead of “conceived.”]*

Indeed, whatever worthy thing he ever wished concerning anyone outside his own person, it would be wrong to suppose that he did not wish it concerning you, O most blessed of women. For he wished you to become his mother, and because he wished it, he made you so. As though one were to say: That Lord, Creator and governor of all things, [Col. 0306A] made you his mother; Lord, I say, of all things—not only of intelligible things but also of those transcending every intellect. He established you as lady and empress of heaven and earth, and thus you were and are lady and empress of the sea and of all the elements, together with everything in them. And in order that you might be such, you were created in your mother’s womb from the beginnings of your conception, with the Holy Spirit working. *[Note: The printed edition reads “created” instead of “you were created.”]*

So it is, good Lady, and we rejoice that it is so. Therefore, sweetest Lady, since you were destined for such greatness—for the unique Mother of the Most High and, after your Son, the wise and noble empress of all that was, is, or will be—[Col. 0306B] should you at your beginning have been such that you could have been subjected either to the impurity or to the dominion of any of those over whom we most certainly know that you exercise dominion? *[Note: The printed edition reads “in such great future glory” instead of “destined for such greatness.”]*

That champion of pure truth, whom your Son, now presiding in heaven, called the vessel of election, confesses that all human beings sinned in Adam. This is certainly a true judgment, and I declare that it is unlawful to contradict it. But when I consider the eminence of God’s grace in you, just as I contemplate you in an immeasurable manner not within all things but above all things that have been made, so I believe that at your conception you were not bound by the law of nature as others are, but were made entirely free from every association with sin through the singular and impenetrable power and operation of divinity.

For sin alone separated human beings from God’s side. And in order that the Son of God [Col. 0306C] might abolish it and thus restore the human race to pleasing God, he wished to become human—and such a human that there would be no agreement in him with that by which humanity was at variance with God. Since this therefore had to happen, it was fitting that the mother from whom such a one would be created should be pure from every sin. Otherwise, how could flesh be united to that supreme purity in so close a conjunction that the assumed human being would become one, so that the things belonging to God would belong equally to man, and the things belonging to man to God? *[Note: The printed edition reads “from whom such a one would be taken” instead of “from whom such a one would be created.”]*

*[Note: The Corbie manuscript ends here: “Anselm’s exposition of the Conception of Blessed Mary the Virgin is finished.”]*

Furthermore, imagine someone wishing to build a palace specially suited to his own uses, in which he himself would spend time more frequently and ceremoniously, and would respond with a gentler and happier countenance to all who needed his aid and assistance, helping them. Would he, I ask, tolerate at the beginning [Col. 0306D] a foundation of the palace that was weak, unsuitable for the structure to be built, and not properly joined to it? I do not think so, if he were wise and wished to bring his purpose to completion.

Therefore we hold with undoubted faith that Wisdom, before all ages, likewise purposed to build for itself a dwelling which it would inhabit specially. It has long been made known what this dwelling was: we confess [Col. 0307A] that it was the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, in which and through which that same Wisdom wished to be joined and incorporated with human nature, and to spare and show mercy to all who confess it with pure minds.

If, while that sanctuary—namely, the universal hall of propitiation—was being built with the Holy Spirit working, its foundation, that is, the beginning or origin of the formation of blessed Mary, was corrupt, then it certainly neither suited nor cohered with the structure itself.

Was the wisdom of God ignorant and powerless to make for itself a dwelling free from every stain of human condition? When other angels sinned, it preserved the good from sins; and was it unable to preserve the woman who was immediately to become its mother free from the sins of others? In the eternity of his counsel he firmly established that she would be the ruler and queen of the angels, [Col. 0307B] and now shall we believe that she was born lower than the angels and admitted into the fellowship of all sinners?

Let whoever wishes think this and prove it by his arguments. I, until God shows me that something more worthy of the excellence of our Lady can be said, continue to say what I have said; I do not change what I have written. For the rest, I entrust myself and my intention to her Son and to her.

Nothing is equal or comparable to you, Lady. Everything that exists is either above you or beneath you: above you is God alone; beneath you is everything that is not God. Who can look upon, or attain, such excellence as yours? And certainly, in order that you might reach this excellence, you were born in the lowliest place—that is, in your mother’s womb—in the utmost purity. If you had not been conceived and ordered in such a way, [Col. 0307C] you would not have grown to such height.

Whoever therefore rejoices and exults in the greatness of your growth ought reasonably to rejoice in the ordering of that growth itself. Whoever, then, removes from the Church of God the joy of your conception from the day of your blessed conception either does not pay proper attention, neglects to pay attention, or does not know the good that proceeded from it for every creature of God. *[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “let it be celebrated” instead of “removes … the joy.”]*

But who could explain the immensity of that good? I confess that I cannot. Such salvation is far from me and from those like me—that is, from sinners. Nevertheless, as I think, it may be perceived to some extent, as though in a riddle, if the evil into which human nature fell through Adam’s sin is set before the eyes of the mind, and the mind of one who wishes to consider it is then fixed upon the opposite of that evil—namely, [Col. 0307D] the good that came to the world through this Lady.

For humanity lost in Adam every good for which it had been created, and in Mary human nature recovered that same good in a far more excellent form. We know that there are two beatitudes and two miseries. One of these beatitudes and miseries is greater, the other lesser. The greater beatitude is the kingdom of heaven; the lesser is that which the first human being possessed before sin. The greater misery is the punishment of hell; the lesser consists in the continual tribulations in which we live.

We are completely ignorant by experience of those beatitudes, while through experience of miseries we feel ourselves weighed down everywhere: we groan beneath one and fear the other, lest it seize us. For [Col. 0308A] if we keep watch and apply our minds to considering the lesser misery, we can to some extent infer what the greater misery is, although it is far beyond what we can comprehend. We cannot easily perceive the nature of even the lesser beatitude except through the contrary misery in which we are.

Concerning the greater beatitude, I think it was said: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

We were therefore entirely separated from these beatitudes by the transgression of our first parent and made unhappily subject to both miseries. For through Adam’s sin death entered the world, and so passed into all human beings (Rom. 5:12); nor could anyone be freed from it before the coming of the Son of the holy Mary [Col. 0308B]. And what death? First, the death of the soul, by which humanity lost eternal life—namely, God, in whose likeness it had been made. Unhappy is the loss—loss of what is supremely and truly existent, without which nothing is ever possessed or exists well! This wretched death, incomparable to every evil, was also followed by the death of the body, through which the soul, having already lost the breath of heavenly life while dwelling in the body, perished, plunged into the much more miserable prison of hell.

No one existed who could escape this immeasurable condemnation, no one who could be freed from it; throughout creation the power of liberation belonged to no being. It remained with God alone, who had made humanity and against whom humanity had sinned. But who? He himself, the one offended, the one despised, was not worthily asked by anyone to spare; crimes multiplied day by day, and God’s anger was provoked more toward punishment than toward pardon. Yet he whose compassion cannot be exhausted, whose mercy cannot be emptied, whose goodness never fails, whose majesty accomplishes whatever it wills, determined to free the human being created in his likeness, lest humanity perish wholly in eternal condemnation. In an order more gracious than any other, he himself—who alone could accomplish this through himself—willed to become human, and not such a human as other human beings are, but so that he himself and the humanity assumed might be perfect God and perfect human being in one person, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.

But the whole of human nature had been corrupted and defiled at its root [Col. 0308D], and God cannot be joined to corruption and the vice of sin. It was therefore necessary that the nature from which he wished to make himself human should be both human and clean from every contagion of sin. He would not find such a nature, since, as I have said, nothing incorrupt remained when the root of all had been corrupted. Yet he who purposed to come to the aid of humanity’s ruin is called the power and wisdom of God. Thus he possesses the ability to do all that he wills, and there is no number to his wisdom, which reaches from end to end and orders all things (Wis. 8:1).

He could therefore make human nature, taken from the sinful mass, free from every stain of sin, so that he might assume it into one person of himself, being a complete human being without diminishing anything of his divinity. Predestined and preordained for this wondrous work [Col. 0309A]—superior to all the works of God and beyond description—was Mary: that most noble star of the great sea, that is, the illumination of the whole world; the unfailing relief and consolation of all who waver amid the storms of varied misfortunes; and also the secure aid and redemption of those who fear the destruction of eternal death and flee beneath her protection.

Would I therefore, O Lady, believe that you—whom divine power predestined and raised to so great a height, whom the wisdom of God, ordering all things, endowed with so many prerogatives, whom the ineffable mercy of all who are to be saved chose as its mother in order to come to the world’s aid—could at your conception have been burdened by the death of sin that, through the envy of the devil, took possession of the world? For as I consider again and again the very arguments I recalled above, my mind avoids believing this, my intention recoils from it, and my tongue does not dare confess it.

But if it is said that, had you been overtaken by bodily death before the birth of your blessed Son, you could not have escaped the law of original sin in the manner of other people, this is foolishly said and is not worth answering. For how could you have been preordained to become the Mother of God if God, who preordained you for this, had not brought you to it? In God there is no “is” and “is not”; in him there is only a simple “is.” Could death have been stronger than God, from whose hand no one can snatch anything?

But now, because you are so greatly esteemed by God above every creature that you deserved most worthily to become his Mother, just as he is not merely supremely chaste and clean but chastity itself [Col. 0309C] and purity itself, so you were to give birth in the flesh to a true human being and therefore ought by right to have been clean above all others. The beginnings of your creation ought accordingly to be venerated by the sons of holy Church, if they believe that they were holy and chaste, separated from every corruption and wrinkle of sin.

Let those who think otherwise believe what they judge better. I, O most merciful Lady, I, your insignificant little servant, know, believe, and confess that you came forth from the root of Jesse most beautiful and therefore alien to every wound of sin that could in any way disfigure you; and, remaining utterly pure, you brought forth the most beautiful flower. A flower, I say, you brought forth—not just any flower, but one upon whom the sevenfold Holy Spirit [Col. 0309D] rested, and whose fragrance of everlasting life and fragrance of eternal salvation, through the grace of his divinity, sprinkled and filled every creature.

Through him we are freed from the sin of our first parent and escape the death that entered the world through it. The flesh redeemed through the blood of that flower, namely, your only and beloved Son, now tramples underfoot—some already in reality, others in hope—the miseries by which all flesh was oppressed because of that offense. Through him, moreover, we are restored not only to paradise, from which Adam was expelled, but also, much more happily and worthily, we are brought into the kingdom of heaven, which he would not have possessed but was going to possess had he not sinned. For if he had not disobeyed God, the Son of God would never have become human; and in him, or for him, by suffering death and rising again, he would have entered the kingdom of heaven in the substance of our flesh [Col. 0310A] with the right to rule.

What glory, then, what honor, what jubilation of heart, what joy of mind, what security of eternal blessedness will belong to human nature when it sees him joined bodily to itself—him whom the whole army of heaven worships above them as the true God, ruling all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit, commanding all, consubstantial and co-omnipotent with his eternal Father? Human nature would never attain this glory, this possession of such great blessings, if God himself had not been born in human flesh for the expiation of Adam’s sin.

We shall therefore be in the kingdom of heaven much more happily and worthily than we would have been had Adam not sinned. And what will it be—perhaps someone [lacuna]—concerning the memory of the evils whose utterly complete abolition will prompt them to give unending thanks to him whom they will always have present, their most merciful Redeemer, whoever will be human beings there? For it is certain that everyone’s conscience will be disclosed to everyone—not only to human beings, but the consciences of angels and human beings to angels and human beings.

When, therefore, the cherubim and seraphim, thrones and dominations, and the other powers of heaven know in each person’s conscience their sins, and see themselves entirely innocent of such things, how will it be possible for them not to reckon those people thereafter more contemptible than they would have been had no such errors ever ruled over them? How, then, will they be happier and more worthy in the fellowship of the angels, whose contemptibility, in their own estimation, is named from their participation in Adam’s sin [Col. 0310C]? For sin is accompanied by unhappiness and unworthiness, whereas not sinning is accompanied by happiness and worthiness.

If anyone says this, he seems indeed to be guided by reason, but human reason. For one who considers heavenly things encounters a consideration different from these. Those angelic spirits, whose likeness all righteous human beings will attain after this age according to the Lord’s promise, will not consider what such people were, but what they are—even though these people will retain in their memory what they were, for the praise and glory of their Savior.

Certainly, if someone living in this mortal flesh had been struck by some serious illness—for example, leprosy—and his whole body swarmed with worms, so that he was horribly repulsive and stank terribly to all who looked upon him; if by some circumstance, such as the help of physicians or the regard of God who performs wonders, he had been restored to complete health, and this change became known to those who had previously known him, then those who had formerly loathed him, if charity remained firm in them, would desire to see him, speak with him, behold in him the grace of God, marvel at it, venerate it, and consider him worthy of double honor.

He himself, nevertheless, not forgetting his illness, would report it freely—even if others did not know of it—and with a certain enhancement of his own honor, so that it might be proclaimed that, first and above all, the grace of God, or the skilled knowledge of physicians, or his own perseverance, or the persistence of devoted prayers together with the long practice of good works, or the severity inflicted by those who treated him, had not turned aside from the desired outcome of health [Col. 0311A].

If, then, such things happen among human beings, what do you think happens in divine matters among those who are in a certain way like them? It is well known that sins, by which God’s countenance is offended, are wounds and putrefactions of the human mind. From where do they proceed except from the innate corruption of their condition? When this corruption has passed into incorruption, there will be nothing further that can grieve, nothing that can offend anyone, nothing that can offend the eyes of God, who sees all things.

There will therefore be peace between God and human beings, a peace enclosed by no end, severed by no circumstance, obscured by no offense. For he who is will himself be seen, and he will rejoice together in that same being and toward him, since nothing wholly other than what he is can exist apart from him.

[Col. 0311B]

My God, my God, teach my heart to understand what will happen there to all who have loved you here; who embraced your death as their life in the ordering of their ways; who clung to you by following your will through the keeping of your commandments. Truly, good Lord, according to the word of your blessed Apostle, you will eternally be the highest and most excellent of all good things in all things (1 Cor. 15:28).

And what good could be lacking to anyone who possesses you, who are the source and perfection of every good? How, then, will those beloved of yours who love you—by “angelic spirits” I mean those who rejoice with everlasting joy at the sight of your glory—how, I say, will they be unable to judge worthy of special honor, and love as themselves, those whom they see joined bodily to you and consubstantial with you in the form of humanity [Col. 0311C]?

How will they not embrace with immeasurable sweetness those whose wondrous power of mind, while they lived in mortal flesh, was so strong in subduing their desires for love of you that it becomes evident to every creature that you did not gratuitously become human, were born, suffered, and died for them? For they won you this praise: those whom, having become human on earth, you sought when they were lost, heard you, loved you, obeyed your admonitions, and came joyfully to you. Thus they showed that you had neither been deceived in your counsel nor suffered uselessly on their behalf.

I have therefore not said, Lord, altogether irrationally, as I judge, that they will be in your kingdom more worthily and happily than they would have been had Adam not sinned.

[Col. 0311D]

This dignity and happiness also present themselves to my consideration—things from which human nature would nevertheless have remained alien had the first human being, on account of his sin, not lost paradise.

When the multitude of human beings gathered in that kingdom of blessedness sees the Virgin Mary—who is today venerated and proclaimed blessed and blessed above all women, whom the supreme and almighty God took as his Mother and appointed to reign with him over all who come after her—standing at the right hand of her one and blessed Son, will it not judge its own condition, honored in her contemplation and presence, to be happy, joyful, and beyond what anyone could estimate?

I say, they will have before their eyes the Virgin sprung from their own stock, like themselves according to the condition of one nature, presiding over angels and archangels, ordering everything with her Son as queen of all, and embracing them with sweet affection, rejoicing with them over the glory bestowed upon her. And will it be possible for them not to exult immeasurably at this, not to celebrate with them in an ineffable joy of glorification?

Indeed, neither the most blessed of virgins nor the multitude of the elect would ever have risen to this dignity if the Son of God, in order to destroy Adam’s sin, had not descended from the Father’s bosom to assume humanity from that Virgin.

Thus Mary became Mother of God because of sinners. Since no one in the human race could be found chaster, holier, or humbler than she, she rightly ought to have been raised to such excellence by him than whom nothing is chaster, nothing holier, and nothing more sublime. And to what greater excellence could she have been raised than that, remaining perpetually a virgin, she should give birth from her flesh to God made flesh?

God conferred this excellence upon the Virgin Mary because he knew that in the purity of heart and body she clung to him above every creature. O happy clinging! O happy to cling to him who alone truly is, who alone supremely is, who never fails anyone who clings to him with an undivided heart!

Because you clung to him, pious Lady, as I have said, he also clung to you, and in a manner sweeter than any other possible. For what can be sweeter or more worthy between two persons than the relation of mother to son, or of son to mother? And both of these relations belong to you, as is clear to all.

But should these honors, these dignities, these joys—which the assembly of human beings mingled with the assembly of angels enjoys because of the transgression of the first human beings—be attributed to them? Should they thereafter rightly have been graciously granted to them? I do not think so. For they did not transgress God’s command with the intention that so many good things should proceed from it, but so that, despising God, they might proudly exceed the measure of their condition.

When they heard the devil say that they would become gods, they did not intend that the Son of God should one day become human from their stock in order to destroy the divinity by which they hoped to be exalted. Perhaps Eve thought she would immediately become God, and that Adam, consenting to her, would become a participant in her divinity.

O intolerable pride! O immeasurable folly! O vanity incomparable to every vanity! O Eve, how much nearer you would have been to true and supreme divinity if you had remained subject to God in the humility of your state!

For Adam, as the Apostle says, was not deceived in your transgression (1 Tim. 2:14), because he understood that what the serpent promised was a lie. But you, most wretchedly deceived (ibid.), and immediately steeped in the many seeds of perverse desires, enticed him by seductive eloquence to consent to you, foreshadowing in this deed of yours the truth of the future saying of the man of God: “Women make even the wise apostate” (Sir. 19:2).

For he had not yet been placed over you by God’s sentence, and therefore, to the destruction of yourself, of him, and of all our posterity, you prevailed through that womanly solicitation. For he obeyed your voice, setting aside obedience to the voice of God.

Woe to obey; woe not to obey; woe to obey a woman’s voice against the voice of God; woe not to obey God’s voice for the sake of a woman’s voice. This evil, this evil!

From this arose all the tribulations and miseries that the world has suffered, suffers, and will suffer. From this they were cast down; from this they lost strength and perseverance; from this came ignorance of every good; from this, knowledge and execution of every evil; from this, contempt of God; from this, the most abominable worship of demons under the form of idols; from this, the death of the present life; from this, that more miserable death, with the losses of the life to come.

Human nature therefore ought not to thank you because it has been so exalted and honored in the Son of God; rather, it ought indeed to blame you because through you it has been cast down and plunged into innumerable evils and into the double death of body and soul. Nor would there be any hope of escaping these great evils in any measure if that most beautiful flower had not begun to be born through the most glorious branch nobly sprung from the root of Jesse.

But he, born into the world in the order he willed, distributed gifts to his hearers, with the Holy Spirit resting upon him in the fullness of his graces; he powerfully led the world out of ignorance of the true good and of the other evils flowing from it, which it incurred through Adam; and he mercifully restored some already in reality and others in hope to the lost fellowship of the kingdom of heaven.

It is therefore clear what the human race owes to each one: what it owes to those by whom it was humbled and cast down to the lowest place, and what it owes to the one by whom it was exalted and glorified to the highest.

You, therefore, O Adam and Eve—you, you are accused. Your offspring imputes to you the evils it endures; with miserable lamentation it deplores that through you it was excluded from paradise and thrust into continual miseries—and not without reason. The cause is evident and cannot be contradicted.

What, then, O God of all, what would the work of your hands, made subject to everlasting punishments and eternal death through the transgression of these parents, have done if you had not come? If you had not come to its aid, where would it have fled, where hidden itself, where escaped? Certainly there would have been no counsel, no remedy, no protection anywhere. But you came and effectively showed how we might attain all these things.

If, therefore, those who came after your advent, Lord, are not saved, they have no one besides themselves against whom they may justly complain about it.

What, then, will they do? It seems to me, Lord, that the final and only counsel for all who wish to be saved is this: first to offer you heartfelt thanks for all your benefits, to love you, and finally to obey your commandments; and thus to hope with secure confidence that they will come to you.

But for this, merciful Father, who is capable? Certainly no one unless supported by your help. For you are the highest of all goods, indeed you are the highest good itself; and nothing good can exist, come to be, or be possessed except either from you, through you, or of you. No one, therefore, can do anything good without you.

You redeemed us, Lord, God of truth. Do not, because of our crimes, exercise against us the judgment of your severity [Col. 0314A]. You willed to become human for us; look upon us, so that we may be able to be what you became one of us in order that we might be. For what we ask is an honor to you if it comes to pass. If it does not, you will seem in some way to have failed in your purpose.

Yet we have no dispute with you, because you are Lord, and one word of yours is stronger than a thousand of ours. For if all our righteousnesses before you are like a menstruating woman’s cloth (Isa. 64:6), what will our injustices be when stripped bare before your face by themselves and by our enemies? Woe, woe! Who could disturb the confusion of mind emerging from this? Who could unfold the enormity of this terrifying horror? And if the enormity of confused horror and horrible confusion is now inexplicable to us, to whom will the strict examination of evils at the future judgment be tolerable [Col. 0314B]?

Alas, sinful human beings, whom all these evils touch through Adam’s stock—what shall we do amid them? Shall we despair? Far be it! What then?

O fountain of David opened for cleansing (Zech. 13:1), flow to us for the cleansing of the menstruous woman and advise what is expedient for us.

O compassion! Truly good Lord, I see, and seeing I rejoice; rejoicing, I embrace the counsel that, through your singular mercy, you have provided as more salutary for us. And what counsel, or of what kind? Surely, in mind, countenance, and voice, to return to her whom we mentioned above, your most beloved Mother, namely, our most merciful Lady; from the sweetness of whose contemplation, from contemplation of whose chastity, from consideration of whose dignity, and from reflection upon whose exaltedness we have reached these straits while recalling to mind certain things that must not be erased [Col. 0314C]; and to beseech her with pure devotion, so that she may advise us and come to our aid with the surpassing grace by which she surpasses all others with you.

Without doubt we know that she has such standing with you that nothing she wishes to accomplish could in any way be without effect. Our salvation therefore rests in her will, provided that what she wills she powerfully brings about.

What more salutary counsel could the Son of God, the end of all things, give us, whom the end of the age encompasses, than to run to her who gave birth from her flesh to that very one without whom there is no remission of sins, who is truly good, truly merciful, and truly willing to show mercy?

And you, Lady, to whose aid your most beloved Son sends us—what do you say to us [Col. 0314D]? For he himself is our mercy, and you are the mother of that same mercy. What, I ask, do you say to us?

Perhaps, Lady, that we should flee beneath the protection of his wings. Good. Yet although we gratefully embrace his mercy, as is fitting, we nevertheless fear his justice greatly. Therefore, lest he present his justice to those seeking mercy, we beg you: stand by us and plead our case for us.

The supreme Angel of the great counsel himself advised us to come to you. Certainly we acknowledge that we are sinners and deserve condemnation—and justly so; we do not deny it. But we equally confess that it is just that he should fulfill his will who does not refuse to agree with his own will in all that he does.

And who has ever been more in accord with his will than you, whose existence was never idle in fulfilling his will? Therefore, Lady, merely will that the most just Judge have mercy upon us. It will surely be just, with no reason standing in the way, that your will be fulfilled.

Do not, therefore, do not, because of the mercy of which you are proved to be the mother, fail us. For he who became our brother through you in order that we might be saved will not set aside your will in our salvation.

O wondrous work of the Creator! O immeasurable consolation of the sinner! O Lady, if your Son became our brother through you, have you not also through him become our mother? For, about to undergo death for us on the cross, he said this to John—indeed to John, who had nothing other than we have in the nature of his condition: “Behold, your mother” (John 19:27).

O sinful human being, rejoice, rejoice, and exult! There is no reason for you to despair; there is nothing for you to fear. Whatever is judged concerning you depends entirely on the verdict of your brother and mother. Do not therefore turn the ear of your heart away from their counsel.

Your Judge—namely, your brother—taught you to flee to the aid of his mother; and that same mother of yours urged you confidently to cling to the protection of her Son’s wings. Nor did she refuse to stand by you, lest you be burdened by his justice.

Mary, what shall we say? With what instrument of the voice, or with what jubilation of the heart, shall we express how much we owe you? Certainly, Lady, whatever we understand, whatever we conceive in our minds, whatever we utter with our mouths, is little—almost nothing—compared with what we owe you in equal measure.

For before every creature you were preordained in the mind of God: to bring forth the true God as human from your flesh, as the chaste one above all women; to reign gloriously as Queen of Heaven over all after your Son; and to prepare for the world, once lost, the way of restoration and the benefit of eternal life.

You restored the human race, stripped of the glory of eternity, to its former state through the virgin birth of your blessed fertility. You overturned the laws of hell by conquering through the death of your Son the prince of death. Finally, you displayed to all the visible and propitiatory God and Lord whom they did not know.

Through you, Lady, we recovered lost life in your only-begotten Son. Through you we are, if we are anything good; through you we can do or possess anything good; through you, whoever we are who are destined to reach eternal glory, we shall reach it [Col. 0315D]. After God, you are our supreme and singular consolation. You are our happy and blessed glorying; you are our guide and conveyance to the kingdoms of heaven. We ask you: be in that heavenly kingdom of blessedness our receiver and our perpetual exultation.

Therefore, in accordance with the blessed and merciful counsel of the special mercy—namely, your sweetest offspring—we flee to you. See to it that we have not done this in vain. For in truth, if you fail us, nothing will be secure for us.

Do not therefore attend so exclusively to our injustices that you set aside your mercies, with which you have been endowed above all others until now. You are eternally joined to him who is supremely all things and cannot in any way be changed from what he is; therefore we ask you not to be other than the one we most certainly know you to be in your perpetual mercy, which you have hitherto shown toward all.

And certainly, Lady, it does not become you to differ from the will of your Son, who never ceases to display himself before his Father’s face as a participant in our nature, in order to have mercy on the human race. And what else is this display of our nature than an ineffable incitement of compassion, calling forth his mercy upon us?

For the Father himself testifies that he was well pleased in him; and it cannot be that he does not have mercy on those upon whom he wishes to have mercy. The supreme Father therefore wishes to have mercy on the sharers in his Son; and the Son himself presents them before his Father’s merciful gaze in place of himself.

Would you, the one Mother of that one Son of God, drive away from the breasts of your mercy [Col. 0316B] those whom, as I have said, both the Father of the Son and the Son himself call and recall into the bosom of your grace?

Would you be angered against us because of our iniquities when your Son, whom we have offended most gravely, surrendered himself to death to erase our iniquities? Would you be more severe toward us than he, when you share the same condition as we do—exceeding your own nature, Lady?

Perhaps you love God’s justice against those who sin against him so greatly that you would rather have him exercise vengeance than display mercy. But if that is so, Lady, why did you once reply in a gentle voice to someone greatly in need of your help and unaware of what you were, calling yourself the mother of mercy rather than of justice, when your Son is no less true and unchanging justice than true and desirable mercy?

Perhaps you did so because, if you called yourself the mother of justice, you would remove hope of pardon not only from the one whom you knew to be in distress and in need of every mercy, with the severity of justice set aside, but also from us, your poor ones; and you would in some way close the door of singular refuge to those fleeing as enemies from the cruel persecutor of the human race.

For who, undergoing God’s judgment, would not be crushed like a garment, devoured more thoroughly than by a moth? Therefore, merciful Lady, sweet and most gracious Mother of the Lord, consider the grave necessity of our frailty, and show by your action that you are what you have recognized yourself to be in joyful affection. If you do this, you will undoubtedly be in accord with your Son and his Father in saving us.

For your most kind Son desires our salvation, and to make it unchangeable and eternal he clothed himself with our momentary mutability, taking on our nature. His truthful and most just Father is so pleased with him in all things that he wills nothing of what he understands him to will.

Therefore, will only what he himself wills, and nothing will remain that can obstruct our salvation. But it is impious even to imagine that you do not will what God wills.

Rejoice, therefore, and exult, human nature! For Christ, the Son of holy Mary, prepared every prosperity for you when, for your sake, he created himself from her in the truth of your substance.

Lady, Lady, forgive and have mercy, I beg you, forgive and have mercy, because I, an insignificant little man and truly a great sinner, dared to meditate upon you with this impure heart, to utter these things with my foul mouth, and to write them with polluted fingers [Col. 0317A].

For you know, merciful Lady, that I presumed to do this because I confess myself to be such that I do not judge myself worthy of either heaven or earth. Therefore, in the greatest anxiety, I would strive, if I could in any way, to the extent that God might look upon me with some regard for his mercy, and kindle in me even a small affection of holy love toward the sweetness of your kindness.

For I trust that, if you did this, his mercy and your aid might perhaps rescue me from the punishments of hell that I have deserved. Therefore, Lady, do not be indignant with me as though I were bold and presumptuous. If anything of this kind seems to be present in these words, my grave necessity compelled it, and your great goodness, proved by the whole world, prompted it.

The final and highest intention of my prayers is this: even if, at the last judgment of your most just Son, he should, with mercy removed, hand me over by a severe sentence to the cruel torturer for condemnation, come to my aid; meet me as I am dragged to hell; and, protecting me beneath the mantle of your most merciful defense, rescue me so that I may not be damned forever [Col. 0317B].

Indeed, Lady, I remember that this was once done for little children—and perhaps for me, if I am not mistaken—by married women when the children were being dragged to receive blows from their schoolmaster. Some people were greatly grateful to those women for this, and loudly praised the compassion by which they brought about their pious liberation.

If, then, a favor so small received such praise, with what praises, I ask, will you be proclaimed by the citizens of heaven, who rejoice in the salvation of sinners, when you have shown mercy to me, a great sinner, as I have said?

Certainly your blessed and good Son, the Lord Jesus, says that there is joy in heaven among the angels of God over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance (Luke 15:7, 10). Since, then, there is joy in heaven over one who repents, because by regretting his evils he advances toward salvation, what joy will there be, Lady, when someone freed from every evil reaches salvation itself?

If, therefore, you free me from the punishments I have deserved and make me a participant in eternal salvation, you will greatly gladden the whole court of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, most merciful Lady and Mother, do not regard the enormous enormity of my crimes as so important that you set aside the magnitude of the joy of the angels who rejoice together in their remission [Col. 0317D].

Lady, Lady [Col. 0318A], I am utterly ignorant of what I shall become or what I shall do. Therefore, whatever is to happen concerning me, I beg you, by the most merciful love with which you love your only Son, do not consign this present petition to oblivion: transfer me, a sinner, from the lot of the author of death into the portion of eternal life.

And you, the singular protection of all who flee to you, true and only Son of this most chaste Virgin, my Lady, I ask you, by the love with which you love that sweetest Mother of yours, to let me at some time experience in fact what I ask to be bestowed upon me through that same most merciful Mother of yours—though my affection is lukewarm and of whatever quality it may be.

But if the multitude of my crimes has raised your justice more strongly to condemn me than the piety of your Mother has inclined your mercy to spare me, you who are present everywhere and equally powerful in every place, find for me some obstacle of your protection in which I may be hidden from my enemies. Do not let me, made the prey of demons, be thrust into the depths of hell’s evils.

And if I deserve to be heard in nothing, at least, once placed in hell, do not allow me to be deprived of the memory and knowledge of your holy name, lest, becoming like Satan and his companion, I reproach your justice and thus bear the examination of your equity more heavily through the obstinacy of perverse murmuring.

Good Lord, good Lord, if in all these things you close the ears of your mercy to me, I truly do not see what more I can ask that might bring me the generosity of your mercies. This ignorance, of course, comes to me from the multitude of my iniquities.

For if I were not wrapped in the dense darkness of those iniquities, you, who are unfailing light, would not fail me; rather, you would drive away the darkness of my ignorance with a ray of your brightness. Thus, established in your light, I would see that you are not a God who wills iniquity (Ps. 5:5), and yet I would know that you possess, and are able, with a merciful will, to aid in immeasurable ways those overcome and oppressed by misery and iniquity.

And this, Lord, I most firmly believe to be so; therefore I hold it in my inmost heart and confess it with my mouth: whatever you do with me, whatever burden of evils you press upon me, you are not drawn into these things by any taint of injustice.

So, when our sins have been erased and forgiven, be toward us, because of the sweet love of your most beloved Mother, such that [lacuna].

[Note: Some things are missing here.]

[Col. 0318D] that the Virgin gave birth to a true human being from the substance of her flesh. Amen.

[Col. 0319]

SERMON ON THE CONCEPTION OF THE BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0319A]

Let your affection hear me as I recount how the conception of the venerable Mother of God, the perpetual Virgin Mary, was declared worthy of celebration through many manifestations of signs in England and France and in the other regions of the world.

At the time when divine mercy was pleased to correct the English people for their sins and bind them more closely to the duties of His service, the most glorious duke of the Northmen, William, subdued that same country by war. This William, who at that time became king of the English, reformed for the better, by God’s power and through his own diligence, all the honors of ecclesiastical dignity. The devil, the enemy of every good thing, envying the works of his pious purpose, often tried to obstruct his successes, sometimes through the deceitfulness of his household, sometimes through the attacks of outsiders [Col. 0319B]. But with the Lord protecting him and glorifying the king who feared Him, the wicked one was brought to nothing (Ps. XIV, 4).

When the Danes heard that England had been subjected to the Northmen, they were deeply indignant. Deprived, as they supposed, of their hereditary right, they prepared weapons and outfitted a fleet, intending to approach them and expel them from the homeland divinely granted to them. When the most prudent William learned of this, he summoned and sent to Denmark a certain religious abbot, Helsin, of the monastery of Ramesey, to investigate the truth of the matter. That man, being of keen intelligence, vigorously carried out the king’s business.

When he had faithfully completed it and wished to return to England, he put out to sea. After he had already crossed most of the sea with a favorable wind, suddenly dense winds arose everywhere [Col. 0319C]; a dreadful storm disturbed both sky and waves. The sailors, exhausted and no longer able to resist, their oars broken, their ropes snapped, and their sails falling, lost hope of safety and miserably awaited nothing but the disaster of drowning.

And when, despairing of the safety of their bodies, they commended only the salvation of their souls to their Creator with great cries, and devoutly called upon the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, refuge of the wretched and hope of the despairing, behold, they suddenly saw near the ship a man of extremely venerable appearance, adorned with a bishop’s mitre, as though standing amid the waves. Calling the abbot Helsin to him, he began to address him in these words:

“Do you wish,” he said, “to escape the danger of the sea? Do you wish to return safely to your homeland?”

When the abbot replied with tears that he desired this with all his heart and awaited nothing else, the other said:

“Know that I have been sent to you by our Lady, Mary the Mother of God, whom you have sweetly called upon. If you are willing to obey my words, you will escape the impending danger of the sea safely with your companions.”

He immediately promised that he would obey him in everything if he escaped that shipwreck [Col. 0320A].

“Promise,” said the other, “to God and to me that you will solemnly celebrate and preach for celebration the day of the conception and creation of the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“But,” replied the most prudent man, “which day is to be celebrated for this feast?”

“On the sixth day before the Ides of December,” he said, “you shall keep this feast as a solemnity.”

“And,” asked the abbot, “what office shall we use in the ecclesiastical service?”

“All the office,” he replied, “that is said at her Nativity shall be said at her Conception, except that the word ‘nativity’ shall be changed to the word ‘conception.’”

After these words, the figure disappeared. The storm was calmed sooner than one could say, and the abbot, unharmed, swiftly reached the English shores with a favorable wind. He made known what he had seen and heard to all whom he could. He also established that the same feast should be celebrated in the monastery of Ramesey [Col. 0320B], and celebrated it himself with devout observances for as long as he lived.

Therefore we also, dearest brothers, if we wish to reach the harbor of salvation, shall celebrate the Conception of the Mother of God with worthy observances and offices, so that we may be rewarded with a fitting recompense by her Son.

This solemnity is also related elsewhere in another way. In the time of Charles, the most illustrious king of the Franks, a certain cleric, a deacon by rank and brother of the king of Hungary, loved the Mother of Jesus with all his heart and diligently sang her hours. At the advice of his parents, wishing to marry a very beautiful young woman, he received the nuptial blessing from a priest. One day, after Mass had also been celebrated, he remembered that on that day he had not sung the hours of the same most blessed Virgin according to his usual custom. Sending the bride home, he compelled everyone to leave the church and remained alone beside the Virgin’s altar.

As he was singing the hours of the Lady, and was reciting the antiphon, “You are beautiful and lovely, daughter of Jerusalem,” the Virgin Mary suddenly appeared to him with two angels, holding his right and left hands, and said:

“If I am beautiful and lovely, why do you abandon me and take another bride? Am I not exceedingly beautiful? Am I not more beautiful than she? Where have you seen anyone so beautiful?”

Stupefied, he replied:

“My sweetest Lady, your splendor surpasses all the beauty of the world. What do you wish me to do, my Lady?”

She said:

“If, for love of me, you abandon the earthly bride to whom you wish to cling, you shall have me as your bride in the heavenly kingdom. And if you solemnly celebrate each year, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, the feast of my Conception, and preach that it should be celebrated, you shall be crowned with me in the kingdom of my Son.”

After these words, the blessed Virgin disappeared. The cleric refused to go home and, without consulting his parents, went to an abbey outside that country [Col. 0321A]. There he was clothed in the monastic habit. After a short time, by the merits of blessed Mary ever-Virgin—who always adorns and blesses those who love her—he became bishop and patriarch of Aquileia. He diligently celebrated the feast of the Blessed Virgin’s Conception on the aforesaid day, with its proper octave, every year for as long as he lived, and preached everywhere that it should be celebrated.

Another miracle of this feast is also proclaimed elsewhere through the inspiration of divine grace. In the Gallic sea, a certain canon, a priest by rank, who was accustomed to sing the canonical hours of the Blessed Virgin Mary, was returning from a village where he had committed fornication with another man’s wife. As he made his way toward the town where he lived and wished to cross the Seine, he entered a boat alone and began to sing the hours of the Lady while sailing [Col. 0321B].

When he was reciting the invitatory, “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you,” and was already in the middle of the river, behold, a great crowd of demons plunged him into the depths of the sea together with his little boat, seized his soul, and carried it off to torment.

On the third day, the Mother of Jesus came to the place where the demons were tormenting him, accompanied by a great host of angels, and said to them:

“Why are you tormenting the soul of our servant so unjustly?”

“We ought to have it,” they replied, “and rightly, because it was caught in our works.”

The Mother of Jesus said to them:

“If it ought to belong to the one whose works he was doing, then it ought to belong to us, because he was singing our Matins while you killed him. Therefore you are all the more guilty, since you have acted wickedly against me.”

After these words, the demons scattered here and there and fled. Blessed Mary restored the soul to the body, seized the man, raised from both deaths, by the arm, and commanded the water to stand like a wall on his right and left. Thus she led him safely from the depths of the sea to the harbor.

Rejoicing, he fell at the feet of the Blessed Virgin and said:

“My dearest Lady, beautiful Virgin, most pleasing to Christ, what shall I give you in return for the many benefits you have bestowed upon me? You have delivered me from the lion’s mouth and from the most grievous torments of hell.”

The Mother of Jesus said to him:

“I beg you, do not fall again into the sin of adultery, lest your last error be worse than the first. I ask you again that henceforth you devoutly celebrate each year, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, the feast of my Conception, and preach everywhere that it should be celebrated” [Col. 0321D].

As soon as the Blessed Virgin Mary had said this, she ascended into heaven before his eyes. He himself thereafter led the life of a hermit and recounted what had happened to him to all who wished to hear. For as long as he lived, he solemnly and devoutly celebrated that feast of the Conception and preached that it should be celebrated.

And we, dearest brothers, by our archiepiscopal authority confirm and command that none of us should be so despairing because of temporal affairs or his own sins that he does not celebrate the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary every year. For just as her Nativity is exalted in the holy Church, so her Conception ought to be exalted; for unless she had been conceived, she would never have been born. Just as her Nativity was once necessary for the salvation of the human race, so was her Conception necessary; by God’s command she is conceived and born. Therefore, if the divine reasoning is considered, it is approved that the day of her spiritual conception is greater than that of her nativity.

It was a greater deed for God to create Adam than for Adam’s sons to be born from a mother; it is not surprising that a human being is born from a mother through God. Let those foolish men therefore be thoroughly ashamed who, blinded by the darkness of ignorance, reject the celebration of such great sacraments and mysteries because the union of man and woman took place in the Virgin’s conception. If her conception does not please fools to celebrate today because it was carnal, nevertheless let it please them to celebrate today that worthy day and night—though unknown to many—and the time and hour of her spiritual conception, when the Creator of souls Himself, with angels ministering, joined the soul of His mother, worthy and most holy, to her virginal body [Col. 0322B].

The arranger of our salvation made that day the first of our restoration and salvation among all days, chose it, and sanctified it.
