For there are two conceptions of a human being, as all learned people know: one, by which the carnal union of man and woman takes place; the other, by which a new and pure soul, through God’s action, is divinely joined to a body. If it does not please someone to celebrate the carnal conception of the Mother of the Lord, let it at least please him to celebrate the spiritual creation of her soul and the joining of her body with her soul.

O how great is that day on which the soul of our Restorer is created and sanctified and united to her most holy body! He is not a true lover of the Virgin who refuses to honor the day of her conception.

Let the mad be ashamed once again who do not wish to honor this day because the holy Church is not accustomed to honor the conceptions of other saints. For it is the height of rusticity to compare her in this matter with other saints, since God assumed human flesh in her and exalted her above all the angels and archangels in heaven. Although the day of the conception of other saints has not been granted to them for celebration, it has nevertheless been granted by the Holy Spirit to her, who is greater and more excellent than all.

Beautifully and fittingly she ought to have dominion over the other saints, through whom all the saints are sanctified. For Christ is called the Holy One of the holy, and she the Holy One of the saints. And just as the supreme Disposer of all things granted her, beyond all precedent, the dignity that the Virgin should conceive and bear the Word made flesh and remain a virgin after giving birth, so He Himself, beyond all precedent, granted her above all others this dignity: that we should celebrate in the holy Church the most sacred solemnities of her Conception and Nativity.

What more need be said? To honor the Conception of the Mother of the Lord is to commemorate the generation of Christ, for her conception is the line of Christ’s generation. Therefore, on that day, as at the Nativity of the Lord, we properly sing the Gospel, “The Book of the Generation” (Matt. I, 1), before the praises of Matins, and read it at Mass. Rightly, then, both the generation of the Son and the conception of the Mother are honored, since the conception and nativity of the Mother are the generation of the Son.

Let us therefore, dearest ones, celebrate today with worthy offices both of her venerable conceptions, namely, the spiritual and the human, so that through her merits and prayers we may deserve to be rescued from worldly [Col. 0324A] cares and from all evils and led to eternal joys, through our Lord Jesus Christ, her Son, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0323A]

## MIRACLE OF THE CONCEPTION OF SAINT MARY

*(From the Gem. Metz manuscript, c. 40. [Col. 0323D] In the same manuscript, written in the same hand, several other miracles wrought through the prayers of the Blessed Mary are found; they are no more credible than these. Among them is one concerning a religious abbess who, after violating her resolve of virginity and chastity and becoming pregnant, poured out prayers to the Blessed Mary and was delivered by angels assisting at the birth.)*

[Col. 0323B]

At the time when William, the most powerful duke of the Normans, had struck down Harold, king of the English, and had subjected the English to himself by vigorously defeating them in war, a certain abbot named Elsinus was residing in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Augustine, the apostle of the English. In that church the bodies of Augustine himself and of the other archbishops who succeeded him rest.

This Elsinus, promoted for certain reasons to the Church of Ramesey, served the Lord Jesus Christ with the greatest devotion and venerated His Mother with equal devotion by rendering her service. It happened that, when the king of the Danes heard of Harold’s death and the subjection of the English, he hastened to come to England and subject it to his rule, overthrowing William, the new king, whom he called an invader of that land, so that he might possess it forever [Col. 0323C].

When William heard this, he prepared to defend himself. He gathered a great many soldiers from the surrounding regions and, being shrewd, vigorously fortified the cities and castles and filled them most abundantly with everything necessary. After taking counsel, King William sent to Denmark the vigorous abbot Elsinus, whom we mentioned above, to investigate carefully their plans and actions and, as far as he could, prevent their arrival in England.

Having boarded a vessel, he came to Denmark with a favorable wind and presented himself to the king of that country. He offered greetings, gifts, and services on behalf of King William. Then he investigated everything as he had been ordered, never ceasing to ask what they were saying and how they were preparing to act [Col. 0323D]. When he had most vigorously completed everything for which he had gone there, and had burdened the nobles of the land with gifts and promises, he wished to return to England, but the king of Denmark permitted him to return with him. He immediately boarded the ship with his companions. They gathered the ship’s fittings, spread the sails into the open sea, and directed their course across the roaring waters.

As they proceeded over the depths of the sea, an opposing wind rose against them, stirred the sea from its foundations, and filled all [the men—word obscured in the transmitted text] who were in the ship with fear [Col. 0324B]. Broken and exceedingly terrified by fear of death, they poured out prayers to God with tears and miserably lamented that they had gravely sinned.

While they were placed in such great danger, still greater perils confronted them: they saw shoals before their eyes, which sailors call *scamma*. Then, more anxious and uncertain, as though already placed in death, they cried out more fervently to God:

“O most merciful God, Father of mercy, deign to look upon us, sunk because of our crime. Look upon us, most merciful one, from the seat of your glory; visit us, now placed in the utmost danger of life. Let your grace be present now! Let your kindness be present! Let your supreme goodness be present! Let good gratuitous gifts be present! Come to the aid of us wretched ones, O ineffable compassion, lest hell now swallow us for our sins.

“Merciful God, we acknowledge that we have grievously sinned and deserved worse things, because we have sinned greatly. May your kindly grace forgive those who confess; we confess our crimes—erase them by your grace. You promised that the wretched would immediately be saved at the hour when they groaned and their hearts repented. Spare us now as we confess; have mercy on us who groan; have mercy now on us who weep and truly repent.

“Mary, Mother of the Lord, pray for us wretched ones. O Lady, commend our lives to your Son. Our miserable bodies have been handed over to the sea; may your Son receive our souls into rest.”

As they cried out in desperation, they saw someone standing beside the ship, clothed in episcopal garments. He addressed the abbot Elsinus by his own name and said:

“O Abbot Elsinus, come, rise, and speak with me.”

While everyone wondered what sort of person this might be, Abbot Elsinus rose. The aforesaid figure, angelic, as we believe, then said to him:

“If you wish to escape safely, if you wish to evade death, if you wish to see your homeland and visit your own hearths, promise most faithfully to the most merciful Mother of Christ that you will celebrate the solemn feast day of her Conception, on which that incomparable Virgin, destined to become the Mother of God, was conceived in her mother’s womb. Teach whomever you can that they should celebrate the most solemn day of this feast” [Col. 0325A].

Then Abbot Elsinus, being most prudent, immediately replied:

“How shall I do this, when I am completely ignorant of the day on which I should do it?”

The messenger of God answered:

“The sixth day before the Ides of December is the most celebrated day of this Conception. I urge you to celebrate it, and tell those to whom you can speak, and those who wish to know, that it should be celebrated.”

Then Abbot Elsinus asked:

“And what service do you command us to use on this feast?”

The divine messenger answered him without delay:

“All the service that is said at her Nativity is also said at her Conception. Thus, wherever the Nativity is said at the Nativity, ‘Conception’ is said at this celebration.”

[Col. 0326A]

After the aforementioned abbot had heard these things, he gave thanks to God and most devoutly vowed that he would keep what he had heard commanded by divine authority. As soon as he made this vow, the storm subsided and calm returned.

With a favorable wind, therefore, they returned and came joyfully to England. He also established in the Church of Ramesey, over which he presided as abbot, that this feast should be solemnly celebrated every year on the sixth day before the Ides of December, and he most devoutly invited many people to celebrate it.

May peace and long life be granted by the Son of that Virgin, our Lord Jesus Christ, to those who celebrate this solemnity, and after the passing of this life may eternal rest be granted them. Amen.

The miracle of the Conception of Saint Mary ends here.

[Col. 0325A]

## PASSION OF THE HOLY GUINERUS, FINGAR, PIALA, AND THEIR COMPANIONS

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Collated with the Victorine manuscript M M M. 18, in which there is no division into chapters.]

[Col. 0325B]

You faithfully ask, dearest one, that the remarkable life of the holy martyr Guinerus and his companions, which you formerly retained in brief notes, and the triumph of their victory, be explained to you in fuller speech. I earnestly desire to comply with your devotion in a devoted spirit. And although I may not do so worthily, as the greatness of their mighty deeds demands, I shall nevertheless apply myself to the praises of the saints as far as my ability permits, since the praise of the soldier is the glory of the emperor, and when the virtues of the saints are recounted, the glory of Christ is proclaimed.

Devotion therefore promises what learning denies, and the faith of the saints promises what ability does not; I shall presume everything from their merits. Nor shall I be ashamed of the poverty of my eloquence, since the one who chose uneducated men and fishermen to proclaim His glory has shown with certainty that the kingdom of God does not consist in the polish of speech.

[Col. 0325C]

## CHAPTER I. Saint Patrick’s preaching in Ireland and the conversion of Prince Fingar

The glorious and everywhere-praised confessor of the Lord, Patrick, was engaged in holy deeds in the regions of Cornwall when he was warned by an angelic voice to go to the island of Ireland to preach the faith of Christ there. Then the faithful and prudent servant, having learned this through a vision from the Lord, rose without delay and sought the place assigned to him by God, fearing in no way the savagery of the barbarous and unbelieving people.

When his arrival had been foretold and made known by rumor, the seven kings of that already-mentioned island came to meet the saint, together with the priests of the idols, the nobles, and a very considerable multitude of that people. The saint of the Lord, sound in faith and full of devotion, approached them and began confidently to preach the Gospel of Christ and to proclaim salvation in Jesus.

But just as a vessel full of wormwood does not admit the sweetness of another liquid unless its bitterness has first been driven out, so those men, still full of a proud spirit, refused to receive the teaching of salvation. Seeing his humility and observing the lowliness of his clothing, but not the treasure hidden within, they utterly despised the holy and truly apostolic man.

Among the kings already mentioned there was one nobler and more powerful than all the others, named Clito. He had a young son of good character, named Fingar, known in advance by divine election and already filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Of all the others, Fingar alone rose to meet Saint Patrick, received the man of God with whatever honor he could offer, and yielded to him, making him sit in the place where he himself had been seated.

[Col. 0326C]

## CHAPTER II. Fingar and his companions exiled for the faith

His stern father, angered and greatly inflamed against his son, saying that he intended to abolish the worship of their gods and introduce through Saint Patrick the new law of the Christians, expelled him from the kingdom and made him disinherited from his paternal land.

Several young men born of the nobility of Ireland, joined to him by the sweetest affection, departed together with him as fellow exiles and, traveling by land and sea, reached Lesser Britain. When the ruler of Britain heard that new settlers had arrived in his land, he ordered them to be brought before him [Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscript reads “he perceived that they were brought before him,” rather than “he ordered them to be brought before him”]. Carefully investigating who they were, for what purpose and from where they had come, they replied that they had been driven out of Ireland. After seriously explaining the reason for their banishment, they asked him, in his clemency, to grant them a place to live in his province [Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscript reads “if in the province,” rather than “in his province”]. [Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscript reads *sua locum atque* (“a place in his [province] and”) rather than *sua locum habitandi atque* (“a place in his [province] to live and”).]

When the ruler learned of the young men’s noble character and also recognized the cause of their exile, he granted their request with the greatest generosity. He gave them as much land for habitation as one man could ride through in a day, and ordered that they be held in honor. In particular, he judged that Fingar should be honored.

Having thus obtained the Lord’s grace in all things, they were loved by everyone and honored by everyone. From then on they began to live familiarly with the native inhabitants as new guests.

## CHAPTER III. The occasion of Fingar’s withdrawal from the world

But when the providence of the most high God wished to attach His recruit Fingar more closely to His service, He separated him from the world by the following means.

One day, when Fingar had gone out hunting with his companions, they found a stag and set the dogs upon it. As the animal fled with the speed customary to its kind, while the dogs harassed it relentlessly, Fingar alone pursued it with the dogs, leaving his companions behind.

What more need be said? He caught and killed the stag; then, stripping off its hide and cutting the flesh into pieces [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript reads *frustratim* rather than *frustatim*], he placed it upon his horse, intending to return to his companions, who had lost him when the mist covered them.

When he wished to wash his blood-stained garment and bloody hands, he looked around but found no water. He planted the tip of his staff in the earth, and suddenly a most welcome stream of a new spring flowed forth. Astonished at the stream of fresh water, he attributed the deed to Him who had given drink to the ancient people by striking the rock.

If one wishes, let this deed be compared with the ancient miracle of Saint Clement [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript omits *cum* (“with”): “Let it be compared with the ancient miracle of Saint Clement”]. The difference is that the former recognized the treasure of a spring by the foot of a lamb, while the latter discovered a bubbling stream by the point of a weapon [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript reads “for he who…” rather than “the former…”].

Finally, when he prepared to wash himself at the spring, he leaned over the water and, observing the beauty of his handsome face reflected there—for he was exceedingly beautiful and pleasing in appearance—began to praise and bless God, who had bestowed such grace upon him.

From that hour he promised with complete devotion that he would serve Him. He loosened the bridle from the horse’s head and let it go wherever it wished. He himself hid among the rocks beneath a kind of cave and lived for some time on acorns.

His companions, meanwhile, dispersed through the region and sought him with all their efforts. When they did not find him, they returned to their dwelling extremely anxious and sorrowful.

When the ruler of Britain heard that Fingar was missing, he summoned his companions and asked them [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript reads “asked them” rather than “asked of them”] where he had gone and what had happened to him. He handed them over to be held in custody and threatened, swearing that he would kill them all unless they told him the truth [Col. 0327D]. He supposed that they had killed him in a quarrel or dispute.

But why would they have killed the man for whose love they had left their native land, endured endless labors, and faced many dangers by land and sea? Indeed, the sorrow that they suffered on his account showed them to be not murderers but true friends—men who should be trusted not because of hatred but because of friendship.

Nevertheless, after explaining how they had become separated from him while pursuing the stag, they offered to search for him again. They said that they would show the places where they had lost their companion if the ruler would send men who knew how to seek him more skillfully.

They went out, and after much labor he was found and brought honorably into the ruler’s presence [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript reads “brought to the ruler,” omitting “with honor”]. The ruler, delighted at his discovery, kindly asked the reason for what had happened. Fingar replied that he had wholly dedicated himself to divine service and could never thereafter return by any means to the duties of the world.

If the ruler, in his kindness, wished to grant him a place where he could serve God more quietly after building an oratory, he said that he would gladly accept it.

The kind ruler agreed to favor his wish, assigned him a place, and moreover granted him as a perpetual endowment all the land that he had previously given to Fingar and his companions for habitation, free from every tribute [Col. 0328B].

The chosen servant of the Lord, Fingar, therefore entered the place assigned by the ruler’s clemency. It was richly endowed and enriched with estates and possessions. With his whole mind and devotion directed toward the dwelling of the heavenly throne, he established there a habitation of sanctification in which God would be praised forever.

From then on the servant of God girded himself more strongly for greater works. He subdued his flesh, strengthened his spirit, and, by pursuing himself, perfected himself in the Lord.

## CHAPTER IV. Fingar’s return to his homeland and refusal of the kingdom

After some time, he was ordered by an angelic exhortation to return to the place of his birth. When he had returned, supported in all things by the Lord’s protection, he found Ireland subjected to the laws of Christ, rejoicing in the confession of the Christian name, and wholly washed in the sacred font.

The servants rejoiced that they had received a lord; the Christian faithful rejoiced to have a companion and patron. Since his father Clito had died, they asked him to accept the kingdom, desiring to have such a defender that the kingdom might be governed by his providence and the still-new Christian faith protected.

“You are owed royal honor by birth,” they said, “apart from the fact that we wish to have you as a supporter of the Christian faith. The inheritance belongs to you; by hereditary right the possession passes to you” [Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript reads *regis* (“of the king”) rather than *regius* (“royal”)].

But he replied:

“Spare me, dearest ones. I have been dedicated to Christ once for all, and I have vowed to serve Him alone. I cannot thereafter return to the duties of the world, because no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX, 62). No one serving God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has devoted himself (II Tim. II, 4).”

When they persisted in asking him with pious insistence, he said:

“You labor in vain, brothers, with such petitions. I cannot remain with you any longer. But if you wish to follow my advice, choose an industrious and faithful man from among the nobles of the country, whose providence may govern the kingdom and protect the Christian faith. Give him my sister Piala in marriage together with the kingdom.”

Piala was a most distinguished virgin, the daughter of the most noble King Clito and the sister of Saint Guinerus. She had already been reborn in Christ through the bath of purification [Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscript reads *lavacro* (“by the bath”) rather than the transmitted phrase with *iam lavacro*].

The saints, instructed by this counsel, spoke to the holy virgin concerning a bridegroom. She, wholly grounded in the love of Christ, replied:

“My bridegroom is Christ, who by His grace chose me as a sharer in His kingdom. To Him I have promised faith, which I must not violate; and therefore I cannot accept another bridegroom besides Him.

“I despise the glory of this kingdom, which ought not to be called glory because it cannot be free from misery. I long for the kingdom that the Lord Jesus Christ promises, where there is neither pain nor sadness but perpetual delight and everlasting joy.”

When the saint saw that the virgin’s purpose was firmly established in the love of Christ, so that she could not by any means be bent to consent to marriage, he said:

“Let her be, brothers. Do not struggle against God’s good pleasure. He has willed it so and has provided that it should be so. Let us entrust this kingdom to God’s providence; He Himself will provide a guardian and defender according to His will.”

After bidding farewell to everyone, he prepared to depart.

## CHAPTER V. Fingar again leaves his native land with a distinguished company

Seven hundred and seventy men followed him, together with seven bishops whom Saint Patrick had begotten for Christ through the water of incorruption. They were filled with God and instructed in divine law, desiring to share in his blessed pilgrimage in the Lord. Among them was the aforementioned virgin Piala, sister of blessed Guinerus.

Thus all united in holy fellowship in the Lord, they proceeded together with their patron as far as the shore. Having found a ship suitable for their purpose, they all boarded it together.

They had already sailed a little farther from the land when, behold, a certain virgin named Hya arrived at the shore. Born of noble blood, she desired to join the blessed company of the saints. Seeing that they were already far from the shore, she was greatly distressed. Kneeling upon the ground, she raised her hands and eyes toward heaven and devoutly sought counsel from heaven in her mind.

Then, lowering her gaze somewhat, she observed upon the water a small leaf. Touching it with the slender rod that she carried in her hand, she wished to test whether it would sink. Behold, before her eyes it began to grow and spread, so that she could not doubt that this service had been sent to her by God.

Strong in faith, she boldly stepped upon the leaf, and by God’s power was wondrously carried [Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscript reads *prolata* rather than *perlata*]. She reached the shore before the others.

There must be no hesitation concerning the works of God. He who powerfully divided the Red Sea for the people crossing it, opened the Jordan for Elijah, and caused Peter to run upon the waters, Himself carried His virgin across in whatever way He willed.

[Col. 0330A]

## CHAPTER VI. The landing in Cornwall

The companions, setting their sails and cutting through the waves of the sea, reached Cornwall with a favorable course, at a harbor called Heul. There the holy virgin Hya had already arrived, carried across by God’s power.

After disembarking from the ship, they found not far from the shore a dwelling in which a certain holy virgin lived enclosed. Saint Guinerus did not wish to disturb her. After greeting the virgin, they went on to another place to eat.

When the saint saw that there was no water, he confidently trusted in Jesus Christ. After offering a prayer, he planted his staff in the earth, and immediately the clearest water sprang forth for the saints to drink.

After the meal, they departed and came to a certain village called Conetconia. There a faithful woman who feared the Lord, named Coruria, showed them no small kindness.

Since all of them could not fit into her dwellings, and she did not have enough straw on which they could all rest, she uncovered the houses and lent them the thatch with which they had been roofed, so that the saints might lie upon it. The woman, full of charity, gave them one cow for food. They killed it, carefully prepared its flesh as was fitting, and ate together.

When the supper had been completed with thanksgiving, Saint Fingar ordered all the bones, stripped of flesh, to be gathered into one place and the hide of the same cow to be laid over them.

Then he invited all the confessors of Christ who were with him to prayer, saying:

“Let us pray, brothers, that God, for whose love this woman has most devotedly served us this cow, may restore it to her.”

When the prayer was complete, the cow appeared standing before everyone’s eyes, more beautiful than it had been before.

He then ordered that milk be brought to him from it. After drinking it, he simply prayed to God that its flow of milk might be three times more abundant than that of other cows. It is said that this happened not only to that cow but also to all those descended from it [Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscript reads *sed omnibus* rather than *sed in omnibus*].

When morning came and they wished to resume their journey, they looked back and saw that all the dwellings had been rethatched and repaired, as though they had never been uncovered.

Then the faithful who followed in the footsteps of Christ under the leadership of Saint Guinerus, seeing God’s wonders multiplied in every place, were strengthened more and more and confirmed in faith and love [Col. 0330D] of Christ.

And rightly Christ should strengthen and console His witnesses with such consolations, since He had arranged to crown them shortly thereafter with the palm of martyrdom.

When morning came, they proceeded through certain wooded regions.

## CHAPTER VII. The martyrdom of Fingar and his companions
The news had already sounded in the ears of King Theodoric of Cornwall—that is, that a Christian multitude had arrived in his land. Fearing that the tyrant, hateful to God, might see his people converted to the faith [Col. 0331A] of Christ, he gathered his soldiers and ran like a savage beast, more ferocious still, to the place where he learned that the saints were. He did not wait for a pretext, seek a reason, or wish to hear any speech; arriving unexpectedly from behind, he suddenly attacked Christ’s sheep like a bloodstained lion, killing, slaughtering, and laying them low. The saints were cut down, dismembered, and torn apart: some had their heads cut off, others were inhumanly pierced with swords, and others slaughtered. All, becoming Christ’s martyrs on the same day, received the prize of eternal life through the swift passage of sacred death.

At that time Saint Fingar, perhaps separated for a short while from his companions, sat in a certain valley awaiting those who followed. When he had driven into the ground the staff he carried in his hand, as soon as he drew the staff back toward himself [Note: one manuscript reads “the elder-wood staff toward himself” instead of “the staff toward himself”], a fertile spring burst forth from the earth [Col. 0331B]. Enclosed decorously on both sides by a double stone, it has not ceased to flow in abundant volume down to the present day.

Suddenly hearing a murmur arising among the company, he wondered what it was and hurried back to the saints. Seeing the victims of Christ being sacrificed everywhere, and the hostile sword running confusedly through the saints’ limbs [Note: one manuscript reads “the sword through” instead of “the hostile sword running confusedly through”], he said to the few who were with him:

“Behold, brothers, this is the place of our repose; here God has provided an end to our labors. Come, therefore, brothers, and let us willingly be sacrificed for him who gave his life as a redemption for many (Matthew 20:28). Let us not fear those who kill the body, but rather him who has power to cast both body and soul into Gehenna (Luke 12:3; Matthew 10:28).”

Meeting the tyrant, he said: “You are doing, son of the devil, the works of your father” [Col. 0331C]. And the tyrant replied to him: “You shall not escape my hands; you shall not evade the sword.”

Then the saint, cheerfully offering an acceptable sacrifice to God, fixed the staff he carried in his hand beside him and fearlessly presented his neck to receive the blow of the striker [Note: one manuscript reads “presented it to receive the blow” instead of “presented his neck fearlessly”]. But the most savage tyrant seized his sword [Note: one manuscript reads “having seized” instead of “seized”] and struck the bare neck with all his strength. Cutting off his head, he made him Christ’s martyr.

Immediately the sacred body’s trunk took up from the ground the head, severed from the neck by the swordsman’s own blade, and, walking with firm knees, carried it in his own hands to a mountain not far from the place. A certain village lay on the side of that mountain. When he heard women quarreling there, he pronounced an eternal curse upon the place, so that those living there would never cease quarreling among themselves. Hence, so it is said, although the earth remains fertile, it is uninhabitable: in one respect it retains the gift of fertility, but in another it lies subject to the saint’s curse.

The holy martyr, therefore, unwilling to rest in a place of tumult, took up his head again and carried it to another place. There, setting it down, he carefully washed the bloodied head. In that place a most welcome spring has continued to flow in an unbroken stream down to the present day. Taking up the head again after washing it carefully, he carried it to another place. This place lies a short distance from the place where the holy martyrs had suffered, separated from it by a small stretch of woodland [Note: one manuscript reads “the woodland is separated” instead of “separated by a small stretch of woodland”].

The place that received the stream of blood flowing from the saint’s body immediately opened and produced a fertile spring, which is still shown to those who see it [Note: one manuscript reads “flowing back” instead of “flowing down”]. One of the soldiers wished to seize the saintly martyr’s staff from the place where he had first driven it into the ground shortly before his passion. He saw that a double branch had already burst forth into foliage, and, shaken by so great a miracle, did not dare touch it. To this day a lofty tree is seen there, as they say, as a testimony to the saint: it grew from the staff through God’s power, though its species is unknown.

[Col. 0332B]

## CHAPTER VIII. The Burial of the Holy Martyrs

The bodies of the saints still lay unburied across the field. Then, one night, the witness of Christ appeared in a vision for the third time to a certain man named Gur, in the same form in which he had carried his own head in his arms over the mountain, and admonished him to bury him.

When the man awoke, he recounted the vision in order to his wife—namely, how he had been persuaded by the saint to undertake the burial. But the woman opposed it, lest he incur the king’s anger and thereby deserve a sentence of death.

The next day, as the man went out into the field to hunt with dogs, he found a stag which, pursued by the dogs’ speed, fled and fell before the holy martyr’s burial place, as though seeking the protection of his sanctity. The dogs ceased barking and stopped pursuing the stag. Abandoning all their fierceness, they lay down together with the stag, as though venerating the saint.

The man contemplated the great spectacle. His mind struck by what he saw, he came to himself, and, recalling what he had seen during the night, considered himself brought there by divine command. Taking up the body of the most holy martyr, he buried it with whatever reverence he could offer. Then he diligently searched the field for the bodies of the holy martyrs and buried them in the field just as they lay.

## CHAPTER IX. The Basilica Built in Their Honor, and Miracles Divinely Performed There

After some time, when the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth—that is, the Church—had begun to occupy the borders of Cornwall, a basilica was begun through the devotion of the faithful [Col. 0332D] over the tomb of the holy martyr.

When the artisans laboring on the construction of the oratory lacked the necessary supplies and no one provided them, the saint, mindful of his own people, who served him with devoted offices, appeared at night in visions to the people of the surrounding region [Note: one manuscript reads “the saint, mindful of their people” instead of “the saint, mindful of his own people”], instructing each of them to bring food and necessary assistance to the workmen.

At last he came to a certain man who possessed an untamed bull, and instructed him to have it led to the workmen and give it to them for food [Note: one manuscript reads “to have it led to them” instead of “to have it led to the workmen”].

When morning came, the man, troubled by the saint’s vision, began to consider how he could subdue the very high-necked and proud animal and lead it, fastened with ropes, as the holy martyr had commanded. Mounting his horse and going out to look for the bull, he first saw the previously untamed animal standing at the door, now made exceedingly gentle by God’s power. It went quietly before its master and proceeded by the straight road to the place where the artisans were laboring on the oratory.

The beast was slaughtered [Note: one manuscript reads “was being slaughtered” instead of “was slaughtered”]. When the artisans saw that the martyr’s assistance was present for them, they devoted themselves more earnestly than before to the work.

Another memorable and worthy miracle is also said to have occurred during the construction of the same basilica. One of the artisans laboring on the work was using an axe when it broke and split into two pieces. The man was distressed [Col. 0333B] and began to swear and protest that he would do no more work on the building.

When the overseer of the work heard this—a good man who had undertaken responsibility for the basilica for God’s sake and had devoted himself faithfully to the saint’s service—he began to console the man and soothe his sadness with gentle words. Taking the pieces in the name of Jesus Christ and joining the fragments of the break, he immediately restored and solidified the tool through the merits of the glorious martyr, so that no trace of the break remained afterward [Note: one manuscript reads “no traces” instead of “no trace”].

God was praised and blessed by all, and the man who had sworn that he would do no more work, strengthened by so great a miracle, now persevered in the work with greater courage.

[Col. 0333C]

## CHAPTER X. Punishments Brought from Heaven upon Sacrilegious Persons

But since I have begun to recount the saints’ powers, I have thought it should be inserted into this reading—something that strikes fear into unbelievers and instructs everyone concerning reverence for the saints.

When two soldiers, in contempt of the holy martyr, urinated upon a certain stone that had been the anchor of his ship, divine vengeance immediately struck both of them. For both were seized by a demon: one chewed his tongue, cut into pieces, with his teeth; the other’s intestines were all spilled out through his hind parts. Thus each breathed his last in a horrible manner.

Behold, from this one may sufficiently judge how greatly God wishes the saints to be honored with reverence, since he arranges that contempt for them be expiated by so strict a judgment.

A certain corrupt man dared to violate the embraces of a woman on the sarcophagus of a venerable bishop who had been one of King Cliton’s companions. In the very act of their shame, they became inseparably joined together like dogs and could not be separated from one another by any means. At last they were brought to the shrine of the glorious martyr Guignerus, where, as was fitting, they were freed through the witness of Christ and the intercession of the faithful.

Moreover, the sacristan of the holy martyr possessed a cow [Note: one manuscript reads “the entrance” instead of “the sacristan”]. When certain wicked men had stolen it and were leading it away, they suddenly saw two burning lights above its horns. Shaken by so great a spectacle, they returned the next day and restored the cow to the sacristan, giving another as satisfaction for their offense and at the same time asking pardon.

Earth taken from the saint’s tomb, with faith and devotion, drives away illnesses through the martyr’s merit and brings about cures.

I, Anselm, servant of Christ Jesus, have arranged in a brief style, according to the testimony of those who tell it, this account of the passion of the saints and the powers of the precious martyr Guignerus, so that the faithful who glory in his special title [Note: one manuscript reads “spiritual title” instead of “special title”] may have readings with which to occupy themselves and may learn the brave deeds of their own patron. For this reason I have appended my name at the end, so that through the martyr’s merit and the prayers of the faithful I may deserve the mercy of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Redeemer, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages.

[Col. 0333C]

## JUDGMENT CONCERNING A MONK’S STABILITY IN THE PLACE WHERE HE HAS BEEN SET

[Col. 0333D]

There are three circumstances for which religious persons may change the places in which they have promised to remain stable. The first is excessive poverty; the second, excessive persecution; the third, irreligiousness.

For stability in a place is promised only for the sake of observing the Rule. The Rule does not consist, as many think, in precepts, but in institutions. Otherwise all who did not observe the Rule in every respect would be transgressors, and the matter of precepts would not be left to discretion.

Institutions, however, may be changed and established by the abbot if they are more useful for purity of mind, which alone is to be sought before God and for which alone one must labor. One should not be concerned with the entire external habit, whatever it may be, provided that it causes no scandal.

Thus Lanfrancus said to a certain monk:

“It has been reported to me that you wish to leave your monastery, but that you are troubled about the stability you promised, lest you offend God more by the very thing through which you ought to please him. Concerning this I shall show you the reason, and in showing it I shall offer myself as an example.

“If I, Lanfrancus, had sworn with my own hand that I would not leave some monastery, and I saw that I could not save my soul there, I would leave and would not incur the crime of perjury. For whoever is bound to God for God’s sake is not released from him except against him [Col. 0334D–0335A]. But he is not released from him against him who, for love of him and in order to please him well, moves from the sons of pride and distrust, from the sons of discord—or, to speak more plainly, from the sons of the devil—to the sons of peace and hope, whom I call the sons of humility, the sons of God.

“For one who passes over in this way, is he not fleeing from the seat of the devil to the seat of God? Who would judge him condemned by God when, fleeing to the Father, to God, and to his friend, he flees to God himself?

“Furthermore, one who passes over in this way does not pass from one Church to another. There are not many Churches, but one Church spread throughout the whole world; everywhere one God is served, and one king is served as a soldier.

“Finally, blessed Benedict, who commanded that a monk’s stability be made firm, orders that a person coming from one monastery to another be received; and if he has led a good life, he encourages him to make his stability firm.

“Remember continually how uncertain and brief human life is, and how infinite are the good or evil things that follow it.”

[Col. 0335A]

## A MIRACLE OF SAINT JAMES, SET FORTH BY LORD ANSELM

### Concerning a soldier whom the blessed apostle, during his death agony when demons oppressed him, freed through a beggar’s staff and a little woman’s sack

*(From the Sangermanensis manuscript, no. 608.)*

[Note: This is falsely attributed to Saint Anselm.]

[Col. 0335B]

Three soldiers of the diocese of the Church of Laon, from the town of Dumezai, agreed that they would go for the sake of prayer to visit the apostle James on the shores of Galicia, and they set out.

While they were on that pilgrimage route, they found a little woman carrying the things she needed in a certain sack. When she saw the horsemen, she asked them, out of pity for her, to transport on their mounts the little bundle she was carrying, for love of the blessed apostle, and thereby lighten for her the burden of so long a journey. One of them agreed to the pilgrim woman’s request, took her bag, and carried it.

When evening came, the woman followed the soldiers and took from her bundle what she needed. At the first cockcrow, when pilgrims on foot usually set out, she returned the sack to the rider, and thus, relieved of her burden, she continued on more happily.

In this way the soldier, serving the little woman for love of the apostle, hastened toward the desired place of prayer. But when they were twelve days’ journey from the city of Saint James, he found a poor sick man on the road. The man began to ask him to lend him his horse to ride, so that he might reach the saint; otherwise he would die on the road, because he could no longer walk.

The soldier consented, dismounted, placed the beggar upon his horse, and took the beggar’s staff in his own hand. He also carried around his own neck the little woman’s bundle that he had taken.

As he continued in this way, however, he began to fall ill, overcome by the excessive heat of the sun and the loneliness of the long journey. When he perceived this, remembering that he had often and greatly offended in many ways, he endured his illness, walking on foot out of love for the apostle as far as his threshold [lacuna] [Col. 0335D]. There, after praying to the apostle and being received as a guest, he lay down in bed with the same illness that had seized him on the road. His sickness grew worse, and he lay there for several days.

When the other soldiers who had been his companions saw this, they approached him and advised him to confess his sins, seek what a Christian ought to ask for, and prepare more promptly for his departure from this life.

Hearing this, he turned his face away and could not answer. Thus he lay for three days without uttering a word. His companions were greatly saddened, both because they had despaired of his salvation and especially because he could not take care of the salvation of his soul.

One day, when they thought he was about to breathe out his spirit, they sat around him awaiting his death. He sighed deeply and spoke:

“I give thanks,” he said, “to God and to Saint James, my lord, because I have been freed.”

Those who were present asked what he meant. He replied:

“From the moment I felt myself weighed down by sickness, I silently began to think that I wished to confess my sins, be anointed with the sacred unction, and be strengthened by receiving the Lord’s body. But while I was considering these things in silence, a crowd of dreadful spirits suddenly came and oppressed me so completely that from that moment I could indicate by neither word nor sign anything that concerned my salvation.

“I understood well what you were saying, but I could not answer in any way. The demons who had gathered around me were doing this: some were holding my tongue, others were closing my eyes, and some were turning my head and body here and there at their will, against my will.

“But shortly before I began to speak, Saint James entered here. In his left hand he carried the little woman’s sack that I had borne on the road, and in his right he held the beggar’s staff that I had carried while the beggar rode my horse, the very staff that was in my hand when the sickness seized me [Col. 0336D]. He had the staff as a lance and the sack as a palm branch.

“Coming upon me at once as though in the indignation of fury, he raised the staff and seemed to strike the demons who had held me. They immediately fled in terror. He pursued them and forced them to leave through that corner there.

“And behold, by the grace of God and of blessed James, freed from those who oppressed me, I can speak. Send quickly and call a priest to give me the viaticum of holy communion, for I have no permission to remain longer in this life.”

They sent for one. While the priest delayed in coming, the soldier publicly admonished one of his companions, saying:

“Friend, do not henceforth serve your lord Girinus surnamed Calvus, to whom you have hitherto clung. He is truly condemned and will soon die a bad death.”

The truth of what happened made this clear [Col. 0338A]. After the pilgrim had died peacefully by that good end and had been committed to burial, his companions returned and recounted what had happened. The aforementioned Girinus, surnamed Calvus, who had been a wealthy man, treated their report as though it were a dream and made no correction whatever in his wickedness. Thus, not many days later, while killing a soldier with weapons, he too was pierced by that same soldier’s lance and died.

Therefore, to the King of kings, the Lord Jesus Christ, be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0337A]

## THE GREAT MIRACLE OF SAINT JAMES

### Set forth by Lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning a pilgrim who killed himself for love of the apostle, and whom blessed James, with the help of blessed Mary, Mother of God, restored from death to life

*(From a manuscript codex.)*

[Note: This tale is falsely attributed to Saint Anselm.]

[Col. 0337B]

Near the city of Laon there is a village in which a certain young man named Giraldus lived. Trained in the craft of working skins, he lived by the labor of his hands; after his father’s death, he supported his mother by his own work.

He loved Saint James intensely. Every year he used to go to the apostle’s threshold and offer him his obedience. He had no wife, but lived chastely alone with his elderly mother.

After restraining himself for a long time, however, he was finally overcome by carnal desire and fornicated with a certain young woman. Since he had already planned a pilgrimage, he set out the next morning with two of his neighbors, taking his donkey with him, and began to go to Saint James.

While they were on the road, they found a beggar traveling to Saint James. They took him with them both for companionship and, more especially, for love of the holy apostle, supplying him with what he needed for food. Thus they proceeded, doing this for several days with joy.

Because the devil envies peaceful and charitable companionship, he secretly approached the young man who had fornicated in a house, taking on a sufficiently respectable human form. He said to him:

“Do you know who I am?”

The young man replied: “Not at all.”

The demon said: “I am the apostle James, whom for a long time you have been accustomed to visit every year and honor with your gifts. Know that I rejoiced greatly over you, because I hoped for great good from you. But recently, before you left your home, you fornicated with a woman. You have not repented of it until now, nor have you wished to confess it. Thus you set out on pilgrimage with your sin, as though your pilgrimage were acceptable to God and to me.

“This must not be done. Whoever wishes to make a pilgrimage for love of me must first reveal his sins through humble confession, and afterward punish those sins by undertaking the pilgrimage. Anyone who does otherwise will not have a pleasing pilgrimage.”

After saying this, he vanished from the man’s sight.

When he heard these things, the man began to grieve and resolved in his heart to return home and confess to his priest. He therefore turned back along the road he had begun.

While he was considering this within himself, the demon came again in the same form in which he had appeared before and said:

“What is this that you are thinking in your heart—to return home and do penance so that afterward you may be able to return to me more worthily? Do you think that you can wipe away so great a crime through your fasts or tears? You are very foolish. Believe my counsel and you will be saved; otherwise you cannot be saved.

“Although you have sinned, I nevertheless love you. For that reason I have come to you, to give you such advice that you can be saved if you are willing to believe me.”

The pilgrim replied:

“Yes, I was thinking as you say. But since you assert that this will not help my salvation, tell me what pleases you, by which I may be saved, and I shall willingly carry it out.”

The demon said:

“If you desire to be completely cleansed from your offense, cut off at once the organs with which you sinned.”

Terrified by this advice, the man said:

“If I do what you advise, I shall not be able to live, and I shall become my own murderer—something I have often heard is damnable before God.”

Then the demon mocked him:

“O foolish man, how little you understand what can benefit you for salvation! If you die in this way, you will undoubtedly pass over to me, because by punishing your offense you will be a martyr. If only you were wise enough not to hesitate to kill yourself! I would certainly come to you at once with a multitude of my companions and joyfully receive your soul to remain with me.

“I am the apostle James, who gives you this advice. Do as I have said if you wish to join my company and find a remedy for your offense.”

After these words, the pilgrim was stirred to the deed. At night, while his companions slept, he drew a small knife and cut off everything masculine in those parts. Then, turning the blade in his hand, he raised it and, thrusting himself upon its point, stabbed his belly.

When the blood began to flow and he writhed in agony, his companions awoke and called him, asking what was wrong. When he gave them no answer but anxiously drew his last breath, they rose in confusion and haste, lit lamps, and found their companion half alive and no longer able to answer them. Astonished and struck by great fear that they might be accused of his death if they were found in the same place in the morning, they fled, abandoning him rolling in his own blood, as well as the donkey and the poor man whom they had begun to support.

In the morning, when the household of the house had risen and found the murdered man, not knowing who had killed him, they called the neighbors and carried the dead man to the church for burial. While a grave was being prepared before its doors, they laid him there because of the flow of blood.

After only a short delay, the man who had been dead returned to life and sat up on the funeral bier. Those who were present, seeing this, fled in terror and shouted. Their cries stirred the people, who hurried there, asked what had happened, and heard that the dead man had been restored to life.

When they drew near and began to speak to him, he narrated aloud before everyone everything that had happened around him:

“I am the man whom you see raised from death. From childhood I loved Saint James and, insofar as I could, was accustomed to serve him. But just now, when I had resolved to go to him and had reached this village, the devil came and deceived me, saying that he was Saint James.”

He recounted the entire sequence as described above, and added:

“After I had taken my own life and my soul was being forced from my body, the same evil spirit who had deceived me came to me, bringing with him a great crowd of demons. They immediately seized me without mercy and carried me, weeping and uttering pitiful cries, to the place of torment.

“They set out toward Rome. But when we had reached the forest situated between the city and the village called Labicau, Saint James pursued us and flew up behind us. Having seized the demons, he said to them:

“‘Where have you come from, and where are you going?’

“They replied:

“‘O holy James, this is none of your concern. He trusted us so completely that he killed himself. We advised him; we deceived him; we have the right to keep him.’

“He said to them:

“‘You answer nothing concerning what I ask, but boast joyfully that you have deceived a Christian. You will receive bad thanks for this. He is my pilgrim, whom you boast of possessing, and you will certainly not take him without a struggle.’

“To me, James appeared young and handsome, lean, of a medium complexion, which is commonly called brown.

“Forcing us to turn aside toward Rome, he brought us to a place near the church of blessed Peter the apostle. There was a green and spacious place on a level expanse of air, where an indescribable multitude of saints had gathered for a council. The venerable Lady Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, presided over it, with many distinguished nobles seated at her right and left.

“I began to gaze upon her with great affection of heart, for never in my life had I seen such a beautiful creature anywhere. She was not tall but of medium stature, with an exceedingly beautiful face and a desirable appearance.

“Immediately my blessed apostle, my most merciful advocate, appeared before everyone and loudly declared how Satan’s deception had overcome me. She then turned to the demons and said:

“‘Wretched ones, what were you seeking in the pilgrim of the Lord and of my Son, and of his faithful James? Your punishment ought to have been sufficient for you; there was no need for you to increase it by your wickedness.’

“After that most blessed Lady had spoken, she mercifully turned her eyes upon me. The demons were overcome by great fear, and everyone at the council declared that they had acted unjustly against the apostle by deceiving me. The Lady commanded that I be returned to my body.

“Then Saint James received me and immediately restored me to this place. Thus I have died and been raised again.”

When the inhabitants of the place heard this, they rejoiced greatly. They immediately carried him to their house, kept him with them for three days, and proclaimed and displayed the man in whom God, through the blessed apostle James, had performed so unusual and marvelous a deed.

His wounds were healed without delay, leaving only scars in place of the injuries. In place of his genitals, flesh grew like a wart, through which urine was discharged.

When the days had passed during which the inhabitants had kept him with them out of joy, he prepared his donkey and set out with the poor companion whom he had taken up on the road [Col. 0340C].

As he approached the threshold of blessed James, behold, the companions who had abandoned him met him on their return. When they were still some distance away and saw the two men urging along the donkey, they said to one another:

“They resemble the companions we left behind: one dead and the other alive. Nor does the animal they are driving appear different from the one that, so far as we can see, was left with them.”

When they came nearer and began to recognize one another through mutual acknowledgment, they recognized what had happened, rejoiced exceedingly, and returned home, where they related the event in order.

The man who had been raised, after returning from Saint James, confirmed in reality what his companions had previously reported. He spread the event everywhere, displayed his scars, and even showed what was in the more secret place to many who wished to see it.

The most reverend Hugh, holy abbot of Cluny, saw this man and all the signs of his death together with many others. Out of wonder, he declared that he had often seen such a thing in the place where it had been reported. We, out of love for the apostle, committed the event to writing so that it would not be erased from memory. We instruct everyone to celebrate throughout all the Churches, with worthy annual observances, on the fifth day before the Nones of October, the feast of so great a miracle and of the other miracles of Saint James.

“It was done by the Lord,” and so forth.

[Col. 0341]

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1121: EADMER, CANTERBURY MONK OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 0341]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Warton, Anglia Sacra, vol. II, preface, p. XII.)*

[Col. 0341A]

Eadmer, a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, disciple and constant companion of Archbishop Anselm, transmitted a very large number of writings to posterity. Selden discusses him at length in the preface to *Historia Novorum*, as does Bale in century II, chapter 68, and others.

Elected to the bishopric of Saint Andrews in the year 1120, he resigned the bishopric and returned to Canterbury in 1121. Bale distinguishes him from Elmer, prior of the Church of Canterbury, and assigns different works to each of them. Gervase supports this distinction: when he frequently cites Eadmer’s *History*, he honors him by no other title than that of Cantor. The Canterbury Obituary likewise says: “Edmerus, precentor of Canterbury, died on the Ides of January.”

A note added at the end of the Life of Anselm in the Lambeth manuscript, codex 159, folio [Col. 0342A], reads as follows:

“Here ends the Life of Anselm, edited by Edmer, his disciple and monk of this holy Church of Canterbury, and afterward prior of Christ Church, Canterbury.”

An equivalent statement appears there at the end of the metrical Life of Anselm.

I showed in the preceding volume that Elmer presided over the monks of Canterbury from 1128 to 1157. The Canterbury Obituary, however, assigns him a different day of death from that of Edmer the Cantor. It therefore seems that Bale correctly distinguished Eadmer the historian from Elmer the prior.

Nevertheless, among the works that the same author attributes to Elmer, there are some that I think should rather be assigned to Eadmer. John Selden published Eadmer’s more notable *History*, called *Historia Novorum*, which deals with the acts of the archbishops Lanfranc, Anselm, and Ralph, in London in 1623, folio.

Most of Eadmer’s remaining works are preserved in a very old and elegantly written manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, volume 338, quarto, arranged in the following order [Col. 0343A]:

A poem on Saint Dunstan.

A poem on Saint Edward, king and martyr.

A letter from another author to Edmer concerning the mother of Saint Edward.

A letter from Nicholas to Edmer asking whether the Church of York has primacy over the Scots. You will find it transcribed from this very manuscript below. I believe its author was Nicholas, prior of the Church of Worcester, who died in 1124.

For it is clear that Eadmer had a very close friendship with the monks of the Church of Worcester, as appears from the letter he wrote to them in 1123 concerning the election of a bishop. Indeed, Nicholas, who had been educated in the Canterbury monastery under Archbishop Lanfranc, had Eadmer as a fellow student, according to William of Malmesbury (*Life of Wulfstan*, book III, chapter 17).

Jocelin saw this letter and included an abridgment of it in his *British Antiquities*. He was seriously mistaken, however: he both rendered the author’s opinion incorrectly (p. 19) and misunderstood his homeland. For he believed that the author was a Scot.

What the men of Glastonbury say concerning their possession of the body of Saint Dunstan. Two copies of this work exist in the frequently mentioned Lambeth manuscript. The same manuscript contains letters of William Warham, archbishop and abbot of Glastonbury, concerning the body of Saint Dunstan. We have appended them because of the similarity of their subject. The register of the Church of Canterbury also contains them.

The Life of Saint Wilfrid, archbishop of York. Mabillon published this in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, century III, part I, p. 196.

The Life of Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury. It exists in this volume and in Mabillon, century V, p. 283, where it is incorrectly attributed to Osbern.

The Life of Saint Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury. Surius published this, together with the following work on Dunstan’s miracles reduced to an abridgment, on 10 May, omitting only most of the Preface [Col. 0343C].

The author’s name had been erased from Surius’s manuscript. Surius had read, however, in several sources that a certain Osbern had composed a Life of Dunstan. He therefore assigned the work to him, although, with his memory somewhat at fault, he substituted the name Osbert for Osbern.

He dated this Osbert to the year 1020, a disgraceful error, since almost all of Dunstan’s miracles published by him under the same author’s name mention Archbishop Lanfranc, and some are even said to have occurred in Anselm’s time. Others easily followed Surius in this error, among them Baronius, who repeatedly cited this Life under the name Osbern, and Spelmannus (*English Councils*, p. 492), who correctly maintained that Surius’s Osbert should be called Osbern by our writers.

After the genuine work of Osbern appeared, Surius’s Life began to be attributed to Osbert of Clare, prior of Westminster. Osbert flourished from 1108 to 1140, as is established by his letters preserved in the Cotton Library [Col. 0343D]. Thus the Antwerp editors of the *Acta Sanctorum*, May, volume IV, p. 344.

In truth, however, the work belongs to Eadmer. He never saw Osbern’s work on the same subject and appears to have composed this one at approximately the same time. Nevertheless, having used some ancient author of a Life of Dunstan—the same source used by Osbern—he has much in common with Osbern.

**Book on the Miracles of Saint Dunstan.** Eadmer had promised at the end of the preceding book that he would commit these to writing [Col. 0344A]. They exist in abridged form in Surius.

**A Writing on the Ordination of Blessed Gregory.**

**On the Excellence of Blessed Mary.** It is found at the end of the works of Anselm edited by Gabriel Gerberon, Paris, 1675, folio [page reference incomplete in the source].

**Life and Miracles of Saint Oswald, Archbishop of York.** I have had this printed. There was indeed in the Cottonian manuscript Nero E 1 an older Life of Oswald, from which Eadmer drew everything that he wrote about Oswald; it had been written by a monk of Ramsey in the time of Ælfric, Archbishop of Canterbury. I rejected it, however, both because of its excessive length and because of its affected style of expression. It begins: “Although the Iliad and Odyssey and Virgil’s Aeneid have been skillfully written out.” Eadmer greatly abridged it, but retained everything worth knowing, and produced a work much more useful.

Furthermore, Senatus, formerly of Worcester, is said by Baleus (*century* III, chapter 10) to have written a Life of Oswald, and the monk Folcard of Canterbury is said by Orderic Vitalis [Col. 0344B] (*book* II, under the year 1108) to have done the same. The work of each has perished. Mabillon published another from the Ramsey Chronicle, *Acta Benedictina*, century V, p. 735. A different Life is found in Capgrave, taken from the compilation of Tinmouth, with the style altered. Tinmouth saw Eadmer’s book and imitated it in many places. Finally, a Life of this same Oswald, among other legends of the saints, survives in a Saxon composition by Ælfric.

**On the Blessedness of Eternal Life.** It exists at the end of Anselm’s works in the recent Paris edition.

**Life of Saint Bregwin, Archbishop of Canterbury.** It was written after the death of Archbishop Ralph, who died in 1122. John of Tinmouth made an abridgment of it, which was wrongly attributed to Osbern and is published in this volume. Later, when a copy of the Cambridge manuscript had been obtained, we did not wish to withhold from the public a more complete Life of Bregwin written by Eadmer.

[Col. 0344C]

**Life of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in Two Books.** It is found in almost all editions of Anselm’s works, and in Surius under 21 February. Everywhere, however, the final two chapters are lacking, although they are found in all the manuscript copies of this work that I have seen, and are cited by Eadmer in the Prologue to the *Book on the Miracles of Saint Anselm*. There Eadmer says that he dealt with the miracles of Count Arnulf and the monk Robert at the end of the books *On the Life of Anselm*.

**Book on the Miracles of Saint Anselm.** The often-mentioned Lambeth manuscript contains it.

**On the Conception of Saint Mary.**

**Life of Peter, First Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury.**

**A Judgment concerning the Memory of the Saints Whom You Venerate.**

**On Drawing the Hand of Saint Peter the Apostle upon Oneself.**

**On the Relics of Saint Ouen and Other Saints in Christ Church, Canterbury.** [Col. 0344D]

**On the Archangel Gabriel.**

Baleus (*century* II, chapter 68) lists other writings of Eadmer, and Gerberon published several others at the end of Anselm’s works. The Lambeth manuscript contains a *Life of Saint Anselm* written in heroic verse; an old Cottonian manuscript, Otho A 12, contains several letters of Eadmer.

# THE WORKS OF EADMER, RESTORED AND CORRECTED THROUGH THE LABOR AND CARE OF THE MONKS OF THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT MAUR

[Col. 0345]

## PREFACE TO THE NEW EDITION OF EADMER’S WORKS

(*Works of Saint Anselm*, Paris edition, 1721)

[Col. 0345A]

Eadmer, whom the English pronounce “Edmer,” while later writers corruptly write “Edinerus,” surnamed Cantor, was born in England and raised in Kent. At length he became a Canterbury monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the monastery of the Savior belonging to the Cluniac congregation. From childhood it had been his custom always to examine carefully and commit to memory whatever new matters happened to arise, especially in ecclesiastical affairs, as he himself says (*Book II of the New History*). Through this pursuit he became highly learned, distinguished above others by historical truthfulness and eloquence of speech.

He was first the hearer and disciple of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, then his companion and friend, and his inseparable companion in exile and hardship. Terrified neither by the king’s anger nor by his hatred, he never withdrew from Anselm. He traveled with him to Rome, where Urban II received him courteously and held him in great honor, so much so that he placed Eadmer over Anselm, who depended wholly upon Eadmer’s commands. Anselm himself had earnestly requested this, lest, by being placed above the others, he lose the merit of obedience [Col. 0345B].

After Anselm’s death, Eadmer lived for some time in retirement; but later, it is said, he was made bishop of the Church of Saint Andrew in Scotland (Malmesbury, *Book I of the Deeds of the Pontiffs*). Selden correctly observes that this Eadmer was not the one who presided over the monastery of Saint Albans and died at the beginning of King Æthelred’s reign, around the year 980. In this he rightly corrects Baleus, his copyist Leland, and Pitsaeus, since this Eadmer flourished no less than a century later and died in the year 1121, according to Simeon of Durham.

This close relationship between Anselm and Eadmer led to their works being published together in a more corrected form: first, lest the press divide into separate parts men who agreed in every respect; and second, so that works written in Eadmer’s style, which had hitherto been catalogued among Anselm’s writings, might be restored to Eadmer himself.

Eadmer wrote the following:

**The Life of Saint Anselm**, arranged in two books.

[Col. 0345C]

**The History of Recent Events**, divided into six books.

**The Life of Saint Wilfrid, Archbishop**, contained in one book.

**A Collection of Histories**, written in one book.

**One Book on the Deeds of His Own Time.**

**On Ecclesiastical Liberty, or On the Dispute between William Rufus, King of the English, and Anselm**, one volume. [Col. 0346A]

**A Lament on the Death of Saint Anselm**, in elegiac verse.

**On the Praises of Saint Mary the Virgin**, one book.

**On the Institutions of the Christian Life**, one book.

**On Saint Dunstan**, a poem.

He wrote many letters and received others from correspondents.

Pitsaeus concludes from Leland and Simeon of Durham that Eadmer briefly treated English history from King Edgar to William I, and later expanded his account down to his own time. I think, however, that this is no different from the *History of Recent Events*, in which he descends in a few words from King Edgar to William.

Of all these works, only the following have been made public: the two books *On the Life of Anselm*, which we corrected against the manuscripts; the *History of Recent Events*; a sermon, or book, *On Heavenly Blessedness*; the book *On the Excellence or Praises of the Virgin*; and the *Institutions of the Christian Life*, or *Book on Morals*, which, in my opinion, is none other than Anselm’s *Book of Similitudes*, collected by Eadmer [Col. 0346B].

The rest lie hidden in the libraries of England. Despite all our efforts, the assistance of our friends, and every expenditure we could make, we have not been able to bring them forth, although we sent letters on the subject to various people. Eadmer’s letters in manuscript are preserved at Cambridge in the College of Saint Benedict. The book *On Ecclesiastical Liberty* exists in manuscript in the library of the Archbishop of Canterbury. A manuscript of the *History of Recent Events* is preserved at Cambridge in the library of the College of Saint Benedict, number 78. The *Life of Saint Wilfrid* is preserved in London among the Cottonian manuscripts. A manuscript of the *Life of Saint Dunstan* is held at Cambridge in the College of Saint Benedict, where other manuscripts of his short works also exist, *On the Mountain of Humility* and *On the Two Guardians of That Mountain*; but we have given these in corrected form in the *Book of Similitudes*.

We therefore do not merely refrain from begrudging those who may more successfully search out these treasures of Eadmer hidden in their chests, and who may more easily bring them forth; we earnestly encourage them to do so.

Notable testimonies concerning Eadmer are found in Malmesbury’s prologue to the *Deeds of the Kings*, and frequently elsewhere [Col. 0346C], where, in recounting the events of his own time, he praises Eadmer’s truthfulness and eloquence at length; in Pitsaeus’s *Accounts of English Affairs*, age 12; in Trithemius, who calls him “Emondus”; and in others who have discussed ecclesiastical writers or written more carefully about English affairs.

[Col. 0345C]

# EADMER’S LIFE OF SAINT ANSELM

(See above under Anselm.)

# [HISTORY OF RECENT EVENTS]

[Col. 0347]

# EADMER’S HISTORY OF RECENT EVENTS

[Col. 0347]

## PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 0545]

**(16*)** This note is printed at the foot of column 545, but its callout number, “(16*),” does not appear in the text.

He instructed Augustine concerning men of the same order to which he himself is known to belong—namely, Benedictine monks. G. of Malmesbury, in a manuscript copy of *On the Antiquities of the Church of Glastonbury*, writes before Augustine that “the monks of the Church of Glastonbury—and it is surely reasonable to believe that the others did likewise—lived according to the manner of the Egyptian monks. Hence,” he says, “after the arrival of Augustine, episcopal sees were established in various places, and monasteries were built, serving God according to the Rule of the Blessed Father Benedict, so that afterward no monks were found among the English who had not professed the Rule of Saint Benedict. From that time the same rule first began to be practiced in the monastery of Glastonbury, whereas previously it had followed the manner of the Egyptian monasteries.”

The manuscript, which our studies gratefully acknowledge as having been of great value because of his distinguished generosity, was once shared with me by the most learned and highly accomplished Thomas Allen, of the Gloucester fellowship and a most eminent ornament of the celebrated University of Oxford.

Some, however, are unwilling to believe that the institutions of the Egyptian monks—whose full measure is preserved in Cassian—were ever received in the West. On this matter, if desired, consult Henri Vandenzypius, part III of *On the Monastic Order of Saint Gregory*, chapter 5. He discusses the matter more fully in part III, chapter 4 of the same work, concerning the religious family of our Augustine, which, I think, everyone agrees was none other than that in which Saint Gregory had made his profession.

Gregory himself gives sufficient testimony to this in Book VII, Letter 114, to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, where he calls Augustine “formerly the superior of my monastery.” Baronius, however, maintains that Gregory’s family was Equitian, not Benedictine. If I am not mistaken, he was the first to maintain this and dared to oppose the opinion of the most widely accepted antiquity, being led by conjectures that are neither contemptible nor, in truth, especially weighty. See his *Annals*, volume VIII, under the year 596, and what Vandenzypius wrote against him in the places already mentioned.

I admit that the ancient compilers of our history do not, as far as I remember, expressly state anywhere that Augustine belonged to the Benedictine fellowship. They frequently call him simply a monk. Yet we read in Bede, whom most writers follow, of Augustine and several other monks with him. Likewise, in an old manuscript Saxon Chronicle under the year 596:

“Her Gregorius papa sende to Britene Agustinum mid wel manegum munecum tha godes word Anglatheode godspelledan.”

That is: “In this year Pope Gregory sent the monk Augustine to Britain with very many monks, who preached the word of God to the English people.”

Nor do I find him mentioned otherwise in this connection by the ancient writers. Meanwhile, the word *monachus*, when no designation of a particular family is added, always—unless my memory deceives me—means a Benedictine when used of those who are mentioned under that name by our forefathers, just as among the Greeks it generally means a Basilian.

Moreover, the inhabitants of the monastery of the Savior at Canterbury have always, from its very beginnings, been regarded among us as belonging to the Benedictine family. At least, nothing appears in the ancient monuments that can serve as evidence here which either suggests or even implies that they ever assumed or discarded the name of any other family.

Especially relevant is the statement of Boniface, the Roman pontiff, in his letter to Æthelberht:

“Glorious son,” he says, “what you have requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus, we willingly grant: namely, that your Benevolence may establish in the monastery located in the city of Canterbury—which your holy teacher Augustine, of blessed memory, the disciple of Gregory, consecrated to the name of the Savior, and over which our beloved brother Laurence is now known to preside—a dwelling for monks living according to a rule, in complete freedom. By apostolic authority we decree that your monk-preachers associate with themselves a flock of monks and adorn their life with the conduct of holy men.

If any of your successors, whether kings or bishops, clerics or laymen, should attempt to invalidate these decrees of ours, let him be subject to an anathema from the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, and from all his successors, until he repents of what he has rashly done with an expiation pleasing to the Lord and makes a true correction of his disturbance.”

Therefore, either the fellowship of this monastery was Equitian or Benedictine from its first foundation, whose author was Augustine. Baronius himself does not doubt that both Augustine and Gregory were Equitian, if not Benedictine.

If it was originally Equitian, it was plainly necessary that a subsequent innovation should have taken place, transforming it into a Benedictine institution. Yet not only is nothing of the sort found; even at its very beginnings, the aforesaid Boniface establishes that the monks instituted there by Augustine—as the text previously reads—should associate with themselves a flock of monks and adorn their life with the conduct of holy men. He also provided, by the most severe threat, that no one should oppose that decree, as though he had ordered that all members of the same family and fellowship in which they had first been instituted should preserve there forever both its name and its customs.

Nor, unless credence is to be given to mere fictions, is there any trace at all of such a change, whether of name or of rule. On this matter I also carefully consulted the records of the aforesaid monastery, where I found very many and extremely ancient papal documents by which it is fortified; yet I found neither the slightest trace nor any indication of such a transformation. See also Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, pp. 516–517.

But if that monastery was Benedictine from its earliest beginnings, the very same line of reasoning that Baronius used in his conjectures about Gregory would demonstrate that Augustine belonged to the Benedictine family. For he himself does not doubt that the prelate was of the same kind as the associates whom that prelate had admitted. Let those who are concerned with the matter decide the rest.]**

[Col. 0347A]

When I observe the people of the present age, overcome by various misfortunes, anxiously investigating the deeds of those who came before them—eager, clearly, to find in them something by which they may console and strengthen themselves—yet unable to attain their desire because the scarcity of writings has allowed a fleeting oblivion to destroy those deeds, I seem to see that the men who, concerned for the benefit of the future, committed the events of their own times to the memory of letters have rendered a great service to posterity.

If, indeed, they labored at such work with good zeal, I believe that they will receive from God a good reward for it. Considering this, I resolved to record in writing, striving for brevity, the things that I saw or heard with my own eyes and ears. I wished both to comply with the desire of my friends, who strongly urged me to undertake this task, and, if perhaps something should arise among posterity that could in some way be assisted by the example of these events, to offer a small gift to their industry [Col. 0347B].
