The principal purpose of this work is therefore to describe how Anselm became Archbishop after having been abbot of the monastery of Bec; why, when a division arose between the kings of the English and him, he was so often and for so long exiled from the kingdom; and what outcome that very cause of division eventually had between them.

Finally, the cause itself appears to be a new matter for our age and, from the time when the Normans began to rule in England—not, I say, before that time—unheard-of among the English. For from the time when William, Count of Normandy, conquered and subdued that land for himself, no bishop or abbot in it had been appointed before Anselm [Col. 0348A]

[Note: [Col. 0523]

**(1)** Who had not first been the king’s man and received the investiture of the bishopric or abbey from his hand.

In that earlier age there prevailed a solemn custom, and one very common here even before the arrival of the Normans: the chief prelates of the greater peoples—namely, bishops and abbots, at least those under royal patronage—were elected by the sacred bodies of the churches, or often even designated at court with complete disregard for the votes of those sacred bodies. They were then sent by our kings, relying on ancestral right, into possession of their dignity through the delivery of the ring and pastoral staff or crozier.

In the privileges of the monastery of Glastonbury, in G. of Malmesbury’s *Deeds of the Kings*, Book II, chapter 5, King Edgar declares that the monks’ election of their abbot shall remain perpetual, but reserves to himself and his heirs the power to give the elected brother the pastoral staff.

Yet the same author writes elsewhere that in the time of the English the election of bishops and abbots belonged to clerics and monks, as may be seen in Book III of his *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, where he discusses Edmund, Bishop of Lindisfarne [Col. 0523D]. In the later years of the Saxon age, however, whether through the favor of the kings alone or through the influence of court factions, such sacred honors were conferred and, with the right of voting entirely neglected, bestowed by the same rite.

Ingulphus, Abbot of Crowland, a contemporary of William I, gives exceptionally clear testimony on this matter. “For many years past,” he says, “there had been no election of prelates that was wholly free and canonical. Rather, the royal court conferred all dignities, both of bishops and abbots, at its pleasure, by the ring and staff of the king.”

He then adds an excellent example of this rite in the case of the abbot of Wegeland, who was appointed to Crowland in this manner by Edward the Confessor. From this it is clear that it was also customary, after the death of a bishop, for the pastoral staff—and, I think, the ring as well—to be presented by a messenger of the sacred body appointed for this purpose to the king, who would invest with those insignia the bishop he chose to substitute.

Gervase of Canterbury likewise writes in a manuscript declamation—or, as he himself calls it, an “imagination”—against Robert, Abbot of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury: “Lanfranc asked the king”—namely, William I—“to grant him the donation of the abbey”—that is, Saint Augustine’s—“as it is known that all his predecessors had possessed it. The king replied that he wished to hold all the pastoral staffs of England in his hand.”

The manuscript annals of the Church of Lichfield likewise state: “Up to that time”—the words concern the age of Henry I—“the kings conferred all the bishoprics in England by the investiture of the ring and staff.” Many examples of this kind occur throughout the sources.

How controversial the matter was is more fully evident from this author of ours and from others who narrate the events of the same century. However, although Henry I is said to have renounced this right, it nevertheless appears to have remained in use for a long time afterward [Col. 0524D]. This may be inferred from a charter of King John, by which he transferred to William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke, the right to deliver the pastoral staff when appointing the abbot of Nutley.

This, unless I am mistaken, was what legal scholars later called the right of patronage over a monastery. Here are the very words of the charter, copied from the royal records, or charters, of the second year of King John, membrane 26, number 118:

“John, by the grace of God, etc. Know that, for the love which we have borne toward our beloved and faithful William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke, and for the good and faithful service which he has rendered to us, we have given and granted, and by this our charter have confirmed to him and his heirs, the donation of the pastoral staff of the abbey of Nutley, which is in his fief, to have and to hold forever, with all things, liberties, and free customs pertaining to the donation of the pastoral staff.

Therefore we will and firmly command that the aforesaid William Marshal, and his heirs after him, shall have and hold from us and our heirs the aforesaid donation of the pastoral staff properly, peacefully, freely, wholly, fully, and honorably, with all its liberties and free customs.

Witnesses: R., Count of Meulan; and R., Count of Chester; R., Count of Leicester. Given by the hand of S., Archdeacon of Wells, at Reading, on 16 August, in the second year of our reign.”

Nor did this custom prevail only among the English. It is frequently found in the Roman Empire, in the kingdom of Gaul, and elsewhere. On this matter, besides Otto of Freising, Sigebert, and many other ancient historians—especially those who wrote the history of the Emperor Henry IV and of the English King Henry I—the following authors should principally be consulted: Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book IV, chapters 9, 10, and 11; Baronius, volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 1077, and frequently afterward; Cherubinus of Nursia, *Bullarium*, volume I, pp. 16–17; Binius, *Councils*, volume III, part II, under Urban, Calixtus, and Paschal II; Renatus Choppinus, *On the Domain of France*, Book II, title 1, §6 and following sections, and *On Sacred Government*, Book I, title 7, §§22–23; together with what is incidentally read on this subject in Ivo of Chartres’s letters, in Geoffrey of Vendôme’s short works and letters, and in Cujas’s commentary on Book II of *On Feuds*, title 3.

Cujas writes that “bishoprics, indeed all fiefs, were conferred according to the ancient French custom by the ring and staff, which was called *par rain* and *par baston*: *rain* for the ring, just as among the Germans today it is *reing*. The English word *ring* is plainly the same.”

One may also consult Gratian, Distinction 63, chapter 22, “Adrianus.” Further observations on this right may be found in the exhortation of the most serene king to Christian princes.

The same must be said of the Eastern Empire, at least with respect to the delivery of the crozier. This is clearly shown both by George Phrantzes in Book III, chapter 19 of the *Chronicle of Constantinople*, and by Malaxus the Peloponnesian in his *History of the Patriarchs*.

When the patriarch-elect Gennadius Scholarius was appointed, the Emperor Muhammad II of the Turks asked the sacred orders of the City about the rites customarily used in creating a patriarch. They replied:

“ἔδειδε τοῦ ὁ Βασιλεὺς με τὸ χέρη τοῦ τὸ δικανίχη, καὶ ἔτζη ἔλαβεν ὀ Σουλτάνος με τὸ χέρη τοῦ τὸ δικανίκη, καὶ τὸ ἔδοκεν εἰς τὸ χέρη τοῦ πατριάρχου.”

That is: “The emperor used to give the patriarch the staff, or crozier, into his hand”—the object called here *dikanikē* and sometimes *patriarchikon dekanikion*—“and so the sultan took the crozier into his own hand and placed it into the hand of the patriarch.”

See the same Malaxus on Patriarch Jeremiah.

The older right of investitures, as our forefathers called it, is also relevant to what appears in the letters of King Edward III to the Roman pontiff and the College of Cardinals. In those letters Edward rightly asserted that a Roman pontiff acted contrary to the right transmitted to him by his ancestors when he confirmed an elected bishop in England in his dignity by sacred ceremonies before, even at that time, the king’s assent to the election had been given.

“For,” he says, “our progenitors, who long ago founded and endowed the churches, formerly freely conferred each vacant cathedral church of our kingdom by their royal right”—which itself was the ancient right of investiture. “Later, however, at the petition of the clergy and out of reverence for, and in response to the request of, the supreme pontiff who then presided over the universal Church, the lord King of England who then was granted to the chapters of the cathedral churches that, when the bishop of the place resigned or died, another should be designated by the votes of the sacred bodies, although that person would necessarily await the solemn assent of the king, though not the form of investiture that we have described” [Col. 0526A].

Those letters are found in the Roman records under the ninth and tenth years of Edward III, numbers 3 and 4. The predecessor whom this Edward has in mind, I think, is King John. On him, if desired, see Matthew Paris, p. 342 of the London edition.

We deliberately omit more recent matters relating to this subject.]**

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The reader is referred below to the fuller notes of John Selden. EDITOR.]

who had not first been the king’s man and received the investiture of the bishopric or abbey from his hand through the delivery of the pastoral staff [Col. 0526].

**(2)** Except for two bishops, namely Ernest and Gundulf. For the right of appointing the bishops to be substituted in the see of Rochester formerly belonged to the Archbishops of Canterbury. This singular privilege—for by common law the patron of bishoprics among us was always held to be the king alone—occurs frequently in the ancient records of the Church of Canterbury. See also Jocelin, *On the Ancient British Church*, in his *Life of Chichele*; Charter 16 of the reign of King John, membrane 6, dorse 5, in the Royal Archive; and Bracton, Book V, *On Exceptions*, chapter 4, §8.

In a manuscript codex of the monastery of Dunstable we likewise read: “In the year 1182 Walter, Bishop of Rochester, died. Waleran the archdeacon was substituted for him; through the text of the Gospel he received from the hand of the archbishop”—namely, Richard, who presided under King Henry II—“the spiritual jurisdiction of the bishopric, but through the ring he received possession of its royal holdings.”

The patron of the Church of Llandaff was formerly the Earl of Gloucester, as appears in an old manuscript codex in the treasury archive of charters—namely, papal documents—p. 166, and elsewhere more than once. The patron of the bishopric of Sodor in the Isle of Man is likewise today said to be the Earl of Derby, since by hereditary right he is lord of the island.]

Except for two bishops, namely Ernest and Gundulf. These men, each successively presiding over the Church of Rochester, were, according to custom, personally invested with the bishopric by Archbishop Lanfranc of Canterbury, of venerable memory, in the chapter of the brothers at Canterbury.

This custom, therefore, as though contrary [Col. 0348A]

**(3)** To God and the sacred canons.

The ancient canons meant here are, I think, Canon 31 among those attributed to the Apostles, and Canon 3 of the Seventh Ecumenical Council held at Nicaea, besides other canons of an earlier age found in Gratian, Distinction 63; Canon 5 of the Roman Council under Gregory VII; and Canon 23 of the Council of Antioch, together with Cause XVI, Question 7, chapter 16. There are other, more recent canons, of which something will shortly be said in passing.

Yet, however carefully the ancient canons provided that princes should neither appoint bishops nor designate them nor place those designated or elected in possession of their dignity, imperial right in both empires, East and West, nevertheless opposed those provisions, as did the laws or customs of the English, French, and other kingdoms; and bishops appointed by kings are found very frequently.

The matter concerning the West and the other kingdoms is sufficiently well known from the passages noted above concerning the rite of investitures. Concerning the East, see Theodore Balsamon, Patriarch of Antioch and a highly learned authority in law, on Canon 16 of the Council of Carthage:

“The Emperor,” he says, “has the right to transfer a bishopric to a metropolitan see, to separate it from its proper metropolitan church, to divide the dioceses of bishops, and to appoint bishops and metropolitans anew.”

See the same Theodore also on Canon 4 of the Council of Chalcedon.]

Anselm, wishing to abolish this practice as contrary to God and the sacred canons, and thereby to cut away the injustices flowing from it, became hateful to the kings themselves and was forced to leave his homeland. There were also other causes of his departure, as the sequence of events will make clear.

Other matters that occurred in England before, during, and after these events will also be described. We have judged that, as far as we are able, those who come after us should not be entirely deprived of knowledge of them. But it will be enough to have mentioned these matters briefly in the preface.

As we now undertake the order of the narrative, we think that we must begin somewhat farther back and proceed with a brief account from the very root, so to speak, from which the shoot of the events to be related grew.

[Col. 0347B]

# BOOK ONE

When the most glorious King Edgar reigned in England and vigorously governed the whole kingdom by holy laws, Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, a man wholly formed by the virtues [Col. 0347C], directed all Britain according to the rule of Christian law.

Through this man’s weighty activity and counsel, the same king became devoted to God and, with unconquered courage, defeated, overcame, and suppressed the attacks of barbarians rushing in from every side. Thus England obtained peace and happy days throughout the land while it was deemed worthy to enjoy the bodily presence of that king and Father Dunstan.

When this king perceived that the final day of his life was approaching, he entrusted the reins of the kingdom to his son Edward. The glorious Edward, therefore, successor to his glorious father and instructed by Saint Dunstan, ruled the kingdom with the greatest vigor for as long as he lived.

But after a few years of his reign had passed, he was killed through the wicked treachery of his stepmother. As his successor in the kingdom he received his brother, named Æthelred, the son of that evil woman, who was indeed heir to the kingdom but to no virtue. Because he had aspired to the kingdom through his brother’s blood, the aforesaid archbishop threatened him with a grave denunciation, declaring that he would live in blood, suffer the barbarian invasions under cruel oppression, and see the kingdom itself crushed by countless and bloody devastations [Col. 0348C].

How true this prophecy of the man of God proved to be can easily be seen both in the Chronicles, by those who wish to read them, and in our own tribulations, by those who know how to take notice—without mentioning what the course of this work will demonstrate at various points under the direction of truth.

When blessed Dunstan had therefore been translated to the heavenly realms, England immediately lay open, as he himself had foretold, to the invasion of the barbarians. For the king’s negligence became known everywhere, and therefore the greed of foreigners, desiring the wealth of the English rather than their customs, began to invade here and there by sea and land. First they devastated the towns and cities near the sea, then those farther inland, and finally the whole province with miserable destruction.

When the king, struck by excessive fear, did not dare to confront them with arms but instead shamelessly sought peace from them by giving money, they took the payment and returned home, so that they might come back fiercer with their numbers increased and receive multiplied rewards for a renewed invasion. Thus at one time they obtained ten thousand pounds of silver, at another sixteen thousand, at another twenty-four thousand, and at another thirty thousand, the aforesaid King Æthelred granting everything to them and oppressing the entire kingdom with a heavy levy.

Amid these evils, Ælfeah, fourth after blessed Dunstan [Col. 0526D],

**(4)** Bishop of Winchester. Winchester is called *Venta Belgarum* by Ptolemy and Antoninus, and is still called *Caer-guent* by the Welsh Britons. Hence *Ventanus* and *Wentanus* frequently occur among older monks, while *Wenlanus* is a corrupt form found in printed manuscripts of William of Malmesbury’s *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, Book I, p. 117b, London edition.]

Bishop of Winchester undertook the governance of the Church of Canterbury. He was a vigorous man, adorned from childhood with the life and habit of sacred religion.

When he considered the countless evils by which the whole kingdom was being devastated beyond measure, he shuddered. He began to seek by every means available to him how he might oppose the savagery of wicked men.

When they perceived this, and took thought for themselves and their own people lest they be deprived of their customary plunder, they became inflamed against him with bitter hatred. Thus, after the city of Canterbury had been devastated and burned, and its citizens condemned by the invaders to a lamentable fate, the Church of the Savior standing there was also consumed by fire.

Meanwhile the Father himself was bound and led away by the hands of the raging men. First, almost all the monks who under his rule served the Lord Christ in that church were slaughtered before his eyes.

Then Ælfeah was thrown into a small boat and carried to Greenwich. There he was confined in cruel custody for seven months. Since he refused to yield to the wickedness of the evil men, and could not be overcome by any threats, he was stoned by them in the most savage manner and died.

I have mentioned these events briefly, not weaving a history, but laying open to the understanding of those who wish to know how truly Father Dunstan prophesied the evils that would come upon England [Col. 0349C].

Nor was this the end of the evils. After these events, other great disasters occurred throughout England, and for many years matters continually went from bad to worse for them. Among them, too, were the monasteries of the servants and handmaids of God, [Note: [Col. 0526]

Source preparation: Embedded foreign-language text recovered from the supplied local archive; the Old English and Latin recensions are translated separately.

(5) Which, up to the number of forty-eight, had newly arisen in the time of King Edgar . . . . .

[5] “Which, up to forty-eight in King Edgar’s time … had newly arisen.”

For Edgar was an excellent restorer and founder of monasteries, and, formed by Dunstan’s exhortation, was exceedingly devoted to those who had enrolled themselves in the solitary life, while he was extremely hostile to gatherings of priests or other clerics. Deliberately passing over whatever is read on this subject in published historians, I note here, not inappropriately, the Institutions promulgated by that same king, which at that time provided a rule of life for the monastic commonwealth—or communities of both sexes—of the Benedictines, restored throughout England. Of these there still exists a very ancient copy, beautifully written both in Saxon and in Latin characters. I have thought it appropriate to present it here, faithfully transcribed in both languages, and in no other form than that found in the exemplar itself, where word is rendered by word, apparently so as to indicate not so much the proper syntax and order of the Saxon language as the meaning of the individual words.

## The Prologue of the Regular Concord of the Monks and Nuns of the English Nation begins

### Old English (Saxon) recension, translated separately

“By Christ’s assisting grace, the nobly born king of the English and of the other peoples dwelling within the circuit of the island of Britain, from the beginning of his childhood—although, as that age commonly does, he followed diverse customs—yet, touched by divine inspiration and repeatedly admonished by a zealous abbot who showed him the royal way of the faith, began earnestly to fear, love, and honour God. As the small spark of faith shone, lest it should be extinguished by the sloth of idleness, he began anxiously to inquire by what merits of holy works he might be kindled to the hot perfection of fulfilment.

“When he found that the holy monasteries, scattered in various places of his kingdom, were ruined and almost negligently abandoned from the service of our Lord Jesus Christ, moved by the Lord’s grace, he hastened with great joy of heart fittingly to restore every place. Having expelled the filth of careless priests, he established not only monks but nuns also, with fathers and mothers appointed, everywhere throughout the wide extent of his realm for God’s service, and gladly enriched them with every good thing.

“Exercising his royal office like the Shepherd of shepherds, he carefully protected the sheep whom he had diligently gathered by the Lord’s granting grace from the ravening nets of faithless men and the gaping mouths of wolves. He most wisely commanded his consort, Queen Ælfthryth, to protect the nunneries as a fearless guardian, so that men should help men and women women, without any suspicion of doubt.

“The rule of the holy Father Benedict having been worthily received, very many abbots and abbesses with the communities of brothers and sisters subject to them joyfully strove together to follow the saints’ footsteps in one faith, though not in one customary usage.”

[Col. 0528B — Old English recension]

“The aforesaid king, greatly pleased with this great zeal, searching out every hidden matter with diligent care, decreed that a synodal meeting should be held at Winchester. He humbly set down and sent words of exhortation and peace, plainly written on a book-leaf, and by Christ’s grace urged all to maintain, in one equal customary practice, the firmly anchored precepts of the Rule while imitating holy and approved fathers, never differing in discord; lest the unequal and diverse customs of one Rule and one people disgrace holy life.

“At the spiritual prompting and careful admonition of this most high king, not bishops only, but abbots and abbesses too, because they had obtained so excellent and great a teacher, raised their hands to heaven and gladly gave immeasurable thanks to the Most High.

“They promptly obeyed his commands with all their minds. Remembering the teaching of our holy patron Gregory, who directed blessed Augustine to establish in the young English church the worthy customs not only of Roman churches but also of Frankish churches, they summoned monks of Fleury, of blessed Benedict, and monks of the famous great monastery called Gent. From their worthy practices they gathered every honourable custom, as bees make one honeycomb from the different blossoms of many fields. Thus, aided by Christ the Saviour of the world, they set these customs down in this little book for the dignity of life and the sweetness of regular observance, so that those who still humbly walk the royal way of the Lord’s commandments, without the blemish of boasting, might lawfully drink them without disgust or complaint, and be fittingly filled with loving desire through the nation’s great and profitable discernment.

“Lest any person, which may God prevent, should confidently choose his own invention and thus lose the excellent fruit of holy obedience, miserably deceived by vain opposition, or should be thought Sarabaites or beasts rather than monks or human beings, they unanimously promised our Lord Jesus Christ, and strengthened the pledge with a spiritual covenant, that while life remained they would openly keep, in a common manner of life under the Rule’s yoke, these noted customs.”

[Col. 0529D — Old English recension]

“Moreover, let each use private prayers in the secret places of the oratory, as gently prompted by the grace of the Holy Spirit, with God as witness and with watchfulness in good works.

“The noble archbishop of this people, Dunstan, inspired with prophetic spirit, wisely added this to strengthen the aforesaid synodal assembly: that no monk, man of higher rank, or man of lower rank should dare enter the nuns’ private places to inspect them; and that those who hold the precedence of spiritual authority over them for instruction, not for worldly power, should govern access to their private places with moderation, as blessed Isidore teaches, so that they do not in any respect oppose their regular observance.

“We judge that those subject to the regular yoke should take heed that, in singing the customary intercessions for the king and benefactors by whose good gifts Christ feeds us, they do not by singing too quickly provoke God to anger rather than thoughtfully call upon him for forgiveness of sins. Therefore, as our father Benedict exhorts, let all sing in measured fashion, so that our mind may agree with our voice and the apostolic saying be fulfilled: ‘I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding.’ If necessity requires something outside the common regular custom to be added, let it be done until the purpose for which it was done is bettered by Christ’s aiding grace; and let the welcome fruit of obedience be gained after prideful opposition has been rejected. Let the regular degree be preserved, in which a monk is commanded to do nothing except what the Rule of the common monastery or the examples of elders commend.”

[Col. 0530D — Old English recension]

“Let no one thereafter keep a presumptuous custom through boldness unless it has been chosen by synodal counsel and committed with the discernment that is the mother of all virtues by all who are faithful. At the aforesaid synodal council all judged with great care that the election of abbots and abbesses should be carried out with the king’s leave and according to the counsel and teaching of the holy Rule.

“The election of bishops also, like that of abbots, wherever regular monks live at an episcopal see, is to be made in the same way if, by the Lord’s granting grace, a monk fit for such advancement can be found. It is to be done in that same manner and in no other, while they are of the same manner of life; the printed Old English then has a lacuna: [lacuna].”

[Col. 0531B — Old English recension]

“But if, through hindering ignorance or sins deserved, no one worthy of the honour of so great an office can be found in that congregation, let one be chosen from another known monastery of monks by the unanimous counsel of the king and of the brothers to whom he is to be consecrated. When ordained bishop, he is continually and without interruption to keep among his monks, with careful and surpassing diligence, the same regular custom which the abbot keeps; he must not, under the pretext of the episcopal dignity, presumptuously break or forget the Rule’s commands, but surpass them in deed.

“They wisely forbade the admission of secular authority in holy monasteries, with careful examination and anathema, lest, as had happened, it bring great harm and ruin. They commanded that only the lordship of king and queen should always be sought by desired petition for the protection of the holy place and aid to ecclesiastical property. Whenever it benefits the holy monastery over which they preside, fathers and mothers of monasteries are to approach king and queen humbly, with fear of God and the Rule’s observance. They may meet powerful people within or outside the monastery, not for feasting but for the monastery’s advantage and protection, whenever that is useful and permitted.

“When riding or travelling on foot, they are not to occupy themselves with idle tales, but either serve in psalm-singing or speak at a permitted time of a necessary matter. They are to fulfil the canonical hours not on horseback but after dismounting and kneeling, unless it is a feast day, as fittingly as they can with divine compunction. Travellers are to take not boys but mature persons whose admonition may improve them.”

[Col. 0532B — Old English recension]

“Those who stay at home are to be improved in the company not of young people but of mature members. Abbots, no less than brothers, are not to embrace young people or boys in their arms or lightly kiss them with their lips; they are to love them reverently, with great caution, in affectionate purpose of mind and without words. They must not presume to lead any of them away alone for obedience, nor under the appearance of a spiritual concern; but each is to remain continually under the watching care of the shepherd or guardian, as the Rule commands.

“Nor may the guardian go with any one boy without a third person present as witness. As customary, he is to go with the whole school, where a reasonable need requires it, in silence or serving in psalmody, and with a blessing. They are not to make frequent rounds of villages unless great necessity compels and sound discretion directs it. Neither superiors nor those subject to them may with boldness visit secular people’s feasts, except when the hospitality of a journey unexpectedly arises.

“Let us keep with all our strength, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, food in weight, measure, and number; clothing; fasting; abstinence; vigils; silence; the good of obedience; and every other thing which we have willingly received from the ordinances of our patron, blessed Benedict.”

[Col. 0533A — Old English recension]

“Concerning the customary practices of the holy Rule, both those of the aforesaid father Benedict and those of his holy followers and imitators, kept partly under the great discernment of judgment and in continual practice, let us, strengthened by the aforesaid king’s admonition and the commands of the fathers, carefully set them out in writing as we have promised, so far as strength helps and the Holy Spirit’s grace prompts, for the preservation of loving brotherly unity. Thus, all keeping them in one accord and joyfully, may receive from him the reward of eternal life: he who makes those of one disposition to dwell in a house, the King, God, Son of God and of the Virgin, who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever. Amen.”

[Col. 0533C — Old English royal sanction, translated separately]

“The aforesaid king, who began this little book with the faithful and prudent admonition of a prologue, also rightly concluded its epilogue with wise deliberation. With the great authority of royal power he most strictly forbade that any abbot or abbess should hoard for himself or herself an earthly treasure, namely the customary payment which the natives call Heregeat, which after the death of the powerful men of this land is customarily given to kings. They must not possess it so that it may be given in imitation of worldly people; otherwise, falling into the anathema of Ananias and Sapphira, they would destroy, to their souls’ great peril, the commands of the holy Rule that forbid all private possessions.

“But in the name of Christ, whose servants they are, and of his mother Mary and of all saints, he forbade for ever, for himself and all his successors, that such payment should be given for an abbot or abbess.

[Col. 0534A — Old English royal sanction]

“With benevolent instruction he taught the fathers and mothers of monasteries to lay up through the hands of the poor, with great and continual compunction, whatever remains above necessary uses as treasure in heaven, so that while the body dwells on earth, the mind, living there in conduct, may remain where it has sent its treasure in the better and more righteous order. If, when an elder dies, anything remains, the following abbot, as the grace of the Holy Spirit prompts, must not divide it according to the former ruler’s direction among fleshly kinsfolk or worldly magnates, but must wisely dispose of it with the brothers’ counsel, helping the brothers’ needs and the poor.”

### Latin recension, translated separately

[Col. 0527A]

For the illustrious Edgar, king of the English and of the other peoples dwelling within the bounds of the island of Britain, aided by Christ’s grace, although from the earliest age of his boyhood he used various customs—as that age is accustomed to do—nevertheless, touched by divine consideration, began, through the constant admonition of a certain abbot who showed him the royal road of the Catholic faith, greatly to fear, love, and venerate God. As the spark of faith gradually shone forth, lest it should be extinguished by bodily idleness and remain hidden, he began anxiously and diligently to inquire by what merits of holy works he might be kindled into the fervent heat of perfection.

[Col. 0527B]

When he had discovered that the sacred monasteries, in various places of his realm, were lying ruined and almost negligently abandoned by the service of our Lord Jesus Christ, he, touched by the grace of the Lord, hastened with great alacrity of spirit to restore them most suitably wherever they were. Having expelled the filth of negligent clerics, he established everywhere throughout the vast extent of his kingdom not only monks but also nuns, appointing fathers and mothers for them, and devotedly assigning them to the service of God; rejoicing, he enriched them with every good thing.

[Col. 0527C]

As a royal ruler, like the Shepherd of shepherds, he carefully rescued and protected the sheep whom, by the Lord’s granting grace, he had diligently gathered, from the ravenous nets of the treacherous and the gaping jaws of wolves. He most cautiously instructed his wife, Alfritha, to defend the folds of the nuns in the fearless manner of a guardian, namely, so that men might assist men and women women, without any suspicion or scruple.

Having therefore most honourably received the regular rule of the holy Father Benedict, very many abbots and abbesses, together with the communities of brothers and sisters subject to them, strove eagerly to follow the footsteps of the saints in one faith, though not in one customary practice, with great joy.

[Col. 0528B]

The aforesaid king was greatly delighted by such zeal and by so great an undertaking. Examining everything hidden with diligent care, he decreed that a synodal council should be held at Winchester. He humbly sent there words of exhortation and peace, clearly written on a small written tablet, and, touched by Christ’s grace, admonished all that, agreeing in an equal customary practice, and imitating holy and approved Fathers, they should hold the regular precepts with the firm anchor of their minds and in no way disagree through dissension, lest the unequal and varied observance of one Rule and one nation should bring shameful reproach upon holy conduct.

[Col. 0528C]

Touched spiritually by the wise admonition of this most excellent king, not only the bishops but also the abbots and abbesses—who had deserved to possess such a great and eminent teacher—did not delay to raise their hands toward heaven and offer immense thanks to the lofty throne, having obtained their desire.

[Col. 0528D]

For immediately, obeying his commands cheerfully with all the strength of their minds, and recalling the instructions of our holy patron Gregory, by which he had sought to admonish blessed Augustine to establish in the still inexperienced English Church not only the honourable customs of the Roman churches but also those of the churches of Gaul, they summoned monks from the monastery of blessed Benedict at Fleury, as well as from the outstanding monastery called by the famous name of Gent. Gathering what was honourable from their worthy customs, as bees gather a honeycomb from the varied flowers of the meadows in one hive, they set down these customs of conduct—by the aid of Christ, the Saviour of the world—for the honour of life and the sweetness of regular observance, so that those who humbly walk the royal road of the Lord’s commandments, still free from the disgust of boastfulness, might taste them lawfully and with the greatest pleasure, and be temperately filled with loving devotion, by means of the great and subtle discernment of the nation, in this little book.

[Editorial note: *studuerunt* (“they strove”).]

[Editorial note: Perhaps read *depulso* (“having driven away”).]

[Editorial note: Read *Codicello* (“little booklet”).]

[Col. 0529C]

Lest individuals, if—God forbid—they should presumptuously choose an invention of their own, should unexpectedly and miserably lose the excellent fruit of holy obedience through the arrogance of pride, and should appear to be Sarabaites or wild men rather than monks or human beings, they unanimously vowed to our Lord Jesus Christ and confirmed by a spiritual pledge that, as long as life lasted, they would devote themselves to the yoke of the Rule and openly observe these recorded customs of conduct in a common way of life.

[Col. 0529D]

Moreover, let each person, in the secret places of the oratory, use private prayers with God as witness, prudently and with vigilance in good works, insofar as the grace of the Holy Spirit may mercifully prompt him.

This the excellent Dunstan, archbishop of this nation, filled with prophetic spirit, wisely and prudently added to strengthen the assembly of the aforesaid synodal gathering: namely, that no monk, nor any man of a higher or lower rank, should dare enter the secret places of the nuns and inspect them; and that those who exercise the primacy of spiritual authority over them for the benefit of discipline, not for secular tyranny or domination, should regulate their access to their private places with moderation, as blessed Isidore advises, so that they may in no way contradict their regular observance.

[Col. 0530A]

We have judged that this alone should be attended to by Catholics devoted to the regular yoke: lest, by chanting too swiftly, they should thoughtlessly provoke God to anger—God forbid—rather than wisely invite forgiveness of sins, when according to the custom of the Fathers they usually sing prayers of intercession for the king and benefactors by whose gifts, through Christ’s generosity, we are nourished.

Thus, at the exhortation of our Father Benedict, let all things be regulated by distinct psalmody, so that our mind may agree with our voice and the apostolic saying may be fulfilled: “I shall sing with the spirit; I shall sing also with the mind.”

If, however, for any necessity something must be added beyond the common usage of the Rule, let it be done for as long as the matter for which it is done is improved, by Christ’s assisting grace. And, despising the arrogance of pride, let the most welcome fruit of obedience be acquired. Let that regular degree be most diligently observed in which it is prescribed that a monk do nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of his elders encourage.

[Col. 0530B]

Let no practice thereafter be rashly maintained with presumptuous temerity unless it has been chosen and handed down by the synodal council, with the discretion that is the mother of all virtues, by all the Catholics.

At the aforesaid synodal assembly all resolved that this should be attended to with the greatest care: that the election of abbots and abbesses should take place with the king’s consent and counsel, according to the teaching of the Holy Rule.

The election of bishops also, like that of abbots, wherever regular monks live in an episcopal see, should be conducted in the same manner, if, by the Lord’s granting grace, a monk of such advancement can be found there; and, while they share the same manner of life, no one should presume to proceed in any other way.

[Col. 0531B]

But if, because of ignorance or because sins have deserved it, no one worthy of the honour of so great a rank can be found in that congregation, he shall be chosen from another known monastery of monks, by the unanimous counsel of the king and of the brothers to whom he is to be dedicated.

When he has been ordained bishop, he shall diligently and continually preserve in all things the same regular manner among his monks that the regular abbot observes, with the greatest care and excellence. Nor, on the pretext of the episcopate, shall he timidly or forgetfully interrupt the precepts of the Rule, but shall show in his works how much he excels.

[Col. 0531C]

As for the authority of secular persons, lest it should come miserably to great ruin and damage, as formerly happened, they wisely prohibited its reception in the sacred monasteries, with severe admonition and anathema. They prudently commanded that only the dominion of the king and queen should always be sought by desired petition, for the protection of the sacred place and the increase of ecclesiastical possessions.

[Col. 0531D]

As often as necessity requires, the fathers and mothers of the monasteries should humbly approach the king and queen, in fear of God and observance of the Rule, for the benefit of the sacred monastery over which they preside.

They may go to meet the powerful, not for the sake of feasting, but for the benefit and defence of the monastery, whenever necessity requires, within or outside the monastery, with permission.

[Col. 0532A]

When travelling on horseback or on foot, let them not give themselves to idle stories, but either attend to psalmody or speak at a suitable time about necessary matters.

Considering this, let them complete the canonical hours not while riding but by dismounting from their horses and kneeling, unless it is a feast day, suitably, as they are able, with divine compunction.

When travelling, let them take with them not young boys but adults, by whose admonition they may be improved.

[Col. 0532B]

Those remaining at home should love not only the brothers: abbots too should love adolescents or boys—not by embracing them in their arms or lightly kissing them with their lips, but with charitable affection of spirit; without flattering words, let them love them reverently and with great caution.

Let them presume neither to lead any of them away for private service, nor even under the pretext of a spiritual matter; but, as the Rule commands, let each remain continually under the vigilance of his guardian.

[The manuscript reading is uncertain; the Latin ends with “let him remain.”]

[Col. 0532C]

Nor may the guardian himself have permission to depart with any single boy without a third person standing by as witness. Rather, according to custom, with the whole school, if a reasonable matter so requires, let him go where necessity demands, either in silence or attending to psalmody, with a blessing.

Let them by no means make frequent circuits of the villages, unless great necessity compels them and the discernment of necessary reason dictates it.

[Col. 0532D]

As for secular banquets, unless perhaps the hospitality of a journey should unexpectedly arise, neither superiors nor subjects should presume to attend them in any way with rash boldness.

Let us preserve with all our strength, with the assent of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, food with due weight, measure, and number; clothing; fasting; abstinence; vigils; silence; the good of obedience; and all the other practices which we have voluntarily received through the teaching of our patron, blessed Benedict.

[Col. 0533A]

Concerning the customary practices of the holy Rule, received partly from the aforesaid Father Benedict and partly from his holy followers and imitators, and maintained with great examination and discernment, relying on the admonition of the aforesaid king and trusting in the commands of the Fathers, let us carefully clarify in writing, as we have promised, insofar as our strength permits and the grace of the Holy Spirit prompts us, for the preservation of charitable brotherly unity.

[Col. 0533B]

Thus let all receive together and joyfully the reward of eternal life from him who makes them dwell in one accord, that is, in one manner, in a house: where the King is God, the Son of God and of the Virgin, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, world without end. Amen.

## [Col. 0533B]

The twelve chapters concerning the sacred and solemn offices of the monks follow, adapted to the Benedictine precepts; from them, moreover, the very wording of the prayer, prologue, and chapters is sometimes taken.

When these chapters have been completed, a royal sanction is appended, by which it was provided that, when monastery rulers died, what the Greek jurists call *Εἰσδεκτικά* (“entrance dues”), and what our people call *Relevia* or *Hereota*, should not be paid into the treasury by those who succeeded them. Formerly they were commonly paid, as is clear from the sanction itself, which we add here.

[Col. 0533C]

“The aforesaid king, so as to conclude the epilogue of this little book orthodoxly, just as he had begun its prologue with a faithful and reasonable exhortation, examined the matter with prudent scrutiny. With the full authority of his royal power, he expressly forbade and commanded that no abbot or [Col. 0533D] abbess should store up for himself or herself a little earthly treasury, so as to possess the customary tax which the natives usually call *Heria tua*—the customary payment which, after the death of the powerful men of this country, is ordinarily given to kings—in order that it might be given on their behalf in imitation of secular persons. Thus they would fall under the anathema of Ananias and Sapphira and, to the great detriment of their souls, abolish the precepts of the Holy Rule, which prohibit all private possessions.

“But he forever forbade, both for himself and for all his successors, that anything should be given for an abbot or abbess in the name of Christ, whose vicars they are, and of his mother Mary and all the saints.

[Col. 0534A]

“He urged and taught them with benevolent intention that the fathers and mothers of monasteries should place whatever remained beyond necessary uses, through the hands of the poor, in heavenly treasuries, with great and continual contrition; so that, while the body dwells on earth, the mind may remain there by its conduct, where the most just order promised that treasures would be.

“If anything remained when a prior died, the succeeding abbot, as the grace of the Holy Spirit should inspire him, should not distribute it to blood relatives or secular tyrants according to the former ruler’s dictate, but should wisely arrange it, with the counsel of the brothers, by assisting the needs of the brothers and the poor.”

[Col. 0534B]

The same law afterward remained in use among us, except where a particular custom or agreement required such a payment. On this matter, if desired, consult Bracton, *On Acquiring Dominion over Things*, chapter 35, § 4; the code called *Breton*, chapter “On Homages,” 3 Edward III, folio 76 verso; 20 Edward III, title “Avowry,” 124, and title “Relief,” 8; 3 Henry IV, folio 2 recto; 8 Richard II, title “Relief,” 14.

Concerning the Saxon *Hereoto* or *Hergeate*, or *Relevamentum*, *Relevatio*, or *Relevamen*—as it was called—see chapters 68 and 69 of the Laws of King Cnut, and the Laws of Edward the Confessor, chapter “On Heretochies.”

Add to these the following from the tax records of England, written under William I with public authority and still preserved in the royal treasury archive:

“In Kent, when an allodial holder dies”—so those records state—“the king shall have the relief of the land, except the land of Holy Trinity, Saint Augustine, and Saint Martin, and except the lands of Godric of Burnes, Godric of Carlesone, Aelnod Cilt, Esber Biga, Seret of Cilleham, Turgis, Norman, and Aror. Over these the king has forfeiture only of their persons, while from their lands he has the relief, since they have their own soke and sake.”

And in the city of Hereford:

“When a burgess serving with a horse dies, the king has his horse and weapons. If one who has no horse dies, the king has either ten shillings or his land with its houses.”

Likewise, in Archenfield—which we now call Irchenfield—a district of Herefordshire, the king has, as those records state, three churches. The priests of these churches carry the king’s messages into Wales; each of them sings two masses for the king every week. If any one of them dies, the king receives twenty shillings from him by custom.

See also Camden, in the county of Berkshire, on the relief of *thegns*. Other examples of this kind are also found; but this is merely by the way.

[Col. 0534C]

As for Edgar’s diligent care and devoted labour in renewing the institutions of the solitary life, there still exists a book beautifully written in letters of gold at his command, in which he restored these institutions at the new monastery of Winchester. Passing over its preface, sufficiently inflated according to the custom of that age—which occupies several pages but is not entirely relevant—we present what follows:

“‘I, Edgar, by the favour of divine grace,’ etc.” See Edgar’s Ecclesiastical Laws, *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVIII, col. 486 and following.

[Col. 0535A]

That this remarkable restoration of the solitary life is intended is shown by the words of Henry of Huntingdon in his eulogy of King Edgar:

> He gave temples to God, monks to the temples, and lands to the monks.

Our historians pass lightly over the same matter. Among them, if desired, consult Florence of Worcester under the years 964, 969, and 970, as well as Matthew Florilegus. What they assign to the year 964 concerning that new monastery at Winchester must be transferred to 966, if credence is to be placed—and it must fully be placed—in the royal charter which we have already taken care to insert above.

[Col. 0535B]

See also what appears in Surius under 5 October and in Baronius, volume X, year 970, where sanctions that repeatedly and most clearly acknowledge Edgar as their author in the plainest words are briefly mentioned as though they had Dunstan alone and Pope John XIII as their authors.

Moreover, Edgar’s address to the bishops concerning the restoration mentioned above is found in Ailred, abbot of Rievaulx, in the manuscript epistolary history addressed to Henry II. It is particularly worthy of attention, for it is the very address praised by the distinguished Isaac Casaubon in the letter prefixed to the *Exercitationes*, and it runs as follows, faithfully transcribed from the same manuscripts that he used:

> “Since the Lord has magnified his mercy,” etc.

It appears above in the ecclesiastical laws of King Edgar.

These new foundations, which had arisen up to the number of forty-eight in the time of King Edgar through Father Dunstan, with the assistance of the holy bishops Oswald of York and Æthelwold of Winchester, were largely destroyed, and the religious observance of the monastic order was almost reduced to nothing. Several years passed during these events.

[Editorial note: This passage is cited here, and from the very exemplar that we used, by the distinguished Isaac Casaubon in the dedicatory letter prefixed to the *Baronian Exercitations*.]

While Edward was reigning—Edward, to whom the aforesaid king of the English, Æthelred, had fathered a son by Emma, the sister of Richard, count of the Normans—many monasteries that had survived until that time were destroyed. At that period the magnanimous Godwin, earl of Kent, was held in great esteem throughout England by land and sea. When a serious quarrel arose between him and the king, he was condemned to exile from England together with almost all his followers. He therefore went to Count Baldwin in Flanders, while his son Harold went to Ireland.

Then, after Emma, the king’s mother, had died, Godwin and Harold returned to England, each protected by numerous ships and a strong force of soldiers. Many of the leading men of the kingdom, recognizing this and dreading that war might break out on both sides, pressed for peace to be established between them. But the king, suspecting Godwin’s craftiness, resisted and would not agree to peace unless he first had hostages who could secure his safety.

Godwin’s son Wulfnoth, and Hakon, the son of his son Sweyn, were therefore given as hostages and sent to Normandy to be held by Count William, namely the son of Robert, son of Richard, his mother’s brother. After this, Godwin, being an enemy of the Church of Canterbury—for after seducing Archbishop Eadsige he had seized from that Church its estate called Folkestone—died a bad death after a short time. His son Harold succeeded him as earl of Kent.

After a little while Harold asked the king for permission to go to Normandy, to free his brother and nephew, who were being held as hostages, and to bring them back once they had been released. The king replied:

> “This will not be done through me. Nevertheless, lest I seem to wish to prevent you, I allow you to go wherever you wish and to discover what you can accomplish. I foresee, however, that you are aiming at nothing other than the injury of the whole English kingdom and your own disgrace. For I do not know the count to be so lacking in judgment that he would grant them to you in any respect unless he had first perceived that this would bring him great advantage.”

Harold therefore boarded a ship, trusting his own judgment rather than the king’s advice, accompanied by his wealthier and more respectable men, nobly equipped with gold, silver, and costly clothing. As they sailed, the turbulent sea terrified them, and a mass of waves violently battered the ship. At last, after it had been cast out with everything it carried into the river of Ponthieu called the Maye, the lord of that land, following the custom of the place, delivered him into captivity; and the men who were in the ship were committed to stricter custody.

[Note: [Col. 0535] (6) “With everything it carried,” etc.; according to the custom of the place, he is delivered into captivity. An ancient custom still survives on almost every shore of the Christian world: the goods of shipwrecked persons are appropriated to the treasury. Among the English, however, this applies only where not a single human being, nor even a living dog or cat, has escaped. On the French coast, see Bertrand d’Argentré, *Consuetudines Britanniae*, title “Des droits du prince,” art. 56 § 45; Charles de Grassaille, *De jure Franciae*, book 20, “De Neapolitano”; Andreas de Isernia on the Neapolitan Constitutions, book I; and Matthaeus Afflictus, on the Neapolitan Constitutions, book I, title 59. On other regions, see the same Bertrand; Choppinus, *De dominio*, book I, title 15; Bodin, *De republica*, book I, chapter 10. Imperial law, however, is different. For what right, says the Emperor Antoninus, does the treasury have in another’s misfortune, so as to seek profit from so grievous a calamity? *Code*, “De naufragiis,” book I. And pontifical law strikes with anathema those who plunder the goods of Christian shipwreck victims, in the *Extravagantes*, title “De raptoribus,” chapter 3, “Excommunicationi,” and in that pontifical sanction called the *Bulla Coenae Domini*; on this see Bartholomeus Ugolinus, *De censuris*. Here understand “the lord of the land” to mean Guido, count of Ponthieu—or of Ponthieu, that is, of the maritime province of Picardy, neighboring Normandy.]

Harold, therefore, being confined, secretly sent to the count of Normandy one of the common people, enticed by a promised reward, to explain what had happened to him. William then sent messengers in haste to the lord of Ponthieu, ordering him to send Harold and his companions to him as quickly as possible, free from every charge, if he wished henceforth to enjoy their former friendship according to custom. But when the man refused to release him, he received a second command: he must necessarily send Harold, or else he should know for certain that William, duke of Normandy, would come armed to Ponthieu to recover him.

He therefore sent the man with his companions, though he first confiscated the better things they had brought with them. When Harold came to William, he was honorably received. After hearing why he had left his homeland, William replied that matters would indeed turn out well, provided that Harold did not remain in William’s power.

He therefore kept the man with him for several days, and during that delay, like a prudent man, revealed to him what he had in mind. He said that when King Edward, then still a young man, had once lived with him in Normandy, Edward had pledged his faith that, if he became king of England, he would transfer the right of the kingdom to William by hereditary right after his own death.

He continued:

> “If you too promise that you will support me in this very matter, and, in addition, that you will build for my use the castle of Dover together with its water-well; that you will later send your sister to me to be married to one of my leading men, at the time mutually agreed upon; and that you promise to take my daughter as your wife, then both now you shall receive your nephew, and, when I come to reign in England, you shall receive your brother unharmed. If, in that kingdom, I am ever confirmed through your favor, I promise that you shall obtain whatever you reasonably ask me to grant you.”

Harold perceived danger on every side in these conditions and saw no way to escape except by yielding to William’s will in all of them. He therefore agreed. But William, so that everything might remain binding, brought out relics of the saints and compelled Harold to swear over them that he would fulfill in action everything they had agreed upon, unless he were taken from the present life by the common lot of mortals.

When this had been done, Harold, having obtained his nephew, returned to his homeland. When the king asked him what had happened and what he had done, he told him. The king said:

> “Did I not tell you that I knew William, and that on your journey many evils might befall this kingdom?”

Shortly afterward Edward died. In accordance with what he had arranged there before his death, Harold succeeded him in the kingdom.

Then a messenger sent by the aforesaid William came to England, requesting Harold’s sister, in accordance with the agreement between William and him. He also brought charges concerning other matters which, although sworn to, had not been fulfilled.

Harold is said to have answered him as follows:

> “My sister, whom you request according to our agreement, is dead. If the count wishes to have her body as it now is, I shall send it, lest I be judged to have violated the oath I made. The castle of Dover, and the water-well in it, he has completed—though I do not know for whom—in accordance with what you agreed. The kingdom, which was not yet mine, by what right could I give or permit it to be given? If he is speaking of his daughter, whom I was supposedly bound to take as my wife, let him know that I neither ought nor can bring a foreign woman into the kingdom of England, without consulting the leading men, and without great injury.”

The messenger returned and reported these replies to his lord. After hearing them, William again sent a friendly message, asking that, leaving the other matters aside and keeping faith with his pledge, Harold should at least take his daughter as his wife. Otherwise, he said, Harold should know for certain that he would claim by force of arms the succession to the kingdom which had been promised to him.

Harold replied that he neither wished to do that nor feared this. William was therefore angered, and Harold’s injustice filled him with great hope of winning the war. He prepared his fleet, set out for England, and, after a great battle had been joined, Harold fell in the field and William, victorious, obtained the kingdom.

The Frenchmen who had been present still bear witness to that battle. Although fortune had varied on both sides, such was the slaughter and flight of the Normans that the victory they gained must truly and without doubt be attributed solely to the miracle of God, who, by punishing Harold’s wicked crime of perjury through this event, showed that he is not a lord who desires iniquity.

When William had thus become king, I omit, since it would serve no purpose, relating what he did to the English nobles who had survived so great a disaster. From the time when he made use of the victory—which occurred on the day before the Ides of October—he remained anointed, and at Christmas he was anointed king at Westminster by Ealdred, archbishop of York, of blessed memory, together with several bishops of England.

Although the king himself and everyone else knew very well that this consecration ought properly and specially to be performed by the archbishop of Canterbury, nevertheless, because many evil and horrifying crimes were being reported about Stigand, who was at that time the pontiff there, William wished to receive it from him, lest he seem to assume a curse in place of a blessing.

Therefore, wishing to observe in England the customs and laws that his fathers and he himself had been accustomed to have in Normandy, he appointed bishops, abbots, and other leading men of this kind throughout the whole country. It would have been considered wrong for them not to obey his laws in every respect, setting aside all other consideration; and if any one of them, because of any earthly power or honor, dared to raise his head against him, all were to know from what source, for what purpose, and to what end they had been appointed.

Thus everything, both divine and human, awaited his command. To make all this more readily understood, I shall set down some of the measures he established for observance throughout England, judging that knowledge of them is necessary for understanding the matters on account of which above all we have undertaken this burden of writing.

He therefore would not permit anyone established anywhere within his dominion to receive the pontiff of the city of Rome as apostolic unless he ordered it.

[Note: [Col. 0535] (7) “That no one established anywhere within his dominion should receive the pontiff of the city of Rome as apostolic unless he gave the order.” William II recognizes this same provision in the same book and declares anyone who violates this ordinance guilty of lèse-majesté or treason. To this belongs the letter of William I, in which, relying on ancestral right, he refuses the profession of obedience and fealty requested through a messenger by Gregory VII, pontiff of Rome. It reads as follows in the manuscript collection of the letters of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury:

> “William, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of the Normans, to Gregory, most excellent shepherd of the holy Church: greeting with friendship.
>
> “Your legate Hubert, reverend Father,” etc.

See under William the Conqueror, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIX.

The money mentioned is the tax formerly granted to the Roman pontiff by Ina, king of the West Saxons, commonly called Peter’s Pence. It is surprising, meanwhile, how Bertold of Constance could have so falsely asserted in his continuation of Hermannus Contractus under the year 1084 that William the Conqueror had made the whole land of the English tributary to the Roman pontiff, and had permitted no one under his authority to buy or sell anything if he was found disobedient to the Apostolic See. He is plainly mistaken, and the events of that age among the English most clearly contradict him.

Here the Roman pontiff is called “apostolic,” as is frequently the case both with this author and with those who were his contemporaries or earlier. In antiquity the word was applied indiscriminately to other bishops as well. Later it became a proper designation of the Roman pontiff. On this matter see Gregory the Great, book VI, indiction XV, letter 37, and the observations of the most learned Isaac Casaubon in his *Exercitations on the Annals of Baronius*, § 4, Annals 32, no. 5.

In the commentaries of our jurists, compiled in the ancient language of the Gauls, *l’apostëille* frequently has the same meaning. The same usage is found more than once in Geoffrey of Villehardouin’s old history of Constantinople, written in French. It is a common development for names that were originally shared by many to become restricted later to signify a particular dignity. This may be seen in *dux*, *comes*, *miles*, *presbyter*, *diaconus*, and also *papa*.

For *papa* was formerly applied to all bishops in the Western Empire, as may be seen in Sidonius and elsewhere. John, patriarch of Alexandria, is called ὁ παππᾶς Ἀλεξανδρείας—“the pope of Alexandria”—in the heading of an epigram in the *Anthology*, book III, chapter 1.

Moreover, in the later period of the Eastern Empire, *papa* still designated nothing more than the first or lowest grade of the sacred order. This is clear from the ordinance of the emperor Isaac Comnenus, by which he enacted a law concerning the *κανονικόν*—the honorarium of a person being admitted to holy orders. He decreed that no bishop should receive more than seven gold coins under that name: one, namely, ὅτε ποιεῖ αὐτὸν λιτὸν παπᾶν ἢτοι ἀναγνώστην—“when he makes him a simple *papa*, that is, a reader”; three, ὅτε χειροτονεῖ αὐτὸν διάκονον—“when he ordains him deacon”; and the remaining three, ὅτε κληροῖ αὐτὸν ἱερέα ἤτοι πρεσβύτερον—“when he appoints him priest, that is, presbyter.” A *πρωτοπαππᾶς* was called one who, whether by reading or by performing other ministries, discharged the functions of the patriarch of Constantinople, or τὰ δευτερεῖα τοῦ ἀρχιερέως—“the second place of the high priest,” as Codinus puts it. The ordinance of Comnenus mentioned here is found in Theodorus Balsamon’s commentary on the title “On Faith” in the *Nomocanon* of Photius.]

or to accept his letters in any way if they had not first been shown to him.

[Note: [Col. 0536] (8) Nor did he permit the primate of his kingdom to establish or prohibit anything except what accorded with his will. How great William was in the authority he exercised over sacred matters may plainly be seen in his charter by which he imperiously granted to the monastery that he wished to be named after the battle in which he defeated Harold, on the Sussex coast, numerous privileges derogating both from sacred offices and from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Chichester. I shall append the relevant passage from the original document, which is still preserved with the king’s seal attached in the priceless Cottonian Library:

> “William, by the grace of God king of the English, to all clergy and laity established throughout England, greeting.
>
> “Let it be known to you that I have granted and confirmed,” etc.

See the reference given above.

The same kind of measure is William’s enactment distinguishing the ecclesiastical from the civil court. For while the Saxon realm flourished, the bishop of the diocese and the governor or sheriff of the shire mutually assisted one another in administering justice, and used the same court twice each year; they called the latter *shire-reeve*—whence our present “sheriff”—and sometimes *ealdorman*. In that age their court was scarcely other than what it would now be if every bishop’s synod were joined to the sheriff’s court, or held in the same court and before the same tribunal.

In chapter 5 of King Edgar’s laws:

> “*Haebbe mon thriwa on gear Burhgemote and twa scyre gemote; and thaer scyre gemote Bisceop and se Ealdorman and thaer aegther taecon ge godes rihte ge woruldes rihte*.”

This is rendered in the manuscript history of John Brampton, abbot of Jervaulx—where almost all the old English laws are found translated from Saxon into the barbarous language of that age—as follows:

> “Let a borough-court be held three times in the year, and a shire-court twice; and let the bishop of the shire, namely at the shire-court or half-yearly assembly, and the alderman be present, and let each teach the law of God and of the world.”

Nearly the same words occur there in King Cnut’s laws.

Perhaps from this comes the rule that even today the half-yearly sessions of inquiry presided over by the sheriff—called *tourns* and *hundreds*, that is, courts of the hundreds—are to be held ceremonially before a month has elapsed from Easter and from the feast of St Michael, by most ancient custom, as is clear from Magna Carta, chapter 35, and Statute 31 Edward III, chapter 4. For a temporary law enacted at the council of Antioch ordered bishops to summon such synods twice yearly, at the same seasons mentioned above. It is not implausible that in the earlier age the custom arose for sheriff and bishop first to hold their courts together at these fixed times, and that subsequently, when William separated their tribunals, the sheriff retained the ancient and long-established arrangement as to the time. See the Council of Antioch, canon 20; Distinction 18, chapter 4. It is well known that the canons of that council, held in A.D. 341, also had a place in the Church’s most ancient collection of canons. Indeed the same is read in the so-called apostolic canon 38.

In both, τῇ τετάρτῃ ἑβδομάδι τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς, “in the fourth week of Pentecost,” means the fourth week within the stated period after Easter. For *Pentecost* there denotes the interval between Easter Day and the feast of Pentecost, not the feast itself, as the word is commonly used. Hence Gratian, in the place cited, Burchard, book I, chapter 44, and Ivo, book V, chapter 154, explain it as the period between Easter and Pentecost, in accordance with the law still in use.

The month Hyperberetaeus—absurdly printed *Beritheon* in printed copies of Burchard—is plainly October, the month of the Syrians or Syro-Macedonians, from which they both began the year and reckoned the Alexandrian era, called by the Arabs *Tarik Dhi lkarnain*, that is, the Era of the Two-Horned One. Alexander is known by that name, being depicted thus on coins, adorned with the likeness of Jupiter Ammon, his horned father. I would not have thought it worth mentioning this, had I not observed that otherwise learned men had doubted whether Hyperberetaeus here meant September or October, despite sufficient instruction not only from ancient interpreters but from the canons themselves. See the notes to the Gregorian edition of Gratian, Distinction 18, chapter 4. They failed to notice the difference between the old Olympiadic year—in which Hyperberetaeus now fell in September, sometimes in other months—and the Alexandrian year, which permanently joined Hyperberetaeus to October. See the incomparable Joseph Scaliger, *De emendatione temporum*, book I, § “On the Macedonian summer period.”

The enactment of King William mentioned above reads as follows in his rescript to Remigius, bishop of Lincoln:

> “William, by the grace of God king of the English, to the counts, sheriffs, and all Frenchmen and Englishmen who hold lands in the bishopric of Bishop Remigius, greeting.
>
> “Know all of you,” etc.

See under William.

It was copied from the royal archive in the Tower of London, where it is found among the royal privileges formerly granted to the Church of Lincoln and confirmed by Richard II: namely, Charter 2 Richard II, membrane 12, no. 5. It is also found in English in Foxe, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, p. 154; see also his book III, p. 135, and chapter 14, § 1, of our history *On Tithes*, where I would prefer to substitute the sheriff’s half-yearly court for the monthly one.

Moreover, in the register, or public manuscript records, of Robert Winchelsey, archbishop of Canterbury, substantially the same words occur as are here attributed to King William. For, as those records state, the clergy presented King Edward I in parliament with a petition complaining of numerous injuries inflicted by the civil court upon their jurisdiction. This is none other than the articles containing the grievances of the English Church, mentioned in the preamble to the Constitutions commonly called *Articuli Cleri*. In the petition the clergy say:

> “Since William, formerly king of England, with the common counsel of the archbishops, abbots, and all the magnates of his realm, judged that episcopal laws, which were not, as they are not in these days, duly observed in the kingdom of England according to the precepts of the holy canons, should be inviolably observed; and therefore ordered and commanded that no bishop or archdeacon should bring before hundreds or secular courts anything concerning episcopal laws or causes belonging to the government of souls, but that everyone charged with any cause or offence according to episcopal laws should come to the ecclesiastical and ordinary place chosen by the bishop, and there answer for the cause or offence according to canonical and episcopal laws; and that, if he refused to abide by the bishop’s judgment, the king’s power and justice, or the sheriff, should, if necessary, be employed to compel him; and nevertheless defended and prohibited any sheriff, reeve, or servant of the king, or any layman, from meddling in laws belonging to the bishop, as these and other matters are more fully set out in the charter of the aforesaid King William,” etc.

For further evidence of William’s royal authority in regulating sacred matters, see, if you please, the *Life of Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, fol. 454; and Gregory VII, book IX, letter 5, where he says that William “compelled priests to put away their wives, and laymen to relinquish, even on oath, the tithes which they retained.”]

Nor did he permit the primate of his kingdom—that is, the archbishop of Canterbury—if he presided over a council convened by all the bishops, to establish or prohibit anything unless it was agreeable to his will and had first been ordered by him.

[Note: [Col. 0538] (9) “He did not permit any of the bishops to publicly excommunicate one of his barons or officials.” Almost the same provision is found among the articles of the councils of Clarendon, restored by Henry II in the year 1164. From this it may perhaps be learned what “barons” means here: the word is being used in a sense other than the common one. It signifies not merely those who today have a place in the special assembly of the estates, but all those who, at least as the more prosperous class, possessed large estates by royal munificence, according to the form of our feudal law, which concerns not the land of any royal township but the king himself alone—what we call in legal French *tenure en chief*, or tenure in chief.

For in the articles mentioned above we read:

> “No one who holds directly of the king, nor any of the king’s household officials, shall be excommunicated, nor shall any of their lands be placed under interdict, unless the lord king, if he is in the kingdom, is first summoned, or, if he is outside the kingdom, his justiciar—who at that time exercised the king’s functions like a prefect of the praetorium or a proconsul, and was also called the chief justiciar of England—be summoned, so that justice may be done concerning him; and so that whatever belongs to the king’s court may be settled there, while whatever pertains to the ecclesiastical court may be sent to that court to be settled there.”

The articles of those councils are found both in the manuscripts of Gervase of Canterbury and Roger of Wendover, and in Matthew Paris, though in corrupt form. The earlier part of his history, extending from the beginnings of William I to the nineteenth year of Henry III, is entirely owed to Wendover, from whom it was copied. Other copies of them are also found elsewhere. Robert of Gloucester understood this law to encompass everyone who held royal lands under any kind of feudal tenure. For, having treated our history in English verse down to his own age—that is, I think, that of Edward I—he recounts the clauses against which Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, resisted under Henry II, and, placing this fourth, believed that he rendered it into the antiquated language of his age as follows:

> “The fourth was that no man who held anything of the king,
> In chief or in any service, should be brought to excommunication,
> Except that the wardens of Holy Church who brought him thereto [should tell]
> The king, or his bailiffs, whether he had done wrong;
> And they were first to see whether they would bring it to amendment;
> And unless they would, they should, with their leave, make the excommunication.”

[See John of Salisbury, letter 159, and the *Life of Thomas of Canterbury* which we call the *Quadrilogus*.]

It is especially worth observing that Radulfus de Diceto, dean of London, relates the following under the year 1163:

> “Thomas, archbishop, conferred the vacant church of Ainfords upon Laurence. William, lord of the town, claiming the right of patronage in that church, expelled Laurence. The archbishop excommunicated him, and because he had done this without first informing the king, he incurred the king’s greatest displeasure. For the king asserts, in accordance with the dignity of the kingdom, that no captain, no one serving the king, no royal official—in ordinary language, no one holding directly of the king a castle, town, or estate—may be excommunicated by anyone without the king’s knowledge. Otherwise, if the king were not informed of the matter, he might unknowingly associate with the excommunicated man, either inviting his captain to a kiss or receiving him into his counsel.”

Here the reason for the law just cited is supplied, and what “barons” and “officials” signify in it is explained more clearly.

Nor do I consider it inappropriate here to record some evidence concerning the barons under William, so that the meaning of the word *census*, which was in use in that age and in this context, may become more certain. William I’s fiscal records mention barons in Dorset in the following manner:

> “In Warham, from the holding of Saint-Wandrille, there are forty-five inhabited houses and seventeen that are waste. From the holdings of the other barons there are twenty inhabited houses and sixty that are destroyed. And in the borough of Warwick”—so those records say in the survey of the county of Warwick—“the king has in his demesne 113 houses, and the king’s barons have 112, from all of which the king receives his geld.”

The bishop of Worcester has | 9 messuages.

The bishop of Chester has | 7.

The abbot of Coventry has | 36.

The bishop of Coutances has | 1.

The count of Meulan has | 12.

Count Alberic has | 4.

Hugh de Grentemaisnil has | 4; the monks hold 1 from him.

Henry de Ferrers has | 2.

Harold has | 2.

Robert of Stafford has | 6.

Roger de Lacy has | 2.

Richard the Hunter has | 1.

Ralph de Limesy has | 9.

The abbot of Malmesbury has | 1.

William Bonvallet has | 1.

William son of Corbucion has | 2.

Geoffrey de Mandeville has | 1.

Geoffrey of Worcester has | 1.

Gilbert de Gant has | 2.

Gilbert Buili has | 1.

Nicholas the Archer has | 1.

Stephen Stirman has | 1.

Turchil has | 4.

Harold has | 2.

Osbern son of Richard has | 1.

Christiana has | 1.

Luith the nun has | 2.
