These messuages belong to lands which the barons themselves hold outside the borough, and they have been assessed there. Except for Christiana and Luith, all were the king’s barons; that is, they were among those who possessed the 112 houses mentioned above.

Other matters noted shortly afterward in another place, relating to these times, will shed light here on the meaning of “baron” in that age. By “officials” here I understand those who, serving in palatine, urban, or rural offices, were regarded as the king’s servants. I do not think that the *thegns* and royal servants called *servientes* in William’s fiscal records were any different from the thanes.

For many are mentioned there by the name *thegns*, that is, *thegens*, whence the Latin *thani*, which means “officials.” Nor is the word, if its origin is considered, anything other than the Belgian *diender*, derived from *dienen*, “to serve,” and it preserves clear traces of *thegen*. Hence *dienst-knecht* means “servant,” and *dienstmaeght*, “maidservant.” For *knecht* denotes a male, as it does among our Saxons.

I recall an example in some prognostications concerning childbirth, written in Saxon. The anonymous manuscript author says to extend a lily and a rose to a pregnant woman, so that she may choose whichever of the two she prefers:

> “*gyf heo nymth Lilian, heo caenth cnyth, gyf heo nymth rosan, heo caenth maeden*.”

That is: “If she takes the lily, she will give birth to a male child—that is, a boy; if she takes the rose, she will give birth to a female child.”

The royal officials, whether *thegns* or *servientes*, are recorded in those fiscal documents as follows: Cola the huntsman, Ulviet the huntsman, Godwin the falconer, Hugh the interpreter, Milo the porter, Herbert the chamberlain, and others of the same kind.

*Latinarius* means the same as “interpreter”; hence *Latimer* is also used in this sense. The person skilled in the Latin language was thought to know the other languages in use so well that the general designation “interpreter” could reasonably be bestowed upon him.

Nor is it at all doubtful that servants were at that time no different from thanes, as is clear from the same records so often cited. In the survey of Surrey, Oswald, Theodoric, and others are mentioned under the name of servants; yet immediately afterward they are called *thegns* indiscriminately. Similarly, in the survey of Wiltshire, Herveus and other officials are called servants, but they are at once identified as those also called *thegns*. The same is to be observed concerning Coluinus and the other servants in the survey of Devon. There, too, they are called *thegns*, without distinction of class.

Hence the word *tainlande* also occurs in those records—that is, “the land of the thanes,” or an estate specifically belonging to thanes. In Wiltshire we read:

> “Count William gave Wintone, Swindon, and Cheverel, which were *tainlande*, in exchange for the land of the Isle of Wight, which belonged to the farm of Amesbury.”

And in Somerset, concerning Robert of Odberville, a *thegn* or royal official:

> “This Robert held one virgate which Dodo held freely in the time of King Edward. To this was added Dolvertone, a royal manor. It has now been adjudged to be *tainland*.”

To this belongs the legal phrase *Glamare ad Tainland*, which occurs in the survey of Cheshire. To claim an estate under that designation is what the phrase means.]

Nevertheless, he did not permit any of his bishops to bring a public legal action against, excommunicate, or constrain with any ecclesiastical penalty anyone among his barons or officials who was accused of incest, adultery, or any capital crime, unless he ordered it.

[Note: [Col. 0540] (10) “What he promulgated concerning secular matters,” etc. Here Selden gives the laws of William the Conqueror. Since we have already published them under William, under the year 1085, in *Patrologia*, volume CXLIX, we have thought it unnecessary to reprint them here.]

As for what he promulgated concerning secular matters, we shall refrain from committing those provisions to literary memory, since writing about them contributes nothing to our office, and since the character of those measures may, I think, be discerned from the divine matters he ordered, in accordance with what we have briefly surveyed. To complete the course we have begun, enough has been said on these matters.

In the fifth year of this kingdom, Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen—a vigorous man, endowed with outstanding knowledge of divine and human affairs—came to England at the command of Pope Alexander and the aforesaid king. Shortly afterward he undertook the governance of the archbishopric of Canterbury. He was consecrated in that metropolitan see on the fourth day before the Kalends of September by almost all the bishops of England.

When he went to Rome to receive the pallium owed to him, he had as companions on the journey Thomas, archbishop of York—whom he himself had consecrated at Canterbury after Thomas had made him a canonical profession of obedience—and Remigius, bishop of Lincoln. When they arrived together at Rome, they were received courteously, each with the honor appropriate to him.

After this, on the appointed day, Father Lanfranc was presented to Alexander, pontiff of the Apostolic See. To him the pope himself, rising as he entered—a gesture that may perhaps seem strange to those acquainted with Roman custom—gently urged him to stand still. Then he added:

> “We have shown honor, not to your archbishopric, but to the master to whom we owe what we know, having been instructed in those matters through his learning. As for what concerns you, it is proper that you should carry it out in reverence for blessed Peter.”

When the pope had taken his seat, Lanfranc advanced and humbled himself at his feet, but was immediately raised by him to receive his kiss. They sat together, and that day passed joyfully between them.

On the following day, when various matters were already being brought forward, Lanfranc accused the aforementioned Thomas, together with the aforesaid Remigius, before the pope, alleging that neither of them had been lawfully promoted to the episcopate. The first, for that reason [Note: [Col. 0540]...

### (11) That the sacred canons exclude from advancement to the sacred orders the sons of priests whom the religious state does not adorn

The same account is related in exactly the same words by Radulph of Diceto, dean, during the reign of John, bishop of London, [Col. 0541A] who evidently inserted into his *History*, preserved in manuscript copies, a considerable amount drawn from Eadmer. But which canons were these—canons in which this was prescribed, together with the added condition concerning the state of religion, as they call it? Were they issued under Alexander II or under one of his predecessors?

The year was 1071, when Lanfranc went to Rome accompanied by these bishops; and it was then, they relate, that the archbishop of York was deprived of his office by Alexander for this reason. But no such canon, if I remember correctly, is found either in the commentaries on pontifical law or elsewhere whose origins are earlier than the Council of Clermont, held approximately five years after Lanfranc’s death, namely in 1095 under Urban II. See canon 25 of that council, and Distinction 56, *Extra*, title *On the Sons of Priests*, besides Bernard of Pavia, book I, title 9; John of Wales, book I, title 9; and Ivo, part VI, chapter 410.

Nor dare we assert anything further than that the matter is unclear, unless Eadmer may be permitted to plead a lapse of memory and an anticipation of the date. For when he wrote, such a papal law was in force, although it had certainly not yet arisen in Lanfranc’s time. William of Malmesbury therefore proceeds more cautiously: he does not add a canon of this kind, but writes that the archbishop of York was deprived under Lanfranc merely because he was the son of a priest, as do others whose works have not yet been published.

For at Rome, even in that age, the sons of priests were regarded as illegitimate; this is sufficiently evident from the older pontifical law preserved in Gratian, Distinctions 32 and 33. The Roman pontiffs then relied on Jewish law in this matter, as in several others, and excluded illegitimate persons from the dignity of the sacred order. Hence this son of a priest was stripped of his office. The Jewish law they wished to follow as their example is found in Deuteronomy, chapter 23, Commentary 2: “A mamzer shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord.” There *manzer*—from which the Greek form μανζήρ derives, and which is used somewhere for an illegitimate person, both by Gregentius and by Cedrenus—is rendered by the Greek translators as ἔκ πόρνης natus, “born of a prostitute”; and in Arabic, in the sacred books, it is rendered *pharuch alzani*, that is, “a prostitute’s offspring,” as it is also in the Chaldean version attributed to Jonathan son of Uziel. See further, if desired, Distinction 56, chapter 12, *Apostolica*, and 13, *per venerabilem*, *Extra*, title *Who Are Legitimate Children*.

, that the sacred canons exclude from advancement to the sacred orders the sons of priests whom the religious state does not adorn. The following case, however, was so decided because, after an agreement, he had purchased it from William, once he had become king, by the service in which he had attended on him as he hastened to England’s destruction, with manifold effort and great expense. Since these men had no plausible excuse by which they could be acquitted, they returned their staffs and rings together with the episcopal care entrusted to them and turned to seek mercy.

Lanfranc intervened on their behalf. Being a man outstanding in piety and wisdom, he demonstrated that they were supported by knowledge of many matters, were indispensable to the new king in the new arrangements of the kingdom, and surpassed many in eloquence. When the supreme pontiff heard this, he turned to Lanfranc and said:

“You appear, father, to be the father of that country; therefore let your diligence consider what is expedient. Here are the pastoral staffs which they have returned. Take them and distribute them as you judge will be most useful to the Christianity of that region.”

Lanfranc received them and immediately, in the pope’s presence, reinvested the men mentioned above, each with his own office. Then Lanfranc, having received from the pope the pallium of the supreme pontificate, returned joyfully with his companions on the journey to England. He was received by the men of Canterbury with the reverence due to him and was confirmed as primate of all Britain. After this, when a short period of time had passed, the fame of his name and the greatness of his wisdom resounded everywhere and made him renowned and esteemed in the minds of men.

Among others—and indeed before others—he was esteemed by the aforementioned King William, and he devoted himself with no ordinary care to the affairs of God. Therefore he always labored greatly both to make the king devoted to God and to renew the religion of good morals among all classes of people throughout the kingdom. Nor was he deprived of his desire: through his diligence and teaching religion was greatly increased throughout that entire land, and new monastic buildings were constructed everywhere, as is evident today.

Of these builders he himself first gave an example. He built the Church of Christ at Canterbury, together with all the workshops and buildings located within the wall of its court, including the wall itself. But who could ever fully describe with what wisdom and fatherly care he raised the monks residing in that church from the secular life, in which he found them excessively involved; imbued them with every path of holy conduct; increased their number; and cherished them with what kindness throughout his life?

To say nothing meanwhile of other matters: because he desired them always to devote themselves to the service of God without poverty or anxiety, he used his skill and diligence with the king to ensure that almost all the lands which the Normans, when they first took possession of the country, had seized from the rightful property of that church—and also certain others which had been lost before their arrival through various circumstances—were restored to the church.

Although I need not write about these and innumerable other good works by which he completed his life through labor—for his works are so evident that they themselves demonstrate their character more clearly than writing [Note: [Col. 0541]

### (12) And that he himself wrote

A work written by him on these matters is missing. See Bale’s *Centuria* XIII, writer XII, where his writings are listed; most of them have perished through the injustice of time.

—and since he himself wrote, in a most truthful and concise style, about the ecclesiastical affairs carried out in his own time—yet, for the sweetness of remembering him, we have thought it pleasant briefly to explain what we have already touched upon.

When this Lanfranc first came to Canterbury and found the church of the Savior, whose governance he had undertaken, almost entirely destroyed by fire and ruins, he was overwhelmed in mind. But when the magnitude of the disaster compelled him to despair, he recovered himself and, relying on the courage of his spirit, set aside his own convenience and rapidly completed the houses necessary for the monks’ work.

After they had used these for several years and their community had grown, the buildings seemed far too small. He therefore demolished them and built others greatly surpassing the former in beauty and size. He also built a residence for himself and, in addition, a church, which in the course of seven years he brought almost entirely to completion from its foundations. He nobly adorned it with copes, chasubles, dalmatics, tunics magnificently marked with gold, pallia, and many other costly ornaments.

How good, pious, and generous he was toward the brothers of that church may be gathered to some extent from this: he could not bear that any of their parents or brothers should be afflicted by any want. And what you may perhaps find even more remarkable, he had made it his practice not to wait until he was asked to provide assistance. Full of the bowels of mercy, now to one, now to another, he spontaneously offered what might serve an impoverished relative as aid for a very long time. Yet in this he was always guided by exceptional discernment, considering within himself the merit and need of each person.

Moreover, one brother of that monastery used to receive thirty shillings of pennies from the Father every year for the support of his mother. On one occasion, five of those shillings—for they were given in separate installments at different times—were given to him at Lanfranc’s command. He tied them in a cloth and, speaking to his mother, placed them in her hand secretly, as he thought. But she, with her mind occupied elsewhere, did not notice what her son was doing; and when the coins fell, mother and son were separated from one another.

Afterward the woman sent word to her son, wishing to know what had happened to the coins which he had promised to give her. Astonished, he had her come to him. When he heard what had happened, he became sad—not only because of the loss that had befallen his mother, but also because he feared that, if the archbishop learned of it, he might be angered by his negligence and deprive him to some extent of his favor.

Meanwhile the pious Father, entering the cloister as was his custom, sat down. Seeing the brother returning sadly from his conversation with his mother, he dismissed the others and privately asked the cause of his sorrow. He heard it and, with the most kindly expression—for he was always so toward the afflicted—replied:

“And are you troubled by that, my dearest son? God destined and gave those pennies to another who perhaps needed them more than your mother. Be silent, and take careful care not to speak of it to anyone. And lest what has happened burden your spirit even slightly, I shall order seven shillings to be given to you today for your mother’s benefit in place of those five. But, as I said, let no one know of it.”

In giving, he had made it his practice to give what was to be given cheerfully, and to permit no one to reveal either what had been given or the identity of the giver.

Let this suffice concerning the monks of his mother church. But who among the poor ever cried out to him and was rejected? Who among travelers, from whatever class of people, asked his help and failed to obtain it? What community of monks or clerics ever sent to him asking assistance and did not experience the abundance of his generosity beyond what it had hoped?

Italy, Gaul, and Britain bear witness to these things, for to this day they mourn the death of Lanfranc with compassionate sighs. What shall I say about the abbey of Saint Alban, which he found almost completely ruined within and without, and which he rebuilt from its foundations, appointing over it Paul, a man of good memory [Note: [Col. 0541]

### (13) Having appointed Paul abbot over it

Matthew Paris left the following account of this abbot in his manuscripts of the lives of the abbots of that monastery:

“King William, having been informed of the death of Abbot Faritius, held the vacant monastery of Saint Alban in his own hand; after cutting down its woods and impoverishing its people, he oppressed it. And unless he had been restrained by Lanfranc’s corrections, he would have destroyed the entire monastery beyond repair. Lanfranc therefore effectively arranged that Paul, his kinsman, whom he had brought with him to England, should be placed in charge as abbot.

This man, a native of Neustria, closely related to Archbishop Lanfranc—and, as some maintain, his son—was a monk of the Church of Caen. He undertook the governance of the church of Saint Alban through the agency of the aforesaid Archbishop Lanfranc, who loved that same Paul with paternal affection. He was promoted to the abbacy in the year of grace 1077, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the time of King William, the elder king and conqueror, in the eleventh year of his reign.

He was the first abbot of this church after England had been completely subjected to the Normans. He rebuilt this church and the other buildings, except Pistorium and Pinsinochium, from the stones and tiles of the ancient city of Verulamium and from the timber which he found collected and preserved by his predecessors. For Archbishop Lanfranc had enriched him and made him abundant in manifold treasure.

This Abbot Paul was also a religious man, liberally educated, strict and prudent in observing the regular order. The discipline of the whole monastic religion—which the seductive pleasure of the more relaxed life of both prelates and subjects had long since driven out—he cautiously and gradually reformed, lest he burden the community with upheaval through a sudden change.

Thus the church of Saint Alban became, as it were, a school of religious and disciplined observance throughout the whole kingdom of England. For he had brought with him Lanfranc’s customs and the monastic statutes, written down and rightly approved by the lord pope. Hence the fragrance of this church’s good reputation flew ahead, illuminating the Roman court and distant kingdoms.”

And it happily inclined many, both prelates and nobles, in its favor.]

He enlarged and honored it within through great religious devotion and enriched it without by gifts of many kinds.

In the bishopric of Rochester he found, under Bishop Siward, scarcely more than four canons, and those living a wretched life. When that bishop and Ernest, whom Lanfranc had appointed as his successor, had been removed from the present life, a monk of pious memory named Gundulf was appointed bishop there by the same man [Note: [Col. 0542]

### (14) Named Gundulf, appointed there by the same man

The following account given by the ancient anonymous author of the manuscript *Life of Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester*, concerning his election, is relevant here:

“When Lanfranc held and wisely administered the highest ecclesiastical dignity in England, the Church of Rochester was deprived of its pastor by the death of Bishop Ernest, who had succeeded the monk Siward—and had indeed succeeded that monk in the episcopate—but had lived in it for only half a year.

The pontiff, wishing a monk to succeed a monk according to the custom of the ancients, began to consider which monk he might select above all others who would be able to bear this burden imposed upon him. While he was considering this, the holiness of Gundulf came to his mind more quickly; it had already been sufficiently approved to him by reliable tests.

Having therefore taken counsel with wise men, he chose him for the episcopate. To secure the king’s consent to his election, he sent him across the sea to the king. The king, filled with no little joy because he had found an opportunity to exalt a man of God, whose holiness had already become known to him through a sufficiently clear reputation, willingly gave his assent to the bishop’s just requests and judged the man of God most worthy of episcopal honor.

Having received royal authority, Lanfranc summoned the bishops and sent word to the leading men of Rochester. He made the king’s will and his own known to all; and, when everyone gave assent and rejoiced, he appointed him the faithful steward of the house of God. There was no power to resist, since the authority of so great a king and so great a prelate pressed upon them. The voice of the man crying out that he was unworthy was silenced, since, in proportion as he declared himself more unworthy, he was acclaimed as more worthy.

Thus the truly most worthy man, Gundulf, was ordained to the episcopate in the Church of Canterbury on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1077, the eleventh year after the coming of the Normans into England under Count William, afterward the most noble king of England.

After being consecrated according to custom, he set out to visit his own see. The crowds rejoicing, he entered the city of Rochester; he was conducted in and enthroned in the episcopal seat, and thereafter the prelate was held in all reverence.

Finally, certain possessions of the Church of Rochester were restored to him, possessions which Lanfranc had held under his control while his predecessors were bishops. They were restored on the condition that, as both prelates had already decided, monks should be installed in the Church of Rochester. For they had heard that monks had once been there; returning, therefore, to the ancient practices, they decreed that an order of monks should be established there.

After a short time had passed, a new church was begun after the old one had been demolished; the circuit of the buildings was suitably arranged, and the entire work was completed within a few days, Lanfranc supplying large sums of money.

When everything had been completed, certain of the only five clerics found there came over to the religious habit. Joined by many others, they quickly grew under the teaching of Father Gundulf to a number exceeding sixty monks. To these Gundulf became a mirror of life; to these he became an example of the whole religious life.”

Thus far the anonymous manuscript author.]

Lanfranc appointed Gundulf bishop there. Through him he demolished the ancient church of the bishopric together with its adjoining structure and built everything anew. The clerics who lived there, as we have said, he either raised in that same place to the summit of the religious life or transferred to other places, giving them other possessions from which they might have a more abundant livelihood and clothing than usual.

For he established the episcopal see with the discipline of the monastic order and, assigning lands and other resources appropriate for the support of those serving God there, made it rich from poor, exalted from humble, as it is seen at the present day.

Nor do I think that what he did for the poor outside the walls of the city of Canterbury should be omitted from this work. Outside the city’s northern gate he built a handsome and spacious stone house, and added to it, according to the various needs and conveniences of the people, several lodgings with a spacious courtyard.

He divided this residence into two parts: he assigned one to men afflicted by various kinds of illness and the other to women who were unwell. He also provided them from his own resources with clothing and daily food, as well as attendants and guardians who would ensure in every way that nothing was lacking to them and that the men had no opportunity to approach the women, nor the women the men.

On the opposite side of the road he arranged a church in honor of blessed Pope Gregory. In it he placed canons who would live according to a rule and would provide the aforementioned sick people with whatever was suitable for the salvation of their souls, together with burial. He bestowed upon these canons such ample lands, tithes, and other revenues that they appeared sufficient for their support.

Farther away from the northern gate, on the western side of the city, he built wooden houses on the slope of a hill and assigned them for the use of lepers. In these, as in the others, men were separated from the company of women. For these people also, according to the nature of their illness, he ordered that everything they needed should be supplied from his resources, appointing men for this purpose whose skill, kindness, and patience, as he judged, no one could doubt.

In addition, in the villages belonging to the bishopric he built many honorable houses, partly of stone and partly of wood, for himself and his successors.

As for the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, which certain bishops—and especially Thomas, archbishop of York, as a new citizen of England—tried excessively to humble in order to exalt his own church, it is unnecessary and tedious to write here how many labors Lanfranc endured and how he humbled Thomas himself to the measure of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0542]

### (15) He himself left writings concerning the matter

He left written records concerning it, confirmed under the testimony of the royal seal. Acts concerning this matter are found both in the manuscript collection of Lanfranc’s letters and in William of Malmesbury, *De gestis regum*, book III, and *De gestis pontificum*, book I, as well as in the *Antiquitates Ecclesiae Britannicae*, p. 111 [Col. 0543A], and elsewhere.

In the letter of Lanfranc which Malmesbury includes as having been written to Alexander II, it was unjust to omit matters most worthy of reading, which Baronius first brought to light from a manuscript. See him, volume II, under the year 1072; and part II, volume III of the *Councils*, in the latest Binius edition, p. 251.]

For he himself left a truthful account of the matter, confirmed by the agreement of the entire kingdom under the testimony of the royal seal. He labored all the more in these matters because almost all the ancient privileges of that church had perished in the conflagration which consumed the same church three years before his arrival.

He recovered through his wisdom other customs which the kings of England, in ancient times, had granted to the Church of Canterbury by their munificence so that it might be completely free in all things, and which they had established by the most sacred sanction as permanently valid, but which had been lost through the imprudence of certain men.

Odo, bishop of Bayeux—to say nothing of others—brother of the aforesaid King William and earl of Kent, was considered great and exceedingly powerful throughout the kingdom before Lanfranc entered England. Raised to immense power by the domination he exercised, he had seized, oppressed, and held not only lands but also the liberty of the aforesaid church, in many ways, without anyone resisting him.

When Lanfranc learned how matters stood, he dealt with them before the king as he knew was proper. The king therefore ordered that, after the leading men and upright persons not only from the county of Kent but also from the other counties of England had been assembled, Lanfranc’s complaint should be brought forward, examined, and decided [Note: [Col. 0543]

### (16) After a gathering of the leading men had been arranged at Pinnedene

What was done at that gathering, and by what form of judgment, is explained more clearly by a brief history which we found in a manuscript of the Church of Rochester. We append it together with the heading under which it appears in that manuscript.

#### Concerning the plea at Pinenden between Lanfranc, archbishop, and Odo, bishop of Bayeux

“In the time of the great King William, who conquered the English kingdom by arms and subjected it to his dominion, it happened that Odo, bishop of Bayeux and brother of that same king, came to England much earlier than Archbishop Lanfranc and settled in the county of Kent with great power, exercising considerable authority there.

Since in those days there was no one in that county who could resist a man of such strength, because of the great power he possessed he seized and usurped several lands of the archbishopric of Canterbury and certain customs, and assigned them to his own dominion.

Afterward, not long thereafter, it happened that the aforesaid Lanfranc, abbot of the church of Caen, also came to England at the king’s command and, by God’s providence, was raised in the archbishopric of Canterbury to be primate of the entire kingdom of England.

When he had resided there for some time and discovered that many ancient lands of his church were missing, and that through the negligence of his predecessors they had been distributed and alienated, he diligently investigated the truth and, as soon as he could and without delay, petitioned the king concerning the matter.

The king therefore ordered the whole county to assemble without delay and all the men of the county—Frenchmen and especially Englishmen skilled in the ancient laws and customs—to come together. When they had assembled at Pinenden, they all sat down together.

Since many pleas concerning the accounting of lands and many arguments concerning the customs of the laws arose there between the archbishop and the aforesaid bishop of Bayeux, as well as concerning the royal and archiepiscopal customs, and these matters could not be settled on the first day, the whole county was detained there for three days.

During those three days Archbishop Lanfranc established his claim to several lands then held by that bishop and his men, namely by Herbert son of Ivo, Turold of Rochester, Ralph of Curva Spina, and Hugh of Montfort, together with all the customs and things belonging to those lands: namely Raculfe, Sandwic, Rateburg, Wedetune, the monastery of Lunning with the lands and customs belonging to that monastery, Saltwood with the borough of Hythe belonging to Saltwood, Langport, Hiwenden, Rokinge, Detling, Preston, Sunderherst, Cahethe, Orpington, and Finesford.

Four prebends: Broche, Riwentune, Stokes, and Devintune. In Surrey, with the favor of King William, the archbishop himself established his claim to Murtelache. In London, the monastery of Saint Mary, with the lands and houses which Living the priest and his wife had held; in Middlesex, Herghas and Heïsam; in Buckinghamshire, Risebergam and Haulton; in Oxfordshire, Riwentune; in Essex, Stisted; in Suffolk, Frachenham.

Likewise, against Ralph of Curva Spina, sixty shillings’ worth of pasture at Green.

And he established his claim to all those lands and others, together with all the customs and things belonging to those lands, so freely and securely that on the day on which that plea ended there was no man anywhere in the entire kingdom of England who challenged anything belonging to them, nor anyone who laid even the slightest claim against those lands.

He returned Stokes, Devintune, and Frachenham to the church of Saint Andrew, because they had anciently belonged by right to that church.

In the same plea he renewed not only these lands named above and others, but also all the liberties of his church and all its customs, and established them by judgment there after their renewal: sake and soke, toll, team, flymena, fyrmthe, grithbreche, foresteal, haunfate, infangthief, together with all other customs equal or inferior to these, in lands and waters, woods, roads, meadows, and all other things within and outside the city, within and outside the borough, and in every other place.

Before all the upright and wise men who were present, it was there established by judgment; and it was also acknowledged and adjudged by the whole county, that just as the king holds his lands free and quit in his demesne, so the archbishop of Canterbury holds his lands entirely free and quit in his demesne.

The following were present at this plea: Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, who stood in the king’s place and administered that justice; Lanfranc, archbishop, who, as has been said, pleaded and established the whole matter; the earl of Kent, namely the aforesaid Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Ernest, bishop of Rochester; Aelric, bishop of Chichester, a very old man and exceedingly learned in the laws of the land, who was brought by the king’s command in a four-wheeled carriage to examine and explain the ancient customs of the laws; Richard of Tunbridge; Hugh of Montfort; William of Arques; Haymo the sheriff; and many other barons of the king, as well as many men of the archbishop and of those bishops, together with men from the other counties and with the whole county assembled—men of great authority, both French and English.

In the presence of all these, it was demonstrated by many clear and manifest arguments that the king of the English had no customs in all the lands of the Church of Canterbury except three.

These three customs were as follows.

First: if any man of the archbishop dug up the royal road which runs from one city to another.

Second: if anyone cut down a tree beside the royal road and threw it down across the road.

Those found guilty and detained while doing these two things—whether bail had been taken from them or not—would nevertheless, through pursuit by the king’s officer and by means of bail, make amends for whatever must be compensated as a wrong.

The third custom was this: if anyone shed blood on the royal road, or committed homicide or anything else there which was in no way permitted, and was caught and detained while doing it, he would make amends to the king. But if he was not caught there and departed once without giving a pledge, the king could justly exact nothing from him.

It was likewise demonstrated in the same plea that the archbishop of Canterbury ought justly to possess many customs in all the lands of the king and the earl.

For from the day on which the Alleluia is closed until the octave of Easter, whoever sheds blood shall make amends to the archbishop. And at every time, both outside and during Lent, whoever commits the offense called *childwite*, the archbishop shall have either the whole or half of the amercement. During Lent, the whole; outside Lent, either the whole or half of the amercement.

He also has in all those lands everything that appears to pertain to the care and salvation of souls.

After the king heard the conclusion of this plea, determined by many witnesses and many arguments, he approved it; and, approving it with the consent of all his leading men, he confirmed it and firmly ordered that it should thereafter remain uncorrupted.

This has therefore been written here so that it may contribute to the eternal memory of the future, and so that future successors of the same Church of Christ at Canterbury may know what and how great dignities they ought to hold from God and what they ought to claim by perpetual right from the kings and princes of this kingdom.”

Nor is it inappropriate to recall here what has been discovered in the often-mentioned records of William’s *Domesday* concerning both the alleged right of the individual archbishop at that time and the judgment delivered in favor of the churches of the Holy Trinity and Saint Augustine.

“The archbishop claims”—so those records say in the survey of Kent—“the forfeiture on the roads outside the city on both sides wherever his land lies.

A certain reeve named Brumannus, in the time of King Edward, began to take customs from foreign merchants on the land of the Holy Trinity and Saint Augustine. Later, in the time of King William, before Archbishop Lanfranc and the Bishop of Bayeux, he acknowledged that he had taken them unjustly and, having given an oath, swore that those churches had held their customs free and quit in the time of King Edward.

From that time both churches held their customs in their own land by the judgment of the king’s barons who held the plea.

The judgment already mentioned as delivered at Pinenden is also recorded in those records, in the survey of Kent, under the heading of the extensive lands of the bishop of Rochester:

‘The manor of Estoches’—for that is how it is read there, although it is called Stokes in the history of the judgment mentioned above—‘was and is of the bishopric of Rochester. But Earl Godwin, in the time of King Edward, bought it from the men who held it from the bishop, and the sale was made without the bishop’s knowledge. Later, when King William was reigning, Lanfranc established his claim to it against the Bishop of Bayeux. Therefore the Church of Rochester is now seised of it.’

The following is also recorded there concerning the digging of the public roads which serve Canterbury and the fines imposed for violating their rights:

‘It was agreed concerning the straight roads which have an entrance into and an exit from the city: whoever commits a forfeiture on them shall make amends to the king. Likewise concerning the straight roads outside the city, extending for one league, three perches, and three feet.

Therefore, if anyone inside or outside the city digs up or places a stake in any of these public roads, the king’s reeve follows him wherever he goes and takes the amercement for the king.’”]

When the gathering of the leading men had therefore been arranged at Pinenden, Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, a man extremely wealthy in England at that time, was ordered to administer justice most vigorously on Lanfranc’s complaints in the king’s place; and he did so.

For Lanfranc, supported by a strong argument and with the common affirmation and judgment of all, recovered there everything that was shown to have belonged anciently to the rights of the Church of Christ at Canterbury, both lands and various customs.

At another time the same Odo, with the king’s permission, instituted a plea against the aforesaid church and its protector, Father Lanfranc. He knowingly brought there all those whom he knew to be most skilled in the laws and customs of the English kingdom.

When the discussion of the cases began, all who had gathered there to defend the church’s causes were so defeated at the first encounter that they simultaneously lost the very matters in whose defense they had assembled. Lanfranc himself was not present. For it was not his custom to attend such proceedings unless the greatest necessity compelled him.

While he was occupied in his chamber with divine reading, he was informed of what had happened. He was not at all frightened in his heart, but asserted that the statements of his adversaries had not proceeded correctly and therefore ordered that the whole matter be adjourned until the following day.

On the following night blessed Dunstan appeared in a vision to the bishop, warning him not to let the crowd disturb him, but, secure in the saint’s presence, to enter the plea himself cheerfully in the morning. He did so.

Beginning his defense with a certain introduction apparently wholly unrelated to the matters that had been discussed or were to be discussed, to the amazement of all he proceeded in such a way that he defeated the statements made against him the previous day and showed them to be empty. As long as he remained in this present life, no one arose who would open his mouth against him concerning that matter.

Thus much concerning these events.

[Col. 0357C] In addition to these matters, and at approximately the same time, nearly all those who, from the clerical order, had been appointed bishops in England by King William attempted to expel the monks who had long been living in certain English bishoprics. They induced the king himself to agree with them in this. They were confident that they would achieve their purpose, so much so that Bishop Walchelin had nearly forty clerics assembled, tonsured and clothed in the manner of canons, whom he intended, once the monks had been expelled, immediately to introduce into the Church of Winchester over which he presided.

The only delay in carrying this out was that permission had not yet been requested from Archbishop Lanfranc. He had no doubt that he would obtain it even more quickly than he wished. But the outcome was different from what his mind had promised him. For when news reached Lanfranc’s ears of what the bishop was attempting, he immediately recoiled from the deed and declared that, as long as he lived, he would never consent to such a plan being carried out in any manner.

Thus both the clerics whom Walchelin had gathered to succeed the monks were dismissed and sent away, and the monks, who had been condemned to yield to the clerics by a kind of prejudicial judgment, were, through the grace of God and the persistence of the good Lanfranc, restored to possession of their former way of life in their Church.

Nor could this suffice to calm the resentment of certain men who had conceived the expulsion of the monks. For with equal determination, similar effort, one accord, and a united mind, the bishops whom the religious order had not bound to it began striving at least to eradicate the monks from the primatial Church of Canterbury, intending by this act to exclude the others elsewhere with the greatest ease. They were supported in undertaking this by reasons which seemed to them especially weighty: partly because of the eminence of the primatial see, which must oversee and correct the Churches throughout England through its representatives; partly because of many other considerations whose execution, according to the fiction they devised, belonged more properly to clerics than to monks.

The king and the other princes of the realm were drawn into this opinion, while Lanfranc, as was his custom, resisted with all his strength and manfully opposed the entire effort and hostility. Yet, lest after his death something should be done which, while he lived, he knew could by God’s help never be accomplished, and since he did not know the day or hour of his death, he acted with the wisdom and industry in which he excelled. Through the authority of the Roman and apostolic see, he secured the confirmation of the monks’ residence in that Church and established it permanently and immovably for all time, as long as the world should endure.

The supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, Alexander, strengthened this by a privilege written in the following terms:

> “Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother in Christ, Lanfranc, venerable archbishop of the Cantuarians: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We have received from certain persons …” etc. See under Alexander II.

[Col. 0358C] From what we have briefly indicated, and from the letter which we shall quote below, it will be sufficiently clear to anyone wishing to know how securely and with what unrestricted freedom the aforesaid Father Lanfranc sought to possess everything belonging to the rights of the Church of Canterbury. We have chosen to insert this letter, written concerning ecclesiastical matters, into the present work, omitting other material, because those who are not wholly inexperienced in such affairs may observe, from the customs of other Churches, with what dignity this Church itself stands pre-eminent among the rest.

The letter is as follows:

> “Lanfranc, archbishop by the grace of God, to his beloved brother Stigand, bishop of Chichester: greeting.
>
> “The clerics of our villages who are in your diocese have complained to us that your archdeacons, when they have found opportunities, demand money from them, and have already received it from some. Your Fraternity ought to remember that, contrary to the custom of our predecessors and yours, we made this concession to you and ordered them to attend your synods, and to hear from you, without any interruption or examination, whatever might contribute to knowledge of the Christian religion.
>
> “If any faults were found in them, the punishment was meanwhile to be suspended and the matters reserved for our judgment; and they were to remain subject to us, whether for mercy or for punishment, as has always been the custom. We therefore command you to order without delay that whatever has been wrongly taken be returned, and, in the interest of preserving charity, to forbid your ministers to presume to do such a thing again. We, for our part, strictly command our priests who are established outside Kent not to attend your synod or that of any other bishop again, nor to answer either you or any of your ministers for any fault. For when we come to our villages, we must investigate by pastoral authority what sort of men they are, both in their conduct and in their knowledge of their order.

> [Note: [Col. 0547]
>
> (17) Nevertheless, they are to receive chrism from you. This same letter exists in a manuscript codex of Lanfranc’s letters and differs from this one in no respect except that it reads *tantum non tamen* (“only not, nevertheless”) in place of *tamen* (“nevertheless”).]

> “Nevertheless, they are to receive chrism from you and pay what has anciently been established in connection with the reception of chrism. For just as we earnestly desire to preserve inviolate whatever our predecessors possessed from ancient times down to our own day, so, God forbid, we do not wish to deny by usurpation anything that is owed to others.”

As for the ingenuity with which the memorable Father Lanfranc acted with King William—this was mentioned a little earlier, and we do not think it out of place briefly to repeat it—in order that, through the inspiration of God’s grace, the king might be brought, while still living, to restore, for the redemption of his soul, many lands belonging to the aforesaid Church of Canterbury that had been taken from it by various claims and human violence, I have judged it lengthy and unnecessary to relate it.

The number and names of those lands are well known to that Church; and the revenues from them, by which those who serve that place under its lord are sustained, are presented by those very men before the eyes of the just Judge, day and night, for the king’s eternal salvation. What, then, should be done by the successors of so great a provider concerning the other lands of that Church which still remain in the same unjust plunder by which they were formerly taken? The fruit which he obtained from those that he restored will teach them, according to the care they devote to their charge.

For in truth he would have restored those lands as well, had he lived somewhat longer. The wise prudence of Prince Lanfranc had led him to this purpose, and he had promised that he would do so at an appointed time. But since he was not able to attain the fulfillment of his promise, he warned by his example how earnestly one ought, while able, to devote oneself to good works.

These and similar deeds, which the glorious Father Lanfranc magnificently performed, would provide abundant material sufficient for a great work if anyone wished to describe them as they were. But since, for a credible and firm reason, I am being led—as I began—to another subject, I shall say only this much more about him: that he was truly a great and unconquerable defender of the Church of Christ, a pious prince of all England, and, insofar as it was permitted him, a good shepherd to all who lived there during his lifetime.

At that same time there was a certain abbot of Bec named Anselm, a truly good man, eminently learned in literary knowledge. He devoted himself entirely to the contemplative life. [Col. 0360A] Because of the excellence of his holiness, he was known, loved, and welcomed throughout Normandy and France; he was also held in great fame in England and was joined by the closest holy friendship to the aforesaid king and to Archbishop Lanfranc.

Whenever he came to the king’s court on various ecclesiastical or other business, the king himself, laying aside the ferocity by which he seemed savage and fearsome to many, became so gentle and approachable that, in Anselm’s presence, he became, to everyone’s amazement, altogether different from the man he usually was.

He always regarded Anselm and Lanfranc—men supported alike by divine and human wisdom—as highly distinguished, and in everything that had to be done for him, insofar as their office required it, he listened to them with a more gracious attention than to others. Therefore, by their counsel, he often and greatly descended from the severity of his mind toward certain people, and he diligently worked to ensure that monasteries should arise throughout his dominion for the observance of religion.

To prevent this religious observance, once begun, from failing, he took care to protect the peace of the Churches everywhere and to give from his own resources whatever might benefit those serving God: lands, tithes, and other revenues. Yet he directed this benevolence particularly toward the Churches of Normandy.

When this William, therefore, in the twenty-first year of his reign, had been detained at Rouen by the illness from which he died, and had resolved in every way to commend himself to Anselm’s merits and intercession, he summoned Anselm from Bec and arranged for him to lodge not far away. But he delayed speaking to him about the salvation of his soul because he felt his illness somewhat relieved. Then the prince’s body happened to be so oppressed by severe sickness that he could not endure the disturbances of the court in any way.

After crossing the Seine, he took to his bed in the villa of Ermentrude [Note: [Col. 0359D] It is now called Sotteville, as if “lower town” or “lower village”], which lies opposite Rouen on the other side of the river. Whatever delicacies were brought to the sick king, half of them were sent by him to Anselm, who was also ill.

Nevertheless, he was not granted either to see Anselm again in this life or to speak to him about his soul as he had intended. For such illness seized both men that neither Anselm could reach King William nor William reach Abbot Anselm.

William did indeed die in this way, though not, as is said, without confession [Note: [Col. 0359D] Simeon of Durham says that William I, king of England, departed “fortified by heavenly viaticum”; nevertheless, both he and the others imply that the king was punished, because, after capturing a certain town in France, he burned all the churches located there, together with two holy recluses].

Anselm, however, was immediately relieved of his illness and restored shortly thereafter to his former health.

As for those who attended the royal funeral, the ceremony with which his body was carried to Caen, and how freely—or rather, with what servile calumny—it was buried in the church of Saint Stephen, we confess that the account is grievous to relate and pitiable to hear.

What condition of human fortune would not move one to compassion on hearing that this king, who in his lifetime had possessed such power that no one in all England, all Normandy, or all the land of Maine dared raise a hand against his authority, was immediately, once he had been laid upon the ground to breathe out his spirit, abandoned by everyone—as we have learned, except for a single servant—and that his corpse was carried across the Seine in a little boat without any ceremony? When he was to be buried, the very ground of his burial was challenged by a peasant, who, claiming it by hereditary right, complained that the king had long before wrongfully taken it from him [Note: [Col. 0361D] John Bromton describes the event quite movingly in his *Chronicle* and adds “that the complaint moved everyone so greatly that they first satisfied the complaining man according to his wish and only then completed the dead man’s funeral rites”].

Who could say how great a grief struck Lanfranc at his death, when we who were around him at the time the news of the king’s death arrived immediately feared that Lanfranc himself would die from the anguish of his heart?

[Col. 0361B]

When King William had died, his son William succeeded him in the kingdom. Since he desired to seize the highest honors of the kingdom from his brother Robert [Note: [Col. 0361D] The other writers say that this occurred according to their father’s arrangement, because Robert, the elder son, had rebelled against his father over Normandy, which had not been left to him freely, and was staying with Philip, king of France], and since he found that he could not enter upon the kingdom without Lanfranc’s consent and that Lanfranc was not altogether disposed to agree with him in fulfilling this desire, he feared that delay in his consecration would deprive him of the honor he sought.

He therefore began, both personally and through everyone he could employ, to promise Lanfranc under oath and by pledge of faith that, if he became king, he would preserve justice, equity, and mercy throughout the kingdom in every matter; that he would defend the peace, liberty, and security of the Churches against all men; and that he would obey Lanfranc’s commands and counsels in every respect and in all things.

But after he had been confirmed in the kingdom, he abandoned his promise and fell into the opposite course. When Lanfranc gently reproved him for this and confronted him with his unkept pledge of faith, he was inflamed with anger and said: “Who is there who can fulfill everything he promises?”

From that time he could not look upon the bishop with favor, although, out of respect for Lanfranc, he restrained himself during Lanfranc’s lifetime from some of the things toward which his will was drawing him. For Lanfranc was a man highly skilled in both divine and human law, and the gaze of the entire kingdom was directed according to his will.

When he had been transferred from this life [Note: [Col. 0362D] Lanfranc died in the year 1089, in the second year of William II; according to some, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, and according to others, on the ninth], I have thought it worthwhile, passing over much, to show briefly how grievous a calamity his death brought upon the Churches of England.

The king immediately brought into the open what he had kept concealed in his heart while Lanfranc lived. For as soon as—as I omit his other wrongful acts—he invaded the mother of all England, Scotland, and Ireland, as well as the neighboring islands, namely the Church of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0547]

(18) “The mother of all England, Scotland, and Ireland, as well as the neighboring islands.” Two letters found in a manuscript codex of Lanfranc’s letters are relevant here. One is from Thomas, archbishop of York, to Lanfranc; the other is from Lanfranc to the bishops of Worcester and Chester. Both concern the solemn elevation to episcopal dignity of Ralph, the elected bishop of the Orkneys. We learn his name—although it does not occur in the letters just mentioned—from Thomas Stubbs, an old and as yet unpublished writer on the lives of the archbishops of York.

“Letter of Thomas, archbishop of York, to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the consecration of Ralph, bishop of the Orkneys.

“‘To the most pious and holy archbishop of the Cantuarians and supreme shepherd of all Britain, Lanfranc, Thomas, his faithful servant, etc.

“‘Unless it should seem presumptuous to his holiness …’ etc. See under Lanfranc, *Patrologia*, vol. CL.

“Lanfranc writes to the bishops of Chester and Worcester that they should attend the consecration of Ralph, bishop of the Orkneys.

“‘Lanfranc, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy Church of Dorobernia, to his venerable brothers Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, and Peter, bishop of Chester [Col. 0547C], greeting.

“‘Our venerable brother Thomas has informed us …’ etc. See the same work.

“Concerning the ancient right of the archbishops of Canterbury in Ireland, which had not yet been added to English rule, there is also clear evidence in those letters of Lanfranc to Gothric and Terdelvac, kings of Ireland, which are preserved complete in the aforementioned book of his letters and were first published by Baronius under the year 1089, volume II. Other evidence is found in Eadmer, who explains this matter more fully. See Saint Bernard, *Life of Malachy*.

“Furthermore, in the inscription of Queen Matilda’s letter to Anselm, Anselm is greeted as ‘archbishop of the first see, primate of all the Irish and of all the northern islands called the Orkneys,’ as found in Anselm, Book III, Letter 55. On Ireland in relation to this matter, see Camden’s *Britannia*, pages 755 and 765. On Scotland, consult the same work, page 703, and, if more is desired, Polydore’s *History of England*, Book XXIV, under Edward IV, in the year 1471, as well as Roger of Hoveden under the years 1180 and 1192, whose words Baronius almost transcribes in volume XII under those same years.”]

he ordered everything belonging to its jurisdiction, within and outside the Church, to be inventoried through his agents. After assessing the provisions of the monks serving God there, he ordered the remainder to be placed under a tax and reduced to his own dominion.

Thus he made the Church of Christ a thing for sale, granting the right to dominate it above others to the man who, by offering a higher price to its detriment, outbid another. Consequently, by a wretched succession, the price was renewed every year. The king allowed no agreement to remain permanent; rather, whoever promised more excluded the one who gave less, unless perhaps the earlier party rose to the amount offered later, after the first agreement had been annulled.

Moreover, every day one could see the most impious men, disregarding the religion of God’s servants, demanding the king’s money as they proceeded through the monastery cloister with grim and threatening faces—issuing orders here and there, making threats, and displaying their domination and power without limit.

It is painful to recall how many scandals, dissensions, and disorders arose from this. In addition, some monks of that Church, as evils gathered upon them, were dispersed and sent to other monasteries; those who remained suffered many tribulations and reproaches.

What should I say about the men of the Church, who were crushed by such immense misery and miserable devastation that, had the evils that followed not occurred, I would doubt whether they could have been more wretchedly oppressed while still alive?

Nor did these things happen only in the Church of Canterbury. This savage brutality raged also in all its daughter Churches throughout England whenever, at the death of their own men—namely, bishops or abbots—they fell into widowhood at that time. Indeed, he himself was the first to impose this mournful oppression upon the Churches of God, accepting no exemption from it on the basis of paternal tradition.

He therefore kept the widowed Churches solely under his own control. He did not wish to appoint anyone else in his place as long as he could extract from them, through his ministers, something that he considered worth any price. Thus it was plain everywhere to see misery.

This same misery lasted for nearly five years over the Church of Canterbury—always worsening, and growing more miserable and more grievous in itself, as I say nothing of the other Churches [Note: [Col. 0362D] In the year of Christ 1082].

In the fourth year of this period, Hugh, earl of Chester [Note: [Col. 0362D] Hugh, earl of Chester, nephew through his sister of William I, lived until the year 1106, according to Knyghton, Book II, chapter 8, *On the Events of England*], wishing to establish an abbey of monks in one of his churches, sent messengers to Bec and asked Abbot Anselm to come to England, inspect the place, and furnish it with monks trained in a regular way of life.

Anselm refused and did not wish to come. For certain minds were already being touched by something like a presentiment, and although some spoke secretly among themselves, it was said that, if he went to England, he would become archbishop of Canterbury. Although this was entirely contrary to his will, and the firmness of his purpose assured his mind that he would never undertake such a burden, nevertheless, because not everyone understood this—for he wished to provide what was good not only before God but also before all people—he did not wish to enter England, lest anyone suspect that he had entered for this reason.

Meanwhile it happened that the earl himself was afflicted by a severe illness. He immediately sent word to Anselm and earnestly begged him, considering their long-standing friendship, to come without delay to advise him concerning his soul.

“If,” he said, “fear of accepting the archbishopric is keeping you from coming, I confess on my faith that the rumor being spread about this is nothing. Let him therefore know that it would be unbecoming to his holiness if, held back by no other consideration, he should refuse to assist my great need.”

Anselm persisted in not coming, and the earl likewise continued to summon him. So, for the third time, he sent him this message:

> “If you do not come, know for certain that in eternal life you will never be in such repose that you will not perpetually grieve that you did not come to me.”

When Anselm heard this, he said:

> “I am surrounded by anxieties on every side. If I go to England, I fear that some evil suspicion may arise in someone’s mind, and that people may think I am going there to obtain the archbishopric. If I do not go, I shall violate brotherly charity, which we are commanded to show not only to a friend but also to an enemy. If violating it toward an enemy is a sin, what is it toward a friend? Certainly my long-standing intimate friend, Hugh, earl of Chester, is now, as he says, in need of me. A friend is proved in adversity.
>
> “If, then, because of the distorted opinion which people may perhaps hold about me, I do not assist my friend in his need, I incur a certain sin of my own for the sake of the doubtful opinions of others. Commending myself and my conscience, emptied of all ambition for earthly honor, to God, I shall, out of regard for his holy love, comply with my friend. Let God himself dispose of the rest, and in his mercy keep me, while preserving his grace, free from every entanglement in secular affairs.”

At that time, certain very urgent affairs of his Church also required him to go to England; but because the fear mentioned above restrained him, he was unwilling to undertake the journey for their sake under any circumstances.

Meanwhile, it happened that he went to Boulogne to speak with Countess Ida [Note: [Col. 0363D] This is the blessed Ida, mother of Godfrey of Bouillon, later king of Jerusalem. We have illustrated her life on 13 April. Saint Anselm wrote several letters to her]. While he was necessarily detained there for several days, a message was sent to him by the men of Bec that, if he did not wish to be marked by the sin of disobedience, he should not return to the monastery until, after crossing the sea, he had assisted his affairs in England.

He therefore set out, crossed the sea, and landed at Dover. From there he went at a rapid pace to the earl and found him already recovering from his illness. Nevertheless, he was detained in England for nearly five months, detained not only by the abbey which he had come to arrange but also by many other matters, which, as we have said, were no less a reason for his arrival.

Thus this period passed without anything being said or done concerning the archbishopric of Canterbury, either to him or about him; and he became secure both from any danger to himself and from his former fear.

After this, wishing to return to Normandy, he could not obtain the opportunity, because the king denied him permission.

Meanwhile, when, according to custom, all the leading men of the kingdom had come to the king’s court for the grace of the Nativity of the Lord, it happened that the best of them, with one accord, complained among themselves about the common mother of the kingdom: she had been deprived of her shepherd for so long and oppressed by such unheard-of affliction.

They therefore took this counsel concerning the matter: they would approach their lord the king with humble prayer, asking him to permit prayers to be offered to the Lord throughout the Churches of England—a thing that perhaps posterity will find astonishing to relate—so that God, in his mercy, might inspire the king to appoint a worthy shepherd and thereby relieve her from such great ruin, and through her relieve the other Churches as well.

When they had jointly made this suggestion to him, he was somewhat angered by it, but nevertheless permitted what they requested to be done, saying that, whatever the Church asked, he would undoubtedly do everything it wished and would not abandon the matter for any reason.

After receiving this answer, the bishops chiefly concerned with the matter consulted Anselm himself. They could scarcely obtain from him, despite their prayers, that he should determine the manner and substance of the prayers to be offered. For the abbot himself avoided being placed before the bishops in such an arrangement.

Compelled, therefore, and acting according to what he knew would most benefit the Church of God, he set out the manner of praying in the hearing of all. The entire nobility of the kingdom that had assembled praised his judgment and insight, and, once the court was dissolved, departed to its homes. The prayers were consequently established and offered throughout all the Churches of the English.

While these things were happening, one day a certain prince of the land, speaking familiarly with the king, said among other things in the course of conversation—as often happens:

“We know no man of such holiness as that possessed, as we truly recognize, by Anselm, abbot of Bec. For he loves nothing except God, and desires nothing transitory, as is clear in all his conduct.”

The king replied mockingly:

> “Nor the archbishopric of Canterbury.”

When the other answered, “Nor that either, at least according to my opinion and that of many others,” the king swore that, clapping his hands and feet, he would run to embrace Anselm if he had any confidence that he could in any way aspire to him.

He added:

> “But by the Holy Face of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0365D]
>
> The Holy Face of Lucca is an image of the crucified Lord, believed to have been carved by Nicodemus and transferred from Syria to Etruria around the year 702. It is venerated at Lucca and is famous for its miracles. On it, see the historians of Lucca and, after them, Franciottus, *On the Saints of Lucca*, page 155],
>
> —for that is how he was accustomed to swear—neither he nor anyone else will be archbishop at this time, except me.”

Immediately after saying this, a severe illness seized him, laid him upon his bed, and, increasing day by day, continued almost until the breathing out of his spirit.

What more is there to say? All the princes of the entire kingdom assembled; the bishops, abbots, and nobles all awaited nothing but his death. The sick man was urged to think about the salvation of his soul, to open the prisons, release the captives, free those held in bonds, forgive debts owed for money that had been demanded, and restore to liberty the Churches that had been subjected to his dominion and servitude by appointing shepherds over them—especially the Church of Canterbury, whose oppression, they said, made the disgraceful fall of all Christianity in England evident.

At this time Anselm, unaware of these events, was staying in a certain village not far from Gloucester, where the king lay ill. A message was therefore sent to him that he should come to the king with all speed and, by his presence, support and strengthen him at his death.

When Anselm heard this news, he hastened to come, and he arrived. He entered the king’s presence and was asked what counsel he judged most beneficial for the soul of a dying man. First, he asked that he be told what counsel had been given by those attending the sick man while he was absent.

He heard it, approved it, and added:

> “It is written: ‘Begin with confession to the Lord.’ It therefore seems to me that he should first make a pure confession of everything he recognizes himself to have done against God, and sincerely promise that, if he recovers, he will amend everything. Then he should order, without delay, that the measures you have advised be carried out.”

This summary of the counsel was praised, and Anselm was charged with receiving the confession.

What Anselm had said was more beneficial to the salvation of the king’s soul was reported to him. Without delay he consented, and, his heart struck with remorse, promised that he would do everything the man had decreed and would henceforth preserve his whole life in gentleness and justice.

He pledged his faith to this and made his bishops guarantors between himself and God, sending them to promise this vow to God in his place upon the altar.

An edict was written and confirmed with the royal seal, ordering that all captives throughout his entire dominion should be released, that all debts should be irrevocably remitted, and that all offenses previously committed should, by an accompanying grant of pardon, be consigned to perpetual oblivion.

Moreover, good and holy laws were promised to the entire people, inviolate observance of justice, and a rigorous investigation of wrongs—one that would terrify the rest.

Everyone rejoiced, God was blessed for these things, and fervent prayers were offered for the salvation of such a great and powerful king.

Meanwhile, good men advised the king to free the common mother of the entire kingdom from her former widowhood by appointing a shepherd for her. He willingly agreed and admitted that his mind was occupied with this matter. It was therefore asked who could more worthily undertake this honor. But while all were waiting upon the king’s nod, he himself announced [Col. 0366A], and the acclamation of all followed with one accord, that Abbot Anselm was most worthy of such an honor.

Anselm was terrified at these words and grew pale. When he was hurried to the king so that he might receive the investiture of the archbishopric from his hand by the pastoral staff, he resisted with all his strength and maintained that this could in no way be done, despite the many reasons urged against him. The bishops therefore took him aside from the crowd and said to him:

“What are you doing? What do you intend? Why are you striving to oppose God? You see that nearly all Christianity in England has perished, that everything has fallen into confusion, that every abomination has emerged, and that everywhere we ourselves and the Churches of God which we ought to govern have fallen through this man’s tyranny into peril of eternal death. And you, when you can provide assistance, despise it? What are you thinking, extraordinary man? Where has your judgment fled? The Church of Canterbury, through whose oppression we have all been oppressed and destroyed, calls for you; anxiously it seeks you as its deliverer and ours. Yet, setting aside its freedom and likewise our relief, you reject participation in your brothers’ labor and seek for yourself alone an idle repose.”

To this he replied: “Wait, I beg you; wait and listen. I admit that it is true: there are many tribulations, and they need assistance. But consider, I beg you. I am already an old man [Note: [Col. 0365D] He was sixty years old.], and incapable of enduring every worldly labor. Since, therefore, I am unable to labor even for myself, how can I undertake the labor of the entire Church established throughout England? Moreover, as my conscience itself bears witness, ever since I became a monk I have avoided secular affairs, nor have I ever been able, by my own inclination, to devote myself to them, because it is clear that they contain nothing capable of bending me toward love or delight in them. Therefore let me have peace, and do not entangle me in a business which I have never loved, lest it prove unsuitable.”

“But you,” they replied, “should accept the primacy of the Church without hesitation. Lead us in the way of God, telling and commanding us what we ought to do; and behold, we will give you our hands, so that by following and obeying what you order we will not fail. Turn your attention to God on our behalf, and we will arrange your secular affairs for you.”

“What you say is impossible,” he said. I am abbot of a monastery belonging to another kingdom, with an archbishop to whom I owe obedience, and a worldly prince [Note: [Col. 0365D] This Robert was duke of Normandy, the firstborn of William the Conqueror, as has been said. His father left Normandy to him at his death, since by hereditary right it belonged to him. But concerning the other territories he had acquired by arms, William believed that, since Robert had been excluded on account of his rebellion, he could dispose of them at his pleasure. Robert did not even possess Normandy peacefully, however, for William did everything possible to exclude his brother from that region as well, and did so. The Normans and English discuss these matters at length elsewhere.] to whom I owe subjection, and monks to whom I owe the provision of counsel and assistance. I am so bound by all these obligations that I cannot abandon the monks without their permission, nor can I free myself from the rule of my prince without his permission, nor can I evade obedience to my bishop, at the cost of my soul’s salvation, without his absolution.”

“On all these matters,” they said, “the advice is easy and everyone’s consent will readily be obtained.”

He replied: “It is entirely impossible; what you intend will not happen.” [Col. 0367A]

They therefore hurried the man to the sick king and disclosed his obstinacy. The king was saddened almost to the point of tears and said to him:

“O Anselm, what are you doing? Why are you handing me over to be tortured by eternal punishments? Remember, I beg you, the faithful friendship which my father and mother had toward you, and you always had toward them; and by that friendship I beg you not to allow their son to perish in body and soul together. For I am certain that I shall perish if I end my life while holding the archbishopric within my dominion. Come to my aid, therefore; come to my aid, lord Father, and accept the pontificate, for retaining which I am now deeply ashamed, and fear that I shall be still more ashamed forever.”

Those present were moved by these words. They attacked Anselm, who was excusing himself and still unwilling to undertake so great a burden, pressing upon him with a certain indignation and agitation words such as these:

“What madness has seized your mind? You disturb the king; you utterly destroy the disturbed man, since you do not fear to aggravate him, already dying, by your obstinacy. Know, therefore, that all the disturbances, all the oppressions, and all the crimes that will henceforth weigh upon England will be imputed to you if today, by accepting pastoral responsibility, you do not prevent them.”

Placed in these straits, Anselm turned to the two monks who were with him, namely Baldwin and Eustace, and said to them: “Ah, my brothers, why do you not help me?” He said this—before God, for I do not lie—in such anxiety, as he used to affirm, that if he had then been given a choice, he would have chosen far more gladly to die, with due reverence for God’s will, than to be exalted to the dignity of archbishop.

Baldwin therefore answered: “If it is God’s will that this should happen, shall we oppose God’s will?”

Tears followed Baldwin’s words, and then blood flowed abundantly from his nostrils, openly showing all from what contrition of heart the words had issued together with the tears.

On hearing this response, Anselm said: “Alas, how quickly your staff has been broken.”

The king, perceiving that everyone’s efforts were being spent in vain, ordered them all to fall at Anselm’s feet, in case even by this means he might be enticed into consenting. But what happened? When they fell down, he himself fell before Anselm, yet Anselm would not fall away from his first judgment.

They, however, becoming angry with him and reproaching themselves with cowardice because they had endured the delay caused by attending to his objections, began to shout: “The pastoral staff! The pastoral staff!” Seizing his right arm, some began to pull him while he resisted, others to push him, and they began bringing the staff toward the hand of the man lying there.

When the king extended the staff to him, Anselm closed his hand against it and in no way consented to receive it. The bishops tried to raise his fingers, which were tightly pressed into his palm, so that the staff might at least in this way be inserted into his hand. But after they had spent some time unsuccessfully exerting themselves in this attempt, while he uttered words of pain because of the injury he was suffering, at last, with his index finger raised but immediately bent back by him, the staff was placed against his closed hand and was pressed and held there by the hands of the bishops together with his own hand. [Col. 0368A]

While the crowd shouted, “Long live the bishop! Long live the bishops with the clergy!”, they began singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* in a loud voice. They carried the chosen pontiff—rather than led him—to a nearby church, while he resisted in every way he could and kept saying: “What you are doing is nothing; what you are doing is nothing.”

After the ceremonies customary in such a case had been performed in the Church, Anselm returned to the king and said to him: “I tell you, my lord king, that you will not die from this illness. For this reason, I want you to know how well you will be able to correct what has now been done concerning me, because I have neither consented nor do I consent that it should stand.”

Having said this, he turned away and departed from him. As the bishops led him away, he left the chamber together with all the nobility of the kingdom. Turning to them, he asked them in these words:

“Do you understand what you are attempting? You are preparing to join an untamed bull and an old and feeble sheep to the plow under one yoke. What will result from this?
