Surely the bull’s ungovernable ferocity will tear the sheep—fertile in wool, milk, and lambs—dragging it here and there through thorns and thistles, unless it throws off the yoke, so that it will be useful neither to itself nor to anyone, since it will be able to provide none of these things.

“Why is this so? You have inconsiderately yoked the sheep to the bull. Consider the plow as the Church, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: ‘You are God’s field, God’s building’ (1 Cor. 3:9). In England this plow is drawn in governing, and governs in drawing, by two oxen superior to all others: namely, the king and the archbishop of Canterbury—the former by secular justice and authority, the latter by divine teaching and instruction.

“One of these oxen, namely Archbishop Lanfranc, has died; and the other, possessing the ferocity of an untamed bull, is now found placed over the plow. Yet you wish, in place of the dead ox, to join an old and feeble sheep like me to an untamed bull. You understand well enough what I am saying; therefore, when considering whom you wish to associate with whom, I wish you would reflect and, after reflecting, desist from your undertaking.

“If you do not desist, I foretell this to you: the royal ferocity, having wearied me—of whom some might obtain wool and milk of the word of God, and lambs for God’s service—by various injuries, will crush me, far beyond what you now imagine. And the joy which you now feel on my account, as though hoping for relief, will be turned into sorrow, when you lament that you were unable to obtain through me any of the counsel ordinarily given or the assistance you expected.

“You will thus bring it about that the Church which you are striving so earnestly to free from widowhood will one day, even while her shepherd is alive, relapse into widowhood—which is worse. And to whom will these evils be attributed, unless to you, who have so thoughtlessly joined the king’s ferocity to my weakness? Once I have been crushed, none of you will dare oppose him in anything; and therefore he will surely trample you everywhere according to his pleasure.”

Saying this, and unable to conceal the grief of his heart as tears burst forth, he went to his lodging, leaving the court.

These events took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, on the day before the Nones of March, the First Sunday of Lent [Note: [Col. 0369D] In that year the lunar cycle was XI, the solar cycle X, and the Dominical Letter B. Easter was celebrated on 17 April; Ash Wednesday, or the beginning of Lent, was 2 March.].

The king therefore ordered that Anselm should immediately and without diminution be invested with everything belonging to the archbishopric, both within and outside the city; and that the city of Canterbury, which Lanfranc had held from the king in benefice during his lifetime, and the abbey of Saint Alban [Note: [Col. 0369D] The Abbey of Saint Alban, in Hertfordshire, was founded by Offa, king of the Mercians, and restored and enlarged with possessions by Archbishop Lanfranc. Saint Alban is commemorated on 22 June, the day on which he was crowned with martyrdom under Diocletian.], which not only Lanfranc but also his predecessors are known to have possessed, should pass into *allodium* [Note: [Col. 0369D] *Allodium* is a free estate, subject to no servitude, or property granted outright without burden; this is indicated by the etymology of the word *Al-od*, meaning “entirely empty.” Consult Selden and Spelman’s *Glossary*.] [Note: [Col. 0547]

(19) “To pass into allodium,” and so forth. In that age, *to pass into allodium* also meant to be granted outright. William of Malmesbury, Book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops*, speaking of Rufus’s generosity toward Anselm, says: “He granted to him outright the city of Canterbury, which Archbishop Lanfranc had held in benefice.” Nearly the same statement is found in the charters of the monastery of Saint Augustine, cited by the distinguished William Camden in *Kent*, p. 238.

The terms *allodium* and *to hold in allodium* occur frequently in the fiscal records of William I. In the survey of Henton: “The king holds Roncelle; Ulffet held it from Count Tosti, but it was not allodium.” Likewise: “The king holds Warochselle. Countess Gueda held it from Count Godwin in allodium; at that time it paid geld for five hides, now for two hides and a half. The land is ten plowlands.”

In the survey of Kent, at Benindene: “Godric remained and holds twenty acres in his allodium.” In Sussex: “Almar held Cetingley from King Edward, as allodium.” Hence those who possess estates under this right of clientship, called allodia, are also called *alodarii* and *aloarii*.

In the Sussex survey: “Godwin holds Lansewice from the count of Eu, and from him [there are] six *aloarii*.” And when an *alodarius* dies, as is read in the survey of Kent, the king receives the relief of the land, except for the land of the Holy Trinity.

In the survey of Hampshire:

“​​Hugh de Port holds Cerdeford, and William from him. Two free men held it in allodium as two manors from King Edward; at that time and now it paid geld for five hides. The land is four plowlands. In the demesne are two plowlands, and twenty bordars and four slaves with one plowland and eighty acres of meadow. In the time of King Edward and now it is worth four pounds, with an additional one hundred shillings received. The same William holds from Hugh one virgate and a half at Clatinges. Two free men held it from Alwin, but it was not allodium. There are two bordars and six acres of meadow; it was worth ten shillings, now seven shillings.

“In this hundred and in this manor Picot holds two virgates and a half from the king. Phitelet held it in allodium from King Edward as a manor; at that time and now it paid geld for two virgates and a half. The land is half a plowland, and there are one villein, two bordars, and ten acres of meadow. William of Chernet claims this land, saying that it belongs to the manor of Cerdeford, the fief of Hugh de Port, by inheritance from his ancestor. In support of this he produced the testimony of the best and oldest men of the entire county and hundred; Picot produced contrary testimony from villeins, common people, and reeves who wished to defend under oath, or by the judgment of God, that the man who held the land was a free man and could go with his land wherever he wished.

“But William’s witnesses refuse to accept any law except that of King Edward until the matter is decided by the king. It was worth fifteen shillings, afterward eight shillings, and now ten shillings.”

There are other examples of this kind. What precisely was the right of allodium among our ancestors in that age is uncertain. What other peoples—especially Germans, Franks, and Italians—understood by this term may be learned from Cujacius’s preface to Book I of *On Fiefs* and to Book II, title 17, as well as from Hotoman’s *Feudal Words* and other works of this kind common among legal scholars.

The frequency of the word, carefully recorded from ancient sources, is also available in the *Glossary of the Code of Ancient Laws* of the very learned Frederick Lundebrog, under the word *Alode*.

Foreign jurists generally distinguish an allodium from a benefice or fief in this way: whereas benefices are subject to solemn obligations and conditions, whether imposed by law or agreement, allodia—like *κτήματα ἰδιοπεριόριστα* (“estates with a self-limited proprietary right”; I remember that some Greek writer used this expression)—recognize merely the right of those who possess the land as their own and, without any declaration of the kind of loyalty usually professed by oath, are entirely free from every form of service.

Yet in the commentaries on our own law there is absolutely nothing in which any trace of this form of ownership appears, except perhaps the single arrangement that we call frankalmoign, or free alms. This applies only to the sacred order and requires from clients neither a rent nor the declaration of loyalty mentioned above, but merely the duty of offering prayers for the welfare of patrons or lords; nevertheless, in a civil court the client cannot be resisted on account of it.

In all the other forms which either still remain intact among us or have left their traces, a solemn declaration of loyalty, confirmed by oath, is legally required. Accordingly, almost all our lands, like benefices or fiefs, properly and plainly either acknowledge, or ought to acknowledge, the clientship of some lord.

Moreover, the ancient right of the archbishops at Canterbury mentioned here may perhaps also concern an old coin, one side of which bears the name of Archbishop Plegmund and the other that of Eicmund the moneyer, marked in the following manner [Col. 0549A]. The original is preserved in the Cottonian Library. I also remember having seen there a coin bearing both the name and image of Archbishop Celnoth.

The right of coining money, which is properly regarded as an attribute of majesty, apparently belonged at that time to the archbishop as lord of the city, and perhaps also to other lords or magistrates of the more important towns which we call boroughs or cities. In that age, I think, every such lord not only enjoyed the right of coining but also marked the coin at his discretion with his own name or image.

Later—for Celnoth flourished under King Ethelwulf and Plegmund under Alfred—it was decreed, during the reign of Athelstan, that there should be only one kind of money throughout the English realm and that it should be the same everywhere. I believe this abolished the earlier promiscuous practice of marking coins, and that thereafter no coin was struck without the ruler’s image or name, sometimes supplemented by the name of the provincial count, the lord of the city or borough, or even the moneyer.

Athelstan’s law reads as follows, chapter 14: “*we cwaethon that an myret sy oser ealle thaes Cynges anwealde and nan man ne mynetige butan port*”; that is: “We decree that there shall be one kind of coin throughout the king’s dominion, and that no one shall mint it outside a borough.”

We also learn from his laws that Canterbury had more official moneyers than anywhere else in England except the city of London: London had eight, Canterbury seven. Four of Canterbury’s moneyers belonged to the king, two served the archbishop, and one the abbot. See also Edgar’s law, chapter 8, and Cnut’s, chapter 8.]

of Christ Church, Canterbury, in perpetual right, for the redemption of his soul.

After this, Anselm remained in the villages belonging to the archbishopric at the king’s command, while the venerable Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, lived with him and provided whatever was necessary for his sustenance. [Note: [Col. 0370D] Gundulf had been taken from the monastery of Bec through the efforts of Blessed Lanfranc in 1077; he held the bishopric with great distinction until 7 March 1108.]

[Col. 0369B]

Meanwhile the king sent messengers with letters to Normandy, to the count, to the archbishop of Rouen, and to the monks of Bec, so that each might give his assent, insofar as it concerned him, to what had been done in England concerning the abbot of Bec. But what happened? Although many things were undertaken in this way, they accomplished nothing with those men. At last, however, overcome by persistent and reasonable insistence, God so disposing, they allowed what had been begun concerning Anselm to be completed, and imposed it upon him under obedience, lest he evade the burden laid upon him.

Accordingly, each of them wrote a separate letter [Note: [Col. 0370D] Maurilius, the archbishop of Rouen mentioned above, who had ordered Anselm not to refuse any great prelacy, was succeeded by John in 1067; John by this William in 1079, and William held the see until 1110.]. Since these letters agreed in one and the same conclusion, they were sent by messengers to Anselm and the king. Of all of them I shall insert one in this little work, so that its meaning and that of the others may become clear. Let it therefore be this:

“Brother William, archbishop, to his lord and friend Anselm: the blessing of God and our own.

“Concerning what the king asked me about you, and about which you yourself wrote to me, I have considered the matter at length and for a long time, as was proper for so important a question, and I have sought the advice of my friends and of yours concerning it. Both sides would have wished, if it had been possible, always to have your presence among them as in former times, and not to do anything that would offend the divine will.

“But since matters have reached the point at which both wishes cannot be fulfilled, we place the divine will before our own and subject our will to the divine. Therefore, in the name of God and Saint Peter, and of all my friends and yours who love you according to God’s will, I command you to accept the pastoral care of the Church of Canterbury and, in accordance with ecclesiastical custom, the episcopal blessing; and thereafter to watch over the salvation of your sheep, who, as we believe, have been divinely entrusted to you.

“Farewell, my inmost heart.”

[Col. 0370A]

These letters, together with the others addressed to Anselm, were brought first to him rather than to the king. Meanwhile, just as Anselm had foretold, the king recovered from his illness. Immediately, therefore, he dissolved all the good measures he had established while sick and ordered them annulled.

He ordered that the prisoners who had not yet been released should be guarded more strictly than usual; those who had been released were to be confined again if they could be captured; debts that had already been forgiven were to be exacted in full; pleas and offenses were to be restored to their former status; and they were to be handled and judged by men who were more concerned to overturn justice than to preserve or defend it, for the oppression of the wretched and the extortion of money rather than for the correction of any sin.

Thus a misery so vast and a devastation so grievous arose throughout the kingdom that, in my estimation, anyone who remembers it will not recall having seen its equal in England before this. Indeed, every evil the king had committed before his illness appeared good in comparison with the evils he committed after being restored to health.

If anyone wishes to know from what source these evils flowed, he may judge from the following. When the king, after recovering his health, admonished the aforesaid bishop of Rochester in familiar conversation to conduct himself more watchfully according to God’s will in all things, he replied:

“Know, O bishop, that, by the holy face of Lucca, God will never regard me as good for the evil he has inflicted upon me.”

For the present, let this brief account of the king suffice; let the narrative now return to its intended order.

When Anselm had received, as we have mentioned, the letters sent from Normandy, and the king had come from Dover—after conferring with Count Robert of Flanders—to Rochester, where Anselm then was, Anselm took the king aside to a private place and addressed him as follows:

“My lord king, my mind still hangs in doubt on both sides as to whether I should agree to accept the pontificate or not. But if reason leads me to accept it, I want you to know briefly what I wish you to do.

“I wish you to restore without any plea or controversy to the Church of Canterbury, which I have been chosen to govern, all the lands that the Church held in the time of Archbishop Lanfranc of blessed memory. As for the other lands which the same Church possessed before his time but lost and has not yet recovered, I want you to grant me right and judgment concerning them.

“Moreover, I wish you to trust me, above all others, in matters concerning God and Christianity; and just as I desire to have you as my earthly lord and defender, so you should have me as a spiritual father and guardian of your soul.

“Concerning Pope Urban of Rome, whom until now you have not accepted as apostolic, but whom I have already accepted and do accept, and to whom I wish to offer the obedience and submission due to him, I warn you to take precautions lest any scandal arise from this in the future.

“Please declare your will concerning these matters, so that, once I know it, I may be certain where to turn.”

The king therefore summoned William, bishop of Durham [Note: [Col. 0371D] Malmesbury portrays this William of Durham as a vile flatterer of the king and the leader of all the disturbances stirred up against Saint Anselm, though otherwise useful in his episcopate, which he held with varying fortunes until 1097.], and Count Robert of Meulan, and ordered Anselm to repeat in their presence what he had said. Anselm did what was commanded, and the king replied to him through their advice:

“The lands of which the Church had indeed been in possession under Lanfranc I shall restore to you, and to the Church, in the condition in which they then were. But concerning those which it did not possess under him, I make no agreement with you at present. Nevertheless, concerning these and the others, I shall trust you as I ought.”

The king ended his speech there, and they parted from one another.

Then, after a few days had passed, the king himself received by letter the consent concerning Anselm which he had requested from the Normans, as we have said. Coming to his estate called Windsor [Note: [Col. 0371D] More will be said about the village of Windlefora on 23 April, in the *Analecta* following the Acts of Saint George, chapter 11, as the birthplace of the Order of the Garter.], he met Anselm in person, together with his own attendants, so that Anselm would no longer refuse to become pontiff in accordance with the election made concerning him by the whole kingdom, and so that he might grant to the king’s men, to be held by hereditary right, the lands of the Church which the king himself had given them after Lanfranc’s death in return for fixed service, as a token of his affection.

But Anselm, unwilling to despoil the Church, which he had not yet invested with any property, refused in any way to grant the lands as requested. A quarrel therefore arose between him and the king, and the matter concerning his pontificate, which had already been under discussion, remained unresolved.

Anselm was consequently extremely glad, hoping that by this opportunity he might, through God’s grace, be freed from the burden of the prelacy. For he had already returned to Bec, with the pastoral staff, the care which he had undertaken over Bec as abbot, in accordance with the absolution described above. And now, because he was unwilling to give away the Church’s lands unjustly, he happily saw himself escaping the burden of episcopal office.

But when, after a considerable period had passed, the king could no longer endure the outcry of everyone lamenting the destruction of the Churches, he had the man come to him at Winchester, where an assembly of nobles had gathered. By many promises that would benefit good men and the Church of God, he persuaded and prevailed upon him to accept the primacy of the Church of the English.

Anselm therefore, led by the custom and example of his predecessor, became the king’s man for the use of the land and, as Lanfranc had been in his time, was ordered to be put in possession of the entire archbishopric.

After this he came to Canterbury on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. Received with immense joy by the monks, the clergy, and the entire people, he ascended with great honor to the pontifical seat in order to govern the Church of God.

On the same day there came to Canterbury, sent by the king, a certain man named Ranulf [Note: [Col. 0371D] Malmesbury portrays Ranulf of Durham in his true colors, as the adviser and executor of all the trafficking in sacred offices throughout England. He purchased the bishopric of Durham for a price in 1099 and held it for twenty-nine years.], the chief executor of the king’s will. Disregarding all consideration of piety and modesty, he brought a legal action against Anselm on that very day, and, fierce and arrogant, did not fear to disturb so great a joy of the Church.

This matter gravely wounded everyone’s spirit. They complained and regarded it as utterly unworthy that so great an injury should be inflicted upon so great a man, so that he was not even permitted to pass the first day of his dignity in peace. Their indignation was increased not a little by the fact that the business at issue belonged to the rights of the Church and did not in any respect await the decision of a royal court.

At that time, therefore, the members of the Church were struck by an exceedingly grievous blow. Anselm, suffering the deepest pain but unable to oppose the king, inferred the future from present events; he understood and foretold that he would endure many hardships in his pontificate.

As he approached this new and unfamiliar form of serving God, he stood in fear, according to Solomon, and prepared his soul for temptation, knowing that all who desire to live devoutly in Christ must necessarily suffer tribulation.

When the time of his consecration approached, Thomas, archbishop of York [Note: [Col. 0372D] Thomas, the first archbishop of York of that name, appointed in 1070 and deceased in 1100, is highly praised by the writers.], came according to custom, together with all the bishops of England, to Canterbury, and there they consecrated him pontiff with due reverence on the day before the Nones of December.

Two bishops, however—namely the bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0372D] The bishop of Worcester was Saint Wulfstan, consecrated in 1062 and deceased on 19 January 1095, when we published his Acts.] and the bishop of Exeter [Note: [Col. 0372D] Osbern, bishop of Exeter, held the see from 1074 to 1103; the letter to him appears below, Book III, no. 15.]—were prevented by illness from attending this consecration. But by sending messengers and letters, they declared that in this matter their absence would be present and consonant with the presence of their fellow bishops.

Before the examination of the pontiff to be ordained, however, when Walchelin, bishop of Winchester [Note: [Col. 0372D] Walchelin was made bishop of Winchester in 1070 and held the see until 1097, a praiseworthy prelate except that he was rather harsh toward monks; elsewhere he is called Walchemus, perhaps more correctly.] [Col. 0373A], at the request of Maurice [Note: [Col. 0373D] Maurice was appointed bishop of London in 1087; he held the see for twenty years and, restoring Saint Paul’s Church after it had burned, produced a work famous throughout England, later consumed in the recent fire of London.], bishop of London, whose office this was, was reading the written election in ecclesiastical fashion, Thomas of York was immediately and seriously offended at the first line and complained that it had not been lawfully composed.

For when it said: “Brothers and my fellow bishops, your fraternity knows how long it has been since, through various intervening events, this Church of Dorobernia, the metropolitan Church of all Britain, has been deprived of its shepherd,” he interrupted, saying:

“‘The metropolitan Church of all Britain’? If it is the metropolitan Church of all Britain, then the Church of York, which is known to be metropolitan, is not metropolitan. We know, indeed, that the Church of Canterbury is the primate Church of all Britain, not the metropolitan Church.”

When it was understood that what he said was supported by reason [Col. 0373B], the written text itself was immediately changed. In place of “the metropolitan Church of all Britain,” it was written “the primate Church of all Britain,” and every controversy fell silent. Thus he consecrated Anselm as primate of all Britain.

When, during the consecration, the text of the Gospel had, according to the rite of the Church, been opened over him by the bishops, held there, and inspected after the consecration had been completed, this sentence was found at the top of the page:

“He called many, and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready; and they all began together to make excuses.”

Then, on the eighth day after the completion of his ordination, as Anselm was leaving Canterbury, he went to the king’s court because of the approaching Nativity of the Lord. When he arrived there, he was received cheerfully by the king and by the entire nobility of the kingdom.

At that time the king was striving with all his strength to take Normandy away from his brother Robert, and was spending on this effort a great and immense sum of money gathered from every source, to such an extent that he even suffered certain difficulties, which seemed unbecoming to royal dignity.

His friends therefore persuaded the new pontiff, and he offered the king five hundred pounds of silver, hoping—and trusting the promises made to him—that by this act he would thereafter secure the king’s firm favor; that he would have him as a supporter in all matters while wishing to attend to the things of God; and that he would obtain his peace and protection for ecclesiastical affairs, both within and outside the Church, against all opponents.

When the king heard of this offer, he praised the proposal as a good one; but certain men of malicious disposition led the king, as often happens, to the point at which he would not consent to receive the money offered, but despised it.

“‘You,’ they say, ‘honored, enriched, and exalted him above all the other nobles of England; and now, when in view of your need he ought to give you two thousand—or, to put it as mildly as possible, one thousand—pounds in gratitude for your generosity, he offers five hundred (for shame!). But wait a little, change your expression toward him, and you will see that, driven by his customary fear of others, he will joyfully add as many again to the five hundred he offers in order to recover your favor.’”

Indeed, the king himself had this practice toward all those under his rule: whenever any of them offered him money, even merely to obtain his favor, he would reject the offering unless its amount corresponded to his desire. Nor would he thereafter admit the offerer to his friendship if he did not increase the gift to his satisfaction.

Those wicked men therefore supposed that Anselm too could be frightened by this practice and immediately induced, through an increased payment, to fulfill the king’s will. But wickedness lied to itself (Psalm 26:12). Accordingly, Anselm was instructed to refuse the money offered to the king, and he was astonished. He approached the king and asked whether such an order had proceeded from him or not. When he heard that it truly had, he immediately said:

“‘Please, my lord, do not refuse to accept what I am offering at present. Although it is the first gift, it will not be the last from your archbishop. And I confess that it is more useful and honorable for you to receive a little from me with friendly freedom, and to receive it often, than to seize much from me all at once by forcible exaction under servile conditions. For with friendly freedom you will be able to have me and all that is mine for your benefit; under servile conditions, you will have neither me nor what is mine.’”

At this the angry king said: “Let your possessions remain with you, together with your quarrelling; what is mine is sufficient for me. Go.”

He therefore rose and departed, reflecting to himself—perhaps not without divine warning—that at the beginning of his entrance into the see the Gospel had first been read: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). Coming back to himself more cheerfully, he said:

“‘Blessed be almighty God, who in his mercy has kept me free from every disgrace. For if the king had graciously accepted what I offered, it would certainly have been thought by the wicked men who abound that what had earlier been promised for the bishopric had now been returned under the guise of a clever offering. But what shall I do now? I shall give the gift already designated for the redemption of his soul to Christ’s poor, not to him; and I shall devoutly pray that God pour his favor upon him and defend me from every evil.’”

He then sought the king’s favor through intermediaries, but because he refused to double the money, he did not obtain it. When the festival was over, he left the court, anxiously intent on using the gift he had offered to refresh Christ’s poor, as he had resolved.

Coming to his estate called Herga [or Berga], he dedicated there a church which Lanfranc had built but, prevented by death, had been unable to consecrate. During this dedication, two canons from Saint Paul’s, sent by the bishop of London, came there carrying letters from the bishop. In them the bishop begged him to postpone the dedication until they could discuss the matter together. He said that the church was in his parish and that, although it stood on the archbishop’s land, its dedication belonged to him.

When Anselm heard this, and knew the ancient custom of his predecessors, he judged that he ought not to withdraw from the ministry because of human requests, and he did not do so. For it was and had long been the custom of the archbishops of Canterbury that, wherever their lands might be throughout England, none of the bishops possessed any jurisdiction apart from them; rather, all human and divine affairs remained under their authority as though in their own diocese.

Nevertheless, Anselm did not wish to injure anyone by exercising what seemed to be unrestricted power. He therefore carefully investigated the certainty of this custom, so that if it proved not to have been valid he might henceforth refrain from it.

There still survived one and only one bishop of blessed memory from among the ancient fathers of the English: a man distinguished in every form of religious life and exceptionally learned in the ancient customs of England. This was Wulstan. Anselm consulted him about the matter and asked him to make the simple truth known to him. Wulstan received the request and wrote to him as follows:

“To the most reverend and most blessed Anselm, distinguished by holiness of life and the dignity of the highest see, archbishop; Wulstan, the least of the servants of God, and, by merit, the unworthy bishop of the church of Worcester: the service of prayers and faithful offices of charity.

[Col. 0375C]

“Your prudence knows the daily labors and oppressions of holy Church: the wicked oppress her, and those who ought to protect her are themselves the instigators. Your holiness has been placed in the highest stronghold to repel such men and defend holy Church against them. Therefore let no fear of secular power humble you, nor favor bend you; rather, begin courageously and, with God’s help, complete what you have begun. Resist those who rise against you, restrain the oppressors, and defend our holy mother against them.

“As for the matter about which your dignity has deigned to write to us and seek the counsel of our insignificance, we shall not fail to say what we can remember. We have never heard this case debated, because no one ever wished to deprive the archbishop of Canterbury of this power or prevent him from publicly dedicating only his own churches.

“For there are altars in our own diocese, and also certain churches in those villages which Stigand, the predecessor of your excellency, possessed—not by right of ecclesiastical inheritance, but by gift of secular power—which he dedicated during the times of ourselves and our predecessor, without consulting us. Neither before nor afterward did we bring any accusation concerning this, since we knew that this spiritual authority belonged to that same metropolitan bishop.

“Yet we have never heard that a judgment was brought concerning this matter, or that he was judged to possess this right. But since we recognize that he freely exercised it in our diocese, we believe that he could exercise it in the dioceses of others as well. Behold, we have made known to your prudence as much as we could recall or know; let your prudence now consider what ought to be done. May your fatherhood prosper, and pray for us.”

[Note: Stigand seized the see of Canterbury in 1052; after being deposed, he died toward the end of 1070.]

Strengthened by this testimony, and by that of many others whom it would take too long to enumerate, Anselm thereafter confidently followed the custom of his predecessors. He not only consecrated churches without consulting the bishops, but also personally or through his own agents administered all divine offices throughout his lands.

[Col. 0376B]

After some days had passed, nearly all the bishops, together with the nobles of England, assembled at Hastings [Note: Ferrarius, following Camden, thinks that Harlinges was not far from Camulodunum, in Essex, where the very broad estuary of the River Idumanus affords a convenient anchorage for a fleet of any size.] at the king’s command, accompanying the king with their blessing and support as he prepared to cross over to Normandy.

Father Anselm also came, intending to protect the king through his prayers amid the dangers of the sea. The king and the nobles remained there for more than a month, because the wind prevented the king’s crossing. During this delay Anselm consecrated Robert to govern the church of Lincoln, in the church of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, which stood in the castle itself. Seven of his suffragan bishops assisted him in this office.

[Note: Robert held the bishopric of Lincoln until the year 1122.]

[Note: The suffragan sees of the church of Canterbury are reckoned altogether as eleven.]

Some of the bishops and nobles, however, attempted to provoke a scandal against Anselm over this consecration, intending that he should consecrate the same bishop absolutely, without the required profession. They undertook this without any legal support, solely because they thought that, by troubling Anselm, they could offer the king something that would please him, knowing that he was greatly disturbed against Anselm on account of the matter described above.

But Anselm conceived no resentment over this. With a calm expression, he refused in every way to consent to them, and he would not consecrate the bishop until he had first received from him a profession of submission and obedience.

When the king heard what the bishops were attempting, he declared that he would in no way consent to anyone detracting from the dignity of his mother, the church of Canterbury, because of the hostility he himself bore toward the archbishop.

[Col. 0376D]

At that time almost the entire body of young men at court wore their hair long in the manner of young women. Every day they combed it, glanced around with irreligious looks, and were accustomed to walk about with delicate steps and a soft gait. When this same Father preached about them on the day of the beginning of the fast, to the people who had gathered for his Mass and for the reception of ashes, he led a large crowd of them to repentance and, having their hair cut, restored them to a manly appearance.

Those whom he could not recall from this disgrace he excluded from receiving the ashes and from the blessing of his absolution. In these and similar matters he acted prudently and freely. Nor did he keep before his eyes in all things only the demands of justice; he strove still more earnestly to urge the king to serve God and cultivate justice.

One day, therefore, he went to him as usual and, sitting beside him, began to address him:

“‘My lord king, you have resolved to cross the sea and subject Normandy to your rule. But so that this and the other things you desire may prosper for you, I beg you first to give help and counsel concerning how Christianity in this kingdom—which has now almost entirely perished in many respects—may be restored to its proper condition.’”

The king replied: “What help, what counsel?”

“‘If it pleases you,’” he said, “‘order the councils to be renewed according to ancient custom; let matters wrongly conducted be brought into the open, let those brought into the open be examined, those examined be censured, and those censured be settled. Certainly no general council of bishops has been held in England since you became king, nor for many years previously.’

[Note: In his Catalogue of Councils, Spelmann places the last general council at Enham. It was summoned by King Ethelred in 1009 at the urging of Ælfheah of Canterbury and Wulstan of York. Under the new rule of the Normans, ecclesiastical affairs had meanwhile declined remarkably and stood in great need of reform. Nevertheless, below, in Book III, chapter 6, a general council under Lanfranc appears to be indicated.]

“‘For this reason many crimes have broken out, and, since no one existed to cut them back, they have grown through corrupt custom to excessive strength.’”

The king replied: “When it seems right to me, I shall deal with these matters—not according to your will, but according to mine. But this will take place at another time.” He added mockingly: “But what will you speak about in the council?”

Then Anselm said:

“‘The most abominable crime of Sodom—to say nothing of illicit unions among blood relatives and many other criminal matters involving detestable practices—this crime of Sodom, I say, has recently spread throughout this land and already grown greatly, defiling many by its enormity. Unless, I confess, a judgment issued more strictly by you and the force of ecclesiastical discipline quickly oppose it, the whole land will shortly become Sodom. But let us try together, I beg you—you by royal authority and I by pontifical authority—to establish a measure concerning it which, once proclaimed throughout the kingdom, will cause every supporter of it to tremble and be subdued even by hearing it.’”

These words did not settle in the prince’s mind, and he replied briefly: “And what would be done for you in this matter?”

“If not for me,” Anselm said, “I hope it would be done for God and for you.”

“That is enough,” said the king. “I do not want you to speak further about it.”

Anselm fell silent, but soon turned his words to another subject:

“‘There is also another matter to which I would like you to direct your attention and, by directing it, extend the hand of your counsel. There are many abbeys in this land deprived of their pastors. Consequently, the monks abandon their order, pursue worldly luxury, and depart this life without confession. Therefore I advise, beg, and urge you, after carefully examining so serious a matter, to appoint abbots for them according to God’s will, lest, through the destruction of the monasteries and the ruin of the monks, you acquire condemnation for yourself—God forbid.’”

The king could no longer restrain his anger. Greatly disturbed, he said indignantly:

“What is that to you? Are the abbeys not mine? You do what you wish with your estates; shall I not do what I wish with my abbeys?”

Anselm replied:

“‘They are yours so that, as their advocate, you may defend and protect them; they are not yours to invade or devastate. We know that they belong to God, so that his ministers may live from them, not so that your expeditions and wars may be carried on from them. Besides, you possess many estates and revenues from which you can fully administer your affairs. If it pleases you, leave the churches what belongs to them.’”

“Know for certain,” said the king, “that what you say is very much opposed to me. Your predecessor would never have dared to say such things to my father; and I shall do nothing for you.”

Anselm therefore understood that he was casting his words to the wind, and he rose and departed.

[Col. 0378B]

Reflecting that his former anger had some part in such replies, and considering that peace could in no way be restored to affairs while the prince’s mind was offended, Anselm—so that he might both serve the interests of those affairs and, with the favor of royal providence, bear fruit more freely for God—humbly asked the king through the bishops to admit him freely into his friendship.

“‘If he does not wish to do so,’” he said, “‘let him explain why; and if I have offended him, I am ready to make satisfaction.’”

This was reported to the king, who replied: “I accuse him of nothing, but I do not wish to grant him my favor, since I do not hear why I should do so.”

When the bishops reported this to the man, he asked what it was that the king did not hear and for which reason he refused to hear his requests.

“They say this is clear. For if you wish to have his peace, you must necessarily provide him generously with your money. Recently you offered him five hundred pounds, but because it seemed too little to him, he refused to accept it. Now, if you are willing to trust our advice—and we urge you to do what we do in a similar matter—give him the same five hundred pounds for the present, and promise him an equal amount of money which you will collect from your men. We are confident that he will both restore his friendship to you and allow you to enjoy your peace as you wish. We see no other way out for you, nor, trapped in the same difficulty, do we have another way out ourselves.”

Immediately understanding what this advice was intended to achieve, Anselm said:

“‘Away with such an escape from me! For since he brings no charge of any offense against me, according to what you say, and yet is so angry with me that he can be reconciled only by a thousand pounds of silver, perhaps if I now appeased him, as a new bishop, with this gift, he would on another occasion become angry in the same way, so that he could again be appeased by an equal payment.

“‘Furthermore, after the death of my venerable predecessor Lanfranc, my men were plundered and stripped. Since I have so far contributed nothing to them with which they might clothe themselves, should I now strip them naked—or rather flay those already stripped? Away with this from me as well!

“‘No less should it be far from me to demonstrate by my action that the love of my lord is for sale. I owe him faith and honor, and should I inflict this disgrace upon him—that I should buy his favor as though it were a horse or a donkey with cheap coins? Having bought his love, I would afterward value it only according to the price I had paid for it. But far be it from me to purchase the greatness of so great a matter at a low price.

“‘Rather, make every effort so that he may freely and honorably love me as archbishop of Canterbury and his spiritual father; and for my part I shall take care to present myself and what is mine for his service and will, as I ought.’”

They said: “We know that at least you will not refuse to give him the five hundred pounds already offered.”

He replied: “I certainly shall not give him even that again, because when I offered it to him he refused to accept it, and I have already given a very large part of it to the poor, as I promised.”

This was reported to the king, who ordered the following reply to be delivered to him:

“Yesterday I hated him greatly, and today I hate him even more; let him know for certain that tomorrow and thereafter I shall always hate him with a sharper and more bitter hatred. I shall no longer regard him as father or archbishop; I utterly reject and curse his blessings and prayers. Let him go wherever he wishes, and let him not wait any longer for me to cross over in order to receive his blessing.”

We therefore departed from the court with all speed and left him to his own will. He himself crossed over into Normandy, but although he spent an immense amount of money, he was entirely unable to subjugate it to himself. His undertaking thus unsuccessful, he returned to England.

While he was staying in a certain estate called Ilingheham, three miles from Shaftesbury, Anselm approached him and made known that he intended to visit the Roman pontiff to request his pallium.

The king asked: “From which pope do you wish to request it?”

At that time there were two men—so it was reported in England—who were called Roman pontiffs, in disagreement with one another and drawing the divided church of God after them: Urban, formerly called Odo, bishop of Ostia; and Clement, formerly called Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna.

[Note: This schism had begun under Saint Gregory VII, as will be related on his feast day, May 25. His opponent was Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, who had been created pope by Emperor Henry in 1083 and was called Clement. After Saint Gregory’s death, Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, succeeded him in 1086 and was called Victor III. He was succeeded in 1088 by Odo, bishop of Ostia, who was called Urban II.]

To say nothing of other regions of the world, this situation occupied the church of England for many years, so that after the death of Gregory of venerable memory, previously called Hildebrand, it wished to submit or render obedience to no one in place of the pope until this time.

But since Urban had long been accepted in Italy and Gaul as the vicar of blessed Peter, Anselm too, as an abbot from Normandy, had accepted him as pope. As a man of great renown and authority, he had received Urban’s letters and had addressed his own letters to him as the supreme pastor of holy Church.

When the king therefore asked from which pope he wished to request the use of the pallium, he replied: “From Urban.”

When the king heard this, he said that he had not yet accepted Urban as the apostolic pontiff. Nor had it ever been the custom, either in his own time or in that of his father, for anyone in the kingdom of England to name a pope without his permission or election. Whoever wished to seize this power of dignity from him would be doing the same as if he were attempting to take his crown from him.

Anselm, astonished at this, brought forward what we have related above: namely, that before he had consented to become a bishop, he had told the king at Rochester that, while he was abbot of Bec, he had accepted Urban as pope and had no intention of departing in any way from his obedience and submission to him.

When the king heard this, provoked by the goads of anger, he declared that Anselm could not at the same time preserve the allegiance he owed to the king and obedience to the apostolic see against the king’s will.

Anselm therefore, while maintaining the position he had advanced concerning submission and obedience to the Roman Church, asked for a delay to examine the matter. He requested that the bishops, abbots, and all the nobles of the kingdom assemble together and determine by common agreement whether, without compromising reverence and obedience to the apostolic see, he could preserve his allegiance to an earthly king or not.

“If it is proved,” he said, “that the two cannot at all be reconciled, I confess that I would rather avoid your land by leaving it until you accept the apostolic pontiff than deny, even for an hour, the obedience owed to blessed Peter and his vicar.”

A delay was therefore granted, and by royal order nearly all the nobility of the kingdom assembled at Rockingham on the fifth day before the Ides of March to debate this case.

[Col. 0380C]

A gathering of everyone therefore took place on Sunday [Note: [Col. 0380D] The fifth Sunday of Lent, commonly called Passion Sunday, fell in the year 1095 on the cited fifth day before the Ides of March—that is, on March 11—and Easter was then celebrated on March 25 of that same month, the Dominical Letter being G.] in the church situated within the castle, from the first hour onward, while the king and his men were secretly and diligently devising their plans against Anselm. Anselm, however, having summoned to himself from the king’s secret council the bishops, abbots, and princes, addressed them, together with the numerous crowd of monks, clerics, and laymen standing by, in these words:

“My brothers, sons of the Church of God—I mean all of you who are gathered here in the name of the Lord—I beg you to listen and to give, as far as you can, the help of your counsel concerning the case for whose discussion you have been assembled. What that case is, let those who have not yet heard it fully now hear briefly, if it please you.

“Certain words have arisen between our lord the king and me which seem to be producing a certain disagreement. For when recently I had asked permission to approach Urban, the prelate of the apostolic see, according to the custom of my predecessors, in order to receive my pallium from him, he said that he had not yet received Urban himself as pope, and therefore did not wish me to hasten to him for that purpose. Moreover, he said that if I received that same Urban, or anyone else, as pope in my kingdom without his election and authorization, or retained him after having received him, I would be acting against the fidelity I owed him, and that in this I would offend him no less than if I were trying to take his crown from him. Therefore, he said, know that you shall have no share in my kingdom unless I prove by explicit assertions that, according to my desire, you will deny every form of obedience and subjection to the Urban in question.

“When I heard this, I was astonished. For, as you know, I was an abbot, living in another kingdom by the mercy of God, without complaint from anyone. I was compelled to come into this land not by any hope or desire for the episcopate, but by certain reasonable causes which I could in no way disregard. When the king himself fell ill, all of you who were then present advised him, as your mother and indeed your own Church of Canterbury, to provide for it by appointing a bishop before his death, and you advised him according to your wishes. What shall I say? Having accepted the advice, it pleased him and you to choose me for this work. I raised many objections, eagerly wishing to withdraw from the episcopate, but you did not yield.

“Among other things, I declared that I had received this Urban, about whom the present dispute is being raised, as the apostolic prelate, and that I did not wish to depart from his subjection for as long as he lived, or even for an hour; and at that time no one contradicted me in this. But what happened? You seized me and forced me to take up the burden of all, although I was exhausted by bodily weakness and could scarcely carry myself. In doing this, perhaps you thought you were serving my wishes. But how much I desired it, how grateful I found it, and how much delight I took in it, I judge it superfluous to say at present, since it serves no purpose.

“Yet, lest anyone, unaware of my conscience in this matter, be scandalized by me, I confess that I speak the truth: without offending the will of God, if I had been given a choice on that day, I would rather have been thrown into a blazing fire and burned than raised to the dignity of an archbishop. Nevertheless, seeing your persistent will, I believed you and accepted the burden you imposed, trusting in the hope of your assistance, which you promised.

“Now, therefore, behold, the time has come when the case has arisen in which you may lift my burden by the hand of your counsel. To obtain that counsel, I asked him for a delay from the day on which the words I have mentioned were spoken to me until this day, so that you might come together and investigate by common counsel whether I can, while preserving fidelity to the king, maintain obedience to the apostolic see. I asked for a delay, and I received it; and behold, by God’s grace, you are present.

“Therefore I beg and exhort all of you—but especially you, my brothers and fellow bishops—to examine these matters carefully and diligently and to give me such counsel as you think I can rely upon, so that I may do nothing against obedience to the pope and yet not violate the fidelity I owe to the lord king. It is indeed grievous for me to deny, by despising him, the vicar of blessed Peter; it is grievous to violate the fidelity which I promised, after God, to maintain toward the king; and it is no less grievous to be told that it is impossible for me to preserve one of these without violating the other.”

The bishops replied:

“The counsel you ask from us lies with you. We know you to be prudent in God and a lover of goodness, and for that reason you do not need our counsel in so profound a matter. Yet, if you wished to transfer the whole substance of your counsel simply and without any other condition to the will of our lord the king, we would readily advise you as we would ourselves. Nevertheless, if you command it, we shall report your words to our lord himself, and when we have heard what he thinks of them, we shall tell you.”

He assented, and they did as they had said. The king therefore ordered everything to be postponed until the following day, since it was Sunday, and Anselm was to return to his lodging, intending to come back to the court in the morning. It was done accordingly.

In the morning, as agreed, we returned. Anselm, seated among the nobles and the gathered crowd, began:

“If you were now willing to give the counsel concerning the present case which I asked from you, my lords and brothers, yesterday, I would accept it.”

They replied:

“What we answered yesterday, we answer now: namely, if you are willing to transfer the entire substance of your counsel purely to the will of the lord king, you shall receive from us a ready counsel, one which we have learned to be useful even for ourselves. But if you expect counsel from us according to God which might in any way oppose the king’s will, you strive in vain, because in such matters you will never see us support you.”

Having said this, they fell silent and lowered their heads, as though in anticipation of what he was about to say. Then Father Anselm, raising his eyes upward, his face full of life, spoke in a reverent voice:

“When you who are called shepherds of the Christian people, and you who are called princes of the peoples, are willing to give counsel to me, your prince, only according to the will of one man, I shall hasten to the supreme Shepherd and Prince of all; in my affair—or rather in his and his Church’s affair—I shall receive from him the counsel which I am to follow.

“He says to the most blessed apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16:18–19). He says likewise to all the apostles together: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke 10:16); and, ‘Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zechariah 2:8).

“Just as we understand these words to have been spoken principally to blessed Peter, and through him to the other apostles, so we hold that the same words were spoken principally to the vicar of blessed Peter, and through him to the other bishops who exercise the apostles’ functions—not to any emperor, not to any king, not to any duke, and not to any count.

“Nevertheless, that we must be subject to and serve earthly princes, the same Angel of Great Counsel teaches and instructs us, saying: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matthew 22:21). These words, these counsels, are God’s. I approve them; I accept them; in no way will I depart from them.

“Therefore, let everyone know openly that in the things which belong to God I shall give obedience to the vicar of blessed Peter, and in the things which lawfully belong to the earthly dignity of my lord the king I shall offer, according to the capacity of my understanding, faithful counsel and assistance.”

Father had finished these words. All who were sitting there were therefore extremely disturbed and rose in haste amid great tumult, expressing their agitation in confused voices, so that one might have thought they were all shouting that he was guilty of death. Turning toward him, they said angrily:

“Know that we will not carry these words of yours to our lord in your place.”

Having said this, they returned to the king. Since no one remained with Anselm to whom it would be safe to entrust the delivery of his words to the king, Anselm himself entered and reported aloud what he had said, then immediately returned.

The king, greatly angered by this, began with the bishops and princes to search most intently for what objection he could make to Anselm’s words, but found none. Thus scandalized among themselves, they divided into groups: two here, three there, four elsewhere, consulting together and diligently seeking whether they could somehow compose an answer to these words which would both soothe the king’s anger and not openly oppose the divine sentences quoted above.

Meanwhile Anselm alone sat there, placing his trust in the innocence of his heart and in the mercy of the Lord God. While his adversaries prolonged their councils, he leaned against the wall and rested in a gentle sleep.

After a long delay, the bishops returned from the king with some of the princes and said to the man:

“Our lord the king wishes to hear your judgment quickly, leaving aside all other words—specifically concerning what was said between him and you at Ilingheham, for which you asked to have a delay until this day in order to answer. The matter is known and requires no explanation. Nevertheless, know that the entire kingdom complains against you because you are attempting to deprive our common lord of the honor of his empire and of his crown. Whoever takes away from him the customs belonging to royal dignity takes away his crown and kingdom at the same time. We are convinced that one cannot properly be possessed without the other.

“But reconsider, we beg you, and cast off the obedience to that Urban, who can do you no good because he has offended the king, nor can his offense harm you. Shake off the yoke of subjection, and, as befits the archbishop of Canterbury, await the king’s will and command in all your actions, free from restraint. Or rather, acknowledge as a fault what you have done otherwise, and, so that he may forgive you, wisely comply with his wish in whatever he asks of you for this purpose, so that your enemies, who now mock your misfortunes, may blush when they see your dignity restored.

“These things, we say, these things we ask, these things we advise, and we declare and affirm that they are necessary for you and yours.”

He replied:

“I hear what you say. But, to say nothing of other matters, I do not at all wish to deny obedience to the lord pope. The day is already declining toward evening. Let this case be postponed until tomorrow, if it please you, so that after discussing it with myself I may answer what God will deign to inspire.”

They therefore suspected either that he did not know what more to say or that, overcome by fear, he was already prepared to abandon what he had begun. They returned to the king and persuaded him that no delay should be granted under any circumstances, but that, after the case had been examined on the spot, he should order the ultimate judgment to be pronounced against Anselm if he refused to accept their counsel.

The principal man and spokesman for the king in this affair was the aforementioned William, bishop of Durham, a man gifted more with a glib and witty tongue than with sound wisdom. He was also a chief author and instigator of the quarrel between the king and Anselm, and had promised the king that he would bring Anselm either to deny utterly the obedience owed to the Roman pontiff or to renounce the archbishopric after returning the staff and ring.

Relying on this promise, the king applauded himself, hoping that Anselm, once he had abjured the apostolic prelate, would remain disgraced in his kingdom. He desired this because he wished to deprive Anselm of all authority for exercising Christianity. For he did not believe that he fully possessed royal dignity so long as anyone anywhere in the whole land was said to have or be able to have anything—even anything according to God—except through him.

Understanding this desire of the king’s heart, the bishop of Durham exerted every effort to discover whether he could drive Anselm from the kingdom by exhausting him with slanderous objections, believing, as was said, that once Anselm had departed he himself would be raised to the archiepiscopal throne.

When he had therefore persuaded the king that the requested delay should not be granted to Anselm, he entered the man’s presence accompanied by many who would support his words with their testimony and said:

“I have heard the king’s complaint against you. He says that, insofar as you are concerned, you have stripped him of his dignity by making Odo, bishop of Ostia, pope in his England without the authority of his command, and that, having stripped him in this way, you now ask him to grant you a delay so that you may demonstrate by your devices that this same act of dispossession was justified.

“First restore to him, if you please, the imperial dignity that belongs to him, and only then discuss the matter of delay. Otherwise know that he calls down upon himself the hatred of almighty God, and that we, his faithful servants, applaud his curse by our acquiescence, if he grants you even an hour’s delay—the delay you are begging to receive until tomorrow.

“Therefore answer the words of our lord immediately, or without doubt you will presently experience the judgment that will avenge your presumption. Do not think that what is being done is a jest; rather, we are being driven by the goads of great grief. Nor is this surprising. Whatever your lord and ours held pre-eminent in all his dominion, and by which it was certain that he surpassed all kings, you are, insofar as you can, unjustly taking from him; and by taking it away you pollute the fidelity and oath which you had given him, involving all his friends in great confusion.”

Anselm heard this patiently and then briefly replied to the enormity of so great a slander:

“Let the man who wishes to prove that, because I do not wish to deny obedience to the venerable supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, I am violating the fidelity and oath which I owe to an earthly king, come forward. In the name of the Lord he will find me ready to answer him as I ought and where I ought.”

When they heard this, they looked at one another, unable to find anything to say in response, and returned to their lord. At once they understood what they had not previously noticed—and what they had not thought he himself could notice—namely, that the archbishop of Canterbury could be judged or condemned by no human being except the pope alone, and that no one except the pope could compel him, under any accusation whatsoever, to answer anyone against his will.

Meanwhile a murmur arose throughout the crowd. In subdued voices they complained among themselves about the injury done to so great a man. No one dared speak openly on his behalf, for fear of the tyrant.

Nevertheless, one soldier came forward from the crowd and stood before the man on bended knees, saying:

“Lord Father, your suppliant sons beg you through me not to let your heart be troubled by what you have heard. Remember instead blessed Job, who conquered the devil on the dunghill, and who avenged Adam, whom the devil had conquered in paradise.”

When Father had accepted these words with a gracious expression, he understood that the heart of the people shared his judgment. We therefore rejoiced and became more courageous, trusting, according to Scripture, that the voice of the people is the voice of God.

What shall I do? If I wished to describe one by one the threats, insults, outrages, and lies directed against the man, I fear I would be judged excessive. Yet he endured them all with equanimity for the sake of fidelity to the apostolic see, and, with God’s help, destroyed every one of them by unconquerable reasoning, showing that he stood upon the truth and that God was the author of all that concerned the substance of the case.

When the king learned all this, he became enraged to the point of division of spirit and said to the bishops:

“What is this? Did you not promise me that you would handle, judge, and condemn him entirely according to my will?”

The bishop of Durham responded to him, speaking about each matter at first so faintly and quietly that he seemed to be ignorant of and lacking all human prudence. Then he added:

“It is night. Let him be ordered to go to his lodging, and we shall now, having fully understood his reasoning, think on your behalf until morning.”

At the king’s command we then returned to our lodging. In the morning we came back and sat in our customary place, awaiting the king’s command.

The king, however, was searching with his men in every possible way for something that could be brought forward to condemn Anselm, but found nothing. When William, bishop of Durham, was asked what he had done privately during the night as agreed, he replied:

“No reasonable argument can be brought forward to weaken Anselm’s reasoning, especially since, as he says, all his reasoning rests upon the words of God and the authority of blessed Peter. Yet it seems to me that he must be crushed by force; and if he will not submit to the royal will, he must be driven from the kingdom after his staff and ring have been taken from him.”

The princes did not approve these words. The king said:

“What do you approve, if you do not approve this? As long as I live, I certainly do not wish to tolerate an equal to myself in my kingdom. And if you knew that he was supported by such strength in his case, why did you allow me to begin this suit against him? Go, go, consult together; for, by the face of God, if you do not condemn him according to my will, I shall condemn you.”

A certain Robert, who was very close to the king, replied:

“What shall I say about our counsels? I confess that I do not know. For while we spend the whole day discussing those matters among ourselves with every effort, and while by discussing them we discuss them again to see whether they can somehow hold together, he, thinking of no evil against us, sleeps; and what is brought before him he immediately tears apart with a single movement of his lips, like spiders’ webs.”

“And you, my bishops, what do you say?”

They answered:

“We grieve that we are unable to satisfy your mind, lord. He is primate not only of this kingdom but also of Scotland and Ireland, as well as of the neighboring islands, and we are his suffragans. Therefore it is clear that we can in no way reasonably judge or condemn him, even if some fault could be shown in him—which cannot now be done.”

He said:

“What, then, remains? If you cannot judge him, can you not at least deny him every bond of obedience and the friendship of fraternal fellowship?”

“This we can do,” they replied, “because you command it.”

“Then hurry,” he said, “and do more quickly what you say, so that when he sees himself despised and deserted by everyone, he may be ashamed and groan that he followed Urban while despising me, his lord. And so that you may do this more securely, behold, I now entirely remove from him all security and confidence in me throughout my dominion, and henceforth I do not wish to trust him in any matter, or concerning any matter, or to regard him as archbishop or spiritual father.”

After they had made many and various plots against the man, seeking to draw him away from the course of his undertaking, and had achieved nothing by any of them, the bishops, having joined the abbots to themselves, reported to Father what the king had said, urging upon him the denial mentioned above, in accordance with the king’s desire.

He replied:

“I hear what you say. But because I hold to the subjection and fidelity owed to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you deny me all the subjection, fidelity, and friendship which you owe to your primate and spiritual father. You are not acting rightly.

“Yet far be it from me to repay you in kind. Rather, showing you fraternal and paternal charity, I shall strive—if you do not refuse to endure it—to turn you, as brothers and sons of the holy mother Church of Canterbury, from this fearful error into which you have fallen, and by the power given to me by the Lord to recall you to the path of righteousness.

“As for the king, who deprives me of all security in his kingdom and says that henceforth he does not wish to regard me as archbishop or spiritual father, I promise him, insofar as it concerns me, every security together with faithful service; and, in a fatherly manner, I retain care for his soul and diligence on his behalf, if he will deign to bear it, while always retaining with me, for the service of God, the power, name, and office of the archbishopric of Canterbury, whatever oppression may happen to afflict my external circumstances.”

The king replied:

“What he says is wholly contrary to my mind, and whoever chooses to belong to him shall not belong to me. Therefore you who are the princes of my kingdom must deny him all fidelity and friendship, as the bishops have done, so that it may become clear what he gains from that fidelity in which, against my offended will, he maintains obedience to the apostolic see.”

They answered:

“We were never his men, and we cannot abjure a fidelity which we never gave him. He is our archbishop; he has the responsibility of governing Christianity in this land; and for that reason we who are Christians cannot avoid his teaching while we live here, especially since no stain of offense touches him which would compel you to act otherwise toward him.”

He restrained his anger and openly refrained from opposing their reasoning, lest they be excessively offended.

The bishops, seeing this, were covered with shame on their faces, understanding that everyone’s eyes were turned toward them and that their apostasy was rightly detested by all. If you had been present, you would have heard one bishop or another marked by this or that nickname, sometimes by one person and sometimes by another, with indignant interjections—namely, “Judas the traitor,” “Pilate,” or “Herod,” and similar names.

A little later, when the king separately asked them whether they had denied Anselm every form of subjection and obedience without any condition, or only that subjection and obedience which they claimed to owe him on the authority of the Roman pontiff, some answering that they had done one thing and some the other, he ordered those who professed that, without any condition, they had utterly abjured everything they owed him as their prelate to sit honorably beside him as his faithful men and friends. But those who had dared to say that they had denied him subjection and obedience only in what they claimed was commanded on behalf of the apostolic prelate, he ordered, as treacherous men and enemies of his will, to await the sentence of their condemnation far away in a corner of the house, moved by anger.

Terrified and clothed in confusion upon confusion, they withdrew into the corner of the house. But they immediately found the wholesome domestic counsel upon which they were accustomed to rely—namely, the payment of a large sum of money—and were received back into the king’s friendship.

Anselm, knowing that the king had removed all security from him in England, sent word asking him to provide a safe-conduct by which he and his men might safely reach a seaport and depart from the kingdom until God should graciously put an end to so great a disturbance.

When the king heard this, he languished in severe distress of heart. For although he greatly desired Anselm’s departure, he did not wish him to leave while still in possession of the dignity of the pontificate, lest the final scandal that might arise from this become worse than the first. Yet it seemed impossible for him to deprive Anselm of the pontificate.

Thus troubled, and setting aside the counsel of the bishops by which he complained that he had been brought into these straits, he consulted the princes and asked what ought to be done. They advised that the man should be peacefully instructed to return to his lodging and receive the king’s answer to his request in the morning.

It was done as they said, and, although many of the courtiers were also disturbed, we returned to our lodging. They thought that the man was about to leave the land and groaned over it. But he, joyful and cheerful, hoped that by crossing the sea he would escape the disturbances and burdens of the world, as he had always desired.

While his mind wavered between the hope of leaving the kingdom and the fear of remaining in it, behold, in the morning the princes were sent from the king’s side:

“Our lord the king asks you to come to him.”

We mounted, went, and eagerly awaited the final judgment concerning our case. We sat in our customary place. Before long, the nobles of the kingdom arrived to Father, accompanied by some bishops, and said:

“Moved by our ancient friendship with you, we grieve that this disagreement has arisen between the lord king and you. Therefore, wishing to restore you to your former harmony, we have judged it useful at present that a delay concerning the case be granted to both sides, so that, with peace established between you from now until some fixed time, neither you or yours may do anything against him or his men, nor he or his men against you or yours, that exceeds the limits of concord.

“This, I say, we have judged useful, and we wish you to say whether you are willing to agree to this with us.”

He replied:

“I do not reject peace and concord. Nevertheless, I seem to see what this peace you offer contains within itself. Yet, lest anyone judge that in this matter I prefer my own judgment to that of others, I agree to accept whatever the lord king and you decide should be established, according to God, for the preservation of peace, while always retaining with me the reverence and obedience owed to the lord Urban, prelate of the apostolic see.”

They approved his statement and reported it to the king. A delay was therefore granted until the octave of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0387D] The feast of Pentecost fell in that same year on May 3.], and the king’s word guaranteed that in the meantime everything on both sides would remain at peace, as had been stated.

The king added:

“If the integrity of perfect peace does not settle the dispute between us before this deadline, then the matter, exactly as it stands on this day, must be brought forward for settlement at the appointed end of the delay.”

After these things had been done, Anselm obtained permission from the king and returned to his own see, knowing inwardly that the peace and delay were an empty and momentary veil over the hatred and oppression that were soon to come. This became clear shortly afterward. For after a few days had passed, the king himself expelled from England Baldwin, a monk upon whose counsel the greater part of Anselm’s party depended, and two of Anselm’s clerics, because of the dispute already described; and by this act he struck Anselm with a grievous blow of sorrow.

What should I say of Anselm’s chamberlain, seized in his own chamber before his eyes, or of his other men condemned by unjust judgment, plundered, and afflicted with countless evils? All this the royal constancy of faith inflicted upon the man within the days of the delay and the stipulated peace.

At that time, therefore, the Church of Canterbury suffered so savage a storm in all its affairs that almost everyone cried out that it would have been better for them to have been without a pastor long ago than to be under such a pastor now. We shall restrain ourselves from describing this storm and bring the present volume to an end, taking care lest excessive foolishness and foolish excess in our speech afflict readers or hearers—if there should happen to be any—with excessive weariness.

[Col. 0389]

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0389A]

As the day of the granted truce was awaited, and while the fidelity of both sides—namely, that of King William and that of Archbishop Anselm—was revealed by clear indications, the king by turning everything he had promised into its opposite, and the prelate by patiently enduring the injuries inflicted upon him while keeping his promise, Walter by name, bishop of Albano [Note: [Col. 0389D] The bishop of the Church of Albano is one of the seven collateral bishops and serves the supreme pontiff with a rank of dignity closer to him.] [Note: [Col. 0390D] To this Walter, a cardinal legate then in England, St Anselm wrote two letters, nos. 25 and 26 of book III, in Raynaud.], was sent by Urban, prelate of the apostolic see, from Rome to England, conducted by two clerics, Gerard and William, who belonged to the king’s chapel.

For when the king perceived that Anselm was unwilling to obey his will in the affair described above, he had secretly sent those same clerics to Rome, without Anselm’s knowledge, wishing through them to learn with certainty the condition of the Roman Church. In those days, as we have already said, there were two pontiffs at Rome, each called apostolic by different parties; but the English were still unaware which of them had been canonically appointed and which otherwise.

These two clerics were therefore sent to Rome to learn the truth about this matter. Once they had learned it, they were ordered, if they could, to induce the pope by sacred promises to send the pallium to the king for the use of the archbishop of Canterbury, without mentioning Anselm by name. After Anselm had been expelled from both the pontificate and the kingdom, the king intended to give the pallium, together with the pontificate and acting as the apostolic representative, to whomever he wished. This was what he had arranged in his own mind; he suspected, not without reason, that it could be granted to him; and he promised himself with complete confidence that it would be done according to his expectation.

The bishop mentioned above therefore came to England, secretly bringing with him the archiepiscopal pallium sent by the pope. Passing silently through the city of Canterbury and avoiding Anselm, he hastened to the king, saying nothing to anyone about the pallium he carried and conversing familiarly with no one unless his guides were present. The king had indeed ordered that this be done, unwilling for the secret of his plan to become public.

When the bishop had therefore come to the king some days before Pentecost, and had answered him with the confidence of a good hope concerning each matter which he had learned would be agreeable to the king’s will, he said absolutely nothing on Anselm’s behalf—nothing that might reconcile peace between them, mitigate the tribulations he was enduring for fidelity to the apostolic see, or strengthen him to advance the practice of the Christian religion in England.

Many who had previously been filled with great hope of good from his arrival were exceedingly astonished and said:

“What shall we say to the pope? If Rome prefers gold and silver to justice, what aid, what counsel, what consolation will those henceforth find there in their oppression who have nothing to give in order to obtain the rightness of their cause?”
