The king perceived that the bishop was reporting from Urban everything favorable to the king’s will, and that Urban wished, if the king would receive him as pope in his kingdom, to promulgate by apostolic authority a privilege for the king for the duration of his life. He therefore accepted the arrangement and ordered Urban to be regarded as the apostolic prelate throughout his entire dominion, and to be obeyed in matters of Christian religion as the representative of blessed Peter.

After this, the king dealt with the bishop by whatever means he could so that, supported by royal power, he might depose Anselm from the episcopate by the authority of the Roman pontiff. He promised to give him and the Roman Church an immense sum of money every year if he satisfied this desire of his.

But when, instructed by the bishop, he learned that this could be done by no means, he lost heart, reflecting that he had achieved nothing by seeking or receiving the Roman prelate. Nevertheless, considering what had been irrevocably done, he consulted with his men and sought how, while preserving the singular height of his own dignity, he might at least outwardly restore his affection to the man against whom he had credulously become angry, since he could not, as he wished, inflict the condemnation he desired.

Therefore, when the appointed day on which the truce between them was to expire drew near, Anselm—then staying in his own village, called Murtelac, and celebrating there the solemnity of Pentecost—was sent instructions to proceed to another of his villages, called Heisa. There, at Windlesora, the king’s messengers were holding his court during that festival, so that Anselm could come to them and they could convey the king’s words to him and his words to the king. [Col. 0390C]

So we went there, and on the following day nearly all the bishops of England came to him. After first exchanging greetings, they gradually began to investigate whether they could in any way entice him into this: that, driven by so many and such great adversities, he might at that point, by offering money, secure the king’s friendship for himself. When they found him, as usual, inflexible, they finally ceased addressing him with such entreaties, adding these words:

“If, then, you are unwilling to give anything of your own in order to gain his friendship, tell us, we beg you, in a brief and simple word what you want.”

He said: “I have already told you that I will never inflict this insult upon my lord, namely, prove by my action that his friendship is for sale. But if he wishes to love me freely, as he ought, as his father, and to permit me to live in England, as the archbishop of Canterbury, under the obedience of my lord Pope Urban, I shall gratefully accept this, and, enjoying his peace and security, shall faithfully and dutifully serve him as my lord and king. If he does not wish this, you know what was agreed between us for this day: namely, that he should provide me safe conduct until I reach the sea, and afterward I shall do what I understand I ought to do.”

“Will you tell us nothing else?” they said.

He replied: “Nothing further.”

“The lord Pope Urban,” they said, “at the request of our lord the king, sent him the pallium of the archbishopric through the bishop who came from Rome. It will therefore be your responsibility to consider what repayment worthy of so great a benefit you will make to the king. For what you could not have obtained without many dangers, great toil, and expense [Note: [Col. 0391D] *Kosten* in German and *coûter* in French mean ‘to cost’; in the barbarian language it is said to be *constare*. Hence *constamen*, the expense and outlay that must be incurred.], behold, you now possess without any intervening burden—unless the matter has remained unresolved in your case.”

Anselm perceived that in this they were contriving a matter deeply entangled against him, and, troubled in spirit, said: “O benefit! The Lord, who examines my conscience, knows what estimation it has in my eyes.”

They said: “Whatever your feelings may be about the execution of this undertaking, we praise and advise you at least to give the king what you would spend on the journey if you went to Rome for this purpose, lest, if you do nothing, you be judged injurious.”

“Not even that,” he said, “nor will I give or do anything for this matter at all. It is being directed toward nothing. Leave it alone.”

Moreover, I am reluctant to relate what was done and how much was done about these matters. After all this, the king, as we have said, following the counsel of his leading men, set aside every cause of the former quarrel, freely restored his favor to Anselm, and permitted him to exercise throughout England whatever belonged to his office as the spiritual father of the kingdom and archbishop of Canterbury. [Col. 0391C]

When the gracious Father had accepted this, and, with the complaints of the past forgiven on both sides, had presented himself at the king’s court at Windlesora, he kept the king engaged in familiar conversation in the presence of the nobles and the assembled multitude. Then that Roman Walter arrived. On entering, he said jokingly: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. CXXXII, 1). Then, sitting down, he spoke some words from the Lord concerning peace, praising the fact that he had restored peace among them, although he was ashamed that his own efforts had not planted it in them.

When the reception of the pallium was being discussed, certain people, in order to win the king’s favor, tried to persuade the man to receive it from the king’s hand, as a mark of honor for the royal majesty. He did not agree, showing reasonably that this gift belonged not to royal dignity but to the singular authority of blessed Peter. [Col. 0392A] Accordingly, when all had fallen silent and held their tongues, it was decided that the one by whom the pallium had been brought into England should carry it to Canterbury and place it upon the altar of the Savior; then Anselm should take it from there, as though from the hand of blessed Peter, in honor of the supreme pontificate which he held. Everyone agreed to this arrangement, and a day was fixed for its execution.

Afterward, as Anselm was departing from the court, two bishops followed him: Robert of Hereford [Note: [Col. 0391D] This Robert of Hereford was very dear to St. Wulstan. After Wulstan’s death in 1097, Robert too, warned by him of his own approaching death, showed by this lapse of his how difficult it is for one who depends upon the court not to be harmed at some time or other.], and Osmund [Note: [Col. 0391D] Elsewhere called Sarum or Sherborne; Osmund is venerated as a saint on 3 December. But where are the other nineteen who had renounced obedience to their archbishop? These two holy men eagerly embraced the first opportunity to amend their fault; the others openly showed how little they cared about the censure they had deserved by neglecting to seek absolution.] of Salisbury. They did penance before him for the guilt of their renunciation, which they had committed with their fellow bishops at Rockingham. He took pity on them and absolved them in a small church that presented itself to us as we walked along the road before us. [Col. 0392B] There too, at that very hour, he restored episcopal office to Bishop Wilfrid of St. David’s in Wales, commonly called Dewi. Because of his fault, Anselm himself had previously suspended him from that office.

Then we hurried to Canterbury, where we were to await the arrival of the Roman bishop. As agreed, that bishop came on Sunday, which was the fourth day before the Ides of June, carrying the pallium most suitably in a silver case. The monks serving the Lord Christ at the metropolitan church, together with the community of brothers from the neighboring monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, went out to meet him, accompanied by a numerous gathering of clergy and an immense multitude of laypeople of different sexes and ages. [Note: [Col. 0392D] In the year indicated above, 1095; the Dominical Letter was G.] The Father himself, surrounded and supported on his right and left by the bishops who had come to Canterbury for this purpose, went devoutly to meet the sacred gift of the blessed chief of the apostles barefoot, but dressed in sacred vestments. [Col. 0392C]

With this form of devotional worship, the pallium, which had been carried to the altar, was taken up by Anselm and reverently kissed by all in honor of St. Peter. The supreme pontiff, having put it on, was then led with great honor to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass and was presented at the altar. At that Mass, as the liturgical reading for that day, the Gospel passage was recited which, as we said at the consecration of that same pontiff, had been found above his head—namely:

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many. And at supper time he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready. And they all began at once to make excuses” (Luke XIV, 16), and so forth.

That this happened in this way was a matter of wonder to some people, especially since it was clear that the event had been carried out without anyone previously reflecting upon it or arranging it in advance. Nevertheless, we shall refrain from saying what some people said about it and what they proclaimed. [Col. 0393A] But from what, with God’s help, we shall state in its proper place concerning the truth of the events, it will plainly be possible to see that the Lord’s words did not occur concerning this event, first, at his consecration, nor, second, were they read during the confirmation of his consecration before the people.

After the aforesaid Baldwin had been recalled to England and matters had been quieted to some extent by the restoration of peace, a certain monk of the monastery of St. Albans, an Irishman named Samuel, came to Anselm. When Donatus of Dublin, the bishop of that city, of blessed memory, had died [Note: [Col. 0393D] After Donatus had been appointed bishop of Dublin, Anselm subsequently wrote Letter 72 to Samuel and rebuked him because “you dispose as you please of the books, vestments, and other ornaments of the church—which Lord Archbishop Lanfranc gave to your uncle, Lord Bishop Donatus, for the use of the church over which your brotherhood presides—and give them to outsiders.” Donatus is reported to have been ordained by Lanfranc in 1085 and to have died in 1095. His nephew Samuel died, according to Ware, in 1121.], Samuel was elected bishop of the same city by the king of Ireland, named Murierdach [Note: [Col. 0393D] St. Anselm wrote several letters to this King Murierdach and addresses him as “Muriardach, glorious king of Ireland.”], and by the clergy and people. [Col. 0393B] In accordance with ancient custom, he was sent to Anselm, by common decree, to be consecrated.

Anselm consenting to their election and petition, kept the man with him for some time and honorably instructed him carefully in how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God. After receiving from him, according to ancient custom, a profession concerning his canonical subjection, he promoted him to the episcopal office at Wiptonia, on the eighth day after the following Easter. [Note: [Col. 0394D] That is, in the year 1096, on 20 April.] Four of his suffragan bishops assisted him in this ministry. Strengthened by the blessing of so great a prelate and by letters written to the aforesaid king, as well as to the clergy and people of Ireland, in testimony to his consecration, the new bishop returned joyfully to his homeland and was honorably received into his see, in accordance with the custom of that land.

In the same year—that is, the third year of Anselm’s pontificate—Samson was elected to the episcopate of the church of Worcester, and Girardus, whom we mentioned above, to govern the church of Hereford. [Note: [Col. 0394D] The printed edition adds “whom we mentioned above,” but there is nowhere any previous mention of Giraldus in the entire preceding history. Therefore correct it as follows: “and Giraldus [nephew of Walkelin, bishop of Winchester], whom we mentioned above.” He was promoted to the archbishopric of York in 1101.]

When they came to Anselm, according to custom, to be promoted to the highest priestly order, and did not yet possess all the lower orders, he ordained them according to their immediate needs: one to the diaconate and priesthood, and the other to the priesthood, on the Saturday of the fast of the fourth month, at the village of St. Andrew of Rochester, which lies near London and is called Lambeth. [Note: [Col. 0394D] Lambeth is still the familiar name across the Thames, on the southern bank in Surrey, two miles from the city. Many other estates, such as Rockingham, Ilingham, Shaftesbury, which have already occurred, and many more to follow, could have been explained by indicating the locations of the places, if it had seemed worthwhile to search through the maps of the entire English kingdom for their sake, and if there were someone to indicate where the now obsolete names should be sought. At some later time a more curious person may remedy this defect.]

On the following day he consecrated them in London at the episcopal see to the honor of the pontificate. Four of his suffragans assisted him in this: namely, Thomas, archbishop of York; Maurice, bishop of London; Robert of Thetford, or Norwich; and Gundulf of Rochester. [Col. 0394A]

At that time Robert, count of Normandy, preparing to depart on the expedition to Jerusalem, transferred Normandy to his brother William, king of England, for three years, in return for money, freely giving him dominion over it. This money, partly given and partly exacted throughout England, devastated the entire kingdom without measure. In this matter the desire to dominate spared nothing: neither the ornaments of the churches, nor the sacred vessels of the altars, nor the reliquaries, nor the books of the Gospels furnished with gold or silver.

Anselm too was approached during this period, and some of his friends advised him to extend to the king a helping hand in so reasonable a cause. He understood that doing so was both reasonable and honorable, but, constrained by the smallness of his own resources, he had nothing from which he could supply what he saw had to be done. Therefore, following the advice of great men—namely, Bishop Walkelin of Winchester and Gundulf of Rochester, together with others whose judgment was considered equally weighty in the counsel over this matter—he accepted from the treasury of the church of Canterbury, with the consent of most of the community, two hundred marks’ worth of silver, partly in gold and partly in silver. He contributed this to the aforesaid king, together with whatever he could obtain from his own resources, to meet the immediate need and assist the situation.

But, unwilling to leave his successors any example in this deed that they might imitate, he immediately granted his own manorial estate, called Peckham, to the rights of the same church for a period of seven years, so that the loss inflicted upon the church might be restored from the revenues of that estate, which in those days amounted to approximately thirty pounds in coin. Indeed, during that same period the church possessed the estate itself; and its woodland, villages, and entire revenues were consumed in the new work that extends eastward from the greater tower and that Father Anselm is known to have begun.

We state these things according to the truth of what happened, so that, if possible, we may silence the mouths of those who even to this day accuse Anselm of having plundered the church. We wish that they would cease disparaging so great a man, lest they wound themselves with a wound of sin that will not profit them. At that same time he also decreed that the same church should thereafter possess its property under his authority with greater freedom than it had usually enjoyed, and he granted to the church, to be possessed in perpetuity, certain other properties that his predecessors had held in their own dominion.

Having said these things briefly by way of digression—but, as I think, not needlessly—let us return to what we began. Accordingly, after an agreement had been made between the brothers, namely King William and Count Robert, concerning the aforesaid matter, William crossed the sea and brought the Normandy handed over to him by Robert under his own rule.

While he was staying there, the king of Ireland, named Murchertach, and the bishop Domnald [Note: [Col. 0395D] Rather, Domnaldus, bishop of Armagh and primate of Ireland, from 1091 until 1105, when he died, according to Colgan in the chronological index to the Triad of Saints.], together with the other bishops, and all the nobles with the clergy and people of that island, sent messengers and letters to Anselm. [Col. 0395B] They informed him that in one of their provinces there was a city called Waterford [Note: [Col. 0396D] More correctly *Waterfodia*, an episcopal city in Munster under the archbishop of Cashel. Because of the convenience of its harbor, it is now, after Dublin, almost the chief city of Ireland, at the mouth of the River Suir.], in which, because of the large number of its citizens, it would be expedient to establish a bishop. At the same time they asked him, since he exercised primatial authority over them and the authority of an apostolic legate, to assist the holy Christian community and the necessary welfare of the people by appointing a bishop for them.

For many centuries had already passed during which that city, existing without episcopal oversight and care, had been tossed about through the diverse dangers of temptation. They themselves had chosen for this office a certain man of their own nation, named Malchus, and by common decree sent him to Anselm to be consecrated. [Col. 0395C] Their decree was as follows:

“To Anselm, archbishop of the English by the grace of God, the clergy and people of the town of Waterford, together with King Murchertach and Bishop Domnald, greetings in the Lord.

“Holy Father, the blindness of ignorance has long compelled us to endure the losses of our salvation, because we preferred to withdraw our necks slavishly from the Lord’s yoke rather than freely submit to pastoral obedience. Now, however, we have recognized how greatly the cause of shepherds advances matters, when we recall analogies from other affairs: for without leadership neither an army dares undertake a war nor a ship a maritime danger. How, then, will our little ship, given over to worldly waves, fight against the crafty enemy without a shepherd?

“Therefore we—our king Murchertach, Bishop Domnald, and our duke Dermeth, the king’s brother—choose this priest Malchus, a monk of Bishop Walkelin of Winchester, whom we know most fully; noble by birth and character; instructed in apostolic and ecclesiastical discipline; prudent in the Catholic faith; temperate in conduct; chaste in life; sober, humble, approachable, merciful, learned, hospitable, well ordered in his household; not a novice; and possessing a good testimony in every grade of office (1 Tim. III, 2–7). We ask your fatherhood to ordain him bishop for us, so that he may be able regularly to preside over us and benefit us, and so that under his governance we may serve the Lord safely.

“Now, so that you may know that all our wishes agree in this election, we have each subscribed to this canonical decree, readily confirming it with our own hands. I, Murchertach, king of Ireland, have subscribed. I, Dermeth, duke, the king’s brother, have subscribed. I, Domnald, bishop, have subscribed. I, Idunan, bishop of Meath, have subscribed. I, Samuel, bishop of Duleek, have subscribed. I, Ferdumnach, bishop of Leinster, have subscribed.

“Many more subscribed with these, whom, being concerned for brevity, we have not thought it necessary to record.” [Col. 0396B]

Accordingly, Anselm, considering and understanding that they were asking for what was just and useful, willingly granted their petition. After carefully examining the chosen bishop concerning the matters required by sacred authority, and after proving him worthy of the episcopate through the testimony of many regarding his life, he received from him, according to custom, a profession of obedient subjection and consecrated him at Canterbury on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. Two of his bishops, Radulf of Chichester and Gundulf of Rochester, assisted and cooperated with him in this ministry.

After these events, the king, having subdued and organized Normandy according to his desire, returned to England. After a short interval he led an army against the Welsh, who had risen against him, and shortly afterward received their submission. Thus he gained peace everywhere.

But what then? When many were already hoping that this peace would serve the service of God, and were eagerly awaiting some great measure for the correction of Christianity, to be proclaimed with the king’s assent by the archbishop, behold, the king, returning from Wales, sent the archbishop letters that disturbed this hope and expectation. In them he ordered that, concerning the soldiers whom Anselm had sent on his expedition, he had no thanks for him except bad ones, because, as he said, they had neither been suitably equipped nor been fit for battle in proportion to the nature of the undertaking. He also ordered Anselm to be prepared to render him justice concerning these matters, according to the judgment of his court, whenever it pleased him to summon him on that account.

To this Anselm replied: “We hoped for peace, and it is not good; for a time of healing, and behold, disturbance.”

Although he had long known that, while this king lived, he would not bear much fruit for Christ in England, he had nevertheless sometimes been accustomed to answer, when asked about assisting Christianity, that he could not devote himself to that task because of the enemies he had hostilely surrounding him on every side. Now that the king had obtained peace, Anselm had thought of approaching him concerning this matter and, by whatever means he could, gently drawing him at least toward consenting to the accomplishment of some good and fruitful work. [Col. 0397A]

But, so that the desire of his heart might not come to fulfillment, the cause of the quarrel I have mentioned arose through the instigation of the evil one—not produced by the truth of the matter, but maliciously contrived to block Anselm from every opportunity to speak for God. Recognizing this, and knowing with complete certainty that all the judgments of the royal court depended upon the king’s will, and that nothing in them was considered except his desire, Anselm thought it unbecoming to contend, in the manner of litigants, over the calumny brought against him, or to introduce his case of truth for examination by a court whose judgment was supported by no law, equity, or reason.

He therefore remained silent and answered the messenger nothing, considering that this kind of command belonged to those forms of disturbance which he remembered had often been inflicted upon him in the past. For that reason he did only this: pray to God with a humble heart that such things might be quieted. [Col. 0397B]

Moreover, seeing churches and monasteries being stripped of their possessions, inside and out, more than usual; all religious observance being destroyed in them; secular people, both great and small, following many paths of corrupt living; evil being done everywhere; and these things multiplying and gaining strength from day to day as discipline ceased, he feared that these matters might, by God’s judgment, become a source of harm to him if he did not attend to opposing them by whatever means he could. But he saw that it was impossible for him to oppose them, since it was evident that the ruler of the entire kingdom either did these things himself or favored those who did them. It therefore seemed necessary to him to seek the authority and judgment of the apostolic see concerning these matters.

When, therefore, at Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0397D] In the year 1097, as is indicated below.] he had presented himself at the royal court for the sake of the festival, and had carefully investigated—sometimes while dining, sometimes on other occasions, as opportunity offered—what the king’s state of mind was toward cultivating justice, and had found him entirely as he had formerly been, no hope remained in Anselm that the king would amend in the future.

After the more festive days had passed, cases involving various matters began, as usual, to be brought forward. They were also considering by what strategy the previously mentioned case against Anselm might be conducted so that, condemned as guilty, he would either pay the king an enormous sum of money or, in order to implore his mercy, devote himself wholly to him, never again raising his head.

Meanwhile, Anselm summoned to himself whichever of the king’s leading men he wished and instructed them to tell the king that he was compelled by the greatest necessity and wished, with the king’s permission, to go to Rome. At this the king was astonished and said: “By no means. We do not believe that he is guilty of any such sin that he needs to seek from the apostolic authority a special absolution for it; nor do we believe him so devoid of counsel that we should not know that he could assist an apostolic man in giving counsel more than an apostolic man could assist him.”

These words were reported to Anselm, and he replied: “Power is in his hands; he says what pleases him. But if he does not wish to grant permission now, perhaps he will grant it on another occasion. I shall multiply my prayers.”

After these words had been spoken concerning permission, all the plotting to bring Anselm to trial was immediately suppressed and abandoned, and we departed from the court free from that accusation. [Col. 0398A]

In the following month, August, when the king had summoned the bishops, abbots, and all the nobles of the kingdom into one assembly by the authority of his command, in order to deal with the condition of the realm, and when, after the matters that had occasioned their gathering had been settled, each man was preparing to return to his own place, Anselm, not forgetting the petition he had begun, asked the king not to refuse even then, in response to repeated prayers, the permission he had sought long before. But for the second time he refused, just as he had refused the first.

After the assembly had been dissolved, in October we came by appointment to the king at Winchester. The pontiff therefore pleaded with the king more insistently, both personally and through others, that he graciously grant him what his necessity compelled him to request for the third time. At this the king, wearied and deeply provoked, said:

“It troubles me, and, though I understand that what he requests ought not to be granted, his grievous importunity exhausts me. Therefore I order him to cease from such petitions, and let him who has already vexed me so often make whatever amends I shall judge appropriate.”

To this Anselm replied:

“Let him know rather that I am prepared to demonstrate that my request is just, and that he himself ought not justly to oppose me in this matter.”

The king answered:

“I will not admit his arguments. But if he goes, let him know for certain that I shall reduce the entire archbishopric to my own dominion and shall no longer receive him as archbishop.”

A great storm therefore arose from these words, with different people shouting on opposite sides. For this reason, some, being moved by the disturbance, advised that the matter be postponed until the following day, hoping that it might then be settled in another way. Both sides agreed to this, and we withdrew to our lodging.

In the morning, when we had returned and were seated in a suitable place, behold, certain bishops with several nobles came to Anselm and asked what he had considered within himself concerning the matter since the preceding day.

He said:

“I did not agree to have the matter you are discussing postponed yesterday because I was ignorant of what I would answer about it today, but so that I should not seem to trust my own judgment so completely that I would not deign to yield even for one night to the counsel of others for its examination. Let it now be known that I remain in the position in which I was. Therefore I ask my lord to grant me the permission I request with a good disposition and cheerful countenance, as befits him, knowing without doubt that I intend to go for the sake of my salvation, for the sake of holy Christianity, and, if he is willing to believe it, truly for the sake of his own honor and advancement.”

They said:

“If you have anything else to say, bring it forward. As for permission, you speak uselessly. He will not grant it.”

“If he does not wish to grant it,” he said, “I shall nevertheless take upon myself what is written: ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29).”

At this, Bishop Walchelin of Winchester looked at him and said:

“Indeed, my lord the king and his nobles believe you to be the sort of man who is not easily moved from anything you have once firmly begun. Yet in this matter—namely, that you should despise the honor and usefulness of so great an episcopate and seek Rome—it is not easy to believe that you will remain steadfast.”

But Anselm, knowing the man’s mind, answered with a lively expression and his eyes fixed upon him:

“Indeed.”

After saying this, they returned to the king and reported what they had heard.

While the king was prolonging his deliberations and the pontiff was sitting with his companions, it occurred to him that the bishops ought to be more equitable in the matter that belonged to God than in the counsel of an earthly king. He therefore sent orders for them to come to him.

They were Bishop Walchelin of Winchester, Robert of Lincoln, Osmund of Salisbury, and John of Bath. [Note: John of Bath held the episcopal see from 1088 to 1122 and transferred the episcopal seat from the city of Wells to Bath.]

When, at his command, they had sat down on his left and right, he said to them:

“Brothers, I have had you come to me because it is your office above all to consider, arrange, and preserve the things that belong to God. For you are bishops; you are prelates in the Church of God. If, therefore, you are willing to consider and defend justice on my side as faithfully and strictly as, on the other side, you weigh and defend the rights and customs of a mortal man, and if you promise me this, I shall explain to you, as faithful men and sons of God, the direction of the whole purpose of my present counsel; and I shall hear and follow the counsel that your faithful industry, devoted to God, gives me concerning it.”

They said:

“We shall speak together, if it pleases you, and report a common judgment to you.”

They then rose and withdrew to one side. After exchanging a few words among themselves, they sent Bishop Walchelin and the Bishop of Lincoln to the king to ask his will and command concerning the matter. Once they had been informed of the reason for which they had been sent, they returned to their companions and told them what they had learned.

Why say more? They jointly decided to follow the will of the earthly man. Returning immediately together to Anselm, they said to him:

“Lord Father, we know that you are a religious and holy man, and that your way of life is in heaven. But we confess that, being hindered by our relatives, whom we support, and by the many affairs of the world, which we love, we cannot rise to the height of your life, nor can we mock this world together with you. But if you are willing to descend to us and proceed with us along the road on which we walk, we shall advise you as we would advise ourselves, and in all your affairs, whatever they may be, wherever there is need, we shall assist you as we would assist ourselves. If, however, you choose to hold fast to God alone, as you have begun, we shall not exceed the loyalty that we owe the king, whether in what has been or in what will be.”

He said to them:

“You have spoken well. Go, then, to your lord; I shall hold fast to God.”

They did as he had said, and Anselm remained almost alone.

After a short while, when each of us who remained with him—we were very few—had sat separately at his command, praying to God for the resolution of the matter, the aforesaid bishops came with several barons of the kingdom and brought the following message to the man:

“The king commands you to know that you have often assailed, angered, and tormented him with various complaints. Yet finally, after the assembly held against you at Rockingham by the whole kingdom, when you wisely sought to be reconciled to him as your lord, and when, aided by the merits and prayers of many who earnestly intervened on your behalf, you obtained the fulfillment of your petition, you promised him that thereafter you would observe his customs and laws in every respect and faithfully defend them for him against all men. Trusting in this promise, he hoped that he would henceforth have peace. But behold, you are openly departing from this promise and this pledge, when you threaten to go to Rome without awaiting his permission. It is unheard of in his kingdom and wholly contrary to its customs for any of his nobles—and especially for you—to presume to do such a thing. Therefore, so that he may not be troubled further in such a matter, either by you or by anyone else who might perhaps wish to imitate you when he has been injured in some way, he wills and commands you either to promise by oath that you will never again appeal to the See of Saint Peter or to his vicar for any cause that may be brought against you, or to depart from his land with all speed. And if you prefer to remain after taking this oath rather than depart, he then commands you to make amends before his court for having dared so often to trouble him about a matter concerning which you were not certain that you would persevere.”

They delivered this message and immediately returned to the king.

Then Anselm spoke briefly with his companions, rose, and entered to the king, with us following him. As was customary, he sat down at the king’s right hand. He then recapitulated, one by one, in the king’s hearing, the commands he had received from the messengers, and asked whether they had truly proceeded from the king himself in the manner in which they had been reported to him. When he had heard that they had indeed proceeded from him, he immediately added what he thought about the matter, speaking as follows:

“What you say—that I promised to observe your customs and usages and to defend them faithfully with you against all men—I confess is true. I would recognize it if you stated them with the distinction according to which I remember without doubt that they were distinguished at the time when the promise of which you speak was made. For I know that I pledged to observe your customs—namely, those which you possess in your kingdom by right and according to God—according to God, and to defend them against all men by justice and to the best of my ability.”

When the king and his nobles, in their blindness, objected to these words and confirmed their objection by interposing an oath, insisting that no mention of God or of justice had been made in that pledge, Anselm broke off their voices and said:

“Indeed! If, as you say, no mention was made of God or of justice, of what then was mention made? Far be it from any Christian to hold or defend laws or customs known to be contrary to God and to justice!”

When they murmured against the man and shook their heads at these words, yet did not say anything definite aloud, the Father continued what he had begun:

“But why do you assert that it is not your custom for me, for the sake of the salvation of my soul and for the sake of the governance of the Church of God that I have undertaken, to seek blessed Peter and his vicar? I declare that such a custom is contrary to God and to justice, and therefore I profess that it must be despised and rejected by every servant of God. If anyone should say that by what I am saying he will prove that I am not keeping faith with you, he will find me prepared to demonstrate, as and where I ought, that in this I am more faithful to you than I would be if I acted otherwise. But I do not now intend to demonstrate this.

“It is nevertheless known that every pledge lawfully made to any man is strengthened by faith in God. Thus a man pledges himself to another: ‘By the faith I owe to God, I shall be faithful to you.’ Since, therefore, the faith given to a man is strengthened by faith in God, it is clear that the same faith is weakened whenever it admits something contrary to the faith of God. But this is not the time for debating that matter.

“Thus the faith that I owe, and his service, compel me to approach the pope, the head of Christianity, and to seek from him counsel that is absolutely necessary for the Church of God and for me. It does not seem that anyone who fears offending God ought to forbid this. For you, king, would not bear with equanimity if some powerful and wealthy man among your subjects hindered one of your men devoted to your fidelity and service, and, once he had been hindered, prevented him by threats and terrors from carrying out what was useful to you. Rather, you would punish him with due vengeance for the guilt of violating the fidelity he owed you.”

Then the king and Robert, count of Meulan, interrupting his words, said:

“Oh, oh! What he says is preaching—preaching, not any argument concerning the matter at hand that prudent men should accept.”

As all the nobles shouted in agreement and tried to close the Father’s mouth with their voices, he himself, amid the mouths of those who were shouting, sat quietly with his face lowered, and disregarded their cries as though with a deaf ear.

When they had been wearied by their own shouting and the tumult had subsided, Anselm returned to his words, saying:

“As for your command that, so that you may henceforth be secure about me, I should swear to you that I will never again, for any cause, appeal in England to blessed Peter or to his vicar, I say that such a command, coming from one who is a Christian, ought in every respect not to be given. For to swear this is to renounce blessed Peter. Whoever renounces blessed Peter undoubtedly renounces Christ, who made him the prince over His Church. Therefore, if on your account, O king, I should deny Christ, I confess that I shall not be slow to make amends, according to the judgment of your court, for the sin I committed in seeking permission.”

At these words the aforesaid count, indignantly adding his own remark, said:

“Go on, go on; you will present yourself to Peter and the pope, and what we know will certainly not pass us by.”

The Father replied:

“God indeed knows what will remain for you, and He will be able to help me, if it pleases Him, as I hasten to the thresholds of His apostles.”

After this he rose. When we had returned to the place from which we had come, the king’s messengers immediately followed us and brought the man this message:

“Behold, you will go. Nevertheless, know that our lord does not wish you to take anything belonging to him away with you as you depart.”

He replied:

“I have riding animals, and also clothing and household goods. Perhaps someone will say that these belong to him? If he does not permit me to take them with me, let him know that I would sooner go on foot and naked than abandon what I have begun.”

At this, the prince, overcome with embarrassment, replied that he had not meant his statement in that way:

“For I did not say,” he said, “that you should go naked or on foot. Nevertheless, on the eleventh day from this one, I order you to be at the port in order to cross the sea. There my messenger will meet you and will tell you what, by my permission, you or your men may take away with you.”

When these matters had been settled in this way, we immediately wished to withdraw to our lodging. But Anselm, instructed to possess his soul in patience, returned to the king with a pleasant and cheerful expression and said to him:

“Lord, I am going. If it pleased you that this should happen with your good will, it would certainly be more fitting for you and more acceptable to every good man. But now that the matter has fallen into the opposite course, although it is grievous as far as you are concerned, I shall nevertheless bear it as calmly as I can, insofar as it concerns me; nor, because of this, shall I withdraw, by the Lord’s mercy, from love for the salvation of your soul.

“Since I do not know when I shall see you again, I commend you to God. And, as a spiritual Father to a beloved son, and as the Archbishop of Canterbury to the king of England, I wish to give you God’s blessing and my own before I depart, if you do not reject it.”

Then the king said:

“I do not reject your blessing.”

Immediately Anselm rose, lifted his right hand, and made the sign of the holy cross over the king, who bowed his head for this purpose. Then he departed, while the king and his men marveled at the man’s cheerfulness.

These events took place in the year from the Incarnation of the Son of God 1097, on Thursday, which was the Ides of October.

Anselm then came to Canterbury, where the pontifical see and the head and primacy of the whole kingdom are situated. On the following day, after addressing and greatly consoling his sons concerning the matter at hand, in the presence of a multitude of monks, clerics, and common people, he received a pouch and staff before the altar in the manner of pilgrims. After commending everyone to Christ, he departed amid great weeping and lamentation.

That same day we went to the port of Dover, where we found a certain cleric named William, sent by the king by appointment, as we have said. We were detained there for fifteen days, because the wind prevented our crossing. During this delay, the same William entered and left with the Father and ate daily at his table, but he was unwilling to do anything concerning the matter for which he had been sent.

On the fifteenth day, when the sailors were urging us to board the ships and we, eager to cross, were being wearied by the delay, behold, you would have seen a pitiable spectacle. That William detained the Father, the father of his country and primate of all Britain, on the shore like a fugitive or a man guilty of some monstrous crime, and, on behalf of his lord, ordered that he not cross the sea until he had disclosed to him, one by one, everything he was carrying with him.

His bags were therefore brought before him and his packs opened, and all his belongings were overturned and searched in the hope of finding money. A great crowd of common people stood around, gazing in wonder at the wicked deed because of its novelty, and, as they watched it, cursing it.

When everything had been overturned, but none of the things for whose sake it had been overturned had been found, the searcher’s anxious care was mocked, and Anselm and his companions were permitted to depart. We therefore boarded the ship, the sails were spread to the winds, and, after a little difficulty arose but was quickly calmed through God’s mercy, we crossed the waves most successfully and, according to our wish, landed at Wissant. [Note: Wissant, once a celebrated port and now a modest village between Boulogne and Calais, commonly called Visan.]

When King William heard that Anselm had crossed the sea, he immediately ordered everything that had belonged to Anselm’s jurisdiction to be transferred into his own dominion, and all the arrangements that could be shown to have been changed or established by Anselm from the time when he had first come to the archbishopric to be declared void.

A storm then raged so fiercely throughout the episcopate that the tribulations inflicted upon it after the death of the venerable Lanfranc, before the arrival of Father Anselm, were considered insignificant in comparison with the tribulations inflicted during these days.

We therefore departed from Wissant in the morning and, after some days, came to Saint Bertin. [Note: The monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu, now enclosed within the same walls as the castle of Saint-Omer and forming the strongly fortified town of Artois, lies approximately ten French leagues from the port mentioned above. Perhaps the text should read “after a day,” or at most “after two days.”] We were received with great enthusiasm by the people and with veneration by the monks, and remained there for five days.

Meanwhile, when Anselm was asked by the canons of Saint-Omer to visit their church and dedicate there the altar they had made in honor of Saint Lawrence the martyr, he consented to their requests. After completing the service appropriately, he dined and returned to the abbey, replying to the clerics who asked him to remain with them with the Lord’s saying that commands His disciples not to pass from house to house.

After this, as we hastened the journey we had begun, the man’s fame ran ahead much more swiftly and filled the peoples with many voices. Thus crowds of common people, gatherings of clerics, and armies of monks came to meet him wherever he went: some resounding with joy and exultation, others joining together in song for God’s sake at his arrival, with banners and harmonious music.

Yet just as some prepared with every effort to honor and serve him, so others, driven by a different spirit, plotted to seize him and strip him of his possessions. But where divine protection is present, what can human plotting accomplish?

After crossing France, we entered Burgundy. The duke of that land had heard reports that the Archbishop of Canterbury, wishing to pass through his territory, was wealthy. [Note: This duke was Odo I, by whom Cîteaux was founded in the following year, 1098, reportedly on 29 April, according to the Life of Saint Robert, abbot of Molesme. Odo was the son of Henry, grandson of Robert, dukes of Burgundy, and great-grandson of Robert, king of France.] Inflamed by his love of money, since rumor had spread that Anselm was carrying a great deal of it, he resolved to take it from him.

One day, therefore, while we were on the road and had turned aside from it for a short while to refresh ourselves, behold, that same duke, accompanied by an armed band of soldiers, rode swiftly up and with a loud cry asked who and where the archbishop was.

As soon as he caught sight of Anselm, who had been pointed out to him and was sitting on horseback, he looked at him with a grim expression. Suddenly struck with shame, he lowered his face, blushed, and found nothing to say.

The Father said to him:

“Lord Duke, if it pleases you, I shall kiss you.”

And he replied:

“I am ready to kiss and serve you, lord, and I rejoice gratefully in God at your arrival.”

After the kiss of peace had been given, the Father said to him:

“Venerable sir, I left England for the sake of the Christian religion and, by God’s mercy, intend to go to Rome. But now I rejoice and am glad to see you, both because I desire to have your acquaintance and friendship and because, through you, I wish henceforth to have security and peace in your land for myself and my companions.”

He replied:

“I greatly love and desire what you say, and I commend myself to your prayers and blessing.”

After saying this, he ordered one of his more powerful men who was present there to escort the man through his territory and to provide for him wherever necessary no less than he would for the duke himself.

As he departed, he invoked the hatred of almighty God upon all who had stirred him up to pursue the man of God.

“For,” he said, “it is not a human face but the face of an angel of God that shines in him.”

Therefore, let all who knowingly show hostility toward him know that they are accursed by God.

We, giving heartfelt thanks to God for His mercy, continued along the journey we had begun.

We came to Cluny on the third day before the Nativity of the Lord. There the Father was received with the greatest veneration by the entire host of the monastery’s monks, and the whole place was filled with joy and gladness. What more? As long as he remained there, to put it briefly, he was treated with an honor surpassing that shown to all others who came to that place.

Meanwhile, he sent a messenger to inform the venerable Hugh, Archbishop of Lyon, of his arrival. [Note: Several letters of Saint Anselm to Hugh the archbishop, and of Hugh to Saint Anselm, survive. He died in 1106.] That man had long been known to Anselm from many previous years and, inflamed by the fire of his holy affection, was tormented by a great desire to see him. Anselm also loved him so greatly and valued his prudence and authority in counsel so highly that he had decided within himself to entrust the entire consideration and disposition of his affair to him and to the reverend Hugh, Abbot of Cluny. [Note: We commemorate the life of Saint Hugh on April 29, with an illustrious mention of Saint Anselm.]

When this pontiff heard that Anselm had approached his territory, he was exceedingly glad. Sending to him those whom he had around him as his more intimate and distinguished associates, he earnestly begged Anselm to deign to visit both his church and himself without delay. He also ordered the Bishop of Mâcon to meet the man with appropriate honor and to serve him with the greatest attentiveness. [Note: Cluny is approximately five leagues from Mâcon; from there Lyon is reached by descending the Rhône in one day. The Bishop of Mâcon at that time was Raynaldus, who died within two years.]

The bishop carefully carried this out.

When we came to Lyon, the honor with which we were received by the pontiff himself and all his people is difficult to describe and perhaps incredible to relate. While we remained there, Anselm learned from what rumor reported that it would not greatly benefit his cause if he proceeded farther. The weakness of his body also shrank from the labor of the remaining journey, and the ambushes laid by the inhabitants of those regions at that time against travelers, especially men of the religious orders, held him back somewhat. Thus he remained at Lyon, greatly welcomed and honored by all.

He then sent a written letter to the prelate of the apostolic see, in which he set out what he had suggested to him concerning the events that had occurred and toward what desire of his heart he had directed himself. The tenor of that letter we reproduce below:

> To the supreme pontiff Urban, lord and Father to be revered with love and loved with reverence, Brother Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission and the devotion of his prayers.
>
> We know, reverend lord and beloved Father, that our Lord Jesus Christ has exalted your holiness in His Church to counsel and assist those who, longing for the rest of their heavenly homeland, are wearied by various tribulations in the exile of this present age.
>
> With this hope and reflection, I, your humble servant, resolved in the distress of my heart to flee, by presenting myself, to the bosom of your paternal and apostolic compassion. But I cannot do this as I desire. Why I cannot do so, you will learn from the bearer of this letter.
>
> Since, therefore, I cannot be in your presence in person as I desire, I communicate my distress to your clemency in writing as best I can, so that the same distress may be eased by its consolation, and that my soul may rejoice that, through the affection of your compassion, it has obtained the tranquility it desires.
>
> The tribulation of my heart is so great that I cannot adequately express it either in words or in writing. But I pray God, who knows what is hidden, to make you understand it, and through the depths of His mercy to move your depths toward compassion according to my desire and need.
>
> Nevertheless, I shall disclose something of my need and desire by which I do not doubt that your prudence can understand what is expedient for me. It is known to many, pious Father, with what violence, how unwillingly, and despite my opposition I was seized and detained for the episcopate in England, and how I pleaded my unsuitability for such an office on account of my nature, age, weakness, and ignorance—qualities that wholly flee from all the activities of the world and steadfastly abhor them, so that I cannot endure them without the salvation of my soul.
>
> Having now remained in that archbishopric for four years, I have produced no fruit. Rather, I have lived uselessly amid immense and detestable tribulations of soul, so that each day I desire more to die outside England than to live there. For if I were to end my present life there as I was living it, I saw damnation rather than salvation for my soul.
>
> I saw many evils in that land which I could neither tolerate nor correct with episcopal liberty. The king himself also did certain things concerning churches that ought not to have been done; after the death of their prelates, he treated them otherwise than he should have. He burdened me and the Church of Canterbury in many ways.
>
> For he did not return to me the lands of that Church which, after the death of Archbishop Lanfranc, when he held the archbishopric in his own hand, he had given to his knights, as the same archbishop had held them. Moreover, against my will, he granted other lands according to his own pleasure. He demanded from me burdensome services, unprecedented for my predecessors, beyond what I could or ought to bear.
>
> I saw the law of God, and canonical and apostolic authorities, being buried beneath arbitrary customs. Whenever I spoke about these matters, I accomplished nothing; and not simple justice but arbitrary customs were put forward as a pretext.
>
> Knowing, therefore, that if I tolerated these things to the end I would confirm such a depraved custom for my successors to the damnation of my soul, and since I could not litigate these matters—for no one dared give me either counsel or assistance—I asked the king for permission to visit your fatherhood, so that I might show him the distress of my heart and then, with his counsel and assistance, do what would be more beneficial for my soul.
>
> Angered by this, he demanded that, as though for a serious offense, I should make satisfaction to him concerning my request for this permission and assure him that thereafter I would in no way seek the Apostolic See for any necessity, nor even speak about it; or, if I intended ever to do so, that I should do it at once.
>
> Thus I crossed the sea in order to come to you. Yet, as I have said, I cannot do what I intended. For it is impossible for me to conform to such a life or for my soul to be saved in such an episcopate, both because of the qualities of the circumstances I have described and because of my many weaknesses of understanding, character, nature, and age.
>
> This is the substance of my supplication, for which I wished to come to you: since you desire God for my soul and my soul for God, through the paternal and apostolic compassion that dwells in your heart, release my soul from the bondage of so great a servitude and restore to it the freedom to serve God in tranquility, lest it be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, as it has already suffered too much, and be dragged from temporal grief into eternal grief.
>
> Then, according to the prudence and authority of your apostolate, counsel the Church of the English. May the almighty Lord preserve your holiness unharmed for a long time in the prosperity of His grace, and may He crush Satan and the gates of hell beneath your feet. Amen.

Meanwhile, the report spread as far as Rome that the Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of Britain, had crossed the sea laden with a great weight of gold and silver and was traveling to Rome. Some men, therefore, kindled by an evil desire, watched the road, set scouts, and prepared snares in order to seize him.

The men of the Alemannic king were especially intent upon this because of the dispute that had existed in those days between the pope and that king. [Note: This was Henry, the fourth king of Germany of that name and the third emperor. In 1094, at the Council of Autun, excommunication had been renewed against him and against the other supporters of the Guibertine schism.]

At that time Wibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, was still alive. Having been expelled from the apostolate that he had invaded contrary to law, he and his followers laid ambushes by whatever means they could against every religious person traveling to Rome. As a result, certain bishops, monks, and religious clerics were captured during that persecution, robbed, subjected to many insults, and killed.

Thus the wicked band, placing the greatest confidence in its hope, expected to condemn Anselm by a similar form of punishment. But he, as we have said, remained at Lyon, awaiting there the return of his messengers.

When those malicious men, contrary to their expectation, were forced to endure delay because of his arrival, they learned from pilgrims that he was suffering from a serious bodily illness and would proceed no farther from Lyon. What the pilgrims said was not wholly contrary to the truth. He had indeed fallen ill, so that we were held by no small despair concerning his recovery.

When they heard this, they were dismayed in spirit and lost the hope they had entertained of disturbing Anselm. But when the illness had been largely subdued and the rumor that had filled the peoples everywhere concerning his progress had died out, behold, the messengers whom he had sent to Rome arrived and reported that the pope, removing every excuse, had ordered him to hurry to him.

Why delay? Unaware of any delay, he obeyed the apostolic commands, committing himself to the dangers of the road and not fearing death for God’s sake.

We therefore departed from Lyon on the Tuesday before Palm Sunday and, on the following Saturday, came to a certain village called Aspera. [Note: In the year 1098. The village called Aspera here is called Secusia in the earlier Life, commonly Susa; there was a monastery of Saint Justus there, as we noted in that place.] After we had been lodged and refreshed there, it seemed better to the Father that we spend that night among the monks who lived in the same village rather than among the villagers, both because of the religious character of the monastic order and because of the duties of the approaching night and day.

The monks were therefore sent a message about this, and they gladly consented. We were three monks who sought this arrangement: namely, our lord and Father Anselm, the aforementioned Baldwin, and I, Brother Eadmer, who write this account. We went along as though we were equals, with no right of domination over our Father leading him before others.

When those monks spoke with us in the evening, as with pilgrims, and asked where we had come from, we replied that we had come from the regions of France and wished, if God granted it, to go as far as Rome.

They said:

“You are heading nowhere. For no one can travel along the road you are undertaking in religious dress without being captured and subjected to many injuries. The Archbishop of Canterbury understood this and acted with wise counsel. That man recently proposed, as is reported, to go to Rome for his own cause, and he traveled as far as Piacenza. But when he learned there of the danger of the road ahead, he turned back, and now he remains at Lyon.”

At this Baldwin said:

“He acted well. But because the service of God and the obedience owed to our spiritual Father compel us to go, we shall proceed as far as we are able, with the Lord guiding us. When we can go no farther, we shall return with our obedience intact. May the gracious God guide us.”

After the office of the night and day had been celebrated among them, we returned to the road.

From there, when we had reached Rome by a prosperous journey, Anselm was received by the pope with fitting honor and was asked about the reason for his arrival. He related it in the same order in which, as we have said, he had set it out in his letter from Lyon.

The pope heard what was reported and promised assistance. He wrote a letter to William, king of England, in which he advised, urged, and commanded him to set Anselm’s affairs at liberty in his kingdom and to reinstate him in all his possessions.

Anselm also wrote a letter on the same subject and sent it to the king together with the pope’s letter.

We therefore remained at Rome for ten days, living with the pope in the Lateran palace.

At that time a certain abbot named John presided over the monastery of the Savior, situated near the city of Telesia. [Note: Telesia was a Samnite episcopal city under the archbishopric of Benevento, not far from the confluence of the rivers Volturnus and Sabaris, in what is now the Terra di Lavoro. It was formerly famous but is now almost deserted.] This John, a Roman by birth, had formerly come to France out of a desire to study letters. There, moved by the reputation of Anselm, who was then abbot of Bec, he approached him, fervent in his religious purpose, and, having heard him, became a monk of Bec. When this had reached the ears of the supreme pontiff Urban after some years, he summoned John himself and made him abbot of the aforesaid monastery.

When John therefore learned that his father Anselm had come to Rome, he sent messengers and earnestly begged him to come to him and, in one of his estates, where a healthful breeze prevailed, to deign to spend the approaching summer, so as to avoid the illnesses of the city of Rome. When Anselm heard this, he gave thanks to heavenly compassion and to his brother’s solicitude, and informed the supreme pontiff that the request had been made. But the pope said:

“O predestination of divine mercy! Truly God sent Joseph ahead into Egypt before his father Jacob. Therefore, although I have proposed that everything I possess should serve your needs—you who, for the sake of justice and the fidelity owed to blessed Peter, are an exile—nevertheless, since the air of this city is exceedingly unhealthy for many people from distant and especially foreign regions, I approve your going where you are being invited, lest you seem to neglect what heavenly favor has provided for you.”

Anselm agreed to the pope’s words, and, while he awaited what the king of England would answer to the pope’s and his own letters, he set out for the region to which he had been invited. He was received with joy and honor in every place he entered, and everywhere people vied with one another to prepare themselves to serve him. When he had approached the place to which he was going, John went out to meet him with a company of brothers. Like a good son, he received his father with great reverence and rejoicing and brought him into the monastery.

Since the heat there scorched everything, he then led him to his own estate, called Sclavia, situated high in the mountains and continually suitable for those dwelling there because of its healthy air.

Around these same days Roger, duke of Apulia, having gathered a large army, was besieging the city of Capua, which had revolted from his authority. [Note: In 1098, “Capua was taken by Roger in the month of March.” Thus Lupus Protospata in his *Chronicle*. But it seems that May should be read: otherwise Anselm, who reached Rome only at the end of March, could not have been present.] [Note: Roger, son of Robert Guiscard, the Norman duke of Apulia, succeeded his father in 1086.] Having heard of Anselm’s reputation, he sent messengers to ask him to come to him, wishing to see and speak with him and, through him, to receive instruction in matters that could contribute to his salvation.

The Father therefore went to him. We were still some distance away when, behold, the duke himself, surrounded by a great multitude of soldiers, came out to meet the Father. Throwing himself upon him with kisses, he gave him thanks for his arrival. For several days thereafter we remained in the siege, withdrawn into tents away from the crowds and tumult of the loudly clamoring army.

Meanwhile, when Urban, pontiff of the Apostolic See, came there, Anselm and the leaders of the entire army went out to meet him. He was escorted with the great pomp of worldly splendor and led into a tent, situated near ours, which had been furnished more splendidly than the others. Thus, until the city surrendered, the siege had the lord pope and Anselm as neighbors, so that their households seemed more like one than two, and scarcely anyone went to the pope without also turning aside to Anselm.

But what am I to do? If I wished to linger in writing over each separate expression of the affection, reverence, and honor shown to Anselm by all among whom he dwelt and to whom he came at that time, I could rightly be accused of indiscretion. I will say only this: although the king of England, who, as has been said, expelled him from his kingdom, tried by letters and lavish gifts to stir against him all whom he thought might be harmful to him, nevertheless he accomplished nothing. On the contrary, it was clearly understood from these events that the man was following the path of simple justice and was being utterly harassed contrary to equity.

For when the letters that had been sent accused him of no fault for which he could justly be blamed, and when their bearers did not contradict those letters by saying anything worse, it came about both that the man’s justice was believed more firmly and that the injustice of the man who was harassing him without fair judgment was increasingly exposed and hated. Accordingly, everyone began to favor his cause and to devote themselves and their resources eagerly, according to their wishes, to his advantage and honor.

The duke himself, to whom those commands had been directed above all others, paid no attention to them. Instead, he tried by many entreaties to persuade the Father to remain with him, and to accept as a gift the finest lands in his territories, both in villages and in castles or cities, according to his own choice, and to claim them by his own right for his use and that of his people for as long as he lived.

The king’s efforts against Anselm therefore turned out otherwise than he had supposed. When the siege had been lifted, Anselm went with the pope to the city of Aversa. [Note: Aversa was a city between Capua and Naples.] The pope entered the city, while Anselm, invited by much pleading, went to the abbey of Saint Lawrence to lodge there. The brothers of that monastery therefore showed Anselm the service of perfect charity, and, as was customary, listened attentively while he spoke of the things of God.

Anselm considered within himself how great an unrest and disturbance of mind he had suffered in England, and how no one, except certain monks, had been willing to listen to him so that he might bear fruit for God; and how, after he had left England, he had attained such tranquility of mind and had been heard by everyone with such fruitful attention. He burned with the desire to abandon the care of England together with his episcopate and to renounce it forever.

This desire was also greatly strengthened by the fact that, with all doubt removed, he saw that his own character and that of King William could no longer agree in any way. For, in addition to what we had learned that the king usually did while in England, new reports were publicly brought each day by those arriving from there. From these it was understood that he was so obstinately opposed to God’s justice that many men and women of those regions held a different opinion of him from that which the Christian law teaches Christians to hold of a Christian.

It seemed worthwhile to touch briefly on a few of these matters, lest it be thought that what people say is being reported merely in bare words. I shall set them down simply, just as we received them, without asserting whether they were true or otherwise.

Those who came reported, then, that at about the same time, while the same king was staying at Rouen, people living in that city were seen coming to him and complaining that some of their own people, having rejected Judaism, had recently become Christians. They asked him to accept a payment and compel them, after rejecting Christianity, to return to Judaism. He agreed, accepted the price of their apostasy, and ordered that they be brought to him from among the Jews themselves. What more need be said? He broke several of them by threats and terrors and made them deny Christ and resume their former error.

Moreover, in those days there was a certain Jewish youth. One day, as he was traveling along the road, another young man appeared to him, handsome in face and clothing. When asked where he came from and who he was, he said that he was Stephen the protomartyr, who had long ago been made a Christian from Judaism.

“But,” he said, “for this reason I have now come down from heaven to earth: so that you may cast aside Jewish superstition, become a Christian, and, baptized in Christ, be called by my name.”

He said this and slipped from the youth’s sight, disappearing. The young man, seized with fear, immediately went to a priest, clearly announced what he had seen and heard, confessed that he believed in Christ, and at once received the grace of baptism.

When his father learned what had happened, he was afflicted with bitter grief of heart. Agitated about how he might restore his son to his ancestral rites, he learned how William, king of the English, had recently restored certain people of this kind to Judaism in return for money. He therefore went to him and related in a lamenting voice how he had lost his son. He begged the king to pity him and asked that the only child whom he loved, as fathers do, be restored to him under the authority of an imperial decree.

The king was silent in response to his request, not yet understanding why he should involve himself in such a matter. The Jew perceived the reason why the king did not answer his pleas and immediately promised to give him sixty marks of silver if he restored his son to Judaism.

At the king’s command the young man himself was brought into his presence, and the king addressed him in these words:

“Your father complains of you because you became a Christian without his permission. If this is so, I command you to satisfy his will and, without any evasion, return to Judaism without delay.”

The young man answered him:

“My lord king, I think you are joking.”

But the king, angered, said:

“Would I joke with you, son of filth? Rather go away and carry out my command quickly; otherwise, by the face of Lucca, I will have your eyes torn out.”

Then the youth, becoming calmer in spirit, answered in a steady voice:

“Certainly I shall not do so. But know that, if you were a good Christian, you would never utter such words. It is the duty of Christians to join to Christ those who have been separated from him through unbelief, not to separate from him those who have been joined to him through faith.”

The prince, confounded by these words, ordered that the youth, after being insulted, be removed dishonorably from his presence. After being expelled, he found his father waiting outside the doors for the outcome.

Enraged against him, he said:

“Son of death and food for eternal destruction, is your own damnation not enough for you unless you also plunge me into it with you? But now that Christ has been revealed to me, far be it from me ever to acknowledge you as my father, for your father is the devil!”

While these words were being spoken, the Jew was brought before the king at his command. The king said to him:

“See, I have done what you asked. Give me what you promised.”

But he replied:

“My son is now both more steadfast in confessing Christ and more hostile to me than usual, and you say, ‘I have done what you asked; give me what you promised’? No: first complete what you began, and only then speak of your promise. That was the agreement between us. ‘I have done,’ you say, ‘as much as I could’; but although I have not succeeded, I will certainly not endure having labored without profit.”

The Jew, distressed by this, scarcely obtained that, after giving half of the promised money, the other half might be remitted to him.

Besides these things, it was also reported at that time that he had fallen into such an elevation of mind that he could not patiently hear anyone say that any matter which was to be done either by him or at his command should be carried out subject to the will of God. Rather, he wanted every action, whether already completed or still to be undertaken, to be attributed solely to his own ability and strength.

This pride of mind grew in him so far that, as was said, he believed and publicly asserted that none of the saints could help anyone with God, and that therefore he neither wished to invoke blessed Peter or any other saint for assistance, nor did any wise person ought to do so.

As this belief advanced in him, he also fell into disbelief in God’s judgment. Accusing it of injustice, he maintained that God either did not know human actions or did not wish to weigh them on the scales of equity.

For example, about fifty men who still appeared, in those days, to possess some remnants of wealth inherited from the ancient free status of the English were seized and accused of having captured and killed and eaten the king’s deer. [Note: “They are judged,” says William of Malmesbury, “to have been brought to trial for capturing the king’s deer.” “The hunts,” he writes concerning William II, “which he had at first permitted, he so completely prohibited that the penalty for taking a deer was capital.” I believe that John of Salisbury had this chiefly in mind in Book I, chapter 4 of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, where he speaks of hunting: “Some, driven by the impulse of this madness, burst into such insanity that they became enemies of nature, forgetful of their condition, despisers of divine judgment, while, in revenge for beasts, they subjected the image of God to carefully devised punishments. Nor did they hesitate to destroy a human being for the sake of a little animal, one whom the Only-Begotten of God had redeemed with his blood.”]

They denied it. Therefore they were immediately dragged to trial and judged guilty of the accusation that had been brought against them.

[Note: “By examination with heated iron.” This type of ordeal for clearing oneself of a charge is found among our ancestors both in the well-known trial of Emma, mother of King Edward the Confessor, accused of violated chastity with Aldwin, bishop of Winchester, and in the enactments of the ancient kings of England, such as Athelstan, Cnut, William I, and their successors. The solemn rites employed in it may be learned from the explanation of the words prefixed by William Lambard to his *Archaeonomia*, and from the *Life of Robert of Jumièges, Archbishop of Canterbury*, in the *Antiquities of the British Church*, besides the glossary of Peter Pithaeus serving the Carolingian and Ludovician capitularies. Public judgments were conducted not only by heated iron but also by water, sometimes boiling and sometimes cold. This is established both in the places mentioned above and in the author of the little book commonly attributed, perhaps incorrectly, to Ranulf de Glanvill. See Book XIV, chapter 1 of that work; Roger Hoveden, *Annals*, Part I, under the years 1176 and following, pp. 547 and 566 of the Frankfurt edition; and Henry Bracton, Book III, *On the Crown*, chapter 16, §3. We deliberately omit what concerns the custom of this kind among other peoples.

In England the use of these examinations lasted until the time of Henry III, when it entirely disappeared both through enacted law and through disuse, out of respect for pontifical law, by which it had long before been prohibited. I do not think that anything else concerning this matter was enacted among our ancestors, whether in the king’s records or elsewhere, apart from that single provision found in the public records of the third year of Henry III. There, certain itinerant judges are ordered to abstain from the form of trial that was then pending, since this type of examination had been condemned by pontifical authority. This is as certain an indication that a permanent law had not yet prevailed as it is that the judicial rite itself soon afterward fell into disuse. The royal command in question is found in Patent Roll 3 Henry III, membrane 5, from which we have faithfully transcribed it.

“ The king to his beloved and faithful Philip of Uletot and his fellow justices itinerant in the counties of Cumberland, Westmorland, and Lancaster, greeting.

“Because before the beginning of your eyre it was doubtful and undetermined by what judgment those accused of robbery, homicide, arson, and similar offenses were to be dealt with, since judgment by fire and water has been prohibited by the Roman Church, our council has presently provided that, during this eyre, the following shall be done with those accused of such excesses: namely, that those accused of the aforesaid greater crimes, and suspected of being guilty of that of which they are accused—concerning whom, even if they abjured our realm, there would still be suspicion that they might thereafter do evil—shall be held in our prison and safely guarded, so that they do not incur danger to life or limb by reason of our imprisonment.

“Those, however, who have been accused of intermediate crimes, for which judgment by fire or water would be appropriate if it were not prohibited, and concerning whom, if they abjured our realm, there would thereafter be no suspicion of their committing wrongdoing, shall abjure our realm.

“Those who have been accused of lesser crimes, and concerning whom there is no suspicion of evil, shall find safe and secure pledges for maintaining our fidelity and peace, and shall then be released in our land.

“Since our council has at present provided nothing more certain in this matter, we leave it to your discretion to observe the aforesaid procedure during this eyre. Since you will be better able to know the persons involved, the form of the offense, and the truth of the matters themselves, proceed in such cases according to this order and according to your discretion and consciences.

“And in testimony of this matter, etc. Witness the lord P., bishop of Winchester, at Westminster, on the twenty-sixth day of January in the third year of our reign. By the same and H. de Burgh, justiciar.”

The same formula is recorded as having been written to several other provincial judges, namely those of Somerset, Dorset, Kent, Essex, and Hereford. It is highly probable that the other judges who presided over the provinces at that time received commands of this kind as well.

It should meanwhile be observed that long before the beginning of Henry III’s reign such examinations had been forbidden by pontifical law. The third year of Henry III was the year 1219 of human salvation.
