Yet not only are such examinations condemned as unlawful in a letter of Alexander II to Raynald, bishop of Como—written before Henry’s time, more than one hundred and fifty years earlier—but the very words of the letter concerning this matter had also found a place in the *Corpus of Canons*, then thoroughly familiar to pontifical jurists and esteemed above all for its authority, a place for which we owe thanks to Gratian’s work. See, if you wish, *Causa* II, question 5, chapter 7, section “Purgationem”; Ivo, Part X, chapter 15; and the *Extra*, title *On Vulgar Purgation*, chapter 3, “Dilecti.”

These and other kinds of examinations used in judicial proceedings were anciently called *ordalium*, or *ordalla*, as the Latin form has it, since they are nothing other than judgments. Hence, even today, among the Alemanni and Belgians—whose language is the best interpreter in many matters of our ancient speech—*Urtheyl* and *dordeel* mean judgments, *Urtheylen* and *dordeelen* mean to judge, and *urtheyler* and *dordeeler* mean a judge.

This is expressly asserted in the canons of the synod held at Enham under King Ethelred:

“Judgment, which in English is called ordeal, and common oaths, shall not be administered during festive times and lawful fasts, nor from Advent of the Lord until after the octave of Epiphany, nor from Septuagesima until fifteen days after Easter.”

Wulfstan, archbishop of York, who governed under Ethelred together with Aelfheah, archbishop of Canterbury, committed the canons of that synod to writing. They may still be read intact in a manuscript codex of considerable antiquity and elegance, written in the script of that period.]

[Note: We have already seen an example of a similar ordeal on the preceding day in the *Life of Blessed Hildegundis*. In his *Spicilegium*, Selden notes at this passage that the use of this and similar judgments, which the ancient Saxons called *ordaldum* (the Germans call it *urtheil*, the Belgians *Ordeel*), became obsolete in the time of Henry III; and he prints the command issued in 1219, by which the king directs certain justices how they are to proceed in cases “for which judgment by fire or water would be appropriate, if it were not prohibited.”] They were required to repel the heated iron from themselves by the ordeal. On the appointed day, therefore, all alike were subjected to the prescribed penalty of the judgment, with pity and mercy set aside. It was a wretched spectacle.

But almighty God, of whom the Davidic psalm sings that he is merciful and just, displayed their innocence to everyone by mercifully preserving all their hands from burning, and by a just judgment declared how unjust had been the malice of the men who impiously wished to destroy them.

When the prince was told that, on the third day of the judgment, all those condemned had appeared with their hands unburned, he is said to have replied angrily:

“What is this? Is God a just judge? Let whoever hereafter believes this perish. Why should this and that be answered by my judgment from now on? Not by God’s, which is twisted this way and that according to everyone’s wishes.” [Note: “By this and that” is an oath formula, which the same king also uses below.]

These and many other reports, even more atrocious, which men of no obscure reputation brought at that time concerning William, greatly inflamed Anselm—as we have said—to renounce the episcopate of England, since he knew that his own character could no longer in any way agree with the king’s.

Wishing therefore to ask the supreme pontiff for release from the bond by which he lamented that he was too tightly bound, he approached him, made known to him the anxiety of his heart, and begged him to have pity on him—that is, he earnestly asked to be relieved of the burden of pastoral care, which he saw as unbearable because fruitless.

The pope heard what he requested and immediately exclaimed in astonishment:

“O bishop! O shepherd! You have not yet suffered slaughter or wounds, and already you seek to evade the care of the Lord’s flock? Christ tests Peter’s love for him in the care of his sheep, and Anselm—Anselm, I say, that holy and eminent man—merely wishing to rest, does not fear exposing Christ’s sheep, even before the battle, to be torn apart by the bites of wolves? Ah, what am I to say? With what love does he hope to be joined to the Lord who flees what the Lord himself, by his own testimony, proves to be the means by which he is loved?

“Let such things be far from you; let them be far from your religious calling, dearest brother Anselm! But so that you may not trouble me any further in this matter, know that I not only do not grant you what you ask, but, in the name of almighty God and in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I command you under holy obedience not to abandon the care of the English kingdom entrusted to you, for as long as you are able to retain it as you have done until now.

“If, because of the tyranny of the prince who now rules there, you are not permitted to return to that land, nevertheless, by the right of your Christianity, always remain its archbishop. You shall retain authority to bind and loose over it for as long as you live, and, wherever you may be, you shall use the pontifical insignia as the supreme pontiff does.”

To this he replied:

“Father, I do not reject obedience. But, if it does not displease you, I will briefly disclose what I have in mind. Let your excellence believe, if you will, that if slaughter, wounds, or death itself were threatened against me for the protection and defense of Christ’s sheep, I hope I would not flee, if my conscience does not deceive me.

“But, to say nothing of the king himself, who, as is known, expelled me from his kingdom, those whom I was supposed to have as sheep, and the bishops whom I was supposed to have as helpers, and who had professed obedience to me, were all jointly trying to lead me to act against justice under the pretext of justice—that is, to renounce obedience to blessed Peter, lest I violate the faith I owed to the earthly king.

“When I tried to persuade them that I could preserve both obligations, provided that I violated neither—since the Lord commands us to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s [Matthew 22:21]—they replied that such a practice was not customary among them, and that they were unwilling to endure this injury from their lord: that anyone in his kingdom should intend anything against anyone, except with or through him. And I, Father, what was I to do among such men?”

The pope answered:

“You are guided by reason. So that I may not seem careless about these and other matters wrongfully inflicted upon you, or unwilling to avenge them with the sword of Saint Peter, I advise you to present yourself at the council which I have decided to celebrate at Bari before the body of blessed Nicholas on the first of October. There you will hear and see what I have determined to do, by the judgment of equity, concerning that English king, his people, and those like him who have risen against the liberty of the Church of God.”

Anselm then returned to his estate at Sclavia, preferring rest and poverty to the riches that had been offered him.

When the time of the council approached, he returned to the pope and traveled with him as far as Bari. [Note: “In October Pope Urban assembled the entire synod in the city of Bari, at which there were 183 bishops.” Thus Lupus Protospata, though he wrongly gives the year as 1099, unless he begins the year in the Greek manner from September.] At the council itself, after the supreme pontiff had discussed many matters concerning the Catholic faith with eloquent reason and rational eloquence, a question arose from the Greeks, who wished to prove by evangelical authority that “the Holy Spirit has procession from the Father alone.”

The pope tried to oppose this error with many arguments and numerous lines of reasoning. Among other things, he introduced, by way of example, a point from a letter concerning the Incarnation of the Word that Anselm had once composed and sent to him. [Note: The letter exists in volume III of Anselm’s works. Most of what follows concerning the Council of Bari had hitherto been entirely lacking. A considerable addition can therefore be made from the very diligent and learned Binius, who admits that he found nothing concerning the acts of this council except what Eadmer briefly records in Anselm’s *Life* and William of Malmesbury in the first book of *De gestis pontificum*. The same may be said of the second Roman council held under Urban, about which our author writes below, pp. 53, 54, and 55. See Binius, *Councils*, vol. III, part II, pp. 421–422. The work *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* is found in Part I of Anselm’s works.]

This brought considerable clarity and strength to his argument. But when certain objections were raised and the reasons already given were requested to be explained more fully—as is customary with unstable minds—the supreme pontiff himself first broke the imposed silence and said in a loud voice:

“Father and teacher Anselm, archbishop of the English, where are you?”

The Father was sitting among the other leading fathers of the council, and I was at his feet. When he heard that he was being sought, he immediately rose and answered:

“Lord Father, what do you command? Here I am.”

The pope said:

“What are you doing, I ask? Why do you remain silent among the others? Come, come, I beg you; come up to us, and, fighting for your Mother and ours, help us. You see these Greeks trying to deprive her of her integrity, and, if they are given the opportunity, to plunge us into the same wickedness. Come to our aid, therefore, as though you had truly been sent here by God for this purpose.”

You would then have seen everyone bustling around the pope’s throne, changing seats, and preparing a place for the man to sit. At last they lifted him with honor and seated him near the pope, while the council marveled at this and asked who he was and where he came from.

When the tumult had been silenced, the pope explained to everyone together the man’s holiness and ability. In a voice worthy of reverence he also made known that Anselm had suffered many persecutions for the sake of justice and had been unjustly expelled from his own land.

When Anselm was therefore ready, at the pope’s command, to answer the question that had been raised, some thought it better to defer the matter until the next day, so that the points to be made might be presented more freely and efficiently.

On the following day, when the assembly had been arranged early, Anselm was asked to discharge the duty agreed upon. He rose and, standing in an elevated place before everyone, treated, discussed, and resolved the matter, with the Holy Spirit guiding his heart and tongue, so effectively that no one in the assembly remained who did not acknowledge himself satisfied.

But we shall refrain from writing by what arguments, reasons, authorities, and examples from divine Scripture he proceeded, because Anselm himself afterward treated the matter more carefully and subtly and wrote an outstanding work on it. [Note: This is the short work mentioned in the *Life*, Book II, no. 10, as having been praised at the Council of Bari. Is it the work entitled *Why God Became Man*, whose composition in Campania is mentioned in the same Book II, no. 43?]

He sent that work, at the request of his friends, to many regions where the reputation of the same error had spread. When he had finished speaking, the supreme pontiff gazed at him and said:

“Blessed be your heart and understanding, and blessed be your mouth and the word of your mouth.”

From that point the assembly lingered in praise of the man. His faith and prudence were proclaimed and magnified, while the perfidy of any who might refuse to accept and believe what he had taught concerning the question was reproached, struck down by perpetual anathema, and overthrown.

As the proceedings continued, discussion began concerning the king of the English, and certain unfavorable things were publicly proclaimed about him. During this, Anselm sat with downcast face and showed no favor toward the speakers.

At length, concerning the selling and oppression of churches—among the other charges brought against him—and concerning the injuries inflicted upon Anselm, the pope complained bitterly:

“For this reason also,” he said, “he made him an exile from his kingdom, because he could not separate him from the fidelity and obedience owed to blessed Peter.”

He added:

“Behold what the life of that tyrant is like, as it has often been reported to the Apostolic See. We have repeatedly sent him many exhortatory and at the same time corrective messages for his amendment, but the affliction and expulsion of this great man, whom you see before you, sufficiently shows how much we have accomplished.

“What, then, brothers, is your judgment? What do you decree?”

They replied:

“The sentence is plain and the judgment evident. If you summoned him once, twice, and three times, and he refused to listen, refused to accept discipline, what remains except that, struck by the sword of Saint Peter under the blow of anathema, he should suffer what he deserves until he abandons his wickedness?”

The pope answered:

“So it is.”

When Anselm heard this, he immediately rose and, kneeling before the pope, who was already prepared to excommunicate the aforesaid king, scarcely succeeded in preventing him from doing to the king what the common judgment of all had proclaimed.

Those who had previously learned of the man’s goodness by hearsay alone now rejoiced to experience it in action: they saw him return good for evil and sincerely intercede for the one who persecuted him. Thus he became an object of admiration to everyone.

Meanwhile I was present with the Father in every respect, evidently ready to serve him. Since from childhood I had been accustomed to observe with careful attention and commit to memory whatever new things came my way, especially in ecclesiastical matters, I examined the council that had been convened—the places and ranks of the persons, the procedures and investigations of the cases—with perhaps more curiosity than discernment, looking modestly this way and that, since I had never before witnessed anything of the kind.

As I was concentrating on these matters, I noticed the archbishop of Benevento, whom I had previously known well, adorned with a cope more splendid than that of anyone else attending the assembly.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] This was Roffridus, of the princes of the Lombards, who sat from the year 1076 until the year 1107.]

[Col. 0416B] For the pope presided over the council not in a cope but in a chasuble, with a pallium over it. As I looked at the cope of the Beneventan prelate and perceived, as I have said, that it surpassed the others, I recalled words that, as a boy, I had once heard from the elders of our church—namely, Edwius, a magnificent man of Blacheman, and Farmannus, together with several others.

Those memorable men often used to relate that, when they were beginning their adolescence, Queen Imma, who was mentioned at the beginning of this work, had exalted the Church of Christ at Canterbury, among the many good gifts she bestowed upon it, by the arm of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, through the arrangement of her lord, King Cnut of the English.

[Note: [Col. 0416D] Imma was the mother of Saint Edward. Much concerning him and King Cnut can be read in the account of his life on 5 January. Eadmer, moreover, at the beginning of Book I, merely calls him “Edward.”]

How this was done, they reported in the following manner—please bear patiently with what may seem an excessive digression from the narrative begun—for they agreed in meaning and followed the same order.

“At the time,” they said, “when that lady was held to be a great and powerful queen in the English kingdom, the bishop of the Church of Benevento came to England. As he himself related, a terrible famine, which he had foreseen by certain signs would afflict all Apulia, had brought him there, since he wished somehow to avert so great an evil, if not from the whole province, at least from his own fellow citizens.

“When he set out on his journey, he carried with him the arm of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, confidently hoping that through it he would obtain many benefits. This arm had been kept apart from the rest of the body in the church at Benevento in order to procure assistance for such a necessity.

“The bishop therefore crossed Italy and came to Gaul, gratefully accepting everywhere whatever gifts were offered to him. When he heard of the fame of the wealthy kingdom of the English, he decided that he ought to proceed there, hoping from the experiences of others to gain more there than in the other regions.

“The aforesaid queen was also held in great renown and widespread fame, which her goodness and her generosity toward the churches had won for her.

[Col. 0417A] “When the prelate therefore came to England, he approached the queen. Having obtained an audience with her, he explained what he had brought and for what reason he had come to such distant parts of the world. Moved to compassion by the charitable labor of the man, she gave him generously from her possessions and urged him to return to his homeland and to assist those whom he feared were threatened by the danger of famine.

“But he, realizing that what he possessed was insufficient for his purpose, asked those whom he understood to be especially close to the lady at court whether the queen might be willing, in exchange for a price, to transfer into her own possession the bone he had brought.

“What more need be said? The lady’s mind was sounded out, and it was found to be most ready—provided that the bishop could assure her that the bone of the aforementioned apostle really was his, and could satisfy her in such a way that she herself would testify that every doubt had been removed.”

To this he replied: “In what manner?”

“Upon the Lord’s body,” she said, “and upon the relics of the saints that I shall place before him, let him swear that the relic in question truly comes from the body of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, and let him do so without any equivocation or sophistry.”

“This,” said the bishop, “I promise to do securely.”

He therefore came to Canterbury with the arm, and, as the king and queen had directed, was received with due honor. With the queen herself present, and an immense company of monks and clerics surrounding her—including the men mentioned above, from whom we received this account, who testified that they had been present—and with a great multitude of both sexes and all ages gathering for this purpose and listening, he solemnly affirmed by oath upon the altar and the body of Christ, as well as upon the relics of the saints that Saint Gregory is known to have sent to Saint Augustine and other Roman pontiffs to other archbishops, that the bone under discussion truly belonged to the blessed apostle Bartholomew, and that his assertion contained absolutely no sophistry or equivocation.

When this had been done, the memorable lady gave the prelate several pounds of silver and, having obtained the bone, granted it by solemn donation to the Church of Christ at Canterbury on behalf of King Cnut and herself. In those days, the English custom was to place the patronage of the saints above all worldly concerns.

The prelate of that see, whose name was Aegelnothus, gave the man, among other things, a very costly cope, ornamented on every side with gold embroidery. It was to serve both as an adornment of that church and, in future times, as evidence and proof for the Church of Canterbury of so important a transaction.

[Col. 0417D] Thus, when—as I said—I saw at the council the Beneventan prelate adorned with a cope surpassing the others, and recognized it perfectly from what I had heard long ago, I was greatly pleased. I showed both the cope and the words that had then been told to me as a boy to Father Anselm.

Soon after the council had been held, I approached the Beneventan himself and, amid other conversations expressing our mutual affection, began to speak about the same cope. I asked him where he had obtained it, as though I did not know. He explained the whole matter and declared that his church had acquired it from the Church of Canterbury in precisely the order I have described.

Having thus become more certain about the matter, I thought it would please some readers to insert it into this little work, although I was aware that in doing so I was exceeding the course of the narrative I had undertaken. This completed, let us return to the journey we began. When the council was finished, we departed from Bari, without leaving the pope’s company until Rome.

Meanwhile, the messenger whom we mentioned above as having been sent from Rome to the king of England returned. He reported that, although the king had somehow received the pope’s letters, he had refused in every way to receive Anselm’s letters; indeed, after learning that Anselm was his man, he had sworn by the face of God that, unless Anselm quickly left his land, he would have his eyes torn out without possibility of reprieve.

[Col. 0418B] But several days after we had returned to Rome, a man sent by King William arrived, the same William whose departure from England we mentioned earlier, to answer the lord pope concerning the letters he had sent on Anselm’s behalf.

He said to the pontiff: “My lord the king instructs you that he is greatly astonished that it could even have entered your mind to address him concerning the restoration of Anselm’s possessions.”

He added: “If you seek the reason, it is this: when Anselm wished to leave his land, he openly threatened that, once he had departed, he would take the whole archbishopric into his own control. Since, therefore, he did not allow himself to be restrained by these threats from leaving, the king believes that he acted justly in doing what he did, and that he is being unjustly blamed.”

To this the pope replied: “Does he accuse him of anything else?”

“No, pope!” he said. “Who has ever heard of such things? For this one reason alone he stripped the kingdom’s primate of all his possessions: because Anselm refused to abandon his intention of visiting the holy mother Church of Rome? Truly and without the slightest doubt we can say that nothing of this kind has ever been heard of. And have you worn yourself out coming here for an answer like that, you extraordinary man? Return—return as quickly as possible—and order him, on behalf of blessed Peter, to restore him fully to all his possessions without any opposition, if he refuses to be excommunicated. See to it, therefore, that he lets me know before the council what he wishes to do, which I shall celebrate in this city in the third week after Easter.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] In the year 1099, therefore, when Easter was celebrated on 10 April, and when the Sunday letter was B, the third Sunday fell on the 24th of that month.]

[Col. 0418D] “Otherwise, know with absolute certainty that at that same council he will be punished by the sentence of condemnation which he has deserved.”

But the man replied: “Before I leave, I shall speak with you more privately.”

William therefore remained there for many days, prudently working to make this person and that supporters of his cause, distributing gifts to those whom he perceived were won by them, and freely making promises in order to satisfy his master’s will.

The Roman pontiff was thus diverted from his judgment, and, at William’s request, granted the king a delay until the feast of Saint Michael.

This took place during the very solemn celebrations of the Nativity of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] It is therefore incorrect for some writers to place here a Roman council held in the year 1098 at which this delay was granted. After the Council of Bari, there appears to have been no other council held in Urban’s presence except the one at which, after Easter of the following year, 1099, the pontiff threatened to pronounce the sentence of excommunication. Nevertheless, beyond that council he granted a delay until the feast of Saint Michael. Was the first feast intended, recurring on 8 May, or the more solemn second one, on 29 September? I believe the second, because although the earlier date would have been sufficient to ensure that nothing had to be feared from the council, the author later, when discussing Urban’s death, says that he died before the answer from England was expected to arrive. This clearly indicates that he understood the later date, since Urban died two months after the first date, namely on 29 July.]

[Col. 0419A] Seeing this, we understood that we were vainly waiting there for counsel or assistance. After requesting permission, we decided to return to Lyons. But when we were entirely unable to obtain that permission, we remained in Rome until the appointed time of the council, living continually near the pope and, as it were, sharing a common household. For there did not seem to be two courts, but one.

Accordingly, the pope himself often came to Anselm, spending time happily with him and making his court at Anselm’s side. He also gave him the lodging in which we were staying, with the right that, if Anselm ever returned to Rome, he could claim it against all other persons.

In gatherings of nobles, in processions, in stations, always and everywhere, Anselm was second only to the pope: honored above all, welcomed by all, and himself submissive to everyone with simple humility.

When the council was about to begin, the bishops who had come from Italy and Gaul were claiming their customary seats. No one could be found who said that he had either heard of or seen the archbishop of Canterbury attending a Roman council before this time, or who knew where he ought then to sit. At the pope’s command, a seat was therefore placed for him in the circle.

[Note: [Col. 0551]

(23) A seat was placed for him in the circle, a position of no slight honor. Gervase of Canterbury, in a manuscript in his declamation against Robert, abbot of Saint Augustine’s—an imaginative composition, as he calls that sort of work elsewhere—says: “Anselm, consecrated in the city of Canterbury, received the pallium from Pope Urban and enjoyed such favor with him that Urban called him the pope of another world, and, after Anselm’s return to England, sent the pallium to be given to the archbishop of York.” Thus far Gervase. He judged that one worthy of so great a title should also rightly be placed in a position of the highest honor. See further the distinguished William Camden, Britannia, p. 239.]

[Col. 0419D] This position is customarily regarded as one of no small honor in such an assembly.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] The paintings that depict the Council of Trent or similar synods show seats arranged so that, at the head, the pontiff sits with his attendants, or the papal legates; on each side, benches extend and finally meet in a semicircle. This semicircle appears here to be called the “circle,” and thus Anselm seems to have sat directly opposite the pope. Gervase of Canterbury writes of him in a manuscript preserved by Selden that Urban called him “the pope of another world.”]

While many matters were being discussed in the council, many arrangements made, and many rules decreed for observance, they were nevertheless not clearly understood by everyone, partly because of the immense size of the gathering and partly because of the noise and clamor of those entering and leaving the body of Saint Peter.

The supreme pontiff therefore ordered the bishop of Lucca, named Reinger, to stand in the middle, higher than the others, and to set forth clearly for all ears, in the strong voice with which he was endowed, what had been decreed.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] Reinger, also called Ringer and Ranger by others, lived until the year 1112. Letters from Queen Matilda to him are extant.]

The bishop obeyed the command of the presiding pontiff. But after several of the decrees had been clearly expounded by him in the hearing of everyone, suddenly, to the astonishment of all, his face, voice, and bodily gesture changed into another manner. Directing the sharpness of his eyes toward those seated around him, he could no longer conceal the anguish of his wounded mind.

Breaking off the sequence of the decrees that he had undertaken to explain, he began as follows:

“But what, then, are we to do? We burden subjects with commands, yet we do not resist the unjust savagery of tyrants. The oppressions that they inflict upon churches through their tyranny, and the dispossessions of persons who were appointed to protect those churches, are reported daily to this see; counsel and assistance are sought from it as from the head of all things. But the outcome to which these matters come—alas, the whole world knows and complains of it!

“From the most distant parts of that world, here among us sits one man, resting in modest silence. His silence is a great cry; his humility and patience, the more lowly and gentle they are, the more exalted they are before God and the more ardent toward us. This one man—this one, I say—most cruelly afflicted and most unjustly stripped of all his possessions, has come here imploring the judgment and equity of the apostolic see concerning his case.

“It is now the second year since he came here.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] “The second year” must here be understood as the second year from Saint Anselm’s arrival in Rome—not a year completed, but merely begun, as is clear from what has been said.]

“But what assistance has he found here up to now? If not all of you recognize the man of whom I speak, he is Anselm, archbishop of the English region.”

[Col. 0420B] After saying this, he struck the pastoral staff he held in his hand three times against the pavement, openly displaying the indignation of his spirit, while his lips and teeth suppressed an explosive murmur.

At this, the pope signaled to him and said: “Brother Reinger, enough, enough. Good counsel will be taken concerning this matter.”

But Reinger, breathing heavily toward him, replied: “And indeed it is necessary. For otherwise he who judges justly will not pass by.”

Then, having been instructed to continue reciting the council’s decrees, he resumed his speech. At the end, so that the injury inflicted upon Anselm would not be treated as insignificant, he repeated his warning, admonished them, and took his seat.

When Father Anselm heard all this and finally understood, toward the end of the speech, that the words had been spoken about him, he was exceedingly astonished. He knew that he had spoken to no one about the matter, and that neither he nor any of his men had prompted Reinger to speak in this way. He remained seated as usual, listening silently.

At the conclusion of the synod, after the matters that needed to be removed had been removed and those that seemed worth establishing had been decreed, the pope, together with the whole council, pronounced the sentence of excommunication against the enemies of the holy Church.

The sentence included all laymen who granted investitures of churches, all who received those investitures from their hands, and all who consecrated persons to the office connected with such honors when they had been granted in this manner.

He likewise bound under the same bond of anathema those who, for the sake of ecclesiastical honors, became the men of laymen. He declared that it seemed supremely abominable for hands that had grown to such eminence that—something not granted to any Englishman—they created in their ministry the God who creates all things and offered that same God before the sight of God the Father for the redemption and salvation of the whole world, to be degraded so as to become servants of hands polluted day and night by obscene contaminations and stained by devotion to robbery and the unjust shedding of blood.

We were present for these proceedings, witnessed them, and heard everyone acclaim, “Let it be so, let it be so!” We know that the council was concluded in these matters.

The next day, having received permission, we departed from Rome, having obtained no judgment or assistance from the Roman prelate beyond what we have described. The road by which we returned was then exposed to many dangers; but with the Lord protecting us, we escaped all of them and reached Lyons unharmed.

There we were received with the greatest reverence and joy. The bishop of the city detained us, and we established our residence there, having lost all hope of returning to England during the time of King William.

Anselm was treated there not as a guest or a stranger but as a native and, truly, as the lord of the place. While he was present, the bishop of that city never wished to preside in his own place; instead, with Anselm presiding everywhere, he performed both the role and the duties of an inferior and suffragan, moved by remarkable humility.

Anselm celebrated festivals, sacred ordinations, and church dedications, and performed every kind of pontifical office.

But when many people, having recognized the breadth of his benevolence, flocked to him and asked that the sacrament of the laying on of the bishop’s hand be conferred by him upon themselves and their families, he—who, in administering episcopal offices, always awaited the bishop’s direction—replied with easy friendliness that it was not his place to presume to do such a thing in another bishop’s parish without consulting him.

When they understood that he was acting reasonably, they immediately sent messengers to their own bishop. They informed him with what kindness Anselm had responded to their requests and asked that he be petitioned on their behalf.

The bishop therefore summoned Anselm concerning the matter—or rather, concerning this and the other pontifical offices throughout his entire diocese—and, placing everything in Anselm’s discretion, would not allow anyone to be admitted without permitting him to receive the benefit of the sacrament.

Thus there was a constant gathering of the people, and sometimes the entire day was spent on this alone, so that we who ministered to him were often exhausted by great weariness, while he always remained cheerful and bright-faced.

From this there grew in everyone an extraordinary and unprecedented affection for him, and his goodness was proclaimed throughout the surrounding region.

Meanwhile, rumor spread among the people that Urban, the pontiff of the apostolic see, had completed the course of his present life. He had died before receiving the replies he was expecting from the king of the English concerning Anselm’s affairs.

When the king heard the news of Urban’s death, he replied: “And may God hate whoever cares about that.”

He added: “But what sort of man is the one who is now pope?”

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Paschal II, elected on 12 August.]

When he was told that Paschal was in some respects like Archbishop Anselm, he said: “By the face of God, if he is such a man, he is no good. Nevertheless, let him be himself for now, because by this and that his papacy will not at this time rise above me. Meanwhile, now that I possess freedom, I shall do as I please.”

For he did not believe that the apostolic authority could possess any jurisdiction in his kingdom unless he himself permitted it.

It is not appropriate, as I hasten toward other matters, to write how he conducted himself thereafter. Nevertheless, he was not permitted to enjoy for long the freedom of which he had boasted. Before a year had passed, he lost it when he was struck by an unexpected and sudden death.

October heard him boast; the second day of the following August saw him breathe his last. For on that morning, after dining, he went hunting in the forest.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] The authors call it the New Forest.]

There he was struck in the heart by an arrow and died immediately, unrepentant and without confession, and was soon abandoned by everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0551]

(24) Whether the arrow itself was shot at him and struck him is uncertain. Most of the old writers state that the king was pierced by an arrow which Walter Tirel, a Frenchman, had aimed with an unlucky shot in the animal preserve we call the New Forest. This is the generally accepted account.

But Suger, who was a contemporary of this king and apparently connected with Tirel by friendship, speaks of his death as follows: “Some people laid it to the charge of a certain nobleman, Walter Tirel, that he had pierced him with the arrow. Yet, although he neither feared nor hoped for anything from this accusation, we repeatedly heard him affirm under oath, as though the assertion were sacred, that on that day he had neither come to the part of the forest where the king was hunting nor seen him anywhere in the forest. We read this in the Life of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks.” But Orderic Vitalis, in Ecclesiastical History, Book X, p. 783, relates far more carefully all the individual details concerning the miserable killing of the king and Tirel’s fatal shot.]

Whether the arrow struck him, as some say, because it was shot at him, or whether, as more people affirm, it killed him when he stumbled over it and fell upon it, we consider it pointless to investigate. It is enough to know that he was struck down and killed by the just judgment of God.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Orderic Vitalis describes the matter at greater length in Book X. Abbot Suger, who was his contemporary, carefully excuses Walter Tirel, a noble Frenchman to whom some attributed the blow; Tirel asserted under oath that on that day he had neither come to that part of the forest nor seen the king.]

At this point, I recall what this king once said, as we related above, to the bishop of Rochester: “God would never regard him as good for the evil he inflicted upon him.”

I consider what God afterward did with him for the remainder of his present life. It is known that, from the time when he spoke those words—after his illness had been removed, with which we know he had been afflicted—he prospered so greatly in crushing and subjugating his enemies, acquiring lands, and pursuing his pleasures, that one might have thought everything smiled upon him.

Even the wind and the sea itself seemed to obey him. I speak the truth and do not lie: whenever he wished to cross from England to Normandy, or to return from there according to his desire, as soon as he arrived and approached the sea, every storm—which sometimes raged with terrible violence—was calmed and served his crossing with marvelous tranquility.

What more can I say? I confess that he was so fortunate in everything, as though God had answered his words in this manner:

“If, as you say, I shall never regard you as good for evil, I shall test whether I can at least regard you as good for good. Therefore, in everything you consider good, I shall fulfill your desire.”

But what was the result? He advanced so far through his successes that, as those who were present with him day and night in his actions testify, he never rose from bed or lay down in bed without always being worse than when he had lain down or risen.

[Col. 0423A] Therefore, since he would not be corrected by evil and could not be drawn by good toward good action, the just Arbiter removed him from this life by a swift and momentary death, lest he should rage for a long time to the destruction of the good.

[Col. 0423A]

# BOOK THREE

In the second year [Note: [Col. 0423D] The year of Christ 1100] after we came from Rome to Lyons—which was the third year of our exile—two monks came to Anselm, who was then spending his third day in the monastery called Casa-Dei.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Casa-Dei, a monastery in Auvergne, will be discussed below on 24 April, in the Life of Saint Robert, its first abbot and founder.]

One was from Canterbury and the other from Bec. They announced to him the death of the often-mentioned King William.

Struck by intense astonishment, Anselm was immediately shaken into the most bitter weeping. We were greatly astonished when we saw this.

But, with sobs interrupting his words, he declared—upon the very truth which a servant of God ought not to violate—that, if he could bring it about, he would much rather that he himself were dead in body than that the king should be dead as he was.

When we returned to Lyons after this, behold, another of the brothers of the Church of Canterbury arrived, carrying letters and conveying petitions in which the mother Church of the English earnestly implored him, now that the tyrant was dead, to return without delay to visit and console his children.

After taking counsel concerning the matter with the aforementioned venerable Hugh, bishop of that city, Anselm began his journey back to England. The bishop himself and the entire people of the land grieved over this and, if it had not been contrary to reason, wished by every means to prevent it.

In the end, they saw themselves deprived of great consolation at his departure. Men and women followed him from village to village for several days, each one running eagerly and uttering groaning cries over his own desolation.

We had not yet reached Cluny when another messenger, sent by the new king of England and the nobles of the kingdom, met Father Anselm and reproved him for delaying his arrival. He reported that the whole country was astonished at his coming and that all the affairs of the kingdom had been postponed pending his hearing and direction.

The letters of the king that he had brought confirmed his words and explained them more fully. They contained the prayers and wishes of the king, who urgently requested that the man come quickly and promised to subject himself and his kingdom to Anselm’s counsel and governance.

These words, and many others of the same kind that I would like to relate, compelled us to hurry toward our homeland.

Thus, after crossing the perils of the sea with the greatest success, we landed at Dover on the ninth day before the Kalends of October and found the whole country rejoicing with immense joy at Anselm’s arrival.

A kind of hope of a new resurrection arose in the minds of individuals. Through it, each person promised himself deliverance from the oppression of the calamity that was still burning, and an entrance into the desired condition of prosperity.

This hope arose chiefly from the fact that Henry, who had recently succeeded his deceased brother in the kingdom, had promised on the very day of his consecration that he would observe good and holy laws for the whole people and would prohibit and overturn throughout his dominion all the oppressions and injustices that had arisen under his brother, both in the churches and in secular affairs.

He had ordered all this to be proclaimed throughout the kingdom, confirmed by oath and strengthened by the testimony of letters bearing his seal.

The presence, moreover, of the common father of all added no little strength to this hope in the minds of the people. They recognized his steadfast integrity and, with their senses alert, awaited the emergence from him of something holy for the reform of the state of the Christian religion, which had declined in many respects after the death of Archbishop Lanfranc, whose memory was revered.

But a few days after his return, when Anselm had come to Serberia to see the king and had been received by him with joy, he accepted the king’s explanation of why, in assuming the blessing of royal dignity, he had not waited for the man whom he knew had the right to confer it.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] A reasonable cause may have been fear of Robert, his firstborn brother, who was undoubtedly plotting something to recover their father’s kingdom. Archbishop Thomas of York therefore blessed the king in the year 1100, on 5 August, the third day after William’s death; Thomas himself died soon afterward, in the following November.]

Anselm was then asked, according to the custom of his predecessors, to pay homage to the king and receive the archbishopric from his hand.

When Anselm replied that he could neither wish nor be able to consent to these things, they asked him why. He immediately made known, in a clear account, what he had received concerning these and certain other matters at the Roman council, and then added:

“If the lord king is willing to accept these things and preserve what he has accepted, there will be good and firm peace between us. But if not, I do not see that it would be useful or honorable for me to remain in England, especially since, if he gives bishoprics or abbeys, I must be entirely deprived of communion both with him and with those who receive them.

“For I did not return to England for this purpose: to remain there if he refuses to obey the Roman pontiff. Therefore, I beg him to say what he wishes, so that I may know where to turn.”

When the king heard these words, he was gravely troubled. It seemed serious to him to lose the investitures of churches and the homage of prelates; it also seemed serious to allow Anselm to depart from the kingdom when he himself was not yet fully established in it.

In the one matter, he seemed to himself to be losing almost half the kingdom. In the other, he feared that Anselm might approach his brother Robert, who had then returned from Jerusalem to Normandy, and make him king of England by bringing him under the authority of the apostolic see—a thing he knew would be very easy to accomplish.

Accordingly, after words had been exchanged on both sides, a delay until Easter was requested, so that both parties might send messengers to Rome to alter the apostolic decrees to suit the kingdom’s former practice.

In the meantime, while the churches of England remained in the condition in which they were, Anselm would be restored to all his possessions by the return of the lands that the dead king had taken from the Church of Canterbury. In this way, if the pope could not be moved from his judgment, the whole matter would return to the condition in which it then stood.

Although Anselm knew and declared that these proposals were frivolous and tended toward no useful result, he nevertheless allowed himself to be overcome by their entreaties, lest he arouse in the new king or the princes any suspicion against him concerning the transfer of the kingdom or anything else. He agreed to what they wished, left the court in peace, and withdrew to his own affairs.

A few days having elapsed, Mathilda, daughter of Malcolm, the most noble king of the Scots, and of Margaret [Note: [Col. 0425D] Saint Margaret, queen, is commemorated on 10 June and is also entered in the Roman Martyrology], who is known to have sprung from the stock of the English kings, married the aforementioned Henry, king of the English. This Margaret was the daughter of Edward, son of King Edmund, who was the son of King Ethelred, son of the most glorious King Edgar, mentioned shortly before at the beginning of this work.

Although the matter of this marriage does not, as some may perhaps think, at all belong to the purpose of the work undertaken, nevertheless, since it was administered by Anselm—for he both blessed them in marriage and consecrated her as queen—I think it should briefly be described, so that it may be known how the matter was conducted. This has especially pleased us to do because, as we have heard, some people blasphemed Anselm, alleging that in this matter he had deviated from rectitude.

For this same Mathilda, brought up among nuns in a monastery from childhood and having reached adulthood, was believed by many to have been offered by her parents for the service of God, because she had publicly been seen veiled in the manner of those among whom she lived. While she was being loved by the king, who had long since discarded the veil, and this greatly relaxed the tongues of those people and held them back from the embraces they desired, she herself approached Anselm, whose decision in the matter everyone awaited, and humbly begged him for advice and assistance.

He, bringing forward the report that was circulating, declared that he could never in any way consent to take away a bride of God and join her in marriage to an earthly man. She replied, and emphatically denied that she had been offered; she also denied that she had ever once been veiled of her own will, and offered, if he did not wish to believe her otherwise, to prove this before the judgment of the whole English Church:

“Nevertheless,” she said, “I do not deny that I wore a veil. For when I was a young girl, and was being raised under the rod of my friend Christina, whom you know well, she used, in order to preserve my chastity against the raging lust of the Northmen—who at that time lay in wait for everyone's modesty—to place a black cloth upon my head, and, whenever I cast it off, to torment and disgrace me with severe blows and exceedingly obscene verbal abuse. I carried that cloth, groaning and trembling, in her presence; but as soon as I could remove myself from her sight, I used to snatch it up, throw it on the ground, trample it under my feet, and, though foolishly, rage against it as fiercely as I hated it.

“In this way, and no other, as my conscience bears witness, I was veiled. And if anyone says that I was offered to God, this too may be inferred from the following circumstance. As many who still survive know, when my father happened to see me veiled in the manner I have described, he was inflamed with anger, seized the veil with his hand, tore it apart, and called down God’s hatred upon the person who had placed it upon me. He declared that he had destined me for Count Alan as a wife, rather than for the common life of nuns.” [Note: [Col. 0425D] Alan, count of the Breton Armoricans, is famous among historians. He lived at the beginning of Norman rule in France and was born of a Norman mother. A plausible conjecture seems to rest upon the common hatred of the English and Scots toward the Bretons: either this Count Alan is mentioned proverbially as a great enemy of the Scottish name, or perhaps one of his early descendants, equally hated by the Scots, is intended.]

“This is the basis of the accusation brought against me. I beg your wisdom to weigh it and to act on my behalf as your fatherhood knows should be done.”

What more is there to say? Anselm postponed giving judgment and declared that the case should be determined by the judgment of the religious persons of the kingdom.

Accordingly, on the appointed day, at the summons of that bishop, noble abbots and men of the religious orders assembled in the village of Saint Andrew of Rochester, which is called Lambeth, where the circumstances of the present case had also brought Anselm himself. The case was therefore presented according to the sequence already stated. Suitable witnesses came forward on both sides, declaring that the girl’s words were supported by pure truth. Two archdeacons also appeared, namely William of Canterbury and Humbald of Sherborne. Father Anselm had sent them to Wilton [Note: [Col. 0426D] Wilton was the seat of a bishop before it was transferred under the Norman kings to Salisbury. The aforementioned King Edgar had founded there, with great zeal, a monastery for virgins, as Ethelred, abbot of Rievaulx, writes in his *Genealogy of the Kings of England*, published among the *Ten Writers], where she had been brought up, to investigate the certainty of the matter. They publicly testified that they had most carefully examined the matter with the sisters and had been unable to learn anything from them that contradicted the account given.

Anselm therefore warned everyone, and commanded them in the name of Christian obedience, not to allow favor or fear to turn anyone away from the truth, but for each person to assist to the best of his ability in the cause of God, so that it might be justly determined. Otherwise, he said, God forbid that a judgment should emerge whose example in future ages might deprive anyone unjustly of his freedom, or allow God to be wrongfully defrauded of what ought to belong to him.

All acclaimed that this should be done and promised that they would act in no other way. The father alone having withdrawn from the assembly, the Church of England, which had gathered together, deliberated on the judgment to be pronounced. Then, when he had been reverently brought into their midst, they explained what the common agreement of all had found concerning the case.

They said that, having examined the matter, the judgment seemed to them well founded, and that to confirm it they were prepared to declare that the girl could not lawfully be compelled on account of her case by any judgment to remain bound, but could use the freedom of her body in whatever legally permissible way she wished. Although, they said, they could prove this by a slight argument, they would refrain from doing so since there was no need; instead, they relied upon the firmer authority of a judgment in an equal case, promulgated by their predecessor of venerable memory, their father and teacher Lanfranc.

“For when that great William first conquered this land, many of his men, applauding themselves for so great a victory and believing that everything ought to obey and submit to their desires and lusts, began to rage with wicked desire not only against the possessions of the conquered, but also against married women and virgins themselves, wherever opportunity presented itself. Some women, foreseeing this and fearing for their chastity, sought out monasteries of virgins and, having accepted the veil, protected themselves among them from so great a disgrace.

“When that disaster had later subsided and peace had been restored to affairs according to the circumstances of the time, the same Father Lanfranc was asked what he thought about those women who had preserved their chastity by such a refuge—whether they ought to be compelled to retain in the monastery the veil they had accepted or not. He resolved the question by the judgment of a general council in this manner: for the chastity that they had shown themselves to love by so clear an indication, he judged that they deserved to be shown greater reverence than that anyone should violently impose upon them any obligation of religious continence, unless they sought it of their own will.

“We were present at these proceedings; we heard wise men approve them; and we wish these principles to have force and to be confirmed in the present case. Although we know that the case of those women was more serious than this one, since they wore the veil voluntarily whereas this girl wore it under compulsion for the same reason, nevertheless, so that no one may think that we are being led by favor toward anyone, we do not wish to proceed further in judgment. We are content that what prevailed in the greater case should prevail in the lesser.”

Anselm then said:

“You know what I advised, what I commanded, and what you promised. Since, therefore, you have judged collectively according to what seemed to you more just, as you assert, I do not reject your judgment; rather, I accept it all the more confidently because I hear that it is supported by the authority of so great a Father.”

The girl was then brought into their midst. With a gracious expression she heard and accepted the proceedings and begged that she be allowed to speak briefly. She therefore declared that she was prepared to prove, either by oath or by whatever other ecclesiastical procedure they preferred, that the account she had given, already defined, rested upon solid truth. She admitted that she was not doing this because she thought herself disbelieved, but in order to cut off every future opportunity for malicious people to blaspheme.

She was told that none of this was necessary, since, if an evil person brought evil out of the evil treasury of his heart, the truth itself, already proved and confirmed by the testimony of so many persons, would quickly overwhelm him.

After receiving Anselm’s address and blessing, she departed. A few days later, as I have said, she became queen and wife.

But when the marriage was to be celebrated and confirmed according to the rite of the Church, the Father himself, standing higher than the others, instructed all the nobility of the kingdom and the common people who had gathered around for this very purpose, as well as the king and the girl, who stood around the church doors, about the manner in which the case of the virgin, which rumor had made public, had been examined and determined by the bishops and religious persons.

Having done this, he warned them and commanded them by God’s authority that if anyone thought differently about the matter and had reached a different judgment—so that it could be shown that the union ought not to take place according to Christian law—he should declare it openly before all, without hesitation and without disturbing anyone’s peace.

At this, everyone cried out together that the matter had been justly decided and that there was nothing in it from which anyone could lawfully raise an accusation, unless perhaps driven by malice. They were therefore lawfully joined, with the honor appropriate to a king and queen.

Here is the order of what happened, as attested by the truth of my conscience. I heard and saw it in person and have described it without turning aside in any direction, placing the girl’s words before the reader only in such a way that I do not assert whether they were true or not. If anyone therefore wishes to go on saying that Anselm did anything in this matter contrary to justice, let him look to it himself.

But we, who have recognized his heart in this and in many other matters, bear witness for him: as he himself used to admit, at that time he neither knew nor was able to do anything in this matter better or more justly than he did.

[Note: [Col. 0427A] Hermann, the third abbot of Saint Martin in the city of Tournai, testifies in a manuscript treatise on the restoration of his monastery that, as a young man, he was present and heard what Saint Anselm said to dissuade this marriage, and how truly he prophesied that it would not be happy. It is useful to append his words in full, because they contain certain details differing from Eadmer’s account and cast further light on the whole matter to Anselm’s praise. He writes as follows:]

“Since I have mentioned Henry, and there will be no other opportunity to speak of him, although I may seem to depart far from the narrative I began, I shall nevertheless relate something worthy of remembrance.

“This Henry, then, having been established in the kingdom, wished to have as his wife a certain girl, the daughter of the king of Scotland. He told the lord Anselm, then the venerable archbishop of the city of Canterbury, to bless her for him and, once she had been blessed in a solemn wedding, to join her to him in marriage.

“The archbishop replied that he did not wish to bless her, nor, on his advice, would he join her to the king in marriage, since, as he himself had reliably heard, she had worn the veil of nuns upon her head, thereby showing herself to be the bride of a heavenly rather than an earthly king.

“The king, on the other hand, said that he had promised her father, and had even confirmed the promise by oath, that he would take her as his wife. Therefore, to preserve his oath, he would not abandon her unless the matter were determined by canonical judgment. He ordered that, after the archbishop of York had been summoned, a council of the bishops, abbots, and ecclesiastical persons of all England should be assembled to determine so important an ecclesiastical matter.

“At the general council, therefore, the abbess in whose monastery the girl had been brought up was asked whether she had in fact been consecrated according to the custom of nuns, with a veil placed upon her head and with episcopal blessing.

“The abbess replied publicly before everyone:

“‘In truth, her father entrusted her to me, not so that she would become a nun, but merely so that, for the sake of precaution, she might be brought up in our church with our other foreign girls and instructed in letters. When she had grown older, it was reported to me one day that King William, my lord Henry’s brother, who was then alive, had come to see her; that he had already dismounted with his knights before the door of our church; and that he had ordered the doors to be opened to him for the purpose of praying.

“‘When I heard this, I was exceedingly frightened lest, being young, she might please the king, and lest the untamed king, who wished immediately to do whatever came before him, might, upon seeing the girl’s beauty, offer her some unlawful violence, since he had come so unexpectedly and unannounced to see her. I brought her into a private room, explained the situation to her as it was, and, with her consent, placed a veil upon her head, so that the sight of it might restrain the king from an unlawful embrace.

“‘My hope did not deceive me. The king entered our cloister to look at the roses and other flowering plants; but as soon as he saw her wearing a veil on her head with our other girls, he went out and withdrew from the church, plainly showing that he had come only because of her. When the girl’s father came to our church within that same week and saw the veil upon his daughter’s head, he angrily tore the veil apart, threw it to the ground, trampled it under his feet, and took his daughter away with him.’”

The abbess was then asked how old the girl had been at the time. She replied that she might have been twelve.

The king then urged the archbishop to order that the marriage be celebrated according to this judgment. After taking counsel and reading various chapters of the canons, the bishops and abbots judged collectively that a marriage should not be prohibited on account of such an act, since, while she had been under the guardianship of her father and below the legal age, she could do nothing without his consent.

When the judgment had ended, the king asked the archbishop whether he wished to raise any objection to it. The lord Anselm replied that he would not object to it, since they had judged according to the decrees of the canons.

Then the king said: “Since you approve the judgment, I wish you to betroth the girl to me.”

But the lord Anselm replied: “I do not criticize the judgment. But if your majesty were willing to trust my advice, I would advise you not to take her, since, whatever the circumstances, she did wear a veil upon her head, and you could find for yourself a sufficient number of the daughters of kings or counts.”

When the king persisted in what he had undertaken, that most holy man added:

“You, my lord king, will disregard my advice and do what pleases you. But I think that whichever of us lives longer will see that England will not long rejoice in the offspring born of her.”

I heard him say these things as a young man; now I see that a large part of them has already come to pass.

The king therefore had by her two sons and one daughter. The sons, already young men, perished with many others at sea when their ship was wrecked as they were returning from Normandy to England. The emperor Henry took the daughter as his wife, with much wealth sent to her by her father, and celebrated the wedding at Liège with great splendor. But after she had borne him one son, he was overtaken by a swift death and left her a widow. She then married the count of Anjou.

When her father suddenly died in the city of Rouen, the English nobles established Stephen, count of Boulogne and brother of Theobald, count of Champagne, as king over them. Robert, son of King Henry by a concubine, was therefore deeply angered and openly rebelled against him. He captured him in a certain castle that his father had given him and shut him up in chains. He then sent word to his sister to cross quickly into England with her son and take possession of her father’s kingdom.

She crossed over quickly, thinking that she would find everything prosperous; but she found things otherwise than she had expected. For Stephen’s wife, having joined the nobles to herself, resisted her vigorously. Stephen himself, after a few days, was reconciled to Robert by certain agreements and released from his bonds, and once again obtained the kingdom of the English. Thus the daughter of King Henry lamented that she had been deceived by a vain hope.

We are uncertain about what the future will bring. But this one thing we clearly see: in accordance with the prophecy of the lord Anselm, England did not long rejoice in the offspring of that queen who, after wearing the veil, had married Henry. Indeed, after being devastated and oppressed by prolonged civil strife, it fell from its former wealth into great poverty.

The words of wise men and prelates of the Church are therefore not to be despised, but rather revered and feared, since it is evident that both the prophecy mentioned above of Pope Leo concerning Count Baldwin of Flanders, who married his kinswoman, and the following prophecy of the lord Anselm concerning the king of the English, proved true.”

Thus far Hermann, who was certainly writing before the year 1153, when King Stephen died. There is no time to linger over the elucidation of his words. We shall say only that we had them transcribed from the original by Joseph Ignatius of Saint Anthony, a Discalced Carmelite, and that an error had to be corrected in them: the girl’s father was repeatedly called King David, although David was her brother. He did not obtain the kingdom until the twenty-fourth year after his father’s death, and the twentieth year after this marriage, namely in the year of Christ 1121; he was the youngest of all Malcolm’s sons.

[Col. 0428D]

In the same year Guido, archbishop of Vienne, came to England, claiming that he was to exercise a legation over all Britain by command and authority of the apostolic see. When this became known throughout England, everyone was astonished, for all knew that it was unheard of in Britain for any man to exercise the apostolic office over them except the archbishop of Canterbury. Accordingly, he returned as he had come, accepted by no one as legate and performing none of the functions of a legate.

After this, when the time of the truce had reached Easter [Note: [Col. 0430D] In the year 1101 Easter was celebrated on 21 April], and the messengers who had been sent to Rome had not yet returned, the truce was extended until their arrival.

At the following celebration of Pentecost, the arrival in England of Robert, the king’s brother, having been announced beforehand by rumor, stirred up the entire royal court and, as later became clear, moved the minds of certain people in different directions. The king therefore suspected the nobles, and the nobles suspected the king: he feared that they might, as often happens, abandon him because of their unstable loyalty, while they feared that, once he had obtained peace on every side, he might rage savagely against them under harsh laws. It was therefore deliberately arranged that assurances should be given on both sides which would exclude what each party feared.

When the matter came to the king’s pledge of loyalty, all the nobility of the kingdom, together with a great multitude of the people, placed Anselm between themselves and the king, so that he, on their behalf, extending his hand into the king’s hand, might promise that the king would administer the whole kingdom in all things according to just and holy laws for as long as he lived. When this had been done, everyone congratulated himself as though he were secure.

But when the king learned with certainty that his brother had arrived, he immediately assembled an army from the whole land and decided without delay to meet him in war. The army was large and strong, and Father Anselm faithfully kept watch with his men beside the king on the expedition.

When it was announced that Robert himself and his companions had crossed the sea, the leading men of the kingdom, as though they had forgotten their pledge, prepared to go over to him, abandoning the king. When Anselm learned through a reliable report that this was happening, he was distressed; and, all the more because he feared that some misfortune might befall the king, he began to devote himself to the matter.

But such a man did not know what to do in such circumstances. He could bring no public accusation of such a crime, since there were no witnesses; yet he did not dare to nourish the crime by keeping silent, lest they, having become perjurers, lead the king astray.

The king himself, fearing not only the loss of his kingdom but also for his life, could trust no one and rely on no one except Anselm. He therefore often came to him and brought with him the nobles whom he most feared might fall away from him, so that, after hearing Anselm’s words, he himself might be relieved of his fear and those men might be struck with fear if they should in any degree fall away from the loyalty they had pledged to him.

The king repeatedly promised Anselm that he would leave to him the exercise of all the rights of Christianity in England and would perpetually obey the decrees and commands of the apostolic see.

While matters stood thus, Anselm, with all the nobles assembled, addressed both the entire multitude surrounding the army and the nobles themselves. With every calumny silenced, he explained how detestable to God and to every good person those would be who violated in any way the loyalty they owed their prince. His argument was so indissoluble that all, recognizing that he was walking in the way of virtue, immediately chose, with contempt for life, to fall in death rather than seduce the king by violating their pledge.

We may therefore state with complete confidence that, if Anselm’s fidelity and prudence had not intervened after God’s grace, King Henry would at that time have lost his right to the English kingdom.

Robert, having lost the confidence he had placed in the treachery of the nobles, and considering Anselm’s excommunication no light matter—since he knew for certain that Anselm would inflict it upon him as an invader unless he abandoned the undertaking—accepted peace and returned to brotherly affection. The army was dismissed to its homes.

After this, while everyone eagerly awaited some action by the king toward Anselm worthy of so great a service, Anselm was suddenly ordered to come to the king’s court to answer concerning the matter for which the truce had been extended. The messengers who had now returned from Rome had brought a letter from Pope Paschal, who had succeeded Urban, addressed to the king. What it contained will be made clear by the text of the letter appended below.

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing. The words of your embassy, dearest son,” etc. See in *Paschal II*.

When we had therefore come to the court, the king, acting on the advice of his brother and of his brother’s friends, who were inflamed with bitter hatred against Anselm because of the loss of the kingdom, demanded of him that he either become his man and, according to the custom of his predecessors, consecrate those to whom he said he would give bishoprics or abbacies, or leave his land immediately and without reconsideration.

Anselm replied:

“I have explained how I took part in the Roman council and what I received there from the see of blessed Peter. If, therefore, I submit myself to the excommunication of which I have been the proclaimer in this kingdom on account of anything, to what, I ask, shall I henceforth be able to adhere, since in my own judgment I shall be excommunicated? The messengers sent to alter these very matters have returned having accomplished nothing. It does not seem sound counsel that I should make myself a transgressor of things which I cannot violate without endangering my salvation and honor.”

The king replied:

“What is that to me? I do not wish to abandon the custom of my predecessors, nor to tolerate in my kingdom anyone who is not my man.”

Anselm said:

“I understand where these words are tending; I have experience of such things. Nevertheless, for the present I shall go not outside the land, as he commands, but to my Church. By doing what I understand myself bound to do, I shall see who wishes to inflict violence upon me or upon mine.”

Many things were conducted in this way concerning these matters, but this was the substance of them all. While the bishops and nobles of the kingdom exchanged arguments on both sides, as they used to do under another king, and strove in every matter to obey the royal will—indeed, they insisted with all their might that they should not be subjected to obedience to the Roman pontiff—Anselm returned to his own, striving to please God in all things and lamenting with deep contrition of heart the oppression of the churches of England.

Not much time had passed when, although the Father himself was unconcerned about his own injuries, he feared somewhat for the losses of the Church, and letters of friendship from the king were brought to him. In them, after an opening greeting accompanied by an offer of complete peace, the king asked him to come, wishing to moderate the judgment in the matter at issue by another policy.

Anselm therefore went to Winchester, to hear whether perhaps God had touched the king’s heart by his grace. There, after the bishops and nobles of the land had been assembled, it was agreed with Anselm’s approval that, under another truce, other messengers, more distinguished than the previous ones, should be sent to Rome from both sides. They would explain to the Roman pontiff in person that he must either necessarily withdraw from his judgment or, if Anselm and his companions were expelled from England, lose the submission of the entire kingdom and the revenue that he used to receive from it each year.

The archbishop therefore sent two monks: the aforementioned Baldwin of Bec and Alexander of Canterbury. They were not sent so that, at their urging, the Roman pontiff might in any way abandon the rigor of justice in Anselm’s case, but partly so that they might offer testimony concerning the threats made at court, testimony which the pope could trust without hesitation, and partly so that they might bring Anselm a definite judgment of the apostolic see concerning the matter.

Three bishops were sent by the king to conclude the matter itself: Gerard of Hereford, recently made archbishop of York; Herbert of Thetford; and Robert of Chester.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] Malmesbury describes Herbert of Norwich’s entry into simony, corrected by genuine repentance and a better subsequent course. Shortly below he is called bishop of Norwich because he established his see at Norwich—the see which Herfast had transferred to Thetford not many years earlier—and he died in 1119.]

[Note: [Col. 0433D] Robert of Chester likewise continued to use the title of Chester, although his predecessor Peter had transferred the see, which had been moved from Lichfield to Chester, to Coventry as early as 1095. The see was later extinguished and finally renewed by Henry VIII during the schism; the see that had been subject to Canterbury became subject to York.]

Two of these bishops also had their own reasons for going to Rome: Gerard, to obtain the pallium, and Herbert, to seek the recovery of the jurisdiction over the Christians attached to the abbey of Saint Edmund, which had been taken from his church.

[Note: [Col. 0434D] This abbey of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, is in Suffolk. It was built by King Canute. See volume I, page 284, of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*. Saint Edmund is commemorated on 20 November.]

A few years earlier, Baldwin, the abbot of that monastery, had gone to Rome and obtained from Pope Alexander a privilege for the abbey [Note: [Col. 0434D] Selden gives this privilege, granted in the eleventh year of Pope Alexander, A.D. 1071, in his notes on page 206], by which he had freed it from subjection to all bishops, while preserving obedience to the primate. Archbishop Lanfranc, displeased by this act, took the privilege away from the abbot and was unwilling to return it to him until near the end of his life, when he was moved by the prayers of many.

The aforementioned bishop, therefore, taking it hard that the bishopric of Thetford, or Norwich—within whose parish that abbey is known to lie—had wrongfully been deprived of its rightful jurisdiction, was, as we have said, planning to go to Rome, hoping that, with justice assisting him, he might perhaps restore the church over which he presided to its ancient dignity.

This Herbert, then, after leaving his companions and entering Burgundy with his men, and after reaching the regions of the province of Lyon, was captured by a certain Guido, a powerful and savage man. Guido accused him of being a bishop from England and of going to Rome on account of the injury done to his lord, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

Herbert denied it, but was not believed. He persisted in denying it and swearing oaths, but in vain. At last, after relics of the saints had been brought out, he was compelled to swear upon them and affirm that he would knowingly do nothing at Rome that could appear in any way contrary to the honor or will of Father Anselm.

After this, so that he might deserve to have the man escorted along the road in peace and security, Herbert left Guido nearly forty silver marks, as is reported, not as a gift willingly bestowed. As he left England, he judged that these would assist his business concerning the Church of Saint Edmund at Rome.

[Col. 0434A]

After they had completed the long journey, the messengers arrived together at Rome. They explained to the ears of the apostolic authority the reason for their arrival, according to the position they had been sent to advance, and humbly requested counsel for resolving so great an evil.

The pope heard what they reported and found no words with which to express how greatly he was astonished by it. When the bishops nevertheless earnestly begged him to take precautions for their interests and to temper the rigor of his predecessor’s defined judgment so that peace might exist everywhere, he declared that he would not do so even to save his own head.

“Would I,” he said indignantly, “destroy the decrees and institutions of the holy Fathers at the threats of one man?”

He ended with these words. In addition, he sent letters to the king and to Anselm, each his own. To the king he prohibited, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, the investiture of churches; to Anselm he affectionately urged him to continue doing what he was doing and saying what he was saying, firm and strengthened in all things by the authority of the apostolic see and by the dignity of his primacy.

To make these matters clearer, we now place the letters themselves before the eyes of the reader.

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Henry, king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing. We give thanks to the Lord, King of kings,” etc., up to the following words:

“We prohibit the investiture of churches, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, to kings and princes, indeed to all laymen.
