For it is not fitting that a mother should be delivered into slavery by her son, or that she should accept a bridegroom whom she did not choose. She has her own bridegroom, our King and Lord, who may preserve you by his mercy in power and virtue and lead you from an earthly kingdom to a heavenly one. Amen.”

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Anselm, greetings and apostolic blessing. You are not unaware that the plan of the divine will is,” etc. See in *Paschal II*, below.

At about the same time he also wrote a letter to the bishop and clergy of the Church of Exeter [Note: [Col. 0434D] Exeter is a church and bishopric in Devon. The city lies on the River Exe and is called Exeter by the English. It is mentioned above, book I, note 13, and below, note 19, where the bishop is called bishop of Exeter]. We do not think it altogether foreign to insert it into this work, since we hope that at some future time it may perhaps be useful to someone in a particular matter. It is as follows:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Osbern, bishop, and to the clergy of the Church of Exeter, greetings and apostolic blessing. The authority of the Fathers has also decreed,” etc. See in *Paschal II*.

[Col. 0435A]

On the return of the bishops and of the others who, as we have said, had been sent to Rome, the king, having assembled the kingdom’s princes at London, approached Anselm through intermediaries in the customary manner, demanding that he either cease any longer to deny the customs of his father or cease to be a subject of his kingdom. He replied:

“Let the letters that have been brought be examined, if it pleases you; and, preserving my honor and obedience to the Apostolic See, I shall try, as far as I can, to comply with his wishes. If he wishes,” he said, “let his own letters be displayed; but let him know that mine will not be displayed on this occasion.”

He reports: “When, therefore, he pleases to show them to himself on another occasion, he will then also find me ready to examine those that he now has.”

He replied: “I am not, and will not be, dealing with the letters; but let him state, so that I may hear it, whether, putting aside all ambiguity, he is willing to agree with my will in everything.”

This was heard with great astonishment by many, who said among themselves that, if the letters agreed with his own prohibition, he would publish them voluntarily, even against Anselm’s will. Thus they were not known to us at that time. Yet the more carefully they had been concealed, the more widely they were circulated after several days.

When the letters sent to Anselm had been read and reread before everyone willing to listen, the bishops who had come from Rome added that they had heard other things at Rome from the Apostolic Lord than were contained either in the letters themselves or in those that they had brought to the king. When questioned, they declared under episcopal oath that the pope himself had expressly commanded the king, through them, that, so long as he lived elsewhere as a good prince, he would tolerate him peaceably concerning the investitures of churches, and would not bind him with any bond of excommunication if he invested religious persons in those churches by the delivery of the pastoral staff. They reported that the reason why he had not wished to delegate this authority to him by an inscription in a document was almost certainly that, if it were brought to the knowledge of other princes, they themselves might claim it, disregarding the authority of the Roman pontiff.

When those who had been sent on Anselm’s behalf testified orally that the pope had commanded nothing to anyone in words that in any respect contradicted the letters, the bishops objected that they had dealt with those men secretly in one way and openly in another. When Baldwin heard this, and could not bear the notorious inconsistency attributed to the Apostolic See, he—being zealous in spirit and a lover of what was good—accused them of acting, in such statements, not a little against the faith and the oaths that they had made before the pope at Rome.

A considerable disagreement therefore arose among the nobles. The former tried to establish that, once the uncertainty of words had been removed, one must place complete trust in writings sealed with the pope’s seal and in the words of monks. The latter, on the contrary, maintained that greater credence should be given to the assertions of three bishops than to sheep skins blackened with ink and weighed down by a lump of lead. They rejected the testimony of the little monks, saying that, once those men had professed their renunciation of the world, they had forfeited all testimony in secular affairs.

“But,” said Baldwin, “this is not a secular matter.”

They said: “Indeed, we know you to be a prudent and energetic man, but the very order of things requires us to judge that one archbishop and two pontiffs possess greater testimonial authority than you.”

“And what,” he said, “of the testimony of the letters?”

They replied: “We do not accept the testimony of monks against bishops, and should we accept a sheep’s skin?”

“Woe, woe,” religious men say in response to such things. “Are not the Gospels also written on sheep skins? Oh, here the whole confusion of the dispute has been exposed!”

For some time Anselm was uncertain what he should do in this matter and which course he should take. He judged it serious, in whatever way he might reveal it, to show that he did not trust the Apostolic letters; and he saw that it would provide fuel for a grave scandal to refute openly the words of such eminent persons, who were insisting under episcopal oath that those words were true.

The text of the letters, however, is as follows:

**[Col. 0436B]**

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Against …” etc. See under Paschal II, for the year 1118.

The king, therefore, having been emboldened in his own position by what the bishops said, began firmly to insist—with the bishops and the princes of the kingdom simultaneously favoring and urging him—that Anselm should do homage to him without retractation and promise that he would consecrate those whom he said he would immediately appoint to bishoprics, while preserving in every respect the custom of his predecessors.

Then Anselm said: “If the letters agreed with the words of his bishops, perhaps, once the reason had been understood, I would do what it required. But now, so that I may not be deceived in any respect, it seems preferable to consult the Roman pontiff about these matters than to rush to a decision in so ambiguous a matter.”

The bishops who had come from Rome replied: “What we have said, we say; what we have testified, we confirm; and in all these matters, if you do not believe us, we appeal to the testimony of the Apostolic See. Moreover, on behalf of the lord pope, who ordered this, we declare to you that you should believe our counsel without hesitation; for, whenever you wish, you will find us ready to prove in fact that there is no duplicity in what we say.”

He replied: “I do not wish to engage in litigation against what you assert. But because I perceive from what I have learned more privately by hearsay that the will of the princes has become one on this point—namely, that if the king gives the investitures of churches, as he threatens to do, although he will do so neither with my approval nor with my consent, I should not, for your sake, withdraw my communion from either the giver or the recipient as though they were excommunicated, until the messengers whom I shall send to Rome to investigate this matter have returned and I know for certain what I should do—I do not wish to differ from them alone. Meanwhile, let this be observed by me: under no circumstances will I consecrate anyone to the office of an honor thus received, nor order or permit anyone else to consecrate him.”

The controversy was settled on these terms, and the matter was put to rest on both sides.

Then the king, as though he had been granted the power he desired, exultant and cheerful, immediately invested two of his clerks in two bishoprics by the delivery of the pastoral staff: namely, Roger, his chancellor, in the bishopric of Salisbury, and another Roger, his larderarius, in the bishopric of Hereford.

**[Note: [Col. 0437C–D]]** Roger of Salisbury’s father, Roger, rose from being a poor priest to the power of chief justiciar under this Henry, whose favor he had obtained by unworthy arts; he also secured for his illegitimate son the dignity of chancellor. Now endowed with a bishopric, that son later proved faithless to Henry’s final wishes and was responsible for the election of Stephen as king, with Henry’s daughter Matilda excluded.

**[Note: [Col. 0437D]]** *Larderarius* means “keeper of the storeroom,” from *larderium*, which means “storeroom,” so called because bacon (*lardum*) is kept there. Such an unworthy promoter could hardly have begun with more worthy candidates.

At about the same time, a general council of all the bishops and abbots of the kingdom was held in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, situated in the western part of London. The council was presided over by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, with Gerard, archbishop of York, Maurice, bishop of London, William, the elected bishop of Winchester, Robert, bishop of Lincoln, Samson of Worcester, Robert of Chester, John of Bath, Herbert of Norwich, Ralph of Chichester, Gundulf of Rochester, Hervey of Bangor, and the two recently appointed bishops, namely Roger of Salisbury and Roger of Hereford, sitting with him.

Osbern of Exeter, however, being confined by illness, could not attend.

**[Note: [Col. 0437D]]** “Osbern, deprived of his sight for no few years, lived until the fourth year of King Henry.” So says William of Malmesbury. From this we established above that he died in the year 1103.

At this council Anselm instituted the observance of many provisions necessary for ecclesiastical discipline, which the pontiff of the Apostolic See later confirmed by his authority. We have judged it appropriate to insert into this work the proceedings of that council, as they were written by Father Anselm himself. He writes as follows:

In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1102, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Paschal, the supreme pontiff, and the third year of the reign of the glorious king of the English, with his assent, a council was held in the church of blessed Peter, situated in the western part near London, by the common agreement of the bishops, abbots, and princes of the whole kingdom.

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, presided, with the venerable men Gerard, archbishop of York, Maurice, bishop of London, William, elected bishop of Winchester, and others, both bishops and abbots, sitting with him.

At Anselm’s request to the king, the primates of the kingdom attended this assembly, so that whatever might be decreed by the authority of the council would be securely preserved by the concordant care and concern of both orders. This was necessary because, after the cultivation of synodal discipline had ceased for many years, the thorns of vices had grown up, and the fervor of Christian religion had become excessively cold in England.

First, therefore, by the authority of the holy Fathers, the intrusion of the Simoniac heresy was condemned in that council. Those found guilty of it were deposed: Guido, abbot of Pershore; Wimund of Tavistock; and Ealdwin of Ramsey. Others, not yet consecrated, were removed from their abbeys: namely Godric of Peterborough, Haimo of Cernel, and Egelric of Middleton.

Without simony, however, the following were removed from their abbeys, each for his own reason: Richard of Ely, Robert of St Edmunds, and the man who was at Michelney.

**[Note: [Col. 0437D–0438D]]** There were abbeys at Pershore in Worcestershire, Tavistock in Devon, Ramsey in Huntingdonshire, Burgh or Peterborough in Northamptonshire, Cernel in Somersetshire, and Middleton in Dorsetshire. For the foundation and other matters concerning these monasteries, consult the *Monasticum Anglicanum*.

It was also decreed that bishops should not undertake the office of secular lawsuits; that they should have properly ordered laws, not as laymen do, but as is fitting for religious persons; and that they should always and everywhere have reputable persons as witnesses to their manner of life.

That archdeaconries should not be given *ad firmam*.

**[Note: [Col. 0438C–D]]** Spelman collects much learned material in his *Glossary* to show that a property or benefice is given *ad firmam* when it is transferred under an obligation to provide annually a banquet or feast, assessed at a fixed sum of money and for a fixed number of days. Hence *firma* is used by Anglo-Saxon authors not only for a village or estate leased for an annual payment, but also for a banquet. Something of this sort seems to be prohibited here, as greatly injurious to ecclesiastical propriety, unless immediately below, in a similar phrase and with an entirely clear meaning, monks are prohibited from holding estates *ad firmam*, that is, leased at an annual price.

That archdeacons should be deacons.

That no archdeacon, priest, deacon, or canon should marry a wife or retain one whom he has married. Any subdeacon who is not a canon, if he marries after professing chastity, is likewise to be bound by the same rule.

That a priest, so long as he has an illicit relationship with a woman, should not be *legalis*, nor celebrate Mass; and, if he celebrates it, his Mass should not be heard.

**[Note: [Col. 0438D]]** *Legalis* is one who has no impediment preventing him from pleading or being pleaded for in court according to law, such as an excommunicated or infamous person. In this sense, judicial formulas call such people “upright and legally qualified men”; hence *legalitas* is derived to designate this sort of honorable qualification.

That no one should be ordained to the subdiaconate or above without a profession of chastity.

That priests’ sons should not be heirs of their fathers’ churches.

That no clerics should be secular officials, procurators, or judges in matters of blood.

That priests should not go to drinking parties, nor drink at *pinnas*.

**[Note: [Col. 0438D–0439D]]** *Pinn* in English signifies a pin or even a wooden peg; but what relevance does that word have to communal drinking? I fear that, through scribal error, the word *popina* may have been truncated and changed into *pinnas*. Certainly the synodical letter of Racher, bishop of Verona, in volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 261, expressly urges priests, saying: “Do not drink in taverns.”

That clerics’ clothing should be of one color and their footwear orderly.

That monks and clerics who have abandoned their order should either return to it or be excommunicated.

That clerics should wear open tonsures.

That tithes should be given only to churches.

That churches or prebends should not be bought.

That new chapels should not be built without the bishop’s consent.

That a church should not be consecrated until the necessary provisions have been made both for the priest and for the church.

**[Col. 0439A]**

**[Note: [Col. 0551]]**

**(25)** That abbots should not make knights. Formerly, recruits were granted the dignity of knighthood or the equestrian order by distinguished prelates of the Church, with solemn rites. An old codex concerning matters relating to the monastery of St Martin of Battle, in the archive of royal revenues called the Augmentations, states:

“Let him [the abbot] not give taxable lands as a fief. Nor let him make knights except in sacred vesture.”

An old charter likewise granted to the abbot of Reading by Henry I and later confirmed by John states:

“Let him [the abbot] not give taxable lands as a fief. Nor let him make knights except in the sacred garment of Christ, in which he should carefully and modestly receive little children. But mature or discerning persons, both clerics and laymen, he should receive with due care.”

**[Col. 0551D]** For sometimes even men who belonged to the sacred order transferred themselves to the dignity of armed knighthood. See Matthew Paris, p. 882 of the London edition.

I find the same matter in Part I of Henry IV, Part II, membrane 26, no. 10, and in the records of the public courts, Trinity II Edward III, roll 106, Berkshire. Anyone wishing to consult the matter more carefully should turn to Ingulf in his *History of Crowland*, John of Salisbury, *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, book VI, chapters 10 and 13, Peter of Blois, letter 94, and the rites of an earlier age for consecrating the arms of those who were to be created knights, which are found in the rituals—called pontificals and manuals among our churches—and in similar works.

All these materials sufficiently show that, in the creation of knights—not merely knights of the Bath, as they are called, but all knights—men of the sacred order performed a solemn service in the churches. This may perhaps have arisen from the fact that, in an earlier age, they were regarded as the very authors of the dignity itself. For we read that the archbishop of Canterbury also created a knight: namely Lanfranc created William II.

The monk of Malmesbury, book IV of *The Deeds of the Kings*, writes of William: “The archbishop Lanfranc, because he had brought him up and had made him a knight, contributed greatly to his favor.”

Moreover, concerning Abbot Brand of Bury St Edmunds and the brave young man Hereward, Ingulf, p. 512 of the London edition, says:

“He approached his uncle, the abbot of Burgh, a very religious man named Brand, and most earnestly begged him to make him a legitimate knight, after first confessing all his sins and receiving absolution for them.”

See also the *Britannia* of the distinguished scholar William Camden, p. 126.

That abbots should not make knights, and that they should eat and sleep in the same house as their monks, unless some necessity prevents it.

**[Note: [Col. 0439D–0440D]]** How the more distinguished prelates claimed for themselves the right, with solemn ceremony, to gird knights or enroll them in the equestrian order is demonstrated at length by Selden in his note on this passage. From William of Malmesbury he shows that William Rufus, relying on the favor of Blessed Lanfranc, did so “because Lanfranc himself had brought him up and had made him a knight.”

That monks should not impose penance on anyone without the permission of their abbot; and that abbots cannot give them permission to do this except concerning those whose souls are in their care.

That monks should not become godfathers, nor nuns godmothers.

That monks should not hold estates *ad firmam*.

That monks should receive churches only through bishops, and should not strip churches entrusted to them of their revenues, so that the priests serving there suffer want in what is necessary for themselves and for the churches.

That a pledge of faith concerning marriage made secretly and without witnesses between a man and a woman should be considered invalid if denied by either party.

That long-haired men should be tonsured so that part of their ears is visible and their eyes are not covered.

That relatives up to the seventh generation should not be joined in marriage, nor, if joined, remain together; and that anyone who is aware of such incest and does not disclose it should know that he is a participant in the same crime.

That the bodies of the dead should not be carried outside their own parish for burial.

That the parish priest should lose what is justly owed to him from it.

That no one should, through rash innovation, confer the reverence of sanctity upon dead bodies, fonts, or other things—something which we know to have occurred—without episcopal authority.

That no one should henceforth presume to carry out that abominable business by which, until now, people in England were accustomed to be sold like brute animals.

**[Note: [Col. 0552]]**

**(26)** As though they were brute animals. If this canon is not speaking about the sale of slaves—whom we call *villeins* in forensic language—I do not understand it at all. For the ownership of them, as of any other things called *mancipi* under Caesar’s law, was lawfully transferred by sale or donation both in the time of the Saxons and under the Normans. See the charter of Thorold of Bukenhale in Ingulf, near the end.

Nor, in fact, has either this canon or any other law enacted among us so completely abolished that right that it is not everywhere recognized in the commentaries of our lawyers as consonant with the laws that we use. On the law of servitude, see the discussions of Bodin, *On the Republic*, book I, chapter 5, and Albericus Gentilis, *On the Law of War*, book III, chapter 9.

Those committing the Sodomitic crime, and those voluntarily assisting them in it, were condemned in this same council under a grave anathema, until they should merit absolution through penance and confession.

If anyone should be publicly accused of this crime, it was decreed that, if he were a person of religious order, he should not be promoted to any further rank and, if he held one, should be deposed from it. But if he were a layman, he was to be deprived throughout the whole kingdom of England of the legal dignity of his condition.

It was also decreed that no one should presume to absolve those who do not know how to live under a rule from this crime, unless he were a bishop.

It was also decreed that throughout England the aforesaid excommunication should be renewed on every Sunday.

This, indeed, is the text of the council of London, which, within not many days after its promulgation, produced many transgressors of its provisions among every class of people.

The final provision, concerning the renewal of excommunication on Sundays, Anselm himself, exercising reasonable dispensation, allowed to be postponed. When the council was finished, Anselm departed from London.

The aforementioned Roger, who, as we have said, had been appointed to the bishopric of Hereford, was immediately struck by a grave illness in London itself and brought to the point of death. When he felt that he was near death, he sent a messenger with a letter asking Anselm to order his two bishops—namely the bishops of London and Rochester—to consecrate him as bishop quickly, while he was still alive.

When Anselm heard this, he marveled at the man’s foolishness and smiled slightly; without answering the request, he sent the messenger away from him empty-handed, just as he had come.

Roger soon died in London, and the queen’s chancellor, named Reinelm, was substituted in his place with a similar investiture.

The king therefore sent to ask Anselm to consecrate, according to his right, these newly elected men together with William, who had long been elected bishop of the city of Winchester.

Anselm replied: “I shall gladly consecrate William, but I shall not alter what has been agreed between him and me concerning those who have recently received investiture.”

The king, somewhat shaken in his peace of mind, declared under oath that, as long as he lived, he would not allow William to be consecrated without the others.

William had been elected to the bishopric of Winchester, as we mentioned earlier, before Anselm had been recalled from exile. But William himself was unwilling either to consent to the election, or to accept the staff extended to him by the king, or to attend in any way to episcopal affairs or causes.

After Anselm’s recall, the clergy and people pressed him and began to petition earnestly that he should set their elected bishop over them. Anselm delayed and did not give an immediate assent. At last, however, moved both by their persistence and by consideration of ecclesiastical necessity, and with the king’s agreement, he brought William into the Church, while everyone rejoiced and the monks of that church proceeded festively; in the presence of the whole multitude, he gave him the pastoral staff and entrusted to him the care of the bishopric of Winchester.

Since William had thus been elected, it seemed that he should not lawfully be deprived of episcopal blessing. But because the king absolutely refused to allow him to be consecrated without the others, while Anselm was wholly unwilling to consecrate them with him, the king ordered Gerard of York to consecrate them all together.

When the aforementioned Reinelm perceived this, he returned to the king the staff and ring which he regretted having received unjustly, knowing that he would receive a curse instead of a blessing if he submitted himself to Gerard’s hands to be blessed in such an order.

The king was therefore extremely angry and deprived him of his favor and of his court.

Gerard, having joined all the bishops of England to himself, wished to consecrate the remaining two—William and Roger—at London on the appointed day, disregarding all equity. Anselm was staying in a village not far away called [Murtclac], awaiting the outcome.

But when the bishops had, according to custom, prepared and arranged themselves for the consecration of those to be ordained, William, moved by love of justice, immediately recoiled. He chose to be stripped of all that he possessed rather than bow his neck to such an abominable ministry under the administration of so great a mystery.

The bishops, struck by their own confusion, immediately separated from one another, with the matter unfinished.

Then a cry arose from the whole multitude that had gathered to watch the outcome. With one voice they shouted that William was a lover of what was right, while the bishops were not bishops but destroyers of justice.

The bishops, revealing the bitterness of their minds by the alteration of their faces, approached the king and complained before him of the insult inflicted upon them.

William was brought forward and accused as guilty of the offense he had committed. He was shaken on every side by serious threats. He stood firm and could not be torn away from what was right; consequently, stripped of all his possessions, he was expelled from the kingdom.

Anselm sought judgment and justice from the king concerning these matters, but in vain. Again and again he offered prayers and complaints suited to the nature of the case, but the king, moved neither by prayer nor complaint, refused to abandon what he had begun.

**[Col. 0441C]**

Then, approximately in the middle of the following Lent, the king came to Canterbury, supposedly to conduct certain affairs of the kingdom at Dover with the count of Flanders. He remained at Canterbury for three days, but it became known that nothing concerning the count’s arrival had in fact been arranged.

The reason for his coming, however, became known, and the opportunity revealed his customary behavior. During those days he approached Anselm through his men, demanding that, now that Anselm had been worn down by his long patience, he should no longer deny him anything concerning the customs of his fathers, lest, provoked, he should be forced to show in action how he felt about what Anselm was doing against him.

For, as some who were aware of his secrets later made known, he had resolved either to injure Anselm with some serious bodily harm or certainly to drive him dishonorably across the sea, and finally to seize everything belonging by right to the Church, if he did not find him completely prepared to carry out his will in the matter of the well-known dispute.

When Father Anselm learned this, he replied:

“The messengers whom I sent to Rome concerning the words reported by the bishops have now returned and, as they say, have brought letters attesting to the truth. Let the letters themselves, I beg you, be examined, in case something may be found in them that permits me to yield to his will.”

“By no means,” he said, “will I tolerate such evasions any longer. I wish to have a final decision in the case. What have I to do with the pope concerning my possessions? Whatever my predecessors possessed in this kingdom is mine. If anyone wishes to take these things from me, let everyone who loves me know with certainty that he is my enemy.”

The prelate then replied:

“I neither take from him, nor wish to take from him, anything that I know to be his. Nevertheless, let him know that, not even to ransom my own life, will I consent to his doing what I have now heard is prohibited in the Roman council, unless a sentence of absolution from the prohibitions proceeds from that same See from which the binding force of those decrees proceeded.”

The words of this division multiplied and became so grievous that the sons of the Church greatly feared that they would immediately lose their Father.

We saw the very princes on whose counsels the king relied, groaning as they considered the future evils, wet with tears.

The Church offered prayers and supplications to Christ, and with devout lamentation appealed to him to look upon his own mercy and halt the impending evils.

Meanwhile, in a subdued voice, the king sent word to the prelate and begged him with many prayers that he himself should go to Rome and, by his own resourcefulness, try to obtain for him what the others had been unable to obtain, lest the king, by losing the rights of his predecessors, become less worthy in their eyes.

The Father perceived where this was leading and replied:

“If it pleases you, let these matters be deferred until Easter, so that, after hearing the counsel of the bishops and the primates of the kingdom who are not now present, they may answer this matter.”

The case was concluded on those terms for that occasion, and they departed from one another in peace.

**[Note: [Col. 0441D]]** The year, as is demonstrated shortly afterward, was 1103, when Easter fell on 29 March.

At Easter, therefore, he came to the court. He consulted the nobility of the kingdom, who were present, concerning the matter, and received the unanimous opinion of the council: namely, that it would be equitable for him, on account of so important a matter, not to shrink from the hardship of the journey.

He reports:

“Since you all wish me to go, I, although weak in body and near to old age, shall undertake the journey to which you advise me to go, as far as God grants me strength. Its outcome will be in his hands. Nevertheless, if I am able to reach the Apostolic Lord, know that he will do nothing at my request or on my advice that could conflict either with the liberty of the churches or with my honor.”

They said:

“Our lord the king will send his legate with you to present his prayers and the affairs of the kingdom to Apostolic ears; you need only bear witness to what he says is true.”

He replied:

“What I have said, I say; and, God’s mercy assisting me, I shall not contradict one who speaks the truth.”

When the Easter festivities were over, Anselm departed from the court, hastening to leave England as quickly as possible.

For his mind had been wounded in some way by the fact that the king, as I have said, was unwilling either personally or through his men to hear what the letters recently brought from Rome contained.

Some people thought that the king acted thus because they gradually realized that the contents of those same letters had already been revealed to him by one of those whom Anselm had sent to Rome.

Anselm therefore feared that, if the pope did not agree in the letters themselves with the words of the bishops, the oft-mentioned sentence of excommunication might entangle certain persons on account of the investitures of churches that had taken place and also on account of the consecrations of certain abbots whom, at that time, Bishop Robert of Lincoln and John of Bath had invested and consecrated. He would not be able to abstain from communion with them without causing a grave scandal.

He had not yet examined the letters, taking care that, if the king should perhaps change his mind and demand that they be examined, and should find them closed by their seal, he would not have something which he could justly object against their authority.

He therefore judged that he must hasten out of England, lest, by communicating with excommunicated persons there, he should become implicated in some offense of excommunication.

We therefore came to Canterbury. After staying there no more than four days, and receiving permission for the sacred blessing from the monks, his most beloved sons, as well as being followed with immense devotion by the great multitude of citizens and surrounding peoples, we hastened to the seaport.

We boarded ships and landed at Wissant.

These events took place in the year of the incarnate Word 1103, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April].

Thus, invested with the king’s peace and all his possessions, he crossed the sea and took the open route through Boulogne in order to reach Normandy, relying on the generous service of certain nobles of that land.

When he had arrived at Bec—where, with what devotion, affection, joy, and every kind of delight he was received, I shall pass over, since I think no one could adequately express it—he there unsealed the letters mentioned above.

What he found in them will therefore be made clear by the text of the letters, which we reproduce below:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable brother and fellow bishop of Canterbury: greetings and blessing.

“We received your most pleasing letters of affection …” etc. See under Paschal II.

When Anselm had come from Bec to Chartres at the feast of Pentecost, intending to undertake his journey from there, he received advice from Ivo, bishop of that city, and from many men whose counsel was not to be despised: it would be better to defer the journey he had begun to another time than, in that season, to expose himself and his companions to the torments of Italian heat.

For the heat of summer was then burning everything everywhere, but especially, as was reported, in Italy, so that it was scarcely tolerable for the inhabitants and harsh and unbearable for travelers.

Understanding this, and trusting the advice, the Father returned to Bec. He remained there until the middle of August, tirelessly attending to the edification of the monks.

**[Note: [Col. 0443D–0444D]]** This is that Ivo of Chartres, famous for his writings and virtues, ordained in 1092 and deceased in 1115. A brief collection of his praises from the *Martyrology of Chartres* may be found in the work of the Sammarthani.

Afterward he returned to the road to Chartres.

What should I do? If I were to undertake to describe one by one the meetings with powerful men, the honors, and the services offered to him beyond what he wished to receive, I would certainly burden others, already occupied with other matters, by my excessive prolixity.

Let it therefore suffice to say briefly that, everywhere protected by divine assistance, he completed the journey in the greatest peace and prosperity and reached Rome safely with all his companions.

Accordingly, when he arrived, a certain William, sent by the king of the English, had preceded the Romans by several days, intending through his own efforts to bring the case he knew was to be argued to the king’s desired outcome. This William had come to Rome in the same way, sent against that same man by another king; and, as the sequence of events outlined above indicates, he had exerted all his strength in support of the ecclesiastical affairs then being conducted.

When Anselm’s arrival was announced to the pontiff of the Apostolic See, he immediately sent word and begged him to spend that day and the following one resting from the fatigue of his journey at Saint Peter’s, and then to present himself at the Lateran. That fatherly command Anselm graciously received and obeyed. On the third day he entered the lodging that Pope Urban had assigned him in the Lateran palace, as we mentioned above. He was then honorably presented to the pope, who declared that both he himself and the Roman Curia, which had gathered there, were exceedingly glad at his arrival.

On the day appointed thereafter, the matter for which he had come especially to Rome was ordered to be brought forward. William too was present, devoting his full attention to the embassy he was undertaking: namely, to secure by apostolic authority for King Henry all the customs and practices of his father and brother. He also set forth the condition of the kingdom and the king’s generosity toward the Romans, by which he attempted to prove that, through an even greater and more distinguished elevation than that enjoyed by other kings, the kings of the English had anciently made use of the Apostolic See’s liberality. For that reason, he argued, it would not only be burdensome and dishonorable for the present king to lose the rights of his predecessors, but, as he claimed to know with certainty, it would also bring great harm to the Romans if this occurred; and, should they perhaps find no opportunity to recover their position, they would later have cause to lament it.

What more is needed? Some Romans were persuaded by these and other arguments, and were drawn into the king’s case, loudly asserting that the reasoning being advanced ought to be admitted and that the wishes of so great a man should not be set aside for any consideration.

Throughout this, Anselm remained silent, awaiting in everything the judgment of the supreme pontiff. He did not wish to offer his words as a means by which a mortal man might become the door of God’s Church. Otherwise, Christ would be set aside—Christ who declares that he is the door of the sheep, and through whom, if anyone enters, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture (John 10:9)—and those wishing to enter the sheepfold would climb in by another way, becoming, as it were, not shepherds of the sheep but thieves and robbers (ibid., 10:1).

Nevertheless, the shepherd of the pontiffs himself, while remaining silent about everything and examining with prudent judgment what each person said, concluded that William, assuming that Roman favor meant the pope would now deny him none of what he sought, burst out and said:

“Whatever may be said on either side, I wish all who are present to know that my lord, the king of the English, will not allow himself to lose the investitures of the churches, even at the cost of losing his kingdom.”

Then the apostolic man spoke these few words:

“If, as you say, your king will not suffer the grants of churches to be taken from him even at the cost of losing his kingdom, know this—for I say it before God—that Pope Paschal will never allow him to retain them with impunity, even for the redemption of his own life.”

When William heard this, he was greatly disturbed. But the Romans, applauding the pontiff’s words, unanimously expressed the wish that such a judgment should be far removed from all the sons of the Church—namely, that the Apostolic See would never make any layman the door of God’s sheepfold. Therefore, they said, another answer should be given to the king, one that would both gradually soothe him and lead him toward proper conduct, and prevent Rome from incurring the offense of other princes.

Accordingly, on the advice of the Romans, the pope granted the king certain of his paternal customs, while entirely prohibiting ecclesiastical investitures. He also temporarily declared him free from the excommunication which, as we stated above, his predecessor had imposed, but retained under the chain of excommunication, in order to preserve the discipline of ecclesiastical severity, those alone who had received investitures from the king’s hand or would thereafter receive them, until they had made worthy satisfaction for so great an offense.

Thus the royal case that was being heard was brought to a conclusion at Rome in this manner. The pope entrusted the satisfaction of the invested persons to the judgment and disposition of Anselm.

After this, Anselm, having discussed with the pontiff many matters concerning the observance of the Christian religion—matters which, after the principal business of his journey, were not insignificant—asked that his return be protected by the apostolic blessing. The pope said to him:

“May the blessing you desire accompany you everywhere, just as you yourself wish. And, so that you may not seem to depart immune from the thresholds of the Church’s shepherds, behold, we present you with letters written in their name and strengthened by the seal of their authority; with our own hand we give them to you, and by their testimony we confirm forever, for you and your successors, what they contain.”

When the letters had been given, Anselm kissed the Father, commended us who were with him to God, and was thus dismissed in peace. The text of the letters is as follows:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, bishop of Canterbury: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the petitions of your fraternity,” etc. See [the text] in Paschal II.

When we were therefore leaving Rome, William remained behind, claiming that he had bound himself by a vow to visit Saint Nicholas. In reality, he intended to stay in Rome and, if possible, in Anselm’s absence to divert the pontiff from the judgment he had been unable to overturn while Anselm was present. Since he could not do this at all, he obtained from the pope persuasive letters to be delivered to the king, so that he would not appear to have accomplished nothing; and thus he changed his route for returning from Roman territory.

As we were traveling through the Alps under the guidance of the glorious Countess Matilda,

[Note: [Col. 0445D] This is the celebrated Countess Matilda, most faithful to the Apostolic See. Francis Maria Florentinius published her Life in Italian. We have often discussed her, especially on 18 March, in the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca.]

we found him at Piacenza. We were greatly astonished at how swiftly the man had traveled from Saint Nicholas.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] By “the Alps,” as often elsewhere, the Apennine mountain is meant.]

The text of the letter that he carried to the king is as follows:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious and glorious king of the English, Henry: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“In the letters that you recently sent to us,” etc. See [the text] in Paschal.

We, together with William, then left the territory of Piacenza and, protected by God’s grace, reached Lyon safe and unharmed, intending to celebrate there the approaching feast of the Nativity of the Lord. But William was in haste and did not wish to turn aside with us to Lyon. Separating himself from the Father’s company, he said to him:

“I thought that our case would proceed differently at Rome, and for that reason I have until now delayed disclosing what my lord the king ordered me to say to you. But now, since I am preparing to return to him with all speed, I do not wish to conceal any longer what he commands. He says that if you return to him in such a way as to make yourself in every respect the kind of man whom your predecessors are known to have made themselves toward his predecessors, then he will gladly desire and welcome your return to England.”

The Father replied:

“Will you say no more?”

“I am speaking prudently,” he said.

Nothing further was said about this matter. But he replied:

“I know what you are saying, and I understand.”

Thus they separated from one another over these matters. Anselm, received with the highest honor and joy by the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and by the entire clergy, was led into the greater church, where everyone treated him as the Father and lord of the place.

Meanwhile, messengers and letters were sent to the king of England, informing him of the substance of what had happened; and Anselm did not conceal, among other matters, what he had received from William on the king’s behalf. The letter was as follows:

“To his reverend lord, Henry, king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.

“Although you know through William of Warelwast what we did at Rome, I shall nevertheless briefly explain what concerns me. I came to Rome and set before the lord pope the case for which I had come. He replied that he in no way wished to depart from the decisions of his predecessors. Moreover, he ordered me to have no communion with those who, after learning of this prohibition, had received investitures of churches from your hand, unless they did penance and abandoned, without hope of recovery, what they had received; nor was I to have communion with the bishops who had consecrated such men, unless they presented themselves for judgment before the Apostolic See. The aforesaid William can bear witness to all this, if he wishes.

“When William and I parted from one another, he recalled on your behalf the love and kindness that you have always shown me. He then admonished me, as your archbishop, to make myself such that I might enter England in a condition in which I could be with you as my predecessor was with your father, and that you might treat me with the same honor and freedom with which your father treated my predecessor. From these words I understood that, unless I made myself such a man, you would not wish me to return to England.

“For your love and kindness I give thanks. But to be with you as my predecessor was with your father I cannot, since I neither dare do homage to you nor, because of the aforesaid prohibition issued in my hearing, dare communicate with those who have received investitures of churches from your hand.

“I therefore ask you, if it pleases you, to let me know your will: whether, in the manner I have described, I may return to England in your peace and in possession of my office. I am ready to offer faithfully to you and to the people entrusted to me by divine disposition the service of my office, to the extent of my ability and knowledge, while preserving regular obedience.

“But if this does not please you, I think that, if any harm to souls should result from it, it will not be my fault. May Almighty God so reign in your heart that you may in all things reign in his grace.”

When these matters had taken place, Anselm remained at Lyon, retaining only a few of his own people with him, and inhabiting the house of the aforementioned pontiff in complete peace and quiet. He awaited his messengers and did not withdraw, even for an hour, in word or deed from the things that belong to God.

[Col. 0447B]

## BOOK FOUR

When William reached England and explained the sequence of events to King Henry, the king immediately ordered all the revenues of the archbishopric of Canterbury to be diverted to his own uses. He did, however, entrust the collection of those revenues to two men belonging to the archbishop, with this understanding: a person can scarcely believe it without reflection, but they were to show so much care that they would devote themselves all the more diligently to the other men and possessions of their lord, ensuring that they were not harassed, oppressed, or plundered, the greater the faith and oath by which they were known to be bound to him.

Whether or not they obeyed such considerate piety and such pious consideration, since the matter does not greatly concern me, I would spend my effort at writing in vain by discussing it. For the Lord will come to illuminate hidden things and to distribute to each person his rewards with an impartial balance. With God as my guide, I shall proceed along the path of narration that I have begun.

After some time had passed, one of the Canterbury monks, named Everard, came to us carrying a letter from the king to Anselm. In it the king plainly testified that he was the author of what William had said when departing from Anselm, as we have stated above—namely, that Anselm should not return to England unless he first promised that he would observe for the king all the customs of his father and brother.

When Anselm refused to do this, he remained at Lyon, stripped of his possessions, living near the often-mentioned venerable Hugh, bishop of that city, for a full year and four months. What evils arose throughout England from this prolonged exile, or with what intention some people, desiring his return and therefore paying insufficient attention to the truth of the matter, may have attributed his exile to him, will, I think, become clearer if I insert briefly into this work some of the things committed to writing and sent to him by religious men who loved God.

A certain servant of God wrote to him as follows:

“To the venerable lord and holy Father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, his most devoted servant and servant of the whole household of the Lord: greetings in the Lord.

“Considering the poverty of our place and of my understanding, I might rightly have decided, holy Father, not to interrupt even once or twice with the words of a simple mind the activity of your holy intellect, in which the mark of religion shines forth and a certain companion of virtue, the brightness of wisdom, gleams. Yet the calm and blessed grace of your good opinion lifts me even above myself, so that our speech, whatever it may be, may be directed to you—not that I should teach you, who scarcely need human instruction, but that I might recall with you both our sorrow and your own.

“At the beginning of this speech of ours, I ask respectfully that you agree to allow me for the moment to claim the gentler role of one who reproves piously, not the bitter deceptions of a flatterer. I would have your holiness know that immoderate grief is consuming our hearts, whose affection for you is the same, because of your absence. If I am not mistaken, you would have been more useful to our danger had you been present, at least showing yourself a sharer in your sons’ peril, than by remaining absent and, as it were, forgetting the injury done to us and to the Church, while allowing us to be troubled by impure and cruel enemies who spare neither chastity nor safety.

“I plainly consider you, holy Father, unhappy for this very reason. For if you, who once trusted in the hope of your holy purpose among your people, now found it burdensome to see England pressed by such an unexpected enemy, how deeply would you groan, how earnestly would you desire to come to our aid or to undergo with us new kinds of bitterness? Of your own accord, with no one forcing you at all, you have escaped our dangers—perhaps so that you would not feel what we are compelled to suffer and, more grievously still, to witness: certain courtiers being raised to the sacred orders, although neither canonical election nor justice [Col. 0449A] consents to this.

“For there is no doubt that, if the true doorkeeper of the Church—who is Christ—admitted these men to sacred rights, the things we daily observe in our province could not be perpetrated: the unjust and savage tyranny of princes, the plundering of the poor, and the destruction of churches, to such an extent that the place of the Lord’s body and blood loses its freedom. Widows groan; old men weep over their hardships because the very narrow portion of their livelihood, which they scarcely deserve, is torn from them. Virgins are carried off and violated in unlawful intercourse; and, what is the first evil of all, priests take wives.

“Apart from these, there are many other crimes which it is wicked or impossible even to remember or recount. If you had carefully considered the rule of ecclesiastical dispensation and the order of ancient custom, neither would any cause for exile have withdrawn you, nor would others have incurred so grave a danger because of your absence.

“Do you therefore think that you can bend the obstinacy of the enemies of God, men who would not believe God and would grant a place to truth only unwillingly? By what reasoning your fatherhood aspires to this, I do not know. For the one who has undertaken to steer a ship must keep watch all the more carefully the more he fears the storms.

“But perhaps you will be ashamed to have fled merely because of the will of envious men when, before the tribunal of Christ, you see those mighty rams of the divine flock leading choirs of souls—men whom no wolf harmed and no terror of anyone drove into flight. How blessed then will be the memory, among the others, of that most holy Father of ours, Ambrose, who, as ecclesiastical history relates, was not ashamed to stand face to face against the emperor Theodosius and to deny him the thresholds of the church on account of his guilt. What could such devotion and such steadfastness not obtain?

“Even, holy Father, if someone had been imprisoned, afflicted, and disemboweled, you ought not to have withdrawn in this manner. How much less when you have experienced none of these things, and your see has not been denied to you, but you decided to flee because of a single word spoken by a certain William, abandoning the enemy and leaving your sheep to be torn apart by the impious.

“I am therefore ashamed to recall what happened, since all, or nearly all, whom the present affliction of the churches had been awaiting for the relief of their need, taking the opportunity of fear, chose rather to succumb with you than to resist uselessly without you. What could those do who lacked a father, who had no head to support them?

“Your holiness should therefore be admonished, not instructed, to hasten your arrival at the holy mother Church, to remove the disgrace, and to extend speedy aid against our enemies, who have already pressed into the innermost chambers. It is still possible to drive out the disease while the wound appears open on the surface.

“For I know that, if you wished to return to your see, you would find many ready, as they say, to defend God’s cause bravely alongside you—unless the weakness caused by the failure of your fatherhood has enervated them.

“If, as we have heard, you wish to place England under an interdict or excommunicate it, what are my brothers and I to do? We have always been ready to obey you. I beg you to send us your instructions.

“Farewell.”

While these things, and some even worse than them, were taking place throughout England during Anselm’s exile, and certain men, distressed by the magnitude of the evils, were pressing the king to recall him—the Father of his country, so to speak—so that he might correct them, the king, moved both by the man’s religious character and by the abundance of the monstrous evils, admitted that he willingly desired what they requested, namely, the man’s return. He insisted, however, that he would in no way allow any of his paternal customs to be taken from him.

Accordingly, while we were still living at Lyon, the king himself sent messengers to Rome to work by every means to persuade the apostolic pontiff to order Anselm to return to England and submit and obey the royal will in everything. Since they were entirely unable to bend him to this, they returned as they had come, their business unsuccessful.

In those days Bishop Gualo of Paris,

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Gualo, or Galo, formerly bishop of Beauvais, became bishop of Paris in 1105. Consult the Sammarthani. Moreover, these events have already been recounted at length above in the Life of Saint Anselm, and we set them all out together on 18 January in the Life of Saint Prisca.]

coming from Rome to us, brought relics of the body of the blessed martyr Prisca that had been given to him at Rome. He gave me a very small portion of them in the presence of Father Anselm. Since the portion seemed quite small to me, I asked the bishop to increase the gift, but Anselm restrained me, saying that what I had was sufficient.

“For,” he said, “since this is itself a bone from her body, as long as it is absent from that body, the body does not possess its integrity. Therefore, if you preserve it worthily and serve in it the lady whose relic it is with whatever devotion you can, she will receive the service of your duty as gratefully as if you were serving her whole body.”

I accepted his words and carefully preserve what I received.

In the second year of our arrival from Rome at Lyon,

[Note: [Col. 0449D] This was undoubtedly the year 1105, when there is no other mention of that Lateran council except in the author of the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, under the year 1109, in these words: “In this year a council was held in the Lateran church, with Lord Paschal II presiding, in the third indiction, on the Nones of March.” If you believe that an error entered into the number of the indiction and misled the writer, so that “thirteenth” should be read instead of “third,” this year will be understood as 1105. In that same year Sabellicus and Antoninus also write that a council of 340 bishops was convened, but at Florence, which we do not readily believe; still less do we believe that the error concerning the Antichrist, said to have already been born and condemned there, belonged to Florentius, bishop of Florence, for there was never any bishop of Florence named Florentius, while Rainerius was still alive and presiding, as is mentioned elsewhere.]

Pope Paschal convened a general council at the Lateran. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit he expelled from the thresholds of the holy Church Count of Meulan, who has often been mentioned above, and his accomplices, who, as was said, were urging the king toward the crime of investiture, as well as those who had been invested by him. He quickly made this known to Anselm in the letter that we insert here:

[Col. 0451A]

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the injury inflicted upon you,” etc. See [the text] in Paschal.

When Anselm received this letter, he examined it and understood that he was waiting in vain for Roman assistance at Lyon, especially since he had already sent envoys and letters repeatedly to the pontiff of the Roman See concerning the completion of his case, and had so far received from him nothing except a certain promise of consoling expectation, postponing the matter from one appointed time to another.

He had also sent his letters to the king of England for the restoration of his possessions for the third time, and had received no reply from him except one that imposed a flattering delay. Therefore, after consulting the venerable bishop of the city of Lyon, he departed from Lyon to travel to France, while that pontiff himself and all the people of the land mourned his departure.

When we came to Charité near Cluny,

[Note: [Col. 0451D] In the Cluniac Library, column 1711, the priory of Saint Mary of Charité on the Loire, in the diocese of Auxerre, is mentioned as having been offered to Hugh of Cluny by Gaudrius, bishop.]

Anselm learned that the Countess of Blois, the elder daughter of King William, named Adela,

[Note: [Col. 0451D] How long-standing the intimacy between Adela and Anselm had already been, learn from Anselm’s letter to Adela, which is the last of Book I.]

was ill at her castle at Blois.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Blois, commonly called Blois, lies between Orléans and Tours on the Loire mentioned above.]

He therefore changed the route by which he had planned to go to Reims—since Manasses,

[Note: [Col. 0452D] This was Manasses II, elected to Reims in 1096 and deceased in 1107.]

the bishop of that city, had repeatedly and earnestly petitioned him through intermediaries—and went to Blois to visit the countess, as was his custom everywhere, avoiding every mark of reproach.

The countess had indeed ministered to him with magnificent generosity both on this occasion and during his other exile, and had chosen him, after God, as a holy and religious man, to be the instructor and guardian of her life. If, therefore, he failed to visit her when she was, as was reported, at the point of death, he would not escape the mark of just reproach.

When we came to her and found that, after her illness had subsided, she had nearly recovered, she detained us most courteously in the castle for several days. During those days the bishop and the countess often conversed with one another: the bishop diligently urging her, in accordance with his office, toward good conduct, while she questioned the bishop, as a father, about matters that she knew she ought to inquire into, according to the quality of his life.

When Anselm was asked by the countess about the reason for his return to France, he informed her of it and did not conceal that he had come to excommunicate her brother Henry, king of the English, because of the injury he had inflicted upon God and upon Anselm for two years and more. When she heard this, she was deeply grieved at her brother’s condemnation and resolved to work toward reconciling him with the pontiff. She therefore persuaded the man to go with her to Chartres.

At that time the king himself was in Normandy and had brought almost the whole region under his control. The power of Robert, count of the Normans—that is, of the king’s brother—had then become so despised by everyone that scarcely anyone was willing to do for him anything that is ordinarily done for the prince of a land among all peoples. His pious heart and his slight desire for earthly things, which flourished together in him, had brought this upon him.

Almost all the leading men of Normandy therefore immediately went over to the king on his arrival, despising their own lord the count and setting aside the loyalty they owed him. They ran after the king’s gold and silver and handed over to him their cities, castles, and towns.

When the king learned through the countess’s messengers of Anselm’s arrival and of why he had left Burgundy and come to France, he investigated how he might turn the man’s mind away from his declared intention. After consulting with his own men, he begged the countess through messengers to bring the man to Normandy to speak with him, promising that, for the sake of peace, he would yield in many respects to his wishes concerning the former dispute.

What more is needed? When the appointed time arrived, the archbishop and the countess came together to the castle called Aigle for the king’s conference, as he had requested. They found that the king was rejoicing with intense happiness at Anselm’s arrival and had descended considerably from his former harshness.

After they had conferred, the king restored to Anselm the revenues of his pontificate, and they received one another back into their former friendship. Since certain people were diligently working to ensure that the bishop would immediately return to England, the king agreed, but only on the condition that Anselm withdraw his communion in no respect from any of those who had received investitures of churches from him or from those who had consecrated them.

Anselm did not at all accept this condition, since he did not wish to transgress the pope’s command in anything. He therefore chose to remain outside England until those whom they had agreed to send to Rome to settle this matter and certain other matters that they could not resolve between themselves on that occasion had returned.

These events took place in the third year after our departure from England, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August.

Because of the great joy that the king felt within himself over Anselm’s reconciliation, you would have seen him, while we remained in the aforementioned castle, scarcely ever allow Anselm to come to him. Whenever there was anything to be done between them, he himself always went to Anselm.

For rumor had already spread widely in many places throughout England, France, and Normandy that the king himself was about to be excommunicated by Anselm. Consequently, since the king’s power was not especially loved, many evils were being plotted against him, and people thought that these would be inflicted upon him more effectively once he had been excommunicated by so great a man.

Knowing this, he rejoiced greatly that the sentence of the man had been turned away from him. In the end, every evil that had been awaiting him was turned away from him when Anselm, who had been estranged, returned to his friendship.

Therefore, so that the man might return more quickly to his bishopric, to the joy of his people and the restoration of the entire country, the king promised that he would send his messengers to Rome in such a way that Anselm could be present with his court in England at the next Nativity of Christ.

He also sent letters to England, ordering that all Anselm’s possessions and people, wherever they might be, should remain in peace and quiet; that no one should trouble or prosecute them; that, freed from every debt, they should retain honorably what they held; and that in everything they should depend upon Anselm’s wish and command.

When these orders became known to the people connected with the archbishopric, a kind of unexpected ray of sunlight immediately shone upon them, bringing them out to a considerable degree from the cruelty and darkness of their former oppression.

Afterward, Anselm returned to the monastery at Bec, and the king to England. Certain minor obstacles arose, however, and the envoys who were supposed to be sent to Rome remained for a long time beyond the appointed date. This shook the hearts of many with intense astonishment. They thought that such a delay in the man’s return was a deception of the devil, and they clearly saw that the whole of Christianity in England was being savagely destroyed.

This will, I think, become clearer if I briefly add below some writings concerning matters sent to us during this delay by a man of no negligible authority. He writes, among other things, as follows:

“Most beloved Father and lord, although you know very well what you ought to do and what you wish to do, nevertheless it seems to almost every person of sound and wise judgment that what is being conducted between you and the king under such prolonged expectation is nothing other than a deceitful illusion and mocking delay of the devil. To speak more plainly, it is the daily diminution and complete destruction of the entire Church of the English, of Christian religion, and of Christian law.

“The possessions of churches that have remained deprived of pastors for so long are being plundered. The order of holy religion within them is neglected and destroyed. The rulers of Christian law are no longer rulers but destroyers, and, according to the will and pleasure of the king, have become almost entirely subverters of all justice.

“What shall I say about the clergy, who have almost all been turned back to their former wickedness? What about the laity? They, and especially the princes, scarcely take wives except from among their own relations; they secretly betroth them, knowingly keep and defend those to whom they are betrothed in violation of ecclesiastical law.

“What shall be said about the Sodomites, whom you yourself excommunicated in the great council until they should do penance and confess, and about the long-haired men whom, later, at the solemnity of Easter, clothed in your pontifical vestment and before the whole people, you removed from the thresholds of the holy Church? You do not come to their aid as you ought, and there is not even one person in the entire kingdom who dares, on our behalf, to rebuke or attempt to correct these and many other things contrary to God and to every servant of God.

“If you wish to hear the truth, I confess that all these things are being done much worse than can be set down in writing, to such an extent that the king himself declares that there has never been such a forceful display of wickedness in this country as there is now.

“All these things unquestionably concern you alone and are imputed to your holiness. Consider, therefore, and attend to the burden you undertook and the one to whom you entrusted the care of it in your place, when you, who were appointed to oppose such things, remain for so long absent from the kingdom in which they are practiced for no reason.

“Consider also, if it pleases you, whether your heart is so free for God alone and whether you are now preserved in such security that you ought not to devote another vigilance to such misery of souls.

“I know, and I know well, that you know perfectly what you are doing; but your very knowledge benefits us exceedingly little. For we still see no fruit advancing toward the common good from your business, prolonged for so long, while every day we observe on all sides evils multiplying in the Church and among God’s people solely because of your absence.”

This man, hating so many evils, wrote these things because he believed that Anselm was delaying his entry into England solely by his own choice. In reality, however, King Henry would not allow him to enter in any manner unless he set aside obedience to the pope, as we mentioned above, and communicated with bishops and abbots who had been excommunicated.

While Anselm was staying at Reims—for he had gone there after being overcome by the earnest prayers of the bishop and canons of that place, and had been received with greater honor and festive welcome than can be expressed in writing by all who lived there, and was being detained for several days near Bishop Manasses with great and dutiful affection—the same king sent him a letter, which we insert here:

“To the most reverend and beloved Father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, Henry, by the grace of God king of the English: greetings and the affection of every good will.

“Venerable Father, do not be displeased that the journey of those whom I have decided to send to Rome to conduct my business has been delayed for so long. As soon as William of Warelwast reaches you, he will explain the matter to you; I am sending him to Rome to conduct this business, as we have decided.

“I therefore humbly beg and devoutly beseech you to send Baldwin of Tournai to Rome together with the same William, to negotiate our affair and, God willing, bring it to completion.

“Farewell.”

To this Anselm wrote the following letter:

“To his most beloved lord, Henry, glorious king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: faithful service with prayers.

“Since your greatness greets me in your letter so honorably and with such an expression of goodwill, I give you great thanks, as I ought. But since you so earnestly ask me not to be displeased that your envoy, who is to be sent to Rome, has been delayed so long, I certainly ought not, insofar as it lies within my power, to disregard your request; yet the matter concerns God more than me. Therefore, with a faithful heart and kindly disposition, I tell you what I ought not to keep silent.

For me to be displeased by something is not a great matter, unless I am displeased for God’s sake; but to displease God in anything is by no means to be disregarded. Certainly God is not a little displeased when a bishop is deprived of his possessions—something which, by God’s grace inspiring you, you have already corrected. But he judges it exceedingly grave when a bishop is separated from his office and a Church from its bishop without a cause approved by God.

It is therefore advantageous for your soul that you earnestly strive to have me—whatever sort of bishop I may be—restored more quickly, in peace and honor, to the Church which God entrusted to your royal authority to protect, and to your kingdom; and that the opportunity to exercise, according to my ability, the office for which I was placed there not be impeded any longer [Col. 0455B].

I must also greatly fear that this may displease God and that the lord pope may justly rebuke me, because, after you and I met together at the castle called Eagle, I have not sent him our envoy in so long a time—someone through whom he might learn what had been done between us concerning such an important matter and what remained to be done, and through whom I might receive his counsel and command.

Therefore it is dangerous for me to wait so long for your envoy, whom, as I understood from your words, I hoped would return to Rome before the coming Nativity of the Lord—especially since, for some reason and by some plan unknown to me, you now set no deadline for me. Since, then, my inability to be present with the Church entrusted to me ought to matter more to me than any earthly possession, I ask you to name for me, in your letters, some near date when I may expect your envoy to go to Rome; for I dare not delay—if I may put it strongly—beyond the coming Nativity of the Lord without sending my own envoy.”

He also wrote to the often-mentioned Robert, count of Meulan, at that time the man by whose counsel the king himself arranged all his affairs, in the following manner:

“Anselm the archbishop to his lord and friend Robert, count of Meulan, greetings.

“You know that, when the king and I met at the castle of Eagle, it was said that the king would send his envoy to Rome concerning those matters on which we could not agree except through the lord pope. I understood this to mean that the envoy would return before the coming Nativity of the Lord. But you see that my lord the king is delaying in doing what he then said he would do.

“He commands me only this: although I wished to send my envoy with his, I should not be displeased that his envoy alone is delayed, while he sets no date for me to know when that envoy will come. Hence some think and say that the king does not greatly care to hasten my return to England, so that the Church of God—which God entrusted to him to protect and which has now been desolate for almost three years—may, by the return and presence of its living pastor, be consoled, and may rejoice in those who love and desire the counsel for their souls of which it has long been deprived.

“Therefore I tell you that I greatly fear he may call down God’s anger upon himself and upon those by whose counsel he delays responding to so necessary and reasonable a matter, since it lies with him, and he is able to ensure that he loses nothing of what, according to God, belongs to the royal authority [Col. 0456B].

“As a friend, and as an archbishop—whatever sort of one I may be—I advise him and those around him not to strive more to satisfy his will than God’s will, since God will at some point satisfy his own will against the will of those who act in this way. Advise him, then, and yourselves, before God displays the anger which he has so far held back, waiting for you to humble yourselves before his will. May God direct him and his counselors toward his true honor and true advantage.”

We have recorded these things in this way so that anyone who reads or hears them may clearly understand to whom he ought chiefly to attribute the evils that occurred in England while Anselm was in exile, and the prolongation of his exile.

Accordingly, envoys were afterward sent to Rome: on Anselm’s behalf, the monk Baldwin, a man who was genuinely a lover of the holy liberty of the Church and of every good thing; and on the king’s behalf, the often-mentioned William, who would act for the liberty of the Church as he was accustomed to do.

How many and how great were the oppressions with which all England was oppressed during this period, I know is difficult to describe. The king himself, having departed from Normandy because he had been unable to subjugate the whole of it to himself in the manner described above, returned to England so that, relying on greater wealth when he came back, he might subdue what remained, after disinheriting his brother.

In collecting this money, there was no consideration of piety or mercy among the collectors; rather, as those who came from there testified to us, cruel exaction raged against everyone [Col. 0456D]. In the end, they said, one could see people who had nothing to give either driven from their little houses, or exposed to complete plunder after the doors of their homes had been torn off and carried away [Note: [Col. 0455D] A similar practice, once used in Belgium, is attested by a custom still existing in the United Provinces: when someone does not immediately produce a publicly imposed monetary contribution, even after being warned, officials tear his door from its hinges and carry it away; it is not restored until money or security has been provided.], or reduced to utter poverty after their scant household goods had been taken away, or certainly afflicted and tormented in other pitiable ways. [Note: [Col. 0456D] That is, enormous offenses, committed as though openly, or outside all justice or excuse. In French, forfait; concerning this word and several terms derived from it, Spelmann writes much in his Glossary, as do many others. Yet none touches upon its etymology. A little below, forisfactura is used for a monetary penalty exacted for an offense.]

Against those who appeared to possess something, certain new and contrived forfeitures were brought forward; and since they did not dare enter into a legal proceeding in which they would have to defend themselves against the king of the land, their possessions were taken away and they were plunged into severe misery.

Some may perhaps regard these matters as trivial to recount, since many such things were done not only under King Henry but also under his brother, to say nothing of their father, King William. Yet these seemed to them more serious and intolerable because far less than usual could be found to take from people who had already been stripped and exhausted.

Moreover, at the Council of London, as we said above, the association of women had been forbidden to all the priests and canons of England; and while Anselm was in exile, many of them had violated that prohibition by retaining—or certainly by taking back—their women.

Since the king would not tolerate this sin going unpunished, he ordered his ministers to prosecute them and to collect their money as expiation for this sin. But when very many of them were found to be free from that transgression, the money sought for the prince’s use supplied less than the collectors had hoped. Therefore the judgment was changed—or rather turned against the innocent along with the guilty: all the Churches that possessed parishes were placed under a financial obligation, and each was ordered to redeem itself by a specified sum of money, paid by the person serving God in it.

It was therefore a wretched spectacle. When the storm of this exaction was raging, some who either had nothing to give or, abhorring this unheard-of demand, wished to give nothing for such a cause, were shamefully seized, imprisoned, and tortured. Then it happened that the king himself came to London.

Nearly two hundred priests, it is said, assembled, dressed in white and in priestly stoles, and went barefoot to meet the king as he proceeded to his palace, imploring mercy with one voice. But he, perhaps distracted—as often happens—by many matters, was moved by no compassion at their prayers; or at least, treating them as men devoid of all religion, he did not deign to give them any gracious reply, but ordered them to be swiftly driven from his sight.
