Covered in confusion upon confusion, they approached the queen and begged her to intervene. She, it is said, moved by compassion, burst into tears, but, restrained by fear, was prevented from intervening.

At that time many other things of this kind were reported as having been done throughout England. But, pursuing brevity, we think that the few matters related here may suffice for the purpose of the present little work.

Nevertheless, it must be said that evils inundated England in those days to such an extent that the bishops themselves—who had always attempted to suppress the liberty of the Church, and Anselm, who strove to uphold and defend that same liberty, as can be understood from what has preceded—were compelled by the immensity of such evils to send Anselm a message with a letter, to request that his assistance be offered to them, and to promise that henceforth they would follow him in the affairs of God, as their father.

But, in my opinion, these matters will become clearer if the letter itself which they sent him is set down. It is as follows:

“To their most beloved father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, Gerard, archbishop of York, and Robert of Chester, Herbert of Norwich, Ralph of Chichester, and Samson, bishops of Worcester, and William, elect of Winchester, greetings.

“We have endured peace, and it has withdrawn farther away; we sought good things, and turmoil has prevailed. The roads of Zion mourn (Lam. 1:4), because the uncircumcised trample them. The Temple grieves, because laymen have burst into the Holy of Holies and even upon the altar itself.

“Rise up, as once did that old man Mattathias (1 Macc. 2:1). In your sons you have the strength of Judas, the vigor of Jonathan, and the wisdom of Simon (ibid., 3–5). These men will fight the Lord’s battle with you; and, if you are gathered to your fathers before us, we shall receive from your hand the inheritance of your labor.

“But now you must no longer be sluggish. Why do you wander abroad while your sheep perish without a shepherd? You have no excuse remaining before God. We are ready not only to follow you but, if you command it, to go before you. Come, then, to us; come quickly—or order us, or some of us, to come to you—lest, while we are separated from you, the counsels of those who seek their own interests incline you toward the wrong side.

“For in this matter we now seek not what is ours, but what is God’s.”

Anselm’s reply to them:

“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friends and fellow bishops whose letter he has received, greetings.

“I grieve and inwardly share the sufferings which you and the Church of England endure. But for the present I cannot assist you according to either my will or yours, because I am not yet certain what, or how much, I may rely upon until I learn through our envoys—whom I expect to return from Rome shortly—what they have accomplished with the lord pope.

“Nevertheless, it is good and pleasing to me that at last you recognize what your patience has brought you to—or, to put it more mildly, that you recognize the consequences of your patience—and that you promise me your help, not in my cause but in God’s, and invite me to come to you without delay.

“For although I cannot act in this way because the king does not yet wish me to be in England unless I disagree with the pope’s command and agree with the king’s will, and although, as I have said, I am not yet certain what I can do, I nevertheless rejoice in your goodwill, in the episcopal steadfastness which you promise, and in the exhortation which you give me.

“As for sending some of you to me, as you request, lest, while we are separated from one another, those who seek their own interests distort my counsel, I do not presently think it necessary. For I hope in God that no one will be able to turn my heart away from the truth, insofar as I understand it; and I hope that God will soon show me what I can do, and that I shall inform you as quickly as I can.

“As for what you should do in the meantime, your prudence understands well enough. Nevertheless, I say this: insofar as, by hoping in God, I perceive it in my conscience, I would not consent to redeem my life, nor would I make myself the minister or executor of that evil which I hear has recently been promulgated against the Churches of England.

“Farewell.”

Meanwhile, as frequent messengers came to Normandy from England, what the king was doing to the priests of England became widely known. It brought not only those who were nourished by his infamy but also those who were nourished by his praise into hatred and reproach of him.

But Anselm, unable to endure such an evil reputation for the king and desiring to recall him from so great an injustice, wrote to him about the matter once, and again, and received written replies from him each time. He thought these letters ought to be recorded below in the order in which they were sent, believing that they might serve future generations as an example, unless God, in his deeper counsel, should calm the great evils now taking place before his eyes in the kingdom of the English.

In this connection, however, we hope that those who read or hear these things will not be angry with us because we are so occupied with writing letters. For this is a certain—and substantial—part of the matter we are handling, and no affair can be known in its entirety when its parts are unknown.

The text of the letters themselves is therefore as follows:

“To his most beloved lord Henry, by God’s grace king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, faithful prayers with faithful service.

“It is my duty, if I hear that you are doing something which is not beneficial to your soul, not to keep silent about it to you, lest—God forbid—God become angry both with you, if you do what displeases him, and with me because of my silence.

“I hear that your excellence is exercising vengeance upon the priests of England and exacting forfeitures from those who did not observe the command of the council which, with your support, I held at London together with the other bishops and religious persons. Until now, this has been unheard of and unprecedented in the Church of God, whether by any king or any prince.

“For according to God’s law, it does not belong to anyone to punish such a fault except the individual bishops within their own parishes; or, if the bishops themselves should be negligent in this, the archbishop and primate.

“I therefore beg you, as my most beloved lord, whose soul I love more than the present life of my body, and I advise you, as one truly faithful to your body and soul, not to plunge yourself into so grave a sin against ecclesiastical custom; and, if you have already begun, to desist completely.

“For I tell you that you ought greatly to fear that money taken in this manner—quite apart from how much harm it does to the soul—will not, when it is spent, help your earthly affairs as much as it will later disturb them.

“Finally, you know that you received me in Normandy into your peace, and restored me to possession of my archbishopric; and the care and punishment of such an offense belongs especially to the archbishopric, since I am a bishop more for spiritual care than for earthly possession.

“May almighty God direct your heart in this and in your other actions according to his will, so that after this life he may lead you to his glory. Amen.”

“Henry, by God’s grace king of the English, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings.

“On the day of Saint Gregory, letters sealed with your seal were delivered to me at Tunbridge. Through them you commanded me concerning matters which greatly surprise me, because I believe that what I did, I did through you.

“On the day of the Ascension of the Lord I shall have all my barons gathered with me, and, following their counsel, I shall give you such a suitable reply that, when I speak with you, I do not think you will blaspheme me on that account [Note: [Col. 0459D] You will often find blasphemare used in medieval writers for ‘to rebuke,’ ‘to reprimand,’ or ‘to disparage.’ Hence, by contraction, the French words blâme and blâmer—meaning ‘reproach’ and ‘to reproach’—are derived from this word, which elsewhere refers to God and the gods but here is restricted to human insults. The Normans, transferred from Gaul to England, adopted the terms.].

“And whatever may happen elsewhere, know that your people, whatever the others may do, will remain in peace throughout all your lands.”

“To his most beloved lord Henry, by God’s grace king of the English, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, faithful service and faithful prayers.

“I give thanks to God and to your graciousness, which in your letter promised to give me a suitable reply concerning the matter about which I had asked you in my letter regarding the priests of England. I pray the Lord, whose counsel endures forever, to counsel you to reply and act as pleases him, and in such a way that those who faithfully love your soul may rejoice.

“As for what I read in your letter—that you believe you are doing through me what you are doing—know for certain, my lord, that it is not through me; for if it were through me, I would be acting against God.

“Therefore I still beg you, with great and faithful affection, not to persist in such an undertaking on anyone’s advice.

“Farewell.”

“Henry, king of the English, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and friendship.

“Concerning what you wrote to me about the priests, know that I have acted properly, as I think, and according to what I ought to have done. Nor should it be unknown to you that I shall cross over shortly.

“And after I have spoken with you, if I have committed any faults in these matters, I shall correct them according to the counsel of almighty God and of yourself.

“Witnessed by Waldrich the chancellor at Marlborough.”

While these things were taking place, the men who had been sent to Rome returned. William, archbishop of Rouen, had already long been suspended from episcopal office [Col. 0460D], and through these messengers Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, had interceded for him with the lord pope.

The lord pope therefore instructed Anselm to do, in his place, whatever he understood ought to be done concerning the case, knowing that no intervention in any matter could knowingly divert him from the paths of justice.

He therefore went to Rouen and explained the reason for his arrival in a synod of clergy that was then assembled. William the king’s envoy produced the letters which he had brought from Rome concerning the matter on behalf of the pope, and they were read aloud before everyone as follows:

[Col. 0461A]

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother William, bishop of Rouen, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Although the nature of your case …” etc. See in Paschal II.

The lord pope also sent this letter to Anselm:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“That the heart of the English king …” etc. See in the same place.

In those days Bohemond came to Rouen [Note: [Col. 0461D] Bohemond, prince of Antioch, married at Chartres, in 1106 after Easter, Constance, daughter of Philip, king of the French, who had previously been married to Hugh, count of Troyes.], one of the most renowned princes of the road to Jerusalem. In his company was a certain cardinal of the Roman Church named Bruno [Note: [Col. 0461D] This is Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, whose feast is celebrated on 18 July; but neither he nor any other Bruno of that period appears to have been a cardinal.].

His master of soldiers was a man named Hgyrus [Note: [Col. 0461D] As far as I know, however, the name Ilgyrus does not occur in Eastern history.], an energetic man of no insignificant reputation among his own people. He had been known to Anselm from his youth and had received many benefits from him.

Thus, while conversing familiarly with him, he discussed at length, among many other subjects, the wars he had won, the cities he had captured, the situation of places, and various other matters he had learned during the expedition to Jerusalem, all in an enjoyable conversation. He disclosed that he possessed many relics of the saints and explained how he had acquired them.

Among these—or rather, above all the others he possessed—he especially boasted of hairs of the blessed mother of God, Mary. He said that some of them had been given to him by the patriarch of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0461D] After Antioch was captured in 1098, John, the patriarch, an outstanding confessor under the Saracens, was left in his dignity. But within two years he voluntarily resigned, seeing that, as a Greek, he could not suitably preside over Latins. Bernard, a Frenchman from Valence and chaplain to the apostolic legate, was then elected, as William of Tyre records at the end of Book VI. The relics were received from one or the other of these men.], when he himself was serving as Bohemond’s master of soldiers.

Then he added:

“Confessing the truth, I would not have dared to receive these hairs if the love of that homeland in which I was born and raised had not inspired me to do so. For I hoped that I would one day reach this place and exalt that homeland of mine.

“Since, therefore, by the Lord’s protection I have not been deprived of that hope, I have decided to give two of them to this Church which holds primacy throughout all Christian Normandy; two to the abbey of Saint Peter and Saint Ouen; two to the monastery of that Virgin of virgins, in which, under your patronage, I grew to manhood; and two to you.

“For the aforesaid bishop gave me twelve of them in number, affirming that they had been plucked from the Lady herself as she stood beside the cross of her Son and a sword pierced her soul, according to what, as he asserted, he had found written in ancient records of great authority among them and preserved in the archives of the Church over which he presided.”

So much for his account.

Anselm was greatly delighted by these matters. After doing with the bishop of Rouen, Bohemond, and the men of Jerusalem what seemed necessary, he returned to Bec.

Since the hairs about which the aforementioned soldier had spoken had remained at Chartres, where Bohemond’s family and almost all his belongings were awaiting his return, the archbishop of Rouen and the abbot of Bec sent religious men to transport them [Note: [Col. 0462D] Although I do not believe this story, regarding it as a fabrication of an unsophisticated later age, I nevertheless honor the hairs themselves with reverence.].

And so it happened. As those who were bringing the relics that Rouen was to receive approached the city, the bishop, accompanied by the canons and the entire clergy of the city, by the monks of Saint Ouen, and by an immeasurable multitude of the whole people, went out to meet them in a long procession. He received them with as much honor as he could, carried them into the church, and placed them in the most sacred location.

Four of them were brought to Bec. Of these, Anselm reverently received two for the place itself and entrusted them to me for safekeeping, since I was the keeper and administrator of that chapel; and I have continued to do so to this day.

I do not know what other people think about these matters. But I know with complete certainty that the lord and reverend Father Anselm always held them in great veneration, and I myself have learned through a sacred and profound experience that they possess something great and a remarkable holiness worthy of the world’s embrace. So much for this matter.

Accordingly, when William [Note: [Col. 0462D] This William of Montfort was a cousin of the frequently mentioned Robert, count of Meulan. Anselm himself commended him by letter to the monks of Bec as exceptionally well suited to the prelacy, which he held until the year 1124. See more in Arthur du Monstier’s Neustria pia.] came to the king in England and recounted to him what had been done with the Roman pontiff concerning his business [Col. 0462C], the king was delighted by what he heard and immediately asked Anselm, through that same William, to return to his Church.

William returned to us a few days later and found Anselm ill, which greatly distressed him. By then his heart was devoted to the liberty of the Church of God, and, insofar as he could, he was diligently working to have Anselm restored to his see in peace and honor.

Fearing, therefore, that the love of the man for the place and the brothers, no less than the bodily illness by which he was weighed down, might prevent his journey to England, he began, by every means available—both personally and through us who were with him—to devise how he might draw the man away from the place and set him on the journey he desired.

First he offered prayers, appealing to him on behalf of his lord, the king of the English, asking him to visit England, desolated by his absence, by making a prompt return [Col. 0462D–0463A]. He affirmed—and by his affirmation promised—that the king himself would henceforth have an entirely ready mind to follow Anselm’s wishes in everything he might command, and would no longer wish to disagree with the Roman Church.

Then he added:

“For this reason I beg you to break off all delay in coming, lest perhaps some worldly breeze should burst forth from the opposite direction and overturn him from these resolutions.”

Hearing this, Anselm gave thanks to God for his extraordinary gift. Having obtained permission from the brothers among whom we had long been held in great love and honor, he set out for England and came to Jumièges [Note: [Col. 0463D] Jumièges, commonly called Gemmeticum, below Rouen: a large monastery, where Anselm was likewise intending to board a ship in order to cross over to England.].

There, when the illness with which he had been afflicted at Bec, as we have mentioned, returned, he was entirely unable to proceed from the place. Therefore he sent messengers to England [Col. 0463B] to inform the king of what was preventing his return.

The king was troubled by the news and deeply grieved, swearing by the word of God that he would endure all losses with greater equanimity than Anselm’s death. He therefore sent messengers back with all speed, asking the man to spare himself and to devote himself entirely to rest.

He also ordered him to take whatever he wished from what belonged to him in Normandy and to have enough supplied from it for himself and his companions; and to await the king’s own crossing in the near future. Anselm gratefully accepted this and remained there for about a month.

When his illness had then abated, he returned to Bec, thinking it would be more convenient and honorable for him to await the king’s arrival there than elsewhere. While everyone rejoiced at his return with marvelous enthusiasm, behold, a grievous calamity shook and overturned that very joy [Col. 0463C].

For such a serious illness again attacked Anselm that we expected nothing from him except death. The bishops and abbots of that land gathered and began discussing his funeral. But almighty God, in his mercy, restored him to health contrary to everyone’s expectation and thereafter filled many with great joy.

Accordingly, on the feast of the Assumption of blessed Mary, the king came to Bec. After Anselm had celebrated the solemn office of Mass, the king and Anselm met together, and at last all the matters that had drawn them in different directions found peace and agreement.

Indeed, the Churches of England which King William, King Henry’s brother, had first subjected to a tax, as I reported much earlier, the king restored to Anselm’s hands free from that exaction. He promised that, while he lived, he would take nothing from them so long as they remained without a pastor [Col. 0463D].

As for the money which he had received from the priests, as we have said, he promised this remedy: those who had not yet paid anything would pay nothing, while those who had paid would possess all their property freely, in peace and quiet, for three years.

As for everything that had been taken by his command from the archbishopric while Anselm was in exile [Col. 0464A], he promised, upon giving security, that he would return it when he had gone back to England.

When these and other matters required by the situation had been settled between the men, Anselm began his journey back to England. Relying on divine protection, he arrived safely and cheerfully at Dover with all his companions.

The exultation, joy, and hope for good with which he came to England and was received there may, I think, be understood to some extent from consideration of the evils which, as we briefly touched upon, had occurred there before his return. Therefore, leaving aside the joys of people of different ages and ranks, I shall say this briefly about the queen herself: neither earthly affairs nor any pomp of worldly glory could detain her from going ahead of the man as he visited different places [Col. 0464B]. When monks or canons customarily went out to meet him, she herself would proceed with them and, through her own arrangements, furnish his lodgings with suitable provisions.

After these events, the men who had been installed in the Churches and monasteries to exact the king’s money were expelled, and the property within and outside each church was entrusted to the persons of that church for the common benefit.

The cases of the priests were also settled, as we said the king had promised Anselm, and this was proclaimed throughout the entire kingdom.

Meanwhile, the king himself subdued Normandy by war [Note: [Col. 0463D] In the autumn of the same year, 1106. Consult Orderic Vitalis under that year, where he also lists the captives, as do Simon of Durham and other writers.], and informed Anselm of it in the following letter, which we now set down:

“Henry, king of the English, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and friendship.

“We inform your fatherhood and holiness that Robert, count of Normandy, with all the forces of cavalry and infantry whom he could assemble by entreaty and payment, fought fiercely with me on the appointed and fixed day before Tinchebray [Note: [Col. 0464D] This was the castle of the count of Mortain. The enemies attacked the king, who was besieging it, on the eve of Saint Michael’s Day, and thereby surrendered victory to him, as the already cited Simon of Durham writes.].

“At last, by God’s mercy, we conquered, without great slaughter among our own men. What more need be said? By divine mercy, God gave into our hands the duke of Normandy and the count of Mortain, William Crispin, William de Ferrières, the elder Robert de Stuteville, and others—up to four hundred knights—and ten thousand foot soldiers; and he gave us Normandy. As for those whom the sword destroyed, there is no number.

“I do not attribute this to pride or arrogance, nor to my own strength, but to the gift of divine dispensation [Col. 0464D]. Therefore, reverend Father, falling humbly and devoutly upon the knees of your holiness, I beg you to pray to the heavenly Judge, by whose decision and will this glorious and useful triumph has come to me, that it may not be for my loss and detriment but be established and strengthened as the beginning of good works and service to God and to the holy Church of God, to be maintained in tranquil peace, so that from now on it may live freely and be shaken by no storm of wars.”

Accordingly, many testified that the king had gained this victory because of the peace he had made with Anselm.

With Normandy thus organized under the king’s peace, and Duke Robert and the count of Mortain sent into England in captivity as stated above, the king himself returned to his kingdom.

When the leading men of the land had assembled at his court at Easter, the arrangement of the Churches—which the king had decided to carry out—was postponed because Paschal, the supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, had come to France [Note: [Col. 0465D] In the following year, 1107, Easter fell on 14 April.], and had ordered King Henry and Archbishop Anselm to send to the council [Note: [Col. 0465D] That is, the council held on the Ides of May, or around the Ascension of the Lord.] which he was to celebrate at Troyes the men often mentioned above, William and Baldwin [Col. 0465B].

The king therefore thought that on their return he might receive some new decision concerning the matter, and postponed everything until the following feast of Pentecost, so that, once they had returned, he might arrange matters more securely after learning the pontiff’s will.

When the court had therefore dispersed, Anselm went to the abbey of Saint Edmund to consecrate a great cross there and to perform certain other episcopal offices. When these had been completed, and he already thought he would be returning, he was seized by a severe bodily illness; as his sickness worsened, he was brought almost to the point of death.

He was detained there because of this illness until the octave of Pentecost, and the council—which, as we said, had been postponed—received a postponement until the Kalends of August because of his illness.

[Col. 0465C]

Meanwhile, this letter was brought to Anselm on behalf of the pope:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the sons of priests …” etc. See in Paschal II.

On the Kalends of August, therefore, an assembly of the bishops, abbots, and nobles of the kingdom was held at London in the king’s palace. For three successive days, while Anselm was absent, the king and the bishops discussed the investiture of churches. Some were striving to have the king carry this out in the manner of his father and brother, contrary to the command and obedience of the apostolic pope. For the pope, standing less firmly by the judgment that had subsequently been promulgated, had granted the homages which Pope Urban had likewise forbidden along with investitures; and by this means he had made the king agree with him concerning investitures, as may be gathered from the letter that we transcribed above.

Thereafter, in Anselm’s presence and with a multitude standing by, the king gave his assent and decreed that from that time forward no one in England should ever be invested by the king or by any lay hand with a bishopric or abbey through the delivery of a pastoral staff or ring. Anselm also granted that no one elected to a prelacy should be deprived of the consecration of the dignity he had received on account of the homage that he rendered to the king.

After these arrangements had been made, nearly all the churches of England, which had long been widowed of their pastors, received their fathers through the counsel of Anselm and the nobles of the kingdom, without any investiture by pastoral staff or ring. At the same time and in the same place, the king himself also appointed certain men to govern certain churches in Normandy, which likewise had been left without their fathers.

During these events Anselm began, before the king and the bishops and princes of the kingdom, to demand from Gerard, archbishop of York, a profession of his obedience and subjection, which he had not made since, as we have mentioned above, he had been transferred from the bishopric of Hereford to the archbishopric of York.

When the king himself said that it did not seem necessary to him for Gerard to add another profession to the one he had made at the time of his ordination—especially since, although he had changed churches, he had remained the same person and had not been released from his first profession—Anselm, for the moment, yielded to the present king’s words, on the condition that Gerard should give him his hand and promise that he would maintain in the archbishopric the same subjection that he had professed in the episcopate.

Gerard assented, and, placing his hand in Anselm’s hand, pledged his faith that he would show to Anselm and his successors in the archbishopric the same subjection and obedience that, when consecrated bishop, he had promised to the Church of Hereford.

It was then decreed that those who had been elected to bishoprics should go to Canterbury and there, according to custom, receive the blessing of that dignity. Accordingly, William of Winchester, Roger of Salisbury, and Reinhelm, then newly restored as bishop of the Church of Hereford, whom we have mentioned above, as well as William, who had usually served as the king’s legate but was then elected bishop of the Church of Exeter, and Urban, likewise elected bishop of the Church of Glamorgan, which is in Wales [Note: [Col. 0465D] Glamorgan is the southern part of Wales, at the estuary of the Severn. The episcopal see was Llandaff [Col. 0466D] (hence others discuss these men under the name of the bishops of Llandaff), concerning which see there is an entry for 9 February, where Saint Teilo, bishop of that place, is treated.], all came together to Canterbury. On Sunday, which was the third day before the Ides of August, [Note: [Col. 0466D] That is, with the Sunday letter F.] they were consecrated together by Anselm, with the suffragans of that see assisting and concelebrating with him in this office: namely, Gerard, archbishop of York; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; John of Bath; Herbert of Norwich; Robert of Chester; Ralph of Chichester; and Ranulf of Durham.

On that same day, before Anselm performed the consecration of those bishops, and in the presence of them and of the bishops who had gathered in accordance with the command of the lord pope—for he had formerly ordered this by letter—he returned to Ealdwin the pastoral staff of the abbey of Ramsey, which, as we mentioned above, Ealdwin had lost at the council of London.

On the following Thursday he also consecrated Robert, a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter at Westminster, in that same see, for the governance of the abbey of Saint Edmund.

The ordination of the abbot of Saint Augustine’s was delayed at that time, so to speak, for the reason that the man who had been elected abbot—namely, Hugh, a monk of Bec—did not yet possess holy orders. He was ordained to the diaconate by the archbishop in his chapel at Canterbury, together with many others, during the fast of the seventh month, and then to the priesthood [Col. 0467B] by William, bishop of Exeter, in the same chapel, during the fast of the tenth month.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] These fasts are commonly called the Ember Days, because they occur four times a year. The names of the seventh and tenth months indicate September and December, respectively; below, the fourth month is called June.]

Anselm was ill, and partly for that reason and partly because the feast of the Nativity of Christ was approaching, the same bishop had been ordered to come to Canterbury to Anselm. Afterward, when Anselm wished to hasten the ordination of that abbot, because the affairs of the Church were deteriorating and every day were declining both within and outside it to its own detriment, he wanted the aforesaid bishop solemnly to consecrate him abbot at the altar of Christ at Canterbury, with Anselm himself standing by.

But when the monks of Saint Augustine’s learned of this, they were stirred to oppose it. They claimed that their church possessed privileges by which they would clearly prove that their abbot ought to be ordained only in his own see. This story of theirs lasted for several days, while Anselm remained entirely unwilling to yield to their assertion.

At last, at the beginning of Lent, [Note: [Col. 0468D] In the leap year 1108, when Easter fell on 5 April and Ash Wednesday on 19 February, with the Sunday letters E and D.] when Anselm had come near London for a conference with the king, certain of the monks whom those who had remained at home had selected by common agreement and sent there to pursue the matter, abandoning their privileges—which had been proved and condemned by the king and the nobles as either nonexistent or invalid—persuaded the king through their advocates to order Anselm to consecrate the abbot in the church of Saint Augustine according to ancient custom.

The messengers who carried this command were William, bishop of Winchester; Roger of Salisbury; William of Exeter; and Abbot Gilbert of Westminster, whom the king sent to Anselm. Anselm therefore replied:

“If the king were to ask me, for love of him, to ordain that abbot in his church, perhaps I would do so, considering that it was the right of my predecessors and is mine equally throughout England, wherever the will directs, to exercise episcopal office. But since he orders me to do it on the ground of custom, I say that it is not a matter of custom.”

They replied: “If it is recognized not to be contrary to the faith, he absolutely wishes him to be consecrated in his own see.”

He answered: “Not everything must be done that is not contrary to the faith; otherwise many things that are inappropriate would be done. Although the matter under discussion, if carried out, would not be contrary to the faith, it nevertheless ought not to be done as a matter of custom, since it would be exceedingly inappropriate. For I would thereby become subject, contrary to order, to one who ought canonically to be subject in every respect to me and to our Church.

“Furthermore, the archbishop of Canterbury is primate of all England, Scotland, Ireland, and the neighboring islands, and by custom he does not leave his see for the consecration of any person except the king and queen. Therefore, if the king wishes me to show the abbot of Saint Augustine’s the same honor that I show him, he wishes to make the abbot his equal in his kingdom. I advise him, as one to whom I owe loyalty, not to allow this to happen, but to restrain himself from this desire. For I say in all truth that if such a great disorder should ever be introduced into England, it will be a great disgrace not only to the king but also to the archbishops, bishops, princes, and the whole kingdom.”

They said: “Well then, if you do not wish to ordain him in his own see for these reasons, he orders you to allow him to be ordained in his chapel, in his presence, by whichever of the bishops he commands.”

He replied: “Why should I permit him to be ordained by another bishop when, by the grace of God, I am able to ordain him myself, as I ought to do by my right?”

“Even this,” they said, “he would prefer: that you yourself consecrate him there.”

He said: “If I do this, I shall do some injury to my lord himself. It is not mine to celebrate Mass in his chapel except when he is to be crowned by me. Therefore, if I do this for the consecration of an abbot, royal honor will be diminished, and thereafter, by my example, what has hitherto been done at the appointed time solely for the king’s honor will be demanded as a custom.

“Yet because he wishes the man to be consecrated soon, since the affairs of the abbey are unsettled while the abbot has not yet been confirmed, if he wishes, I will ordain him here in the chapel of my lodging, since it is not easy for me, for so slight a matter, to go to Canterbury on this occasion.”

These words were reported to the king. Approving Anselm’s reasoning, he praised the proposal that, omitting all the circumstantial objections, the abbot should be consecrated as Anselm had said. Accordingly, Anselm ordained him on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, the Thursday of the first week of Lent, at Lambeth, in the chapel of the church of Rochester, where Anselm was then staying.

After receiving his profession according to custom, in which he promised that he would obey in every respect the Church of Canterbury and its archbishops according to canon law, those who were present said that he could have been consecrated much more honorably at Canterbury and that, for the abbot’s greater honor, he should have asked the father of the country for his blessing in the metropolitan see rather than in the chapel of the church of Rochester.

In the meantime Anselm sent this letter to the lord pope:

[Col. 0469A]

“To Paschal, revered lord and father, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, due obedience together with constant prayers.

“I ought not to conceal from Your Excellency what, by God’s grace, is being accomplished through you in England and Normandy. The king who rules the English and Normans, obediently receiving your command, has entirely abandoned the investiture of churches, despite the resistance of many. To bring this about, Count Robert of Meulan and Richard of Redvers, as your faithful men and sons of the Church devoted to the truth, pressed him strongly with their advice.

“The king himself makes no use whatever of his own will in choosing persons, but entrusts himself entirely to the counsel of religious men. As for myself, I cannot sufficiently express in writing how many thanks I owe to your paternal kindness; rather, I continually read them written on the tablet of my heart.

“For when, as your beloved servants and our brothers, William and Baldwin, reported, you command that, with such kind solicitude, care be taken for my corruptible life so that it may not quickly fail, you show that Your Greatness possesses no small affection of compassion toward my lowliness. May Almighty God preserve your life for a long time in every prosperity.”

We have thought it appropriate to insert this letter into the present work so that, by its testimony, we might demonstrate that what we have said concerning the investiture of churches is confirmed. It also seemed fitting to indicate by this testimony that Count Meulan was brought to the correction described above on account of the letters that the pope had sent him, as we wrote above.

For in truth he had been changed to some extent from those among whom he had formerly moved. Since he loved justice, he often offered counsel to some, assistance to others, and both to still others, according as reason required. King Henry himself, believing his counsel in affairs of the kingdom to be superior and more effective than that of the others, dreaded following in the footsteps of his deceased brother, the king, as he admitted. Nevertheless, the aforesaid count neither loved the English nor allowed any of them to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignity.

After Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, whom we mentioned above, had been taken from this life, Anselm went to Rochester to bury him. When the burial rites had been decently completed amid the service of a great multitude of mourning monks, clerics, and laypeople, Anselm arranged the affairs of that bishopric, both within and outside it, for the benefit of the Church, as he best understood was expedient.

The episcopal staff was then carried to Canterbury, according to custom, by Ernulf, a monk of Rochester who had been that bishop’s chaplain, and was presented in the presence of the brothers upon the altar of the Lord and Savior.

Meanwhile King Henry, considering that almost the entire kingdom had fallen into serious misery for many reasons, began, through the counsel of Anselm and the nobles of the kingdom, to take measures as to how and by what means the evils that most oppressed the poor might be alleviated.

Knowing that the beginning of this good work should start with his own court, he began there. In the time of his brother the king, the multitude of those who followed his court had the custom of plundering whatever they could destroy, and, with no discipline restraining them, laying waste the entire land through which the king traveled.

Another evil was added to this. Many of them, made drunk by their own wickedness [Note: [Col. 0469D] The word *debriare*, instead of *inebriari*, frequently occurs in the Acts of the Saints. It is certainly an appropriate word, although unknown in the Golden Age, since, as some maintain, *bria* signified a fixed measure of wine. Thus *ebrius* and *debrius* would mean, as it were, “from” or “beyond the measure of drink”; *sobrius* would mean “under the measure.”] [variant: *inebriati*, “made drunk”], when they could not entirely consume what they found in the lodgings they invaded, used either to carry it to the market and sell it for their own profit, even though it belonged to the owners, or to burn it after setting fire beneath it, or, if it was drink, to wash their horses’ feet with it and pour the remainder onto the ground, or certainly to waste it in some other way.

It is shameful to recall what cruelties they committed against householders and what indecencies against their wives and daughters. For these reasons, whenever they learned beforehand that the king was approaching, people fled from their dwellings and did what they could for themselves and their families in woods or other places where they hoped they could protect themselves.

Desiring to remedy this evil, King Henry issued an edict that all who could be proved to have done any of the things I have described should, with unwavering justice and severity, either have their eyes gouged out or their hands, feet, or other limbs amputated. When this justice had been seen in the case of many, it deterred the others who loved to preserve their own integrity from injuring anyone else.

Likewise, debased and counterfeit coin afflicted many people in many ways. The king determined to correct this under such severe punishment that no one who could be caught making false coins would be able to obtain any reprieve from losing his eyes and the lower parts of his body.

And because coins were very often bent, broken, or rejected while they were being examined, he decreed that no penny or halfpenny should remain whole. From this measure great benefit was created for the whole kingdom for a time. These were the measures the king meanwhile took in secular affairs to relieve the sufferings of the land.

Nevertheless, since the divine offices were being handled unworthily by the hands of certain priests to such an extent, he took care to ensure that they too should be celebrated chastely according to their proper rite. For many priests, setting aside the decrees of the council of London and also the punishment that the king had inflicted upon them, of which we spoke above, retained their women, or had taken women whom they previously did not have.

Desiring to overturn this crime of incontinence, the king summoned all the leading men of the kingdom to his court at London on the solemnity of Pentecost. He discussed the matter with Archbishop Anselm and the other bishops of England, and strengthened them, supported by royal authority and power, to eradicate that evil.

Accordingly, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; Thomas, elected archbishop of York—for Gerard had then recently departed for that same court—together with all the other bishops of England, decreed in the presence of that glorious king Henry and with the assent of all his barons that priests, deacons, and subdeacons should live chastely and should not have women in their houses, except those closely related to them by blood, in accordance with the definition of the holy Council of Nicaea.

Those priests, deacons, and subdeacons who, after the prohibition of the Council of London, had retained their women or taken others, if they wished to celebrate Mass thereafter, were to make them entirely separate from themselves, so that neither the women should enter their houses nor they the women’s houses. They were not to meet knowingly in any house, nor were such women to live within the territory of the church. If, however, some respectable matter required them to speak with one another, they were to converse outside the house in the presence of at least two lawful witnesses.

If any of them were accused, on the testimony of two or three lawful witnesses or by the public report of the parishioners, of violating this statute, he was to clear himself with suitable witnesses of his own order: six, if he were a priest; five, if a deacon; four, if a subdeacon. If he failed in this purgation, he was to be judged a violator of the sacred statute.

Those priests who, scorning the divine altar and holy orders, preferred to live with women were to be removed from the divine office, deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice, and, having been declared infamous, expelled from the choir.

But whoever, being rebellious and contemptuous, refused to abandon his woman and dared to celebrate Mass, was to be summoned to make satisfaction; if he neglected to do so, he was to be excommunicated on the eighth day.

The same sentence included archdeacons [Note: [Col. 0552]

(27) *Archidiacones.* Thus the manuscript reads. The expression *atque archidiacones* is found in Anselm, Book III of the Letters, “Concerning Archdeacons,” and likewise in Roger of Hoveden, Part I, p. 270.

I believe that the author said *archidiacones* in the same way as others say *hypodiacones*. Isidore, in Gratian, Distinction 21, chapter 1, “Cleros,” says: “*Hypodiacones* in Greek, whom we call *subdeacons*.” That is how the passage is read there, although in the copy of Isidore that we use, namely the edition published by Bonaventura Vulcanius, *hypodiaconi* is found. The passage occurs in Book VII of the *Etymologies*, in the chapter “On Clerics.”

In any event, the word *diacones* and the forms derived from it are frequently used in ancient councils. Council of Agde, canon 39: “Priests, deacons, subdeacons, and others thereafter who are not permitted to marry wives should also avoid the banquets of other people’s weddings.” Canon 49: “Deacons or priests,” and so forth. Canon 65: “Since a deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a priest,” and so forth.

The nominative *diacones* is also found in canon 18 of the Council of Elvira and canon 38 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, and incidentally in Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian. It is not worth adding more examples. Hence later Greeks also use *διάκων* for *διάκονος*.

Malaxus of the Peloponnese, in his *History of the Patriarchs*, has: “*Ἀρσένιος διάκων*,” “Arsenius the deacon,” and later, “*ὁτὶ, ὅποιος γένει ἀρχιερεὺς ἡ ἱερεὺς ἤ διὰκων*,” “[materially uncertain:] ‘that, whatever [a person is] by birth—a high priest, priest, or deacon,’” and so forth.

Nor, indeed, is *diaconus* avoided in the nominative. Both among the Latin authors of the councils mentioned above and in Malaxus, the two forms are used indiscriminately.

By the same analogy the Greeks formed *Πάτρων* for *patrono*. Hesychius, in his *Lexicon*, has: “*πάτωνες οἱ πρῶτοι τῶν ἀξιωθέντων τῆς Ῥωμαίων πολιτείας ὑπὸ Ῥωμύλου ἑκατὸν ὄντες*,” meaning: “*Patōnes* were the first hundred who were deemed worthy by Romulus of Roman citizenship.”

Theophilus the Antecessor, *Institutes*, Book I, title 17, writes: “*Ὁ νόμος ὁ δωδεκάδελτος τοὺς πάτρωνας καὶ τοὺς τῶν πατρώνων παῖδας ἐπὶ τὴν τούτων ἐπιτροπὴν καλεῖ*”: “The Law of the Twelve Tables calls patrons and the children of patrons to the guardianship of these persons,” namely, the freedmen.

The same form is also very frequently found in the author of the *Basilica*, Book XLIX, titles 1 and 2, where he says: “*Ἀπελεύθερος κατὰ πάτρωνος ἀτιμοποιὸν ἀγωγὴν οὐ δύναται κινῆσαι*”: “A freedman cannot bring an action for infamy against his patron.”

Harmeuopolus and other Greek jurists very often use the same form, and ancient inscriptions in Greece have *τὸν πάτρωνα* for *patronum*. We read this in Janus Gruter, p. 595, nos. 11 and 12.]

and also all the canons, both with regard to abandoning the women and avoiding their company, and with regard to the strictness of the penalty if the statutes were violated.

Moreover, all the archdeacons were to swear that they would not accept money for tolerating a violation of this statute, nor tolerate priests whom they knew to have women, to sing, or to have vicars; and if they heard them being accused, they were to investigate the truth of the matter. The deans were likewise to swear in every respect to the same things.

Any archdeacon or dean who refused to take this oath was to lose his archdeaconry or deanery irrevocably.

Those priests who, after abandoning their women, chose to serve God and the sacred altars were to abstain from office for forty days as penance for the violation of the aforesaid council, while they were to have vicars acting for them in the meantime, and penance was to be imposed upon them according to the judgment of their bishops.

All the movable goods of priests, deacons, subdeacons, and canons who thereafter fell into this offense were to be handed over to the bishops, and the concubines, together with their possessions, were to be treated as adulteresses.

[Col. 0472A]

In those days there was discussion of the parish of the bishop of Lincoln, which was excessively extensive. The matter proceeded to the point [Note: [Col. 0553]

(28) “Since the principle of Christianity advised that this would be useful.”

The terms *Christianitas* and those relating to Christianity occur frequently in Eadmer and other writers of that age. They denote the episcopal function and the activity and administration of the sacred court, or the episcopal office, as it is more commonly called.

At column 366, see: “Almost all *Christianitas* in England had perished.” At column 381: “He wished to take away from him all authority for exercising *Christianitas*.” There are other examples of the same kind.

By the general name “Christians,” some jurists wish bishops specifically to be designated in the edicts of the ancient emperors, in relation to the law “Christians,” Code, concerning episcopal jurisdiction, Book 11. Hence among us the sacred courts over which bishops preside, or those who in their name defer to bishops, since appeals may be made to them, are still called the Courts of *Christianitas*, that is, Christian courts.

Originally, the word *Christianitas* meant Christian law, or Christian reverence, and Christian worship in general, as may be seen in the Code, title “Concerning Apostates,” law 4; in the Theodosian Code, title “Concerning Spectacles,” law 5; in the same Code, title “Concerning Decurions,” law 112; in the same Code, title “Concerning Jews and Celestial Beings,” Book XIX; and elsewhere.

Later, however, that function and jurisdiction which are chiefly exercised in the care of the Christian religion, or of Christianity and ecclesiastical polity, were also specifically called *Christianitas*. From this arose the name “Courts of Christianity” for the sacred courts.]

so that, since the principle of Christianity advised that this would be useful, the king, the archbishop, and the other princes of the kingdom decided that a portion should be taken from that parish from which another bishopric could be formed [Note: [Col. 0553]

(29) “Whose cathedral see was to be established in the abbey of Ely.”

Concerning the beginnings of the bishopric of Ely, there is a manuscript fragment of an ancient history of that church in which I have found the measures taken and the royal and papal documents concerning the matter:

“After the death of Abbot Richard,” says that history, “Hervey, bishop of Bangor, who had been violently expelled from his bishopric, was sent by the king to the monastery of Ely, so that he might temporarily be supported there from the resources of the Church until the king had more fully deliberated what he should do with him.

“Bangor is a monastery in Wales so full of inhabitants that, as Bede reports, if it were divided into seven parts, each portion would contain no fewer than three hundred men. When Hervey held that bishopric, he treated the savage people with excessive severity. Seeing such perversity in their conduct—something that no one could easily tolerate, and because of which they showed no reverence for episcopal authority—he wielded a two-edged sword to subdue them, restraining them now by frequent anathema, now by the multitude of their relatives and other men.

“Their rebellion against him was no less serious. They pressed upon him with such danger that they killed his brother and would have killed him in the same way if they could have laid hands upon him. The bishop was terrified by the misfortune that threatened him. When many of his men had been killed or seriously wounded, and seeing that his life was being sought and that he had no suitable defenders, he fled to the protection of the king of England and thereby secured a useful exile.

“The king, kindly receiving his arrival as that of a bishop who was at that time famous and religious, sent him to the church of Ely and appointed him to receive sustenance from its resources. When Hervey came there, he so won the affection of nearly all the monks by his graciousness, way of life, and remarkable prudence that, if it could be done, they would have adopted him as their bishop.

“When he saw how greatly they were attached to him, he gradually began, through various circumlocutions, to set before them the advantage of the place, to test the minds of the brothers, and to promise many pleasant things if they were willing to promote the abbey into a bishopric and receive him as bishop. He also promised them his assistance in bringing this about, provided that they gave him their assent.

“When they had readily turned toward him, he approached the king. The king granted his request and invited Robert, bishop of Lincoln, to a conference, so that this change might not be made without his concurrence, since that place seemed to lie within his bishopric and his diocese might suffer injury if another bishopric were introduced there without consulting its bishop.

“For this reason it was necessary that the future bishopric should possess a parish, which, according to canonical justice, he demanded should be granted to it from the Church of Lincoln with an equitable compensation.

“Accordingly, the manor of Spaldwick was given to the Church of Lincoln in perpetual right in exchange for the episcopal jurisdiction over the district of Grantbridge. When this secret business between the king and Bishop Robert had been concluded—without the monks being consulted at all, and while the sons of the Church remained ignorant of it—Bishop Hervey was sent to Rome with letters from the king to confirm the proposal.

“When he arrived there, he obtained what he had requested and returned with apostolic letters addressed to the king, the archbishop, and the bishops of the province concerning his case, of the kind he desired. It is neither useless nor burdensome to append their text here.”

[Col. 0554B] [ [Col. 0553D] These are the words of the author whom we are transcribing, as are the other passages inserted in this little history.]

The mandate obtained by Hervey from the lord pope to King Henry concerning the promotion of the abbey of Ely into a bishopric and his appointment there as bishop:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Henry, glorious king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We give thanks to Almighty God,” and so forth. See this in Paschal II, below, under the year 1118.

“The pope also sent another letter to the same king, whose text is as follows.

That by apostolic authority a bishopric is established at Ely:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and to the other bishops of the province, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Among the other kingdoms of the earth,” and so forth. See the same place.

“After Hervey had received these letters of his confirmation, he hastened to England with the apostolic blessing. He approached the king and the archbishop, showed them the letters, and obtained their assent. In the following year he completed the entire undertaking, namely, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1108, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

“In that same year King Henry changed the abbey of Ely into an episcopal see and placed Hervey of Bangor, the bishop, over that church, confirming him with the following charters.”

The charter of King Henry concerning how he transformed the abbey of Ely into a bishopric:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1108, indiction [lacuna], in the tenth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Paschal II, and likewise in the tenth year of my reign, I, Henry, by the providence of divine mercy king of the English and duke of the Normans, son of William the great king, who succeeded King Edward by hereditary right in the kingdom, seeing that the harvest of the Church in my kingdom is abundant, while the laborers are few and therefore labor greatly in the harvest, and that the Church of Lincoln itself is fertile in a multitude of people, by the authority and counsel of the aforesaid Pope Paschal, and with the assent and at the request of Robert, bishop of Lincoln, who then presided over the aforesaid Church, and of his entire chapter, with the assent of the lord Anselm, of blessed memory, archbishop of Canterbury, and of all the bishops and abbots of the whole of England, as well as of all the dukes, counts, and princes of my kingdom, establish and confirm perpetually as a free and fully independent episcopal see the monastery of Ely—which until my time had possessed abbots—together with the province of Cambridge, insofar as it pertained to the right of the Church of Lincoln, and with the two abbeys, namely Thorney and Chatteris, just like the other bishoprics of my kingdom.

“And in order to release it from subjection and all episcopal customs belonging to the aforesaid Church of Lincoln, by the counsel and assent of the aforesaid Pope Paschal, I have given, to be held in perpetual right, to the aforesaid Church of Lincoln, to Robert, bishop of that see, and to his successors, from the revenues of the same monastery, the town called Spaldwick, with all its appurtenances, situated in the territory of Huntingdon, together with all the customs belonging to the aforesaid town, just as the monastery of Ely ever held it more freely and peacefully.

“First, at London, in Westminster, during the solemnity of Pentecost, this matter was discussed in my presence before Anselm, archbishop of blessed memory, and all the bishops, abbots, and nobles of my kingdom, and the favorable common assent of them all was obtained. After the death of the aforesaid pontiff Anselm, by the authority of the lord Pope Paschal, as has already been said, it was happily concluded and settled by the mercy of God at the council held at the castle of Rockingham on the feast of the translation of blessed Etheldreda the virgin, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.”

I have read this little history in two copies, which are nearly identical and both were written more than three hundred years ago. Yet they may rightly appear of doubtful reliability.

For King Henry’s charter does not possess the character of the documentary style that was in use in that age. It begins with a wholly unusual display of words, woven together—though I do not know with what sort of pomp—in honor of the Roman pontiff. It mentions “dukes” as though this were an honorary title, clearly distinguished from counts, although it is certain that no one among us was designated by such a title from the time of William I until Edward III.

Nor, although I have searched diligently, do I find anything of this kind in the royal archives, where instruments of ancient privileges granted to the bishopric of Ely, as well as those granted to other churches, are frequently repeated. Anselm likewise died in 1109, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Yet this document, which is assigned to the year 1108, mentions the deceased Anselm.

Furthermore, 1108 is here made the tenth year of King Henry, although it plainly could not have exceeded the ninth. These are unmistakably gross chronological errors. It is enough that I have mentioned them in passing. I leave the rest to the judgment of more discerning readers.]

whose cathedral see was to be established in the abbey of Ely. But Anselm, upon whom the chief responsibility for the matter rested, knowing that a new bishopric could nowhere be properly established without the consent and authority of the Roman pontiff, wrote to him as follows:

“To Paschal, revered lord and father, supreme pontiff, Anselm of the Church of Canterbury, due obedience with faithful service and prayers.

“Since the strength of arrangements that are beneficially made [Col. 0472B] in the Church of God depends upon the authority of your prudence, whenever such arrangements are made they ought to be referred to your knowledge and judgment, so that, once they have been confirmed with apostolic assent, no later presumption may violate what has been salutarily established, but that it may remain ratified forever.

“In England there is a certain bishopric, namely Lincoln, whose diocese is so extensive that one bishop cannot fully suffice for those matters that can be carried out only by an episcopal person. When the king, the bishops, the princes, and the other reasonable and religious men of the kingdom of the English considered this, it seemed useful for the Church to divide the aforesaid bishopric into two, so that an episcopal see might be established in a certain abbey situated on an island called Ely and lying within the aforesaid diocese, while the monks there remained, as there are many bishoprics that have monks in the mother church rather than canons. The bishop of Lincoln himself, Robert by name, willingly grants this, because from those things taken from his Church to establish the new bishopric at Ely, so much is restored to the Church of Lincoln [Note: [Col. 0471D] Namely, one manor of Ely Abbey, Spaldwich, to which Godwin, in his *On the Bishops of England*, adds two others below, Bicclesworth and Bokden; asserting that Ely Abbey was so wealthy that it yielded more to its abbot than the bishops of two or three English sees yielded to their bishops.] that he acknowledges it to be sufficient and pleasing to him.

“Because of this, both on account of the necessity mentioned above and on account of the multitude of those who agree to it, it seemed to me that I should give my assent, without prejudice to your authority. My smallness therefore humbly entreats you that what has thus been arranged for the benefit of the Church may be strengthened forever by your authority, lest later presumption violate [Col. 0472D] what has been well established. We pray the almighty Lord to preserve you for his Church in lasting prosperity.”

[Note: [Col. 0472D] The pope granted Anselm’s request, but Anselm died before the matter was completed.]

When the court was dismissed, Anselm went to his own estate, called Murtelac, and there, during the fast of the fourth month, promoted many men to sacred orders. Among them he ordained to the priesthood Richard, who had been elected at the preceding and most recent solemnity of Pentecost to the episcopate of the Church of London.

[Col. 0473A]

Then, coming to Canterbury for the feast of the most glorious apostles Peter and Paul, on the day of the feast itself, in the chapter house, in the presence of the brothers of the Church and of many others—monks, clerics, and also laymen—he gave the bishopric of Rochester to Ralph, abbot of Séez [Note: [Col. 0473D] The Abbey of Séez is in Normandy, commonly called Saint-Martin de-Séez; concerning its foundation, said to have taken place in 1050, see the *Pious Neustria* of Arthur. Ralph was transferred to the archbishopric of Canterbury in 1114.], a good and religious man, and very close to that church. First, however, he received from him, before everyone, homage and fidelity. Ralph promised that he would perpetually preserve this fidelity toward Anselm, toward all his lawful successors, and toward the Church of Canterbury, and he confirmed this by swearing upon the four Gospels.

On the following day Anselm sent him to Rochester, together with his archdeacon William, so that William might invest him with that bishopric on Anselm’s behalf. For the same business he also sent Anthony [Col. 0473B], a monk who was serving as subprior in the monastery at Canterbury. For after Aernulf, the prior of that Church, had been made abbot at Burgh [Note: [Col. 0473D] Peterborough, a monastery in Northamptonshire, concerning which see the notices on 6 March, where the saints Kyneburga [Col. 0474D] and Kyneswitha, daughters of Penda and sisters of Peada, kings of the Mercians, are discussed.], no one had succeeded to the priorship up to that time.

At the same time the king was preparing to go to Normandy. Anselm, invited by him to bless him at the seaport from which he was to cross, came there. But during the night, when on the following morning he was supposed to cross the arm of the sea separating the king’s lodging from Anselm’s lodging in order to speak with the king, he became so ill that he was in no way able to approach him.

When this was reported to the king, he sent orders through William, bishop of Winchester, and the bishop of Exeter of the same name that Anselm should not come to him at all, but should give himself fully to rest. Through these same men he also commended himself as he went, and his son, whom he was leaving in the kingdom, together with the whole kingdom, to Anselm’s protection, so that whatever Anselm decided might be valid and whatever he prohibited might be void.

He also asked Anselm, for love of him, to consecrate at Chichester the aforementioned Richard, elected bishop of the Church of London, since Chichester was nearby and the bishops whom he could have as assistants and ministers in that office were present. The reason why he wished this to be done in such haste was said to be that he was planning to send the same Richard, who was very influential in secular affairs, far toward the western borders of England to conduct his business.

But Anselm, having considered certain reasonable causes [Col. 0473D], refused and did not agree to consecrate the bishop at Chichester, as requested. Nevertheless, so that he would not appear to do nothing for the king, who at that time was doing everything Anselm had asked, he consecrated the same bishop for love of the king in his own chapel at Pagham, on 26 July, with William, bishop of Winchester, Roger of Salisbury, Ralph of Chichester, and William of Exeter assisting him in this office. First, as customary, he received from Richard his profession concerning obedience and submission.

After this Anselm came to Canterbury and there, with great honor, consecrated the aforementioned Ralph, bishop-elect of Rochester, on 9 August, with William, bishop of Winchester, Ralph of Chichester, and Richard of London assisting him. Richard, following the custom of his predecessors [f, *morem*], honored his mother Church of Canterbury on that very day with an honorable gift, in accordance with what had been stipulated by the king when he obtained from Anselm that Richard should be consecrated at Pagham, as we have said.

Meanwhile, a certain monk of Durham, named Turgot [Note: [Col. 0474D] This is Turgot, formerly prior of Durham, to whom we attributed the *History of Durham*, published under the name of Simeon of Durham, on 20 March, before the *Translation of the Body of St Cuthbert*, p. 125.], was elected by Alexander, king of Scotland, and by the clergy and people, to the bishopric of St Andrews in Scotland.

When his consecration was delayed longer than was expedient—partly because Thomas, elected bishop of the Church of York, had not yet been consecrated, and partly because of certain other matters that would take too long to recount—Ranulf, bishop of Durham, proposed to consecrate the same elect in Thomas’s presence at York, with the bishops of Scotland and of the Orkney Islands associated with him.

But because he knew that this could not lawfully be done without the consent and authority of the bishop of Canterbury, he informed Anselm of the matter through a certain knight and begged that the consecration be carried out with Anselm’s counsel and permission. In response Anselm wrote him this letter:

[Col. 0474C]

“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to Ralph, bishop of Durham, greetings.

“You sent word to me through a certain knight named Scollard that you wished the bishop-elect of the Church of St Andrews in Scotland to be consecrated, and that you wished this to be done with my counsel and permission. But this may neither properly nor canonically be done by that elected archbishop, nor by anyone else on his behalf, before he himself has become archbishop through canonical consecration. Therefore I neither advise nor permit it—indeed, I forbid it—before the consecration of that elected archbishop, unless it should be required by necessity and I myself perform it. Farewell.”

After this, Anselm, considering that Thomas was not seeking his episcopal blessing as earnestly as he ought, sent him the following letter:

“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friend Thomas, elected archbishop of the Church of York, greetings.

“Canonical authority commands [Note: [Col. 0555]

(30) that a bishop’s church should not remain without a shepherd for more than three months. The Council of Chalcedon, *Acts* 15, canon 25, gives this command concerning a consecrated shepherd: ‘Since certain metropolitans, as we have learned, neglect the flocks entrusted to them and defer the ordinations of bishops, it has seemed good to the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops should take place within three months.’ It is also found in Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 75, chapter 2. See also Burchard, book I, chapters 24 and 25; Ivo, part VI, chapter 5; and Gratian, distinction 100, chapter 1.]

“that a bishop’s church should not remain without a shepherd for more than three months. Since it has pleased our lord the king, with the counsel of his barons [Col. 0475A] and our permission, that your person should be elected to the archbishopric of York, you ought not to defer longer the salutary time limit that has been established. Therefore I am surprised that after your election you did not request to be consecrated to that office for which you were elected.

“I therefore command you to be at your mother Church of Canterbury on 6 September, to do what you ought to do and to receive your consecration. If you do not do this, it pertains to me to take charge and to perform what belongs to episcopal office in the archbishopric of York.

“Furthermore, I have heard that before you are consecrated you wish the bishop-elect of St Andrews in Scotland to be consecrated at York. You ought not to do this, nor do I permit it; indeed, I absolutely forbid it, whether concerning him or concerning any person who ought to be advanced by the archbishop of York to the governance of souls. For it does not belong to you to give or grant anyone the governance or care of souls, since you have not yet received it. Farewell.”

The following letter was written in reply:

“To the most beloved Father and venerable lord Anselm, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, Thomas, elected—though unworthy—to the metropolitan see of York, greetings and the service of friendly fidelity.

“I thank you, reverend Father, because you have always loved me and listened to me, rejoiced at my advancement, and your heart rejoiced in the Lord. May the Lord God repay you on my behalf!

“As for the reason why I delayed coming for my consecration, it was not one reason, nor a small one, that detained me. The money that I had contracted, according to my means, for the expense of coming to you—large for me—was spent at Winchester beyond my expectation and after I had remained there too long, although I had intended to leave more quickly and come to you.

“Moreover, it pleased our lord the king that when he was sending envoys to Rome on his own business, I should send one of mine with them to request the pallium for our Church. Therefore, returning hastily to my own affairs at the king’s advice, I sought money for this purpose, and I am still seeking it, but I find little unless I borrow heavily, because Lord Gerard, the archbishop, has greatly impoverished our churches, our men, and our own lordship.

“Indeed, the king promised me that he would speak with you and excuse my delay to you. By the deadline you have set, with the Lord’s help, I shall be at the holy Church of Canterbury, if I can come at a suitable time, to receive and do what I ought. But if I cannot, since your fatherhood commanded me to notify you fifteen days beforehand, I ask that your kindness grant me permission to notify you ten days beforehand [Note: [Col. 0475D] This must have been done either by another letter or verbally through messengers, since the limitation is not expressed above.].

“I also request letters from your fatherhood as testimony to our person and election, of the kind that you ought to provide and know should be provided. In this way your holiness owes something to my smallness, and your Church ought not to deny it to ours.

[Col. 0476A]

“As for the bishop-elect of St Andrews in Scotland, what you have heard is rumor, which ought not to be believed. It is therefore easy to forbid something that was not devised by me in order that it should happen.

“May your holiness live healthy and joyful for a long time; our Church beseeches God, our Lord, on your behalf. I greet the congregation of the holy Church of Canterbury and ask it to pray for me. Farewell.”

Anselm’s reply to the same Thomas:

“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friend Thomas, elected archbishop of York, greetings.

“You wrote to me in your letter that, by the deadline I had set for you, you would be at Canterbury, with God’s help, if you could come at a suitable time, to receive and do what you ought. You also asked that, if you were unable to accomplish this, I should grant you permission to notify me ten days beforehand [Col. 0476B].

“Your cleric and messenger William also asked me on your behalf to extend the deadline for your arrival somewhat, so that you might come to us at a more suitable time. I gladly do this, out of love for you and for the sake of convenience. Therefore, so that you need not notify me in advance of your arrival, I urge you to be at Canterbury on Sunday, 27 September, to do what you ought to do and to receive your consecration.

“Furthermore, when you say in your letter that you are seeking money to send to Rome for the pallium of your Church, I do not permit this. I think you would do it in vain, since no one ought to have the pallium before he has been consecrated.

“As for the letters you request as testimony to your person [Col. 0476C] and election, when you have spoken with me and shown me to whom I ought to address them, I shall gladly do for you, as for a friend, what I ought to do. Farewell.”

Anselm therefore judged that it was not inappropriate to forewarn the lord pope about the matter of the pallium, which Thomas had written that he intended to request. He wrote him the following letter:

“To the truly beloved and reverend lord and Father Paschal, supreme pontiff, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due obedience with faithful prayers.

“Since the strength and direction of the Churches of God depend above all, after the Lord, upon the authority of your fatherhood, whenever reason requires it we gladly have recourse to your help and counsel.

“Gerard, archbishop of York, has departed this life, and another, named Thomas, has been elected in his place. There is a report that the pallium is being sought for him before he has been consecrated and before he makes to me the profession required by the ancient custom of my predecessors and his.

“This, then, is the substance of my prayers in this matter: that before he is consecrated and makes the obedience due to me, as I have said, and before you learn from our letters that this has been done, he should not receive the pallium from your authority.

“I do not say this because I begrudge him the pallium, but because some people assert [Col. 0477A] and are also working to ensure that, if this is granted by you, he will trust that he can refuse to make the profession due to me. If this should happen, know that the Church of England would be torn apart and, according to the saying of the Lord, ‘Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste’ (Luke 11:17), would be devastated; and the force of apostolic discipline in it would be seriously weakened. Nor would I remain in England under any circumstances. For I ought not, and could not, endure the destruction of the primacy of our Church while I was living in it.

“I make the same recommendation to your reverence, with the same concern, regarding London, if the pallium is being requested for its bishop—which he has never possessed—that is, that you should in no way consent to this. For certain people are contriving, under the appearance of something good, to humble the dignity of Canterbury’s primacy in a manner that is improper.

“This year, after Pentecost, I sent letters to your holiness through Bernard, the servant of your chamberlain Lord Peter, saying that the king of England complains that you tolerate the German king’s giving investitures of churches without excommunication, and therefore threatens without doubt to resume his own investitures, since that man holds his in peace. Let your prudence therefore see without delay what you ought to do about this, lest what you have built so well be irreparably destroyed. For our king is carefully inquiring what you are doing concerning that king.

“We pray the Lord God to gladden us with your lasting prosperity.”

The lord pope’s reply to Anselm:

[Col. 0477C]

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“We have received the letters of your affection, through which we recognized the sweetness of your graciousness, etc., up to: ‘But if the king persists in the path of his father’s wickedness, he will undoubtedly experience the sword of blessed Peter, which we have already begun to draw’ [Note: [Col. 0477D] And he did experience it—not from Paschal, from whom Henry V, king of Germany, extorted the investitures in 1111, while the same king futilely sought to retract the acts at Sutri after he had been released [Col. 0478D]; but from Callistus II, to whom he himself was compelled to restore them in 1122 at the Council of Worms.].

“Given at Benevento, 12 October.”

The aforementioned Thomas, meanwhile, having changed his earlier plan, was unable to come to Canterbury at the appointed time, being forbidden by his canons, as he informed Anselm by letter; and for this reason he asked Anselm’s advice about what should be done.

Those canons, knowing that Anselm was exhausted both by age and by weakness, thought that he would soon be taken from this life. They therefore stirred up a dispute and wrote to Anselm that the Church of York was equal to Canterbury. Yet in this they acknowledged that the elected bishop of their Church ought to go to Canterbury for his blessing; but they denied that he was required to make a profession of submission to the bishop of Canterbury, and, as far as they could, forbade him, in the name of God and of the Roman Church, to make it.
