What reputation this brought upon the canons in the minds of many, those who know what legal authority the Church of Canterbury has always customarily possessed over York from ancient times can infer without my saying anything. Anselm, however, postponing his reply to the clerics’ letter, wrote the following to Thomas:

“Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, to his friend Thomas, elected archbishop of York, greetings.

“I have instructed you charitably more than once to come to your mother Church of Canterbury, to receive your blessing and to do what you ought to do, but you have not come. Therefore, with the same affection, I still command you to be at that same mother Church on 8 November, so that you may do what you ought and receive our blessing.

“Furthermore, since you ask for advice, I advise you not to begin anything that you ought not to begin against the Church of Canterbury. For know with certainty that I shall devote myself to this by every means in my power: that in my time that Church may lose nothing of its dignity. Farewell.”

Thomas did not come, but among other things he wrote in a letter that was sent:

“The cause for which my consecration is being delayed—something that no one would more earnestly than I wish to hasten—those who have postponed it do not cease to strengthen. Therefore let your discernment recognize how dangerous and shameful it would be to invade the governance of the Church to which I ought to be appointed, against the consent of that Church.

“And recognize also how dreadful it is, and how much it must be avoided, to put on a curse under the guise of a blessing!” [Col. 0478C]

From this Anselm perceived that Thomas was adhering more to the counsel of his clerics than to the counsel he himself had requested. He therefore summoned the bishops to him and, discussing the matter with them, investigated what most particularly ought to be done.

They approved sending two more bishops to Thomas, who would warn him on behalf of Anselm and all the bishops of England to renounce the rebellion he had begun, and, if he refused to do so, would persuade him to come to Canterbury for his blessing, according to what he knew he ought to do. There, if he could, he could prove that he ought to be free from the submission Anselm demanded; and if he could accomplish this, he could return home consecrated and at peace.

These proposals pleased the Father. The two bishops sent to carry them out were the bishop of London, because he was dean of the Church of Canterbury, and the bishop of Rochester, who was known to be particularly attached and close to that Church.

They therefore set out and sent word to Thomas. He met them at Southwell, his own estate. They explained why they had come. He replied that he was awaiting his messenger, whom he had sent to Normandy to the king, and several of his own men, whom he had ordered to come to him from a distant place. “When they have arrived,” he said, “I shall hear their counsel and do whatever they commend as most necessary for me to do.” The bishops returned with this report.

[Col. 0479A]

After this, when a short time had passed, a messenger sent to Anselm on Thomas’s behalf brought him the following letter, enclosed with the king’s seal:

“Henry, by the grace of God king of the English, to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, his dear Father, greetings and friendship.

“I command you to await, with a patient mind and good will, the blessing of Thomas, archbishop of York, until Easter, together with whatever has been done between you concerning this matter. For if I return to England within the aforesaid period, I shall, with the counsel of my bishops and barons, reconcile you concerning it justly and honorably. But if I do not return so soon, I shall act concerning it in such a way that fraternal peace and good harmony will exist between you.”

[Col. 0479B]

When the messenger asked what response Anselm wished to give, Anselm said: “I shall respond to the king who sent me the letter, not to Thomas.”

He therefore entrusted this embassy to Odo, dean of the Church of Chichester, and to Albold, a monk of the monastery of Saint Mary of Bec, and sent them to Normandy to tell the king everything that had taken place between Anselm and the men of York throughout the present dispute.

They were also to ask him, through the freedom and foresight of his authority, to take care that the integrity of Christianity in England not be split into two, being certain that, according to the Lord’s saying, division would be followed by devastation (Luke 11:17).

As for the truce that he had ordered to be granted to Thomas, archbishop of York, he should know for certain that Anselm would rather suffer being cut to pieces limb by limb [Col. 0479C] than ever grant that truce, even for an hour, in a matter in which he knew that Thomas had raised himself unjustly and against God, contrary to the ancient decrees of the holy Fathers.

When the messengers returned, they reported that the king had received Anselm’s words with a calm and kindly spirit and had promised that, with God’s help and mercy, he would demonstrate in deed that he loved the integrity of Christianity in England, not its division.

Meanwhile, the illness that was gravely afflicting Father Anselm’s body grew heavier for him day by day. Nevertheless, not forgetting the rebellion that had become notorious, he wrote Thomas the following letter:

“Anselm, minister of the Church of Canterbury, to Thomas, elected archbishop of York.

“To you, Thomas, in the sight of almighty God, I, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, speak. Speaking on behalf of that same God, I forbid you the priestly office that you received in my parish at my command through my suffragan [Note: [Col. 0479D] I would prefer to read *injussu*, ‘without my command’; otherwise it is not clear why he could canonically have been prohibited from exercising the priesthood he had received. He had not yet been condemned for contumacy.], and I command you not to presume in any way to undertake pastoral care until you withdraw from the rebellion that you have begun against the Church of Canterbury and profess to it the submission that your predecessors, namely the archbishops Thomas and Gerard, professed according to the ancient custom of their predecessors.

“But if you choose to persist in what you have begun rather than withdraw from it, I forbid all the bishops of Britain, under perpetual anathema, to lay hands upon you for promotion to the episcopate, or, if you are promoted by outsiders, to receive you as a bishop or into any Christian communion.

“To you also, Thomas, under the same anathema, I forbid, on God’s behalf, ever to receive the episcopal blessing of York unless you first make the profession that your predecessors Thomas and Gerard made to the Church of Canterbury.

“But if you entirely relinquish the bishopric of York, I grant you permission to exercise the priestly office that you have already received.”

He sent this letter to all the bishops of England, one separately to each, with his own seal, commanding and ordering each of them, by the holy obedience they owed to the Church of Canterbury, to conduct himself thereafter toward Thomas according to what was written in it.

After this, on 21 April, the glorious Father Anselm died at Canterbury, in the metropolitan see. On the following day, which was Maundy Thursday, he was honorably buried in the major church at the head of Lanfranc, his predecessor of venerable memory, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1109, in the ninth year of the reign of Henry, glorious king of the English, in the sixteenth year of Anselm’s pontificate, and at the age of seventy-six.

Thus, a few days later, a certain cleric named Ulric, cardinal of the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0480D] Ulric, or Ulfric, is said to have been made cardinal in 1105 and to have been English by nationality.], came to England, sent by the venerable supreme pontiff Paschal. Carrying with him the pallium for the Church of York, when he learned that Anselm had died—for the certainty of his death, which had just occurred, had carried the news not far beyond England—he was thrown into confusion and wondered what he ought most appropriately to do.

For he had received the pallium itself from the Roman pontiff to deliver first to Anselm, and he had received instructions from the same pontiff to act thereafter according to Anselm’s counsel and arrangement.

At the next celebration of Pentecost, King Henry held his court at London with great worldly magnificence and lavish display. When the more festive days of his coronation had passed, he began to discuss with the bishops [Col. 0480D] and princes of the kingdom what should be done concerning the consecration of the elect of the Church of York.

The letter that we wrote immediately above, which Anselm had sent to the elect forbidding him the blessing unless he first made his profession to the Church of Canterbury, was read before the king. When Robert, count of Meulan, understood its contents as they were explained to him, he asked which of the bishops had dared to receive that letter without the assent and command of the lord king.

As the bishops realized from this question that the count intended to stir up a charge by which he could make them liable to the royal majesty, they withdrew from the crowd and, after taking counsel, resolved among themselves that, if the king’s judgment should happen to be dictated at the count’s prompting, they would rather be stripped of everything than disobey what Anselm had commanded concerning the dispute then before them.

They were Richard of London, William of Winchester, Robert of Lincoln, Herbert of Norwich, Roger of Salisbury, Ralph of Rochester, Reinhelm of Hereford, Robert of Chester, John of Bath, Ralph of Chichester, and William of Exeter.

Having thus confirmed their resolve among themselves, they decided that Samson, bishop of Worcester, should be summoned and that they should also inquire what judgment he would give concerning the matter. This was done, and he replied:

“Although I once fathered as a son, through his wife, the man who has been elected to the archbishopric of York, and although, according to the standards of the world and the nature of the flesh, I ought most justly to owe him advancement in honor and dignity, I owe much more to my mother Church of Canterbury, which advanced me to the honor in which I now stand and, through the episcopal ministry, made me a participant in the grace it merited from Christ the Lord.

“Therefore I wish it to be known to all that I shall obey in every way the letters of our Father Anselm concerning the matter now at issue between us, and that I shall never consent to the consecration in any way of the man elected to the bishopric of York until he professes the due and canonical obedience of submission to the Church of Canterbury.

“For I myself was present when my brother Thomas, archbishop of York, compelled by both ancient customs and irrefutable arguments, made that same profession to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and to all his successors.”

After these words, all the bishops immediately returned together to the king, firmly asserting both that they had received the letters about which the count had inquired and that they would act against them in no way whatsoever.

When the same count shook his head, apparently thinking that a charge of contempt of the king could now be brought against them, the king said:

“Whatever the judgment of others may be in this matter, let it be clear concerning me that I agree with the bishops, and that I do not wish, even for an hour, to be subject in any way to Anselm’s excommunication.”

When they heard this, everyone rejoiced. Together they gave thanks to the Lord and proclaimed that Anselm was present, and that, although absent from the world in body, he had now settled the case of his Church, which he could no longer settle while living in the flesh.

They then continued in praise of the outstanding prince and asked that he himself permit no one to humble the dignity of the primacy of the Church of Canterbury. Otherwise, they said, the ancient customs and their confirmations, made with the support of the whole kingdom under the great King William, as well as the privileges previously granted to that Church by the apostolic see, would be corrupted, torn apart, and annihilated.

The king agreed to this and ordered that the written records of those authorities, which the Church of Canterbury possessed, should also be brought promptly and read aloud. When this had been done, he said:

“What more is being sought? The authorities and privileges of the apostolic see, and the provisions determined in the presence of my father and mother, under the testimony and confirmation of the bishops, abbots, and nobles of the kingdom—should I, as though Anselm’s letter were entirely silent, put these matters in question or permit them to be disturbed by new evasions? No. Let Thomas know that he must either profess submission and obedience to the Church of Canterbury and its primates, as his predecessors professed, or entirely withdraw from the archbishopric of York. Let him therefore choose what he wants.”

Thomas, having considered the authorities by which he saw that the Church of Canterbury was supported and surrounded, and having rejected his clerics, whose counsel he regretted having trusted too late, said that he did not wish to oppose those authorities, but that, following the custom of his predecessors, he wished to accept them and to love and honor that Church forever thereafter.

“The king therefore ordered that the profession Thomas was to make should be dictated and written in his presence. It was to be impressed with his seal, with the round character, as they call it, and kept enclosed so that it could not be altered by any device before Thomas read it while making his profession.

And this was done.

On Sunday, 27 June [Note: [Col. 0481D] It had been printed incorrectly as 28 June; in the year 1109, the Sunday letter C fell on Monday.], therefore, at the king’s command, Richard of London, William [Col. 0482C] of Winchester, Ralph of Rochester, Herbert of Norwich, Ralph of Chichester, Ranulf of Durham, and Hervey of Bangor, bishops, assembled in the church of St Paul at London for Thomas’s consecration.

During the customary examination, at the appropriate point, Richard, bishop of London, who was to consecrate Thomas, demanded from him the profession of submission and obedience to the holy Church of Canterbury.

The profession, sealed as it was, was presented to Richard in the presence of everyone. The seal was broken, the document unfolded, and he read it as follows:

“I, Thomas, being about to be consecrated metropolitan of the Church of York, profess submission and canonical obedience to the holy Church of Canterbury, to the canonically elected and consecrated primate of that same Church, and to his canonically enthroned successors, saving the fidelity owed to my lord King Henry of the English, and saving the obedience which, on my part, Thomas my predecessor professed on his part to the holy Roman Church.”

The prior of the Church of Canterbury (Conrad by name) was present at this ceremony, together with a considerable number of monks from the same place, who had assembled there precisely for this matter, since it affected them most directly. When Richard, bishop of London, had received the profession offered to him by Thomas, he handed it to the prior and the brethren, saying:

> “Brothers and my lords, receive this profession, as a testimony to the authority of your Church, and preserve it for yourselves as a memorial for posterity.”

Then Bishop Ralph of Chichester declared publicly that the consecration ought, by right and ancient custom, to take place at Canterbury. He added:

> “Yet because that city, after the death of our father Anselm, is at present without a pontiff, it has seemed good to the king, to the consecrated orders of the realm, and to the leading men that the ceremony should be performed here, and most especially by the bishop of this see, for this reason and on this account: the bishop of London is dean among the other bishops of the Church of Canterbury, and therefore ought to be preferred to the others by a particular dignity.”

Thus Thomas was consecrated to the bishopric of York, receiving from a minister what he had refused to receive from his master. As long as he remained alive in this present life, remorse for this action did not leave his heart; he declared that he had been unfortunate and unworthy of the blessing of so great a father.

[Note: Thomas survived until February of the year 1114. He is also worthy of praise for this: when the physicians said that his fatal illness could not be cured without intercourse with a woman, he preferred to die chaste rather than contaminate his episcopal dignity with such a stain.]

When these matters had been completed, the aforesaid cardinal of the Roman Church, after hearing the king and consulting the king’s court, carried the pallium that he had brought to York, and invested its pontiff with it; then he resumed his journey back to Rome.

Meanwhile Bishop Hervey of Bangor, whom we mentioned above, was completely transferred from his Church, which he had formerly abandoned, and was enthroned in the new bishopric which the king and the leading men had long before decided should be established at Ely, as was mentioned above. He was scarcely able to obtain this privilege after the death of the vigorous Father Anselm, despite much pleading, many promises of many things, and the performance of many services.

That same year a star appeared, which very many people called a comet. It was seen in the month of December near the Milky Circle, directing its tail toward the southern region of the sky.

At the following Nativity of the Lord Christ, the kingdom of England assembled, as usual, at the king’s court in London, and a great and splendid solemnity was held. On that very day the archbishop of York, hoping to crown the king in the place of the primate of Canterbury and to celebrate the Mass, presented himself fully prepared for this purpose. The bishop of London, however, did not agree to this. He placed the crown upon the king’s head, led him by the right hand into the church, and performed the service of the day.

When they came to the king’s table and a dispute arose between the same bishops over their places of seating, the king refused to hear them. Instead, he excluded both of them from his meal and ordered them to go to their lodgings to eat. The bishop of London acted as he did—among other reasons—because he was both dean of the Church of Canterbury and, according to the institution of blessed Gregory, apostle of the English, at that time the senior of the two, since he had been ordained before the other. It was precisely because of the privilege of this seniority that he knowingly sought to be ordained to the pontificate with such haste, as we said above, although something else was being proclaimed publicly. Those who undoubtedly knew the secrets of his mind testified to this for us, and he himself, when I questioned him, affirmed it in familiar conversation.

But concerning the seating at the royal meal, the matter between the bishops remained to be determined by the judgment of the future pontiff of Canterbury.

During this period the case of the priests of England was dealt with, and more strictly than in the time of Father Anselm: they were restrained from associating with women. For very many of them, greatly heartened by the death of Father Anselm, had promised themselves that, once he had been removed, what they had grieved to be forbidden while he lived would be lawful for them. But the matter turned out otherwise.

For the king, who was feared by many more than God, bound them by his law so that, whether they wished it or not, they would at least in the eyes of men become executors of the London council, which we mentioned above. But if the priests themselves tried to act more wickedly, as though they had labored for this purpose in condemnation and insult of Anselm, let them look to it themselves. Each person will bear his own burden.

For I know that if the Lord judges fornicators and adulterers, those who violate their own kinswomen—not to mention sisters or daughters—will not escape his judgment. Nor will the fact that Anselm prohibited them from illicit embraces provide any excuse for their iniquities; surely each person will receive according to what he has done.

If someone should say that Anselm would have acted better by remaining silent and tolerating what he prohibited, although it might perhaps have grown worse, he could likewise say that the rich evangelical man who invited many people to the dinner he had prepared ought not to have sent his servant to summon the invited guests, since it happened that all of them found excuses not to come. It is not unreasonable to believe that this very Gospel reading, found over Anselm at his consecration and also read publicly at the reception of his pallium, perhaps foreshadowed these events.

For an excuse was raised against almost everything he taught by preaching or prohibited by instruction, and his words were effectively obeyed in nothing. Let whoever wishes read the text of the London council; having examined its statutes and commands, let him consider who obeys them, who proves their executor, and who treats them as though they were empty.

To say nothing of many other matters, certain abbots who had been deposed at that council on account of simony obtained, by paying money to laymen, either the abbeys they had lost or other abbeys. Likewise, those called priests or canons, now that the king’s edict was growing cold, arranged with their bishops and archdeacons, by infamous commerce, that they might freely take as their wives little prostitutes—either those whom they had left behind or others whom they preferred—while rejecting their former wives.

Furthermore, the long-haired men whom we know with certainty to have been excommunicated by Father Anselm from the thresholds of the holy churches now abound in such numbers, and boast so extravagantly of the feminine and shameful length of their hair, that anyone who is not long-haired is branded with the disgraceful name of “rustic” or “priest.”

I shall suppress in silence the other matters, no less disgraceful than the indignity of these men, lest I needlessly offend their admirers, since they are of no concern to me. I say only this: I do not know what the future day will bring forth; but at present I know how few—speaking of secular people—are found who strive to hasten with a pure and simple heart toward the Lord’s dinner by the road which the illustrious Father Anselm showed through his teaching.

He left England once, and he left it a second time, in accordance with the command that the Lord gave to his evangelical servant. In those departures, we who were his companions on his journey and in his labor know beyond all doubt that, by preaching, warning, and correcting, he brought an immense multitude of foreigners into the Lord’s dinner.

Therefore may almighty God turn away from those who were invited, to whom he was first sent to bring them, the sentence which that same Lord pronounced:

> “I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my dinner” (Luke 14:24).

These matters having been set in order, I shall bring the present work—which I undertook chiefly because heavenly piety granted me, unworthy as I am, a sincere love for Father Anselm of blessed memory—to its conclusion.

Before doing so, however, I ask briefly that those who are now, and those who after us will by God’s gift become, sons of the Church of Canterbury, that is, Dorobernia, do not grow angry with us who have written these things, as though we had labored for nothing. They might perhaps judge that what the glorious and magnificent Father Lanfranc is known to have done in his time was sufficient, indeed more than sufficient, to protect and preserve the dignity of the Church named above.

As for us, concerning what he himself did—so far as the affairs for which he did those things are concerned—we have no judgment, nor have we ever had any judgment, other than theirs. Therefore it seems madness for anyone to suppose that, by assuming so great a burden of writing, we imagined that our work could in some degree support his work. This is especially so since what we have written, being connected with his deeds, receives from them its only strength and foundation, without prejudice to the truth of the matters we have described.

Nevertheless—said with everyone’s goodwill—I ask that it be accepted that, among other things, the letter which Pope Paschal of pious memory sent to Girard, bishop of York, concerning the profession which he was bound to make to the bishop of Canterbury on Anselm’s behalf, contributed not a little to destroying the scandal which the men of York had stirred up against that Church and have not ceased to strengthen.

For that same letter remained at Canterbury with the pope’s seal. Girard, as a man educated in ecclesiastical disciplines and not requiring an instruction from such an authority, had already confirmed by his oath the profession made in the episcopate to Anselm, as the reference made above declared.

We shall therefore set down here the text of that letter, so that it may become known to all who deign to read or hear these things; and we shall make it the conclusion of this work, to the praise of God.

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Girard, bishop of York, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Although wickedly against us, etc.”

See the letter in the section on Paschal.

Here, then, and throughout all his work, let Him be praised and blessed who, while remaining the same in himself, renews all things, transfers kingdoms, and establishes over them whomsoever he wills—God, living and reigning before and beyond all ages. Amen.

## BOOK FIVE. And This in Abundance

The conclusion of the fourth book of the History, to which we gave the title *Recent Events in England*, clearly indicates that we had there deliberated about bringing the whole work to an end—indeed, that we had resolved in every way to do so.

For when he whose love had been the chief reason for composing this History, namely the lord and most glorious Father Anselm, supreme pontiff of the English, had been translated from this life, I judged that, in view of the delay in appointing his successor, if I continued writing I might either be writing empty things or, while living in private, fail fully to recognize many matters which the purpose of writing would require, given the silent uncertainty of my life, which is no more certain to me now than it was then.

Yet meanwhile, since I had learned with certainty from what I had written that I had complied with the wishes and affection of many, I decided to attach to it an account of subsequent events, insofar as God, the end of all things, should deign to inspire me. I hoped that, just as I had discovered the earlier material to be acceptable to many, this additional material would not prove burdensome.

Before undertaking it, however, I thought it appropriate to offer a brief explanation to certain people who still do not hesitate to disparage the aforesaid pontiff, on the grounds, as they say, that he did not devote himself to the construction of secular or ecclesiastical works, while keeping everything in his own hands, as his predecessor, Father Lanfranc of venerable memory, had done in his time. I wish them, after considering the nature of the circumstances, to judge from the truth itself whether they should now remain silent on this matter.

When Anselm first undertook to govern the archbishopric of Canterbury, he found all the lands belonging to that dignity devastated and all its revenues seized by William, son of William the elder, the king, so that he had nothing from which to support himself—I speak literally. Thus, deprived of the revenues by which he should have lived from the feast of Saint Michael—for he had come to Canterbury shortly before that feast—until the Nativity of the Lord, he was compelled by extreme necessity to have food supplied to him from the revenues by which he was to live from that solemnity until Easter.

By gradually drawing upon the revenues of later periods during earlier periods, with moderation and restraint, he was scarcely able, in the third year after his arrival, to bring them back to the condition established by his predecessors. What hardships, besides these, he suffered from King William and his followers during those three years and the fourth that followed, we have set out in some detail in the first and second books of the History, since we were present with him.

Thus, after living in England for four years amid tribulation and savage persecution, he was driven out by that same king in the fifth year. The entire archbishopric was invaded and, for three continuous years—that is, until the same king perished by an arrow—devastated beyond measure.

Meanwhile Anselm, expelled from his homeland and unable to obtain anything from England with which to support himself and his companions, borrowed what was necessary from foreigners. He did not wish to be a burden to those among whom he lived, nor to accept gratuitously everything that was offered to him.

Then, recalled by King Henry, who had succeeded his brother in the kingdom, he found his property reduced to the utmost poverty. He did not consider it honorable, given the circumstances, to send away empty-handed the collectors of the money he had borrowed, who came across the sea every day. If he was distressed by these matters, no one should wonder.

Moreover, peace between him and the king did not last with lasting firmness. He was therefore grievously harassed for two years and finally induced to leave the country. He departed and, as we have described, was unable to return until almost four years after his departure had elapsed.

At last he returned and survived for two years; in the third he died, with the debts by which he had supported himself in a foreign land scarcely paid. Since matters stood thus, by what reasoning, I ask, could he devote himself to earthly works when such constant oppressions and the destruction of his property never ceased to weary him?

Nevertheless, what he could not accomplish personally he carried out through the faithful sons of his Church, without envy and seeking nothing of secular glory. He placed the monks’ affairs in their own administration, appointing as prior after Henry, Ernulf, and after Ernulf, Conrad—monks of that place—so that all the affairs of the Church would be referred to their direction and treated, arranged, and concluded by the common counsel of the brethren.

Through the freedom which the monks obtained over their own possessions through the good Anselm, the Church was greatly increased in every respect: in the recovery of many lands which certain lay holders claimed for themselves as hereditary possessions; in various ornaments; and in every form of beauty in the house of God. Thus the ornaments of the Church appeared few and unattractive in comparison with the beauty and abundance brought into it in those days.

Moreover, the oratory itself, in the section extending eastward from the great tower, was enlarged through the provision and direction of Father Anselm. All these things were done from the Church’s resources, just as many things had been done by Lanfranc; and Anselm, from his own property, contributed a very large sum of money toward the enlargement of the house of God.

From what he possessed in his own right, he granted to the Church in perpetuity the half of the offerings of the high altar—the other half having been contributed by Father Lanfranc—as well as certain lands formerly belonging to the monks’ support but then diverted to other uses, many excellent pallia, and several other things appropriate to the beauty of the house of God.

Furthermore, after he had been recalled from his second exile, when he had obtained a certain degree of peace, he assigned to the works of the Church the pennies which are customarily paid at Easter each year by the parish churches to the mother church. He judged it more equitable that these payments should be possessed by the Church to which they were offered as a sign of due subjection than that secular power should take them away as its own when the bishop died, since earlier pontiffs had also claimed them as belonging to their own right in accordance with their office.

After his death, the king acted no differently in this matter from the arrangement Anselm himself had made. Throughout the entire period during which the Church lacked a pastor, the king preserved it in the condition in which Father Anselm, at his death, had left it, judging that he ought not to alter its institutions.

It is therefore sufficiently clear to whom the peace which the Church enjoyed should be attributed after God. I beg the detractors of so great a man and so magnificent a benefactor of Christ’s Church to spare their tongues—indeed, I beg them to spare their souls. For if God persecutes those who secretly slander their neighbor, I confess that it is to be feared that God will destroy those who publicly and unjustly gnaw at their father with wicked words.

Having briefly set these matters forth as the circumstances require, let us proceed to the events themselves, taking the beginning of our narrative from the matters we have described.

When the blessed and fortunate Bishop Anselm had been translated from the troubles of passing life to the blessedness of enduring life, King Henry, following the practice of his brother, King William, ordered everything belonging to the archbishopric of Canterbury to be brought under his own control, while the monks’ possessions remained in the freedom and under the protection in which Father Anselm had placed them.

Accordingly, many things were then done for the beauty of the house of the Lord Christ. When certain malicious people suggested to the king that the monks were mad and that they were daily squandering on superfluous uses what could have been magnificently employed at royal expense, he, as a man conspicuous for prudent goodness, said:

> “What do the monks spend of their resources on foreign expenses, on secular matters, or on vain works contrary to their order? But if they spend them on the enlargement and glory of the house of God, let God be blessed, who both inspired them with such a mind and granted me by his gift this grace: that in my days my mother Church should receive increase rather than loss.”

Thus the Church prospered, and royal authority took care that it should not be harassed by anyone.

Bishop Ralph of Rochester also exercised the care of pontifical office in it, and, both within and beyond it, was a constant defender and faithful supporter whenever any matter arose. He dedicated, as circumstances required, the churches in all the lands of the entire archbishopric of Canterbury, both within and outside Kent, without consulting the bishops.

He diligently administered in those same lands whatever pertained to Christianity, as circumstances demanded. These things were thus done in the Church’s children and possessions throughout the full five-year period during which the Church itself remained bereft after Father Anselm’s death.

When nearly that period had elapsed, King Henry, moved both by the admonitions of the lord pope and by the pleas of the Canterbury brethren and many others—and, most importantly, by the prompting of God—caused the bishops and leading men of England to assemble at Windsor, wishing to have their counsel in appointing a pontiff for Canterbury.

The aforesaid Bishop Ralph of Rochester, together with the prior and several Canterbury brethren, were also summoned to come to court, though they did not know the precise reason for which they had been invited. We therefore went there. Many people came to meet us on the way, asserting that they had just come from court and that, without any opposition, we would have Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, as archbishop.

Since we knew the man’s proven ability, we welcomed this news gladly, provided only that God’s will might be pleasing—God in whom we had placed all our hope.

What more need be said? We came to court, and behold, everything was full of the abbot, exactly as we had heard. In fact, the royal will had proposed this, and the same abbot, ordered by the king, had presented himself at court for that very purpose.

Nevertheless, the minds of the bishops and of certain leading men were inclined in another direction. They preferred either any bishop from the clerical order or some cleric from the king’s chapel to be taken up for that office.

But when it was pointed out to them that no one had ever presided over the archbishopric of Canterbury unless he was from the monastic order, with only one exception—

[Note: [Col. 0555]

(31) “Unless from the monastic order, etc., with only one exception.” He unquestionably meant Stigand, who is also expressly named by William of Malmesbury. But those who wish to examine this matter more carefully should consider Nothelm and the archbishops before and after Nothelm; they should also consult Jocelin in the *Antiquities of the British Church*, and Francis Godwin, bishop—of Llandaff when he wrote, now of Hereford—in his lives of our bishops. Arnold Wion, a distinguished and by no means negligent student of the monastic order, while laboring to discover which archbishops of the most celebrated Churches had entered the Benedictine brotherhood, omits among the archbishops of Canterbury Nothelm, Cuthbert, Bregwin, and others as well—although, to speak truthfully, he omits several whom it is absolutely certain were Benedictines. See Arnold in *The Tree of Life*, book II, chapter 20, and William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Bishops*, book I, in the section on Odo.]

—and that this one had been deposed by the Roman pontiff both for this presumption and for certain other wrongs committed by him, they were compelled to abandon the undertaking which they had been laboring with great effort to complete, since no reason or necessity required that such an ancient and authoritative custom be overturned.

Accordingly, by the providence of almighty God, the opinion of the bishops was suddenly turned toward the previously mentioned bishop of Rochester. They wished him to be appointed primate of all Britain and asked that the king’s assent cooperate with them in this.

The king immediately changed the mind he had held concerning the promotion of the abbot and willingly turned his attention to what was being proposed concerning the bishop, provided only that the monks and the leading men and people of Canterbury were willing.

There was no delay. Their willingness was sought, and everyone’s wishes were found to be one. The substance of the matter was announced to the crowd, and all mouths were opened in praise of God on this account.

Thus Bishop Ralph of Rochester was elected to the archbishopric of Canterbury, and an immeasurable joy was thereby produced in the entire multitude that had assembled. For there was in him a remarkable affability toward everyone, which made each good person greatly love him and rejoice together in his honor.

Meanwhile, if you had been present, you would have heard many people cry out together:

> “Truly, the king’s heart is in the hand of God; he inclines it wherever he wills” (Proverbs 21:1).

These events took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, on the fifth day after the completion of five years since the death of the most glorious Father Anselm.

He came to Canterbury on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June and was gloriously received by clergy and people; then, by the bishops who had assembled for this purpose, he was elevated to the pontifical seat.

He spent the first days of his arrival amid great glory and abundant resources, while everyone rejoiced and praised God because at last, after a long period of waiting, he had deigned to provide his Church with a pastor not from outside but from among its own household.

After this, removing from positions of authority those who had been accustomed to dominate the pontificate, he appointed his own people as seemed best to him. The opinions and perhaps the goodwill of many toward him changed from what they had previously been, and his reputation, which everyone had formerly proclaimed, was criticized by many in the unfavorable manner of the crowd.

Meanwhile King Henry was preparing to go to Normandy, wishing by his skill to subject to the peace he enjoyed the French and his other neighbors who were creating hostilities against him. But so that nothing in England would remain disordered during his absence, he arranged all the monasteries, which had long been deprived of pastoral care, by appointing persons to this office with the counsel of his bishops and leading men.

If some of them became wolves rather than shepherds, let them look to it themselves. The king appointed them as shepherds, not as wolves—as one is rightly entitled to believe. This arrangement might perhaps appear more credible if he had appointed not all foreigners but at least some natives of the land, even if they were not entirely English.

For merit of life, observance of regular discipline, and the prudence required for administering affairs were present no less in those who were rejected than in those who were appointed. Only their nationality separated them. If a man was English, no virtue could help him to be judged worthy of any honor; if he was a foreigner, he was immediately judged worthy of exceptional honor if his friends’ testimony attributed to him merely those qualities which could suggest the appearance of some goodness.

Yet no one should accuse God of injustice in these matters, since everything is subject to his ordering, since he never orders anything unjustly, and since nothing happens without cause. Since these things are so, let no one applaud himself for what God does not approve, for by the same measure by which he knows how to grant a crown to one, he also knows how to assign punishment to another in equitable judgment.

But for the present, let this suffice concerning these matters. The days are evil.

While the king was thus, as we have said, attending to the arrangement of the Churches, the archbishop of Canterbury requested that he return to him a monk of the Church of Canterbury, then abbot of Bury, named Ernulf, so that he might appoint him in his own place as pontiff of the Church of Rochester.

He did this both because he had discovered the man’s wisdom and religious character, because he did not wish to introduce an unknown person into that Church or among the Canterbury brethren, and also because he greatly hoped to be helped by his proximity in the administration of his own affairs.

When the king understood this, he readily agreed. The abbot was therefore taken from Bury, and at Canterbury, in the chapter of the brethren, he was invested by the archbishop with the bishopric of Rochester on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, according to ancient custom. The monks, clergy, and laymen belonging to that bishopric, together with a large multitude of other people, assembled for this purpose and elected him.

Although he was a professed monk of the Church of Canterbury, before he was invested with the bishopric by the pastoral staff he nevertheless touched the Gospels and promised that he would preserve in every respect his fidelity to the Church of Canterbury and to its bishop, and that he would never by any scheme or pretext interfere, or give his assent to anyone’s interference, in such a way that the Church of Canterbury should in any manner lose the dignity or power which it had hitherto held over the Church of Rochester.

The archbishop—who had previously been bishop of Rochester—knew that it was entirely necessary for this pledge to be made.

The newly elected bishop remained at Canterbury for nearly fifteen days after this. Finally, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, he was led by the archbishop to Rochester and received by clergy and people into the pontifical seat with due honor.

On that same day the river called the Medway failed so greatly on the southern side of the bridge, near the city’s castle, for several miles, that even the smallest boats could not move through the middle of its bed because of the lack of water. Nor was that river alone afflicted by this failure on that day.

The Thames likewise displayed the same deficiency. Between the bridge and the royal tower, and even beneath the bridge, the water of the river diminished so greatly that not only horses but also an innumerable multitude of men and boys crossed it on foot, the water scarcely reaching their knees.

This shortage of water lasted from midnight of the preceding night until deep darkness on the following night, as those who were present and saw these events—and who accompanied those crossing the river—testified and continue to testify to this day.

We have also learned by reliable report that a similar shortage of water occurred on that very day at Yarmouth and in other places throughout England.

Afterward, on the Kalends of November, Archbishop Ralph consecrated at Canterbury, in the metropolitan church, Albold, a monk of the monastery of Bec, whom we mentioned in the fourth book of the aforesaid History, to govern the abbey of Saint Edmund.

During these days messengers were sent to Rome to bring the pallium from the apostolic see for the archbishop of Canterbury. They were John, a monk of Séez, who shortly before these days had been elected and consecrated abbot of Bury after the aforesaid Ernulf; Warner, a Canterbury monk; and John, a cleric who was the archbishop’s sister’s son.

When they came to Rome, they delivered to the lord pope letters from the king of the English, from the archbishop, from the assembly of the brethren of the Church of Canterbury, and separately from nearly all the bishops of England. We judged it worthwhile to include here one of these letters, so that the meaning of the others might also be understood through it. It was as follows:

> “To Paschal, supreme shepherd of the holy universal Church, the assembly of Christ’s Church of Canterbury offers faithful prayers and the service of complete holy devotion.
>
> “We do not doubt that it is known, etc.”

See the letter in the section on Paschal II.

The men who had been sent then presented the business of their embassy to the apostolic ears with all the prudence they possessed. At first, however, they did not deserve to receive an answer that offered them any hope of accomplishing their purpose. They spoke with people unknown to them, and they were answered as strangers. They were therefore uncertain and did not know where they could safely turn.

In those days Anselm, nephew of the lord archbishop Anselm, was in Rome. He was familiar with the lord pope, who had made him abbot of Saint Sabas the Confessor. Having lived in England for a long time during the days of his blessed uncle, he was loved by the natives of the land as one of their own because of his gentleness.

When he heard that the aforesaid messengers had arrived, he came eagerly to them at the Lateran. Following toward them the conduct of a true friend in everything required by the substance of their business, he worked on their behalf.

What more need be said? By persistent advocacy, he made the Roman pontiff and those whose counsel supported him into such supporters of their cause that they obtained their wish entirely without payment. The same supreme pontiff handed over the pallium for which they had gone—Anselm himself was to carry it to Canterbury on behalf of blessed Peter and the lord pope—and they received it from his hand.

When these matters had been completed, the messengers returned from Rome, leaving Anselm with the pope to attend to the affairs that concerned him. They came to the king in Normandy, explained what they had done, and received the deserved praise for their diligence.

Then they sent a messenger to England to report their actions to the archbishop, while they themselves awaited the arrival of the aforesaid Anselm across the sea. When he arrived, the king received him with honor and gave him worthy thanks for the care he had devoted to the dignity of the kingdom of England.

After handing over the letters addressed to him by the pope and spending several days with him, the messengers who had come from Rome set out eagerly for England in his company. The text of the letters which he had brought to the king was as follows:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, illustrious king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Since from the hand of the Lord, etc.”

See the letter in the section on Paschal.

When Anselm had entered England, he approached the archbishop, who received him appropriately and then kept him with him for a considerable time in an equally fitting manner.

On the Sunday which fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, bishops, abbots, all the nobles, and an innumerable multitude of people gathered from every direction at the metropolitan see of Kent. Therefore, in accordance with what had been arranged beforehand, the aforesaid Anselm came to Canterbury, honorably carrying the pallium in a silver vessel.

Both communities—the archbishopric and the neighboring abbey of Saint Augustine—went out to meet him as far as the city gate, together with all who had gathered there for this purpose. The Father, surrounded by bishops and wearing sacred vestments like the others, came forward barefoot in devotion.

The pallium was then carried to the altar of the Savior and received there by the pontiff, after he had first made to the Roman pontiff a profession of fidelity and canonical obedience. Then everyone kissed it in reverence for blessed Peter, and the supreme pontiff, clothed in it, was solemnly led to the chair of the patriarchate of the English and enthroned.

Before that chair, after the prayers had been said and the other rites which the sacred custom of that Church has established had been performed, the newly elected bishop of Worcester, named Theobald, was immediately presented to him for consecration.

After being examined by him and making, according to the usual custom, a profession of canonical obedience to him and to his successors, he was honorably consecrated to the pontificate for which he had been designated.

The bishops who had assembled were present at and assisted in this consecration: Richard of London, Roger of Salisbury, Herbert of Norwich, Ralph of Chichester, John of Bath, and Hervey of Ely.

The bishop of Rochester was present that day but was not consecrated. He remained there, detained by a consideration which persuaded his mind that it would be more expedient to defer the matter to another time.

During this period the lord pope also sent a letter to the brethren of Christ Church, Canterbury. I have thought it appropriate to include it here; it is as follows:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the sons of the Church of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Your Church’s legates, etc.”

See the letter in the same section.

After these days Archbishop Ralph, on the advice and at the request of the bishops named immediately above, granted the archdeaconry of that Church to his nephew John, with the consent and approval of the Canterbury monks. John was a cleric of honorable conduct and gentle behavior toward everyone. The grant was made in the chapter, in the presence of the community of the brethren, with a large gathering of clergy and laity brought together for this very purpose. First, before them all, John touched the Gospels and swore that, for as long as he lived, he would show fidelity to the Church in every respect and in all things. [Col. 0494A]

In the same year King Henry ordered all the bishops and princes of the entire kingdom to come together to his court. Consequently, a rumor spread throughout the land that the Archbishop of Canterbury would celebrate a general council, in the presence of the lord pope’s legate whom we mentioned above, and would promulgate certain new measures worthy of so great an assembly for the correction of the Christian religion in every order. Accordingly, as the king had ordered, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October [16 September], an assembly of everyone was held at Westminster in the king’s palace. At last the gathered multitude realized that the rumor concerning the celebration of a council and the reform of Christianity had amounted to nothing.

Nevertheless, the often-mentioned Anselm, who had brought the pallium to Canterbury, came there, carrying a letter from the pope to the king and the bishops of England, containing the following text:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, illustrious king, and to the bishops of the English kingdom: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> How the Church of God was founded,” etc. See under Paschal II.

In response, after consulting the bishops about what he should answer the pope concerning these matters and certain others that greatly offended him, the king and the bishops jointly decided that he should send his own messengers, through whom he could communicate to the pope more securely whatever he wished.

For shortly before this, a certain cardinal of the Roman Church, named Cono, who was serving as legate of the Apostolic See, had come to France. [Col. 0494C] There, in accordance with the duty of his legation, while celebrating general councils, he excommunicated the bishops of Normandy and suspended them from episcopal office because, although summoned to three councils, they had refused to attend. This excommunication of the bishops greatly disturbed the king, and he thought it appropriate to take the matter up with the pope, especially since Cono appeared to have torn up, undeservedly, the privileges long ago granted by the Roman Church to the king’s father and brother and to the king himself.

William, bishop of Exeter, was therefore sent to carry out these matters. He was well known to the pope, since, in the time of the glorious Father Anselm, he had often been sent by the kings themselves concerning the affairs then pending between the kings of England and that same Father. Nor could the blindness that had taken away his sight excuse him from the journey, for his previous actions gave the king confidence that, as far as possible, he would faithfully pursue the king’s cause in his customary manner.

Meanwhile, the clerics of the Church of Menevia—which was founded in Wales under the patronage of the blessed Andrew and Saint David—asked King Henry for a bishop to replace their deceased bishop, Walfrid. A certain Bernard was chosen for this office, the queen’s chaplain, an upright man and, in the judgment of many, worthy of the priesthood. He was elected on the Saturday of the fast of the seventh month [the Ember Saturday in September], and on that same day he was ordained to the priesthood by William, bishop of Winchester, at Southwark.

As for the promotion to the episcopate, which both the king and several others wished to take place on the following day, while they were considering where it could be done most suitably, Robert, count of Meulan, unnecessarily introduced doubt about the place. Since it was clear, he said, that a bishop elected on such an occasion ought, according to custom, to be consecrated in the king’s chapel, he declared that he would prove this if necessary.

Father Ralph, unable to tolerate this unfair statement with equanimity, said that by such an allegation the count could easily bring it about that the bishop would be consecrated neither there nor anywhere else, but only at Canterbury, whatever the reason might be. The count himself should know, however, that since he had spoken only of the king’s chapel, Ralph would on no account consecrate him there.

The king then turned to the count and said: “There is nothing in what you are proposing. Neither I nor anyone else can in any way compel the Archbishop of Canterbury to consecrate a bishop of Britain elsewhere than where he himself wishes. So let him decide. It is his affair. Let him consecrate his bishop wherever he wishes.”

He therefore proposed to consecrate him in the church of his lodging at Lambeth. But because the queen wished to attend the ceremony herself, he was requested by her and consecrated the bishop in the church of Saint Peter at Westminster, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October [19 September]. He received from him the customary profession, together with the submission and obedience to be shown to the Church of Canterbury and its bishops.

The suffragans of the Church of Canterbury attended this consecration and assisted in it: namely, William, bishop of Winchester; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; Roger, bishop of Salisbury; John, bishop of Bath; Urban, bishop of Llandaff; and Gilbert, bishop of Limerick in Ireland. [Col. 0495C]

At this same time Alexander, king of the Scots, sent Ralph the following letter:

> “To the most beloved lord and Father Ralph, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, Alexander, by the mercy of God king of the Scots, greetings and the service of devoted fidelity.
>
> We inform you, most gracious Father, that the bishop of the church of the apostle Saint Andrew, namely Lord Turgod, departed from this world on the second day before the Kalends of September [31 August]. We are therefore greatly saddened, deprived as we are of so great a consolation.
>
> We consequently seek your counsel and assistance, as we trust in you, so that, according to God’s will, we may be able to appoint in his place someone who will know how to govern and instruct us and our people usefully by a manner of life pleasing to God.
>
> We also ask you to remember what we once brought to your attention concerning the bishops of the Church of Saint Andrew: in ancient times they were not accustomed to be consecrated except by the Roman pontiff himself or by the archbishop of Canterbury. We maintained this practice and, through successive generations, kept it confirmed by authority, until Lord Archbishop Lanfranc, we do not know by what arrangement, relaxed it for a time in favor of Thomas, archbishop of York, while we and our people were absent.
>
> We do not consent that this should continue any longer, relying entirely, if it please you, upon your authority to restore the matter to its former state. Now, therefore, if we may hope for your assistance in repairing this matter for us and for our Church—as we desire and request with our most humble prayers—please send us privately, in a worthy letter of your own, a clear assurance.
>
> Farewell.”

In that same year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December], Archbishop Ralph consecrated the aforementioned Ernulf to the episcopate of the Church of Rochester, and Geoffrey to the governance of the Church of Hereford. They were consecrated together at Canterbury, in the metropolitan church, with the suffragans of that see assembling and assisting in the office: William, bishop of Winchester; Herbert, bishop of Norwich; Ralph, bishop of Chichester; and Bernard, bishop of Menevia.

After this, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April [20 March], an assembly of the bishops, abbots, and princes of the whole kingdom was held at Salisbury, compelled to gather there by a royal order of King Henry. He had decided to cross to Normandy shortly afterward and, not knowing what might happen to him, wished to appoint as heir to the kingdom William, the son born to him by his lawful wife.

Accordingly, as soon as they learned the king’s will, all the princes became William’s men at his command, confirmed by faith and oath. Archbishop Ralph of Canterbury, together with the other bishops and abbots of the kingdom of the English, professed by faith and oath that, if they survived his father’s death, they would transfer to William both the kingdom and the crown of the kingdom, without any complaint or pretext, and that, once he became king, they would perform homage to him with faithful intent.

So much concerning this matter.

During these days a case was also heard concerning the dispute that had existed for almost an entire year between the Archbishop of Canterbury and the elected archbishop of York. After Thomas’s death—of whom sufficient mention was made above, near the end of the fourth book of the aforementioned History—a certain Thurstan, one of the king’s clerics, had been elected to govern the said archbishopric, with the connivance of Archbishop Ralph and with an opinion of him different from that which the outcome of the matter later justified.

When this elected man was admonished by the archbishop himself to do for the Church of Canterbury what he owed it and to receive his blessing according to ecclesiastical custom, he replied that he was indeed willing to receive the blessing, but that he would in no way make the profession which the archbishop demanded and which he knew his predecessors had made.

Because Ralph was unwilling to listen calmly to these words, the matter remained unresolved for so long. Thurstan himself had also sent his representatives to Rome, seeking from the pope an exemption from the required profession by the methods he knew ought to be used in dealing with the Romans, but he had accomplished nothing.

When King Henry noticed that Thurstan persisted in his obstinacy and supported and maintained that obstinacy as though relying on the king’s protection, he broke the bonds of that confidence. He openly declared that Thurstan would either observe the custom of his predecessors, both in making the profession and in other matters belonging by ancient right to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, or would be deprived entirely of the archbishopric of York, together with its blessing.

At this, while clerics were acclaiming him with a pretended reverence for the freedom of his dignity, and while he rashly trusted the counsel of his own heart, he resigned the archbishopric. He promised the king and the archbishop that, for as long as he lived, he would not protest against whoever was appointed in his place or raise any complaint on that account.

But after some days had passed and the customary services and former honors shown to him had greatly diminished, he began to waste away inwardly and bitterly regretted what he had done. He therefore changed his mind and followed the king across the sea, hoping to recover the archbishopric that had been taken from him and to act toward the king in such a way that, at the king’s command, he might obtain the archbishop’s blessing without being required to make the profession.

Since the king was unwilling to intervene in the matter except by delaying it, knowing that the archbishop regarded it as abominable to make himself permanently liable through such precipitancy, the matter was suspended, and neither Thurstan nor anyone else was appointed to the archbishopric of York.

In that same year, around the month of August, the aforementioned Anselm returned from Rome and came to Normandy to King Henry, bringing letters from the pope granting him permission to exercise the pope’s legatine authority in England. This soon became known throughout the kingdom of England.

The bishops, abbots, and nobles were therefore stirred and assembled at London, in the presence of the queen, to deliberate by common counsel about these matters and certain others. What more need be said? It was agreed by all that the Archbishop of Canterbury, whom the matter chiefly concerned, should approach the king and explain both the ancient custom and the liberty of the kingdom; if the king approved, he should go to Rome and annul these new measures.

The archbishop embraced this counsel. Burning with the greatest desire to visit the thresholds of the apostles, he crossed the sea and found the king at Rouen. The king and the Church of the bishopric of that city received him with the greatest joy and honor, and the king kept him there for several days.

There too we found the aforementioned Anselm waiting to cross into England to exercise his legation. But King Henry, unwilling to allow the ancient customs of England to be prejudiced, prevented him from entering England. Nevertheless, since he was the messenger of blessed Peter, the king had him supplied generously and courteously.

Archbishop Ralph therefore dealt carefully with the king, in the proper order of events, concerning the affairs for which he had come, and set out upon the route for his journey to Rome. When he reached France, however, he was struck in the face by a serious ulcer, and, as his entire head swelled, he was brought almost to the point of death.

For this reason he lay in bed for an entire month in a castle called Feritas a freno [reading uncertain], while we who were with him scarcely dared promise that he would live. At last, when he had improved from his illness, he gradually resumed his journey toward Rome, as far as he was able to endure it.

He traveled with a large and wealthy retinue and, impressive in appearance, was magnificently received by everyone to whom he came.

When we reached Lyons, where the lord and illustrious Father Anselm, once driven from England for the sake of justice, had formerly been treated by everyone not as an exile or stranger but as a resident and truly as the bishop and lord of that place, we were received there with exceptional honor and affection. We remained for some time, attracted by the sincere affection of everyone with whom I associated, constrained by the severity of the winter, and detained by the approaching solemnity of the Nativity of Christ.

During those days, because I was familiar with the place and its people, I once went up to Saint Irenaeus and turned aside to the oratory of blessed Mary Magdalene to speak with two servants of God who had been enclosed there beside the oratory for God’s sake. These women had once been known to Father Anselm on account of their religious life and had been instructed in many things by his most sacred teaching.

Among them, after the lord Anselm’s departure, a very serious disagreement arose at the instigation of the Evil One, produced—as commonly happens—by the evil of envy. Since disputes, reproaches, and many things unbecoming their vocation passed between them on almost every day, one night, according to what I learned from the women themselves, Father Anselm appeared to one of them, the one whom the greater blame for the division marked out.

He rebuked her harshly and complained that they had badly observed his teaching, for whose sake he had journeyed from distant parts of the world to them. Nevertheless, he ordered them to abandon their undertaking and, if they did not wish to lose his peace—which was God’s peace—to return to peace with all haste, abandoning every evasion.

What the admirable bishop advised was done. And behold, they dwell as one in the house of God, nor do they doubt that he is present to them, since they have beneficially experienced his correction. [Col. 0498C]

Moreover, one of these women, named Achaleid, told me in familiar conversation, under the testimony of truth, that after the death of the memorable Father Anselm, she had once devoted herself to prayers and tears more than usual through the gift of God’s grace. Suddenly, as though in an ecstasy of mind, she was carried outside herself and brought by certain reverend persons before the tribunal of the most glorious Queen of Heaven.

After greeting her with due reverence and falling at her feet at her command, she saw and heard many wondrous proclamations of the heavenly homeland. As though thereby made more steadfast in confidence, she asked the Lady of all things, among other matters—which she was unwilling to tell me—about the venerable Hugh, bishop of Lyons: namely, how, or in what lot of God’s judgment, he stood, now that he had departed from this world.

She replied: “He will be well, daughter; indeed, through the mercy of God he will be well.”

“And concerning my lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury,” she said, “pious Lady, if it please you, I beg you to reveal what we may think.”

She answered: “Be absolutely certain concerning him that he is in the great glory of God.”

At this she returned to herself. The sweetness and dignity of the vision will teach anyone who considers what she did and how she spent the remainder of the night.

We have spoken of these matters, as it were, in ecstasy, led by our love for the most worthy Father Anselm. By the Lord’s mercy we are deeply imbued with that love, and it is always a pleasure for us to write or speak about him.

From here we return to the order of our narrative.

When we reached Piacenza, Herbert, bishop of Norwich, who had left England intending to travel with us to Rome, was seized by a severe illness. As his sickness worsened, he lay for ten uninterrupted days mute, without food or voice. We consequently spent four weeks there, uncertain what God would do with the bishop.

When we clearly observed that he was recovering, our Father, at his request and on his advice, resumed the journey he had begun. Herbert himself, exhausted by extreme weakness, remained there, intending either to await the archbishop there or, if he recovered and the archbishop delayed, to precede him on the return journey.

We therefore reached Rome, while he reached Normandy, after some days, as far as the Lord granted us strength.

Since the lord pope, because of the disagreement then existing between himself, the emperor, and the Romans, was staying at Benevento, Ralph could not approach him at all—partly because of his bodily weakness and partly because of the aforementioned conflict, on account of which the inhabitants laid serious ambushes for everyone wishing to go to the pope.

He therefore sent messengers with letters to inform the pope at Rome both of his arrival and of the reason for his arrival. The pope received them graciously and weighed their carefully measured words on the scales of equity. In accordance with the nature of the matter, he wrote to the bishops of England and to the king as follows:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brothers, the bishops of England, and to our most beloved son Henry, illustrious king: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> When he came to us,” etc. See under Paschal II.

After leaving the pope, the messengers returned to us at Rome. We, however, had gone out from Rome as far as Sutri. Several days later, Archbishop Ralph, invited by the emperor, visited him with the pope’s approval and spent eight days with him in his army, which the emperor had brought near Rome.

From there Ralph returned again to Rome and stayed many days at Sutri. For a report had spread everywhere that the Roman pontiff would soon come to the city, and Ralph thought that he would more conveniently await him there, since he greatly desired an interview with him.

But when it became clear that matters stood otherwise, he set out on the journey home. We therefore came to Rouen to the king of the English, and he detained us in Normandy for a long time.

During these days, the clerics of York, wishing to have the aforementioned Thurstan, their elected archbishop, restored to their Church and insisting by every means that he should not make a profession of subjection to the Archbishop of Canterbury, sent their most prudent representatives to the pope. They desired that their wish should be established by his authority and command as a new law.

They undertook the journey and proceeded all the way to the pope. How truthful they proved as reporters of their cause, the outcome itself—which, I confess, has been set out above in a truthful account—and the text of the letter that the pope himself sent on behalf of Thurstan will make clear to anyone who wishes to know. It is as follows:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, illustrious king of the English: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> With God as our author,” etc. See under Paschal.

Thurstan, restored to the archbishopric, came to England around the month of February, in the second year after he himself had come to the king in Normandy.

The venerable Father Ralph, still unable to separate himself from the king’s company, remained in Normandy, awaiting a suitable time for his return. The aforementioned Anselm likewise remained at Rouen with the king, wishing to take with him to Rome the money customarily paid each year from England to blessed Peter.

But, as we have said, the king was unwilling to consent to his crossing into England to exercise the legation entrusted to him, for the reason we have already mentioned, as well as for others no less reasonable.

So that posterity may perceive what ought to be done in such circumstances, should they perhaps arise, we have briefly touched upon what happened in our own days, without prescribing any course that anyone who prefers it must follow.

After this—namely, in the second year after Archbishop Ralph had left England to travel to Rome, and after Anselm had come from Rome to Normandy to the king of England, hoping to enter England to exercise his legation—Pope Paschal, whose memory is sacred, died. A certain John, born at Gaeta, was appointed in his place.

John had been raised and educated as a monk from childhood in the monastery of Monte Cassino, and had served continually as chancellor in the ministry of the venerable apostolic lords Desiderius, Urban, and Paschal. Having therefore been appointed successor to the supreme pontiff, he changed his name and was called Gelasius.

The Teutonic king, who was also Roman emperor, heard that the pope had departed this life, hastened to Rome, and, after Gelasius withdrew from the city, installed as his own pope the bishop of Braga, whom the same pope had excommunicated at Benevento the previous year. Taking the name Gregory from Burdinus, he appointed him.

So that all these events may be clear to those who wish to know them, let them read the letter that Gelasius himself sent concerning them to Gaul, and which we reproduce here with his subscription:

> “Gelasius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, princes, and all the other faithful throughout Gaul: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> Since you are members of the Roman Church,” etc. See under Gelasius II, below.

During these days England was struck by a grave loss: the death of the queen. She died at Westminster on the Kalends of May [1 May] and was decently buried in that same monastery. By what judgment of God this occurred, we do not know.

Immediately afterward, many of the Normans who had sworn fidelity to the king abandoned it and transferred themselves to the king of France and to his princes, not fearing the justice of their own natural lord. What evils, and how great, arose from this, we know to be difficult to conceive, let alone describe.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned Pope Gelasius crossed the sea and came to Burgundy, and his arrival soon became known throughout Gaul. All the powerful, together with people of more modest standing, were stirred to meet him, and people eagerly prepared to attend the council that he had arranged to celebrate at Rheims in the middle of Lent.

When Archbishop Ralph heard of the pope’s arrival, he left Rouen, where he had remained until then, and resolutely decided to meet him. But after he had completed part of the journey, he learned from certain people that the pope had gone much farther away and intended to proceed toward Spain.

Because the journey was difficult on account of its labor and length, Ralph, on the advice of his friends, turned back and postponed his departure, intending, as he thought, to resume the same journey not long afterward and, God willing, to meet the pope when he came to Cluny. Nevertheless, thinking it advisable, he sent his representatives to the pope to investigate carefully both the certainty of his route and his disposition toward Ralph, as well as what he might be able to entrust to him concerning his affairs.

When these events became known to Thurstan of York, he left England, crossed the sea, and came to Rouen, intending, as he hoped, to seek the pope for the sake of his cause. The king rebuked him for having crossed without consulting him and forbade him to proceed farther until he learned a more certain account of the pope’s movements.

But after not much time had passed, the representatives whom the archbishop had sent returned and announced that they had reached the pope, who had been proposing to undertake many things new and unheard of in our age, but had been overtaken by death and buried at Cluny.

After this, therefore, the cardinals and other Romans who had followed the pope to Gaul, deliberating for themselves as though they were far removed from their own people, appointed in place of the deceased pope Guido, archbishop of Vienne, supported by the authority and resources of that place, so that they might be safer in a foreign province. Changing his name, they called him Calixtus.

While these ecclesiastical affairs were being arranged in Burgundy, the apostolate of the Roman Church was being administered with the aforementioned Gregory presiding over the See of blessed Peter.

England was therefore shaken by many rumors concerning these matters, some asserting that this man, others that that man, and others that neither was rightfully prelate of the Church of God. The Gauls, however, and the king of the English, together with the Archbishop of Canterbury, transferred their allegiance to Calixtus and, rejecting Gregory, accepted him as pope.

Whether anything authentic and worthy of remembrance was sent in those days by Calixtus to the king and the primate of England, or by them to Calixtus, no certainty has so far come to light for us. We who devoted ourselves to writing these matters were in England; those about whom we are speaking were at that time outside England.

When Father Ralph, after returning from Rome, was living with King Henry in Normandy, and noticed that I—who had been the constant companion of blessed Anselm while he lived, and who, from the time he had been elevated to the archbishopric of Canterbury, had remained continually in his service—was somewhat ill, he grieved for me with paternal affection.

He could not endure that I, who had been nurtured from infancy within the Church, should be exposed to any danger of death outside it. He therefore advised and persuaded me to go to Canterbury, writing, in his goodness, the following letter to the community of the brethren of our Church and sending it by his messenger:
