> “To his most beloved brothers and sons, Prior Conrad and the other servants of God who are at Canterbury in Christ Church, their most faithful brother Ralph, priest of that same Church and its devoted minister: greetings and love, with the blessing of God and of himself.
>
> I have longed with great longing to see your faces, all the more because I thought that you were somewhat saddened by the prolonged delay of my pilgrimage. Since I shall soon be coming to you, I am sending ahead our brother and friend, Lord Eadmer, who is aware of and has shared all our labors and actions. He can lay my heart completely open to you and reveal more precisely everything that is happening around me and all that I desire than I have judged it possible to entrust to any written document.
>
> I earnestly ask you to remember once and often to give him thanks for the service and honor that, out of true love, as a prudent and perfect man, he has shown me, and for the labor and burden that he has borne sorrowfully for my sake, without murmuring, while making no complaint for himself.
>
> Remember, therefore, to repay him with equal gratitude, showing me the love that you have for me by serving him and giving him the honor and love that you would wish to give me, knowing that I endure his absence with difficulty.
>
> But I was frightened by what seemed to be a recurrence of the illness by which he was afflicted last year, and for this reason I was compelled to send him ahead. Take care, therefore, to be most compassionate brothers to him and the most diligent administrators of all those things that you see to be suitable and beneficial for his health.
>
> Farewell, and remember us.”

I have recorded this letter here not to commend my own person—for I know with absolute certainty that I am worthy of no praise—but so that, by describing the event in a straightforward style, I may present the matter to those who hold and assert that I abandoned my father as though he were placed among strangers and deprived him of the comfort of my service in the manner of an illegitimate child.

Indeed, when I saw that he was delaying his return beyond the appointed time, I would certainly have gone back to him if I had not been forbidden to do so on his behalf. For, repeatedly instructing his people in England that his arrival was now imminent, he did not wish to be wearied out of consideration for his own affection. Instead, he ordered me to await him where I was, since he thought he would arrive as quickly as possible.

The truth itself knows that matters stood thus. Since, therefore, I am for the present separated from that father of mine not in any other way but this, I do not think anyone should be angry with me if I fail to write what is being done or has been done in the meantime, when it is worthy of remembrance.

Until now I have wished to state nothing uncertain as though it were certain, and even now I do not wish to write such things. Nevertheless, I cannot doubt that he did something, or intended to do something, concerning the affair that had continued between him and the aforementioned Thurstan of York.

With great insistence he ordered that a privilege promulgated concerning this matter in the time of Archbishop Lanfranc, under the great King William, and confirmed by that king’s seal, which is carefully preserved in Christ Church at Canterbury, should be sent to him during those days.

I would not readily believe that so great a man had done this without good reason. When Father Ralph had received this privilege, brought to him at his command, he would have presented himself to the pope, as we were told in England, in order to transact with him concerning his own and certain other ecclesiastical affairs, unless he had been held back from proceeding by King Henry’s promise: namely, that when the king returned to his kingdom, he would do Ralph full justice and would ensure that the often-mentioned Thurstan submitted himself to Ralph’s will and authority.

This promise did indeed detain him to some degree in the lands across the sea and persuaded him patiently to await the outcome. The king, too, was occupied everywhere by the tumult of war and could neither deliberate as he wished nor, while abandoning these affairs, return to England with honor intact.

Meanwhile, in the very year of his election, Pope Calixtus appointed a general council at Rheims, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October]. This was the year 1119 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the fourth year since Archbishop Ralph had left England to travel to Rome.

For this council there was a great gathering of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and princes from various provinces, together with a numerous multitude of clergy and common people.

Among them:

[Note: [Col. 0556]]

(32) Representatives were also sent by Henry, king of the English, to that council, etc.: William of Exeter, Ranulf of Durham, etc. There were four bishops. For an ancient solemn custom once prevailed that only four bishops should be sent from England to a general council. The same practice was observed at the Lateran Council held under Alexander III in the year 1179.

When a council was held in England at that time concerning the sending of bishops to Rome to attend the council there, the bishops of England consistently asserted—and these are the words of Roger of Howden, of the manuscript of Simon of Durham, and of others who deal with the matter—that only four bishops from England were to be sent to the lord pope’s general council at Rome.

In more recent councils, however, the practice varies and is often changed according to royal discretion and the circumstances of the case. Concerning legates or envoys sent from England to general councils, one may consult Matthew Paris under the year 1245, where the entire body of the English citizenry—that is, the three orders—also sent letters and envoys to the Council of Lyons held under Innocent IV; and Thomas Walsingham’s *Ypodigma Neustriae* under the same year, p. 466; and the same author under the year 1409.

To these may be added, from the archives, what Henry IV, king of England, is said to have decreed in order to repair the schism that was then excessively dividing the Roman factions at the Council of Pisa [ [Col. 0555D] See the Council of Constance, session 20, in Binius, vol. III, part II, p. 913.]. He wrote as follows in a letter to the estates of Aquitaine:

> “We have ordained that our solemn envoys”—thus he wrote—“shall be sent to the day and place of the said council; and that two archbishops, accompanied by four doctors, and five bishops, accompanied by an equal number of doctors, shall personally attend there with them.
>
> Each of the other bishops of both our aforesaid kingdom and our land of Ireland who, for certain reasons, may not go to the said council shall send one doctor in his place, for himself and for the clergy of his diocese. Each of our universities shall also send two doctors, one of whom shall be a theologian and the other a doctor of canon or civil law.
>
> The Black Monks shall send four abbots; the Cistercians, two; the regular canons, likewise two abbots; the Cluniacs, two abbots or priors; the Carthusians, one prior; and the Premonstratensians, one abbot. Each chapter of a cathedral church shall also send one doctor to the said council.
>
> The prior of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem residing in England shall go there in person.
>
> We wish these ordinances of ours, and any others already made or still to be made concerning the aforesaid matter of schism or union, to be observed not only in our aforesaid kingdom and the said land of Ireland, but also in our duchy of Aquitaine.”

So we read in the Gascon Rolls, nos. 9 and 10, Henry IV, membrane 4.

I have also thought it worthwhile to add the form by which King Henry VI appointed his legates—some of them laymen, others members of the sacred order—to attend the Council of Basel. Since such a thing occurs very rarely, it is appropriate to include it from the French Rolls, no. 12, Henry VI, membrane 2. The heading in the margin is: “Concerning the authority entrusted to the king’s ambassadors to attend the Council of Basel.”

The instrument itself is worded as follows:

> “The king, to all to whom these presents shall come, etc., greetings.”

“Know that, since, in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Constance [ [Col. 0555D] See the Council of Constance, session 19, p. 935 in Binius, vol. III, part II, and the Council of Basel in the same author, vol. IV, part I, p. 14.] the present Council of Basel is now actually being held under the most holy Father, Lord Pope Eugene IV, and have been repeatedly urged to attend that council—not only on the part of the council itself, through its envoys specially sent to us for this purpose, but also by apostolic and imperial letters and by letters of many other fathers of Holy Mother Church and secular princes—and desiring to attend it for the praise of God, the desired prosperity and honor of Holy Mother Church, and especially for the advancement of the Catholic faith, being reasonably hindered by various and differing causes from attending it in person as we would wish, we hereby constitute, appoint, and deputize the venerable Fathers Robert, bishop of London; Philip, bishop of Lisieux; John, bishop of Rochester; John, bishop of Bayeux; and Bernard, bishop of Aix; as well as our dearest kinsman Edmund, count of Mortain; our beloved Nicholas, abbot of Glastonbury; William, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of York; and William, prior of Norwich; and also our beloved and faithful Henry Broumflete, knight; Master Thomas Broun, doctor of both laws, [Col. 0557B] dean of Salisbury; John Colluelle, knight; Master Peter Mauricii, doctor of theology; and Master Nicholas David, archdeacon of Coutances and licentiate in both laws, as our ambassadors, true and undisputed envoys, procurators, agents, representatives, and special messengers. By these presents we give and grant to them and to the greater part of them authority and mandate, both general and special, in our name and on our behalf, to attend, deliberate, communicate, and conclude in the said council concerning matters that may relate both to the reformation of the universal Church in head and members and to the strengthening of the orthodox faith and the pacification of kings and princes, and also concerning and regarding perpetual peace or abstention from war between us and Charles, our adversary of France; and likewise to deliberate, communicate, arrange, consent to, and, if necessary, dissent from whatever may happen to be established and ordained there in accordance with the deliberation of the said council. We promise, and do promise in good faith, that we shall perpetually hold as ratified, acceptable, and firm the whole of whatever shall have been agreed, done, or conducted in the matters aforesaid and in each of them by our said ambassadors, envoys, and procurators, or by the greater part of them; and, once we have been informed concerning these matters, we shall, insofar as it concerns us and a Christian prince, ensure that due execution is carried out. In testimony of this matter we have caused these letters of ours to be made patent. Given under the testimony of our great seal in our palace at Westminster, on 10 July.”

“By the council.”

The forms of the papal letters by which religious orders are summoned to general councils may be found in Binius, vol. III, part II, p. 674, in the apparatus to the Lateran Council held under Innocent III; in Matthew Paris, under the year 1245, p. 886 of the London edition, namely the letters sent to the abbots and priors of the Church of England at Lyons on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the second year of Innocent IV, although I also find them in the ancient manuscript Annals of Burton monastery, where, though the syllables otherwise scarcely differ, the fifth day before the Ides of June is substituted; likewise in Binius, the aforesaid volume III, pp. 768 ff., in preparation for the Council of Vienne under Clement V, and in vol. IV, part II, p. 276.]

Bishops and abbots of Normandy were also sent by Henry, king of the English, to that council, as well as the bishops of England who at that time were living with him in Normandy—namely William of Exeter, Ranulf of Durham, Bernard of Menevia, and Urban of Glamorgan. Ranulf, archbishop of Canterbury, was prevented from attending that assembly, partly by bodily weakness and partly by other considerations. The aforementioned Thurstan, having asked the king’s permission to go there, could in no way obtain it until, having pledged his faith by which he was bound to him as his lord, he promised him that he would do nothing before the pope whereby the Church of Canterbury might suffer any diminution of its ancient dignity, nor would he, for any reason or upon any persuasion, receive episcopal benediction from him. Thus bound by such a pledge, he set out and came eagerly to the pope, as he knew would best serve his own business.

Why say more? Setting aside his pledge of faith, he transferred the Romans to his own cause, as they are accustomed to be drawn into every sort of business, by the service of his generosity; and through them, with his own assistance, he obtained that he should be consecrated bishop by the pope. Indeed, before this the king had sent his messenger to the pope, warning him about the dispute that had until then continued between Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thurstan himself. The messenger and executor of this mission was Sieffred, surnamed Pelochinus, the archbishop’s brother, [Col. 0504A] a monk in habit, clever in understanding, prudent in foresight, and bound to both king and pope by the ties of familiarity.

Among the other matters that the king instructed this man to say to the pope, he particularly ordered him to tell him that he should take care that, without the intervention of any favor or consideration, either he himself consecrated Thurstan, or ordered or permitted him to be consecrated by anyone other than the archbishop of Canterbury, as was customary; otherwise, he would never again receive him into any place under his dominion. And if the pope himself should perhaps wish to press the contrary view, as though by the authority of his apostolate, he should know for certain that not even for the loss of his crown—though I have been excommunicated for a period of seven years—would the king change his purpose in this matter.

He replied: “Let the king not suppose that I shall in any respect act otherwise in the matter of which he speaks than he himself wishes. Nor has my will ever inclined me to humble in any way the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, over which so many illustrious Fathers have presided, as is known almost throughout the whole world.”

When the royal messenger believed these apostolic words and became confident in the outcome of his mission, he therefore came to Reims. There, on the morning of the Sunday preceding the appointed day of the council, while at Saint Remigius with his companions from Canterbury he heard certain men protesting to him that Thurstan and his associates were eagerly preparing for the benediction of the pontificate in the episcopal seat, he was astonished beyond measure and could not in the least believe what was being said. But when the truth of the matter became publicly known, John, the archdeacon of Canterbury (whom the course of this business had brought there), stood before the pope and, in the presence of many bishops and other distinguished persons, protested aloud that the benediction ought to be given by the archbishop of Canterbury; nor could the pope himself, although he was exercising the papal office, lawfully take away the right of the Church of Canterbury, since it was evident that it had thus far denied nothing that it justly owed.

In reply he said: “We do not wish to commit any injustice against the Church of Canterbury; but, with its justice and dignity preserved, we shall carry out what we have proposed.”

Everyone who heard this judged it astonishing, seeing him contradict with an adverse expression what he was saying by an act of the greatest injustice. For Thurstan was consecrated to the archiepiscopate of York [Col. 0504D], and in this way was cheated of the pledge which he had made under God to his lord. After this act the hearts of many were shaken with astonishment. They judged that he could never have dared such a thing if he had not perceived that the royal will was favorable to him in it.

Since, at the pope’s command, several bishops from Gaul attended this consecration, Hubald, archbishop of Lyons, of revered memory, absolutely refused to be present, not even when the pope ordered him to do so. He perceived that the matter was proceeding by an improper path and was horrified that so great an injury should be inflicted unjustly upon the Church of Canterbury, to which he was joined by particular friendship and fraternal intimacy. The bishops of the kingdom of the English, whom we have said were sent to the council by King Henry, had not yet arrived there, and so, in their absence, these things were completed.

When the king learned of them with certainty, he issued orders and absolutely forbade Thurstan and his associates to return to Normandy, England, or any place under his dominion. Everyone who heard of these events concluded that what had been done had been done without the king’s consent.

After this, Calixtus came to Gisors, and King Henry went there to speak with him. Many matters were then conducted between them, for the sake of which such great persons had reasonably assembled. Among other things, the king obtained from the pope that he should grant him all the customs that his father had possessed in England and Normandy, and especially that he should never permit anyone to exercise the office of legate in England unless the king himself, compelled by some special complaint that could not be resolved by the archbishop of Canterbury and the other bishops of the kingdom, should request the pope to do so.

When all these matters had been settled according to the circumstances of the time, the pope asked the king to become Thurstan’s friend and, for love of him, restore him to the archiepiscopate to which he had consecrated him. But the king confessed that he had pledged on his faith that he would never do this while he lived.

He said: “I am the apostolicus, and, if you do what I ask, I shall absolve you from this pledge of faith. I shall deliberate on these matters,” he said, “and shall inform Your Paternity of whatever the tenor of my counsel discovers.”

Then the king withdrew from the pope and sent him the following reply through his intermediaries:

“As he says that, because he is the apostolicus, he will absolve me from the faith that I pledged if I receive Thurstan at York, it does not seem fitting to royal honor to consent to such an absolution. For who would thereafter believe anyone pledging his faith, when he saw from my example that it could so easily be destroyed by absolution? Nevertheless, since he so earnestly requests that Thurstan be admitted to the archiepiscopate, insofar as it concerns me I grant this for love of him, on the condition that Thurstan first come to Canterbury and make, in writing and according to custom, the due profession of obedience and submission which Thomas, Gerard, and the other Thomas made to the Church of Canterbury and its primate. If he fails to do this, let him know that, while I reign in England, he will preside over the Church of York without any edict compelling me to allow it. For I have promised to maintain this and have pledged my faith as surety, lest I ever become a transgressor of this promise.”

[Col. 0505D]

When these matters concerning the legation of England and the archbishop of York had been settled, Father Ralph returned to England. Having landed at Dover, he was received into his seat at Canterbury on 12 January with the greatest honor and joy. Anselm, however, who, as we have described, boasted of the legation of England, was judged unworthy either to enter England or to exercise any office of legate. Thus deprived of all this authority, he returned from Normandy to his own country.

Thurstan followed the pope, but was not detained by him for long, lest his presence become burdensome. King Henry, however, persisting in his decision, would not allow him to be admitted either to the archiepiscopate of York or to any place under his authority. [Col. 0506A]

During these days many were stirred to investigate the authorities and ancient privileges of the primacy that the Church of Canterbury, which is Dorobernensis, claims over the Church of York. This happened chiefly because the dispute that, as we have described, had continued between Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thurstan of York had been brought to the attention of the bishops overseas, Thurstan himself soliciting their support against Father Ralph by every means.

They, being ignorant of the customs and privileges of the Church of Christ at Canterbury, favored Thurstan excessively. They asserted, as he reported it, that Ralph relied in his assertions more on force and an abundance of wealth than on ancient authority and the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. But when it was said in response that it was vain to hold such an opinion, and that, for determining this dispute, what had been done concerning the matter since the time of King William, who had conquered England by arms, ought to be sufficient—especially since, from the days of his reign, almost everything that the English had anciently revered as virtually sacred was now, in the judgment of some, scarcely regarded as possessing even the lowest authority—they said:

“It is not so; rather, the new matters introduced in these times must, if they are to stand as valid, be supported by the testimony of ancient writers.”

Therefore, as we have said, the concern of many awoke for investigating these matters. Trusting in the justice of the Church of God, they searched more diligently the hidden recesses of ancient archives and the volumes of the Holy Gospels, which until then had served only for the adornment of the house of the Lord. And behold: so that the will of those who love justice might not be deprived of its desired effect, God revealing it, certain privileges were found, firm on every side and supported by apostolic authority. They are as follows:

“Pope Boniface to Æthelbert, king of the English.

“Since the integrity of your Christianity has grown so greatly in the worship of its Creator that it shines far and wide, and since its increase in works worthy of God, proclaimed throughout the whole world, is reported, we render enormous thanks to God, the giver of all good things,” etc.

“Pope Boniface to Justus, archbishop of Dorobernum.

“Having received the writings of Your Affection, in which, among other things, we find that very many of the pagans dwelling there have been converted, with the help of Almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and especially that in the regions of Kent they have been led by your labors to faith in our true God, we have greatly rejoiced.”

“Pope Honorius to Honorius, archbishop of Dorobernum.

“Having received the letters of Your Affection, we find in them the concern of your labor, occupied with much toil on behalf of the flock entrusted to you,” etc.

“Pope Vitalian to Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury.

“Among the many matters that you have instructed us to learn through your letters, we have also come to know your desire concerning the confirmation of your diocese, which lies under your authority and which you desire to shine in all things by the privilege of our apostolic authority,” etc.

“Pope Sergius to the kings of the English.

“The gift of spiritual grace, which kindles the hearts of the faithful through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, restores them by renewal, strengthens them with wondrous steadfastness of virtue, establishes them perpetually to merit the assistance of heavenly blessings, and nevertheless guards them beforehand against the destruction of passing things,” etc.

“The same pope to the bishops of England.

“Just as the gracious dignity and governance of divine mercy has brought before us, though unknown to us as brothers, the presence of those to whom it has granted the pastoral care of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so also the recognized well-being of your most devout college of bishops has brought a twofold gift of rejoicing. For we offer immense thanks to the Lord our God, author of all good things, when we find in the bosom of Holy Mother Church the devoted steadfastness of unity among faithful brothers and a fervent fellowship of love and affection among them.

“For by such shrewd diligence they are known to please God, offering him pure libations: while they refresh the altar of the heart with the splendor of true light, they do not deceive the mind with any enticements, do not spur on the hearts of their brothers with any goads, and do not assent in their minds to anything harmful to their neighbors. Rather, as ministers of God, they present themselves to their subjects as a mirror of life and moral integrity. Thus they will find God prospering them in adversity, nor will the enemy’s ambush be able to steal any opportunity to harm them. For whenever the Lord’s help is present, every hostile force of evil spirits is driven away. And since this is so,” etc.

“Pope Gregory to the bishops of England.

“We praise together the immense greatness of the mercy of Almighty God, who has deigned to spread the glory of his majesty in such a way that the sound of his preachers has already gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world,” etc.

“Pope Leo to Athelard, archbishop.

“It is especially fitting for pontifical discernment to grant the bishops a hearing in accordance with their blameless faith, and to grant favorable consideration to what they desire to carry out through blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and through us, provided that it does not conflict with canonical decrees.”

“Bishop Formosus to the bishops of England.

“Having heard that the rites of the impious pagans have revived in your regions, and that you have kept silence like dogs unable to bark, we have decided to strike you with the sword of separation from the body of the Church of God,” etc.

“Pope John to Dunstan, archbishop.

“John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother Dunstan, bishop of Dorobernum: greeting in Christ, for the continuation of eternal life.

“If shepherds of sheep are willing to endure heat and frost day and night in guarding their flock, and keep watch with vigilant eyes lest any of the sheep perish by straying or be carried off, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much toil and care ought we to remain constantly vigilant for the salvation of souls, we who are called their shepherds?

“Let us therefore attend to performing our duty in guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest, frightened as though by a wolf’s coming, we flee, and lest on the day of divine judgment we be tortured before the supreme Shepherd because of our sloth and negligence, although now, with the reverence of honor, we are judged above others in a higher station.

“Therefore we fully confirm your primacy, in which, according to the custom of your predecessors, it is fitting for you to exercise the functions of the apostolic see, just as blessed Augustine and his successors, the pontiffs of the aforesaid Church, are known to have possessed it more fully. We entrust to Your Fraternity, according to custom, the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, not intending that you use it in any other way than your predecessors have handed down, while the privileges of your Church remain in their proper condition.

“Nor is this unknown to your prudence or to anyone else, since the honor of the garment will be awe-inspiring according to the moderation of one’s actions. These ornaments are suited to the uprightness of your conduct, so that, with God as author, you may be conspicuous, and so that your life may be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness is found in them, let it be corrected by looking at you, and let them always advance by considering in you what they should imitate, so that through having lived well they may deserve, together with you, to see God.

“Therefore let your heart be lifted up neither by prosperous circumstances, which flatter only temporarily, nor cast down by adversities. Whatever adversity it may be, let it be conquered by you through the virtue of patience in Christ. Let no undiscerning favor find a place with you; in all things let others recognize discernment in you. Let no evil suggestion make an innocent person guilty before you, nor let favor excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders; nor permit them to perpetrate what would not benefit them. Thus let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the severe strictness of a judge: the one, that you cherish the innocent; the other, that by striking the restless you restrain them from wickedness.

“But since sometimes the zeal of superiors, while it is too strict in avenging the wicked, passes into cruelty, restrain correction by judgment and examine the severity of discipline, so that you may strike at faults but not depart from love of the perverse whom you correct.

“Show mercy to the poor insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed. Oppose their oppressors with measured reason. Do not accept anyone’s person against justice. Do not despise anyone seeking what is just. Excel in guarding equity, so that you neither hear the rich, because of his power, in any accusation outside its proper course, nor allow the poor man’s lowliness to make him despair, so that, by God’s mercy, you may be such as Holy Scripture commands when it says: ‘A bishop must be blameless’ (1 Tim. 3:2).

“You will be able to use all these things beneficially if you possess charity as your teacher; whoever follows it does not depart from the straight path. Behold, dearest brother, among many other matters, these are the duties of priests; these are the rights of the pallium. If you diligently observe them, you possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.

“May the Holy Trinity surround Your Fraternity with the protection of its grace and direct you in the way of its fear, so that, after the bitterness of this life, we may together deserve to reach the sweetness of eternal life.”

“And this was written by the hand of Leo, notary of the apostolic see, in the month of October, in the third indiction, dated on the first day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth year of the supreme pontificate of John.”

These documents, as we have mentioned, were found in the archives of the church of the Lord Savior, and we judged it not inappropriate to commend them to future memory. Indeed, more were found, but some had been effaced by excessive age, while others were written on sheets made from papyrus and inscribed in foreign characters; these too, for the most part worn away, did not disclose themselves fully to our knowledge. Since we shudder to write unknown things as though they were known, we necessarily excluded them from this work.

Indeed, what some are not ashamed to assert—that blessed Gregory granted solely to the person of blessed Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, not only the bishops whom he was to ordain, nor merely those who were to be ordained by the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain, subject to him, with the Lord our God Jesus Christ as author—is sufficiently demonstrated by the sacred decrees of his successors, addressed to Augustine’s successors, which we have briefly noted above.

For in these it is clear that they understood it not to be a great privilege if Gregory had said those things only to Augustine, since, to say nothing of other matters, in his days the province of York had neither received the faith of Christ [Col. 0509C] nor had anyone been sent there to preach it. Augustine and his companions had so much to do in the preaching of the name of Christ in Kent and the neighboring regions that they had to refrain from regions so distant.

Blessed Paulinus, who first preached the Gospel to the Northumbrians and first obtained the episcopal chair at York, was not chosen, ordained, and sent there by blessed Augustine, but by Justus, who was the fourth archbishop of Canterbury after Augustine, as the venerable Bede set forth in truthful prose in his *History of the English People*, and as is known to all.

Therefore, what blessed Gregory said to Augustine, he said to Augustine’s successors, through whom it pleased God to fulfill what, by his own arrangement, he had willed to fulfill through Augustine. Those who preside over Augustine’s see and have served in the office of carrying out his functions are therefore not lawfully to be deprived of the privilege conferred upon Augustine.

As for what they say—that blessed Gregory could have said and known well enough, if he had wished, “your Fraternity and your successors”—we fully admit that this is true. Likewise, we do not doubt that the Lord Christ, saying to blessed Peter, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19), knew how to say, if he had wished, “your successors.”

Those, therefore, who strive to deprive the successors of blessed Augustine of the power and dignity that blessed Gregory granted to Augustine should, if they dare, deprive the successors of blessed Peter of the power and dignity that the holy and just Lord granted to Peter. For in the same way that the Lord spoke to others through his apostle Peter, Gregory spoke to his successors through his disciple Augustine: “Judge rightly, you sons of men, and consider that the same judgment applies to similar cases.”

I also thought it should be added that the aforementioned Bede reports Theodore, who was seventh after blessed Augustine to succeed to his see, to have been the first among the archbishops to whom the whole Church of the English consented to submit. When he first came to Britain to exercise his pontificate, he removed Ceadda, the prelate of York, from the episcopate because, having not been lawfully consecrated, he had been unjustly placed over that Church through the priestly office. He immediately installed Wilfrid and, relying on the authority of the Roman see, entrusted to him the archiepiscopate of York in its entirety.

Afterward he caused him to come to his councils and made full use of his obedience and submission according to the circumstances of the times. Later, when complaints arose—too lengthy to recount—he deprived him not only of the episcopate in his own Church at York but also, exercising his free authority, divided his diocese among three bishops. Then, once the knot of that dispute had been untied, according to the pleasure of his will, he removed those bishops and restored the same Wilfrid to his former dignity.

Nothing new is being said; these are ancient matters, and they are utterly clear to those who know the deeds of the ancients. It is also evident with no less clarity that Brithwald, the successor of Theodore, deposed that same Wilfrid from the episcopate a second time, after he had been accused of a certain disobedience; and that afterward, moved by compassion for his old age and religious devotion, he restored him to the rank of his pontificate when appealed to by the apostolic see.

But why weave together an endless account? Let this suffice concerning these matters, so that those who do not fear to detract from the authority of the Church of Christ at Canterbury may at least blush that, placed in the light, they cannot see, and may henceforth close their mouths, lest by speaking perversely they become a reproach to those who love what is right.

In the very year in which Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, returned to England from overseas—that is, the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Word of God—certain honorable and vigorous men came to him as envoys from Alexander, king of the Scots. One of them was a monk and prior of the Church of Dunfermline, named Peter; there were also two clerics and one knight. Whoever wishes to know the business of their embassy should read or hear the letter that they brought, reproduced below.

“Alexander, by the grace of God king of the Scots, to Ralph, reverend archbishop of Canterbury and one to be loved with reverence: greetings.

“Having learned through a clear report of your prosperous arrival in England, which I had long desired, I rejoice in your safety and prosperity and render thanks for them to the supreme Protector. Since the occupation of temporal cares on every side prevents me from undertaking a journey so that I may at present enjoy your presence, I wish to make the affection of my heart known to your goodness both by this letter and through the report of my envoys.

“For, relying on the counsel of so discerning a person, I do not doubt that, with God’s assent, I shall be able very successfully to bring a good purpose to the accomplishment of a good work. I therefore do not wish Your Excellence to be unaware that I desire to console the Church of Saint Andrew, which exists in my kingdom and has long been deprived of pastoral care, by providing it, through God’s providence and your kindness, with a suitable pastor.

“Therefore I ask the clemency of your piety to grant me freely a certain person, praised by many—namely the monk Eadmer—if he seems suitable to you, so that he may be enthroned in pontifical dignity. For I fear that I have gravely offended the supreme Shepherd by allowing his flock, desolated for a long time by the lack of a pastor, with my negligence and perhaps other sins standing in the way, and having strayed in many respects from the path of truth.

“Fearing also, with filial fear, that I might from now on offend him in this matter, I have recourse to the fountain of your discernment, so that, remembering the former affection that existed between us, you may, with paternal feeling, protect me in this matter—me, your son, whom you adopted spiritually long ago—by the shelter of your counsel. Farewell.”

Father Ralph was astonished by these things and judged that the word had come from God, especially because it was entirely certain that the same brother had never spoken to anyone about this matter in any way, either personally or through anyone else, although he disliked his absence. For just as he had been assiduous in the service of his blessed predecessor Anselm, so also he was accustomed to be assiduous in Ralph’s service.

Nevertheless, he did not wish to refuse assent to the royal petition, lest he seem to resist God’s ordering. Since, therefore, he had learned that the envoys had come for this same matter and would approach the king of the English on their lord’s behalf concerning other matters as well, he and the assembly of the Canterbury brothers sent the following letter to that king through them:

“To Henry, king of the English, his dear lord and one to be revered with the highest honor, Brother Ralph, unworthy priest of the holy Church of Canterbury, and the whole assembly of that Church: greetings, prayers, and faithful service.

“We make known to Your Highness that Alexander, king of the Scots, with the consent of the clergy and people of his kingdom, has sent his envoys to us and has sought from our Church counsel concerning pastoral care for the Church of Saint Andrew.

“Therefore, considering their just petition and attending both to reverence for divine love and to the benefit of Holy Mother Church, we have piously assented to their praiseworthy desires. In accordance with their petition, we have granted them the person from our Church whom they named, Lord Eadmer, whom we know to have been nobly instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines from childhood and suitably adorned with holy conduct, and to be wholly suitable for the priestly office.

“We therefore humbly beseech Your Venerable Highness that, through the pious will and authority of Your Majesty, both their God-worthy petition and the grant of our humility concerning so necessary a matter for the Church of God [Col. 0512A] may be strengthened. May Almighty God deign to preserve Your Highness safe for long ages, to the honor of his name and the protection of his Church, and after your temporal kingdom to exalt you with the dignity of the eternal kingdom.

“The king’s reply to this:

“‘Henry, king of the English, to Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury: greetings.

“‘I wish and grant that you freely give him that monk concerning whom the king of Scotland has petitioned you, according to the custom of his land, for the episcopate of Saint Andrew.’

“‘Witnessed by Everard of Calne at Rouen.’”

After this he sent the same brother, as he thought proper, to the king of Scotland, writing to that king as follows:

“To my dear lord and friend Alexander, by the grace of God [Col. 0512B] king of the Scots, Archbishop Ralph: greetings and prayers.

“We render countless thanks to God, who, dispelling the clouds, has opened the eyes of your mind to recognize and request what you ought. We also thank Your Magnanimity, who by your legitimate petitions have made us, from friends most friendly, from intimates most intimate, and from associates most closely joined to you.

“For although by these petitions you seek, as it were, to tear an eye or a right hand from our body, I must nevertheless praise your just desire and, insofar as I can, obey it according to God. Willingly—if it may be said with God’s and your peace—and yet unwillingly, I assent to your good will: willingly, because I dare not resist God’s will, whom I see present and favorable in this act, nor embitter your heart against us; unwillingly, because I am deprived, as though alone, of the consolation of a father, of constant assistance and relief, and of the counsel and aid of a wise son in our infirmity and old age.

“O wise man’s counsel—if you had not deprived us of him, and while you deprive us of him—that you should strive to place over your land, in matters pertaining to God, so great a man, so famous, so useful to the Church of God, instructed from childhood in life, morals, sacred learning, and, if necessary, secular learning as well.

“If someone from distant regions had requested what you request, know for certain that I would not have allowed the secret treasure of our heart to be taken far from us. But there is nothing, according to God, that we wish to refuse you.

“We therefore send you the person you request, entirely free, so that he may learn more certainly from you whether your petition concerns the honor of God and of the holy mother Church of Canterbury. Deal cautiously and with counsel concerning what you are undertaking, because there are many who would gladly obstruct this man’s consecration and, if they were able, would make it void by obstructing it.

“Therefore our counsel would be that the man to be consecrated be sent back to us as quickly as possible, lest through delay what we fear, or what we would not wish, should occur. The assembly of the brothers of our Church, truly your faithful servants and altogether ready for your service, sends you greetings.

“Collectively we ask that you conduct yourself toward our brothers who are in your kingdom in such a way that God and we may give you thanks for it. Farewell.”

[Col. 0513A]

And so, when the brother himself came to Scotland, on the third day after his arrival—the feast day of the most glorious apostles Peter and Paul—he accepted the bishopric of Saint Andrew of Chenrimunt, the clergy and people of the land having chosen him and the king having granted his consent. This was accomplished by God’s arrangement in such a way that he was neither invested by the king with pastoral staff or ring, nor did he render him homage. Thus the day was celebrated joyfully and spent eagerly in the praise of God.

On the following day, however, the king spoke privately with the elected man about his consecration, and, being utterly opposed to having him consecrated by the archbishop of York, learned from him that the authority of the Church of Canterbury had, from ancient times, precedence over all Britain. For that reason, he said, he wished to seek the episcopal blessing at Canterbury. The king, disturbed in mind, rose and departed from him. He did not want the Church of Canterbury to be preferred to the Church of Saint Andrew in Scotland.

He therefore summoned William, a monk of Saint Edmund’s, who, after Thurgod, had been placed in charge of that bishopric and had almost emptied it of its substance, and ordered him to conduct himself in the bishopric as usual, after stripping the newly invested man of his possessions.

When, after this, a full month had passed and the lands that remained to the bishopric had already been completely emptied, King Alexander, at the request of the princes of the realm, approached the elected man. With difficulty he obtained from him that, since he intended to lead an army against his enemies, he would take the pastoral staff from above the altar, as though receiving it from the hand of the Lord, and would thereafter, throughout the whole kingdom, devote himself as far as he was able to the care of all souls.

After this he came to the church of Saint Andrew. When the queen met him, he was received by the scholars and the common people and succeeded to the place of bishop.

Meanwhile, Thurstan of York was still staying overseas. Vigorously pursuing the affair mentioned above, he also provoked the king of the English to the point that he sent written instructions once to the archbishop of Canterbury and three times to the king of the Scots, directing that the one should not consecrate the elected bishop of Saint Andrew, nor the other permit him to be consecrated in any way.

This wounded many minds and drew them apart in different directions; it also greatly weakened the elected man, lest he should undertake the correction of Christianity by episcopal authority. Consequently, those who cared more about obeying their own pleasures than God’s commands were strengthened, and, because they feared correction of their morals, they now mocked him without fear.

What more is there to say? The king himself, alarmed by the commands of the king of the English, began from this point to hold the man in lower esteem and gradually to diminish his possessions. When the elected man noticed this, and knew with absolute certainty that, while the king was hostile to him, he could make little progress in God’s service in that kingdom, he resolved to go to Canterbury and seek there advice about what would most appropriately be done in such a case.

When the king learned of this, he declared that the man was entirely released from the Church of Canterbury and had no share whatsoever in it, and that during his lifetime he would never consent to the bishop of Scotland being subject to the archbishop of Canterbury. When Eadmer told him that he would not, for all Scotland, deny that he was a monk of Canterbury, the king replied in a troubled spirit: “We did nothing wrong in asking Canterbury for a bishop for ourselves.”

From this point, bound by the rancor of his heart, the king began to harass the man in many ways, secretly and openly assailing him with many injuries and stripping him of his dignity and of the revenues of the bishopric. He could not look upon him with a favorable eye or patiently hear his words, even when they concerned God; and this could not remain hidden from the common people. Many rumors therefore arose, drawing opposing parties in different directions.

Perceiving this, and judging, as we have said, that his position in such circumstances was of no benefit, the elected man sent him this message through intermediaries: “Since I see that you are not favorably disposed toward me, as would be expedient for me, and do not know why I have deserved this from you, while it is certain that, with you offended, I can be of little use in correcting Christianity in your kingdom, I ask you, with your favor, to allow me to go to Canterbury. There I may seek advice about what I ought to do, and receive episcopal blessing from there, to the honor of God and the exaltation of the kingdom of the Scots.”

These words did not please the king. He declared that he would by no means consent to the request, maintaining that the kingdom of Scotland owed no subjection to the Church of Canterbury and that Eadmer had been given to him wholly free from it. Eadmer replied that he had not known this hitherto, especially since the archbishop’s letter to him had stated, among other things, that he had sent him to Scotland to discover whether the request by which he had recommended his election pertained to the honor of God and of the holy mother, namely the Church of Canterbury, and not so that he himself, as a foster son, should destroy a dignity which that Church had securely possessed for five hundred years. The king, exceedingly angry, swore that he did not know how to enter every day into new arrangements in this affair.

Then the man, calling into his council John, bishop of Glasgow, and two Canterbury monks whom he then had with him, asked what they thought would be best for him to do in his situation. They approached the king and, after learning more fully the state of his mind concerning the man, presented the following advice to him, as though its substance had come not from the king but simply from themselves:

“If you wish to live in peace as a son of peace, seek peace elsewhere. As long as this man reigns, you will have no communion with him or with peace. We know the man. In his kingdom he wishes to be everything by himself, and he will not tolerate any power being able to do anything in any matter without his direction. He is already embittered against you, and he does not know why; he will never be fully reconciled to you, even if he sees the reason. Therefore, either understand that you must abandon everything, or live forever among the Scots, following their customs, in disgrace and against the salvation of your soul.

“But if you prefer to depart, you will be compelled to return to him both the ring that you received from his hand and the staff that you took from above the altar. Otherwise, you will not leave his land unless you are able to fly over it.”

It pains me to write how many things were said and how many accusations were made on both sides as the discussion moved toward other matters. After all this, the elected man himself considered the order in which the events concerning him had taken place—namely, how he had received the ring from the king’s hand, how he had been invested with the bishopric, and how he had taken the staff from above the altar—and replied briefly as follows:

“I will willingly return the ring that I received from his hand, because I received from it none of the power that the ring signifies, since it was given by a layman, to whom such a thing does not pertain.

“As for the staff, which I took from above the altar in the presence of two bishops, I will place it where I took it from and commend it to the disposition of Jesus Christ.

“As for abandoning the entire bishopric, I agree to do so under this condition: because force is being used against me, I will not reclaim it during the time of King Alexander, unless the archbishop and the Canterbury community, together with the king of the English, give me different advice concerning these matters.”

Thus they parted in peace. Eadmer, coming to Canterbury, was joyfully received by the bishop and his brothers. He was loved by everyone, and those who had been saddened by his absence were greatly delighted by his presence.

The king, however, sent his messenger to the archbishop with a letter accusing Eadmer, containing the following:

“Alexander, by the grace of God king of the Scots, to Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury: may you always live in him who is life.

“Your immense goodness, which condescended to my request by sending me the person who was to be raised to the bishopric of Saint Andrew, has earned from my grateful affection, as is just, countless thanks. But when the person had been placed in the bishopric, he refused to accommodate himself to the customs of the land and the ways of its people, as circumstances and the time required, and as justice and necessity demanded.

“Finally, in the presence of certain bishops and earls and of good men of my land, this same person asked me to grant him permission to depart and release him from the fidelity that he had sworn to me, since he was unwilling to remain in any way unless I detained him in captivity.

“When I heard this, I replied that, if he could show that I had inflicted upon him any injuries in word or deed, or that I had failed in anything I ought to have done for him, I would most willingly make amends for the love of God and for my honor.

“In the presence of all who stood there, he replied that I had inflicted no injury upon him in word or deed, nor had I ever failed in anything I ought to have done for him.

“Moreover, I myself, together with the bishops and counselors and other good men of my land who were present, offered him obedience in reverence, wherever it was just to do so, with great kindness of heart. We firmly urged that it was not necessary for him to abandon the bishopric because of any lack of an honorable provision for his maintenance, and we earnestly begged him to remain until I had informed the king of England and you, so that I might benefit from the advice of you both.

“After hearing this, he replied that he would remain in no way unless I detained him in captivity. He knew, he said, that he was neither useful nor suitable for governing the bishopric, and he saw that, if he remained, harm threatened his own soul and the souls of others.

“Finally, by common counsel, I was unwilling to retain him by force. Although unwillingly, I consented to his request; he returned the bishopric and confirmed the pact of friendship between us with a kiss.

“This is the truth of the matter, which I wished to make known to you in writing, so that, if something else should reach your ears, you would not believe it.

“Finally, let your goodness know that I desire to be wholly subject to you, as a faithful friend, and that I wish to submit to your counsel and also to your affection. I earnestly ask you to show honor to Lord Eadmer.

“Farewell.”

Whether the king himself sent to that great Father a true, sophistical, or false account in these matters will not escape the knowledge of him who, in his own time, will expose the plans, inventions, and deceptions of each person and repay each according to his deeds.

Father Ralph nevertheless wrote the following letter in reply:

“To Alexander, illustrious king of the Scots, Brother Ralph, minister of the Church of Canterbury: may you so reign in the earthly kingdom that you may reign with Christ in heaven.

“We return to your eminence, venerable lord, such thanks as we can for the gift of affection and honor that, as we learn from messengers and letters, you are known to extend toward our humble selves. In this matter you will undoubtedly always find us as devoted as we are able to be; and if, by the Lord’s generosity, anything fruitful should be found in our life, know with confidence that it belongs to you.

“We also offer you our thanks, arising from our goodwill, for your reception of our dearest son, namely Eadmer, your elected bishop, whom we sent to you at your request and whom you treated honorably. When he returned to us, we too received him with the respect due to so great a person, and we rejoiced considerably at his arrival.

“Afterward, when conversation took place privately between us, we heard that he understood certain matters differently from the meaning of your letters, which we had previously heard, and that he did not entirely agree with everything we had heard. Since, therefore, we now read one thing in your written account and learned another from our brother himself, we think it advisable to retain this same son of ours with us until, with the Lord’s guidance, you come to England, unless you should previously send us some other instruction about what ought to be done.

“When, by God’s gift, we are able to speak with you in person and hear the causes of the matter from both sides, if the life and teaching of this friend of ours seem useful to you and to your country, he will be able to return to the place of his election, under the obedience imposed upon him, if you wish to receive him. But if something else should seem preferable in your sight, we shall retain him with great joy as a man richly instructed in the law of the Lord and fit for every good work; and, placing good hope in God’s mercy, we shall have his return be fruitful.

“Farewell.”

Such, then, were the events concerning this matter.

But while these things were being done in Scotland concerning the Canterbury monk, something unheard-of in our age occurred in England. William, son of King Henry, whom we mentioned in several places earlier in this work, eager to follow his father when he returned from Normandy to England, boarded a ship accompanied by a great multitude of nobles, soldiers, boys, and women.

After they had quickly passed out from the sea-port, relying on the remarkable calmness of the weather, and had escaped the strait, the ship in which they were traveling struck a rock in a shallow place and was overturned. All who were aboard it were swallowed by the waves of the sea, except one peasant, who himself—so it was reported—was scarcely worthy even of a name, and who escaped alive through the wondrous grace of God.

This event terrified and disturbed the minds of many and shook them with wonder at the hidden judgments of the just God. Yet the enormity of this disturbance was all the sooner quieted in the minds of most because they saw the king, whom this misfortune affected above all, conduct himself with manly courage and attribute the matter to the equity of God’s judgments, which no one can resist, with submissive bearing and voice.

For, consoling himself in this way, he said with humble spirit and mouth what he understood all Christians ought to say in all their circumstances: “Blessed be the name of the Lord forever. Amen” (Job 1:21).

[Col. 0517A]

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0517B]

Anyone who remembers that time can perceive, even without my saying so, with what joy and exultation the kingdom of England was gladdened at the king’s return. Great hope of great good arose from it in the minds of many, promising them relief and assistance from the great evils with which, through weariness of them, they had previously seemed to be thoroughly infected.

But when the report rang out that William, long ago designated heir to the kingdom, had been taken from their midst, no small portion of this good hope perished, once the injustices that were emerging among every class of people in those days had been taken into account.

Nevertheless, the lawful king, having long since been released from the bond of marriage, resolved, on the advice of Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and of the princes of the kingdom—all of whom he gathered together at London on the Epiphany of the Lord—to take as his wife Atheleide, daughter of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine: a virgin girl, distinguished by good morals and by the becoming beauty of a modest countenance.

Messengers were therefore sent to complete this union. They hurried together with those whom the aforementioned duke had sent to England for this very purpose, and brought the future lady of the kingdom with the highest honor, as was fitting. When she arrived, a great gathering of the kingdom’s bishops and nobles met her at Dover, where she landed, and from there she was escorted to the king’s court.

While these matters were being arranged, and the assembly of princes that had been convened to meet the queen had not yet dispersed, much discussion took place about the dispute that had continued up to that time between Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thurstan of York.

For Thurstan himself, as we described above, having been ordained bishop by Calixtus, had obtained letters from that same Calixtus in the customary manner by which everything is procured at Rome. They ordered that Thurstan should obtain possession of his bishopric, or that the king should be punished with anathema and Ralph with suspension from episcopal office.

The judgments of the privileges that we included in the preceding book were read aloud, and everyone understood how worthily these apostolic arrangements had been made by God. Nevertheless, lest the proposed threat of punishment disturb the king or the archbishop in any way, Thurstan was permitted by common counsel to return to England and come to York by the king’s road.

This was done on the condition that he should celebrate no divine office outside the parish of York until, after renouncing the obstinacy of his heart, he had made satisfaction to the Church of Canterbury for the injury he had inflicted upon it.

Meanwhile, the kingdom’s leading men discussed the queen’s marriage and whether she should be advanced into the kingdom, and it was decided that the matter should be carried out at Windsor.

There, when the bishop of Salisbury, because the castle itself lay within his diocese, attempted to administer the service of the marriage, the others contradicted and disproved him. They maintained that the matter belonged rather to the archbishop of Canterbury, on the grounds that the king and queen were his special and domestic parishioners, and that the diocese of any other bishop could not take from him what was recognized as belonging to his jurisdiction. For, by the law of primacy, the entire land was his parish of Canterbury, and all the bishops of the island held the parishes they possessed from him and through him alone.

The controversy over these matters was therefore settled. Since Archbishop Ralph, weighed down by bodily weakness, was unable to perform the service himself at a suitable time, he entrusted it to the bishop of Winchester, lest, if the bishop of Salisbury administered it, someone in later times should claim such a right on the authority of his own parish rather than from obedience to the bishop of Canterbury.

On the following day, when this rite was to be performed and the girl blessed as queen, Father Ralph had already taken his place at the sacred altars to celebrate the service at the appointed entrance of the Mass, when he noticed the king sitting crowned on his throne. He was astonished, knowing that he had not placed the crown on him and that the king ought not, in his presence, to wear one placed there by another.

The archbishop therefore turned away from the altar, wearing his mitre and girded with the stole of his patriarchate, and approached the king. The king rose respectfully before him, and the archbishop asked who had placed the crown on his head.

The king replied in a modest voice, with downcast face, that he had not paid much attention to the matter and that it had therefore slipped his memory.

“Whoever placed it there,” said the archbishop, “certainly did not do so lawfully; and as long as it remains on your head in this manner, I shall not be the executor of the undertaking begun.”

The king replied: “If it was not placed there lawfully, as you assert, do what you recognize ought justly to be done; you will find no opposition from me.”

The archbishop then raised his hands and removed the crown from the king’s head. The king himself loosened the clasp tied beneath his chin so that the crown would not slip while it rested on his head.

When those standing around saw this, they all begged the archbishop in loud voices to show mercy and restore the crown to the royal head. He consented, and then, standing beside the crowned king, began the “Gloria in excelsis Deo” at the Mass that had been begun. As the choir sang the continuation, he returned to the altar.

The queen was therefore consecrated as queen, and the day was celebrated as festive and joyful by all the people who had gathered.

After this, the archbishop came with the king to Abingdon and there consecrated Robert, who regularly and diligently served that lord king in the care of food and drink, to the bishopric of the Church of Chester or Coventry. Beforehand he received from him a profession by which, according to ancient custom, Robert devoted himself to being subject and obedient to the holy mother Church of Canterbury and to its bishops.

He was consecrated on the third day before the Ides of March, with William, bishop of Winchester, William of Exeter, and the Welsh bishops Urban and Bernard assisting and cooperating in this sacrament.

[Col. 0519C]

While these matters were being arranged in England in this order, reliable news reached there that Pope Calixtus, having gathered forces from every direction, had captured the aforementioned Maurice, surnamed Burdinus, whom the emperor, together with his supporters, had named Gregory and established as pope in the Apostolic See. Stripped of all his possessions, Calixtus had disgracefully thrust him into a monastery to live as a monk.

Having accomplished this, Calixtus himself, secure in possession of the apostolic summit, exercised freely in every direction through his legates the authority with which it is considered fitting that the Roman pontiff should be supported.

One of these legates, a certain Peter by name, Roman by birth and a Cluniac monk by profession, came to Gaul. He had been sent by the pope himself and, as was reported, held a legation for Gaul, all Britain, Ireland, and the Orkney Islands.

The fame of this man surpassed that of all who had previously been sent to these regions from the Roman see. Abbots and certain other men of distinction were sent ahead by him to announce his arrival in England.

He was the son of Peter, a most renowned and powerful Roman prince, whose faith and conduct were customarily regarded as matters of great wisdom and courage by those who, canonically established in the apostolic see, were considered the Fathers of the world.

Since the whole country was struck with awe in expectation of so great an arrival, King Henry sent Bernard, bishop of Saint David’s in Wales, and John, the son of his paternal uncle, a cleric, across the sea to the place where Peter was then staying and awaiting the will and command of the king of the English concerning his entry into England, so that they might bring him to the king.

The king himself, acting with prudent counsel, instructed them to arrange Peter’s journey in such a way that, after entering England, he would not enter any churches or monasteries on his way to lodge there, and that the necessities of food and sustenance would be supplied to him only from the king’s own resources.

He was therefore brought to the king and received by him with due honor. After explaining the reason for his arrival, the king, having completed the campaign in which he was then engaged—for at that time he had led an army against the Welsh—said that he could not at that moment devote himself to so great a matter. It was clear that the authority of Peter’s legation could be firmly established only through the assent of the bishops, abbots, and nobles and through an assembly of the whole kingdom.

Moreover, the king declared that he would by no means calmly allow the loss of the ancient customs granted to him by the apostolic see—among which was one of the most important, namely, the provision that the kingdom of England should be free from the authority of every legate—as long as he remained alive.

With royal eloquence he honored Peter greatly in these and similar matters, promising in complete good faith that he would in every way ensure that nothing of his ancient dignity was diminished, and indeed that the glory of his dignity would be increased in every direction. [Variant: “in every way”; alternatively, “in no way.”]

A firm peace was therefore established between them. The man who had come to exercise the office of legate throughout Britain was sent by the king, with great ceremony, out of England by the same road on which he had arrived, free from every such office.

As he was about to cross the sea at Dover, he was received magnificently by the brothers at Canterbury at the urging of the king and the archbishop, and he stayed among them joyfully for three days.

During that time a complaint was brought before him concerning the serious injury by which Pope Calixtus had not hesitated to humiliate the Church of Canterbury in the case of Thurstan of York, and to reinforce that humiliation by his letters, leaving aside every consideration of justice.

Peter received the complaint with an untroubled expression and a gentle mind. He asked that the privileges formerly possessed by the ancient Fathers from the Roman see be shown to him, and promised that, if they proved valid, he would work to reduce to nothing whatever had recently been established.

After careful examination by prudent men, it was established that the ancient charters bearing seals had been destroyed in the fire that, less than fifty years earlier, had completely consumed the entire church. A few of them had been hastily copied and preserved in some way in ancient documents or old books; their authenticity was demonstrated both by the style of Roman eloquence and by the authority that the Church itself had possessed securely for more than four hundred years.

After examining and weighing these documents, Peter himself also declared that the Church of Canterbury had suffered a very serious and excessive prejudice, and promised that he would employ every means to have it corrected as quickly as possible.

After this he left England, crossing the stormy sea with a favorable voyage.

While these matters were taking different turns, the aforementioned bishop of Scotland continued to reside at Canterbury, just as he had formerly done before he was elected to the episcopate. He did not readily leave the monks’ community but conducted himself in every respect like the others.

A full year and a half passed in this way. Meanwhile, various bishops, abbots, and nobles who had known the man through his former association with Father Anselm came to Canterbury and questioned him about his affairs.

When they had learned the course of events, they unanimously declared that, according to the canonical statutes, he could not in any way abandon without legal judgment the Church that he had canonically been elected to govern, even though he had not been consecrated. They asserted that his election in some sense took the place of consecration.

Following the advice of these men and of certain others—and perhaps also encouraged by the example of his blessed father Anselm, whose holy conduct had formerly instructed him in many matters, and who had once been driven from England for a similar reason in the same manner as Eadmer had been driven from Scotland, as was mentioned much earlier—he sent the following letter to the king of the Scots:

“To Alexander, illustrious king of the Scots, Eadmer, formerly elected bishop of Scotland: greetings and service.

“For the gracious goodwill that your excellence once deigned to show toward me, I offer you such thanks as I can. I know, indeed, that your kindness was not the result of my merits, since, passing over countless men distinguished both by the integrity of their lives and by the authority of their wisdom and prudence, you chose me for the bishopric and wished me to preside over your kingdom in the matters that belong to God.

“May almighty God repay you for so good a will with the reward that good will deserves from him. This is what my soul daily prays for and desires.

“But that the affair has taken an outcome different from the course intended by our common purpose must, I do not doubt, be attributed to God’s ordering, which no one can penetrate or evade.

“Yet, if I were granted the opportunity to speak with you privately, I would make known to your holy faith what I have learned from my departure from the episcopate.

“Although I have departed from you in body, know with certainty that, with God’s help, I shall not violate the fidelity that I owe you. Therefore, wherever I am able, I shall faithfully seek the honor of yourself and your kingdom, if you do not despise it, with him as my witness who alone and truly examines my conscience.

“I do not say this because I greatly desire to become bishop in your kingdom; nevertheless, I would prefer the dignity of your land to be increased rather than diminished.

“Moreover, let your blessedness know that all who hear how I was elected, received, installed in possession of the bishopric, and substituted in the bishop’s place assert with one voice that I could not justly have abandoned the bishopric, nor can another be substituted for me during my lifetime according to the law of the Lord.

“For a husband cannot lawfully dismiss his wife so that another may marry her, nor can a wife dismiss her husband for another man. But perhaps you say: ‘You dismissed it.’ I did indeed dismiss it, but—let this be said with your peace—under force inflicted upon me, which I could not resist.

“For when continual discord and endless hostilities were directed against me from your side by those whom I knew to be your intimates, unless I entirely yielded the bishopric, both your conduct toward me and the dispossession by which you twice stripped me, without law or judgment, of the possessions belonging to the episcopate bore witness to this. I necessarily gave up what, once it had been taken away, I could not retain.

“But it is not suitable to investigate these matters at length in the brevity of a letter. Therefore, leaving them aside, I briefly submit this: if you permit it in your peace and are willing to lend assistance—as befits your royal highness—so that I may return honorably to you to fulfill God’s service and yours, I shall undertake the journey according to God’s will and strive to obey your will in all things, unless, which God forbid, it should appear to resist God’s will.

“If you are entirely unwilling to accept this, I can do no more. I entrust the cause of his Church to God. Let him see; let him dispose; let him repay each person in this matter according to what each deserves.

“I have, as I believe, freed my soul. As I ought, I have set forth my case before him, ready in all things to follow his will.

“Nevertheless, do not suppose that I wish in any way to diminish the liberty or dignity of the kingdom of the Scots. I want you to be assured that, concerning what you once asked of me and to which I then refused to consent—thinking that I ought to judge differently from what I later learned—namely, concerning the king of the English, the archbishop of Canterbury, and the priestly blessing: if you still persist in your opinion, you will no longer find me opposing you.

“Nor will these matters in any way separate me from God’s service or from love for you, so that I may not do whatever you wish, provided only that I am permitted, with your good will, to administer the other matters that belong by right to the bishop of Saint Andrew.

“I would have made this known to you earlier; but because a report was circulating everywhere that you would come to England then or then—indeed, certainly then—I delayed writing, since I preferred to explain it to you in a private conversation.

“Whether, therefore, you accept these things or defer them to a higher counsel, I have done what concerns me with a pure and simple conscience, under the gaze and examination of him who knows what he must repay to each person with just measure.

“Since, then, the hearts even of all kings are in his hand, I ask him from my inmost heart to direct your heart and your actions toward himself by his grace, so that his Church, which dwells as a stranger in your kingdom, may by your assistance advance day by day in holy conduct, and so that from this may come to your soul, after this life, the reward of eternal blessedness. Amen.

“Please, in your kindness, deign to inform your faithful servant by letter what your excellence thinks of these matters.

“Farewell.”

In those same days, Archbishop Ralph and the brothers of the Church of Canterbury also sent the king a letter containing, among other things, the following:

“To Alexander, illustrious king of the Scots, Ralph, minister of the Church of Canterbury, and the community of brothers serving the Lord Christ in it: through him may you reign on earth whom all the heavenly host serves.

“Your wisdom knows how long the episcopal see that is regarded as preeminent in your homeland has lacked its shepherd. Without doubt, the longer it has been deprived of its proper strength, the more grievously the ruin of its subjects will result from this.

“Therefore we exhort your serenity, whom divine mercy has thus far honored among other kings without notable reproach, so that you are considered praiseworthy by all, to put an end to so great a religious loss and, of your goodwill, recall to his see the shepherd whom you canonically elected and whom we lawfully sent to you.

“Since no fault is apparent either in you or in him that would prevent this from being rightly done, we do not understand, on the authority of the Fathers, how your aforementioned Church can obtain another bishop while this man lives. For the bride of God, while her husband survives, must not become adulterous unless she wholly rejects her lawful husband.

“Therefore, however long this has hitherto been delayed, recall to the first place of your affection and to the office entrusted to him—as we hope he will be useful to you—a man nobly instructed in the law of God from his youth, for your glory.

“May the God of peace and love, from whom every good counsel proceeds, always be with you. We ask that you have written back to us what you think of the matters we have communicated to you.

“May your affection flourish gloriously, with the lady queen, your wife, and with all who desire what is just and love you—glorious lord and honored son of the holy mother Church.

“Amen.”

In that same year, which was the year 1122 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the ninth year since he had been transferred from the bishopric of Rochester to the patriarchate of Canterbury, Archbishop Ralph died at Canterbury, in the metropolitan see, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the presence of his sons, namely the glorious company of monks of that place. On the third day afterward he was decently buried in the middle of the hall of the greater church.

[Col. 0557B]

## EADMER THE MONK, BOOK ON THE EXCELLENCE OF THE VIRGIN MARY

[Note: It has been collated with manuscripts Corb. E. 10 and S. 62. Manuscript E. 10 reads: “Written by Eadmer the Monk, disciple of blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. Concerning Mary, the most devout and sweetest Mother of the Lord.” Manuscript S. 62 reads: “Here begins a sermon on Saint Mary.” This manuscript does not distinguish the chapters.]

(G)*

## CHAPTER ONE

### That Mary surpasses all creatures
