Eager to contemplate, however dimly and at least with the bleary eye of the heart, the excellence of the blessed Mother of God, surpassing that of everything created after God became man, and desiring, through contemplation, to bring into common knowledge whatever I am granted to grasp from it, I shudder at the enormity of the sins under which I am oppressed, and greatly fear lest, when I immediately seek such heights, that saying of Sacred Scripture be brought against me: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he may not see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10).

[Note: Col. 0557D: “Petenti mox” (“when seeking immediately”) is the reading of manuscript S.; “petenti misero” (“when I, wretched, seek”) is another reading.]

Truly, when I reflect that her holy Son became her son for this purpose—that he might heal the sins of mankind—I conceive some hope that I may perceive at least a little of the sublimity of so great a mother, knowing that she was made the Mother of God more for sinners than for the righteous.

[Note: Col. 0557D: The manuscripts variously read “Quod vel parum concipiendi de sublimitate tantae matris, Dei scilicet Genitricis, omniumque tam Angelorum quam hominum Reginae, sciens” (“that, knowing her to be so great a mother—namely the Mother of God and Queen of all angels and human beings—I may conceive at least a little of her sublimity”) and “quid vel parum percipiendi de sublimitate tantae matris, sciens” (“what, or at least a little, of perceiving the sublimity of so great a mother, knowing”).] For her good Son himself says that he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners (Matt. 9:13). The Apostle also testifies that Christ came into the world to save sinners, among whom he confesses himself to be the first (1 Tim. 1:2, 15).

[Note: Col. 0557D: “Verum cum” (“but when”) is the reading of the manuscripts; “vere cum” (“truly when”) is another reading.]

If, then, she became the Lord’s Mother for sinners—that is, for me and those like me—how can the enormity of my sins compel me to despair of their forgiveness, when so ineffable a gift was made from her for their healing?

[Note: Col. 0557D: “Cogere me poterit” (“can compel me”) is the reading of the manuscripts; “cogere poterit” (“can compel”) is another reading.]

[Note: Col. 0557D: “Ineffabile donum” (“ineffable gift”) is the reading of the text; the manuscripts read “ineffabile bonum” (“ineffable good”).]

But to whom will that healing advance more effectively, or in whom will it operate more mercifully, than in those by whom so great a good is loved, embraced, and venerated?

Let us therefore arouse our minds, my brothers, and strive, as far as we can, to attend to the loftiness of so great a Virgin. Whatever mercy her Son deigns to reveal to us concerning her, let us proclaim in her praise, and let us meditate upon what we have proclaimed. For this itself may perhaps become no small cause of the salvation we desire, and a healthful medicine for minds wounded by the stings of vices.

[Note: Col. 0559D: “Laude ejus prolata ruminemus” (“let us meditate upon what we have proclaimed in her praise”) is the reading of the manuscripts; “laude ejus proferamus, prolata ruminemus” (“let us proclaim her praise and meditate upon what we have proclaimed”) is another reading.]

[Note: Col. 0559D: “Optatae nobis” (“of the salvation desired by us”) is the reading of the text; the manuscripts read “optare nobis” (“for us to desire”).]

How could salvation fail to proceed to a sinner from remembering the praise of her whose womb became the way for the Savior, who came to heal the sinner?

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “peccatorum, cujus uterus factus est via ad sanandum peccatores venienti” (“of sinners, whose womb became the way for him coming to heal sinners”), rather than “peccatori, cujus uterus factus est via ipsi ad sanandum peccatorem venienti” (“for the sinner, whose womb became the way for him himself, coming to heal the sinner”).]

What have I said—“the way”—when that same womb was made the chamber of God, the palace of God in which he was to dwell? For he truly dwelt in it, since in it and from it he himself made himself, who previously was not, into what he became.

O wondrous dwelling-place! O ineffable indwelling!

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts omit “O wondrous dwelling-place!”]

The womb of the blessed Mary received him whom the heavens of heavens and all the structures of created things cannot contain, when it conceived and gave birth to that very same true and perfect God and man in one person. Yet that womb was also a way, because through it God, made man, came visibly into the world.

## CHAPTER II. On the origin of the Virgin Mary

Although the single fact preached concerning the holy Virgin—that she is the Mother of God—surpasses every height that can be spoken or conceived after God, and although the human mind that longs for her has in this fact something supremely lofty to contemplate and meditate upon, nevertheless, since it has come into my mind to say something about her, I wish first to speak a little about her origin and thereafter to bring forward whatever my feeble understanding may have been able to grasp concerning her which I judge not to be contrary to her dignity.

[Note: Col. 0559D: “Quae Dei mater est” (“that she is the Mother of God”) is the reading of the manuscripts; the text has “quod Dei mater est” (“that she is the Mother of God”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: “Ad eam anhelat” (“longs for her”) is the reading of the text; the manuscripts read “ad Dominum anhelat” (“longs for the Lord”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “quoniam modo venit” (“since now it has come”) rather than “tamen quoniam mihi venit” (“nevertheless, since it has come to me”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts omit “parum” (“a little”) in “primo parum de ejus origine” (“first, a little about her origin”).]

Be present, therefore, O Lady, and deign to look favorably upon not my merits, which I abhor, but yours, which I venerate. You know that my mind is occupied with this conviction: I consider myself wholly unworthy to speak about you or to write anything at all.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “quae vereor” (“which I fear”) rather than “quae veneror” (“which I venerate”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “aliquid scribere” (“to write something”) rather than “quidquam scribere” (“to write anything at all”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: Manuscript B reads “tua, precor” (“yours, I pray”) rather than “tua, quae precor” (“yours, which I pray”).]

But since I know that, with the eye of your innate piety, you have looked upon many like me, I would wish to offer you some service of my devotion, however unworthy of your dignity, so that with that accustomed eye of your mercy you may at some time deign to look upon me also.

[Note: Col. 0559D: Manuscript B reads “insitae tibi” (“inherent in you”) rather than “insitae tuae” (“your inherent”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: “Vellem agere” (“I would wish to offer”) is the reading of the text; the manuscripts read “velim agere” (“I may wish to offer”).]

Setting aside, therefore, those things prophesied about this Virgin from the beginning of every creature until the coming of her holy Son—both by those who were righteous before the Law and by those who were righteous under the Law—I infer for myself that her birth (which I know descended from the line of human generation) was preceded by certain great and wondrous indications of divine signs.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “illis ab initio” (“those things from the beginning”) rather than “illis quae ab initio” (“those things which from the beginning”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “sanctum sui adventum” (“his holy coming”) rather than “sanctum filii sui adventum” (“the holy coming of her Son”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts omit “sicut” (“just as”).]

What those signs were, however, he alone knows without uncertainty who chose her for himself as Mother before she was born. This, as I suppose, and not implausibly, may be believed to have been done so that the greater the sublimity of so great a matter was hidden in a higher secret, the greater would be the veneration of the faithful surrounding her birth.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “eam antequam” (“her before”) rather than “eam sibi antequam” (“her for himself before”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “quod in ea re” (“because in that matter”) rather than “quod ea re” (“because by that matter”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts omit “actum” (“done”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “quod enim alio modo sublimitatem” (“for in another way the sublimity”) rather than “quo sublimitatem” (“so that the sublimity”).]

Nor does the Church of God regard as possessing unshakable authority the writing that reports her birth as foretold by an angel. For although blessed Jerome, following the subject matter of another writing—which he says he read in his youth and whose author he confesses that he does not know—produced it in revised form, he nevertheless says that he did not write what he wrote in such a way as to wish to impose upon the Churches any certainty concerning the matter described, but only so that, in simplicity, he might comply with the requests of his friends.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “eam refecerit” (“revised it”) rather than “eam fecerit” (“produced it”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The Picard edition reads “similem morem” (“a similar manner”); the manuscripts read “humilem morem” (“a humble manner”), while the text reads “simpliciter morem” (“a simple manner”).]

Hence, as I have said, the Church did not wish to receive that writing as authoritative, considering it unbecoming that anything doubtful should be recited in praise of the blessed Mother of God, when the things that unquestionably exist concerning her are so full of material for praise that anyone who wishes to linger in praising her must necessarily find his capacity unequal to the greatness and truth of the matter.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “magnitudini rei” (“to the greatness of the matter”) rather than “ejus magnitudini” (“to its greatness”).]

For just as she alone, above all others, shone with singular merit, so whatever concerns her is worthy to shine with a particular firmness of truth.

[Col. 0560C]

## CHAPTER III. On the angelic annunciation

After she was born and had passed beyond the years of infancy, who could conjecture—even in thought, let alone in speech—how chastely, how holily, and how worthily of God she ordered and conducted her life?

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “non dicam … conjecturare” (“I will not say … to conjecture”) rather than “non dico … conjectare” (“I do not say … to conjecture”).]

No one, surely, could doubt that her most chaste body and most holy soul were wholly free from every stain of sin and protected by the constant guardianship of angels, since she was the palace that her God, the Creator of himself and of all things, was to inhabit bodily, and from which, through an ineffable operation, he was to take man into the unity of his person.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “protecta” (“protected”) rather than “protectam” (“having been protected”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “unitate” (“unity”) rather than “unitatem” (“into the unity”).]

And why is this surprising? Among human beings too, there is an established practice—if any comparison between heavenly and earthly things can be made—that when some eminent and wealthy person goes somewhere to lodge, his retainers run ahead to secure, cleanse, adorn, and guard the place, so that it may be suitable and fitting for his lord, who is coming, to inhabit.

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts read “nam inter” (“for among”) rather than “nam et inter” (“for also among”).]

[Note: Col. 0559D: The manuscripts omit “ut” (“so that”).]

If such preparations are made for the arrival of an earthly man and a power lasting only for a moment, what preparations for every good do we think were made for the arrival of the heavenly and eternal King in the heart of the most sacred Virgin? He was not merely going to lodge temporarily within her; he was also to be born from her substance as man.

Accordingly, when “the fullness of time came” (Gal. 4:4)—the time which God himself had predestined before the ages for his coming—he sent the angel Gabriel, one of the chief princes of his kingdom, to announce to you, O most blessed of women, that the salvation of the human race was at hand, that he himself would accomplish that salvation, and that from you, most chaste through the operation of the Holy Spirit, a true man would be born.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “suo adventu” (“at his coming”) rather than “suo adventui” (“for his coming”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “principibus suis, scilicet regni” (“his princes, namely of the kingdom”) rather than “principibus regni” (“princes of the kingdom”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “verum Deum et hominem” (“true God and man”) rather than “verum hominem” (“a true man”).]

You hear what is announced, and you tremble and marvel at something unheard-of throughout the ages. Yet you are not moved by any disbelief; rather, you hold firmly within yourself the conviction that it would be altogether impossible for what the angel said would happen not to happen. She therefore believed and most certainly understood that God was so good, so compassionate, and so full of every mercy that he wished to descend from his heavenly seat to earth and, having become man, to rescue the human race from the perpetual death by which it was held, through a death not owed by him.

Answering the messenger, therefore, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

O faith pleasing to God! O humility dear to him! O obedience offered to God, more pleasing than every sacrifice! What, then, could remain in her to offend the eyes of the coming God, when, as he came, he found in her the insignia of such great virtues, exhaling their fragrance?

Certainly Abraham is said to have pleased God by faith alone, and this alone—that he believed God—was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gal. 3:6). God asserts that his Spirit rests upon the humble and peaceful, and those who tremble at his words (Isa. 66:2), and that he prefers obedience to sacrifices (1 Sam. 15:22).

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “prae sacrificiis” (“above sacrifices”) rather than “pro sacrificiis” (“instead of sacrifices”).]

Since, therefore, holy Mary pleased him so excellently in those things that please God so greatly, I believe that she could not possibly have pleased him more excellently in any way.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “crederet quis illam aliqua” (“would anyone believe that she in any way”) rather than “crediderim ipsam ulla” (“I believe that she in any way”).]

We therefore rightly hold by faith that her heart was so cleansed from whatever original or actual sin still remained in her, that the Spirit of God—namely, the Spirit resting upon the humble, the peaceful, and the one who trembles at his words—rested wholly upon her, that he accepted her obedience to the Lord’s will with a chaste and simple heart as more pleasing than every whole burnt offering, and that, overshadowed by the power of the Most High, he incorporated the Son of God from her.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “ut nec super” (“so that not even upon”) rather than “ut vere super” (“so that truly upon”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “sua ortus” (“his arising”) rather than “sua totus” (“wholly upon his words”). The wording is materially uncertain.]

Here let the attention of the human mind raise itself, and, as far as it can, attend briefly to how greatly almighty God valued the merits of this most blessed Virgin. Let it attend, I say, contemplate, see, and marvel: the one Son consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with himself, whom God the Father, God without beginning, begot from his own nature, and through whom he made all visible and invisible creatures from nothing.

This Son, so uniquely his own, so dearly beloved, and in every respect entirely equal to himself, he did not permit to remain his alone. Rather, he willed that this same Son should in truth be the unique, beloved, and natural Son of blessed Mary—not in such a way that there would be two sons, one the Son of God and another the son of Mary, but that the very one who was the Son of God should, in one person, be the son of Mary, and that the one who was the son of Mary should, one and the same, be the Son of God in one person.

Who, hearing this, would not be astonished, and would not judge it more wondrous than anything that can be said—that God could will such a thing?

A girl born from Adam’s stock, sprung from a sinful lineage, is suddenly proclaimed, by an astonishing reversal of the curse of Eve, blessed above all women. She conceives, carries, and gives birth to God as man, who would drive away all transgressions from the sons of Adam and establish as his co-heirs in his heavenly kingdom those who obeyed him.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “ac parit Deum omnes praevaricationes ab Adae filiis propulsurum, eosque in coelesti” (“and gives birth to God, who would drive away all transgressions from the sons of Adam and establish them in the heavenly kingdom”) rather than the fuller text “et parit hominem Deum omnes praevaricationes propulsaturum, eosque qui sibi obtemperarent in coelesti” (“and gives birth to God as man, who would drive away all transgressions and establish in the heavenly kingdom those who would obey him”).]

## CHAPTER IV. On the Virgin’s love for her Son

Let those who in some degree love one another with the fervour of a singular affection—mother, that is, loving son and son loving mother—consider, if they can, how wonderful and ineffable is the affection of love between such a son of so great a mother and such a mother of so great a son. Let some good mother consider, I say, with what affection she is bound to a good and only son; and let a good son similarly consider with what devotion he is moved toward his good and most sweet mother. Let them try, insofar as they can conjecture this within themselves, to conceive the love of this good mother for her truly good and only Son, and of this good Son for his truly good and most sweet mother.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “tentet” (“let him or her try”) rather than “tentent” (“let them try”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “eum autem” (“but him”) rather than “cum autem” (“but when”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “mirabilis natura et ineffabilis affectus amoris” (“the wondrous nature and ineffable affection of love”) rather than “mirabilis itaque et ineffabilis amoris affectus” (“the wonderful and ineffable affection of love”).]

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscript reads “aliqua mater” (“some mother”) rather than “aliqua bona mater” (“some good mother”).]

All human beings, indeed, are begotten from the union of two persons, male and female, and those thus begotten naturally owe their love to both persons, that is, father and mother; and both parents who begot them likewise owe them their love.

[Note: Col. 0561D: The manuscripts read “ipsumque nihilominus amorem suum parentes” (“and likewise their parents their own love”) rather than the grammatically difficult “ipsisque nihilominus suum parentes.”]

But the love which father and mother severally owe their son, this most blessed of mothers alone owed her Son; and the love which every son owes jointly to father and mother, that Son, truly the Son of the Virgin, owed to his mother alone. For as other sons are born of father and mother, so her Son was born of her alone. Therefore the love of this mother for her Son and of this Son for his mother surpasses every love of parents for children or of children for parents.

These things are so according to the reason of a sonship shown to exist outside the law of human generation. Let us also, if it please you, investigate the love of this Son and this mother, and contemplate it, as far as is granted us and as we can.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “concessum, prout” (“granted, insofar as”) rather than “concessum fuerit, prout” (“may have been granted, insofar as”).]

Certainly, she who gives birth is a virgin born in time; he who is born is God, through whom all times exist and by whom the virgin herself was created. He first showed the love which he bore toward the Virgin—a love than which we think none greater exists: he made her his mother and did not take virginity from her.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “generat, est” (“she gives birth, is”) rather than “generat virgo, est” (“she who gives birth is a virgin”).]

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “ipse prius” (“he first”) rather than “ipse primus” (“he first”).]

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “putemus esse posse majorem” (“let us think that there can be a greater”) rather than “putemus esse majorem” (“let us think there is a greater”).]

She herself loved these two things most sweetly, namely virginity and fruitfulness: virginity, because she understood that it pleased God in every respect; fruitfulness, because without it she feared that she would incur the curse of the Law, which was still observed carnally. Yet love of preserving virginity prevailed in her and drove out fear of incurring the curse. Thus, a tender and delicate virgin, of royal descent and most beautiful, directed all her purpose, all her love, and all her zeal to consecrating body and soul to God in perpetual virginity.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “Deo pro virginitate” (“to God for virginity”) rather than “Deo virginitate” (“to God in virginity”).]

For she knew that the more holily she preserved it, the more sublimely she would draw near to him who is most chaste of all—indeed, who is Chastity itself.

Embracing what she knew to be more acceptable to the Lord than the Law, she hoped and believed that she would wholly escape the curse imposed by the Law. She considered that he whom she sought to please was of such goodness and wisdom that, since she saw that according to her conscience she neither knew nor could do anything better than what she did, he would find a sure counsel so that she should incur no sin in these matters.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read: “What she knew to be more acceptable to the Lord, she surpassed the Law and despised the curse of the Law, and believed, reasoning with herself, that he whom she sought to please was of such goodness and wisdom …” The text has “what she knew to be more acceptable to the Lord than the Law …”]

Nor was she deceived. For who has hoped in the Lord and been forsaken by him? (Ps. 30:2).

When, therefore, he saw her purpose so holy, her resolve so chaste, her faith so firm, her hope steadfast, and her charity unfailing, he looked upon her with such mercy that neither the holiness of her purpose was frustrated nor the chastity of her resolve violated; neither was the firmness of faith weakened and made to waver from the constancy of hope, nor did the fullness of charity fail in her.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “ejus misericordiae” (“of his mercy”) rather than the text’s “ejus, eo misericordiae” (“of his mercy, with such mercy”).]

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “aut sanitas” (“or the soundness”) rather than “aut firmitas” (“or the firmness”).]

Therefore he granted her both to remain a virgin, which she desired more, and to become fruitful, so that none might doubt that she was free from the curse of the Law. And how fruitful? Fruitful through the Holy Spirit, who makes all things fruitful, gives life to all things, and nourishes all things; fruitful, I say, through him without whom every fruitfulness is turned into barrenness and is cut down to be consumed by fire.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read: “How fruitful? From him without whom … it is turned into barrenness” rather than “How fruitful? Fruitful through the Holy Spirit, etc.”]

And indeed it was fitting that, when he came upon the Virgin, she should become fruitful—the Virgin who was to bear the God through whom the whole world would be saved.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “eo in Virgine” (“when he came upon the Virgin”) rather than “eo in Virginem” (“when he came upon the Virgin”).]

What, then, shall we say here? Do you suppose that there is any human mind able to penetrate the measure of the love which God bore toward this Virgin, when he so wholly preserved for her what she loved most dearly and, making her fruitfully and chastely so worthy, made her the mother of himself?

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “servabat ut” (“he preserved so that”) rather than “servavit, ac” (“he preserved, and”).]

Can any human being or angel comprehend, even in thought, anything comparable to the immensity of that love or the dignity of that honour?

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “amoris immensitatem penetrare vel” (“to penetrate the immensity of the love, or”) rather than “amoris immensitati aut” (“to the immensity of the love, or”).]

Lift up, I beseech you, my brothers, lift up the gaze of your minds to contemplate so marvellous a work of divine condescension, so ineffable and astonishing a grace and exaltation of this woman throughout all ages.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “contemplandum tam ineffabilem” (“to contemplate so ineffable a thing”) rather than “contemplandum tam miram divinae dignationis operationem, tam ineffabilem” (“to contemplate so marvellous a work of divine condescension, so ineffable a thing”).]

And you, O most blessed of women, into whom there flowed so copious and surpassing a grace, the sum of all graces: what disposition, I ask, did you bear toward him who did these great things for you, by which, as you yourself said, you deserved henceforth to be called blessed by every generation? (Luke 1:48). Truly your soul magnified the Lord, and your spirit rejoiced in God your Saviour (ibid. 46–47).

O wonderful salvation, which not only, Lady, exalted you with inestimable salvation, but, coming forth from you, by a marvellous dispensation healed the whole world, rotten with the wounds of sins.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “prodiens mirabili” (“coming forth wondrously”) rather than “prodiens mira” (“coming forth by a marvellous dispensation”).]

But when you saw him who had done these wonders for you handled as a little child in your arms, hanging at your breasts, and crying after the manner of little children because of the small injuries of his little body, with what affection, I pray, was your most loving soul moved?

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “et ad verba” (“and at words”) rather than “et ad ubera” (“and at your breasts”).]

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “ad parvi ac teneri” (“of the small and tender [body]”) rather than “ad parvas parvi” (“at the small [injuries] of the little [body]”).]

With what care did you prepare yourself to meet every discomfort which you feared might befall his most chaste body?

O God, Son of this most blessed mother, who are the power and true wisdom of the highest Father, we pray you that, by that same mercy through which you became man for us, you may deign to show our hearts with what spirit and what thought this your sweetest mother was occupied when she held you, so great and yet so little, rejoicing and glad in her arms; when she rejoiced with you, an eager infant, in sweet and frequent kisses; when she consoled you, weeping on her knees, by whatever means she could; and when at last, by various other attentions to which motherly tenderness prompted her, she diligently caressed you according to the changing circumstances.

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “intentione ferebatur” (“was directed by her intention”) rather than “cogitatione ferebatur” (“was occupied in thought”).]

[Note: Col. 0563D: The manuscripts read “tibi infantulo dulcibus” (“with sweet things for you, an infant”) rather than “tibi ut infantulo gestienti dulcibus” (“with sweet things for you as an eager infant”).]

Teach us, I say, to perceive in mind even a little of the affection that filled her heart, so that, if we who are overwhelmed by the filth of our sins do not deserve fully to attain its greatness, we may at least deserve, by understanding something of it, to breathe a little amid our miseries.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “pauca mereamur” (“we may deserve a few things”) rather than “pauca de illo intelligendo mereamur” (“we may deserve, by understanding something of it, a few things”).]

Nor should anyone think it contemptible for a person to feel even a little within himself of this mother’s affection for her Son.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “nec putet” (“nor should he think”) rather than “nec putetur” (“nor should it be thought”).]

For I could by no means believe that one who has deserved to advance to understanding it can remain altogether a stranger to the sweetness of that love. Whoever enters into the sweetness of love need not at all despair that he will also enter into a share of its reward.

All Christendom knows what reward of her love she has obtained, for it most certainly believes that she has been exalted above all heavens and set before the angelic choirs.

Come then, brothers: let us strive as far as we can to recognize in some measure the affection of this so good a mother, and, at least by yielding in ourselves to the greatness of the matter, taste it; so that, aided by her merits and refreshed by the sweetness of her love, we may deserve to be exalted by some recompense of future consolation.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “meritis adjuvari” (“to be aided by her merits”) rather than “meritis adjuti” (“aided by her merits”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “salutaris” (“salutary”) rather than “suavitate” (“sweetness”).]

Whoever loves anyone with a sincere and sweet affection of love and desires that every advantage and joy may come to that person, groans sorrowfully over that person’s misfortunes, if any occur. Let such a one turn and return this affection in his mind, and consider what it would be if the same affection became greater in him, multiplied by whatever number he chooses to imagine.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “adhuc quem” (“still whom”) rather than “adhuc numero quem” (“still by whatever number”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts have the corrupt reading “fingere multiplicatus in se sedem major existeret”; the text reads “fingere libet multiplicatus in se idem affectus major existeret” (“if the same affection, multiplied in him, became greater, by whatever number he chooses to imagine”).]

When he has done this, and thinks that his own love, however magnified in his understanding, can in some degree be compared with the love of this most loving Lady and mother for God her Son, I do not know whether he should be heard in such an estimate.

Nor is this surprising. The Spirit of God himself, the love of the almighty Father and Son himself, he through whom and in whom everything that is rightly loved is loved—he himself, I say, bodily, so to speak, came into her and rested in her with singular grace above all created things, whether in heaven or on earth. He made her queen and empress of heaven and earth and of everything in them.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “ut bene dicam” (“so that I may speak well”) rather than “ut ita dixerim” (“so to speak”).]

Shall anyone, drunk for a time with a kindly affection, conceive that he possesses any love which can be judged comparable with that love which this most blessed of mothers bore toward him by whom she knew herself raised to so ineffable a dignity?

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “tempus affectu debriato” (“time, being drunk with affection”) rather than “tempus debriato affectu” (“being drunk for a time with affection”).]

Therefore the greatness of this Virgin’s love for her Son surpasses all the loves and delights of all created things, as does the immensity of the sweetness in which her soul rejoiced and melted toward the same Lord her God.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “in finem” (“unto the end”) rather than “in filium” (“for her Son”).]

Thus, to anyone to whom it is granted frequently to think of her in this way with sweet devotion, it may be conjectured to be a great sign of salvation to be won.

But what shall I say? If her love toward this most beloved Son was so great, with what or how great a joy was her whole being filled when she had with her the one whom she loved so greatly, whom she knew to be the Creator and Ruler of all things, living with her, eating with her, and sweetly teaching her whatever he wished her to know?

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “fuerit amor ejus et vere major erga” (“her love was, and truly greater toward”) rather than “fuit amor ejus erga” (“her love was toward”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “secum egentem” (“in need with her”) rather than “secum degentem” (“living with her”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “quid caperet” (“what would contain it?”) rather than “quis capiet” (“who will contain it?”).]

## CHAPTER V. On the compassion of blessed Mary for her crucified Son

When she was gladdened by so great a love and such exultation at his presence and companionship, let whoever can consider by what pains, what groans, and what sighs she was tortured when she saw him torn away from her by cruel hands, handed over to be condemned, and set before the tribunal of an unjust judge to undergo death.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “When, therefore, the blessed Mother of God was gladdened by so great a love and such exultation at his presence and companionship” rather than the text’s “gladdened by so great a love and such exultation at his presence and companionship.”]

Perhaps, amid these events, she could still have had, to speak in human fashion, some consolation of hope for his escape, while she heard the sentence of his death still hanging in the dispute between the governor seeking to release him—

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “pendere conspiceret audiretque subaltercationes praesidiis” (“she saw and heard it hanging amid the disputes of the governors”) rather than “pendere audiret sub altercatione praesidis” (“she heard it hanging amid the dispute of the governor”).]

—and the wicked Jewish people, appealing against the governor to Caesar’s sovereignty lest he be released.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “quaerentis, et Judaeorum” (“of him seeking, and of the Jews”) rather than “quaerentis” (“of him seeking”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “contra praesidentem” (“against the presiding authority”) rather than “contra praesidem” (“against the governor”).]

But when, after the definite sentence of his death had been pronounced, every hope of escape forsook her, and she saw with groans that he was carrying on his shoulders to the place of his passion the cross upon which he was to hang, is there, I ask, anyone who can comprehend the condition of her heart?

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “prolata certe” (“after the sentence had certainly been pronounced”) rather than “prolata certa” (“after the definite sentence had been pronounced”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “humeris usque ad” (“on his shoulders all the way to”) rather than “humeris ad” (“on his shoulders to”).]

To these pains another pain was added: Peter and the other disciples, chosen by him out of nothing for the apostleship and already raised to such a height of power that they even commanded demons, and made privy to his secrets and intimate with him in all things, took flight when the hour of his betrayal came.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “discipuli ejus ab” (“his disciples, from him”) rather than “discipuli ab” (“the disciples, from him”).]

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “ut jam daemonibus” (“so that they already commanded demons”) rather than “ut etiam daemonibus” (“so that they even commanded demons”).]

Forgetting so many benefits and their promise, they left him alone—him for whom shortly before they had promised to undergo death—while she alone looked on.

Therefore, groaning, she followed him as he went to his passion deprived of all friends, saying: “You go, O propitiator, to be sacrificed for all. Peter, who said, ‘I will die for you’ (Matt. 26:35), does not come to meet you; Thomas, who said, ‘Let us all go and die with him’ (John 11:16), has left you. Of all these, none is led away except you alone, you who kept me chaste, my Son and my God.”

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “Vide ipsum” (“see him”) rather than “Unde ipsum” (“therefore him”).]

It is enough to have recalled these words, drawn from the fountain of great love, briefly for this purpose: that the eye which attends to them with compassion, sympathizing with the groaning affections of so great a mother, may someday deserve to be rewarded with the fruit of that pious love.

[Note: Col. 0565D: The manuscripts read “ad haec commemorasse” (“to have recalled these things”) rather than “ad hoc memorasse” (“to have recalled these for this purpose”).]

But when the moment of his passion itself had come, and he, fixed to the cross, looked on one side at his mother and on the other at the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he substituted for her, lest he leave his mother utterly bereft, the disciple who was present in his place as a son: “Woman,” he said, “behold your son” (John 19:26).

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscripts read “praesentem discipulorum” (“the disciple of the disciples who was present”) rather than “praesentem discipulum” (“the disciple who was present”).]

O exchange! In place of the eternal and unchangeable God, she received as a son a pure yet corruptible human being; in place of her natural and only Son, a servant.

O Lady, what thoughts, I ask, succeeded one another in you when you heard that so inestimable an exchange was being made for you by him whom you loved above all things?

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscript reads “quae, precor, in te” (“what, I ask, in you”) rather than “qui, precor, cogitatus in te” (“what thoughts, I ask, in you”).]

Truly the sword of sorrow passed through your soul, a sword more bitter to you than all the pains of any bodily suffering. Whatever cruelty was inflicted on the bodies of martyrs was slight—or rather nothing—in comparison with your own passion, which by its very immensity pierced every inner recess of your most loving heart.

And certainly, loving Lady, I could not believe that you could in any way have endured the thrusts of so great a torment without losing your life, unless the Spirit of life, the Spirit of all consolation—the Spirit, namely, of your most sweet Son, for whose death you were so grievously tormented—had strengthened you, consoled you, and taught you inwardly that the death consuming him was not death, but rather a triumph subjecting all things to him, which you saw accomplished in him before you, as you were dying.

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscripts read “coram moribundo” (“before him, as he was dying”) rather than “coram moribunda” (“before you, as you were dying”).]

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscripts read “moriente conquerebaris” (“you complained while he was dying”) rather than “moriente tantopere torquebaris” (“you were so grievously tormented while he was dying”).]

Nevertheless he died and, while you looked on, was shut in the tomb and taken from your eyes.

I pass over the rest in silence, wholly ignorant where or whence I might take anything to say by which I could set before anyone the extent of your mourning, O most chaste Virgin.

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscripts read “virgo, alicui” (“Virgin, to anyone”) rather than “virgo, considerandum alicui” (“Virgin, to anyone for consideration”).]

For when you saw him whom you knew that you, while a virgin, had conceived, had borne as a virgin, and had remained a virgin after giving birth to; and through whom you understood that you had deserved to be called blessed by every generation—when you saw him slain by the savage cruelty of the wicked in so cruel a death, so suddenly withdrawn from your sight and shut in the cave of the tomb—what could I, an unknown man, have, or where could I find anything to disclose to anyone for contemplation the state of mind which you bore at that time?

[Note: Col. 0567D: The manuscripts read “videbas” (“you saw”) rather than “videres” (“when you saw”).]

But after the resurrection of that same Son of yours, the bitterness of mourning was turned into joy. And into what and what kind of joy, let us consider, my brothers.

## CHAPTER VI. On the joy of the resurrection.

Above, when we tried to contemplate the exultation of her joy, with which she was filled in her intercourse with this son of hers, still dwelling with her in mortal flesh [Col. 0568A]—the manuscripts read *degentibus istius* rather than *degentis istius*—we failed in this very effort of ours (the manuscripts read *nostri animi nisu*, “by the exertion of our mind,” for *nostrae annisu*), and perceived that it was immense and wondrous beyond all human understanding. If, then, her joy was so great at that time, when she knew well that he would die shortly afterward, how great and what kind of joy do you suppose it was now, when she saw him, having trampled upon the laws of death, rise again—not only to live forever, but also to rule eternally, by perpetual right, over heaven, earth, and every creature? I do not want anyone to try to penetrate the immensity of her joy, since what is wondrous and impenetrable even to God’s angels, I would hardly believe could be penetrable to any mortal human being.

But if someone asks why the evangelists do not report that the most loving Lord, rising from death, appeared first and especially to this sweetest mother of his [Col. 0568B]—the manuscripts read “to his sweetest and most beloved mother”—in order to relieve her sufferings, we reply what we heard from a certain wise man when we questioned him about this very matter. He said, then, that the authority of the Gospel narrative is known to be so great that nothing dependent upon it, nothing empty, and nothing superfluous is found in it. Therefore, if it were written that her own Son, as he rose from the underworld, appeared to the Lord’s Mother, the Lady of the world, and taught her of his resurrection just as he appeared to any other person, who would not regard such a statement as superfluous? It would place the queen of heaven and earth and of every creature on an equal footing with that man or woman to whom he appeared. [The manuscripts read *coaequare illis quibus*, “to make her equal to those to whom,” rather than *coaequaret illi vel illi quibus*, “would make her equal to this or that person to whom.”]

His Spirit rested fully and perfectly in her, revealing to her both his being and all his deeds more clearly than light; and the evangelists would have written that at that time or another he presented himself to her in such and such a manner. [The manuscripts read “that he presented himself in such a manner,” omitting the repeated qualification.]

With these few words, perhaps answering someone’s inquiry as we received the answer—the manuscripts read *his itaque*, “with these things,” rather than *his ita*, “with these things thus”—let us still place before our eyes, by contemplation, something of the joy of this most blessed Virgin Mother—not in the hope that we, living in this mortality, shall perfectly understand its measure, but so that, tasting something of it as far as we can, we may venerate it with whatever devotion is possible. For when it is contemplated and tasted, it usually produces great progress in those who long for her love [the manuscripts read *proficuum*, “benefit,” rather than *profectum*, “progress”].

Come, then: if she had joy while her own son was dwelling with her in the flesh; if she had joy when that same son, having trampled down death, rose from the underworld; did she exult with any lesser joy when she saw her son, in the flesh which she knew he had assumed from her, penetrating the heavens before her eyes [Col. 0568D]? Who could say this? Rather, who would not believe that her joy surpassed all the joys that preceded it? [The manuscripts read *num minori … penetrante?*, “with no lesser joy … penetrating?” rather than the principal reading.]

Good mothers commonly rejoice greatly in this world when they see their sons raised to earthly honors [Col. 0569A]. Surely this mother, undoubtedly a good one, would rejoice with ineffable joy when she saw her only-begotten Son enter heaven by right of dominion over all the heavens and reach, by his ascent, the presence of God the almighty Father? Indeed, what has ever been heard like this joy [Col. 0569D]? What has ever been brought forth that could, at least in some measure, direct the human mind toward it?

Moreover, the magnitude of her joys received some increase when, after the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, so great a multitude of people, as you know, accepted the faith of her Son at once through their preaching [the manuscripts read “so great a multitude of people,” without “as you know”]. Nor should anyone find it strange that I say her joy increased through the conversion of believers [the manuscripts read *incrementum sumpsisse*, “received an increase,” rather than *crevisse*, “increased”]. For there, apart from the joy she conceived at the salvation of the human race in the conversion of these people, she saw that her Son had not died in vain, since she saw faith in his death working so effectively even in those who had been the authors of that death [the manuscripts read “the faith in his love, even in those who were his lovers”].

Thus she had joy in heaven, joy on earth, and joy also in every creature. Joy in heaven, because the fruit of her womb, now victor over death and the world, reigned in heaven and glorified God the almighty Father by his victory, while he gladdened all the hosts of the heavenly court with immeasurable magnificence. [The manuscripts read: “Her blessed womb’s fruit had already become victor over death and the world; he reigned in heaven, and all …”]

She had joy on earth, because she saw those for whose salvation she knew herself to have become the Mother of God running freely toward salvation after casting off the yoke of the devil, by whom they had been held captive [the manuscripts read: “because she saw their freedom …”]. She also had joy in every creature, because she saw that creation had been freed from its former oppression and restored to the condition for which it had been made.

For after man despised God and, swollen with pride, did not fear to oppose his commands, he ought, by a just judgment, to have no further right in any creature that God had established for his assistance. Yet when he persisted in his defiance against God, the Lord of all things, and did not cease to turn the use of created things to his own advantage, he inflicted injustice upon the Lord God and violence and oppression upon God’s creature.

But now, when man, reconciled through the death of the Son of this most blessed Mother [Col. 0569D]—the manuscripts read “through the death of the daughter”—returns to God’s favor, he also returns to the rights of that freedom for which God’s creature was made: namely, to serve the one for whom it recognized itself to have been established. [The manuscripts read: “returns to the grace of God, to serve”; another reading has: “returns also to the right of freedom, for which God’s creature was made, namely, to serve him.”]

These things, most sacred Lady, you saw; these things you understood; these things you greatly rejoiced to see fulfilled through you in such a manner. We say these things, brothers, because we delight in repeatedly turning over and recalling them in our memory, and because we desire you to delight in doing the same: the love and joy of this Lady, by which her whole being rejoiced in God and in things concerning God with continual abundance [Col. 0570A]. For after God there is nothing more useful than the memory of the Mother of God; nothing more salutary than the mediation of the devoted love with which she burned in remembering and contemplating her Son; nothing more pleasing than the savor of reflecting upon her blessed joy, with which she was nourished in manifold ways in and through that same Son.

Often we have seen and heard many people, in their dangers, remember the name of this good Mary, and immediately escape the evil of every danger [the manuscripts read “remember this, and …”]. Sometimes salvation is swifter when her name is remembered than when the name of the Lord Jesus, her only Son, is invoked [the manuscripts read “more favorable salvation” rather than “swifter salvation”]. This does not happen because she is greater or more powerful than he—for he is not great or powerful through her; rather, she is so through him.

Why, then, is salvation often received more promptly through remembrance of her than of her Son? I shall say what I think. Her Son is Lord and Judge of all, discerning the merits of each person. Therefore, when he is invoked by anyone under his own name and does not immediately hear, he certainly does so by a just judgment [the manuscripts read “he does so justly”]. But when the name of his mother is invoked, even if the merits of the person invoking do not deserve to be heard, the merits of the mother nevertheless intervene so that the prayer may be heard.

Human custom proves this every day: when someone puts forward the name of his friend, he effectively obtains from that friend something that he could in no way obtain simply by his own request [the manuscripts read “putting forward the name of his lord” rather than “the name of his friend”]. Therefore, if remembrance of the name of the Mother of God is so useful in bringing help [the manuscripts read “is useful at some time”], it is not surprising if frequent meditation upon her holy love bears the fruit of great salvation, and if the sweet practice of thinking upon and recalling the immensity of her joy gives complete delight.

## CHAPTER VII. On the joy of blessed Mary at her Son’s ascension

Let us therefore still turn our words toward contemplating her joy, and for a little while nourish our minds with its sweetness. Let us consider, then, since so great a magnitude of joy filled the innermost heart of this most devoted Lady, as we have been able to taste by briefly contemplating what has already been said, whether anything further could have been added to her joy: namely, that, as the Holy Spirit revealed to her without any uncertainty, once the course of her fleeting life had been completed she would ascend into the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom; there she would see her Son, equal in his divinity to God the almighty Father, as he is, in unfailing contemplation, and would rule after him, by perpetual right, over every heavenly, earthly, and infernal creature.

But who could contemplate the immensity of this joy without being utterly overwhelmed by the contemplation itself [Col. 0570D]? And if the cause of her joy was such and so great, what was the joy itself like, and how great?

But, O good Jesus, most loving Son of this sweetest mother of yours, how could you endure that, when you returned to the kingdom of your glory, you should leave her as though bereft amid the wretchedness of the world, rather than take her up immediately to reign with you? Perhaps, Lord, you wished to prevent your heavenly court from being uncertain about whom it ought rather to go out to meet: you, its Lord, then for the first time seeking your kingdom in the flesh you had assumed, or your own Lady, ascending into that kingdom already hers by maternal right. [The manuscripts read *cum post*, “when afterward,” rather than *tum primo*, “then for the first time.”]

For I do not think it would have been fitting for the court to be divided by going out to meet both, so that one part might attend you and another her at your first arrival—especially since the heavenly court is yours, entirely yours through you, and is likewise hers.

You therefore used the wiser and more fitting plan: you wished to precede her in order to prepare for her a place of immortality in your kingdom, and thus, accompanied by your entire court, to go out to meet her with greater festivity and raise her more sublimely to yourself, as was fitting for your mother.

Indeed, it is not unreasonable to believe that the only-begotten Son of this most blessed Virgin preceded his mother for these reasons, since he himself promised his disciples that, if he departed, he would prepare a place for them in the heavenly dwelling and afterward receive them to himself. [The manuscripts read: “would prepare a place, and afterward receive them to himself. If …”]

If, then, he prepared a place for the glory and honor of his disciples, how would he not prepare one for the honor and glory of his Mother, the Lady and Queen of the angels?

Moreover, as it seems to me [the manuscripts read “as it seems here”], her presence among his apostles after the Lord’s ascension was useful and necessary for our faith [Col. 0571C]. Although they had been taught all truth through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, she understood the depth of that very truth incomparably more eminently and clearly through the same Spirit [the manuscripts read “the Spirit of the truth of that very truth”]. Consequently, through her many things were revealed to them which she had learned concerning the mysteries of that same Lord Jesus Christ not merely by simple knowledge, but by the very effect and experience of them.

Nor could the delay of her assumption in any way diminish the immensity of her love and joy, since the perfection of her love and joy so refreshed her with its fullness that this very circumstance became for her a great increase of love and joy: she saw that she was there where she knew that the one whom she loved above all things wished her to be.

Thus, wherever she was, she was in God, and God was in her; and, happy through this very joy, she wished above all that what she understood to be most pleasing to God’s wisdom should everywhere take place.

This most holy Virgin was endowed with this immeasurable immensity of love and joy for as long as the wisest Son of hers was pleased to let her remain in mortal flesh [Col. 0572A]. [The manuscripts read: “for as long as it pleased the wisest one that she should remain even in mortal flesh.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the assumption of blessed Mary, Mother of God

But when he had determined to take her into his kingdom and show her the magnificence of his glory [the manuscripts read “the magnificence of the glory of the kingdom,” with *of the kingdom* omitted in the principal text], what rank and honor, I ask, was the whole angelic court intent upon displaying? With what voices of exultation and salvation [the manuscripts read “of exultation and greeting”] did the numerous dwellings of the ancient Fathers, newly joined to that court [the manuscripts read “then joined to that court”], resound?

Certainly, I would believe that all the citizens of that blessed homeland were prepared for the arrival of their Lord’s mother with a more festive celebration than usual and a more exalted splendor of beauty, and that, in expectation of so great an event, they rejoiced together with a new and ineffable grace of delight.

And what is surprising in this? Jesus himself, God and Lord of all, the son of this most chaste Virgin and Lady of all things [the manuscripts read “her blessed Son”], wished to go out to meet her in full festivity, as his unique mother. Would any member of his household withdraw from the immensity of so great a joy [Col. 0572B]? [The manuscript reads “his household withdrew from …” rather than “any member of his household.”]

Among human beings, it is known to be customary for every good servant of any powerful lord to rejoice with greater joy at the arrival of his master’s friend, the more he knows his own lord to love that friend. But when the arrival of the lord’s parents is concerned—whose special affection no one can doubt—he considers himself happier if he gives freer rein to joy through a greater jubilation and a more festive welcome.

If this is so among human beings, in whom whatever goodness exists is nevertheless far inferior to the goodness of the citizens above [the manuscripts read simply “to the goodness of those above”], let whoever can contemplate in his mind with what joy, what festivity, and with what songs of jubilation all the orders of blessed spirits rejoiced when they saw both the unique mother of their Lord approaching and their Lord and God himself wishing to go out to meet her adorned with all his glory.

Thus God himself, surrounded by thousands upon thousands—indeed, innumerable hosts—of angels, went out to meet this most devoted Mother as she departed from this world. He exalted her above all the heavens and placed her upon a throne [the manuscript adds “of glory”] to rule with him, by perpetual right, over every creature.

O glorious and blessed day of so great a meeting! Blessed and renowned day of so splendid an exaltation! Festive day of so sublime a glorification, wondrous to every age! For that day not only raised you, Lady, ineffably on high; it also adorned heaven itself, which you entered, and all that is in it, with a new and ineffable glory.

It adorned heaven with a new glory, because through your presence it magnified its former glory beyond anything that can be said or imagined. For when you ascended there, Lady, you illuminated it with the new and surpassing dignity of your virtues, and suffused it with the immense light of your mercies and graces.

That same day of your ascent clothed those who from the beginning of creation had deserved to be its citizens [Col. 0573A]—the manuscripts read “those of them who had deserved to be its citizens”—with a more festive joy of exultation than usual. Through the glorious fruit of your fruitful virginity they saw their half-ruined city restored.

Truly, at your arrival, through whom they had merited so great a blessing, the greatness of their joy rightly had to increase.

The day of your exaltation also watered the earth with wondrous grace, O most blessed of women. For when it recognized that you, whom it knew to have been begotten from it and in it according to the law of other human births, had been exalted to the throne of the Creator of all, it undoubtedly believed that, through the abundance of so great a blessing of yours, it had escaped the punishment of the ancient curse which it knew itself rightly to have incurred in the sin of its first children.

What more can I say, Lady? For when I wish to contemplate the immensity of your grace and glory, my understanding fails and my tongue falters [Col. 0573B]. Just as everything in heaven is ineffably adorned through your glorification, so through that same glorification everything that exists on earth is ineffably exalted.

Each thing advanced into the splendor of immense dignity when, through your blessed and inviolate virginity, created beings were granted to know, worship, and love their Lord God, whom they had not known. When they learned that you had ascended above all the heavens and had been exalted at the right hand of the Lord God, your blessed Son, they also learned in him that they owed everything they are to that same God, since you, who were one among them and from them, had deserved such eminent dignity. [The manuscripts read: “Since they learned that she had ascended above all the heavens and had been worthily exalted at the right hand of the Lord God, her blessed Son, they also learned in him … when she, who was one among them and from them, had deserved such …”]

Thus human beings understood that they owed nothing either to idols or to any other kind of thing belonging to creation for the worship paid by idolaters, since they received their unique Creator, begotten from your most chaste womb for the restoration of their original creation, and since they learned that you, through whom they recovered their lost dignity, had been placed so sublimely above every creature.

## CHAPTER IX. How greatly blessed Mary benefited human nature

What praises, then, and what acts of thanksgiving does not only human nature, but every creature, owe to this most holy Virgin? For the pure holiness and most holy purity of her most devoted heart, surpassing every purity or holiness of every creature with incomparable sublimity, deserved that she should most worthily become the restorer of the lost world [Col. 0573D].

Therefore, the world itself, restored through her, is utterly unable to estimate what praise it rightly owes her for so ineffable a blessing with the heart of anyone living under mortal flesh [Col. 0574A]. [The manuscripts read: “The restored world is utterly unable to estimate with the heart of anyone living under mortal flesh what praise it rightly owes her. Yet, lest anyone …”]

Nevertheless, lest anyone suppose that in what we say we are speaking too extravagantly, more in the manner of indiscriminate flatterers than with a desire to set the matter before the consideration of the faithful as it truly is [the manuscripts read “to consider it as it is”], it is useful to recall more fully the good things that have come to human nature through her. In this way we shall also be pleased, as far as we can, to bring forward how all the forms of other things have been reformed through her [the manuscript says “have been restored or reformed” rather than simply “have been reformed”].

We wish to do this so that, with the singular benefits she has bestowed placed to some extent before their eyes, no one may be left whose reflection is not overwhelmed by the immensity of the praise she has deserved.

Know, then: I shall speak for every age, and, as far as I am able, I shall declare from what condition and to what advancement we have come through this Lady’s merits [Col. 0574B].

Our nature was created in the beginning in the likeness of God, so that it might continually enjoy God himself and at some time possess his glory without any corruption or change. Nature immediately lost this such great blessing in the first human beings, and, wretched and headlong, plunged into the miseries of this world; thereafter, when the brief course of its fleeting life had been completed, it was destined to plunge still more wretchedly into eternal miseries [the manuscripts read “then into eternal miseries,” omitting “was destined to”].

Many ages passed, and the enormity of this condemnation was always strengthened for the worse over all the children of mankind. For the wisdom of the Most High did not establish any way in the mass of human creation [the manuscripts read *viam invenit*, “found a way,” rather than *viam constituit*, “established a way”] by which, coming into the world as he had ordained, he might aid so grievous a ruin, until the Virgin of whom we are speaking was reached.

But as soon as she came into the world through the line of human generation, she shone forth perfectly with such strength and constancy in every good [the manuscripts read “with virtue and substance” rather than “with virtue and constancy”] that the Wisdom of God itself, as it had predestined her from the ages, judged her truly worthy to be the one through whom, coming into human nature, it would not only erase the guilt of the first human beings but also the sins of the whole world, and would crush the devil, the enemy of his works, together with his own [the manuscripts read “would elude him” rather than “would crush him”]. It would also restore the losses of the heavenly homeland by leading man there [the manuscripts read *redintegret*, “restore,” rather than *redintegraret*, “would restore”].

Who, then, considering these things, could estimate how much praise she deserves, who alone, before all others, merited to become the mediator of such great blessings?

Freed, therefore, from the law of death by which we were held, we rise again into the glory that we lost in our first parent—indeed, into a greater glory than either he lost in himself or we lost in him. For those of us who, while still in mortal flesh, strive by faith toward the grace or homeland we lost, pass into adoption as sons of God through the blessed Son of the blessed mother Mary; and, with that same Son himself as author, we adopt him as our brother [Col. 0575A]. [The manuscript reads *arcessimus*, “we summon [him],” rather than *asciscimus*, “we adopt [him].”]

For when he rose from death, he called us his brothers, and he ordered it to be made known to us in familiar speech [the manuscripts read “with familiar affection”] that he would ascend to his Father and our Father, his God and our God (John 20:17).

Since, then, we have received so great a Father and so great a brother, we must certainly ascribe this to blessed Mary, through whose inviolate fruitfulness we rose to so great a dignity. Human nature would never have attained that dignity if her fruitful virginity had not given birth to God from her own substance.

Since, therefore, human nature, even while dwelling amid the squalor of this world, has been exalted through the merits of the devout Mother of God, Mary, let whoever can consider what glory will adorn it when it has received this same brother, equal to his almighty Father, reigning in his majesty, and when, as a co-heir of his kingdom, it stands perpetually and unchangeably in his presence [Col. 0575B]. [The manuscripts read “when it has established itself in his presence,” rather than “when it stands in his presence.”]

Let him consider—I say, let him consider—what glory, what joy, and what jubilation there will be for all those who, taken up into the kingdom of eternal blessedness, shall see the God and Lord of all things like themselves in the substance of his flesh, and shall see all that exists in heaven, on earth, or in the underworld depend upon his will. They shall see him love them with brotherly affection—indeed, with an affection beyond every brotherly love—and see whatever they can wish supplied to them eternally, without delay, contradiction, or failure [Col. 0575C].

Beyond this, when they have before their eyes the Lady through whom such great blessings came to them, seated beside God whom, as a Virgin, she had borne from her womb as her Son [the manuscripts read “whom she bore” rather than “whom she had borne”], and presiding by maternal right with that same Son over heaven and earth, let us consider with what exultation they will exult over her such great glory, and to what honor they will be raised through her such great power.

Every creature would certainly pay them honor, not only because it would see their Creator to be a sharer in their nature, but also because it would see its own Lady, one of their number, made Queen of the angels [the manuscripts read: “because they will see Mary, their supreme Lady and the one and only ruler of heaven and earth, made Queen from among them.”]

With these things considered, whoever you are, born from the human race, raise the eye of your mind as much as and as far as you can, and attend knowingly to what thanks, what praises, and what services you owe perpetually to her through whose blessed and inviolate fruitfulness you have been advanced from so great an evil to so great a good, as we have briefly shown. Let no pleasure of this world move you away from considering these things; let no indolence arising from any vain love hold you back from offering the praises you owe [Col. 0576A].

## CHAPTER X. How greatly she benefited every creature, including those beyond the human

But since we have now observed, at least briefly, what good we have obtained through the merits of the most excellent blessed Mother of God, Mary [the manuscript reads “through the excellence” rather than “through the merits of the most excellent”], let us also consider, as we proposed and as far as we can, what the other kinds of created things have obtained through those same merits of hers.

I know that I have mentioned some of these matters above, but, in order to commend the eminence of so great a Lady to devout ears, it does not seem superfluous to present the same point again. No one of sound judgment doubts that every creature, heavenly as well as earthly, was established for the praise and glory of its Creator; no wise person remains silent about this [the manuscripts read “no one of sound mind” rather than “no one of sound judgment”].

Therefore, if anything in anyone detracts in any way from his praise, glory, or honor, it is clear to those who observe rightly that it thereby wounds the other creatures—which preserve the integrity of their subjection to him—with a kind of blow of confusion. For they would not hold fast with complete fidelity to their Lord if they endured with equanimity and unshaken tranquility the dishonor of their author [the manuscripts read “of their Lord and author,” omitting “of their Lord” in the principal text]. [The manuscripts read “endured” rather than “held fast.”]

Man, then, who was created by God with a sublime nature among the other creatures, dishonored God through the guilt of his disobedience [the manuscripts read “was created while dishonoring God”]. He lost everything that had previously been under his jurisdiction, and, insofar as it depended upon him, wounded with a certain confusion everything that preserved the integrity of its condition through the enormity of his guilt.

A further confusion was added to them on top of this confusion: although they saw this man departing from his Creator through the merits of an evil life, they could never, by the law of their creation, refuse him the service of their ministry. Thus a certain insulting oppression was inflicted upon the works of God, and a grave and injurious abuse was made of them. For one who does not fear opposing God’s will through evil actions ought justly to have no right in the things that belong to God.

Thus, when man, guilty, enjoyed the light of heaven and the movement of the stars for his own uses, heaven itself and the stars suffered the loss of great honor [Col. 0576D]. They served one for whom they knew they had not been established. They had been created for the service of a just man, not of the unjust man whom he then was [the manuscripts read “for the service or obedience of a just man”].

The same may be said and understood of the air, of the earth and what it produces, of the sea and all waters, and of the things they contain. All the forms of created things were covered with a kind of shapeless and insulting obscurity, because they were compelled without interruption to minister and submit to the very one who continually offended his God [Col. 0577A]. [The manuscripts read “who had shown” rather than “who continually offended.”]

This injury remained in the substances of created things until the blessed Virgin Mary, of whom we are speaking, came in the flesh. But when she came, incorporated the Son of God within herself, and human nature recovered its original dignity in the God who was being born, no confusion or injury remained any longer in any kind of thing. Rather, it immediately deserved to receive again the freedom of its first creation [the manuscripts read “its ancestral creation” rather than “its first creation”].

For when she, to whom by the law of her condition the greatest right of freedom belonged—namely, to obey the one whom she knew to have been created in the image of God—saw man return through good works to the likeness of his Creator, which he had corrupted in himself through sin, it is no wonder that thereafter, by obeying his dominion, she shook off the yoke of an insulting servitude [Col. 0577B].

## CHAPTER XI. On the same subject
In another way too, if you please, let us consider how every creature was created for the benefit of humankind, and how that same benefit somehow vanished because of the sin of the first human being, and by what means, through the blessed Mother of God, the virgin Mary, it recovered the first dignity of its usefulness.

Certainly, the human being, existing through the reasoning of the mind yet weighed down by the frailty of the flesh, was created for this purpose: that with the eye of contemplation he might continually fix his attention upon the form of his Creator. But since his Creator is an unbounded spirit, and no one enclosed within corruptible flesh can ever attain knowledge of his greatness or contemplation of that wondrous divinity as it truly is, the existence of other things was set before him, so that through consideration of them he might behold, understood by himself, the sublimity of God, which cannot be seen in itself, once he had understood it.

[Note: The manuscripts read “pressed down by the incorruptibility of the flesh” instead of “weighed down by the frailty of the flesh.” They also read “the dignity of that one” instead of “his divinity,” and “a mirror” instead of “contemplation.” One manuscript omits “which cannot be seen.”]

But when, after the sin of the first human beings, the offspring of humankind had fallen into the desires of its heart and become befouled by vices, not only contemplation of the Creator but also the saving meditation upon the wondrous ordering of created things vanished far from it. You see, therefore, in what manner the dignity of things fell in the fall of humankind. For in considering them, the human being ought to have risen to the recognition of God, and they ought thus to have become, as it were, steps for him by which he might reach his Creator and theirs; but this dignity perished in them when no one remained who would use them worthily.

Nor did they in any way recover the lost eminence of so great a good from the time when the first human being fell, until that Lamb who would take away the sins of the world appeared to the world through Mary, in the person of God and human being.

[Note: The manuscripts read “appeared” rather than “appeared to the world.”]

But when, through this Lamb, the human being had been recalled to the knowledge of God, every other creature too was recalled to the state of its creation and to the honor of its own innate and natural beauty.

[Note: The manuscripts read “was renewed in the state ...” rather than “was recalled in the state ...”]

[Col. 0578A]

We therefore rightly judge that the effect of so great a good must be attributed to her through whose virginal womb he came into the world who, by his wisdom, recalled human nature to such an excellence of dignity as we have described, and at the same time, by a wondrous dispensation, restored to every creature the privilege of the honor it had lost.

What, then, every rational as well as irrational creature rightly owes to this most sacred lady—whoever is able may perceive it with an expanded understanding from what we have touched upon briefly. Certainly, all things that God made good and useful ceased to remain in the state in which they had been created, as we have shown, and through this most blessed Virgin they were recalled and restored to their original state.

Therefore, just as God, by his power in preparing all things, is Father and Lord of all, so blessed Mary, by her merits in restoring all things, is mother and lady of created things. For God is Lord of all, establishing each thing in its proper nature by his command; and Mary is lady of created things, restoring each one to its innate dignity through the grace she merited.

And just as God begot from his own substance him through whom he gave all things their origin, so Mary from her flesh

[Note: The manuscripts omit “most pure flesh.”]

gave birth to him who restored everything to the beauty of the first creation.

[Note: The manuscripts read “restored all things to the beauty ...” rather than “restored everything ...”]

Again, just as no kind of thing exists except through the Son of God, so the law of deserved condemnation abandons no one except the person whom the Son of Mary absolves.

Who, therefore, weighing these matters with sound understanding and sincere heart, could fully grasp the excellence of this lady, through whom the world has been raised from so estimable a degradation by so ineffable a grace?

[Note: The manuscripts read: “through whom nature has such immeasurable goods, through whom the world has been raised from such ineffable degradation by such immeasurable grace”; another reads “through whom the world has been raised from such ineffable degradation by such ineffable grace.”]

Who, I ask, gazing with the eye of the mind upon so wondrous a grace of this woman, wholly unheard-of in every other respect, would not be astonished—and not merely become speechless, but be utterly incapable of comprehending so great a matter?

## CHAPTER XII. Prayer to the Most Blessed Virgin Mary

Therefore, leaving aside those matters that are impenetrable to us, let us endeavor to obtain through prayers what we cannot grasp with the understanding, so that at least by a saving affection we may deserve to attain it.

We therefore ask you, lady, by that very grace through which the merciful and almighty God so exalted you and granted that all things might be possible for you together with him, obtain this for us from him: that the fullness of the grace you merited may so work in us

[Col. 0578D]

that we may one day, in his mercy, be granted a share in his blessed reward.

[Note: The manuscripts read “may be pardoned” rather than “may be granted.”]

For this reason, after all, our God became our brother through you: so that, just as he deigned to become a sharer in our humanity, we too might deserve to become sharers in his divinity.

Look, therefore, most merciful lady, to the fulfillment of that for which our God came among human beings as a human being, made from your most chaste womb. We ask you, do not be difficult to persuade, for undoubtedly your most gracious Son will be ready and willing to grant whatever you wish.

Only will our salvation, and truly we shall in no way be unable to be saved. What, then, will restrain the generous depths of your mercy, lady, in regard to us, so that you should not wish us to be saved? Certainly our God is our mercy, as the Prophet testifies (Psalm 58:18), and you are without doubt the true mother of that same Lord of ours.

If you, then, who are the Mother of God and therefore truly the mother of mercy,

[Note: The manuscripts read “mother of mercy and grace,” omitting “and therefore.”]

deny us the effect of the mercy of which you have been made the mother so wondrously, what shall we do when that same Son of yours comes to judge all people with impartial judgment?

For although he himself, through you, has become our brother, your Son will nevertheless observe where he sees the will of his sweetest mother especially extended—provided, of course, that he preserves the rule of equity, from which he will see that you in no way wish to differ—

[Note: The manuscripts read “from which he will see that you do not differ,” omitting “wish to.”]

and he will pronounce the sentence of his judgment, bending it either toward mercy or directing it toward justice.
