[Note: The manuscripts read “our brother: where ...” rather than “our brother. Your Son will nevertheless observe where ...”; they also read “her will, namely,” rather than “your will ...”]

Come to our aid, therefore, lady, and, without considering the multitude of our sins, bend your will toward showing us mercy. Think, I ask you, and think again within yourself: our Creator became human from you not to condemn but to save the sinner.

Why, then, will you not help us sinners, when for our sake you have been raised to such a height that every creature alike has you as its lady

[Note: The manuscripts read “has you, Lady,” with the title capitalized.]

and venerates you?

Or will you no longer care whether we perish, because whatever misery may thereafter befall us will bring no loss to your glory?

This could perhaps be said in some sense, good lady, if you had become the Mother of God solely for your own exaltation and salvation,

[Note: The manuscripts read “and benefit” rather than “and salvation.”]

if, that is, God, who assumed humanity from your most chaste flesh, had done this for your salvation and ours in common.

[Note: The manuscripts read “for the salvation of us all” rather than “for your salvation and ours in common.”]

If, therefore, you, who have obtained salvation in its fullness, do not intend that this same salvation should, according to our measure, reach us also, you will appear already satisfied with your own advantages and negligent of ours. And when you, who merited becoming the Mother of the Most High for the salvation of the whole world, place before yourself us, whom the end of the age has enveloped,

[Note: The manuscripts read “when you put us after yourself” rather than “when you place us before yourself.”]

what benefit, I ask, will your glorious and blessed exaltation bring us, and what of the sweet and affectionate joy that we possess from it?

[Note: The manuscripts read “and what benefit do we possess from it?” rather than “and what of the sweet and affectionate joy that we possess from it?”]

Therefore, so that we may truly recognize your Son as the Savior of the whole world and you as his reconciler, help us and cherish us with the more ardent devotion, we pray, the more clearly you see that we, born and raised in the filth of the world,

[Note: The manuscripts read “raised” rather than “raised and nourished.”]

need greater assistance.

From the beginning, finally, of the renewal of humankind, you have come to the aid of all who have fled beneath your protection, even to this day. For that reason you have deserved to be called, and to be, more worthy of every praise than all creation.

Come, then, help us, we pray, so that the praise you have rightly possessed for so many ages

[Note: The manuscripts omit “rightly.”]

may endure for you continuously in the grace itself through which you came to the aid of the lost world.

[Note: The manuscripts omit “of the lost world.”]

To you, therefore, we commend ourselves. Take care that we do not perish; rather, bring it about that our salvation may increase from day to day, and that our life may serve your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in continual devotion.

He lives, rules, and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout infinite ages.

[Col. 0580C]

[Note: Manuscript Corbie E. 10 ends: “Here ends Eadmer the Monk’s Writing on Mary, the Most Pious Mother of God.” Manuscript S. 62 ends: “Here ends the Sermon on Holy Mary.”]

[Col. 0579C]

# ON THE FOUR VIRTUES THAT WERE IN BLESSED MARY, AND ON HER SUBLIMITY (G)*

[Col. 0579D]

## CHAPTER I. On These Virtues in General

Many who have attempted to shape the praises of the holy lady Mary in writing have gladly set before the human race, according to their abilities, how great an abundance of virtues once flowed together in her, how readily she now comes to the aid of mortal needs, how sublime and wondrous was then the grace of her gifts, and how powerfully singular and singularly sweet is her compassion now.

For since philosophers have not failed to say that there are four virtues—justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance—from which, as though from the boundary of a crossroads [the text reads *gaudio*; perhaps *quadrivio*, “a four-way crossing,” is intended], the whole host of virtues shines forth, our predecessors taught that these four primary virtues reigned in her. It was therefore very easy for them to show that certain appendages of these virtues had been perfectly fitted together in her mind.

They asserted her justice in this way: she clung so tenaciously to God’s commandments through the Law that she did not think those practices should be abandoned which are known to arise from its integrity [the text is corrupt; perhaps read *posse non observari*, “cannot fail to be observed”]—for example, purification after childbirth, a sacrifice for a child, and the annual ascent to the Temple. Who among the faithful could doubt that she performed these things out of an abundance of devotion?

Her prudence was shown in this: she was the first among women to recognize, in a matter that lacked precedent, how pleasing to God was the sacrifice of chastity that she herself had vowed, leaving the curse of the Law standing in the midst of the matter. Moreover, after the angel’s greeting, how prudently she spoke, how readily she believed! Her faith and belief were indeed the equipment of prudence: she believed that through the Holy Spirit she could produce a son without sexual embrace and without danger to her chastity, with the thorn of lust banished.

[Col. 0581B]

Her fortitude was shown in this: what she prudently understood ought justly to be done, she vowed without hesitation and steadfastly pursued her vow. It is just that what one holds more gracious and more beautiful should be offered, at God’s command, to him who is the giver of all good things. The prudent Virgin wisely gathered this conclusion and bravely vowed to God her virginity, which she considered nothing more lovable and nothing more beautiful, and preserved it with the greatest courage.

Her temperance was shown in this: she continued the virtues mentioned above through devoted humility, preserving by it whatever the devotion of an upright mind and heavenly grace had accumulated in her. Thus it was justice that she did what was good; prudence that she understood how it ought to be done; fortitude that she persevered; and temperance

[Col. 0581C]

that, placed at such a height, she avoided falling through a humble mind.

## CHAPTER II. On Justice and Its Appendages

These virtues, as I said, also have other appendages and companions; they have attendants and associates. If I faithfully remember their arrangement in the Mother of the Lord, their effects were as follows.

Justice, they say, is accompanied by religion, which is purity of life, through which one pleases God; piety, through which one loves one’s neighbor; gratitude, which is remembrance of a benefit received; obedience, which obeys the one whom it rightly ought to obey; and truth, which teaches one to live according to nature and to speak according to the matter at hand.

The blessed Mother of the Lord exercised these virtues so completely that, through religious purity of life, she built a temple for the Lord God in her body; through piety, she honored her neighbor; and, not ungrateful to God for the benefits bestowed upon her, she in turn offered him soul and body as a living sacrifice.

She was diligent in obeying those greater and worthy of obedience, so much so that when she heard from the angel’s proclamation that she would be the Mother of God, she promptly climbed into the hill country (Luke 1:39), to serve her elderly kinswoman and assist her in childbirth.

As the mother of truth, leaning upon truth and accustomed to living according to nature, she carried within her intact womb the very maker of nature. She knew how to speak according to the matter: she examined the angel’s promise on the careful scales of reason, so that she might clearly learn how it was to be done, while having no doubt that it could and ought to be done.

[Col. 0582A]

## CHAPTER III. On Prudence and Its Followers

Prudence is followed by foresight, which looks ahead to what may beneficially occur in the future; understanding, which understands what may beneficially occur in the present; and memory, which gathers completely what has been done well or badly and what has been said concerning the past.

No one was more provident than this lady. Before she vowed her virginity to God, she clearly foresaw how much progress that vow, if made and carefully observed, would bring to herself and to the whole world. She would not have vowed something so extraordinary unless she had foreseen that incomparable glory would thereby be accumulated for herself and for others.

No one was more understanding than she. With the ready acuity of her mind and consciousness of the divinity itself, she fully understood, in the Lord’s birth, passion, and resurrection,

[Col. 0582B]

how great was the good present in those events and how incomparably fruitful it would be in the future.

She possessed a tenacious and unique memory. Everything she alone knew about her Son, gathering it into a heap through a secret counsel known only to herself, she impressed upon the consciousness of human beings. Hence it is said of her: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).

The whole world therefore owes her full knowledge of its salvation, since she did not begrudge the apostles the knowledge of the most complete understanding. Therefore, because the progress of the Gospel could not grow from a small beginning unless the character of its origin were known, she is rightly called both the apostle of the apostles and the evangelist of the evangelists, through whom the foundational teaching shone upon those very leaders of the faith.

[Col. 0582C]

## CHAPTER IV. On Fortitude and Its Followers

Fortitude is joined by magnificence, which endeavors to undertake something magnificent; confidence, which trustfully seizes upon thoughts splendidly conceived; perseverance, which steadily presses forward a good work begun; and patience, which endures difficulties for the sake of benefit.

The “benefit” which I mentioned here and above is to be understood, according to blessed Ambrose’s *On Duties*, in the sense that what is useful is the same as what is honorable, and what is honorable the same as what is useful, although in secular schools these are defined differently.

The happy girl acted with great magnificence in seeking out the good that was to be begun, which she began confidently and completed perseveringly. She did not break under insults directed either against herself or against her Son.

Magnificence was shown in her words: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47).

Confidence was shown in: “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (ibid., 48).

Perseverance was shown in: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name, and his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him” (ibid., 49, 51).

Of her patience it was said: “And a sword will pierce your own soul” (Luke 2:35).

## CHAPTER V. On Temperance and Its Followers

Continence is closely allied to temperance; through it, the chief desire of the mind is governed by the direction of counsel. Clemency is also allied to it, by which the mind, rashly stirred to hatred of someone, is restrained; and modesty, by which whatever is in some way excessive is carefully and cautiously cut away.

It is plainly evident that the blessed lady exercised these virtues, since it is certain that she was neither incontinent under the stimulus of any pleasure, nor rash through hatred, nor immodest in spirit. For how could she commit what was unlawful, when she abstained even from what was lawful?

Added to the precepts of continence are the habits that befit a virgin, as Ambrose teaches in that familiar and, for others, inimitable nectar of his words:

“Let her be a virgin who, by no deceitful maneuver, adulterates a sincere effect; humble in heart, serious in speech, prudent in mind; if there is any pleasure in food, satisfying it only in small measure; completely restraining the vices of the flesh; sparing in speech, more devoted to reading. Let her manner be neither overly affected, her walk neither too loose, her voice neither too wanton, so that the very appearance of her body may be

[Col. 0583B]

an image of her mind and a representation of her integrity.”

No Christian will deny that these qualities were present in the Mother of the Lord, since her illustrious life, as the hymn says, enlightens and shapes all the churches.

## CHAPTER VI. Christ Confirmed These Virtues of Saint Mary

The Son of God poured himself entirely into this girl, crowned as she was with the diadem of virtues, preserving by his own coming the good qualities of her virginal soul above all.

For he is not only just but justice itself, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness” (Psalm 44:8). Therefore, penetrating his already just mother with the justice of God, he anointed her with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—above all his companions, that is, above all virgins.

In granting fecundity to his mother without taking away her virginity, he is not only wise but Wisdom itself, and in him all the treasures of wisdom dwell bodily. Finding a wise girl, Wisdom itself preserved wisdom: that is, it kept her pure in heart and body. For it is written: “Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4).

He is temperate, and temperance itself, as he says in the Song of Songs: “I am the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1), that is, the flower of the humble. Likewise in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Therefore, accepting the virgin’s humility through his gracious condescension, he poured his fullness of divinity into her womb, as the prophet says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and peaceful?” (Isaiah 66:2). Likewise, she herself says in the Gospel: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48).

He is also not only strong but the strength of God, through whom God the Father made all things from nothing. Coming as the strong one, stronger than the devil, he stripped the halls and divided the spoils (Luke 11:22).

He did not, therefore, weaken his mother’s strength, but exalted it by his own power, so that she might be the commanding lady of all creation, reconciling and soothing those above, casting down and terrifying those below.

The God who searches hearts and kidneys (Psalm 7:10), choosing from among all the virgins whom the world contained, chose and sanctified her so that he might dwell bodily in her—her whom he had long before cherished and embraced spiritually, already filled with the virtues described above.

[Col. 0584A]

## CHAPTER VII. That God Could Not Have Become Human from Another Virgin

For this reason, those who say that God could have brought about human salvation either through another virgin or through something other than a virgin seem to me to depart from the truth.

To those who think that God could have become incarnate in some other virgin, I reply briefly: Rather, he could not, because he did not wish to. And conversely: he did not wish to, because he could not.

For although he is almighty, there are nevertheless many things that he is said not to be able to do. Thus he cannot lie or die, because he does not wish to. For if he wished to lie or die, he would not be almighty, because lying is not power but sin—that is, the incapacity for good—and dying is a falling away from power.

Therefore it is said of God: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Psalm 113:3), because he willed nothing except what was fitting.

In the same way I say that he could neither have been able nor ought to have been born from another virgin. And therefore, as I said, he could not, because he did not wish to.

Moreover, he did not wish to because there was no reason. It is obvious that God, the author of reason, could neither will, do, nor even be able to do anything contrary to reason.

Who would not see that God had departed from reason if, while observing that all women without exception were beneath the holiness of blessed Mary, he chose some other woman as mother and rejected her? I think that anyone who considers what has been said above understands that she surpassed all women in holiness. For the others received only portions of grace, whereas she was greeted by the angel as full of grace.

Furthermore, whoever says that God ought or could have repaired the sin of Adam in some other way than through the virgin birth is as though he were saying that God ought to have done it better, or could have done it just as well in another way.

But if he ought to have done it better, or could have done it just as well in another way, and yet did not do so, then either he was unwilling or he did not know how.

If he was unwilling to do what was better, though he could have done it, he was envious or sluggish. If he did not know how to do it better, though he ought to have done so, he was ignorant.

Anyone who sees how shameful it is to attribute these vices to any honorable human being acknowledges how far envy, sluggishness, and ignorance are from God’s nature.

It therefore remains that whoever blushes to assign these qualities to God, and does not reject the preceding arguments, must confess that God could restore the world only through a virgin—and especially through this virgin.

He could not do otherwise because he did not wish to; he did not wish to because there was no reason; and because there was no reason, he ought not to have done otherwise.

If someone reverses this sequence, it will not be invalid in the following form: He ought not to have saved the human race in another way, because there was no reason; and because there was no reason, he did not wish to; and because he did not wish to, he could not, since he could neither wish nor be able to act contrary to reason.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Sublimity of the Blessed Virgin Is Explained

Having briefly culled and gathered together into one account the views of the ancient Fathers concerning the virtues of blessed Mary, my discourse will now attend to commending her sublimity, which she attained on account of the grace of her virtues.

To explain this more perceptively, I shall set before you the love of the Son for his mother and of the mother for her Son.

[Col. 0585A]

God the Son, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with the Father, begotten from the Father before time without a mother, willed to be born in time from a mother without a father. He chose this girl out of the love he had for her, so that the whole divinity might flow into her and she might become the mother of God and human being.

He loved her, therefore, before he was born from her, so that she might be one from whom he could be worthily born. Is it a small love that made a mother from a daughter, and from a creature the mother of the Creator?

Nor did love fail after the birth; rather, it received incomparable increase. For just as all human beings, born from both parents, divide their love between both parents, so the Lord Jesus, born from a mother without a father, owed and paid the love due from a father and mother to his mother alone.

Moreover, there were two things contending in the Virgin’s mind in an invisible but great battle: love of virginity and fear of the curse of the Law. Nevertheless, after long and careful deliberation, love, which outweighed the other, conquered, and fear gave way.

Then God’s help intervened: he would take away from her what she feared, while not taking away what she loved, and would preserve its seal intact. He therefore granted her both fruitfulness in offspring and freedom from the loss of virginity.

And what of her? Did she not respond with a love worthy of such benefits from her Son, filled with the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father, and with the tender and sweet love of a child—love not fleeting but eternal?

Did she not love him who made her lady of all creation, queen of heaven and earth, granting fruitfulness, as I have said, without diminishing integrity?

Indeed, with all her marrow and all her strength she was suspended in love of him; and the love that father and mother owe their offspring, this one sweet earthly mother alone bestowed upon her Lord and Son.

No knowledge can penetrate, no eloquence proclaim, how assiduously she cherished the little child; with what care and service she brought up the adolescent as he advanced toward the strength of maturity; with what joy she heard and saw the young man performing miracles and made famous by their glory; with what sorrow she sighed over him as he suffered and died.

And these things are almost as inconceivable to us as they are unfamiliar.

But when he rose and ascended, with what joyful eyes did the blessed Virgin behold him, with what delight were her blessed inmost parts moved—especially when she already understood that what had been labored for through so long a time was now coming into effect?

She saw the human race being called to salvation through the apostles, for the sake of which she had earlier understood that the Son of God, made flesh from her and suffering on the cross, had come.

Therefore she rejoiced that the hope she had previously conceived, and that which she had hoped through the vow of her virginity would be salvific for the whole world, was already passing into actual reality.

The angels too rejoiced. They saw the number of their fellow citizens, once diminished through sin, now restored through her blessed childbirth.

Human beings rejoiced and rejoice because what they lost through the first woman they receive again through Mary, with the profit of a hundredfold recompense.

Servants fell; brothers and children rise—brothers of the Lord, children of Mary.

That joy will grow into an incomparable increase when, in heaven, they enjoy the joy then present through the presence of those by whom they have obtained such great joys!

Every creature rejoiced and rejoices, because those things that, at the beginning of the world, were made by God to serve humankind, when humankind had withdrawn from knowledge and service of God, grieved to be subjected to the degenerate service of one who was rebellious against its Creator.

But when the human being was saved through blessed Mary, creation escaped into its ancient dignity and shone again in its former splendor, while serving the one who obeys his Creator in faith and in works.

Therefore, just as God is the Father and Creator of all things, so this Virgin is the mother and restorer of all things. For just as nothing exists except what God makes, so nothing is restored except what the Son of Saint Mary redeems.

Let the faithful soul therefore ascend to the watchtower of the mind and, as far as it can, behold how sublime is the position of the lady Mary.

Every nature was made by God, and God was made from Mary. The maker of all things made himself from Mary, and thus remade all things.

He who was able to make everything from nothing did not wish to restore what had been violated without Mary.

God is therefore the Father of created things, and Mary is the mother of restored things. God begot him through whom all things were made, and Mary begot him through whom all things were restored and saved.

Through these arguments it is impossible that anyone who turns to her and is regarded by her should be condemned. For she gave birth to him through whom the dead revive, through whom human beings are saved from sin; there is no justification except that which she fostered in her womb, and no salvation except that which she gave birth to.

She is therefore the mother of the one who justifies and of those who are justified; she is the mother of the one who saves and of those who are saved.

Thus the Mother of God, who alone condemns and who alone saves, whom alone we fear and in whom alone we hope, is our mother.

Our Judge and Savior is our brother.

How, then, can we despair, when our salvation—or our condemnation—depends upon the judgment of a good brother and a merciful mother?

Will a good brother endure the punishment of his brothers whom he redeemed? Will a good mother endure the condemnation of her children whose Redeemer she herself bore?

The sweet mother will ask her sweet Son, our merciful brother: the Son on behalf of his sons, the Only-Begotten on behalf of his adopted children.

The merciful Son will gladly hear his mother on behalf of her children, the Only-Begotten on behalf of those whom he adopted, and the Lord on behalf of those whom he liberated.

[Col. 0587]

# EADMER THE MONK’S BOOK ON THE BLESSEDNESS OF THE HEAVENLY HOMELAND

[Note: It was collated with manuscripts Corbie S. 62, E. 10, and 605. These manuscripts place before it a letter from Eadmer to William, but do not distinguish the chapters.]

(G)*

[Col. 0587A]

To his reverend lord, his brother and friend, the monk William—whom he loves greatly for his gentleness, modesty, and uprightness of life—Brother Eadmer, the least of the monks of Christ Church, Canterbury: what God has promised to those who love him.

Your holiness, honored brother, will, I believe, remember that when the venerable Father Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, was recently staying for several days at the monastery of Cluny, and was speaking while being heard with the greatest devotion by the religious community of that place out of reverence for him, you asked me to present to you in writing the discourse that he delivered in the chapter house before the assembled brothers concerning eternal blessedness.

Since I gladly wished to comply, to the best of my ability, with your desire, I immediately undertook the work, thinking that it would prove easier to explain than I later discovered.

[Col. 0588A]

Let your beloved affection therefore know that it was solely for your sake that I did not abandon what I had begun, although perhaps it would have been better to abandon it entirely.

A beautiful and desirable subject, when recounted in an unpolished and contemptible style, sometimes tends to offend the listener’s mind more than to delight it. I therefore fear that the same may happen in my work: that a worthy subject, arranged in an unworthy style, may produce this effect in people’s minds, namely, that what previously pleased them in itself, without writing, may afterward be made cheap by the ugliness of the written form.

But certainly I wrote what I wrote to you because your sincere affection moved me to do so, intending only to state simply what I remembered having heard from the mouth of that Father at that chapter meeting, or elsewhere, concerning the same matter at that time.

[Col. 0588B]

May your holiness prosper, and pray for me.

[Col. 0587B]

# PROLOGUE

[Note: Manuscript E says: “The following little work is the work of the venerable Anselm on the Beatitudes.” Manuscript 62 says: “Here begins the Prologue of Eadmer the Monk to the book on eternal blessedness, which he composed from the words of blessed Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.”]

Many people, when good conduct and righteous works are sometimes set before them, and when they are urged to practice them after setting aside the vanity of the world, are accustomed to ask why they should do so, with what reward, and with what recompense.

They are therefore answered with what is written: “For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of a human being what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

When they cannot clearly perceive what this means, the same thing is repeated to them in other words, and they are told: The reward that is repaid in the future life to those who serve God in this life is eternal life, eternal blessedness, eternal joy—namely, the sufficiency of every good according to the will and without any need.

When these things are said to them in this way, they certainly appear to be good and great, as they are. But because they do not understand what they will possess in eternal life itself, and cannot immediately grasp what it means to have the sufficiency of every good according to the will and without any need, they remain mentally suspended and are not drawn with much effective relish toward what they have heard.

What, then, should be done so that these things may become somewhat pleasing to them and they may thus awaken to good works?

I think we should feed them in the manner of children. When children receive a large apple to eat, they cannot consume it because of the tenderness of their teeth and the narrowness of their mouths unless it is first divided into small pieces according to their capacity.

Let us therefore divide into parts the great things we have mentioned, so that from them those about whom we are speaking may be nourished toward life.

To make these matters shine forth more clearly,

[Col. 0588C]

let us consider what the human mind loves in this life, and from these things, as far as we can conjecture, let us infer that they will possess them much more excellently in the future life—if, amid the dangers of worldly temptations, they have followed the Lord’s commandments, and if, once they have obtained them there in their fullness, they realize that they have in no way been defrauded of their desire.

Let us do this, I say, and proceed gradually from the smallest matters.

Behold, first, let us briefly enumerate the goods that pertain to the body. In my judgment, these are the things that people seek for their own sake and for which they seek everything else: beauty, speed, strength, freedom, health, pleasure, and length of life.

But if there are among these things some that servants of God at times not only do not desire but also carefully avoid pursuing in this life—such as, for example, bodily beauty and pleasure—they do this not because they naturally do not want them, but so that they may not in any way offend God through them.

For if they were certain that no offense against God could be incurred through these things, or did not fear that they would be hindered by them from loving eternal things, they would undoubtedly conduct themselves more joyfully in their possession than in their opposites.

Having briefly introduced these matters, let us now treat individually the things we have proposed, and, as the Lord grants, explain how we shall enjoy them after the resurrection of our bodies.

[Col. 0589A]

# CHAPTER ONE  
## On the Beauty of the Bodies of the Blessed

Beauty is therefore a certain good, and one that all naturally desire to possess. In that life, then, the beauty of the righteous will be equal to the beauty of the sun, which will be seven times more splendid than it is now, just as divine Scripture testifies: “The righteous,” it says, “will shine like the sun in the presence of God” [Col. 0589B] (Matthew 13:43). Moreover, I do not know whether anyone could doubt that the Lord’s body surpasses the sun in glory. And, as the Apostle testifies, we shall be like him; for he says: “He will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21). Authority affirms this, and it is known to be impious to contradict it. Yet if anyone wishes this to be demonstrated by reason, I believe that no one ought to find it incredible that in that life the righteous will obtain the beauty of the sun, where “this mortal nature will be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4). For they will truly be called and will be the temple and dwelling of God—whereas nowhere in the divine text do we remember reading this said of this visible sun alone.

[Col. 0589B]

# CHAPTER TWO  
## On Swiftness

Swiftness, which is loved no less than beauty, will accompany us to such an extent that we shall be as swift as God’s angels, who move from heaven to earth and from earth to heaven more quickly than a word can be spoken. If it were necessary to prove whether such speed exists in angels [manuscripts: “it is necessary to prove” rather than “it were necessary to prove”], one might perhaps offer as an example a man still weighed down by mortal flesh who was at once carried by an angel from Judaea to Chaldaea and, after delivering the meal he was carrying, brought back without delay. Therefore, since those who will possess the equality promised to them will be altogether equal to the angels, they will possess the same swiftness.

The Apostle likewise, when he asserts that our bodies, however far apart in place their members may have been and however dispersed, will rise “in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Corinthians 15:52), sufficiently indicates what swiftness those same bodies, now incorruptible, will possess. For “this corruptible body,” as he himself testifies, “will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality” (ibid., 53).

An example of this swiftness may also be observed in a ray of the sun. As soon as the sun has risen in the eastern region, the ray reaches the farthest region of the west [manuscript: “of the eastern region” rather than “of the western region”]. Thus we may judge that what we say about our future swiftness is not impossible, especially since living things are usually endowed with greater speed than lifeless things.

We have a similar example of this solar-ray swiftness in ourselves. For the ray of our eyes reaches as far as heaven when our eyelids are raised, and in the blink of the eyes it returns wholly and intact into itself.

It is also certain that the souls of the saints, which already possess the heavenly realms, do not yet enjoy complete happiness until they obtain the incorruptibility of their bodies. When they have obtained this [manuscripts: adepti fuerint, “when they [masculine] have obtained,” rather than adeptae fuerint, “when they [feminine] have obtained,” agreeing with souls], there will be nothing more for them to desire. Therefore, if these bodies were to make them slower or heavier than their own swiftness, they would surely recoil from their companionship rather than desire it. Accordingly, we shall be endowed with the swiftness of which we speak when we have entered the true life.

[Col. 0590A]

# CHAPTER THREE  
## On Strength

After these qualities we named strength, which most people love all the more because they hate weakness. Therefore, all who have deserved to be joined to the citizens above will be endowed with such power that nothing at all will be able to resist them if they wish, by moving or overturning it, to alter anything in any way from its position, without its immediately yielding.

Nor will they labor with greater effort in what we are describing than we now do in moving our eyes [manuscripts: “in the movement of our eyes” rather than “in moving our eyes”]. Please do not let the likeness we shall attain to the angels slip from your mind [manuscripts: excitat animo, “stirs the mind,” rather than excidat animo, “slip from the mind”]. Thus, if no example presents itself here or in what we are about to say [manuscripts: quatenus hic, “thus here,” rather than quatenus si hic, “thus, if here”], that likeness itself will present one, and will prove and affirm that we too possess in equal measure whatever it is established that the angels possess.

I think that no one doubts that angels exercise the strength they desire. But perhaps someone will ask what that strength will provide for us, since everything will be so suitably arranged—indeed, incapable of being arranged more suitably—that there will be nothing to change, nothing to overturn, and nothing to stand against, in which anyone could exercise his strength.

Whoever says this should consider with us, briefly, what use human experience has in such matters, and he will see that we do not always actively use everything we possess and in which we greatly rejoice in possessing—for example, sight itself, some power, knowledge of certain things, and many things of this kind. So too then there will be the strength of which we are speaking [manuscript: “strength” rather than “the strength”]. Its mere possession will be pleasing to us, and there will be great exultation, even though we will not need to exercise it, since everything, as has been said, will be established in its proper place.

This same question, whether it concerns swiftness or any of the matters that we shall discuss for the purpose of the proposed work [manuscripts: praepositi, “preceding,” rather than propositi, “proposed”], if it troubles anyone, may receive the solution by which it has been resolved here, unless he has a clearer one [manuscripts: “a more suitable one” rather than “a clearer one”].

[Col. 0590D]

# CHAPTER FOUR  
## On Freedom

Next, in the order we proposed, comes freedom, which is loved no less than the qualities already mentioned. Therefore, all who have attained the likeness of the angels will necessarily attain their freedom as well.

Just as nothing obstructs the angels, and nothing can impede or restrain them from penetrating all things with complete freedom, according to their will, so there will be no obstacle to delay us, no enclosure to hold us, and no element that will not be entirely accessible to us according to our will.

For example, the Lord’s body, to which Paul testifies that our bodies are to be conformed (Philippians 3:21), and which we mentioned above, rose from the dead while the tomb was closed; and afterward it entered through locked doors so that the disciples might touch it (John 20:26–27). Thus it left us a great proof of the freedom that will be ours.

[Col. 0591A]

# CHAPTER FIVE  
## On Impassibility

Above, we said that human beings love health. And what better can be said about it than what the Psalmist sings: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 36:39)? But when someone has true health from the Lord, what weakness will be able to steal upon him?

Yet concerning this health that we shall have in the age to come, I do not see what example I can offer by which its nature may be understood, because neither I nor anyone living under mortal flesh has experienced in himself anything that I could compare with it.

Here we think ourselves healthy when we feel nothing painful in us. Yet we are sometimes deceived in this. For we are often ill in some part of the body and nevertheless perceive this only through bodily movement or through some kind of touch.

But what shall we say about those who are not even ill in this way, but seem to themselves healthy in every respect? How shall we determine whether or not they are healthy? Imagine for yourself someone extremely healthy in body, and ask him about his health: according to his own judgment, he is healthy. Now let such a person be touched somewhat more firmly, or be tightly constricted in some part of his body, and you will immediately see that he cries out: “Stop, you are hurting me; you are tormenting me.”

What is this? Did he not previously say that he was healthy? And now, touched only slightly, he cries out so painfully. Does this man seem healthy to you? I do not think so.

Therefore, we shall certainly not be given a salvation of this kind, since our salvation is expressly promised to be from the Lord. For God “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his own” [manuscripts omit “of his own saints”], “and there will no longer be mourning, or crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). “They will hunger no more, nor thirst anymore; neither will the sun strike them, nor any heat” (Isaiah 49:10; Revelation 7:16). For God will shelter them with his right hand and defend them with his holy arm (Wisdom 5:2, 17).

What, then, can harm those for whom God’s right hand will be a shelter?

What that health will be like, I certainly know that I have not learned either through my own experience or through anyone else’s senses or experience. If anyone asked me about the nature of fevers and various illnesses, I could perhaps easily explain what they are, both because I have experienced them in myself and because I have learned from those who have experienced them what they are. But concerning what I have not perceived through my own senses, nor, as I said, learned from anyone who has perceived it, I cannot speak in the same way.

Nevertheless, I may believe and confidently affirm, as I think, that the health of the future life will be so continuous, unchangeable, and inviolable that it will fill the whole person with an ineffable and perceptible sweetness of delight, and will drive far away and repel everything that might suggest the suspicion of any alteration, change, or injury in him. Let this suffice concerning health.

[Col. 0592A]

# CHAPTER SIX  
## On Pleasure

Next, in the order in which we proposed to discuss each of the subjects before us, we added pleasure, which we also call the delight of the bodily senses.

This is greatly loved because each bodily sense takes pleasure in what it judges beneficial to itself. Thus, to give a brief example, the sense of smell delights in various fragrances, and taste in the differing flavors of different things; likewise each of the other senses delights in this or that, according to the natural appetite proper to each [manuscripts: “because each bodily sense is loved” rather than “because each bodily sense takes pleasure”; “let them be said” rather than “let it be said”; “each sense” rather than “each of the other senses”; “each generally tends” rather than “according to the natural appetite proper to each”].

Yet these pleasures do not always give pleasure; they sometimes bring weariness even to those who love them. For they are transient and brutish. Those pleasures, however, which will be fully administered to the righteous in the age to come [manuscripts: “those pleasures in the future age” rather than “those pleasures which will be fully administered to the righteous in the age to come”], are perpetual and rational.

Therefore, I do not see how their nature can be explained so as to be understood, especially since no example can be found among the pleasures of the present life by which we might represent them. For the more anyone enjoys those pleasures, the more fervently he will embrace them, because their satiety creates disgust in no one.

I think that no one living in this mortality, nor anyone who has lived in it, has experienced or tasted these pleasures [manuscripts: “and anyone who has experienced them” rather than “or anyone who has lived in it”], so as to be able to explain their flavor or character by comparison with other things.

For we know that there are two kinds of blessedness, and likewise two kinds of misery: a greater and a lesser. We call the greater blessedness the kingdom of God; the lesser is the joy of paradise in which Adam was first placed. Likewise, we acknowledge the greater misery to be the eternal fire of Gehenna; the lesser consists of the hardships that we continually suffer in the present life.

We have never experienced either kind of blessedness. But if we had at least experienced that lesser blessedness which Adam possessed when placed in paradise, perhaps through it we could in some way conjecture the greater, just as now, born, nurtured, and grown up in lesser misery, we can whenever we wish describe and explain many things about the greater misery.

Since, then, the pleasure of which we are speaking is a large portion of the greater blessedness, I do not see how we can explain it in a way that will make it intelligible, unless perhaps we attempt this by means of some contrary likeness to the great misery that we conjecture from the lesser.

Let us therefore place before the eyes of the heart, by way of example, some person who has burning and glowing iron fixed both in the pupils of his eyes and in each of his limbs, so that neither his marrow, nor his intestines, nor anything at all throughout his whole body is free from the enormity of that torment, or feels it in any part less severely than in his eyes.

What shall I say? He is in anguish. Who would consider this man sane amid such circumstances?

In the same way, but with a wholly opposite consideration, an ineffable pleasure will intoxicate the good in that future life and satisfy them entirely with an immeasurable abundance of its sweetness.

Why did I say “entirely”? Their eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, hands, feet, throat, heart, liver, lungs, bones, marrow, and even their innermost organs—in short, each of their members individually and all of them together—will be filled with such a marvelous sensation of pleasure and sweetness that truly the whole person will drink from the torrent of God’s pleasure and be intoxicated by the abundance of his house (Psalm 35:9).

[Col. 0593B]

# CHAPTER SEVEN  
## On the Eternity of Life

Whoever, then, has attained these goods, I do not understand why his desire should extend any further for the sake of bodily well-being [manuscripts: “of his body” rather than “of bodily well-being”]. Let him merely possess the duration of life, which, as we have said, everyone desires. Yet this will certainly not be lacking to him, because “the righteous will live forever,” as Scripture says (Wisdom 5:16).

There are also other things, which are loved no less than those we have set out [manuscripts: “the things which we have set out up to this point”], but which relate to the soul as those relate to the body. These too, established in the number seven [Col. 0593C], greatly please the mind that has been imbued with their savor.

They are wisdom, friendship, concord, power, honor, security, and joy.

[Col. 0593C]

# CHAPTER EIGHT  
## On Wisdom

Wisdom, then, which everyone loves even in this life, though not courageously [the Latin phrase is textually awkward], will be so great for the good in the future life that there will be nothing they wish to know that they will not know. For they will know all the things that God has made to be known, both those belonging to the past and those that are to come in this age.

There each person will be known by all, and all by each; and no one at all will be ignorant of the homeland, nation, or lineage from which anyone was born, or of what he did in life.

Someone may perhaps say here: “What is this? Will everyone know the sins I committed? I confessed them so that they might be erased, forgotten, and no longer disclosed to anyone.”

Quite right. But when, in that glory, you stand present before the face of God, cleansed of every stain of crime, will you be able to be ungrateful to him for the great mercy he showed you, having remitted those sins and those offenses of yours [manuscripts: “having remitted those offenses of yours”; another manuscript: “having remitted also those offenses of yours”]? And how will you give thanks if you retain in your memory none of the things for which you ought rightly to give thanks?

Therefore, so that you may rejoice eternally in his praises, you will, I think, always have before you the remembrance of how great a misery you were rescued from. Since, then, the consciences of each will be open to each, I dare to say that those things will also be open to all for the healing of which you will continually give thanks to God—not for your confusion, but for the great glorification of God and for the shared rejoicing of others with you.

For then you will not be weighed down by greater anguish of heart on account of your sins, nor will you be more ashamed of your crimes, than a man once afflicted with great wounds, now healed in every respect, is weighed down by the distress of an illness that has been eliminated, or than a grown man is ashamed of what he did as an infant lying in the cradle [manuscripts: “as an infant placed on the road” rather than “as an infant lying in the cradle”].

For when complete health, perfect purity, full remission, and secure immunity from all offenses have certainly smiled upon you, knowledge of those sins will be able to cause you no more horror than the apostasy by which Peter, the most blessed prince of the apostles, denied Christ; than the enormity by which blessed Paul persecuted; than blessed Mary Magdalene’s sins; or than the many crimes of many others now known to have been forgiven [manuscript: quia Christum, “because [of] Christ,” rather than qua Christum, “by which [he denied] Christ”].

Indeed, once your offenses have been recognized as a monstrous and shameful illness, the piety, power, and wisdom of the physician who healed you will be admired, praised, and magnified all the more by everyone. And the praise and magnificence of God’s glory is, if you consider it well, your glory [manuscripts: “the praise and magnificence belong to God’s glory, and yours, if you consider it well”].

But you will say: “I certainly agree that the praise of God is my glory. Yet when so many others come forth, innocent in comparison with me, who, considering the obscenities of my life, will judge that I ought rightly to be regarded with horror, what shall I say? Justice demands its own reward, and injustice its own.”

Brother, do not fear in this matter; it will be otherwise than you imagine. You will not find there the one whom you judge to be entirely innocent, and who, as you suppose, will feel that way about you. For when the person of whom you speak sees you, he will clearly understand that when you sinned you offended not him but God.

Therefore, when he sees that God has entirely forgiven you the debt you owed him, it will not even enter his heart to judge you in any way. For he would recognize that he was offending God himself if he thought that you, reconciled to God in every respect, ought to be despised on account of what you once did.

Rather, he will gratefully admire God’s ineffable clemency, not only toward you but also toward himself: toward you, because God rescued you from so deep a pit of iniquity; toward himself, because by God’s grace alone he was held back from falling into that same depth [manuscripts: “if, having been abandoned by God, he had fallen in the same way, he perhaps would not have escaped so well” rather than “because by God’s grace alone he was held back from falling into that same depth”].

Thus, in praising God, he will magnify in you, after God’s grace, the strength and steadfastness by which, striving, you courageously escaped the abyss of so great an evil—a pit into which, as he himself will consider, he might perhaps not have escaped so well had he been abandoned by God and fallen into it in the same way.

You see, then, how the public knowledge of your sin will produce no reproach, but rather how much praise and thanksgiving the knowledge of its remission will generate.

Even the angels, if they wished to judge you unworthy of their fellowship because of your sins, would provide you with a lawful defense against them.

“How?” you ask. Listen. Imagine an angel reproaching you in words such as these:

“You are a human being made from dust; you are dust that will one day be dust. You exalted yourself against God, and, swollen with every sin and impurity, cast yourself into the mire against his commandments. And now you seek to be like us, whom you see never to have acted against God’s will in anything.”

You may answer him as follows:

“If, as you say, I was made from dust, perhaps it is not surprising that, driven by the wind of temptation, I slipped into the filth of crimes. But once I had recognized and believed in Christ’s mercy, I rejected everything that I could know he did not want and exercised myself in everything that I understood he did want.

“For his honor I did not hesitate to endure tribulations and anguish—hunger, thirst, vigils, beatings, insults, and countless other forms of suffering. And, considering every worldly thing worthless according to my strength, I desired to be reconciled in every respect solely by his grace.

“But what of you? What of these things have you ever endured for your own sake? Glory always accompanied you; delight always accompanied you; God’s right hand always held you and defended you from the assault of every sin, so that no stain of sin ever defiled you [manuscripts: “so that no stain could steal upon you”; manuscripts 62 and E. 10: “so that no stain could defile you”].

“Therefore, if you did not fall away from his will, this is his gift, since you were continually upheld by him.”

But since this argument concerns only those who did violence to their own destruction and seized the kingdom of heaven by force (Matthew 11:12), others who are in that kingdom but will enter it by another way will claim equality with the angels by another argument.

If you ask what that argument might be, perhaps it will be this. They will say to the angels:

“That we seek to be blessed in the kingdom of God with an equality to yours, we ascribe to the gift and grace of Christ Jesus our Lord, who deigned to become human, suffer, and die for this purpose: that, having justified us from every offense in his blood, he might make us sharers in his kingdom.

“Consider, then, whether the blood of Christ, which was poured out for us, can be for us the perfect cause of salvation.”

What would the angels say to this—angels who, because they are good, willingly wish to yield to reason—except that what has been said rests on reason, and that such human beings rightly ought to possess equality with them [manuscripts: “they willingly say” rather than “they willingly wish to yield”]?

When, therefore, the angels and those human beings whom you had judged more innocent than yourself agree with you, and in all matters defer to you in accordance with the truth of reason, consider, if you can, how pleasing that wisdom will be by which, in that life, you will thus know everyone and everyone will know you [manuscripts: “by which you will thus be known by everyone, and all will be known by you”].

[Col. 0596A]

# CHAPTER NINE  
## On Friendship

Will not an immeasurable friendship necessarily arise from this wisdom, which will be common to all, and which will so completely fill the inmost being of each toward every other with its own warmth that each person’s love will suffice for every other [manuscripts: “which will fill them only so greatly” rather than “which will so completely fill”; “the innermost being” rather than “the inmost being”; “their own warmth” rather than “its own warmth”]?

For I do not see how it could be otherwise, especially since all are one body in Christ, and Christ, who is peace itself, is the head of all [manuscripts: “since they are one” rather than “since all are one”; “peace of all” rather than “peace itself, is the head of all”]. Nor will they embrace one another with any lesser affection than the members of one body are joined to one another [manuscripts: “we may embrace” rather than “they will embrace”].

You will therefore love everyone as yourself, and everyone will love you as they love themselves [manuscripts: “as they love her” rather than “as they love themselves”].

Do you think that you will abound in love when you possess this? Yet pass beyond this and contemplate the one through whom these goods have come to you. You will perceive that he will love you incomparably more than you love yourself and more than all the others do; and you will love him with an ineffable sweetness beyond yourself and beyond all others.

[Col. 0596B]

# CHAPTER TEN  
## On Concord

But since it sometimes happens among human beings that those who love one another wholeheartedly do not agree in everything and everywhere—when one person sees something differently from another, and what one desires the other avoids—concord must necessarily be added to the love described above, lest, if it should be absent in any way, even for a moment, some injury creep into so great a good.

There will therefore be such concord among all that you will perceive no one disagreeing in anything with what you are established to desire. We shall be one body; we shall be one Church; we shall be the Bride of Christ, all of us who shall be there.

There will therefore be no greater discord among us then than now exists among the members of one body. But just as you see in the movement of the eyes that wherever one turns, the other immediately follows, so wherever your will turns, you will immediately have the will of everyone at your disposal, without dispute.

What did I say—of everyone? God’s will itself will not differ from yours. Just as you will desire whatever he desires, so he will desire in everything whatever you desire [Col. 0596D]. For how could the head disagree with its own body?

Here someone may perhaps ask secretly in his heart, saying:

“Come now! If God and that entire company of the blessed will desire what I desire, then they will also desire with me an increase of my good; and I shall be among the greatest in heaven, according to my desire, since I will not be able not to desire this there.”

I answer him: if he should even wish to be equal in glory to blessed Peter, he will be. I say “in glory,” because he will not be able to wish to be Peter in person. For if he wished this, he would wish himself not to exist—which he cannot wish.

Nor will he be able to wish to equal Peter in glory if he is unequal to him in merits, because he will love the splendid composition of Peter’s body more than any advantage to himself; and he would see that this composition was violated by such a change.

For in the human body neither does the foot wish to perform the function of the hand in the hand’s place, nor the hand that of the foot; nor does the mouth or nose wish to be where the eyes are, nor the eyes where the mouth or nose is; nor, if they were transferred, would they endure it patiently.

In the same way, in that marvelous and glorified arrangement of God’s blessed city, each person will love what he possesses in such a way that he will not wish his own position to be changed to a higher rank.

Why? Because each person’s own happiness and blessedness will be sufficient for him.

Moreover, if those who have already been placed in the unity of that body were to desire greater things than they have attained [manuscripts omit “also”], they would be miserable precisely because they did not yet possess what they desired [manuscripts: “because they desire what they do not yet have”]. For wherever anything desired is lacking to someone, there he must be miserable.

But may all misery be far from that kingdom. Therefore, complete sufficiency will be present for everyone, perfected in each person by unanimous and complete concord.

[Col. 0597B]

# CHAPTER ELEVEN  
## On Power

When, therefore, you have God and everyone in agreement with your will, you will certainly desire nothing that you cannot do. You will therefore be omnipotent with respect to your will [manuscripts: “your will will be omnipotent”], because you will have the Omnipotent One agreeing with your will in everything.

[Col. 0597C]

# CHAPTER TWELVE  
## On Honor

When such great power is present to you, fitting honor will certainly not be lacking to that power. Let us briefly consider what sort of honor it will be by means of an example [manuscripts: “by a brief example” rather than “briefly by means of an example”].

Imagine before our eyes some poor person, deprived of every comfort, disfigured by ulcers and other illnesses, and naked, without any covering to protect him even from the discomfort of cold. If some very powerful king, passing by, saw such a person lying in this condition, unable to help himself in any way; if, moved by pity, he ordered his wounds to be treated and the man to be clothed in the king’s own ornaments; if he brought him to himself and adopted him as a son; if he ordered everyone in his kingdom to regard him as his son and no one to oppose anything he commanded; if he appointed him his heir and a co-heir with his own son; and if he ordered him to be called by his own name—would you not say that this man had been greatly honored? [manuscripts: “would you not be called” rather than “would you not say”]

Certainly God will do all these things for us. Born from the corruption of flesh, we are filled with many miseries (Job 14:1). While we are established in these miseries, deprived of every comfort, subject to the sufferings of every illness, and full of the ulcers of sin and corruption, he, moved solely by mercy, will receive us and heal us [manuscripts: “and will help us” rather than “and will heal us”]. When restored to health, he will adorn us with the ornaments of perfect righteousness and incorruptibility; he will adopt us as sons when we have been brought to him; he will make us sharers and heirs of his kingdom; and he will establish us as members of the body and co-heirs with his only-begotten Son, equal to him in every respect and co-omnipotent.

He will command every creature to obey us in everything we desire [manuscripts: “in everything we desire” rather than “in everything we may desire”]. He will call us by his own name and make us gods. For he himself says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 82:6; John 10:34).

But God himself is the one who deifies; you, however, will be a deified god.

Perhaps you will say: “Your argument may indeed prove valid in the case of those great apostles or martyrs; but how it could hold true for me, who—if only I might deserve to be the very last—I do not understand.”

Pay attention and understand: God excluded no righteous person from this divinity when he said: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

But so that these words may become clearer, consider by means of an example the nature of fire and the nature of things set on fire, if perhaps you may thereby imagine to some extent how you can be deified, according to your capacity, by participating in that supreme divinity.

There is one fire, hot in its own nature. Place in this fire, all at once, some wood, lead, and iron. When the wood has been turned into coals and the lead has melted, so that nothing but fire appears in the coals and no more heat can be added to the lead, the iron nevertheless will not yet be able to equal them in heat, because perhaps it has not yet become thoroughly glowing with fire.

Although one thing has advanced further than another in heat, each, while retaining its own nature, is nevertheless, in the ordinary manner of speaking, called fire in itself because it has been set on fire.

So it will be in that blessed fellowship of the citizens above of which we are speaking. Just as those who are nearer to the supreme majesty of God, and therefore superior to others, will be called gods, so those who are lower than them will also be called gods, because they participate according to their capacity in the one and same divinity in which the others participate [manuscripts: “in the divinity by which they themselves participate” rather than “in the one and same divinity in which the others participate”].

When, therefore, you have attained this honor together with so great a good, I do not see how you could desire anything greater.

Therefore, when you are happy in possessing the goods we have set out, will you not seem sufficient to yourself?

“Most certainly,” you say.

Come, then: if you could enjoy all these things in reality for even one day, just as they have been described, would you rejoice?

Without a doubt [manuscripts: “Would you rejoice? Without a doubt”].

But if for one month or one year, would you be made glad? I think that the measure of your joy could not even be expressed.

And if for the whole duration of your life, what would you do? You would willingly give whatever you had as a reward [manuscript: “as the price” rather than “as the reward”], and even yourself, if you could attain these things in that way and no other.

[Col. 0599A]

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN  
## On Security

But if, in addition to all this, you were entirely secure that you would not lose these things through any event while you lived, I will not even ask whether you could imagine what your exultation would be.

Since your life will endure forever in that life, and since, possessing all these things, you will also enjoy the security of certainly never losing them, I ask you: what do you think your state will be? I believe that even at the mere mention of security a certain rejoicing of heart has stirred within you, and that you eagerly desire to learn whether you will possess such great goods securely and forever.

I say, then, that if you are going to lose them, either you yourself will willingly wish to lose them, or God will take them from you against your will, or someone else, stronger than God, will come and take them away, though neither God nor you desire it [manuscripts: “though neither God nor you desire it” rather than “though both God and you desire it”].

But surely you will not wish, having cast away so great a good, to fall back into the miseries from which you will gratefully rejoice to have escaped. Nor will God, who gave it to you with such abundant and merciful goodness, ever wish to take it away from you. Nor will anyone stronger than God come who, while God protects you, could in any way take it from you against your will.

You will therefore be secure forever in possessing such great goods [manuscripts: “you will be secure in possessing it forever”], and you will fear no attack from anyone who wishes to oppose you.

What, then, do you think your state will be when you possess forever all these things—beauty, swiftness, pleasure, the duration of life, strength, freedom, health, wisdom, friendship, concord, power, honor, and security—in the manner in which we have described them, indeed more gloriously and sublimely than any human estimation can conceive, and in a way more exalted than can be written or spoken?

Will there not be joy, which will be the consummation of all these things? For, truly, I cannot see how immeasurable joy could fail to surround the person whom so many advantages of blessed happiness and happy blessedness surround without end [manuscripts: “surrounds” rather than “surround”].

Then you too will enjoy this joy, because you will possess nothing from which you ought not to rejoice.

[Col. 0599C]

# CHAPTER FOURTEEN  
## On Joy
Therefore, if you had someone whom you loved utterly as yourself, and whose good you rejoiced in altogether as in your own [Note: *Omnino penitus* (“altogether utterly”); the manuscripts omit *penitus*], and if you saw him supported in every respect by a happiness no less than yours, would you not have your joy doubled in his joy? But if you possessed two, or three, or more who were your equals in love, and saw them distinguished by equal happiness [Note: The manuscripts read: “or three, or more, possessing those equal to himself in love, and …”], would not the magnitude of your joy be multiplied within you in proportion to their number? Indeed, when we were discussing friendship above, we showed that all the citizens of that homeland will love you as they will love themselves, and you will love them [Col. 0600A] as you love yourself. Can the measure of that joy, then, be grasped by any human being [Note: The manuscripts read *a quoquam homine* (“by any human being”), rather than *a quodam homine*]?—when there are there more than a thousand times a thousand and ten times a hundred thousand innumerable people, all enjoying the same blessedness, and not one of them rejoicing in another’s good any less than in his own? Moreover, seeing that God himself loves them beyond the measure in which they themselves will love themselves, and understanding that they love him indescribably more than themselves, they will exult in his glory with wondrous and ineffable rejoicing. Thus there will be joy for them within and without, joy above and below, joy all around and everywhere; and this, as we think, is what God has prepared for those who love him, as I said at the beginning of this little work. This, then, according to what my present judgment [Col. 0600B] tells me, may in some fashion be called that eternal blessedness, that eternal happiness [Note: The manuscripts read “how it may be called,” rather than “may in some fashion be called”]—namely, the sufficiency of all goods according to the will and without any want—which all the friends of God will fully possess in eternal life. For we do not wish to affirm that it is not far greater than the blessedness we have described [Note: The manuscripts read *at quam* (“but greater than that”), rather than *hac quam* (“than this which”)].

[Col. 0600B]

## CHAPTER XV. On the misery of the reprobate

Since, then, the just will be blessed with such great happiness, it remains that the unjust, by contrast, will be miserable with a certain immeasurable unhappiness. For just as the former, according to what we have described as best we could with God’s help, will be made joyful and exultant by wondrous beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, and pleasure [Note: The manuscripts read *sicut enim justos* (“just as the just”), rather than *sicut enim istos* (“just as these”)], so the latter will be made sorrowful and wailing by a certain monstrous and immeasurable ugliness, slowness, weakness, servitude, sickness, and pain [Col. 0600C]. Indeed, the length of life, which the former will embrace with the greatest love in order to enjoy such great goods, the latter will curse with the greatest hatred because it will be theirs for the endless punishment by which they will be tormented [Note: One manuscript reads *summo odio exurabunt*; the printed reading is *summo odio exsecrabuntur* (“they will curse with the greatest hatred”)]. What shall I say about wisdom? I find nothing to say except that, just as for the just whatever they know will be turned into joy and honor, so for the unjust it will be turned into sorrow and confusion. As for the friendship by which the devout will be joined to one another in the greatest delight, if there is any such friendship among the impious, it will be a torment to them [Note: The manuscripts read *in tormentis* (“in torments”), rather than *in tormentum* (“into a torment”)]. For the more they love each other, the more grievously they will suffer over one another’s punishment. If it is asked whether they will possess concord, they will have discord with every creature, and every creature will be at odds with the others [Col. 0600D]. Thus, in place of the power of the good, such powerlessness will follow them [Note: The manuscripts read *tanta impotentia ejus sequetur* (“such powerlessness will follow him”), rather than *tanta impotentia eos sequetur* (“will follow them”)], that they will be utterly unable to do anything they wish, and will not wish for whatever they possess. Therefore, in place of the honor of the saints, they will obtain perpetual disgrace. And with what end will these things be closed [Note: The manuscripts read *et haec quoque sive claudentur* (“and whether these things too will be closed”), rather than *et haec quo fine claudentur* (“and with what end these things will be closed”)]? Truly, just as the friends of God will be secure that they will never lose their goods, so these enemies of God will utterly despair of ever again losing these evils of theirs. In place, therefore, of the eternal and ineffable joy of the blessed, all who, because of their impenitent guilt, are destined to pass into the fellowship of demons will inherit eternal and inconceivable sorrow. [Note: In manuscripts EE. 10 and S. 62, more follows, which has hitherto been unpublished.]

When these matters have been considered and examined, it can be understood how useful it is for a person to exercise his life in good morals and righteous works, and how harmful it is, when these are neglected, to overflow with vices and iniquities.

If we consider the matter more broadly—namely, how useful it is for any human being to be good—we shall see that it is useful not only to the one who is good, but also to God himself, to the angels, to every just person, and, moreover, to every creature. A good person is said to be useful to God—not because anything beneficial or harmful can happen to God’s person, but because he assists in completing God’s city, which God has established to be completed from good people, with the zeal by which he strives toward it. Human practice indeed has this feature: a person judges someone useful to him when that person helps him toward something without which he does not wish to accomplish what he rightly desires.

How a good person is also useful to the angels is recognized from the fact that, through the fellowship of good people, the number of the angels, which had been diminished, is restored. When someone therefore runs into their fellowship through a good life, he renders them a great service [Col. 0601C], because, insofar as it depends on him, he fills out and completes their number. We have likewise said that a just person is useful to every just person and to every creature. He is useful to a just person because the more ardently he strives toward the heavenly homeland, the more swiftly that homeland will be completed in its citizens; and when each person has obtained the resurrection of his body, which he greatly desires, he will enjoy doubled joy and honor in the kingdom of God. He is useful to every creature because, while the city of God rises through his goodness, he no longer delays the renewal by which creation itself is to be changed for the better; rather, insofar as it concerns him, he breaks and removes every delay to its perfection.

Let anyone who can consider how earnestly each person must strive to be good [Col. 0601D], since both the completion of the heavenly kingdom and the universal restoration predestined for the whole creation depend upon human goodness. None of these things will be completed in every respect until the number of the elect has been fulfilled. Therefore, the more rarely those who are worthy of eternal life are found, the longer this good will be delayed.

To every individual who reaches the kingdom of God, God himself, as well as the angels and just people, will be gracious because he has shown himself to be such that he will reach that place; and they will unanimously wish all their goods to be his [Col. 0602A], loving him forever as a fellow heir and fellow participant in the heavenly kingdom, as though he were themselves. For, insofar as it depended on him, he has completed the city of God, the number of the angels, and the holy people. But since those who attain eternal life deserve so much, it is clear, by contrast, what wicked people deserve, since by their own merit they become exiles from the kingdom of God. For as far as they are concerned, neither the city of God, nor the multitude of the angels, nor the predetermined fullness of the elect will advance toward completion; indeed, although they were created for the perfection of these things, they do not strive to attain it and, by their deeds, work toward its never being completed.

Therefore, just as any person grieves and complains when he in some way loses what he acquired for his own advantage [Col. 0602B], so God in some way grieves and complains when he sees the devil snatching away the human being whom he had created for his work and causing him to perish eternally for himself. For this reason, those who are condemned are also called “lost,” because they perish, having been hurled by the devil into eternal confusion, away from God, for whose kingdom and honor they were created.

Behold, in some fashion, the blessedness of perpetual life and, conversely, the misery of eternal death have been set before us. Therefore, in order that the latter may be escaped and the former acquired, one must labor all the more because this misery torments the wicked with interminable punishment, while that blessedness delights the good with unfailing joy.

Let the person who is good persevere until he receives the rewards of blessedness owed to him; but let the person who is evil cease to be what he is, so that he may be able to escape the misery he deserves [Col. 0602C]. Goodness, because it is light, plainly instructs the person in whom it dwells how to walk so as to reach life; but wickedness, because it is darkness, blinds the person intoxicated by it, so that he does not see where he is rushing and may perish. But suppose there is someone who is perhaps evil, who is ashamed of being what he is and says that he wishes to become good. He must first of all understand that he is evil—that is, a sinner—and therefore enveloped in darkness, so that he may see himself where he was lying. For there are many so wrapped in the dense darkness of sins that they are unable by any means to notice that they are even in darkness.

It is therefore established as the first and great good that a person can understand in what condition or fall he remains [Col. 0602D]. For insofar as he understands himself, he approaches the light. When, then, he understands that he is evil, if he wishes to become good he must grieve that he is evil. Otherwise he falsely says that he wishes to be other than he is.

To the knowledge by which he knows himself, therefore, pain must necessarily be added, as Scripture says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). But if he wishes to apply a remedy to the pain he feels, it is fitting that he disclose it to one whom he knows understands it and is able to heal it. For a wound that has already festered and gathered within itself a dreadful poison from its putrefaction cannot be freed from pain, nor can it be healed in any way, until it is opened [Col. 0603A] and the corrupt fluid is squeezed out. Thus, the person who grieves over the wound of sin inflicted upon him should expose it through true confession and, after the deadly fluid that lay hidden has been expelled, take the medicine of repentance, following the counsel of his superior, so that he may be healed. Let him not fear human tongues; let him not conceal the practice of repentance. Rather, let him firmly hold this in his mind: if he did not fear that scandal concerning his sin might thereby creep in among others, he would make himself known to everyone as he sees himself to be in the sight of God whom he has offended. This contributes greatly to a worthy fruit of repentance: a person grieves over his sin, by which he offended God, so much that he does not shrink from being known by other people as he recognizes himself to be in the eyes of his Creator. [Col. 0603B] Although this must not be permitted in deed, lest any scandal thereby arise in the Church of God, nevertheless a person should neither deny nor be disturbed if others accuse him of what he himself voluntarily confesses about himself. For there are many who are deeply disturbed when others say about them what they themselves do not shrink from publicly confessing about themselves. It therefore belongs to a great height of perfection when someone can patiently and with undisturbed tranquility of mind endure having the evil he proclaims about himself spoken against him by others.
