For by this it can be proved that he stands at the true level of humility, just as, conversely, the person who cannot endure it has a mind possessed by a certain boastfulness and desire for eminence. The just person, indeed, wishes to be regarded as just. For it is written: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning” (Proverbs 18:17).

When, then, he accuses himself but refuses to be accused of that same thing by others, what else is he seeking except to show himself humble, while showing others to be marked by falsehood or hatred?

If, therefore, he wishes to reach the height of true humility, he must consent patiently to hear from others what he himself does not fear to utter openly and willingly about himself, and he must allow himself to be tested as he confesses himself to be worthy of being tested.

When a person has reached this state of humility, then, if he turns the eyes of his heart back upon his former way of life, he will truly see that he had been in dreadful evil and darkness, and, gratefully, with ineffable joy and exultation, he will marvel that he is now in great goodness and light [Col. 0603D].

Let him therefore guard his heart; let him guard his body, lest his enemies steal from him what he has acquired through God’s grace and cast him, guilty, back into the former darkness that he left. Let him attribute none of the virtues he has acquired to his own strength, nor in any way exalt himself over those who have not yet advanced to this point.

At the summit of humility to which he has arrived, let him always guard himself carefully, and believe—not falsely, but with his inmost heart—that he is lower than all human beings. “But,” you say, “how can anyone do this—believe himself more worthless than someone whom it is undoubtedly clear is inferior not only to himself but also to others in good actions?” For example, you may see someone who is sober, humble, patient [Col. 0604A], generous toward those in need, diligent in God’s service, kindly doing for others what he wishes done for himself, and many other things of this kind; and yet this person will judge himself more worthless than any person who is luxurious, proud, injurious, predatory, avoiding God’s service as much as he can or dares, and striving as far as possible to do the opposite of these things to others. It must be so; it is necessary. Otherwise, by exceeding the limits of humility set by the divine Scriptures, he does not obey. Nor should anyone think that Holy Scripture commands anyone to judge something impossible to do.

Since it is written, then, that each person should not only declare with his mouth that he is more worthless than everyone else, but also believe this with the inmost affection of his heart, consider how this can be fulfilled, and strive to understand whose mind the divine Spirit has touched so that he may wish to exercise himself in such a practice [Col. 0604B]. For it is difficult, while living a good and holy life, to judge oneself from the inmost heart inferior to a person of perverse heart and conduct, when both natural and divine law decree that the good is always superior to the evil, and that an eternal reward of glory is prepared for the one, while a punishment of everlasting disgrace is prepared for the other. From the result of the reward of each, therefore, it is clear what is superior to what. If the good person judges himself inferior to the evil, he makes the evil superior to himself in an inverted order. Nature does not admit that this is true. Either, then, the person who believes himself inferior to the evil is opposed to the truth, or, if he does not believe it, he will be disobedient to the divine Scriptures, which command this. Neither alternative is acceptable.

[Col. 0604C]

We must therefore see how it can be done so that neither truth is abandoned nor the divine command disobeyed. Whenever anyone wishes to compare himself with another, let him consider what he has from himself and what the other has not from himself but through God’s grace. From himself no one has anything except evil; through God’s grace, he has whatever good he has. Let him therefore set his own evil alongside the other person’s evil, and he will immediately see which of the two is superior. Let him also consider carefully that everything is preserved together for the future, and let him be aware that perhaps he himself may fall from goodness by God’s hidden judgment, while the other may rise from evil.

Whoever, then, diligently examines himself by such consideration will certainly not retain in his mind any basis for magnifying himself above others. And the more closely he clings to God, the more he will think humbly of himself, despise no one, and strive under God to obtain the true love of all.

I have written these things as I received them from the mouth of the blessed Father Anselm, wishing to satisfy the will of my friend, who earnestly begged me to do this. To him I also sent the letter that I did not omit to place at the beginning of this little work, taking care that no one, observing the beauty of the subject matter and the ugliness of the style, should think it strange that Anselm composed it with such beauty of subject matter, while the meanness of the style caused the clarity of his mind and the elegance of his speech to vanish.

Nevertheless, let anyone who deigns to pass this work into his own knowledge know that the Father himself often read and heard it, and, having examined it with his own holy hand and authority, commended it to posterity for transcription and reading. Therefore, may God be blessed in all things. Amen.

[Col. 605A]

# EADMER THE MONK’S BOOK ON THE SIMILITUDES OF SAINT ANSELM [Note: This was collated with the manuscripts Gem., Bec., Corb. 307, Victorinus EE. 13, and San-Germanensis A. 1, which I myself noted, and with the Cologne edition of 1573. The Victorinus manuscript begins: “The book of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Similitudes.” The Corbie manuscript begins: “The treatise of Saint Anselm on the Similitudes.” The Saint-Germain manuscript begins: “The treatise composed by the venerable Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the Threefold Will.” In that manuscript this treatise is not divided into chapters.] (G)*

## CHAPTER I. On the threefold will [Note: The manuscripts read “On the division of the will,” rather than “On the threefold will.”]

The will is understood in three ways [Note: The Saint-Germain manuscript reads: “The will is understood in three ways. For will is called …”]. For “will” means the instrument of the soul by which it wills, and the affection of that same instrument of willing. This will, which is called an affection [Note: The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “which is an affection,” rather than “which is called an affection”], is for a time as though asleep, because it concerns things which the mind does not remember; but as soon as the mind recalls them, the instrument of willing also desires them. Furthermore, “will” means willing, or the use of that instrument.

[Col. 0605B]

## CHAPTER II. The likeness between a woman and the will

The will, then, which is the instrument of willing, is related to God and the devil as a woman is related to her lawful husband and to an adulterer. The husband commands her to be joined to him alone [Note: The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “For the husband commands her,” rather than “The husband commands her”]; the adulterer, however, persuades her to be united to him as well [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads “to be united to him,” rather than “to be united to him as well”]. If, therefore, she joins herself to her lawful husband alone, she is a lawful wife and bears legitimate children [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads “she is lawful, and she bears children,” rather than “she is a lawful wife and bears legitimate children”]; but if she joins herself to the adulterer, she is an adulteress and bears adulterine children [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads “she is an adulteress, and she herself bears children,” rather than “and bears adulterine children”].

Similarly, therefore, God commands the will to be joined to him alone [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads “to be joined to himself alone,” rather than “to be joined to him alone”]; but the devil, on the other hand, suggests that it should be joined to him as well. If, then, it joins itself to God alone—that is, if it receives the prompting of the Holy Spirit like good seed—it becomes his lawful spouse and bears legitimate children, that is, virtues and good works [Col. 0605C]. At once, in obedience to its command, all the senses of soul and body are opened to fulfill what God commands [Note: The Victorinus and A.1 manuscripts read “what God commanded,” rather than “what God commands”].

## CHAPTER III. On the senses of the soul

The will itself is opened to affection for the virtues [Note: A.1 reads “the will itself is also opened to affection for the virtues”; Corbie reads “the will itself is also opened, and the will to affection for the virtues”], and to willing what ought to be desired [Note: The Corbie manuscript adds “and is raised up”]; the memory, to remembering what ought to be remembered; thought, to thinking what ought to be thought; the intellect, to discerning what ought to be willed, remembered, or thought. The mind is also raised toward charity [Note: Manuscripts A.1, Bec, and Gemmet read “is directed toward charity,” rather than “is raised toward charity”], disposed toward humility, strengthened for patience, and opened to generate other virtues.

## CHAPTER IV. On the senses of the body

Similarly, the bodily senses are opened at its command [Col. 0606B]: sight, for seeing [Note: The manuscripts read “for living rightly” or “for living,” rather than “for seeing”]; hearing, for hearing God’s words; taste, for tasting; smell (*odoratus*), for smelling; touch, for touching; olfaction (*olfactus*), for smelling; the eyes also, for watching and weeping; the mouth, for speaking well; the hands, for acting rightly; the feet, for walking where they ought. Thus one will alone, after it has been joined to God’s will, generates so many virtues and good works.

## CHAPTER V. On obedience

The affection or use of this will is called an obedient will, or obedience, because, being obedient to God’s will, it has that will as its advocate if someone asks [Note: A.1 reads “if it is required,” rather than “if it is asked”] why it wills this or that. But if this will, which is called the instrument of willing, joins itself to the devil [Col. 0606C], receiving his suggestion like disordered seed, it becomes an adulterous mother and bears adulterine children, that is, vices and evil works [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads “receiving it,” rather than “receiving his suggestion”]. For, closing all the senses of the human being to what God commands [Note: The Victorinus and A.1 manuscripts read “to what God commanded,” rather than “to what God commands”], it opens them to what the devil orders. It is first opened to affection for vices and to willing them, and then it opens the human senses to perpetrating them.

## CHAPTER VI. On disobedience and self-will

The affection or use of this will is called a disobedient will, or disobedience, or also self-will [Note: The manuscripts read “or self-will,” rather than “or also self-will”]. Self-will is that which cannot have God’s will as its advocate, so that, if someone asks [Note: A.1 reads “if it is required”] why it wills this or that, it cannot truthfully answer, “Because God also wills that it should will this.” But the affection or use of the will arising from a diabolical suggestion cannot have God’s will as its advocate [Note: The manuscripts read “cannot have it,” rather than “cannot have it as its advocate”]. Both wills, therefore, are undoubtedly self-will; because they are deprived of God’s will, they are rightly called self-will for this reason [Note: The manuscripts read “Self-will: because it is deprived…”]. This self-will is pride, which Scripture calls the beginning of every sin [Note: The manuscripts of Bec., Gem., and A.1 read “which Scripture announces,” rather than “which Scripture calls”].

## CHAPTER VII. On pride

It is called pride because it walks above what it ought to. For pride means transgression or overstepping. Self-will, therefore, because it is not subject to God’s will but exalts itself above it, is rightly called pride. It is also the beginning of every sin, because every sin arises from it. And because a person has it from himself and does not wish to have above him another will—God’s will—to follow, he takes away from God what God properly and uniquely ought to have.

## CHAPTER VIII. That self-will belongs to God alone

God alone ought to will whatever he wills by his own will, so that he has no other will above him to follow. When, therefore, a human being wills something by self-will, he takes from God, as it were, his crown [Col. 0607C]. For just as a crown belongs only to a king, so self-will belongs only to God. And just as someone would dishonor a king by taking his crown from him, so a human being dishonors God by taking away the privilege of self-will from him and possessing what God alone ought to possess. But just as God’s self-will is the fountain and origin of every good, so human self-will is the beginning of every evil.

## CHAPTER IX. The likeness between self-will and a fountain

For self-will is like a certain fountain divided into three heads, from which diverse and innumerable streams flow; in some places they are separated from one another, but in others two and two, or several, are joined to several [Col. 0607D] [Note: The manuscripts read “from which, however,” rather than “but in others”]. In the same way, self-will is divided into three kinds, from which diverse and numberless vices arise; sometimes they are separated in a person, but at other times two or more are joined together [Note: The manuscripts read “so that there are more,” rather than “or more are joined together”].

## CHAPTER X. On the three kinds of self-will

Self-will is either in pleasure, or in exaltation, or in curiosity.

## CHAPTER XI. On pleasure

There are two principal kinds of pleasure: one external, in the five bodily senses; the other internal, in the affections of the soul [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “kinds of pleasure,” rather than “kinds of pleasures”].

## CHAPTER XII. On the five bodily senses

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. They are called senses because through them external things are perceived. Through sight they perceive forms and colors; through hearing, sounds; through taste, flavors; through smell, odors; through touch, hard or soft, hot or cold, rough or smooth [Note: The manuscripts read “rough and smooth,” rather than “rough or smooth”], heavy or light things. The pleasure of these senses is rarely good [Note: A.1 reads “more rarely good,” rather than “rarely good”], but more often evil. It is good when it has God’s will as its advocate; it is evil when it cannot have God’s will as its advocate.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the kinds of evil pleasure

There are thirty-one kinds of this evil pleasure: five are simple, ten double, ten triple, another five quadruple [Col. 0608C], and one consists of all five parts.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the five simple kinds

There are five simple kinds because each of the five senses usually takes pleasure by itself. Sometimes sight alone takes empty pleasure, as when one watches horses running in competition [Note: A.1 omits “and contemplating”] or hawks flying and catching other birds [Note: A.1 reads “running together in competition,” rather than “running in competition”]. Sometimes hearing alone does so, as when a person takes pleasure in striking a bell [*nola*] beside his ear for a long time [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads “a small bell or *nola* for a long time,” rather than “a bell for a long time”], listening to its sweet sound. Sometimes taste alone does so, as in eating honey immoderately, though without taking pleasure in its appearance. Sometimes smell alone does so, as when someone carries fennel suspended before his nostrils so that it may smell sweet to him [Note: The manuscripts read “suspended from his ears,” rather than “suspended before his nostrils”]. Sometimes touch alone does so [Note: The manuscripts read “traction alone,” rather than “touch alone”], as when it delights someone who has eaten to excess to handle his own belly [Note: The manuscripts read “delights the belly,” rather than “delights someone to handle his own belly”] [Col. 0608D].

## CHAPTER XV. On the ten double kinds

There are ten double kinds because usually two senses, and the same two senses, take pleasure together [Note: The manuscripts read “two—that is, the senses,” and the Victorinus manuscript reads “two senses are together”]. Sometimes sight and hearing take pleasure together, as when someone takes excessive pleasure in seeing dogs pursue wild beasts and hearing them shout after them [Note: A.1 reads “and shout,” rather than “and hear them shouting”]. Sometimes sight and taste do so, as when one gazes with great pleasure at very clear wine in a sapphire-colored cup and drinks it. Sometimes sight and smell do so, as when one excessively looks at and smells very red roses. Sometimes sight and touch do so, as when one looks at and smooths a white mouse [*muriceps*]. Sometimes hearing and taste do so, as when someone takes pleasure in drinking in such a way that he makes a certain sound between his lips by sipping [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads “by striking,” rather than “by sipping”]. Sometimes hearing and smell do so, as when, from eagerness to drink, someone takes pleasure in listening with his ear held near fermenting must and drawing its odor into his nostrils. Sometimes hearing and touch do so, as when someone takes excessive pleasure in hearing a lyre resounding and touching it by striking it [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “hearing a lyre,” rather than “hearing and touching”]. Sometimes taste and smell do so, as when hens carefully seasoned with pepper and cumin are eaten immoderately. Sometimes taste and touch do so, as when ripe figs, sweet to eat and soft and smooth to touch, are devoured with gluttony. Sometimes smell and touch do so, as when someone is anointed with a fragrant ointment.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the ten triple kinds

There are also ten triple kinds, because the bodily senses mentioned above often take pleasure three at a time. Sometimes sight, hearing, and taste take pleasure together [Col. 0609C], as when wafers or pastries [*collyridae*], which appear white as snow, are eaten with excessive eagerness and are rubbed by the hands or teeth so that they can be heard to sound. Sometimes sight, hearing, and smell do so, as when someone sits in a garden in such a way that he looks at green grass, listens to stories, and smells flowers. Sometimes sight, hearing, and touch do so, as when a beautiful woman is looked at for the sake of pleasure, heard speaking lustfully, and meanwhile touched. Sometimes sight, taste, and smell do so, as when someone takes pleasure in looking at wine made with herbs sparkling, drinking it, and smelling it [Note: The manuscripts read “they delight someone,” rather than “someone takes pleasure”]. Sometimes sight, taste, and touch do so, as when someone, though filled with grapes, walks through a vineyard so that he may see how beautifully the bunches hang there, and, touching some bunches or others, tastes them [Note: A.1 reads “although the vineyard,” rather than “although the vineyard nevertheless”]. Sometimes sight, smell, and touch do so, as when someone for a long time looks at, smells, and touches lilies. Sometimes hearing, taste, and smell do so, as when the rich take pleasure in hearing deer calling in the forest and meanwhile eating the flesh of some already captured deer, seasoned with pepper. Sometimes hearing, taste, and touch do so, as when someone sitting in a bath listens to stories, eats and drinks, and touches the warmth of the water all around [Note: One manuscript reads “and the warmth of the water,” rather than “and touches the warmth of the water”]. Sometimes hearing, smell, and touch do so, as when someone listens to songs while resting on a soft bed, where he also smells herbs scattered everywhere. Sometimes taste, smell, and touch do so, as when, at night, tasty, fragrant, and soft apples are eaten immoderately.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the five quadruple kinds

There are five quadruple kinds because usually four senses at a time take pleasure together [Note: A.1 reads “usually four at a time take pleasure together,” rather than “usually four senses and four senses take pleasure together”]. Sometimes sight, taste, hearing, and smell take pleasure together, as when at weddings games are watched, songs are heard [Col. 00610B], delicious food and drink are consumed, and their odor is perceived. Sometimes hearing, taste, smell, and touch do so, as when at night nothing is seen there in which sight can take pleasure, but hearing, taste, smell, and touch take pleasure—for example, when a bridegroom embraces his bride or one person is touched lustfully by another [Note: A.1 reads “touch takes pleasure in smell,” rather than “smell and touch take pleasure”]. Sometimes taste, smell, touch, and sight do so, as when nothing pleasing to hearing is heard there, but other things are present in which the remaining senses each take pleasure in their own way [Note: The manuscripts read “each takes pleasure in its own way,” rather than “each take pleasure in their own way”]. Sometimes smell, touch, sight, and hearing do so, as when nothing is tasted there, but guests take pleasure in smelling, touching, and looking at flowers scattered about, and in listening to various musical sounds [Note: A.1 reads “of various musicians,” rather than “various musical sounds”]. Sometimes touch, sight, hearing, and taste do so, as when there is nothing by which smell may take pleasure, but there are things in which the other four senses take pleasure together [Note: A.1 reads “the senses take pleasure”; the Cologne edition of 1573 reads “the senses are delighted,” rather than “take pleasure together”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the final kind of evil pleasure

One kind consists of all five parts, because at times all these bodily senses take pleasure together [Note: The manuscripts read “all the senses of the bodies,” rather than “all these bodily senses”]. Sometimes it delights a person to look at a house decorated inside, to hear drunken people singing in it, to drink wine there from gilded horns [Note: One manuscript reads “wine from horns,” rather than “wine from gilded horns”], to smell flowers scattered throughout the house [Note: The manuscripts read “scattered about,” rather than “scattered throughout the house”], and to handle the flowers themselves, the golden horns, or other things pleasing to touch. Thus there are thirty-one kinds of pleasure belonging to the five bodily senses; these [Note: The manuscripts read *quia his* (“because by these”), rather than *qua his* (“by which these”)] are enjoyed in thirty-one ways. Of these, the double kinds are worse than the simple, the triple than the double, the quadruple than the triple, and that which consists of five parts is worse than the quadruple. For the more senses are joined in a pleasure, the worse that pleasure becomes. [Col. 0611A] Nevertheless, at times the pleasure of one sense is worse than the pleasure of all the senses together.

## CHAPTER XIX. Pleasure is worse when it delights more senses or graver ones.

For it is more serious to listen willingly to slander than to look at, touch, and smell beautiful flowers; meanwhile to drink once or twice more than is necessary; and to hear some idle word. But in equal or similar sins, it is worse when more senses take delight than fewer. For it is worse to take delight through sight and hearing in a shameful object than through sight alone or hearing alone. Likewise, it is worse to take immoderate delight through taste and smell in a prepared drink than through taste alone or smell alone in some delicious food. Thus, of these thirty-one kinds of delight, some are bad and others worse. The bad are those in which fewer senses take delight, or, if more are involved, they take pleasure in lesser matters. The worse are those in which more senses take delight, or, if fewer are involved, they take delight in more serious matters. Such, then, and so numerous, are the kinds of delight in which the five bodily senses take pleasure.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Delight of the Soul

The kinds of that delight in which the soul takes pleasure are far more numerous. For whatever the external senses perceive, by perceiving they indicate to the soul what the thing they perceive is like. Thus, when they have represented to themselves the quality of the thing and have ceased to perceive what they had perceived, it delights the soul to think about the same thing, and in as many ways as the senses represented it to the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *ut cum qualitatem* (“thus, when [they have represented] the quality”); manuscript A.1 reads *ut quae qualitatem* (“thus, what quality”); another reading is *utique qualitatem* (“indeed the quality”).]

[Note: [Col. 0611D] *Cogitare: totidem*: Victorius, A.1, and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *cogitare et totidem* (“to think, and in as many [ways]”).]

[Note: [Col. 0611D] *Repraesentavere*: manuscript A.1 reads *repraesentare* (“to represent”).]

For just as it delights the individual senses, or two, or three, or four, or all of them together, to perceive this or that and represent it to the soul, so it delights the soul to think that the senses perceived this or that in the same ways and, by perceiving, represented it to the soul. The soul is also delighted to think about what the senses have never represented to it because they have never perceived it, but which, had they perceived it, they would have been able to represent.

The soul is delighted to think in as many ways as the senses would have been able to represent the thing to it. For sight has never represented to it an entire golden house, because it has not seen one; nor hearing a sound spread throughout the whole world, because it has not heard one; nor taste bread sweeter than honey, because it has not tasted it; nor smell wine more fragrant than balsam, because it has not smelled it; nor touch woolen garments softer than linen, because it has not touched them.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *Nolfacit* (“does not smell”) for *non olfecit* (“has not smelled”).] Nor have the senses represented many other things to it, because they have not perceived them; but if they had perceived them, they could have represented them. And yet it delights the soul to imagine these or other such empty things as if the senses had perceived them and had represented them to it individually, in pairs, in threes,

[Col. 0612A]

in fours, or all together.

There are also other kinds of the soul’s delight which the senses cannot represent to it, nor can the soul itself think of them through imagination—for example, when it takes pleasure in pride, without any imagination. The senses cannot represent this to it, since sight cannot discern whether it is white or black; hearing, whether it is resonant or hoarse; taste, whether it is sweet or bitter; smell, whether it is fragrant or foul; or touch, whether it is soft or hard, smooth or rough, hot or cold.

The soul itself also cannot imagine whether that pride is of one kind or another, because it consists solely in the elevation of thought. There are therefore far more kinds of delight in which the soul takes pleasure than of that in which the five bodily senses take pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *illius quinque . . . delectantur* (“than that in which the five . . . take delight”) for *illius qua quinque . . . oblectantur* (“than that in which the five . . . are delighted”).]

[Col. 0612B]

For the soul is delighted both to remember what the senses perceived, and in as many ways as they represented it to themselves;

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Manuscript A.1 reads *et eandem delectat illam* (“and the same thing delights it”) for *et eamdem delectat illa* (“and that thing delights it”).]

to imagine other things which the senses did not represent to it because they never perceived them, but which, had they perceived them, they could have represented;

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Manuscript A.1 reads *quae illos sentire* (“which [delights] them to perceive”) for *quae et illos sentire* (“which also [delights] them to perceive”).]

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Manuscripts A.1 and Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *quae sibi non* (“which [they] did not represent to themselves”) for *quae illi sibi non* (“which they did not represent to themselves”).]

and to think about certain things which the senses themselves cannot perceive, nor can the soul think of them through imagination, but which it thinks about simply, without any imagination.

## CHAPTER XXI [Note: [Col. 0611D] In manuscript A.1, the material from here through Chapter 37, exclusively, is absent.] On the Kinds of Exaltation

There are fifteen kinds of exaltation: four are simple, six double, four triple, and one quadruple.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Four Simple Kinds

[Col. 0612C]

There are therefore four simple kinds, because exaltation sometimes consists in opinion alone—for example, if someone thinks himself worthy of the episcopate but nevertheless does not wish to become a bishop; sometimes in will alone—for example, if he wishes to become a bishop but nevertheless does not think himself worthy of the episcopate; sometimes in speech alone—for example, if he boasts that he is worthy but does not wish to become a bishop, although he knows himself to be worthy; and sometimes in action alone—for example, if some lowly person, through ignorance, sits beside a king.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] “If some lowly person”: the manuscripts Victorius, Gembloux, Bec, and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “if some infirm person.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Six Double Kinds

There are six double kinds,

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *sex sunt* (“there are six”) for *sex vero sunt* (“there are indeed six”).] because sometimes a person is lifted up simultaneously in opinion and will—for example, when he considers himself worthy of some priorship and wishes to become prior;

[Note: [Col. 0611D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *Vi prior* (materially uncertain; apparently *ut prior*, “that he may become prior”) for *ut prior* (“that he may become prior”).]

sometimes in opinion and speech, but not in will—for example, when someone does not want some office of authority that is offered to him, and, exalting himself on this account, considers himself better than others and therefore boasts of himself, yet in such a way that he is not turned away;

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *ne avertatur* (“lest he be turned away”) for *ut non avertatur* (“so that he is not turned away”).]

sometimes in opinion and action—for example, if someone considers himself worthy to sit beside a bishop and, somewhere, through ignorance, sits beside him;

sometimes in will and speech—for example, when someone who wishes to become a bishop boasts that he is worthy of it,

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *jactat se esse non indignum* (“boasts that he is not unworthy”) for *jactat inde se esse dignum* (“boasts that he is worthy of it”).]

although he knows himself to be unworthy;

sometimes in will and action—for example, when someone wishes to sit in the higher place at a banquet and forces his way there without being invited, although he considers himself unworthy of so high a place;

and sometimes in speech and action—for example, when a prelate sees some weakness in himself on account of which, if he could do so honorably, he would abandon the office itself, yet in his words and actions displays a certain arrogance so that no one notices that weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Corbie reads *ostendit: aut ipsam* (“he displays: or that very [weakness]”); the Cologne edition of 1573 reads *ostendit ne ipsam* (“he displays [it], lest that very [weakness]…”); another reading is *ostendat: nec ipsam* (“may display [it]: nor that very [weakness]…”).]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Four Triple Kinds

There are four triple kinds. Sometimes a person takes pleasure in opinion, will, and speech—for example, when he considers himself worthy of an office, wishes to have it, and boasts about it.

Sometimes it consists in will, speech, and action—for example, when, because he wishes to hold an office, he pretends in word, deed, and conduct that he is worthy of it, although he knows himself to be unworthy.

Sometimes it consists in speech, action, and opinion—for example, when someone, although he boasts that he is worthy of an office, willingly performs the things by which he might appear worthy, and thinks the same of himself, nevertheless does not wish to hold the office, so that he may be judged more holy.

Sometimes it consists in action, opinion, and will—for example, when a prelate oppresses his subjects immoderately so that he may possess without any obstacle the office of which he considers himself worthy, for as long as he wishes.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the One Quadruple Kind

[Col. 0613C]

There is one quadruple kind, because a person often lifts himself up in opinion, will, speech, and action—for example, when he considers himself worthy of praise and desires it, praises himself, and performs certain great deeds in order to acquire praise.

There are therefore fifteen kinds of self-exaltation: four simple kinds, which are bad; six double kinds, which are worse; four triple kinds, which are worst; and one quadruple kind, which is worse than all the others.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] The manuscripts read *sed duplicia* (“but double [kinds]”) for *sex duplicia* (“six double [kinds]”).]

For the more aspects in which a person exalts himself, the worse that exaltation becomes.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius reads *excellentia* (“excellence”) for *extollentia* (“self-exaltation”).]

It should also be understood that exaltation consisting in action alone,

[Note: [Col. 0613D] The manuscripts read “excellence of action.”]

which always occurs through ignorance, is bad; that consisting in speech alone is worse; that consisting in opinion alone is worst; but that consisting in will alone is worse than all the others.

For it is foolish when some insignificant person, through ignorance, sits beside one who is worthy; but it is more foolish when he consequently boasts that he is worthy;

[Note: [Col. 0613D] The manuscripts read *se jactat dignum* (“he boasts himself worthy”) for *se jactat dignam* (“he boasts himself worthy,” with the feminine form).]

and it is most foolish when he considers himself worthy of this position;

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Corbie reads “when he considers himself worthy of these things.”]

but it is much more foolish when he wishes to sit beside her, although he knows himself to be unworthy of that place.

Against the exaltation that consists in action, the Lord himself says: “When you are invited to a wedding, recline in the lowest place” (Luke 14:10).

Against that which consists in speech, Solomon says: “Let someone else praise you, and not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27:2).

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Corbie reads *te alienus et* (“a stranger [praises] you, and”); another reading is *te alienum et* (“you, a stranger, and”), preserving the differing inflection.]

Against that which consists in opinion, the Apostle says: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20).

Against that which consists in will, the Lord again says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant” (Matthew XXIX, 27).

Against all the kinds of exaltation he likewise says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Curiosity and Its Sixteen Kinds

[Col. 0614B]

Curiosity is the effort to investigate things which there is no usefulness in knowing. It has sixteen kinds, of which five are simple, six double, four triple, and one quadruple.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Five Simple Kinds

There are therefore five simple kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in thought alone—for example, when someone carefully considers how he might learn another person’s secret.

Sometimes it consists in speech—for example, when he inquisitively asks about it.

Sometimes in action—for example, when he walks around that person as though he were looking for something else, in case he might be able to discover what he seeks by some indication.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “by some indication”; another reading is “by some judgment.”]

Sometimes in sight—for example, when he anxiously observes where that person is going,

[Col. 0614C]

what he is doing, and how he conducts himself while sitting, standing, walking, or in some other way.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius reads “where that person is directing himself.”]

Sometimes in hearing—for example, when he listens intently to what that person says about someone else, or someone else says about him.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “listens attentively.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Six Double Kinds

There are six double kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in speech and action—for example, when he addresses the person amicably

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “speaks amicably to him.”]

and meanwhile does something for him, in order to extort from him through flattering words and the service he performs what he is seeking.

Sometimes it consists in speech and sight—for example, when he asks another person to look at him with him, saying: “Do you think this man would act in this way or that if he were not such-and-such a person?”

Sometimes in speech and hearing—for example, when he sits near that person and speaks to someone else sitting on the other side of him, yet listens attentively to what the first person says behind him.

Sometimes in action and sight—for example, when he does something so that he will not be noticed while looking at the person, but will always be thought to be concentrating on the task he is performing.

Sometimes in action and hearing—for example, when he goes and comes in front of that person while listening to what he says.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “to listen to what he says.”]

Sometimes in sight and

[Col. 0615A]

hearing—for example, when he inquisitively observes what the person is doing and carefully listens to what he says, so that by this means he may learn the secrets he is seeking.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Four Triple Kinds

There are four triple kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in speech, action, and sight—for example, when someone calculates, measures, and considers how far the sun and moon are from the earth and how large those heavenly bodies are.

Sometimes in action, sight, and hearing—for example, when someone hides himself in order to see and hear the secrets of others.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “the secrets of some others.”]

Sometimes in sight, hearing, and speech—for example, when someone sits beside the roads in order to see passersby, hear rumors, and ask about them.

Sometimes in hearing, speech, and action—for example, when, in order to hear and inquire about future things, he sacrifices to demons.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the One Quadruple Kind

There is one quadruple kind, because curiosity sometimes consists in sight, hearing, speech, and action—for example, when someone watches and listens to certain people whom he sees taking counsel and of whom he suspects some evil, so that he may somehow learn their counsel. He approaches them and asks whether they have seen something which he pretends to have lost around them; meanwhile, by looking and listening, he seeks around them what he has nowhere lost.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Twenty-Eight Kinds of Curiosity

There are likewise twenty-eight kinds of curiosity, of which

[Col. 0615C]

three are simple, nine double, ten triple, and five quadruple; but one consists of five parts.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Three Simple Kinds

There are three simple kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in taste alone—for example, when a fish is brought to someone who is eating peas, and before he has consumed the peas themselves, he tastes the fish to find out what flavor it has.

Sometimes in smell—for example, when he brings it to his nose to discover what odor it has.

Sometimes in touch—for example, when someone, seeing a new cloth, handles it merely to find out whether it is rough or smooth, thick or fine.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Nine Double Kinds

[Col. 0615D]

There are nine double kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in taste and sight—for example, when someone tastes a dish placed before him before he has finished the first one, and meanwhile considers whether the person sitting beside him has a better dish.

Sometimes in taste and speech—for example, when he tastes it and asks whether it has been seasoned with pepper.

[Col. 0616A]

Sometimes in taste and smell—for example, when he tastes and smells it.

Sometimes in taste and touch—for example, when he seeks to discover by taste whether it is flavorful, and by touch whether it is hot, cold, or lukewarm.

Sometimes in smell and sight—for example, when someone, while reading, finds beside him an unfamiliar herb;

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Manuscript Corbie and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “an herb near him.”]

ceasing to read, he brings it to his nose and smells it; then, looking at it, he tries to identify what it is.

Sometimes in smell and speech—for example, when, smelling it, he asks another person what it is.

Sometimes in smell and touch—for example, when he smells and handles it to find out whether it is soft or hard, smooth or rough.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] The manuscripts read “light or rough.”]

He does all this not because it is necessary for him, but merely to know what it is or what sort of thing it is.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] This sentence is absent from the Cologne edition of 1573.]

Sometimes in sight and touch—for example, when someone comes to the table where he is going to dine, immediately lifts the cloth under which the bread is covered, and looks to see whether it is white,

[Col. 0616B]

and touches it to find out whether it is hot.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] A manuscript and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “looks to see whether it is hot.”]

Sometimes in speech and touch—for example, when he does not uncover it, but asks whether it is hot or how long ago it was baked, and touches and presses it while it is covered to find out whether it is hot.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Ten Triple Kinds

There are ten triple kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in sight, speech, and taste—for example, when someone is sitting somewhere and sees a drink being carried before him in a cup; he immediately rises, looks at what color it is, also asks what drink it is, and tastes whether it is good.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “someone sits.”]

Sometimes in sight, speech, and smell—for example, when he does not taste it, but smells it and, by asking questions, considers what it is like.

Sometimes in sight, speech, and touch—for example, when food is brought to someone eating, between two bowls; before he has finished what he was previously eating, he opens the bowls and considers what kind of food it is, investigates whether it has been well cooked, and touches it to determine whether it is hot or cold.

Sometimes in sight, taste, and smell—for example, when he asks nothing about it and does not touch it, but, curious to see it, tastes and smells it.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Manuscript Victorius reads: “He asks nothing and does not touch it, but is curious to see it, and tastes and smells it.” Another reading is: “He investigates nothing and does not smell it, but out of curiosity to see it, he tastes and smells it.”]

Sometimes in sight, taste, and touch—for example, when he inquires about nothing and does not smell it, but out of curiosity to see it, tastes and handles it for the reason I have mentioned.

Sometimes in sight, smell, and touch—for example, when he inquires about nothing and does not taste it, but merely looks at it, smells it, and handles it.

[Col. 0616D]

Sometimes in speech, taste, and smell—for example, when someone comes upon people dining and asks whether the food and drink they have are good, tasting some and smelling others.

Sometimes in speech, taste, and touch—for example, when he does not smell them, but handles the bread or other foods; tasting some, he asks about others.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Manuscript Corbie, manuscript Victorius, and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “the foods; tasting some, he asks about others.” Another reading has only “the foods.”]

Sometimes in speech, smell, and touch—for example, when he does not taste them, but smells, asks about, and handles them.

[Col. 0617A]

Conversely,

[Note: [Col. 0617D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “but smells them, asks about them, and handles them. Conversely.”]

sometimes curiosity consists in taste, smell, and touch—for example, when he asks nothing about them, but nevertheless tastes, smells, and handles them.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Five Triple Kinds

There are five quadruple kinds. Sometimes curiosity consists in sight, speech, taste, and smell—for example, when someone walking through a marketplace examines these or those goods, investigates what price these or those are worth, tastes grapes, apples, or other fruits, and smells pepper, cumin, or other fragrant things; doing all this merely to know what these or those things are, or what sort they are.

Sometimes in sight, speech, taste, and touch—for example, when he does the things mentioned above, except that he smells nothing there,

[Col. 0617B]

but, handling the goods, turns them over and over.

Sometimes in sight, speech, smell, and touch—for example, when he tastes nothing there, but does the other things mentioned above.

Sometimes in sight, taste, smell, and touch—for example, when he does not investigate what price these or those things are worth, but does the other things we have mentioned.

Sometimes in speech, taste, smell, and touch—for example, when he is not curious to see them because he has often seen such things, but does the other things mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Last Kind of Curiosity

There is one kind consisting of five parts, because curiosity sometimes consists in sight, speech, taste, smell, and touch—for example, when someone inquisitively turns his eyes toward these or those things and does all the other things we have mentioned above.

[Col. 0617C]

There are therefore forty-four kinds of curiosity: eight are simple, fifteen double, fourteen triple, and six quadruple; but one consists of five parts.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscripts read *ex partibus consistit quinque* (“it consists of five parts”) for *ex quinque partibus consistit* (“it consists of five parts”); the distinction is word order.]

This multifaceted curiosity, like the exaltation and delight about which we spoke above, all arises from one’s own will. For unless a person first has the will to take pleasure, to exalt himself, or to investigate inquisitively what it is of no use for him to know, he will never take pleasure, exalt himself, or inquisitively scrutinize useless things.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] Manuscript Victorius reads: “He would never take pleasure, or exalt himself, or scrutinize ...”]

Nevertheless, the evil of these vices is preceded by the will, and they themselves follow it; thus they arise from it, and from them all the others arise.

For from delight arise luxury, adultery, fornication,

[Col. 0617D]

uncleanness, gluttony of the belly, drunkenness, and other vices of this kind.

From exaltation arise vainglory, envy, anger, sorrow, avarice, and other similar vices.

From curiosity arise restlessness, whispering, slander, and all the rest.

All of them exist in the household of one’s own will,

[Col. 0618A]

and some of them form a great army out of themselves; they obey that will as though it were a mistress.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “form a great exercise.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Note: [Col. 0617D] Manuscript A.1 has: “Likewise, a treatise of the same Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, on one’s own will.”] A Comparison between One’s Own Will and an Adulterous Queen

One’s own will is like an adulterous queen who has joined herself to an adulterous king, by whom she has also had three sons. From these three,

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *in his vero* (“but in these”) for *ex his vero* (“but from these”).]

so many other sons and grandsons have been begotten and multiplied

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscripts read *itaque quoque* (“and therefore also”); the Cologne edition of 1573 omits *quoque* (“also”).]

that they cannot be counted. All of them belong to the household of that king and queen, and each of them fulfills their commands in his own way.

The king, then,

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “the king, however.”]

when, together with this queen, he opposes another king, gathers an army of sons and grandsons, attacks that king’s realm,

[Col. 0618B]

and plunders it. This army attacks the servants of that king in such a way that either many attack many, one attacks one, many attack one, or one attacks many.

Whomever they are able to defeat, they bind and carry away and thrust into prison, exacting from them what they can never repay; afflicted by every misery, they waste away in that prison.

This queen is one’s own will, the mistress of all who disobey.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] Manuscript A.1 reads *haec itaque regina* (“this queen, therefore”) for *haec autem regina* (“this queen, however”).]

She is called adulterous because she separates herself from God, to whom she ought to be joined, and joins herself to the devil, from whom she ought to be separated.

The devil himself is called king and adulterer because, reigning in human beings through their own will, he abuses their souls, who are the spouses of God. After one’s own will has joined itself to him, it conceives from his seed—that is, from his perverse suggestion—his three principal vices,

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscripts read *tria principalia vilia* (“three principal worthless things”; apparently a corrupted reading) for *tria principalia ejus vitia* (“his three principal vices”).]

namely, delight, exaltation, and curiosity; and, as though giving birth to them, it brings them forth through the five bodily senses.

From these three so many other vices are born and multiply that they are beyond counting. All of them belong to the household of the devil and one’s own will, and from themselves they produce a certain astonishing multitude.

The devil and one’s own will therefore oppose God, the King of kings; and, gathering the army of vices, attack and plunder his kingdom, namely, this world.

This army

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The manuscript and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “this household.”]

attacks the human race in such a way that either several vices seize several people, one vice seizes one person, several vices seize one person, or one vice seizes several people, in different ways.

[Col. 0618D]

Whomever they are able to overcome, they thrust into hell, bound by evil habit. There each vice demands from that person whatever he has ever committed through it. Since he will never be able to repay it, misery will never be absent from him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. A Comparison between One’s Own Will and a Poisonous Herb

[Col. 0619A]

Again, one’s own will is likened to a poisonous and deadly herb.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts read *assimilatur et comparatur* (“is likened and compared”); the Cologne edition of 1573 omits *et comparatur* (“and compared”).]

A highly skilled physician forbade a certain ancestry—namely, the first parents—to eat from it, threatening them that if they ate from it

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts read “having threatened them that if.”]

they would undoubtedly become lepers and perish.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript Victorius reads *ex ea comederint* (“if they eat from it”) for *ex ea comederent* (“if they should eat from it”).]

But they refused to obey his commands and ate from the same herb. As a result, they became lepers, begot leprous children, and, just as the physician had threatened them, died.

Although their children knew that their fathers had been weakened and killed by that herb, and that they themselves had been struck by leprosy and killed,

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscripts Gembloux, Bec, A.1, and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “struck and destined to die.”]

they nevertheless love that same herb above all others and season all their food with it.

When they rise in the morning,

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “rising in the morning.”]

they also take it as though it were medicine; and when they are about to sleep at night, they do the same.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts read “and the dream.”]

Anyone who hears this can recognize how insane they are. But no less insane are those who use their own will. For it is the devil’s herb, poisoned by poisonous suggestion and deadly to all who use it.

God, who mercifully heals our sins, forbade this herb to the first parents of the human race when he prohibited them from eating the fruit under threat of death. Because they transgressed his command and ate from it, they immediately became sinners and died in soul; after they had begotten other sinners,

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript Victorius reads “after they had begotten other sinners”; another reading is “after they had begotten others.”]

they themselves also died in the flesh.

Yet human beings love the same will above all else and mix it into almost everything they do. There is therefore nothing more insane than these people, who willingly use nothing more than their own death.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. An Explanation of How All Vices Serve or Minister to One’s Own Will

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript Victorius has: “How all vices minister to one’s own will.”]

Finally, after this own will has established its seat in a person,

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript A.1 and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “after it has built its seat.”]

other kinds of vices serve it: some like soldiers holding lands, others like soldiers serving for pay.

Those vices which are like holders of lands obey it when they exist in human beings for their own sake, as adultery does.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *ille etenim* (“for that one indeed”) for *illa etenim* (“for those indeed”).] For whoever commits adultery does so for no other reason than that the vice itself delights him.

Those, however, serve it like soldiers serving for pay, which exist in a person for the sake of other vices,

[Col. 0619D]

such as the desire for expensive clothing for the sake of vainglory. For no one seeks expensive clothes except for vainglory.

Likewise, one vice sometimes serves this vice and sometimes that one: avarice sometimes serves gluttony, sometimes exaltation.

Again, sometimes one vice yields to another, as luxury yields to vainglory. For luxury is sometimes driven away so that the desired praise may not be lost.

All of them, whether in this way or that, serve one’s own will and the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript A.1 reads “the vices which serve the devil”; manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read “and also serve the devil.”]

From these arise vices produced in a human being in three ways.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript Victorius reads *peccata nascuntur* (“sins arise”) for *procreata nascuntur* (“things produced are born”).]

For each vice is brought to completion by the devil’s suggestion, the pleasure of the flesh, and the consent of the spirit.

## CHAPTER XL [Note: [Col. 0619D] Omitted in manuscript A.1.] A Comparison between Suggestion, Delight, Consent, and a Dog

From these three—namely, suggestion, delight, and consent—suggestion is like a heavy dog; delight like a light and fierce puppy; and consent like a strong and enormous dog.

For when the heavy dog hears someone passing close by, it barks once or twice after him and immediately grows quiet, provided that the passerby keeps straight on his way. But if he looks back and provokes it, the dog follows him barking, although it does not bite him.

The light and fierce puppy presses forward fiercely; and unless it is struck quickly, it bites more fiercely.

But the strong and enormous dog presses forward with strength; and unless it is overwhelmed by great force, it strangles the man.

Therefore, the heavy dog must not be looked back at; the puppy must immediately be struck back; and the enormous dog must be overwhelmed manfully.

Likewise, if the suggestion of sin strikes the mind which is moving from love of present things toward eternal ones, it soon leaves that mind, provided that the mind holds firmly to its purpose. But if, attending to it, the mind receives it into itself and, by thinking, turns it over as though inciting it, then it repeatedly harasses the mind, although it does not wound it, so long as it is suggestion alone.

But if the mind repeats it for too long, the heavy dog passes into the puppy—that is, suggestion passes into delight, which presses forward fiercely; and unless it is quickly rejected, it wounds the soul.

Therefore, as soon as it begins to come, the soul, the bride of Christ, ought to repel it, thinking that it is a great disgrace for her to appear before him stained by such a shameful delight.

If she does not repel the delight, the puppy passes into the enormous dog—that is, delight passes into consent. When it seizes the soul, it kills her unless it is overwhelmed by great force.

But as soon as it begins to make its attack,

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts Victorius and the Cologne edition read “as soon as it begins to approach.”]

the soul must overwhelm it with great force—that is, destroy it within herself through an immense dread of eternal death.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] The manuscripts read “the soul must overwhelm him.”]

Let us therefore not attend to suggestion, let us immediately restrain delight, and let us forcefully overwhelm consent. In this way let us strive to guard our heart, so that the devil may not be able to violate it with even one superfluous thought.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Manuscript Victorius and the Cologne edition of 1573 read *ut neque una* (“so that not even one”) for *ut nec una* (“so that not even one”).]

## CHAPTER XLI. A Comparison between the Human Heart and a Mill

[Col. 0621A]

Our heart, therefore, is like a mill that is always grinding. A certain master entrusted such a mill to one of his servants to guard, commanding him to grind in it only his own grain—namely, wheat, barley, or even oats—and to live from what he had ground.

But someone is hostile to that servant, and he is always lying in wait for the mill. If he should ever find it empty, he immediately throws into it either sand, which destroys it; or pitch, which makes things stick together; or something that soils it; or straw, which merely occupies it. Therefore, if that servant guards his mill well and grinds in it only his master’s grain, clean flour comes out of it [Col. 0621B], according to the kind of grain that is ground inside. From what he has ground he both serves his master and acquires food for himself.

But if he allows his enemy to violate his mill, bad flour comes out of it, because the grain he grinds is bad. That flour both greatly displeases the master, and the servant gains from it not food for himself but hunger.

This mill, then, always grinding something, is the human heart, constantly thinking about something. God has entrusted it to every human being to guard, commanding that he turn in it only those thoughts that God himself suggests. Of these thoughts, some are like wheat, some like barley, and some like oats.

Those thoughts are pure like wheat which the soul turns over when, placed in contemplation, it thinks purely about God [Col. 0621C]. Those are compared to barley which contemplate ascending from virtue to virtue, as though through various labors. For although these thoughts are good, they are nevertheless less perfect than the former. Those, however, are like oats by which a person aims to abandon his vices. These too are good, but they are nevertheless less perfect than those already mentioned.

God therefore wishes a person to turn all these thoughts over with his whole heart and to acquire eternal food for himself from them. But because the devil is always opposed to humanity and always lies in wait for the human heart, if he ever finds it empty of good thoughts, he immediately fills it, if he can, with evil ones.

Of these evil thoughts, some destroy the heart, such as anger and envy. Others make it stick together and defile it, such as gluttony and lust. Others merely occupy it, such as vainglory [Col. 0621D], which is not excessively harmful.

This person, then, if he guards his heart well and turns holy thoughts over within it, sends out clean words through his mouth, as through the opening of a mill; clean sight through his eyes; clean hearing through his ears; clean taste through his mouth; clean smell through his nostrils; and clean touch through his whole body [Col. 0622A], according to the kinds of pure thoughts that are turned over within.

Through these pure thoughts he both serves God by thinking about them and acquires eternal life for himself. But if he allows the devil to corrupt his heart, vices immediately advance through the senses, according to the kinds of evil thoughts that are turned over within. These things greatly displease God, and from them a person acquires not food for himself but death.

For when each person has reached the end, he will find prepared for himself for life or death as much as he has now ground, whether good or evil. It must, however, be understood that there are three kinds of these millers—that is, of those who labor in this life.

## CHAPTER XLII. The comparison between millers and those who labor.

These three kinds are like three men grinding by hand from morning until evening. The first of them receives and stores in a sack whatever he grinds. The second takes one part, allows another part to fall through negligence into the river, and the wind carries off another part. The third loses whatever he grinds: the force of the river carries it away, or the wind scatters it.

When evening comes, when work ceases and the fruit of labor is sought, what do you suppose each will possess? The one who preserved all the flour has rightly accounted for all his labor. The one who gathered only part of it rejoices over what he has; but over what he lost to the wind or in the river he is sad. The one who lost everything is sadder still.

The river signifies the course of the world, while the wind signifies empty glory [Col. 0622C]. The mill that grinds all day signifies the present labor of this world, which never ends from morning until evening.

It was morning for us when we were born; evening will be when we depart from here through the debt of death. The present time, then, is the day in which we must labor so that we may live in the evening. And just as a millstone, drawn around in a circle, always returns to the same place, so this labor is repeated every year in the customary manner. Now the land is plowed, sown, harvested, made into bread, and eaten; then the process returns again to the same point.

At evening, therefore, when it is said, “Call the laborers and give them their wage” (Matthew 20:8), the righteous will rejoice, having preserved all the flour—that is, their life. Others, who did not preserve it all, will be sad about this; nevertheless, they will rejoice that through part of their labor they recognized God [Col. 0622D].

But others, who spend all their time in vanity and do not conceal what they do from human praise, as though they cast all the effort of their life into the course of the river and entrusted their flour to the wind, will therefore lack the bread of eternal life at the end [Note: [Col. 0621D] The manuscript of Victor has *panae vitae aeternae*; the eternal bread]. Woe to them!

## CHAPTER XLIII. That the goodness of each faithful person is useful to God and to all good things [Note: [Col. 0623D] In the manuscript of Victor and in the Cologne edition: “That the goodness of each faithful person is useful to God and to all good things.”]

The more abundant the fruit that is shown to come from the pursuit of goodness, the more diligently each person is brought to pursue it. It must therefore be understood that the goodness of each person is useful and beneficial to every creature, except demons and condemned human beings.

It also seems, in a certain sense, to benefit God, who needs nothing. It is useful to human beings: whenever someone reaches eternal blessedness through the merit of his life, the number of the elect increases. The more that number grows, the sooner the eternal reward is to be expected. For when that number of saints has been completed [Note: [Col. 0623D] Namely, “when that number of the saints has been completed,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “when the number of the saints has been filled,” in another reading], the reward of the righteous will immediately be received [Col. 0623B]—then, indeed, in their bodies as well as in their souls, which already possess it.

But if each faithful person, as soon as he left this life, were to attain eternal blessedness in body and soul at once, everyone who saw this would be compelled to imitate his holiness; thus the merit of faith would seem in some way to be nullified.

Goodness is therefore useful to those who are good and with God, because their merit increases through the good person’s presence. It is also beneficial to those who are in the present life and to those who are still to come, because he fills a place in that company of the blessed which can in no way be empty at the end.

It also accomplishes something else: by the example of his goodness, he restrains the wickedness of the perverse [Note: [Col. 0623D] “The military service of the perverse,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “the wickedness of the perverse,” in the main text; the Victor manuscript and Cologne edition instead read, “indeed, he excludes it by the example of his goodness.”].

A good person is useful to the sun and the moon, and to the other creatures, because at the completion of the righteous everything belonging to all creatures will be changed for the better [Col. 0623C]. For the sun, as the prophet says, “will shine sevenfold, like the light of seven days,” and the moon “will be like the sun” (Isaiah 30:26). Other creatures, although beautiful, will be changed for the better when God changes them into a state that thereafter will not be changed.

A good person is also useful to the angels, because he makes himself a friend to all of them. If someone acquired for me a friend who loved me as himself, and whom I loved as myself, I would owe him great thanks. Whoever therefore strives to be good will enter into the friendship of the good, so that he will love each one as himself, and all will hold him dear in the same way. For such love and harmony will exist among all that all the friends of one will be friends of another.

Let us see, however, how a good person is also useful to God. Almighty God built a great and exceedingly spacious city for his glory [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Exceedingly spacious,” in the manuscript of Corbie, Victor, and the Cologne edition; “exceedingly beautiful,” in another reading], and filled it with a large multitude of citizens [Col. 0624A] [Note: [Col. 0623D] “How beautiful a multitude of citizens,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “how large a multitude of citizens,” in the main text].

Some of these, when they chose to do their own will rather than remain under God’s will and ordering, fell miserably, and the great and spacious houses and buildings remained partly empty. Thus, if someone had planned to make a great city, had built many palaces in it, and had made many dwellings for the construction of the city but had no inhabitants, and had invited to himself all whom he could, so does the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0623D] “So does the Lord God,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “so does God,” in another reading]. For he begs, admonishes, and invites everyone to come to him and to help him in building his city, promising good laws and offering peace and security.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Praise of the heavenly Jerusalem.

There the ordinances of the laws are unchanging, and the customs are excellent. There the citizens do not conceal their possessions through fear of anyone; rather, they rejoice while these possessions appear openly to all. No attack of evils is there, no plague, no violence, and every kind of robbery is far removed from that place.

Moreover, the place is pleasant and refreshed with great sweetness; the houses are prepared, the buildings spacious, and the dwellings of various kinds. Hence the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwellings.” And the prophet Baruch says: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast is the place of his possession!” (Baruch 3:24). It is great and has no end; it is exalted and immeasurable.

There are no darknesses there, for unfailing light shines all around; no weakness, but tireless health; nothing harmful, and everything according to one’s desire. The Lord therefore invites us to this building, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

Whoever wishes to come will undoubtedly be, in a certain sense, God’s helper. Hence the Apostle says: “We are God’s helpers; you are God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

Therefore, whoever perseveres in goodness will be useful not only to himself and to every creature, but also, as we have said, will render a benefit to God himself, the Creator of him and of all things. For this holy city, to which he has freely joined himself [Note: [Col. 0623D] “And to every creature … to every creature to which he freely joined himself,” in the manuscripts and Cologne edition; “and to every creature to which he freely joined himself,” in the main text], will never be completed if even one good person is absent.

## CHAPTER XLV. That the goodness of a good person is useless to the condemned and to demons [Note: [Col. 0623D] “That the goodness of a good person is useless to the condemned and to demons,” in the main text; “That the goodness of a good person is useful to the condemned and to demons,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition.]

It must also be noted that, just as the goodness of a good person is an increase of joy to everyone [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Is an increase to everyone,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “is an increase to human beings,” in another reading], so to demons and condemned human beings it is a detriment [Col. 0625A]. For to demons and condemned human beings the completion of the saints will be endless grief and eternal condemnation.

When these people obtain everlasting joy of body and soul, then those others likewise will go into eternal punishment [Note: [Col. 0625D] “When the righteous obtain it,” in the manuscript of Victor]. Since this is not hidden from the demons, they labor by every means to hinder the increase of the saints. For until the last of them has been joined to their company, they are not shut in; instead, they have the power to tempt God’s elect, so that those who are found approved may be crowned with worthy reward, while those who are defeated and rejected may be punished forever.

Let us therefore keep watch, as the Savior admonishes us, because “our adversary goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). He devours the person whom he hardens in evil deeds through his suggestion.

It must also be noted that whoever rejoices in another’s good consents to the saints, while whoever envies them sides with the devils. Indeed, I think that the salvation of one who does little good but favors the good deeds of others is more hopeful than that of one who does much but envies.

For if the person who takes pleasure in the good deeds of others were even condemned, he could justly complain in this way: “O saints, I always rejoiced justly in your justice. Therefore, if I do not share in your blessedness, I will receive condemnation for the very thing over which I always rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0625D] “I will not receive condemnation,” in the manuscripts and Cologne edition; “I will receive condemnation,” in the main text].

## CHAPTER XLVI. The comparison between God and any king judging his subjects [Note: [Col. 0625D] “The comparison between God and some king who will judge his subjects,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “the comparison between God and any king judging his subjects,” in the main text.]

God distinguishes between those who will be saved and those who will be condemned just as a certain king distinguishes between the faithful and unfaithful members of his realm.

This king, having prepared on one side a great banquet [Col. 0625C] and on the other a dark prison [Note: [Col. 0625D] “A certain banquet,” omitted by the manuscripts of Victor and the Cologne edition], decreed that, after all had been gathered, he would make all whom he could prove faithful to him recline together; but all whom he could prove unfaithful to him, after they too had been gathered, he would have thrown together into that dark prison [Note: [Col. 0625D] “That he would make all …,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “he decreed that all …,” in the main text].

He therefore invites everyone to himself [Note: [Col. 0625D] “He invites them to himself,” in the manuscript of A.1, Victor, and the Cologne edition], so that he may recognize who is faithful and who is unfaithful. Among these faithful and unfaithful people, all of whom are invited, some arrive earlier and others later.

Whenever one of the faithful arrives, after he has truly been proved faithful, he is given a mixture of food in the meantime, until all who are to dine with him have assembled, so that they may all begin feasting together.

Whenever one of the unfaithful arrives, after he has been convicted of being unfaithful, he is meanwhile scourged until the others who are to be thrown with him into prison have gathered, so that they may all begin to suffer there together [Col. 0626A].

As soon, therefore, as all have been gathered and proved to be either faithful or unfaithful, the faithful are all placed together at the banquet and are satisfied [Note: [Col. 0625D] “These, namely, together,” in the manuscript of A.1 and the Cologne edition; “they are placed together and satisfied,” in the main text; “they are placed together and associated,” in the manuscript of Victor]. But the others [Note: [Col. 0625D] “The others, namely the unfaithful,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition], thrust into prison, die of hunger and thirst.

This king, then, is God himself, who thus distinguishes between the good and the evil of this world. Having prepared paradise on one side and hell on the other, he has decreed that all whom he can find faithfully serving him, after all who pass to him from this world have been gathered, he will place together in paradise in body and soul [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Into paradise, in body and soul,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “in paradise, in body and soul,” in the main text].

But all whom he can find resisting his commandments, after they have assembled, he will thrust together horribly into hell with the devil [Col. 0626B]. He therefore invites everyone to himself through his preachers, so that he may recognize how each person wishes to obey him. Some obey his commandments, while others resist them.

Of both groups, some are brought before his judgment earlier, and others later when they die [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Some die later,” in the manuscripts; “others are brought later when they die,” in the main text]. Whoever is proved to have obeyed him is meanwhile given rest—but in the soul alone. Whoever is convicted of disobedience is likewise tortured—but in the soul alone.

After all have died and, as was said, have been examined individually [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Examined individually,” in the manuscripts; “deprived of life individually,” in the main text], and after the world has ended, all have been resurrected, and that general judgment has also been completed, all the good, transferred into heaven, will rejoice together in soul and body. But the evil, thrust into hell [Col. 0626C], will likewise be tormented in soul and body.

And just as the good will then obtain perfect blessedness of body and soul for the first time, so the evil, conversely, will then for the first time be subjected to perfect misery of body and soul [Note: [Col. 0625D] The manuscript of A.1 reads: “They were being tormented. And just as the good then first obtained perfect blessedness of body and soul, so the evil, conversely, would then first be subjected to perfect misery of body and soul.”]

## CHAPTER XLVII. The fourteen blessed conditions of body and soul.

Many people [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Many people, etc.” The manuscript of A.1 adds: “For there are fourteen parts of blessedness, etc., which in substance are entirely the same as in the printed editions, but in wording are completely different. For in the manuscripts the sayings of Saint Anselm on blessedness are abridged, whereas in the printed editions we read them expanded. The Sagiensis manuscript, folio 16, condensed these same sayings still more briefly.]—to whom good conduct and righteous works are sometimes proposed, so that they may be admonished to exercise themselves in them after setting aside the vanity of the world—are accustomed to ask what the reward or recompense will be.

They are answered with what is written: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 0625D] “For those who love him,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “for those who love him,” in the main text] (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9) [Col. 0626D].
