When they cannot clearly perceive what this means [Col. 0627A], the same matter is repeated to them in other words, and they are told: The reward that is repaid in the future life to those who serve God in this life is eternal life, eternal blessedness, eternal joy, and the sufficiency of all good things at once according to one’s will and without any want [Note: [Col. 0627D] “They are recompensed; it is life,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “they are recompensed, eternal life,” in the main text].

When these things are expressed to them in this way, they certainly appear to be good and great, as they are. But because they do not understand what they will possess in that life, and cannot immediately grasp what it means to have all good things according to one’s will, with complete sufficiency and without any want, they remain inwardly uncertain. They are not greatly moved by the savor of what they have heard [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Not greatly affected,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “not greatly effective,” in another reading], nor are they drawn away from the vanity of the world [Note: [Col. 0627D] “And from the vanity of the world,” omitted by the manuscripts of Victor and the Cologne edition].

What, then, should be done so that these things may in some measure become perceptible to them and they may thus awaken to good works? I think they should be fed like children. If they are given some large apple to eat, they cannot consume it because of the tenderness of their teeth and the narrowness of their mouths [Note: [Col. 0627D] “They cannot swallow it,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “they cannot consume it,” in the main text], unless it is first divided into small pieces according to their capacity [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Unless it has first been divided for their capacity,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “if it has first been divided for their capacity,” in another reading].

Let us therefore divide into parts the great things we have mentioned, so that from them those of whom we speak may be nourished toward life. To make these things shine forth more clearly, let us consider what the human mind loves most eagerly in this life, and from these things, insofar as we can, infer that they will possess them in eternal life in a far more excellent manner.

For if, placed amid the many dangers of the world, they have followed the Lord’s commandments and have attained these things there, they will perceive that they have in no way been deprived of the fullness of their desire [Note: [Col. 0627D] “When they have attained fullness,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “when they have attained it in fullness,” in the main text].

Let us therefore do as we have indicated, and proceed gradually from the least. There are fourteen parts of blessedness [Col. 0627C], which, after the general judgment has ended, all the elect will possess more perfectly; and there are an equal number of kinds of misery, which the wicked will then endure. These parts of blessedness and kinds of misery are altogether opposed to one another, just as those who receive them are opposed in their recompense.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. These are the fourteen parts of blessedness.

The parts of blessedness are beauty, agility, strength, freedom, health, pleasure, longevity, wisdom, friendship, harmony, honor, power, security, and joy.

These, I think, are the things which human beings seek for their own sake and for the sake of which they seek all other things. If there are among them some things that the servants of God in this life not only do not seek but even carefully avoid caring about, such as bodily beauty and pleasure, they do not flee these things because they naturally dislike them [Col. 0628A]. Rather, they avoid them so that they may not in any way offend God.

For if they were certain that through these things no offense against God could be incurred, or did not fear being hindered by them from the love of eternal goods, they would certainly take greater pleasure in them than in their opposites [Note: [Col. 0627D] “If they were certainly convinced,” in the manuscript of Victor; “if they were convinced with certainty,” in the main text].

## CHAPTER XLIX. These are the fourteen parts of misery.

The fourteen parts of misery, opposed to the blessednesses just mentioned, are these: ugliness, heaviness, weakness, servitude, sickness, anxiety, brevity of life, foolishness, enmity, discord, disgrace, powerlessness, fear, and sadness.

It must be noted that just as the first seven parts of that blessedness pertain to the blessedness of the body, while the seven later parts [Note: [Col. 0627D] “And the seven later parts,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition] pertain to the blessedness of the soul [Col. 0628B], so the first seven parts of this misery belong to the body, while the last seven complete the misery of the mind.

Whoever is able to possess all those parts of blessedness will possess perfect blessedness of body and soul. But whoever happens to endure all these parts of misery will be subjected to the greatest misery of body and soul.

In this life, however, no one can possess even one part of that blessedness and of this misery perfectly, nor again can anyone be entirely without them. In the other life, either one who possesses perfect blessedness will in no way be subjected to misery, or one subjected to the greatest misery will be entirely deprived of blessedness.

To establish all this, let us proceed through the individual parts of blessedness and [Col. 0628C] misery.

## CHAPTER L. On beauty and ugliness.

The first part of blessedness is beauty; the corresponding part of misery is ugliness. Everyone desires to possess the former and to be free from the latter. Yet here no one can possess either perfectly, nor can anyone be entirely without either [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Here no one can possess either of them perfectly,” in the manuscript of A.1; “here no one can possess either one perfectly,” in the manuscripts of Victor and the Cologne edition; “here neither can be possessed perfectly,” in the main text].

For what human beauty is there that is not far inferior to the beauty of a little flower [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Of a little flower?” in the manuscript of A.1 and Victor; “of the flower of God,” in the Cologne edition; “of the flower of the world,” in another reading]? Who shines white like a lily? Who is red like a rose? Yet because a person possesses however little beauty, he is not subject to the greatest ugliness.

Therefore, in this life he can neither possess the one or the other perfectly, nor be wholly without them. In the other life he will possess one perfectly and be entirely without the other.

Beauty is a good thing, and naturally all creatures love to possess it. In that life the beauty of the righteous will equal the beauty of the sun, which will be more splendid than it is now by sevenfold brightness. Hence it is written: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the presence of God” (Matthew 13:43).

Moreover, I do not know whether anyone could doubt that the body of Christ can shine more brightly than the sun [Note: [Col. 0629D] “The body of Christ,” in the manuscript of Victor]. We shall be like him, according to the Apostle, who says: “He will transform the body of our humiliation, configured to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21).

Once this has been established by authority [Note: [Col. 0629D] “This, moreover,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition], if someone also wishes it to be established by reason, I believe no one should find it incredible that in that life, where this mortal condition will be swallowed up, the righteous will possess the beauty of the sun, especially since they are truly called and are the temple and dwelling-place of God. We never find in the divine writings that this visible sun is called that.

With such great beauty, therefore, the righteous person will shine. But if he has been unrighteous, he will be fouler than mud and every corpse, and uglier than every soot-blackened thing [Col. 0629B]. There, therefore, he will possess perfect beauty or the highest ugliness.

## CHAPTER LI. On agility and heaviness.

The second part of blessedness is agility; its opposite in misery is heaviness. Here a human being can possess neither of these completely, nor can he be entirely without either. For how great is human agility when the smallest of sparrows surpasses it? Yet because a person can move himself in some manner, he is not subject to the greatest heaviness.

Thus here he possesses neither perfect agility nor the greatest heaviness. In the future, however, he will either be perfectly agile or so heavy that he will be entirely unable to move himself.

In that blessed life, however, a speed no less loved than beauty will accompany us to such a degree that we will be as swift as the angels themselves [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Angels,” in the manuscripts; “the angels,” in the main text] of God, who dart from heaven to earth [Note: [Col. 0629D] “To the lands,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition] and back again more quickly than a word can be spoken [Col. 0629C].

If it were necessary to prove that such speed exists in angels, one could say, by way of example, that a man still weighed down by mortal flesh might immediately be carried by an angel from Judea to Chaldea, and from there, after handing over the meal he was carrying, be brought back without delay.

Therefore, we shall possess speed entirely equal to theirs, since, as has been promised, their equality will be ours. The Apostle also, by asserting that our bodies, however far apart their members may have been separated or scattered, will rise in the blink of an eye, sufficiently indicates the speed that those same incorruptible bodies will possess.

For, as he himself testifies, “This corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

One may also observe an example of this speed in a ray of the sun [Col. 0629D]. As soon as the sun has risen in the eastern region, the ray reaches to the farthest limits of the western region [Note: [Col. 0629D] “To the farthest limit of the region,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “to the farthest limits of the region,” in the main text]. Thus we may understand that what we say about our future speed is not impossible, especially since living things are accustomed to possess greater speed than lifeless things.

We also have in ourselves an example of speed resembling that of a sunbeam [Note: [Col. 0629D] “We also have this example,” in the manuscripts]. The ray of our eyes, when the eyelids are raised, reaches all the way to heaven, and with the striking of the eyelids it returns wholly and intact into itself [Note: [Col. 0629D] “And with the striking of them,” in the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; “and their striking,” in the main text].

Moreover, it is certain that the souls of the saints, which already possess heavenly things, do not yet enjoy complete happiness until they possess the incorruptibility of their bodies. When they have obtained this, there will be nothing more for them to desire.

Therefore, if these bodies were to make them in any way slower or heavier than their own speed, they would surely shrink from their company rather than desire it. Thus the holy person, when transferred to the true life, will be endowed with the speed we have described.

But the wicked person will be weighed down by such a burden of punishments that he will be unable to move even a foot, a hand, or any part of his body. Hence also the saying in the Gospel: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:23) [Col. 0630B] [Note: [Col. 0629D] “And his feet, cast him,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition; “and his feet, cast him,” in the main text].

## CHAPTER LII. On strength and weakness.

The third part of blessedness is called strength; its opposing misery is weakness. But what strength do human beings possess in this life, when a sea-urchin can hold back a fully laden ship at sea?

Yet because a human being is able to overcome certain weaknesses, he is not entirely subject to weakness. Thus here he possesses neither perfect strength nor the greatest weakness.

Those who have deserved to be joined to the citizens above will, however, be endowed with such power that nothing at all will be able to resist them, even if they wish to move or overturn something from its position; it will immediately yield [Col. 0630C]. Nor will they need greater exertion for what we are describing than we now need for the movement of our eyes.

Let us not, I beg, allow that likeness to the angels which we will acquire in the future to slip from our minds [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Which we will possess,” in the manuscript and the Cologne edition]. If an example does not arise for this strength or for the things we are about to discuss, let that very likeness, by which we will be made equal to the angels, serve to establish them.

Thus our strength will be no less effective in those matters in which angels are known to be powerful. No one, however, should doubt that angels possess the strength by which they carry out whatever they wish. Since we shall be like them, we shall never be weaker than they are.

But perhaps someone will ask: What use will that strength provide us then, when all things have been so fittingly arranged everywhere that nothing needs to be changed, overturned, or established, in which anyone could exercise his strength?

Let the person who asks this consider with us briefly how human experience operates in such matters, and he will see that we do not always actively use everything we possess and in which we take no small delight—for example, sight itself, some power of knowing things, and many things of this kind. So it will also be with the strength under discussion.

Its possession alone will be pleasing to us and a great cause for rejoicing, even though it will not at all be necessary for us in action, since, as has been said, everything will be suitably placed in its proper state. The same question, if it is raised about speed or about any other part of blessedness, may be resolved by this answer, unless the reader finds a more suitable one.

In the future, therefore, as we have already indicated, the righteous will be so strong that, if he wishes, he will even be able to move the earth [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Thus the righteous,” in the manuscript of Victor and the Cologne edition]. Conversely, the unrighteous will be so weak that he will not even be able to remove worms from his eyes.

### Additional textual apparatus

[Col. 0621D] At the opening, the manuscripts read *in ea molat*, “grinds in it,” for *in eo molat*; manuscripts A.1, Victor 13, and the Cologne edition read *ut ex eodem*, “so that from that same [mill],” for *et ex eodem*, “and from that same [mill].” They read *Servus autem ille*, “but that servant,” for *Servus igitur ille*, “therefore that servant”; *ut in eo molat*, “that he may grind in it,” for *ut in eo volvat*, “that he may turn over in it”; and *tantum cogitans*, “thinking only,” for *tantum cogitatus*, “only those thoughts.” For the last class of evil thoughts, A.1 and Victor 13 read *ut vanae gloriae non nimis nocivae*, “such as vainglories, which are not excessively harmful,” for *ut vanae non nimis nocivae*, “such as vain [things] which are not excessively harmful.” In A.1 the section begins with *Verum sciendum*, “But it must be understood.”

[Col. 0621D, Chapter XLII] Victor and the Cologne edition read *Haec autem velut*, “These, however, are as it were,” for *Haec autem tria genera velut*, “These three kinds are as it were”; and the manuscripts read *praesens est labor hujus saeculi*, “the present labor of this world is,” for *praesens labor hujus saeculi*, “the present labor of this world.”

[Col. 0623D] Victor and the Cologne edition read *in praesentiarum sunt vel adhuc*, “are at present, or are still [to come],” for *in praesenti vita sunt, et adhuc futuri sunt*, “are in the present life and are still to come.” In the closing sentence of Chapter XLIV, the corrupt transmitted alternatives are: manuscripts and the Cologne edition, *et omni creaturae cui sponte associavit* (“and to every creature to which he freely joined [himself]”); Corbie and the Cologne edition, *cui se sponte associavit* (“to which he freely joined himself”).

[Col. 0623D, Chapter XLV] Victor and the Cologne edition read *damnatis erit ad detrimentum*, “will be a detriment to the condemned,” for *damnatis est ad detrimentum*, “is a detriment to the condemned.”

[Col. 0625D, Chapter XLVI] A.1 reads *Inter salvandos siquidem*, “For among those to be saved,” for *Inter salvandos autem*, “But among those to be saved.”

[Col. 0625D–0627D, Chapter XLVII] Victor and the Cologne edition read *reperitur hoc ipsum*, “this same thing is found,” for *repetitur hoc ipsum*, “this same thing is repeated.” At the scriptural quotation, the main text has *diligentibus se*, “for those who love him [God himself],” while Victor and the Cologne edition read *diligentibus eum*, “for those who love him.” At the child-and-apple comparison, Victor and the Cologne edition read *absorbere nequeunt*, “cannot swallow,” for *absumere nequeunt*, “cannot consume,” and *assumere nequeunt*, “cannot take,” for *absumere nequeunt*; they also read *si pro illorum capacitate*, “if [it is divided] according to their capacity,” for *nisi pro illorum capacitate*, “unless [it is divided] according to their capacity,” and *prius non fuerit particulatim divisum*, “has not first been divided into small pieces,” for *prius fuerit particulatim divisum*, “has first been divided into small pieces.” Victor and the Cologne edition read *fuerint plenitudinem*, “have attained fullness,” for *fuerint plenitudine desiderii sui*, “have attained [them] with the fullness of their desire.”

[Col. 0627D, Chapter XLIX] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition transpose the words: *Quod totum ut*, “So that we may establish all this,” for *Quod ut totum*, with the same sense.

[Col. 0627D–0629D, Chapters L–LI] The Cologne edition’s *floris Dei*, “flower of God,” and another reading’s *foris saeculi*, “outside of the world,” stand against the main text’s *flosculi*, “little flower.” A.1 reads *Quia cum quantulacunque*, “For although [one has] however little,” and Victor 13 *quae tamen quantulamcunque*, “which nevertheless [has] however little,” for *Quia tamen quantulamcunque*, “Yet because [one has] however little.” The Cologne edition reads *subjacere, nec*, “to be subject, nor,” for *subjacet. Non*, “is subject. Therefore not.” The manuscripts and Cologne edition read *invenimus legi*, “we find written,” for *meminimus legi*, “we remember having read.” In Chapter LI, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *qui tamen*, “who nevertheless,” for *quia tamen*, “because nevertheless.”

[Col. 0629D–0631D, Chapter LII] Victor and the Cologne edition read *quam habituri sumus*, “which we shall possess,” for *quam adepturi sumus*, “which we shall acquire.” They read *sumus ad exemplum*, “we are [to take it] as an example,” for *sumus, exemplum*, “we are—an example”; *si igitur*, “if therefore,” for *sic igitur*, “thus therefore”; and *fortitudo valebit neminem qui dubitet*, “strength will prevail; let no one doubt,” for *fortitudo valeat; neminem autem qui dubitet*, “let strength avail; but let no one doubt.”

## CHAPTER LIII. On freedom and servitude.

## Chapter LIII. On Freedom and Servitude

The fourth part of blessedness is called freedom; of misery, servitude. That person is free  who cannot be compelled [Col. 0631B] to do what he does not wish, nor prevented from doing what he wishes. But who in this life can be such as to possess this freedom? Who does not daily suffer what he would not wish? Who can attain everything he would wish? Yet because a person is not compelled to everything he does not wish, nor prevented from everything he wishes, he is neither wholly deprived of freedom nor wholly subjected to servitude.

In the future, however, a person will either possess perfect freedom or enter into complete servitude  But, as we have already stated and confirmed the same by apostolic authority , we shall be like the angels . Whoever is made like the angels will necessarily also attain their freedom. Thus, just as nothing obstructs the angels, and nothing can hinder or constrain them so that they may freely penetrate everything according to their will, so there will be no obstacle to delay us, no enclosure [Col. 0631C] that can in any way impede us, and no element that will not be entirely accessible to us according to our will 

Moreover, the Lord’s body, to which Paul testifies that our bodies are to be conformed (Philippians 3:21), as we have already mentioned above, rose from the dead with the tomb closed and finally entered among the disciples through locked doors so that it could be touched (John 20:26). In this it left us a great proof of future freedom. For in that life, if a person is good, he will suffer nothing he does not wish, but will be permitted to do whatever he wishes. If, however, he is evil, he will be compelled to everything he does not wish and prevented from everything he wishes.

## Chapter LIV. On Health and Illness

[Col. 0631D]

The fifth part of blessedness is health; of misery, illness. From his birth a person begins to lack the former and to endure the latter . As soon as he is born, his first cry indicates that he is suffering. Immediately he begins to hunger, thirst, grow weary , and become dirty in his garments. From this point he becomes ill—blind or deaf, mute or lame, afflicted with heart disease or scabies, leprosy, paralysis , or some other disease .

Yet because his illness can be eased by certain medicines, he is not subject to the utmost degree of illness . But in the future he will be so healthy that he will never become ill in any way, but will enjoy perfect health.

What better can be said about this health than what the Psalmist sings? “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 37:39). But once true health has been given by the Lord, what illness will be able to steal it away?

Yet concerning this health that we shall possess in the future age, I do not see what example I could offer by which its nature might be understood. For there is nothing comparable to it that either I or anyone living in mortal flesh has experienced in himself [Col. 0632B]

Here we think ourselves healthy when we feel nothing painful in ourselves. Yet we are sometimes deceived in this. Frequently we become ill in some part of the body, but experience it in no way except through some movement of the body or through touch. And what shall we say about those who are not even ill in this limited way, but seem to themselves to be healthy in every respect? How shall we determine whether they are healthy or not?

[Cols. 0632B–C] Imagine for yourself someone in the soundest bodily health, and ask him about his health. In his own judgment he is healthy. Now let such a person be touched somewhat more harshly or be squeezed more tightly in some part of his body, and you will immediately see him cry out: “Stop—you are hurting me; you are tormenting me.” What is this? Did he not previously say that he was healthy? And now, touched only slightly, does he cry out so painfully? Does this person seem healthy to you? I do not think so.

No such health will be given to us, whose salvation is promised to be from the Lord. For God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and “there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). They will no longer hunger or thirst, nor will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat (Isaiah 49:10; Revelation 7:16); for God will cover them with his right hand and defend them with his holy arm (Wisdom 5:17). What, then, will be able to harm those for whom God’s right hand will be a covering?

[Cols. 0632D–0633A] As for what that health will be like, I certainly know that I have learned it neither through anyone’s sensation nor through experience. If someone were to ask me what fevers and the various kinds of illnesses are like, he might easily understand my explanation, both because I have experienced them in myself and because I have learned of them from those who know them through having experienced them in themselves. But something that I have not perceived through sensation, nor learned, as I said, from anyone who has perceived it, cannot be described in the same way.

Nevertheless, I may believe and confidently assert, so far as my judgment allows, that the health of the future life will be so continuous, unchangeable, and inviolate that it will fill the whole person with an ineffable sweetness of delight and drive far away and repel everything that could suggest even the suspicion of any alteration, change, or injury 

Thus the righteous will be healthy. But know that every unjust person there will be afflicted with such great illness that afterward no medicine will be able to cure him.

## Chapter LV. On Pleasure and Anxiety

The sixth part of blessedness is pleasure; of misery, anxiety. People desire the former and avoid the latter. Yet while they seek pleasure in this life, they can find it only through anxiety. And when they reach what they think is pleasure, they can enjoy it only by laboring. If they indulge in it excessively, it turns back into anxiety  Nevertheless, because they take some kind of delight in it, they do not suffer complete anxiety.

After this life, however, they will either be in complete pleasure  or will be completely filled with anxiety.

## Chapter LVI. The Simile of Red-Hot Iron

For just as red-hot iron contains fire in every part of itself, so the good will feel pleasure in themselves, while the evil will feel anxiety. I do not think that anyone living or having lived in this mortality has experienced or tasted this pleasure as it is, in such a way that he could explain its flavor or character to others 

## Chapter LVII. On Two Blessed States and an Equal Number of Miseries



Nevertheless, let us say something to make this clear. Let us say that there are two blessed states and likewise two miseries, namely a greater and a lesser. The greater blessed state is the kingdom of God; the lesser is the joy of paradise, in which Adam was first placed. Likewise, we call the greater misery the eternal fire of Gehenna; the lesser misery we acknowledge to be the sufferings of the present life, which we endure continually while we live.

[Cols. 0633C–D] We have never experienced either blessed state. But if at least we had experienced that lesser blessedness which Adam possessed when placed in paradise, perhaps through it we could somehow conjecture and see the greater, just as now, born, nourished, and grown up in the lesser misery, we can whenever we wish describe and explain many things about the greater misery.

[Col. 0634A] Since, then, the pleasure of which we are speaking is one portion of supreme blessedness, I do not see how to explain it so that it may be grasped [Col. 0634A], unless perhaps we undertake this through some great contrary likeness of the misery that we conjecture from the lesser 

Let a certain person, for example, be placed before the eyes of the heart: someone who has red-hot, glowing iron fixed not only in the pupils of his eyes but also in each of his limbs, so that neither his marrow nor his intestines, nor anything at all in his entire body, is free from the enormity of that torture or feels it in any lesser degree than in his eyes.

What shall I say—that he is distressed? Who would judge him to be sane amid such things?

[Cols. 0634A–B] In the same way, but with the consideration entirely reversed, in that future life an ineffable delight will intoxicate the good and satisfy them wholly with its immeasurable sweetness and indescribable abundance. What did I say—wholly? Their eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, hands, feet, throat, heart, liver, lungs, bones, marrow, even their very inward parts , and all their limbs individually and separately, will be filled with a common and wondrous sense of delight and sweetness, so that truly the whole person will drink from the torrent of God’s pleasure and be intoxicated by the abundance of his house (Psalm 35:9).

But, as has been said, we believe the opposite concerning the unjust.

## Chapter LVIII. On Longevity and the Brevity of Life

The seventh part of blessedness is longevity; of misery, the brevity of life. The former perfects the blessedness of the body, while the latter perfects its misery. For the body can first possess the aforementioned parts of blessedness when it is able to retain them for a long time. If it possessed them all and immediately lost them by dying, what benefit would it have gained from possessing them?

But no one who is destined to die can possess perfect longevity. However long he may live, what he has lived seems to him, when he dies, like a dream  Therefore a person does not possess longevity here, where he is destined at some point to die. Yet because he could die sooner, he does not possess an entirely brief life here either. In the future, however, he will have either the longest life or the briefest life.

For if he has lived well now, then he will live as long as God, because it is written: “But the righteous will live forever” (Wisdom 5:16)  But if he has lived badly, then he will be able to live there only by dying. Nothing, therefore, is briefer than that life to which death is always joined 

Now it should be noted that the seven aforementioned parts of blessedness and misery [Col. 0634D] pertain to the body; the remaining parts that follow pertain to the soul.

## Chapter LIX. On Wisdom and Folly

The eighth part of blessedness pertaining to the soul is wisdom; of misery, folly  A person thinks that he possesses wisdom and lacks folly if he has recognized something that another person does not know. But what wisdom does someone possess who does not know himself? For who can perfectly recognize what sort of thing his soul is? Or who knows what his body is like internally, or behind, or even externally?

Yet because he can in some way know both himself and other things, he is not altogether foolish. But in the future he will either be perfectly wise or entirely foolish.

Wisdom, then, which all do not uselessly love in this life , will be so great in the good in the future life that they will be ignorant of nothing they wish to know. For the good person will be filled with the perfect wisdom that God is and will behold it face to face. When he has thus looked upon it, he will see the nature of the whole creation , which exists better in God than in itself.

Then the righteous will know everything that God has made knowable: both the things that are past and those that will afterward be future. There each will be known by all, and all by each. No one will be ignorant of the homeland, nation, or lineage from which anyone was born, or even of what he did in his life.

## Chapter LX. That the Sins of Individuals Are Revealed to All



Here perhaps someone will say: “What is this? Will everyone know the sins I committed? I confessed them so that they might be erased and forgotten, so that they might no longer be disclosed to anyone.”

[Cols. 0635B–C] Good. But when you stand present before God’s face in that glory, cleansed of every stain of wrongdoing, will you be able to be ungrateful to him for the great mercy he showed you by forgiving those sins and those offenses?

“No,” you will say.

“And how,” I ask, “will you give thanks if you retain in your memory none of the things for which you rightly ought to give thanks?” 

Thus, in order that you may delight eternally in his praises, you will, as I think, always have before you how great a misery you were rescued from.

Therefore, when the consciences of individuals are open to each other, I dare to say that those sins too will be open to all the elect, for whose healing you will continually be grateful to God—not for your confusion, but for the great mercy of God, for his glorification, and for your own shared rejoicing.

For you will not then be more distressed in heart on account of your sins, nor more ashamed of your crimes, than someone who was once wounded by great injuries and is now healed in every respect is distressed by the discomfort of an illness that has been abolished. Or does an old man now feel ashamed of something he did as an infant in the cradle?

[Cols. 0635D–0636A] For then, when complete health, perfect purity, full forgiveness, and secure impunity from all offenses have certainly smiled upon you , the recognition or recollection of your sins will be no more a horror or source of shame to you than the denial of Christ is now to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; than the sins of blessed Mary Magdalene are to her; or than the many crimes of many others that have already been forgiven 

Moreover, when your offenses have been recognized, the piety, power, and wisdom of the physician who healed you will be more sublimely admired, praised, and magnified by all, just as in your enormous and foul illness  But the praise and magnificence of God’s glory is, if you understand it well, your glory.

“But,” you will say, “I certainly agree that the praise of God is my glory. Yet when so many and such great innocent people appear here and there in comparison with me—people who, considering the obscenities of my life, will rightly judge me to be altogether an object of horror—what shall I say?”

Justice demands its own reward, and injustice its own reward.

Brother, do not be afraid in this matter. It will be otherwise than you think. You will not find there the person whom you judge innocent in comparison with yourself thinking about you in the way you suppose. For the person of whom you speak clearly understands that when you sinned you offended not him but God  When, therefore, he sees that God has entirely forgiven you what was owed, it will not enter his heart to judge you in any way on that account. For he would recognize that he was offending God himself if he thought that you, reconciled to God in every respect, ought in any way to be despised for what you once did.

[Col. 0636C] Rather, he will marvel at God’s ineffable clemency, not only in your case , but also in his own. In you, because God rescued you from such a profound depth of iniquity; in himself, because God’s grace alone held him back from falling into the same depth.

Thus, in praising God, he will magnify in you, after God’s grace, the strength and steadfastness by which, striving, you bravely escaped so great an abyss of evil. He will also consider that, unless he had been aided by God, he perhaps would not have remained so firmly on the path of righteousness 

You see, then, how the public knowledge of your sin contains no reproach; indeed, how much praise and thanksgiving the knowledge of its forgiveness will produce.

## Chapter LXI. A Debate between a Righteous Person and an Angel



[Col. 0636D]

Even if the angels wished to judge you unworthy of their fellowship because of your sins, you would have a legitimate defense against them.

“How?” you ask.

[Col. 0637A] Listen. Imagine an angel reproaching you with words such as these:

“You, human being made from dust, you dust who will one day become dust again—you exalted yourself against God, against his commandment; swollen with every sin and impurity, you cast yourself into filth, and now you seek to be like us, whom you see never having acted against God’s will in anything?”

To this you should reply:

“If I, as you say, was made from dust , then certainly it is not surprising that, driven by the wind of temptation, I fell into the filth of crimes. But once I had recognized and believed in Christ’s mercy, rejecting everything that I could know he did not wish, I exercised myself in everything I understood he did wish.

“Therefore I did not refuse to endure, for his honor, tribulations and anguish, hunger and thirst, vigils, beatings, insults, and countless other forms of suffering. Making light, to the extent of my strength, of everything worldly , I strove at every point to be reconciled solely through his grace [Col. 0637B].

“But what of these things have you ever endured for his sake? Glory has always accompanied you; delight has always accompanied you; God’s right hand has always held and defended you from the assault of every sin, so that no stain of sin could steal upon you.

“Therefore, if you have not departed from his will, that is his gift, since you have continually been held by him . But because this argument concerns only those who did violence to their own destruction  and seized the kingdom of heaven by force (Matthew 11:12), others who are there but will enter by another way will claim the purity of the angels for another reason.”

“But how?” you ask. “Perhaps in this way?”

They will say to them:

“That we seek to be blessed equally in the kingdom of God, we ascribe to the gift and grace of Jesus Christ our Lord, who deigned to become human, suffer, and die for this purpose: to make us, justified from every offense by his blood, sharers in that kingdom.

“You, therefore, consider whether the blood of Christ, which was poured out for us, can fail to be the perfect cause of our salvation.”

What could the angels say in response—angels who, because they are good, willingly wish to yield to reason—except that what had been said was grounded in reason , and that such people rightly ought to receive their equality?

Therefore, when the angels and the people whom you had judged more innocent  agree with you, and when in all things they grant honor to the truth of reason, consider, if you can, how pleasing that wisdom will be by which in that life you will be known by all, just as all will be known by you .

But if you are evil, and indeed entirely deprived of wisdom , you will be pressed by such great pains that you will become not merely foolish, but altogether insane.

## Chapter LXII. On Friendship and Enmity

[Col. 0638A]

The ninth part of blessedness is friendship; of misery, enmity. Perfect friendship is friendship that cannot be turned into enmity. But who here possesses such great friendship—even a son toward his father? Yet because no one here possesses such great enmity that it cannot be turned into friendship , no one here possesses complete enmity. In the future, however, each person will find either perfect friendship or complete enmity 

For God and all the other good people will love every good person in such a way that they can no longer hate him. For each person will love another as much and for as long as he loves himself. Nor do I see how it could be otherwise, especially since all are one body in Christ, and Christ, who is peace itself, is the head of all. They will embrace one another with no less affection than the members of one body are joined to one another.

How abundant in love do you think you will be when this has come into your possession? 

Nevertheless, pass beyond these things and contemplate him through whom these good things have come to you. You will perceive that he loves you incomparably more than you love yourself and than all others love themselves, and that you will love him, above yourself and above all others, with an ineffable sweetness.

But God and all the good will hate every evil person in such a way that not even a son will feel affection for his father when he sees him in punishment.

## Chapter LXIII. On Concord and Discord

[Col. 0638C]

The tenth part of blessedness is concord; of misery, discord. A person possesses concord here so rarely that he is not always even in agreement with himself . For body and soul disagree with each other, so that what one desires the other does not wish. Yet because they do not always act this way , but sometimes desire the same thing, they do not remain in complete discord.

In the other life they will persist either in concord or in complete discord. The body and soul of every saint—or rather, all the righteous—will possess such great concord as our eyes now possess. For just as one eye cannot turn in a direction in which the other does not also turn, but both are always moved toward the same place, so the body and soul, or that society of the righteous, will never be able to desire different things , but will always have the same will.

For we shall be one body. We shall be one Church, the bride of Christ, whoever we may be who are there. God’s will will not differ from yours; rather, just as you will what he wills, so he will will in all things what you will. For how could the head differ from its own body?

## Chapter LXIV. That All the Righteous Will Desire the Same Thing

Here perhaps you will say:

“Come now! If God and the whole company of the blessed will then desire what I desire, and will desire an increase of my good along with me—something that I will not be able not to desire there—then, according to my will, I shall be among the greater ones in heaven.”

I answer this weakness of yours. If you wish to be equal in glory even to blessed Peter, you will be. I say “in glory,” because you will not be able to wish to be Peter in person. For if you wished this, you would wish yourself to be nothing, which you will not be able to wish.

Nor will you be able to wish to equal him in glory if you are inferior to him in merits, because you will love the most beautiful arrangement of his body, which you would see violated by such a change, more than any advantage. Even in the human body, the foot does not wish to perform the place or function of the hand, nor the hand that of the foot; nor does the mouth or nose wish to be where the eyes are, nor the eyes where the mouth is. Nor does the nose, leaving its own place, desire to be transferred; and if it were transferred, it would not endure it suitably or without injury.

In the same way, in that wondrous and glorified arrangement, and in the equally ordered glorification of God’s blessed city, each person will love whatever he has attained in such a way that he will not wish his condition to be changed to a higher rank.

Why? Because each person’s happiness and blessedness, mercifully allotted to him according to his merits, will be sufficient for him.

Moreover, if those who have already been placed in the unity of that body desired greater things than they had attained, they would be miserable for the very reason that they did not yet possess what they wanted  For whenever something a person desires is lacking, he must be miserable in that respect. But may all misery be absent from that kingdom. Thus everyone will have complete sufficiency, which unanimous and perfect concord will bring to completion in each person.

But the evil will persist in such great discord that their body and soul will always disagree. For the body will hate the soul because it once conceived evil thoughts, and the soul will hate the body because it carried those evil thoughts into action; and for all these things they will be tortured in punishments 

## Chapter LXV. On Honor and Dishonor

The eleventh part of blessedness is called honor; of misery, dishonor. A person desires to be honored by everyone , either in their words or in their actions. In words, so that they may praise him; in actions, so that they may place him before themselves.

But when he desires such honor, it is as though one worm sought to be praised by other worms and to be placed above them in rule  Nevertheless, although this honor is almost nothing, no one here can possess it fully. For no emperor is praised by everyone or placed above all others. Yet because no one here is cursed by everyone or placed beneath all others, he is not wholly without honor.

In the future, however, a person will either be honored or, conversely, be utterly dishonored  Let us briefly consider what sort of honor this is through an example.

## Chapter LXVI. On a Poor Man Adopted into the Kingdom



Let some poor man be placed before our eyes, deprived of every comfort, corrupted by the foulness of ulcers and other illnesses, and stripped of every covering by which he might be protected from the harshness of the cold. Suppose that a very powerful king, passing by, sees this man lying in such a condition and unable to help himself in any way [Col. 0640B]. Taking pity on him, the king orders his ulcers to be treated; once he has been cured, he commands that the man be brought before him dressed in royal ornaments; then he adopts him as a son. Afterward he orders that throughout his kingdom he be regarded by everyone as his son, that no one contradict him in anything he commands, and he appoints him his heir and co-heir with his own son, wishing him to be called by his own name.

Would you not say that this man had been magnificently and unexpectedly honored?

Certainly God will do all these things for us. Born from the rottenness of flesh, we are filled with many miseries (Job 14). Finding us established in these miseries, deprived of every comfort, subject to the sufferings of every illness, and full of the ulcers of sins and corruptibility, he will receive and heal us, moved solely by mercy. Restored to health, he will adorn us with the ornaments of perfect righteousness and incorruptibility; then he will adopt us as his sons, make us sharers and heirs of his kingdom, and establish us as members of the body and co-heirs with his only-begotten Son, who is equal to him in every respect and co-omnipotent. He will command every creature to obey us in everything we wish, and, called by his name, he will make us gods.

For he himself says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 82:6).

But God himself is the one who deifies; you, by contrast, are a deified god.

Perhaps, however, you say:

“Your argument may indeed hold true for those great apostles or martyrs, but in my case—if only I might deserve to be even the least among them!—I do not understand how it can stand.”

To this, please attend and understand: God excluded no righteous person from this divinity when he said: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

## Chapter LXVII. The Simile between God and Fire



But so that what has been said may become clearer, consider, by way of an example, the nature of fire and the nature of things made fiery. Perhaps there you may to some extent imagine how, according to your capacity, you can be deified by participating in that supreme majesty 

Behold: fire is one, and in its own nature hot. Put wood, lead, and iron together into this fire. When the wood has been turned into coals and the lead melted, so that nothing but fire appears in the coals and no further heat can be added to the lead, they still cannot be equal to the iron in heat, since perhaps it has not yet been thoroughly inflamed by the fire.

Thus, although one thing may have advanced further than another in heat, while the nature of each remains preserved, in the customary manner of speaking, that which is fiery is said to be fire in itself.

So it will be in that blessed society of the citizens above of which we are speaking  For just as those who are nearer to the supreme Divinity, and therefore superior to others, will be called gods, so those who are lower than them—because they participate, according to their capacity, in the one and same supreme Divinity in which the others participate—must likewise be called gods.

Such honor, as we stated earlier, will be displayed to the righteous according to the measure of their merits. But whoever is evil will, by contrast, be so dishonored  that, cast down amid every stench, he will even be subjected to the dominion of worms.

## Textual apparatus

The readings below follow the supplied apparatus in source order. Sigla identify the witnesses named there; “manuscripts” means the apparatus does not identify individual witnesses. Source forms are retained where English alone would hide a distinction.

**LIII, freedom (Cols. 0631B–C; notes at 0631D).** A.1 has *Liber est qui*, “Free is one who,” for *liber est ille, qui*, “Free is that person who.” The manuscripts and Cologne read *Cum tamen*, “Yet since/although,” for *Quia tamen*, “Yet because.” A.1 has *omnimodam inibit servitutem*, “will enter complete servitude,” contrasted in the note with *omnino servituti subjacebit*, “will be wholly subject to servitude.” Vict. and Cologne read *ut praediximus auctoritate*, “as we stated by authority,” for *ut jam praediximus, et auctoritate*, “as we have already stated, and by authority.” They have *angelis enim consimiles*, “for [we shall be] like the angels”; the text omits *enim*, “for.” The manuscripts have *clausula*, “a closure,” for *clausura*, “an enclosure.” They read *non extet*, “may not exist,” Cologne *non esset*, “would not exist”; the contrasting form recorded in the note is anomalous *non exercet*, “does not exercise,” while the narrative prints *non exstet*.

**LIV, health (Cols. 0631D–0632D).** The manuscripts insert *autem*, “however,” in *illa autem homo*, “that, however, a person ….” They read *lacessere*, “to provoke/assail,” for *lacescere*, “to grow weary”; the variant infinitive is anomalous in the list of an infant's sufferings. They omit *vel*, “or,” before *paralyticus*, “paralyzed.” A.1, Vict.13, and Cologne read *afficitur infirmus*, “is afflicted, ill,” for *efficitur infirmus*, “becomes ill.” A.1 has *nec summae*, “nor [subject] to the utmost,” against *non summae*, “not [subject] to the utmost.” At the comparison with true health, Vict. reads *nihil sanitatis quod ei*, “nothing of health which to it …”; Cologne has *nihil est sanitatis quod ei*, “there is nothing of health which to it …”; the contrasting apparatus wording is *nil sanitatis quod est, ei*, “nothing of health which exists, to it ….” The narrative's own *nihil est sanitas* is grammatically disrupted; these readings concern the claim that mortal experience provides no comparable health. At the explanation from experience, Vict. and Cologne have *tum quia illas in me*, “then because those [illnesses] in me …,” against the apparatus's *tamen quia ego illas in me*, “yet because I [experienced] those in myself”; the narrative prints *tum quia ergo illas in me*, with an additional *ergo*, “therefore.”

**LIV–LVI, health's permanence and pleasure (Cols. 0633A–C; notes at 0633D).** Vict. and Cologne read *vicissitudinis, immutabilitatis*, “of alteration, of immutability,” against *vicissitudinis, mutabilitatis*, “of alteration, of mutability”; the contradictory “immutability” is the witness reading. The manuscripts have *quo si etiam*, “and if even by/in which,” for *quod si etiam*, “but if even.” A.1, Vict.13, and Cologne have *vertitur*, “is turned,” against *convertitur*, “is transformed.” The apparatus records *aut in omnimoda voluptate erunt, aut*, “either they will be in complete pleasure, or,” in manuscripts A.; Vict. and Cologne have *aut voluptate, aut*, “either in pleasure, or”; the contrasting text is *aut in omnimoda voluptate sunt*, “either they are in complete pleasure.” The manuscripts and Cologne read *qui eum ut est*, “who [has experienced] him/it as he/it is,” with masculine *eum*, for feminine *qui eam, ut est*, “who [has experienced] it as it is,” referring to pleasure.

**LVII, the two blessednesses and miseries (Cols. 0633C–0634B; notes at 0633D).** S. Germ. A.1 omits this entire chapter. Vict. and Cologne omit *illud*, “that,” from *forte illud agamus*, “perhaps we might do that.” The manuscript and Cologne have *conjecturamus* for *conjectamus*, both “we conjecture,” with different verbal forms. The manuscripts read *extra etiam*, “even outside,” for *exta etiam*, “even the entrails.” At *homo de torrente*, “the person from the torrent,” the note attributes exactly that same form to Vict. and Cologne and repeats it as the contrasting reading: no difference is discernible in the supplied note.

**LVIII, length of life (Cols. 0634B–D; notes at 0633D).** A.1 reads *somnium sibi*, “a dream to himself”; Vict.13 has *somnia sibi*, “dreams to himself”; the contrasting form in the apparatus is *somnum sibi*, “sleep to himself.” Vict.13 has *unde scriptum est*, “whence it is written,” for *quia scriptum est*, “because it is written.” The manuscripts and Cologne omit *ergo*, “therefore,” from *nihil ergo brevius illa*, “therefore nothing [is] shorter than that [life].”

**LIX, wisdom (Cols. 0634D–0635B).** A.1 has *ad animam pertinens*, “pertaining to the soul,” in the nominative, for genitive *ad animam pertinentis*, “of [blessedness] pertaining to the soul.” Vict.13 reads *vita non inutiliter amant*, “they do not uselessly love [it] in life”; Cologne *vita amant*, “they love [it] in life”; the contrasting form is *vita non utiliter amat*, “he/she does not usefully love [it] in life.” A.1, Vict., and Cologne have *natura videbit*, “nature will see,” with nominative *natura*, for *naturam videbit*, “[the person] will see nature,” with an accusative object; the variant's case is irregular in this context.

**LX, the disclosure of sins (Cols. 0635B–0636C; notes at 0635D).** A.1 omits the entire chapter. The manuscript and Cologne read *gratias agens*, “giving thanks,” for *gratias ages*, “you will give thanks.” The manuscripts and Cologne have *audeo eo quoque*, “I dare by/for that also …,” for *audeo ea quoque*, “I dare [to say] those things also ….” They read *scelerumque magis*, “and more [ashamed] of crimes,” for *scelerumve tuorum magis*, “or more [ashamed] of your crimes.” They have *tibi recto arris[erit]*, an anomalous *recto*, “straight/right,” at “has smiled upon you,” for *tibi certo arriserit*, “has certainly smiled upon you.” Vict.13 has *abnegatio sua*, “his own denial,” for *abjuratio sua*, “his own renunciation.” Vict. and Cologne include *tuis*, “your,” in *delictis tuis velut*, “your sins, as if …,” against *delictis velut*, “sins, as if ….” They have *infirmitate tua*, “in your illness,” for *infirmitate sua*, “in his own illness.” The manuscripts and Cologne have *illud quidem*, “that indeed,” for *illum siquidem*, “for that man ….” Vict. and Cologne read *namque videas*, “for you may see,” for *namque videns*, “for, seeing ….” The manuscripts, Vict., and Cologne read *plane intelligit te, neque*, “he clearly understands you, and not …”; the contrasting apparatus form is *plane nequaquam intelliget te, nequaquam*, “he will clearly not understand you at all, not at all ….” The narrative itself prints *plane intelligit te nequaquam*, “he clearly understands that you in no way ….” Vict. and Cologne have *nec solum in te*, “nor only in you,” for *non solum in te*, “not only in you.” They read *juxta quam, et*, “beside which, and,” for *juxta quam, quod et*, “beside which, which also …,” in the comparison with the abyss of evil.

The description *tu Deo gratiosus existes* can mean “you will be pleasing to God” or, in the context of remembering his mercy and giving thanks, “you will be grateful to God”; the translation follows the surrounding thanksgiving argument without suppressing that lexical ambiguity.

**LXI, the righteous person and the angel (Cols. 0636D–0638A; notes at 0637D).** A.1 has only the final words of this chapter. The manuscripts and Cologne have *contra voluntatem Dei*, “against God's will,” for *voluntati Dei*, “to God's will,” in the clause about opposing it. Vict. and Cologne omit *tu*, “you,” from *ut tu dicis*, “as you say.” They have *nihil pendens*, literally “weighing nothing,” for *nihili pendens*, “reckoning [worldly things] of no account.” They read *non recessistis, illius*, “you have not departed; of him …,” for *non cecidistis, ipsius*, “you have not fallen; of that same one ….” The manuscripts and Cologne read *qui salvationi suae*, “who to their own salvation …,” against *qui perditioni suae*, “who to their own perdition …,” before “did violence.” They have *rapuerunt: ideo alii*, “seized; therefore others,” for *rapuerunt. Alii*, “seized. Others.” At *aequalitate beati*, “blessed in equality,” the apparatus repeats the same reading on both sides; the narrative instead has *aequaliter beari*, “to be blessed equally.” The manuscripts and Cologne have *rationi veri acquiescere*, “to assent to the reasoning of truth,” for *rationi acquiescere*, “to assent to reasoning.” Vict. and Cologne read *ratione moti*, “moved by reason,” for *ratione niti*, “to rest upon reason.” L. transposes *magis judicaveras te*, “[whom] you had judged more [innocent] than yourself,” against *magis te judicaveras*, with *te* placed before the verb. Vict. and Cologne include *etiam*, “also,” in *verum etiam omnino*, “but also entirely,” against *verum omnino*, “but entirely.”

**LXII, friendship (Cols. 0638A–B; notes at 0637D).** The manuscripts omit *hic*, “here,” in *sed quis hic habet*, “but who here possesses …?” The manuscripts and Cologne read *amicitiam tantam quae converti non possit in inimicitiam*, “such great friendship that it cannot be turned into enmity,” for *inimicitiam tantam quae converti non possit in amicitiam*, “such great enmity that it cannot be turned into friendship.” This is a reversal of the two nouns, not “enmity turned into enmity.” They have *nec ullus omnino habet hic inimicitiam summam, aut amicitiam. In futuro*, “nor does anyone here possess complete enmity or friendship. In the future …,” against *nec omnino habet hic inimicitiam summam. In futuro*, “nor does [a person] here possess complete enmity. In the future ….” They read *autem perfectam, aut inimicitiam quisque*, “however, perfect [friendship], or enmity, each person …,” against *autem aut amicitiam magnam vel perfectam, aut inimicitiam quisque*, “however, either great or perfect friendship, or enmity, each person ….” Vict. and Cologne omit *quantum*, “how much,” at *quantum putas*, “how much do you think …?”

**LXIII–LXIV, concord and discord (Cols. 0638C–0639C).** A.1 omits *vero*, “however,” from *concordiam vero homo*, “concord, however, a person ….” It reads plural *non semper haec*, “not always these things,” for singular *non semper hoc*, “not always this.” The manuscripts and Cologne have *vel diversum*, “or something different,” for *velle diversum*, “to wish something different.” Vict. and Cologne read *quod nondum haberent*, “because they would not yet possess,” for *quo nondum haberent*, “whereby they would not yet possess.” The manuscript reads present *torquentur in*, “they are tormented in,” for future *torquebuntur in*, “they will be tormented in.”

**LXV, honor (Cols. 0639D–0640A).** A.1 reads *ab omnibus appetit*, “desires [honor] from everyone,” for *ab hominibus appetit*, “desires [it] from people.” A.1 and Cologne have *unus vermis*, “one worm,” for *mus unus*, “one mouse.” Vict. and Cologne read *inhonorabitur* for *exhonorabitur*, both “will be dishonored,” with different prefixes.

**LXVI–LXVII, adoption and participation (Cols. 0640A–0641B).** Vict. and Cologne title LXVI *De paupere in regnum adoptata*, “On a poor person adopted into a kingdom,” with anomalous feminine *adoptata*; the contrasting heading is *De paupere in regem adoptato*, “On a poor man adopted as king.” The narrative heading has *in regnum adoptato*, “adopted into a kingdom,” with masculine *adoptato*. Vict. and Cologne omit *illum*, “him,” from *illum videret*, “[the king] saw him.” They title LXVII *Similitudo inter Deum et ignem*, “A likeness between God and fire,” against *similitudine inter ignem et Deitatem*, “By/in a likeness between fire and divinity.” They read *summae majestati*, “in/to the supreme majesty,” for *summae Deitati*, “in/to the supreme divinity.” The manuscripts and Cologne have *de qua loquitur*, “of which he speaks,” for *de qua loquimur*, “of which we speak.” Vict. and Cologne insert *sit*, “may be,” in *malus sit, econtra*, “may be evil, on the contrary,” against *malus, econtra*, “evil, on the contrary.”

The twelfth part of blessedness is power; of misery, powerlessness. Truly, he possesses power who can do whatever he wishes. Since no one here is capable of doing this, no one here can possess true power [Note: [Col. 0641D] “wishes, can do”: manuscript A.1 reads, “wishes, can.”]. Yet because at times he can do what he wishes, he is not altogether subject to powerlessness. In the future, however, he will either be truly all-powerful or altogether and perpetually powerless.

The good person will be able to do whatever he wishes, because he will have the Almighty himself agreeing with his will in everything [Note: “But the good person, whatever he wishes”: manuscript A.1 reads, “But the good person, whatever he wishes.”]. The wicked person, however, will be able to do nothing that he wishes. When, therefore, you have acquired this omnipotence with so great an honor and together with all the other things mentioned above, I do not see how you could desire anything greater.

Therefore, while you are happy in possessing these blessed states that we have set out, will you not seem sufficient to yourself?

“Especially so,” you say.

“Come, then. If you were to live securely in all these things for even one day, just as they have been described, you would doubtless rejoice. But if you were made joyful for a month, or for one year, or for the whole period of your life, what would you do? It cannot even be said, I think, what limit there would be to your joy. I would gladly give the price—whatever I possessed, and even myself besides—if by this means, and no other, I could obtain these things” [Note: “What would you do? Nor can the measure of joy even be stated, I think. I would give the price”: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “What would you do? Would you give the price?”].

But if you were still entirely secure that, while you lived, you would lose them through no event whatsoever, I shall not say whether you could even imagine what exultation would be lacking to you [Note: “Whether you could imagine”: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “whether you could also imagine.”].

## CHAPTER LXIX. On security and fear

Receive as the thirteenth part of blessedness security, and as the corresponding misery, fear. This indeed confirms all the other parts of blessedness, and they cannot be possessed perfectly without it. For a person possesses them perfectly when he fears losing them nowhere.

In this life, however, no one can possess anything by which he can be secure. At the same moment, a rich man may become poor and a living man dead. Therefore here he possesses neither the other parts of blessedness nor perfect security [Note: “They cannot be possessed firmly and perfectly without it. Yet”: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “They cannot be possessed perfectly without it. Yet”; the manuscripts of Bec and A.1 read, “They cannot be possessed perfectly without it. Then a person possesses them perfectly when he fears losing them nowhere. Yet”].

Nevertheless, since a person does not always fear what he suffers [Note: “He does not always suffer what he fears”: the manuscripts read, “He does not always fear what he suffers.”], but can sometimes escape it, he does not here have the greatest fear. In the future, however, he will have either perfect security or, conversely, the greatest fear. The good person will have whatever he wishes and will fear losing nothing of it.

## CHAPTER LXX. That no one loses the goods once acquired

I say that, if he is going to lose them, either he himself will wish of his own accord to lose them, or God will wish to take them away from him when he wishes to lose them, or someone stronger than God will come and take them from him against the will both of God and of the person himself.

But certainly neither will he himself wish, after casting away so great a good, to fall back into the miseries from which he will rejoice gratefully to have escaped; nor will God, who bestowed it upon him with such generous and merciful goodness, wish ever to take it away from him [Note: “He will ever take it away from him”: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “He will ever take these things away from him”]; nor will anyone stronger than God come along who, while God protects what is just, could in any way take this from him against his will.

The wicked person, however, will both always fear the torments that he will suffer and never be able to escape from them.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On joy and sadness

The fourteenth part of blessedness is joy, and of misery, sadness [Note: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “Therefore the fourteenth part of blessedness.”]. Only the person who can obtain all the aforementioned parts of blessedness can possess perfect joy. Since no one here can possess any one of them, it is clear that here he cannot retain the greatest joy [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “cannot possess the greatest joy,” instead of “cannot retain the greatest joy.”].

Likewise, only the person whom all the aforementioned parts of misery entirely constrain truly suffers the greatest sadness [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “only he can suffer the greatest sadness.”]. But since no one here suffers all of them completely, it is evident that here no one possesses the greatest sadness [Note: Manuscripts A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “nor is the greatest sadness possessed here.”].

In the future age, however, each person will be filled either with the greatest joy or with the greatest sadness. For every good person will then be able to rejoice completely [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “will then be able to rejoice perfectly”], because he will possess all the aforementioned parts of blessedness perfectly.

What, then, is more blessed than the person who will be filled with such great joy [Note: The manuscripts read, “With what joy will the just person then be filled?”]? Yet he will have something else in addition, by which he may rejoice even more. Since each person will love another as himself, it is clear that he will rejoice in the other’s happiness as in his own. How many, then, and how great will be the joys of the person who will exult in so many and such great blessednesses of the saints? And if he will rejoice so greatly over others, whom he will love as himself, how greatly will he exult over God, whom he will love above himself?

For joy will be within him and outside him; joy above and below; joy all around him—joy everywhere, complete joy.

The wicked person, on the other hand, will be filled with the greatest sadness, because he will inevitably and without end suffer all the parts of misery by which he will nevertheless feel himself surrounded, and will suffer them without interruption [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “mentally” (mentaliter); the printed text reads inevitabiliter, with the spacing “inevita biliter.”].

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the desire for worldly honor

Those who desire the honors of this world act like children who chase butterflies [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “For this is how they act.”]. When butterflies fly, they never keep to a straight path but dart here and there; and when they seem to settle somewhere [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “when they seem to be settling”; manuscript L reads, “when they have settled”], they do not remain there long. When children wish to catch them, they hasten to run after them; and because they look not at their own feet but at the butterflies, they sometimes fall into a pit and grievously injure themselves.

Often, however, when they see the butterflies settled somewhere [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor, together with the Cologne edition, read, “settled somewhere”], they proceed gently and cautiously so that they may be able to seize them. While doing this, they also clap their hands and say to one another in a soft voice: “Look, now we shall have them; look, now we shall have them” [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “Look, now we shall have them, look, now we shall have them.”]. But when they draw nearer and try to grasp them, the butterflies fly away.

If they do happen to catch them, they rejoice over nothing, as though they had acquired something great. In the same way act those who desire the honors of this world. The honors of this world never follow a fixed course; rather, by uncertain byways, they fly from one person to another. When they have come to rest under someone’s power, they cannot remain there long.

While foolish people desire to pursue them, they hurry after them by whatever means they can. And because they do not consider how they might attain them but only how they might obtain them by any means whatsoever [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “but only how they might obtain them”], they often fall into serious crimes, by which they gravely injure their souls.

Sometimes, when they see the honors somewhere as though prepared for them, they approach secretly and very craftily, so that they may obtain them as though no one knew. As they draw near, they rejoice and exult greatly. But when they have come closer and think that they can now grasp them, the honors shake themselves from their hands and for some reason transfer themselves to others.

If they should ever obtain them, they congratulate themselves as though they had achieved some true honor, although they cannot reach the summit of true honor unless they have abandoned these honors in satisfaction for the offenses they have committed [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “in accordance with their offenses,” instead of “in satisfaction for their offenses.”].

## CHAPTER LXXIII. A likeness between God and a certain master

Thus matters stand between God and human beings as they do between a certain master and his servants, who are commonly called “natural” servants.

If a master commands something to a natural servant and the servant willingly obeys his master, the servant does what he ought and what pleases his master [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “and what pleases the master.”]. But if he resists the commands of his master, he immediately loses the master’s favor.

If he wishes to regain it and thereafter to serve his master faithfully, as he ought naturally to have done from the beginning, then, if the master commands him, he swears that he will obey his commands and serve him more faithfully for as long as he lives [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “and will serve him faithfully.”]. Once he has done this, the master forgives him what he has done wrong and, if it pleases the master, permits him to possess some property from which he may live [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “if it pleases him,” instead of “if it pleases the master.”].

After some time has passed, however, the servant gradually begins to forget what he had sworn and grows lukewarm in his love for his master. And because what the master commands seems harsh to him, he first transgresses some things and afterward more, until he is considered almost perjured in everything. Thus he again loses the favor of his master, which he had previously regained by promising to amend his ways.

What more, then, will he do [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “What will he do?”]? What else can he promise? He has corrupted his natural right and violated his oath.

Yet the servant finds something else that can still be done. By his master’s permission, he had retained some property [Note: The manuscripts read, “he had retained some property”; the Cologne edition reads, “he had retained something in his property”; Victor 13 reads, “he had retained something from the property”; another reading is, “he had retained it as property”], from which he could reconcile himself as before.

After he recognizes that he has erred [Note: Victor’s manuscript reads, “recognizes that he has sinned”], he returns to his master, entreating him with words such as these [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “praying to him”]:

“Master,” he says, “I confess my wrongdoing: what I naturally owed you, and what afterward I promised by oath, I have wholly transgressed to my own misery. But, if it pleases you, forgive me once more for whatever I have done wrong [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “forgive me still, if it pleases you,” instead of “forgive me once more”]. I shall return to you whatever property I have retained until now by your permission [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “whatever property I have retained until now”; Victor’s manuscript reads, “whatever property I have retained from you until now”].

“I shall bind myself to your service in such a way that I will abandon my own will altogether and, insofar as I can, do your will. And, so that I may always be able to fulfill it, I shall place myself under the authority of those who know and wish to teach it to me [Note: Manuscript A. reads, “who know how to teach it to me”], and who by admonishing, reproving, and chastising will make me keep it. I will swear all these things to you, if you forgive me whatever I have done wrong until now.”

Then the master says: “I still forgive you everything that you ask, if you do everything that you promise. But know this: unless you keep this agreement, or if you violate it in any way by accident [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “if by some accident”], and unless you return to the same agreement through repentance [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “unless you return to the same repentance”], you will not be able to appease me by another agreement.”

In the same way, then, matters stand between God and human beings. God gave the first man a command; if he had obeyed it, he would certainly have pleased God [Note: The manuscripts read, “if he had obeyed, he would certainly have done what he ought to do and what would have pleased God.”]. But because he transgressed that command, he immediately lost God’s favor.

If a human being wishes to regain it, he swears in baptism, as God commands, what we heard that servant swear. But because he repeatedly transgresses this as well [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits “repeatedly”], he becomes a monk, abandoning everything together with his own will [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “abandoning everything, a monk.”]. Therefore either the monk will be saved, or else he will be damned [Note: The Cologne edition reads, “or else he will be damned”; another reading, judged erroneous, is “he will be damned in another way.”].

## CHAPTER LXXIV. A likeness between the devil and an unscrupulous litigant

It must be understood that the devil litigates against a human being as an unjust litigant does against another person [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “But it must be understood by him that …”].

An unscrupulous litigant, although he does not have a right case [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “although he does not have a just case”], nevertheless, because of his wickedness, comes to court and tries to present what is unjust as just and what is just as unjust.

But when a legal expert hears him and recognizes that he does not have a right case, he judges as unjust what the litigant had called just, and as just what the litigant had asserted to be unjust. Thus, defeated in court, the man departs sorrowfully, since he will not be able to do anything [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “since he could not do anything else.”].

After some time has passed, however, when he thinks that this judgment has been consigned to oblivion, he begins his case again, saying that he is being wronged. If someone tells him that the matter has already been settled, he says that it was not judged correctly [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “that it was not properly adjudicated.”].

But the person who has already won once should not pay attention to what he says; he should merely say: “What has once been properly settled must not be begun again” [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “He does not pay attention … but merely says that it must not be begun again.”]. In this way he will always be able to free himself from his enemy without difficulty [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “he will always be able to free himself from his enemy without difficulty.”].

Likewise, the devil litigates against a human being. The court of this litigation, however, is the human being’s own heart [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “the heart of some person.”]. The devil comes to this court to litigate. Although he knows that he does not have a just case, he nevertheless asserts there that what is false is true and what is true is false [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “and conversely.”].

There he says that the thought he instills is true—namely, that a person ought to love the world, desire riches and honors, fulfill the desires of the flesh, and do these and similar things. This is indeed false.

On the other hand, he says that it is false that a person ought to abandon the world, despise riches and honors, cut off the desires of the flesh, redeem his sins by almsgiving [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits “redeem his sins by almsgiving”], finally embrace monasticism [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “approach monasticism”], and do these and many other things. All of this is shown to be true.

But when someone who knows how to distinguish between right and wrong thoughts hears the devil saying these things in his heart, he judges the thought that the devil called just to be unjust, and the thought that the devil affirmed to be unjust to be just.

Having made this judgment, he rejects what is unjust and follows what is just. He despises the world [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “despising the world”] and approaches monasticism [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “embraces monasticism.”]. Thus the devil, defeated in the court of the heart, withdraws and is saddened because he could not prevail.

But after the devil hopes that the person has forgotten how he had judged previously [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “how he had judged previously”], thinking that he may find him unprotected in some respect [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits this clause], he returns to the same court of the heart. Renewing the litigation as though it had not been properly settled, he brings his complaint.

If the person knows with certainty that he judged rightly when he decided that the world ought to be abandoned, the devil immediately replies that it was not right for him to desert it so quickly or so completely; that he can still indulge himself by remaining in the world and assist the poor or his relatives who look to him [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits this passage].

But the person who has once rightly overcome both the world and the devil should pay no attention to the things the devil deceitfully says to him [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13 read, “should not care about these things”]. He should hold firmly to the conviction that what has once been justly and firmly settled must not be destroyed again [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13 read, “that what has once been justly settled must not be destroyed again”], and that what he has finally determined rightly to abandon must not be desired again [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “must not be desired again.”].
