In this way, with God’s help, he will always be able easily to overcome the devil [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “he will always be able to overcome the devil.”].

## CHAPTER LXXV. A likeness between God and any king

[Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “and a certain king,” instead of “and any king.”]

God himself wages war against the devil as a certain king does against a certain enemy prince of his. This king has a very large village in his kingdom.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the kingdom, the village, the castle, and the dungeon

[Note: The Cologne edition reads “and the dongeon”; another reading is “and the divigione.”]

In the village the king has a certain castle, and above the castle a dungeon [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “one dungeon”; the Cologne edition reads, “one dungion”; another reading is “one fortified tower.”]. In the village there are some strong houses and many weak ones.

In the castle there is such great strength that, if anyone takes refuge there, he cannot be harmed by anyone unless he comes back out. There is such security in the dungeon [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “in the dungeon”; the Cologne edition reads, “in the dungion”; another reading is “in the fortified tower”] that, if anyone can once climb there, he will never wish to return from it.

The same king has all these things in his power. His enemy, however, is so strong that whatever he finds outside the village he seizes without any obstacle and carries away [Note: The manuscripts read, “he carries away,” instead of “he seizes and carries away.”].

He frequently enters the village itself and violates the houses he finds to be weak, carrying away as captives those who live in them together with their households [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “carrying away the captives.”]. But those that he finds strong, when he cannot break into them, he finally leaves unwillingly.

He cannot climb into the castle or do anything evil to those who flee there for refuge, unless they return to the battle in the village. But if, out of love for their relatives, they return because they hear them being killed and mistreated [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “or being mistreated”], and if they look out curiously through a hole or a window, then he will easily be able to kill or wound them.

Therefore they must never pay attention to the cries of their relatives, nor return to the battle [Note: The Cologne edition reads, “nor return to fight”], nor look back, but must always flee as they began until they reach the top of the dungeon [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “of the dungeon”; the Cologne edition reads, “of the dungion”; another reading is “of the fortified tower.”]. For after they have reached it, they will be entirely secure.

That king, then, is God, who is at war with the devil. In his kingdom he has Christianity; within Christianity, monasticism; above monasticism, the manner of life of the angels alone [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits “alone.”].

Within Christianity some are strong in virtues, but many are weak. In monasticism there is such great strength that, if someone takes refuge there and becomes a monk, the devil cannot harm him unless he returns from it through repentance.

In the manner of life of the angels, however, there is the joy of such great security that whoever ascends there will never wish to return from it.

The same king, God, has all these things in his power. His enemy, that is, the devil, has such power that he seizes all Jews and pagans whom he finds outside Christianity, with no one resisting, and casts them into hell [Note: Manuscripts read, “he seizes … he casts,” instead of the subjunctive forms “he may seize … he may cast.”].

He frequently enters Christianity itself and, by tempting those whom he finds weak, violates them and carries away as captives the souls dwelling in their bodies [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “he also carries away the souls”].

But those whom he finds strong and well fortified, when he cannot overcome them [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “those whom he finds strong, when he cannot overcome them”], he finally, though sorrowfully, leaves.

He cannot break into monasticism or do anything evil to those who have become monks, unless they return to the world bodily, or in their hearts, or through some affection for their relatives [Note: A manuscript reads, “or in their hearts, or through some affection for their relatives”; A.1 reads, “or through an affection of the heart.”].

## CHAPTER LXXVII. A likeness between the monk and a potion, and between the abbot and a physician

But since this often tends to happen to novices, let them take heed: the person who undertakes the difficulty of monasticism acts like a sick person who takes a powerful potion [Note: The manuscripts read, “Let novices take heed, since …”].

It often happens that someone suffering from a bodily illness seeks a potion by which he may be healed of that illness. When the physician tells him to take this or that potion and that he can thus be healed, he buys it or receives it when it is given to him freely [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “or it is given to him, and he receives it.”].

But when the strong potion searches through his entrails, passes through all his limbs, draws out the bad humors, takes away his strength, dissolves his body, and throws him to the ground [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “throws him down to the ground”], it kindles in him a powerful desire to drink, or to sleep, or to go outside into the wind; and the physician forbids him these things [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read simply, “the physician forbids them”], threatening that he will die if he does them.

“Alas!” says the sick man. “Why did I take this potion? I was ill before, and now I am worse. Alas! What misery it was for me to encounter those who gave me this advice, since they did not tell me that I would have to suffer this and that. If I had known this, I would never have taken the potion.”

Thus and in these terms he complains while he is afflicted by the potion. But when the bad humors begin to flow out and his whole body gradually becomes lighter, he rejoices and exults because he has taken such a potion, through which he feels that he is returning to his former health; and he blesses the people who gave him this advice [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “and everyone who gave him this advice”].

In the same way, it often happens that someone who considers the sickness of his soul seeks a spiritual medicine by which he may be cleansed of the sickness of his vices. When some spiritual person tells him that he could be saved through monasticism, he gives whatever he has so that he may be received into some monastery, or he is sometimes granted admission freely and is received.

But when the difficulty of the order forces him to keep vigil when he wishes to sleep; to hunger when he wishes to eat; to thirst when he wishes to drink; to keep silent when he wishes to speak; to read or sing when he wishes to rest; to sit when he wishes to stand or walk; or to stand or walk when he wishes to sit; to endure many injuries; and to abandon his own will entirely, he says:

“Wretched me! Why did I assume this habit? Before, I was doing badly, but now I am doing worse, because I am unable to fulfill so many and such great things that are commanded to me; and I can scarcely accomplish anything good except unwillingly. What, then [Note: Manuscript A.1 omits the sentence fragment “What, then?”]? Woe is me, woe is me! Why did I trust those who gave me this advice? I thought that all these people were saints.”

The novice says these and similar things while the order initially seems burdensome to him [Note: The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “at the beginning”]. But after he has sensed and considered within himself [Note: Manuscript A.1 abbreviates this passage, beginning, “He senses and considers within himself that …”] that, by enduring these things in a united spirit, all his sins can thus be wiped away and the health of his soul recovered more quickly, everything that had previously seemed burdensome gradually becomes easy. And, as though he now had no illness at all, he begins to rejoice and gives thanks to God because he has deserved to embrace monasticism. He blesses all who gave him such advice.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. The dispute between converted monks and those brought up in the monastery

[Note: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “between converted monks and those brought up in the monastery”; another reading reverses the order: “between monks brought up in the monastery and converts.”]

But since the monastic order is composed of converts and those brought up in it, it must be said that a certain dispute tends to exist between monks brought up in the monastery and converts.

Those brought up in the monastery assert [Note: Victor 13 reads, “They maintain”] that they have committed no crimes and have not defiled themselves in the filth of the world; rather, they have led a pure life from childhood and have always labored in God’s service. They observe, on the other hand, that the converts have always lived in the opposite way [Note: The manuscripts read, “have lived in the opposite way”; another reading is, “have always lived contrary to this”], and therefore judge that the converts are rightly inferior.

The converts, however, reply that they possess knowledge of external matters and manage the monastery’s affairs wisely; they procure what those brought up in the monastery need and, for the most part, observe their order more fervently. They observe that the others have little ability in these matters and therefore consider themselves better than them.

Thus each group prefers itself to the other, while attending not to its own weakness but to that of the others.

But if they were truly monks, the relationship between them would be like that between the angels in heaven and holy human beings. The angels are, as it were, those brought up in the monastery, while holy human beings are, as it were, converts.

Yet the angels do not despise the saints because they have sometimes been overcome by temptations, nor do the saints despise the angels because they have suffered no temptation that they had to overcome. If Michael were to say to Peter, “You denied the Lord,” Peter could reply, “What you say is true, but you never endured even one slap for the Lord.”

They do nothing of this kind; rather, they exist in such harmony as though all were angels or all human beings. So these men should likewise be as though they were all those brought up in the monastery or all converts [Note: Manuscript A.1 reads, “So let these men be.”].

## CHAPTER LXXIX. A likeness between monks, angels, and God

[Note: The manuscripts of Victor and A.1, together with the Cologne edition, omit “and God.”]

The relationship between the congregation of monks on earth and the congregation of angels in heaven is like that between those who are still outside in the novices’ cell and those who are already inside in the congregation of monks, who, as far as they are able [Note: The manuscripts read, “as far as they may be able”], keep themselves perfectly in everything.

The abbot has already taught the latter by himself everything that he wishes them to observe. For the former, however, he appoints masters from among the latter, to teach them what they ought to keep.

The latter have already been tested in all humility, obedience, patience, and observance of everything that the order requires. The former must still be tested [Note: Victor 13 reads, “must still be tested for these things”] to see whether they wish to be humble, obedient, patient, and to observe everything that the order requires.

The person appointed as master over each of them tests him by admonishing and reproving him. Often he also tests him by flogging him, to see whether he is fit to be received [Note: Manuscript A.1 and the Cologne edition, as well as manuscript Victor 13, read, “to be received”] into the congregation of the others.

If he sees that the novice patiently endures everything and is in every respect worthy of the companionship of the others, he comes to the abbot and announces to him before the whole congregation:

“Lord,” he says, “that novice whom you entrusted to me [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “whom you commended to me”] is behaving so perfectly in every respect that he is now worthy to be among us, if you so command.”

After hearing this, the abbot either receives him, with the common counsel of the brothers, or leaves him still, as an example to the other novices.

Thus the appropriate procedure is followed with this novice, who is now considered worthy of the companionship of God’s servants.

But if the master sees that another novice is disobedient, impatient, proud, and unworthy of reception, after tolerating him for a long time and trying in many ways to amend him [Note: Manuscripts A.1, Victor 13, and the Cologne edition read, “tried,” instead of “has tried”], he finally comes to the abbot, if he can make no progress, and reports to him as follows:

“Lord,” he says, “that novice whom I had in my keeping [Note: The manuscripts of A.1 and Victor 13, together with the Cologne edition, read, “whom I had in my keeping”; another reading is, “whom I was keeping”], so that I might teach him how he could become worthy of our manner of life, behaves so perversely in everything he does that he is not even worthy to live among the other novices. It is therefore fitting for you to consider what ought rather to be done with him.”

In response, the abbot urges the master to continue trying by every means to correct him, saying that it is better to tolerate him among the others than to dismiss him and allow him to return to the world [Note: The manuscripts of A.1, Victor 13, and the Cologne edition read, “to dismiss him so that he may return.”].

Thus this novice is neither received into the congregation nor expelled from the novices’ cell.

In the same way, therefore, one must consider in every respect the relationship among God, the angels, and the monks, as it is between that abbot, the master, and the novice monks.

## CHAPTER LXXX. A likeness between God and any emperor

[Note: Victor’s manuscript and the Cologne edition read, “and a certain emperor,” instead of “and any emperor.”]

Source preparation: Native Terra repair and review used only the supplied local canonical source; embedded foreign-language text is translated as part of this section.

It must also be considered that the relation among God, angels, and human beings is like that between an earthly emperor and those obedient to him. [Note: At Col. 0651D, the manuscript reads, “It must be considered thus”; A.1, “it must also be considered thus.” The manuscript has “human beings and angels”; the received text, “angels and human beings.”] For there are three classes of people who serve an earthly emperor. Some serve him for the lands they possess, seeking nothing else than what they hold; others because they wish to recover lands which their parents lost through some fault of their own; while others serve only for pay. [Col. 0651B] [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read, “Others who possess lands,” rather than “others because they wish to recover lands.” A.1 reads *per solidatis*, “for pay,” rather than *pro solidis*, “for coins/pay.”]

The lord, therefore, treats more honourably those who have never committed any offence and seek nothing other than what they possess. These are rooted and founded, and do not fear being uprooted so long as they preserve themselves in the will of their lord. [Note: At Col. 0651D, the transposed section runs from “The lord, therefore” to “and that they may be well fed.” Some manuscripts read, “These are rooted and founded, and do not fear being uprooted so long as they preserve you in the will of their lord”; this sentence is absent from A.1.]

But those whose parents sinned against him, and who serve him for the sake of their parents’ inheritance, he treats somewhat more harshly and tests in various ways: by insulting them, threatening them, imposing certain severe commands, and sometimes even flogging them. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1, Victorinus, and the Cologne edition read *quinque pro illorum* (“five for/of those”) for *quique pro illorum* (“and who for their”); the Cologne edition has *quinque illorum* (“five of those”). A.1 omits *sibi*, “to him,” in “serve him.” A.1 reads *aliquando vilius*, “sometimes more poorly,” for *aliquanto vilius*, “somewhat more poorly.”] If they endure all these things humbly and patiently await their lord’s mercy, at last the lord restores to them their fathers’ inheritance. But if they refuse to tolerate these things, they can neither recover their inheritance nor does the lord wish to give them anything else. [Col. 0651C]

Those, however, who seek nothing other than their pay and good nourishment serve the emperor only so long as he grants them these things. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 reads *quam solidos*, “than coins/pay,” for *quam solidatas*, “than pay.”] If he gives these things to them abundantly, they praise him and say that such a lord truly ought to be served, since he bestows such things upon those who serve him. [Note: At Col. 0651D, Victorinus and the Cologne edition read, “They say: ‘Truly …’”; A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *qui talia*, “who bestows such things,” rather than *quia talia*, “because [he bestows] such things.”] But if he ceases to give them these things, they immediately depart, reproaching him, and begin to serve his enemy.

These, then, are the three classes of people serving an earthly emperor. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 reads, “These are three classes,” omitting *igitur*, “then.”] Likewise there are three classes of those who serve the heavenly King. The first class is the angels, who, steadfast in eternal blessedness, serve him without any interruption. [Col. 0651D] The second class is good human beings, who, so far as they can, obey their own will and thus strive to attain, by hereditary right, the kingdom of heaven lost through the fault of their father Adam. [Col. 0652A] The third consists of those who serve only for earthly advantages, like mercenary soldiers. Thus, in every respect, the relation between these three classes and God must be considered like that between the other three classes mentioned above and their emperor.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. That it benefits a monk if he does some good unwillingly

It sometimes happens that someone is so full of evil humours that, unless he is cut open, he cannot otherwise be healed. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 begins instead: “But someone may say that nothing benefits a monk which he is compelled to do unwillingly. To him one must reply that it sometimes happens that someone …”] Therefore, so that he may be wholly cleansed of them, he first willingly has himself bound, asking even those who are to cut him not to release him, whatever he himself may say, until they have cut him completely. [Col. 0652B] When they begin to lance and cut away the putrefaction, he cries out and says that he previously had no illness at all, and threatens to kill them unless they release him. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 reads *se nihil mali habere*, “that he has no illness,” omitting *prius*, “previously.”] But those who know that pain makes him speak thus pay no attention to his words, but completely cut away the putrefaction, as they had begun.

When he has been fully cleansed and is better, he thanks those very persons whom he had earlier threatened to kill because they had not released him to follow his own will. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 reads *quibus antea*, “those whom/to whom earlier,” for *quos antea*, “those whom earlier”; it omits *occidere*, “to kill.”] What then? Does not the cutting benefit the man who endured it unwillingly, since he willingly had himself bound in order to endure it? [Note: At Col. 0651D, the manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *voluntarius*, “willingly/voluntarily,” for *spontaneus*, “of his own accord.”] It certainly benefits him, because by it his illness has been cut away and his health restored. [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 reads *reparata sanitas*, “health restored,” rather than *reparata est sanitas*, “health was restored.”]

Likewise, it often happens that someone abounds in vices and understands that he cannot otherwise be saved unless they are cut away from him by the sword of stricter penitence. [Col. 0652C] [Note: At Col. 0651D, A.1 omits “by the sword of stricter penitence.”] Therefore, that he may be wholly purified of them, he willingly binds himself to someone in a monastery. For in making profession he promises stability and conversion of his conduct, and confines himself within the monastery’s enclosure on this condition: that the spiritual physicians, namely his shepherds, who ought to correct him, will not release him afterwards, whatever he may say, but will cut away and amend his vices.

Yet often, when they begin to spur him toward better things and to cut away his vices by rebuking him, he kicks against them and becomes angry, saying that he is not guilty of the thing for which he is reproved; and sometimes he even threatens to kill those who rebuke him. [Col. 0652D] But they know that he says this because of the strictness of discipline; they therefore do not release him, but strictly cut away his folly from him, as far as they are able, now in one way, now in another. [Col. 0653A] [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1 reads, “they prevail, [and] cut [it] away,” for “as far as they are able, now in one way, now in another, they cut [it] away.”]

When, therefore, he has been corrected of his vices and made gentler, and has returned to himself, he gives thanks to those at whom he was angry because they corrected him when he was reproved. [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *eum reprehendendo*, “by rebuking him,” for *eum reprehensum*, “him when rebuked.”] What then? Will that great strictness not benefit him because, through the weakness of the flesh, he unwillingly endured it for a time, since he willingly bound himself in the monastery in order to endure it? [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts read *infirmitatem carnis*, “the weakness of the flesh,” for *infirmitate carnis*, “through the weakness of the flesh”; they read *invitus sustinuit*, “he endured unwillingly,” while A.1 reads *ad horam sustinuit*, “he endured for a time.”] It will indeed benefit him, because by it he is freed from every infirmity of vice and returns to the true health of the virtues.

But someone will say: “It would be better for him to serve God willingly without profession than, after binding himself by profession in a monastery, to be compelled to serve unwillingly.” [Col. 0653B] [Note: At Col. 0653D, Chapter LXXXII begins at this point in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER LXXXII. How great is the hope of a professed monk

[Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts and the Cologne edition read, “That the hope of a professed monk is great,” for “How great is the hope …”]

The answer must be that there is as much difference between one who does not wish to make God a promise of serving him and one who gladly makes it, as there is between two men both bound by obligation to serve one lord. [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *ad serviendum sibi*, “to serve him,” for *serviendi sibi*, “of serving him.”] But one of them approaches his lord and says:

“Lord, I wish to serve you with all my heart, but I do not wish to promise that I shall be faithful to you. For if I made you this promise and afterwards sinned, I should commit a graver offence and deserve a heavier punishment. Nevertheless, I shall serve you as well as I can; but if I ever sin against you, judge me as one who did not at all promise to be faithful to you.”

[Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts read, “If I promise you this and afterwards sin against you,” for “if this having been promised to you, I afterwards sinned.”]

The other comes and says:

“Lord, I love you with all my heart, and I promise you fidelity and submission, so that, if I ever act against your command, you may not judge me as a stranger, but correct me as your own servant.”

After these things have been said, it happens that both later commit the same sin and then, repentant, come to their lord’s mercy. [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *deinde poenitenter*, “then repentantly,” for *deinde poenitentes*, “then repentant.”] The lord says to him who refused to promise fidelity:

“Why did you do this?”

And he replies: “Lord, I confess that I sinned; but I did not promise you that I would not sin.”

But the lord says: “Did you refuse to promise me fidelity in order that you might sin against me more freely? Then I too shall act against you, not as toward one who belongs to me, but as against a stranger; and I shall exact everything that is mine by right, down to the last farthing.” [Col. 0653C–D] [Note: At Col. 0653D, B.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *meri juris*, “of strict/pure legal right,” for *mei juris*, “of my legal right.”]

Once this judgment has been rendered, he turns to the other and says: [Col. 0654A] [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts read, “When this, therefore, has been judged,” for “Once this has been judged”; and, “Turning to the other, he says,” for “he turns to the other and says.”]

“And you, wicked servant, who had promised me fidelity, and therefore ought to have guarded yourself more carefully, why did you do this?” [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts read, “And you, servant,” omitting *male*, “wicked.”]

He replies: “Lord, I truly confess that I sinned and promised you fidelity. But now that I repent that I sinned, ought I to suffer worse because I promised you fidelity before I sinned than that man who wishes to promise it to you even after he has sinned? For I wished to be yours so that, if I ever sinned, you would not judge me as a stranger but correct me as your own.”

[Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts read *poenitet, quia deliqui*, “I repent because I sinned,” for *poenitet me deliquisse*, “I repent of having sinned.”]

The lord says: “It is as you say. Therefore, whenever I wish, I shall take vengeance upon you as upon one who is mine.”

Thus God also judges between a professed monk and one unwilling to profess, if they repent of having sinned against him. [Col. 0654B] He judges the professed monk not only more gently than the unprofessed, but also more gently than any layperson still living in the world. [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1 and Victorinus 13 read *melius judicat*, “judges more favourably,” for *mitius judicat*, “judges more gently.”] For although both commit the same sin, nevertheless, if the monk repents of his offence with all his heart and guards with ardent love the order to which he has subjected himself, he will obtain greater mercy than a layperson, however much that layperson may repent while still detained by worldly affairs. [Note: At Col. 0653D, the manuscripts have a differently ordered reading: “Although the monk repents with all his heart that he sinned, and guards with ardent [love] the order to which he has subjected himself …”; the received wording is uncertain only in this ordering.] But if he refuses to repent, he will be subject to a greater condemnation than the layperson.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. The likeness between a sinning monk and a layperson

That we may see this more clearly by analogy, let us consider two men, servants of one lord. Let both receive personal possessions from that lord, under an oath-promised assurance that they will be faithful to him. [Col. 0654C] [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *sibi jurejurando*, “to themselves, under oath,” for *sub jurejurando promisso*, “under an oath-promised assurance.”] Let one of them do so on this condition: that if he ever commits an offence against his lord, he shall make amends to him from his own goods, as justice requires. [Note: At Col. 0653D, Victorinus and the Cologne edition read *ut si quid*, “that if he should …,” for *quod si quid*, “but if he should …”; A.1 reads *deliquerit*, “has offended,” for *delinquat*, “offends.”] But let the other love his lord so greatly that he prefers to keep nothing as his own and, after surrendering everything to him, to serve him more intimately. [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1 reads *familiarius velit*, “wishes to serve more intimately,” for *familiarius malit*, “prefers to serve more intimately.”]

Let him also make this agreement with him: that, if he ever commits anything against him, the lord may take whatever vengeance he wishes on the man himself, not from another’s property, but as from what belongs to him personally. [Note: At Col. 0653D, A.1 reads *cum eo componat*, “make an agreement with him,” for *cum eo faciat*, “make [this] with him”; the manuscripts read *ut si aliquando*, “that if at any time,” for *quod si aliquando*, “but if at any time”; A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *non ut de re*, “not as from a thing/property,” for *non de re*, “not from property.”]

When these arrangements have been made, if both commit the same offence and afterwards, moved by repentance, wish to make amends—one from his own property, which he is still unwilling to give wholly in satisfaction for that offence, the other from himself, whom he had previously enslaved wholly to his lord—let the lord see that the first is unwilling, even after offending him, to do as much as the second did before he offended him. [Col. 0654D–0655A] [Note: At Col. 0655C, the manuscripts read: “from himself, because he had already wholly enslaved himself to the power of his lord; and let [the lord] see”; the Cologne edition reads *totum*, “wholly,” where some witnesses have *toti*, an uncertain inflection. The received text reads, “from himself, whom he had previously wholly enslaved to his lord.” A.1 reads, “was unwilling,” and the other witnesses, “is unwilling,” for *nolit*, “is unwilling.”]

Of which, I ask, does he appear to wish to have greater mercy? Or does he appear to wish to deal more gently with the one whose deeds prove that he loves him less? [Note: At Col. 0655C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read, “or to deal more gently than with the one whose deeds …,” for “or does he appear to wish to deal more gently with the one whose deeds …”; A.1 reads *ac cum illo*, “and with that one,” for *an cum illo*, “or with that one.”]

But if he wishes to rebuke the latter more harshly than the former, saying, “Wicked servant, the more intimate you were with me, the more culpable you are,” he can answer him thus: [Note: At Col. 0655C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read, “If he wishes to rebuke this one more harshly than the other”; A.1 reads, “if he wishes to rebuke this latter one more harshly.”]

“Lord, what you say is true, but while I was unwilling to repent. Now, however, that I repent with all my heart and surrender myself for correction, ought I to suffer worse than he who is unwilling to give you even all that he possesses in satisfaction for his offence? Does it seem just to you that, because I loved you more, I should obtain less mercy? On the contrary, ought you not to show me greater mercy, since I can offer you no greater satisfaction?” [Col. 0655B] [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1 reads *ac postquam*, “and after,” for *at postquam*, “but after”; A.1 reads *facere debere*, “ought to show,” for *facere deberes*, “oughtest to show.”]

What else would the lord say than what truth requires? He judges this man more gently, as wholly his own; but the other more severely, as less exclusively his. Thus God more readily forgives the monk who commits himself wholly to him than the layperson unwilling to give himself or his possessions for the things he has done. [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1, Victorinus, and the Cologne edition read *sic enim Deus*, “thus indeed God,” for *sic ergo Deus*, “thus therefore God”; they read *nolenti se vel sua*, “unwilling to give himself or his possessions,” for *nolenti vel sua*, “unwilling [to give] even his possessions.”]

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. The likeness between a monk and a tree

Again, it may be seen by analogy that a monk’s good work is more acceptable to God than that of some secular person. It often happens that two men under one lord each possess a tree in his own ground. [Col. 0655C] Both trees bear good fruit. But because the two love their lord unequally, they also serve him unequally from their fruit.

For one of them, because he loves him less, when the fruit of his tree is ripe gathers it and brings his lord as much of it as he sees fit. But the other loves his lord so much that, coming to him, he offers him the tree itself:

“Lord,” he says, “I have a certain tree which bears very good fruit. Since it is fitting to your dignity, I prefer that it should belong to you rather than to me. I therefore offer it to you, that henceforth it may bear fruit for you alone. [Col. 0656A] I shall also assign it to your steward, that he may gather fruit from it and thereby diligently serve you according to what he knows you wish. And I too will take care, as diligently as I can, to keep it for your benefit.” [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *quae si vestrae*, “which, if [it is] fitting to yours,” for *quae quia vestrae*, “which, because [it is] fitting to yours.” A.1 reads, “I shall keep [it] according to your will”; Victorinus 13 and the Cologne edition, “I shall keep [it] for our benefit,” for “I shall take care to keep [it] for your benefit.”]

Whose service, then, appears more acceptable to that lord? That of the man who gives him fruit from his own tree whenever and in whatever quantity he wishes, or that of the man who offers him the tree and its fruit altogether? [Note: At Col. 0655C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read, “Whose service appears more acceptable to the lord?” A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *qui quantumcunque voluerit*, “who [gives] however much he wishes,” for *qui quando quantumque voluerit*, “who [gives] whenever and however much he wishes.”] Surely that of the man who gives him the whole tree with its fruit is more acceptable. [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1, Victorinus, and the Cologne edition transpose and repeat the phrase: “the tree? Or the one who offers the tree and its fruit entirely? Rather …”; A.1 continues only, “the tree? Rather …”]

Thus the service of a monk is more acceptable to God than that of a secular person. [Note: At Col. 0655C, Victorinus 13 reads *sic ergo et servitium*, “thus also the service,” for *sic ergo servitium*, “thus the service.”] For these are the two men who, under God, have themselves as certain trees. Both alike are suited to bear the fruit of good work. But because they do not love God in the same way, they do not serve him equally by doing good works. [Col. 0656B]

For the secular person, because he loves God less, offers God, only when he has a desire to do good, as much good work as he wishes. But the monk loves him so much that, coming to him, he offers himself wholly, addressing him in word and deed thus: [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1 reads, “the monk, however, when he loved him so much that, coming to him, he offered himself wholly”; the Cologne edition reads, “when he loves him so much, coming [to him], he offers himself wholly.”]

“Lord, until now I was under my own authority, and did such good and evil as pleased me. But because I ought to be wholly yours and bear fruit only in good works for you alone, I surrender my whole self to your power, that henceforth I may bear fruit for you alone. That I may be better able to do this, I shall submit myself to one of the prelates of the Church, who, keeping watch over me, may teach me to do only those works which he knows please you more. [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read “one of the prelates of your Church,” for “one of the prelates of the Church.”] And I too shall strive, according to my measure, to keep watch over myself.”

Whose gift, therefore, is more acceptable to God? [Col. 0656C] [Note: At Col. 0655C, the manuscripts read, “Whose gift is more acceptable to God?”] That of the person who offers him some of his works but withholds most, or that of the one who gives him himself with his works? Surely the latter’s: the one who gives himself with all his works. [Note: At Col. 0655C, A.1 reads *operibus suis cunctis*, “with all his works”; the Cologne edition omits *cunctis*, “all.”]

Nor is he deprived of his own reward because he is often compelled to do a good work. For just as one who has entrusted the whole tree to his lord’s steward, that he may gather fruit from it and thereby serve his lord according as he knows his lord wishes, does not lose his own merit if the steward gathers the fruit before it is ripe or, on the other hand, leaves it on the tree until it rots— [Note: At Col. 0655C, L. reads *velle noscet*, “knows [him] to wish,” for *velle nosset*, “knew [him] to wish”; Victorinus 13 omits *econtra*, “on the other hand.”]—so the monk who has entrusted his whole self to his superior, that he may keep watch over him and require him to perform only those works [Col. 0657A] which he knows please God more, does not lose his own reward if he is compelled to do some good work before he wishes, or on the other hand is forbidden to do it when he wishes, until he even loses the will to do it. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *ea opera tantum*, “only those works,” for *eaque opera tantum*, “and only those works”; the manuscripts read *exiget*, “will require,” for *exigeret*, “would require”; and *potius noscet*, “knows [them] rather to please,” for *potius nosset*, “knew [them] rather to please.” A.1 reads *propriam non perdit*, “does not lose his own [reward],” for *propriam non perdet*, “will not lose his own [reward].”]

Therefore he must not omit any good thing his superior commands him, nor presume to do what the superior forbids him. For it belongs to the superior to foresee what he ought to command and forbid; but it belongs to the subordinate to follow him in every good thing. [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1, Victorinus 13, read *sit enim illius praevidere*, “for it should belong to him to foresee,” for *est enim illius praevidere*, “for it belongs to him to foresee”; A.1 and Victorinus 13 read *cum in bono*, “with him in good,” for *eum in bono*, “him in good.”] But that he may do this with willing obedience, let him learn by analogy how many kinds of disposition there are among subordinates. [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1 repeats, “in every respect. But that he may do this obediently in will, let him learn by analogy how many kinds of disposition there are among subordinates.”]

## CHAPTER LXXXV. The likeness between a matron and the divine will

It sometimes happens that a matron entrusts daughters together with maidservants to a female teacher, that she may teach them tasks appropriate to women. [Col. 0657B] [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *filiam cum*, “a daughter together with,” for *filias cum*, “daughters together with.”] She commands them all to obey her and promptly perform whatever she assigns them to do. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *praecepit*, “commanded,” for *praecipit*, “commands”; Victorinus and the Cologne edition read *quodque faciendum*, “and whatever is to be done,” for *quodque sibi faciendum*, “and whatever she assigns to them to do.”] Once this has been arranged, the teacher gathers them all together, assigns each what she ought to do, and watches that they do not go outside.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Concerning the matron’s daughters

When they have thus been bound under her instruction, the good daughters obey her in every respect; nor do they trouble themselves to ask permission to go outside. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *sub magisterio*, “under instruction,” for *sub ejus magisterio*, “under her instruction”; Victorinus and the Cologne edition read *quaerere curent*, “should trouble themselves to ask,” for *quaerere curant*, “do trouble themselves to ask.”]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Concerning her good maidservants

The maidservants likewise do the same, except that they are more unstable. [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *ancillae vero*, “but the maidservants,” for *ancillae quoque*, “the maidservants likewise.”] Since they become weary of remaining in confinement for a long time, they sometimes ask permission to go outside. [Col. 0657C] [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *licentia foras*, “permission outside,” for *licentiam foras*, “permission to go outside.”] If they cannot obtain it, they do not become sad or murmur on that account, but merely say that they would gladly accept it if it were granted. [Note: At Col. 0657C, Victorinus 13 reads *sed tantum dicunt*, “but merely say,” for *tantum dicunt*, “merely say.”] If it is granted, they go out wherever they see fit and meanwhile cease from their work. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts read, “If perhaps they cannot obtain it,” omitting *forte*, “perhaps,” in the received text; the manuscripts read *concessum fuerit*, “if permission has been granted,” for *concessa fuerit*, “if it has been granted”; Victorinus reads *concessa egrediuntur*, “when it is granted, they go out”; A.1, Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read *cessant interim*, “they meanwhile cease,” for *cessantque interim*, “and meanwhile cease.”]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Concerning the thieving maidservant

Among them there is sometimes a certain female thief, scarcely willing to obey the teacher’s commands. [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1 and Victorinus 13 read, “This one, therefore, because confinement is always wearisome to her,” for “This one because confinement …”; a witness reads *haec qui custodia*, an apparently defective form, “this one who/by confinement.”] Because confinement is always burdensome to her, she frequently seeks permission to go out and invents reasons that appear plausible. If she cannot obtain it, she is greatly distressed and grieved, and, if she dares, replies rather harshly to her teacher. [Col. 0658A]

If she has not dared openly, she secretly speaks ill of her and stops the work she was doing. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts have the corrupt/variant reading, “But if an open cause is not available to her, she secretly …”; the received text means, “If she has not dared openly, she secretly …”] If she is ordered to work, she immediately pretends to be ill. Or whenever she finds herself alone, she immediately leaps up, goes to the door, looks in every direction, and tells this or that person to ask permission to speak with her. [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1 reads *ac si quando*, “and if ever,” for *aut si quando*, “or if ever.”]

If she is discovered in this and rebuked, she immediately bursts out in words of this kind: “What,” she says, “have I done, that I ought to be rebuked so? What extraordinary thing have I been seen to do, that so many insults are inflicted upon me? But now it seems sufficiently plain how unjustly I am treated.” [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1 and Victorinus 13 read *quo sic debeam*, “wherefore I ought thus,” for *quod sic debeam*, “that I ought thus”; the manuscripts read *inferuntur mihi*, “are inflicted upon me,” for *inferuntur tot mihi*, “so many are inflicted upon me”; the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *contra me agant*, “they act against me,” for *contra me agatur*, “I am treated.”]

Accordingly she sits down sad and grieving that she has been rebuked in this manner. But after that pain has subsided somewhat, she pretends to a certain maturity. [Col. 0658B] When she thinks that she is considered mature by the others, she again tries to ask permission. If she cannot obtain it, she immediately adds: “A man is foolish,” she says, “if he does good, when good and bad are treated alike.” [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *tractentur ut mali*, “are treated as wicked,” for *tractentur et mali*, “and the wicked are treated.”] But if she can obtain permission, she immediately goes outside, wanders here and there, seeks the company of young men, and commits many things which ought not to be done. Thus it may be gathered from this analogy that there are three kinds of disposition in subordinates.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Concerning obedience, permission, and disobedience

The first of these may be called obedience, the second permission, the third disobedience. All these kinds can be found among monks whom a certain matron entrusted to a certain teacher—that is, whom the divine will subjected to the will of their abbot. [Col. 0658C] [Note: At Col. 0657C, A.1 omits the remainder of this chapter.]

For permission deceives many. [Note: At Col. 0657C, Victorinus 13 and the Cologne edition read *licentia igitur*, “therefore permission,” for *licentia quippe*, “for permission.”] Obedience and disobedience are opposites; permission lies between them. Therefore, one whom obedience binds not to leave the enclosure nevertheless wishes to go out and freely evade the strictness of the rule; although he does not wish to presume to do so without permission, and therefore tries, as far as he can, to defend his action by permission, he undoubtedly sins through that unlawful desire. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *libenter*, “willingly,” for *licenter*, “freely/licentiously.”]

For once he has died to the world and entered the enclosure, he ought by no means to return to worldly affairs, even in desire; nevertheless, he wished to fulfil his desire in deed only when permission had been granted. [Note: At Col. 0657C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *implere vult*, “he wishes to fulfil,” for *implere voluit*, “he wished to fulfil.”] Thus the obedience he embraced in this case excuses the action itself; but his will, which he held contrary to obedience, will be dangerous to him unless he repents. Because some pay too little heed to this, they are often deceived by the permission which they seek to fulfil their own desire.

To speak briefly and concisely: those who live under obedience itself are daughters of the royal matron. [Col. 0659A] [Note: At Col. 0659C, Victorinus 13 reads *regales filiae*, “royal daughters,” for *regalis filiae*, “daughters of the royal [matron].”] Under the name of maidservants understand those who adhere to permission. By disobedience, which itself is called a thief, are designated those rebellious in the monastic order. [Note: At Col. 0659C, Victorinus 13 and the Cologne edition read *rebelliones signantur*, “rebellions are marked/designated,” for *rebelles designantur*, “rebellious persons are designated.”]

## CHAPTER XC. The likeness between a monk and a denarius

Again, by analogy we can see how many things ought to be in a perfect monk. [Note: At Col. 0659C, the manuscripts read *quae in perfecto*, “which [things] in a perfect [monk],” for *quot in perfecto*, “how many [things] in a perfect [monk].”] Three things belong to every good denarius, and these three ought to belong to every good monk. [Col. 0659B] [Note: At Col. 0659C, the manuscripts read “every good and perfect [monk/denarius]”; the received text reads simply “every good.”]

A good denarius must consist of pure copper, correct weight, and lawful coinage; for if one of these is lacking, it cannot be marketable. Therefore, to be marketable it must possess all three together. A monk must likewise have these three if he is to be accounted truly a monk. The purity of its metal is his pure obedience: no impurity of disobedience ought to be in him, but obedience alone. Its correct weight is the stability of his purpose. He ought not to be lightly blown away from what he has begun, but to remain steadfast and persevere to the end. [Note: At Col. 0659C, the Cologne edition reads *non ergo leviter*, “therefore not lightly,” for *non enim leviter*, “for not lightly.”]

Its coinage is the monastic habit, the tonsure in front and behind, and similar marks. For just as a denarius is recognized from its coinage as belonging to a particular region, so a monk is recognized by these marks as belonging to a particular order. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *sit regiminis*, “is of what rule/governance,” for *sit regionis*, “is of what region.”]

But a monk so old that he can no longer bend forward or backward resembles a denarius whose coinage has been worn away by age. [Col. 0659C] The person, however, who has assumed not yet the monastic habit but the monastic life, and therefore does not yet have the name of monk, resembles a weighty coin lacking coinage, and therefore not equally marketable. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads: “who has not yet assumed [the habit], and therefore does not have the name of monk, resembles a coin which does not yet have coinage and is therefore not yet marketable”; the received text is “has assumed not yet [the habit], but [the] life.”]

Yet just as someone who wishes to amass treasure loves such a coin no less than one bearing coinage, so God, who desires to place us all in the heavenly treasury, places there such a person no less than one possessing the monastic habit. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *recuperare cupit*, “wishes to recover [us],” for *reponere cupit*, “wishes to place [us].”]

But if he sees someone possessing the monastic habit while made of impure metal—that is, disobedient—he never places him in the heavenly treasury, just as no one seeks to place a false denarius in his own treasury, even if it is properly coined. [Col. 0660A] [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *monachalem*, “monastic,” for *monachicum*, “monkish/monastic”; A.1 reads *hunc in thesauro*, “him in the treasury,” for *hunc thesauro*, “him [in] the treasury”; it also reads “a false [coin] in his [treasury],” omitting “though properly coined.”]

But if he sees one who is obedient, even though he sometimes sins through human frailty, he does not reject him, if he truly repents. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *si statim poeniteat*, “if he immediately repents,” for *si vere poeniteat*, “if he truly repents.”] For as a false denarius differs from a weak denarius, so a false monk differs from a weak monk. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads, “as an imperfect monk differs from a perfect [one],” for “as a false monk differs from a weak [one].”]

A weak denarius has less weight than it ought, but what it has consists of pure copper. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads, “than it ought, but …”; one witness has *puto ex aere*, “I think, of copper,” for *puro ex aere*, “of pure copper.”] A false denarius displays the same coinage as a good one, but the falsity of its metal lies hidden within. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads “the same [coinage] as a perfect [coin]” for “as a good [coin].”] So the false monk has the same habit as the good monk, but the falsity of disobedience is hidden within. The weak but obedient monk, although he does not possess such stability that he never falls, nevertheless retains the purity of obedience. [Col. 0660B] He soon repents because he has sinned, and in pure obedience does what is commanded him.

Therefore the former, like a false denarius, is rejected from the heavenly treasury; the latter, according to the measure of his strength, is placed there. Thus it benefits no one to possess the external habit of a monk unless he also strives to retain the inner one. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *interiorem habere*, “to have the inner [habit],” for *interiorem retinere*, “to retain the inner [habit].”]

For there are two kinds of order fitting for a religious man. One is external, by which he appears religious; the other is internal, by which he is religious. [Note: At Col. 0659C, Victorinus 13 reads *religiosus habetur*, “is considered religious,” for *religiosus videtur*, “appears religious”; A.1 reads *religiosus habeatur*, “may be considered religious,” for *religiosus habetur*, “is considered religious.”] The external is an artificial order, the internal a natural order. [Note: At Col. 0659C, the manuscripts, Bec., Victorinus 13, and the Cologne edition read, “For the artificial order consists of artificial customs,” for “the external is of an artificial order.”]

The customs of the artificial order are artificial, as many are found in the monastic order. Men devised these and established that they should be observed for certain reasonable causes. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *de causis irrationabilibus*, “for unreasonable causes,” for *de causis rationabilibus*, “for reasonable causes.”] But the virtues of the natural order are natural: humility, charity, and many others. [Col. 0660C] [Note: At Col. 0659C, the manuscripts and Cologne edition read *naturali vero*, “but of the natural [order],” for *naturalis vero*, “but natural [virtues].”] For God himself implanted these naturally in human beings and commanded that they be observed for the sake of their salvation. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *Deus, ipsi*, “God, to them,” an apparently defective variant, for *Deus ipse*, “God himself.”]

That artificial order, therefore, benefits a person nothing without this natural order; but this natural order can save a person even without the artificial one. Yet, if the natural order is to be preserved, the artificial order is very necessary to it. [Note: At Col. 0659C, A.1 reads *est ille*, “that [order] is necessary,” for *est et ille*, “that order too is necessary.”]

## CHAPTER XCI. Concerning the likeness between a strap and a shoe, and between artificial and natural order.

Thus it is with the artificial and natural orders as it is with the strap and the shoe. For a strap, when tied by itself around the foot, provides the foot with no protection [Note: [Col. 0659C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “aid” (*juvamento*) instead of “protection” (*munimento*)] [Col. 0661A]; indeed, it seems even more unsuitable if it is wrapped around the foot by itself. But a shoe, even by itself, sufficiently protects the foot and fits it quite properly; nevertheless, so that it may not fall off or become twisted, it needs a strap to be fastened to it. So, although the artificial order by itself is of no benefit, and rather brings disgrace, while the natural order is both beneficial and becoming without it, nevertheless, so that the latter may be kept firm, the former is necessary to it.

For this reason, whoever desires to preserve religion inwardly binds himself outwardly by the monastic habit, so that what he displays outwardly may always reproach him [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “may admonish him” (*eum arguat*) instead of “may reproach him” (*eum coarguat*)], because, if afterward he should be unwilling to be what it signifies, that habit brings him greater disgrace [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts read “because, if afterward he should be unwilling to be, it brings him greater disgrace”; the Cologne edition reads “but if afterward he should be unwilling to be, it brings him greater disgrace”; the source text reads “if afterward he should be unwilling to be this, it brings him greater disgrace”]. For if, for example, a monk is proud while by his outward habit he professes humility, he seems to be much more incongruous than if he lacked the habit of humility. [Col. 0661B] Therefore, he ought to strive to possess inwardly what he displays outwardly. For scarcely anything does he have outwardly in habit, profession, or custom [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “in habit, possession, or custom”; other manuscripts read “in habit or custom”; manuscripts Vict. and Gemmet., and the Cologne edition, read “in habit, profession, or custom”] that does not remind him to possess something inwardly.

## CHAPTER XCII. On the monk’s clothing

That he wears cheap [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “that he avoids” (*quod enim vitem*) instead of “that he wears cheap” (*quod enim viles*); another reading is “Why do you avoid?” (*Quid enim vites*)] and black garments [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “garments, unless” (*vestes nisi ut*) instead of “garments, so that” (*vestes ut*)] reminds him to regard himself as lowly and a sinner [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “reminds him of sinners” (*peccatorum commonet*) instead of “reminds him to regard himself as a sinner” (*peccatoremque commonet*)]; and the fact that he is covered by these garments from head to foot urges him to do this from the beginning of life to its end [Note: [Col. 0661C] The manuscripts omit: “For this is the ankle-length, multicolored tunic which the patriarch Jacob is read to have made for his son Joseph”]. But their being made in the form of a cross constantly reminds him to retain the memory of the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the monk’s crown and tonsure

[Col. 0661C]

Finally, the crown and the tonsure of his hair show that he ought to be a priest [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “that he is a priest” instead of “that he ought to be a priest”] and a king. For under the Law priests covered their heads with a mitre, after the likeness of which this man’s head is shaved. Kings, however, use a crown [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “crowns” (*coronis utuntur*) instead of “a crown” (*corona utuntur*)], after the likeness of which this man’s hair is cut [Note: [Col. 0661C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *tonduntur* (“are cut”) instead of *tondentur* (“are cut”)]. These things, therefore, exhort him to perform the office of a priest and a king [Note: [Col. 0661C] The manuscripts read “constrain him” (*coactant eum*) instead of “exhort him” (*cohortantur eum*)].

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the monks’ spiritual sacrifice

The office of a priest under the Law was to slaughter animals of various kinds [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “the office likewise of a priest” instead of simply “the office of a priest”]. Accordingly, his office also ought to be to kill within himself the lion of anger and cruelty, the wolf of rapacity, the bull of ferocity [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13 read “the bull of sheer ferocity” (*tantum ferocitatis*), and the Cologne edition reads “the bull of ferocity” (*taurum feritatis*)], the fox of cunning, [Col. 0662A] the goat of uncleanness, the dormouse of sleepiness, the horse and mule of lust, the donkey of sluggishness, and the other bestial vices [Note: [Col. 0661C] The manuscripts read simply “to kill vices” instead of “to kill bestial vices within himself”].

The proper office of a king, however, is to rule his kingdom, drive its enemies from it, take care that the unjust do not injure the just, and, when the wicked have been brought low, raise up the good. Therefore, the monk’s office ought to be to rule the kingdom of his mind and of his body [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript Vict. 13 omits “and of his body”]. For from it [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “for here” (*hic enim*) instead of “for from it” (*hinc enim*)] he ought to drive out all vices, take care that an evil appetite does not resist a good one, and ensure that the good appetite always subjugates the evil. Finally, whatever he displays outwardly in habit or custom [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 adds “or in the profession itself”], he should also strive to possess inwardly. Otherwise, neither the crown nor the tonsure, nor any monastic habit or custom [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 reads simply “the monastic habit”], will benefit him.

Yet there are many who blame the artificial order for not preserving the natural one. For they say [Col. 0662B] that, with good intentions, they cannot endure having such customs imposed upon them [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “which are imposed upon them” (*eis imponuntur*) instead of “which they have imposed upon them” (*eis imponantur*)]. They also complain that they were better in the world and that monastic life has made them worse. But whoever says this resembles a counterfeit coin.

## CHAPTER XCV. The comparison between monastic life and fire

A counterfeit coin often seems to be good; but if it is put into the fire, it is immediately proved counterfeit. So a badly behaved person often seems to have good conduct in the world; but if he becomes a monk and afterward is regularly rebuked as his faults require [Note: [Col. 0661C] Some manuscripts read: “But if, under some prompting, he should take up the severity of monastic life, and afterward, as his faults require…” instead of “But if he should become a monk and afterward, as his faults require…”], he is immediately proved not to be what he seemed [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “to be what he seemed” (*videbatur esse*) instead of “what he seemed” (*videbatur*)]. For he who seemed humble [Col. 0662C] and patient is soon found to be proud and impatient.

If he blames the order for this, it is as though the coin were to say to the fire, “You made me counterfeit.” For the fire did not make it counterfeit; it revealed what it was. Thus, monastic life did not make this man badly behaved; it declared that he already was so. Let him therefore accuse not the order but himself, and change his perverse conduct into good conduct. For unless he seems to have good conduct, the good things he does outwardly [Note: [Col. 0661C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “whatever he does outwardly” instead of “the good things he does outwardly”] are of little account.

## CHAPTER XCVI. On inward and outward virtue

There are two kinds of virtue, differing from each other as body and soul. One is inward [Col. 0663A] and invisible, while the other is outward and visible. Inward are charity, humility, patience, kindness, and the other virtues of this kind; outward are fasting, giving alms, keeping vigils in prayer, shedding tears, and similar practices.

But just as a body cannot long endure without a soul, whereas a soul can exist without a body [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “can be without a body” instead of “can exist without a body”], so the outward kind of virtue does not long endure without the inward, whereas the inward can exist without the outward. A person can possess charity for a long time even if he does not fast, since he cannot fast for God for long if he does not love him.

Yet just as an evil spirit often assumes a body and makes it endure by animating it, so vainglory enters the human heart and feigns that outward kind of virtue. For just as charity makes one fast, so does vainglory. But just as an inanimate body [Col. 0663B] soon stinks and is despised, so the outward kind of virtue without the inward is despised [Note: [Col. 0663C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “is displeasing to the inward virtue, to God, and to the angels” instead of “is despised without the inward”].

For when someone is devoted to fasting but seems quick to anger, if someone praises him for his fasting, another immediately replies, “Who,” he says, “cares about the fasting of one who is so inflamed” [Note: [Col. 0663C] The manuscript reads “so puffed up” (*sic inflatur*) instead of “so inflamed” (*sic inflammatur*)] “over nothing?” But if he eats more frequently while seeming humble and patient, and if someone reproaches him because he does not fast [Note: [Col. 0663C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read: “but if he were humble and patient, he would rightly seem so; but if someone reproached him because he did not fast”], another immediately replies, “He certainly deserves to eat,” [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “It is good, he says”] “for he deserves it, since he is so patient and kind” [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “who is so patient” instead of “since he is so patient”].

## CHAPTER XCVII. The comparison between the monk and a gardener

[Col. 0663C]

It should be understood that one who strives toward the virtues [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “It should be understood” (*sciendum est*) instead of “It should be understood that one strives” (*sciendum est ad*); manuscript A. 1 reads “But it should truly be understood that one strives”] ought to act like a gardener [Col. 0664A] [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “like a good gardener” instead of “like a gardener”]. For a gardener who wishes to plant herbs first considers the nature of the soil and of the herbs [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13 read “the nature of the soil and of them” instead of “the nature of the soil and of the herbs”], and where he should plant them. For unless the nature of the soil and of the herbs agrees, they will in no way be able to grow or bear fruit.

So one who wishes to make a plantation of virtues must foresee in what place he should plant them within himself [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “in what place he should plant them” instead of “in what place within himself he should plant them”]. For if the place is vicious, the virtues themselves will also be turned into vices.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On one who builds a house

Again, he ought to act like one who must build a house. For whoever wishes to make a stable building first considers the firmness of the soil, so that he may safely lay a solid foundation, raise a wall, place a roof above it, and dwell within it securely [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “and may safely dwell inside” instead of “and dwell within it securely”]. [Col. 0664B]

So one who wishes to construct a building of virtues, in which he may dwell securely against the ambushes of demons, must foresee in what place within himself he should build it [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “build it” (*construat illud*) instead of “establish it” (*constituat illud*)]. For if the place is not firm [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscripts A. 1 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “if its place is not firm”], neither will the building be able to endure for long.

This good soil, or pure soil [Note: [Col. 0663C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “pure soil” instead of “good soil”], is humility, whose nature accords with all the virtues and sustains them like a firm foundation.

## CHAPTER XCIX. That pride is a great valley full of beasts of the vices

In the Bec and Saint-Germain manuscripts, the passage from “It is not elevated on high,” etc., through Chapter 109, “But because,” etc., is omitted. For the other virtues can endure only as long as they retain the support of humility. Humility itself is like a great mountain: on its summit is a most splendid light, while in the valley below there is a great density of darkness; above, moreover, dwell persons of great honor, while below, in the valley, very wicked beasts dwell. There are arranged steps by which one ascends from the valley to the summit of the mountain.

Whoever remains in the valley is blinded by the density of the darkness and is often attacked by beasts. But whoever leaves it and begins to climb, the higher he ascends, the more the darkness thins and the more brightly the light shines for him; the beasts also cease to pursue him, and honorable persons come to meet him. When he has reached the summit of the mountain, he rests among those persons in clear light.

The deep valley, therefore, is pride, which, the more it is exalted, lies the lower. The density of darkness is ignorance of oneself—that is, the condition of one who does not recognize that he is contemptible. The wicked beasts are the vices that trample down those who do not know themselves. The steps by which one ascends to the summit of the mountain are the seven degrees of humility by which one reaches its perfection.

Whoever, therefore, remains in the valley of pride is blinded by the darkness of ignorance of himself and is often trampled by various vices. But whoever, having abandoned pride, begins to ascend through the degrees of humility, the more of them he ascends, the more, as ignorance thins, the knowledge of himself is opened to him. The vices no longer assail him as before; rather, honorable persons—that is, the virtues—draw near to him. When he has ascended to the highest degree of humility, he rests among the virtues in clear self-knowledge.

The first degree of humility, then, is to recognize that one is contemptible. And because there are some who recognize that they are contemptible but do not grieve over it, the second is to grieve that one is contemptible. Since there are others who grieve that they are contemptible but refuse to confess it, the third is to confess that one is contemptible. And because, again, there are others who confess that they are contemptible but do not want this to be believed, the fourth is to persuade others that one is contemptible. But because some wish to be believed contemptible but do not want this said to them, the fifth is to endure being called contemptible. Since some endure this but nevertheless do not want to be treated contemptibly, the sixth is to receive an injury so patiently that it seems to be a great advantage. But since some of these endure it unwillingly, the seventh is to love being treated contemptibly.

When someone has ascended there, he dwells in clear light—that is, in perfect self-knowledge—and among honorable persons, that is, the virtues, all of which are founded upon this mountain of humility like a certain building.

All these degrees of humility are necessary, as can clearly be seen from a comparison. If some master had a servant whom, because of his fault, he ought to deliver to death, and, after having reasoned with him, the servant wished to conceal his fault as though in darkness; or, if he recognized it, did not grieve over it; or, if he grieved before others, refused to confess it although his master ordered him to; or, if he confessed it, refused to persuade others that it should be believed; or, if he wished to be believed guilty, nevertheless did not want to endure being called guilty; or, if he endured having this said of him, still did not want to endure being treated as guilty; or, while enduring this, did not love being treated in that way, although he knew that his master wished it—surely the master would not forgive him that fault, but would instead punish him as an unjust servant. So the Lord will not forgive us our faults if we do not humble ourselves through these same degrees, as he commands.]

Pride, therefore, is not elevated on high, as some suppose, but is brought low; it is a great valley full of beasts [Col. 0664C] of the vices and of the densest darkness. [Col. 0665A] For the more someone is enveloped in pride, the less he sees the light of truth. As long as he lies in darkness—that is, in the blindness of his heart—the proud person cannot clearly distinguish the just from the unjust [Note: [Col. 0665C] The manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “the proud” (*superbis*) instead of “the proud person” (*superbus*); the Cologne edition reads “the proud” (*superbos*)]; rather, he pursues crooked things just as though they were straight.

Hence it happens that in this dark valley of the vices there is an abundance, as it were, of a great multitude of savage beasts. For lions of cruelty, foxes of cunning, poisonous serpents of envy, frogs of garrulousness and anger, and the other animals of the vices also commonly abound there. The more familiar these become to each person, the less cruel they seem. For it is characteristic of vice that it is not easily seen by the one oppressed by it; but as soon as he has ceased from it and separated himself from it, only then does he consider in what foulness [Col. 0665B] and misery he had lain [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “will have lain” (*jacuerit*) instead of “had lain” (*jacuerat*)], and what grievous bites of evil beasts he had endured [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “will have endured” (*toleraverit*) instead of “had endured” (*toleraverat*)].

## CHAPTER C. On the mountain of humility and its seven degrees

Humility, however, is a great mountain, on whose summit there is no small light and a most beautiful throng of honorable persons—that is, of holy virtues. But whoever desires to reach it [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “he who desires to reach it” (*qui ad hunc*) instead of “whoever desires to reach it” (*quicunque ad hunc*)] must ascend by certain steps, if he longs to recognize and inhabit this mountain.

## CHAPTER CI. The first degree of humility

The first degree on the mountain of humility is self-knowledge. Everyone ought to possess it in such a way that he judges himself inferior to all, imitating [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “judges himself, imitating” instead of “judges himself to be inferior to all, imitating”] the Apostle, who said that he was the least of all his fellow apostles (1 Cor. 15:9).

For if there were someone who had sinned so greatly that his master could, by just judgment, cut off his hands and feet, tear out his eyes, and tear his whole body apart, yet did not do so but tolerated him out of mercy, he ought to recognize himself as greatly indebted to his master and to humble himself all the more, the less he considered himself to have deserved to be so tolerated by his master.

We, therefore, have all offended our Lord in many ways (Jas. 3:2), and to such an extent that, in punishment according to his justice, he could tear us limb from limb, afflict us in the present with continual illness, or afterward deliver us to eternal punishments.

## CHAPTER CII. That whoever sins against God stirs up every creature against himself

[Col. 0666A]

Because of this offense, we have not only merited God’s anger but have also stirred up the whole creation against us. For if a servant were to withdraw from his master and attach himself to the master’s enemy, he would not only provoke the master himself but would also, with complete justice, anger his entire household.

Since, then, we have offended the Lord, the Creator of all things, we have moved every creature to anger against us, insofar as our deserts are concerned. The earth can therefore say to us with just consideration: “I ought not to sustain you, but rather to swallow you up, because [Col. 0666B] by sinning you did not fear to withdraw from my Creator and attach yourselves to his enemy, namely the devil” [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “to serve and attach yourselves to the devil”; manuscript Corb. 307 reads “to the devil, namely, to attach yourselves”].

Food and drink can also say: “You have not deserved that we should nourish you, but rather that we should prepare confusion and death for you. For by sinning you withdrew from him through whom not even a bird hungers.”

The sun also can say: “I ought not to shine upon you for your salvation, but, in vengeance for my Lord, who is light of light and the source of illumination, to restrain you completely.”

And so each and every created thing can rise against us by an unanswerable argument [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “each and every creature” instead of “each and every created thing”]. It is therefore advantageous for us to humble ourselves, lest, after vengeance has been long deferred, it punish our evils all the more harshly when it comes, the longer it has tolerated what it was able to punish [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “the longer it tolerated” instead of “the longer it will have tolerated”].

Therefore, in order that we may be humbled, let us consider in our minds what and what sort of people we have been born, and what we have done [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “what, or what sort of people, we have been born” instead of “what we have been born”], and let us recognize that we are vile sinners and worthy of very great punishment. Whoever judges himself to be such already stands on the first degree of humility.

## CHAPTER CIII. The second degree of humility

The second degree is grief. For there are some who recognize and confess that they are sinners [Note: [Col. 0665C] Manuscript Corb. 307 reads “confess that they are sinners, but” (*esse fatentur, sed*); manuscript Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “recognize that they are sinners, but” (*esse cognoscunt, sed*)], but are seen to feel no grief over it. They must grieve if they desire to merit pardon, because it does not avail for salvation for someone to recognize that he is a sinner unless he also grieves over it.

For if someone sinned against his master and did not grieve over it, what do you think his master would say about him [Note: [Col. 0665C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “what he would say about him” instead of “what his master would say about him”]? How could he forgive him the offense as long as he did not know that he felt any grief over his offense? It would seem ridiculous rather than anything else if he asked pardon for something about which he admitted that he did not grieve [Note: [Col. 0667D] Manuscript Vict. and the Cologne edition read “for something about which he did not admit that he grieved”]. For whoever desires to obtain pardon for sins committed must feel grief.

## CHAPTER CIV. The third degree of humility

Next comes confession, by which he should strive to confess how he recognizes and grieves that he is a sinner [Note: [Col. 0667D] The manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition, read “so that he may confess how” instead of “by which he should confess how”].

For there are many who recognize and grieve that they have sinned, yet conceal it because, ashamed to confess it, they do not dare. And because they know that confession is necessary for salvation, they repent in their hearts before God and intend to confess to him, undergoing much greater repentance than if one of the priests imposed it upon them [Col. 0667B]. But in this they are utterly deceived, because no one can confess anything to God that he does not know. For all things are naked and open to him (Heb. 4:13).

God therefore wills that whoever has sinned against him should not, as though he himself did not know, refuse to confess it in its proper place to another who does not know, so that by this judgment he may plainly prove that, if God did not know it, he himself would truly reveal it to him [Note: [Col. 0667D] Manuscripts Corb. 307 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “For if God” instead of “so that, if God”].

Moreover, if someone who has not confessed wishes, by his own choice, to perform greater penance than anyone would wish to impose upon him if he confessed, let him consider within himself what has cost him more: to confess and perform a small penance, or to repent for a long time by his own spontaneous will without confession.
