And when he chooses to prolong his penance freely rather than reveal his guilt through confession, let him know for certain that he has not yet equated that spontaneous penance of his, however serious it may have been [Note: [Col. 0667D] The manuscripts Corb. 307 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “however great it may have been” instead of “however serious it may have been”], with true confession, since he has not yet found it as costly to repent secretly with such gravity as to make the confession that he ought to have made. Therefore, it is always less for anyone to repent gravely without confession than to make confession with a pure heart.

## CHAPTER CV. The fourth degree of humility

Since, then, we have three degrees on the mountain of humility, persuasion follows, which must be possessed by everyone as the fourth degree of the virtue already mentioned. Since it is necessary that we confess, it should be understood that we must confess in such a way that we persuade others that the very thing we confess is truly so. For confession is pure when voluntary persuasion follows it.

## CHAPTER CVI. The fifth degree of humility

At the fifth degree, therefore, confession must be added [Note: [Col. 0667D] The manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition, read “to the fifth degree” instead of “at the fifth degree”], so that one who recognizes, grieves, confesses, and persuades that he is such-and-such a person may also allow himself to be judged by others as such. For there are many who judge themselves sufficiently, but are in no way able to endure being judged and blamed by others. If they are to ascend the mountain of true humility, they must learn to endure others’ contempt when others despise them in judging them, just as they judge themselves deserving of contempt. In this matter patience is necessary, and it must be added in the sixth place [Note: [Col. 0667D] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition, read “must be explained and added” instead of “must be added”].

## CHAPTER CVII. The sixth degree of humility

[Col. 0668B]

This must become so familiar to everyone that whenever some injury is inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0667D] Manuscript Vict. reads “however great” (*quantuncunque*) instead of “whenever” (*quandocunque*)], he receives it patiently, as though a great advantage were being granted him. Indeed, if a servant of some prudent man had sinned and, while many troubles resulted for him from it, did not protest but rather said that he deserved to suffer such things justly, he would more quickly find mercy with his master.

We, therefore, who have committed many offenses against our Creator must humble ourselves with all the greater zeal, the more we see that we need his indulgence.

## CHAPTER CVIII. The seventh degree of humility

[Col. 0668C]

We must not only endure troubles without murmuring, but must also love being severely punished as vengeance from God. For love seems to be the highest degree of the mountain of humility, since satisfaction is pleasing to God when no murmuring remains in the mind of the one who makes satisfaction, but a devout love continually burns there.

## CHAPTER CIX. Recapitulation of the degrees of humility

What we explained above at length and in parts, let us now gather briefly and summarily by means of an example. If some master had a servant whom, because of his fault, he ought to deliver to death, and, after having reasoned with him, the servant wished to conceal his fault as though in darkness; or, if he recognized it [Col. 0668D]—which is the first degree of humility—did not grieve over it; or, if he grieved over it—which is the second—refused to confess it before others, although his master ordered him to; or, if he confessed it—which is the third—refused to persuade others that it should be believed; or, if he wished to be believed guilty because of it—which is the fourth—nevertheless did not want to endure being called guilty; or, if he endured having this said of him—which is the fifth—still did not want to endure being treated as guilty; or, while enduring this—which is the sixth—did not nevertheless love being treated in that way—which is the seventh [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition, read “or could not love being treated in that way” instead of “did not nevertheless love being treated in that way”]—although he knew that his master wished it, surely the master would not forgive him that fault, but would instead punish him as an unjust servant.

So the Lord will not forgive us our faults if we do not humble ourselves through these same degrees, as he commands.

## CHAPTER CX. How each person should regard himself as inferior to all

But because we are sometimes elated because we do not compare ourselves rightly with others, we must consider how we ought to do so. If we wish to compare ourselves with others, we ought to consider only those things that come from us and are in us [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read “those things that are ours and in us” instead of “those things that come from us and are in us”], not those granted to us as gifts by God [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read “those granted to us” instead of “those that are granted to us”].

For this is what someone does who exalts himself above another on account of the good things granted and bestowed upon him by God [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “the good things conferred and granted to him” instead of “the good things granted to him”], like someone who boasts while dressed in another’s garments.

We ought not, therefore, compare these things with the good qualities of others, but only our own evils, which we have from ourselves and within ourselves [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read “which are ours and in us” instead of “which we have from ourselves and within ourselves”]. If we do this—that is, compare our evils with the good qualities of others—we ourselves shall seem inferior to all others [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read “if we do this, namely, compare our evils with the good qualities of others, we shall seem inferior to all”].

By contrast, because the proud do this, even if they are worse than everyone, they nevertheless judge themselves better than all. For they consider only their own good qualities and compare them with the evils of others, whose evils they ought in no way to consider.

## CHAPTER CXI. That consideration of another’s sin is harmful

Consideration, or knowledge, of another’s sin produces many evils in different people. If the person who considers another’s fault is a sinner, he perseveres in his own sin by the other’s bad example. If he has repented of sin, he grows cold toward repentance because of the same example. If he is being tempted by the same sin, or even by another [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “or even by another’s sin” instead of “or even by another”], he is more easily overcome by the other’s example. But if he is free from temptation, he is tempted by the very fact that he considers the other’s vice.

If he is just [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read simply “but if just” instead of “but if he is just”], by placing himself above the other he is lifted up into pride. If he loved that person in God, he now begins to hate him [Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts read “if he loved him, he now begins to hate him”; manuscript A. 1 reads “if he loved him in God, he begins to hate him”; the Cologne edition reads “if he loved him even in God, he now begins to hate him”].

Another’s fault, therefore, should not readily be considered, since its consideration produces so many [Col. 0670A] evils. His virtue, however, should always be attended to, because consideration of it has the opposite effect [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “proceeds in the opposite direction” instead of “has the opposite effect”; the Bec manuscripts read “has the opposite effect”]. For it makes the sinner convert, the penitent repent, the more greatly tempted resist temptation, the untempted remain steadfast, the just become humble, and the one who loves love more [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “but makes the one who loves love more” instead of “and makes the one who loves love more”].

Whoever strives to ascend to the summit of humility should therefore attend to another’s virtue, not his vice, and to his own vice, not his virtue [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript A. 1 reads “the virtue of another, not his vice, and his own vice”].

## CHAPTER CXII. On the two sisters who guard this mountain

[Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript A. 1 omits this chapter and the following chapters up to Chapter 117, whose likeness it expresses in other words.]

The guards of this most beautiful mountain of humility are two sisters: namely, the shame that exists before God and the shame that exists before human beings. For when someone is tempted, if he firmly brings these two sisters before the eyes of his mind, he will easily overcome the temptation. He ought to speak to himself in this way.

## CHAPTER CXIII. On the shame that exists before God

If I commit this sin or that, how will I be able to lift my eyes before God and his holy angels, who see me [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “who see this” instead of “who see me”]? What shall I say when all creation sees my guilt [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition, read “my sin” instead of “my guilt”] on the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscripts Corb. 307 and Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition, read “all my guilt” instead of “all creation sees my guilt”]? Angels and devils [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript Vict. 13, manuscript Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “angels, that is, devils” instead of “angels and devils”] will accuse me. I will certainly not sin; rather, for your sake, Lord, I will be put to death all day long, and I will guard my ways so that I do not sin [Note: [Col. 0669C] The Cologne edition reads “my ways so that I do not sin in my soul” instead of “my ways so that I do not sin”].

Let everyone set this before himself, let him consider himself in this way, and let him rescue himself from the beasts rushing upon him [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript Vict. reads “let him rescue himself from the beasts”; manuscript Corb. 307 reads “let him rescue himself from his enemies”; the source text reads “let him rescue himself from the beasts”]. But it must be considered that the shame which exists before God [Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript Vict. 13 reads “before God” instead of “before God” in the sense of “in God’s presence”] is always free and a faithful guardian.

## CHAPTER CXIV. On the shame that exists before human beings
Nevertheless, the shame that is before human beings is sometimes deceptive and a most evil thief. For it often happens that, when the mountain of humility—of which we have so often spoken—is to be established in someone’s mind, a goat of lust, a wolf of rapacity, or some other beast of the vices attempts to break in [Note: [Col. 0669C] *Tenet irrumpere* (“keeps breaking in”), manuscript and Edit. Col.; *tentet irrumpere* (“attempts to break in”).]. When the shame that exists before human beings ought to prevent it from entering, it sometimes speaks to itself, giving itself bad advice, as follows:

“There will be great disgrace,” it says, “if I give this temptation of lust access, so that it may later become known. But no human being will see this, and I shall conceal myself well; it will no longer be known. Let me consent to pleasure just a little now, and, whenever I wish, I shall correct myself. Then, by repenting, I shall become much better than I am now. For many have risen after a fall and afterward have become better.”

Thus the shame that exists before human beings, through its bad counsel, is sometimes deceived and deceives; it permits the evil beast of vice to enter the mountain that it ought to guard. Once it has been permitted to enter, it cannot easily be expelled. For if the person who committed the crime later wishes to confess it, that thought which had previously promised him that he would amend himself as soon as he wished now says, after the fault has been committed:

“How shall I confess? With what face shall I disclose my guilt? I shall no longer have honor if I reveal myself; rather, I, who am now esteemed, shall be contemptible forever. What, then, shall I do? I shall satisfy myself by living voluptuously; I am not yet able to keep to the way of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Tenere valeo* (“I am able to keep to it”), manuscript Vict. 13; *tenere volo* (“I wish to keep to it”).].

See how the wretched man is deceived [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Homo in his decipitur* (“the man is deceived in these matters”), manuscripts Corb. 307 and Vict. 13 and Edit. Col.; *homo decipitur* (“the man is deceived”).]. How craftily he is defeated, how subtly overcome! He himself had gradually established the mountain of humility by making progress; he himself had appointed guardians of that mountain; he himself drove those guardians from the mountain’s defenses; and afterward, by guarding himself badly, he handed himself over as a captive to his enemies.

In me, indeed, lies that by which I make progress with God’s grace; in me also lies that by which I fail. No one forces me to make progress. No one compels me to come to failure. God suggests, reason suggests, virtue suggests that I live rightly; and there is in me the substance of free choice, namely freedom, and I can do this [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Quod et hoc facere* (“and that I can do this”), manuscript Corb. 307; *et hoc facere* (“and I can do this”), manuscript Vict. 13 and Edit. Col.; *quod hoc facere* (“that I can do this”).] if I wish. But, on the other hand, the devil suggests, appetite suggests, and vice suggests that I live voluptuously; and I have the power to do this [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Potestatem hoc faciendi* (“the power to do this”), manuscript Vict. 13 and Edit. Col.; *possibilitatem hoc faciendi* (“the possibility of doing this”), manuscript Corb. 307; *potestatem faciendi* (“the power to do it”).], but I do not wish to oppose them [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Sed contradicere nolo* (“but I do not wish to oppose them”), manuscript Corb. 307; *si contradicere volo* (“if I wish to oppose them”).].

## CHAPTER CXV. On the Consultation of the Two Sisters Mentioned Above

[Note: [Col. 0671C] *Confabulatio* (“conversation”), manuscript Vict. 13 and Edit. Col., instead of *de consultatione* (“on consultation”).]

It must be understood that the shame that exists before human beings sometimes deceives, and through it the hearing of vices reaches us in many ways. The shame that exists before God neither deceives nor is deceived. For when it is summoned back to the mountain, it finds afterward that its own place—namely, humility, which it ought to guard—has been overthrown by vices through the deception of its sister, as though scattered by the snouts of pigs [Note: [Col. 0671C] *Dejectum* (“cast down”), Edit. Col.; *disjectum* (“scattered”), manuscript Vict. 13; *dissectum* (“cut to pieces”).]. It is violently disturbed, grieves, groans, and often even pours forth tears; wretched, it miserably asks itself how the destructive beast entered, what the cause was, what its beginning was, and what its entrance was. And while it vehemently curses it, behold, its deceptive sister often deceptively consoles it in this way:

“Come now, why do you grieve so much? Why do you afflict yourself with so many and such great tears? That person or that person sinned more seriously than you, and obtained pardon. It is human to sin, and sin is not as great a burden as you make it.”

By giving such bad advice, she attempts to lessen its grief. But the faithful guardian, who fears being accused before God, just as she does not know how to deceive, so she scorns to admit bad counsel. For she laments what has been committed with grief, and by lamenting continually seeks the forgiveness of her Creator; thereafter she guards her own place with still greater care.

## CHAPTER CXVI. That God’s Mercy Should Not Always Be Considered

[Note: [Col. 0671C] “That God’s mercy should not always be considered at the time of temptation,” manuscripts Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “That God’s mercy should not always be considered.”] [Col. 0672B]

It must therefore be noted that, at the time of temptation, before the fault has been committed, God’s mercy should never be considered; rather, his justice and judgment, his fury and indignation. These must be weighed [Note: [Col. 0671C] “These must be weighed,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “These should be weighed.”], these must be brought back before the eyes of the mind, and these must very often be recalled with great horror.

When someone is tempted, he should not say, “The mercy of the Lord is great,” but rather this: “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31). When the appetite of lust strikes someone, he should not then think, “On whatever day the sinner groans, all his sins will be consigned to oblivion” (Ezekiel 1:4), but rather, by repeatedly reflecting, he should consider that everyone who sins in hope is accursed; and Isaiah’s words:

“Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, wicked children, a depraved seed” (Isaiah 1:4).

But if the admission of sin has occurred through an injury, then God’s mercy should finally be considered more earnestly, lest despair of forgiveness supervene. At the time of temptation, therefore, everyone must strive by every means [Note: [Col. 0671C] “Must strive vehemently,” manuscripts Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “must strive.”] not to be overcome. For although God has promised forgiveness to the penitent, he has not promised the delinquent that he would give him the will to repent.

Since it is certain that whoever turns away from evil and does good earns God’s grace, while everyone who practices sin incurs his anger and indignation [Note: [Col. 0671C] “And incurs anger and indignation,” manuscript Vict. 13; “and incurs the anger of indignation.”], we must take the greatest care both to avoid vices and to cling to virtues.

## CHAPTER CXVII. What Comparison Exists among Those Who Ascend

Three things are necessary for one who ascends: innocence, beneficence, and placing oneself beneath others. Innocence must be such that it harms no one; beneficence, such that it benefits everyone; and placing oneself beneath others, such that one judges oneself inferior to everyone [Note: [Col. 0671C] “Inferior to all others,” manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 and Edit. Col.; “inferior to everyone.”]. Hence the Apostle says: “Considering one another superior” (Philippians 2:13).

Everyone ought to offer these three things to others and demand none of them from anyone as a debt. For if someone’s servant had sinned against his master in many ways, he would not only provoke his master’s anger [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Would provoke the master’s anger,” manuscripts Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 and Edit. Col.; “would serve the master’s anger.”], but would also incur the indignation of all his fellow servants; and if some injury were meanwhile done to him, he ought not to complain justly.

Someone says: “I gladly offer innocence and beneficence to others, but I cannot believe myself inferior to everyone else. For they are murderers, adulterers, robbers, and the like.”

The answer is this: Whenever you make a comparison between yourself and another, do not place on the scales what is not yours; rather, place there what is yours—namely, your own evils—and afterward his good qualities. Such comparison, or such consideration, should always exist among those who ascend [Col. 0673B]. If you see any good in yourself, attribute it not to yourself but to God. Hence the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

## CHAPTER CXVIII. A Comparison between the *Coenovexia* and Charity

Thus we ought to use innocence, beneficence, and placing oneself beneath others in giving and receiving, just as a *coenovexia* is customarily carried [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Thus therefore we ought to use innocence, beneficence, and placing oneself beneath others, etc.” Manuscript A. 1 sets down the contrary of these things.]. Those who carry it upward [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Quippe illam, qui* (“indeed, those who carry it”), manuscript Vict. 13; *quippe qui illam* (“indeed, those who carry it”), manuscript Corb. 307; *quippe illi qui* (“indeed, those who”).] [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Subvehunt* (“carry upward”), manuscripts Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; *subeunt* (“undertake it”).] turn their faces toward the place to which they are going; toward the place from which they come, they turn their backs. For it can be carried in three other ways, though not suitably: with faces turned face-to-face, with back to back, or with faces turned toward the place from which they wish to proceed and backs toward the place where they ought to go [Col. 0673C].

It must also be noted that a *coenovexia* is not carried in operation by fewer than two people; nor can charity—what we wish the *coenovexia* to signify—exist between fewer than two. If, then, several people were building a house for themselves on some mountain, and stones, cement, and other things belonging to the construction of the house had to be carried upward from the valley by *coenovexiae* [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Coenovexia sursum* (“the *coenovexia* upward”), manuscript Vict. 13 and Edit. Col.; *coenovexiis sursum* (“by *coenovexiae* upward”).], into the mountain, and if, I say, those carriers took up that instrument in such a way that either each turned his back toward the place to which they were going, or their faces toward it, and their backs toward the place from which they wished to proceed; and while they could not go properly in this manner, they began to quarrel with words, and from quarrelling [Note: [Col. 0673D] *De litigio* (“from quarrelling”), manuscript Vict. 13; *et de litigio* (“and from quarrelling”), manuscript Corb. 307; *litigio* (“quarrelling”).] came to blows and hair-pulling, and then to weapons—tell me, what would a passerby say if he found them fighting for this reason? Certainly, that they were insane.

Let us therefore consider all these things in ourselves, because we ought to maintain such a disposition in fraternal charity that we carry, as it were, a kind of spiritual *coenovexia*. For we ought to strive to build a house for ourselves on the lofty mountain—namely, in the heavenly homeland—which is constructed solely by the practice of virtues and to which one ascends by the steps of humility.

These steps must be made through innocence, beneficence, and placing oneself beneath others: namely, that I harm no one, serve everyone, and prefer anyone whatsoever to myself. When I frequently offer these things to others, even if they are not offered to me, I endure it patiently. I make for myself steps suitable for proceeding up the mountain of virtues toward the house of the heavenly homeland, and I carry the *coenovexia* well.

But if I refuse to offer these things to others, I turn my back against their back, as it were, by turning my face away from the one who is proceeding and whom I ought to follow as though he were going ahead [Col. 0674B]. But if I seek to have these things done for me as though they were owed, and he does what I ask, although unwillingly because I demand it, I turn my face against his face in the carrying [Note: [Col. 0673D] *In subvectionem* (“in the carrying”), manuscripts; *in subvectione* (“in the carrying”), manuscript and Edit. Col.; *in subjectione* (“in subjection”).] of the *coenovexia*. But when I demand and he refuses what is demanded, because I irritate him through my demands, we turn our backs toward the place to which we ought to go and our faces toward the place from which we proceed.

Thus, whoever attempts to carry the *coenovexia* in these three ways will generally endure quarrels and disagreements. Therefore, let us always direct our faces—that is, our intention—toward innocence, beneficence, and placing oneself beneath others, so that we may offer these things to everyone and demand the same from no one. For this is to turn one’s back toward those things, namely, toward the present and passing things, and one’s face toward the future and toward those things that are themselves everlasting.

## CHAPTER CXIX. A Comparison between the Qualities of the Body and of the Soul

Just as there are two kinds of bodily quality, so also there are two kinds of quality of the soul [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Just as there are two qualities,” manuscripts A. 1, Vict. 13, and Corb. 307; “just as there is one quality.”]. Bodily quality is sometimes sudden and sometimes continuous. It is sudden when, for example, a person suddenly becomes dark through a sudden illness or blushes from shame, but as soon as either of these passes, he returns to his former color. It is continuous when someone suffers a lasting illness [Note: [Col. 0673D] “When someone suffers a lasting illness,” manuscripts A. 1, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “when he suffers a lasting illness,” manuscript Vict. 13; “when a person suffers a lasting illness.”], which produces a continual pallor.

So too the quality of the soul is sometimes sudden and sometimes continuous. It is sudden when, as a sudden temptation rushes in, the soul suddenly grows dark in sin, but immediately returns through confession and repentance to its former beauty [Col. 0674D]. It is continuous when it lies continually in sin, through which it continually appears deformed before God.

These two kinds of quality of the soul are two kinds of its unworthiness. One who is unworthy according to a sudden quality nevertheless does not for that reason take Christ’s body and blood to his own judgment. But whoever, being unworthy according to a continuous quality, presents himself, takes them to his own judgment [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Being unworthy according to a continuous quality, he exists,” manuscripts; “being unworthy according to a continuous quality, he presents himself.”].

## CHAPTER CXX. On the Impurities of the Heart

Let the person who intends to examine his weakness also know that there are three kinds of impurity of the heart. The first kind is love of things that ought not to be loved, such as lust and similar things. The second is hatred of things that ought not to be hated, such as hatred of another’s prosperity. The third is neither love nor hatred, but a certain vanity of thought, as when we think about where this person is coming from or where that person is going [Col. 0675B].

## CHAPTER CXXI. A Comparison between Bodily and Spiritual Illnesses

Again, it must be observed [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Let him observe,” manuscript A. 1; “it must be observed.”] that there are two kinds of illness of the soul, just as there are of bodily illness [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Of bodily illness,” manuscripts A. 1, Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “of corporeal illness.”].

Bodily illness is sometimes, as it were, natural illness and sometimes accidental. It is, as it were, natural when someone has suffered a continual weakness from the very infancy of human life [Note: [Col. 0675D] “As though from the infancy of human life, a continual weakness,” manuscript Vict. 13; “as though from the infancy of human life, a continual illness,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “as though from the infancy of human life, a continual [condition].”]. It is accidental, as with a fever, which comes upon a person through sudden cold or some other accident. Since this illness occurs through an external cause, it can be cured more easily with a single remedy. The other, because it clings to a person as though naturally, cannot be cured by one sudden treatment; it can be diminished and alleviated through frequent treatment, until it can be borne more easily.

So too among vices, which are illnesses of the soul, some are, as it were, natural, while others are, as it were, accidental. As it were natural are gluttony and lust, which grow out of the flesh itself in a person from infancy. Accidental are such things as lying, which is often produced by some external cause, even when it has not been premeditated. Since these arise from external causes, they can be avoided by lighter vigilance. The others, because they are joined inwardly to nature, cannot indeed be entirely erased by a single abstinence; nevertheless, through continual effort they can be diminished to the point at which they can be tolerated quite easily [Note: [Col. 0675D] “So that they can be tolerated sufficiently easily,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “to the point at which they can be tolerated quite easily.”].

We must always persist in eradicating these things, even if we cannot erase them entirely. For just as a person suffering from a natural bodily illness acts foolishly if he neglects to apply medicine because, after applying it once or twice, he has not immediately been cured, so one held by the natural illness of vices acts foolishly if he ceases to apply vigilance because, after applying it several times, he has not immediately been freed from temptation.

## CHAPTER CXXII. On Appetite, and the Difference between Appetite and Will

No one can be entirely without the appetite for vices; instead, he naturally retains it in the place of an appetite for true benefit. For after human nature lost perfect blessedness, it also lost its perfect benefit. Nevertheless, it always naturally possesses an affection for that same benefit [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Yet a natural affection,” manuscripts Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “yet it naturally possesses an affection,” manuscript A. 1; “yet an affection.”].

And because it cannot possess perfect benefit, it cannot lose the appetite for perfect benefit either. Thus it has an appetite for gluttony and lust and for other false benefits, and through these it proceeds, seeking that perfect benefit whose appetite it naturally retains.

The devil sometimes inflames these appetites through false benefits, and through them suggests some sin to the will; at other times he persuades the will by himself, so as to incite those same appetites toward sin. For example, he suggests to a drunkard who can no longer drink more that he should wish to eat some roasted food [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Aliquid ad suum* (“something for himself”), manuscripts; *aliquid assum* (“some roasted food”).], so that he may acquire an appetite for drinking more.

Thus the devil incites the will to sin either through these appetites or by himself. It is as if a robber were to incite someone to strip himself by some device with which he would warm his flesh [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Or warm his own flesh,” manuscripts; “with which he would warm his flesh.”], or simply by telling him to undress. When the man approaches him, suspecting no trickery, he is suddenly seized, beaten, stripped in turn, and eventually killed.

These appetites are nothing other than certain necessities of benefit. For appetite is not the same thing as will. The appetite for evil is not evil [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Is not evil,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “is not bad.”], but the will for evil is evil. Since the devil always inflames these appetites, they must be restrained with great diligence and vigilance.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. A Comparison between Water and Human Nature

Human nature spreads through vices as easily as water spreads over level ground [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Profunditur* (“is poured out deeply”), manuscripts; *diffunditur* (“spreads”), manuscript Corb. 307; *effunditur* (“is poured out”).]. Therefore, the person who wishes to restrain it must act like one who struggles to hold back flowing water.

Just as such a person confines and restrains water in a pond [Note: [Col. 0675D] “He who confines water,” manuscripts; “he confines water.”], so this person must restrain wandering human nature within some rule [Note: [Col. 0677C] “This person must restrain wandering human nature within,” manuscript Corb. 307; “he must restrain human nature within,” manuscript A. 1; “he must restrain nature.”]. And just as the first person takes care that the pond does not break open anywhere through which its water might flow away, so it is fitting for the other to take care [Note: [Col. 0677C] “So it is fitting for the just person to foresee,” manuscripts; “so this person must take care,” manuscript Corb. 307 and Vict. 13; “so it is fitting for him to take care.”] that he does not violate his rule in any respect, through which he might rush into sin [Note: [Col. 0677C] *Quoad peccatum* (“with regard to sin”), manuscripts; *quo ad peccatum* (“by which toward sin”).].

For in this way the appetites of the flesh can be restrained, which is to establish a certain peace between the flesh itself and the spirit. No one will be able to possess this peace better within himself than the person who has endeavored to subject himself to the strictness of the monastic order. For that order is, as it were, a kind of enclosure or pond of a fish-pond. Just as fish die when the water of the fish-pond runs out through the enclosure’s small and frequent breaches and those breaches are not repaired, so every religious community of the monastic order perishes completely if its discipline gradually grows lukewarm through contempt for minor faults, as Scripture testifies, saying: “He who despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1).

[Note: [Col. 0677C] Manuscript A. 1 omits this passage to the end of the chapter; manuscript Vict. 13 omits *quidem* (“indeed”).]

## CHAPTER CXXIV. That Peace Is Achieved in Four Ways

Peace is achieved in four ways, by which a person is brought to true rest. It is either made by someone between two others, or between oneself and another, or between the flesh and the spirit, or between our corruptibility and the incorruptibility that we await by God’s gift [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Which, nevertheless, is received as a reward after this present life alone,” manuscript A. 1.].

If we now possess the three higher forms, then at last we shall reach that peace of which the Apostle says: “Have peace with God” (Romans 6) [Note: [Col. 0677C] Manuscript A. 1 omits this passage down to “The first two forms,” which it also abridges.].

The first two forms are achieved through concord. There is a carnal peace, and there is also a spiritual one. Concord likewise may be carnal or spiritual. Carnal peace and concord are what unbelievers, or even false Christians, possess when they agree in sin and thereby obtain a certain peace. Christ did not commend this peace when he said: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). By “earth” he can mean earthly people, and by “sword” the separation by which we are separated from carnality [Note: [Col. 0677C] “You can understand,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “you can understand.”].

The third form occurs through the spirit’s victory, by which it subjects the flesh to itself. Concerning this the same Lord says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27); and the prophet: “Great peace for those who love your law” (Psalm 118:165); and: “His place was established in peace” (Psalm 11:13); and: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 33:15).

The fourth form will occur through recompense, when our corruption has been transformed into incorruption, as we have already said.

## CHAPTER CXXV. On the Fourfold State of Human Nature

It must be noted, then, that human nature has four states [Note: [Col. 0677C] “It must be noted, then, that human nature has four states,” manuscript A. 1; “There are indeed four states of human nature.”], through which it is made blessed or wretched according to different merits. The first two are blessed, while the last two are wretched [Note: [Col. 0677C] “A blessed or wretched life,” manuscripts A. 1 and Corb. 307; “blessed or wretched.”] [Note: [Col. 0677C] “The last [are] wretched,” manuscript A. 1; “the last are wretched.”]. Among the blessed, one is less blessed and the other most blessed. So too among the wretched, one is less wretched and the other most wretched.

The less blessed state was that in which Adam stood in paradise before sin. The most blessed is the state in which the souls of the saints are now in heaven. Our state is the less wretched one, in which we are, while we live, in this world [Col. 0678B]. The most wretched will be the state in which the reprobate will remain in the punishments of hell. Therefore, in order that we may rest eternally in the most blessed state, let us labor temporarily in God’s service [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Let us labor temporarily,” manuscript A. 1 adds: “For an eternal reward would also have to be earned through eternal service, if both could exist simultaneously.”].

## CHAPTER CXXVI. A Comparison between Human Service and Reward

Since a human being could not have an eternal reward if he rendered eternal service to God by laboring, God compares the reward of his own life, which is eternal, with the service of human life, which is temporal [Note: [Col. 0677C] “If God required eternal service by laboring. But God,” manuscripts; “if he rendered eternal service to God by laboring, God,” Edit. Col.; “Unless [he rendered service] to God,” etc., as in the manuscripts.]. If a person serves God for as long as he lives, and God assists him in this [Note: [Col. 0677C] “And God assists him,” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “and God assists him in this.”], then God will repay him.

But if someone did not begin to serve God from the beginning of his life [Note: [Col. 0677C] *Qui vero non a* (“but he who did not from”), manuscript A. 1; *quod si non a* (“but if not from”).], yet, from the time he began, persevered until the end, God will not demand from him the service of his earlier life, just as he himself will not demand from God the reward of that earlier life [Note: [Col. 0677C] “He demands from him the reward of his earlier life,” manuscripts A. 1 and Corb. 307; “the reward of the earlier life.”].

But if, on the contrary, a person serves God badly for as long as he lives, God will repay him with an evil recompense for as long as he himself lives. If he did not begin to serve God badly from the beginning of his life, but, from the time he began, wished to persevere until the end of his life, God will not recompense him with evil for the good service of his earlier life, just as he himself will not wish to have the evil reward of that earlier life [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Will recompense with evil, just as,” manuscript A. 1; “will recompense. Just as.”] [Note: [Col. 0677C] “He will wish to have,” manuscript A. 1; “he will not wish to have.”]. For he will lack both the reward for the good of his earlier life and God’s evil recompense for his earlier life [Note: [Col. 0677C] “He will not lack [it],” manuscripts and Edit. Col.; “he will lack the reward,” manuscript Corb. 307; “he will lack the reward of eternal life.”].

Therefore, let every human being always serve God in whatever order God has appointed him.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. On the Three Classes or Orders of Human Beings

There are three orders of human beings: those who pray, cultivators, and defenders. God has arranged these orders in this world for different duties, just as a certain head of a household distributes sheep, oxen, and large dogs throughout his household.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. The Example of Sheep, Oxen, and Dogs

He keeps sheep so that they may bring him milk and wool; oxen so that they may work the earth; and dogs so that they may defend both sheep and oxen from wolves.

If each of these animals performs its own duty, the Lord preserves it for life, because its life is useful to him [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Because its life is useful to him,” manuscript A. 1; “because its life is useful to him.”]. But if it does not perform the duty that is its own, it is judged worthy of death alone, because its life produces no fruit [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Produces no fruit,” manuscript Vict. 13; “makes no [fruit].”]. For if a sheep brings neither milk nor wool [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Milk and wool,” manuscripts A. 1, Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “either milk or wool.”], and an ox does not work the earth, what other fruit can they produce [Note: [Col. 0679D] “What other fruit can they produce?” manuscripts A. 1 and Edit. Col.; “what other fruit could they produce?” manuscript Corb. 307; “what other fruit might they produce?” manuscript Vict. 13; “what other duty could they perform?”]?

Again, if a dog assigned to guard the livestock permits wolves to tear them apart, or begins to strangle them itself or to strangle other dogs, what else should its master do except crush it?

So God acts concerning those orders whom he has appointed in this world for different duties. He has appointed some—clerics and monks, for example—to pray for others and, gentle like sheep, to nourish them with the milk of preaching and to make them fervent in the love of God through the wool of their good example [Col. 0679C]. He has appointed others, such as cultivators, so that they and others may live from their own labor, like that of oxen. He has also established some, such as soldiers, so that they may display severity as necessity requires and defend both those who pray and the cultivators from hostile peoples, as from wolves.

If each person fulfills the duty of his order, he earns a long life, because he lives for the benefit of the others. But if he refuses to do this, he is unworthy of life itself, because he produces no fruit for which he lives. For if clerics and monks do not offer prayer or preaching to others, or even present a good example, or if cultivators refuse to cultivate the earth, what other duty can they fulfill [Col. 0679D]? Again, if soldiers refuse to defend others, or even, like rabid dogs, kill or oppress those same people or themselves, what should be done with them other than what should be done with rabid dogs [Col. 0680A]?

Let everyone perform the duty of his own order, lest everything for which he lives be considered a lie.

## CHAPTER CXXIX. On Lying

For if someone does not perform what belongs to his order, all his outward appearance lies, since it testifies that he belongs to that order [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Which testifies that he belongs to that order,” manuscripts A. 1, Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “which testifies that he is of that order.”]. His action, his words, and his very thought also lie, because they testify to a lie as though it were truth.

For when someone does or says or thinks something, he indicates to others that it ought to be done, said, or thought in that way [Note: [Col. 0679D] “He judges for others,” manuscripts; “he indicates to others.”]. Indeed, a person often speaks more through action than through words, as can be seen from the following example.

## CHAPTER CXXX. The Example of a Physician

If a physician were to say that some herb was beneficial to a sick person and did not eat from it [Note: [Col. 0679D] “If a physician were to say that some herb was beneficial for a sick person,” manuscript A. 1; “if he were to say that a certain one was beneficial.”] [Note: [Col. 0679D] *Aegroto salutiferam esse, ac ut ea comederet* (“that it was health-giving for the sick person, and that he should eat it”), manuscript Vict. 13; *cognosco salutiferam esse. Et non ex ea comederet* (“I know it to be health-giving. And he did not eat from it”).], but were to taste another, a deadly one, he would advise the sick person more through his action than through his word that he should eat the latter, since by action more than by word he would urge him to eat it [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Than he would urge him to eat it by word,” manuscripts A. 1 and Corb. 307; “than by word.”].

When someone does, says, or thinks something, he therefore makes it clear to others that it ought to be done, said, or thought in that way [Note: [Col. 0679D] “He makes it clear to others,” manuscripts Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and Edit. Col.; “he makes it clear to the rest,” manuscript A. 1; “he indicates to the rest.”]. If this is indeed the case, he speaks truthfully in action, word, and mind. But if it is not the case, he lies in all these respects. Thus, insofar as truth is spoken, life is good; but insofar as a lie is uttered, life is evil, because every sin is proved to be a lie. For sin is committed only in thought, word, and deed; and whenever we sin through these, we lie to God and to human beings [Note: [Col. 0679D] “We lie to God and to human beings,” manuscript A. 1 omits “to God and to human beings.”].

Let us therefore place the fear of God as a guardian over these three, because Scripture testifies: “The fear of the Lord will expel sin” (Ecclesiasticus 1:27). Indeed, fear is the gift of the Holy Spirit and the first of all the others.

## CHAPTER CXXXI. On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit

There are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. Of these gifts, as has been said, fear is the first and, as it were, the foundation of the others. The Holy Spirit lays this beneath the field of the mind and superimposes the other gifts in their order [Note: [Col. 0679D] “In its order,” manuscript A. 1; “also in its order,” manuscripts Corb. 307, Vict. 13, and Edit. Col.; “in its order.”], as though in a building.

First, he makes the mind fearful, lest it be separated from God because of its sins and be tormented with the devil in the punishments of hell. Upon this fear he then superimposes piety, when he breathes into the mind that fears in this way compassion for itself and makes it piously recall how wretched it will be if, separated from God, it is tormented with the devil in hell [Col. 0680D–0681A].

Then he superimposes knowledge upon piety [Note: [Col. 0681D] “He superimposes it upon the mind,” manuscripts; “he superimposes it upon piety.”], when the mind that fears in this way and has compassion for itself searches for the manner in which it may be saved, and the Holy Spirit grants it knowledge of this matter. Thereafter he superimposes fortitude upon knowledge, when the mind, fearful and compassionate toward itself, now knowing what it ought to do, becomes strong through the gift of the Holy Spirit to perform what it has learned and through which it trusts that it can be saved.

After this he builds counsel upon fortitude, when the mind, already strong for performing what it has learned through pious fear to be necessary, learns through its own experience, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, what counsel it ought to give others concerning all these matters.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. That Five Gifts of the Holy Spirit Belong to the Active Life, but Two to the Contemplative Life

[Col. 0681B]

These five gifts of the Holy Spirit pertain to the active life, whereas the two that follow—namely, understanding and wisdom—pertain to the contemplative life. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit adds [these gifts] to the first five, so that the edifice of his gifts may be fully completed. For after the Holy Spirit makes the mind fearful, compassionate toward itself, energetically performing what it knows must be done, and advising others about these matters by its own example, he kindles that same mind to understand why God commands this or that, and why a person, even if he does good to another, ought to demand no repayment from him. When the Holy Spirit breathes understanding of these things into the mind, [Col. 0681C] he finally heaps wisdom upon it: that is, what the mind understands by reason becomes most pleasing and sweet to it, and solely out of love for righteousness it follows what it understands must be followed. Yet from this wisdom, which we have placed last, the Holy Spirit begins, through the Prophet, to enumerate his gifts, and by enumerating them descends all the way to fear, from which we began to ascend. Hence we should note that, by descending, he indicates to us how, from these same gifts, he constructs an edifice in us by ascending. When this edifice has thus been put together, the Holy Spirit dwells in it, governs the whole household of the inner house—that is, all the faculties of the soul—and orders them for service.

[Note: A.1 reads *ipse tamen* (“he nevertheless”) for *ipsa tamen* (“the Spirit nevertheless”); manuscripts read *primus quinque* (“the first five”) for *primis quinque* (“upon the first five”). A.1 reads “consulting others from his own examples,” Corb. 307 “consulting others by his own example,” and another witness “consulting others from his example.” Manuscripts read “he kindles, and the same [mind]” for “he kindles that same [mind],” while the Cologne edition reads “he approaches that same [mind].” Several manuscripts add *tamen* (“nevertheless”) after “from him.” A.1 and Corb. 307 read “may breathe understanding into the mind; finally” for “breathes understanding into the mind, finally.” A.1 and Vict. 13 read “so that what indeed,” and Corb. 307 “and since indeed,” for “when what indeed.” A.1 and Corb. 307 read “may become sweet to it” for “becomes sweet to it.” A.1 reads “it is necessary to know, indeed” for “it should be noted that.” A.1 reads “governs the faculties and orders [them]” for “governs all the faculties and orders them.”]

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. On the qualities and dispositions of the soul

[Col. 0681D]

From this point he reduces the qualities of the soul, which had previously been unstable, to good dispositions. For dispositions are qualities of the soul that have already been formed into habits. [Col. 0682A] They are not called dispositions when they arrive quickly and quickly depart, but when they exist stably in the soul.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. Some dispositions are good, others evil

Of these dispositions, some are good and others evil. The good are therefore called virtues, and the evil vices.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. On virtue and vice

Virtues produce good external actions, whereas vices produce evil ones. Yet a person is not properly said to possess virtue or vice every time an act of virtue or vice is performed. They are properly possessed only when they are held by habitual practice; hence people are called just or vicious. When they are possessed perfectly, although virtue and vice are wholly unlike each other, their actions are nevertheless not always unlike. [Col. 0682B]

[Note: A.1 has the corrupt reading “they always have unlike [actions]”; other readings give “they have unlike [actions].”]

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. On wisdom and folly, sometimes coinciding

Some of these qualities—for example, perfect wisdom or folly—often cause the same actions to be performed. For just as a perfectly wise person does not wish to abandon what seems good to him, so too does one who is perfectly foolish. The wise person does this because he knows that it is not good to abandon it; the fool does it because he thinks so. There is also an intermediate person, neither so wise that he does not fear being deceived, nor so foolish that he wishes to persist in the evil he has begun. This person often abandons what seems good to him, because he trusts another’s advice more than his own. [Col. 0682C]

[Note: A.1, Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition read “or folly” for “and folly.” The same witnesses read “For just as a perfectly wise person” for “Just as a perfectly wise person”; the Cologne edition reads “this then seems good to him” for “what then seems good to him.”]

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. On hatred and love of sin

Likewise, perfect hatred of sin and perfect love of it often display the same external action. For just as one who perfectly hates sin in himself does not care who has discovered it, so also does one who perfectly loves it in himself. The former does this so that God may forgive him; the latter does it out of his own shamelessness. There is also an intermediate person, who neither hates sin so much that he wants everyone to know it, nor loves it so much that he wants everyone to remain ignorant of it. He therefore conceals it from many, yet discloses it to one person through confession. [Col. 0682D]

[Note: Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “hatred of sin” for “hatred of the sin.”]

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. On humility and pride

Again, perfect humility and perfect pride have certain similar actions. For just as a perfectly humble person, when he sins, wants his superior to punish his fault severely, so does a very proud person. But the humble person wants this for the remission of the same fault, whereas the proud person wants to suffer out of indignation. He disdains it when his superior, taking pity on him, spares him even a little; rather, he desires that his fault be punished immoderately. [Col. 0683A]

[Note: The manuscripts add: “For here he possesses that kind of shame which is partly before God and partly before human beings.”]

There is also an intermediate person who wants neither to be punished with complete severity nor to have his fault entirely forgiven. Thus, when he sometimes sins, he desires that his fault be partly punished and partly forgiven. For here he possesses that kind of shame which is partly before God and partly before human beings.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On the three kinds of shame

[Col. 0683B]

There are three kinds of shame, which also produce different external effects. One exists before God alone, another before human beings alone, and the third partly before God and partly before human beings. Shame before God alone occurs when we are ashamed because we are what we ought not to be, and, if our sins did not harm others, we would confess them before human beings. Shame before human beings alone occurs when, because we recognize what we ought not to be, we are ashamed, and are ashamed to disclose our offenses even to one person through confession. Shame partly before God and partly before human beings occurs when we are not so ashamed of our sins before God that we would also be willing to confess them before human beings, and yet are not so ashamed before human beings that we would be embarrassed to disclose them even to one person through confession. [Col. 0683C]

The shame that exists only before human beings is therefore good; that which exists partly before God and partly before human beings is better; and that which exists before God alone is best. For this last kind, as has been said, would make people confess their fault before everyone, if doing so did not harm others. The intermediate kind is neither so perfect that a person wants to confess before everyone, nor so imperfect that he might at least be ashamed to confess his fault before one person. The first kind is ashamed to confess the fault even before one person; nevertheless, it too is good, because, although with blushing, a person sometimes does confess the fault to at least one person. [Col. 0683D]

[Note: The manuscripts read “which also produces it” for “which also produce [different effects].” A.1 omits the text from “Shame before God alone” to the end of the chapter. Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “because we recognize what we ought not to be, we are ashamed” for “because we recognize what we ought not to be, we are ashamed and embarrassed.” Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “perfect, that he might at least be ashamed to confess his fault before one [person]” for “perfect, that he might be ashamed to confess his fault before one person.”]

## CHAPTER CXL. On the three things observed in a young person

[Col. 0683D]

Three things are observed in a young person, by which it may be foreseen that he will attain uprightness. These are silence, bodily restraint, and shame. Silence means that he should first be silent and speak afterward. Bodily restraint means that he should not lightly move his eyes here and there, nor move his hands or feet, but should keep all the members of his body decorously under control. Shame means that he should blush before human beings when he does something forbidden, and, suffused with redness, show openly that he is ashamed. Let every young person strive for these three things, because through each of them he is advanced toward higher things. By keeping silent and listening to the teaching of the wise, he gradually acquires knowledge and, through their words, reaches spiritual life by successive stages. [Col. 0684A]

[Note: Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition title the chapter “On the three kinds which are observed.” A.1, Vict. 13, and the Cologne edition read “three kinds are observed” for “three things are observed.” The manuscripts read “when he does something forbidden,” A.1 “when he does something forbidden,” and another reading “when he does something illicit.”]

## CHAPTER CXLI. A comparison between different kinds of nourishment and commandments

[Col. 0684B]

Just as a person is brought to full bodily maturity by different kinds of nourishment, so he is brought to spiritual life by dissimilar commandments. For he is first nourished with his mother’s simple milk, then with something else, thereafter with food mixed with flour, later with pieces of bread, and afterward even with crusts, until he is able to use solid food of any kind. In the same way, he is first commanded to believe in God, then to love him, afterward to fear him, later to do good, and finally even to endure adversity, until any commandment may safely be imposed upon him. [Col. 0684B]

[Note: A.1 omits this and all the other material that follows concerning the Comparisons. It attaches to the preceding material comparisons of the spiritual soldier and the temporal soldier, and of the Lord’s storeroom; these do not occur this far in the printed editions. Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “Thus he is first commanded” for “Thus it is first commanded to him,” and “endure diverse things” for “endure adversities.”]

## CHAPTER CXLII. The example of a new vessel once imbued

Because a person once fully imbued with spiritual teaching seems like a new vessel. For just as a new vessel, once filled with a good drink, scarcely loses its flavor, even if it is afterward filled with another drink of a different taste, so a young heart once imbued with spiritual teaching scarcely loses its sweetness, even when it is afterward occupied with a secular task because of the office to which it attends. [Col. 0684C] But if, by remaining silent, it scorns listening to the words of the wise, it will not rise to any knowledge of spiritual life.

[Note: Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 omit “afterward occupied with a secular task because of the office to which it attends.”]

## CHAPTER CXLIII. The example of a knife

Just as one who lacks his own knife is rightly hungry if he refuses to cut with another’s knife, so one who lacks knowledge of his own rightly perishes from spiritual hunger when he refuses, by remaining silent, to make use of another’s knowledge. Therefore, by remaining silent, let him attend to the words of the wise, so that through their teaching he may attain knowledge of spiritual life. By restraining the members of his body, as was said above, he also makes progress toward what is better, because in this way he makes the mind more stable [Col. 0685A] and calm. A stable and calm mind, in turn, produces calm words externally as well.

[Note: Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “cut with another’s [knife]” for “cut with another’s.”]

## CHAPTER CXLIV. An example from still water and the rays of the sun

Just as still water, when it receives a ray of the sun on one side, reflects an equally still ray onto some wall on the other side, so a peaceful mind, receiving someone’s word through the ear, sends it back equally peacefully through the mouth. But just as agitated water reflects an agitated ray, so a troubled mind returns a troubled word, as well as every external action. Therefore, if a young person is to make progress toward tranquility of mind, speech, and conduct, he should restrain each of his members decorously. By blushing, as was also said, he makes progress toward what is better, because shame produces repentance, of which one kind is dry and another [Col. 0685B] moist.

## CHAPTER CXLV. On dry and moist repentance

Repentance is dry when someone is indeed sorry for his sin, but lacks the moisture of compassion and remorse. It is moist when he possesses both, and mourns his sin with great contrition of heart. Therefore, in order to make progress toward this repentance, not only a young person but every human being should feel shame when he does something unlawful. [Col. 0685D]

[Note: Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “may benefit him” for “may make progress.”]

## CHAPTER CXLVI. The example of one wishing to cut down a great tree

It must be understood that, if someone repents of a great crime, he must act like a person wishing to cut down a large tree. For just as that person first takes care to cut down the smaller shrubs around it, lest they hinder him while cutting down the tree itself, so someone in this situation must first uproot the lesser vices adjacent to that crime, lest they offer him some impediment when he is destroying the crime itself. [Col. 0685C]

[Note: Corb. 306 reads “if anyone repents of a great [crime]”; the Cologne edition has both “if anyone repents of a great [crime]” and “how greatly [someone repents].”]

## CHAPTER CXLVII. On detraction

The vice of detraction, which generally arises from idleness, must be avoided with great care, because it is a pernicious evil. Hence blessed Clement, among the other things he confesses to have learned from the mouth of blessed Peter, writes as follows.

## CHAPTER CXLVIII. On the three kinds of murder

[Col. 0685D]

There are three kinds of murder, which are punished with equal penalties: the killing of brothers, detraction, and hatred. Paul also says of this: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15). One person devours another and, as it were, bites him whenever someone makes another person lesser by speaking evil of him. Hence it is necessary that they be consumed by one another—that is, that they be thrust into the punishments of Gehenna and most wretchedly tormented. Thus the person who devours another through detraction is himself consumed by the one whom he strives to consume with the bites of detraction. For when he tears apart that person’s life through detraction, he condemns himself before God, the just judge. And so it often happens that the person who disparages another, unless he repents, falls into condemnation before God, although the person who is slandered feels no harm from the detraction itself. But let us inquire what detraction accomplishes, or what it is, and, by inquiring, briefly state what the Lord grants—not because it is unknown, but so that what is known may be held more firmly. [Col. 0686A]

[Note: Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “tears apart” for “dilacerates.”]

## CHAPTER CXLIX. An example from fire, wind, and the human mind

[Col. 0686B]

It often happens that a fire burns for a while in some material; and if it is driven by the wind, it grows into a greater blaze. In the same way also the human mind, struck by a salutary admonition to perform an action, rises more quickly after the suggestion to do what it had previously neglected to undertake. Thus, just as fire is moved by the wind, so the mind is aroused from the sluggishness of torpor by an admonition.

[Note: The supplied text has *si* (“if”) before “driven by wind.” Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “in the same way also the human mind”; Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “more quickly rises.” Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “let the mind be,” while Corb. 307 reads “if the mind be,” for “thus the mind is.” The Cologne edition reads “sluggishness of the body” for “sluggishness of torpor.”]

## CHAPTER CL. A definition of detraction

Detraction occurs whenever someone says something about another with the intention that the person himself may thereby be loved or esteemed less. Detraction offers the wicked hardness, the repentant refreshment, and the one about to be tempted an example of sinning, as though it were fuel for wickedness. For it is natural that, just as I fear doing what I hear no one do, so I more readily presume to do what I perceive many—or even a few—doing; and the more people I know to have done the same thing, the less hesitant I am to do it.

Even a good person, if he has neither repented of some serious offense nor experienced any temptation regarding it, may hear through detraction that another has committed this or that serious offense. Unless he provides beforehand with the eye of vigilance, he receives material for pride. For it is characteristic of pride always to rejoice in being exceptional. Therefore the sin of detraction must be avoided with the utmost care, because it is the fuel of such great destruction. [Col. 0686C]

[Note: Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read *refrigerium*, “refreshment,” for *refrigerationem*, “a cooling.” Corb. 307 reads “one about to be tempted” for “the tempted.” Vict. 13, Corb. 307, and the Cologne edition read “unless he provides beforehand with the eye of vigilance” for “unless he guards himself with a watchful eye.”]

## CHAPTER CLI. A commendation of charity

[Col. 0686D]

For detraction takes away charity, without which it is impossible for anyone to please God (Heb. 11:6). “He who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). The person who diminishes love of neighbor in another’s heart therefore sins more seriously than one who snatches food from a poor person’s mouth. [Col. 0687A] For just as the soul is more precious than the body, so it is more serious to take away the soul’s food than the body’s. The food of the soul is the love of God and neighbor: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8). Therefore whoever removes the love by which the soul ought to be nourished kills the soul, insofar as it lies within him.

For this reason, care must be taken that no one presume to speak anything harmful about another, unless he does so for the purpose of correcting him. To a superior, or to someone whom I think capable of advising the sinner and healing the wounds of his vices, I ought to disclose another’s wrongdoing for the sake of correction when I cannot correct it myself. And lest someone else be corrupted by that person’s offense, I may also briefly warn him not to enter into an especially close association with such a person. Otherwise, I must in no way speak anything adverse about anyone. [Col. 0687B]

## CHAPTER CLII. What harm detraction causes and what benefit comes from hearing good things

Moreover, just as speaking evil about anyone harms many, so hearing good things about others usually benefits many. For when good things are reported about someone, good people imitate his deeds, and they strive more eagerly to persevere in their own goodness insofar as other followers of the same goodness are praised. If they are repentant, they carry out their repentance more diligently in order to become good, insofar as they hear through careful reports how much more glorious good people are than the wicked. If they are wicked, they are ashamed when they hear good things reported about others, since they recognize that they themselves are empty of such things; and they are more easily recalled to repentance when they are told that many—and perhaps people weaker than themselves—perform good works. [Col. 0687C]

Let it therefore be the constant practice of every Christian always to think good things about others, speak good things, believe nothing evil, and say nothing evil.

[Note: Vict. 13 and Corb. 307 read “Moreover, just as”; Vict. 13 reads “how much more gracious” for “how much more glorious.”]

## CHAPTER CLIII. On knowledge, will, and practice

Since with all our actions we must seek with the greatest care to be good—for otherwise we cannot be blessed—we must also ask what things we ought rather to use in order to become good. Three things therefore seem to me necessary for anyone who wishes to become good: knowledge, will, and practice. For unless someone possesses knowledge of how to do good, he will in no way be able to perform the good by which he may attain salvation. And if he possesses knowledge but does not have the will to act, he will in no way be good. But if he has acquired recognition of the good and the will to act, yet has not completed it in practice, he will not be good, even though he is able to act. [Col. 0687D]

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “with all [our actions]” for “in all [our actions].” Vict. reads “must be sought,” and another witness “must also be sought,” for “must be sought.” Vict. and Corb. read “will in no way be” for “will in no way be good.”]

## CHAPTER CLIV. The example of a harpist

[Col. 0688A]

If someone who ought to be a harpist did not recognize the harp, how could he be a harpist? If he did not recognize that instrument, and, even if he recognized it, did not wish to touch it, how could he be a harpist? If he recognized it and touched it, but scorned to acquire skill in its use, he would never become proficient in this art merely through knowledge and willingness, without practice. In the same way, even if someone possesses knowledge of living well and the will to do so, he will not be good unless he also maintains the practice of good works according to his ability.

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “did not recognize” for “did not know.”]

## CHAPTER CLV. A comparison between the idle and sinners

[Col. 0688B]

Some people are ignorant of the sacred Scriptures. When they hear something from them that they could retain for their own edification, they also say contemptuously: “Why should I retain this tiny thing? I will not become wise because of something so small; why then should I impose this labor upon myself?” They say: “I shall rest now and live as I can, because I shall study wisdom further in vain. For not everyone who is not wise will perish.”

The lazy and foolish person proposes these and similar thoughts to himself, and does not perceive that the ancient enemy suggests such things to him, so that throughout his whole life he may devote himself to no useful purpose, but may always live and perish in negligence and torpor. Moreover, they say: “There are enough wise people in the world, enough writers, enough people who possess skill in the arts; there is no need for me to weary myself by speaking. Besides, I have already passed beyond childhood and am approaching old age; I can no longer attain great fruit of knowledge if I begin to labor now.” In this way the lazy person reasons with himself and persists in the sluggishness of his torpor. [Col. 0688C]

In a similar way, the sinner is sometimes ensnared so that he does not rise at some point to the exercise of good works. It often happens that a person who is defiled by the pollution of lust comes to recognize himself and regrets what he has done. But when temptation returns and an opportunity for sinning is present, he says: “Why should I lose this pleasure? I can certainly allow myself this one, just as I have allowed myself many others. In the future, when I have had my fill, I shall confess everything all at once, and thus become good. I shall therefore satisfy myself until I make satisfaction to God for everything; then I shall fast, then chastise my body with so many afflictions and so many beatings, and devote myself so greatly to almsgivings and frugalities, that nothing deserving punishment will remain in me. Since this and that still remain in me without confession, why should I restrain myself from this pleasure alone?” [Col. 0689A]

Some people sometimes give themselves such wicked advice, and in their misery do not consider how deeply they are darkened inwardly by the blindness of error. For the more heavily they are bound by serious sins, and the poorer they are in goodness, the more ardently they ought to shake off every pleasure suggested by the devil. For just as virtue added to virtue is beneficial, so vice added to vice is harmful.

Therefore, whoever can perform some good work today must not postpone it in any way. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it promptly, for there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld” (Eccles. 9:10).

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “they also say contemptuously”; they also read “suggests such things to him” for “suggests such things to him for his destruction.” Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “Moreover they say: ‘There are enough …’” Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “I can no longer” for “I could no longer”; Vict. reads “until [I make satisfaction] to God for everything.” Vict. and Corb. read “and frugalities” for “and frugality.” Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “perform some good work” for “perform some good.”]

## CHAPTER CLVI. A comparison between the poor, the foolish, and the negligent

[Col. 0689B]

Such people, negligent in sinning, also imitate foolish poor people. A foolish poor person, when he acquires a small coin or some other little gift, says: “Why should I save such a tiny thing? I will not become rich because of it. I shall spend it on apples, or nuts, or anything else that gives me pleasure. I do not want to be considered anxious by guarding this.” In this way the foolish person, while he considers small things worthless, never progresses to greater ones.

But the wise poor person guards the small things he obtains, and the less he considers himself to possess, the more eagerly he wishes to retain what he has acquired, so that he may at some time reach greater things by gathering little ones together. In the same way, a person who feels himself poor in knowledge and goodness must act if he wishes to arrive at some attainment of knowledge and goodness. For just as many grains make a mass, drops a river, and many coins a rich person, so many judgments of knowledge make a wise person, and many actions of goodness make anyone good. [Col. 0689C]

[Note: Vict. reads “may seek at some time to reach [greater things]”; Corb. reads “may reach [them]”; the supplied text reads “may at some time reach [them].” Vict. reads “many judgments of knowledge,” Corb. “many knowledges of judgments,” and another reading “many knowledges,” for “many judgments of knowledge.”]

## CHAPTER CLVII. On knowledge and its three parts

Since knowledge is necessary for someone to become good, and it is evident that no one can comprehend it who neglects to gather even its smallest parts—unless perhaps someone is suddenly enlightened, as were the apostles and prophets—we must ask how, by God’s grace, we can acquire it. It seems to me that it can be attained through three causes: teaching, experience, and reasoning.

## CHAPTER CLVIII. On teaching

[Col. 0689D]

Knowledge is acquired through teaching, which is received through reading and conversation. For whoever reads, or hears someone reading or speaking, applies himself so that he may possess knowledge of what is read or reported. [Col. 0690A]

[Note: Vict. 13 and the Cologne edition read “For whoever reads”; Corb. 307 reads “because when someone reads.”]

## CHAPTER CLIX. On experience and reasoning

Knowledge is acquired through experience when someone possesses certain knowledge of a matter that he has tested. And through reasoning it is also acquired, when, through the natural discernment of the mind, a person is made firm in those things that must either be done or avoided. Knowledge is therefore acquired through these three things.

But because knowledge puffs up unless charity builds up, it accomplishes absolutely nothing without the will to goodness. The good will is therefore one that is subject to God’s will. It is subject to God’s will when it wills what God wills it ought to will; and it is called just or upright when it embraces what God wills it ought to will. [Col. 0690B]

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “And through reasoning” for “Through reasoning.”]

## CHAPTER CLX. That we ought not always to will what God wills

We ought not always to will what God wills, but what God wills that we ought to will. For God willed to take blessed Martin from this life; but if his disciples had then willed this, they would certainly have been cruel. They did not will what God willed; rather, they willed what God willed that they ought to will, and they maintained the life of righteousness. [Col. 0690C]

Therefore whoever carries together with knowledge the will to do good approaches goodness for the most part. Hence it must be understood that whoever desires to have a good will must strive to withdraw himself from vanity. For just as one action excludes another action different from itself, so one thought drives out another thought, and one will likewise repels another will. Thus, when I write with my hand, I am not sowing a field; then, when I have sown, I exclude writing. In the same way, when I am thinking about something empty, I am not meanwhile considering what is useful; and when afterward I have considered something useful, I drive out emptiness. Having passed briefly over what we have said about knowledge and will, let us also see how necessary the practice of good action is. [Col. 0690D]

[Note: Vict. and Corb. read “but we should will that which God wills.” The manuscripts and the Cologne edition have the corrupt *viam* (“way”) for *vitam* (“life”) in the following sentence; one manuscript reads “But they willed what God willed them to ought to will, and the way [of righteousness].” Vict. reads “Thus, when he himself thinks,” and Corb. “Thus, when he thinks,” for “Thus, when I think.” Vict. and the Cologne edition read “I drive out virtue” for “I drive out emptiness.”]

## CHAPTER CLXI. On practice

[Col. 0690D]

Just as the human body cannot subsist without the frequent use of food, so the soul cannot live without the frequent practice of the virtues. Therefore whoever desires to attain the effect of goodness must possess practice itself together with knowledge and will. [Col. 0691A]

## CHAPTER CLXII. That a good person makes good use of everything

A good person derives benefit for himself from all good and evil things. For when he hears something good about a good or evil person, he rejoices and gives God thanks for it. By doing this, he receives from God the reward of a good will, as though he had been a fellow-worker in that same deed. If he hears something evil, he grieves, and this is reckoned to him as a reward, as though he had been the destroyer or diminisher of that same evil.

But someone says: “I cannot rejoice in the goodness and prosperity of my enemy, nor grieve over his misfortune; and if I confess this with my mouth, I condemn myself, for in my heart I am lying.” [Col. 0691B]

[Note: Vict. and the Cologne edition title the chapter “That good persons …” Vict. reads “from all good and evil people” for “from all good and evil things,” and “is reckoned” for “is counted.”]

## CHAPTER CLXIII. How enemies can be loved

For the purpose of considering this, we must understand how a person who desires to progress in goodness must do violence to himself so that he may be able to advance.
