Although my carnal or natural appetite desires harm for my enemy, I ought not confess this with my mouth, but rather mourn his harm and, against the appetite of my flesh, favor his prosperity. I should show, at least in words alone if I cannot do so in my heart as well, that his harm displeases me. For if we consider reason, we act more rightly when we obey God than when we consent to carnal pleasure.

The Lord’s command is that we love our enemies. If, therefore, I cannot love them with affection, because I am still unable to bend my carnality toward loving them, nevertheless I ought to wish that I might be able to love them; and until I can do this, I should proclaim what is good, and not evil, about them—the word that lies within my power. When I do this, I am not lying when I say that I love them, because I possess the will, but not the ability to accomplish it (Rom. 7:18). Yet, according to the reason of my spirit, I take delight in the Lord’s command that I love them, although the corruptibility of my flesh resists. For now it is no longer I who do this, but the sin that reigns in me (ibid. 7:20). It is one thing to experience something, another to consent to it. [Col. 0691C]

The evil person, by contrast, heaps sin upon himself from all good and evil people, since he envies all good people but shows favor to the wicked. His end inwardly is death and tribulation, whereas the end of the just person is Christ, life, and exultation.

[Note: Corb., Vict., and the Cologne edition read “my carnal or natural appetite”; Vict. and the Cologne edition read “confess” for “profess.” Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “and his harm” for “his harm.” Vict. reads “from good and evil,” rather than “from all good and evil things.”]

## CHAPTER CLXIV. On understanding, love, and practice

God is perceived in three ways: through understanding, love, and practice. Through understanding we become wise; through love we are justified; through practice we are blessed. To the extent that someone understands God, he is wise; to the extent that he loves him, he is just; but to the extent that he experiences him, he is blessed. But when we see what is upright, we perceive God through the understanding of the mind, since whatever uprightness exists comes from him. [Col. 0692A]

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “But when” for “When.”]

## CHAPTER CLXV. A comparison between God and the sun

Just as, from the sun’s radiance, we perceive the sun itself before we see it clearly, so we perceive God from the contemplation of our mind when, by the very light of truth, we perceive something true. Thus, by understanding and loving him, we perceive him in the present through faith and hope. In the future, however, we shall perceive him through vision, because “we shall see him as he is” (II John 3:2). Nevertheless, not everyone will see him equally, nor will everyone burn equally with love for him. [Col. 0692B]

[Note: Corb. reads “not now through hope,” and Vict. “not now through vision,” for “through vision.”]

## CHAPTER CLXVI. A comparison between fire and the love of God

Just as wood and iron become hot in different ways through the heat of fire, so the heavenly spirits and the souls of the blessed burn unequally with the love of God.

## CHAPTER CLXVII. How the saints will see God

Now “we see him in a riddle” (1 Cor. 13:12), and, as it were, in a painting: just as if we were looking at a painted sun or sea. When we see the sun or sea depicted, we do not possess them as they exist in reality. But when we clearly see the shining sun, or behold the sea as turbulent or calm, we truly contemplate the thing as it is, although we cannot contemplate it as fully as it exists in itself. Thus the saints of God will see God in his glory, but they will not be able to comprehend the magnitude of his divinity or the immensity of his power. For he would not be immeasurable if he could be comprehended by anyone’s understanding. [Col. 0692C]

[Note: Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “if he could be comprehended by anyone’s understanding” for “if he could be comprehended by someone’s understanding.”]

## CHAPTER CLXVIII. On the four ways of commanding and the corresponding four ways of obeying
Sometimes a command is good and obedience is good; conversely, sometimes a command is bad and obedience is bad; sometimes a command is good and obedience is bad; sometimes a command is bad and obedience is good. [Column 0691D. Note: “Sometimes a command is bad and obedience is good” is omitted by manuscript Vict.]

[Column 0692D] It is a good command and good obedience when someone is commanded not to violate chastity and this is observed. [Note: “And let it be observed”: manuscripts Vict. and Corb., and the Cologne edition.] It is a bad order and bad obedience if someone is commanded to steal, or something of that kind, and does it. It is good to command and bad to obey, as, for example, if someone is taken captive and brought to execution, and is bound so that he may not flee. If someone should say to him, “Flee; I shall put myself in these chains in your place and undergo the punishment for you,” [Column 0693A] such a command is indeed good, because it proceeds from perfect charity; but consent to it is bad, because it wholly opposes charity. [Note: *Pro poenam te accipiam*: “I shall accept the punishment in your place,” manuscript Vict.; *poenam pro te excipiam*: “I shall undergo the punishment for you,” manuscript Corb.; *pro te eripiam*: “I shall rescue you.”] For where it is said, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), it is not said, “Lay burdens upon one another.”

An order is bad and obedience good, as when a superior orders someone to bring him citron apples, or something else that could not be obtained without danger. Thus David ordered water to be brought to him from the cistern; but because it was brought at the risk of his men, he repented of the order and refused to drink it, instead pouring it out as a libation to the Lord.

## CHAPTER CLXIX. On Fear, Advantage, and Love

[Column 0693B] People serve God for three reasons: namely, fear, advantage, and love. There are indeed some who, if they knew that the punishments of hell did not exist, would give up none of their pleasures for any promise of eternal goods. [Note: *Cessarent*, “they would cease,” manuscript Vict.; *cessassent*, “they would have ceased.”] Although they escape the punishments of those who do not fear God at all, they will nevertheless not find a full reward.

Others serve God in order to gain great advantage from it, either in the present life or both in this life and in the future. [Column 0693D. Note: “Either in this life”: manuscripts Vict. and Corb.] To them, if God wills, he might reasonably say: “For the sake of your advantage you kept my commandments—not because you loved me purely, but because you wanted to profit from me.” It is like those who serve a king: many do not love the king, but the king’s gifts. [Note: *Non quia regem*, “not because they love the king,” manuscripts Corb. and Vict.; *non regem*, “not the king.”]

There is another who truly loves God and keeps his commandments solely out of love for him. He serves lawfully [Column 0693C] and acquires for himself a good and perfect reward. Therefore, just as that man placed nothing above God, so God ought, in a just recompense, to give himself to him, since he surpasses all things.

## CHAPTER CLXX. On Reason, Will, and Appetite

There are three faculties in the soul: reason, will, and appetite. By reason the soul resembles the angels; by appetite, brute animals; by will, both. [Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read: “By reason it resembles … by appetite … by will.”]

The will stands midway between reason and appetite; for sometimes it turns toward reason and sometimes toward appetite. But when it turns toward reason, because it savors what is rational and spiritual, a person is called rational and spiritual. When, however, it adheres to appetite, because it savors what is carnal and belongs to irrational animals, a person is called carnal or animal.

Hence it is written: “The animal person does not perceive the things that are of God. But the spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Since, then, a person is called carnal or spiritual according to the disposition of the will, it must be understood that sometimes certain sensations are experienced in the flesh to which the will gives no consent.

## CHAPTER CLXXI. On Suggestion, Pleasure, and Consent

[Column 0694A]

There are three kinds of pleasure. The first is felt in the flesh apart from the will; this is called suggestion. The second is felt in the will of thought, though not in the will of action; this is called pleasure. [Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. and the Cologne edition read “in the will of suggestion”; the printed text reads “in the will of thought.”] The third is felt together with the will to act and is called consent. [Note: “With the will to act”; manuscript Vict. reads “in the will to act.”]

But the sensation called suggestion is accompanied by no punishment. For where there is no consent of the will, no punishment follows from the pleasure. Hence the Apostle says: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh” (Romans 8:1). And elsewhere: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:22).

[Column 0694B] He calls the inner person reason itself; the law of the members, pleasure without the will; the law of God, observance of his commandments, which is also called the law of the mind because it is kept by the mind; and the law of sin, which he had earlier called the law of the members.

## CHAPTER CLXXII. On the Names of the Soul

[Column 0694C] Note that the soul has many names. It is sometimes called spirit, mind, soul (*animus*), reason, understanding, or the inner person. It is also called vegetative, sensitive, and rational soul. But although it has many names, let us return to those about which we spoke earlier. For the will will either conduct itself rightly in relation to them and be legitimate, or, by abandoning them, become adulterous, base, and rejected.

If the will, which stands midway between reason and appetite, agrees with reason, it lives legitimately; but if it agrees with appetite, it will be adulterous. Thus reason, or spirit, is like a husband; the will like a bride; and the appetite of the flesh like an adulterer. Therefore the will must consent to it in nothing. For it is written: “Desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and when sin has been completed, it brings forth death” (James 1:15).

## CHAPTER CLXXIII. An Example of Filth

[Column 0694D] Just as, if some filthy person covered with every stench approached someone and said that he wished to consult with him, a clean person ought not to remain there, [Note: *Non debet qui mundus est subsistere*, “a clean person should not remain,” manuscript Vict.; *non deberet mundus sustinere*, “a clean person should not endure it,” Cologne edition; *non debet mundus subsistere*, “the clean person should not remain.”] so the will must not yield to carnal appetite.

## CHAPTER CLXXIV. On the Square Stone

A square stone has six equal sides; whichever of these it falls upon, it will lie firmly. So a righteous man must take care to remain steadfast in his purpose. Its six sides are these: prosperity, adversity, self-possession or freedom (*sui libertas*), subjection, being in private, and being in public. [Column 0695A] In each of these circumstances, if he is pushed by the devil, he must stand firm and not be moved from his purpose.

## CHAPTER CLXXV. On Sin

We speak of sin in three ways. According to nature—that is, strict justice—as in the statement: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22). According to grace, as in: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, his sin shall be forgiven him” (Ezekiel 18). And: “Turn to me, says the Lord, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3).

According to discipline, as when a person is commanded to repent to a certain degree. Discipline is under grace, because no one could repent or make satisfaction unless grace went before him. [Column 0695B]

## CHAPTER CLXXVI. An Analogy of Wax

[Column 0695D] You may see a person [Note: Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *videns hominem*, “seeing a person,” for *videas hominem*, “you may see a person.”] who has lived in vanity from childhood into extreme old age, who understands only earthly things and has become completely hardened in them. Engage him on spiritual matters, speak to him about the subtlety of divine contemplation, and teach him to examine heavenly secrets; you will see that he is wholly unable to perceive these things. [Note: *Ad haec videre*, “to perceive these things,” is read by the manuscripts; manuscript Vict. has *hoc videre*, “to perceive this.”]

Nor is this surprising: the wax has hardened. He has spent his life cultivating these things and has learned to pursue what is foreign to them.

Conversely, consider a boy tender in age and knowledge, unable to distinguish good from evil and unable even to understand you when you discuss such matters. [Column 0695C] Nor is this surprising. The wax is soft, almost liquid, and does not receive the image of a seal in any way.

Between these stands the adolescent and young man, suitably tempered in his tenderness and hardness, as though from old age and childhood. If you instruct him, you will be able to shape him appropriately toward whatever useful achievement you wish, whether of moral excellence (*honestatis*) or another kind.

## CHAPTER CLXXVII. The Devil’s Assault on a Novice

When the devil cannot overwhelm a monk with hatred of the life he has professed, he tries to undermine him through disgust with the way of life in which he finds himself. [Note: Manuscript Gem. G. 40 reads: “When the devil cannot make someone hate the monastic state, he tries …”]

Although he seems to grant him permission to maintain his monastic purpose, he nevertheless never ceases, by many deceptions, to accuse him of being exceedingly foolish and imprudent because he began it under such conditions, or among such people, or in such a place. [Note: Manuscripts read “monastic state” (*monachatum propositum*) for “monastic purpose”; manuscript Vict. reads “undertook it in such a place” (*loco suscepit*).]

Thus, by persuading him that he is ungrateful for the beginning granted by God, he ensures that, by God’s just judgment, he neither advances toward better things nor long maintains what he has received, nor remains usefully steadfast in it. [Column 0696A. Note: Manuscript Gem. G. 40 reads: “By many deceptions he never ceases to accuse him of being exceedingly foolish and imprudent; so that, by persuading him that he is ungrateful for the benefit of God’s beginning, he may neither advance toward better things by God’s just judgment nor …” Manuscript Gem. omits “long maintains”; its reading is “or remains in it.”]

For while he is constantly occupied with burdensome thoughts about changing his purpose—or, if he cannot change it, at least about condemning it—he never meanwhile attempts to advance toward perfection’s goal. [Column 0695D. Note: Manuscript Gem. reads “about condemning the beginning”; “he never attempts to advance toward the goal of perfection.”] Since he dislikes the foundation he has laid, he has no desire to build upon it the structure of a good life. [Note: Manuscript Vict. reads “the fruit of a good life” rather than “the structure of a good life.”]

Hence it happens that, just as a little tree, if it is repeatedly transplanted, or, newly planted in the same place, is disturbed by frequent uprooting and cannot take root, soon becomes dry and never reaches any fertility of fruit, so the unhappy monk, if he is repeatedly moved from place to place by his own desire, [Column 0696B. Note: Manuscript Gem. reads “is changed by his own desire,” rather than “is moved by his own desire,”] or, while remaining in one place, is frequently shaken by hatred of it.

[Note: Manuscript Gem. reads *conculcatione*, “trampling,” where the printed text has *convulsione*, “uprooting.”]

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII. Children Compared with Plants

Tell me, I ask, if you planted a tree in your garden and immediately enclosed it on every side so that it could not extend its branches at all, then released it after some years, what sort of tree would emerge from it? [Note: Manuscript Gem. reads, “What sort of branches do you suppose it would extend?”]

Certainly, a useless tree, rough and full of knots, with its branches crooked and tangled. This is precisely what you do, O teachers of boys, to your pupils, who have been planted in the garden of the Church through their offering, so that they may grow [Column 0696C] and bear fruit for God. [Note: The manuscripts Vict. and Corb. and the Cologne edition omit *scilicet*, “namely,” in “namely, so that they may grow.”]

But you hem them in on every side with so many terrors, threats, and blows that they are given no opportunity whatsoever to enjoy freedom. Thus, oppressed without discernment, they pile up, cherish, and nourish within themselves crooked thoughts, tangled like thorns.

The result is that, because they perceive no love, pity, or goodwill toward them in us, they likewise have no expectation of any good from you. Whatever there is of hatred, impiety, and ill will becomes their hope for the future. And so, miserably, it happens that just as they grow in body, so fear alone, envy, and every suspicion of evil grow within them because of you. They are always bent and inclined toward vices, considering among themselves either how they might avoid your snares and schemes or how they might afterward return to the world.

## CHAPTER CLXXIX. An Example of a Gold Leaf

[Column 0696D] Have you ever, I ask, seen an artisan fashion a beautiful image from a sheet of gold or silver by striking it alone? I do not think so. What, then, does he do? To shape the sheet into a suitable form, he now presses and strikes it lightly with his instrument, and afterward smooths it; now, with a measured gentleness, he raises and forms it more lightly. [Column 0697A. Note: Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read *minceam suo* [a materially uncertain, apparently corrupt reading] where the printed text has *nunc eam* (“now [he] it”).]

So you too, if you wish your boys to be adorned with good character, must combine the depressions caused by blows with the relief and support of paternal compassion and gentleness. Give tender things to the tender, just as they themselves are tender—milk, that is, rather than solid food—to those who have not yet reached mature age. [Note: “You hold tender things tenderly”: manuscripts Corb. and Vict. and the Cologne edition; the printed text reads “Give tender things to the tender.”]

## CHAPTER CLXXX. On Charity

[Column 0697B] Whoever retains charity in his heart has something for which to give thanks to God. [Note: The printed reading, *hoc unde Deus gratias scit ei*, is evidently corrupt; the variant reads *hic unde gratias Deo agat*, “he has something for which he may give thanks to God.”] But the person toward whom charity is merely directed does not possess it. [Note: Manuscript Vict. and the Cologne edition read *illi vero* (“but to him”) for *ille vero* (“but the person”), and *misericordiae* (“of mercy”) for *minime* (“not at all”).]

What thanks does God owe me if someone loves me? Moreover, the person to whom another’s love is service receives it perfunctorily as a benefit of convenience: one favor, one honor, one meal, or some other service of this kind. But another person, who has displayed charity as though it were a benefit of convenience, retains it within himself. [Column 0697C. Note: “As a service”: manuscripts and the Cologne edition; the printed text reads “perfunctorily.”]

For the service of charity passes from the one who receives it. But charity itself, which is God, remains in the one who bestows it upon others; and a good that remains is better than a good that passes away. Reflecting on this, we shall certainly see that we ought to rejoice more if we love others than if we are loved by others. No one owes me anything, nor do I owe anyone anything; therefore charity is to be offered, not demanded.

## CHAPTER CLXXXI. Everything Is Loved for Three Reasons

[Column 0697D] Whatever is loved is loved either by nature, rightly, or in hope of advantage. By nature, we love every good and useful thing. [Note: “For it is natural”: manuscripts Corb. and Vict. read *naturale enim est* rather than *natura enim est*.] Rightly, we love one who does good to us. Sometimes a thing is loved in hope of advantage.

One thing is loved for its usefulness, such as honey, because it is good and sweet, including in its use. Another is loved for its effect, such as wormwood and certain natural medicines, which, although they give health, provide no sweetness in their use.

## CHAPTER CLXXXII. That God Is to Be Loved in Three Ways

God too is to be loved in these three ways. [Column 0698A]

By nature, because he is better and more useful than all things, and therefore is to be loved more than all others.

By righteousness, because he gives us everything we possess, including the very fact that we exist. We ought to love him all the more, and more than ourselves, by how much greater he is who gave himself for us and will give himself to us again. And since we cannot personally return that gift to him—for his person has no need of these things—he shows us to whom we ought to repay it, saying: “I command you to love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:17). And the Apostle says: “Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so you ought to lay down your lives for your brothers” (1 John 3:16).

[Column 0698B] Therefore we ought to love one another: first, because even certain brute animals do this; second, because we belong to one family, namely Christ’s; third, because in his kingdom we shall love each person as ourselves; and fourth, because there we shall be loved equally by them. For it is unfitting if in this world we hate those whom there we shall hold most dear. We must understand that all who will be present there will repay us for the love we show in the present.

God is also to be loved in hope of advantage or recompense, because he promises us immortality and incorruption.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII. On Three Kinds of Freedom

We say that there are three kinds of freedom: namely, freedom of action, which everyone desires—that is, to be able freely to do what they wish. There is also freedom of understanding, which not everyone desires. And there is freedom of a right will, which is always good: very few desire this, namely, to will what they ought.

It must be noted that freedom of action without freedom of a good will is always evil. Freedom of understanding, however, is intermediate: it is good whenever it adheres to freedom of a right will, but evil when it exists without it.

At first a person possesses however little freedom of understanding—that is, he knows how to understand what is useful to him. Let him will that understanding toward the good, and so he will deserve to attain the freedom to understand whatever is useful, to will whatever he ought, and to do whatever benefits him. Under the freedom of willing stands freedom of choice. [Column 0698C]

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV. The Devil’s Hunt

Through the suggestion of sin, the devil goes hunting every day. He keeps within his nets those whom no sorrow for their own sin afflicts. He begins to lose those whom he already sees grieving over the disorder of the flesh. But he utterly loses those of the third order—that is, those healed of carnal and spiritual sins. [Column 0698D] Let the first grieve completely, the second grieve still, but let the third rejoice.

## CHAPTER CLXXXV. That God Does Not Abhor Sin

God is said to abhor the sinful soul, not because he abhors sin, which is nothing, but because the due righteousness that he would love is not present there. It is like our saying that we abhor a house in which there is nothing we love—though this and similar expressions are used improperly. [Column 0699A]

Let us therefore cling to the virtues, setting vices aside, and embrace this patience with constant practice. For patience, or any virtue without practice, is like a leaden spear.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI. Anselm’s Vision of a River

Anselm, as he used to relate, saw while lying ill and, as it were, carried outside himself in ecstasy—he saw, I say, one swift and precipitous river into which flowed the runoff of every purification and the washings of all earthly things. The water itself appeared exceedingly turbulent and filthy, dreadful with the foulness of every impurity.

It swept into itself whatever it could touch [Column 0699B] and rolled beneath its surface men and women alike, rich and poor together. The water was indeed foul, yet, as the one who guided him said, they lived from it and took pleasure in it. [Note: The Cologne edition reads *ille vero ab ipso* (“but he [was questioned] by him”) for *illo vero ab ipso* (“while he was questioning him”).]

When he asked what that torrent was, or what the multitude wallowing in it signified, that guide, the leader of our Father, added and said: “Do not be surprised. The torrent signifies the world, into which they are swept and in whose seductive impurities all who love it are entangled.” And having said this, he continued.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII. On True Monasticism

“Do you wish to see what true monasticism is?” [Column 0699C]

The other replied, “I do.”

He therefore led him as though into the sight of a certain great cloister, exceedingly spacious and beautiful. And he said, “Look around.” He looked, and behold: the walls of that cloister were covered with the purest silver. In the middle there was green grass, itself also silver, soft, fragrant, and more delightful than human imagination could conceive. Like ordinary grass, it bent gently beneath those who rested upon it, and when they rose, it too rose again. [Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read, “It too rose.”]

Why should I linger? Every kind of delight was there. When Anselm had chosen to dwell there forever, his guide promised him that, if he wished, he would show him true patience. But, as usually happens, he awoke in the meantime and lost both the promise and the one who was to show the promised true patience. [Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read simply, “He awoke and lost the promise.”]

Let us therefore willingly hear these two visions, related to us by holy fatherhood and paternal holiness; and, hearing them, let us devoutly retain them; retaining them, let us continually turn them over in our minds, so that, whenever possible, we may flee the horror of the one and devote ourselves to the pleasant delight and delightful beauty of the other—we who maintain the monastic life. [Column 0699D. Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read “the other,” without *vero*, “indeed.”]

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII. On Security and Peace in Religion

Just as an owl, while it is in a cave with its young, is happy and, in its own way, is well; but when it is among crows, jackdaws, or other birds, it is attacked and torn apart and is altogether ill-treated—one bird striking it viciously with its beak [Note: Manuscript Vict. reads *rostro percutit*, “strikes with its beak,” for *rostro male percutit*, “strikes viciously with its beak.”], another rushing upon it with its wings, and another tearing it with its claws—so it is with me. [Column 0700A]

When I can associate with the monks, my sons, I am well, and this singular consolation of my life is dear to me. But when I am separated from them and live among secular people, attacks from various concerns tear me apart on every side, and secular affairs that I do not love harass me. I am therefore ill at ease when I am thus situated, and trembling, I fear for the loss of my soul.

On one occasion this same Father of ours approached King William the Younger after the king had returned from across the sea. He humbly and gently asked him to grant permission for him to go to Rome to Pope Urban to obtain the pallium of his archbishopric. [Column 0700B] But the king, disturbed at the name of Urban, said that he did not regard him as pope and that it was not his custom to permit anyone in his kingdom to name a pope without his election.

From this there arose a serious disagreement between the kingdom and the priesthood, so great that he himself left England without the king’s consent [Note: Manuscripts Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read, “He himself left without the king’s consent”; they also read *Angliam exivit*, “he left England,” rather than *Anglia exivit*.] and set out for Rome. There he remained for some time in great honor and reverence, exalted both by the pope himself and by the Romans. At length, through the entreaties of the king and the whole kingdom, he returned to England [Note: Manuscript Vict. reads *tandem precatu*, “at length through entreaty,” for *ac tandem precatu*, “and at length through entreaty.”] and, with God’s assent and the favor of the people, was restored to his own see.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX. An Example of a Hare

[Column 0700C] On one occasion, as our same Father was departing from the court of the aforesaid king, the boys whom he was raising pursued with dogs a hare that had encountered them on the road. They caught up with it even after it had taken refuge beneath the feet of the horse on which the Father himself was riding. [Note: Manuscripts Vict. and Corb. read, “They caught up with it beneath the horse on which he was riding.”]

Knowing that the poor little creature had thus sought refuge, he held the reins, stopped the horse in place, and did not wish to deny the animal the protection it had sought. The dogs surrounded it and, with eager service, repeatedly licked it from every side [Note: The manuscripts read *hanc grato obsequia* [uncertain]; manuscript Vict. reads *ac grato obsequio* (“and with pleasing service”), for the printed *hanc grato obsequio* (“with pleasing service toward it”).]; yet they could neither drive it out from beneath the horse [Note: Manuscript Vict. reads *nec se sub equo*, “nor could they [drive] themselves under the horse,” for *nec de sub equo*, “nor [could they drive it] from beneath the horse.”] nor harm it in any way. Those who were present marveled when they saw this.

But when the merciful Father noticed some of the soldiers laughing and, as though over the capture of the animal, giving free rein to their joy, he burst into tears and said: “You are laughing; yet this unhappy creature has no laughter and no joy. Its enemies are around it, and, concerned only for its life, it has fled to us, seeking protection in its own way. This, my sons, is precisely an image of a human being and a dying soul.

“For when it leaves the body, its enemies immediately appear—the evil spirits, that is, who, while it lived in the body, persecuted it in many ways through the winding paths of vices. [Column 0701A] They are ready to seize it and hurl it into eternal death. But the soul, exceedingly anxious, looks around in every direction and longs with ineffable desire for a hand of defense and aid to be extended to it, by which it may protect itself. The demons, on the contrary, laugh and rejoice with immense delight if they can find it supported by no assistance.” [Note: *Parati sunt eum*, “they are ready to seize him,” manuscripts Vict. and Corb.; the printed text has *parati eam*, “they are ready to seize it.”]

Having said this, he loosened the reins, resumed his journey, and with a loud voice forbade the dogs to pursue the animal any farther. Then, safe from all injury, the hare, exultant and joyful, swiftly returned to the fields and woods.

## CHAPTER CXC. An Example of a Little Bird

On another occasion he saw a boy playing on the road with a little bird that had its foot tied with a thread. [Column 0701B. Note: Manuscript Vict. and the Cologne edition read “having its foot tied,” *annexum habens*.] Whenever it was allowed to go a little farther, it tried to fly away, wishing to secure its escape. But the boy held the thread in his hand and, pulling it back, dragged the entangled bird toward him, providing himself with great amusement and a beautiful spectacle.

This happened once, then again, and then repeatedly. When the kindly Father saw it, he took pity on the little bird and ordered that the thread be broken and it be restored to freedom. And behold, the thread breaks and the bird flies away: the boy weeps, the Father rejoices.

Calling those who were present, he said: “Have you noticed the boy’s game?” When they admitted that they had, he said: “The devil plays a similar game with many people, whom he has entangled in his snares and drags at will into various impediments of vice. [Column 0701C]

“For there are some—for example, let me say—who are inflamed by the fires of avarice, lust, or similar passions and, through bad habit, have become enslaved to them. Sometimes it happens that, considering their deeds, they weep and promise aloud that henceforth they will cease from such things; and, like an entangled bird, they imagine that they are free to fly. [Note: Manuscript Vict. and the Cologne edition read *si more avis*, “as in the manner of a bird,” for *et more avis*, “and in the manner of a bird”; they also read *autumant*, “they suppose,” for *autument*, “they suppose.”]

“But because they are entangled by perverse habit and held by the enemy, they are thrown unwillingly back into the same vices. This happens again and again, and they are not completely freed unless, through great effort and the grace of God, the cord of evil habit is broken.” [Note: Manuscripts Vict., Corb., and the Cologne edition read “and grace”; the printed text reads “and the grace of God.”]

## CHAPTER CXCI. On the Malice and Foulness of Sin

“If I saw here,” said Anselm, “the shame of sin, and there the horror of hell, and necessarily had to be plunged into one of them, I would plunge myself into hell before allowing sin to enter me. [Column 0701D. Note: Manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “If I saw this,” *si hic*, rather than “If I saw here,” *si hinc*.] For I would rather enter Gehenna pure and innocent of sin than possess the kingdoms of heaven polluted by the filth of sin, since it is certain that only the wicked are tormented in hell and only the good are cherished in heavenly blessedness.”

## CHAPTER CXCII. The Words of a Dead Man

[Column 0702A]

These are the words of the deceased monk Osbern, conveyed in spirit to Anselm and later explained by Anselm himself:

“Three times,” said the dead man, “the ancient serpent rose up against me, but the Bearer of my Lord (*Ursarius domini mei*) delivered me.” Saying this, he vanished.

Our blessed Father, having awakened from sleep and recalled that vision to mind, examining each detail more carefully, explained it as follows whenever and to whomever he wished:

“First, the ancient enemy rose up against him on account of the sins by which he had been bound before baptism; second, on account of the sins he committed after the sacrament of baptism and before his profession; third, on account of those he committed after his profession and before his death. [Column 0702B]

“But he fell three times. The sins by which he had been bound before baptism were removed in the sacrament itself through the faith of his parents, and the devil found them there. [Note: Manuscript Vict. reads “through the faith of his parents in him”; manuscript Corb. reads “through faith in him”; manuscript Corb. 307 reads “through the faith of his parents in him.”] Those also which he committed in the world or in the monastery before his profession were likewise abolished in his monastic profession, and that ancient serpent found them there. But the sins he committed after his profession were erased by the monk through true confession before his death.”

He said that the order of angels was signified by that lordly Bearer. For just as bear-keepers restrain bears, so angels restrain and suppress evil spirits from their savagery, preventing them from harming us as much as they wish.

*Here ends the book of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, On Analogies.*

In manuscript Bec, two additional *Analogies* are read: one concerning a Soldier and another concerning a Cellarer; these are also found in manuscript San-Germani A. 1.

## CHAPTER CXCIII. The Analogy of a Soldier

[Column 0702C]

[The supplied source ends here.]

As the temporal soldier is equipped with temporal weapons, so the spiritual soldier ought to be equipped with spiritual weapons. For whatever things are necessary to the temporal soldier against a visible enemy, those same things, understood spiritually, are entirely necessary to the spiritual soldier against an invisible enemy.

But what are the things necessary to the temporal soldier? First of all, a horse, which is so necessary to him that it may rightly be called his most faithful companion. With it he attacks the enemy who comes against him, pursues the one who flees, and, when circumstances require, flees from the one pursuing him. Next, a bridle is added, by which the horse itself is guided; for it would not keep to a straight path if the soldier did not guide it with the bridle. A saddle is also supplied, highly suitable for the soldier himself, because he will be able to mount his horse decorously for the first time and sit firmly upon it when he sees that it has a saddle on its back. Spurs are also added, very necessary for urging that same horse onward; for it would often not move its step if the soldier did not press it with spurs, one of which is on the right and the other on the left.

Then the soldier is clothed in his armor, by which he is protected from the assault of his enemy. He is dressed in a breastplate, lest any part of his body be wounded. His head is adorned with a helmet, both so that he himself may thereby be decorated and so that his principal part may be kept safe. A shield is held out before him, so that he may be protected by it in his entirety. A lance is held in his hands, so that with it the enemy, while still far away, may be pierced. He is girded with a sword, with which that same enemy may be slain at close quarters.

All these things, then, are very necessary to the temporal soldier. For he can in no way be well armed if even one of them, however small, is lacking; nor can he properly be called a legitimate soldier, since he will still be imperfect.

Yet all these things, as we have said, understood spiritually, are likewise necessary to the spiritual soldier. We call our spiritual soldier the inner man, for he ought at all times to serve his Creator as a soldier. The horse of this soldier is his own body. For just as a horse is necessary to the soldier, so the body is necessary to the inner man. As the soldier fights against his adversary with his horse, so the inner man fights against the devil with his body.

With his body he defeats the devil who comes against him by resisting his temptations courageously; he torments the devil who flees by pursuing him steadfastly; and, when reason requires, he wisely mocks the one pursuing him by fleeing. For when a person begins to live well, the devil immediately strives with all his strength to deceive him. If the person does not consent to him, but resists his temptations courageously in mind and body, he immediately conquers the devil. For this is to conquer the devil: to resist his suggestions firmly.

If the person also perseveres steadfastly in good works, both in mind and body, he strikes the devil himself with the great torment of persecution. The soldier of Christ pursues the devil, therefore, when he embraces perseverance in doing good. But when, by God’s supreme providence arranging all things justly, power over a person is granted to the devil, the devil is said to pursue that person.

Yet for the most part the soldier of Christ yields for a little while to the devil’s madness, so that he may still bear fruit for his Lord, in accordance with what that same Lord himself warned his disciples concerning the devil’s members, saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23). When the soldier of Christ does this, he wisely mocks the devil himself. He does not flee because he fears him, but so that he may still acquire prey for his Lord.

Thus the external body is exceedingly necessary to our soldier, that is, to the inner man. It must be understood, however, that it is proper to the soldier to command and to the horse to submit; to the soldier to order and to the horse to obey. For the soldier will in no way be able to fight decorously against his adversary unless his horse is subject to him and obeys him in everything. But because the horse is a mute animal and lacks understanding, the soldier places a bridle on its head, by which he can turn it here and there according to his own will, even against its inclination.

Nor will he be able to fight efficiently against his adversary unless he has a bridle on his horse. For how could he resist the enemy bravely if his own horse often resisted him? It is therefore fitting that he have a bridle on his horse if he wishes to fight efficiently against his adversary.

He ought, however, to provide a bridle proportionate to the quality of the horse. If he has an obedient and quiet horse, he should place upon it a small and gentle bridle. If, however, he has a rebellious and untamed horse, he must place upon it a large and harsh bridle. If he has one of moderate temperament, he should likewise provide moderation in the bridle.

Similarly, if the soldier of Christ wishes to contend lawfully against the devil, he ought to have a bridle on his horse. The bridle by which this sort of horse is governed is called abstinence. For through abstinence the inner man ought to restrain the wantonness of the outer man and turn him here and there according to his own will. Without the governance of such a bridle, he will in no way be able to fight efficiently against the devil.

But abstinence itself ought to be discerning. According to the condition of his body, the inner man should provide the proper measure of abstinence; otherwise it will be of no help to him, but rather a very great hindrance.

It should also be noted that a bridle usually has two reins, which the soldier ought to hold in his hand and by which he should guide his horse. But if he pulls one more strongly than the other, the horse will in no way be able to keep to a straight path. For it to keep to a straight path, the soldier must pull both reins straight.

What, then, are we to understand by the two reins of the bridle except the two forms of abstinence? One form of abstinence is excessively lax, the other excessively strict. If the inner man imposes these unequally upon the outer man—that is, if he enjoins one more than the other—the latter will in no way be able to keep to the straight path. Either he will grow proud because of excessive laxity, or he will fail because of excessive severity. It therefore remains that he impose neither upon his body indiscreetly, but hold to moderation with the hand of discernment.

This soldier ought also to have a saddle upon his horse. We believe the saddle to be gentleness. The inner man ought to place this upon the outer man, so that he may sit more firmly upon him and guide him more decorously: namely, so that no member may move here or there disorderly, but that he may restrain all things decorously and gently, doing nothing arrogantly but everything calmly.

Spurs are also entirely necessary to this soldier for urging on his horse. These spurs are the two kinds of exhortation. There are two kinds of exhortation by which the inner man ought to stir the outer man to good work: some exhortations concern fear, others love. Those concerning fear are called left-hand spurs; those concerning love are called right-hand spurs.

But fear of what, and love of what? Fear of Gehenna and love of eternal life; fear of dreadful calamity and love of delightful joy; fear of perpetual misery and love of everlasting glory.

Since, therefore, our outer man is weak and corruptible, he would often wish to cease from good work when some serious difficulty arises. But when the inner man perceives him wishing to grow sluggish on the path of good action that he has begun, he ought immediately, like a soldier, to exercise him with the spurs mentioned above—that is, with these exhortations—sometimes with the right-hand ones, sometimes with the left-hand ones, namely now by fear, now by love, and at times by both together.

We have discussed the horse and the things that pertain to it. Now let us return to our soldier and inquire more carefully with what weapons he ought to be armed.

As we said, we believe our soldier to be our inner man. Therefore, just as it is clear that a temporal soldier cannot lawfully contend with his adversary without weapons of war, so this soldier cannot contend without them. For how could he keep his members unharmed from the deadly arrows of the devil if he were not clothed in a breastplate? What security could he obtain for his principal part, or what fear could he instill in the enemy, if he did not have a helmet on his head? How could he defend both himself and his horse from the poisonous blows of the ancient serpent unless he held out a shield? With what would he pierce the enemy if he did not hold a lance in his hands? Or with what would that enemy be slain if the soldier of Christ were not girded with a sword?

His weapons, then, are exceedingly necessary to our soldier. Although these weapons are weapons of war, they are not temporal but spiritual; they are not carnal but intellectual. As the Apostle teaches, “we must compare spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:13). Our soldier is called spiritual, and his adversary is likewise believed to be spiritual. What, then, could be more fitting than that such adversaries should fight against one another with spiritual weapons?

Therefore, so that the soldier of Christ may protect himself on every side against the devil’s fiery arrows, let him immediately put on his breastplate. According to the testimony of Scripture, his breastplate is called justice (Ephesians 6:14). For just as a breastplate is woven from rings, so justice is completed through good works. The works of justice are like the rings of the breastplate, but justice itself ought to be continuous.

It is evident concerning a breastplate that, if it is broken, it is less suitable for protecting the soldier. Understand the same thing concerning justice if it too is interrupted. Justice is said to be interrupted when it is sometimes discontinued. Whoever therefore discontinues justice puts on a breastplate that is, as it were, broken. This soldier, then, will in no way be able to fight bravely against his adversary.

Therefore, so that the soldier of Christ may courageously resist the ancient enemy, let him preserve the breastplate of justice inviolate; that is, let him apply himself without interruption to works of justice.

This soldier ought also to adorn his head with a helmet, so that he himself may appear beautiful through it and may inspire the enemy with at least some terror through such a sign of security. The head of this soldier may appropriately be understood as the intention of the inner man. For just as the head presides over the other members of the body, so intention appears to preside over the other faculties of the inner man. As experience itself teaches us, intention usually precedes in us; then come care, concern, diligence, and other such things, so that intention may be demonstrated in action. Certain members then ordinarily follow.

What are we to understand by the helmet except blessed hope? For just as a helmet is directed upward, so blessed hope is always raised toward things above. The soldier of Christ therefore places a helmet upon his head when he fortifies his intention with blessed hope: that is, when whatever good he intends to do, he does solely for the hope of blessed and everlasting glory.

A shield is also very necessary to our soldier. He ought to hold it out before him so that he may be able to defend both himself and his horse from the poisonous arrows of the devil. The Apostle teaches that the shield of this soldier is faith: “Take,” he says, “the shield of faith” (Ephesians 6:16), and so forth. For faith, like an unconquerable shield, usually receives the most burning missiles of the vices and extinguishes them by mortifying them through fear of Gehenna and belief in the heavenly kingdom.

We may also most appropriately understand patience by the shield. Just as a shield, by receiving the enemy’s missiles, preserves the temporal soldier unharmed, so patience, by receiving the devil’s deadly darts, preserves the spiritual soldier.

It should also be noted that the soldier usually holds the shield before his left side. By the left side we may understand adversity. The soldier of Christ therefore holds his shield before his left side when, in adversity, he embraces patience both in mind and body. For the virtue of patience is never exercised in prosperity. A person is truly believed to be patient when he is worn down by adversity and yet is not turned aside from the straightness of hope.

It remains, then, that this soldier should immediately seize the lance in his hands, gird himself with the sword, and thus approach the single combat boldly, courageously presenting himself to his enemy.

He ought to seize the lance so that he may pierce his enemy with it; he ought to be girded with the sword so that with it that same enemy may be slain. What are we to understand by the lance except providence? Just as a temporal adversary is pierced by a lance while still far away, so the ancient enemy, as though still separated at a distance, is pierced by a certain providence.

Therefore, as we said, our soldier ought to hold this lance in his hands. In the divine Scriptures, because we usually act through them, works are often signified by hands. To hold a lance in one’s hands therefore means to exercise providence in one’s works.

When the soldier of Christ proposes to do something, he ought immediately to direct the gaze of his mind toward the action itself and, with careful foresight, examine what end it is tending toward. If he sees that it tends toward an evil end, he should immediately reject it as deadly poison, cursing it. But if it appears to tend toward a good end, whether the action is light or serious, he ought to undertake it fearlessly and complete it with cheerful devotion.

If, therefore, the soldier of Christ diligently strives to have this provident concern continually in all his works, he will be able very easily to overcome his adversary, as though that adversary had been pierced by the lance of providence.

What the sword signifies the Apostle thought worthy to explain to us: “And the sword,” he says, “of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). And again: “The word of God is living and effective” (Hebrews 4:12), and so forth.

The word of God is appropriately called a sword, namely a spiritual sword, or a two-edged sword, because what such a sword does corporeally, the word of God appears to do spiritually. A two-edged sword usually cuts on both sides. Thus the divine word appears to cut on both sides when it ordinarily pierces human hearts in two ways: sometimes by terrifying, sometimes by comforting; sometimes by threatening eternal death, sometimes by promising everlasting life.

When the soldier of Christ is able to exercise this reading of God’s word both upon himself and upon others, he appears in a certain way to slay the ancient enemy with the sword. For, as though slaughtering him, he casts him down to utter destruction when he violently drives him with the sword of God’s word far from his own territories—namely, the hearts in which he had previously dwelt.

Thus, as we said, the weapons of the spiritual soldier are exceedingly necessary.

## CHAPTER CXCIV. The Simile of the Steward of the Wine Cellar

Solomon speaks in the person of the bride in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into the wine cellar” (Song of Songs 2:4).

Let us see how a prudent steward ordinarily arranges the casks in a wine cellar. He places near the door the cask containing the weakest wine; beside it he places another containing somewhat better wine; and beside that a third, containing wine better still. Thus, the farther the casks are from the door, the better the wine they contain. Finally—that is, in the corner—he places the cask containing the most precious wine.

With the utmost prudence, the best wine is not placed near the door, but that which is cheapest. Why? Because of those entering and leaving. If good wine were near the door, the steward himself would suffer no small loss from those entering or leaving; for whatever is found close to hand is seized most quickly. Therefore he puts the cheaper drink first and the better drink farther back.

He also ordinarily exercises another prudence: when he brings someone into his wine cellar, he gives him wine to drink according to the measure of his affection for him. To one whom he loves little, he gives the lighter drink; to one whom he loves somewhat, he gives the moderate drink; but to one whom he loves very greatly, he gives drink from the best cask.

The bride therefore says: “The king brought me into the wine cellar.”

This king is the King of kings. He has a wine cellar into which his bride—that is, the faithful soul—rejoices that she has been brought. His wine cellar is called sacred Scripture.

In this cellar there are four casks filled with honeyed sweetness, whose names are these: simple history, allegory, morality, and anagoge—that is, understanding directed toward higher things.

These casks are arranged in the manner described above. First in sacred Scripture, as though beside the door, is simple history; next comes allegory; afterward morality; and finally, as though in the corner, anagoge—that is, contemplation.

History is a very sweet drink, but allegory is sweeter; the sweetest is morality; and far, incomparably sweeter, is anagoge, that is, contemplation.

The drink contained in the first cask, history, consists of the simple deeds and examples of the saints. When we attend to these, we in a certain way give our souls a drink of great sweetness.

In the second cask, allegory, there is instruction in faith. Through allegory we are instructed in faith and, in our inner man, imbued with a taste of wonderful sweetness.

In the third cask, morality, there is the ordering of conduct. Through morality we order our ways and, refreshed as though by a drink of marvelous sweetness, appear cheerful and agreeable to our neighbors.

The drink contained in the fourth cask, the one standing in the corner—that is, in anagoge—is a most sweet affection of divine love. When our soul is refreshed by its ineffable sweetness, it is in a certain way united with the highest divinity.

When this steward therefore brings people into his cellar—that is, into sacred Scripture—he gives them drink in the manner described above. He ordinarily gives the simpler and less instructed in faith and in its love drink from the first cask, that is, from history; those with greater capacity receive allegory; the more perfect receive morality; and the most perfect receive anagoge, that is, contemplation.

It should be known that whoever drinks from the fourth cask, the one standing in the corner—that is, from anagoge—will immediately become drunk, however little he may taste from it, because of the extraordinary sweetness of that drink. This is the drunkenness to which the bridegroom invites his elect in the Song of Songs: “Eat, friends, and drink, and become drunk, my beloved.”

Whoever becomes drunk with the sweetest flavor of the drink in this cask is immediately rendered insensible, like a drunkard, to the storms of this world.

This wine cellar also has a door within it; and in this door there is a key by which it is closed to unbelievers and opened to the faithful. The door of this cellar, that is, of sacred Scripture, is right faith; the key is humility.

Whoever therefore wishes to enter the Lord’s cellar, that is, sacred Scripture, must enter through the door and the key—through faith and humility. He must most firmly believe that whatever sacred Scripture says is true. Then he must humbly investigate the meaning of that Scripture, as though knocking at the door.

No one can enter the Lord’s cellar for his own benefit without faith and humility. He may indeed break in like a thief and, by a kind of force of secular learning, lick a few drops from the first casks; but he will be utterly unable to reach the last cask, which contains the wine that makes the human heart glad (Psalm 103:15)—that is, anagoge.

Whoever therefore desires to drink sufficiently from all the casks in the Lord’s cellar—that is, from history, allegory, morality, and contemplation—should strive to possess right faith together with the greatest humility.

[Col. 0709]

# LIFE OF SAINT WILFRID, BISHOP OF YORK, BY EADMER

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume III, part I, page 170.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

### 1.

Many authors have celebrated Wilfrid, the first bishop of York by that name, in their writings. Above all, Bede the Venerable describes the deeds performed by him in various passages of his *History*, especially in Book III, chapter 25, and Book V, chapter 20.

There follows Bede’s contemporary, Eddi or Heddius, surnamed Stephen, who is said, according to John Pitseus and other more recent writers, to have composed a book *On the Life of Saint Wilfrid*. He had been invited from Kent by the most reverend Wilfrid to be the first teacher of singing for the churches of the Northumbrians after James, as Bede testifies in Book IV, chapter 2 of his *History*. From this association he could certainly have learned the deeds of Wilfrid.

After Heddius comes Fridegod, to whom Odo, bishop of Canterbury, ordered that the life of the same saint be composed in heroic verse. William, the monk of Malmesbury, had read Fridegod’s composition and gives this judgment concerning it in Book I of his *On the Bishops of Canterbury*:

“Fridegod, a certain man, carried out this task in verses not to be condemned—except that, hating Latin, he loves Greek.

“He frequently uses Greek words, so that the Plautine saying may deservedly be applied to his statements:

> ‘No one will read these things except the Sibyl.’”

Fridegod began this labor immediately after the translation of Wilfrid’s relics to the church of Canterbury.

Odo himself, who governed the church of Canterbury for twenty-four years from the year 934, is also said by Eadmer to have described the deeds of Wilfrid. Eadmer, or Edmer, a monk and secretary to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, later accomplished this work in the year 1121. Thus the heading prefixed to a manuscript codex in the Cottonian Library reads:

> “The Life of Saint Wilfrid, Archbishop, by Eadmer of Canterbury, in the year 1121.”

At the beginning and end of his work the author commends the deeds he has described by the authority of the venerable men Odo, archbishop, and Bede, priest, without mentioning Heddius or Fridegod, although he quite often uses Fridegod’s very words.

This gives rise to the suspicion that Fridegod’s offspring may have been attributed to Odo, who encouraged the work. Nevertheless, from the prologue of Odo himself, which Eadmer quotes at the end of the *Life* he composed, it is conjectured that Odo’s composition was different from Fridegod’s labor.

Gervasius of Canterbury, a monk, cites Eadmer’s fragment concerning the translation of the body of Saint Wilfrid in his book *On the Burning and Restoration of the Church of Canterbury*. This fragment was taken from another work by Eadmer.

Eadmer’s contemporary was William, the monk of Malmesbury, who likewise recounted the deeds of Saint Wilfrid in Book II of his *On the Bishops of the English*, in the section concerning the bishops of York.

After all these men, Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, composed a book *On the Life of Saint Wilfrid* and dedicated it to Geoffrey, archbishop of York, as is read in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, page 172, where a fragment from this Peter is quoted.

To all these must be added the English writers, among them Thomas Stubbs, in his book *On the Bishops of York*. An old catalogue of them is found in Labbe, volume I of the *New Library*, page 322.

Among the authors mentioned above, Bede and William are accessible to everyone. Here we present two hitherto unpublished authors: Fridegod, mutilated at its end [see *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXIII, under FRIDEGOD]; and Eadmer, whose labor we received from England through the kindness of the most distinguished gentleman, Mr. Joseph Williamson, confidential secretary to the king.

If it should happen that, with the help of friends, we recover the long-awaited Heddius, we shall publish him, God willing, in the Appendix to this century or the next, together with the surviving remains of Fridegod’s poems.

### 2.

Wilfrid’s feast day is given both by the more recent martyrologies and by Bede’s widely circulated *History* as 12 October, although these words have been inserted into Bede’s text. Abraham Wheloc enclosed them in parentheses, and they are absent from our German copy, as they are also absent from Alfred’s Saxon translation.

The date mentioned above is certainly the date of the translation, on which, according to Eadmer, Lanfranc placed the body of Saint Wilfrid in a more suitable location.

But on what day the holy man departed to the heavenly realms, all the writers of his *Life* are silent. One among the ancient compilers of sacred calendars assigns the day 24 April—namely, the author of the metrical *Martyrology* published under Bede’s name in volume X of the *Spicilegium*. He writes in these verses:

> Egbert, resplendent with worthy praise of virtues,  
> Reverently ascends the star-bearing Olympus on the eighth day before the Kalends.  
> On that same day the holy bishop Wilfrid entered,  
> Carried beyond the stars of heaven by an angelic company.

Nevertheless, the solemnity of the translation on 12 October appears to have been the more celebrated, as is clear from the title that Eadmer placed after the prologue of the *Life*.

### 3.

Wilfrid lived the life of a monk from the fourteenth year of his age and wonderfully propagated the rule of Saint Benedict. In what place he first assumed the monastic habit is not entirely clear.

First, at fourteen years of age, he diligently sought both to learn and to practice among the monks of Lindisfarne whatever belonged to monastic chastity and piety, says Bede in Book V, chapter 19:

> “Not yet tonsured, but distinguished by virtues of humility and obedience not inferior to those who are his elders in tonsure. While he served God in that monastery for several years, he realized that the path of virtue taught by the Scots was far from perfect. He resolved to go to Rome and see what ecclesiastical or monastic rites were observed at the apostolic see. There he acquired the perfect pattern of the monastic life, that is, of the Benedictine life. Returning to Lyons, he was tonsured by Dalfinus, or Annemundus, the bishop of that place.”

Afterward Alchfrid, son of Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, made Wilfrid, who had returned to Britain, his teacher in Christian learning. Bede calls him “a most learned man.” Alchfrid knew that Wilfrid’s teaching was rightly preferable to all the traditions of the Scots, and therefore he had also given him a monastery of forty households at a place called Ripon.

This is what Bede says in Book III, chapter 25. He consequently calls Wilfrid an abbot, so that it must be said that he assumed the monastic insignia in that monastery. Shortly afterward, at the request of Alchfrid, he was made a priest in that monastery by the Gaul Agilbert, bishop of the West Saxons.

After the Scots had been refuted at the synod of Streaneshalch, he brought our monks into the monastery of Lindisfarne, where the Scottish monks lived. Hence, according to William, he boasts that he was the first in Northumbria who, after expelling the Scots, “taught the true Easter and ordered the Rule of the most holy Benedict to be observed by the monks.”

He built several monasteries: Ripon and Hexham in his own bishopric; others in Kent; Selsey among the South Saxons; and others in the kingdom of the Mercians.

The following verses from his epitaph refer to this:

> In these places he gathers frequent companies of monks,  
> And diligently establishes them by the precepts prescribed by the Rule of the Fathers.

In this passage the rule of Saint Benedict, which Wilfrid learned and cultivated both in Britain and at Rome, is called the “Rule of the Fathers,” as it is also explicitly called by Ambrose Autpert in his book *On the Life of Saint Paldo, Abbot, and His Successors*.

### 4.

As for the sequence of Wilfrid’s deeds, he was born in the year 634 or the following year, since he died in 709 at the age of seventy-five.

At fourteen he went to the monastery of Lindisfarne, where he remained for several years. From there he went to Rome around the year 653, shortly before or certainly shortly after the death of Honorius, bishop of Canterbury, which Bede places in that year in Book III, chapter 20.

After spending nearly four years partly at Lyons and partly at Rome, he returned to Britain, built the monastery of Ripon, and governed it under the title of abbot.

Around the year 660 he refuted Colman, the leader of the Scots, at the synod of Streaneshalch, although Bede, in Book III, chapter 26, assigns the year 664.

Yet Bede is not sufficiently consistent with himself when he writes there that Agilbert, a Gaulish bishop, took part in this synod and that, at his command, Wilfrid, still a priest, opposed Colman; and yet, according to chapter 28, Wilfrid was ordained bishop in that very year, 664, at Compiègne in Gaul by Agilbert, now bishop of Paris, who, after the assembly had ended and been dismissed, is said in chapter 26 to have returned home—that is, to his own bishopric, which he held among the West Saxons.

Certainly, in the Saxon epitome appended to Bede’s *History*, Agilbert is said to have departed from Cenwalh in the year 660 and to have assumed the bishopric of Paris in Gaul, on the river Seine.

Wilfrid, ordained bishop of York in 664, learned upon his return from Gaul that Chad had been consecrated bishop of his church and withdrew to the monastery of Ripon.

Then, summoned by Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, he later came to Kent, where he ordained priests and deacons until Theodore arrived. This is reported in Bede, Book III, chapter 28, and Book IV, chapter 2. Theodore expelled Chad from York and installed Wilfrid in his see.

In the year 670, when Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, wished to go to Rome, he asked Wilfrid to become his guide on the journey; but, with the matter unfinished, he died, according to Bede, Book IV, chapter 5.

In the year 673 Wilfrid is recorded as having been present at the council of Hertford, presided over by Theodore, through his own representatives; the same source states:

> “In the year 677, a disagreement arose between him and King Ecgfrith. The same bishop was expelled from the seat of his bishopric, and two bishops were substituted in his place: Bosa, who was to govern the province of Deira, and Eata, who was to govern that of Bernicia” (chapter 12).

Meanwhile, after two years Wilfrid went to Rome to present his case. Once the matter had been settled, he converted the province of the South Saxons to Christ and built the monastery of Selsey with the support of King Æthelwalh. With Cædwalla likewise conspiring, he instructed the people of the Isle of Wight in Christian observances (chapter 16).

In the year 687, after the death of Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, the venerable bishop Wilfrid administered the episcopate of that church for one year, until someone was chosen who should be ordained bishop in Cuthbert’s place (chapter 29).

“After a long exile, lasting more than ten years, he was received into the bishopric of the church of Hexham,” according to Book V, chapter 3.

In the second year—or, preferably, the twelfth year—of Aldfrith, who reigned after Ecgfrith and was a different man from Alchfrid, that is, in the year 697, he recovered his see and bishopric at the invitation of the king himself.

But after five years he was again accused by that same king and many bishops, and was expelled from the episcopate. Coming to Rome around the year 703, he was acquitted by Pope John and returned to Gaul.

At Meaux, when he had been brought to the point of death, he obtained from God a reprieve of five years. Later, he was restored at the council of Nidd, at the beginning of the reign of Osred, son of Aldfrith—that is, in the year 705.

He died in the fourth year of that same King Osred, after forty-five years in the episcopate, according to Bede, Book V, chapter 20, specifically on 24 April at the beginning of the year 709.

Certainly, his epitaph, reported by Bede, says that the bishop completed fifteen times three years in the episcopate.

[Col. 0713]

# AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

### 1.

[Note: This is not infrequently found written as *Brittania* among the ancients; likewise, among the Greeks, Βρεττανία (*Brettanía*) is sometimes found.]

Britain, which the Angles, after defeating and driving out the Britons, call and inhabit as England, is surrounded on every side by the ocean. From ancient times it abounded in marvelous profusion not only in native riches but also in wealth brought in from every quarter. Just as it was powerful in earthly resources, so too it was fruitful in a great abundance of most holy men.

In response to their merits, the grace of almighty God adorned the whole island with such generosity that worship in the service of God multiplied everywhere, and both public affairs and private households enjoyed great peace and fortunate prosperity.

2. But since nature has granted nothing in worldly affairs perfect in every respect, blind and destructive desire of soul, having at times driven certain people so far that they did not know how to be content with their own possessions, shattered the defenses of peace. Peace once shattered produced plunder, fires, seditions, wars, and the destruction of every good thing. These evils were sometimes worn down by holy men of that province; at other times, when the evils themselves grew without measure, those who endeavored to restrain them were crushed by the varied turmoil of misfortunes. For while they devoted their principal effort to ensuring that, having lost the uprightness of their station, they would not yield to the perversity of wicked men, and while the latter on the other hand labored by every means to prevent themselves from submitting even slightly to the uprightness of the former for the sake of correction, the same wicked men, exercising their depravity now by force, now by fraud, were wholly unwilling to have as companions in common life those whom they had been unable to overcome in wickedness.

[Col. 0713C]

Hence many were deprived of their proper dignity, many expelled from their homeland, and many also killed by the most savage death, yet most gloriously crowned by God, the just Judge. These things the Church of the English experienced at the beginning of the faith as it grew, partly from preachers who came from elsewhere; these things it endured in the progress of that same faith, partly from preachers born within it and from its own people; and these things, once that same faith had been firmly established, the Church of the English suffered with equal cruelty from its own and from foreign enemies, in the persons of its fathers.

[Col. 0714A]

To say nothing of other matters, this is why the venerable bishops Mellitus and Justus, expelled from England, went to Gaul; this is why the most holy Father Wilfrid was so often driven from the seat of his own dignity; this is why also the most glorious king Edmund and the most blessed bishop Ælfheah, condemned to an unjust death, were most worthily crowned with the glory of martyrdom; and this is why, beyond doubt, the most illustrious man and Father of outstanding holiness, Dunstan, is known to have been driven into exile. But it will suffice that I have touched on these matters briefly. For our ancestors learned many things about them worthy of remembrance, and thereafter left their descendants writings marked by the light of truth.

3. And since what has been written about the aforesaid Wilfrid is not found together in a single work, but scattered among different authors, I undertook, at the request of certain people—whom I considered it improper to contradict, or rather, to speak truthfully, compelled by love for that most holy Father—to bring together in my own work what had been written about him in scattered form.

Indeed, Bede, the most distinguished historian of our people, discusses this same Father in several places throughout his history; and Odo, of blessed memory, bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, composed a small book about his life and conduct after he had taken up the relics of that saint from the place where they had first been laid and transferred them, with great reverence and devotion, to the church that is the mother of all Britain, situated in the city of Canterbury.

Following the statements of these men in every respect, I trust that I shall say almost nothing that cannot be supported by their authority, and absolutely nothing contrary to it. Certainly, whoever deigns either to read or to hear these things, I ask not to understand that I have written them as though I wished to set my own writings above whatever the ancients have written on this subject; rather, let that person consider that I wished both to accommodate my friends, who, as I have said, requested this of me, and to offer the saint of God some service of my love and reverence.

[Col. 0713C]

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF THE MOST HOLY CONFESSOR AND BISHOP OF CHRIST, WILFRID, WHOSE FEAST IS CELEBRATED ON THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF OCTOBER

[Col. 0713D]

4. In the six hundred and thirty-fourth year, therefore, from the Incarnation of the Word of God, when Eadbald, son of the most glorious King Æthelberht of the men of Kent, ruled in Kent, and the most holy King Oswald, successor of the most noble Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, ruled in Northumbria, the boy of God Wilfrid was born of the noble lineage of the English people; and from the very beginning he was most nobly marked out for the world by a heavenly prodigy.

For when the blessed child came forth from his mother’s womb in the silence of the dead of night, a column of fire sent down from heaven above the house in which he was being born wiped away all the surrounding darkness of night with the ray of its light.

Those neighbors, therefore, who were suddenly terrified by the magnitude of so great a light rushed out of their houses. Struck with astonishment, each seized whatever he could first grasp, and, gathering into a crowd, hurried toward the fire with confused murmuring. When they reached the house, they found the flame sending out rays just as it had begun to do; but they looked on in wonder that neither the house nor anything nearby had suffered any harm.

Terrified by such overwhelming astonishment, they said: “Good heavens! What sign do you suppose this is indicating to us? Surely it is an omen of the divine power.”

As they were wanting to rush into the house, women came out to meet them, saying: “Wait, wait, we beg you! Where are you rushing? Are you hastening so eagerly to discover the cause of the fire that you see before your eyes? Know for certain that it is nothing other than a child just now brought forth from his mother’s womb.”

When they learned this, they turned back and returned to their homes, reverently honoring the great deeds of God.

What is there to say about these events? We see the ancient miracle shown to Moses, the servant of God, in the bush: behold, fire blazes in the house of the boy of God, yet does not burn; flame leaps forth, yet consumes nothing. What sign that event of old produced, the world has now learned. But what this event signified, nearly the whole nobility of the English kingdom, having experienced it in its own midst, came to understand.

For the event itself proved that, just as formerly the Lord, when he was about to free his people from Egyptian slavery, entrusted Moses with the ministry of that liberation through the fire of the bush, so now the same Lord, intending to lead another people of his own out of the darkness of vices, designated through fire sent down from heaven the one whom he had chosen to exercise the ministry of that deliverance.

5. Thus the most blessed Father Wilfrid received the beginnings of his life with the sign of such nobility. Since he was a boy of good character, he strove by his own diligence to add nobility of conduct to his noble birth. Therefore, advancing beyond his years in character, he wished to admit nothing childish, nothing insolent, into his behavior. Rather, even while still of tender age, he conducted himself in all things so modestly and prudently that, deservedly, he was loved, honored, and embraced by his elders as one of themselves.

His face was of great beauty, but the character of his conduct was far more beautiful than the appearance of his face. As far as the capacity of his age permitted, he took care to devote the duties of his tongue not to chatter, detraction, or contention, but with the greatest zeal to the things of God.

6. But after he reached the threshold of more mature age, and his mother had died, he resolved to leave the boundaries of his birthplace, so that he might devote himself more freely to the service of the Lord. When he reported this to his father, his father willingly assented to his heavenly vows and desires and ordered him to persist in his salutary undertaking.

When he had completed his fourteenth year, he came, under the protection of God as his companion, to a queen named Eanflæd. She received him kindly and kept him for some time with great honor. He made known to her that the chief purpose of his mind was to abandon the world and devote himself to the service of God.

When the venerable queen recognized this, she rejoiced greatly in the strength of his spirit and, with devoted eagerness, offered both counsel and assistance for accomplishing so great a thing. And because she learned that this man preferred the singular life of a monk, she arranged for him, as he desired, to come to the island of Lindisfarne and to be associated with the monastery of monks.

Once established there, he diligently sought to learn and practice whatever belonged to monastic chastity and piety.
