Since he was sharp of intellect, he learned the psalms and several books with great speed, although he had not yet been tonsured; yet he was already distinguished to no small degree by virtues greater than tonsure, namely humility and obedience. For this reason he was rightly honored by his elders and peers.

[Col. 0716B]

7. While he served Christ for several years in that monastery, the young man gradually perceived that the way of virtue taught by the Scots was by no means perfect. He therefore resolved to come to Rome and see what ecclesiastical or monastic rites were observed at the apostolic see.

When he reported this to the brothers, they praised his plan and encouraged him to carry out what he had decided in his mind. He immediately came to the aforesaid queen and told her that he desired to visit the thresholds of the apostles.

Delighted by the young man’s good purpose, she sent him to Kent, to King Eorcenberht, who was the son of her uncle, asking him to send Wilfrid honorably to Rome. At that time, Honorius, one of the disciples of the blessed Pope Gregory, held the rank of archbishop there—a man thoroughly trained in ecclesiastical matters.

While the young man of keen mind remained there for some time and diligently applied himself to learning the things he observed, another young man named Biscop, surnamed Benedict, of noble English stock, arrived, himself wishing to come to Rome. The king therefore joined the blessed Wilfrid to his company and ordered Benedict to bring him with him to Rome.

8. When they reached Lyon, they were honorably received by the venerable Dalfinus, archbishop of that city. Wilfrid was detained by the bishop, while Benedict proceeded as far as Rome.

The bishop delighted in the exceptionally capable young man’s wisdom in speech, the grace of his handsome appearance, the liveliness of his conduct, his steadfastness, and the maturity of his purpose. Accordingly, whatever necessities he had, he provided abundantly for him and his companions so long as they wished to remain with him.

Indeed, he offered the blessed Wilfrid a considerable part of Gaul to govern and promised that, if Wilfrid wished to take his niece as a wife, he would give her to him, so that the bishop might be a father to Wilfrid and Wilfrid, through such a union, a son to him.

But Wilfrid, giving thanks for the kindness that the bishop deigned to show him while he was a foreigner, replied that he had set his mind on a different way of life and that for this reason he had begun to leave his homeland and go to Rome.

When the bishop heard this, he supplied him with a guide for the journey and generously provided whatever the needs of so long a road required. He then sent him on to Rome, earnestly begging and repeatedly entreating him that, on his return from Rome, he should turn aside to visit him.

9. When he came to Rome, he sought the shrine of the most blessed prince of the apostles for the sake of prayer. On leaving it, he entered the oratory of the blessed Peter’s brother, being led there for the same purpose. Prostrating himself on the ground, he is said to have openly addressed the devout apostle, whom he saw present in spirit, with this prayer:

“Most holy apostle of God, brother of the most blessed Apostle Peter, behold, I, a citizen of a foreign province, have come to your threshold to seek pardon for my sins. I therefore beseech you, by the compassion that, as the testimony of the whole world proves, you show to others, that I may not seek in vain the forgiveness of sins which I trust to obtain through you, lest the progress of so great a journey prove fruitless for me.

“Rather, that I may experience the bonds of my wickedness being loosed through your merits, loosen, I beg you, the impediments of my understanding and my tongue, so that I may grasp the mysteries of the word of God in my heart and be able to communicate them to others in eloquent speech.”

O faith of the servant of God! O remarkable sign of the piety of God’s apostle! O abundant kindness and kindly abundance of God’s mercy! No sooner had he completed the words of his prayer than he recognized that he had received a most lively understanding and a most ready manner of speech.

He returned to himself and, gratefully, marvelled that he was no longer the man he had been.

10. While he was living in Rome, devoted, as he had resolved, to daily perseverance in prayer and meditation on ecclesiastical matters, he came to the notice of a most holy and learned man, namely Boniface the archdeacon, who was also a counselor of the apostolic see.

Through his instruction and friendship, Wilfrid was fortunate enough to learn from him the four books of the Gospels, the proper calculation of the date of Easter, and several other things that he had been unable to learn in his homeland.

11. Thus magnificently imbued with ecclesiastical discipline and filled with apostolic blessing, he returned to his journey. He joyfully visited Bishop Dalfinus, who had been very doubtful of his return, and remained with him in faithful companionship for three years.

The bishop tonsured him and held him in such great affection that he considered making him his heir. But, to prevent this from happening, the bishop was killed by a cruel death, and Wilfrid was reserved instead for the episcopate of his own people—that is, the English nation.

For at that time the queen of the Franks had brought a savage storm upon the Church of Christ. Inflamed by the fire of demonic fury, she coveted the possessions of all good people; coveting them, she seethed with plunder and devastation; seething, she condemned many through a cruel ordeal and, once condemned, killed them with the savagery of a monstrous death.

Therefore, to say nothing of the other cruelties she inflicted upon countless people of lesser rank, she slew eight fathers of churches by the sword, and among them removed the venerable bishop mentioned above from this life by the same kind of death.

Wilfrid followed him as far as the place appointed for his execution, wishing either, if it were granted, to die by the sword in his place, or at least, if permitted, to die together with him. But the bishop forbade this by every means, and the mercy of Christ, as well as the pilgrimage of the holy man, prevented the sword-wielders from adding so great a crime to their crimes. What at that time was a source of great terror to many also prevented it—namely, Wilfrid’s English nationality.

He nevertheless buried the murdered man with the honor due to him, and thus returned safely to England.

12. At that time the most Christian King Oswiu governed the people of the Northumbrians. He was the successor of the most blessed King and martyr Oswald. Oswiu made his son Alfrid his partner in the kingdom.

Both kings were fervent in the Christian religion, most diligent worshipers of the churches, and exceptionally devoted hearers, lovers, and followers of Catholic teaching.

When the blessed man of God Wilfrid had returned to his homeland, the fame of his holiness and prudence, and the fame of his eloquence and apostolic learning, became known everywhere with astonishing speed and reached the ears of the aforesaid rulers with great praise.

The holiness and distinguished love of Christianity that filled the kings’ hearts could not fail to take notice of the saint. Accordingly, he was presented at the court of King Alfrid, received graciously, and, within a short time, was known by actual experience to possess what had previously been known of him only by hearsay. He was then familiarly admitted into the king’s friendship.

The integrity of his life, which fame had first proclaimed, and the prudent simplicity, or simple prudence, which flourished in him toward all in humility [the Latin is uncertain], made him dear not only to the king but to all. From that time he served at the royal court for three years and won for himself favor, glory, and honor by the virtue of his spirit.

He was therefore enriched by royal gifts with both movable and immovable possessions, and he was also distinguished among worldly men. In addition, the church at Ripon was bestowed upon him by royal generosity, together with whatever belonged to its rights.

From that time he took the greatest care that his wealth should pass more toward feeding the needy than be preserved, after the manner of misers who hide away their possessions.

13. Meanwhile there came to the king the bishop of the West Saxons, named Ailbert, a holy man thoroughly trained in ecclesiastical disciplines, who was also joined to the king by a strong bond of friendship.

At the king’s request, Ailbert promoted Wilfrid to the office of presbyter, since he recognized him as supremely worthy to exercise the priesthood.

At that time a question arose concerning the observance of Easter, a question that had long been widespread and serious. Those who had come from Kent and Gaul simultaneously demonstrated and confirmed that the Scots celebrated Easter Sunday contrary to the custom of the universal Church.

For up to that time the Scots, not yet fully instructed by the sequence of Scripture’s teaching on this subject, often celebrated Easter Sunday when that Sunday fell on Palm Sunday, because on that day itself there was a fourteenth moon, which is the limit of the paschal day.

Aidan, a man of the holiest life, had in his time been a great support for this sect, to such an extent that all tolerated it with something like equanimity while they observed his exceptional conduct in the work of God. But after his death, Finan, following the traces of that sect in every respect, was appointed to his episcopate. When he too had brought his life to an end, Colman succeeded to both the sect and the see.

In his time a more serious controversy arose concerning the observance of Easter and other disciplines of ecclesiastical life. For this reason the question rightly stirred the minds and hearts of many, who feared that perhaps, having taken the name of Christianity, they were running—or had run—in vain.

The matter also reached the ears of the rulers themselves, namely King Oswiu and his son Alfrid. The former, instructed by the Scots and imbued with the sacraments of baptism, believed that nothing better could exist than what he had received from his teachers. The latter, following the privilege of the stronger faith and thus surpassing his predecessor, held it established that the rite of the Roman and universal Church excelled all others.

For the most Christian and learned man Wilfrid—who, as we have said, had received many lessons in ecclesiastical discipline at Rome and had been instructed in certain matters by Dalfinus, bishop of Gaul, at Lyon—had formed him through rational teaching and Catholic instruction, and, once instructed, had established him firmly in the stability of the true faith by removing every scruple.

When, therefore, as we have said, the question concerning the observance of Easter had arisen, it was decided that a synod should be convened and that the question should be debated and settled. Both kings came there—the father and the son—and earnestly begged that the Holy Spirit might deign to be present with them.

The aforementioned Bishop Ailbert, the friend of King Alfrid, therefore came with the blessed Wilfrid and his own presbyter Agatho. Against them Colman came with his clerics and brought with him to the synod Abbess Hild, a supporter of his sect, along with several others.

14. When silence had been made, King Oswiu is said to have spoken first, after a preface, in this manner:

“Until now, venerable Fathers, the schism that has arisen in the churches of Christ has led certain people who were less devoted to truth so far that holy Easter has been celebrated twice in one year—something which is shown to be forbidden even to say. Yet, for those who consider the cause carefully, this does not seem so very surprising. For when the rams themselves take different paths, they also drag their flocks behind them along divided tracks.

“Here indeed it is pitiable to see them striving toward the kingdom by paths contrary to one another, although they seek to hasten toward it with a common purpose of faith. And since Christ alone is known to be the indivisible way of reaching life, it is plainly discordant and absurd to wish to divide Christ himself in his mysteries by divergent observance.

“For this reason the very necessity of reason has chiefly led me to this decision: that my command should compel the defenders of both sides to come together, so that, once the reasoning of both parties has been heard, we may, after examining the error, discern what ought to be followed and what ought to be avoided.

“Therefore you, Colman, who are chiefly accused by certain people of celebrating Easter contrary to the custom of the universal Church, stand forth, I say, as the first defender of your case—and I too am accused with you of the same observance—so that, once the authority on which it rests has been recognized, our observance under that same authority may henceforth be freed from such great accusations, if that authority is as strong as you claim.

“But if you are defeated by the lesser strength of the authority on which you rely, then surely you will no longer have either me or any of my people as a follower of your sect.”

15. Then Colman said:

“We celebrate Easter from the fourteenth moon through the twentieth, and we affirm that it ought to be celebrated in this way; we prove by the support of powerful authority that it must be so.

“For the most blessed Apostle and Evangelist John, such an intimate companion of the Lord Jesus that he reclined upon his breast at the Supper, celebrated it in the same order as we do, and by his authority established that it should be celebrated in all the churches over which he presided.

“This has been handed down to us through a succession of wise and equally holy men; this has been founded in us with stable firmness by the teaching of our forefathers; this has been observed by us until now with inviolable practice; and we affirm that it must continue to be observed, without any consideration to the contrary.”

16. After Colman had said these and several similar things, the king ordered Ailbert also to present the rule of his observance, so that it might be known on what principle and upon whose authoritative institution it rested.

Ailbert replied:

“Let Presbyter Wilfrid speak in my place, I beg you, because both of us, together with the other guardians of ecclesiastical tradition who sit here, hold the same understanding; and he can explain what we believe better and more clearly in the language of the English than I can through an interpreter.”

Then Wilfrid began to speak at the king’s command. He demonstrated by clear reasoning not only that Colman falsely relied upon the authority of the blessed John, but also proved that, in his observance of Easter, Colman held an opinion contrary to John, contrary to the Law and the Gospel, contrary to the teaching of the apostles, and indeed contrary to the custom of the universal Church.

We have therefore passed over writing out this proof, lest we impose upon readers some tedium in a matter unnecessary to this little work. Anyone who wishes to find it will discover it in our history—that is, the history of the English people.

Having omitted this, let us continue the life of the blessed man in order, as we began, insofar as he of whom we speak deigns to assist us. When the conflict had ended and the dispute had been settled, Ailbert returned home. Colman, however, relinquished the episcopate of his see and went to Scotland, because he was unwilling to place his traditions after the traditions of the Church.

[Col. 0720D]

17. From that time the man of the Lord Wilfrid was held in great veneration by everyone, since he was both splendidly imbued with divine learning and shown to be magnificently supported by the works of the Lord.

Therefore, by the acclamation of the whole people, he was elected by King Alfrid to the episcopate. But Wilfrid himself resisted the appointment with strenuous and grave protest. At last, overcome by the importunity of everyone, he asked the king not to permit him to be ordained irregularly in Britain. Rather, so that so great a matter might be completed according to the decrees of the canons, he asked that the king send him to Gaul to be ordained.

For the venerable Deusdedit, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, had already been taken from this life, and throughout Britain no canonically ordained bishop remained except Wine, bishop of the West Saxons. Ailbert, whom we mentioned shortly before, had left Britain and obtained the episcopate of the city of Paris.

Since this was the state of affairs, the king readily agreed to the request. With the advice of his father Oswiu, he sent the blessed Father to the king of Gaul, asking and earnestly entreating him to receive the man honorably and command that he be elevated to the rank of bishop by his authority.

Accordingly, the king received him honorably, as was fitting, and sent him to Bishop Ailbert with instructions ordering Ailbert to promote the servant of God to the episcopal order with the highest honor. Ailbert willingly obeyed the instructions and, with the cooperation of eleven bishops, consecrated him honorably.

[Col. 0721B]

18. While Wilfrid remained in the lands beyond the sea after his ordination, those whose sectarian perversity had previously been exposed and overthrown by him, thinking that they had now found an opportune time to repay his injuries, approached King Oswiu with fraudulent cunning. By deceiving him, they led him to the conclusion that he should order Ceadda to become bishop of the city of York, lest, while the Church remained without a shepherd any longer, the faith of Christ suffer some loss—especially, they said, since it was entirely unknown where Wilfrid had gone, the man whom Alfrid had sent to Gaul to be ordained for the governance of that Church.

Taken unwarily by their trickery, King Oswiu gave the episcopate of that Church to the aforesaid Ceadda and sent him to Kent to be consecrated to the priestly rank.

When Ceadda arrived there with his companions and found that same see deprived of a shepherd, he turned away from it, approached the aforesaid Bishop Wine, and obtained consecration from him. Then, taking two bishops of the British people who had been ordained contrary to the written canons, he in the same irregular manner ordained Ceadda.

19. Once ordained, Ceadda was placed at the head of the Church of York. Not many days later, the blessed Wilfrid, intending to return to his homeland, boarded a ship, and for some time the vessel carried them across the waves of the sea on a prosperous course.

But when they had already crossed the middle of the sea, and the blessed man with his clerics was intent in heart and mouth upon the things of God, the winds changed and an extremely violent storm arose. After being shaken by great distress, they were finally cast upon a region of the South Saxons that they did not know.

When the waves had been drawn back there into their own gulfs, the inhabitants, still bound by pagan error, rushed upon them, wishing to claim as their own the ship and everything in it. They held firmly to this purpose: either to take the men captive or to destroy by death those who resisted them.

When the venerable man recognized this, he offered them a large sum of money and humbly urged them to withdraw from their intention. But they were made fiercer by his words and proclaimed that they would accept nothing from him in exchange for his release. They even declared that, with no reason preventing them, they would take as their own not only all his possessions but Wilfrid himself.

When the bishop’s companions understood what the situation was leading toward, they first offered a supplication to the Lord and then took up arms. They preferred, like men, to fall bravely in battle rather than prolong their lives by enduring a cowardly captivity.

When the pagans learned this, they hastened to draw up their battle line and direct their weapons against the people of the Lord. The chief priest of idolatry stood before the pagans on a high mound. Through his magical incantations he strove to strengthen his own people as though blessing them and to weaken the companions of the servant of God by cursing them.

While he was devoting his mind, voice, and hand to this task with the greatest zeal, insofar as it mattered to him, a young servant of the man of God cast a stone from a sling and struck the magician in the forehead, knocking him down and killing him.

The ancient miracle performed by David against Goliath immediately returned to the memory of the man of God, when suddenly a remarkable tumult arose among the pagans and all their strength was exerted for the destruction of the Christian side.

What more is there to say? The battle lines advance; the soldier of Christ devotes himself to prayer. But while the Lord fought for his own, the hostile hand departed in confusion and defeat.

After a short while, however, the enemy returned in greater numbers and with greater savagery, formed its battle line, and hurled its weapons into the empty air. It received back weapons that were not empty: the greater part fell, and the remainder fled.

Why delay? When, defeated for the third time, they were preparing with their king for a fourth battle, the sea, through the merits of the blessed Wilfrid, flowed in long before the appointed hour, lifted the ship, and carried the holy man and all his companions safely into the port of Sandwich, with only five of his companions lost.

When the enemies saw this, they returned to their own people in the greatest confusion and mournfully lamented that the servant of the Lord was departing as a victor in joyful serenity.

20. Having thus reached his native port and regained his homeland, Wilfrid immediately learned by report that another bishop had been substituted for him in his see.

He was not at all disturbed by the event. With a calm face and cheerful heart, he went to Ripon, where, intent upon the service of God, he lived for some time with great stability of mind in a more secluded dwelling.

But because a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, many people, especially nobles, visited him, moved by the fame of his exceptional holiness.

The king of the Mercians also, named Wulfhere, a man deeply devoted to God, approached the servant of Christ. With scarcely tolerable persistence he persuaded him to leave the place and remain with him. Having achieved the fulfillment of his desire, the king honored the blessed Father with immense affection and increased him in lands and honors.

21. Meanwhile, the metropolitan see of all England was without a shepherd, since, as we said, Archbishop Deusdedit had died.

And because so great a see could not remain without episcopal care, King Egbert of Kent, having heard of the wisdom and holiness of the blessed Wilfrid, sent to him and addressed him with the most humble entreaty. He asked Wilfrid to deign to visit the widowed Church with his presence, raise it up through the aid of consolation, protect it against spiritual wickedness with the shield of his admonition, and establish within it, by pontifical authority, whatever the course of ecclesiastical tradition required.

Wilfrid did not consider it lawful to resist the royal will in such a matter and gave his consent. He therefore came to the Church and diligently administered there whatever he recognized through the Holy Spirit as needing to be done.

He was the first among the bishops created from the English people to have learned to transmit the Catholic way of life to the churches of the English. Consequently, by his teaching he spread throughout those churches many rules of Catholic observance.

Thus it came about that, as Catholic instruction increased day by day, all the Scots who were then living among the English either submitted to these practices or returned to their own homeland.

22. The blessed Wilfrid, insofar as he had the opportunity, was accustomed to travel here and there, accompanied by a great multitude of people, for the purpose of spreading the word of God.

While he was doing this on one occasion, he came to the place where he had been born and raised. Feeding the inhabitants of that place with the word of heavenly life, he turned many away from love of earthly things and converted them to love of almighty God.

As a result, he established several cells there for those who wished to serve the Lord and prudently instructed each one in how their life ought to be ordered.

For three continuous years he devoted his care and attention sometimes to the administration of the Church of Canterbury, sometimes to the exhortation and correction of those people. Although he nowhere had a proper place belonging to an episcopal throne, he nevertheless applied himself zealously to the episcopal office, striving to snatch the devil’s vessels from him, reconcile them to Christ the Lord, and strengthen them in their purpose of holy conduct.

23. When the period of three years had elapsed, Theodore, consecrated archbishop by Pope Vitalian and sent out by him, came to Kent. Having taken up the episcopal see in the metropolitan city, he immediately strove, with the greatest prudence and pontifical authority, to improve whatever needed correction throughout the region, as ecclesiastical vigor required.

When he discovered that Ceadda had been consecrated to the rank of bishop contrary to the statutes of the canons, he rebuked him publicly and threatened him rather sternly that he ought rightly to be degraded.

But Ceadda, being a man of great humility and gentleness, said:

“If you assert that I was ordained contrary to the decrees of the canons, I willingly consent to be removed from office, since I have certainly never considered myself so important that I ought to preside over this office even for an hour. But when I was ordered to undertake it for the sake of obedience, I consented, though unworthy.”

Theodore received this humble reply and said that he did not at all wish to deprive him of the priestly rank. Yet, because, as we have said, he had been irregularly ordained to so great a ministry, Theodore completed his ordination according to canonical procedure.

But Ceadda, realizing that he had not justly obtained another bishop’s episcopate, was moved by repentance and chose rather to be deprived of such an honor than to continue unjustly presiding over another’s see.

He therefore withdrew from the episcopate and, deprived of office, retired to his monastery at Lestingesei.

24. Theodore restored the blessed Wilfrid to the episcopate of the Church of York and also to that of all the Northumbrians, as well as of the Picts, insofar as King Oswiu had been able to extend his authority.

Thus the most holy man both possessed his soul in patience and, increased in honor, recovered what had been his amid the rejoicing of the whole people.

At that time Wulfhere, whom we mentioned shortly before, ruled the kingdom of the Mercians. When, after Bishop Jaruman’s death, he asked Theodore to provide another bishop for himself and his people, Theodore did not wish to ordain a new bishop for them but gave them the aforementioned venerable Ceadda.

The blessed Wilfrid, restored to his own, applied himself with outstanding perseverance of spirit to ensuring that he would restore in the churches whatever long antiquity or neglect had dissolved, and remove whatever in the conduct of his subjects might offend the eyes of the great God.

The more earnestly he devoted himself to these works, the more strictly he bound himself to the exercise of virtue, so that in his life those subject to him might see with what diligence they ought to receive his verbal teachings.

25. After fully restoring those things he had found destroyed, he completed from the foundations a church in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and consecrated it with great magnificence amid an immense gathering of rulers and peoples. When he came to the duty of preaching, it became clearer than daylight that the Lord’s words were fulfilled in him: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20). This may plainly be recognized from the fact that the people were thereby moved to great love for the Lord, while the hearts of the rulers were kindled with such fear and love of God that they not only confirmed by written charters, at his word, those things that had previously belonged by right to the church, but also bestowed upon the church certain possessions of their own.

Three days afterward, keeping the entire crowd with him, he abundantly refreshed it with the bread of life, both heavenly and earthly. Moreover, he enriched the church with great gifts and with ornaments appropriate to the beauty of God’s house. And while he performed these works most worthy of praise, he fled human praise as though it were a deadly plague; thus, placed amid the peoples, he was for all of them a mirror and an instruction in good works.

26. While these things were taking place, almighty God, wishing to show the world how highly he valued the merits of his servant, determined to adorn the virtues he had first poured forth through the radiance of inward qualities also by the display of outward miracles. Accordingly, one day, while the venerable shepherd was instructing the sheep of God in words and the sacraments of faith, removing from them the ancient enemy of the human race’s right to rule over them, and through the anointing of sacred chrism imparting the Spirit of sevenfold grace to those already baptized, a woman afflicted with overwhelming grief suddenly came through the throng to meet the minister of God, displaying in her arms, in a pitiful procession, the corpse of her dead child.

When the Father saw this, he was astonished and stood rooted to the spot. The bereaved woman, disturbed by the extreme sharpness of her grief, bent forward upon him, as he held back for a little while from the ministry of the work he had begun, and, impeded by sobbing, scarcely managed to utter these words:

“Behold, good lord,” she said, “the child whom I had resolved to carry to the laying on of your hand, that he might be confirmed in Christ. Now I bring him to your holy and devoted compassion not merely for confirmation, but first for resurrection from the dead. You preach that your Christ is almighty; prove this, I beg you, by deeds, and raise my only son from death. And how great a thing is it for his almighty power to raise this little one and dispel the pangs of my grief? Truly, nothing. Therefore I ask you to demonstrate powerfully that what you preach is true, so that you may restore my only son to life for my consolation.”

She repeated her plaintive cries, and all the people, compelled by the force of her lamentation, came running together. Behold, there was a great mourning. At last the venerable servant of the Lord took pity on her. He gave silent thanks in the sanctuary of his heart that the crowd, though not yet perfected in faith, knew how to ask the mercy of the Lord Christ. Then he fell prostrate upon the ground and, his face covered with tears, said:

“O Lord Father, look favorably, I pray, not upon my merits but upon the works of your mercy, and extend the aid of your consolation to this woman in her affliction, restoring her son safe and sound through Jesus Christ, our Lord, your only-begotten Son.”

Having said this, he rose and touched the dead boy’s head by extending his right hand. At his touch, the head began to move; then the man of God reached out his hand to him and presented him to everyone standing upright, alive and unharmed. The crowd burst into cries of overwhelming wonder and praise, and was strengthened in the observance of Christian law with the fullest faith.

The boy, restored to life in Christ through the laying on of hands, was confirmed and returned with joy to his mother, on the condition that, after being raised for seven years under his mother’s care, he would be restored to the man of God. When the appointed time arrived, however, his father forbade it. The mother therefore fled into exile among the foreign Britons with her child, knowing that the boy could not remain with her in his own country contrary to the command of the man of God. Yet this flight brought about the very result intended. After a few days, a certain prefect brought the boy back into the Father’s hands against the wishes of his parents. He immediately devoted him to the service of God and later, after thoroughly instructing him, made him an example for many through his holy way of life.

From this, consider what sign the radiance of a flame sent down from heaven over his cradle must have foreshadowed.

27. At that time the kingdom of the English people shone with a twofold splendor: its kings burned with love for Christianity, and its bishops diligently exercised the divine ministry. Thus royal foresight chiefly concerned itself with drawing subjects away from wicked conduct rather than, through greed, plundering their property and scattering their possessions; their concern was not how they might rule over their subjects, but how they might rule as good men.

Likewise, the summit of the priesthood stood fully equipped for its office, offering its diligent service only in those matters for which God, the founder and author of that order, had established it. As a result, there was profound peace for the people who observed the laws. The land, rich in crops and tranquility, not only removed want from its cultivators [reading: *colebat*; correction: *tollebat*], but also allowed them to devote themselves without anxiety over worldly affairs to the work of God. The dreadful war trumpets were silent, and no one feared the incursions of robbers. What more is there to say? To state everything briefly, the Church flourished, bound together by a peaceful covenant.

When the devil saw this, he envied it with the malignity proper to him and, considering the matter, found causes for disrupting the peace. Through the spirit of his pride he invaded the people of the Picts to such an extent that this nation—which had always been accustomed to endure it—attempted by war to shake off the yoke of the English.

At that time Ecgfrith, son of King Oswiu, ruled the kingdom of the Northumbrians. He had succeeded his father in the kingdom, was a vigorous man in arms, and was strongly bound by friendship with blessed Wilfrid. He therefore explained to the bishop the Pictish threat that confronted him and urged him by humble prayers to bring the aid of his intercession to the situation. Then, fortified by his blessing and accompanied by his most holy prayer, Ecgfrith met the Picts with a small band of soldiers, struck down the Picts who came against him in dense formations, and subdued their arrogance by the sword’s vengeance.

Why delay? He inflicted slaughter far and wide; the chains returned to their necks. Thus, having gained a joyful victory, he returned and offered exceptional thanks to his protector. In this way peace was restored to the English people and remained for several years.

Afterward, when the kingdom of the Mercians had fallen into dissension, the aforesaid king, wishing to restore peace by arms, marched to war against the Mercian king, met him in battle, and obtained the peace he sought after routing the leader and overthrowing his army. This outcome was granted to that king so that God might show that the prayers of blessed Wilfrid could not be wholly nullified before him.

Nor is this surprising. For he who said in the Gospel that everything is possible for one who believes (Mark 9:22) ought rightly to grant that what was justly asked was possible for one whom the Lord’s own wisdom recognized as Catholic in faith and outstanding in the works of that faith. For who could doubt the integrity of his faith, or who could adequately discuss the perfection of his works? Nevertheless, let some of his works be described briefly, so that they may both bear witness to the integrity of his faith and place before the eyes of those who wish to imitate the devotion of his heart examples for imitation.

28. First, it must be said that, trained from childhood in the best conduct, he could never in any way be drawn away from it throughout his life. As a worshiper of unchanging justice, he could not be softened by favor, diverted by detraction, deceived by praise, or provoked into zeal by insults.

By night he devoted himself to divine observances and disciplined his body—which he had kept pure from every contagion from his mother’s womb—with both vigils and cold, dipping it in cold water every night. He did not cease this practice until John, bishop of the apostolic see, ordered him, on account of the burden of his age, to bring it to an end. Neither the heat of summer nor the cold of winter could turn him aside from the persistence of the work of God he had begun.

Moreover, wherever he went, carrying the grace of preaching and proclaiming the grace of God, he was prepared to give his life for the very truth he preached, if a fitting occasion arose that required it. Whenever, on any occasion, he took some delicacy as food—and even then with the greatest restraint—he afterward punished himself for it by severe fasting.

This discipline of life cultivated in his heart the smallest possible inclination toward pride and the greatest zeal for humility. It imposed upon his subjects an example of holy conduct; it led them into the narrow path of continence; and it also brought many who had been converted from their error to the grace of Christ. Consequently, very many nobles, moved by his example, entrusted their sons to the man of God to be dedicated to God’s service. They marveled at his merits, approved them with worthy praises, and eagerly desired in every way that their sons should become imitators of his uprightness.

But just as what happens to some for the advancement of virtue can lead others to the effect of wickedness, so from the very cause by which some advanced into love and veneration for God’s servant, others broke out into hatred and abuse of him. Yet the athlete of God was at peace with those who hated peace (Psalm 119:7), and he repaid their hatred with the service of gentleness.

29. Moreover, in the town of Austerfield he built a church of marvelous workmanship, which he himself dedicated to the Lord in honor of blessed Andrew the apostle, thereby repaying a benefit that the same apostle had long before bestowed upon him.

The envy of the deadly serpent was not absent from the construction of this church. While the masons were plastering the upper parts of the wall, the enemy of the human race caused one of them to fall headlong. He fell so severely that, with all his limbs crushed, he was thought already to be dying.

As he struggled as though in the final exhalation of his spirit, everyone ran out as if to attend his funeral. The man of the Lord Wilfrid, though bodily absent, perceived everything through the presence of his spirit. He immediately burst into tears and, explaining in order to each of those present what had happened, asked them to intercede for the brother’s salvation.

When they reached the sick man, his limbs immediately recovered their former health at the Father’s touch. If it may be said so, death was ashamed when it saw itself driven away by a human being and life restored to a human being. The devil, author of that death, saw that the man was increasing his own confusion both through the inward virtues of his soul and through the display of outward miracles. He was inflamed with the excessive malignity of his fury and sought every means by which he might turn his confusion back upon Wilfrid.

30. King Ecgfrith had taken as his wife a woman named Æthelthryth, who had resolved to pass this life under a vow of virginity rather than be violated by another’s desire. Nevertheless, she was joined to the aforesaid king by the law of marriage, though not by carnal union.

For this reason the king approached blessed Wilfrid, both personally and through his friends, praying, pleading, and attempting to entice him by promises of the greatest rewards to persuade the queen to abandon her resolve of virginity and yield to the royal will. But Wilfrid, knowing that it is written, “Vow and pay to the Lord your God” (Psalm 76:12), preferred not to obey Ecgfrith in this matter rather than deprive the Lord of his sacrifice, lest by doing so he prepare not only for the virgin’s soul but also for his own the loss of eternal life.

As a supporter of the virgin’s vow, he therefore used the vigilance of his discerning mind to ensure that the woman, through any instability of the female mind, would not set aside her resolve and, overcome by earthly allurements, submit her mind to them. Through his own efforts he brought it about that the virgin instead sought a divorce from her husband, so that, having gained her freedom, she might leave the world and happily cleave to the bridal chamber of the eternal King.

And this was done. When the king learned that she could in no way be moved from her resolve, he granted, though unwillingly, that she should leave the world, as she wished, and receive the distinguished veil of virginity. Made happy by this permission, and having received the veil from blessed Wilfrid, she abandoned worldly things with the world, despised them, and cast them far from the desire of her heart.

31. Ermemburgis, however, was joined in a royal marriage. The devil therefore considered her a suitable instrument through whom to vent the hatred he bore against the man of God. He inflamed her mind against him by introducing certain quarrels and strongly urged her to set the snares of his deceits against him.

She yielded all the more readily to this suggestion because the instability of a woman’s mind, the intemperance of slippery ostentation, and the oppression and violent seizure of condemnable rapacity—all of which flourished in her with great arrogance—armed the servant of the Lord repeatedly with bitter denunciations against her.

Accordingly, deeply offended inwardly and further inflamed by demonic fire, she began greatly to envy his glory and dignity and to seek opportunities by which she might strip him of his dignity and cast him away once stripped. Considering, then, the man’s glory and how the abundance of his dignity shone around him on every side, she approached the king with feminine eloquence, as though she were about to discuss certain matters of her own advantage. In reality, she was seeking indirectly to discover whether she could first incline his mind toward whatever she wished.

When she perceived that he was disposed according to her desire, she began, through fraudulent words, to recount his glory to the king with admiring emphasis, so as to bring the man of God into disfavor. After setting forth the abundance of his riches, the multitude of his monasteries, the size of his buildings, the throng of subordinate rulers, and the abundance of his soldiers, equipped with royal garments and arms, she added:

“What more is he to you than you are to him? Your entire kingdom is his bishopric; indeed, if your power is compared with his, it is the lesser. The boundary of your rule is confined within its own limits, whereas the boundary of his bishopric extends beyond your borders in authority.

“And I admit that your faithful men and friends ought to fear that, if your enemies should ever take up arms against you, he might retain those who follow the peace he preaches from taking up arms, and you, inferior to your enemies because of the small number of your men, might be defeated and fall.

“Therefore, consider the matter before the matter arises; and, so that your strength does not fail in the execution itself, arrange in advance what you know to be harmful. There are also many other considerations that can honestly persuade you that it is in no way appropriate to your honor to have anyone in your kingdom—not merely superior, but even equal—to you. I recognize that these things need not even be said, because I know that they are clear not only to your prudence but to anyone, however foolish.”

31. Moved by such words, and wholly attentive to them as though she were advising his interests, the king thought that his affairs could not be better secured than if the man of God were deprived of everything and his bishopric divided among several bishops.

But because this could not be done without the consent of the archbishop of Canterbury, they sent words of malicious accusation against the bishop to Theodore, the bishop of that see, and induced him, once deceived, to bend to their will. Theodore therefore came to the royal court to fulfill the royal will concerning Wilfrid by his authority.

And so it was done. Immediately, in Wilfrid’s absence, he ordained three bishops in his place. The matter could not be concealed from the man. He was led by the greatest astonishment, yet with cheerful heart, joyful countenance, and modest step he entered the king’s palace to inquire into the affair.

He was reportedly given this answer to his questions:

“We do not at present charge you with the commission of any crime, nor will we on this occasion alter the judgment that has been made concerning you.”

Since he acknowledged that such words did not satisfy him, he appealed to the apostolic see and, indignant at their injustice, turned to leave the hall. Seeing certain people insulting him with a laugh at once shameful and malicious, he said:

“Ah, my sons, may you pass long years in fortunate prosperity. But know that hostile fortune will very soon dissolve these joys of yours; and you will not see this year pass before you pay for these mockeries you direct against me with bitter sorrow.”

This prophecy became true. Not long afterward, in a grave battle fought between Ecgfrith and Æthelred, king of the Mercians, near the River Trent, Elfwine, Ecgfrith’s brother, was killed. He was a young man of about eighteen years and greatly loved by both provinces. His death struck Ecgfrith and his people with immense and intolerable grief, and all the joy they had felt at the expulsion of blessed Wilfrid was, by God’s just judgment, turned into sadness.

From the time they did not fear to drive away from them the Lord’s strongest soldier, they never gained a joyful victory. Those who had previously, protected by his intercession and with a small band of soldiers, overthrown immense forces, afterward fell defeated by a few soldiers even when they themselves had a great force. And not unjustly. For once the one through whom they had been victorious had been driven away, there was no reason remaining why they should not be defeated everywhere.

But let us return, through the work of our pen, to the order of the work we have undertaken.

32. Blessed Wilfrid, deprived of the dignity of the episcopal see, returned to his own people. His sons and brothers were deeply saddened by his misfortune, and he addressed to them many words of consolation, patience, and true charity, saying among other things that one must attach no importance to what it was evident would sometimes have to be endured.

After this he set out for Rome, intending to present his case before the apostolic see lest any scandal should threaten the Church of Christ on his account. He was escorted to the sea, surrounded on his right and left by a venerable company of monks; he was placed on a ship and commended with their devout prayers. The sails were spread to favorable winds.

But when the ship had advanced a short distance, the wind changed and drove him to Frisia. There he was honorably received by the barbarians and by their king, Aldgisl, and he conducted himself honorably there. He was held in the highest honor by everyone for as long as he wished to remain, although the entire province still persisted in the worship of idols.

Wishing to repay their kindness, he preached the word of God to them, instructed many thousands in the word of truth, and washed them from the filth of their sins in the saving font. Thus he caused those who had received him to be received by the Lord and to receive the Lord within themselves.

Before the blessed man’s arrival, that land was exceedingly salty and barren, rough like a mass of rock, and consequently very unsuitable for animals of every kind to inhabit. But when that people received the Lord’s faith through the preaching of the man of God, just as their hearts were softened for fruitful good works by the dew of heavenly sweetness and made suitable for the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, so the saltiness of their land was changed into sweetness, its barrenness into fertility, its roughness into softness and richness, and it brought abundant supplies of every kind of benefit to all who inhabited it.

33. Meanwhile, those who, overcome by their wickedness, had driven Christ’s friend from his dignity, possessions, and land sent their envoys to Francia, bound both by the frauds of the most unjust denunciation and weighed down with various gifts, in order to lay snares of deception and capture, plunder, destruction, and death for the man of the Lord, partly through fraud and partly through bribery.

But so that the snare of those who, seduced by gifts, had set a snare for God’s servant might entangle them themselves, by God’s hidden judgment they stripped of everything a certain priest of the Lord named Winfrid, recently deposed from his bishopric and then traveling as a pilgrim for the love of God. They were deceived by the similarity of the name and by their own wickedness.

When they learned of this and discovered where the man of the Lord was staying at that time, Ebroin, the chief of the royal court and of this wickedness, sent a letter with a great gift to King Aldgisl, asking him to strip Wilfrid of all his possessions and kill him by a cruel death.

The king, however, refusing to yield to such wickedness through either prayers or gifts, tore up the letter with great indignation and threw it into the flames. Rebuking the wickedness as it deserved, he ordered the envoys to return immediately, dismissed without honor.

34. The bishop was therefore secure from their plots. He spent the entire winter happily in that province with the new people of God, then resumed his journey to Rome. Reaching Gaul, he entered the familiar stronghold of King Dagobert.

When the king saw him, he immediately recognized him and received him into his hospitality with great joy. He summoned his men and addressed them as follows:

“I commend this man whom you see here before you most earnestly to your affection, asking you to assist him in whatever matter he may need you, if indeed, as it is right to believe, you love me sincerely.

“Through this man’s uprightness and diligence I was restored to you and, as you now see, raised to royal dignity. For long ago, as you yourselves remember, when I had almost perished through the plots of my people, I wandered as an exile wherever I might find deliverance. After being tossed upon the sea, I was even carried to the cowardly Irish.

“From there, brought to him, he kept me with him for some time in great goodwill, protected me from every danger, and gave me the opportunity to be restored safe and unharmed to my native land. Therefore, by your own safety and mine, I implore you: if you have any faith, let us preserve so great a friend, and let us all together hasten to repay him the affection and goodwill he showed me [reading: *procurramus*, “hasten”; correction: *procuremus*, “see to it that we repay”].”

At these words everyone rejoiced and testified to their joy with an emphatic acclamation. For among them it was not considered a small matter for any subject even to murmur against the command or will of his ruler.

Accordingly, the king offered the saint residences, estates, dignities, and various gifts, and he was entreated with many prayers to deign to inhabit lands within his kingdom and, by inhabiting them, claim them as his own.

35. The saint, however, mindful of his purpose, did not yield to the royal will. He took certain necessities with him and, joining to himself a certain bishop named Deodatus, withdrew from the court.

From there he approached the duke of Campania, a man named Berhter, and was nobly received by him. After showing him the duties of true charity and kindness, Berhter sat with the man of God and began to tell him how his enemies had wished to destroy him and attempted to bend Berhter to their purpose by offering gifts.

“But I,” he said, “remembering what loyalty and friendship I once found in a certain pagan king when I was exiled from my homeland and living with him, did not wish to be found less faithful as a Christian to you, a Christian, than a pagan man had been to me, a Christian.

“For a heathen king of the Huns, while keeping me with him for the sake of preserving my life, entered into a pact with me in the name of his gods [reading: *dominorum*, correction: *deorum*], promising that he would never betray me to my enemies on any account.

“After some days, envoys came to him from my enemies and promised him a huge sum of money for my destruction. He said to them: ‘May they cut short my life if, yielding to you for any earthly profit, I should in any way dissolve the pact I made. If an unfaithful man refused to break his pact in order to remain faithful to his false god, shall I, faithful through the grace of Christ, violate the faith I promised to the true God for the sake of any earthly advantage? Far be it, far be it! Rather, I receive you under my protection [reading: *sua*; correction: *mea*, “my”], and I ask you to remain with me for as long as you wish. I also greatly desire to ask this of you: if there is anything among my possessions that you value especially, take it, use it, and possess it.’”

The man of God was greatly delighted both by this man’s goodness and by his kindness, and he disclosed to him what he had resolved in his heart. Thus enriched with possessions and companions, he departed from him with his goodwill.

36. When he reached Rome, the fame of his already well-known holiness immediately spread everywhere, and very many citizens went out to meet him. He was welcomed with great favor by the people and reverently conducted into the basilica of blessed Peter.

At that time the apostolic see was governed by Agatho, of blessed memory, a just and simple man, yet by no means unskilled in ecclesiastical affairs. In his presence and that of many bishops, Wilfrid’s case was debated with his accusers present. By the judgment of all, he was proved to have been accused without guilt and to be worthy of the episcopate.

At that time the same pope was gathering at Rome a synod of one hundred and twenty-five bishops against those who taught that the Lord and Savior had one will and one operation. He ordered blessed Wilfrid to be summoned and, seated among the bishops, to state both his own faith and that of the province from which he had come.

When he was found to be Catholic in faith together with his people, and to have been deprived of his priestly dignity unjustly, it was decided that he should be restored to the episcopate by decree of the Roman see. As a memorial of his Catholic faith, the following was inserted in the acts of that synod:

“Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case, and absolved by this authority from definite and indefinite charges, and appointed by the see to be judged in synod with one hundred and twenty-five other fellow bishops, confessed and confirmed by his subscription the true and Catholic faith for the whole northern part of Britain and Ireland, which are inhabited by the peoples of the English, Britons, Scots, and Picts.”

[Note: The same subscription appears in Bede and William. The acts of the council survive partly in William and partly in Spelman.]

37. Restored to the episcopate by apostolic and synodal decree, and having received letters from the apostolic see addressed to King Ecgfrith and Archbishop Theodore concerning the restoration of his position, the servant of God, enriched by the apostolic see with a great gift of relics of the servants of God, resumed his journey to England.

Because he knew the Scripture, “Whoever walks uprightly walks securely” (Proverbs 10:9), he traveled by the royal road. But beyond what had been expected, a band of robbers ready to kill him came against the man of the Lord in a procession far from welcome.

They were the men who had plotted against King Dagobert and killed him by thrusting a sword into his groin. These men, encountering the man of God and revealing the fury of their minds through the ferocity of their faces, threatened battle at close quarters, brandishing their spears.

One of them, regarded among them as their leader, shook the weapon he held in his hand and reviled Christ’s soldier with foul speech:

“Informer against your homeland, insolent and doomed traveler,” he said, “you once violated the Gallic scepters; you ruined the Gallic countryside; you reduced Gallic freedom to slavery when, through your persistence, you established in the kingdom a tyrant who had long before been exiled by us.

“His cruelty was punished by a most just death, and it declares that you too, as the chief author of his death, must be punished by the same death. Fall, then, pestilent man, fall; and, punished with deserved vengeance, succumb to the very death you fostered against us.”

The Father replied:

“If I acted unjustly when I placed a king unjustly expelled from his kingdom, as far as lay within me, before his hereditary dignity, and if the equity of the most just Judge holds this against me, I confess that I will most willingly pay the penalties of just vengeance.

“But if, in that deed, I was not acting wrongly but rightly—as my very innocence of mind immediately bears witness—then I desire to die all the more willingly, if you wish to kill me, because I recognize that, if I am killed for justice, I shall be crowned with the glory of martyrdom.”

When he had said this, they saw that the man relied upon such firmness of mind that they were struck with overwhelming terror. They threw down their weapons, fell upon the ground, sought the man’s feet with kisses, and asked pardon. Having found pardon according to their desire and been enriched by his blessing, they sent the bishop and all his companions onward in safety; they themselves continued by their appointed route.

38. When the man of God reached Britain, he brought the king the letters he had received from the apostolic see. Supported by the authority of those letters, he defended his case aloud in an assembly of nobles and openly demonstrated that he had been falsely accused and unjustly degraded.

But the more the king recognized that Wilfrid was fortified by the stronger claim of truth, the more he grieved that he himself was supported by the weaker claim. Following the custom of the most wicked, he preferred to persist in his obstinacy against equity rather than temper his obstinacy through reason and justice.

The hardened discord of the earlier informers strongly reinforced this dullness of heart, as those whom it already possessed and filled poured the poisons of their malice into the king’s ears. Blinded by his own anger and drawn away from the truth by the flattery of his seducers, the king looked down upon the apostolic pope’s letters with haughty disdain, mocked them in his contempt, cast them far from him in his mockery, and brought against the servant of God the charge of being a most wicked informer.

Some of the king’s retainers, indeed many of the nobles, were deeply stirred by the king’s indignation. They all rose up in unanimous conspiracy against blessed Wilfrid and inflicted many insults upon him. Wishing to demonstrate that they were completely faithful to the royal majesty, they sought to satisfy his indignation fully and seized the man of God, tearing him away from the king’s presence and thrusting him into prison.

Ermemburgis, the persecutor of all good things and the unyielding author of this schism, plunged into the middle of the plunder. She shamelessly tore the reliquary from his neck and, with ugly chatter and feminine loquacity, mocked and cast him aside.

Thus the illustrious hero, deprived on every side of companions and resources, turned as best he could among the hands of the wicked toward his own people and addressed them briefly in these words:

“Do not let this injury inflicted upon us, my lords, brothers, and sons, disturb you or in any way drive you from the path of truth. Always keep before your eyes that ‘all who desire to live devoutly in Christ must necessarily suffer tribulation’ (2 Timothy 3:2).

“Although the wicked may seem for a time to prevail over the righteous, it will not always be so. A time will come when the tribulation of the righteous will be rewarded with everlasting joy, and the proud exaltation of the wicked punished with everlasting sorrow.

“But lest tribulation drive you into impatience, consider how the venerable succession of our fathers, after suffering many tribulations, merited, with God’s help, to overcome many enemies through patience. Nor do I wish you to forget that, according to the Apostle, no one can be crowned unless he has striven lawfully against the devil (2 Timothy 2:5).

“Certainly, the struggles of this present time are of little account and do not last long; yet through them eternal happiness and the blessed eternity of God’s kingdom are acquired. Love that happiness, brothers, I beg you; desire it, strive toward it, and labor with the full intention of your minds to reach it. If you do this, there will surely be nothing for which you need fear the adversities of this life.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when those in whose hands he was held, inflamed with fiercer fury by his very words, thrust him bound into a dark prison.

39. O steadfastness of the man! Most holy Father, I behold in such a way the cheerfulness of your heart amid so great an adversity; I consider you joyful in just the way you were accustomed to be when everything seemed to smile upon you in prosperity.

Yet, lest you appear to have lost any part of the compassion you owed your sons, you spent your pious tears upon their sufferings rather than your own. When a dark prison enclosed you, you grieved more that the words of life were separated from their ears than that you yourself had been deprived of the presence of bodily light.

For you shone with the radiance of inward light, by which you held the darkness of the prison to be nothing. Therefore, when God saw that the splendor of divine light was active in you, he did not permit you to be oppressed long by human darkness. Instead, after dispersing those darknesses, he sent a ray of his light into the house you inhabited.

And rightly so. Since, watchful before the eternal light, you attended upon it both amid the horror of night and within the prison, he judged it fitting, by the outpouring of his light, to show that your works had nothing in common with the gloom of darkness.

The watchfulness of the guards bears witness to this outpouring of light. Around midnight they testified that they had seen the prison wonderfully shining, though not without great fear. Yet he who regards the merits of your holiness with a faithful eye understood that you had no need of this testimony.

I compare the prison of the blessed apostle Peter with yours and rejoice greatly that, through the manifestation of light, you were granted a liberation like his in the Gospel. Moreover, after these events, you were freed from the danger of death through the angelic visitation of Michael the archangel, so that it might be clear to all that, together with the apostle himself, you have been crowned with the glory of God’s kingdom.

### 40 [Cols. 0735B–0735C]

Meanwhile, the wife of the prefect Offrid, who had the blessed Wilfrid in custody, was seized by a most severe illness and was already being brought to the extremity of life. She lay weakened throughout her whole body, with her joints loosened and deprived of every bodily function; moreover, having lost sensation and with her nerves contracted and lifeless, her internal organs were collapsing. This circumstance inflicted upon her husband the sharp goads of great grief and anxiety, and brought on a state of great exhaustion and horror. Moved by this misfortune, he approached the man of God with tearful pleas; he released the bonds by which he was burdened, inclined himself toward compassion, and, having led him out of prison, brought him as a physician of salvation to his wife.

The man of God arrived and immediately ordered the crowds who had come for the woman’s funeral to withdraw. Then, after offering prayers to the Lord, he blessed water and sprinkled the blessed water over the woman’s prostrate body. Wonderful to relate! No sooner had the water touched the sick woman’s limbs than, every illness having been driven away, complete health returned to her. At this, all who were present gave thanks to God with one voice, and the merits of the blessed Father were proclaimed worthy not of imprisonment but of every honor.

But lest anyone should think that he had performed this sign of power out of a greater desire to escape prison than from compassion, he did not wish to remain outside; rather, intending to enjoy the light of divinity, he returned as quickly as possible within the bounds of the prison guard. The prefect’s wife, who had been granted health, was, a few days later, having renounced the world, clothed with the sacred veil and dedicated to the service of Christ.

### 41 [Cols. 0735D–0736B]

From that time onward, the prefect held the servant of God in great veneration. He approached the king through messengers and said:

> “By your safety and your kingdom I adjure you: do not allow the priest of the Lord Wilfrid to be detained by me any longer, for I confess that it would be better for me to die than to inflict any further injury upon him. But if, disregarding this adjuration, you prefer to persist in your decision, know that I would rather undergo torture and death together with him than keep him in torment.”

At this the king, greatly angered, ordered the saint to be taken to his city, Thymber [Note: William calls the attendant Tumber.], and to the prefect named Tydlin, as a man of even fiercer character. He instructed Tydlin to commit Wilfrid to stricter custody, firmly bound with fetters and chains.

The prefect, not daring to oppose the command, received the man, handed him over to the guard, and had him bound. Yet while the servants were laboring to fasten him, either the same bonds burst apart from his body, or, since they could not be joined, they fell away in disarray. By the wonderful restraint of Christ, the power to bind him became weaker in proportion as hostile ferocity raged more savagely in its attempt to bind him.

Therefore, greatly astonished but driven by royal terror and their own madness into barbarous frenzy, they prepared one set of bonds after another, exhausting themselves completely in their futile labor. Why, mad hands, do you rage, now that the power of binding has been taken away from you? Why do you strive so intensely to attack one whom you will never be able to overcome? Why do you change his bonds so many times in order to fetter him, rather than change the bonds by which you yourselves are deservedly bound because of your wickedness?

Your straps fear to be placed upon the neck of the just man, because they behold with reverent awe that this neck is subject to the yoke of Christ. Your manacles fear to be inserted into his hands, because they observe that those hands have been extended in the care of the poor. Trembling chains avoid binding his feet, because they consider that those feet have been swift to preach peace. Thus you expend all your strength in vain when you strive to torment one whom you are in no way permitted to torment.

Although enveloped in the darkness of prison, the blessed Wilfrid nevertheless enlightened those who came to him with the light of the word of God, insofar as he was able, instructed them, and cleansed them from every stain of sin through baptism.

### 42 [Cols. 0736B–0737A]

Meanwhile, while the king, accompanied by his men, was going wherever he wished in order to fulfill his pleasure and was loosening the reins of joy in great merriment, suddenly—behold!—his happiness was disturbed by an unexpected calamity.

For while the queen, swollen with excessive pride, dared impiously to abuse the relics she had seized, avenging anger immediately arose. Carrying those same relics, and chattering playfully with a lively and wanton mind like a partridge, she suddenly became filled with a demon and, like a little fox, began to yelp with a deranged and ruined mind. The one whom she had previously honored willingly in her insolence, she afterward, unwillingly, cherished within the dwelling of her body.

When these things occurred, and everyone was struck with astonishment, the king’s mother approached the raging woman and rebuked her in these words:

> “Are the deeds of ancient guilt now evident, sister? You drove Wilfrid from the seat of his episcopate through your false accusations, and now, with the situation reversed, you have received a demon into the seat of your heart. Thus you may understand what sin you committed in that deed. You irreverently took the relics of the saints from Wilfrid’s neck, and behold, you have deserved that a demon should subject your neck to his power. You despised Wilfrid’s most holy words, supported by the authority of blessed Peter; and for this reason, with a demon possessing your heart, you have lost the right to your own words. Wilfrid, full of the light of divinity, does not fear the darkness of prison, though you placed him there; but your spirit, filled with demonic fury, is now tortured by a most fitting vengeance.”

The king was present, deeply disturbed and inflamed with the immense fire of rage, breathing through his nostrils as though emitting smoke. His mother addressed him also in these words:

> “Now at last, my son, now at last remember who you are. Divine vengeance is afflicting, as you see, the wife whom you love too greatly; and, believe me, she has deserved to be wearied by such punishment, because, inflamed by diabolical indignation, she did not fear to persecute the servant of the Lord Wilfrid with extraordinary afflictions. Therefore, I beg you, do not doubt that this vengeance has been inflicted upon her on your account. But if you stubbornly refuse to be corrected by this, take care lest you yourself be corrected against your will. Release, then, from prison the man whom we know to be detained without cause of any crime of his own. And if you do not wish him to remain in your kingdom, order him to leave the kingdom, lest, if he is held longer, you should first wish to release him only after you have been punished with a greater penalty.”

Warned by these words, the king himself agreed that the holy man should leave the prison. It was done, and from the darkness light emerged into the world. But the servant of God, preferring to return good for evil rather than evil for evil, prayed to the Lord, and immediately, after the demon had been expelled, restored the queen to health.

### 43 [Cols. 0737A–0737D]

From there he abandoned his homeland and the lands of his kindred, and, intending to travel as a stranger toward the southern territories, set out upon the road leading there. Since no deceit can violate the proclamations of Truth, and since the servant of God was seeking the kingdom of God first, he could not lack anything that the necessities of life required.

Thus it happened that a certain Byrtwaldus, descended from royal stock, received him with great honor when he met him on the road; and, keeping him with him for some time, kindly supplied him with whatever he needed. But diabolical envy could not bear that generosity to continue for long. It infected the aforesaid man with the poison of its perversity and induced him to strip the soldier of Christ of his generosity and drive him out from himself and all his possessions.

He was the brother of King Aedelfred of the Mercians, who had taken in marriage the sister of King Ecfrid.

> [Note: Osdrida, namely, who had married Ethelred in consolation for her murdered brother Elwin, reconciling peace between her husband and her brother, according to William.]

Fearing, therefore, that he would offend his brother if he kept with him a man who was hostile to his wife’s brother, he cast Wilfrid away, not fearing injustice—and not without insult, so that we may understand that in this deed he was not free from a malicious mind. For Wilfrid had previously been afflicted and insulted in many ways both by Byrtwaldus and by King Aedelred, by their wives, and by those who supported their will; he had been urged and driven by many threats to violate his faith and to renounce the catholic and apostolic tradition for which he was chiefly attacked. Yet he was not overthrown. At last, he was driven away in disgrace.

### 44 [Cols. 0737D–0738D]

Thus deprived of every human aid, he did not know where to go or where to turn for lodging. He carried before him only this confidence: that he could in no way be abandoned by God. Trusting greatly in this confidence, he endured with the utmost gladness of heart whatever adversity befell him; and the more he was struck by hardships, the more wholeheartedly he devoted himself to the works of God.

At last he came to the court of a certain king named Kentwin.

> [Note: William passed over this passage untouched; Fridegodus explained it.]

There he was received with sufficient humanity and treated well, but only for a short time. For, as on other occasions, so also there, through the instigation of the demon, he suffered women’s anger. The royal wife was the sister of Ermemburgis, the author of nearly all the evils that were inflicted upon the man of God. Thus, no less malicious in mind than her sister [the text reads “wife”; read “sister”], she expelled the blessed bishop from all his own people after afflicting him with many forms of opposition.

What are you doing, savage fury of the devil? Why do you wander about raging so violently against the servant of the Lord? Why do you attempt to fasten the snares of your deceit upon him, and, in your attempts, weary him with a storm of varied accusations? Why do you strive to turn him away from building up the human heart, and for this reason refuse to let him remain joined to the fellowship of Christians?

Behold: when you drive him away from Christians, he will go freely to pagans, whether you wish it or not. And while you fear that the minds of some Christians might in some way be emptied of your deceptions through his association with them, by these very actions you bring it about far more than you imagine that an entire province is entirely deprived of your domination.

### 45 [Cols. 0738A–0738D]

After this he turned aside to the province of the South Saxons, which at that time was still laboring under pagan rites. There he preached the word of faith and administered the bath of salvation to those who believed.

The king of that people was named Edilwalh and had been baptized not long before in the province of the Mercians; the queen, named Eabe, had been baptized in her own province, that is, the province of the Hwiccii. Accordingly, with the king’s permission—or rather, to his great joy—the blessed Wilfrid washed the chief men and soldiers of the province in the sacred font, while his priests baptized the rest of the people.

Before this, the entire province was ignorant of the divine name and of the faith, apart from the king and queen. There was, however, a certain monk of Scottish nationality, named Diculus, who had a very small monastery in a place called Bosanham, surrounded by woods and sea. In it five or six brothers served the Lord in humble and poor circumstances. Yet none of the provincials cared either to imitate their life or to attend to their preaching.

When the bishop evangelized the people, he rescued them not only from the misery of eternal damnation but also from the appalling disaster of temporal death. For during the three years before his arrival in the province, no rain had fallen in those regions. Consequently, a most bitter famine had invaded the people and struck them down with impious death. Indeed, it is said that often forty or fifty men at once, worn down by hunger, would go to some precipice or to the sea; and, joining their hands in misery, all together would fall, either to perish in the collapse or to be swallowed by the waves.

But on the very day when the people received the baptism of faith, at the prayers of the exceptional Father, gentle yet abundant rain descended. The earth blossomed again; a joyful and fruitful year returned to the green fields. Thus, superstition having been cast aside and ancient idolatry having been expelled, everyone’s heart and flesh rejoiced in the living God (Psalm 83:3), understanding that he who is the true God had enriched them with the goods of heavenly grace, both inwardly and outwardly.

### 46 [Cols. 0738D–0739A]

When the bishop had come into the province and had seen there such punishment from famine, he taught them to seek their livelihood by fishing. For their sea and rivers abounded in fish, but the people had no skill in fishing except for eels.

Accordingly, nets for eels were collected from every side and cast into the sea by the bishop’s men. Aided by the divine generosity through the merits of their Father, they caught three hundred fish of various kinds. Dividing them into three portions, they distributed one hundred for the use of the poor, gave one hundred to those from whom they had received the nets, and kept one hundred for their own use.

By this benefaction the bishop turned everyone’s heart greatly toward love of himself; and, as he preached, they began with greater confidence to hope for heavenly things, since through his ministry they had received earthly goods.

### 47 [Cols. 0739A–0739B]

At that time King Elidwalh gave the servant of God land sufficient for eighty-seven households, called Selesei, which in Latin is said to mean “Island of the Sea-Calf,” where he might receive his people who were wandering as exiles.

When Bishop Wilfrid had received this place, he founded a monastery there and established it in regular observance, especially with those brothers whom he had brought with him. His successors are known to possess that monastery to this day. Later, however, the seat of the episcopal see was transferred to Cicestrum.

The renowned Father Wilfrid administered the office of the episcopate in those regions for five years—that is, until the death of Ecfrid—with extraordinary holiness and prudence, being greatly loved and honored by all. The king gave him, together with the aforementioned possession, all the resources found there, along with the lands and their people.

He baptized all who had been imbued with the faith of Christ, washing them in the baptismal water.
