Among them he baptized two hundred and fifty slaves of both sexes; and just as through baptism he freed them from diabolical slavery, so also, by granting them liberty, he released them from the human yoke of servitude.

### 48 [Cols. 0739B–0739D]

After this, when Cedwalla—who had been recalled from exile through the merits and interventions of the blessed Wilfrid—had obtained the kingdom of the Gewissae, he planned to capture the Isle of Wight by war and, after expelling the natives, to replace them with people from his own province.

That island had previously been devoted to idolatry. When the battle was at hand, however, the aforesaid prince bound himself by a vow, although he had not yet been reborn in Christ: if he captured the island victorious, he would give one-quarter of it, together with its spoils, to Christ the Lord.

Having obtained victory, he fulfilled the vow in this manner: he offered the quarter to the blessed Wilfrid for the Lord’s use. Since the size of the island, according to the reckoning of the English, amounts to twelve hundred households, the bishop was given possession of land containing three hundred households.

He entrusted the portion he had received to one of his clerics named Bernuinus, who was his sister’s son. He gave him a priest named Hildila, instructing both of them to minister the word and the bath of life to all whom they could reach on the island. Having undertaken the ministry of preaching, they subjected that island to the yoke of the Christian faith through the merits and intercession of the blessed Father and through their own persistence.

### 49 [Cols. 0740A–0740B]

In the year 685 of the incarnation of the Word of God, when Ecfrid, king of the Northumbrians, rashly led an army to ravage the province of the Picts, the enemy feigned flight, drew him into the defiles of inaccessible mountains, and destroyed him together with a very great multitude of the army that he had led there.

And rightly so: since he had in no way deemed it worthy to admit the man of life into his friendship or under the rights of his authority, he deserved, after despising him, to die at the hands of those same enemies whom, when he had earlier accepted him as a familiar ally, he had deserved to subject successfully to his rule.

At the very hour when the king was being overwhelmed in a severe battle in the province of the Picts, the servant of almighty God Wilfrid was occupied in the South Saxons with the sacred celebration of Mass. When, after the words “Lift up your hearts,” the response “We have them with the Lord” had been given, he was carried away in an ecstasy of mind and saw, through the Spirit of God, that at that same moment Ecfrid had been struck in the head and was falling dead.

Terrified by this vision, he was struck by a somewhat greater fear. For, as he continued the Mass and himself said in the preface, “Through Christ our Lord,” he looked up—and behold, two evil spirits miserably brought the king’s soul before his eyes, and then, carrying it away with a dreadful groan, led it to the gates of hell.

Immediately he summoned his priest Acca and recounted to him everything he had seen. The priest, stunned by immense astonishment, could scarcely bring himself patiently to believe what he heard from him. But the just man noted the day and hour of the king’s death, and confirmation of the event after several days proved that it had occurred at that very time.

### 50 [Cols. 0740B–0741A]

When report therefore announced the king’s death everywhere, the news quickly reached the ears of Theodore, bishop of the metropolitan see. Wishing to correct through humble satisfaction the offense that he had long before committed against the servant of God—namely, by consenting, as we have said, to his being unjustly afflicted by such disturbances—he sent for him and, having brought him honorably to himself, addressed him as follows:

> “My son—or rather, most holy Father, eminent in the merits of your virtues—I, who above all others had been appointed for this purpose, namely, to oppose every injustice that might arise in this kingdom, was overcome by my own weakness and, I confess, sinned greatly by consenting to the many who opposed you contrary to justice. But as I confess my guilt and repent of it in the depths of my heart, I ask you to assist me as a merciful giver of forgiveness. The final days of my life, as you see, are now at hand; therefore grant what I beg, and, since I humbly ask it of you, intercede for me.”

Terrified by these words, the servant of Jesus Christ the Lord replied:

> “I do not fail to know, venerable pastor, that with your consent I was afflicted by many tribulations. Yet far be it from me to believe that you were induced to do this by any wickedness! Rather, as I suppose, you did it with this intention: you wished me to be exercised in patience through those very tribulations, so that, driven by anxieties, I might be able through the path of patience to attain the summit of perfection. Therefore I ought much more to give you thanks for your good intention than you ought to seek forgiveness from me for it—especially since forgiveness is properly sought only for something from which an offense is thought to have arisen.

> “But since I know that you are watchful on every side like a heavenly creature, I recognize that you consider with keen and subtle judgment the things that must be seen. Therefore, most beloved Father, if you think that you contracted some sin in the things to which you consented against me, I freely forgive you in my mind; and, as I forgive, I also humbly beseech the Judge to show mercy to you.”

From that moment, the firmest and most holy peace was established between the venerable men. By pastoral authority they reconciled one another to Christ, and, rejoicing in spiritual gladness, they discussed the things of God with unanimous affirmation.

### 51 [Cols. 0741A–0741D]

Moreover, Theodore sent letters to Alfrid, who had succeeded Ecfrid among the Northumbrian people after Ecfrid’s death. In them, with rhetorical eloquence, he urged and persuaded him to become a friend to the blessed Wilfrid from the heart and to receive him honorably into the seat of his Church, from which he had been unjustly deposed.

> [Note: William reports these letters, though not those which Theodore sent to Alfrid.]

He also sent instructions concerning the same matter to Ailred, king of the Mercians, and to certain others whom he judged it appropriate to instruct about it. All of them, together with the kings, supporting the messages with equal agreement, sent back word with great joy of heart that they would receive the most noble servant of the Lord into his own place.

Indeed, King Alfrid sent messengers from his own side and ordered them to recall the man with the service of due reverence. Thus, summoned by royal invitation and episcopal command, he returned to his own church.

O how happy that day was for all who lived in those regions, and how great a joy of mind it brought to all the surrounding peoples, since the one who first deserved to see the blessed Wilfrid recalled from exile! Who could fully grasp the form of this joy? Who could pour it into the hearts of others through the service of his mouth?

Frequent companies of monks came out to meet the Father; bands of clerics, together with the entire multitude of the people, hastened eagerly to meet their shepherd; and all, blessing the Lord with raised voices, received him and led him into the church.

There, strengthened, and shortly afterward having removed whatever the judgment of equity showed ought to be removed, he soon recovered whatever lands or revenues belonged by right to the Church. Moreover, through him the words of divinity were poured daily into the hearts of his subjects, and in them a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4:14) arose.

The faith of Christ grew warm through the return of good works, while the work of faithlessness and wickedness everywhere grew cold. Consequently, sincere peace of hearts, tranquil abundance of possessions, great eagerness in the service of God, delightful pleasure, and pleasurable joy advanced in the Lord. All these things aroused great envy against him in the devil.

But the soldier of Christ, now well equipped with the armor of the word of God and having already experienced very many of the devil’s temptations, was more difficult to overthrow the more vigorously he was roused for battle. Imitating the manner of a most courageous warrior, he protected not only himself but also his fellow soldiers by striking down the enemy on the right and on the left. Thus impenetrable to the devil, he remained for five years in the dignity of his position.

### 52 [Cols. 0742A–0742C]

But O the inexterminable envy of the devil! O his violent condemnation—and how difficult it is to evade the right of possession acquired through custom!

When he could find nothing new to bring against the virtuous man for the subversion of peace, he stirred up the persuaders of the ancient disputes into their former agitation and quickly, through them, once peace had been disturbed, armed the king in anger against the bishop.

Inflamed by the words of informers, the king began to burn with sudden desire for his various and numerous possessions and unjustly to take them away from the rights of the churches to which they had been given. Since Bishop Wilfrid did not fear to resist him with episcopal authority, he inflamed the king with severe anger against himself. Thus it happened that the king planned to drive him from his kingdom after stripping him of everything he possessed.

To provide himself with the archbishop of Canterbury as the executor of this plan, he charged Wilfrid with failing to observe the decrees of the bishops of that see, and especially those of the venerable Theodore, who had recently died. Since it was intolerable that a bishop of the English kingdom should be held in authority if he dared even slightly to oppose the statutes of the bishop of Canterbury, the king did not wish Wilfrid, who was unable entirely to clear himself of this accusation, to remain a bishop in his kingdom.

Wilfrid accepted those statutes of Theodore which had been established by the canons and which he had instituted in peace at the beginning and end of his archiepiscopate, and he offered them due obedience. But those which, as was reported, he had established during interrupted periods of peace according to his own will rather than according to reason, he was entirely unwilling to accept or to give his assent to.

Therefore, as though a stain of disobedience and contumacy had been found in him against the see that was the mother of all Britain, he was deprived of his former authority and accused before Archbishop Birtwald, who had succeeded Theodore, on this charge.

Thus rejected, he withdrew to his faithful friend, Ailfred, king of the Mercians. He was gloriously received by him and lived for some time under the protection of God and of that king.

### 53 [Cols. 0742C–0743A]

Meanwhile, at the request of King Alfrid, Archbishop Birtwald ordered a general council of the bishops of all Britain to be assembled in the field called Eastrefeld. Wilfrid was ordered to present himself at this council, and it was promised that he would receive full justice concerning the injury of which he complained, provided that he could demonstrate by sound reasoning that an injury had been done to him.

Why say more? He came to the synod, but he found none of the justice that had been promised him. For certain bishops, favoring the king’s will, immediately began to harass the man of God with false accusations in the council and to disturb him with every form of opposition they could devise.

When they were unable to prove that their charges rested upon any truth, they finally added to their accusations that he did not at all obey the decrees of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. He replied:

> “I wish, with my conscience bearing witness, to submit with devoted mind to the decrees of the venerable Father Theodore that he promulgated in peace and with canonical authority, and, as is just, to obey them in all things. I do not at all refuse to be judged according to them in accordance with reason. Nevertheless, I ask you to tell me why, for so many years now, you have been disobedient to the letters sent from the apostolic see, while you accuse me so vehemently because I do not accept those institutions of Theodore which, as you yourselves know very well, he composed not with canonical authority but at the dictation of discord.”

### 54 [Cols. 0743A–0743D]

When they hurled these words back amid agitated murmuring, although they were entirely devoid of reason, a certain young courtier, well acquainted with the man of God, immersed himself in the surrounding crowd. Reaching Wilfrid, he explained to him the cause of the whole tumultuous council and urged him to take precautions. Immediately he secretly returned to the court by the road from which he had come.

Thus forewarned and fortified by the report of his faithful friend, Wilfrid adopted the defense of equity with all the greater steadfastness because he knew that his judges themselves were knowingly acting against justice. He therefore stood secure amid the missiles of words, since the freedom of his conscience was an impenetrable wall on both his right and his left.

When they discovered this, they tried to bend to their will by threats the man whom they could not overcome with words. Since he was unwilling to give answers according to their wishes, they said:

> “Know that you will be punished by a just sentence of condemnation unless, by the answer you give, you quickly wipe away the charges brought against you.”

He replied:

> “I have already answered the greater charge that I understand you to have brought against me: namely, that I do not wish to obey the decrees of the glorious bishop of the Church of Canterbury. If you wish, I answer it again and again: I wish to submit in all things to his canonical institutions.”

At once they seized these words from his mouth with deceitful cunning and declared that it was his canonical institution that the proud and disobedient should be cast down while the humble and obedient should be raised up.

> “But you have risen up in pride even against your lords, and have nevertheless been proved disobedient to your archbishop. Therefore it has been judged and decreed with sound reason that, stripped of all your possessions, you should pay the penalties of arrogance and disobedience.”

When they heard this, even his enemies were seized by horror, and they said that it was impious for a man honored by every nation to be stripped of everything without any definite crime.

Therefore, after some people had intervened with the king and the archbishop, they granted to him the monastery that the blessed Wilfrid himself had built at HRipis, as we said above, together with everything belonging to it. The condition was imposed that he should remain there in peace, should not leave the monastery’s bounds without the king’s permission, and should no longer administer the care of episcopal office.

### 55 [Cols. 0744A–0744D]

After this altered judgment had been carefully explained before everyone in a merciful speech, efforts were made to persuade Wilfrid, and what was presented to him as useful advice was that he himself should choose, by a pious subscription, to be degraded from episcopal office. In this way, free from the tumult of secular affairs, he could devote himself to contemplation of the heavenly life—especially since, as they said, it would be more advantageous for him to live privately in the service of God alone than to labor in the episcopal ministry and be daily wearied by the disputes of men.

The man’s prudence perceived from what source such advice had come. Astonished by their deceit, he refuted them all in these words:

> “The virtue of true counsel, which is numbered among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, admits no duplicity within itself. Thus, the more simply it proceeds from its source, the more freely it finds a place in the mind of God’s servant where it may be received. But I reject your counsel—which anyone can understand to be without the simplicity of the Holy Spirit—all the farther from me because, from the things you first heaped upon me, I can more clearly see from where it proceeds.

> “The lies that you maliciously fabricated against me could not themselves give birth to the gift of the Spirit of truth. Therefore, according to the counsel of true judgment, I will not cast myself down from the priestly rank, because I confess that, although unworthy, I nevertheless accomplished works not unworthy of the episcopate, aided by the grace of the Lord.

> “Hence it is that, behold, for forty years I have preached the truth of the undefiled faith wherever I could; I have overcome those who contradicted it by unconquerable reasoning; I have corrected those whom I overcame from every error by teaching them the truth; I have illuminated those whom I corrected with the light of the word of God; and I have joined them to the members of the Church of Christ.

> “Yet it was not I, but God himself, who did these things through me. Moreover, supported by apostolic authority, I corrected in many places throughout England the rite of ecclesiastical observance, which had been corrupted by Scottish tradition.

> “Have these and many other things, of which I am presently reluctant to remind you, deserved that I should be allowed nowhere to be safe, as though I were a betrayer of the laws and an informer against my own country? At least obey the commands of the apostolic see, which, when I was accused and condemned by a similar injustice, excused me and decreed that I was acquitted, if you refuse to allow me to remain at peace neither out of love nor out of fear of God.

> “But, as I think, you have either forgotten those commands or, knowing and understanding them, certainly regard them as worthless. Therefore, although I am worn out by old age, know in truth that I shall prove at Rome before the apostolic see that the accusations which, because of the king’s indignation, you bring against me are not true. And know also that I shall no less truly proclaim with what zeal you conduct the priestly ministry, since you prefer to favor human injustice rather than uphold God’s justice.

> “This is sufficiently evident while you attack me with such zeal, contrary to what is fair and true, although you plainly see that I am devoted to truth and justice. Moreover, though my conscience bears witness that I have deserved no adverse judgment for the charges on which you accuse me, you attempt to drive me to the point where, contrary to justice, I pronounce a sentence of condemnation against myself.

> “But in this matter know that I will in no way agree with you; rather, I confidently appeal to the apostolic see. Whoever wishes to deal with me, let him, invited by me today, go there with me for judgment.”

At these words the king was violently inflamed with anger and planned to crush him by the force of his army and compel him to submit to the king’s judgment, if only he could obtain the archbishop’s agreement in the matter.

### 56 [Cols. 0745A–0745B]

After the assembly had been dismissed, the man of God returned to King Ailred and disclosed to him the whole substance of the affair. Astonished by the wickedness of such great deceit, Ailred deeply grieved over the injury inflicted upon him.

Since Alfrid had been unable to deal with Wilfrid according to his will, he nevertheless decided, so that he would not seem powerless in this matter, to uproot, scatter, and dispose of everything that he himself had provided for the servants of Christ as their sustenance, and to make their dwelling-place itself entirely deserted.

But the disposition of the Judge who does not know how to yield to human fury did not permit the place of his servants to pass into the hands of sinners.

Finally, before the Father Wilfrid set out on the road to Rome, he came to the place, urged the brothers to commend themselves entirely to God, and strongly commanded them not to fear human anger. He said that nothing at all could harm them if they deserved to have God as their protector; and they would have him as protector if they truly loved him and always served him with a sincere heart.

They received the words of their Father in obedience, and through God they deserved to have God as their protector against all adversaries.

### 57

When blessed Wilfrid had arrived at Rome, he was received with great honor both by John, bishop of the apostolic see, and by the Roman people. When the reason for his arrival had to be discussed before the apostolic bishop and many bishops, he was granted the opportunity to defend himself in the presence of his accusers. Accordingly, he rose and stated his case before everyone; and he proved, by firm reasoning grounded in truth, that matters were as he had said. Thus, by the common judgment, the innocence of the man of God was confirmed, while the false accusations of his accusers were rejected.

Moreover, the venerable Pope John was earnestly entreated by all that, through apostolic authority, the just man might be raised to the honor due to him by justice, and that the injustice of those resisting him might be punished with an appropriate condemnation.

His cause was also aided by the reading of the synod of the venerable Pope Agatho, which had once been conducted in his presence, as we have said, while he himself sat among the bishops in council. For when that synod was read at the pope’s command, as the matter required, and recited for several days before an assembly of nobles and common people, they came to the passage where it was written: “Wilfrid, beloved of God, bishop of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case,” followed by the other words that we have set out above.

When this had been read, astonishment seized the listeners. While the reader was silent, they began asking one another who that bishop Wilfrid was. Then Boniface, counselor of the apostolic pope, and many others who had seen him there in the time of Pope Agatho, said that he was the very bishop who, accused by his own people and awaiting judgment from the apostolic see, had recently come to Rome. They said that, when he had come there earlier under accusation, his case and the dispute between the two parties had soon been heard and judged; and that Pope Agatho, of blessed memory, had declared that he had been unlawfully expelled from his bishopric. For this reason, they continued, he had been held in such high esteem by Agatho that the pope had ordered him to sit in the council of bishops that he had assembled, as a man of incorruptible faith and upright character.

On hearing this, everyone, together with the supreme pontiff, declared that a man of such authority, who had exercised the episcopate for nearly forty years, ought by no means to be condemned, but should return to his homeland acquitted and honored, as one free from every fault.

Accordingly, letters were written to the English kings Aethelred and Alfrid, instructing them that, if they did not wish to be struck with anathema, they were to restore him without delay to the seat of his bishopric, since everyone held it established that he had been unjustly deposed.

*[Note: [Col. 0745D] William records Wilfrid’s letter to Pope John, offered in his own defense, and also Pope John’s letters sent in Wilfrid’s favour to the most eminent lords Aethelred, king of the Mercians, and Alfrid, king of the Deirans and Bernicians.]*

### 58

After this, the servant of God, enriched with many holy relics and refreshed and rejoiced by the veneration of many people, resumed his journey homeward. When he had reached the regions of Gaul, he was suddenly seized by illness. As it grew worse, he was afflicted with such pain that he could not ride a horse at all, but had to be carried on a litter by the hands of his attendants.

Thus he was carried to the city of Meaux in Gaul, where for four days and nights he lay like a dead man, showing by his exceedingly faint breath alone that he had not been wholly deprived of life. When he had remained for four days without food or drink, without speech or hearing, on the fifth day, just as his companions were already mourning him as one about to die, the holy archangel Michael was sent by the Lord, through whom he was restored to his former health.

The Father, paying attention to him and rejoicing inwardly as much as he could, as though he knew him perfectly, lay silently awaiting what he wished to say. The prince of the angels is therefore said to have stood and addressed the man in these words:

“Wilfrid, most worthy fellow citizen, rise—why are you lying there? Although you are numbered among the citizens of heaven, nevertheless, because of the prayers of your sons, you will not die at this time, especially through the merits and intercession of blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin. For she prayed for you because certain works performed by you were pleasing to her. Indeed, she knows what work you did for Peter and what you built for his brother Andrew.

“Therefore, you will now be recalled from death and restored to life and health. But be prepared, because I shall return to visit you after four years. When you reach your homeland, you will recover the greater part of your possessions that were taken from you, and you will end your life in tranquil peace.”

When he had said this, the vision of the conversing angel vanished from his sight. Immediately Wilfrid rose, as though awakening from a deep sleep. He sat up and, opening his eyes, saw around him choirs of brothers singing psalms and weeping. After sighing softly, he asked where the priest Acca was.

Acca was summoned at once and entered. When he saw that Wilfrid was better and able to speak, he knelt with all the brothers who were present and gave thanks to God. After they had sat together for a short time and had begun anxiously discussing certain matters concerning heavenly judgments, the bishop ordered the others to leave for a while. Then, turning to the priest Acca, he recounted everything he had seen in order, binding him by a solemn adjuration not to disclose the vision to anyone while he remained alive.

### 59

The bishop therefore recovered, to everyone’s joy, and, having resumed his journey, came to Britain. When the letters that he had received from the bishop of the Roman see were read at an assembly of nobles, Archbishop Birtuald and Aethelred, formerly king but at that time abbot, gladly supported them.

This Aethelred summoned Coenred, whom he had made king after himself, and urged him always to honor, choose, support, and wholeheartedly cherish the servant of God, and to stand tirelessly as his defender against all adversaries. The king agreed.

King Alfrid of the Northumbrians, however, preferring to succeed his brother alike in his kingdom and in his indignation rather than, after laying aside his resentment, submit to the apostolic command concerning the deposed man, tried by various evasions to show that it was entirely impossible for him to carry out what had been ordered.

But the wisdom of God, which searches out the secrets of every heart, observed his wickedness, examined it after observing it, condemned it after examining it, and so weakened his body by a violent attack of pain that he was immediately confined to bed and deprived of almost every bodily function.

When he realized that he was dying, he summoned witnesses and promised that, if God granted him life, he would obey the apostolic commands and remain submissive to Wilfrid at all times. But he himself departed from life without recalling his hostility, and a certain Aedulf succeeded him in the kingdom, surpassing his predecessor in cruelty and hardness of heart.

For when holy Wilfrid came from Ripon to his court, he sent messengers to ask whether Aedulf would agree to peace. Aedulf answered them harshly, in keeping with the wickedness long inherent in him: “By my salvation I swear that, unless he leaves my kingdom within six days, I shall deprive of life all of his people whom I am able to find.”

Because of this, a conspiracy was formed against him, and he was driven from the kingdom, which he had held for two months.

After him, when Osred, the son of Alfrid, was reigning, a synod was convened near the River Nidd. After some conflict between the two parties, blessed Wilfrid was finally restored to the seat of his church, with everyone’s support.

*[Note: [Col. 0747D] This was chiefly through the efforts of Alfrid’s sister Elfleda, abbess of Streaneshalch after Hilda; the distinguished Berfrid also concurred—according to William, the second prince after the king, in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*.]*

King Ofred was joined to him in close friendship and deep affection. Throughout all the lands of his realm he ordered that no one should oppose Wilfrid in any matter, but that all should obey him in everything as a servant of God. And so it was.

For during the four years that the Father survived thereafter, there was no one who opposed him; no one dared despise his words or interpret them perversely or carelessly. Every form of envy lay crushed everywhere, both by love and by fear. The Father faithfully carried out in every place whatever the care of his ministry required. The more he recognized that the day of his calling was drawing near, the more diligently he labored to return to his Lord the talent entrusted to him, multiplied by fruitful increase.

### 60

He perceived that the time promised by the angelic revelation was now approaching, when suddenly he was seized by a serious illness and, exhausted, was taken to bed. Venerable companies of brothers, together with a large part of the people and their leaders, gathered around him. They surrounded the bed on which he lay with mournful cries, and great fear arose that he might depart from them.

But he understood that he was passing from labor to rest, from misery to blessedness, and from sorrow to everlasting joy. With whatever words he could, he consoled the sorrowful hearts of those around him, telling them that they ought in no way to mourn for one whom they could be completely certain would approach, after death, not mockery but the greatest joys.

Who could set out the whole sequence of words that he spoke both to console them and to exhort them to preserve the purpose of a holy life? The nearer he came to the unchangeableness of true consolation and eternal life, the more fully he drank in its sweetness, and the more freely he poured what he had drunk into the ears of those standing around him.

So that the hearts of his listeners might receive the power of his holy infusion, he confirmed before their eyes, through the wondrous efficacy of signs, that what he spoke in words was true. This power of signs accompanied the man all the more as, departing from the transient frailty of this life, he was eternally joined to Supreme Truth.

I confess that I cannot say how many sick people, through him while he himself was sick, were healed of every illness; how many possessed persons were freed; how many paralytics were strengthened; how many blind were given sight; how many deaf and mute were cured; or how many others afflicted by various calamities were, through the working of God, wonderfully restored by him.

For these and other reasons, a very great multitude of people hastened from distant places and devoutly entrusted themselves and their relatives to him. He, commending them to God with holy affection of heart, urged them to embrace God’s commandments with sincere love and to render them the obedience due in every respect, with reverence.

### 61

The time and hour that no mortal can escape were therefore at hand, and the whole sickness that weighed upon the servant of God entered into his vital organs. Groups of people of various ranks stood around him and offered prayers of praise to God in anticipation of his death. Although they could not help mourning their own desolation, they were nevertheless greatly consoled by the hope that they would never be deprived of his spiritual presence.

The Father himself, breathing faintly because of his great love for the sons surrounding him, raised his weary head for a little while and began to address them in these words:

“Strive with all your strength, dearest brothers, so that the grace of divine love may remain continually in you. In order that you may happily deserve to possess this grace forever, diligently practice the duties of fraternal love toward one another. Pay no attention to anything that might draw you away from such charitable service, lest you fall from the sincerity that is in Christ.

“You know the snares that the malicious deceiver lays for the faithful, seeking to capture their souls through deceptive fictions. Guard against these fictions with every care, as you have often heard me say, and cast them far from you, as you have seen me do. Do this, and the God of peace will be with you.

“And now, my dearest brothers, do not delay the one who is departing. You indeed—you yourselves—once recalled me to life when I was going away; but now, I beg you, spare me. It gives me joy, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, to follow the Lamb of God. You will see me no more in this flesh until Christ raises me with you at the end of this age. O my inmost being, farewell. I am pressed hard; soon I shall depart. And, O brothers, keep watch, lest the sleep of perpetual death envelop you.”

He said this and laid his limbs down in the hard repose of death. While the brothers were chanting the Psalter in order and had already reached the verse of the hundred-and-third psalm, “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm 103:30), he happily surrendered his spirit into the hands of the Creator and so entered the banquet of the Lamb, there to be forever refreshed.

He passed away in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 709, which was the seventy-fifth year of his life and the forty-fifth of his episcopate.

*[Note: He died in his monastery in the province of Undalum, under the governance of Abbot Cudbald. Through the ministry of the brothers, his body was carried to his first monastery, called in-H Ripon, and placed in the church of Saint Peter beside the altar, according to Bede. From the statements here and from the old calendar of the Missal of Gemeticum, granted by Robert, bishop of London, six hundred years ago, the date of his death was 24 April. Abbot Bacula is said, according to the Monasticum Anglicanum, to have wrapped Wilfrid’s body in a shroud among the other brothers.]*

He was buried in his monastery, which he himself had founded from the foundations at Ripon and consecrated to God in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There, to show mortals that he had not lost life but exchanged it for something better, he does not cease, when circumstances require, to perform miracles in this life even after being taken from it.

### 62

His garments were distributed as he had arranged before his death. One of them, a tunic damp with the sweat of his most holy body, was received by a servant to be taken to a certain devout abbess. A woman afflicted with paralysis earnestly begged to be allowed to touch it. But she was not granted the opportunity to touch the garment itself. Instead, she received as a drink the water in which the garment had been dipped, and she was immediately healed.

After this, certain enemies of the man of God, inflamed by the fire of their own wickedness, tried to set fire to the house in which he had ended this life. But the power of the dead man terrified the living fire, saved the house unharmed, and put the enemies to flight, thereby showing that he truly lived.

### 63

When a year had passed from the day of his burial, a great multitude of people gathered from every direction to keep a vigil in memory of his holy deposition. While the crowd spent the night offering vows to the Lord and lamented that it had irretrievably lost the affection of their father’s consolation, they saw that a light sent down from heaven in the east illuminated the entire place of the servant of God with wondrous splendor and drove away all the horror of night and darkness by its presence.

Those who saw it were greatly rejoiced. They fixed firmly in their minds that they ought not to grieve much over the bodily absence of the Father, since they had learned through so evident a manifestation of light that his spiritual presence was with them and therefore knew that they ought rather to rejoice greatly.

From this event, the veneration of all people for the most blessed Father Wilfrid grew intensely. They held it entirely certain that, just as the most holy bishop had been gentle and approachable to everyone during his temporal life in this transitory world, so now, living eternally with Christ in that everlasting life, he was gracious and ready to intercede for all who loved him.

### 64

The greatness of the signs that the Lord performed day after day at his body declared his merits far and wide and brought countless peoples, moved by his renowned reputation, together at his memorial. For this reason, the place itself was held in the highest honor for a long time and was greatly beneficial for those afflicted by every kind of illness who came there to recover their health.

The Lord had also calmed hostile attacks on every side, because he did not wish the devotion that his people had toward the veneration of his servant to be disturbed. But when certain neighbors began to be wearied by the continual arrival of the crowds and therefore gradually started to restrain themselves from visiting the place, it happened that, following their example, others also abandoned the fervor of their devotion and no longer visited the place as they had formerly done.

Thus it came about that those who had first kindled others to pious action by their own zeal later, through their laziness, compelled very many to withdraw from works of devotion.

### 65

Meanwhile it happened that a hostile invasion occupied the province. After occupying it, the invaders killed many thousands of people there and devastated all the places surrounding the monastery of blessed Wilfrid, reducing them to the likeness of a wilderness.

The monastery itself was seized and destroyed. Previously it had been glorious with hymns and songs; now it was disgraced by the filth of wild beasts and enemies. Meanwhile, the body of the bishop, deprived of every honor, remained unmoved amid the same filth at the original place of its burial.

But almighty God, who cannot be deprived of his own mercy and justice, stirred the minds of certain truly devout men to consider so great a matter and supplied both the desire and the means to alter it.

At that time a good and holy man, Odo, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, governed Christianity in England. With vigilant care he oversaw the arrangements of all the churches and, as reason required, was accustomed to visit them.

Moved by this concern, when he had come at one time to the province of York, and had diligently completed the matters for which he had come, he proceeded to Ripon to inspect the monastery of blessed Wilfrid. When he arrived and saw the dreadful desolation, he burst into tears.

While he remained in those regions, the men whose hearts, as I have said, God had touched so that the heavenly treasure might be moved, thinking that they had received an opportunity to fulfill their intention, sought, after first offering supplication to the Lord, to accomplish in action what they had long considered in their minds.

And so it happened. On the appointed day they came to the place, opened the ground where the body of blessed Wilfrid lay buried, reverently lifted all the bones together with the dust, and presented them to the venerable Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, so that he might carry them with him to Canterbury and, according to his desire, rebury them in Christ Church, which he governed.

For the monastery itself, where they had been buried, had—as was said above—been reduced to a pitiable wilderness, and no place remained there in which the relics could safely be placed and preserved. Therefore, they judged that they could and should be kept nowhere more safely or more appropriately than in the church of Canterbury.

They had this reason in mind: at that time Kent enjoyed great peace, and the blessed man himself, once displaced through the deceit of certain people and unable to live in the Church of York, had nevertheless continued to care for that same Church of Canterbury through his priestly office. It seemed just to them that he should rest in peace after death in the place where he had lived in peace while alive.

In addition, the sacred affection that they bore toward the venerable Odo was a major reason. Since they knew that he loved such gifts, they understood that by this act they were genuinely complying with his wishes.

Nevertheless, so that the place that blessed Wilfrid had loved above all others while he lived in the body would not be entirely deprived of his relics, they retained a small portion of them with the dust and placed it in a suitable location.

The venerable Odo, enriched by so great a gift, returned to Canterbury. He was received with the great rejoicing of the entire city and led with sacred praise into the house of God. There he placed the most holy relics of blessed Wilfrid that he had brought in the principal altar, which had been consecrated in honor of Jesus Christ our Lord.

*[Note: Read Eadmer’s fragment on this matter in Gervase the monk’s book On the Burning and Repair of the Church of Dorobernia.]*

For the benefit of posterity, so that no doubt might arise, the Father himself who received those relics, transferred them, and, as we have said, reburied them in the altar, proclaimed in a brief statement at the beginning of the work that he wrote about Wilfrid’s life and conduct the facts that we have related.

### 66

We too, who received those bones from the place mentioned above, are not permitted to waver in doubt concerning them. For after they had been preserved there unharmed for many years, and more than a hundred years had passed since the time when they were first placed there, by the fair but hidden judgment of almighty God almost the whole city of Canterbury was burned by fire, and Christ Church, which stood there, was consumed in the same conflagration.

In the third year after that conflagration, Lanfrancus, abbot of the monastery of Caen, of joyful and glorious memory, undertook the governance of that Church. After he had been nobly established in every respect in the patriarchate of the first metropolitan church of the English, he demolished whatever remained of the church’s ancient work, intending to construct everything anew.

When the altar mentioned above was demolished, the relics of blessed Wilfrid were found and lifted out, and placed in a shrine. After some years, when the brothers agreed that they should be enclosed in a more permanent place, a tomb was made for them on the northern side of the altar, and they were reverently enclosed there on 12 October.

### 67

Having now arranged these matters concerning the Father as best we could, let us finally conclude the order of our writing and, giving thanks to God and our Lord Jesus Christ for all his works, bring this little work to an end.

Nevertheless, we thought it necessary to add the following at the conclusion. If anyone who reads or hears these things weighs, without charitable indulgence, the unworthiness and dullness of my intellect, and for that reason refuses to believe what has been said about so great a Father, let him know that we affirm everything we have described about him, however imperfectly, on the authority of venerable men—namely, Archbishop Odo and the priest Bede. We have added nothing of our own except what we ourselves saw with our own eyes.

As for what I said about the condemnation of King Egfrid, I confess that I have never read it anywhere. Yet so many men of such standing confirm that it happened in this way that I consider it great shamelessness not to believe them.

Therefore, praise and thanksgiving be to almighty God the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0753A]

# Life of Blessed Bregwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, by Eadmer the Monk

(Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, II, 184.)

I commend the beginning and course of my undertaking—by which, at the request of certain of my friends, I have resolved to write concerning blessed Bregwin, bishop of the people of Canterbury—to the grace of the Holy Spirit. I pray that, in the abundance of his bounty, he may reveal the matters to be spoken and mercifully open my heart and tongue, according to the good pleasure of his will, to set them forth.

This blessed man was chosen by God in his mother’s womb, having happily received, before all ages, that same election in the ordering of God’s predestination. His parents, sprung, as is reported, from a noble stock of the Saxon people, deserved that the Creator of all should give them such a son: one whom his excellence of character, his mastery of the learning of heavenly doctrine, and the highest rank in ecclesiastical dignities, and the kingdom of everlasting glory, are shown to have deservedly attained.

Amid these works of God there reigned in Kent a vigorous and noble man named Wihtred, imbued with a most sacred devotion to God, who always held God’s servants in God, and God in his servants, in great esteem. In his time Father Birhtuald, of praiseworthy memory, had succeeded blessed Theodore in the patriarchate of the first metropolitan see of the English, and administered it worthily before God in every respect. At his prompting and exhortation the aforesaid king, in a general council, decreed that all the churches of his kingdom should for ever be free from every dominion and exaction of kings or of any earthly power.

*[Note: [Col. 0753C] This was done in the year 694, at the council of Becancelda, whose acts are extant in *Concilia Anglicana*, vol. I, p. 189.]*

In these days the man of whom we have undertaken to write was born in Saxony [Col. 0753C], and was named Bregwin by his parents. He was thereafter reborn in the Christian faith by the sacred font; and when he had passed beyond his infant years, the boy began to show a good disposition, giving his own people confidence, through the modesty of his conduct, of a holy hope concerning him. He was therefore handed over to letters and nurtured in the Lord’s school. Day by day his endeavours in sacred progress increased; and, in keeping with his age, after no long interval he became accomplished in literary learning.

Moreover, throughout England the exercises and studies of letters still flourished, magnificently watering the whole land through the teaching of blessed Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, and of his disciples. Christian religion likewise, which Kent had received through the preaching of the glorious and God-worthy Father Augustine, flourished there especially [Col. 0754A], since his most holy and vigorous successors—whom Rome had sent and who had succeeded him in the patriarchate of Canterbury down to the aforesaid Birhtuald—applied vigilant care lest it should waver in any respect. Indeed, from the arrival of Father Augustine in England until that time, the island itself had not been open to barbarian invasions to the same extent as we learn that it was open thereafter—and rightly so. For the yoke of Christianity, newly received, was borne by many with greater diligence; and for that reason the Lord Christ protected those who clung to him with more ready mercy. Thus a good report spread even into foreign regions and brought many to England after they had left their native soil. Strengthened by the grace of Jesus Christ, Bregwin was among them; on coming there, he soon obtained a place, became beloved by all, and was made a citizen of the country.

Thereafter, free from envy, he taught others what he knew and learned from others what he did not know. Thus, as he advanced in age and learning, so also, by the inspiration of God’s providence, he advanced in holy conduct and heavenly wisdom. Since he had read the Scripture, “He who adds knowledge adds labour” (Ecclesiasticus 1:18), he saw all the more that he must labour in this life, lest, while walking among the innumerable snares of the devil, he should in some way be hindered by them from eternal life. For, endowed with greater knowledge, he understood more clearly where he might tread if, unentangled by any of their hindrances, he persevered in the way of uprightness.

Adopting, therefore, a salutary counsel, he despised the world and all its delights, wishing to follow the examples of those who, following the Lord, left themselves and all that was theirs [Col. 0754C]. Thus, exchanging secular life for monastic life, he cast off secular dress and joined the community of monks who possessed nothing. When his outward man had become a monk, his inward man embraced all that belongs to a true monk, namely the ornaments of virtues. He acquired each of these things in his youth, knowing, according to the saying of the divine utterance, that even when he grew old he would not depart from them. Nor did he. Therefore, persevering in the Lord’s service, he continually commended to that same grace for preservation the heavenly purpose which he had received as a gift of God’s grace.

In those days Bishop Birhtuald was taken from this present life and borne into everlasting life. The place that he left vacant on departing from the world was filled in the same [Col. 0755A] year by a certain Tatwin, exalted to the rank of priesthood, a man of exceptional religion and, what is foremost, distinguished by monastic profession and habit. By the most sacred election of the whole Church he was made archbishop. This is the Tatwin whom the venerable Bede, in the history which he composed—that is, the history of the English people—sets down as the last bishop of Canterbury; and in his time Bede brought both that history and his own life to an end.

The aforesaid most Christian King Wihtred had indeed met his final day some years before and left the reins of the kingdom to Eadbert. In the eleventh year of that reign Archbishop Tatwin rested in a blessed end, namely in the fourth year after he had undertaken the governance of the archbishopric of all England. Nothelm succeeded him and governed Christ’s Church nobly for five years.

*[Note: [Col. 0755D] Tatwin ascended the throne in the middle of 731 and died after the middle of 734. Wightred died in 725, according to Saxon chronology. Tatwin therefore ended his life in the tenth year of Eadbert.]*

Thereafter, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 742, Cuthbert was elected [Col. 0755B] to the see of the bishops named above. He was a man born of the illustrious stock and renowned lineage of the English people, and himself wholly made up of virtues. Among the other good things by which he glorified the whole course of his life before God and men, he built a church in the eastern part of, and almost adjoining, the greater church, and solemnly dedicated it in honour of blessed John the Baptist. He constructed this church so that baptisms and examinations in trials established for different causes—which are customarily held in the Church of God for the correction of criminals—might be celebrated there, and that the bodies of archbishops might be buried in it. Thus the old custom was abolished by which, until then, they had been buried outside the city in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, where the bodies of all his predecessors lie. Having completed the course of his present life, Cuthbert was gathered to his fathers in the fifteenth year of his episcopate and honourably buried in the aforesaid church of blessed John.

*[Note: [Col. 0755D] On Cuthbert’s succession, see the dissertation on the true succession of the archbishop of Canterbury.]*

Accordingly, the Church of God sought with the greatest care someone who might be substituted for the deceased, not inferior in life and holiness of conduct. At that time Aethelberht, son of the above-mentioned King Wihtred, held royal authority in Kent, Eadbert, who had succeeded Wihtred, having long since died. This Aethelberht, knowing blessed Bregwin well from the loftiness of his holy purpose and the gravity of his conduct [Col. 0755D], conferred with those whom the tenor of the whole matter especially required to be consulted in the election of a shepherd of all. He urged them, after considering together the man’s industry, the standard of his holy life, and his perseverance in the purpose he had undertaken, to confirm in him by ecclesiastical election the will of God set before them, if by unanimous assent they judged him fit for the governance of all the churches of the whole of Britain.

The man’s God-worthy conduct from childhood was therefore set before them: his gentleness towards all, humility in everything, gravity of life, and in each of these qualities and in all of them together, continual strength joined with discretion [Col. 0756A]. The matter was referred to the people; all agreed as one that such a servant of the Lord was most worthy to be priest of so great a Church. Why say more? He was taken up and, although he resisted greatly and opposed his advanced age with all the efforts he could, was invested with the patriarchate of Canterbury. At his exaltation God was praised with the loud voice of the whole assembled clergy and with the rejoicing of their hearts. Then, at Canterbury, on the third day before the Kalends of October, he was consecrated with the highest honour and ascended the episcopal chair to govern the Church of God, amid the exultation of all.

*[Note: [Col. 0756D] Saxon chronology establishes that Bregwin was consecrated on that day in the year 759; and I think the year is correctly given. But in that year the day did not fall on a Sunday. It therefore appears that in that age consecrations were celebrated not only on Sundays but also on saints’ feast days.]*

[Col. 0756B]

Set by God as a mirror for all, he shone so brightly in holy works that those who wished to walk in the path of light could see clearly enough in his life the way in which they should walk. If anyone asks concerning the performance of miracles, which more often display holiness than produce it, I will say what I think. I confess that whether he performed any such miracle or not has not, thus far, come to my knowledge. If he did perform any, either a lack of writers, or antiquity, or certainly some occurrence among the various vicissitudes, has removed them from our knowledge.

Yet the things which we have learned on reliable report to have been done at his sacred body after his death show more clearly than light what he might have done while living in the body, had reason or necessity brought him to perform such deeds. But those times, with the faith of Christ established everywhere [Col. 0756C], had no need of miraculous signs, which, as blessed Gregory says, belong rather to unbelievers than to believers. A miracle would be displayed outwardly in vain if that which should work inwardly were lacking. And, as reason persuades me, it appears established that it is greater for each person continually to have within himself, through purity of flesh and spirit, the author of all miracles, than to display miracles which Truth says may, at men’s pleasure and for their amazement, be common even to the reprobate.

Peace also flourished throughout the kingdom in the days of his episcopate, and no hostile attack was feared. Therefore, while all things remained in God’s peace, the God of peace was all things in all things and through all things to all. When the blessed and happy Father preached the word of life among the people [Col. 0756D], he was heard with a gentle and modest spirit; and the things which he enjoined in his exhortations were carried out with willing effect. For true faith either to increase or, if wavering, to recover strength and stability, the Father’s voice alone, strengthened by the increase granted by the Lord, sufficed; nor did anyone demand a miracle to prove it. But these good things did not endure long. For when the blessed man, by whose merits they had come about, was soon removed from this life, after a few years had passed they too were removed [Col. 0757A].

For he lived only three years in the episcopate, filled in every respect with God and endowed with unfailing constancy in every virtue. In the second year of his patriarchate, King Æthelberht, son, as we have said, of the most vigorous King Wihtred, brought his final day to a close.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] The Saxon Chronicle reports that King Ethelbert died in 760, and also records the exceedingly severe winter of the following year.] In the year after this there was a most severe winter, constricting everything with excessive harshness of cold and destroying animals of various kinds both through the density of the snows and through the savage severity of the winter. But when, according to the words of the true Solomon speaking in the Song of Songs, “the winter had passed, the rain had gone away and departed” (Song of Songs 2:11), the flowers of the Lord appeared. Hence, when the vineyard of the Lord of hosts sent forth a flower of the sweetest fragrance, at the voice of the turtle-dove and of the bridegroom saying, “Arise, hasten, my beloved; come from Lebanon, come, you shall be crowned” (Song of Songs 4:8), the soul of the most blessed Father, the sweet beloved of the supreme Father, arose—that is, to be crowned by her bridegroom Jesus Christ. She left the world and the body and, supported by the assistance of the angels, joyfully and gladly ascended to where she might eternally behold God himself, the God of gods, in Zion.

He was indeed buried in the aforesaid church of the blessed John the Baptist, near the body of the revered Bishop Cuthbert, the founder of that church and, as we have said, his most worthy predecessor. After him Father Jambertus, abbot of the neighboring and aforementioned abbey of the glorious apostles Peter and Paul, was appointed to the episcopate of the bereaved Church.

## [Col. 0757C]

After a few years had passed, the savage people of the Danes, learning that England was deviating from its former condition in almost every class of people and devoting itself more than usual to riches and pleasures, began, as though gradually testing the matter, by first sending three ships there, to discover what they might accomplish if they sent more ships and more men came. When they heard that these had succeeded in certain respects, they were encouraged; and, with a fleet prepared, they acquired the practice of coming to England not once or twice but very frequently.

At a certain time, etc. Several miracles follow, an epitome of which was given above, in Eadmer’s abridged words, by the *Life of Bregwin* falsely ascribed to Osbern. Many more accounts of this kind are reported concerning the blessed man, all of which it would be excessively burdensome to write down. Turning therefore to other matters, we shall set an end to these here.

## [Col. 0757D]

Many years passed, and his body remained undisturbed in its place under the veneration of many. Some of his successors, too, when departing this life, received a place of burial in the same basilica. After this, when many evils were increasing throughout England, it happened that the city of Canterbury, through the negligence of certain people who were managing their property less carefully, was set on fire; and, as the flames grew, the fire was carried to the mother church standing there. What shall I say? It was entirely burned, together with nearly all the buildings of the monks dwelling there, and likewise the church of the blessed John the Baptist, where, as was stated above, the remains of the archbishops lay buried.

No one can say what or how great were the losses that place suffered in this conflagration. To touch upon some of them, whatever it possessed that was more precious in gold, silver, ornaments of various other materials, sacred and secular books, the tongue of fire devoured and absorbed almost entirely. Since these things, however, were recoverable, perhaps they are less to be lamented. But an immense grief, one that cannot be brought to an end, still weighs upon that same church: the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, and the privileges of the kings and princes of the realm, carefully sealed and granted to that church, by which it ought to have fortified and protected itself and its possessions by perpetual right, were entirely reduced to nothing and destroyed. If any of them were recovered, they were found and obtained in various places where they had been copied out, since the bulls and seals—which could not be recreated in any other way—had been consumed by the fire together with the church in which they were kept.

## [Col. 0758B]

As a result, the strength and power of its enemies against justice increased down to the present, and the audacity of insurgent sons built up against it many evils, oppressions, and scandals. But since these matters are known to everyone, we vainly indicate them in writing as though they were information for others. Therefore, omitting them, let us say that after this lamentable fire the bodies of the aforementioned bishops continued to rest undisturbed in their own tombs, until that most vigorous and entirely honorable man, Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen, became archbishop of Canterbury.

He leveled with the ground all the buildings of the burned monastery that he found, and the worn remains of its buildings, and dug out all the foundations that lay beneath the earth. Then he constructed everything anew and ordered that the aforesaid bishops be raised and placed in safety until the church he had begun should be completed, in which they could be decently deposited. And so it was done. After some years they were brought into the church that had now been founded and placed on the northern side, above the vault, each beneath a separate little wooden shrine, where the mystery of the saving sacrifice is celebrated every day.

When these arrangements had been made, it happened that one day one of the brothers of the church, sitting on a bench before the tomb of the blessed Bregwin, etc. Two miracles follow; for these, see the epitome falsely attributed to Osbern above. Indeed, as many assert, the Saxons observe among themselves this custom with particular distinction: that they honor their elders more worthily and do not spare the irreverence of their subjects, lest they grow insolent. Thus, even after being removed from the world, the good father sought to display the custom of his people to his sons, so that he might teach them with what reverence they ought to treat their elders.

## [Col. 0758D]

Amid such events in the life of the most holy man, a certain monk named Lambert came to Canterbury from the land of the German emperor. He was known to the queen whom King Henry had taken from Saxony as his wife after the death of his first wife. This Lambert lived for a long time at Canterbury, at the queen’s request, with the brothers, and was regarded by everyone almost as a monk of the place.

Thus, having also gained their familiarity, he began frequently to visit the place where the remains of the bishops rested; there he prayed, there he celebrated Masses, and there he conducted himself familiarly. He would ask this man and that who this or that person was, or by what name the one enclosed in this or that shrine was called. When he heard about the blessed Bregwin, he was inflamed with the desire to possess him and transfer him to his own land, perhaps remembering the ancient reputation for goodness that he had learned about him in his homeland.

But when it seemed impossible for him to fulfill his desire either secretly or openly by his own efforts, he suggested to the archbishop then in office, a man named Ralph who was seriously afflicted by paralysis, that he should grant him the bones of the aforesaid Father. He assured him that the leading men of his people had granted him a site for building a monastery, which he and his followers intended to construct under the patronage of Father Bregwin and to organize wholly for the service of God.

What more is there to say? The bishop consented, for he did not know what was being done; and therefore he was easily moved by the petitioner’s requests. The matter was brought before the monks. Some praised the grant most fully, so that the bishop’s concession might be carried out; others, on the contrary, rejected it by every means. After some days the archbishop died. Accordingly, many of those who, while he was alive, had approved that what he had granted to the requesting brother should be done, now changed sides and agreed with those who opposed it. With one mind they all insisted that the Church should not be deprived of its shepherd, whom while alive it had loved with devoted affection.

Nevertheless, so that the bishop’s concession would not appear to be altogether disregarded, it was decided by common agreement—and some testified that the archbishop himself had consented to this—that one bone, namely the left arm, should be given to the brother from the sacred body.

He considered this of little value and could not endure being cheated of what he said had been promised him. He suspected that, through the queen, he could prevail with the king, so that he himself might by royal authority forcibly wrest from the monks the grant of what he sought. He therefore came to London to speak with the queen about the matter and to visit her while she was staying with the king in Woodstock Park. There he was struck by a severe illness and could not proceed farther.

As his sickness increased day by day, he was carried back to Canterbury, where, after living for a short time, he died and was buried among the deceased brothers.

## [Col. 0759D]

On the following night, a man of medium stature, distinguished in appearance, dressed as a monk but unknown in face, appeared in a vision to one of the brothers of the community, a thoroughly religious man who feared God. He said to him:

“Do you know for what reason that Saxon Lambert was taken away by such an unexpected death?”

When the brother replied that he did not know, the man said:

“Know that it was because he attempted to remove Bregwin’s body from its place and claim it for himself. For he was not of such merit in the sight of God that he ought rightfully to possess either the presence or the possession of so great a bishop.”

## [Col. 0760A]

Considering these matters, therefore, the prudent concern of the servants of God, and judging from what that brother had attempted that something similar might in the future be attempted by foreign newcomers, moved the relics of that Father from the aforementioned place, together with the relics of the blessed Archbishop Plegemund, to the southern part of the church, lest such people should more easily achieve their purpose. There they were most decently buried behind the altar of Pope Gregory the blessed.

One of the monks, named William, made himself, with the consent of the others, the principal intermediary in all these matters. Through his efforts and provision, nearly everything required for the transfer of the relics and the arrangement of the tombs was procured.

Afterward, on one solemn occasion, while devoting himself with all his strength to the service of the church and forcing his voice beyond its capacity in singing, he suffered an internal rupture. Soon he was violently afflicted by vomiting blood and other serious ailments. What, then, was he to do? He did not know. For he knew that the same thing had already happened in that church to certain others for the same reason: some had paid for it with their lives, while others had been tormented for many years by severe illness, as he knew beyond all doubt.

Then he remembered what service, what care, and what honor he had recently bestowed upon those two bishops, Bregwin and Plegemund. Therefore, with a contrite heart and humbled spirit, his cheeks drenched with tears, he prayed that they would have mercy on him, so that, having obtained from Christ Jesus the restoration of his former bodily health, he might understand what should henceforth be thought about them by himself and by others, and with what confidence he might call upon them to intervene for his eternal salvation.

Wonderful is God’s goodness, wonderful his power! Immediately, as he himself reports, he felt himself cured of every illness and thereafter suffered no further trouble from any new pain or discomfort.

I, who possess little wisdom, have published these things about the blessed Bregwin, which I learned from older and truthful men. They report that they themselves experienced some of these things, while others they received either from those who were present or from people who had received them from eyewitnesses; and they repeatedly affirm them with consistent testimony.

Therefore, so as not to offend the feelings of my friends who urged me to undertake this work, I yielded to their wishes. What I have written, I have written for them; let them judge for themselves. If I have proceeded well in any respect, thanks be to God; if in any respect otherwise, I beg them to pray more earnestly for my offense.

The memory of the departure of the most blessed man is commemorated on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, so that there the name of the Lord, who honored him, may be more readily magnified. Therefore, may he who lives, rules, and reigns through all things be blessed for ever and ever and beyond. Amen.

*Here ends the Life of the blessed Bregwin, archbishop and confessor of Canterbury.*

## [Col. 0761A]

# LIFE OF SAINT OSWALD, BISHOP OF WORCESTER AND ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, BY EADMER, ON THE SECOND DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MARCH

According to the purpose of God’s grace, the venerable Oswald, bishop of York, chosen by God before the ages, advanced along the path of the present life. Nobly born into the light of this world through the nobility of his lineage, he was initiated into noble character.

His deeds, arranged in various styles by different authors, seem to be more burdensome to read because the material is more extensive and the mind is divided among many matters.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] Ælfric and Folcard had previously committed Oswald’s deeds to writing. Consult the preface concerning them.]

Therefore, those who, as is truthfully believed, love him in this life more sincerely than others, were pleased to urge me by both entreaty and command to undertake this task, so that I might set forth in a concise and new style of narration what has been written about him in many different ways.

In this I confess that I am not a little afraid. When I consider the foolishness of my little intellect within myself, I fear that I may be unable to satisfy those who ask this of me in the work itself, because I know that they desire the one whom they love above all to be presented in the most joyful eloquence.

Yet I judge it wicked not to comply with their wishes: both lest they think that I, their very dear friend, am unwilling to accommodate them, and lest, with their conscience wounded, they suppose that I possess no love for the saint of God.

Hemmed in by these difficulties, I chose rather to meet the desire of my friends in rustic speech than, by urban silence, to despise them and offend through the guilt of disobedience. Since, therefore, my assigned duty is to write the life of so great a man, I invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was always present with him, so that he may graciously grant me, through his merits, to explain without offending the ears of his Church, by whatever arrangement of words I can manage, those things which he deigned to accomplish through him for the praise of his name.

## [Col. 0761C]

At the beginning of his birth, the glorious Oswald, born of the noblest lineage, shone with an elegant appearance. When, carefully brought up, he had passed beyond the years of infancy, he became a boy and began to avoid childish foolishness and, insofar as that age could understand, to shape himself toward works of holiness.

For he resolved, in the sight of him who sees the secrets of the heart, that he would in no way prove degenerate from the noble stock of his family; but those whom he had received as relatives according to the flesh, he would follow in the footsteps of virtue, instructed in faith and armed with the other heavenly weapons.

The good and prominent Father among the English, named Odo, was his father’s brother—a man outstanding in religion, exalted in discernment, grave in character, a cultivator of justice, great in counsel, and pre-eminent in authority, as he was circumspect in all his actions.

We have thought it not inappropriate to touch upon a few of his deeds, which certain older men described to us in a full account, so that it might thereby be shown from what imitable and distinguished lineage the boy of God, Oswald, derived his origin.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] Eadmer had not yet written Odo’s Life. Here he seems to indicate the Life of Odo written by Osbern, and later narrated the same events more fully in Odo’s Life, which is placed above under Osbern’s name, incorrectly.]

This Odo, as the story relates, was very dear and acceptable to Æthelstan, the most victorious king of the English. Because of Odo’s praiseworthy holiness, that king regularly kept him with him and relied greatly upon his counsel.

The king, who loved God and served the laws of equity, governed the kingdom vigorously. Once, armed, he went out to meet an immense army of pagans, taking with him the aforementioned Odo, through whose merits he believed above all that he would conquer the enemy.

When battle was joined, Odo stood at a distance from the fighting, raising his eyes and hands to heaven and praying earnestly to the Lord for the king and his men. The battle raged most fiercely on both sides, and nearly the whole day was consumed in combat.

At last, as the sun was already turning toward setting, a grievous accident occurred: the king’s sword broke near the hilt. What was he to do? He did not want to disarm any of his men in order to arm himself.

What then? When the enemies, who had already begun to turn their backs, saw that the king, with his sword broken, had become almost unarmed, they were encouraged and returned more fiercely to the battle. A shout rang out, urgently calling Odo to hurry forward.

## [Col. 0762C]

He arrived. The king himself urged and entreated him to bring his aid through prayer and action. But Odo said:

“The help you desire is at hand, if only you are willing to use it. What, then, are you doing? Why do you spare the sword that hangs at your side? Why do you keep it from the destruction of the enemy? What do you fear? Without hesitation, seize it; and behold, the hand of the Lord will be with you. The sun will not set before flight or destruction overwhelms your resisting adversaries.”

He spoke, and the king, astonished at his words, immediately turned his right hand to the scabbard and drew out a shining, strong, and splendid sword. With it he terrified, cut down, or struck to the ground all who came against him. In accordance with the word of the servant of God, both the setting of the sun and the king’s triumph came about.

Odo himself, since he presided over the Church of Canterbury in the office and dignity of supreme pontiff, administered the laws of Christianity throughout the entire kingdom, as a father of his country, with the greatest prudence.

During those days, Edwius, who held the scepter of the kingdom of the English and was fourth after the aforementioned Æthelstan, was a lover of pleasures rather than of God, of luxury rather than sobriety, and of lust rather than chastity. He dishonored the royal dignity by shameful deeds and, despising men of virtue, provoked them against justice.

Therefore, the blessed Dunstan, then abbot of Glastonbury, was expelled from his country because, at the suggestion and command of the aforementioned Odo, he had forcibly withdrawn the king himself from illicit embraces. Afterward, innumerable evils were perpetrated throughout England by that king.

Against him Odo rose, girded with the armor of the Holy Spirit, becoming the public enemy of his iniquities. He did not cease until, once the incestuous relations had been suppressed, he cleansed the kingdom of the disgrace of the infamous woman with whom the same king repeatedly consorted after setting aside his wife.

Surrounded by a troop of his soldiers, he forcibly removed her from the royal court where she had been staying, and, once taken away, condemned her to perpetual exile in Ireland.

He was a man supported in every respect by the strength of pure equity. He favored no servant of iniquity and strove in all things to obey the will of God. Therefore God’s mercy was always with him, and he inclined his ears to Odo’s will.

For example, when that Father wished to raise the walls of Christ Church at Canterbury—that is, of his own see—to a height greater than before, after removing the roof, and fulfilled his desire by action, he prayed to the Lord that, as long as that house of God lacked its proper completion, no rain that might keep the people from the service of God would fall within its enclosure.

And so it happened. For one might see the whole city often surrounded by heavy rain, while the temple itself was not even touched by the inundation of that rain.

Again, on one occasion, while that Father was present at the altar administering the sacred mystery, the Lord’s body appeared between his hands, bloody and dripping blood into the chalice. When the minds of those watching had been struck with the greatest fear, it was immediately restored, at the bishop’s prayers, to its customary form.

Other marvelous deeds are also reported of the same man, but we pass over them in silence, lest we be thought to have forgotten the work we have begun.

## [Col. 0763D]

The boy Oswald, therefore, being this Father’s nephew, was entrusted to him by his parents so that he might be imbued with his teachings and formed by his example. Declaring himself fortunate to live in the company of so great a man, he took care to imitate not his miracles—which sometimes occur even among the wicked—but his virtues, without which no one becomes good.

Thus he was loved by everyone, not only because he was joined to Odo by such close kinship of the flesh, but also because his merits had made him worthy of being loved by all.

He was committed to the study of letters and learned diligently under the instruction of a certain man named Frithegod, who was thought to surpass all the learned men of his time in sacred and secular disciplines.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] This monk of Canterbury was distinguished by the publication of many writings, above all by the *Life of St Wilfrid*, composed in verse at Odo’s command.] In a short time he made very great progress.
