For the spirit of wisdom and understanding (Isaiah 11:2) rested upon him, breathing its grace into him and giving him an understanding heart for learning one by one the things he heard.

Thus, fully imbued with knowledge of secular books, he devoted his mind with diligent attention to the pages of sacred letters. From them, kindled by the holy fire of charity toward God and neighbor, he was wholly raised into contempt for the world and meditated at every hour on how he might in every way attain merit through the service of God.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Tinmouth reports that at Winchester Odo placed Oswald in the old monastery and later made him dean. At that time the monastery was occupied by secular canons.]

Meanwhile, his aforementioned uncle, the glorious Odo, sent him to Winchester so that, living there, he might learn and imitate any way of life worthy of imitation that he might perhaps find among the canons.

What more is there to say? He became a canon among those canons—or, if one asks what kind of man he was among such men, a regular man among irregular ones. For he tirelessly carried out what the institution of canonical life teaches and commands; they, having rejected the discipline of their order, walked according to the desires of their hearts.

Therefore, to everyone’s wonder, because of the fullness of God’s grace that shone in his conduct, he was made dean while still a young man and placed over his elders, so that the gray hair of his understanding and his blameless life might cleanse the elders’ stained life, and so that the childish understanding of those men might be emptied through the practice of heavenly discipline.

But they, preferring to follow the ancient paths of their corrupt old age, although they honored him with flattering respect and due favor because he was good and acted well, nevertheless declared that they would in no way listen to him in such matters.

He, caring nothing for the vanity of their praise, daily groaned and prayed night and day that God would provide for his salvation. But when he perceived that they were unwilling on his account to be corrected from their old way of life, and that, through them, if he did not withdraw, he might be corrupted from his purpose, he rejected the worldly pomp with which he was surrounded, rejected the riches in which he abounded, and left the canons whose company he had until then shared. He returned to his uncle, the bishop, to discuss with him the matter of the salvation of his soul.

What more is there to say? When, speaking with the bishop, he had lamented the miseries of mortal life in pious reflection, and when, in their conversation, they had weighed from both sides how difficult it is for a person walking amid the allurements of the world not to be ensnared by those very allurements, the soldier of Christ, Oswald, declared that it had now come into his mind to follow Christ henceforth stripped of all worldly things and truly to become a monk.

The bishop leapt for joy at what he heard. As tears burst forth because of the rejoicing of his heart, he was utterly unable to find words with which to express what he carried within.

O what contemplation of eternal life arose among them from the divine words! O what persuasive and divine discourse, born from contempt for the world! Who could explain it?

Thereafter the old man urged the young man not to turn back, not to look behind him after placing his hand on the plow (Luke 9:62), and not to allow the enemy to entangle him in the snares of the world just as he was beginning to escape its snares.

To this he replied:

“Having broken the bonds of carnal pleasures, I have now, by God’s inspiration, been granted freedom. Should I hand myself over again to the most wretched captivity, to be bound beneath the bonds of those same pleasures? I did not think that I ought to follow Christ in this way. From knowledge of his Scriptures he granted me love of him; and should I now abandon him? Is this the sort of fruit I should gain from meditating upon them? Rather, Father, if you please, tell me; do not doubt that I shall complete what I have resolved wherever you wish. Or, if it is not burdensome to you, let me myself disclose what I have determined.”

He said, “Tell me.”

“I wish,” Oswald replied, “to observe the Rule of the blessed Benedict under obedience. Therefore I have resolved to become a monk in Gaul, at Fleury, where the relics of that Father are said to be kept. For, according to my judgment, nowhere are the institutions established by that Father more rightly to be observed—or perhaps actually observed—than in the place which he himself does not cease to honor perpetually by his bodily presence.”

To this the bishop replied:

“We feel the same; we think the same; our intention tends toward the same goal. I am a monk of that place. For I received from there the religious habit when I was called to the burden of governance beneath which I groan. Therefore, since I love you in a special way, I most earnestly desire that you become a monk there.”

Indeed, this change of homeland pleased the will of both men at that time for this reason: the religious observance of the monastic order, which had almost entirely grown obsolete throughout England both because of the frequent incursions of barbarians and because of the turbulent rebellions of certain evildoers, had not yet been restored to the condition of its former strength and distinction.

The young man was sent to Fleury, there to be supported by the flowers of virtue. Many gifts were also sent with letters of recommendation, commending the young man to the abbot and brothers in word and deed.

He was received, and, having been clothed as a monk, he was adorned from the very beginning with the life of a monk. Although he had come to be taught by others and to imitate others, he presented himself to them in such a way that they found in him enough to teach and imitate.

He was sparing of sleep, temperate in food, discerning in speech, constant in prayer; and from his sincere charity, which was poured out upon everyone beyond human estimation, one may infer how strong, obedient, kindly, and steadfast he was in the other virtues—patience, I mean, humility, kindness, gentleness, and the rest of this kind. As the Apostle says:

“Charity is patient, is kind; it does not envy, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4),

and the rest, which it would be lengthy for me to set out as I strive for brevity.

This same servant of the Lord had received from the abbot a secluded place in the church, where he might draw nearer to God according to the measure of his way of life. There, withdrawn from their disturbance, he was accustomed to devote himself to prayer, meditation, and contemplation of eternal life. By this he provided abundant fuel for the envy and hatred of the enemy of the human race.

For that enemy, observing the diligence of the most vigorous young man and longing to overthrow him through observation, assailed him with many kinds of cunning; by assaulting him, terrified him; by terrifying him, wearied him; and by wearying him, labored to drive him from the place.

Thus, on one occasion, while Oswald was offering himself to God at night in prayer through contrition of heart, the Evil One appeared. Producing terrifying sounds, he attempted to subject the man to fear, both so that he would abandon what he had begun and so that at other times he would attempt a similar work more sluggishly or not at all.

But Oswald, protected by the shield of Christian faith, was no more frightened by the roar of a lion or the hiss of a serpent than by the bleating of a sheep or the squeak of a mouse—for that wicked being imposed upon him the voices of these and other animals. He regarded all such things as worthless and laughed at them all together with their author.

When the demon perceived this, he disappeared; but immediately he was transformed into an angel of light and appeared to the man. He thought that, having now achieved a new victory over himself, he might persuade Oswald that he was rightly being visited by an angel, since the enemy had been unable to entangle a man supported by firm constancy of mind in any of his illusions.

But his wickedness deceived him. For at the sight of this apparition the servant of Christ made the sign of faith, knowing that from that moment the angel of light must not be provoked, while the angel of darkness must be driven away from a distance.

And so it happened. The degenerate angel who had appeared was immediately terrified and fled from the young man fortified by the sign of the cross.

Then Oswald, singing a psalm, said:

“The Lord is at my right hand; I shall not be moved. Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh shall rest in hope” (Psalm 15:8–9).

He also frequently devoted himself to sacred reading, and whatever he learned from it under the Lord’s instruction, he taught the less knowledgeable with a cheerful face and kindly heart.

Amid these exercises, after receiving the lower grades of the ecclesiastical order, he received the rank of deacon. In it he served God with the obedience of the deepest devotion, while he delighted the people through the magnificent harmony of his exceedingly sweet voice.

Indeed, among the marks of virtue that, as we have said, shone in him, a certain manifold and surpassing grace also gleamed in his outward person. In the clothing he displayed to the eyes of those who saw him there was a becoming and attractive order, serving neither pomp, nor dissolution, nor ostentation, nor hypocrisy. His face likewise possessed a broad beauty—not a stimulus to any wicked pleasure, but a great distinction of propriety that surpassed the faces of others.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] This entire section was added to the Benedictine manuscript codex on an inserted folio, written by a later hand, as far as the copyist was able to conjecture. The same passage appears in almost exactly the same words in Tinmouth, book 21, chapter 52.]

By such distinguished gifts the man of God, Oswald, was judged worthy to ascend to the higher grade of the ecclesiastical order, beyond the diaconate, and afterward was elevated to the dignity of priest.

In that rank, offering sacrifice to God, the purity of heart and body with which he cleaved to Christ, and the gracious ear that God lent to his holy prayers, can be clearly understood both from the quality of his life, which is described according to the truth of events, and from the presence of angels, who are shown to have sometimes appeared to him visibly as well.

The place in which, as we said, he used to pray with the abbot’s permission was a certain crypt, constructed with elegant workmanship in the western part. According to custom, that place bore the name of a confession.

Before the doors of that crypt, twelve poor men had from ancient usage been accustomed to live, receiving their daily sustenance from the church itself. These poor men were arranged so that all were companions in letters and all were clerics.

## [Col. 0767B]

From among them the revered Father Oswald had chosen one to assist him whenever he wished to celebrate the solemnity of Mass, so that through his help and ministry he might perform the office of so great a mystery.

One day, as he himself was present at the altar and engaged in the office of the Mass that had begun, and after the Gospel readings took bread and the chalice into his hands for the offering, as is recognized to be the custom of many, he directed his eyes toward heaven and, with attentive mind, sent before God the prayer, “Receive, holy Trinity.”

Then the aforementioned minister saw a person of reverend appearance standing on the right side of the altar, with his face turned toward the altar itself. He held between his hands a very white loaf, though not especially large, and held it with fitting reverence between hands extended upward as far as his head.

Although the minister was struck dumb with excessive fear at the sight, he nevertheless endured it and did not wish to flee suddenly. But when he saw the same loaf gradually growing, in accordance with the priest’s progress through the secret prayers, and becoming of extraordinary size as it grew, he no longer dared remain. He slipped away in flight through the door.

The priest therefore remained alone, together with the angel who appeared to be standing at his right. The minister, whom fear had driven away, stayed outside near the door, hiding, and from time to time thrust his head through the doorway, anxiously investigating what was happening around the altar.

When the servant of God was saying, in the order of the Mass, “through all ages of ages,” and the other words customarily spoken in the hearing of the people, and the minister, because of the marvelous vision appearing to him, did not dare to answer or approach, he heard the angel whom he saw responding to each part and rendering the service of the minister to the priest.

When the entire sacrifice had been completed, the minister, remaining hidden as before, put his head through the doorway and no longer saw the figure he had seen. He therefore entered to the priest, trembling and shaking, and fearing that he had somehow offended him by leaving him apparently alone.

After explaining the reason for his flight, he asked, pale with fear, whether the priest too had seen and heard what he himself claimed to have seen and heard.

But the priest said:

“I both saw and heard well what you describe. But blessed be the name of almighty God, because although I was badly deceived by you, I was not abandoned by him in the holy ministry of his life-giving body and blood.”

Nevertheless, he strictly forbade the man, as far as he could, to tell anyone what had happened for as long as he himself continued to live in the present life.

After the venerable bishop Odo, mentioned above, had learned with certainty from reliable report that his nephew Oswald had grown to the summit of good works, he gave immense thanks to almighty God and prayed for him day and night, asking that God grant him continually to advance toward better things and, perfected in the way of perfection, to see after this life the God of gods in Zion. Moreover, he sent various gifts to the abbot and monks on Oswald’s behalf and, with the prayers he knew to be appropriate, rendered thanks. He also informed them [Col. 0768B] that he greatly desired to enjoy Oswald’s presence, both because he knew that, being close to old age, death was approaching him, and because he intended through Oswald to train men of his nation in the regular way of life.

When this was reported to the brothers, they were cast down in profound grief and declared that, if it could be avoided, they by no means wished to live in this life without him, because they had felt that his way of life had greatly benefited them both in soul and in body. Nevertheless, since they did not dare oppose the bishop’s will, they obeyed and sent the servant of God to the bishop at his command, with the honor due to him. Oswald, however, hastening on his journey to England, was protected from every danger by land and sea. When he arrived at Dover with a cheerful face and joyful mind, he was immediately struck by overwhelming grief [Note: [Col. 0767D] William of Malmesbury gives a somewhat different account, *De gestis pontificum*, book III, fol. 153: he reports that Oswald undertook his journey only after receiving news of his sick uncle, who was already reclining at table.].

For when he heard that the man whom he loved more closely than all others, whose sweet face he longed to see above all, to whom he ardently desired to cling in the deepest charity, and from whom he remembered with no small anguish of heart that he had been separated for so long, had now recently been taken away not only from him but from the world, no one should wonder that he grieved. My God, what groans do we suppose that fosterling of yours uttered at this news? What sighs did he breathe? What tears did he shed? What, I ask, was the confusion of his mind when he learned that the man for whose love and reverence he remembered all embracing him was now to be turned into earth and thrust beneath the earth, removed from the sight of everyone? What grief covered the cheerfulness stamped upon his most devout face when he found England thrown into deep mourning at Odo’s death, though Oswald himself was certainly unequal to the cause of that grief?

Coming therefore to Canterbury, but finding it bereft of its father [Col. 0768D], he hesitated uncertainly, not knowing what to do or where to turn his steps. His tearful sorrow was thereby increased. Those who had previously known him, on seeing him, poured forth tears in remembrance of the deceased Father.

At that time a certain man named Oschetel presided over the Church of Dorchester through the exercise of pastoral office. He was a man of good reputation, skilled in arranging matters that concerned him [Note: [Col. 0768D] It has hitherto escaped all our published English writers that Oskitell, archbishop of York, had previously presided over the Church of Dorchester. See what we noted above in the history of Ralph de Diceto [Col. 0769D], *On the Bishops of England*. But where Eadmer reports that Oskitell presided over the see of Dorchester at that time and was later transferred to York, he is plainly mistaken. Oskitell had in fact obtained the throne of York about two years before Odo’s death. The monk of Ramsey, in Mabillon, *Saeculum Benedictinum* V, p. 735, made the same error.].

The man of God Oswald, since Oschetel was both related to him by ties of flesh and conspicuous through the light of wisdom in which he excelled, approached him in order to live with him [Col. 0769A], wishing, in Solomon’s words, “by walking with the wise to become wiser,” rather than “through the company of fools to be made like them” (Prov. XVI, 20). The same bishop received him most kindly and loved him sincerely; and, while Oswald lived with him, he made him a confidant and partner in his private affairs.

After some days, when the archbishop of York had died, the aforesaid Oschetel was appointed to his see. When he went to Rome for the pallium of the archbishopric, he took Saint Oswald as his companion. Having obtained what he desired, and, as he was leaving Rome, hastening on his journey to return to his homeland, Oswald left his company and turned aside to Fleury, taking with him as a companion from his homeland a certain cleric named Germanus, young in age but old in character.

The abbot and brothers received him with the greatest joy. After several days had passed happily in his company, they granted Germanus, whom Oswald had brought with him, the habit of holy communal life among them, solely because they understood that this was Oswald’s wish. The venerable Oswald remained in that monastery for some time, serving God in every way, in word and deed, and presenting to all who lived there examples of how they should strive toward heavenly things.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned bishop sent messengers asking him to return to England, so that he might instruct the men of his nation in the way of holy religion, whose summit he had certainly recognized Oswald to have reached. Oswald, however, gently obeyed his request and went to England, leaving Germanus behind. Germanus was still inexperienced in the regular disciplines [Col. 0769C], and Oswald would not allow him to leave the place until he had been perfectly instructed.

When Oswald reached the bishop, he lived beside him, as usual, in all holiness and gentleness. For that reason everyone embraced him, cherished him, and venerated him with devout affection, great love, and utmost zeal. During this time that distinguished and glorious friend of God, Dunstan, succeeded the aforementioned Odo in the see of Canterbury. He was a man full of God’s grace from his mother’s womb and, for as long as he remained in this present life, was at one time admitted to heavenly secrets, at another favored with frequent visitations by blessed spirits, and at another supported by celebrated power in the working of miracles.

When Dunstan heard the fame of Oswald’s outstanding holiness, which magnified the blessed man everywhere, he sent for him, eagerly wishing to learn fully from his way of life whether the widespread report was true or not. After a few days, when he had discovered what he was investigating, he rejoiced to find that Oswald far surpassed what rumor had spread, and with devout heart and lips gave himself to thanksgiving to God. Nevertheless, he often tested him—not because he regarded Oswald’s firmness of mind as suspect and wished to examine it, but so that, since he knew it to be firmly established in goodness, he might prove truthfully to others that it was so.

And indeed Oswald was found tested and approved in every adornment of the virtues. He was loved by Dunstan not only sincerely but with an affection surpassing that shown by others. Thus, when the dignity of his blessed uncle had been taken into account, Oswald was found to possess almost everything that his uncle had possessed in the quality of his life and the integrity of his character, apart from age and pontifical dignity alone. Since Oswald’s life and character imitated the dignity of a bishop, blessed Dunstan judged that his life and character ought rightly to be raised to the dignity of a bishop.

For this reason he approached Edgar, under whose kingship England at that time gloried, brought the venerable Oswald with him, commended him to the king on the basis of his merits, and introduced him into the king’s intimacy. What more is there to say? The supreme bishop praised the excellence of Oswald’s mind, the constancy of his purpose, and the integrity of his character. The king himself, believing such testimony, was brought to the point that, by his command and judgment, Oswald, made a bishop, ascended the episcopal chair at Worcester, over which that same Father, Dunstan, had formerly presided [Col. 0770B].

First, however, the will of the clergy and people concerning the matter was sought, and with immense rejoicing and acclamation the voice of all became one. They sounded forth and proclaimed that Oswald was most worthy of the episcopate of so great a see, and with fervent prayer begged that he be consecrated to that ministry as quickly as possible. What the clergy and people of Worcester requested was done, and the blessed Oswald was raised by Father Dunstan to the highest priesthood. By God’s gracious providence it came to pass that, just as blessed Dunstan had succeeded Saint Oswald’s uncle in Canterbury, so blessed Oswald succeeded Saint Dunstan in the episcopate of Worcester.

When the man of God had assumed the pontificate, he showed himself in good works the same man he had been before; indeed, just as he surpassed others in dignity, so he surpassed himself in goodness [Col. 0770C]. Although he was distinguished by every splendor of virtue, he was endowed above all—and beyond what can be expressed—with assiduity in prayer and the most ready generosity in almsgiving. Thus he began, in the Apostle’s words, to be “all things to all people” (I Cor. IX, 22), and no one’s love or anger could in any way turn him aside from the path of justice.

Yet he was especially guided by discretion, knowing that no one who wavered in discretion could fully preserve the laws of justice. He therefore devoted himself vigilantly to the clergy and people placed under his rule and showed them by word and example the road by which they should travel toward life. But when the multitude of those whom he desired to bring back from straying off the path of uprightness into the way of justice sometimes wearied his mind [Col. 0770D], he sent a messenger directly to Gaul and had Germanus, whom we mentioned above, and other men endowed with the fear of God come to him. With their help and religious devotion he wished to correct the irreligiousness of others.

Thus Germanus came to the bishop and was received honorably. He was indeed deeply religious and thoroughly imbued with sacred letters and devout studies.

Moreover, before his arrival, several men born of English lineage had come to blessed Oswald, submitted themselves to his holy instruction, and appointed him their father and guide on the way that leads to life [Col. 0771A]. Among them was a certain man named Ednoth, who, having served in the priestly order, was called “Senior” by the others because of his wisdom and diligence.

The brothers, gathered together to the number of twelve, therefore completed their company. Father Oswald placed them, so that they might serve Christ the Lord day and night according to the rule of their holy purpose, in a village of his bishopric called Westbury. He appointed the aforementioned Germanus as their superior and instructor, and assigned from his own resources whatever was sufficient for their support.

They lived in that place, conducting themselves in every respect and in all things as servants of God. The holy man took extraordinary delight in their endeavors and used frequently to visit them, provide them with admonitions for eternal salvation, console them, live among them, and devote himself with them to divine works, hymns [Col. 0771B], psalms, fasts, vigils, prayers, and holy meditations. Through the inward quiet of his mind he magnificently refreshed himself from external cares and worldly business.

With these arrangements made, the feast of the Lord’s resurrection was approaching, and the nobility of the whole kingdom was hastening to the king’s court. The princes, assembled together, spent joyful and highly solemn days. The court had now been dismissed, and each person was returning home. Then one of the king’s soldiers, rich and powerful, was overcome by death and was mourned by many.

The pious Father Oswald attended his funeral. He himself had come to the court among the foremost nobles of England, was held in favor by the king, and enjoyed his firm friendship. A certain Aegelwin, one of the more powerful leaders of the kingdom, watched him as he followed and chanted at the funeral with modest bearing and downcast face, and was thereby drawn into his friendship.

Previously, having heard of Oswald’s good and gentle character, which he had acquired through his ruling virtue, Aegelwin had long held him in high esteem and had resolved that, if he could obey Oswald’s wishes in any matter, he would gladly do so. Perceiving this intention of his through certain indications, the man of God spoke with him, among other things, about the true love of God and neighbor.

He made known to him that he had certain monks living religiously in his bishopric, but that the place where they lived was too confined for their way of life, especially since almost every day certain people were running to join their number, and Oswald by no means judged that those who were seeking the Lord should be rejected [Col. 0771D]. He added:

“Therefore, if it is not burdensome to your religious devotion, I ask that, if you have under your authority any place suitable for the habitation of monks, you grant it to me either for the sake of your own soul alone or in return for some gift, so that I may build a monastery there and, through the brothers mentioned above, establish the monastic way of life in that place.

“For the life of a monk is a great thing before God and is to be imitated by every Christian. Whoever in this life wishes to advance toward life and to avoid the snares of death can certainly achieve this in no way unless his life agrees in some measure with the life of monks. For the life of a monk—which truly is the life of a monk—admits everything that it teaches. Christian perfection abandons everything that it judges profane and contrary to the footsteps of Christ [Col. 0772A].

“Therefore, if, when we are able, we refrain from multiplying monks in their purpose, or envy their religion, or are shown unwilling to love or follow it, we may be convicted. But may almighty God keep these things far from us. Therefore, dearest son, let no worldly ambition hold you back from establishing and assisting monastic religion. For just as one wishes to reach eternal life, so one ought to strive to lead others with oneself to that same life. There the greater honor and glory will receive the man who here acquires for Christ the greater gain from the salvation of others.”

The duke himself, filled with joy at these words, received them with a friendly face and concluded his reply in a few words:

“I have an estate called Ramsey, surrounded by waters and marshes [Col. 0772B], which, as I judge, is suitable for the way of life of such men as you describe. Three men now live there, fervently devoted to holy religion and earnestly desiring to lead their lives under the Rule of blessed Benedict, if only they had a teacher. If it pleases you, let us go and inspect this place. If it appears suitable for the matter of which you speak, let us take care that, through the work of God, it may become distinguished by a heavenly habitation.”

The man of God embraced this with wonderful eagerness of heart. Then, accompanied by the duke himself, he reached the place and perceived that it was suitable for the habitation of monks. He gave thanks to God and also thanked the venerable man who had brought him there. He therefore pressed to lay hands on the desired work as quickly as possible, fearing that, if the good purpose were delayed, it might later be hindered by some stratagem of the malignant enemy [Col. 0772C]. He suggested this to the duke for his consideration and earnestly urged him to lend the work his assistance with his customary generosity.

What more is there to say? The duke trusted the advice and consented to the exhortation. Workmen were hired, the work was pressed forward, and labor was undertaken. Supported both by the very abundant expenditures of the most holy Father and by his most earnest prayers, the work was completed with astonishing speed.

After some days, in the presence of an immense crowd of people—rich, moderately prosperous, and poor alike—the completed church was solemnly dedicated to God under the patronage of blessed Benedict. The same place was established with monks who had been living at Westbury, and soon others and still others were gathered there. For their food and clothing, as well as for the celebration of divine service [Col. 0772D], very many landed possessions and very many gifts of various ornaments were bestowed upon that place by both men.

Thus a suitable and well-equipped dwelling for monks was established. Oswald appointed as its superior Ednoth, whom we mentioned above, a prudent and religious man who later became bishop of the Church of Lincoln. He himself returned to Worcester, where he lived as a good shepherd, watching over his own sheep and over them.

At that time, by the decree and authority of John, bishop of the apostolic see, blessed Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, whom we mentioned somewhat earlier, summoned a general council and, by issuing a decree, confirmed the decision that all canons, all priests [Col. 0773A], all deacons, and all subdeacons should either live chastely or lose the churches they held together with the property belonging to them.

King Edgar was a faithful supporter, steadfast helper, and firm defender of the matter. Following the advice of this Father, the king entrusted the task of carrying out the decree throughout the whole kingdom to two men: Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and Athelwold, bishop of Winchester.

Inflamed by zeal for the house of God, strengthened by love of divinity, and moreover supported by the aforementioned authority, they carried this out with the greatest vigor. To say nothing of others, blessed Oswald established seven monasteries in his diocese according to regular discipline, expelling clerics who preferred the companionship of women to the churches. He assigned to those monasteries, in addition to what the churches had previously possessed, so much support from the munificence of the king and the other leaders of the kingdom that it would suffice for the food and clothing of those living together there.

At the monastery of Winchcombe, which was one of the seven, he appointed the aforementioned Germanus [Note: [Col. 0773D] The monk of Ramsey reports that Germanus was born at Winchester, was Oswald’s fellow monk in the monastery of Fleury, then became prior of Westbury in order to teach his subjects the rule of monastic discipline. Meanwhile Ednoth Senior was appointed superior to manage external affairs. Germanus soon became prior of Ramsey and finally abbot of Winchcombe. When Germanus was transferred to Winchcombe, Ednoth succeeded him in the priory of Ramsey. After holding the priory for twenty-two years, Ednoth was elected abbot in 993 after the death of Ailwin the founder; he was transferred to the bishopric of Dorchester in 1008 and killed in the battle of Assandun in 1016. The Ramsey Register records these facts about Ednoth in *Monasticon*, vol. I, p. 240.] as abbot, and appointed over each of the others a single abbot proven in religion.

One of these, named Folberht, was appointed abbot over the Church of Pershore, which was one of the seven abbeys. He was a man grave in character and a most fervent cultivator of monastic discipline, but toward his subjects he displayed an excessive and indiscriminate severity, which was strongly censured in him.

When he had been brought to the point of death, had been taken away from this life, and had been placed in a coffin in the manner of the dead, he recovered his spirit and, to the terror of everyone, raised himself [Col. 0773C]. The others fled, but the aforementioned Germanus approached and asked where he had been led, by whom, what he had seen, what had happened to him, and why he had returned.

Folberht replied that he had been led by blessed Benedict into a vision of God, that God had forgiven him his sins through the merits of his beloved Oswald, and that he had been restored to life in order to make known the holiness of that Father. Germanus again asked what form and appearance blessed Father Benedict had possessed and what sort of company attended him. Folberht replied that Benedict’s clothing shone with the brilliance of gems, that his appearance was beautiful beyond human estimation, and that his company consisted of countless thousands of monks and most beautiful holy women dressed in white.

After saying this, he fell silent. Having received the viaticum of the Lord’s body, he lived for half a day [Col. 0773D], and then ended his life by dying a second time.

Afterward, in other parts of England not belonging to his own parish, Oswald emptied distinguished churches of clerics for the aforementioned reason and, supported by the authority already mentioned, elevated men trained in monastic discipline over them. These were the Church of the precious martyr of Christ, Alban; the Church of Saint Æthelthryth, virgin, at Ely; and the church established at Beamfleot, which was regarded as honorable [Col. 0774A].

He appointed individual Fathers over these as well: Aelfric, who later became pastor of the Church of Canterbury, over the church at Alban; Brithtnoth over the church at Ely; and Godemann over the church at Beamfleot. As we have described, the monastery at Ramsey was built from its foundations at his prompting and through his activity.

Thus the observance of regular discipline increased throughout England to such an extent that forty-eight monasteries, partly for men and partly for women, were established through these men: namely, Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury; Oswald, bishop of Worcester; and Athelwold, bishop of Winchester.

Oswald himself always watched over the monasteries he had built with great care and concern—for I have no intention of writing about the others [Col. 0774B]—lest the devil, who “goes about like a lion seeking someone to devour” (I Peter V, 8), should find any brother deviating from the rule of his profession whom he could devour.

For this reason he used to visit those same monasteries and remain in each one for as long as he knew to be useful, supplying the brothers with paternal affection, in word and deed alike, whatever he was able to perceive would benefit each one’s salvation. In addition, when requested by certain churches to which he did not devote himself in the same way as to those mentioned above, he sent them teachers of regular discipline, grammar, and the liberal arts. These teachers had either been educated in Gaul and brought to England by him or had been trained through his own diligence in his monasteries, and they were regarded as wise and distinguished.

Among them was a certain monk of Fleury named Abbo, outstanding for the holiness of his character and thoroughly instructed in knowledge both of secular and of divine letters. Father Oswald placed him in the monastery of Ramsey to teach the monks, direct the schools, and benefit them as far as he could both in the discipline of the rule and in literary knowledge. This he did.

From this it came about that, together with the growth of religion, the liberal arts—which, because of various circumstances, had previously fallen into neglect throughout England—sprang up in many ways wherever Father Oswald’s diligence and care had cultivated them. The aforementioned Abbo, because of his great worth, also became very close to blessed Dunstan. At Dunstan’s prompting and arrangement, he committed to the memory of posterity, in writing, the passion of blessed Edmund, the most glorious king of the English [Col. 0774D].

After these and countless other good works that he had done in England, he returned to his monastery at Fleury, became its abbot, and was later crowned by God with the palm of martyrdom for the sake of justice.

When blessed Oswald began to undertake the correction of the clerics of Worcester, they themselves perceived into what difficulties he intended to force them, insofar as their habits were concerned. They immediately closed the entrance to their hearts against his words and in no way allowed them to penetrate their understanding [Col. 0775A] [Note: [Col. 0775D] At that time, says the monk of Ramsey, chapter 7, the Church of Worcester, following the ancient institution, had secular canons rather than monks. Malmesbury, in the same manner reported by Eadmer, says that the canons were removed from their position. Other historians, however, imply that force was used. So report Florence and the monk of Ramsey. Certainly King Edgar strongly supported Oswald’s efforts by his authority. On this matter there exists a charter of the king, *Concilia Angliae*, vol. I, p. 432, and a speech there, p. 476. Oswald was the first of all to introduce monks into cathedral churches after expelling the secular canons. For this reason the law concerning the expulsion of married clerics was anciently called “Oswald’s Law.” Oswald carried this out in the Church of Worcester in 969, according to Florence, who adds that Winsinus was placed as dean over the monks recently introduced. This is the same man as the Wensinus mentioned shortly afterward. The monk of Ramsey calls him prior; Edgar’s charter calls him superior.].

Therefore, with the approval of Father Dunstan, on whose prudent counsel he was accustomed to rely, and with the consent of the often-mentioned glorious King Edgar, Oswald began to build a monastery within the episcopal see itself, in which he could gather monks to live with him. The walls of the high structure had already been raised and the work was advancing.

Not far from his work lay a certain square stone, entirely suitable and necessary for the construction. Artisans considered capable enough came to move it at the bishop’s command to its proper place and set it into the structure of the church. But although the stone seemed to cling to the earth by its very roots, they were unable to move it even slightly by any effort. Other men were added to them, and then still others, but they too were found to possess no strength at all against the weight of the stone.

Great astonishment seized everyone. The matter was reported to Father Oswald, who was then absent, and he was asked to come as quickly as possible to see what monstrous thing the event signified. He arrived and, seeing the crowd sweating in vain labor around the movement of the aforementioned stone, was amazed. Standing in astonishment and silently praying to God, he saw an Ethiopian sitting upon the stone, mocking the laborers with obscene gestures and derisive laughter.

The man of God immediately traced the sign of the holy cross against the demon and forced him, terrified at once, to seek safety in flight. Then the stone, which eighty men had previously been unable to move [Col. 0775C], was immediately lifted with the greatest ease by a few men and set into the building.

The people who had flowed in from every direction to watch this, observing the powerful virtue displayed in what had happened, gave immense thanks to God for his wonders. They also proclaimed their Father and bishop with extraordinary praise, understanding that he was truly a friend of God, at whose command the adversary of God, struck with such helpless terror, had trembly disappeared.

Oswald himself dedicated the completed church in honor of the holy and perpetual Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and, as he had proposed, gathered monks there to serve Christ in holy communal life. The clerics therefore assembled in the episcopal church, which had anciently been founded under the name of the glorious chief of the apostles, Peter [Col. 0775D], while the monks lived together in the new church under the patronage of Saint Mary.

For some time the people attended both churches in turn, now one and now the other. But after a while, admiring and, in their admiration, venerating the religious life of the monks, they gradually began to absent themselves from the clerical community and to be present at the service of God performed by the monks, because, as the reasoning of their minds told them, that service was carried out more appropriately and more worthily before God.

Thus it came about that, just as the people shifted from one church to the other, so their offerings shifted as well. While the one group lost what the other gained, and while the one declined, the other increased.

Why delay? Wensinus, who was regarded as the senior and more honorable among the clerics, cast aside everything secular, became a monk, and gave himself and all that he possessed to the monks. The servant of God rejoiced greatly over this. After a short time, he sent Wensinus to Ramsey to be fully instructed in heavenly studies. When he brought him back after his instruction, he appointed him among the assembled monks at Worcester as their teacher of conduct.

Oswald knew that, as a cleric, Wensinus had always been a lover of honor according to the ancient customs; he therefore confidently hoped that, as a monk, he would likewise be a supporter and practitioner of what was honorable. His hope was not disappointed. Wensinus himself greatly increased through good works the goodness that the Father had expected of him.

When some of the clerics observed all this and, pierced in heart, understood that “there is no counsel against God” (Prov. XXI, 30), they scorned the world and all worldly pomp, submitted themselves to the yoke of Christ, and became monks among those monks whom shortly before they had excessively detested.

You might hear very many people singing in amazement at this: “O truly, the change of the right hand of the Most High!” In this way, therefore, the episcopal seat was transferred from blessed Peter to the Mother of the Lord and Savior, from clerics to monks.

[Col. 0776C]

While these things were taking place, the aforementioned bishop of the city of York was taken from the present life, and thereafter deep grief arose among the English people. The report of his death, swiftly spreading, reached the royal ears and no more slowly reached blessed Dunstan’s knowledge.

Wishing, in fulfillment of his office, to provide for the widowed Church, Dunstan went to the king and proposed the advice that seemed most beneficial to him concerning the appointment of a successor. He praised the dignity of the venerable Oswald: the nobility of the parent from whom he was descended, the religious manner in which he had been trained from childhood, and the distinctions of virtue with which he had been adorned.

In addition, he explained how vigorously Oswald had governed the episcopal chair over which he had presided until then. From this he disclosed, proved, and asserted on what right and merit Oswald ought to ascend to a higher office [Col. 0776D].

The king approved what was reported and praised what Dunstan proposed should be done concerning Oswald. He wished only that the clergy and people of York should agree. Dunstan wished it, advised it, urged it, and commanded that it be done. Their consent was sought, and all together replied with one voice that they wished Oswald to be placed over them before all others. With every delay broken off, they pressed the matter with great petitions.

There was no delay. The man who had been summoned arrived, but when they asked him to accept the governance of the widowed Church, he did not immediately consent. The voice of the people thundered, so that one might unquestionably have testified that Scripture’s saying is true: “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

Their charity was equal, their judgment harmonious, and the people’s will was one in what was good. Would the God of peace, who “makes the like-minded dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII, 7), and who is among “two or three gathered in his name” (Matt. XVIII, 20), not favor what so great a multitude favored, not think what it thought, and not will what it willed?

Certainly he would not fail to will it; but granted that whatever God wills to be done must necessarily be done. He wills what his faithful people will according to him. Otherwise they could will well without him, and Truth would not be truthful when it says that no one can do anything without him [Col. 0777B] (John XV, 5).

But did his faithful people will, according to God, that Saint Oswald should become bishop of York? Since God willed this very thing to happen, it was necessary in every respect. Therefore Oswald submitted to God by submitting to the will of God’s servants.

Having thus become archbishop of York [Note: [Col. 0777D] Eadmer, Florence, and Malmesbury report that Oswald immediately succeeded Oskitell. Thomas Stubbs and Simeon of Durham, however, insert Adelwold between them. After Adelwold renounced the dignity, Oswald succeeded him in 972. In that year, according to Ingulf, the Worcester chronicler, Hoveden, and the Durham chronicler in *De gestis regum Anglorum*, Oswald obtained the archbishopric of York. In the same year, in September, Pope John died; Eadmer writes that John had given the pallium to Oswald. Simeon of Durham is therefore mistaken when, in his *Letter on the Bishops of York*, he says that the pallium was given by Benedict, John’s successor. Thomas Stubbs is certainly wrong in reporting that Oswald received it from Pope Stephen.], he went to Rome to request from the apostolic see the pallium owed to his Church and to transact with the pope the many affairs of the kingdom that the king had entrusted to him.

Leaving his homeland, crossing the sea and lands filled with various dangers, he reached Rome and entered the Roman walls. There he was presented to John, the apostolic bishop, and obtained what he desired. Finally, after receiving the pallium he had requested and completing the replies concerning the royal embassy he was carrying, he was honorably dismissed by the pope [Col. 0777C] and returned to England. On his return he was gloriously received by the leader of the kingdom and by the kingdom itself.

After delivering his response concerning his embassy to the king, and after everyone had praised him with lofty acclaim because he had acted wisely in all things, he proceeded to his see at York, supported by the king’s great goodwill. There he was received with extraordinary honor, with the rejoicing of the people, and with the ringing harmonies of the clerics, and he took possession of the archiepiscopal chair.

Having done this, he did not feed the multitude that had gathered on that day as an inexperienced or ignorant man, but as a truly seasoned and discerning shepherd of God’s sheep, providing abundantly both the instruction of abiding life and the nourishment of passing life. From then onward, reflecting upon the saying of the Wise Man that “from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required” (Luke XII, 48) [Col. 0777D], he carefully took care at every hour to manage by stewardship and to dispense through careful administration what had been entrusted to him, so that nothing might later be demanded from him that would produce harm for him, but only what would be rewarded with blessed recompense [Col. 0778A].

For this reason he remained the same man he had been in visiting the monasteries he had established; he continued the same in consoling the brothers who lived there; and he remained the same in supporting them and all who needed his help. He therefore suffered no decline in any work of holiness because of the burden of priestly office. Either he accomplished what he had previously accomplished, or, having become greater than himself in such works, he directed the gaze of his mind through unfailing contemplation toward seeing the God of gods in Zion.

Although he had thus been raised to the pontificate of York, he did not lose responsibility for the bishopric of Worcester. Blessed Dunstan, whose concern extended to all the churches established throughout Britain [Col. 0778B], feared that the monks recently instituted by Oswald at Worcester might be shaken by some temptation beyond what they could bear if, deprived of pastoral care, they had no one by whom they could be strengthened. Therefore, by the authority of the supreme Shepherd, he ordered Oswald to attend to them with the diligence he had always shown, until God should reveal to him a person suitable for so great a responsibility whom he could appoint in Oswald’s place.

After this, the days of the Rogations were approaching, and the servant of God, Oswald, set out for Ramsey [Note: [Col. 0777D] The Ramsey Register records that the Ramsey monastery was visited twice by Oswald [Col. 0778D] (in the *Monasticon*, vol. I, p. 240). First, in the year 972, on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John, when he brought with him and settled there twelve monks from Westbury. Then, in the year 974, when together with Dunstan he dedicated the Ramsey church. This occurred in the year 974, on 6 November, with Oswald accompanied not by Dunstan but by Ælfnoth, bishop of Dorchester, according to the Ramsey monk (in Mabillon, fifth century, p. 742). The same source also records Oswald’s first visitation, but implies that it occurred before the year 972. Finally, in the year 991, Oswald again consecrated the Ramsey church, rebuilt by Earl Æthelwin, on 8 November, a Tuesday, according to Florence.], namely to visit and console the brothers whom, as we have mentioned above, he had long before placed there.

He arrived, and the monks, as was customary on the appointed days, proceeded to the church of blessed Mary, which, because of the intervening marsh, could be reached by dry land only by a long circuit. After Mass had been celebrated and the bishop had completed the solemn office of preaching, the monks, wishing to shorten the length of the route by which they had come, boarded a vessel, intending to return to the monastery by the river that flowed between them. But while more people crowded into the boat than the boat could carry, it became excessively burdened and began to sink. Those in the boat were thrown into confusion and feared death. They cried out, asking that blessed Benedict and their father Oswald bring them help.

For the Father himself was still standing on the riverbank, arranging certain useful and necessary matters for those who were with him. But when the shouting struck his ears, he was stunned with astonishment, immediately turned his eyes in that direction, and, seeing his sons placed in peril of death, turned his heart toward God and extended his right hand toward them. When he had made the sign of the holy cross, the boat at once rose up from the depths of the waters and, as though it were carrying no burden, was carried in a most prosperous glide to the farther bank of the river, together with everything it bore. Great security followed great fear, and, in response to what had happened, praise of God issued from everyone’s heart and mouth.

Afterward, he remained there for some time among the monks, as was his custom, devoting himself day and night to their moral edification. And behold, a messenger sent by the monks of Ely arrived and announced that one of them had fallen from the wall of the church and died suddenly. Oswald, overcome with profound grief—for he knew that the man had not led an entirely happy life—immediately rendered him the charitable service that was his duty.

Indeed, he summoned the monks together and disclosed the event, adding prayers in which he earnestly exhorted them to pray more diligently to the Lord for the dead man’s soul. They obeyed his instructions and persisted in vigils, psalms, and tears for their brother’s eternal salvation, knocking at the door of the mercy of the world’s Redeemer. In addition, every day there was offered for him that which surpasses all these things: namely, the sacrifice of praise which the Son of God offered to his Father for us on the altar of the cross.

While these things were being done, one night the same deceased man visibly appeared to the bishop while he was engaged in prayer to Christ at York. When the bishop asked him who he was, he replied that he was the man for whose sake both the bishop himself and others through him were entreating God. Then the bishop sighed and said, “How was it with you, brother, and how is it with you now?” He answered, “Until now, it was very bad, but now it is very good. Through your merits and prayers, God yesterday rescued me by his angel from the punishments by which I was being tormented. I have come to give you thanks by making this known to you, so that you may recognize—although you know it very well—how rightly you ought to give thanks to God for this and for other things.” After saying this, he disappeared.

The man of God, filled with great joy at these words, blessed God for his ineffable mercy. In the morning he reported to his own people what had happened, what he had seen, and what he had heard. Then, exulting and rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, he gave thanks to God the Father for what had occurred, through the offering of the body and blood of his beloved Son, in whom alone, as he himself testifies, he is well pleased (Matthew 12:18). He also instructed his sons, namely the monks of Ramsey and Worcester alike, and admonished and exhorted them to render pious thanks to God for the brother’s release from his soul’s punishment. They carried this out with diligent devotion.

Moreover, as he traveled through his diocese at suitable times, he strove, through paternal correction, to rebuke and amend whatever he could learn in the conduct of his people that offended the eyes of the Most High God. On one such occasion, while engaged in these activities, he happened to come to Ripon, where blessed Wilfrid had once built a noble church, in which he is known to have been buried after being taken from this world.

Before the time of blessed Oswald, this church had been exposed to the incursion of barbarians. They left it largely ruined and made it suitable not for divine services but for the lairs of wild beasts. The man of God entered the enclosure of this church and remained there throughout the night, keeping vigil in prayer. There, enlightened by divine revelation, he learned that the bodies of saints had been buried in that very place; and, searching for them, he found them without a doubt, together with the names of each.

In the morning he summoned his people and recounted to them what he had received during the night. At these words everyone rejoiced. Therefore, at the bishop’s command, the pavement of the half-ruined church was dug up, and the promised treasure was sought with holy curiosity. The bodies of the saints were found, together with a tablet bearing this inscription:

“Here rests Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York, and the venerable abbots Tylbert, Botwin, Albert, Sigred, and Wildengus.”

The servant of the almighty God, filled with joy and gladness at this discovery, placed the relics temporarily in a suitable location. Later, after a suitably fashioned bier had been prepared for the body of Saint Wilfrid, he placed the body in it with great reverence. He knew that Wilfrid was related by blood to the great Wilfrid, the founder of that place; he knew that he had succeeded him in the government of the Church of York, as the Venerable Bede reports, almost in the very words of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*; and he had learned that, as he shared his name, so he had also inherited his life and character.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] Eadmer related more fully the history of the translation of the relics of Wilfrid the Elder in his *Life* of him, printed among the *Acta Benedictinorum*, century III, p. 226. Gervase drew from Eadmer in his *Chronicle*, p. 1291. The men of York, on the other hand, vigorously maintained that it was the body of Wilfrid the Younger, not the Elder, that Odo translated. On this controversy see Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, fol. 153, and vol. I of this collection, p. 66. The prologue of Odo cited by Eadmer is given above, p. 50.]

[Col. 0780C]

As for the body of that elder Wilfrid, it had been separated from the others and possessed a tomb of its own in an elevated place within the church. Bede relates in the same *History* that Wilfrid had honorably adorned it with an epitaph. The body had been transferred to Canterbury by Odo, the glorious bishop of the people of Kent, whom we mentioned briefly at the beginning of this little work, just as Odo himself testifies in the preface to his *Life of Wilfrid*, which he composed in heroic verse. He writes:

“Accordingly, when certain persons, with God’s favor, had transferred from the place of his tomb the most venerable relics of blessed Wilfrid, confessor of Christ—relics that had become foul and decayed through the unseemly filth of a muddy abyss and had been neglected with excessive, indeed almost terrifying, horror by those in charge—I received them reverently and placed them within the enclosure of the metropolitan church over which, by God’s grace, I preside, especially compelled by that testimony of the Gospel, namely my own defense: ‘Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered’ (Luke 17:37). Therefore, delighted by the nearness of so great and God-worthy a relationship, I resolved both to adorn them with a more exalted reliquary and to embellish them with a new work in verse, adorned with flowers gathered from the book of his Life.”

After the relics had been raised and suitably placed, as I have said, blessed Oswald made another bier, in every respect equal and similar to the one he had first made. Having consecrated it himself, he sent it to Worcester. When he was asked, at its consecration, for whose relics it appeared to have been made, he replied that he had fashioned it for the honor of God and that it was perfectly clear whose relics were to be placed in it.

The bier was therefore preserved at Worcester, and many years later, when the relics of that wondrous Father Oswald had been raised from the earth, they were placed in it with great honor.

Having said these things, let us resume the narrative we began. The fame of Saint Oswald’s holiness spread so widely that people afflicted with various illnesses sent word to him from afar, entirely confident that they would receive help from him. Nor were they deceived.

For example, there was a certain powerful man who was known to King Edgar through the service by which he used to serve him. When this man was struck by a serious bodily illness, he simply informed the man of God through a messenger that he was extremely sick. Oswald blessed a loaf of bread, sent it to him, and ordered him to eat from it with complete faith in the recovery of his health. The man did what he had been commanded, and less than an hour passed before, after tasting the bread, he perceived that he was better.

On another occasion, while the same servant of God was seated at York, about to dine amid a large company of his people, and had distributed to those seated there bread marked with his most holy hand, a mouse happened to approach and began gathering up the crumbs that had fallen, biting them eagerly yet fearfully. When it had come out into the middle without being deterred by anyone, it collapsed and could go no farther. For, greedily devouring the remains of the blessed bread, it could not in any way vomit up what it had swallowed, and was suddenly suffocated. It therefore remained dead.

The exceptionally prudent man ordered the lifeless creature to be removed from the sight of those watching, lest anyone attribute the event to his own praise. Finally, he noticed that some people were speaking among themselves about it and extolling the event with more admiration than he wished.

As I consider these two things that we have just related concerning the marked bread, I judge that this too is not unworthy of wonder: the irrational animal was brought from life into death by what raised the rational animal from death into life. Certainly, the nature of the bread was the same in the one case as in the other; and just as a human being is nourished by bread, so is a mouse nourished by bread. What was therefore life-giving to the human being became fatal to the mouse. The cause was not the substance of the bread but the merit of the most holy Father, who, though everywhere and in all things small and humble in his own eyes, was great and exalted in the eyes of God.

Among other proofs of this was the fact that God extended his protection and correction not merely to him but, which is less, to the places in which he was accustomed to stay in turn, lest they be occupied by the unworthy.

But perhaps what we say will not be believed if we do not add an example that makes it clear. There was a certain brother who by profession and habit was a monk, named Aegelricus. After loosening his limbs in the bath, when he needed a place in which his weary body might rest, the first place that presented itself—alas for the wretched man!—was the spot where the venerable bishop Oswald was accustomed most often to sit.

He therefore had no fear of the holiness that the place had acquired through the bishop’s continual presence. He threw himself down there, expecting to enjoy sleep and sweet rest. Already a gentle slumber had enveloped him as he rested, but without delay a multitude of demons rushed upon him and violently dragged him away from his very rest.

Several hideous spirits stood over him and demanded, under strict examination, what madness had seized his mind, and what had induced him to place himself in the seat of so great a bishop. Since he had no answer to offer in his defense, they attacked, tortured, and tore him, dragging him this way and that, snatching him from below upward and hurling him from above down to the ground.

What could the wretched man do? He knew where he was, but, enveloped in such anguish, he could neither tear himself away from the place nor call upon anyone for help. At last, however, by a violent effort he broke into speech and roared out with a dreadful cry.

Those nearby were suddenly terrified by the sound of the sleeper and came running. They struck the shouting man, roused him by their blows, and, once he had awakened, carefully questioned him about what he had suffered in sleep. Trembling and pale, he then related in order what had happened, what he had done, what he had heard and from whom, and what he had endured.

When this became known to everyone, they thereafter showed honor and reverence in every way not only to the man but also to the things that had belonged to him. We could perhaps write at length about these matters, but, lest we become tedious to anyone, we omit them, intent upon the brevity we have resolved to maintain in writing.

Let us therefore turn the service of our pen toward his holy departure and, as God grants, bring to its conclusion the work that we have prolonged thus far. To report how Father Oswald finally left Ramsey—amid how many showers of tears, as I suppose prophetic of the fact that he would never return there again, he was sent away by the brothers—would perhaps be a matter for conjecture. Who could know? Certainly, in the truth of the matter, I declare that no one can know.

As he departed, he was escorted not only by the monks whom he had gathered there but also by the common people assembled from every direction. Each person commended himself to his holiness and begged with humble devotion to receive his blessing.

His departure was followed in the church itself by a terrifying crash. It thundered three times, shaking those who heard it with enormous fear. It taught, warned, and fortified perceptive minds that he would soon be taken from this world and that many would consequently be subjected to a grave disturbance.

Finally, some people who wished to know where the sound they had heard had come from went out of their houses and reached the church. There they found everything sound, everything intact, and everything standing in its usual place, and they marveled.

I pass over what was shown to some in a vision—namely, that the collapse of two towers had occurred—lest, if I say that the fall of those towers foreshadowed the deaths of blessed Oswald and the aforementioned Duke Æthelwin, I be rightly mocked for arrogating to myself, from things I know to have happened, a knowledge of the future that I do not possess.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Oswald again consecrated the church of Ramsey with Æthelwin in the year 991, on 8 November; this is gathered from Florence and the Ramsey monk. Æthelwin died in 992, on 24 April; this is established by the same authorities. Oswald died in the same year, on the day before the Kalends of March. Both agree on this. Florence, however, reports that it occurred on Monday, whereas the Ramsey monk assigns it to the third Sunday of Lent. Florence is more correct.]

Passing over that matter, as we have said, we ask in prayer that the glorious Father Oswald, whom we are about to describe as soon seeking the heavens, may guard and assist us through his prayer.

When Christ’s servant Oswald had left Ramsey, he went to Worcester. The spirit of charity that, through grace, was always more ardent in him toward the people of Worcester is rightly believed to have led him there, because he knew that he ought to be rewarded with a greater prize of eternal life if he happened to be found departing this life in a greater affection of true charity.

He therefore remained there as long as he remained in the body, intent upon God day and night and striving with all his strength to make his journey toward God pure of every obstacle. Because of these efforts, exhausted by labor and, in addition, by old age, he was seized by a serious illness, through which he understood that he was soon to be called from this life.

The sacred days of Lent were at hand—those days, namely, during which what is committed on other days of the year through the various deceptions of demons is washed away in different ways, and during which what is practiced at other times is pursued with more diligent attention.

The same bishop had the custom, every day, besides the countless others whom he fed daily, of washing the feet of twelve poor people, kissing them, drying them with his hair and a linen cloth, pouring water over them with his hands, giving them coins, and providing them with sufficient food and drink at a table set before them. At Easter he also had them dressed in new clothes and honorably kept with him in his household for several days of the feast.

No bodily illness held him back from these acts. The weaker he felt himself to be in body, the more forcefully he compelled himself to serve them.

Already eager to ascend to the kingdom of God, one day he went out from the oratory in which he was continually occupied in God’s service, together with his companions. Standing beneath the open sky, he fixed the gaze of his eyes intensely upon heaven, praying with devout heart and heightened voice to Christ, for whom he longed.

He did not quickly lower his raised eyes, as people ordinarily do. Rather, as though he were contemplating something new and delightful, he kept them fixed for a very long time upon the place where he had directed them. Those present were greatly astonished and asked what he was looking at so intently.

He said to them, “I am considering where I am going. Therefore, my sons, wait, I beg you, so that, insofar as it is granted to me, I may taste in advance the joys that I await. Nevertheless, if you wish to know what the matter about which you ask signifies, tomorrow, even without my speaking, the event itself will make it known to you. For the eternal salvation for which I have labored on earth until now is at hand, and tomorrow will not pass before my Lord, as he has promised, introduces me into it.”

He said this and returned to the oratory from which he had come.

Then, having summoned the brothers, he urged them to provide him with the ministry of holy anointing together with the viaticum of the Lord’s body, which, according to the ordinance of the Church, is owed to Christians departing this life.

When they heard this, they broke into groans and tears—not because they begrudged him the perpetual glory toward which he was hastening, but because they expressed their pious affection for the paternal kindness from which they were about to be deprived, and because they mourned with loving grief their own desolation, which they had no doubt they would suffer when deprived of so great a Father.

Nevertheless, they presented him with what he requested. Overwhelmed by deep sorrow, they wished that the coming night could be prolonged for many ages, if that were possible.

During that night, the Father himself, as though he had forgotten the illness by which he was held, went to the church before the hour of the nocturnal vigil, as it had always been his constant custom to do. There, after completing the office of the night, he spent the remaining time until daybreak, as was his custom, keeping vigil in divine praises.

Thus that night came to its appointed end, and for the brothers dawned the fearful day on which you, revered Father Oswald, were to be received into blessed rest, closed by no limit.

On that day, after chanting the Psalter, which he was accustomed to sing every day with the flowers he received from it, he had the one sacrifice of human redemption offered before God the Father. Refreshed afterward by participation in it, he fortified his approaching death with its unconquerable power.

Finally, after the entire day had been devoted with great solemnity to the honor of God, he rose as though he had recovered from his illness. Although the monks earnestly urged him to spare his weakness, he girded himself with a linen cloth according to his custom, washed the feet of the poor, kissed them, and dried them with his hair and the linen cloth.

After washing them and chanting the fifteen psalms of the Gradual, which he always customarily sang during this ministry, he added, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” When the poor rose before him and offered their customary thanks, he himself, while saying, “To the Holy Spirit,” was released into death. He breathed out his spirit at the feet of the poor into the hands of Christ, whom he himself had served in those poor people. For, as Christ himself testifies, what is done to one of his least is done to him (Matthew 25:40).

Thus, passing from this life, he was received by Christ, so that, according to Christ’s word, he might be where Christ also is (John 14:13). O truly blessed ministry, which made its executor heir of the kingdom of God with such speed! And you, most blessed Father, no less—indeed, far more—blessed, who, having performed your ministry, entered in the very moment in which you faithfully completed it, rewarded with a happy recompense, into the joy of your Lord whom you served (Matthew 25:21).

The glory with which you are crowned shows your sons how much you can benefit them before God, if you are willing. Indeed, illustrious Father, blessed was your life, and blessed also was your death. Would that your foster children might experience within themselves how blessed your memory is, and how salutary and beneficial is the humble devotion they offer to you.

Therefore, when the brothers learned that their Father had died, they ran to him and, clapping their hands, uttered mournful cries. Yet, trembling and groaning, they took up the lifeless body, spread a haircloth beneath it, washed it, and clothed it in priestly garments, as was customary.

From these acts of devotion one could perceive with what pious affection the living shepherd had been loved by his sheep: at his death such an exhibition of love took place that no one was thought to have paid him sufficient honor unless, with tearful eyes, he had impressed devoted kisses upon his hands and feet.

Then the body was placed upon a bier and carried to the church of the most blessed Virgin of virgins, which, as I mentioned above, he himself had built from the foundations.

And behold, while it was being carried aloft, with those who went before it offering praises and prayers to God in sonorous chants, and with the people following behind, mourning with the monks in a pitiful voice the shepherd they had lost, the glory of God appeared and taught discerning minds to understand the merit of the dead man.

Those who had gathered saw a snow-white dove descending from above with outspread wings and protecting the bishop’s body with a slow flight. They also saw a fiery sphere, like a rounded shield, descend from heaven onto the bier.

They marveled at both signs and asked that those who had not noticed them should look. A cry rang out from every side, and the voices of divine praise broke forth. The more that praise broke out, the more it increased: it broke forth in melodious voices and increased in the heart’s jubilation.

They rejoiced in God for the grace that he had deigned to display in such a multitude through his Father. Through the dove he showed the simplicity and innocence of the man’s heart; through the fiery sphere, the fervent zeal with which his spirit was endowed in the love of God and neighbor.

Meanwhile, the venerable body was carried into the oratory, accompanied by the continuing protection of the aforementioned fire and dove. When it had been placed before the altar, the vision that had appeared turned toward the southern part of the church, near the altar, as though indicating the place where the body was to be buried. After this, the vision slipped away, returning to heaven before the eyes of those watching.

The report of his death therefore spread everywhere. On that day and the following night, during which the burial of the body was delayed, people of every age and both sexes flocked from all directions, and their cries, mingled with sighs and lamentations, filled the air.

Among them, the monks and the poor were afflicted by more bitter weeping: the former because they had lost their shepherd, father, and advocate; the latter because they recognized that in him they had lost the support, hope, and consolation of their entire life.

Thus the mourning of all became immeasurable, and the assembled multitude innumerable. As it surrounded the body and pressed in upon itself, the limbs of the most holy bishop were buried in the aforementioned church of the most noble Virgin, namely in the place previously designated by God.

After this, his burial was announced to this person and that—that is, to those whom he had undertaken to govern under his pastoral care, and to those whom he had withdrawn from worldly life and instructed how to follow God in the monastic habit. Therefore, because of the sweetness of his memory, common mourning was proclaimed for all who understood that they had been his sons.

When the often-mentioned Duke Æthelwin learned that the glorious Oswald had brought his life to an end, the bodily illness that at that time perhaps oppressed him grew so strong through the excessive anguish of his heart that, after a short while, he rested in a holy death and entered upon the way of all flesh. He was buried in the church that he and Father Oswald had built at their own expense at Ramsey.

The venerable and beloved bishop Oswald passed from this life to eternal life on the second day before the Kalends of March, after having served in the episcopate—of which he had first been incumbent—for thirty years or more. His venerable body was buried, as we have said, at Worcester, in the church of the most glorious Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary.

Truly, so that the grace of Christ might show mortals that Oswald, dead to the world, lives for God, those who seek him not as one utterly dead find in him signs that he is truly alive and greatly powerful before God.

To prove this with evident arguments, we have thought it appropriate to append briefly the things performed through him after his death that have reached our knowledge. But lest we be judged unworthy of receiving such things if we are found ungrateful for what we have received, for the matters to which we have devoted our mind in writing, and for the outcome we have attained insofar as God has granted it, let praise and thanksgiving be given to almighty God himself, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

The Life of Blessed Oswald, Archbishop and Confessor, ends.

[Col. 0785C]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT DUNSTAN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY. BY EADMER, A MONK.

[Col. 0785C]

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

Because we are commanded by the prophetic voice to praise God, wondrous in his saints (Psalm 67:36), we have resolved to praise him, in the things he deigned wondrously to accomplish in the holy Dunstan, bishop of the first metropolitan see of the English, by the work of our pen and in our customary manner of speech, yielding to the not contemptible wish of certain simple-minded brothers. We leave to the consideration of the learned writings that recount the events in another kind of diction.

Although I am foolish, I would have been content with this, but those same writings attracted me somewhat because they seem in certain respects to have exceeded the bounds of customary narration.
