I was also led to this by the accusations of certain people, who often complained—and do not cease complaining—that the author [Note: [Col. 0787C] The author is the writer of Dunstan’s *Life*, whose errors Eadmer rebukes. He was neither Bridferth nor Osbern. The former made no mention either of the church at Worcester dedicated to the Blessed Virgin or of King Edward’s mother. The latter indeed reports that the Worcester church was consecrated to the Blessed Virgin, but says nothing about Edward’s mother. I therefore think that Eadmer is hinting at another author, whom Osbern states in his preface to have composed the deeds of Dunstan in a lively and well-ordered style. Although this man’s writings were consumed in the burning of the Canterbury church in the year 1070, Osbern declares that they survived in translation into the English language. It is clear, however, that Osbern’s book was not entirely known to Eadmer. Osbern himself had read all the writings of earlier authors concerning Dunstan’s deeds, and the monk of Tynemouth frequently describes him in his manuscript *History*, book XXI, in which he included a fairly extensive *Life of Dunstan*.] of those very writings had not agreed in every respect with the commonly circulated history of events.

We do not, however, admit that this fault had slipped into the miracles written about that Father himself. For example, the author writes that the bishopric of Worcester, when Father Dunstan was elected and consecrated to it, was dedicated to the honor of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, whereas in fact it was dedicated to the honor of the glorious chief of the apostles, Peter. He also reports that the martyr Edward was born from a nun, whereas it is beyond doubt that he was begotten by a lawful wife; and there are certain other matters of this kind.

At the request of my friends, I was so diligently concerned to investigate the pure truth of all these things that, wherever throughout England I knew that studies of this kind flourished and I could not go in person, I did not hesitate to send others for this very purpose. I considered it wholly detestable to provide, whether by word or writing, anything that departed from the limits of fact to those who wished to know the truth.

Therefore, lest anyone judge me to have undertaken these writings out of arrogance or envy, I confess, with my conscience itself bearing witness to me, that I did so in the name of truth itself, from which a Christian may not deviate. Unless the blindness of the human mind deceives me, none of the vices I have mentioned prevailed in this matter; only love of the truth did so—a love by which I wished, without any ambiguity, to commend so great a Father both to those now living and to those who would come after.

Nor did I rely here upon my own judgment, but upon the firm authority of Fathers whom I believed—it would be sacrilegious not to believe them—I remembered as having once testified to me that they had learned the events themselves, just as we describe them, through the reliable report of those who knew them best.

To avoid seeming to act with merely bare words, I resolved to set forward one of these men, Aegelred, while omitting the others. Aegelred had most diligently held the offices of subprior and cantor in the church of Canterbury for a long time. Later, because of his religious prudence and prudent religiousness, he had been placed over the church of Worcester under Bishop Wulstan of blessed memory. He had been well known to many who are still alive.

This Aegelred had formerly been attached for a long time to Aegelric, bishop of Chichester, a man highly skilled in great matters, and had learned many things from him about blessed Dunstan, whose near-contemporary he had been. Aegelric acknowledged that he had received these accounts from those who had been worthy to be present at the events.

In addition, there are writings of the ancients arranged in a simpler style, as well as abbreviated entries in chronicles, and we write in testimony to them. As for the things we report as having been done through Dunstan after his most holy departure, we learned some from written records, some from the confirmation of our own senses, and some from the testimony of truthful men who had learned them partly by sight, partly by hearing, and partly through their own experience. We know these things with every scruple removed.

If anyone therefore deigns to read or hear these matters, let him, I ask, read or hear them in such a way as not to detract from the simplicity of my conscience. For I declare that they have been written not to disparage diligent students, but to condescend, according to my ability, to my own smallness and that of others like me who know and are prepared to do so. Let no one, therefore, occupy himself vainly with what we write if what we ask does not dwell in his mind.

The prologue ends.

[Col. 0787C]

## THE LIFE BEGINS

Blessed Dunstan, therefore, deriving his origin from the noblest lineage of the English people, entered the broad expanse of this world all the nobler because, while he was still enclosed within the narrow confines of his mother’s womb, a divine miracle indicated that through him a brilliant light was to arise for the world.

When his mother was rejoicing, pregnant with the hope of future offspring, the feast day of the Purification of the Blessed Mother of God dawned. A multitude of people of both sexes, gathered from every direction because of the excellence of so great a feast, flowed toward the church that had anciently been built of wood at Glastonbury and consecrated in honor of that same Mother of God.

Among this multitude, Dunstan’s father, Herstan by name, a man surpassing many in nobility and rank, was hastening to the service of God together with his mother, Chynedritha. Both carried candles that they were to offer to God according to the rite of that day. The office of Mass had already begun, etc.

(The historian Eadmer continues in an expansive style. He recounts Dunstan’s deeds in the same order as Osbern and relates the same miracles in the same places, though in a very different style. Eadmer employs a simple and historical manner, while Osbern’s is more affected and almost declamatory. From their agreement in events and order it may be inferred that both drew Dunstan’s deeds chiefly from the same source, namely an English History. Therefore, lest we burden the reader with useless repetition, we have decided to omit everything by Eadmer except what corrects or notably illuminates the accounts of others. We have merely restored in the margin the notes that were anciently added to the manuscript: the death of King Eadred in the year 955 and that of Edwy in 958.)

[Note: [Col. 0789D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, col. 407, under Saint Dunstan.]

From that time, after the bishop of London had died, inquiry was made as to who could worthily succeed to the episcopate. Since some time was spent on this, and no suitable and capable person could be found, at length everyone’s choice turned to Dunstan, and he was compelled by the common acclamation of all to assume the pontificate of the aforesaid Church. Thus both Churches—that is, Worcester and London—gloried in him as their prelate, since, compelled by the greatest necessity, he was for some time bishop of both, devoting himself to the care of both charges, fortifying each within and without by his protection against all rivals, and diligently performing the episcopal office in each at the proper time.

The vision described above was partly fulfilled in the swords of the apostles, when Dunstan was confirmed in the episcopate of London, which is celebrated under the name of the most blessed apostle Paul. For indeed, the one placed over that Church received the sword of that apostle, because, following his example, he infused the word of God excellently into the hearts of his subjects, and used the power in which Paul gloried through the strength of the Lord Christ to terrify the wicked and soothe the godly everywhere. He acted with equal vigor in the Church of Worcester, which he undertook to govern with the sword of blessed Peter. For at that time the same episcopate was regarded as founded in honor of that glorious apostle.

But Oswald, a holy and devout man, whom blessed Dunstan, after becoming archbishop of Canterbury, caused to succeed him in the governance of that Church, was unable either to convert the clerics living there from their depravity or to expel them, since they were noble and powerful according to worldly standards. He therefore built almost adjoining that church another church dedicated to blessed Mary, Mother of God, in which he himself would serve Christ with the monks whom he had resolved to gather together. And so it happened. The religious life of the monks consequently brought contempt upon the clerics and made the gathering of the common people, alienated from them, devoted to itself. What more need be said? The number of clerics steadily diminished, while the community of monks increased day by day. Moreover, some of the clerics themselves were converted and added to their number. In this way the episcopal see was changed into the church of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin.

[Col. 0790A]

When Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, had been translated to the joys of eternal life, his passing brought immense mourning to all the Churches of the English and struck innumerable peoples with bitter sorrow. When Dunstan was asked to succeed Odo in the patriarchal see of the English, he refused, declaring that the burden of the government he had already undertaken was sufficiently heavy for him to bear, without adding a greater one. Consequently, Aelffinus, bishop of Winchester, obtained the archbishopric with the king’s consent through the kingdom’s leading men—some of whom he had made his supporters by present favors, others by the hope of future gifts. A few days after acquiring his dignity, he set out for Rome to request the archiepiscopal pallium, but was seized in the Alps by excessive severity of cold and breathed his last there. After him, Birhtelmus, bishop of the people of Dorset, was appointed to the supreme pontificate of the Church of Canterbury, a man wholly formed by gentleness, humility, and modesty. But when it became clear that he possessed nothing for correcting vices, enforcing ecclesiastical discipline, or, finally, displaying the virtue and firmness needed to protect the good or restrain the wicked, he was ordered to return to his own Church. Thus the see of Canterbury remained vacant for some days.

Then the unanimous choice of all called insistently for Dunstan, declaring loudly that they knew only him whom so great a see could properly have as its ruler—especially since, from the earliest flowering of his life, holiness, gravity of conduct, and an unconquered, steadfast, exemplary authority that no one could oppose had marked his course.

By this acclamation, therefore, Dunstan, as though constrained by a truly divine voice, undertook to govern the primatial see of all Britain, and ascended it amid the immense rejoicing and glory of all the neighboring Churches and peoples. Afterwards, when the proper time had come, he visited the thresholds of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul. The pontiff of the supreme see received him on his arrival with great affection and sincere love; then, associating with him more intimately and recognizing without doubt from his conduct that he was a temple of the Holy Spirit, he honored him magnificently and most fittingly adorned him with the pallium of his apostolate, for which Dunstan had come. He thus appointed him, with a commission from the Apostolic See, shepherd and guardian of the salvation of the English people.

So the man of God returned from Rome and, having been received into the patriarchal dignity of the chief see of Britain, rose up like a giant against the very prince of this world. With steadfast courage he began to brandish against him the armor of the word of God, “on the right hand and on the left” (II Corinthians 6:7), and to defeat, overthrow, and weaken his members everywhere.

Meanwhile, as he recalled the vision that we have described as having formerly appeared to him when the apostolic armor was offered, and as he clearly saw it now firmly fulfilled in his administration of the government of the two Churches—that is, Worcester and London—I think it should be explained by what means the archbishopric of Canterbury, which surpasses those sees in dignity and in which he himself sat more exaltedly, had been prefigured for him.

It was, plainly, through the word of God, which he received inscribed upon the sword of the most blessed Peter, according to the interpretation given by King Eadred when Dunstan himself, as we related above, reported the vision to him. Thus Peter’s sword signified Peter’s Church, and the word of God signified the Church of the Word of God situated at Canterbury.

From this it seems reasonable to ask what the sword of blessed Andrew, offered with the others, signified, since Dunstan sat in no church consecrated under that apostle’s name, as he did in the three Churches mentioned above. As far as we English are concerned, to whom the meaning of this is clearer than daylight, I consider it superfluous to mention it either by word or in writing. For the sake, however, of foreigners, should these matters ever by chance come to their attention, I shall say briefly that he rightly received the sword of Andrew together with Peter’s sword inscribed with the word of God. For the man who presides over the Church of Canterbury by his pontificate also presides over the Church of Rochester, which stands under the patronage of blessed Andrew, through the appointment of its bishop and, whenever circumstances require, through the ordering of its affairs within and without, as a church under his authority.

What, then, Dunstan was in all matters pertaining to religion—what virtue he displayed in suppressing every injustice committed by every kind of person, and in fostering and protecting every good work—the whole of England sings to this day. I do not think it necessary to weary myself with writing all this at length. Nevertheless, I shall append in a concise account certain things that we have learned from those who, through the succession of generations, have come down from his time to ours, so that the truth of the statements we have made may be perceived.

A certain very powerful earl had joined his female relative to himself in an unlawful marriage. Though Dunstan reproved him once, twice, and three times, he refused to expiate his incest by divorce. Therefore, struck by the sword of the Holy Spirit through the man of God, he was separated from the thresholds of the holy Church.

Puffed up by pride, he approached the king, accused Dunstan of excessive and impious harshness, and begged and implored in a plaintive voice that by royal decree he be declared free from Dunstan’s tyranny. The king, yielding to his words, ordered Dunstan to allow the man to remain peacefully with the woman he had taken and to restore him to the sacred thresholds from which he had suspended him.

Dunstan was astonished at what he heard and grieved that the religious king had been misled by the man’s lying tongue before the matter had been investigated and examined. Nevertheless, he called the man to account and reproved him somewhat more harshly both for the crime he had committed and for the unjust accusation he had brought against Dunstan before the ruler of the land, hoping by this means to soften his heart toward repentance and correction.

But when he saw that the man not only refused to accept his words but also raged against him with a rebellious spirit and threatened him, Dunstan imposed upon him, in addition to the exclusion from the house of God mentioned above, a complete prohibition from communion with the faithful until he abandoned his wickedness.

Then the man, becoming worse than himself, was seized by savage fury. Considering nothing that he possessed to be of any importance, he devoted himself entirely to stirring up scandal against Dunstan and to making the yoke of Christian law, by which his lust was restrained, alien to him.

He therefore sent his envoys to Rome and, by lavish gifts and still more lavish promises, won over to his cause the hearts and mouths of certain Romans accustomed to such things. What followed? The prelate of the Apostolic See ordered Dunstan, by words and letters, to yield to the sinful man, and advised, urged, and commanded him to reconcile him fully to the bosom of the Church.

Dunstan replied as follows:

> “Indeed, when I see that the man in question has repented of his offense, I shall gladly obey the commands of the lord pope. But that he should remain in his sin, insult us while exempt from ecclesiastical discipline, and then rejoice in it—God forbid. May God also turn from me the thought that, for the sake of any mortal man or for the redemption of my own life, I should set aside the law that my Lord Christ, the Son of God, established to be observed in his Church!”

When the man heard this reported to him, and knew with certainty that Dunstan was inflexible in what he had firmly declared, he was constrained by the penalty of excommunication—both ashamed before men and terrified by fear of the dangers that sometimes befall such persons. He abandoned the obstinacy of his mind, renounced the unlawful marriage, and imposed upon himself the practice of penance.

When Dunstan was holding a general council of the entire kingdom concerning the observance of Christianity, the man, forgetful of himself, came barefoot, his body clothed in woolen garments and carrying rods in his hand. He thrust himself into the middle of the council and fell groaning and wailing at Dunstan’s feet.

At this sight all who were present were moved to pity, and the Father himself was moved by even greater compassion than the others. Yet, preserving on his face the strictness of discipline, since he desired to reconcile the man fully to God, he sternly withstood his tears for a time. At length, when the whole council pleaded for him, Dunstan too, weeping, forgave his fault. Thus he absolved him from the bond of excommunication and, to the joy of all, restored him to communion with the faithful.

At another time, three moneyers who were under the authority of a certain man were caught with counterfeit coin and sentenced to undergo the punishment publicly decreed throughout the kingdom for such men. This matter could not be concealed from Dunstan.

On Pentecost, therefore, when that Father was about to celebrate the solemn Mass, he asked whether the prescribed justice had been carried out upon those moneyers. The reply was that, out of reverence for so great a day, it had been postponed to another day.

“By no means,” he said, “shall this be done. Moneyers who deliberately make false pennies are thieves, and I know of no theft more harmful than theirs. For by the false coin they make, they rob, deceive, and disturb the whole land. They harm the rich, the middling, and the poor alike, and reduce everyone, according to his circumstances, either to disgrace, poverty, or nothingness.

“Therefore know that I shall not approach today to offer sacrifice to God unless those who have been caught have first undergone the punishment they have deserved by deceiving the whole people. For if, when the matter concerns me, I refrain from appeasing God in requital for so great an evil, how can I hope that he will receive the sacrifice from my hands?

“Yet although this may be attributed to cruelty, my intention is known to God. The tears, groans, and sighs of widows and orphans, and also the cry of the entire populace, weigh upon me and demand the correction of this evil. If I do not intend, insofar as it lies within me, to alleviate their suffering, I both gravely offend God, who sympathizes with their groans, and make others readier and bolder to practice the same evil.”

He spoke, and, moved by compassion for those whose hands were to be lost as punishment, he poured forth tears, so that it was clear from what source the decree that seemed cruel to some had proceeded.

When he heard that the prescribed justice had been carried out, he rose and, his face washed, went cheerfully toward the oratory with a joyful expression, saying:

> “Because today I have obeyed God by observing the established laws of justice, I trust that he too, in his mercy, will receive the sacrifice from my hand today.”

Nor was he deprived of the effect of this confidence. For while, amid the sacred solemnities of the Mass, he extended his sacred hands and entreated God the almighty Father to “grant peace to, guard, unite, and govern” his Catholic Church throughout the whole world, a snow-white dove descended from heaven before many people and remained silently above his head, its wings spread and apparently motionless, until the sacrifice had been completed.

What do you suppose was taking place in the spirit of the servant of God during this? With what love, sweetness, and longing do you think he was nourished in God, when he was cherished by such a visitation through the present grace of God?

When the sacrifice had been completed, the same dove moved toward the southern side of the altar and settled upon the tomb of blessed Odo, whom we mentioned above. It embraced the tomb on either side with its wings and seemed to kiss it with its beak.

When blessed Dunstan saw this, and considered the merit of the man who lay there, he thereafter held him in such reverence that whenever he passed before his tomb, he bent his knees. After this he also always called him by the surname “Good” in the mother tongue, namely, Odo Segode, which in Latin means Odo Bonus, “Odo the Good.” From that time to our own age, the English, and especially the people of Canterbury, have commonly called him by this surname.

When the Mass had been fully sung, Dunstan withdrew from the altar. His ministers, signaling to one another about what had happened and supposing that other brothers would come to assist in the pontifical ministry, dispersed in different directions, leaving the man alone, still soaked by immense showers of tears from the presence of God’s grace.

And behold, while he was removing the chasuble in which he had been vested during the sacred rites, with no one present to receive it, by God’s arrangement it remained suspended in the air, so that, if it fell to the ground, it would not distract the servant of God from his spiritual purpose.

[Col. 0794A]

About this same time, at the request of a certain noble and devout man, Dunstan dedicated a church that the man had built on his own estate. When water was lacking for the ministry, causing the man considerable distress, the servant of God first prayed, then struck the earth with his staff. Immediately a very clear spring burst forth, bringing no small joy to all who were present. Flowing to this day, that spring makes Dunstan’s name and merit renowned.

The same Father, establishing his hospices at suitable intervals from Canterbury toward his more distant estates, built a wooden church at Magaveld, as he did at his other hospices. When he himself dedicated it, he was walking around it according to custom and noticed that it was not at all turned toward the rising of the sun at the equinox. It is said that, as he passed by, he pressed it somewhat with his shoulder, and at once it was moved from its former position and turned, according to his wish, toward the central course of the east.

No one doubts that he could easily have effected this, unless he is unbelieving regarding the words of the Lord Christ, who promises those possessing faith like a grain of mustard seed that they may even transfer a mountain by their command (Luke 17:6).

Amid such works, Dunstan always kept God in mind, ascribed whatever good he did to God rather than to himself, and possessed in every way and in all things a heart full of great humility and very little pride.

Whenever rest was granted him from the occupations of secular affairs, he devoted himself at one time to divine contemplation and prayers, at another to reading the sacred Scriptures and interpreting them, and at another diligently to exhorting the brothers or correcting books.

He was endowed with such grace in the compunction of tears that whenever one saw him standing at the sacred altars or performing some pontifical office, one could not doubt that his mind was kindled by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and that what he administered outwardly he was himself performing inwardly, as was shown by the tears flowing from his eyes.

He caused buildings suitable for himself and his successors to be constructed both within the walls of the city and in every village belonging to the archbishopric; and if any of those already built had been damaged in some part, he had them restored. He understood that in these matters he had been born and lived not merely for himself but also for the benefit of many.

Moreover, he diligently bore responsibility for all the Churches of Britain and the neighboring islands, and he administered their affairs whenever they were brought before him as primate and patriarch. Because he served the Lord Christ in every way with watchful devotion, he was often joined to the joys and harmonies of the heavenly citizens, for which he longed anxiously—sometimes while awake in the body, sometimes while resting in holy sleep.

And, something that you may perhaps find no less astonishing, through a vision he learned certain things from blessed spirits, which he later taught his own people to sing in the service of God.

(There follows the history of the vision concerning his mother, betrothed to a very powerful king; it may be found in Osbern.)

At another time, a king went hunting early on a Sunday morning and asked Dunstan, who happened at that time to be with him, to postpone his Mass until the king returned.

As the third hour approached, therefore, the man of God went to the church and, clothed in the sacred vestments, awaited the king as he had promised. He stood leaning on his elbows against the altar, devoted to prayer and tears. Then, suddenly pressed gently by sleep, he was carried up into heaven. Joining the blessed ranks of angels, he heard them singing praise to the most high Trinity in harmonious voices and saying:

> Kyrie eleison, Kyrie eleison, Kyrie eleison.  
> Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.

Having been taught to contemplate their heavenly melody, he returned to himself. Turning to his attendants, he asked whether the king had arrived. When he learned that the king had not yet come, he returned to his prayers.

After a short interval, he was again led outside himself and heard it proclaimed in the heavens with a high-sounding voice:

> Ite, missa est.  
> Go, the dismissal has been given.

When the response “Thanks be to God” had been made, the king’s clerics came running and cried out that the king was present; they begged the priest to celebrate the Mass more quickly.

But Dunstan turned away from the altar and declared that he had said Mass and would celebrate no other Mass that day. After he had removed his sacred vestments, his attendants questioned him about the matter, and what had been hidden was revealed.

From that time onward he prohibited the king from hunting on Sundays. He taught his own people the Kyrie eleison that he had learned in the heavens, and today the holy Church sings it during the solemnities of the Mass in many places.

It was the man’s custom, when he was staying at Canterbury, to visit the holy places at night accompanied by only one faithful companion, and there to offer himself to God through compunction and contrition of heart.

On one occasion, therefore, he went according to custom, around the silence of midnight, to the monastery of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, where blessed Augustine and several other Fathers of the Church of Christ at Canterbury had been buried. There he prostrated himself in prayer before God for a long time.

Then he went out to the oratory of blessed Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, which stood on the eastern side of that monastery, intending to do the same there. As he approached it, he heard voices inside singing psalms and saying:

> The souls of the saints who followed Christ’s footsteps rejoice in heaven; and because they poured out their blood for his love, therefore they will rejoice with Christ forever.

Astonished at this, he stood at the door and, looking inside through its cracks—for it was barred—saw the entire oratory shining with immense light and a certain company of radiant persons echoing the antiphon in joyful harmonies.

At another time, when at a similar hour he had sought the threshold of the aforesaid Church of the Shepherds with the same devotion, he left there and began to approach the aforementioned building of the most holy Virgin in order to pour out prayers to God there.

And behold, the most blessed Virgin, accompanied by a numerous choir of virgins, came to meet the approaching man. Having received him with the greatest honor, she began to lead him toward her church, where he was heading, while two girls from the choir sang the following poem of Sedulius:

> Let us sing, companions; let us sing honor to the Lord.  
> Let the sweet love of Christ resound from the devout mouth.

[Col. 0796A]

As the choir of virgins repeated these verses in song, the two aforementioned singers continued with the next two verses in order:

> The first, proud from the great light, fell to the depths.  
> So too, when man grew arrogant, the first fell to the depths.

And so, until the man of God had been led into the oratory, the virginal choir sang the first verse, while the two virgins sang two verses each, in accordance with the sequence of the hymn.

From these and similar deeds, you may judge how great were the honor, reverence, and magnificence that the distinguished Father Dunstan enjoyed among all good people. Whoever knows how to embrace such gifts of God will perceive much of this even without my saying more.

But to those who strove to live in wickedness rather than goodness, his face inspired horror and terror, so that they preferred to flee from him rather than approach him. All who desired to abandon their perverse deeds and turn to righteous works felt that he overflowed with true piety and mercy in his heart, and found in him counsel and help for their salvation beyond all human estimation.

People therefore came to him from distant regions of the earth, and wherever it was known that he excelled, the counsel of the Holy Spirit was sought from him.

If the devil’s hatred and envy raged against these things, no one should wonder. But because he already knew with certainty that he could accomplish nothing by disturbing the man except what would increase his own shame and Dunstan’s glory, he restrained himself from the attack with which he had often been accustomed to weary him.

Nevertheless, in order to make him troubled, he set a snare of mournful deception for King Eadgar, whom Dunstan greatly loved out of reverence for him, and entangled him in the stain of a grave sin.

On one occasion, that king came to the monastery of virgins situated at Wilton. There he was captivated by the appearance of a certain girl who, born of the English nobility, was being raised and kept among the nuns without having been veiled. He ordered that she be brought to him privately for conversation.

As she was being led to him, fearing for her modesty, one of the nuns snatched a veil and placed it upon her head. She hoped in this way to protect herself if the king should attempt to demand anything dishonorable from her.

When he saw her veiled, he said: “How suddenly you have become a nun!” Then he seized the veil and pulled it from her head, although she resisted as best she could.

He abused her, and as a result the minds of all the devout throughout England were wounded by grave scandal. The scandal was all the more serious because the same king had a lawful wife, namely Aelfleda, surnamed the White, daughter of Ordinaer, the powerful duke of the East Angles, by whom he had fathered the holy Eadward.

When the matter became known to Dunstan, etc.

(There follows the account of Dunstan’s rebuke and the king’s penance; see Osbern concerning these matters.)

At that time the clerical order was extremely corrupt, and the canons, together with the parish priests, were serving the pleasures of the flesh more than was fitting. Wishing to correct this evil, Dunstan, relying on the authority of John, the prelate of the Apostolic See, obtained from the king that canons who refused to live chastely should be expelled from the Churches they held and that monks should be introduced in their place.

At that time Athelwold, a man of exceptional holiness and one particularly distinguished by his upbringing under Father Dunstan, presided over the Church of Winchester. Having learned Dunstan’s intention concerning the canons of his Church, who were excessively worldly, he warned them once and again to change their conduct and actions and, leaving the women, to take up the paths of a more disciplined life.

But they immediately denied that this was possible for them and, in a croaking voice, continually promised that they would reform on the following day. Dunstan, knowing them, did not tolerate this for long.

On the day when the hymn “Serve the Lord in fear” was sung, he prepared a great many monastic cowls, entered the choir, and had the garments he had prepared carried in with him. Throwing them down in the middle, he said to the canons:

> “Did you notice what you have just sung?”

“We noticed,” they replied.

“Then,” he said, “if you wish to serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling, take hold of discipline—that is, the monastic habit—lest you perish from the righteous way, as you have sung” (Psalm 2:11–12).

Astonished at this, they asked, as usual, for a delay and promised that they would do it in the future. Then he said:

> “Believe me, I shall no longer trust this croaking promise of yours. Either you will take up discipline now, or, expelled from this place’s benefices and way of life, you will depart immediately.”

Accordingly, some of them at once abandoned their clerical dress and became monks, while the others, in accordance with the bishop’s words, were expelled from the Church.

But since those who had thus recently been converted could not skillfully observe the rule of discipline without instruction from others, monks from Abingdon were brought by the same bishop to teach them the path of monastic formation.

The expelled clerics, however, went swiftly to the king and demanded that judgment and justice be done for their expulsion. The matter was referred to Dunstan, and he declared that their demand was just.

Therefore, by order of the king and the archbishop, the nobility of the entire kingdom assembled at Winchester, and the king with his wife was present, to determine the complaints in this case.

Disputes arose on every side, but Dunstan destroyed them all by the arguments he put forward. He showed reasonably to everyone that clerics who had incorrigibly departed from God’s lot through the depravity of their lives could claim no right, by any principle of justice, to those things that had been given to the Churches for the support of those who preserved themselves in pure conduct within the clerical order.

When they had heard this, the king and many of the leading men, abandoning every controversy and moved to pity by the clerics’ pleas, appealed to Dunstan. They asked him, on this one occasion alone, to spare them and, since the clerics had now learned by experience what they would suffer if they did not reform, to restore them to their Church.

He was silent at this and, bowing his head, considered in his mind what should chiefly be done in the matter. A profound silence seized everyone, and they raised their ears attentively, waiting for the bishop’s answer.

Then suddenly the image of the crucified God, affixed high upon the wall of the house, spoke in the hearing of all with the sign of the cross:

> “It shall not be done; it shall not be done. You judged well; you would not change well.”

The entire assembly trembled at this. Father Dunstan then continued and said:

> “What more do you want, my brothers? You have heard the divine judgment by which the present matter has been decided.”

They replied: “We have truly heard it.”

From then on the monks remained securely at Winchester, and as long as those clerics lived, no one troubled them concerning this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Rather, scarcely seven years, certainly not ten, intervened between the councils of Winchester and Calne.]

After the clerics had been taken from this life, their sons, wishing to recover what their fathers had lost, sent to Scotland and brought from there, at great expense, a man named Bernelm, reputed to possess extraordinary eloquence, to defend their case against Dunstan.

The sons of the clerics, gathered together under one banner, found the king and Dunstan staying in an upper room at a village called Calne. Armed with that rhetorician, in whom lay their greatest hope of victory, they brought forward before them the quarrels of the old accusation.

Dunstan replied briefly in these words:

> “We know that this accusation you are raising was long ago decided by the divine voice, and we do not think it should be brought forward again in a new conflict. I too am old, and I know that the remainder of my life is short; I desire, if permitted, to spend it in peace. I have labored as long as I could. Now, weary of every labor, I entrust to the Lord God the defense of his Church against its rising enemies.”

He spoke, and behold, the floor beneath the feet of those who had assembled against the man immediately collapsed, casting them all down and injuring them considerably in their fall. Where Dunstan and his companions were standing, no part of the house collapsed and no accident occurred.

In this way, therefore, the clerics’ accusation was silenced, and the monastic way of life has remained established in that Church to this day. During that period, many other clerics like these were nevertheless expelled from their Churches, and monks were substituted in their place.

Thus religious observance increased throughout England to such an extent that forty-eight monasteries for monks or nuns were established, with blessed Dunstan cooperating in this work with the venerable men Oswald—first bishop of Worcester and later bishop of York—and Athelwold of Winchester, whom we mentioned above.

All who wished to walk according to the paths of their own devices feared the life and deeds of blessed Dunstan (Psalm 80:13).

Meanwhile, when the matter that had prevented King Eadgar from being crowned according to royal custom had been settled, Dunstan assembled the bishops, abbots, and other leading men, together with the whole body of the kingdom’s free-born people, and, with an innumerable multitude of people standing before them, placed the royal crown upon him. All rejoiced and gave jubilant praise to God with a voice of thanksgiving and exultation.

Two years after these events, Eadgar was overtaken by an untimely death and left the entire kingdom by hereditary right to his son Eadward. When this Edward was to be consecrated king, some of the leading men of the land tried to prevent him from becoming king. They suspected the severity of his character, by which he was accustomed to rage harshly against the offenses of his subjects; and they knew that, although his mother had been lawfully married, she had not been consecrated for the kingdom any more than his father had been when he fathered him.

But Dunstan, trusting in the young man’s discernment and ability, fearing nothing on the one hand and disregarding the other consideration in observance of the right of paternal inheritance and testament, seized the banner of the holy cross, stood in the midst of them, and, overturning all the objections by reason, established Edward as king. Once he had established him, he took care throughout his life to provide him with paternal affection, counsel, and assistance in every matter.

The king, for his part, so ordered his conduct in all things and in every respect, and so arranged the whole kingdom according to holy laws, that both his actions pleased God and those who had opposed him when he received the kingdom came to displease themselves.

But after he had been treacherously killed by his stepmother, the son of that wicked woman, Aethelred, was placed upon the throne. He possessed more of his mother’s disgrace than of the prudence of his father Eadgar.

Dunstan was not altogether pleased by his advancement. Nevertheless, because he was the nearest heir to the kingdom, Dunstan fulfilled the royal right toward him, knowing that without offending the laws of the land and its leading men he could not transfer the kingdom to anyone else.

Yet once Aethelred had obtained the royal throne, Dunstan rebuked him with a severe thunder of words because he had acquired the kingdom through his brother’s blood. He foretold that he would live amid bloodshed, that his descendants would be devastated by the cruel invasion of barbarians, and that the entire land would be ravaged for many ages by their savage domination.

Although Dunstan denied that these things would occur during his lifetime, prophecy asserted with great truthfulness that they would certainly occur, as we read in the Chronicles and see today. The omnipotent God will hasten, when it pleases him, the liberation that he has promised will follow through the merits and intercession of so great a prophet of his.

Indeed, we confirm that Dunstan shone with the spirit of prophecy not only from this event but also from several others that he is known to have foretold truthfully, and we prove it by the example that follows.

(There follows Dunstan’s prophecy concerning the deaths of Athelwold of Winchester and the bishops of Rochester; consult Osbern concerning it.)

The death of Athelwold inflicted deep grief upon Dunstan, both because he had lost the great consolation of so eminent a man and because he was uncertain to whom he should entrust the governance of the Church, still tender in age. His mind was troubled by conflicting considerations: on the one hand, the monks who had recently been introduced; on the other, the clerics who had been expelled from that church. The monks preferred to have as bishop a man of their own profession; the clerics desired to have placed over them a man of their own order. The former wished to be firmly established in the church granted to them through a monk; the latter hoped to be restored through a cleric to the church taken from them. But God’s foresight, which is also wise providence, quickly settled the matter. For through the blessed apostle Andrew, to whom God had permitted Dunstan to be attached with a special affection of love, He commanded Dunstan to appoint, without any hesitation, Aelfegus, abbot of Bath, as the high priest of the Church of Winchester. Dunstan rejoiced in these things, and, having given thanks to God for His benefits, carried out in Aelfegus what God Himself had commanded him through His apostle.

We could still commend much about this man to the faithful record of literature in a truthful style, according to what the not-to-be-despised testimonies of many people report. But, lest we burden anyone with the prolixity of an unpolished narrative, let us set those matters aside and prepare heart and tongue to recount his holy passing. Since preparing ourselves for this is beyond our strength, let us pray that, through the intercession of the very man about whom we are speaking, it may be accomplished by Him whose gift and grace we know it to be.

*(What follows is an account of Dunstan’s death and burial, entirely consistent with Osbern, except that Osbern writes that his body was miraculously raised from the earth on Thursday, whereas Eadmer places the event on the Saturday on which he died.)*

[Col. 0799C]

## LIFE OF SAINT ODO, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

*(It exists under the name of Osbern in Patrologia, volume CXXXIII, column 931, under Saint Odo.)*

[Col. 0799C]

## EADMER’S LETTER TO THE GLASTONIANS

### At the time when the Glastonians claimed that they possessed the body of our patron, Saint Dunstan

[Col. 0799D]

To the glorious convent of the monks of the monastery of Glastonbury, Brother Eadmer, one of the least in goodness and learning, sends faithful friendship and charitable service in Christ Jesus our Lord to the sons and brothers of the Church of Christ at Canterbury [Col. 0800D].

I remember that, some time ago, when I came to you on one occasion, I was received with great joy and honor, and that, with still greater delight and rejoicing, I was welcomed and detained among you for as long as I wished to remain. Hence I have remained pleasing to you until now, and I shall be less pleasing while I continue in this present life. Since, therefore, I am such a person toward you and ought rightly to be so, I think no one should wonder if I love your honor, if I approve what benefits you, and finally if I detest and condemn what brings reproach upon you. Otherwise I could not be a faithful friend, nor could I truly be said to observe the law of brotherly love.

How serious this ought to seem to a Christian who wishes to reach the kingdom of God is perceived by anyone who believes the blessed Apostle when he says that a person who does not love his brother is a murderer (1 John III, 15), and that such a person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God (Ephesians V, 5). Understand why I have prefaced these remarks. Some of your number, recently converted among you, as we suppose, preach that your ancient fathers were thieves and robbers, and, what is worse, even sacrilegious men. They count it to the credit of their preaching that those men were such, perhaps intoxicated by the same desire, without considering that the divine page thunders that thieves and robbers will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians VI, 10). Moreover, to make it more firmly believed that this was so, they assert that those men were like Judas the betrayer, who, being entrusted with the Lord’s money-box, most wickedly stole what he ought to have guarded.

O men! O honorers of your brothers! O most attentive hearers of the Lord’s words! A hundred years and more have passed since those whom you proclaim to have been thieves and robbers departed from this present life; yet only now is such reproach brought against them, and the eternal punishment in which, according to the judgment of these men, they are most wretchedly tormented is most unhappily renewed for them. Truly, this is great impiety. For even if they were not what these men want them to have been, the impiety of these accusers is not thereby lessened; rather, with all ambiguity removed, it is greater, since they defame the innocent and reveal themselves to everyone as liars and shameless men.

For God, the truth who knows and disposes all things, is my witness: when I was still a querulous student, at the command of Lanfranc of blessed memory, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, a fast was imposed upon all the people of Kent, and the body of the most blessed Dunstan was raised from the first place of his burial. Scotland, the abbot of Saint Augustine’s, was present, as was Gundulf, later bishop of Rochester, together with the whole company of monks from both churches: our own, that is, the Church of Christ at Canterbury, and the neighboring church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which in common usage is now called the church of Saint Augustine. An innumerable multitude of men and women came together for this event. They all accompanied that heavenly treasure to the place where it was to be reinterred, with an immense harmony of voices and rejoicing of heart, and they spent that day, made joyful and solemn by divine miracles, in celebration.

[Col. 0801D]

**Note:** Concerning the translation of Dunstan’s body carried out by Lanfranc, Osbern says the following in the second book of his Life of Dunstan:

“Not long afterward the church of the Savior was consumed by fire, and the walls fell; nor did anything remain unburned among all the monastery’s buildings except two houses, without which the monks could not remain—namely, the dormitory and the refectory—and that part of the cloister beneath which they could pass from one house to the other without being drenched by rain. From this it could readily be seen how great a care our father Dunstan had for us.

“But this ruin was changed for the better when the venerable man Lanfranc, archbishop, arrived, at once the holiest and wisest of all who in our age had lived on earth. When he wished to lay the foundations of a new church, and could not do so without translating the bodies resting within its boundaries, he proclaimed a fast for all the people, so that the will of the saints might be made known as to whether their bodies ought to be moved elsewhere.

“On the day appointed for this undertaking, while all the people prayed, and the clergy came forward with candles, spices, and every kind of expression of joy, the priests prepared to lift the shrine of the holy Father Dunstan from the earth without touching his body and to carry it with every care to a place prepared for it.

“This fire occurred in the year 1074, on the Nones of September, according to Gervase of Canterbury. Eadmer says that fifty years had elapsed since then. This letter, therefore, was written around the year 1124.”

Now, however, fifty years having passed since that event, some of your number have risen up and, wherever they please, preach that, a hundred years earlier, the monks of your church had been appointed guardians of our church, which, as they say, had fallen into great desolation because of the martyrdom of our glorious Father Elphege, and that there they had fraudulently and secretly stolen what was most precious. Woe to men more wicked than all other men! The church of the entire island of Britain, afflicted by the killing of her Father and sons, fled to her only beloved daughter, and, as though what was alleged had happened in the present, trusted more greatly in her protection, so that she might preserve herself and her relics. And she, as you preach, sent her better sons to the place to which they had been requested; and they, having become guardians of the sacred things there, attacked the womb of their mother, whom they had undertaken to protect, plundered it, ravaged her heart and entrails, seized them, and carried them away.

[Col. 0802C]

When the Jews had taken the dead and buried Lord into their custody, lest He be taken away by the apostles, they did not fail in their guardianship for as long as they could, nor did they attempt to steal or otherwise remove what had been entrusted to them. Rather, they attributed the charge of theft to others while they themselves slept. If the Glastonian guardians had acted in a similar way—that is, if they had said that the sacrilege of which they boast had been committed by others while they themselves were overcome by sleep—they might perhaps have taken some care for their reputation and would not have sinned in so detestable a manner.

But now what shall we say? As we have already indicated, we approve them as being like Judas in theft—not we ourselves, however, but their fellow Glastonians, who follow them. For we truly know that they are entirely free from this sin. What will become of those who, having fabricated so shameless a lie, accuse their brothers—indeed, their fathers? They are surely neither brothers nor fathers. For if they had naturally become their brothers or sons, or at least if human shame taught them to spare their tongues and to take thought for their own reputation, they would have done so.

But let it be granted that the holy Glastonian brothers concealed their theft from everyone by prudent cunning. They are said to have carried away with them the corpse of one of their abbots—whose name is unknown to those who compose this tale—and to have placed it in the shrine of our holy Father Dunstan, lest it remain empty.

O wisdom! Were there no dead men’s bones between Canterbury and Glastonbury, so that they had to transport, for two hundred miles, so to speak, the corpse of someone whom they did not know in order to conceal their theft? Let your Blessedness know that I, who write these things, am not a little ashamed at such evident folly, worthy of every person’s laughter—especially since, as it is said, it was fabricated by Englishmen. Woe to you for not consulting some man from overseas! Such men, having lived among many peoples and been instructed in many things, know how to fabricate many tales. You might at least have paid them to compose for you some plausible lie about so serious a matter. Woe to you, men of my own people, for being marked by such foolish simplicity that you should be condemned to be mocked by everyone forever.

Furthermore, I ask the preachers of this splendid sacrilege to tell me, their fellow countryman, whether they carried the corpse of their recently deceased substitute abbot whole from Glastonbury to Canterbury. And whether, in the manner of a high priest, it was mitred, palliate, clad in a tunic, and shod with sandals? If it possessed all these things, where, I ask, did it obtain the pallium, to say nothing for the moment of the rest? Did Glastonbury’s abbots use the pallium in ancient times? Yet this is granted only to patriarchs, primates, and archbishops by Rome and the Apostolic See. Until now it has never been heard in any age that Glastonbury was a patriarchate or even a bishopric.

Then, to deceive those who would come later, your predecessors brought the corpse, clad in the pallium, to Canterbury. By doing this they made themselves liable to and infamous before the Roman pontiff and every Christian who holds himself to the faith of Christ under the teaching of blessed Peter, and worthy of every reproach. For it is known that they did not receive it from the Apostolic See; rather, with malice as their teacher, they themselves fashioned it—or, if that was what happened, had it fashioned by men like themselves.

[Col. 0803D]

In truth, the body that we found was as follows: apparently entirely whole, mitred, ringed, palliate, clad in a tunic, and most beautifully adorned with sandals. With it was found an inscription engraved on a lead tablet, which clearly testified that the body buried there was that of the blessed Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury.

Do you have, I ask, any written records that prove these things happened in this way? Records, namely, that report the corpse of that abbot dressed in the manner we have described? I ask further: did those ancient fathers and brothers of yours, who, as you say, were brought to protect the relics of our abandoned church, bring that corpse with them to place it beneath the blessed Dunstan, thereby securing themselves against the consequences of their theft? Or did they first come and carry the exhumed body of the blessed Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, to Glastonbury, strip it there of its pontifical insignia, clothe your abbot in those same insignia, and transfer him to be placed in the tomb of the Father who had been removed?

Whichever of these things you say happened, it is easy for anyone—even a blind man—to see how great your madness is in believing it. O unhappy men, so wrapped in empty stupidity that you cannot understand that your very stupidity cannot escape the eyes of anyone prudent!

Christ, who is the truth, says: “The truth will set you free” (John VIII, 32). Yet your prophets say at this time that the theft and sacrilege of your fathers, and your lie, will honor our church and us.

[Col. 0804B]

What lie? “The body,” they say, “of the blessed Dunstan, bishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, was secretly taken from his church by your fathers, and your abbot, purchased by such a sacrilege because he was useless to you, was carried there and placed in his tomb.”

O joy! O grief! O your place, which is to be magnified by so great a return! But, O enemies of pure truth, what will you do, I ask you, when Truth itself comes to destroy all who speak lies (Psalm V, 7)?

It is indeed clearer than daylight to everyone that you falsely accuse your fathers, because, when invited to Canterbury, they brought with them the corpse of their abbot; they did not bring it there after living at Canterbury and carrying away the body of the blessed Dunstan. For that would have been not merely excessive and incredible folly, but madness. And it would have been the result of an audacity impossible to carry out.

For when the blessed man himself ordered that a tomb be dug for him, as his Life most truthfully records, and the depth of the pit reached below ground to the height of a man’s body, what place or opportunity, I ask, could there have been for so empty a theft? The church itself had never been without its resident monks, its own sons, nor had the city of Canterbury ever been emptied of its citizens.

Moreover, it must be considered that, during the passion of the most blessed martyr Elphege, the church itself was neither consumed by fire nor destroyed in roof or walls. We know that it was violated and stripped of many ornaments, and that a fire was set from outside beneath it in an attempt to burn it, so that the frenzied hand might force the bishop, who was defending himself inside, to come out. But when they seized him as he emerged, abandoning the fires and other evils by which they had been occupied in capturing him, they led him away—after killing some monks before his eyes—and, having inflicted many injuries and tortures upon him, brought him to the place intended for his destruction and killed him.

[Col. 0804D]

Since these things were so, with what face can it be said that the church floor was dug up before everyone’s eyes, extending on either side for a full seven feet down to the depth of the tomb—for otherwise it could not have been reached—and that, after the body of the most holy Father Dunstan had been removed, it remained open for fifteen days, so to speak, until the monks secretly entered, hurried to their monastery, and there—not, I say, killing the abbot themselves, but finding him immediately dead on the way—stripped the pontifical ornaments from blessed Dunstan and adorned the corpse with them, then perhaps hastily carried it to Canterbury on some little donkey and placed it in his tomb?

I ask further: was the land between Glastonbury and Canterbury laid waste in those days and turned into a wilderness, so that a clear passage for the bearers of so great a treasure, back and forth in every direction, was open without hindrance—or was it not? Yet, certainly, everywhere and at the time when these things were allegedly being done, Danish savagery was rampant: nowhere was there peace, nowhere security; wars and rebellions raged everywhere.

Moreover, as is known with complete certainty, the body of the blessed Dunstan was buried in the middle of the choir, before the steps by which one ascended to the high altar, in a leaden coffin, and that coffin was placed deep in the earth, as was formerly customary among the English when burying their dead. How, then, did the monks of the Church—who, according to what Lord Osbern reports, were at least four survivors of so great a calamity—

**Note:** Osbern reports this in his Life of Elphege:

“After that mournful slaughter of the monks, the clerics recovered the ancestral possession which they had lost when expelled by Archbishop Alfric nine years earlier, and they retained it until the time of Lanfranc, though monks were admitted among the clerics in smaller numbers.”

—together with the clerics who had been admitted among them and were administering God’s service in that very church, endure that opening in the earth for so many days, until the unnamed abbot was brought and placed in the tomb of the removed Dunstan?

Wonderful patience—and truly even more wonderful was their expectation of the arrival of the future abbot, perhaps called Delsinus or Wlsinus! Therefore, my lords, I ask: is there anyone who could restrain himself from laughing at such great vanity? Certainly, we could still say many more things no less suitable for displaying the ineptness of that vanity, if we were not sparing the reputation of your holy monastery. For when it shelters, nourishes, and embraces men who so defame themselves, this is a source of shame and great reproach to it.

For the Glastonians did not come to Canterbury at the time they claim, nor did they live there. Therefore, the body of the blessed Dunstan was not stolen from us by them and in any way brought to you. Yet you deny that it was brought by others or at another time. You must therefore admit that your prophets have spoken falsely and that you are altogether lying when you say that you possess anything of the body of the blessed Dunstan. Take thought, therefore, for your reputation, and restrain your mouths from this vanity.

Nevertheless, let the truth be recalled to you, if you have forgotten it. Without doubt, you know that Agelnoth, abbot—and indeed abbot of Glastonbury—once lived for a very long time at Canterbury with one or two monks. I call him an abbot because he had been deposed from his abbey by Lanfranc of blessed memory, the high priest of the holy Church of Canterbury, in a general synod of all England, and had been placed at Canterbury, appropriately indeed for so great a man, though in a kind of confinement.

**Note:** This appears to have occurred in the year 1081, when the *Historia Glastoniensis*, in the *Monasticon*, vol. I, p. 17, reports that Thurstan the Norman was appointed by Lanfranc to the abbey of Glastonbury.

At that time the number of monks serving the Lord Christ and blessed Dunstan there had risen to sixty.

[Col. 0805D]

If, then, the Glastonian monks ever stole the body of the blessed Dunstan, I suppose these were the men. But while they were at Canterbury, the body had already, as we said earlier, been translated from its first place of burial to a place to which they had no access. It was not taken by them, therefore, and consequently it was not taken by any of your people.

So remove the bones with which you have burdened the image of our Redeemer, lest He become indignant with you. He has enough in Himself by which He may be honored, and there is no need for His holiness to be increased either by the bones of the dead or by anything else.

My brothers, let your prudence consider and reconsider, I ask, what it is honorable for you to think, appropriate to say, and becoming to do. A hundred years and more have passed since the martyrdom of the blessed Elphege, and no human being who was present at it remains alive—or at least no one who remembers having been present. Nor has it yet come to our knowledge that any of those who truly lived in those days said or wrote anything concerning the matter you are discussing that any sound-minded person would regard as acceptable as a spoken or written account.

Therefore, setting aside childish songs of mourning, as befits wise and mature men, love the blessed Dunstan as your father and patron, speak the truth about him, and then you will truly deserve to be loved by him. He is a member and friend of supreme Truth, and it cannot admit into the embrace of its love those who disagree with it.

God knows—and he himself, our sweetest Father and advocate—that what I say I say for your honor and benefit. My sole intention is that God, who is truth, may be magnified, praised, and proclaimed in the blessed Dunstan, as is right, both by you and by us, and, if I could bring it about, by all the faithful of the entire created world.

I know that I have exceeded the proper manner of letters somewhat in speaking. But such was the subject that, although I had resolved to speak briefly, my discourse nevertheless extended itself into what you see here. Do not, therefore, be surprised. “A man’s way is not his own” (Jeremiah X, 23).

You, then, my lords and brothers, to whom God has opened the understanding necessary for grasping matters of reason, restrain the insolent impudence of foolish young men. They open their mouths merely so that they may seem to know how to speak, saying whatever the volatility of their hearts drives them to say, and imagining themselves to be something when the simplicity of others lends an ear to their words.

I once knew some such men, and perhaps I myself was one; for that reason I do not entirely doubt that some people like them—and like me—exist at this time. But I have grown old and gray, and many things that I greatly valued as a young man I now regard as nothing. May the same happen, by God’s gift, to the young men of this age.

Since the length of the letter now demands an end, I say this last thing: although all your ancient fathers who died in the Glastonian monastery more than a hundred years ago are gone, I think that some may still survive who were brought up there in monastic discipline before the time of the Normans. Ask them, if any such remain, whether they remember that your abbot customarily came each year to Canterbury for the feast of Father Dunstan with four or more monks, and there spent six or more days among the brothers in joy and rejoicing out of reverence for so great a Father—or whether this was not so.

I think that, if any such person has survived to this day, he will not deny that the matter was then conducted in this way. For if he did otherwise, he would undoubtedly contradict the truth. If, then, they knew that the body of the blessed Dunstan was at Glastonbury, why did they seek it in Canterbury on his feast day?

Let these things suffice to refute the error of the imprudent and to confirm the wise in the holy love toward us which we greatly desire them to possess. May your holiness, therefore, prosper in Christ Jesus, and pray for us.

**The letter of Eadmer, monk of the Church of Christ at Canterbury, ends here.**

[Col. 0807A]

## EADMER’S LETTER TO THE MONKS OF WORCESTER

### On the election of a bishop

*(Warton, Anglia sacra, volume II, p. 238, from the Cottonian Library, Claudius A, 1.)*

**Note:** In the same manuscript there precedes this a letter from the prior and convent of Worcester to William, archbishop of Canterbury, asking him to obtain from the king the freedom to elect their new prelate. It is followed by a consolatory response from Archbishop William concerning the death of their shepherd. Of the Worcester bishops, only Theulf died during the time of Archbishop William, namely in the year 1123, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. Simon succeeded him, elected in 1125—not from the flock of monks, as Eadmer earnestly recommends, but from the secular clergy.

[Col. 0807B]

To their lords and brothers, namely to the most beloved lord N., the beloved Prior, and to all the others serving God at Worcester, Brother E., wholly theirs, sends the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding.

Your father, your bishop, as you know, has departed from this age, and you have been left orphans. But would that He who said to His disciples, “I will not leave you orphans” (John XIV, 18), would not leave you orphans! And indeed He will not leave you, if you do not first leave Him. You will not leave Him if you have peace among yourselves. For He is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians II, 14).

Have peace, therefore, among yourselves, and the God of peace will be with you (2 Corinthians XIII, 11). And if God is with you, He will certainly also be for you. And if God is for you, who can be against you?

My beloved, I beg you—I beg you for God’s sake and for the sake of the dignity of your holy way of life—be one in Christ Jesus, rooted in love in Him (Ephesians III, 17). But if you are divided from one another, you and your friends have cause to fear that you may fall into desolation, according to the Lord’s word: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Matthew XII, 24).

Consider into what hatred the monastic order has fallen at this time among certain evil men, and how greatly they strive at least to extirpate it from bishoprics. Take care, therefore, for the sake of your souls, lest you be the first to be extirpated.

If the policies you have followed until now have produced peace among you, and have enabled you to retain with the greatest diligence in your own hands your lands, from which you must obtain food, clothing, and all necessities, and have preserved with sacred care the ornaments of the Church in which you serve God, so that they might not be dispersed elsewhere, then, my lords, hold fast to those policies and do not wish to abandon them for the favor of any friend.

But if any of these things have worked against you, then, for the sake of almighty God, let no love hold you in them, and let no flattering promise deceive you in any way into remaining in them. Serve God, and He will provide all necessities for you.

Let no one say, “I will not serve God unless I first possess everything that pleases my mind.” For the person who says this demands his reward before he is willing to render the service to which the reward is owed. Anyone possessing reason can see how foolish this is even among human beings.

But you yourselves must see what your holiness should do. I have become foolish by admonishing men better and in every way wiser than I. Yet truly your love compelled me. Farewell, then, and pray for me, and forgive me this fault. May almighty God direct you and your deeds according to His good pleasure. Amen.

[Col. 0809A]

## NICHOLAS’S LETTER TO EADMER

### On the primacy of the see of York in Scotland

*(Warton, Anglia sacra, volume II, p. 234.)*

[Col. 0809A]

To Eadmer, elected by God’s grace to the cathedra of Saint Andrew, his Nicholas wishes an eternal passage from adversity toward joyful and prosperous outcomes.

In the adversities which you mention that you are suffering, patience is especially necessary; next, prudence and diligence are needed to overcome the barbarism of the people, whom you can win over more quickly by the generosity of your lavish giving than by any ingenuity. Hence the blessed apostle Peter also admonished Saint Clement, whom he appointed as his successor, among other things in this way:

“The greatest encouragement for receiving and maintaining love will be if you frequently share common food and a common table among yourselves.”

And shortly afterward:

“For this reason, share your food with those who are brothers according to God. For it is chiefly through these things that love is acquired.”

Nor is it surprising if the untamed barbarism of some people, softened by such services, is bent toward civilized morality, since even the fiercest beasts, devoid of reason, become tame when soothed by nourishment and human attractions, to such an extent that they prefer the companionship of human beings to that of their fellow beasts.

Therefore, as a friend concerned for his friend, I suggest, advise, and urge you to strive to win the affection of everyone toward yourself through generosity, even beyond your means, and through lavish gifts. By such services you can soften the most savage hearts and the barbarism of an untamed people, so that they may love you and accept sound teaching and ecclesiastical discipline. Enough on this matter.

Concerning the primacy of the Church of York over the Scots, about which you asked, there is no authority, no reasoning, and no example apparent that establishes this. For although the Church of York has often borrowed from the Scots the faith and teaching of Christianity, as well as the consecration of bishops, the Scots have never borrowed these from York, except in the matter of Thurgod.

**Note:** Turgod, prior of Durham, was elected bishop of Saint Andrews around the year 1107. When the archbishop of York raised a dispute concerning the subjection of the Church of Saint Andrews, his consecration was delayed for some time. He was finally consecrated after the middle of the year 1109—on the Kalends of August according to the Melrose source—by Thomas of York, at the command of King Henry, without any demand for subjection, while preserving the rights of both churches. After returning to Scotland, he governed the Church for nearly six years. When various disputes finally arose between him and the Scots, he asked the king for permission to go to Rome. Having suffered a refusal, he fell into deep anguish of mind and requested and obtained permission to withdraw to Durham. Returning, therefore, he died in the monastery of Wearmouth in the year 1115, on the day before the Kalends of April, a Tuesday, after having occupied the see for eight years, two months, and ten days. Simeon of Durham reports these matters more fully in *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, p. 207, though he was somewhat mistaken in specifying the time of his death. For in the year 1115, the day before the Kalends of April is Wednesday, not Tuesday.

For after the people of York had apostatized from the faith and expelled their first bishop, Paulinus, who had been ordained for them in Kent, Saint Aidan, a Scot sent and ordained by the Scots, vigorously introduced the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the faith throughout all Northumbria. Thereafter, his successors, the prelates of the Church of York, were all, down to the fourth, ordained, instructed, and sent to that Church by the Scots.

**Note:** Aidan was succeeded by Finan, Colman, and Tuda, all Scots and ordained by the Scots. Although they established the episcopal see at Lindisfarne, they nevertheless governed the whole of Northumbria, that is, the province of York. While these men were seated at Lindisfarne, the see of York remained vacant for approximately thirty years.

One of them, judged useless to that Church because of his indiscretion, was deposed by those same Scots.

[Note: He means Wilfrid the Elder, who was repeatedly driven from his see by the kings of Northumbria. After Wilfrid was first expelled in 678, Eata, a Scot by nationality and abbot of Melrose, was appointed in his place to the see of Lindisfarne. I think this is why Nicholas says that Wilfrid was deposed by the Scots.]

The holy Bede bears witness to all these matters in his *History of the English*. But no history, nor even a tale, teaches that any bishop or teacher was sent or ordained by York for the Scots, apart from the aforementioned Thurgod. Let the Church of York therefore cease claiming and seeking for itself the primacy of Scotland. If it possessed that primacy, then, since the bishop of St Andrews is called the supreme pontiff of the Scots—and “supreme” means only one who is over others—what is one who is over other bishops except an archbishop, even if the barbarism of the people is ignorant of the honour of the pallium?

[Note: The bishops of St Andrews did not obtain the use of the pallium before the year 1472.]

If, I say, the bishop of York held precedence over him who is called the supreme pontiff of his people, then the bishop of York would already be not merely metropolitan, but also primate of another kingdom. Nowhere is this read.

What concern is it of yours who the suffragans of the Church of York are? Let it seek others for itself, not from among you. If it cannot find as many as it thinks it ought to have, let it blame itself; let it not attempt to invade what belongs to another. Indeed, this is attributed to its own negligence, or rather to its greed, that it lacks the proper number of suffragans, especially since its kingdom is sufficiently large and adequate for so many bishops. But the bishops of that Church, enticed by desire for possessions, have laboured more to destroy than to establish suffragan sees.

Hence that Church alone claims for itself the parishes of six bishops, all of whom had been distinguished by definite churches and cathedras. First is the see of York; second, beyond the River Ouse, at the Church of Christ near the city—

[Note: The name of the city is missing in the manuscript. I cannot easily guess which city it was. At that time the archbishop of York claimed that the Churches of Worcester and Lincoln ought to be subject to him. Yet each had its own bishop and rendered obedience to the see of Canterbury when this letter was written.]

third, at Ripon—

[Note: The Church of Ripon had one bishop, namely Eata, whom Theodore, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, placed over the Ripon Church after Ethelred, king of the Mercians, had expelled him from his bishopric at Lindsey.]

fourth, at Beverley—

[Note: I have nowhere read that a bishop’s see was established at Beverley. Yet John, archbishop of York, after consecrating Wilfrid the Younger as his successor, withdrew from York and spent the rest of his life at Beverley. I think Nicholas’s error arose from this.]

fifth, the Church of Hexham—

[Note: Today we do not know the ancient boundaries of the diocese of Hexham. Certainly part of that diocese, together with the episcopal see itself, was swallowed up by the diocese of Durham. The other part seems to have passed under the jurisdiction of York. The bishopric of Hexham came to an end with Bishop Tilred, around the year 821, according to Richard of Hexham, Book I, at the end.]

sixth, Whithorn—

[Note: Ninian, bishop of the Southern Picts, first established the episcopal see at the White House, as Bede testifies in Book III, chapter 4. The bishopric did not change its see after the Picts had been expelled and the English had settled in the region; their first bishop was Pecthelm, around the year 730, according to the same author, Book V, chapter 24. For the province of Galloway, which today is regarded as part of Scotland, was formerly subject to the kings of Northumbria and therefore to the archbishops of York. Indeed, the bishops of Galloway remained suffragans of the Church of York long after the inhabitants had thrown off the English yoke. In the year 1176, Christian, bishop of Whithorn, summoned by Vivian, papal legate, to the council of the Scottish bishops, replied that his bishopric belonged by allegiance to the archbishop of York, who had consecrated him bishop, according to the ancient custom of both Churches, as John Bromton reports in his *Chronicle*, p. 1111. The see may have been vacant for several years in Eadmer’s time. Hence Nicholas writes that the parish of Whithorn had been swallowed up by York. A short time later, that is, after the year 1125, Thurstan, archbishop of York, consecrated Gilla Aldan bishop of Whithorn, as Thomas Stubbs testifies, p. 1720.]

By swallowing up all these Churches and their parishes and incorporating them into its own body, York alone possesses them. It has scarcely left itself two suffragans, namely Lindisfarne, now called Durham, and Cumbria, which John now holds.

But where the see of the bishop of the Picts mentioned by the holy Bede was, I entirely do not know.
