[Note: Bede mentions Northern and Southern Picts: the former converted to the faith by the priest Columba in the year 565; the latter converted much earlier by Bishop Ninian, *History*, Book III, chapter 4. I do not remember a bishop of the Northern Picts being mentioned by Bede, nor did that bishop have any connection with the archbishops of York. The bishop of the Southern Picts, however, was none other than the bishop of Whithorn at the White House, mentioned above.]

Yet it ought to be the eighth suffragan. It has never had more, just as the Church of London has never had any, owing to the negligence of the bishops and the instability of a people that has often apostatized from the faith.

[Col. 0812A]

Behold, insofar as I have been able within the brevity of a letter, I have made these matters clear to you. I would disclose many more things face to face, for they are very necessary. But concerning your affair, hear my advice. Dissolve the dispute between yourself, Canterbury and York, and the princes of England and Scotland; and, with the favour of the king of the Scots, seek consecration from the Apostolic See.

[Note: Eadmer, having been chosen for the bishopric of St Andrews, never obtained the office of consecration. Moved by excessive reverence for the Church of Canterbury, of which he was a monk, he wished to subject the Church of St Andrews to Canterbury and to receive consecration from Archbishop Ralph. Against this, Thurstan, archbishop of York, maintained that the Church of Scotland belonged to his jurisdiction. King Alexander did not wish the Church of his kingdom to be subjected to either English archbishop, and advised Eadmer to go to Rome and obtain consecration from the pope. Nicholas therefore advises the king to be obeyed and the liberty of the Scottish Church to be defended. Eadmer accepted this most prudent counsel of his friend far too late, and consequently lost the dignity. His successor Robert acted more cautiously: he obtained consecration from the archbishop of York without any profession of subjection.]

Carry out energetically the business of your Church and people, and, while you are their bishop, do not let them lose their liberty and dignity. If this pleases you, take care not to pass through the king of England’s territory, and do not let the Church of York learn of it, lest your attempt be obstructed. For my part, I am ready—and I also wish you to tell the king of the Scots this—that, if necessary, I shall argue in the Roman council for the liberty and dignity of the kingdom and Church of the Scots against York.

[Col. 0812B]

Furthermore, I ask and earnestly beg you to acquire for me as many white pearls as you can. You may also acquire any very large pearls; I particularly request that at least four be acquired for me through you. If you cannot otherwise manage it, ask the king for them as a gift—he is the richest of all men in this matter. Farewell.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1108

**Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester**

[Col. 0813]

## Historical Notice on Gundulf

*(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 174.)*

Gundulf, bishop of Rochester from the year 1077, whose biblical codex was sold the preceding year, 1734, in the public auction of the library of the distinguished gentleman Hermann van de Wall at Amsterdam. The codex is a large parchment volume, written quite neatly in two columns, and bearing at the front of the volume and of each of its two parts the following notice:

> First part of the Bible, by Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, of blessed memory. A book from the Rochester cloister. Whoever has removed it from there, concealed that it had been removed, or erased this title fraudulently, is excommunicated, the sentence being pronounced by the bishop, the prior, and each of the priests of the Rochester chapter.

[Col. 0813]

## Life of Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester, by a Contemporary Monk of Rochester

*(Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, II, 273.)*

### The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0813A]

[Note: The life of Gundulf is preserved in the Cottonian manuscript Nero A. 8, an exceptionally elegant codex, only slightly later than Gundulf’s lifetime and adorned with illuminated paintings. Numerous passages indicate that it was written by a monk of Rochester; and in the prologue the author testifies that he lived in familiar association with Gundulf.]

It belongs to those endowed with outstanding talent to transmit the lives of earlier Fathers to posterity as examples of living, if they can say as much as those Fathers were able to do. The great men strove to become great by doing great things; these men strive to become great by writing about great things. Yet there is one supreme Spirit, who inspires the former to be able to do great things and the latter to be able to speak of great things.

Therefore, as I prepare to write the life of the venerable Father Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, I implore that same supreme Spirit who granted him the ability to do great things, so that he may also grant me the ability to relate what such a Father accomplished. Everything that I have proposed to write about him I either saw myself while associating with him, or learned by hearing it from those who saw it or heard it from him.

The prologue ends.

**The Prologue Ends**

### The Life Begins

[Col. 0813B]

In the days of William the First, king of the English, there was a man named Gundulf, venerable in life: a Norman by birth, a cleric from childhood, then a monk, and finally a bishop. He transformed the clerical life through monastic conduct and adorned the monastic life with episcopal dignity.

Since we have determined to pursue his whole life in order in truthful writing, let us say first what he did as a cleric, then what he did as a monk, and finally what he did as a bishop, so that each order may select for itself from his life, worthy of imitation, whatever it should take up for imitation by following the man of God.

[Col. 0815A]

## Part I

Born, then, of his father Hatheguin and his mother Adelesia, he brought distinction by his birth to the diocese of Rouen, in the territory of Vexin. He was given over to letters there when he was already flourishing in boyhood, and was instructed in them, insofar as his age permitted, according to the capacity of his intellect.

When he had grown older and was studying the art of grammar at Rouen, inspired by the divine Spirit he began to devote himself much more to a more useful art: namely, to seek with studious intent how he might best please God, learning from him through inward reading how he might become meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11:29).

While he was still a cleric among clerics, devoted to clerical duties in the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, in that same city, he became an example to the others and offered himself as a model of life. Through his own religious devotion he benefited many who sought the path of holiness.

William, then archdeacon and later to become archbishop of that city of Rouen, saw the young cleric, whose youthful age was beautified by the maturity of his conduct. He made him very close both to Archbishop Maurilius and to himself; and, so that he might often enjoy his conversation, he received him at his common table and into his household.

Sweet conversations often passed between them. They spoke of contempt for the world; they discussed eternal blessedness and blessed eternity; and they desired to endure the labour of the present life in exchange for eternal rest.

[Col. 0815C]

At last, therefore, both agreed that, for the sake of exercising their bodies, they should travel to Jerusalem and visit the holy places for the sake of prayer, so that, having recognized the places of the Lord’s incarnation, passion and ascension, they might afterward retain all these things in sweeter memory.

What had been planned was accomplished: they undertook the hardship of a long journey. Willingly, by land and sea, each endured fatigue amid many dangers. At last they reached earthly Jerusalem, lovers of their heavenly homeland; and when they attained their desire, they counted as nothing whatever they had suffered on the way.

Who could worthily relate with what fires of holy love they worshipped in the places where the feet of the Lord had stood (Psalm 131:7), with what longing they looked upon the lands where the salvation of the human race had lived bodily (Baruch 3:38), or how sweetly they kissed the place where the Lord was crucified, where he died and was buried, and where at last he ascended into heaven?

When the purpose of their holy desire had been fulfilled, their fatigue doubled on the return journey. They encountered the difficult passages of the roads just as they had on the outward journey and, as was then customary, feared the terrifying ambushes of the Saracens. They also suffered intolerable bodily illnesses, and, never having security, passed through no place or time without great fear.

It happened that, while they were suffering on the road, Gundulf was afflicted with such bodily weakness and exhaustion that he could neither stand on his feet nor continue walking with his companions. They therefore went farther on, unknowingly leaving him behind, and, after climbing a certain mountain with difficulty because of its steepness, rested for a little while.

There a nobleman who was travelling with them remembered Gundulf and deeply lamented that they had left him alone. Returning at a swift pace, he found him deprived of all assistance, overcome by weakness, and afflicted as though death were near. Since he had no strength either to walk or stand, the nobleman took him upon his shoulders and, mindful of mercy and every virtue, carried him back to his companions, repeating the laborious ascent of the mountain with great effort.

Then, when heavenly clemency looked upon him, Gundulf recovered within a short time. Throughout the rest of his life he held the venerable man who had given him aid dearer to him, repaying him with worthy gratitude.

[Col. 0816B]

Among the other dangers of land and sea, another, more serious than all the rest, threatened them; yet, by God’s providence, as we believe, it gave them the occasion to change their way of life.

As they were being carried across long stretches of sea in an uncertain vessel, an extremely violent storm broke upon them. The whirlwind of winds and waves shook the ship on every side, its framework already almost coming apart, and struck everyone with the terror of death as though it were already imminent.

What more need be said? Since death was already believed to be at hand, they fled to vows. Begging that the Lord’s mercy might restore calm weather, and, instructed by fear and love of God, promising complete perseverance in the religious life they had begun, Gundulf and the archdeacon preferred the monastic life to all the world’s delights by their vow. Through their devout promise they became monks—though they still remained clerics in habit, not willingly.

When the vow had been made, the storm at sea subsided, calm returned, they reached land, and returned to their homeland.

## Part II

Although the archdeacon delayed fulfilling his vow—which he later fulfilled at Caen—Gundulf put on the religious habit at Bec. He was instructed in the rudiments of monastic life under Abbot Herluin and Prior Lanfranc, and from the very beginning he was counted among the perfect monks.

He was a man of great obedience, severe abstinence, constant prayer, and exceptional contrition. If you looked at his eyes streaming with tears, you would say that they were two fountains overflowing in little streams.

By this power of contrition, through which he mortified himself in prayer and in the celebration of Mass, he became so admirable both in monastic life and afterward in the episcopate, both to the lesser and to the greater, that he was regarded almost as a prophet on earth. Everyone honoured him; everyone called him a servant of God.

He also became keeper and sacristan of the church of Blessed Mary at Bec. Thus he became more familiar with that same undefiled Virgin and her close companion in sacred things. He became more devoted in prayer because the place entrusted to him was more suitable for prayer.

In that same year Anselm, whom we later saw raised to the dignity of the archbishopric of Canterbury because of his notable holiness and remarkable learning, also came to Bec for conversion. He became bound to Gundulf by such friendship that he called himself “another Gundulf” and Gundulf “another Anselm,” and rejoiced to be called so.

For in God they had one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). They frequently conversed about spiritual matters; much pouring forth of tears occurred during their conversations; they mutually encouraged each other always to climb to higher things; and they competed in holiness, anticipating one another in the work of God.

Anselm, however, because he was more learned in the Scriptures, spoke more frequently. Gundulf, because he was more abundant in tears, was more thoroughly watered by weeping. The one spoke; the other wept. The one planted; the other watered. The one uttered divine words; the other drew forth deep sighs. The one acted in Christ’s place; the other in Mary’s.

Yet Anselm once said to Gundulf:

“Do you always seek to sharpen your knife on my whetstone, while you never permit me to sharpen my knife on yours? Tell me also, I beg you, from what source I might progress. For, like a whetstone, because of the multitude of my sins I am always blunted by great dullness. But you, directing your mind and intention ardently toward love of the heavenly homeland, remain continually sharp in contemplation of the Lord.”

And Gundulf said whatever good he was able to say. Both were kindled, and so refreshed one another with the sweetness of heavenly desire. Such was their conversation, such their cloistered life.

Far from their hearts and tongues was detraction of their priors or brothers. They were not troubled, as happens so often to many people, by complaints about food, drink or clothing. And because, possessing contempt for the world perfectly in their lives, they earnestly sought God through abstinence—even rejecting permitted things—and through the practice of holy virtues, therefore, as must be believed without doubt, they deserved truly to attain him.

[Col. 0817C]

Gundulf also became so dear and familiar to Lanfranc, prior of Bec and at that time the most renowned of all men, that when William, duke of the Normans, appointed Lanfranc as the first abbot of the monastery at Caen, he took Gundulf with him, brought him along, and had him as his associate and helper in governing that monastery, because of his holiness and prudence.

When Gundulf’s excellence in virtue increased there from day to day, he also had his natural mother come to that place. Enkindled with holy desire, he established her in the monastery of virgins which Matilda, the wife of that prince and future queen of the English, had built in the same town, under a religious rule.

She persevered ardently in observing the holy rule and the commandments of God and ended her life in that place with an excellent death. Thus the same Father commended to God, through the religious habit and holy living, the mother who had given birth to him for the world.

[Col. 0817D]

Finally, when that same count, having subdued England by arms, was reigning there and had raised Lanfranc to the archbishopric of Canterbury and the primacy of all England, he brought Gundulf with him into England. Since Gundulf was also very industrious in external affairs, the king appointed him administrator of his household.

The reputation of the man of God began increasingly to grow, both for his most holy religious life and for his very prudent administration of secular affairs. He divided the hours of the day with such discernment that at some hours he sat at the Lord’s feet with Mary, and at others prepared the Lord’s supper with Martha (Luke 10:39–40).

He is known always to have possessed this virtue of twofold discernment, both before and during his episcopate: at one time wholly devoted to divine contemplation, at another wholly devoted to caring for the poor.

Once, when a severe famine had powerfully oppressed all England, he went to London with much money received from Lanfranc, gathered an innumerable multitude of poor people, and fed them piously and mercifully throughout the entire period of famine.

It is said that he sympathized so deeply with their misery that he would wash their weaker members; and, after washing his hands, he would immediately go to sing Mass, so that, with their memory still fresh, he might torment himself more severely during the Mass.

Although he was so diligently occupied in caring for the poor, either when some obstacle arose in carrying out the administration of affairs, or when there was no place where, hidden from human eyes, he could devote himself in his customary manner to prayer and tears in the presence of God, he would take a candle at night and go out as though to see whether his horses had been properly cared for.

Sitting beside their manger, or hiding himself in some corner, he placed in heaven what he could not or did not wish to place before the eyes of onlookers in daylight—his labours, watered by sighs of prayer and showers of the sweetest contrition—with greater ardour because in greater secrecy.

[Col. 0818C]

At this time, because sins demanded it, one of the brothers at Christ Church, Canterbury, suffered a mental collapse. Filled with an evil spirit, he became alienated from human senses in word and deed. Bound in chains, he gnashed his teeth and behaved disorderly in many ways.

The brothers said to him: “Be quiet, wretched man, and desist from your madness. If you will not do so for our sake, Lord Gundulf will soon come and restrain the uncontrolled movements of your body and tongue.”

But he replied: “Is that Gundulf who provokes me day and night with his tears and the goads of his prayers? Who, by frequent celebration of Mass, fasting and much mortification of his flesh, torturing his body, continually opposes my works and my will? He persecutes me; I shall certainly persecute him. And from the very thing in which he now takes pride, a serious loss will soon arise for him.”

When this was reported to him—for Gundulf had not been present—the venerable man fortified his life with the armour of righteousness and stood with great strength against the camp of spiritual wickedness. Although on a certain day, during the solemn rites of the Mass, he suffered severe disturbance when the chalice fell, he never ceased praising God or giving thanks.

But because he believed that this had happened through the evil spirit’s promise and his own negligence, he afflicted himself even more severely than before with tears and other holy labours, as though he had previously done nothing in God’s service and were only then beginning the rudiments of heavenly life. From this he rose to the summit of holy exaltation, from which the inventor of deceit had sought to cast him into the abyss of confusion.

The same infirm man was afterward healed through Blessed Dunstan, and Gundulf persevered tirelessly in his holy purpose.

In those days Anselm, a distinguished man in learning and religious life who remained at Bec, heard of Gundulf’s life and the nobility of his deeds. Renewing their ancient friendship, he sent him letters. Whoever hears them will be able, from the testimony and authority of so great a man, to recognize most clearly what affection of holy love existed between them and what Gundulf’s life was like.

And so that the fragrance of their holy fellowship might pleasantly spread forth and shine into the knowledge of those who hear it, the author decided to insert some of Anselm’s letters in this little work, in these words:

> [Note: This letter is found among Anselm’s letters, Book I, Letter 4.]
>
> “To the revered lord, most beloved brother, Lord Gundulf: Brother Anselm sends greetings. When I propose to write to you,” etc.

He also sent him another letter, flowing from the treasury of sacred love, which fortified Gundulf’s mind with an admirable admonition against the deception of empty glory, which sometimes fraudulently insinuates itself beneath the cloak of holy virtues. It reads:

> [Note: It is found in the same place, Book I, Letter 7.]
>
> “To Gundulf, Anselm. For this reason I wished to preface my greeting to a friend with such brevity, because I could not communicate my affection to one so beloved as richly as one beloved should be addressed by one who loves him. For whoever,” etc.

Again, because he knew him to be constant in prayer, that same heavenly instrument, Father Anselm, sent him three prayers—or rather meditations—about Blessed Mary, which he himself had composed under the inspiration of the divine Spirit. He also explained how Gundulf ought to study them through meditation, saying:

> [Note: It is found in the same place, Book I, Letter 20.]
>
> “To Lord Gundulf, Brother Anselm: What Gundulf is to Anselm. There is no need,” etc.

Having heard these things, let the reader understand how great a bond of love joined these Fathers together and what sort of conduct they maintained in earthly affairs during their present life.

## Part III

Let us now try, as best we can, to explain how Gundulf was raised to the pontifical chair, how he lived as a bishop, and by what kind of death he left the Church entrusted to him in sorrow.

While Lanfranc held and wisely administered the highest ecclesiastical dignity in England, the Church of Rochester was deprived of its shepherd when Bishop Ernostus died.

[Note: The Saxon Chronicle reports that Ernostus was consecrated at London by Lanfranc in the sixth year of Lanfranc’s archbishopric, that is, between the end of August 1075 and the end of August 1076. Our anonymous author confirms that he presided over the Church of Rochester for approximately half a year. According to the evidence of the manuscript Canterbury Obituary, he died on the Ides of July. He therefore seems to have been consecrated at the beginning of 1076, at the council held in London in the church of St Paul. William of Malmesbury says that the council was held in 1075, folio 117; Bromton says it was held in 1076, column 975. The former reckons the year from the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin, the latter from the Circumcision of the Lord. The following year, the Saxon Chronicle reports, Gundulf was substituted for Ernostus. This corresponds to the year 1077 of Christ and the eleventh year after the arrival of the Normans, which our historian assigned to Gundulf’s consecration. The day assigned by him fell on a Tuesday in that year, so that Gundulf may rather be considered to have been consecrated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. For it is clear from what follows that he was consecrated on the third Sunday of Lent.]

Ernostus, a monk, had succeeded Seward, himself also a monk, in the bishopric, but had held it for only half a year.

The archbishop, wishing a monk to succeed a monk in the Rochester Church, according to the custom of the ancients, began to consider which monk he could choose above all others, one capable of bearing the burden entrusted to him. As he deliberated, however, Gundulf’s holiness quickly came to mind, for it had already been sufficiently proved to him by certain tests.

After consulting with wise men, he therefore chose Gundulf for the bishopric. To secure the king’s consent to his election, he sent him across the sea to the king.

The king was filled with no little joy, since he had found an opportunity to exalt a man of God, whose holiness had already reached him through sufficiently clear report. He willingly assented to the archbishop’s just requests and judged the man of God most worthy of episcopal honour.

Having therefore received royal authority, Lanfranc summoned the bishops and sent instructions to the leading men of Rochester. He disclosed the will of the king and of himself, and, when everyone gave his assent and rejoiced, he appointed Gundulf as a faithful steward of the house of God by consecrating him.

There was no opportunity for resistance, since the authority of so great a king and so great a bishop pressed upon them. The voice of one crying that he was unworthy was silenced; the more unworthy he proclaimed himself, the more worthy he was acclaimed.

Thus the truly most worthy man, Gundulf, was ordained bishop in the church of Canterbury, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1077, the eleventh year after the arrival of the Normans in England under Count William, later the most noble king of the English.

After his consecration, according to custom, he set out to visit his own see. Amid the rejoicing crowds he entered the city of Rochester, was led to the episcopal seat and enthroned, and from that time onward was regarded by all with the greatest reverence.

Certain possessions of the Church of Rochester were also finally restored to him—possessions that Lanfranc had held under his own authority while Gundulf’s predecessors were bishops. They were restored on the condition that monks should be placed in the Church of Rochester, as both bishops had already decided.

For they had heard that monks had once been there. Returning, therefore, to the ancient statutes, they decreed that an order of monks should be established there.

After a short time had passed, the new church was begun after the old one had been destroyed. The surrounding buildings were suitably arranged, and the whole work was completed within a few years, with Lanfranc supplying large sums of money.

When everything had been completed, some of the only five clerics who were found there embraced the religious habit. Joined by many others, they soon grew under the instruction of Father Gundulf into a number exceeding sixty.

For them Gundulf became a mirror of life and an example of the whole religious vocation. To them he was a rod, strictly correcting childish behaviour; to them a staff, mercifully supporting the aged; to them Martha, providing what was necessary; to them Mary, offering himself as a model of attentive contemplation.

At night and in the morning he was especially Mary in prayer; at other hours he was especially Martha.

O how many tears he shed while praying, watering the Lord’s feet! O with what prudence he conducted himself while arranging external affairs! With what generous hand he provided what was necessary for monks and poor people! O how sweet were the kisses he impressed through prayer in contemplation of heavenly things! O how bitter the sobs he drew forth in remembrance of his sins!

Who saw his eyes wet with tears? Who heard him groaning and did not immediately groan himself? Who looked upon his face troubled by a flood of tears and could gaze at it for long?

When everything had been completed, as has been said, that could be necessary for the servants of God dwelling at Rochester, the same venerable Father, after consulting with wise men, gathered an assembly of monks and clerics together with a large multitude of the people. With great solemnity he approached the tomb of the most holy confessor Paulinus, who had been buried in the old church, and caused the treasure of his holy relics to be transferred to the new church and placed in a suitably prepared location.

Meanwhile, a certain matron was afflicted with a grave illness of mind and body. She promised that, if she could recover her health, she would never again repeat a certain crime by which she was shamefully oppressed. Through the merits of Blessed Paulinus she was restored to health, but she did not keep the promised agreement.

For as soon as bodily health returned, the perversity of that repeated crime soon followed in her life. Later, when her husband had been prevented from dealing with certain necessities, she approached the saint of God to seek his aid, bringing her offering.

But she, whom a shameful conscience inwardly defiled, was driven back, as if by a violent blast, through some force of divine indignation. Leaving her offering scorned, she returned home deeply ashamed and, not long afterward, struck by a serious illness, unhappily awaited her final day.

But the merciful Lord, who despises no one and excludes no one from his mercy, inspired her with his grace. She summoned the venerable Bishop Gundulf to her and, through humble confession, disclosed the foulness of her guilt. From the great contrition of her heart she promised an unbroken perseverance in amendment throughout her life.

What more need be said? On the strength of this promise, the merciful bishop received the sick sheep; the saving remedy of penance was applied. At last, when she had recovered perfect health, she humbly presented herself with her offering to God’s holy servant Paulinus.

Transformed by the renewal of her mind into a pure life, she was not driven away from the saint with her gift. Rather, while the joy of her recovery remained, she returned home cheerfully, giving thanks to God and to Bishop Gundulf, by whose counsel she had been freed from so great a danger.

When his beloved Anselm heard these things and learned that Gundulf had been raised to the episcopate, he wished to strengthen his heart and fortify him against the adversities that sometimes arise by shaking the inner peace of the minds of prelates. He therefore sent him a letter of consolation in these words:

> [Note: It is found among Anselm’s letters, Book I, Letter 69.]
>
> “Formerly my most beloved brother, now my sweetest Father,” etc.

The same Father of sacred love also sent him another token of affection in this letter:

> “His own to his own, friend to friend, brother to brother: Anselm to Gundulf—out of love for happiness, perseverance in holiness; as the reward of holiness, eternity in happiness.”

[Note: It is found in the same place, Book I, Letter 33.]

> “Behold my Gundulf,” etc.

Let us therefore return to what we began to say about so great a Father. For his praiseworthy life most sweetly offers to all who seek God a draught of heavenly sweetness. Indeed, on almost every day he was accustomed to celebrate two Masses, between which he scarcely had a dry eye. The first was either of the Sunday, or a Commemoration of Blessed Mary, or of Blessed Andrew, or of some saint whose memory he especially cherished, or else for familiar friends. The second, however, was for the Dead; he wished no one to be present at it except his monks and certain boys, while the others withdrew. [Col. 0822C] When this Mass was being said straight through, without singing, until after the Gospel—which he himself read—and, after *Dominus vobiscum* had been said, he pronounced *Oremus* in a loud voice, the boys immediately followed, singing the offertory *Domine Jesu Christe*, or *O pie Deus*, in sweet melody. Meanwhile he sat in his seat, attentive to the sweetness of the singing, and wholly dissolved in tears at the sweetness of God. Fixing his mind upon the love of the heavenly homeland, with his eyes raised toward heaven, he was wonderfully nourished by the food of heavenly joy, more than anyone could express. After dwelling on this at length, he finally rose and completed what remained of the Mass.

When this was finished, he sought a secluded place, a friend to sorrow, specially assigned to his prayers. In all his villages [Col. 0822D] where he was accustomed to stay, he had a prayer-cell, and whenever he came there his chamberlain placed his prayer book there. He would therefore devote a long time to prayer, just as he had done before Masses, and he never at any time ceased this alternation of praying and celebrating Masses.

Moreover, whenever he heard some sweet melody, or the sound of a bell ringing melodiously, or anything of that kind, it was his custom immediately to sigh deeply from the depths of his heart and say: “Oh, how great is the joy in heaven, where the praise of God is heard eternally and continually, without interruption! When can a human hand or tongue [Col. 0823A], by its own ingenuity, express harmony of such sonority?” Thus he spoke. Then, if he was in a secluded place, he quickly followed the accustomed discipline of compunction.

And what shall we say? How pure was his holy reverence and earnestness in hearing or reciting the service of the Lord! Rarely, when the second nocturn was being recited, did he sit, unless severe illness or great weariness had compelled him to do so. The same was true after they began to say *Laudate Dominum de coelis* until the end of Matins, and likewise at Lauds concerning all the saints.

With what heartfelt attentiveness and fervor of divine love did he recall the memory of the Lord’s Passion! He constantly kept it in mind. He imitated it, afflicting and subduing his flesh [Col. 0823B] by many fasts and sometimes by the harsh mortification of scourging. He also said to us:

“What shall we do, my brothers? What shall we say when the Lord comes? Certainly we know that our Lord Jesus Christ, solely through the mercy of his compassion, without any preceding merits of ours, redeemed us from eternal death through the Passion of the Cross. This is what he did for us; and what do we do for him? What return do we make to him for such great honor? Dying for us, he endured five wounds; five times each day we ought to weep as we recall this most sweetly in the memory of our hearts. And if, because of our weakness—which corrupts us in many ways—we cannot do this so often, at least let us shed five tears each day in remembrance of him.”

In these practices the bishop passed his days [Col. 0823C], deserving praise. On account of all this, therefore, he was regarded as admirable by all and beloved by all. Many gave him many things, but he too gave much to many: sometimes greater gifts to lesser persons because of their need, and lesser gifts to greater persons because of his affection. The lesser, enriched by his gift, believed themselves safer; the greater, safer still. For who ever wore on his finger a ring, however small, given to him by the bishop and did not believe himself more secure? Who commended himself to his prayers and did not depart from him reassured?

When Lanfranc heard that the servant of God was increasing so greatly in virtue and that the fame of his holiness was being raised even to the stars, he was filled with no little joy that so great an ornament of the Church had proceeded from his household. He gladly enjoyed Gundulf’s conversation whenever he summoned him or [Col. 0823D] Gundulf came of his own accord. Yet he scarcely ever sent him away empty-handed, but gave him gifts—sometimes copes, sometimes precious candlesticks, sometimes other ornaments of ecclesiastical splendor.

On one occasion, however, when he had sent him away empty-handed and feared that he might be upset because of it, he said to his attendants: “I fear that the bishop has departed from us displeased. Something must therefore be sent to him that may be acceptable to him.” Accordingly, after preparing certain great gifts worthy of ecclesiastical decoration, he hastened to send them to him, humbly asking him to deign to pray for him to Blessed Andrew, whose vicar he was. He had such great confidence in that apostle that, whenever he sent some special gifts through the bishop, he would earnestly beg him to sing one *Dominica*—that is, one Lord’s Prayer—for him before the altar [Col. 0824A] of that apostle.

Thus the Church of Rochester became very wealthy, chiefly through the gifts of the archbishop himself and also through the many offerings of others.

Afterward, when the Church had been enriched with so many possessions that one portion could suffice for the bishop and another for the monks, it pleased the bishop, and it pleased Lanfranc as well, that the bishop should have his own property separately and that the monks should likewise have their possessions separately. This was done above all so that no bishop in a later age who did not love the monks so greatly might be able to diminish the property divided among them.

Because the monks, being already numerous, needed more—both for their food and clothing and for receiving guests [Col. 0824B]—it was wisely provided again that the monks should possess more and the bishop fewer possessions. Which possessions were the greater ones is set out clearly enough in a charter kept in the Church of Rochester, confirmed by the authority of the kings and nobles, as well as of the bishops of England. It was very easy for the man of God to obtain this from everyone. For none of the kings who reigned in England in his time possessed the power to rule without fearing to offend him.

After the most noble king of the English, William, had died at Rouen, his son William succeeded him in the kingdom. Having received the kingdom, he was burdensome and less agreeable to many because of certain unusual oppressions and the weight of many affairs; nevertheless, he held Father Gundulf in greater veneration than all the bishops [Col. 0824C], having learned from the reports of many that the life of the man of God had long been tested in devotion to heavenly love.

Although in other matters he troubled certain people with various exactions, throughout all his days he kindly spared Father Gundulf and the Church of Rochester. Indeed, he not only spared them, but also greatly and liberally increased the bishop’s possessions with a generous hand. Out of special affection for him, he first granted permission for two manors—Haedreham and Lambeth—to be given, and then bestowed the second through his own generosity.

Lanfranc the archbishop had acquired Haedreham through his own labor and money; the same village had not belonged to the ancient possessions of the archbishopric. With the king’s favor, he granted it to Bishop Gundulf and his Church, to be possessed by them in its entirety for all future time. Lambeth, however, the same king gave [Col. 0824D] of his own free will, as compensation for the damage that the Church of Rochester had suffered during the siege made at that place against Odo, bishop of Bayeux.

When the king was besieging that same Odo in the city, together with other men of the greatest power, because Odo had provoked against him something more than civil war by favoring Count Robert, he nevertheless allowed the man of God both to leave freely and, whenever he wished, to enter the city freely. Gundulf conducted himself between the two sides with such prudence that he pleased the besiegers and was not suspected by the besieged. Why was this so, except that he was believed to possess such holiness that he would harm neither the besieged nor the besiegers? Indeed [Col. 0825A], he was regarded as a friend to both and, because of his religious character, as beneficial to both.

After his enemies had been defeated, the same prince and the other nobles of the kingdom honored him with extraordinary veneration, observing in him especially now the tearful sighs of Mary, now the laborious services of Martha. For who was more attentive to practicing Martha’s labor after Mary’s repose? Who was more diligent in nourishing Christ in his members with food, drink, and clothing?

Often, when he sat at table, he would not touch the food he knew to be more delicate, but immediately sent it to those whom he had learned were in greater need. He carefully inquired who were the poorer and who the weaker people to be found in the village or outside it. Such was the conversation at table; such the discussion of the needs of the poor. [Col. 0825B] To the hungry he sent food; to the thirsty, drink. To those in need of both, he mercifully sent both.

If he had tasted even a little of the food in his own bowl and sensed that it was especially fine, he would often hasten to send it to some sick person, saying that person was more worthy of such nourishment. If he was told of some poor woman who was pregnant or had recently given birth, he gave her all the more generously what was necessary, lamenting their misery.

Moreover, when he dined in his hall, he arranged for at least thirteen poor people to be fed each day, in addition to those prebendaries whom he always maintained at different places. He also took the greatest care to clothe the naked—or rather, to ensure that they would not be naked, especially in the winter season. He ordered many kinds of clothing to be obtained and distributed them to poor men and women according to the needs of each. [Col. 0825C]

He was so compassionate toward their misery that once, as he advanced not far from Rochester, he saw a broad piece of land suitable for bearing crops but overgrown with trees and brambles. Since it belonged to his monastery, he decided, by applying diligent labor, to make it fruitful instead of unproductive for the benefit of the servants of God.

And so that he might not appear before God to be without a share, as though empty-handed, in the reward of this work, on the appointed day he came there with his people. He humbly took a spade in his own hands, which much abstinence had made sufficiently thin, and, undertaking the first labor, the pious farmer pulled out the first thistles and thorns. Then, encouraging his household [Col. 0825D] and the other workers, he soon completed through their hands the fulfillment of his desire. In this way he entrusted the cultivation itself to his almoner, to be held thereafter always for the poor.

These and many other works of mercy he continually bestowed upon those suffering want, as a diligent guardian of the house of his Lord.

In the time of this prince, William the Younger, in the second year after the siege of Rochester, Lanfranc, that distinguished doctor of Christ’s Church, was taken from this life on the fifth day before the Kalends of June [28 May], leaving many—and especially Father Gundulf—sad and gravely desolate at his death.

By the king’s command and according to the custom of the Church of Rochester, Gundulf, a prelate worthy of mention, therefore undertook the care of the archbishopric in matters pertaining to God. [Col. 0826A] He had also held this responsibility during Lanfranc’s lifetime, by Lanfranc’s own order and favor. For Lanfranc rarely performed church dedications, clerical ordinations, or the confirmations of groups of boys in person; instead, he would send his beloved Gundulf in his place and amicably order him to perform these duties.

In those days a vigorous abbot named Guido presided over the monastery of Saint Augustine, the apostle of the English. After completing for the most part the church that his predecessor had begun, he decided that the bodies of Saint Augustine and his companions should be transferred from the ancient church to higher places. Having prepared everything that seemed necessary for so great a ministry, he summoned several men of the highest probity, and especially Father Gundulf. Through the working of Gundulf’s [Col. 0826B] holiness, he completed what had been planned with the greatest rejoicing and deepest devotion.

At that time it was almost customary in England that whenever especially important dedications or translations of holy relics were to take place anywhere, Gundulf was summoned quickly, so that the majesty of such matters might be handled through the purity of his hands. While other bishops rejoiced on such occasions in the gifts given by those who summoned them, as though in payment of thanks, Gundulf rejected this with every effort; instead, in return, he often gladdened the hearts of those who summoned him through his own generosity.

After this, when about four years had passed since Lanfranc’s death, King William was seized by a serious illness and caused almost the entire people [Col. 0826C] of England to become uncertain of his life, with little hope of his recovery.

At that time Father Anselm, whom we mentioned above and who was then abbot of Saint Mary of Bec, had come to England because of certain pressing necessities. The bishops and princes of the kingdom, seeing the danger threatening the king, as well as the desolation and oppression of the Churches, especially that of Canterbury, humbly implored him to appoint a primate for them in so great a crisis.

And so it happened. The king heard their counsel, and, with his consent, by the provident grace of God they all together chose Anselm. They summoned the chosen man and, although he resisted with all his strength, appointed him archbishop.

Gundulf, therefore, who had willingly cooperated [Col. 0826D] in this matter, ardently embracing in the bosom of holy sweetness the long-desired presence of his beloved friend, received with an exhilarated heart the refreshment of inward consolation that he had lost for so long because of Lanfranc’s death.

As for what Anselm’s life was like before and during his episcopate, and what adversities or exiles he endured in his time, like a most steadfast soldier of the Lord, in order to secure the liberty of Holy Church, anyone who wishes to know fully can find a sufficiently clear account in the writings published about his life, his admirable teaching, and his holiness. Let us return to our subject.

Just as these two illustrious princes of the earth, Gundulf and Anselm, had loved one another at the beginning of their conversion at Bec, so, at the ends of the earth, through heavenly clemency joining their bishoprics, they were not separated. [Col. 0827A]

When the other bishops withdrew from communion with Anselm because of certain occasions of discord that had arisen between him and the princes of the kingdom, Gundulf always clung to him sweetly, firmly, and faithfully. Prudently conducting himself between both sides, he preserved complete loyalty to the archbishop in their disputes and in no way offended his adversaries.

Thus, having received the consolation of their former affection, these lovers of the heavenly homeland—whom the distances of land and sea had separated for a long time—were joined together. They did not delay in refreshing one another, now as revered bishops in England, with the sweet conversations of eternal life by which they had formerly been accustomed to refresh one another as monks in the cloister.

They often [Col. 0827B] met in different places and kindled one another’s love for God through mutual conversation. The archbishop, however, more frequently kindled the fire of divine love by speaking, while the bishop, by remaining silent, warmed himself more closely at that already-kindled fire.

On one occasion the bishop asked whether the archbishop attended equally to and retained equally all the things that were said in church. He replied: “I want to retain everything I hear, and so I attend to everything; but, because I want to grasp everything at once, these things more often escape my mind.”

The bishop answered him: “Quite rightly, the one who embraces everything through desiring everything loses everything.” He spoke as though making a play on the words. Then he continued:

“I, however, do not attend equally to everything I hear. Rather, from everything I choose one thing that is more [Col. 0827C] dear to my heart. Clinging to it more attentively, I draw from it some sweetness of heavenly love. It is like what happens when several kinds of food are offered to a sick person: he does not choose all of them, but selects from them one that pleases him more, perhaps an apple, so that by tasting it he may obtain some remedy for his illness.”

So he spoke. But we, who knew his life sufficiently well by experience and by hearing, often observed that this had always been his practice. For sometimes, when he heard sung in church, “Afflicted for our sins, we continually await our end with tears,” or, “That day, the day of wrath,” or something else similarly suited to compunction, he immediately disregarded everything else and devoted himself solely to what he had heard and found most acceptable. Raising his eyes toward heaven [Col. 0827D], he repeated it two, three, or four times with sighs, and wholly dissolved into groans and tearful cries.

We watched him, and we too were compelled to dissolve at least into tears or groans. What happened when he was preaching to the people? Sometimes, when tears interrupted him, he himself could not speak, and the people, attending to nothing except his weeping or groaning, could do nothing else either. The words ceased; the tears completed the sermon.

This happened especially when, on the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, he preached to the people about her repentance or tears. Speaking of her repentance, he urged the people to repent. Recounting her tears, he himself wept and inflamed the others to tears.

He loved her with a certain special affection and always endeavored to celebrate her memory both by daily commemoration and by an annual solemnity. Since [Col. 0828A] he believed himself to be a great sinner, he said that she, who had been a great sinner, knew better what was especially necessary to a great sinner, and believed that she more greatly desired to show mercy.

He therefore continually attended her with prayers and entreated her with tears. He set her before the others as one to be followed, and showed in himself how greatly she ought to be followed.

“O teacher worthy to be followed! What he taught the others to do, he first did himself, so that the others might follow him! O bishop worthy to have obtained his episcopate not through money but through tears!”

Some become bishops by imprudently displaying a pretense beneath the veil of religion; [Col. 0828B]; this man became a bishop by pouring forth many tears from his heart. Yet he made this very fact a subject of tears for himself, namely, that he had become a bishop by displaying a certain appearance of religion. He would say:

“Woe to me, a sinner, because just as some buy the episcopate by the expenditure of money, so I have obtained it through the less cautious display of a certain holiness! O empty glory, what have I to do with you, and what have you to do with me? Why do you urge me to display as mine what is not mine? Rather, since it is nothing, why do you persuade me to display it as though it were something? What can you find in me by which you may rightly exalt me? When you find no material for exalting me, why do you seek to exalt me? You could have approached Archbishop Lanfranc while he lived, or now other men of the highest probity, if you wish to find people worthy of being exalted. There [Col. 0828C] you find wisdom together with knowledge; there riches together with power. There you find men adorned in many ways with the instruments of holy virtues and able to resist most steadfastly your deceitful and malicious schemes. Leave me, a sinner who possesses none of these things, in whom you can find nothing but sin.”

He also added that he greatly feared that what he had heard had happened to a certain man might happen to him. When that man came to his final moment and was about to breathe out his last breath, he said: “O empty glory, how many have you destroyed, of whom I am one!”

Thus he earnestly avoided empty glory, yet feared with no less earnestness that he might not avoid it. He often disputed with it, therefore, as has been said, as with some adversary, in order to drive it away from himself, lest, when all praised him for the merit of his praiseworthy life, it should somehow creep into him.

For who could remain untouched by elation [Col. 0828D] when the nobles of the kingdom, preferring him to other bishops, approached him and sought his friendship; when they familiarly exposed their own sins to him and did not doubt that through him they would become more absolved; when, on the day they were able either to kiss his hand or at least to see him, they believed themselves finally safer?

Indeed, I heard a bishop of good reputation and a lover of truth report that, when he was tormented in his youth by the gravest impulses and temptations of the flesh, as sometimes happens, he had disclosed the clouds of his passions in their entirety to Gundulf with a pure heart, and that ever afterward he had been freer from such impediments to sin through Gundulf’s counsel and prayer.

Such things were said about Gundulf. [Col. 0829A] He himself, however, did not seek himself in the mouths of men; rather, he carefully investigated what he was within himself. They exalted him by raising up his merits; he humbled himself by recalling his sins. Whenever he was carried outside himself by empty praise, he sought and found himself through daily contemplation and quickly returned to himself by guarding humility.

Having said something about his character, let us now turn our pen to the sequence of his works.

After taking counsel with wise men, and with the venerable Archbishop Anselm especially favoring him and providing assistance in many matters, the man of God arranged for a monastery of women [Col. 0829B] to be built on his own estate, in the place called Mellingas, just as he had built a monastery of men in the city of Rochester.

Beloved by both sexes, he strove to benefit both sexes in religious devotion. At the aforesaid place he established a church in honor of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, together with certain buildings arranged as circumstances permitted. With as much diligence as he could, he gathered there a community of nuns, instructing them inwardly with assiduous teaching and providing outwardly, through careful industry, what was necessary for their life.

He took great care that what would benefit their souls should always be fully available to them, and that what their bodies required should never be lacking. He appointed as their prioresses or guardians spiritual mothers chosen from other monasteries. He acquired revenues or lands wherever he could, and took care to adorn their church with varied decoration. [Col. 0829C]

As a result, many noblewomen rejoiced to place themselves under his direction, hoping to obtain through his holiness what, because of the frailty of their own bodies, they could not obtain through their own efforts. He did not initially wish to appoint an abbess over them, but for several years preferred to govern them by his own care.

During those days, great disputes and complaints arose between Father Anselm and the king concerning the liberty of the Church, and Anselm, having left England, lived in exile at Lyon. After several years, however, it happened that the king was struck by an arrow and died a terrible death, and that his brother Henry was raised to the heights of the kingdom.

Henry immediately [Col. 0829D] recalled Anselm to his homeland and, as his predecessors had done, honored the praiseworthy Gundulf with extraordinary veneration, observing in him the holiness of a life long tested and the security of the great devotion and fidelity that Gundulf displayed toward him in prosperity and adversity alike.

When affairs were thrown into confusion by the change of kings, certain princes of the kingdom, showing little loyalty to the security of the new king, caused his authority to totter, as far as they could, through deceitful schemes, scorning submission to him. Gundulf, perceiving such great disturbances, labored intensely to establish bonds of peace between the king and his adversaries.

He therefore often visited the disturbers of peace in person [Col. 0830A], showing them through sacred admonitions what great evils commonly arise from an abundance of discord, and what evil those deserve who become followers of such a scandal. He also showed how close to God and united by kinship with the holy angels are those who receive the seeds of peace in their hearts and make them visible through the execution of their works.

After hearing this, some of them, considering the innocence and holiness of the man of God, devoutly accepted his salutary advice, established concord with the king, and promised thereafter to keep the bonds of peace.

Because of this he became beloved by the king and the princes of the kingdom. Whenever mention was made in the palace or elsewhere, during their conversations, of other nobles of the land, Gundulf was regarded among them not as an equal but as a superior and almost as a father.

The prudent Father, seeing that he had a suitable opportunity and time [Col. 0830B] in which he could benefit both his monasteries in some way, handed over to those same sons of his—the monks—the revenues and possessions that had formerly been separated from his own. These had been confirmed by the authority of King Henry, the nobles of the kingdom, Archbishop Anselm, Gundulf himself, and the other bishops of England, and had been sanctioned by their charter.

It was then decreed that whoever should violate this arrangement by rash presumption, unless he corrected the offense by worthy satisfaction, would be struck by the sword of anathema and receive, together with the traitor Judas, the sentence of condemnation.

At Mellingas, where he had built the women’s monastery, the same village had from ancient times been open country and was rarely inhabited. With the favor of King Henry’s grace, Gundulf made it populous enough, as crowds flowed in from every direction and established their homes there. At that place, as can be seen today, he created a very large village suitable for merchants and useful to the nuns.

Moreover, the noble English queen [Col. 0830C] Mathilda, wife of that prince Henry, having learned of the reverence due to the man’s praiseworthy life and the dignity of his good works, became very familiar with his holiness. She frequently had him come to her and desired to be tirelessly satisfied by his salutary conversation.

She embraced such love for him that, when she had borne a son, she entrusted the child especially to him to baptize and lift from the sacred font. And so it was done.

Thus he was dear to the king and queen [Col. 0830D], and dear also to all the people of England. For when many people were bound to the king or queen by some impediment, Gundulf, summoned by those who were hindered, confidently approached them as a merciful intermediary and often obtained from them the aid of mercy and relief for those who requested his help.

He served God under three kings, dear and acceptable to all of them. Under the first King William, with Lanfranc’s support, he built the Church of Rochester; under the second, he increased it with certain lands; under King Henry, the son of the first and brother of the second, he distinguished and confirmed the monks’ property from the king’s own property by a charter of royal authority.

The first king willingly approved him as he built, the second as he enlarged, and the third as he confirmed; all rejoiced to cooperate with the man of God in his good work.

But how, under the third king, God granted his beloved servant [Col. 0831A] that from this point the Lord’s inheritance should begin for him, I shall now begin to relate, lest by saying too much about what remains to be said I weary the reader. So that this may seem incredible to no one, let all who will hear these things know that, under the testimony of truth, the works of his compunction and mercy were far greater than these.

About one year, more or less, before his death, he began to be chastised by a father’s scourge, oppressed by a serious illness, and increasingly deprived of bodily strength day by day. He was also afflicted by excessive pain in the head, caused, as they said, by the excessive and continual shedding of tears.

He could no longer celebrate the solemn rites of Mass as usual, pour forth rivers of tears, or render his customary measure of prayers. Nevertheless, as far as he could, he strove to overcome his illness by maintaining his good habits.

Since he could not celebrate two Masses as before [Col. 0831B], he first at least tried to celebrate one for as long as he was able. Though he could not perform the whole measure of his prayers, he nevertheless rendered what he could, with tears.

He ordered many alms to be distributed throughout his villages, prudently arranging for some to be set aside so that they might suffice his successor for a long time. When he heard that his beloved and principal friend, Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury, had said that it was not proper for a dying bishop to distribute all the ecclesiastical property entrusted to him, but that he should reserve something for the use of his successor, Gundulf said:

“I give thanks to God, because he has supplied me with such abundant means that I can relieve the needs of the poor and provide my successor—even if he has as many as thirty additional men with him—with an abundance of landed revenue.”

Thus, as he had begun, he continued his fatherly care for the poor until death [Col. 0831C], yet he did not impoverish his bishopric by showing compassion to the poor. Like a faithful and prudent steward, he distributed in the present what was necessary to the servants of his Lord and wisely reserved for the future what could be distributed abundantly.

When the venerable archbishop learned of his prudence, he praised with rejoicing the pious and discerning desire expressed in his distribution, and gave thanks to God for his continuing perseverance in goodness.

And truly his persevering devotion in just works deserved praise. For although he was so weak that he could not even sit on a horse, but had to be carried from village to village in a carriage prepared with two horses whenever necessity required, immediately upon arriving he brought the needs of the poor back to mind, especially those of his prebendaries, whose care he watched over most attentively.

Not fully trusting his attendants [Col. 0831D]—that, in his absence, they had cared for them according to his wishes—he forced himself, setting aside the burden of his illness so that he might complete what he had planned more privately. Toward evening, lest he be recognized by people, and while we looked on in amazement, he was lifted by the hands of his attendants onto a horse. Taking with him only one monk and two servants, he personally visited the cells of the infirm, including those who were wasting away from gout and elephantiasis.

Entering inside and sitting before their rooms [Col. 0832A], he carefully inquired into their needs. With tears pouring from his eyes and compassion for their misery, he supplied each one, according to that person’s condition, with what was needed in food and clothing.

And what shall we say of his guardianship of humility? In the hidden chambers of the king’s daughter, “whose whole glory is within” (Psalm 44:14), he placed the treasures of his virtues under the key of humility, so that he might receive their fruits on the day of need; he did not wish to exalt himself above himself.

To give one example among many: in that very year, on the solemnity of All Saints, after he had celebrated the festive Mass in the principal church at Rochester, he became somewhat disturbed, almost as if angry, over something displeasing to him. One of the brothers who was familiar with him stood beside him and said:

[Col. 0832B] “What is the matter, Father? What causes this disturbance? Why is the serenity of your heart troubled? The whole population of this city is rejoicing today with the greatest delight at the recovery of your strength, as they hope, because your long-desired voice has sounded in their ears—and you are troubled?”

He answered: “Is the people applauding for me?” Repeating this question several times, while sobs and tears interrupted his voice, he remained silent for a long while, absorbed in the thought. Then he said:

“Oh, who is there who ought to rejoice for me? Behold, held by serious illness, I am dying; and what worthy of praise have I done throughout my entire life? Even a single spark of fervor and love of God, such as would have been fitting, have I never been able to grasp, though I have lived so long.”

By developing these thoughts at length [Col. 0832C], he did not cease to fortify his life most prudently, to the very end, with the weapons of justice and mercy.

As the burden of his illness later grew heavier, his dear friend Father Anselm came to him. Seeing that he was beginning to enter upon the way of all flesh, Anselm first heard his pure and simple confession, then absolved him from all his sins in the place of Blessed Peter, and, according to custom, most devoutly anointed him with the oil of sacred unction.

The bishop entrusted both himself and the sons whom he had gathered to Anselm’s venerable hands, asking him both to commend to God in his prayers the man who was departing from this world and, in his place, to guard pastorally those of us whom he was leaving in this age.

At the pious words of the Father, tears arose and flowed from both men [Col. 0832D]; the cheeks of the sons standing around them were wet. Long sighs were drawn, and the unbearable prospect of bereavement was anticipated.

When the office of sacred unction had finally been completed, the archbishop departed, perceiving from certain signs that Gundulf would live for some time yet.

The bishop, however, later fearing that death was already near, preferred to die not as a bishop in the more exalted house, but as a monk among monks in a humbler place. He therefore ordered his attendants to lift him up and carry him to the church of Blessed Andrew the Apostle, whose vicar he was.

There [Col. 0833A], dissolved in tears and groans, he prayed to the merciful apostle of God to take pity on him in his mercy, since he was utterly uncertain whether he would ever return again to his church. He asked that Andrew absolve him from his sins, grant him permission to depart after giving him his blessing, and watch over that place and the monks gathered for his service with vigilant care.

After pouring forth these and similar prayers with a devout mind, he had himself carried to the house of the infirm, so that he might give up his spirit among the hands of the monks. Nevertheless, he survived there for some time afterward, in great contrition of heart and body.

On those same days, when, as he lay bedridden, certain persons urged him to appoint the prioress of the monastery of Melling as abbess above the others, so that, after his death, that place would not remain without governance, nor would someone with no interest in it seize authority over it for himself, he said: “Why do you compel me to do this, when, behold, I am dying? I utterly do not know whether it pleases God.” Yet when the necessity of a just reason had been demonstrated, and those giving counsel had read aloud in his presence the authority of the king and the archbishop conveyed in their letters, [Col. 0833B] with many people standing around his bed, he took the pastoral staff and handed it to that prioress, appointing her the first abbess of that place. She then swore canonical obedience and submission to the bishop and to the Church of Rochester, and swore that neither by herself nor through another would she attempt to withdraw that monastery from subjection to Rochester.

Afterward, provident in every respect, he deliberately distributed to brothers and the needy his clothes and whatever small and poor garments he possessed, down to his leggings, as a free monk, freeing himself from every shameful burden of property. Fearing also to wear the episcopal ring, he entrusted it to a certain brother who served him constantly. When some people asked him to give the same ring to a certain religious man, an abbot—namely, the abbot of Bello—who was staying with him in expectation of his end, he replied: “He is a monk; neither he nor the ring belongs together.”

In those days there was in England a man famous for his great reputation and religion, named Ralph, abbot of Séez. Expelled from his monastery by the harassment of a certain tyrant, he remained with Father Anselm, not as an exile but as a compatriot; he was very well known to Gundulf. Hearing that his friend was ill, he came to him, already awaiting his final day among the sick. After sweet conversations about heavenly life, Ralph received permission for their final separation and his departure. As he proceeded away, shedding abundant rivers of tears on either side, [Col. 0833D] and had reached the doorway of the house, the bishop summoned the brother to whom he had meanwhile entrusted his ring, received it from him, and immediately added: “Call the abbot.”

The man who had been summoned returned, and, at the bishop’s command, after everyone else had withdrawn, the bishop took the abbot’s hand and put the ring into it. Terrified and astonished at this strange event, the abbot said: “What is this, Father Lord? It is not proper to my station to possess a ring; for I am a monk in habit, though not in life. Therefore I fear being burdened with a thing unnecessary to me.”

The bishop replied: “Take it. It will be necessary to you. And do not persist in disobeying by refusing to receive it, since it is fitting that what I wish should be done.” Then the abbot, greatly wondering and entirely unaware of the hidden reason for this act, took the ring and departed. After Gundulf’s death, however, the obscurity of this action became clear, as will be revealed shortly when we set out the matter in its proper order. [Col. 0834A]

Some time afterward, on a certain day he ordered the community to assemble and requested that, in the sight of everyone and on behalf of all his sins, bodily discipline be administered to him. But the brothers, considering his great weakness, thought this a dreadful thing to do. They replied that they could not do this to him, but that they were all willing to do the same to themselves on his behalf.

And so it was done. Behold, on the following Saturday the venerable Father, overcome by the nearness of death, began to grow very weak. Nevertheless, on that very day he ordered certain works of mercy to be performed for those in need. At the Mass celebrated in the chapel of the sick while he listened, he directed his attention most devoutly; and when the Gospel was being read, he had himself raised in reverence for so great a mystery. When evening came, he became mute and, awaiting the hour of midnight, lay without speech but not without awareness. After Matins had been said in his presence, with the portions pertaining to the day and all the Hours of the Blessed Mary, he finally began to draw his last breath.

The customary signal having been struck, and he himself having been laid upon sackcloth, the monks hastened together with the utmost speed. After the Creed had been recited, they began the commendation of the soul, singing psalms and the litany. With tears and prayers they accompanied the Father’s soul as it departed and returned to its Creator. While there was some delay during this fearful expectation, and the brothers were praying and singing psalms, they had reached the seventy-ninth psalm, saying [Col. 0834C] around the words: “God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine,” when, at sunrise, the Father’s spirit left his body. He left to the protection and visitation of the supreme Creator the vine he himself had planted—namely, the congregation of his Church, which he had instructed in many ways in the pursuit of heavenly discipline.

As for the body that remained, incredible to relate, they saw it grow white with a marvelous radiance, although they had always been accustomed to see it black by nature. They therefore attributed the whitening of his hands to the abundance of his almsgiving; and they attributed the whitening of his entire body to the outpouring of his tears and to his holy life. They washed him with the reverence due to his honor, clothed him in pontifical garments, and with weeping and singing carried him into the church of the blessed apostle Andrew, where they laid him before that saint’s altar. [Col. 0834D]

A messenger was immediately sent to announce to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, the death of his dear friend, and to ask him to come and pay the final service of friendship to the body. When Anselm received the message, he came as quickly as possible to Rochester and, carrying out all the rites for his friend’s funeral with sufficiently fitting reverence, as befitted episcopal dignity, buried him before the altar of the Crucified One in the church that Gundulf himself had built from its foundations.

Oh, how great meanwhile was the mourning of the monks whom he himself had gathered! Oh, how great the weeping of the holy women whom he too had withdrawn from the world! Oh, how great the lamentation of the people, over whom he had so often poured his blessing! Oh, how great the groaning of the poor, whom he had fed with fatherly affection! Oh, how great the grief of all whom the good shepherd had governed without complaint for thirty-one years!

This venerable Father died on the eighth day before the Ides of March, on the third Sunday of Lent, when the Office “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” is sung (Psalm 24:15). The same passage was also sung at his consecration, so that through this as well the Lord might indicate to all the pursuits to which his life in the present age had been devoted. He passed well from this world on that day, because, in accordance with what has been said, his eyes were continually fixed upon the Lord through the grace of compunction. Therefore, as we must believe, in recompense for his good works, his feet were drawn out of the snare of miseries (Psalm 24:15), with which the present life abounds.

It was then the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eighth year of the reign of Henry, king of the English, and he was approximately eighty-five years old; he had been a monk for fifty-one years and a bishop, as stated, for thirty-one years.

Some time after the death of our Father had passed, Archbishop Anselm began to consider whom he could appoint as bishop in his place. Taking counsel—a counsel which, as we believe, came forth from the face of God, as we said above—he chose the venerable Ralph, abbot of Séez, for the bishopric of Rochester, with everyone’s support. Once chosen, and with all rejoicing, he devoutly consecrated him according to custom as bishop of that place.

When Ralph had become bishop, he then first understood the significance of the hidden gift of the ring: while still alive, Gundulf had specifically designated it for him after it had been refused to another. Thus it appears that Gundulf possessed foreknowledge during his life of who ought to be raised after him to the pontifical office in his place.

This Ralph, after governing the Church of Rochester for nearly six years, was transferred to the archbishopric when Anselm died. In his place he appointed Ernulf, a man highly worthy of praise, long tested in literary knowledge and religion, formerly prior of Canterbury but then abbot of Burgh. Received by his people with complete approval, on the very day of his election he said to us:

“I knew, brothers, a few days ago that, although unworthy, I was soon to be promoted to the dignity of this office. For, while I was still in my own place, Father Gundulf appeared to me in sleep, offering me a ring of great weight. When my weakness seemed unable to bear its heaviness, and I was foolishly refusing to accept the burden, he rebuked me; after rebuking me, he compelled me to receive the ring. Then he disappeared.”

This is what he said. But we who were present and heard these things from him later understood that the holy man’s dream had not been a fantastical illusion: afterward, when Ernulf became bishop of Rochester, he received the same ring which Bishop Gundulf, while alive, had given to Ralph when he was still an abbot but was destined to become a bishop. [Col. 0836A]

We have now discussed the life of Father Gundulf at greater length in prose, though previously we had briefly gathered it into a few heroic verses. We have decided to append those verses here as well, because we know that some find the force of meter more pleasing than prose. They are therefore twenty lines, arranged in the order written below: [Col. 0836B]

You, Father Gundulf, were born of Normandy your mother,

You spurned the world and sought the cloister of Bec.

The monks’ habit clothed you; the Rule governed you.

It governed and raised you, and no crooked way turned you aside.

First you helped the men of Bec, afterward those of Caen.

You crossed the sea and pleased Lanfranc,

The greatest of teachers, the foremost of teachers.

By his gift bestowed, you governed the pontificate.

You founded the temple and adorned it with gifts.

You gathered the monks whom you placed here.

You lived as their father, and as the father of the peoples.

Both the great and the small loved you.

You were the solace of sinners and the refuge of the wretched.

You lived generous toward the poor and sparing toward yourself. [Col. 0836C]

You wept in prayer and drew out long sighs.

While you mourned in this way, you were accustomed to celebrate Masses.

A fountain of many tears nearly blinded you.

Before the day of death, strong pain came upon you.

While the year granted a delay, it drew you to your final hour.

Death took you as it approached on the eighth day of March.

Thus, in verse and prose, we transmit the life of our venerable Father to posterity as an example for living. And although we have not portrayed in the elegance of composition everything he accomplished, nor as much as we ought, we have nevertheless done what we could—more at another’s request than from our own presumption—for the praise and honor of him who granted both that man to do what he did and us to write what we have written, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0835C]

## Two Letters of Gundulf

### First Letter

To the monks of Bec.—That they should not grieve over their abbot Anselm, who had been taken from them. (See above, among Anselm’s letters, Book III, Letter 3, column 17 of this volume.)

### Letter II

To Anselm residing at Lyon.—That he should relieve by his presence the Church of Canterbury, afflicted by troubles of many kinds. (See above in Eadmer’s *New History*, Book IV, column 453.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1108: Philip I, King of the Franks

[Col. 0837]

## Historical Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 384.)

[Col. 0837A]

Philip I, king of France, who had been crowned in 1059 during the lifetime of his father Henry I and ruled after him until 29 July 1108, the end of his life, was by no means a learned prince, although he possessed eloquence and took care to have his son, Prince Louis—known in history as Louis the Fat—educated. Yet various documents preserved under his name, and several others personally concerning him, prompt us to say a few words about him here, in order to make these documents known as useful sources for history.

Among those of the first class are three letters by this prince: one, the earliest in date, to Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier, and another to Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. The first is all the more important because it contains many indications of the prince’s good sentiments, despite the pleasure-seeking life he was then leading. He begins by admitting to the pious abbot that he had often treated him badly and had until then neglected to make suitable amends, his sins being the cause and great affairs having distracted him, although he had always loved and esteemed his monastery above all others.
