After this admission he earnestly begs Bernard and his entire community to pray fervently for him, and commissions him to reform the abbey of Farmoutiers, where scandalous disorders had arisen. Shortly afterward, the same prince charged Bernard to render the same service to the monastery of Saint-Magloire in Paris. This latter commission is dated February 1093; from this it is clear that the undated letter preceded it by some time. Dom Mabillon, having found the original in the archive of Marmoutier, had it engraved in his *Diplomatics* as a model of the script in use in the eleventh century, and later reprinted it in the body of his *Annals*.

The letter to Saint Anselm is short, but well written in every respect. It forms part of the collection of Anselm’s letters and was sent to him during his second exile at Lyon, in 1104. Philip expresses how deeply he shared Anselm’s sufferings and offers him his protection, if that could ease them for him [Col. 0837C] or even free him from them altogether. Having learned that Anselm’s health was failing and that the constraint of his exile was not conducive to restoring it, Philip urges him to withdraw to his domains—for Lyon was not yet part of them—and assures him that he would there receive proofs of the affection he bore him. M. de La Curne de Sainte-Palaye, during the course of his literary travels in Italy, discovered another letter from the same prince to the emperor Henry IV, which begins with the word “Philippus.”

The solemn oath by which this prince swore to leave his concubine Bertrada permanently has also been preserved. He swore it on 2 December 1104 into the hands of Lambert, bishop of Arras, who had been appointed for this purpose. Bertrada was obliged to do the same, and her oath follows that of King Philip.

There is another public act of this prince confirming the abolition of the pernicious custom by which the episcopal residence and all its dependencies were plundered as soon as the see of that Church became vacant. This act, made in 1105 at the request of Ivo of Chartres, is especially interesting for the detail it provides about everything that was plundered on such an occasion. They spared neither furnishings, livestock, or provisions, nor even the windows, lead, iron, or stones.

As for the documents concerning King Philip’s person—that is, those expressly treating the history of his life or reign—we have only three short pieces of verse, all epitaphs devoted to his memory. The first, in five long lines, contains only the date of his death, and even that is expressed rather obscurely. The second, composed of ten elegiac lines, traces his descent from the ancient Trojans and represents him as a handsome, powerful, warlike, and politically capable prince, possessing piety, gentleness, eloquence, and charm in his speech and manners. Finally, the third, consisting of twelve long lines, without going into such detail, gives a reasonably good characterization of Philip in its first six lines. [Col. 0838C]

## Letters and Charters of King Philip I

### I. Letter of King Philip to Bernard, Abbot of Marmoutier

He urges him to reform the utterly depraved conduct of the nuns of Faremoutiers.

(Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, V, 311.)

PHILIP, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to BERNARD, venerable abbot of Marmoutier, and to the entire community entrusted to him, greetings.

Although I recognize that in many respects I have exasperated your holiness, I nevertheless wish it to be clear to you that I have loved your church above all other churches of the monastic order, and, because of your humility and patience, have resolved henceforth to love it. But because I have been hindered by many and great affairs—my sins, I confess, demanding it—I neglected to make satisfaction to your holiness. Now I earnestly beg you to receive me, although unworthy, in your prayers from this time forward, so that through them I may deserve to be helped in the present and in the future. For I trust that they have great confidence before God.

Now, following the footsteps of our predecessors, we transfer, grant, and by royal authority confirm through this present charter to you, to possess in perpetuity as a cell, the monastery of Saint Mary ever-virgin and Saint Fara, in which, through the weakness and negligence of its inhabitants, all religion and the monastic order have been utterly abolished and—which is more deplorable—we grieve to say has become a brothel. We do this for the salvation of my soul, so that through the prudence of your holiness and the urgency of your prayers the monastic order may be restored there, and the Church of God, which until now—alas!—has been defiled by adulterous embraces and deprived for so long of God’s service, may rejoice to ascend with the sons of your church from the valley of tears and to sing the Song of Ascents.

Therefore, take courage in the Lord, without hesitation, knowing that my assistance will fail you in nothing. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0839C] See Ivo’s Letter 70, to Walter, bishop of Meaux.]

### II. Letter of King Philip to the Same

He entrusts to him the monastery of Saint-Magloire in Paris, to be restored to better condition.

(Mabillon, cited above, p. 316.)

[Col. 0839C]

Let it be known to all that we possess a royal chapel constructed in honor of the blessed apostle Bartholomew and the blessed confessor Magloire, situated in the city of Paris beside the royal palace. Until now it appeared to have been not so much governed as laid waste by its own abbots, especially during the time of Abbot Haimon. Through his negligence it had first been so destroyed in the religion of the monastic order and then so despoiled of its external resources that the few brothers who still remained there could not be supported from the church’s goods in the manner proper to monks. Almost reduced to secular life, each one, as best he could and with great hardship and violation of the order, procured his needs from his own resources. [Col. 0840A]

Accordingly, when we demanded an account of this desolation from the aforementioned Abbot Haimon, and he could not excuse himself but acknowledged that all these things had happened through his negligence, with his consent and at the supplication of the brothers who inhabited that place, as well as at the admonition of our nobles and the recommendation of certain religious men, we found this salutary counsel: that we should hand over that church for restoration to the hands of men living in an orderly and monastic fashion—namely, Abbot Bernard and the monks of Saint Martin of Marmoutier. This we have done for the redemption of our soul, and so forth.

This was done publicly in Paris, in the royal palace, before the witnesses subscribed below, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, indiction 1, epact 26, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, while King Philip was reigning, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign.

(Appended to this document are the signatures or marks of Philip himself, king; Ursion, bishop of Senlis; Hugh, brother of King Philip; Guy, the king’s steward; Adelelm, the king’s constable; Simon of Neauphle; Gozlin, the king’s chamberlain; Walter, the king’s chamberlain; William, the queen’s chamberlain; and Harduin, the queen’s chamberlain, together with those of others. Among the monks present for this enactment were Hilgodus, who was bishop of Soissons, and his brother Andrew; Robert, prior of Paris of the aforesaid monastery; and Robert of Castella, who was steward of the aforesaid King Philip. Hubert, the chancellor, wrote and subscribed it.) [Col. 0840C]

### III. Letter of King Philip to Saint Anselm, Exiled at Lyon

That he might deign to visit Gaul.

(See above, among Anselm’s letters, Book IV, Letter 50, column 230 of this volume.)

## Oath of Philip, King of the Franks

By which he promises, at the command of the Roman pontiff, to dismiss Bertrada, his paramour.

(Labbe, *Councils*, X, 658.)

“Let you, Lambert, bishop of Arras, hear—you who here exercise the apostolic office in his place; let the archbishops and the bishops present hear—that I, Philip, king of the Franks, will no longer practice the sin and custom of carnal and illicit union which I have hitherto practiced with Bertrada. Rather, I renounce this sin and disgrace completely and without any reconsideration. With that same woman I will have neither mutual conversation nor cohabitation, except in the presence of persons who are in no way suspect. All these things, as the pope’s letter states and as you understand, I will observe without any evil intention. So may God help me, and these most holy Gospels of Jesus Christ.”

Likewise, when Bertrada was released from the bond of excommunication, she too swore this same oath personally, touching the most holy Gospels. [Col. 0841A]

This was enacted at Paris in the presence of Lord Daimbert, archbishop of Sens; Radulf, archbishop of Tours; and also Lords Ivo, bishop of Chartres; Humbald, bishop of Auxerre; John, bishop of Orléans; Gualo, bishop of Paris; Manasses, bishop of Meaux; Baldric, bishop of Noyon; Lambert, bishop of Arras; Humbert, bishop of Senlis; as well as the abbots Adam of Paris, likewise Ulric of Paris, Rainald of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Rainald of Étampes; and many archdeacons, distinguished clerics, and laymen assembled there in no small number.

Thus, by the authority of the Apostolic See, Philip, king of the Franks, was restored to communion with his holy Catholic Church, his mother, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of Christ 1104, while Paschal II was presiding in the Roman See, in the sixth year of his pontificate.

[Col. 0841]

## Two Charters of King Philip

### (Year 1072) I. Seal of King Philip concerning Saint-Germain

He grants estates to enlarge the foundation of the cell of Saint-Germain at Laie-la-Nouvelle.

(Martène, *Amplified Collection*, I, 490, from the archive of Colombes.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, PHILIP, by the grace of God king of the Franks, wish it to be made known both to those now living and to posterity that our grandfather, King Robert, constructed a certain monastery in honor of God and Saint Germain beside the forest called Laie, providing there the necessities for the brothers serving in that place. My father, namely King Henry, who governed the empire of Gaul after him, enlarged the place by granting more, in addition to everything that Robert had given.

Therefore, so that I might share in so great a benefit, I gave to the aforesaid monastery and to the monks of Colombes serving God in that same place all the tithe of my wine and grain belonging to the cellar or granary of Poissy—namely, from Trel, from Charla-vana, and from Poissy itself. I also gave the tithe of the wine, grain, vegetables, and oats of Alvers, wherever it might be. Likewise, I gave all the tithe of my grain, oats, vegetables, and all my increases produced there. I also gave the mill of Filioli-Court and the land of Gaudine. I gave as well as many branches of Laie as might be necessary for the monks’ fire, together with as much dead wood as was sufficient for the use of the monks and their guests, and all pasture for the monks’ animals and also for their guests’ animals. I further gave as much living woodland as would be necessary for the monks’ buildings, whether new ones were to be constructed or existing ones repaired.

I also granted to the aforesaid place of blessed Germain a certain Gautier, my collibert, [Note: [Col. 0841D] Colliberts were neither slaves nor free men, but held an intermediate status between the two, though they were closer to slaves than to free men.] together with all his descendants, and five hospites at Rivoldicourt. [Col. 0842B]

And so that memory of this benefit might not be erased, I ordered a document to be made concerning it, which I confirmed with my own hand. I ordered the witnesses to the aforesaid grant to be set down. Considering, however, that day by day charity grows cold among many people and iniquity abounds, I caused all these things to be recorded under the protection and defense of my seal, so that those who come after us may know what I have granted or given, for the redemption of my soul and that of my predecessors, to the monks of Colombes serving God and Saint Germain.

Enacted publicly at Paris, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, while King Philip was reigning, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

The mark of Geoffrey, bishop of Paris; the mark of Hugh, count of Meulan; the mark of Simon of Montfort; the mark of Guy of Montlhéry; the mark of Hugh of Puteaux; the mark of Count Ivo; the mark of William Albanus; the mark of Walter; the mark of Garnerius; the mark of Fromond, his brother; the mark of Geoffrey, son of Nivard; the mark of Nizard, his brother; the mark of Hugh, son of Walter of Poissy; the mark of Walter, his brother, still a child.

### (Year 1105) II. Philip I, King of the Franks, Orders the Goods of Deceased Bishops of Chartres to Be Preserved Untouched

[Acheri, *Spicilegium*, III, 296.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

We wish it to be known to all who in future times will succeed one another in the kingdom of the Franks that Lord Ivo, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Chartres, approached the height of our serenity with humble devotion, earnestly begging that we grant and confirm by our pragmatic enactment the remission and liberty previously granted to the episcopal houses and the goods collected in them from the wicked custom which Count Henry, surnamed Stephen, and his wife Adela had abolished with the consent of their sons William, Theobald, Odo, and Stephen.

Assenting to his pious desire and inclining our ear to his most equitable request, according to the tenor of the document which the aforesaid counts decreed should be made concerning the aforementioned goods, by the authority of our majesty we free the specified goods from the wicked custom. These include the house itself and its iron, lead, glass, wood, stones, and all other furnishings—namely, boards, benches, stools, wine vessels, and beds—as well as kitchens and barns, granaries, cellars, presses, ovens, and the buildings of the ovens, whether in the city or outside it; forests, so that they may not be sold, cut down, or given away; and also grain, wine, hay, sheep, oxen, and other animals, together with all remaining movable goods that have been gathered or collected, whether in the city or outside it, before the death or departure of any bishop. We decree that these must remain untouched, to benefit those to whom the bishop had decided to reserve or give them, either personally or through his steward, so that the chief persons of the Church may act if some circumstance prevents the bishop from doing so.

We also grant that the exaction customarily imposed after the death or departure of bishops upon their servants or peasants shall henceforth never be imposed.

All these things, as they were granted and confirmed by the aforesaid counts, we likewise grant as stated above and confirm by our pragmatic enactment, attested by the written character of our name and by the seal of our majesty.

Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

Enacted and confirmed at Paris in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1105, and in the forty-sixth year of our reign.

## Three Epitaphs of King Philip I

(Duchesne, *Historians of the Franks*, vol. IV, 167.)

### I. From an old manuscript book of Lord Alexandre Petau, senator of Paris

Add seven to a thousand, with a hundred at the same time removed,

And then you will know the year in which King Philip

Entered dreadful death, which refuses no one,

While the world marked the fourth day before the Kalends of August,

On the fourth feria, in the week called Sylvester’s.

### II. From another manuscript of the same Lord Petau

Here lies buried Philip, supreme king of the Franks;

He was a king, descended from great Priam.

Tall in body, serene in face, shining like a star,

In power, a figure fitting for Romulus.

Brave in wars, defender of his ancestral kingdom,

Skillful in counsel, provident in speech.

Distinguished by piety, restrainer of savage anger,

Pleasant in words and gentle in manners.

He ascended to heaven on the third day before the Kalends of August,

Having wielded the scepter for “novem vigies et bis” years [a numerically obscure reading].

### III

I had been a king, rich in wealth and eloquent in speech,

Descended from kings, powerful in virtue, of exalted lineage.

Great was my glory, in which rival excellence was stretched forth.

Buried in this earth, I paid what nature required,

And, given as ashes to ashes, I learned what I was.

Ah! What are honor, wealth, glory, or

[power?

But I sought, O Benedict, your church especially;

Grant me, I beg through my prayers, a heavenly dwelling.

When July had completed its days,

My spirit departed before the Kalends of August. [Col. 0844D]

You who read this, ask that the deserved anger of my Judge be diminished for me;

But favor these prayers, O Christ the Redeemer.

## In the Year of the Lord 1109

## Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny

[Col. 0845] *Life of Saint Hugh* (Bollandists, April, vol. III, day 29)

## Preliminary Commentary

### § I. His Predecessors, Age, Disciples, and Notable Friends

1. We described the first seat and cradle of the Cluniac order, and the head of all the monasteries of that institution, on 13 January in the *Life of Blessed Berno*. He was the first of the abbots of Cluny and, before founding Cluny, had been a most holy archimandrite at Gigny and at the monastery of Baume, where, under its founder Saint Eutychius, he had served his novitiate in the monastic life.

When he died in the year of the Lord 926, Saint Odo succeeded him: a noble Frank, formerly a canon of Saint Martin of Tours, who became a monk and was first made abbot of Tulle. Aymard succeeded Odo; writers variously call him Eymardus, Ademarus, and Ademardus. He was an outstanding cultivator of holy simplicity and innocence, but unfortunately lost his sight in 954. For that reason he voluntarily resigned his dignity and yielded it to Saint Majolus, who had been born of a very noble family in the province of Valence. He was first archdeacon of the Church of Mâcon and finally exchanged this life for death in the year of the Lord 994.

Saint Odilo, called of Mercœur, succeeded the deceased. He was the son of Beraud I, surnamed the Great, lord of Mercœur in Auvergne, and of Gerberga. After his blessed passage to the heavenly realm, which occurred in the year 1049, Saint Hugh, the subject of this account, began to occupy the seat of the abbot of Cluny. The Cluniac library collects many testimonies of distinguished men concerning him. To offer a sample from it, let the following first be that of the author of the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, bishop of Soissons:

“He was most chaste in body and soul, continually intent and devoted to almsgiving and prayer; an exceedingly zealous guardian and promoter of monastic discipline; a perpetual nourisher of perfect monks and of persons suited to ecclesiastical service; and a remarkably fervent protector and propagator of the holy Church.” [Col. 0845C]

This is what Sigebert of Gembloux says under the year 1087:

“Hugh, abbot of Cluny, is regarded as distinguished for piety, outstanding for discernment, and renowned for holiness and religion.”

The curious reader will find many similar statements there, not to repeat them all. We nevertheless add the eulogy offered to us by the *Chronology of the Abbots of Cluny*:

“He was distinguished not only by nobility of flesh but also by nobility of mind, and he enlarged this place—understand Cluny—far beyond all his predecessors in buildings, adornments, possessions, monasteries, and cells, everywhere through his faith and industry beyond what can be believed. Although he was suitably adorned with the exercise of every virtue, with the hand of prudence he restrained more tightly the order of monastic religion, which was flowing too loosely. In two oratories constructed by him, he established that two Masses should be sung daily: one for the deceased brothers and another for the living. He was always so devoted to almsgiving, above all the men of our time, that the saying from Ecclesiasticus may rightly be judged to suit him: ‘The whole assembly of the saints will declare his alms’ (Ecclesiasticus 31:11).

“Having been given to us by God, he was permitted to live for a long time for the advancement of this place. Instructing the flock entrusted to him alike by words and examples, he increased it in many ways. Finally, worn out by old age, he rested in a holy embrace on the third day before the Kalends of May, during Easter week.”

This is taken from there.

## 2. The Year of Saint Hugh’s Birth

The year of Saint Hugh’s birth must be determined from the year of his death and from the events of his life at that time. He died, as the writers of his life relate, in the eighty-fifth year of his age, on the eighth day after Saint Anselm departed this life. Since we have shown that Anselm died on 21 April, around Easter in the year 1109, it is necessary that Saint Hugh’s birth fell in the year of Christ 1024. [Col. 0846C] We therefore state that Saint Hugh was born in the year of Christ 1024.

In 1039, at the age of fifteen, he embraced the institution of Saint Benedict among the Cluniacs and entered monastic life under Saint Odilo, then abbot. Ten years later—at the age of twenty-five, and in the year of Christ 1049—when Odilo had died, he was designated as his successor and invested with the abbatial insignia. He spent the rest of his life in that office, namely sixty years, together with eight days and two months, as is written at the end of the Second Life. This was a long period in the sacred [Col. 0847A] dignity, and one exceedingly beneficial to the many whom he instructed in the precepts of religious life. For from his school emerged bishops, cardinals, pontiffs, and men distinguished by sacred veneration on account of the holiness of their lives.

The Cluniacs owe to him Blessed Morandus and Saint Ulrich, who were enrolled among the choirs of the saints. The former is honored among them on 3 June, the latter on 10 July. Saint Hugh admitted Ulrich to the monastic habit, together with Gerald, who was later made bishop of Ostia. Concerning them, the Cluniac Chronicle says:

> “This Gerald was the schoolmaster of the city of Regensburg. At the request of Saint Ulrich, he went with the aforesaid Ulrich to the city of Rome, and, having obtained absolution for their sins, these explorers of virtue came to Saint Hugh. Under him, in the Cluniac monastery, they received a second regeneration. [Col. 0847B] Gerald himself was outstandingly pre-eminent in wisdom, counsel, and gravity of character. After not many years he was appointed major prior, and afterwards, at the command of the prelate of the Apostolic See—namely Gregory VII—he was raised to the bishopric of the Church of Ostia. He governed that see with the greatest diligence and, returning to his Lord the talent of the entrusted stewardship with doubled interest, deserved to hear: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew 25:21).

> “Saint Ulrich also, magnificent in his divine exercises, Abbot Saint Hugh caused to be promoted to the priestly office, and appointed him his chaplain and counselor. Because he knew that Ulrich was wholly composed of virtue and wisdom, he also prepared for his own flock in him an avenue of confession. [Col. 0847C] Hence both old and young came to him, suffering from various afflictions, and opened their consciences to him all the more sincerely because they did so with greater security. He received everyone with the greatest charity and, in the manner of a most wise physician, treated them with suitable remedies of penance for as long as necessary.

> “This Saint Ulrich, born at Regensburg from the illustrious lineage of the Bannarii, shone among the stars of his family’s noble stock as the morning star among the other lights of heaven. The rest of his merits in virtue and his miracles are contained in the book of his deeds. His feast, or solemnity, is celebrated among us on the tenth day of July.”

This is what is said concerning the bishop Gerald and Saint Ulrich. A short Life of Blessed Morandus exists in the Cluniac Library; it will be given in its proper place, at columns 501 and following. [Col. 0847D]

Among those who must also be counted as illustrious men from the same school are Goderanus, bishop of Saintes; Durannus, archbishop of Toulouse; and Hugh, duke of Burgundy. The last of these was the grandson of Robert II, duke of Burgundy, through Robert’s son Henry. Inflamed by a desire for a holier life, he transferred the duchy to his brother Odo—namely, the man who shortly afterward founded Cîteaux—and received the monastic habit at Cluny under Saint Hugh. After three years there of holy and austere life, he died in the year of Christ 1097. The following epitaph is read on his tomb among the Cluniacs:

> Here rests a man worthy of celebrated remembrance,  
> a great despiser of the world,  
> Hugh, duke of Burgundy,  
> Cluniac monk, later priest.

[Col. 0848A]

## 3. Pontiffs Who Acquired Virtue under So Great a Master

The pontiffs who acquired under so great a master the virtue that first raised them to the sacred purple and then to the summit of ecclesiastical dignity were Urban II and Gregory VII.

Urban, formerly a regular canon of the Order of Saint Augustine, which he had professed in the Roman Lateran monastery, sought a stricter manner of life and received the monastic habit in the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Cava. From there he went to Gaul and, among the Cluniacs, placed himself first under Saint Odilo and then under his successor Saint Hugh for instruction. Gregory VII, with whom he had formed a holy friendship at Cluny while both were still monks, bestowed upon him the cardinal’s purple. Finally, in the year 1088, as ruler of the universal Church, he ascended the pontifical chair of Saint Peter.

The other, namely [Col. 0848B] Gregory VII, called Hildebrand before his pontificate, had been prior of the Cluniac monastery. Nicholas II drew him into the college of cardinals, and in 1073 he was proclaimed pontiff by the unanimous agreement of the Fathers, to the great advantage of the Church. He shone with such virtue and holiness of life that thereafter, his name having been entered in the rolls of the saints, he also received sacred veneration with them.

Many of his letters to Saint Hugh are preserved in volume 26 of the Councils. For during that period of upheaval which the emperor Henry III had provoked through his continual discord against Gregory and the Church, Hugh was an opportune counselor to the pontiff and was placed in charge of difficult affairs undertaken for the common good of Christendom. The pontiff expresses in Letter 62, Book 1, [Col. 0848C] how greatly he desired Hugh’s assistance and how necessary he considered it:

> “Therefore,” he says, “let your religious devotion know that, although until now we have endured with amazement your denied presence, henceforth we cannot bear it without great anxiety and disturbance of mind. You must remember how many and how important matters we have placed in your hands and those of our brother Gerald, bishop of Ostia. Because of your absence, these matters either perish through neglect or cannot reach a suitable conclusion. For when we sent the aforesaid bishop across the mountains to the king in the service of Saint Peter, we expected you to come. Therefore, although moved by concern, we earnestly admonish your affection that, since we are placed amid many and great anxieties, you should take care to visit us as soon as possible,” and so forth.

Thus the [Col. 0848D] pontiff wrote to him, in addition to many other letters of this kind. Hugh handled the pontiff’s most difficult affairs with the aforementioned Henry in such a way that he freed the pontiff for a time from the dangerous storm; and he made Henry, released from the bond of excommunication by which he was held, a friend of the Church.

## 4. His Close Relationship with Blessed Peter Damian

He also had a close relationship with Blessed Peter Damian, whose letters sent to him are collected in the Cluniac Library.

Saint Peter Damian was at Cluny, where he learned from Saint Hugh’s account the following terrifying examples, which are reported in Letter 15, Book II. At Hugh’s urging, he also wrote the Life of Blessed Odilo. Damian speaks thus in its preface:

> “Hugh, ruler of the monastery of Cluny, leader of the spiritual army, and its chief instructor, [Col. 0849A] imposed upon me the task of briefly treating in my own style the Life of Odilo, his predecessor, so that from the matters more fully spread out in the earlier pages I might extract, in a brief summary, whatever was most useful and necessary. Compelled by his command, I shall not pursue the elegance of brilliant eloquence; rather, as I am able to understand from the written pages placed before me, with the help of almighty God I shall endeavor to do justice to the truth as I can.”

Hugh also enjoyed a close friendship with Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, later the supreme pontiff called Victor III. For when Hugh went to Monte Cassino around the year 1083, he established with Desiderius, among his own monks and those of Cassino, a communion of merits. Leo of Ostia reports this in Book III, chapter 50, of the Cassinese Chronicle:

> “At this time the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a man celebrated for his life and reputation, came devoutly to the threshold of Father Benedict. The venerable Desiderius, receiving him with great honor, as befitted so great a man, and joining the fellowship of the Cluniac brothers to our congregation, entered into a pact with him. Those distinguished men decreed that a perpetual remembrance should be maintained both of our congregation among them and of theirs among us.” [Col. 0849B]

## 5. The Bishops of Gaul Bound to the Cluniac Monastery through Saint Hugh

What shall I say now of the bishops of Gaul who were bound to the Cluniac monastery through Saint Hugh? Volume VI of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, in its collection of miscellaneous letters, presents us with two: Araldus and Isembardus. Through them the discipline of the Cluniac Church was notably commended and its resources enlarged to some extent.

> “Araldus, [Col. 0849C] bishop of the Church of Chartres, and the canonical fraternity of that same Church, moved by the good reputation of the virtues of the Cluniac monastery, as though by the sweetest fragrance of lilies and roses from a flourishing garden, and divinely inspired by the desire to maintain fraternity with that monastery, grant a certain prebend to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery for perpetual use,”

as appears in no. 23. Then, in no. 24:

> “Isembardus, by the grace of God bishop of Orléans, and the entire congregation of the Holy Cross … when requested by Hugh, venerable abbot of Cluny, and the most holy congregation entrusted to him, to grant for the sake of the previous agreement and fellowship which they had mutually established a prebend belonging to a certain canon, for perpetual possession by the church of Saint Peter and by the brothers serving there, [Col. 0849D] …”

they consented on the condition that, as the bishop says in his charter, they should:

> “receive us also into their fellowship, and make each of our canons as one of their monks, and grant us a share in their prayers, almsgiving, and other good works; and commend the death and anniversary of the death of each of our canons, as though he were one of their cloistered monks, by prayers, almsgiving, and the other solemn observances. If any of our canons should wish to become a monk, they should receive him freely, even if he were unwilling or unable to give anything. They should also celebrate our anniversary—that is, that of the bishop, as their abbot—and those of my successors every year. We, for our part, should commemorate the living and the dead abbots and monks of that church as though they were our bishops and canons.” [Col. 0850A]

## § II. The Singular Regard of Emperors and Kings for Saint Hugh

### 6. Saint Hugh Was Deeply Dear to the Princes of the Age

Hugh was also deeply dear to the princes of the age. Among these, the first to be named in dignity is Henry, the second emperor of that name and the third king of the Germans. In the year 1051 Hugh had congratulated him by letter “on the restoration of his health and the adoption of a son granted by God.” The emperor, writing to him again, concluded his letter as follows:

> “As for your saying that, because of the length of the journey, you could not come as we had ordered, although we would have gladly welcomed your arrival, we forgive you on the understanding that you come to us at Cologne at Easter, if this is possible, so that—if we may dare to say so—you might receive from the sacred font the same child in whom you have so greatly rejoiced, and mark him as his spiritual father with the gift of your blessing. Thus, purified together from the leaven of sins, may we deserve to enjoy the Easter solemnity with the unleavened bread of heavenly glory.” [Col. 0850B]

This happened the following year. The boy was given the name Henry in honor of his spiritual father; he later became Emperor Henry III of that name and King Henry IV. After his father’s death, his widowed mother wrote to “the most beloved Father and abbot worthy of all acceptance, Hugh,” in the year 1056. [Col. 0850C] The letter is number 14 in the second volume of Acher’s *Spicilegium Miscellanea*, where the preceding letter and others cited shortly afterward are also found. It conveys the following meaning:

> “Because my harp has been turned into mourning (Job 30:31), I return a groan for the joy and a mournful lament for the exultation which your letters had produced. Yet my heart, trembling with grief, shrinks from recounting everything. Therefore, since swift rumor, as is its custom, has announced my sorrow to you, I beg you to commend to God in prayer, together with your community, my lord, whom you did not wish to preserve longer in the flesh, now that he has died. Obtain also that your son may long remain his heir and worthy of God, and strive by your counsel to quiet any disturbances that may arise against him in the neighboring parts of his kingdom. Farewell, Father.”

### 7. Henry III’s Fall and His Appeal to Saint Hugh

Hugh did not fail in his duty toward him. But Henry III was gradually corrupted by the flattering suggestions of the worst counselors. By violating the liberty [Col. 0850D] and rights of the Church, through open defiance and disobedience, he finally deserved to be excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII and, at the assembly of princes at Augsburg, to be deprived of the empire unless within a year he returned to peace with the Church.

Then, seeing himself placed in desperate straits, he began to turn toward Hugh, whose counsels and paternal admonitions he may previously have neglected. He crossed into Italy to seek absolution and, through Hugh’s intervention and guarantee on his behalf, obtained reconciliation in the year 1077.

But he soon returned to his former character—or rather, he cast off the mask of penitence which he had assumed as a deceiver. He went so far as to create an antipope and stir up a most pernicious schism, bringing ruin upon many souls and extreme confusion upon the whole empire. Yet the man who had attempted to drive the common Father of all the faithful from the chair of Peter was himself removed from the empire by his own son, Henry IV, in the year 1105.

Then, lacking counsel, he wrote to “the most dear and beloved Father Hugh, and all the holy brothers of the Cluniac monastery, [Col. 0851A]” offering “the tender affection of a son and the devoted service of a brother, indeed of a servant.” The letter, which is the tenth in the aforementioned *Miscellanea*, begins:

> “Because we have always kindly experienced your piety and paternal concern toward us, so that we believe ourselves to have been freed from many dangers through your holy prayers, therefore, dearest Father, after God we flee to you as to the singular refuge of our necessity. We humbly beg that we may at least find with you consolation in our miseries. Would that it might happen to us to see your angelic face in the body, so that, prostrate at your knees, we might familiarly recline in the lap of your holiness the head which you received from the saving font; and there, weeping over our sins, recount in order the multitude of our tribulations!” [Col. 0851B]

After he had made this complaint at length and with lamentation, he concluded:

> “But now it is time to put an end to the tragedy of our long miseries. We have taken care to lament them before your piety, most loving Father, because in God and in you we have a great and singular hope of counsel and assistance for our salvation and liberty. Therefore, with the whole affection and desire of our heart, we entrust all our counsel to your faith. Whatever you decide must be done concerning our reconciliation with the apostolic see, whatever must be done concerning the peace and unity of the holy Roman Church, while our honor is preserved—we promise without doubt to do it all, before God and before you. Hasten, therefore, dearest Father, to advise us; and, we beg you, do not be displeased to labor for the salvation of your servant, even if not for the liberation of your son, since we have sinned against heaven and before you (Luke 15:18),” [Col. 0851C]

### 8. Further Letters from Henry III

Not content with these letters sent through the Cluniac monks, he added others, to be read immediately afterward, through different messengers. In them he offered “whatever, although a sinner, he could more devoutly and humbly pray for as a spiritual son to his most desired and beloved Father.” He declared that, with the most ardent devotion, he sought the holiness of Hugh’s fatherhood as a refuge for his sins, like the publican, and, [Col. 0851D] like a shipwrecked man, as the harbor of salvation; and that he placed his entire case in Hugh’s counsel and in that of the other religious men whom Hugh might wish to have involved, promising to do whatever Hugh should determine.

Finally, in a third letter, wishing to express his hope of obtaining divine mercy by the example of the people of Israel—who, when they sinned, were punished by the Lord, but when they repented were judged worthy of pardon—he says:

> “It has been a long time since you visited your sick man, as you used to do, and since you healed your crushed man with the consolations and encouragements of your exhortations.”

Afterward he wishes himself to be commended to God through the prayers of Hugh and the Cluniac brothers:

> “May he who anticipated us with the mercy of good will deign to direct us toward the fruitful accomplishment of our works,” [Col. 0852A]

namely, the works concerning which he had made the following promise in the same letter:

> “We make known to your serenity that, for the restoration of the churches which in our time and through our sins have, alas, fallen into ruin, we wish to labor in every way, insofar as God grants us strength, and henceforth to yield to the sound counsels of all good men. If in any way we are able, we shall gather together what has been scattered, unite what has been torn apart by the wedge of schism with the glue of unity, and repair through the restoration of peace and justice the ruin of the Church which has occurred through us.

> “Furthermore, we inform you that, if by God’s favor we are able to gather the kingdom and the priesthood together again, we intend afterward to go to Jerusalem and see the holy land in which our Lord appeared in the flesh and lived among human beings (Baruch 3:38). With his favor, we greatly desire to worship him there more vividly, where we know that he suffered for us slaps, spittle, scourging, the cross, death, and burial.” [Col. 0852B]

These are his words. As Baronius observes, “other statements of this kind could insinuate the mind of a most pious man; but because he was so constituted that, whenever he was brought low, he then craftily put on a mask of piety to deceive others, which he immediately removed once he had accomplished what he had attempted, it was deservedly and rightly the case that those whom he had called holy patrons became his avengers. He was punished by a sudden death in the year 1106, on 10 August.”

### 9. The Repentance of King Philip I of France

It is credible that the repentance of Philip I, king of France, was more sincere. After a ten-year adulterous [Col. 0852C] concubinage, he was finally absolved at Paris in the year 1104. Not out of fear of losing an earthly kingdom, but from a desire to attain the heavenly kingdom more surely, he did not disdain to humble himself for this purpose, as Saint Hugh says in replying to him in Letter 18 of the aforementioned *Miscellanea*:

> “He confessed that he wished to live unanimously and harmoniously with us for whatever time remains.”

Hugh continues:

> “Since God has opened for us the door of a sweet familiarity, through which we may speak with you about him, we now reveal to you for the first time what we did not first begin to think and desire concerning you today: that henceforth you may have a more earnest affection and greater intention toward the good. I mean the true good, the highest good, which is God.

> “O great friend, remember that you once asked me whether any king had ever become a monk. I replied that one had. Even if we knew of no other example, the example of Saint Guntram, king of the Franks, would suffice. He abandoned the pomp, vanities, and allurements of the world and became a monk.

> “Let the lamentable misfortune and mournful death of your contemporaries and neighbors also move and terrify you—namely, William, king of the English, and the emperor Henry. One of them perished in an instant from the blow of a single arrow, not in battle but in a forest; the other, amid many grievous anxieties and hardships which he had long endured, recently died, as we already believe you have heard.” [Col. 0852D]

We believe this was written in the very year in which Henry died. King William, as is described more fully under 21 April in the Life [Col. 0853A] of Saint Anselm and in Book II, no. 43, of Eadmer’s History, had died in October of the year 1100.

Concerning the final period of Saint Guntram’s life, we possess a few details from Fredegar, brought forward under 28 March. Although there is no mention there of his becoming a monk, we nevertheless think it sufficiently plausible that, if he lived and died for some time in the monastery of Saint Marcellus, where he is buried and honored, he at least died in the monastic habit. The same may be said of the emperor Lothair among the Prumians, with this difference: it is certain that Lothair renounced the empire and kingdom through a public abdication, whereas nothing of the kind is recorded concerning Guntram.

Whatever the truth may be, Hugh uses this example. He exhorts the king “to true repentance and perfect conversion, which cannot be embraced by an easier or more certain path than the monastic profession,” and finally concludes:

> “Behold, the princes of the apostles, judges of emperors and kings and of the world, are ready to receive you into this house of theirs at Cluny, which our fathers called an asylum of repentance. And we are ready to have you as king and to treat you as king …” [Col. 0853B]

### 10. The Later Conduct of Philip and the King of Spain

These pious and holy intentions of King Philip, however, as often happens with men long habituated to many great vices, especially carnal ones, were either late or ineffective. The king himself was taken from the earth in the year 1108 before he voluntarily relinquished his earthly kingdom. Yet what he could not or did not wish to obtain while alive, he wished to obtain to some extent after death, [Col. 0853C] ordering in his final will that he be buried in the Benedictine monastery at Fleury.

The will of Alfonso, king of Spain, sixth of that name, was both more suited to royal weakness and more effective. He had long been held captive by his brother Sancho and considered that he owed his life, liberty, and kingdom to the prayers of Blessed Hugh and the Cluniac monks. Accordingly, around the year 1070, he sent Hugh the following letter, which is number 19 in volume VI of Acher’s *Spicilegium Miscellanea*. He addresses it:

> “To Hugh, venerable and most excellent abbot of the Cluniacs, renowned for the flowers of virtue, supported by the nourishment of virtue, and an elder flowing with every sweetness; … and also to the entire most noble congregation of Peter and Paul, Alfonso himself, by the grace of God king of Spain, with every devotion of mind and body … [Col. 0853D] offers, from the depths of his heart and with embracing love in the Lord Jesus Christ, the guardianship of true charity, the joys of eternal life, perpetual prosperity and salvation, and whatever is more exalted.”

He then continues:

> “With what devotion I love you, most glorious Father … Know this, most holy Father: the tribute which my father was accustomed to pay to that most holy place, Cluny, I, with God’s consent, shall double during the days of my life.”

He indicates that he had also taken precautions by testament that the same should be done by the kings who succeeded him. He humbly asks that Robert be left in his kingdom to be at his side in life and death. And, for establishing there the use of the Roman rite—which he had adopted at Hugh’s persuasion—he asks Hugh to obtain Cardinal Gerald for him from the pope.

[Col. 0854A]

### 11. Hugh’s Response to Alfonso’s Benefits

In a manner worthy and grateful of such affection and of the many other great benefits that followed it, Hugh issued a constitution, declaring to all the brothers in the Cluniac monastery, present and future:

> “Let it be known that, concerning Lord Alfonso, king of Spain, our faithful friend, who has done us such great and numerous benefits and continues unceasingly to do so … [Col. 0854B] wishing to add an overflowing abundance to this good measure, pressed down and shaken together, we have given him in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which he appears to have built from his own resources, one of the principal altars, so that the divine mysteries celebrated there may contribute to his salvation. When he has completed the course of this temporal life with its appointed end, then, apart from the offices, Masses, and almsgiving that are to be performed for him, one Mass shall be sung for him specifically at the aforesaid altar for one year.”

I omit what he prescribes for Alfonso’s anniversary, “as for Lord Henry, the august emperor,” namely, the second Henry. He also wishes his most devoted queen and wife to share in everything, and orders that her anniversary be celebrated as that of the empress Agnes.

The individual provisions can be read in no. 20 of the *Miscellanea* of the aforementioned *Spicilegium*. These details are sufficient to make known Hugh’s gratitude toward his benefactors.

### 12. Princes of Lower Rank

I pass to princes of the second rank. Among these were Theobald, by the grace of God count of the Franks, and his wife Adelaide. Moved by faith and devotion toward the holiness and religion [Col. 0854C] which, through divine generosity, were held in higher esteem and celebrated more prominently within the Cluniac community, they sent their son Odo to Hugh, venerable abbot, and his convent, to be renewed in the sacred mysteries of regeneration. They judged that, through the dispensation of heavenly clemency, it would not be without benefit to themselves to have parents in Christ who were more religious rather than more wealthy. For the more earnest attainment and more effective advancement of that grace and protection, they granted and donated to the monastery of Cluny a certain estate called Cossiacus.

The complete charter is found in the *Miscellanea* already cited, no. 22. Immediately afterward, in no. 25, comes the following:

> “Donation of the church in the castle of Avallon, made by Hugh, duke of Burgundy, to the Cluniac monastery, where Lord Hugh the abbot appears both to preside and to benefit others,” [Col. 0854D]

in the year of Christ 1077. The donor wished to imitate “many powerful and wealthy men of this age who, taught by divine preaching, transferred the resources granted to them by the Lord to better uses, disinheriting themselves in this world so that they might become heirs of the heavenly kingdom.”

Soon afterward, in the year 1078, Wido, formerly count of Mâcon, considering how useless all honor in this world is—and indeed how harmful and alluring it is to eternal damnation—when the mercy of Christ visited and inspired him, renounced the world entirely for Christ’s love in the monastery of Cluny, so that there, subject to regular discipline, he might do penance for his sins. He also donated many estates, which the charter [Col. 0855A] lists in no. 26 of the sixth volume of the often-mentioned *Spicilegium Miscellanea*.

These examples are sufficient for our present purpose, for it is not our plan to collect more.

## § III. The Foundation of Marcigny; the Cult of Saint Hugh; the Writers of His Life

### 13. The Foundation of Marcigny

Saint Hugh took care not only to preserve, through both temporal and spiritual means, the monasteries that had already been founded, but also to establish new ones, including monasteries for women. Among these was Marcigny, situated not far from the town of Semur and the river Loire, in the diocese of Autun. The following fragment of its foundation charter survives in the Cluniac Library:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be known to all our brothers and to all the sons of the holy Church of God that I, Brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, [Col. 0855B] with divine assistance preceding and cooperating, and with the agreement and help of our brother, Lord Geoffrey of Semur, founded and built this place, Marcigny, which at first was quite small and almost a kind of refuge, from the ground in our own time.

> “For it seemed good to us that, just as through the foundation of our holy fathers sinful men had Cluny as a refuge if they wished to renounce the world and its pomp, so divine clemency should not close the entrance to the heavenly kingdom to sinful women who flee from the snares of the world to this place and groan from their hearts over their offenses.

> “Let a heavier danger of eternal death threaten those who are not ashamed to harass or attack this house of the servants of God and of the most blessed Virgin,” and so forth.

Peter the Venerable pours himself out at length [Col. 0855C] in praise of this monastery and of the religious life of those who professed it in Book I of his *Miracles*. He says that, when the monastery was suddenly seized by a powerful fire which had already admitted the flames into its innermost chambers, and when Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, invited the enclosed nuns to come out, one of their number, named Gisla, replied to the archbishop:

> “We, Father, have been enclosed within these limits which you see by the fear of God and the command of our abbot, so that we might escape eternal fire, and are to remain here until death. Therefore it is in no way possible for us, under any necessity, to cross even by the step of a foot the boundaries fixed by the bonds of penance, unless we are released by him who, in the name of the Lord, enclosed us in this place.”

[Col. 0855D] The archbishop was thereby raised to such confidence in God that, when the flames were forbidden to advance farther and the fire was extinguished at his command, the remaining part of the religious house was found safe from the conflagration, even though the nuns were enclosed and in such urgent need of leaving.

There is no doubt that Saint Hugh sent them frequent letters filled with salutary admonitions. In the Cluniac Library we found only one, which is as follows.

### 14. Hugh’s Letter to the Nuns of Marcigny

> “To his sweetest daughters and most beloved sisters, stripped of the pomp of the world and gathered at Marcigny for the honor and praise of the holy and undivided Trinity, under the protection of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul: Brother Hugh, [Col. 0856A] abbot of Cluny, sends greeting, grace, and blessing, now and forever.
>
> “Let your heartfelt charity not be unaware, O daughters,” and so forth. See below.

### 15. The Burial and Veneration of Saint Hugh

Saint Hugh was buried, as the Cluniac Chronicle relates, in the larger church which he himself had built in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, behind the morning altar. He was later translated, and his body now rests above the main altar of that basilica.

A few years after his death, during the time of Pontius, his successor as abbot, he was enrolled among the company of the saints by Callixtus II. Concerning this, the monk Hugh wrote the following to Pontius in his letter:

> “This Callixtus, namely Callixtus II, returned to Cluny for the second time and devoutly celebrated there the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision and Epiphany. [Col. 0856B] While he frequently spoke, among other matters, of the life and miracles of Blessed Hugh, he did not attend merely to documents written about these matters by just anyone and in great abundance. Rather, he gladly accepted the testimony of authoritative persons presented in the midst of the Cluniac chapter, whose accounts of what they had seen and heard concerning the saint were more firmly attested. With the bishop and cardinals likewise giving their assent, the pope decreed that the birthday-feast of so great a confessor, approved by so many and such great virtues, should be celebrated to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

Galesinius entered his name in his Martyrology under 5 July; others, such as Crevenus, Maurolycus, Molanus, Menardus, and Miraeus, place him under 29 April. Under that same date he is entered in the Roman Martyrology in these words:

> “In the Cluniac monastery, Saint Hugh, abbot.”

He did indeed [Col. 0856C] die on the Wednesday after Easter mentioned above, as did Saint Anselm. But since that Wednesday fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, or 28 April, and since he died as the day was growing late—or, as others put it, during the night—both the authors of his Lives and the obituaries recorded the date as the third day before the Kalends, which the aforementioned martyrologists followed.

### 16. The Writers of Saint Hugh’s Lives

Gilo and Ezelo, Cluniac monks, were the first to write his Life, as Hildebert, whom we shall shortly mention, testifies. [Col. 0856D] Whether the complete work survives anywhere, we do not know. We appear to possess some abridgment of it, extracted by Father John Gamans in 1640 from a manuscript of the monastery of Bodec.

Although that manuscript does not contain the passage which Hildebert says was the only part he altered, the rest is nevertheless expressed in such terms that it is clear that it was taken from the material which alone he had before his eyes. He adds what he saw and what he heard, and omits certain matters for the reason explained in his preface. Since part of those omissions appears in the aforesaid manuscript, we thought it appropriate, for the greater satisfaction of the curious reader who wishes to form his own judgment concerning the omissions, to give the abridgment itself not first but third, after the more worthy works of the aforementioned Hildebert and of Raynaldus, which are equally deserving of respect.

Hildebert—the same man whose style produced the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt in metrical paraphrase, which we gave under 2 April—was formed in Saint Hugh’s discipline and monastery. He was promoted to direct the schools of Le Mans, then became archdeacon and afterward [Col. 0857A] bishop in the year 1097, and seems to have written around the year 1115. Later, in the year 1125, he was raised to the archbishopric of Tours.

We received from the manuscript collections of our Sirmond a Life of Saint Hugh written by Hildebert and compared it with the editions in Surius’s collection and in the Cluniac Library.

The second Life, which we present from a manuscript belonging to the serene Queen Christina of Sweden and from another of our college at Douai, explains many matters untouched by the first and omits certain things stated there. It was composed by the aforementioned Raynaldus—not a brother, as the Sammarthani write, but, as is clear from the venerable Peter of Cluny, Book III, Letter 2, and from Raynaldus’s own statement, the nephew of Saint Hugh. He was appointed abbot of Vézelay, in the diocese of Autun, where the nuns had been established, in the year 1108. [Col. 0857B] In his preface he says that, if perhaps the work of some man of greater talent had previously labored over this subject—by these words he seems to hint at Hildebert’s composition, which had not come into his hands—such a work should be left to the excellence of greater and wiser men, whereas his own should be assigned to the study of men of lesser ability and understanding.

He cites no earlier authors as his sources, since he treats the subject, as he says at the end, partly from what he saw and partly from what he learned through the report of trustworthy men. What he had written in prose he renders in the same meter, and concludes:

> These words, Father Hugh, of your nephew Raynaldus,  
> receive, I beg you, in piety, and protect me, Father.

And since certain other matters, as well as the time of his death [Col. 0857C] and his governance, are confirmed here more explicitly, and since the account is brief and exists nowhere else, we decided to add this one too from the same manuscript of the queen.

Raynaldus himself was made archbishop [Col. 0858A] of Lyon in 1128; after living one year in that dignity, he was buried at Cluny beneath this epitaph:

> Here lies Raynaldus, formerly abbot and restorer of Vézelay, and afterward archbishop of Lyon.

17. Hugo too, a Cluniac monk, admitted to the order after the death of the saint by his successor Pontius, wrote a letter to that abbot of his sometime after 1120. In it he included much about Saint Hugo. This letter is to be published from the Cluniac Library, first among the *Analecta*. There he also discusses the canonization of Saint Hugo, carried out at Cluny by Pope Callixtus II, supplying certain matters omitted by others.

The Cluniacs, not content with this, compelled him to write a complete Life, which likewise deserved to be given because of the antiquity of its author [Col. 0858B], had it not already been sufficiently preserved in the Cluniac Library and, from there, in the latest edition of Surius. Accordingly, we shall use it only to illuminate the first Life; the distinctive materials found there will form chapter 2 of the *Analecta*.

Finally, a certain anonymous writer described several notable points concerning Blessed Hugo’s governance and holiness. Part of these is reproduced in full in the Lives mentioned above—unless one would rather believe that they were transferred from this account into those Lives—and part will fill chapter 3 of the *Analecta*.

The hymn written in praise of Saint Hugo by the venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny after Pontius, is found among his works in the aforementioned Library, column 135. It is written in the form of a sequence and embraces a summary of the Life. You will also find there, at column 468 and following, testimonies of the ancients concerning the same saint. It did not seem worthwhile to transcribe them here.

[Col. 0857C]

# LIFE BY HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0857D]

To the venerable and most reverend Pontius, abbot by the grace of God:

[Note: Pontius the abbot, having transferred from the monastery of Saint Pons de Tomières to Cluny, governed the monastery with distinction during its first twelve or more years, when all the material that we shall give below was being written. Later, weary of murmurs against him that were gradually increasing, though they had not yet broken out publicly, he asked Pope Callixtus II, around the year 1122, to release him from office. Although with difficulty, he obtained this, and went to Jerusalem. Hugo of Marcigny, the prior, was appointed in his place; he was a different man from the one mentioned by the author of the final Life—for that author had himself been admitted to the order by Pontius, whereas this man’s long life in holy conduct is praised. When he died within a short time, Peter the Venerable was elected. From him, in Book II of the *Miracles*, where he writes Pontius’s Life, we learn that Pontius, having returned from Jerusalem, seized the opportunity to invade Cluny with armed force and acted so that he deserved to be excommunicated with his followers as a schismatic. He was nevertheless summoned to Rome to plead his case, and after sentence had been pronounced, died there soon afterward, unrepentant, under Pope Honorius II, in 1125.

It is therefore unjust that Wion should assign him to the Benedictine Martyrology on 29 January with the title of saint. In this matter Wion acted as rashly as he did negligently when he said that Pontius died at Cluny in 1122, although Pope Honorius himself writes that he died unrepentant at Rome, in a letter cited by Peter the Venerable in the place mentioned.

Peter himself, however, may seem to have spoken under the influence of some animosity, since he dishonors Pontius’s entire ten years before his deposition by branding them as years of disturbances and quarrels, even though these did not erupt publicly. Those years are sufficiently excused by the many distinguished praises bestowed upon Pontius by those who wrote about Saint Hugo and by others reported in the Cluniac Library.]

Hildebert, a priest by profession,

[Note: Although *priest* here means the same as *bishop*, he nevertheless seems, out of humility, to have used the former title rather than the latter.]

a sinner in life, wishes you to attain the common hope.

A fitting outcome for human actions promises that no one should profess beyond his strength. Whoever neglects to consider his strength surely either falls into vice or, failing altogether, hears sadly and shamefacedly: “This man began to build, and was unable to finish” (Luke 14:30).

I feared incurring either of these faults when, compelled by the authority of your request, I resolved to commend the life of Blessed Hugo to memory in whatever style I could. Although I recognized that my talent was unequal to this labor, I preferred to be found a ridiculous writer rather than disobedient to you. I hoped for a reward from obedience and believed that my shame from inadequacy would be forestalled by your correction. I still believe this, I ask it, I beg it; I shall regard it as payment if you remove from public view whatever you perceive to be deserving of censure.

Correction is a dutiful act [Col. 0859B] and pleasing to a prudent writer. I welcome it, provided that the person corrects and not the crowd; for a fault is restrained too late when the people are already mocking the faulty man.

I confess that I must especially ask pardon for daring to undertake this subject after men of greater learning, Ezelo and Gilo, who are said to have written about the most blessed Hugo with vigilance. Following them as though from a distance, I may be found to have painted a monkey in place of a man and fashioned a pitcher in place of an amphora.

[Note: Hezelo, who became a monk from the cathedral chapter of Liège under Peter the Venerable, is praised in Book III, chapter 2, for his exceptional learning and eloquence. We find nothing elsewhere about Gilo.]

The author of this presumption, moreover, is Pontius, who hoped that I possessed an acuity of mind of which I myself am not conscious. Pontius’s words began the case, his authority carried it forward, and his piety pleaded it. It is difficult to resist Pontius, who, by a certain prerogative of grace, is helped even by his silence when seeking to obtain something.

Overcome by these considerations, I attempted to reconsider what I had already read, not to testify about it as though I had seen it myself. Let no one wonder when, in the present work, he sees something added, suppressed, or altered—something that those who wrote about Hugo before me did not add, did not suppress, or wrote differently.

I added things, I admit, but things that I myself saw and things that I heard, to which I bear witness; and my testimony is true. What I suppressed altogether was suppressed because, if what had been read could have provoked calumnies, it might have detracted from the authority of matters that could be written and believed without danger to the faith.

I believe that I altered only this: that Count Geoffrey of Anjou,

[Note: Below, in chapter 33, the events between Hugo and Geoffrey of Anjou are discussed. Geoffrey was not Martel but the son of Martel, surnamed “the Bearded.” Whether the authors mentioned above added some error concerning the name in the actual matter, we cannot determine.]

is said to have arrogated Hugo to himself as abbot. Because the writers mentioned above lacked truthful informants concerning this, they incurred the stigma of falsehood.

Whatever, therefore, I have written as it was granted to me from above, let it either come into your judgment or, if you deem it should be suppressed, disappear completely. Yet I prefer less to produce what has been approved than to conceal what is defective; for it is a more shameful loss to lose a name once acquired than never to have acquired one at all.

May the Lord God preserve you for the children of his adoption, holy Father. Know, moreover, that you repay me in kind if you love me and pray for me.

# CHAPTER I  
## Saint Hugo’s birth, his assumption of the monastic habit, his abbatial dignity, and his virtues in that office

### 1

Blessed Hugo, an Aeduan by nationality,

[Note: Augustodunum was called *Augusta Aeduorum* by the ancients; hence *Aeduan* and *Augustodunensian* are used interchangeably.]

distinguished by noble parents, was still more distinguished by the prerogative of his life and by the titles of his virtues.

When he had escaped the weakness of infancy, his father Dalmatius,

[Note: Dalmatius was lord of the castle formerly called Sinemurum and now Semur, seven or eight leagues north of Augustodunum, approximately halfway between Dijon and Avallon. The Sammarthani assign another town in Brionnais, much farther away.]

a man of consular rank, and his mother, named Aremburgis,

[Note: To Aremburgis the same Sammarthani add the surname “of Vergy” or “of Vergiaco,” a name thereafter often joined to Burgundian marriages.]

held different opinions concerning the education of the boy.

The woman, devoted to God, thought he should be dedicated to the study of letters because, before he was born, she asserted that the dignity of the priesthood had been divinely promised to him. When she was pregnant and feared the pains and danger of childbirth, a certain religious priest of holy reputation approached the altar of the Lord to offer sacrifice for her. Then, while he was celebrating the sacred mystery, the appearance of a certain child seemed to emerge in the chalice, displaying immeasurable radiance.

The priest’s authority caused the vision, when reported to the mother, to be believed. It therefore seemed fitting that he should be dedicated to the ministry of the chalice, since the one promised had appeared in the chalice.

His father, however, desiring an heir to his earthly possessions, destined the insignia of secular knighthood for the boy. Thus, when Hugo had reached the age for elementary schooling, his father pressed him to ride with the young men of his own age, turn a horse in circles, brandish a spear, handle a shield with ease, and—what he abhorred even more deeply—to pursue plunder and booty.

But Hugo had been born for another vocation. Bodily weakness and his mind alike drew him away from knighthood. Unfit for arms, unwilling to plunder, he was already drawn wholly to Christ by both nature and grace.

One day, when the young men mentioned above were taking a cow from a poor man, Christ’s recruit was deeply grieved, sharing in no guilt because he shared in no plunder. Nevertheless, by restoring the loss to his neighbor through an annual repayment, he silenced the man’s complaint and relieved his poverty. Thus the servant of God made both the wrong done to the poor man and the loss itself fruitful.

### 2

While he was still of schoolboy age, he displayed in word and deed the dourness of old age. Already he pursued wantonness without mercy and took humility as the guardian of chastity. Already he despised luxurious dress and delicacies; amid enticements he remained ignorant of enticements.

With young men he had nothing of a young man except his age. He was greatly at odds with plunderers and showed remarkable compassion toward the afflicted. He committed the word of God to a tenacious memory and was a frequent visitor to the church, but secretly, for he feared his father, who attributed the first fruits of virtue to idleness and inactivity.

At that time the bishop of Auxerre, named Hugo,

[Note: Hugo, bishop of Auxerre, was the son of Lambert, count of Chalon. He is said to have attended the council of Anse in 1025 and seems to have lived until about 1040. But how could our Hugo have been his great-grandson? Perhaps he was descended from a sister’s son or daughter, for the bishop of Auxerre was his father’s only son and therefore also heir to the county. As elsewhere often happens, the county is here called the “consulate.”]

also vigorously governed the county of Chalon. For his sake Blessed Hugo scarcely managed to wrest permission from his father to travel to Chalon.

There, having received the first elements of grammar, the young man was opened, as it were, to an entrance into the heights of the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0861B]

At last, tearing off his secular clothing, he chose “to be rejected in the house of his God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Psalm 23:11).

Following, therefore, the evangelical saying, “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:17), he came to Cluny without his father’s knowledge. His father opposed him, both in words and by example, as Hugo longed for his homeland.

He revealed the inclination of his mind to Blessed Odilo,

[Note: We gave the Life of Blessed Odilo on 1 January.]

who at that time was the abbot under whom the monastery flourished. Then, entering the chapter according to custom, when he was declaring his request for admission before the community,

[Note: The printed text has *edisceret* incorrectly; *ediceret* should be read.]

one of the brothers, taught by the Holy Spirit, said: “O happy Cluny, which today has received a treasure more precious than every treasure!”

When his life had therefore been changed together with his habit, he devoutly ascended the first steps of the monastic order—obedience and humility, which hold the primacy among Christian virtues. Surpassing the others in these qualities, he bore without complaint whatever difficulty the profession he had assumed involved.

As though observance of the monastic rules were insufficient for perfection, the servant of God added hardship for his own punishment and the Lord added it for his crown. He took food below the monastic allowance, so that eating broke his fast without at all removing his hunger. He also devoted himself diligently to vigils and often passed the night without sleep in continuous prayer.

His companions were blessed: abundant tears, fasting, and meditation on heavenly joys. Ambition stole nothing from the monk, and pleasure claimed nothing for itself. There was no arrogance in his mouth,

[Col. 0861D]

no vanity in his speech; everything about him spoke holiness, everything spoke of a monk.

Such grace also came to the servant of God from the monastic habit that even his father, who had borne his son’s sacred resolution with great difficulty,

[Note: I would prefer to read *nimis*, “too greatly.”]

would say that Hugo was more handsome than usual.

### 3

Pastoral fullness of concern already shone forth in him. He possessed no less wealth for counsel

[Col. 0862A]

than religious devotion for example. Celebrating him with such praises, Blessed Odilo, with the brothers’ consent, appointed him prior, so that his foresight might benefit both the possessions and the discipline of the order.

The young man undertook responsibility for the elders and carried out the business entrusted to him in such a way that administration did not diminish religion, nor religion impede administration. Promotion brought no arrogance upon him, nor did the fervor of his order grow cold. The dignity imposed upon him became material for virtue, not a loss of virtue.

With such gentleness did he show himself a father, and with such severity a teacher, that against offenders he used neither lax mercy nor excessive discipline.

His good reputation therefore spread like a sweet fragrance, and he acquired the favor of the common people and of princes, although he had sought it least of all. He was consequently sent to the Germans and restored to the monastery of Paterniacum

[Note: The monastery of Paterniacum was a priory in the diocese of Lausanne.]

the favor of the king,

[Note: Henry II is meant, crowned emperor in 1046 and deceased in 1056.]

from which it had fallen.

When Blessed Odilo’s death became known there, Hugo returned to the monastery in bitterness of spirit, bringing with him abundant gifts, which the aforementioned king sent through him to Cluny for the adornment of the house of the Lord.

Received with the reverence due to him, he found the community filled with tears. He urged them to restrain their weeping, although he himself could not restrain his own. He consoled the mourners, though he admitted no consolation for himself. Everyone’s Father was mourned by everyone, and the memory of paternal affection recalled tears that had dried.

The master himself had been buried, but the master’s merits lived unburied in the minds of his disciples. I must fail if I attempt to explain Odilo’s virtues, for by teaching and example alike he made a community of men into a community of virtues.

### 4

The time had come when provision had to be made for the deserted flock. After fasts and prayers had been prescribed, a shepherd was sought from the supreme Shepherd. The children of adoption assembled, concerned only for the salvation of souls.

At last, while they anxiously considered among themselves whom the Lord might deem worthy of pastoral care, a certain Adalmannus, whose authority was greater both by religion and by age, named Hugo as prior. The community, with unanimous assent, supported the one who had named him.

Then, on the day when the holy Church celebrated the chair of Saint Peter, the archbishop of Chrysopolis

[Note: This was also named Hugo, the first bishop of Besançon of that name, who held the see from 1031 to 1070.]

raised him to the abbatial blessing, although Hugo resisted and protested that he was unworthy.

Having undertaken pastoral vigilance, the servant of God drew no insolence from his promotion and allowed no access to vices. Under such a guardian of souls, judgment was not lacking for sin, nor growth for religion.

His entire life was claimed either by Mary or by Martha. Insatiable in reading and devoted to prayers, he was always either benefiting others or progressing himself. It would have been difficult to judge whether he was wiser or simpler. Just as there was nothing idle in his words, so there was nothing suspicious of dishonesty in his works.

He knew no anger except against vices. His teaching, suited to individuals and sufficient for all, possessed more of a father than of a judge, more mercy than censure.

Conspicuous in appearance and tall in stature, he enriched the gifts of his body with the titles of his virtues. Always silent with the Lord, when he spoke he always spoke in the Lord or about the Lord.

Although occupied with many matters, no one found him inattentive to individual concerns; he was wholly absorbed in whatever he had first undertaken to do. He loved God above himself, his neighbor as himself, and earthly things below himself, in an ordered charity.

Gentle and patient alike, he gave thanks for his own circumstances but wept over the injuries suffered by the poor.

[Col. 0863B]

### 5

Because he had read Christ’s saying, “Whatever you have done for one of the least of mine, you have done for me” (Matthew 25:40), he attended to their needs with such urgency as though Christ’s own person were visibly present.

For this reason an immense crowd of needy people surrounded him. As a faithful and prudent steward, he prepared food and obtained clothing for them. He avoided no work of mercy and no form of assistance. He attended to everyone’s requests whenever circumstances permitted their fulfillment.

When he traveled, groups of poor people met him wherever they had heard that he would pass. He distributed gold coins to them with a generous hand, preferring to give what would bring the greater reward when given.

When the food ran out with which he was accustomed to load pack animals for the use of the needy,

[Note: *Summarius*, *saumarius*, and *somarius* mean a beast of burden suited to carrying loads on its back. In the French vernacular: *sommier*.]

messengers were sent here and there to purchase what would both suffice for the crowd and satisfy the desires of the sick.

Moreover, whoever was afflicted either by age or by a serious illness he ordered to be brought nearer. He examined their distress more gently, asking with the greatest attentiveness what they needed or wanted. He shrank from no one’s conversation and feared no one’s discomfort.

Toward querulous elders flowing with bodily corruption, he was moved by compassion to multiply his benefits and to undertake a service full of reward. I speak of small matters: toward lepers dreadful to look upon, he frequently showed distasteful service without distaste.

You might have seen around his bed an immense heap of garments of various kinds. With only a few members of his household assisting, he himself was accustomed to cut and mend them.

You would also have seen bread and meat—everything prepared at hand, so that delay in giving a gift would not torment the poor man waiting for it.

To poor monks also he sent more generous blessings, lest lack of the necessities of life force them to wander either from the monastery or from the monastic life. With this kindness he helped the people of Marseille and many monasteries.
