Furthermore, when the tyranny of princes continually raged against Christ’s poor and exhortation achieved little, he softened it with gifts. To these works and uses he consecrated both silver and gold. He declared that money shone more brightly when spent in this way than when preserved.

And, in accordance with Ambrose’s testimony, “the Church’s chalice is truly a chalice when it ransoms from hunger or from the enemy those whom the blood of the chalice freed from death.”

# CHAPTER II  
## Favor with the Emperor Henry II; a mission undertaken for the pope in Hungary; the Council of Reims; King Alfonso of Spain freed from prison; the foundation of the monastery of Marciniacum

### 6

By these and many other praises of virtue, Blessed Hugo was held in high esteem among the great, who provided for the salvation of their souls by his counsel.

Under him the religious life of the monastery of Cluny increased day by day, and the fragrance of his name was like the fragrance of a full field that the Lord had blessed.

Thus the emperor of the Germans, namely Henry II, desiring to see his face and obtain his friendship, earnestly asked him to come to him. The pious Father granted the request, entered Saxony, and was received with the highest honor and joy alike.

After spending a few days there, at the king’s request he lifted his son from the sacred font, giving the child his father’s name.

[Note: Henry III was born on 10 November 1051. His baptism, delayed until the following year, seems to have taken place on Holy Saturday, since Easter was celebrated on 19 April.]

He celebrated Easter with the emperor at Cologne in Agrippina. The Germans marveled at his maturity of conduct despite his still youthful age, the gentleness of his way of life, the graciousness of his face, and the mildness of his words.

By these signs of virtue the king’s soul became so closely joined to him and to the monastery of Cluny that the king himself seemed to have entered into perpetual friendship with them.

At last, having scarcely obtained permission to return, the pious shepherd went back to his flock, bringing greater gifts sent by the aforementioned king as a pledge of affection.

Thus the servant of God returned and gladdened the sons who had awaited their father in prayer, both by news of the king’s invitation and by his own arrival.

### 7

Later, sent to Hungary at the command of the Roman pontiff, he took charge of restoring peace.

[Note: The disputes probably concerned the conflicts between Andrew, king of Hungary, and his brother Béla after the coronation of the child Solomon. These conflicts were repeatedly settled and repeatedly renewed. See the Hungarian writers under Leo IX and also under later popes.]

He pursued the task he had prudently undertaken and completed the business entrusted to him, carrying it out to the praise of God and glory.

As he was returning, having received both the king’s favor and many gifts, he was captured by a certain tyrant of that region. Everything precious found among his possessions was plundered.

Disturbed by this injury, the servant of God turned to the help of prayer and interceded for his evil-doers. He was less concerned about the loss of property than about the danger to their souls.

To avoid appearing either to trust in his own merits or to ask for pardon for the transgressor and restoration of his property for himself, he entrusted both matters to Blessed Majolus. He asked that he be helped through Majolus’s prayers and merits.

Without delay, the author of the injury was pierced with remorse, threw himself at the abbot’s knees, and with a contrite and humbled heart asked pardon. Everything that had been taken was restored in full. Moreover, so that the offended man might be appeased by an act of service, the one who had committed the robbery provided the abbot with an escort.

In many other matters too, Blessed Hugo’s diligence, requested by the Roman pontiff, earned praise from the pontiff and an eternal reward from the Lord.

For when Pope Stephen was suffering a mortal illness in the city of Florence,

[Note: Pope Stephen X, who died on 28 April 1058, is commonly called Stephen IX. The anonymous author in the Cluniac Library, column 451, gives a fuller account of the assistance provided to him by Saint Hugo, but adds nothing substantive.]

Hugo went there at the sick man’s request, accompanied by monks of consummate holiness, for whom, in Paul’s words, “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

The aforementioned bishop testified that at the servant of God’s arrival the evil spirit had departed, but at his departure it returned. Blessed indeed was the man whose life Satan abhorred and whose presence he feared.

Finally, when the aforementioned pontiff had been brought near death and had entrusted his weary limbs and failing nature to sackcloth and ashes, he received the sacred Viaticum and breathed out his spirit between the holy hands of the abbot.

### 8

When Leo IX had reached Reims in order to transfer the body of Blessed Remigius and was celebrating a general synod there, the holy man was present, full of authority and reverence, and by his presence contributed greatly to the decrees of the council.

[Note: The Council of Reims and the translation of Saint Remigius took place on 1 and 3 October 1049. They are discussed at greater length under 19 April in the preliminary commentary on the Acts of Saint Leo. There Hugo sat second among the abbots, after Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius.]

When the council was dealing with the Simoniacs, and certain bishops, whose consciences had brought them shame or whose ignorance had brought them silence, debated the aforementioned heresy too mildly, Hugo himself, inflamed with zeal for justice, resolutely sought to abolish the commerce of Simon.

He rose up against it and stood as a wall for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 13:5); he was moved neither by the number of those resisting nor by respect for persons.

When he was questioned at that council about his own promotion, he replied: “The flesh desired it; the spirit resisted.”

[Note: The same response is recorded in the Acts of the council as follows: “The deacon turned the course of his speech toward the abbots who were present and urged them to confess, lest they too had entered the Lord’s sheepfold by some way other than the door. First Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius, rose and cleared himself of such guilt with an appropriate response. Then Lord Hugo of Cluny followed and added this account of his purification: ‘With God as my witness, I gave or promised nothing to obtain the honor; the flesh indeed desired it, but mind and reason resisted.’”]

This was surely a sound answer,

[Col. 0866A]

for he was above all a just accuser of himself (Proverbs 18:17). It showed that, though he had been assailed by the temptation of the flesh so that he might fall, he had resisted by the strength of the spirit so that he would not fall.

He possessed such grace in exhortation that, awaiting his speech, the minds of those present hung in suspense. Therefore, at the pope’s command, he delivered a holy speech full of grace. Through it the Simoniacs were expelled from the dignities they had acquired by evil means, and fornicating priests were forbidden the sanctuary of the Lord.

### 9

Another sign of his holiness and merits followed.

Hildebrand, a deacon of the Roman Church who later attained the majesty of that same see, was sent into Gaul and entered the chapter at Cluny. After sitting there for some time, he saw Christ beside Blessed Hugo, suggesting the rules and decrees of the monastic order.

When he had left, he reported to several people what he had seen. From that time he embraced the friendship of the servant of Christ more devotedly and proclaimed his holiness.

Hildephonsus, or Alphonsus,

[Note: Hildephonsus, or Alphonsus—called Andefonsus in Hugo’s Life—was, by the will of his father Ferdinand, king of León. He was attacked in war and captured in 1071 by his ambitious brother Sancius, king of Castile, who is inexplicably called “Santulus” here, and was taken to Burgos for custody.]

king of Spain, was held in chains after being captured by his brother Santulus.

When the abbot of mercy heard this, he ordered that prayer be offered persistently for the king, remembering the affection of his father Fredeleides,

[Note: Fredeleides is called Fredeldanus in the Life by Hugo and Fredelannus by Peter the Venerable. Elsewhere the better form is Fredelandus, for which the forms Fredenandus and finally Ferdinandus later prevailed. The name is Gothic and, according to its different spellings, means “one who makes peace in the land” or “peace-maker.” Instead of the reading found here, we have judged that *multo beneficio*, “by a great benefit,” should be substituted, despite the manuscript’s reading.]

who had bound the monastery of Cluny to himself by a great benefit.

When acceptable offerings were made for him and prayers multiplied, Blessed Peter appeared to him through a certain bishop and indicated that the day of his deliverance was near.

[Note: In the aforementioned Life it is said that the apostle Peter appeared to a certain brother at Cluny and revealed that the Lord had accepted Hugo’s prayers for the restoration of Andefonsus.]

Through the intercession of the abbot and the community of Cluny, he obtained that the king, released from his chains, should recover his rule.

Without delay, the same apostle appeared to Santulus as he slept and threatened him with severe punishments unless, after bringing his brother out of prison, he restored the dignity he had wrongfully taken from him.

Awakened by the vision, Santulus hastened to fulfill whatever the apostle had commanded.

[Note: What Saint Hugo had ordered to be announced to Alphonsus concerning his freedom and kingdom was indeed fulfilled, but not at one and the same time. Rather, Santius responded to the vision shown to him only by releasing his brother from prison and sending him to the monastery of Saint Facundus to live among the monks. But Alphonsus escaped from there, fled to Toledo among the Moors, and did not return to the kingdom until his brother was killed in 1073. Thus Santius may perhaps have paid the penalty for neglecting the command.]

Thus Hildephonsus, restored both to himself and to his kingdom, sent a written petition asking that he might deserve to see his liberator and be granted an interview with him.

The desire of the powerful man was fulfilled. After crossing the Pyrenees,

[Col. 0867A]

the servant of God was received with solemnity and festive ceremony.

The king rejoiced at the arrival of such a guest, finding in his conduct, speech, and dress nothing except instruction in morals.

So that he might not at some time appear ungrateful to his intercessors, he arranged that two hundred ounces of gold should be assigned annually to the monastery of Cluny, double the tribute paid by his father. He desired the day of both deliverances—the day of his release from prison and the day of his release from the body—to be celebrated.

[Note: Peter the Venerable states that Alphonsus customarily paid forty ounces in addition to the two hundred of gold and founded two monasteries for the Cluniacs.]

As the man of God returned with the money mentioned above, he brought with him a Moor who had recently been baptized but was still darker in mind than in skin.

The pious abbot, wishing to show him greater respect because he had accepted the Christian faith, had provided costly garments for him. But the man, like a whitened tomb, thrust sacrilegious hands into the abbot’s pierced saddle-pouches and removed whatever gold or silver he found in them.

He was nevertheless caught while fleeing and brought back to the abbot with the money he had carried away. Thus the fraudulent attempt did not harm the servant of God.

These things are great indeed, but greater are those that follow.

### 10

Near the castle of Bliterium,

[Note: The castle is called Bliterium here; in other Lives it is called Briderium.]

certain men of perverse mind provoked the revered Father by inflicting injuries upon him. Although the pious abbot was inclined to forgive and granted pardon when they asked for it, their presumption was nevertheless severely punished by the Lord.

For immediately, as flames ravaged it, the castle of the wicked was burned.

So that it might be believed that this had happened by divine vengeance rather than by chance, two soldiers who had long been dead appeared to certain inhabitants of the same castle who had gone out on business and knew nothing of the injuries or the fire.

When the inhabitants recognized the two men clearly and, disturbed, marveled at their appearance, the soldiers said: “Return as quickly as possible; you will find Bliterium burned.”

When Blessed Hugo entered it, neither his religious status nor his office received any respect.

The inhabitants, astonished and terrified, returned with great haste and found the matter exactly as they had learned it.

Let no one suppose that the man of God either sought or accepted offered riches as though he were desirous of money. Their abundance served not avarice but mercy, not himself but the needy.

With the Prophet he said: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8). Whatever the devotion of the faithful brought to him, he consecrated all of it either to the adornment of the church or to the expenses of the poor.

The abundance of possessions did not exalt his soul, nor did their loss cast it down. In every condition he placed earthly things after heavenly things, and transitory things after eternal things.

### 11.

Moreover, he was concerned not only with the salvation of men; he also took care to lead women from the shipwreck of this great and spacious sea into the harbor of salvation, making known to them the way of life through instruction and preparing it for them at his own expense. On his own estate, called Marciniacus, he built a monastery and suitable buildings for religious life, where older women, weary of the license of marriage, might purge their former errors and deserve to be bound in the embraces of Christ.

Noble women chose this place. Having experienced the pleasures of marriage as well, they endured the loss of both with all the greater patience because they had learned that the pleasure they brought was both brief and full of sorrow. He established that they should live under rules such as these: none of them, whether because of some domestic necessity or for any other business, was to appear before the sight of men, lest those to whom he had prescribed the vow of continence should be enticed to sin by a gaze. Their administrators were religious and prudent men, under whose guardianship there was no fear either that the property would be dissipated or that their honor would suffer harm.

There was no young woman there—or scarcely any—lest the still-lascivious heat of youth should either bring disgrace upon the place or generate scandal among the sisters.

[Note: In the Cluniac Library, fol. 493 and following, there is preserved a writing of St. Hugh, composed toward the end of his Life, addressed to his successors as a supplication or warning, in which he commands under anathema: “Let the place always remain in the condition in which we began and maintained it: no one of childish age is ever to be received there into the religious habit; nor anyone except one in whom it can be tested whether the spirit is from God, and who has in any case already reached, if not a greater age, at least her twentieth year. If anyone is of a more wanton age, and this has been certainly ascertained, she must not be admitted into this community of women.” Again, in the supplication that follows on fol. 495—or, more truly, in the testament—in which, after asking pardon for the negligent administration of his office, he orders certain things to be supplied annually to the brothers after his death, he finally turns to the abbot who would succeed him and commends this place to him first of all, as though it were unique up to that time, and then the other brothers. Quercetanus presents various fragments of important charters relating to this monastery of Marciniacus in his notes on this passage; there he also teaches that, according to St. Hugh’s institution, two administrators and ten religious men were assigned to its governance.]

For their instruction he appointed an old man named Renchon, a monk of consummate reputation, who knew both how to stir up devotion through mercy and how to restrain excesses through discipline. Moreover, lest the sacred purpose of the handmaids of Christ should fail through lack of food or clothing, he provided them with abundant revenues and acquired estates for them. Thus he cared for their needs, so that neither superfluity might lead them into sin nor want extort a complaint.

Adorning the monastery also with very many ornaments, among other relics he placed there the arm of the blessed virgin and martyr Agnes, clad in silver and gold.

### 12.

Other monasteries were also built under him and through him, and very many cells were constructed.

[Note: In the same supplication he says: “As you see at the present time, God—not through our merits but through his immense clemency—has greatly enlarged this place on every side and enriched it both with brothers and with possessions; and he has extended it not only throughout our own region but also through Italy, Lorraine, England, Normandy, France, Aquitaine, Gascony, Provence, and Spain.” In the privilege of Paschal II, granted to Pontius in the very year in which the saint died, on 16 October, seventy-five priories are enumerated that remained under the administration of Abbot Hugh; many of these grew into abbeys, in addition to the twelve abbeys already established at that time. Hence Hugh may rightly be said, among the first five abbots of Cluny, to have been “later in order, but first in usefulness.”]

Old abbeys, which the negligence of their inhabitants had utterly worn away, were restored to their former dignity both in order and in possessions. For Cluniac religious life flourished so greatly under the aforesaid Father that abbots were sought from it for monasteries lying desolate; at the same time examples of holiness and a standard of discipline were taken from it.

Happy the Church, which deserved to receive from that holy community a supreme priest!

How great his discretion and mercy were is shown by the kindness he extended to the younger monks. Although, according to custom, they were given less than a pound of bread and drink, he nevertheless ordered that an equal amount be given to them, judging it fair that those whom the same burden of the day and the same heat afflicted should receive the same allowance, as though the same wage had already been paid. It was indeed a sound arrangement: it both restrained that age from murmuring and strengthened it for the labor of the obedience it had undertaken.

## CHAPTER III. The secrets of souls discerned by him and future events foretold.

### 13.

To show how pleasing to God he rendered his service in all things, Blessed Hugh is said to have received, together with discernment of spirits, the gift of prophecy. Among those who professed the monastic ascent, he freely discerned with what disposition each person approached him. He perceived who would become a good fish in the net of Blessed Benedict, who would bear the angel of light, and who the angel of darkness.

Lest we seem rather to attribute this grace to him than to report it as bestowed by God, the examples that follow, supported by his testimony, serve as evidence and confirmation.

A certain lord named Maingodus, carrying a wounded spirit because of the delay in his reception—a delay which the prudent Father had suspended for some time in order to test him—resolved to leave and flee. When this was discovered through a revelation of the spirit, the most devout abbot rebuked the aforesaid brother in harsher words, at once pointing out the wounds of his mind and applying to those wounds the medicine of paternal consolation. Thus, coming to his senses, he patiently awaited the reception whose postponement he had regretted.

### 14.

He also foretold, in a clear prophecy, the death of the younger William, who had succeeded his father, William the Great and triumphant conqueror of the English. That servant of God was at Marciniacus, together with Anselm, a man of glorious reputation, the archbishop of Canterbury.

[Note: St. Anselm had been driven into exile in 1096; William was killed on 2 August 1100.]

These were two great lights, whose devotion advanced toward the love of rewards through exhortations and examples offered in turn. Three other monks were there as well—namely Baldwin, Edmer, and Eustace—all sons of light, walking blamelessly in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord (Luke 1:6).

Blessed Hugh turned to them and said: “It is excessive to reveal divine judgments to the archbishop, by which the just Judge casts down the powerful from their throne and exalts the humble (Luke 1:52). But we tell you that during the past night a sentence of condemnation has been pronounced against the king of the English, and that he will reign only a short while longer.”

A few days had passed when, behold, the event followed the prophecy of the blessed man who had foretold it. For the king in question, while engaged in the pursuit of the hunt, was struck in the heart by an arrow shot by a certain soldier, and immediately, overtaken by sudden death, expired.

[Note: On 21 April we gave the Life of St. Anselm, written by the Eadmer named here. In Book II, no. 55, he says that St. Hugh “accused the king before the throne of God, judged him, and pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him”; from the following section it appears that the king died on the third day afterward.]

Thus, when the king’s life had ended, it became clear both that the abbot possessed the grace of prophecy and that the archbishop of Canterbury, who had yielded before the king who persecuted him, received the opportunity to return to his see.

### 15.

Again, while the servant of God was in Aquitaine, he visited the church of Blessed Vivian, as he was solicitous in visiting holy places. There, while carefully reading the acts and Life of the aforementioned confessor, he found mention of a certain good man named Amandus.

[Note: St. Vivian, bishop of Saintes, is commemorated on 18 August. His Life contains no mention of St. Amandus, but says that he had Ambrose, whom he succeeded, as his teacher. We therefore desire to be more fully informed about that Amandus—for someone so solemnly exalted ought to have his own day of cult, even though Saussayus omitted to record him in the Gallican Martyrology.]

Desiring to learn more about him, Hugh asked the clerics present about his reputation and homeland, his way of life and death, and his burial. They replied that Blessed Amandus had been the teacher of St. Vivian, distinguished in merit, eminent in learning, and renowned for his example. His body, as rumor reported, was buried somewhere in Gaul.

The following day, the dean of the canons, intending to build a hospice at the same place, asked Blessed Hugh to designate the foundation for the work he had undertaken. But he, instructed by the Holy Spirit, said: “Lay the foundations here, and you will not regret it.”

Accordingly, at his suggestion, boys digging more deeply discovered a mausoleum of remarkable beauty, marked with the name of Blessed Amandus. When it was found, the clergy rejoiced and the people glorified God, who is wondrous in his saints (Psalm 67:36), no longer doubting the abbot’s merit, which had become clear through the discovery of the confessor.

### 16.

Wonders followed upon wonders. For the sake of consolation, the devout Father was accustomed to visit the places that belonged to the monastery of Cluny. Having therefore entered the cell of St. Mary called “of Charity”—

[Note: St. Mary of Charity, in the region of Nevers, was a priory founded by St. Hugh through the monk Gerard, on the Loire; it is commonly called Charité.]

—he received the brothers gathered there with a kiss. Yet he recoiled from meeting one of them and avoided kissing him. Clearly, taught by the spirit, he had learned that the man’s mouth was full of blasphemy and filth, and was not fit to be honored by a servant of God with the kiss of peace.

Those present were astonished and perplexed by the novelty of the matter. The abbot asked what life the wretched man had led and what religious practice he pursued in private conversation. He replied that he was a layman—

[Note: Here *mechanicus* means “layman”; elsewhere it is ordinarily used for an uneducated person. The marginal addition to Hugh’s Life, no. 6, as though *Manichaeum* ought to be read, is an inept gloss.]

—and that he was polluted by the tricks of necromancy. The shepherd drove him from the fold, since he displayed no sign of conversion either in his words or in his conduct.

Thus, in one and the same matter, both the wolf’s deception and the shepherd’s foresight became known.

### 17.

When the same servant of God had been received at the monastery of Angeriacum—

[Note: The monastery is called Angeliacense, Angeriacense, and, in the Life of St. Genulf, also Ingeriacense. In Hugh’s work it is the monastery of St. John of Angeliacum, commonly Saint-Jean-d’Angély, in the Saintonge region on the river Boutonne. It was founded by Pippin, king of Aquitaine and son of the emperor Louis the Pious. For more about this monastery, especially its two distinguished charters, see Quercetanus’s notes on the Library.]

—with the senses of the flesh briefly laid aside, he saw with a purer gaze of the mind a certain bolt of lightning coming from above, breaking into the chapter house of the monastery of Cluny, and dragging a great ruin along with it.

From this vision the man of God inferred that an offense had been committed at Cluny which, unless cleansed by a most public correction, would provoke the indignation of the heavenly Judge against that place. Without delay he returned to Cluny, preferring the gain of souls to the business that pressed upon him and that he had undertaken to complete.

Then, entering the chapter, by the same spirit through which he had already learned of the guilt, he also recognized the guilty person. Calling him by name, he said:

“Blush, Peter, and do penance while you may, lest you begin to repent at a time when repentance is profitable to no one at all. Reveal yourself completely to the prior; uncover the wound of your mind, so that you may experience care proportionate to the wound from the one who heals. Unhappy man, shake off the yoke of the devil and embrace the yoke of Christ, for his yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30). Since, although you have already been admonished so often, you nevertheless do not cease to resist, let a stricter discipline punish the guilt accompanied by obstinacy. For your sparing of your own offenses works toward the peril of others.”

[Note: The same Hugh, recounting this in no. 15, says: “He hastened back to Cluny and summoned the priors and guardians of the order. He inquired into the negligence of the brothers but could discover nothing of the sort through them. Having dismissed them, he returned as usual to the Lord, fulfilled the vows of his prayers, entered the chapter, and looked around at the brothers. A wondrous thing! By revelation of the Spirit he detected among the others a hidden guilty man; he accused and convicted him. That guilty man was Peter, who had come from Terdiniacum. The merciful Judge duly scourged the penitent and mercifully healed him. At this, each of them looked around at himself, lest the spiritual eye of the Father should discover something improper in him.”]

When blows were added to these words, the obstinate brother was restored both to himself and to the order; and the good of obedience, which exhortation had not produced, was brought forth by correction.

### 18.

At another time a similar vision appeared to him. While he was sleeping, a certain person approached him and said that he ought to undertake the exhausting journey as far as Chalon, because an offense had been committed in the monastery of St. Marcellus—

[Note: The monastery of St. Marcellus at Chalon was founded by King Guntram, concerning whom see the extensive treatment in his Life, 28 March, §2.]

—and that, since it had until then been covered by silence, it ought to be cut away by monastic discipline.

Awakened by this, the servant of God set out on the journey. When he entered the monastery, he learned that the matter was as he had understood it in the vision. Applying medicine to the wound, he drove away an old and difficult-to-cure corruption.

One night, while the man of God was giving his weary limbs a little rest in sleep, he seemed to see a multitude of serpents lying beneath his pillow, along with reptiles of various kinds. Disturbed by them, he could not continue sleeping. Then, removing the pillow, he found a book of Virgil. After throwing it aside, he slept peacefully.

The vision was appropriate to the matter, since the fables of poets are nothing other than certain poisons.

[Note: If this is said of the exceptionally chaste pagan poet Virgil—whom some call “Virgineus,” just as a one-eyed man could be called king among the blind—what shall we say of the more lascivious poets?]

### 19.

It is worthwhile to add to the accounts what we learned both by hearing and by seeing. Our predecessor Hoel—

[Note: Hoel, bishop of Le Mans from the year 1085; this meeting took place in 1094.]

—of blessed episcopal memory, was traveling to Rome and turned aside to Cluny in order to see the holy man of God. After obtaining the opportunity to speak with him, he was led, together with one of his archdeacons, into a small chamber devoted to sacred conversations, made famous more by its occupant than by its furnishings.

When the adopted sons had gathered and were mutually sharing with one another the benefits of their prayers, Blessed Hugh, looking frequently at the aforementioned archdeacon, said:

“Only take care not to fall short of the grace of God, for it has been ordained that you will by no means remain in the rank in which you now serve.”

Not much time had passed when the prophecy was followed by its fulfillment. For the archdeacon received episcopal dignity in the following year.

[Note: No one can be identified by a more suitable conjecture than Geoffrey of Mayenne, born of an illustrious family among the people of Le Mans, elected bishop of Angers in 1093 and consecrated in 1096.]

We heard this; we saw it happen while present; and in that conversation we became participants in the prayers of that blessed man. We had indeed learned, through the revelation of reputation, certain things about his holiness, certain things about his gentleness, and certain things also about those qualities by which judgment is applied to vice and increase is granted to virtue. But we found more: from the conduct of the flock we discerned the vigilance of the shepherd.

### 20.

Other matters remain, by which it is plainly shown that he, the patron of justice, was distinguished among the marks of holiness by the grace of prophecy.

A certain monk named Durannus—

[Note: Durannus was first abbot of Moissac in Quercy and later, around the year 1060, became bishop of Toulouse. He died around 1070, and, according to the Sammarthani, his image with a title of sanctity is displayed in the cloister of Moissac.]

—was accustomed to utter words that provoked laughter, being incapable of laying aside his foolish levity, which had become a prejudice against him. In other respects, however, he had so conducted himself in matters “against which there is no law” that he deserved to advance in life and learning, first to the abbacy and then to the episcopate.

When he was less than obedient to the abbot’s rebuke, the abbot said to him: “Brother, unless you perform worthy penance, after your passage from this life you will appear before the heavenly beings with foaming lips.”

It happened, however, that he neither abandoned his idle words nor failed to experience the fulfillment promised by the abbot’s prophecy. For the aforementioned Durannus, having paid the debt of nature, appeared in the habit that had been foretold to him to a certain Siguinus, a priest and religious man, miserably asking his assistance—though while alive he had scorned to obey him.

When the devout Father learned this from Siguinus’s report, he selected seven brothers and imposed silence upon them for a week, so that the excess of the mouth might be cleansed by obedience of the mouth. The others obeyed, but one of them, violating the command, broke the silence.

Again the bishop, wearing the same habit as before, appeared to the prescribed priest and accused the brother’s disobedience, saying that by breaking the command he had excluded the suffrages of the others. When the most merciful Father heard this, he once more imposed seven days of silence and made good, through obedience, the deficiency caused by its violation.

Thus it happened that, when the bishop appeared for the third time—but now bearing nothing defiled—he gave thanks to the abbot: through his intervention the reproach of the mouth had been wiped away, and the judge’s sentence had been changed.

This account both revealed the Father’s merit and increased among the brothers reverence for the obedience they had undertaken. Thus the discernment of spirits granted to the man of God taught him through effective governance what correction could accomplish, what should be endured with mercy, and what should be punished by discipline.

## CHAPTER IV. Various illnesses healed by him.

### 21.

Let no one suppose that the abbot was distinguished only by prophetic predictions; together with discernment of spirits, he had also received the grace of healings. It is established that some who were oppressed by various illnesses recovered after taking remnants from his table.

A certain Acardus, suffering from the violence of fevers, owed his restored health to the aforesaid remedy. In addition, three brothers who were lying ill with the same disease were restored to their former health through the merit of the blessed man. To two of them he granted complete health through the gift of blessed bread intended for them; the third, after enduring the burning of quartan fever for six months at Bourbon—

[Note: There are three places called Bourbon under various names. One, situated nearer Cluny on the Loire, is now called Bourbon-Lancy.]

—was ordered by the holy Father, who had arrived there at that time, to attend the sacred mysteries. He came while feverish, and, after Mass, drank wine in which the relics of the saints had been washed, as the abbot had commanded. The burning of the fever ceased.

O humility worthy of praise in the Father! What could have been attributed to his own merits, he preferred to assign to the relics of the saints.

Jarento, too, a monk of exemplary reputation, recovered after enduring the long affliction of fevers, having drunk wine with which the sacred fingers of the holy man had been washed after the sacrament had been offered to God.

### 22.

Blessed also was the physician who, together with the health of bodies, labored for the salvation of souls! Blessed, I say, was the soul through whose merits temporal remedy was obtained and through whose exhortation eternal remedy was obtained.

As he was traveling to Crispeium—

[Note: Crispeium, a town in the Vexin, containing the priory called that of St. Arnulf.]

—a fever-stricken soldier met him—

[Note: Hugh calls him Robert in no. 8.]

—and begged to be helped through his most holy intervention. Then, pressing his request more insistently, the abbot said: “Refrain, brother; refrain from robbery, and in this way you will regain the health you have lost.”

The soldier renounced his robberies, and at that very moment, in response to the abbot’s prayers, both the vow was made and the burning of the fever was extinguished.

Let no one wonder that health was granted to bodies through the abbot’s merit, since this grace was also added to him: souls released from the prison of the flesh found, through his intervention, a placated Judge.

A certain brother, having paid the debt of nature but not yet having been buried, appeared to two persons who had acquired a reputation for religious devotion. He said that, without the permission of the sacristan under whom he served, he had taken two solidi and spent them according to his own judgment. Because of this offense, the repose due to him had been postponed, though it could nevertheless be obtained through the abbot’s intercession.

When morning came, although each of the two knew nothing of the other, they nevertheless reported the aforementioned vision in the chapter, in the same order and in the presence of the holy man. The transgression was carefully examined and found to be venial. Through the suffrages of the prayers that the most merciful Father ordered to be offered with greater devotion, and through a more generous distribution of alms, the brother deserved to be released from it.

### 23.

In the city of Paris there was an eminent man named Robert, a soldier by profession, so benumbed by paralysis that in the same man one might have said that one part was alive and another already buried. This long-standing and deadly affliction had long since taken away the sick man’s hope of recovery.

It happened at that same time that the servant of God entered Paris and went up to the church that is famous both for the name and for the body of the most blessed virgin Genevieve. When he heard this, the sick man in question was carried there with the aid of others, threw himself at the abbot’s knees, and entreated him with sighs and tears to deserve his intervention before God.

The Father was moved by the anxiety of the suppliant and, during the sacred solemnities of Mass, sought to obtain the help requested for the paralytic. Yet, presuming nothing upon his own merits, he turned wholly to the prince of the apostles, whose shadow had restored health to the sick and whose prayer had restored life to the dead.

He therefore took the apostle’s chasuble—

[Note: Hugh adds that it was believed to have been brought from Antioch, and says that it provided the occasion for the miracle. After Mass, St. Hugh took the chasuble in his hand and said: “If only the sick man were here, so that we might experience the apostolic power in him!” When Robert heard this, he had himself carried there.]

—which, according to ancient reports, was believed to be in the aforementioned church, and lifted it over the prostrate sick man, crying out: “The apostle Peter said to the paralytic: ‘May the Lord Jesus Christ heal you.’”

At these words Robert immediately recovered as though Peter himself had uttered the prayer on his behalf. He who had arrived half alive returned in good health, and those who were present bore witness that the life of a man whose petition they had seen to be so effective before God was pleasing to him.

[Note: He adds: “This matter is very well known; nearly the whole city is witness to it.”]

### 24.

Perhaps these things would be attributed to apostolic merits, and since it is established that the shadow of Peter restored health to the sick, Robert might accordingly be said to have recovered through Peter’s garment. Yet other works of Hugh are read of, no less great in merit, in which the benefit can be assigned to Hugh without danger to the faith.

While he was visiting the dependent cells in Gascony, as he did those belonging to the monastery of Cluny, he noticed not far from the road a small hut whose inhabitant was poor and leprous. From rich he had become poor, from splendid despised, from healthy leprous; he was leading a life more grievous than death.

The servant of God rejoiced that he had obtained a favorable opportunity to visit Christ in the poor man. While the others went ahead, he entered the shelter with only one monk as companion. He devoted himself entirely to consolation, caressed the torn skin, and repeatedly called him fortunate in his misfortune, since he had been granted to be cleansed by bodily scourges and the fire of poverty.

Finally, as the man of God was about to leave and had nothing to give the poor man, he removed the lambskin garment he was wearing and clothed the poor man with it. An unexpected grace accompanied the garment: as soon as the poor man had put it on, the disfigurement of his skin disappeared. The contagion of leprosy was wiped away, and health and beauty were restored to all his limbs.

The servant of Christ departed, leaving the poor man a blessing that benefited the recipient beyond hope and revealed still more clearly the merit of the giver’s desire.

Others also are said to have received the healing they sought, both from clothing and from water that had dripped from his hands.

### 25.

Wigo, a monk of venerable reputation and a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, had lost the use of his voice. He was extremely sad because, with Christmas approaching, he could not perform the obligation of singing.

While he was resting beside the abbot’s footstool and hoping for the restoration of his voice through the holy man’s merits, he secretly took the strap of the abbot’s cap and placed it around his neck. As soon as it was removed—once the thing that obstructed his arteries had been loosened—the use of his former voice and melody was completely restored to him.

A cancer—a deadly disease—had eaten away the foot joint of a certain Theoderic, a soldier of great power but of even greater devotion before God. Since medical skill had been unable to overcome it, it was also removing his hope of life. Yet through the abbot’s merits the burning of this horrible disease was extinguished in the following manner.

The abbot had sung Mass, and servants, without the abbot’s knowledge, had brought to the sick man, who was present and had requested it, water that had dripped from the abbot’s hands. When it was poured over the parts consumed by the disease, the joint was restored to its proper condition; the loss of flesh that had been eaten away was repaired, and, as the water took the place of medicine, the abbot unknowingly restored health.

For it was harsh and intolerable to the man of God that anything should be carried away from what was around him or remained from his table in the hope of obtaining healing. A man of true virtue, he regarded the courting of others’ tongues as the destruction of virtues; for he had absolutely no desire for praise, except for that whose subject was in his heart and whose witness was in heaven.

Although both his deeds and his words gained this for him, while he longed for another reward, no pride arose in him from the proclamation of miracles.

The servant of God also benefited others without knowing it. Although we have not committed all of them to writing, we have judged it appropriate to set down some of them on these pages.

### 26.

There was in one of the obediences a monk named William who, lying ill with a long-standing disease of the leg, could not perform the duties assigned to him. The illness had increased to such a degree that, after losing its natural form, the leg appeared to be a kind of globe.

When the growing disease seemed to speak of nothing but death, he turned wholly in hope and faith toward the abbot’s merit. Placing his hands upon the swollen leg, he said:

“I command you, affliction, in the name of Jesus Christ, and on behalf of the Father whose commands brought me here: withdraw and allow me to fulfill the obedience assigned to me.”

On the following night, while he was sleeping, two monks in white appeared and said that they had been sent by Blessed Hugh. One of them placed his hands upon the leg and poured in oil; the other seemed to anoint the diseased parts with a gentler touch, as though his hand were suspended above them.

When this was done, the illness itself withdrew as the monks departed, and grace restored the health that medicine had been unable to restore. When the monk awoke and felt that the distress of his illness had been destroyed, he attributed the recovery of his health to his blessed Father.

### 27.

Because of the difficulty of childbirth, a certain woman had lost the use both of her tongue and of her hand, and feared the loss of the other faculties of her body as well. While she lay in this distress, it was suggested to her in a dream that she ought to travel to Laisiacum—

[Note: Laisiacum, perhaps a town in the region of Le Mans, commonly called Lassay?]

—where she would be relieved of both afflictions through the merits of Blessed Hugh.

The woman obeyed. When she had been brought there, and while the aforesaid Father was celebrating the divine mysteries in the presence of the woman herself in the oratory of St. Sulpicius—

[Note: St. Sulpicius, not Suplicius, as it was incorrectly printed. There are several churches of this name throughout Gaul; we discussed him on 17 January.]

—she deserved, through his merits, to obtain a complete remedy for both diseases.

It may be believed that, in relieving the sufferings of human bodies, a grace had been granted from above to this adopted son, a grace that is also reported to have been present in disturbed weather.

For Count Louis and his wife Sophia—both, namely, a man and woman of notable devotion—had received him as a guest at Aldechiarcum—

[Note: Aldechiarcum, called anciently Chirica in Hugh’s Life, was a place not far from Basel; it is therefore Altenkirch, five miles away, on the river Ill. *Kirch* means “church” in German, from the Greek word Κυριακόν, “belonging to the Lord,” as most scholars maintain, though there is no time here to summon them for judgment.]

Then, after a table had been set in the garden, the disturbed air gave warning signs of a storm. The servants ran about in confusion, not knowing what would become of the dishes already set out. But the servant of God raised his hand, made the sign of the cross, and thus drove away the threatening storm.

Lest it seem to have departed by chance rather than through the abbot’s merits, it is reported that, while rain and thunder raged all around, that place remained free from the storm and stayed clear.

At Paredum—

[Note: Paredum was a priory in the diocese of Autun, annexed to the monastery of Cluny by Bishop Hugh in 999, the same Hugh discussed above.]

—a boy consecrated to the monastic warfare was struck down by a board falling from the top of the bell tower. At that time the blessed abbot had come to Paredum to visit the brothers.

The boy, whose pulse examined at the thumbs indicated that death was near, was carried to him half alive. The brothers mourned the boy as though he were already dead, although he had scarcely begun to live in the camp of spiritual warfare.

Finally, the devout abbot, pierced with compassion, touched the stricken boy, attended to him with services rather than funeral rites, and, as a veteran soldier of Christ, ran to the door of divine mercy with such persistence in prayer that both health was restored to the boy and the boy was restored to the community.

### 28.

Many, invited by the fame of such miracles, desired above all to see him, to remain attached to him, and to be instructed by his most holy teachings. For his entire life, equal to sacred institutions, and his entire conduct were a school for blessed living. There were few, if any, monasteries that did not advance through his vigilant instructions or examples.

It is difficult to describe how fatherly his affection was toward the monks or abbots who came to him, how adequately he answered those who sought his counsel, and how piously he opened to those who knocked.

Among them, when the abbot of Soissons approached the chief teacher of monastic perfection, he had as his companion on the journey a certain priest named Peter, who had long enjoyed Blessed Hugh’s familiarity.

[Note: Our manuscript has *Suecionensis*, which is certainly better than *Uccionensis*, as it is printed in the Library. It is unknown which abbots the abbey of St. Crispin at Soissons had before its restoration in 1157. Another abbey there, that of St. Medard, is more famous, but it lies outside the walls and is not usually designated by the name “of Soissons.”]

Because of this familiarity, the priest addressed him with greater confidence:

“We know, most holy Father, that you care for the afflicted and, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, become weak with those who are weak (2 Corinthians 11:29). Therefore, as I knock at the door of your mercy on behalf of one of my brothers, I lament that this wretched man needs to be helped by your holy prayers. A putrid wound, spreading more widely and affecting the healthy parts, has brought him to the danger of despair.”

At last the devout Father yielded to his pitiable entreaties. He ordered that bread left over from his own table be brought to him; when it was brought, he blessed it and gave it, blessed, to the priest. He also gave him a piece of the staff that he was accustomed to carry in his hand and use for support.

Having received these things, the priest returned in hope and faith, as distressed before by anxiety about his brother as he was afterward to rejoice in his recovery. For as soon as the piece of wood was placed upon the ulcer and the sick man ate the bread of blessing, the affliction of the putrid flesh was so completely driven away that no pain and no sign of illness remained there.

## CHAPTER V. Certain evils driven away by the protection of angels; the malevolent divinely punished; his generosity repaid.

29. Furthermore, one day, while the abbot was sleeping for a short while, the monks awakened him because of some pressing matter. The abbot asked: “Why have you brought this boy here?” The monks replied that they had brought no one. The abbot continued, saying: “Do you not see that boy of handsome appearance?” [Col. 0878B] When the monks again expressed their astonishment, affirming that they could see absolutely no one, the abbot realized that something divine had been shown to him and turned the conversation to other matters, making no further mention of the boy. I believe that the angel of God who guarded his body had appeared to him; by that angel’s watchfulness he avoided both the assaults of aerial powers and the dangers threatening his body.

Thus, when he had given himself over to sleep at Berziacum [Note: [Col. 0878D] Berziacum was a priory in the Mâconnais, in a town of the same name.], protected by angelic guardianship, he escaped a manifold danger of death. For suddenly, when the air had been thrown into confusion, winds arose as though they were beginning some kind of combat; flashes of lightning raged with increasing frequency. The house was battered by stones and hail, and lightning bolts flew about, so that not even the father’s dormitory, adjoining the church, remained untouched. For the force of the lightning, bursting in, [Col. 0878C] searched the aforesaid dwelling with such wandering violence that—if I may call it an equal miracle—it preserved three boys in the furnace and the holy man of God amid the raging flames.

The danger was increased by the masonry and stones falling everywhere, which the lightning-struck wall, torn apart, scattered around the sleeping abbot. The servants ran about; the monks lamented, supposing that the abbot had either been buried beneath the collapse and stones or consumed by fire. But he, protected by divine guardianship, lost neither his sleep through the uproar nor his safety through the flames that ravaged the place. Thus the servant of God, surrounded by a dreadful conflagration, was found worthy to be rescued by divine power and emerged unharmed.

30. The same Father is also said to have been preserved from other dangers, and his holy passing—which seemed imminent because of a most serious illness—was postponed into a venerable old age through the community’s intercession and lavish almsgiving. For once, blessed Hugh was afflicted by such a bodily disorder that despair of his life followed upon the impending calamity. From the middle of the mountain adjoining Cluny he was carried to the chapter house, as though he were about to give the brothers his final blessing. [Col. 0879A] The community wept, and whoever tried to console another was himself in need of consolation. The sons cried out for their father; the disciples surrounded their master. The flock recalled the shepherd’s unremitting vigils, and everywhere his deeds of compassion were proclaimed—deeds calculated to provoke tears.

Then, at his own indication, he was brought before images of the saints and apostles, hoping to obtain healing through their merits and imploring it. It was immediately granted, restoring a protector to the orphaned, a father to his sons, and a provider to the poor.

We also believe that what happened when he was traveling to Rome deserves no less to be committed to writing: his life and safety alike were preserved from death. As he was proceeding near the city of Vapingum [Note: [Col. 0879C] Vapingum was an episcopal city of Narbonese Gaul, commonly called Gap.], along precipitous mountain paths and dangerous winding passages, he encountered an even steeper descent by an unguarded approach. [Col. 0879B] When the mule veered toward the valley, on which its first steps rested, it found nothing solid. The monks grew pale [Note: [Col. 0879D] Hugh in his Life describes the event as follows, no. 13: “Once, as Father Hugh was traveling to Rome, he entered a very narrow path along the side of a hanging cliff. Beneath it lay a terrifying depth of precipice, which scarcely any traveler would ever dare to look upon. Thus, while his companions went ahead in single file, overcome with fear, the Father followed, raising his mind, eyes, and right hand alike toward heaven, while with his left he held the reins of his mount, wholly intent upon the Lord in prayer. As they passed by, a poor little woman had taken refuge in a very narrow hollow of the steep rock. When the holy man’s mule, carrying its burden, suddenly saw her hiding there, it was dreadfully frightened and abruptly sprang backward; springing back, it fell entirely into the immense abyss. There the saint, just as before, kept his mind, eyes, and right hand raised toward heaven even as he fell. His body was falling, but in mind he stood unmoved with the Lord. Thus the steadfastness of his mind prevailed, and, seated on his mount, he was invisibly carried back from the depths and restored to the path wholly unharmed.”], despairing that the present danger could be avoided by any human counsel. But the Lord, preparing for his servant an ending full of blessed hope and glory, miraculously drew him out of the open abyss: the mule was divinely guided toward the side where it found a solid path free of obstacles.

Moreover, a certain cleric returning from Spain with the abbot, while going ahead of his companions to the lodging, heedlessly slipped into a dreadful precipice. At the invoked name of the abbot, he was found worthy to be saved by catching hold of a small branch.

It is also reported that the abbot was repeatedly present to a certain Gerald, who was rashly rowing across the Loire. When the little boat sank and matters came to the point of mortal danger, Gerald cried out his name and swam safely to the bank. In this man’s case the abbot’s merit shone forth all the more clearly because Gerald, though earlier confused in mind, had through inexperience boarded the boat, but through grace escaped death.

31. Great indeed were this man’s merits: neither were his friends unrewarded by God, nor his despisers left unpunished—not because he himself desired the death of a sinner or ceased to pray for his enemies, since he knew that no one truly loves Christ until he also loves an enemy for Christ’s sake. Nevertheless, God sometimes wills contempt for the saints to be punished even in this life, lest the righteous grow jealous when they see sinners enjoying peace and say: “Then in vain have I kept my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent” (Psalm LXXII, 3, 13).

There may also be other, more hidden reasons by which the just Judge both repays the rewards of good deeds here and punishes injuries. We shall briefly explain how severely he punished the insults inflicted upon this servant of his.

While Hugh was wholly occupied with efforts to extend the monastic way of life, and was striving to reform it in the monastery of Mauziac [Note: [Col. 0880D] Our manuscript copy and the printed editions read Maudiacensi; in the margin, however, Moysiacensi is noted. But in the privilege of Pope Paschal cited above, Moisiacum is named first, while the abbey of Mauziac is named seventh. The former is in Quercy, the latter in Auvergne; and the similarity of the names favors Mauziac, requiring the correction of only one letter. In the Bibliotheca, col. 534, there is also a charter of Durannus, bishop of Auvergne, granting this abbey to Hugh of Cluny with the consent of Robert, count of Auvergne, together with a confirmation of the same donation by King Philip, in the year 1095.], he endured the envy of certain men and suffered their abuse, being denounced as a seducer and hypocrite, a tyrant and invader.

Among them, a certain cleric went so far in madness as to say that he would gouge out the abbot’s eyes if the desired opportunity were granted him. Even those who slandered the abbot more moderately rebuked him for a presumption deserving punishment, saying that the dignity both of the office and of the person should not be provoked by insults but rather honored by obedience.

And lest anyone doubt that the Lord had been gravely offended in his servant, in accordance with the Gospel saying, “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16), such a fitting vengeance followed the presumption of the poisonous tongue that, before eight days had passed, the eyes of the man who had wickedly desired the power to attack the abbot’s eyes were gouged out at the demand of his guilt.

32. Pontius of Burgeto, a man of condemnable disposition toward the servant of God, heard that the abbot was going to visit the region of Auvergne [Note: [Col. 0880D] The fact that this example is joined consecutively to the preceding one proves that the abbey in question was Mauziac, not Moysiac. What cause could both men have had for hating the saint except that they resented the abbey’s subjection to Cluniac jurisdiction, since previously it had been free?], where Pontius himself lived. Since he neither wished to see the abbot nor would avoid being seen by him out of contempt, he pretended to be ill and took to his bed. But when the abbot arrived there, the illness he had feigned became real; indeed, it increased so greatly that, having lost the power of speech, he was thought to be near death.

The man who had previously refused to see the abbot was later compelled to see him, repeatedly begging through intermediaries that he might deserve to be visited by him. When the sick man was visited, he confessed his guilt with tears and groans; through the contrition of his heart he obtained pardon, and through the abbot’s intervention he obtained healing.

33. The tyrannical presumption of Gaufridus, surnamed the Savage, count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0880D] Quercetanus seems, in his notes, to object that the man called count of Anjou here is known to have been count of Tours. In fact, the title of count of Tours had been added to that of Anjou when King Henry of France transferred this county to the aforesaid Gaufridus in 1037, after taking it from Theobald and Stephen.], severely afflicted the monastery of blessed Martin, called the Great Monastery. [Col. 0881A] [Note: [Col. 0881D] The reference is to Bartholomew, abbot of the Great Monastery, and to the monastery itself, which had enjoyed the privileges of an ancient and hitherto unshaken immunity. Gaufridus wished to subject it to his own authority and required the pastoral staff, or investiture, to be received from him, as is explained at length in the Acts of the Counts of Anjou, among the notes to the Bibliotheca published by Quercetanus.]

The abbot of the aforesaid monastery asked the servant of God to assist the oppressed abbey both with counsel and through the intervention of his prayers. Hugh did not hesitate to undertake the tiring journey as far as Tours, all the more willingly accepting the difficulty of the road because that place had received the foundations of its monastic life from Cluniac discipline.

When he came to the count and accomplished nothing by his words, he was not ashamed either to embrace his knees or to fall at his feet. Every form of supplication was employed by which even gentleness can move cruel powers. Yet the count, hardened in spirit, turned away the supplicating abbot and went so far in madness as to say that he would reduce the community of Saint Martin to the service of a single donkey.

[Col. 0881B] At last the servant of God rose from the dust. As he tried to soften the tyrant, who was wearing a cloak, with words bringing salvation, the count broke the clasp fastening his cloak and departed, disregarding the exhortations. As he left, the man of prophecy, touched by the Spirit, is remembered to have said the words of Samuel: “Your kingdom has been torn from you today” (I Samuel XV, 28).

The outcome of events plainly confirmed this prophecy. For after being expelled from the countship, that contemptuous man was held in prison by his brother Fulco for so long that his body was not released from custody before his spirit was released from his body. To complete his punishment, he also lost his reason and raved in childish foolishness until death.

34. Berardus of the castle of Retortorium [Note: [Col. 0882D] The castle of Retortorium, called Rehorterium by the monk Hugh and commonly Riotier, stood on the Saône River in the territory of Lyon.], having raged with extraordinary exactions against the village of Cavariacum [Note: [Col. 0882D] The same Hugh calls it Chavariacus. I suspect that, with the present r changed to l, this is the place marked Chaufailles on maps, as though Cavaliacum, eight leagues from Cluny between the Saône and Loire.], which belonged to the monastery of Cluny, suffered a similar punishment.

He was tolerated patiently for some time. Then, after being admonished by princes and ecclesiastical persons to cease his tyrannical injuries, he nevertheless despised them all. Blessed Hugh entrusted the entire matter to John the Baptist. Berard turned to him and with tears and groans earnestly begged for his help against the aforesaid Satan. There was no delay: the outcome showed that the abbot’s prayers had been heard.

For Berard, having lost both his reason and his sight, was carried home in the hands of his servants, uttering every kind of confused speech and showing by other signs as well the indignation of the just Judge that had been aroused against him. His bed, having caught fire twice in one night, nearly consumed him in the fire he deserved—him who had consumed the sanctuary’s possessions through unjust exactions and plunder.

Compelled by these scourges, he eventually came to his senses; he renounced the exactions, restored the losses, and promised that henceforth he would presume to take nothing from the sanctuary of the Lord. Thus the man who, by despising the servant of God, had drawn upon himself a double affliction received full health when he repented and divine vengeance had been restrained.

35. Consider, reader, with what affection he sought the salvation of the souls entrusted to him: even toward the killers of his brother and father he expressed and imitated the gentleness of David. In accordance with the Gospel saying, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, 37), he granted pardon to each of the two men guilty of homicide. To the brother’s killer, who had no refuge open to him by which he could avoid the relatives of the slain man, he opened the shelter of his holy protection. Received into it, the man both escaped the danger of his temporal life and entered upon the way of eternal life.

At the abbot’s urging, the homicide, moved to compunction, assumed the final habit of penance. Having successfully completed the necessary pilgrimage of this world in that habit, when he ceased to live he began to live anew.

After his own father had died—the duke of Burgundy, his son-in-law, having killed him with his own hand—Hugh strove to assist him before God by transferring to himself the satisfaction for his sins, which the hostile sword had forestalled. He afflicted himself with continual fasts and offered sacrifices more frequently. He also undertook to wear an iron cuirass, seeking through personal torments to atone for another’s sins.

He interceded as well for the man who had killed his father, lest the ancient enemy should triumph over him, offering victims and prayers to God. Since his charity grew even to the point of loving his enemies, it is not surprising that, as some report, his almsgiving increased while passing through the hands of those who distributed it.

This happened in the case of Ademarus, the dispenser of the servant of God, who later deserved advancement to the abbacy both in learning and in life. Setting aside ten solidi to distribute to the needy at the abbot’s command, he seemed to spend them on the poor throughout the entire month rather than to give them away; nevertheless, he felt no loss in the silver distributed.

Behold the increase and the constancy alike of the oil of Sarepta, the grace and the end of grace. As long as the widow’s vessel was present, the oil flowed; but it stopped when the vessel of the one asking was no longer available. So too for Ademarus: as long as faith remained, what he gave to the poor did not fail; but it failed when he simultaneously began to cease giving glory to God and to grow weak in faith.

[Col. 0882D]

36. On another occasion, although he possessed only nine denarii and had given them to a poor woman, he found fifteen gold pieces in his possession and offered them to the abbot. The magnanimous abbot immediately hastened to place them in the lap of the poor, knowing that no field responds more fruitfully to its cultivator than the lap of the poor.

His chamberlain Jarento proved this when he was traveling with the blessed Father to Valence. [Col. 0883A] After his purses had been exhausted for the needs of the poor, he was distributing, at the abbot’s command, ten solidi that he had reserved for the brothers’ expenses, but he did so with a sorrowful and bitter heart.

“Do not,” said the abbot, “do not fear, my son. We shall not enter the city gate until the field to which we entrusted the seed bears fruit, returning more than it received.”

The promised outcome immediately fulfilled this prophecy. Before they entered the city gate, someone appeared who gave him, in exchange for a few denarii, a considerable weight of gold. The dispenser, filled with wonder, gave glory to God and became more generous toward the poor in proportion as he grew more confident of his reward.

## CHAPTER VI

Many were led by him to a better and monastic life; the Cluniac church was enlarged.

37. Through such and so many praises of virtue, this man of God was regarded as the greatest among the great. He walked in the blameless way and, through the sons of his holy imitation, aroused and exalted the institutions of monastic life.

The branches of this vine extended as far as the sea, and its shoots as far as the river. From these, certain men who became abbots exalted the dignities entrusted to them by example as well as by word. Others, distinguished solely by virtue, lived in the flesh as though beyond the flesh: although necessity required them to take part in human affairs, by their will they took part in the affairs of angels.

To enumerate them and pursue their lives in the present undertaking would be to drive the chariot beyond its course—except that the praise of the disciple is also the glory of the master. To proclaim the devotion of the sons, so as to exalt the merits of the Father, is nothing other than attempting to help the sun’s brightness by bringing torches near it.

There still remain so many distinguished examples of his virtues and works that, in recounting them, it is necessary to pause for a little rest and breathe like a panting horse. Therefore, for the moment we lay down our pen, intending, with the help of the servant of God whom he serves, to undertake the remainder with greater confidence. [Note: [Col. 0883D] The work seems to have been divided into two parts, so that the first book ended here and the second began.]

38. The holy man had already passed through the stumbling blocks of slippery youth with unhindered steps. He was sixty-five years old from his birth and had completed forty years from the time he assumed the governance. The virgin Wisdom warmed him. Like blessed David, the old man embraced her; although his body was failing, he surpassed himself through the maturity of his understanding and the excellence of his counsel.

No decline in religion resulted for him from the bodily troubles that accompany such an age. With the same devotion as before, he taught and observed the monastic rules and sacred practices with undiminished diligence. The more abundant provision by which the love of his sons sought to restore their physically failing father to divine service was for him nothing other than material for virtue.

Some people readily lack delicacies, but few can abstain from what is set before them. Blessed Hugh, however, was accustomed to act in such a way that, when many dishes were placed before him for his meal, he allowed nature a little, but nothing to gluttony. Whatever was added beyond what was necessary for his nourishment served the crowd, not the individual; the poor, not the abbot.

At these meals it was especially remarkable that wine was never set before him. He broke his fast with dry food, as though one were making cement by mixing only lime and sand. Thus, while traversing a feeble old age without himself being feeble, he added something daily to religion. The nearer he felt the end of the service entrusted to him, the more he instructed the Lord’s camp by word and led it by example.

He also decided to lay broader foundations for the Cluniac monastery [Note: [Col. 0883D] Others more correctly read “church,” for the following vision concerns only the church, and only its construction is recorded in the monuments of Cluny. Saint Odilo “had carefully renewed Cluny within and without, except for the walls of the church; and in his final days he built the cloister,” as is reported in his Life.], unable to bear seeing the brothers, who were daily increasing both in merit and in number, burdened by exceedingly cramped buildings.

The Father’s sound plan was shown equally by a revelation and by its fortunate outcome. To one of the brothers, named Gunzo [Note: [Col. 0883D] The anonymous author adds, “having been made a claustral brother from an abbot”—namely, of Balme, as is evident from the following Life.], a man worthy of praise and illustrious memory, but at that time confined by bodily illness, the apostle Peter appeared. He was surrounded by a mitred company [Note: [Col. 0884D] Namely, Saints Paul and Stephen, concerning whom the following Life and the anonymous author provide information.] and displayed the majesty of a being of another order.

He declared his name and the reason for his coming to the sick man: “Brother, hasten to the abbot Hugh and report to him that the pressure upon my sheep is burdensome to me. They are enclosed within the fences of that Cluniac sheepfold, but the narrower space oppresses them. It is time for him to prepare a material dwelling for them, since he has already prepared in them a spiritual dwelling for God.

“You above all have been chosen for this mission, so that the healing granted to you may lend credibility to your words.” He also added that seven years would be added to Gunzo’s life if he faithfully carried out the obedience imposed upon him; but if blessed Hugh delayed obeying, he would suffer the illness from which the messenger himself had escaped.

After saying this, Peter himself seemed to stretch out cords and measure the length and breadth. He also showed him the character of the basilica to be built, commanding that the memory of its dimensions and design remain firmly fixed in his mind.

39. When the brother awoke, he presented himself to the abbot in good health, although illness had threatened him with death. [Col. 0884D] Everything that had been said or shown to the monk was reported in due order. The abbot believed him and, inspired by the divine warning, built for the dwelling of God’s glory such a great and splendid basilica [Note: [Col. 0884D] The same anonymous author adds, “within twenty years.” Quercetanus, in his notes, incorrectly counts twenty-five years. He more reliably reports that its form was “in the shape of a patriarchal cross,” such as we too saw in 1662; it was said to be equal in length to the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter.], that it is difficult to decide whether it is surpassed in size or more marvelous in craftsmanship.

Such is its beauty and glory that, if we may believe that heavenly inhabitants take pleasure in human dwellings made for such purposes, one might call it a kind of ambulatory for angels. In it, as though brought out from prison, the monks are refreshed by a spacious open area, so well adapted to monastic observance that the narrowness of the choir does not require the ranks to be mixed, the stations confused, or anyone to wander outside from time to time.

Much more could be said, were it not that places dedicated to divine service receive more praise from the merit of their inhabitants than from the hands of craftsmen. This certainly applies to the structure of which we are speaking. Although it is most splendid through the skill of its builder, it is much more splendid because of its inhabitant.

Blessed Hugh, solicitous as steward for the glory of both—the flock and the place—labored before God and his angels with a pure conscience, able to say: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm XXV, 8).

Under his most holy leadership, many thousands of souls came out of Egypt and offered in this desert to the God of hosts the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and the sacrifice of praise. They became the sanctification of the Lord and the cord of his inheritance.

For just as a fisherman uses different instruments in catching fish, so the son of wisdom, proceeding by diverse paths for the salvation of souls, became all things to all people, so that he might win them all (I Corinthians IX, 22). A hook was always hanging for him; nets were always cast into the sea; and small and large fish were always brought forth onto the shore of rest and life.

For always under him and through him, in accordance with Isaiah, “the wolf dwelt with the lamb, and the leopard confidently lay down with the kid” (Isaiah XI, 6). With these men who had come from the people, exalted powers bore the yoke of the Lord so patiently that they did not oppress them either through pride of birth or through arrogance of authority. The greater each person had been, the humbler he was in all things.

For those who, through fear of failing, hesitated to profess themselves monks, the prudent Father tempered monastic discipline in such a way that even those accustomed to luxuries endured it without complaint.

40. Guigo the count was both a witness and an example of this. He had been raised indulgently from childhood and was incapable of renouncing the luxuries to which he had been accustomed from the cradle. Even woolen clothing caused him pain, and he tolerated nothing except the skins of foreign mice or silken garments against his naked body.

Nevertheless, blessed Hugh trained him to endure the harshness of any clothing through carefully considered accommodations. Indeed, lest he break a bruised reed, after Guigo became a monk Hugh permitted him to use soft garments, which were covered above by the regular habit. This was surely a sound plan. The wise abbot had foreseen that Christ’s novice would, out of shame, eventually lay aside the softer clothing and would be distressed if he were ever accused of inactivity only in spiritual warfare, when he was said always to have competed with the best in secular life.

The count’s conduct showed that this is what happened. Suddenly transformed, he cast off the clothing allowed by the dispensation, imposed new crosses upon his flesh, and, fighting the good fight, deserved the eternal reward at a blessed end. [Note: [Col. 0885D] The same anonymous author adds the following, first concerning Hugh of Burgundy: “We also saw Hugh, formerly duke of Burgundy and afterward standard-bearer of the spiritual army. He used to oil the brothers’ shoes and despise and humble himself so greatly that all lowly persons were amazed when they saw such a prince prostrate beneath them. After the contest he waged, enduring bodily blindness as well, he finally obtained the eternal light he had deserved and left us examples fragrant with good works.”

“Afterward, concerning the aforesaid Guigo, I believe, he adds: ‘Furthermore, the venerable Guigo, once count of Mâcon and then made a poor man of Christ from the root, offered God the holocaust of so perfect a conversion that he drew his wife and children after him into the fragrance of heavenly virtues. After he had governed the monastery of Silvaniacum for a time, he was released from that office by the will of the holy Father, Lord Hugh, and returned to the cloister. There, after the proper course, he changed rather than ended his religious life, because, departing in a good end, he obtained a share in the highest Good, as we truly believe in faith.’”]

41. Divine signs also taught how great a refuge there was under blessed Hugh for those wishing to emerge from this great and spacious sea. A certain man [Note: [Col. 0886D] He seems to have been Udalricus, discussed in the preceding commentary.] [Col. 0886B] went to Rome as the result of a vow and, prostrating himself before the apostles’ tomb, begged with abundant tears to be taught by what road he should approach God.

While he was engaged in this concern, Peter, the doorkeeper of heaven, appeared to him and advised him to go to Cluny. At Cluny, he said, there was a bath for souls; there he would find salvation if he deserved to obtain the favor of the abbot of that place.

Thus instructed, the petitioner returned joyfully and hurried to Cluny. He asked for the abbot by word and voice; when he found him, he disclosed his sacred desire and opened the story of the divine vision, recounting in order everything that the apostle had commanded him.
