The abbot was moved and did not delay satisfying the petitioner. Having been received, the man arranged his ascents in his heart all the more diligently because, through the divine revelation, he had learned that from the company of human beings he was to advance to the company of angels.

[Col. 0886C]

42. The monk Goderannus had also learned this. After leaving the monastery of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0886D] By the simply named monastery of Saint Remigius, I believe the monastery at Reims is meant. There was also another monastery of the same name in the suburbs of Sens, famous and ancient.], he moved to Cluny for the sake of stricter discipline. There he deserved to hear from the Lord, on account of the distinction of his merits and the excellence of his knowledge: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV, 10).

First he became abbot of Malliacum [Note: [Col. 0886D] The monastery of Malleacum was situated in the territory of Poitiers and was later endowed by John XXII with an episcopal title. Goderannus was placed in charge of it in 1070, became a bishop shortly afterward, and died in 1075.], and afterward he obtained the dignity of the Church of Saintes.

It happened that, while he was present, the Eucharist was being given by the hands of blessed Hugh to a certain leper. Since the man could not swallow the portion of the sacred bread he had received and struggled for a long time in vain, the sacrament fell from his torn mouth together with saliva and foul-looking sputum. Goderannus placed both hands beneath it and swallowed the whole substance that had been brought to his mouth, triumphing more gloriously over himself than over any enemy.

When the blessed abbot saw this, he was astonished and said that the grill of Lawrence was preferable to such a torment of the spirit.

Illustrated by these and other persons as by so many luminaries, the monastery of Cluny was a kind of school of virtue. The Father was present in abundance in their characters and lives, and the entire flock proclaimed by its manner of life what kind of shepherd he was.

We refrain from speaking further about them, judging that it is sufficient for recognizing their devotion that, before us, Ezelo and Gilo—men of the highest distinction—are reported to have written about them with greater diligence.

## CHAPTER VII

His death foreknown and piously undergone; his reception into heaven revealed.

43. The sixtieth year from the ordination of blessed Hugh was drawing toward its end, and the recurring season had brought the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity. On that day, that veteran soldier of Christ was brought by the brothers into the chapter house and, by his most holy exhortation, strengthened them in divine service as they wept, and confirmed those wavering in spirit, though he himself could not stand because his step was failing.

He impressed upon them that their struggle was against the princes of darkness, but that enemies of this kind would readily yield if they found a steadfast fighter. The monk’s purpose, he said, was a kind of fortification, and there would be no other hope of refuge if, through their slackness, the enemy found a place to break in.

Taking occasion from the present day, he began another but not unrelated account: “I know—I know a certain man to whom the Mother of Mercy deigned to appear in an oratory in this form. In her lap was a beautiful boy, displaying divine loveliness; she herself was gentle in her kindly expression, mild and ready to obtain intercession for sinners. The divine Child, assenting to her, said: ‘At this hour this night, made illustrious by my birth, proclaims that glory has come to the angels and peace to humankind. This night, witness to my grace, has opened the obscurities of the Law and fulfilled the prophecy of the prophets. On this night I, born of you, O illustrious Mother, crushed the serpent’s head, abolishing its ancient power by which it preyed upon the human race. Where is the guile of that poisonous serpent? Where are the darts with which, before my birth, it wounded souls unto death?’

“After these words a wicked spirit intruded. When the Child rebuked it rather severely, it was forbidden, in unbridled envy, to disturb the praises and worship with which the devotion of the faithful celebrated his birth; sorrowful and confounded, it departed. Now that it has fled farther away, know that Christ with his Mother is present at your worship, and that, according to the quality of your dispositions, he decrees either punishment or reward. Therefore receive him with sincere devotion of mind; in the person whom he finds pleasing to himself, he will make an everlasting dwelling.”

As he recounted these things with tears, the community understood that the vision he had described had been shown to none other than himself. He had, however, withheld the person’s name so that he might not seem to seek glory for himself rather than report the truth.

44. In the following Lent, when the failure of his strength showed that the day of his death was near, the weary Father added to his labor, and the Lord to his crown. For with fasts multiplied, he pursued sacred severity against his exhausted limbs; crosses were imposed upon his flesh, and tears continually joined with groans declared that he was occupied with longing for another way of life. His vigils became still longer vigils, depriving nature of its due sleep; prayer or reading claimed the remaining time for itself.

It was too little for the man of God that nature should urge his spirit toward departure, unless it were also urged by added torments. For the soul that desired its Creator considered it a choice punishment to remain longer in the prison-house of the flesh.

Having kept this observance throughout Lent until Palm Sunday [Note: [Col. 0887D] In 1109 Easter fell on 25 April, and Palm Sunday consequently fell on the 18th.], a greater crowd both of people and of monks had assembled at Cluny to celebrate the solemnity of that day. The ornaments of the church were taken up for the procession, and the white-clad community went out. When the blessed abbot wished to go out with them, summoned to another departure, he could not accomplish what he wished.

He desired to be present among the white-clad choirs and, by his presence, to exhort Christ’s soldiers in his praises. Since he felt his strength fail him in this, he accompanied with prayers and blessing those whom he could not accompany in body. Already there was in his countenance some share of his future glory, so that one might say that something of the likeness of the angels had been granted to him. [Col. 0888C]

45. While these things were taking place, a certain man of obscure name [Note: Bertinus of Varenne, as Hugh the monk calls him in his Life.] hastened to force his way in to Blessed Hugh, crying out that he had undertaken an important mission to him. On entering, he said:

“Do not despise me, holy Father, a man poor in possessions and obscure in birth, commended only by the authority of him who sends me. I was recently cultivating a field [Note: St. Augustine, Against Faustus: ‘A certain man planted a vineyard and leased it to farmers.’] when suddenly certain persons appeared to me, of venerable dignity and worthy of honor and glory beyond the limits of this present age and beyond the condition of us human beings. A certain Lady went before them; I could not look upon her face because of the speed of her passing, but followed her only by sight of her back. Behind her came an old man, venerable with snow-white hair. Turning his eyes toward me, he said:

‘Ho, you farmer! Whose is this field that you cultivate?’

“I replied: ‘It belongs to the blessed Father and lord, Abbot Hugh.’

“Then he said: ‘The field is mine, and its possessor is mine. For I am Peter the apostle; and the woman who goes before us is Mary, the blessed Mother of God, accompanied by a throng of holy souls. You, therefore, hasten to Abbot Hugh and say to him: “Set your house in order; you are now about to enter upon the way of all flesh.”’

“I delayed obeying such a command, fearing that I might be called a babbler and an interpreter of falsehood. But after being warned again, and rebuked with sterner words because I had delayed reporting the vision mentioned above [Col. 0889A], I hastened to carry out the mission that had long remained suspended.

“After I had said these things, some indeed accused me of falsehood; but the blessed abbot declared that they were a sure indication of his own deposition. From that time onward he awaited the promised summons in tears, saying with the Apostle: ‘I desire to depart and to be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23).”

46. The day of the most sacred Supper had arrived, and behold, the servant of God entered the chapter house—not so much because the time prescribed it as because affection moved him. There, after ordering that abundant alms be distributed for those whom the monastery of Cluny had bound to itself in sacred fellowship, he was asked to absolve the community and wept most copiously. At last, producing a reply while exhausted by sobbing, he said:

“Am I to absolve you, when my own conscience binds me [Col. 0889B]? Shall I lift your burden, prostrate and lying low under the weight of so many offenses? How can prayer, itself subjected to sins, release the yoke of sins? Nevertheless, though unworthy, we shall perform the office required of us; but may the Lord, who loosens those in fetters and raises up those who are bowed down (Ps. 145:7), deign to work inwardly in you what belongs to his mercy.”

Then, raising his eyes toward heaven, his face drenched with tears, he absolved the flock entrusted to him. He added the consolation of a blessing, following Christ the Master, who, as he was about to pass to the Father, blessed the disciples left amid the world’s distress, being always present to them by his grace, although he was leaving them bodily.

After this, when the service of the poor had been completed, the blessed old man returned to the chapter house at the hour of the Mandatum, in imitation of the example of the Lord’s humility. He washed the brothers’ feet, adding a holy sermon from the Gospel reading and calling forth a stream of tears.

On the following Saturday also he took part in the sacred office, greeting the column of the new light [Note: Understand the paschal candle, which the Church also calls a column in the blessing given to it.] and praying with frequent sighs that he might be deemed worthy to reach with unhindered step the land of promise, which he already seemed to behold as though from its border.

47. A few small reserves of strength still remained in his frail body, so that he could celebrate the paschal solemnity in the church, adorned with festive ornaments that in some manner proclaimed both the glory of the day and the purity of that holy soul. There, refreshed by spiritual nourishment, he withdrew to the house in which he was accustomed to stay.

When evening had come, he fell onto his bed, expecting nothing but the end and reward of his labors [Col. 0889D]. On Tuesday, when his eyes were already growing dim, his tongue failing, and the other faculties of his senses proclaiming that his departure was at hand, he was asked whether he recognized the life-giving flesh of the Lord. He replied: “I recognize it, and I adore it.”

When the sign of the saving cross was also offered to him, he earnestly strove to venerate it with most Christian devotion [Col. 0890A].

And so, even as he was dying, he might show how watchful and solicitous he had been concerning the watches of the sheep entrusted to him. As best he could, he announced that the anniversary of Archbishop Gaufridus [Note: Of the several archbishops named Gaufridus or Godifredus listed by the Sammarthani Index, only two, both of Bordeaux, could be brought into consideration here: the first, named in the year 982; and the second, who sat between the years 1027 and 1047. But below we shall demonstrate that among the bishops of Lyon one of this name must be accepted for this period; we think he is certainly the same man as the one mentioned here. He therefore died on 28 April 1072.] and of Abbot Guido [Note: We may suspect that this was the man whom we praised above, Count of Mâcon, who died at Cluny after placing his abbey there.] was at hand, indicating that the benefits owed to deceased brothers ought to be paid. Truly blessed is the soul that could not forget the salvation of its own people even at the hour when forgetfulness of one’s own salvation commonly overtakes some.

48. As the servant of God was about to depart from this Egypt, he asked that the reliquary of Blessed Marcellus be brought to him [Note: Apparently St. Marcellus, pope and martyr, is indicated; some of his relics may have been at Cluny. Among the altars dedicated in the greater church in the year 1131, one was dedicated to this saint, as noted in the Bibliotheca, col. 1639.], piously entreating his merciful advocate through tears that, under his guidance, he might be restored to his homeland after exile.

His sons sat around him weeping, and no one consoled another, since the cause of lamentation was equal and inconsolable for all. To them, signaling his departure, he uttered the word “Benedicite” and then lost the power of speech.

As the day declined toward evening, he was carried into the church of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, and commended his weary limbs and nature now announcing its end to sackcloth and ashes. Then, as the sun set, the sun himself set, and the spirit, released from the burden of the flesh, happily exchanged its temporary dwelling for its everlasting homeland.

The cry of his surviving sons rose up. Awakened by the striking of the board, as was customary, they had gathered to commend that blessed soul. Each had what seemed a particular reason for grief, and as many as there were mouths, so many distinctions of his virtues were brought forth.

Some spoke of the abbot’s unyielding hatred of vices; others recounted his fatherly affection toward penitents [Col. 0890C]. Many lamented that the poor had lost a father, widows an advocate, and orphans a defender. Some recalled the gift of prophecy bestowed upon the Father; more spoke of how he had been marked from above by discernment of spirits.

There were even those who lamented that Hugh had feared Christ would be angry if he saw the sun setting while he was angry. Each person had an abundance of material for praising him, and tongues fell short of recounting his merits, while his merits themselves did not lack tongues to recount them.

Amid these bands and crowds of mourners throwing themselves upon the lifeless body, there was scarcely time to wash it, scarcely time to wrap it in priestly vestments. While the brothers were performing the humane service described above, a small quantity of balsam—which seemed quite insufficient for anointing the head—is said to have increased so greatly that it was enough to anoint certain other parts of the body [Col. 0890D].

49. When these rites had been properly completed, the people were admitted as they pressed forward, showing by their tears and expenditures how much they had prospered under his protection. The neighboring hills echoed with their cries, and the funeral rites were celebrated with costly lights [Col. 0891A].

Everyone recounted how genuine liberty had been under him, how great the advancement of affairs had been, and what glory of morals had flourished under his holy discipline. Meanwhile people hurried to embrace the Father’s feet; garments were drenched with weeping; and each person believed that he had done too little unless he venerated his feet either with a kiss or with an offering.

Thus, after three days had passed in tears, the blessed remains received burial on Saturday with the honor that was due [Note: The three days, since he had died on Wednesday evening.]. Blessed Hugh the abbot passed away on the third day before the Kalends of May, full of authority and grace, leaving his sons joy in his crown, an example in his life, glory in his body, and hope in his intercession. How great his favor with God was became known to many through numerous signs even after his passing.

50. At Cluny there was a certain man named Bernard [Note: Bernard of Narbonne, as Hugh calls him in his Life.], just, holy, and God-fearing, to whom religion had won reverence and renown. When Blessed Hugh migrated to heaven, Bernard was weighed down by sleep and could not be awakened either by the noise of those hurrying about or by excessive shouting. Not long afterward he fell onto his bed, about to yield to the supreme affliction of human existence.

As he was being pressed toward death, he summoned several monks and said:

“Brothers, I have thought it necessary to disclose to you the vision that the Lord has shown me. Do not accuse me, who am reporting it, of falsehood; for if not from love of virtue, then at least from fear of the judgment before which I am summoned in uncertainty, I would fear to lie.

“You know that recently I voluntarily relinquished the obedience of Nogent [Note: ‘Nongent,’ Quercetanus says in his notes, ‘a town and priory of the Perche district, founded in honor of St. Denis.’]; but perhaps you do not know for what reason I relinquished it. As I slept, a venerable person appeared to me, calling himself Dionysius the Areopagite [Note: The aforementioned Hugh omits the title ‘Areopagite,’ which Hildebertus may be judged to have added here because of his own opinion, then commonly held, concerning the apostle of the people of Paris.], and urged me in these words to return to Cluny:

“‘Brother, you must, you must return to Cluny as quickly as possible and greet Abbot Hugh, who is about to enter upon the common journey of pilgrimage. You will also see his successor, to whom, by divine grace sent from the Roman regions, the princes of the apostles have entrusted pastoral watch.’

“Compelled by this exhortation to return, I hastened to Cluny. Woe to me, wretched man! The Father has indeed departed, but I was not worthy to greet him as he departed. Should I blame the sleep that held me, or give thanks? I do not know. It both begrudged and provided. It held back the eyes of my flesh so that I would not see him as he departed; but it showed my inner eyes where he had gone [Note: He adds: ‘I was present in the oratory of Blessed Mary, Virgin and Mother of the Lord, where that same Father, carried there by the brothers, expired at that hour.’].

“I saw—and, with God as my witness, I truly saw—the inhabitants of heaven mingled with mortals, and the most blessed Mother of God, Mary. At a distance certain archers stood; when they recognized the most holy Virgin, they withdrew as though terrified and confused [Note: ‘While they were receiving the soul of the dying Father, certain archers rushed in from a distance. Against them the Mother of Mercy raised her hand and protected him as he departed. When they recognized her, the archers immediately fled, terrified and confused.’ Thus says the aforementioned Hugh.].

“There appeared there a multitude of martyrs and confessors together. I was granted to recognize some of them from above and to distinguish their various ranks. There I recognized Blessed Martial, Martin, and the glory of the abbots, Benedict.

“These two seemed to lead the spirit of Blessed Hugh into a most fertile vineyard and place him there, as though he were to rest after his labor. While I marveled equally at the glory of the saints and at what was taking place, he turned his eyes toward me with gentle kindness and said:

“‘Stand, brother, and eat with us from the white clusters that abound here for us. I shall rest here for a little while [Note: He likewise says: ‘For three days I shall rest here.’], until the swelling of my feet subsides and the dust is shaken off that I gathered by traveling the many circuits of the roads. Then I shall pass to another dwelling that the Lord has prepared for me eternally [Note: Thus even the holiest carry something away from this life which, although it may not deserve punishment, nevertheless delays them for a little from the free enjoyment of God and the fullness of glory; yet they await it in great rest and peace.].

“‘You shall tell my successor Pontius not to tolerate any deviation from humility [Note: ‘Let him preserve innocence for himself and mercy for others,’ says the monk Hugh; but Pontius seems eventually to have departed from both, carried away by an indiscriminate zeal for discipline.]. Let him devote himself to works of mercy; let him be forgetful of his own injuries and moved by those of others. Above all, let him burn with zeal for the law; toward offenders let him be neither lax through indulgence nor immoderate in discipline.’

“He was still speaking when sleep, while the vision soothed my mind, departed from me. But know that I have spoken truthfully if this illness brings the present course of my life to an end; if not, I have summoned the Judge against my own head, because I have fabricated a falsehood.”

These reports moved the listeners, who learned from the man’s death that Brother Bernard had uttered nothing false. For on the third day [Note: ‘On the feast of All Saints,’ as the aforementioned Hugh adds.], he departed from the human world, leaving the brothers both testimony to the abbot’s glory and hope of his own salvation.

51. They report that on the very night when Blessed Hugh migrated to heaven, a similar vision appeared to the abbot of Noyon. He seemed to see two beds carried into heaven by angels, furnished with softer coverings that would summon forgetfulness of care and sleep. The angels carrying the beds cried out in these words:

“We shall place two illustrious men in these beds: namely, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny. After the earth they deserved heaven; after labors, rest; after tears, joy.”

After this, the abbot awoke and related to several people what he had seen, applying the vision mentioned above to the departure of both men. Nor was his interpretation frustrated, since both are reported to have escaped the narrow confines of this body at almost the same time.

Other signs of the blessed man’s merits also became manifest. After his death, they are reported to have been accomplished upon people afflicted with various illnesses. A certain Hincmar had an overgrowing film covered the pupils of his eyes and condemned him to pitiable blindness. When hope of recovering his health depended upon the merits and intervention of the abbot, it is recalled that the servant of Christ appeared to him in a dream and warned him not to seek bodily illumination but that of the mind. Nevertheless, after impressing the sign of the cross upon the eyes of the man praying, the servant of God withdrew, and the blindness was wiped from his eyes [Col. 0894A].

A certain brother also, named Guido, had been deprived at once of peace of mind and body by a new madness. He was led to the tomb of the blessed man and, once the affliction had been driven away, found rest, restored both to himself and to the community through the holy man’s merits. This was granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout infinite ages. Amen.

[Col. 0893A]

ANOTHER LIFE, BY RAYNALD, ABBOT OF VEZELAY AND LATER ARCHBISHOP OF LYON.

(From the manuscript of the most serene Queen Christina of Sweden, and from another manuscript of our College of Douai.)

[Col. 0893B]

PROLOGUE

Brother Raynald, not so much abbot as servant of the Church of Vezelay, sends greetings in the Lord to all the sons of the Church of Cluny.

Since I am pressed by the admonitions of many brothers to describe briefly the Life of the most devout Father, Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, I have decided to serve devotion, not presumption. If perhaps the labor of some man of superior intellect has already been spent on this work before us, I do not undertake this in order to obscure him and make myself conspicuous; rather, I think his work should be left to the excellence of greater and wiser men, while ours should be attributed to the effort of lesser and less capable men. Nor will the humility of an unpolished style be shameful, so long as the style itself serves the truth purely.

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0893C]

His youth spent piously; his apprenticeship in monastic life; his abbatial dignity; his generosity toward the poor; his intimacy with Christ; his power over demons.

1. The blessed man was born from one of the noblest lines of the Burgundian race, fathered by Dalmatius, a man of consular rank, and by his mother Aremburga, a highly religious woman who was not unequal to her husband in birth.

When this venerable matron was pregnant with the happy offspring of whom we speak and the time of delivery was approaching, she decided to ask a certain venerable priest to offer sacrifice to God to ease the distress of her labor. While the man of God was complying with her devout prayers, the priest himself saw in the most sacred chalice, as it were, the image of a little child. In this image he could discern how great before God would be the merit of the boy who was being born [Col. 0893D].

Immediately after the office of the Mass had been completed, the priest hurried to verify the outcome of the event and found the child born, whose destiny he had foreseen and recognized in the mirror of so great a sacrament. He then foretold many things about him and declared that, if he lived, he would become a great man [Col. 0894B].

This was already sufficiently evident from the earliest beginnings of his childhood, when he frequently attended either churches or schools, though during stolen hours, because he feared his father, who wanted to apply him to military pursuits. When more costly clothing, more attractive because of its variety of colors, was fitted for him, he rejected it in favor of what was humbler and simpler. He devoted himself not to the frivolity customary at that age but to innocence and simplicity; he also frequently applied himself to reading, against his parents’ wishes.

Because of all these things and similar qualities, when he was criticized by his father and even by his peers—on the grounds that such pursuits were contrary to a military career—he resolved within himself that he must seek another kind of military service, one in which these things, without which he did not wish to serve, would not be contrary.

2. Therefore, abandoning everything, he escaped naked from the world and submitted himself to the instruction of Blessed Odilo, becoming a monk at Cluny. At his reception, one of the elders is said to have burst out in these words:

“Cluny, what a treasure you have received today!”

What a degree of humility, purity, and integrity he afterward displayed, and how fervent he was in the love of God, is declared not by our speech but by the diligence of Blessed Odilo, who, before he had reached the years of adolescence, appointed him provost of Cluny.

How much mercy and charity, how much energy and vigilance he displayed in the office of that governance is made clear by the devotion of the Cluniac elders. At the first word concerning the election of an abbot, when the man presiding over the election had named him and wished to proceed with the nomination of the others, they immediately snatched him from his seat and raised him to the abbacy amid praises of God.

Of the crosses he then imposed upon himself, one may suffice, brought forward above the rest: that breastplate which, worn next to his flesh, subdued his youthful body. Beneath it he performed penance both for himself, though innocent, and for his father, who had already departed from the world.

As for reading and prayer, to which he devoted himself almost continually, I think they may be characterized briefly in this way: in both he showed himself insatiable, as though, when he read, God were speaking to him visibly, and, when he prayed, he were conversing with God face to face [Col. 0895A].

3. I am not able to set forth the number of his acts of mercy: how devout he was toward his subjects, how generous toward the poor, and how kindly disposed toward strangers as well as toward members of his household.

Indeed, he showed such great charity and gentleness toward his sons that their number increased daily, and each person considered himself fortunate if he came to the grace of conversion under so great a Father.

For who could worthily recount his almsgiving? He labored at it so earnestly that, besides daily food, he purchased clothing suitable for the poor both in winter and in summer, and spent nearly everything he could possess on their needs [Col. 0895B].

O faithful steward of Christ! It was not enough for him to feed the poor with bread unless he also fattened them with meat; it was not enough unless he frequently cheered them with wine; it was not enough unless very often he had them rewarded with silver, and sometimes even with gold.

And what was all this to him unless plentiful clothing followed as well? Woolen garments were prepared to drive away the cold; linen ones were bought to restrain the heat; and, so that nothing might be lacking to perfect charity, he himself often used to make them together with the brothers who assisted him. He also distributed shoes, not without the axle-grease with which they were to be anointed.

You might think him no different from John, who because of the vastness of his almsgiving alone is called in the Church “the Merciful,” when he squandered incomparable treasures on such expenses. What might have been thought sufficient to make some most powerful king wealthy, he himself repeatedly scattered in relieving the misery of the poor [Col. 0895C].

4. What should I say of his remarkable faith, by which he shone before God with such great merit that God both heard his prayers and frequently worked miracles through him, whether he knew it or was absent?

To come to other matters in their proper place, let us first bring forward the miracle concerning the Savior himself. Although Hugh did not see it, Pope Gregory VII, previously called Hildebrand, is known to have been a faithful witness of it.

One day, while Gregory was sitting beside the blessed man in the chapter house at Cluny—for he was still a monk and subdeacon of the Roman Church—he turned and saw the Lord Jesus sitting beside Hugh. Christ appeared cheerful in face and bearing, as though he favored Hugh in each of his judgments.

Immediately, while everyone marveled and was entirely ignorant of the matter, Gregory rose before so great a Judge and wished to seat the Lord in the midst. At last, when the most holy Father asked him why he had risen from his seat, he explained the vision as we have related it, while admitting that he did not know with which eyes he had seen it.

From this we may judge with what purity and equity he examined faults, since he deserved to have the Judge of the ages as his assessor [Col. 0896A].

This man of such great authority and grace, it is said, was called “the kindly judge” on account of the severity of his discipline and the gentleness of his moderation—especially because, like a mother, he was gentle with his sons, and, like a father, he corrected their offenses.

5. As I consider what he did for Pope Stephen, I think it should rightly be inserted into this work.

Stephen was lying ill near Florence, a city of Italy. Visited by the holy man, not without the grace of God, and after a long conversation with him, he prayed that he might deserve to die in his hands.

Then, behold, the enemy of the human race, during the hours when the man of God was absent, thrust himself before the dying pontiff’s eyes, terrifying and disturbing his mind with his horrifying appearance. But at the entrance of the man of God he fled, and as long as Hugh remained with him he did not appear again [Col. 0896B].

When this became known, the pontiff afterward detained Hugh with earnest prayers. Hugh remained with him until his death, washed his body with his own hands, wrapped it in funeral garments, and placed it in the tomb.

6. It is no wonder that the devil fled at the presence of such a man, whose spirit adhered to God so completely that even the Lord Jesus Christ himself deigned to come in person to visit him.

This became clear at another time through a revelation unlike the earlier one, yet not inferior to it. A certain elder—who, as we believe, related the matter about himself as though about another—saw the Redeemer with a harp, singing psalms in the Cluniac choir before each of the brothers.

The song that was heard was the Gospel antiphon:

“But to sit with me is not mine to give you, but [to those] for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. 20:23).

At that time so great a fragrance of heavenly spices seemed to arise that it was thought to surpass the scent of all balsams [Col. 0896C].

CHAPTER II

The dead freed from punishments; the sick freed from illnesses. Churches and monasteries built or restored.

7. I do not think the following should be covered in silence: a certain brother named Pontius nearly experienced the judgment of divine punishment upon himself, had not heavenly mercy come to his aid through this servant of God.

When the brother in question was staying at a certain cell called Mons [Note: Among the deaneries of the diocese of Clermont, one is called de Montibus; it was united to the monastery of Cluny. See the Bibliotheca, col. 1755.], and the revered Father had arrived there, Pontius did not want to see him, since he foolishly murmured against the Father. He therefore withdrew to bed under the pretense of illness.

But the more he tried to withdraw from the man of God, the more rapidly life hastened to depart from his body—not now through pretense but through genuine illness—until his voice clung in his throat and his speech failed.

People hurried to the merciful shepherd so that he might commend the sheep who was nearly departing to the supreme Shepherd. The holy man hastened to him, first pronouncing the absolution of commendation [Col. 0897A]. Then, when the sick man’s strength and voice had been restored for a little while, he confessed his fault, accused himself of rashness, begged forgiveness, and obtained it. At last he recovered from that illness.

8. Another man, after departing from this world, had his body kept unburied in the Cluniac oratory according to custom. On the very night of his death he appeared to two brothers. He confessed to them the crime of having given two solidi to a certain man without permission, and, because he had died without confessing this offense, he asked the holy Father for absolution before being committed to burial.

When morning came, both brothers, as though with one voice, set forth the vision before the entire community and the blessed man. The person whom the dead man had named was then sought, and the matter was found to be as the vision had shown.

Immediately penance was enjoined upon all for the brother, and prayers, psalms, almsgiving, and Masses were added; absolution then followed.

Thus—indeed, thus—not only on earth but also in heaven, his faith daily produced virtue, virtue power, power authority, authority glory, glory humility here and a crown there [Col. 0897B].

9. At a certain time, while traveling through the regions of Gascony, accompanied by Hunald [Note: Hugh the monk in his Life says: ‘Taking with him two of his monks, namely Durandus, who was bishop of Toulouse, and Hunald, who was abbot of Moissac, a most eloquent man,’ the brother of Count Centullus of Béarn. He embraced the monastic life at Cluny under St. Hugh in 1062 and governed the monks of Moissac while that saint was still alive. Concerning Durandus, in addition to the account given in the earlier Life, Hugh cites another witness to the miracle, perhaps a secular cleric: ‘I learned what I have related from the religious man Vincent, who was present at the event, saw it, and gave testimony.’], a most prudent man and his own monk, he noticed not far from the road a certain cell in which a man of noble birth was living, though afflicted with leprosy.

After inquiring into the man’s character and learning that his patience had been tested, Hugh, a man of remarkable piety, turned aside to visit him. Fulfilling the duty of charity through words of consolation, he removed his fur garment and gave it, together with some silver, to the sick man.

After Hugh had departed, the sick man put on the garment and immediately realized that he had been cured of the affliction of leprosy [Col. 0897C].

10. Again, the same most holy man happened to arrive in Paris. He visited the church of Blessed Genevieve, situated outside the city walls, both out of devotion to her most sacred body and in veneration of the chief of the apostles, whose chasuble is believed to be kept there.

At that time a certain soldier named Rothertus, who had contracted paralysis from a wound caused by a blow in battle, was carried there in the hands of attendants and asked Hugh to pray to the Lord for his health.

Hugh took the apostolic mitre and applied it to the afflicted limbs. Then, after imposing the antiphon sung in the Church concerning the healing of the paralytic Aeneas, he changed the name and said: “Rothertus, may the Lord Jesus Christ heal you” (Acts 7) [Col. 0897D].

Immediately, to the sight and amazement of everyone, and amid great rejoicing, the man returned home sound and whole.

But the miracles he performed through the agency of the saints’ relics are as innumerable to us as they are frequent [Col. 0898A]. Yet he always showed such caution that he attributed to the saints whatever health God granted anyone through his ministry.

11. On another occasion, as he was about to enter Valence in Gaul, he encountered a crowd of poor people who were seeking alms from so famous a dispenser throughout the world.

He ordered his steward Jarento, a brother outstanding in every respect, to distribute silver among the entire crowd according to custom. But afterward Jarento said that scarcely ten solidi remained for him, since the rest had been spent on a similar purpose, and that perhaps these should be reserved for a greater necessity.

“Do not be afraid, brother,” Hugh replied. “God is faithful, and trust that, once these have been distributed, our good Rewarder, Jesus, will faithfully repay us in the present, if we are cheerful givers” [Col. 0898B].

The Father’s commands were fulfilled. Before they reached the city, behold, someone from the city offered him gold exceeding the value of ten times as many solidi.

Then Hugh turned to the brother mentioned above and said: “Take it, and do not distrust the good lender any longer.”

It would take a very long time to enumerate how often this man, by the faith through which he was wholly rooted in God, rescued himself and the household over which he presided from great and intolerable poverty.

12. Of what he wrote to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, let one example among many briefly be related.

On one occasion, when scarcity was pressing, a delegation was sent to him by the brothers. He was then at Marcigny [Note: We have treated the monastery of Marcigny above.], and they asked him to provide for them in such great need.

He therefore turned to his singular protectors and sent a letter to the apostles, asking and entreating them to have mercy on their servants; to rescue that place even now from its difficulties, just as they had previously ruled it and advanced it from a small condition to a great one; and to look not upon his sins but upon their many mercies.

The embassy of faith was then carried before their altar. What more is needed? Before many days had passed, such abundance of goods arrived that it relieved not only the scarcity of that time but also the need of the entire year.

And since the occasion has led us to mention the blessed apostles, it is fitting to relate how the blessed man was warned by them concerning the foundation of a new basilica.

13. The abbot of a monastery called Balma [Note: Balma, commonly Baume, in the diocese of Besançon, whose founder was St. Euricius, as is related in his Life on 13 January.], named Gunzo, a man of great integrity and simplicity, was once at Cluny, failing from a severe attack of paralytic illness, so that he thought he had already reached the end.

One night he saw the apostles Peter and Paul themselves standing beside him, together with Stephen the protomartyr. Their first and chief, Blessed Peter, after Gunzo had asked who they were, declared his own name and those of his companions, and began as follows:

“Rise, brother, quickly, and deliver these commands of ours to Hugh, the abbot of this Church: The multitude of the brothers can scarcely endure the narrowness of our basilica, and we wish the abbot himself to build a larger one. Let him not distrust the expense; it will be our task to provide everything that this work requires.”

Gunzo replied: “I do not dare undertake this mission, because no one would believe my words.”

The apostle answered: “Receive this sign of the truth from me: as soon as you have fulfilled the mission, you will find yourself safe from every illness.”

He had spoken, and the vision immediately disappeared from his eyes.

At dawn, Gunzo related the commands to the man of God in order. Through the apostle’s promise he was restored to health [Col. 0899B]. This was the first reason that most strongly inclined the holy Father’s mind to begin so great a work.

The construction displays within itself such grace of beauty and elegance that throughout the entire western region—for I know less about the other parts of the world—there is no basilica more remarkable than this one.

14. But lest I seem to have published this as the only magnificent work of this man of God, passing over his other deeds, here he renewed Cluny; here he increased the number of the brothers, both within and outside, beyond all his predecessors; here he restored the cells with buildings; here he enlarged the possessions by extending their boundaries. Who but this blessed man restored to religious observance the churches of the blessed confessors Martial [Note: [Col. 0899D] The church of Saint Martial at Limoges was transferred from the canons to monks in 848; thereafter it had abbots, the twelfth of whom was Adalbert, under whom the Sammarthani write that the basilica of Saint Martial was recovered. Now secular clergy are there again.] and Giles [Note: [Col. 0899D] Saint Giles’, an ancient monastery in Septimania, still famous today.]? Who but this blessed man restored the church of the blessed Mary Magdalene at Vézelay to its former condition under the regular order?

Who but this blessed man restored that of the blessed Austremonius of Auvergne [Note: [Col. 0899D] Saint Austremonius, apostle of the Arverni, is commemorated on 1 November. His tomb, and afterward his monastery—famous in the time of Gregory of Tours—were at the village of Issiodorum, commonly called Issoire; it has now ceased to be counted among the abbeys.]? Here at Poitiers he founded from the foundations, under religious observance, the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0899D] This monastery of Saint John the Evangelist no longer survives at Poitiers, unless perhaps it was reduced in dignity or converted into a parish church.]; and he adorned with religious observance the church of Saint Bertin the Confessor [Note: [Col. 0900D] The monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu, near the castle of Saint-Omer, was renowned throughout Flanders. Its abbot Iperius relates how Saint Hugh, with the permission of Lambert, bishop of the Morini, brought religious men from various Cluniac monasteries in 1101. When these men lived strictly and religiously, the remaining monks of Sithiu dispersed through fear of the more rigorous discipline, while in a short time more than 120 brothers joined them. It is therefore not surprising that Hugh’s successor, Pontius, attempted to subject this abbey to Cluny.] together with many monasteries of Flanders itself. He also built from the beginning the place known as Charity, through his monk Gerard, a man of wonderful grace before God and human beings.

15. At Paris he transferred the church of Saint Martin, now called “of the Fields,” from the canonical order to the monastic rule. But why should I traverse almost the whole of Gaul, which he so richly adorned with monasteries that, whether you turn toward France, Aquitaine, or Burgundy—or indeed wherever you turn throughout all its regions—you see everywhere the religion of so great a Father shining forth? [Col. 0899D] But should only the lands of Gaul be mentioned, and the western provinces passed over? [Col. 0900A] Their monasteries bear witness to how brightly he illumined each of them with the light of religion: most of them he either built himself or reformed into a far better condition. In his own patrimony, through the diligence and assistance of his brother Gaufred, he founded the monastery of Marcigny for holy women. For them he established the rule both of cenobites and of anchoresses, so that they might emulate the purpose of obedience and imitate the life of anchoresses in the solitude of perpetual enclosure.

## CHAPTER III

### Knowledge of hidden thoughts, predictions of the future, and illnesses cured

[Col. 0900B]

16. Among so many gifts of grace, the most holy man was not without the Spirit of prophecy. At times he possessed such power in discerning the wills and minds of the brothers that he often foretold their character and inclinations. It happened, therefore, that once, while making his rounds to visit his cells and having come to the place called Charity, he refused to kiss one brother among the others. When asked the reason, he replied that an evil spirit dwelt in him. Those present were astonished, and the wretched man was questioned about his conscience. He immediately confessed that he had long celebrated Mass without priestly ordination, that he had undertaken neither confession nor penance, and that he still persisted in that very crime. When he ought to have repented, he had afterward become disgraceful and utterly wicked. [Col. 0900C]

Likewise, near the city of Avignon, when a certain crippled man one day begged alms from him, the man of God looked at the wretch and is said to have addressed him with this reply: “I do give you alms for Christ, whom you profess; but your life, full of drunkenness and lust, displeases him, even though you pretend to be poor for his sake.” At once all the citizens who were present were filled with amazement and affirmed that the man was exactly as the holy man—who had never seen him before—had exposed him to be.

17. There was also a certain novice named Maingodus who, wearied by the delay in receiving the habit and having already decided within himself not to endure any further postponement, was anticipated by the man of God, through the spirit, in this thought of his. [Col. 0900D] For Hugh both revealed how he had wished to depart and warned him not to oppose the regular examination. He afterward became exemplary in his conduct and happily completed the course of his life, [Col. 0901A] as had been divinely told him in a vision at the very moment of his death.

18. There was also a man of remarkable simplicity and grace named Durannus, bishop of Toulouse. Although his life was religious, he sometimes, from a cheerful disposition, uttered words that provoked laughter. Because the holy Father, whose monk he also was, often reproved him for this, he once foretold to him in spirit that, after he had departed this life, he would appear in a vision to one of the brothers with foam on his mouth. This happened.

After his departure, he appeared to one of his chaplains named Higuinus and, just as the man of God had foretold, showed the brother his foaming lips, teaching him that his mouth was disfigured because he was suffering punishment for the fault of idle talk. He begged him to disclose the matter to the pious Father. When the vision had been revealed to him, the man filled with the Holy Spirit imposed silence for a week upon seven brothers. One of them violated it, while six preserved it unbroken. Then the bishop appeared again to the same brother, now with his mouth cleaner, but with saliva still seeming to flow from one part of it. He said that he had been cleansed by the obedience of the brothers who had kept silence, but complained that, through the negligence of the seventh brother, that part remained uncured. The things seen were therefore reported again to the Father, and when the breach of silence had been repaired during a second week, the bishop finally appeared to the same brother a third time, without any disfigurement.

19. I think it should also be committed to memory [Col. 0901C] that a certain Flemish cleric named Lambert, a canon of Saint-Omer the Confessor, had resolved to renounce the world and submit himself to the instruction of the blessed man. The provost of that town, however, detained him by force, both him and his possessions.

One night the aforementioned provost saw a person of great severity approaching him with a pastoral staff. This person called himself the abbot of Cluny and was driving out the cleric, together with his possessions, with many blows. When daylight had restored the earth, the cleric who had been expelled was summoned. After he had explained the vision, and the holy Father’s appearance and clothing had also been described, he was released together with his possessions and became a monk at Cluny.

There was a certain man named William who had been sent by the holy Father to a particular obedience. Soon afterward so severe an illness struck his leg that he could not fulfill the obedience imposed upon him and, with the pain raging, could scarcely bear the leg itself. [Col. 0901D] Then, conceiving faith, he said: “By him who sent me here, I tell you, disease, to allow me to fulfill the obedience imposed upon me.” He said this, and on the following night saw himself visited by two men who said that they had been sent by the holy man. In the guise of physicians they treated and healed him. When he awoke in the morning, he perceived that he was sound and free from every illness.

20. Another man, named Theoderic, was afflicted by what seemed like a fire burning in the great toe of his foot, so that he could scarcely give himself sleep or any bodily rest. He asked the keeper of the sick to receive carefully some water with which the holy Father’s hands had been washed at the hour of Mass and to bring it to him. An opportunity was therefore taken, [Col. 0902A] the water was received from the Father’s hands, and it was poured over the burning foot. Immediately the burning ceased completely.

A certain Auvergnat soldier had been wounded in battle. Because the wound had been carelessly closed by a scar, the deadly pus enclosed within it spread through his whole body. He was tortured daily by immense pains and, despairing of recovery, awaited death. He had a brother who was a cleric. This brother too despaired of human medicine, but did not distrust the mercy of God; he decided that the blessed man should be sought for his suffering brother.

He therefore came to the man of God and begged advice concerning so great an affliction. He also asked him to send the sick man some fragments of his food. He further requested and received a wooden splinter, smoothed by scraping, which the man of God happened then to be holding in his hand. He took the food fragments and gave them to his brother to eat, marking the scar with the splinter in the sign of the cross. Immediately the pain fled so completely that, to the astonishment of all who were present, the sick man left his long-occupied bed and afterward felt none of his former illness. [Col. 0902B]

21. A certain boy who was a monk at the monastery of Paredum was praying with the brothers in the choir when one of the boards joined to the ceiling of the lofty tower fell and crushed him from the crown of his head. People hurried to the venerable Father, who at that moment happened to be occupied with the divine service in another church, that of the Mother of God, and reported to him that the boy had been struck so violently that he was almost lifeless.

When he arrived, he sprinkled the boy’s face with holy water. Then, after prayer, he held back his scarcely throbbing spirit, which was hastening toward departure. [Col. 0902C] His strength gradually returned, he was restored to health, and he lived for a long time afterward.

22. In the territory of Lyon there was a soldier named Berard, lord of the castle of Rehoterium, who was devastating the estate of Saint Peter at Cavaillon and trying to turn it to wicked uses. Because the holy Father repeatedly rebuked him for this, while his wickedness grew ever more violent, he was one day lifted up in pride, uttered threats, and departed from him.

The holy man then resorted to the weapons of faith. He invoked Christ as his protector and earnestly called upon John the Baptist, in whose honor the basilica of that place had been consecrated, as its defender. Immediately, on the road between Cavaillon and his own castle of Lusesium, he was struck by divine judgment and went mad. He was carried away by the hands of his men and dragged to his bed. [Col. 0902D] That very night he was scarcely saved from a fire that seized his bed once and then a second time; he was barely preserved until the satisfaction of the following day. When this had been carried out according to the holy man’s judgment, he ceased to suffer that madness through Hugh’s absolution.

23. Once, while the blessed man was traveling through Aquitaine on certain matters beneficial to his church, some robbers from a castle called Briderium attacked him and carried away his mules together with a large quantity of equipment. Divine vengeance followed this crime. For in the same year their town was destroyed by the Aquitanian duke Guido, who was also called William, and was burned by the fire of divine punishment. [Col. 0903A]

The man of God also possessed such grace in giving counsel that anyone who sought him for advice, whether about divine or worldly matters, was so saturated with the fountain of heavenly teaching that he believed himself to have been instructed almost by an angel.

24. The church of Saint Michael, situated in that part of Cisalpine Gaul called Clusa, gave sufficient proof of this in the driving away of lightning. That place was repeatedly struck by lightning, and a dreadful storm threatened destruction to the monastery on account of the death of certain brothers. At last the blessed man was consulted about changing the site of the monastery.

Then the man filled with God replied that the place ought not to be abandoned, but that the patronage of the blessed martyr Lawrence should be invoked by daily commemoration. The effectiveness of this counsel became so evident [Col. 0903B] that from that time onward, through the merits of the holy martyr and the faith of the most blessed Father, the place was spared the strikes of lightning.

Though he was useful in counsel to others, he was prompt and prudent for himself. It would take too long to demonstrate this in all his affairs. I shall briefly conclude with a few examples.

## CHAPTER IV

### The Council celebrated at Reims, the schism settled, and the pious death

25. At a certain time Pope Leo IX was holding a synod at Reims to eradicate the heresies of the Simonians and Nicolaitans from Gaul, and he was examining the entrance and admission of each of the Fathers. While they answered one by one concerning their elections, the man of God is said to have given this answer about his own conscience: [Col. 0903C] “The flesh consented, but the spirit resisted.”

By these words he was held in such admiration and favor by everyone that, although he was still a young man among so many highly eloquent men and so many elders, he was chosen to address the entire synod.

His advice was sought not only by neighboring peoples but also from remote parts of the world; and not merely by private individuals, but by great orders of people—kings, emperors, and pontiffs, both of the Roman See and of many other sees. He answered them with such moderation and fairness that he placed God before everything while showing himself gracious toward all. This was clearly demonstrated in the schism of the Emperor Henry against the Roman Church. [Col. 0903D]

26. When he had been summoned by the supreme pontiff Gregory VII for the emperor’s reconciliation, and, having passed by the threshold of the apostles—for Caesar was staying there with his army [Note: [Col. 0903D] These events belong to the year 1083 and the following year. Having gained possession of the city, the sacrilegious Guibert was enthroned as antipope, and he in turn received from him the imperial crown—or rather, the pledge of his own condemnation.]—had gone to the supreme pontiff, the king, learning of this, sent an embassy to him, judging it blameworthy that he had passed by a mortal man.

But the man of God replied [Col. 0904A] that he had passed over the place not out of neglect but with good intention: he would obtain pardon from the apostles more quickly if, for the sake of restoring peace, he had approached the severe pontiff before approaching them, than he would return to the favor of that pontiff and be less useful to the cause if, under the appearance of prayer, he seemed to have preferred a royal conversation to a pontifical one.

Although the man of God could not bring them into agreement, the emperor nevertheless, made somewhat more moderate by so reasonable a reply, came to his meeting at Sutri [Note: [Col. 0903D] Sutri is twenty-five miles from Rome.], lest he should see at Rome a second person whom the former had been unable to see. After they had spoken at length with one another, the king, moved by royal zeal, knelt and made satisfaction concerning a certain bishop of Brescia [Note: [Col. 0903D] This was Odalric, who occupied the see of Brescia from 1063. Expelled by his own citizens on account of the schism, he served in Henry’s camp and died there of plague in 1088, as Bernardinus Faynus writes in his *Coelum Brixianum*.], who had inflicted the injury of imprisonment upon the man of God [Note: [Col. 0903D] The same thing happened to various prelates who came to the council convoked by the pope with Henry’s consent—namely, to those whose sincere zeal the schismatics feared most.].

27. I can report still less about his discernment, since it is extremely difficult to go through each of his deeds individually. But just as I have briefly discussed his other virtues, so I shall explain in a few words that virtue which is the mother of them all, without which none of his deeds is found. Since no matter is better demonstrated than by example, I have thought it appropriate to recall how Guigo, count of Albon (Albionensis), was saved by him through a new kind of discernment.

One day, while speaking with the holy Father, Guigo denied among other things that he could become a monk unless he were permitted, whenever he wished, to continue wearing secular clothing. When the man of God heard this, he both satisfied Guigo by yielding to his wish and won his soul for God. After becoming a monk, Guigo first went about wearing softer and more costly garments beneath his cowl. [Col. 0904C] Then, when he saw the humility of the brothers and the simplicity of their life and clothing, he reproached himself for being like a lion among Christ’s sheep. Of his own accord he cast aside all secular and pompous things, and within a short period after his conversion—about twenty days—he died a good death.

28. We shall then praise his religious observance worthily and truthfully if we say that his clothing, gait, bearing, speech—in short, all his works—were holy and irreproachable throughout his entire life. It is unnecessary to describe his patience, humility, chastity, sobriety, and the other virtues that he possessed. They were present in him as though innate and adorned all his actions in every way from his very cradle. [Col. 0904D]

Yet I think it unworthy to omit one thing about his charity, in which no one can deny that he was admirable. When two soldiers had killed one of his brothers and no place of refuge was open to them in Gaul where they could withdraw to safety, this blessed man received them into the asylum of Cluny. [Col. 0905A] After making them monks, he retained one under the rule of the monastic order. The other, who had been the chief author of the crime, escaped and afterward devoted himself to plunder and robbery; because of this he was badly killed, and Hugh lost him.

Since the whole life of the blessed man was nothing other than virtue, and since we cannot collect every detail because of their immensity, let us conclude this work with the death of so great a Father.

29. The holy man, therefore, after the glorious labors of his life, now desired with all his mind to enter upon the way of all flesh, so that he might receive eternal blessedness as a reward from the King whom he had always served. He did not cease daily to practice good works ever more diligently, to pursue mercy, to feed the hungry, to clothe the naked, to put every concern behind the service of God, to maintain the rigor [Col. 0905B] of his order inflexibly, to observe religious discipline both in himself and in those subject to him, and finally to emulate, embrace, and attain every virtue. Thus he continually awaited the day of his calling.

Meanwhile the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection at Easter arrived. The holy old man was about to pass from labor to rest. On the very day of the Lord’s Supper, after he had absolved his brothers, both absent and present, with paternal authority, and after the life-giving Passion and Resurrection had been celebrated, on Wednesday, as evening was already falling, he gave his blessed spirit back to God in the oratory of the blessed Mother of God. His body, embalmed with spices, was buried toward the east in the new basilica that he himself had built.

30. On the very night when he departed to the Lord, a certain religious brother named Baldwin, formerly steward of Lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, saw his funeral from England in a spiritual vision, as he himself related to me. [Col. 0905C] Everywhere incomparable mourning, everywhere wailing, everywhere lamentation resounded. Whatever grief was being enacted at Cluny for the funeral of the holy Father, Baldwin, stationed in Britain, saw it all and understood why it was happening. [Col. 0906A]

Then he summoned the bishop of Rochester, Lord Ralph, who at that time was comforting the Church of Canterbury over the recent death of its lord archbishop Anselm, and explained the vision to him. He foretold that the holy old man had departed from the world. Accordingly, after noting the day and hour, he learned a few days later that the holy man had died, and found that the time corresponded with the vision he had seen.

A certain abbot from the region of Cambrai also saw two biers being carried up to heaven. One was said to be that of the archbishop of Canterbury and the other that of the abbot of Cluny. One ascended on the Wednesday of one week, and the other likewise on the Wednesday of the following week. The event proved the vision after a few days had passed. For the lord [Col. 0906B] archbishop departed at dawn on the Wednesday before the day of the Lord’s Supper, while the holy old man, as stated above, after the Resurrection had been celebrated, was released from the flesh on the same weekday, as evening fell on the eighth day.

These things concerning the life of our holy Father Hugh, abbot of Cluny, I have sketched partly from what I saw myself and partly from what I learned through the credible testimony of reliable men. In his praise let us sing these verses:

> Rule of virtues, Father Hugh, glory of monks,  
> Hope of the needy, despiser of wealth, harbor of the wretched,  
> Vessel and temple of God, offering and sacrifice of Christ,  
> His flesh is laid in the earth, but his spirit has sought the stars.  
>
> O blessed chariot! Blessed driver of your own people! [Col. 0906C]  
> Grant that you may carry to the stars those whom you governed here by your life.  
>
> The final light of his life shone on the penultimate day of April.  
> May God shine eternal light upon you throughout every age.

He governed the Church of Cluny for sixty years, together with eight days and two months [Note: [Col. 0903C] He was therefore consecrated in the year 1049, on 22 February, the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch, which then fell on a Wednesday; he also died on a Wednesday.]. May his merits help us before God for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0905C]

## METRICAL SUMMARY OF THE LIFE

*(By the same Raynaldus, from the aforesaid manuscript.)*

[Col. 0905D]

> We sing of Hugh, distinguished by titles and renowned throughout the world for praise,  
> O Cluny, your hope.  
>
> May God favor these beginnings and fulfill these prayers,  
> So that I may deserve to speak words worthy of so holy a Father.  
>
> From the most noble leaders Burgundy possessed,  
> This distinguished man drew his lineage.  
>
> For Dalmatius never begot anything more illustrious,  
> Unless it was that he himself wished all too eagerly to pursue warfare.  
>
> His mother Aremburgis, no less noble in lineage than her husband,  
> Shone in character and was still nobler in herself. [Col. 0906D]  
>
> Shaken by fear when the danger of childbirth drew near,  
> She thought it right to seek the prayers of priests.  
>
> A thing unheard of through so many ages: while one priest was celebrating,  
> An infant’s form was seen in the chalice.  
>
> What sort of person, and how great, was the one who was being born?  
> The figure seen in so great a mirror reveals it.  
>
> After he had completed the sacraments in the customary manner,  
> The priest proclaimed extraordinary the child whom he found born.  
>
> Thus his prophetic declaration about the boy was not deceived by the course of his life;  
> Nor could the habits of youth corrupt him. [Col. 0907A]  
>
> Already wholly devoted to schools and to the Church,  
> He set amusements aside for the pursuit of virtues.  
>
> He rejected the clothing of nobles in favor of humble dress,  
> And walked simply with the simple.  
>
> But his father, fearing that he might thus withdraw from arms,  
> Rebuked him as though he were guilty of impiety.  
>
> He scarcely feared that the things learned in youth  
> Would harm military service unless they were unlearned;  
>
> He said that he had once appointed him heir to his possessions,  
> That he had always loved him more than the other brothers;  
>
> That therefore he ought to follow his father’s character  
> And his father’s traditions, lest he become like a degenerate.  
>
> This was the father’s speech. But at last the young man accomplished  
> What he had conceived in his mind and, as a fugitive, sought you, Cluny.  
>
> The magnificent Odilo, then shepherd and abbot, [Col. 0907B]  
> Received him among the sheep, instructed him, and cherished him.  
>
> In a short time he proved him so virtuous  
> That he placed him in order over all the brothers.  
>
> Indeed, he afterward raised him to the honor of prior,  
> So that one day he himself might exercise Odilo’s office.  
>
> So humble, so gentle, so fervent, and so severe was he  
> That, when the Father died, he rightly became Father.  
>
> O harmonious, unanimous judgment of the brothers!  
> For everything that sounded there was one voice.  
>
> The entire phalanx of brothers demanded him as abbot.  
> The Fathers had no other choice: it was Father Hugh.  
>
> What crosses he afterward imposed upon himself,  
> The breastplate bears witness, by which he thoroughly subdued himself.  
>
> He wore it against his flesh while mourning his father’s sins;  
> He wore it against his flesh while subduing his own members. [Col. 0907C]  
>
> Believe that, while he held the government, he was almost always praying  
> Or almost always reading,  
>
> Now listening to God, now consulting him.  
> Hope joined him on one side, faith on the other, and love bound both together.  
>
> In writing of the Father’s piety I shall seem culpable  
> If I report the riches he poured out upon poor Christ,  
>
> Since in reality no one was second to him in praise;  
> My measure fails me, my number is too small.  
>
> Yet I can briefly define what I think:  
> In his own time no one distributed more wisely.  
>
> Let us now at last come to the marks of faith.  
> Let signs concerning Christ hold the first place.  
>
> Bear witness to this matter, you seventh Pope Gregory,  
> To whom God wished these secrets to be visible.  
>
> Once, while the illustrious Father was instructing the brothers, [Col. 0907D]  
> Examining their conduct and destroying what was harmful,  
>
> This excellent man—then still Hildebrand,  
> A subdeacon of the city, afterward an apostolic man—  
>
> Then the Father’s assessor, looked upon him, and behold: the Redeemer  
> Was seen seated at the Father’s side.  
>
> He was cheerful, calm, and serene,  
> As though by appearance and expression he approved the judgments.  
>
> Rising before him while the assembly of brothers marveled,  
> The man wished to seat God in the midst of them.  
>
> When asked what had been the reason,  
> He reported the vision, recalling it in order.  
>
> There is a city of Italy called Florence.  
> Here, rumor had it, Pope Stephen was dying.  
>
> The saint visits him, a wise physician of souls, [Col. 0908A]  
> And often ministers to him the word of life.  
>
> But the cruel and envious enemy of our race,  
> When the holy man is absent, is himself deceitfully present.  
>
> He terrifies the pontiff, who looks about in confusion and horror;  
> When the holy man is present, the deceitful one himself is absent.  
>
> Thus the present alternation continued for a long time.  
>
> Then the bishop asks that the Father always be present.  
> He complies with the prayers and no longer withdraws from him,  
> Until he sees him die and buries him.  
>
> Nor should you wonder that he drove away the ancient tyrant,  
> Since his mind and spirit clung to God;  
>
> And since he was fixed upon God, to whom he devoted himself night and day,  
> I shall relate, while there is occasion, Him whom he saw beside Him.  
>
> The brotherly choir was singing psalms to the Lord, and the Father himself  
> Saw Christ singing with a lyre. [Col. 0908B]  
>
> He was seen singing individually through all the voices,  
> And filled the place with a fragrance surpassing balsam.  
>
> Nor shall I pass over the feigned illness,  
> Which that guilty Pontius vainly pretended through resentment.  
>
> Once, so that he might not enjoy conversation with the Father,  
> He fled to his bed and pretended to be ill.  
>
> Yet it did not go unpunished; for immediately he was made so sick  
> That his speech almost failed him.  
>
> And unless the holy man had hastened to visit him,  
> No hope of life would have remained.  
>
> But when he was absolved from his faults by the holy Father,  
> His strength immediately returned, and speech itself returned.  
>
> You too, who gave unauthorized solidi to be held,  
> We know that you experienced the Father’s help.  
>
> You were dead, though not yet buried in the flesh, [Col. 0908C]  
> When a vision warned two brothers together:  
>
> You were to ask to be absolved before being buried;  
> Otherwise, the gift might be harmful to you.  
>
> And so that they might be able to believe the words,  
> The man to whom you had given the solidi was also exposed.  
>
> When these things became known to the Father, what prayers followed  
> You know better, for pardon is granted to you from this.  
>
> It would be wicked to remain silent about the leper healed by the garment  
> Which the saint, in compassion for the wretched man, had given him.  
>
> Nor does the memorable mitre of Peter escape my memory,  
> Through which he restored a suffering man to health.  
>
> Hence I report ten solidi repaid tenfold in gold,  
> Either as praise of you, O King of the needy.  
>
> Peter, together with Paul, this Father’s letter moved you;  
> It moved you often to relieve his poverty. [Col. 0908D]  
>
> And you admonished the Father to found a new church;  
> Through you the messenger himself came safely concerning this matter.  
>
> Tell us, Cluny, the condition in which Father Hugh placed you.  
> Tell us the countless number of brothers he gave you.  
>
> Tell us the cells, tell us the churches that he himself founded.  
> Tell us the many monasteries that he restored.  
>
> Among all these, I ask you especially to cherish Marcigny.  
> He established this place within his paternal jurisdiction.  
>
> Here he ordained holy women to serve God  
> And to continue the song of the Mother of Jesus.  
>
> You too, gracious Spirit, discerner of spirits,  
> Were not absent when minds were being discerned.  
>
> Hence the saint refuses kisses to a certain brother,  
> Whom he discovers to have celebrated Mass without being a priest. [Col. 0909A]  
>
> Hence, zealous for the poor, he rebukes one  
> Who was condemned for luxury and drunkenness.  
>
> Then you, who were meditating flight and whom the blessed man anticipated,  
> You too perceived that your heart lay open.  
>
> That Durannus, bishop of the city of Toulouse,  
> Learned from the Father after death what he had to suffer.  
>
> He learned that he would be seen with foam on his lips  
> Because of words that provoked laughter.  
>
> As soon as he died, he appeared foaming by night  
> To a certain Siguinus, recalling the Father’s words.  
>
> But the pious, wise, and skillful physician of souls  
> Ordered the brothers to keep silence for a week.  
>
> He imposed this upon seven brothers, but one neglected it,  
> While the others kept it; nevertheless, this did not remain hidden.  
>
> For again the bishop sought the same brother [Col. 0909B]  
> And reported that the Father’s command had been transgressed.  
>
> He said that he had been sufficiently helped because six had kept silence,  
> But that what still remained was hindered by the seventh.  
>
> When the Father learned this, he repaired what had been broken  
> Through the same number of brothers and for a week.  
>
> Then the bishop returned, no longer disfigured as before,  
> But retaining a proper and comely appearance:  
>
> O cleric, imprisoned because you were to become a monk,  
> The Father frees you through angelic assistance.  
>
> The man whom pain in his leg prevented from obeying the Father  
> Drove the disease away at the Father’s very name.  
>
> He is said to have healed many through the remains of his table;  
> The thing he touched often became a remedy.  
>
> You, crushed boy, who could scarcely breathe,  
> You were restored to health through the Father’s prayers. [Col. 0909C]  
>
> You whom the burning of your foot allowed no rest,  
> You recovered through the water with which the Father had been washed.  
>
> How vainly you threaten the saint, soldier Berard!  
> He prays, and you go mad, while he grants pardon.  
>
> What did that robbery profit you, Briderium?  
> Through the merits of the saint you perish by heavenly fire.  
>
> Now I shall briefly explain how great this blessed man was in counsel,  
> For brevity is pleasing.  
>
> For a long time repeated lightning struck the people of Clusa,  
> And the holy Father was consulted about it.  
>
> “You, good Lawrence, you, because you overcame well  
> The fires of Caesar, he commands to be remembered. [Col. 0910A]  
>
> He affirms that you can sufficiently drive away these fires  
> If they celebrate your merit night and day.”  
>
> The Father’s commands are fulfilled; immediately the lightning ceases,  
> And that place remains without fear.  
>
> How great and how remarkable was the discernment of the pious Father!  
> Count Guigo, one among many, bears witness to it.  
>
> He swore that he could not become a monk  
> Unless he were allowed to wear clothing like a count.  
>
> The saint gave his consent and won the count.  
> The man died a monk after a short period,  
>
> So that nothing was lacking from perfection in the holy man.  
>
> He is said to have loved the killers of his brother,  
> Becoming an asylum for men stained by fraternal blood.  
>
> I believe that in this deed he was not inferior even to King David.  
>
> Let these things published about the Father’s merits and virtues suffice; [Col. 0910B]  
> Now I shall relate his death.  
>
> When the festivals of the triumph of Easter were being celebrated,  
> Since the Virgin had borne God begotten in the flesh,  
>
> After one thousand one hundred and nine years had been completed,  
> That blessed old man passed into rest.  
>
> At his funeral a certain religious man,  
> Though mentally transported, remained far away in body.  
>
> Across the sea that divides the Northmen and the Britons,  
> He saw what Cluny was doing.  
>
> Everywhere mourning sounded; nowhere was anything heard but lamentation.  
> Nothing was seen without sobbing or groaning.  
>
> He therefore noted the day on which the saint was thought to have died,  
> And within a short time confirmed that it was indeed the day.  
>
> Hence I recall the two biers carried toward the stars, [Col. 0910C]  
> As an old man reported that he had seen them.  
>
> One was said to be that of Archbishop Anselm,  
> Under whose episcopate Canterbury rejoices; it was the first bier.  
>
> The one that was second was intimated to be that of the holy Father,  
> But eight days later.  
>
> The vision’s truth followed, for after the archbishop died,  
> It is established that the saint died on the eighth day.  
>
> He held the sacred governance for twelve lustrums;  
> Add two months and, in addition, eight days.  
>
> Father Hugh, receive these words of your nephew Raynaldus,  
> I beg you, in kindness, and protect me, Father.

[Col. 0909C]

## EPITOME OF THE LIFE

*Written shortly after the saint’s death by the Cluniac monks Ezelon and Gilo, excerpted by an anonymous author.*

*(Recovered from a manuscript at Bodec, in the diocese of Paderborn, by John Gamas, S.J.)*

[Col. 0909D]

1. Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, was a native of Autun and of noble birth. His father was Dalmatius, a consular man devoted to military affairs. When Hugh’s mother, pregnant with him, was suffering greatly in childbirth, she begged a certain religious priest to celebrate Mass for her deliverance and the safety of the child about to be born.

While the priest was solemnly celebrating the Mass with intense attention and, lifted up in contemplation, was raised above himself, he is said to have seen in the chalice upon which he was concentrating with particular fervor the form of an infant, shining beyond ordinary human measure. [Col. 0910D]

It was an entirely worthy vision and truly prophetic of the future: the child who had not yet been born appeared in the chalice. From his youth he would receive the chalice of salvation, imitate the Lord’s Passion in an evangelical manner, turn the words of the Gospel into deeds, and invoke the name of the Lord into old age. [Col. 0911A]

## 2
