Having reached the years of adolescence, he did not, as that age commonly does, loosen the reins of lust, nor, softened by idle luxury, pursue frivolous absurdities; rather, in accordance with what is written of Jacob, “He dwelt innocently at home” (Gen. 25:27). Then, going to Cluny, he placed himself under Blessed Odilo, and, changing his way of life together with his tunic, most devoutly assumed the habit of holy religion. Thereafter, thoroughly purified of the rust of the world in the furnace of discipline, he suddenly overcame the prolonged lukewarmness of many by his ardor. Later he became prior and, after the death of Blessed Odilo the abbot, succeeded him in governance, though he accepted the office with tears. He was good in knowledge, better in conscience, best in self-restraint; angelic in appearance, composed in conduct, remarkable in his natural bearing, gentle in speech without affectation, and distinguished by other such gifts of grace.

At that time Emperor Henry II was governing the summit of the kingdom with great vigor. His father, the Emperor Augustus, had entrusted to Cluny the insignia which he had carried at Rome when he attained the kingdom.

[Note: Emperor Conrad died in 1039; he had been crowned at Rome by John XX on Easter Day in 1027.]

Therefore, cherishing deep in his heart a love for Cluny as though it were an hereditary right, the son resolved to bind the flourishing Father [Hugo] more closely to himself. Accordingly, he invited Saint Hugh, then blossoming in the vigor of youth, to come to him. He received him with honor and gladly obtained from him that he should lift his son Henry III from the sacred font. At that time he also celebrated Easter—the son of the paschal Lamb—together with the emperor in the colony of Agrippina, surrounded by the angelic host of the senior monks of Cluny. Not long afterward, scarcely released from the Emperor’s presence, he returned to Cluny, accompanied by gifts and favor.

## 3

This favor of his did not escape Pope Stephen either. When the pope was lying ill in the city of Florence, he declared to those around him that, when Saint Hugh arrived, the enemy withdrew, and that when Hugh departed, the enemy approached. Therefore, lest he be oppressed by the attacks of the hostile power, he implored the diligence of the man whose presence confounded the ambusher. By then the father’s tears had driven the evil assaults far away, when the apostolic man breathed out his soul in the lap of the presider. Properly prepared by Hugh’s hands, he was handed over for burial.

It also became abundantly clear to the most reverend Hildebrand—later, when both his name and rank had been changed, called Gregory—how much spiritual grace Father Hugh possessed. Before he had yet been adorned with the papal dignity, Hildebrand, while seated in the chapter at Cluny, declared that he had seen the Judge of the world himself at Saint Hugh’s side. Seated at Hugh’s right, he continued to foster regular discipline.

[Note: The Plumali manuscript reads “at the summit”; we have corrected the text by adding the word “summit.”]

After he became pope, Hildebrand habitually called him “the gentle tyrant,” since he showed himself a lion toward the fierce and a lamb toward the gentle, well aware how to spare his subjects and chastise the proud.

## 4

During the time of Pope Leo IX, the body of Blessed Remigius was translated to Reims. The apostolic man presided over so great a translation and celebrated a general council, principally against the Simonians. Father Hugh also attended, armed with faith, followed by a vast procession of distinguished men. But the multitude of the wicked was so great that the good scarcely dared to rebuke them; and even if they had dared, the outcry of those living badly would more easily have burst forth than the free voice of those who held sounder convictions.

Soon, at the synodal urging of a certain very distinguished man, acting by order of the lord pope and at the persuasion of a certain very distinguished man, Saint Constantius, a canon of Reims, together with others, he acted laudably and offered a prudent judgment concerning the evasions of those who were accustomed to uphold falsehood against the truth.

[Note: Besides the cathedral church of Saint Mary, Reims has two collegiate churches, Saint Symphorian and Saint Timothy. If it can be shown that another collegiate church existed there under the title of Saint Constantius, I shall believe that this passage indicates the proper name of a church and not a canon. If not, I shall ask the people of Reims whether they know anything of a certain canon named Saint Constantius; certainly, we have found no other mention of him anywhere.]

## 5

Hildefonsus, king of Spain, remembering the holy father Hugh more than anyone else, obtained through fervent prayers the favor of being worthy to see him. First, because he had emerged from the captivity of his brother Sancho through the prayers of Saint Hugh; and second, because he was planning more firmly to restore the union between his father Fredelandus and the people of Cluny, since otherwise he would have been disobedient to Blessed Peter and ungrateful for his benefits.

[Note: This refers to Saint Peter, as is clearly stated in the Life by Hildebert.]

For while he was being held in the strictest confinement and the Cluniacs were devoting themselves to prayer on his behalf, a certain bishop made known that, pressed by the insistence of Hugh and his followers, Sancho was to restore him shortly to his own power and raise him again to the throne. Without delay the keeper of heaven’s keys appeared terrifyingly by night to Sancho, who had usurped the kingdom, and threatened him with death unless he immediately released his brother.

[Note: These words seem to have given Hildebert occasion to believe that Sancho had been compelled to restore his brother’s dignity. In fact, he merely released him from prison into freer custody in a monastery; and only after dying two years later did he leave the kingdom to be received by Alfonso.]

The tyrant rose at once, terrified, and, having freed him from his bonds, returned to bed. Thus it came about that the liberated king, having doubled his father’s tribute, annually sent various ounces of gold to his intercessors and left our community the anniversary of his liberation as a day of celebration.

## 6

Saint Hugh contributed many things for the use of the poor, regarding them as worthless burdens. He often endured their seizure without anger and even maintained such moderation in issuing commands that neither excessive leniency nor overbearing severity would prevail. By the spirit of prophecy he was accustomed to discern among novices which were to be strengthened with the stability of grain and which, like chaff, were to be scattered by the evil spirit.

On one occasion, while he was at Marcigny with the distinguished Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, who, having been removed from the archbishopric for the sake of justice, took joy in Hugh’s consolation, he was warned by divine revelation and foretold the imminent death of William, king of England. It happened as he had predicted. For while William was eagerly shooting fleeing deer through the woodland glades, he suddenly received in his heart the arrow with which his own soldier was aiming at a stag.

At another time, while the same Father was asleep, he saw in a dream a multitude of serpents and wild beasts lying beneath his head. Shaking them off and examining what had been placed beneath him, he found there a book of Maro. Immediately, having cast away the secular volume, he rested peacefully; and he understood that the nature of the book corresponded to the vision, since a work full of obscenities and pagan rites was unworthy to be placed beneath the couch of a holy man.

A certain brother named Durannus of Brodon—previously appearing to be an uneducated man, later a not unsuitable abbot of Moissac, and afterward advanced to the bishopric of Toulouse by virtue of his wisdom—shone among the workers in God’s cultivation through the excellence of his diligence.

[Note: The Sammarthani did not know this surname, though they were otherwise diligent in recording those known to them.] In other matters he was circumspect, but he often uttered words that provoked laughter with excessive carelessness.

For this reason, the venerable Father Hugh frequently rebuked him. When he made no sufficient progress, Hugh threatened him prophetically with what would happen in the future and said:

“Certainly, dearest brother, unless while you live you abandon your joking words, which are entirely forbidden to a monk, you will appear exceedingly deformed after death.”

This prophecy was indeed fulfilled when he departed. For he appeared with foaming mouth to a certain Siguinus, the Father’s chaplain, and tearfully begged his help, though he had refused to obey him while alive. When Siguinus reported this to the lord abbot, Hugh ordered seven brothers to maintain silence concerning their own mouths for one week on behalf of the dead man; seven brothers were selected for this purpose. All the others obeyed, but one of them, who despised his vow, broke the silence.

Again the bishop was revealed to the same man and bitterly complained about that faithless brother, who, by refusing to remain silent, had interrupted his healing. When most merciful Hugh heard this, he ordered that the breach of silence committed by one man should be repaired by seven more days of silence.

When this had been done, the bishop’s soul appeared for the third time, showing himself in apostolic state, and gave thanks to Hugh—mindful of, and always to remember, his purgatory—for the restoration of his integrity.

[Note: The copy reads, “his purgatory.”]

## 7

Likewise, at Silviniacum, a certain brother named Stephen, overthrown by the snares of the ancient enemy, laid hands upon himself in order to anticipate the crown of martyrdom and killed himself in a certain forest. He was, however, prone to anger; the tempter was stirred by this disposition of his and perhaps prevailed.

When his soul was dragged before judgment, it found an accuser hostile to it, holding out the murderous knife.

[Note: The copy reads “preceding”; but in that case “and preceding” would have to be added.]

The wretched man, prodigal of his own soul and stripped of his cowl, obtained through apostolic intercession that he should remain before the entrance of the Cluniac cloister, holding his cowl in his hands, until by the prayers of Saint Hugh and the brothers he might deserve to put it on and recover his order.

[Note: Silviniacum is commonly called Sauvigny. It is not the place called Saviniacum, founded by Saint Vitalis within the borders of Maine and soon transferred to the Cistercians, but another place, perhaps situated in a town of Burgundy near the boundary between the duchy and the county.]

A certain brother saw these things in a vision and reported them to the lord abbot, though not immediately, as he should have done. Therefore, at the time of the Rogations, because he had delayed reporting what he had seen, he was compelled by blows to disclose it. While the others went to the procession, he alone remained in the choir, being lame.

Saint Odilo appeared visibly to him while he was awake, accompanied by two men. After prayer had been made, Odilo called him and entered the chapter; he rebuked the brother’s sluggishness and, with great harshness, ordered his attendants to discipline him severely.

After the litanies, the brother, having been beaten, reported to the abbot both the vision and his own affliction. Immediately the pious Father ordered that almsgiving, prayers, and offerings should be continued until the apparition appeared in another vision wearing the sacred habit, and the body was judged not unworthy of the cemetery.

[Note: He may have repented of the sin after inflicting the fatal wound upon himself. The apparition requesting help leads one to suppose that this truly happened.]

## 8

Once Saint Hugh happened to administer the Eucharist to a certain leper, who was physically excluded from human communion but was then receiving communion. With swollen lips and ulcerated mouth, he dishonorably chewed the Lord’s body and rejected the small portion with an ill-timed expectoration, followed, of course, by nausea and terrible foaming.

Then the soldier of Christ, Goderannus, who was present, seeing his Lord’s sacraments being treated so unworthily, gathered up what had been expelled with swift service. And behold, the courageous man placed both hands beneath the life-giving sacrament, cast the vomit of the nauseated sick man into his own mouth, and faithfully swallowed it together with the deadly bile.

At this, the pious master was astonished and, stunned by the perfection of his disciple, declared without hesitation that the gridiron of Laurence had been easier to endure. This Goderannus was eventually promoted to the bishopric of Saintes; and the higher he climbed, the more brightly he shone.

## 9

It is the custom of the monastery of Cluny to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord with a particular devotion greater than that shown at other solemnities, and to solemnize it with hymns and melodies, with the lighting of candles, and—what is far more excellent—with spiritual devotion and a great outpouring of tears, together with the angels.

For this festival the brothers prepared themselves and all that belonged to them. That venerable Father Hugh, who still survived in old age, entered the chapter where the brothers were and addressed them all:

“Know, brothers, that the gracious Jesus is present at your solemnities, while the wicked enemy labors in opposition, so that he may mingle some cloud of his darkness with so great a splendor. For a certain brother”—thereby clearly indicating himself—“saw the Mother of Mercy holding in her sweetest lap the very Son whom she had borne the preceding night, while a multitude of holy angels stood beside him amid immense light.

“The same divine child rejoiced and displayed the joy of his heart by the movement of his body and the clapping of his hands. Turning to his Mother, he said: ‘Do you see, Mother, how the night of my birth, which is approaching, is to be illumined with joys? On it the oracles of the prophets and the proclamations of the angels will be renewed, and all things both heavenly and earthly will likewise rejoice in my birth from you. Where now is the condemned treachery of my enemy? Where now is his power, which ruled the world before this singular joy?’

“When the imprudent enemy heard this, he came out of his hiding place and revealed himself from afar. Disgracefully disfigured, with much lamentation and howling, he begged to be admitted:

“‘And if,’ he said, ‘I am admitted into no part of the church, may I at least be received somewhere in one of the remaining buildings.’

“But the Son of the Virgin said: ‘Go, gallows-bird. Do not complain that my power has prejudged you; try whatever you can.’

“Released, he sought the entrance to the chapter. He tried to enter but could not, for he found both himself swollen with pride and the chapter entrance narrow, so that he could not enter in any way. Truly inflamed by the old abscess of pride, he could not pass through the humble entrance.

“From there he turned his steps toward the brothers’ dormitory. Trusting that he could disturb them with his customary fantasies, he attempted to enter; but, repelled from the doorway by the same bulk of his, he withdrew.

“Afterward he placed his hope of causing harm in the refectory. There, suspecting that their slight care for the body meant a greater negligence of mind, he nevertheless found so many barriers formed by the reading of divine words, so many beams formed by the devotion of the listeners, and so many obstacles formed by the charity with which they served one another, that, unable to proceed any farther, he was forced to retreat.

“Thus rejected from all the buildings of the church, that pestilential one withdrew from the presence of the most merciful Redeemer and his most glorious Virgin Mother, with the confusion he deserved.

“Therefore, be watchful, brothers, and give immense thanks to the almighty and most merciful Savior, because he has both driven the most wicked enemy away from you and himself remained with us to celebrate the feast.”

[Note: Something is missing here. For Bernard himself, who is introduced as speaking here in the first person, cannot be said to have written this Life, as appears from Hildebert above, where this vision is said to have been revealed to him only during the saint’s final illness, and indeed not long after the saint’s death.]

## 10

A few days before Saint Hugh died, a vision of saints appeared to a certain peasant laboring in a field. A certain royal lady preceded them; the peasant saw her back as she passed and her face. An old man followed that holy procession. He stopped and said:

“Whose is this field, farmer, which you cultivate?”

He replied: “It belongs to Blessed Peter and the lord abbot of Cluny.”

Then the old man said: “The field is mine, and the abbot is my servant. Hurry and report to our abbot that he should make arrangements for his household, which he has nourished, because after a short time he will meet the end of this life. Tell him that the apostle Peter announced this to you, and proclaim that those who precede me are the Mother of God and the saints who attend her.”

## 11

The same Hugh, placed at the point of death, remembering the anniversaries of Archbishop Gaufridus and Abbot Mendo, admonished those who had forgotten them. He had such tenacious memory and such great charity because he was not forgetful of his brothers’ salvation where scarcely anyone remembers his own.

On the very night on which he died, he bestowed the blessings of the readings upon the readers. His final word to those standing around him was: “Bless.”

His body was washed by the brothers in the chapter, first with water and then with wine. Finally, with the small amount of balsam that remained in a little vessel, his entire body, although large, was abundantly anointed three times. The balsam would scarcely have sufficed for his fair head alone, had it not been multiplied by heavenly blessing and become abundant in the hands of those serving him.

Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite appeared to a certain brother at Nogent and told him to hurry to Cluny so that he might say farewell to Saint Hugh, who was about to die.

[Note: Peter the Venerable transcribed this in Book I, chapter 15, of his *Miracles*, occasionally rendering a few words more elegantly.]

“I came, unhappy man that I am, but I did not greet the departing saint. Yet what was denied to the body was granted to the spirit, as is certain. For I saw the heavenly ones mingled with mortals, and, together with the company of monks, I saw the Mother of God, the star of the sea, flashing more brightly. Her presence so terrified and drove away certain figures appearing as archers, just as a powerful wind is accustomed to strike down the autumn leaves.

“Among them were Martin, the jewel of priests, and Benedict, the sun of abbots. They led the spirit of Saint Hugh into a beautiful and most fertile vineyard and placed him there, so that he might rejoice and remain for a little while. There Saint Hugh himself, seeing me, invited me in these words:

“‘Eat, dearest one, of the white grapes that abound for us, and keep solemn company with me. I shall rest here only briefly, until a certain swelling subsides, which I contracted in my dusty feet during my long circuit through the lands. But immediately afterward, with my steps restored and the worldly dust shaken off, I shall pass freely to better things.

“‘Tell my successor Pontius to guard the treasures of humility and innocence, and, considering the needs of all as his own, to devote himself to mercy. Let him wisely order the zeal of the monastic order according to my example. For by acting manfully he will obtain help from God, who does not abandon those who hope in him.’”

## 12

On the same night on which the blessed Father fell asleep in the Lord, a certain abbot saw two saints, decently adorned in a vision, being lifted to the stars by the hands of angels. He heard voices above saying:

“These two, correctors of themselves and of the world, shall be placed in radiant beds of gold according to the merit of their lives: namely, the archbishop of Canterbury and the abbot of Cluny, who in glory are fathers of many sons.”

These two indeed died at almost the same time.

### Verses on the Cluniac Abbots, from the First up to Blessed Hugh

In order Berno stands; then Odo, blessed in honor:

After these rises holy Majolus, in the form of a man,

Fiery, scarcely restraining his burning soul;

Then holy Odilo, sent from the shores of Auvergne,

Gentler in character than fierce in command;

Next comes Hugh, using discerning reins,

Later in succession, but first in usefulness.

# ANALecta

*(Collected from other materials in the Cluniac library.)*

## Chapter I. From a Letter of the Monk Hugh to Abbot Pontius

### 1

To the most serene Father Pontius, abbot of Cluny, his lord: the servant Hugh.

When I consider your excellence, Father, I do not dare to speak before you unjustly. But since I see that certain matters worthy of remembrance concerning the great Hugh, your holy predecessor, have been left unspoken, if your dignity commands me to speak, I shall briefly set forth a few things from many, small things from great ones.

I am astonished that those prolific writers who composed such extensive volumes about him omitted these matters. What I report is best known to those now living, but, as you command, it has been committed to the memory of posterity.

### 2

Blessed Hugh had once set out to visit the people of France. When he reached the territory of Beauvais, he entered Gournay on the river Arona.

[Note: Gornacum, commonly Gournay-sur-Epte, lies five leagues from Beauvais across the Epte, which strictly separates the Franks—that is, those subject to the government of Paris—from the Normans. Whether the river Epte is also called Arona, or whether Hugh went astray through confusion with another Gournay, Gournay-sur-Marne, situated between Paris and Melun, and whether “Arona” crept in through scribal error for “Matrona,” I do not determine.]

There the illustrious Albert received him with honor. The man’s wife, named Ermengardis, also came reverently to meet so great a guest.

When the saint saw her, filled with the prophetic spirit, he said:

“Lady, you are pregnant. You will give birth to a son who, if it pleases God, will be a monk.”

The woman was astonished to hear what she had not previously known about herself; those present rejoiced, recognizing the prophecy when they heard it. Later, in accordance with the word of the servant of God, the pregnant woman gave birth to a son.

The boy grew up and was assigned to the profession of arms. Having entered military service, he became destructive, as that class of men is unhappily accustomed to do. Meanwhile the saint, full of days as well as virtues, brought his final day to a close in the Lord.

At that time, in Italy at Pavia, there was a distinguished ornament of the bishops, Godefridus, bishop of Amiens, renowned for his learning and conspicuous for his holiness. When Blessed Hugh was dying from the present life and being granted the eternal one, the bishop saw distinguished companies preparing to go forth, with lights and the other things customarily displayed solemnly in a procession.

When the bishop asked who it was for whom a triumph of such glory was waiting, he was told that this festive devotion of the saints was proceeding to escort Lord Hugh, the abbot of Cluny. When the bishop disclosed this to his companions in amazement and recorded the time at which he had seen it, he returned to Gaul and discovered that Saint Hugh had departed at Cluny at the very time in which the vision had been shown to him at Pavia.

[Note: Saint Godefridus, bishop of Amiens, is commemorated on 8 November. He governed his church from 1104 to 1118.]

### 3

After the saint had died, you were happily elected and worthily appointed to the office of so great a Father. Under the Lord’s guidance you descended to the regions of France mentioned above. There, following your noble custom of proclaiming good things to everyone, you found the young man of whom the saint had prophesied; you found him, called him, and brought him away.

We saw him at Cluny for many years, a monk named Landricus, distinguished by good conduct.

[Note: In the Life written later by this same Hugh, the revelation made to Saint Godefridus after the boy’s birth and moral corruption in adulthood is omitted, and his conversion is immediately joined to what precedes in these words: “Meanwhile Blessed Hugh completed the course of the present life. When his pious son, Lord Pontius, succeeded this Father and was appointed abbot of Cluny, he too, intending to visit France, entered it. There, following his noble custom of recalling the erring, he brought many back with him, among them me, a sinner, and this young man of whom we speak. He found him, called him, and made him a monk, as the saint had foretold. He is present at Cluny and performs the priestly office.”]

Thus, most kindly Father, thus your predecessor, the most holy abbot Hugh, whom you loved exceedingly—indeed, whom you love—has been shown, among his other virtues, to have shone also with prophetic power. Thus, at the dissolution of his body, he was revealed to a bishop and is recognized as a fellow citizen of the heavenly realm.

But let my smallness now be silent; let your charity consider more fully how exalted these matters are. For I, so lowly, ought to fear speaking of such height.

### 4

Finally, in the year 1118 of the Word born of the Virgin, after the death of Pope Paschal, who governed the summit of the Roman See for eighteen years and more,

[Note: More precisely, eighteen years, five months, and four days.]

Gelasius was chosen by canonical election and consecrated pope. He was a man of outstanding learning, generous in almsgiving, and prudent in counsel.

When Henry IV, emperor of the Romans, was raging against the Church, Gelasius withdrew and went down to the sea, traveling by ship to Gaul. He first sent word of his coming to you through a messenger dispatched from Pisa, for the Roman pontiff regards you, the abbot of Cluny, as his own special son in the regions of Gaul.

You met him at Saint-Gilles, and for him and his large retinue you most elegantly supplied horses and every other possible provision. When illness had weakened him because of the hardships of the sea, you carefully tended him on the soil of your birthplace, which your father Peter, a powerful and noble count of Melgueil, had contested against the right of the apostles Peter and Paul and had received from them.

[Note: Melgueil, commonly called Mauguio, must be situated in Languedoc not far from the Rhône, since Pontius was born there; at least the place of his birth must be sought in that region, since the pope, after withdrawing to Saint-Gilles, went from there upstream along the Rhône toward Lyon.]

When he had recovered and wished to reach his own Cluny, he passed through Lyon in Gaul and descended to Mâcon.

[Note: He is said to have “descended,” not with reference to the river, which was against him, but with reference to the route, which led from south to north.]

There, overcome by a very grave illness, he urgently ordered that he be carried to Cluny. Transported there and received with the greatest reverence, after completing one year and four days of his pontificate,

[Note: Gelasius II died in 1119, on 29 January.]

he peacefully rested at Cluny in his own house, amid the brothers and surrounded by cardinal bishops, as their own shepherd.

### 5

After him, the reverend Guido, archbishop of Vienne, was elected by the Catholic Church at Cluny and thus ordained Pope Calixtus.

[Note: Calixtus II was crowned on 1 February of the same year.]

He excelled in the loftiness of his earthly nobility,

[Note: He was the son of William II, count of Burgundy.]

but shone more beautifully through the splendor of heavenly gifts. He returned to Cluny for a second time and there devoutly celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision and Epiphany.

[Note: In the year 1120, before he returned to Italy.]

While he frequently spoke, among other matters, about the life and miracles of Blessed Hugh, he did not attend merely to the writings of just anyone, lavishly covered with accounts of these things; rather, he gladly accepted authoritative witnesses presented in the midst of the Cluniac chapter, who gave stronger testimony concerning what they had seen and heard about the saint.

When the bishops and cardinals likewise agreed, the pope decreed that the birthday of so great a confessor, approved by so many and such great virtues, should be made a festival to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: The other things the pontiff did at Cluny may be read in the Cluniac library, column 560.]

Let it suffice that I have said these things, and may your grace grant me pardon.

[Note: The rest of the letter concerns the relics of Saints Peter and Paul brought to Cluny and preserved in the new monastery built by Pontius, beneath an unmoved altar under which they had formerly been placed.]

## Chapter II. From the Life Written by the Same Hugh

### 6

To the holy assembly of the Cluniac fathers: the servant Hugh.

Charity, which freely serves, compels me to obey pious commands. Therefore, at the command and not through presumption, I have undertaken, though unworthy, to say something about Blessed Hugh. Nor do I prejudice those who before me wrote elegantly about the saint; rather, I serve our own people by gathering certain matters omitted by them and abridging what they published at greater length, lest I burden the busy by passing over many things.

“With this protestation prefaced, the author briefly touches upon the saint’s birth, monastic profession, and election. After briefly indicating what happened at Florence, he continues his subject as follows:”

### 7

I append things even more wonderful to the things already wonderful, which I recognize as confirmed by trustworthy men who reported them. These matters are indeed reported by Gaufridus of Mont-Saint-Vincent and Rainaldus of Autun.

Robert, duke of Burgundy, was harassing Haganon, bishop of Autun, with excessive hostility, and Burgundy was suffering everywhere from various incursions by brigands. Therefore the bishops Gaufridus of Lyon, Hugh of Besançon, Accardus of Chalon, and Drogo of Mâcon assembled at Autun and asked the aforementioned Hugh, abbot of Cluny and a man of great counsel, to come.

[Note: The Sammarthani assign this gathering of bishops to the year 1072 in their account of the bishops of Besançon. Their Hugh, number 53, was in the first year of his episcopate in 1071; Drogo of Mâcon, who likewise took part, was in the penultimate year of his episcopate.

A major controversy is raised by the same Sammarthani concerning Gaufridus of Lyon. In their list of the archbishops of Lyon they find no period during which he held the see, nor do they find his name in the catalogues. They reject him on the authority of the chronicle of Flavigny, which states under the year 1077: “Because the see of Lyon was vacant, after Humbert the Simoniac had been expelled and made a monk in the Jura.”

Yet, as they themselves indicate, the earliest record of this Humbert is found in the chartulary of Saint Peter of Mâcon under the year 1072. They suppose that Philip, mentioned by Alberic in his chronicle under the year 1051, is the same man who in 1055 was convicted of simony by a miracle. Why, then, should he not also have been deposed? At least, there is ample space between 1055 and 1072 for Gaufridus to have occupied the see in the interim and to have died shortly after the synod of Autun was held—especially since it is not even certain that the synod took place in 1072 rather than 1071.

Add that, as Querectanus notes, Nicholas Aragonius also remembers this Gaufridus of Lyon in the ancient *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*.]

A great multitude of distinguished men was present, and the people streamed together without number, pleading for peace with tireless cries. The duke himself—or rather the tyrant—arrived and entered Autun, but in malicious arrogance refused to take part in the assembly.

Father Hugh, however, moved by the fervor of charity, went to the tyrant. Rebuking him vehemently, he led him away, to everyone’s amazement, as though he were the gentlest of sheep.

When the bishops begged Father Hugh to speak for the making of peace, while the crowds everywhere fell silent and hung upon his words, he said:

“Let those who seek peace and love God listen to us and act with us. But whoever is not a son of peace, whoever is not from God but is an adversary—I command him in the name of the Almighty to leave us and not hinder the work of God.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when a certain man, tall in stature and savage in face, accompanied by many followers, went out and disappeared. Among so great a multitude of people there was no one who knew any of those who had gone out.

Each person wondered; everyone was astonished. When they questioned one another about what had happened, there was no answer except that, when the saint had forbidden them, demons had visibly gone out and had vanished from the crowd at the same time.

After these had been driven away, the saint’s preaching immediately had such power that, at his command, the duke himself pardoned those who had killed his son,

[Note: Hugh and Henry died before their father. The first perished in 1057 in a war against the duke of Nevers. Henry left behind a son, Hugh, who succeeded his grandfather Robert in the duchy, despite the futile opposition of his uncle Robert, the duke’s third son. If some proof of Henry’s murder could be established, there would be no doubt that he should be understood as the person named here. It is not apparent how Hugh’s death could have given Haganon of Autun reasons for disturbances, unless Haganon belonged to the family of Nevers; and Hugh himself seems to have been killed not so much in battle as through treacherous deceit.]

and the Church recovered peace.

O blessed man, whose presence Satan could not endure, and whose command he obeyed against his will! The event is remarkable, but it was heightened by a still greater miracle. For as long as the holy man taught holy things in that assembly, a white dove appeared visibly above his head. Those who were granted to see it glorified God, for not everyone was worthy to behold this glory.

Stephen, archpriest of Parce,

[Note: Parce, commonly called Parigné, lies in Maine beyond the Sarthe, on the border of the duchy of Anjou.]

also testified under oath that he, unworthy though he was, had seen the same thing.

### 8

Father Hugh had come to Paredum to celebrate the feast of John the Baptist devoutly. A certain woman came to him with a crowd pleading on her behalf, because a violent invasion by a poisonous serpent gripped her womb.

The saint, moved by compassion, ordered water to be brought. He marked it beforehand with holy prayers and blessings; then, taking a spoon, he poured three spoonfuls of that water into the woman’s mouth while praying.

When this had been done, a frightening serpent immediately came out through the woman’s mouth, before the eyes of all who were present. Those who had come in sorrow returned with joy, praising the Lord together.

Gaufridus, a faithful man who was present when the saint drove the demons from the crowd at Autun, regularly testified that he had also seen this serpent expelled by him.

9. At another time, for the sake of arranging peace, the aforementioned father was present together with the bishops Roclenus of Chalon [Note: Roclenus presided over the Council of Chalon in the year 1073, according to the old Chronicle of Mâcon preserved by the Sammarthani. From this it is clear that Aicardus, mentioned above, did not long survive the Council of Autun.], and Drogo of Mâcon, in a hunting field. While crowds stood around, a certain man, defiled by a most wicked crime, did not fear to attend. The saint, instructed by the Holy Spirit, looked at him from a distance and said to those present: “Do you see that wretched man? Do you see him full of a demon?” Immediately he pointed him out and ordered him to come to him. When the man had been brought forward, he said: “How did you enter here among us, when you wished to defile yourself with this crime” (and he specified the crime)? “Why, wretched man, have you presented a demon in yourself to us? We seek peace; we do not want a demon.”

The man, confounded, could not deny it. When many who were present saw what had happened, they said to one another in subdued voices: “Let us turn away from this man, who knows how to see the hidden things of men, lest he also be able to discover us in our sins, as he has discovered this man in his.” Finally, when the saint inquired to whose episcopate the man belonged, he learned that the man was from a certain parish of Chalon. Then the saint laid before Bishop Roclenus both the wretched man and his sin; the bishop took him aside and corrected him as his office required. Witnesses are the venerable men who were present, Rotbertus of Séez and Gaufredus, whom I mentioned above. Let your charity judge how great these things are; my smallness will remain silent within.

10. The Saint was at Nanctoacum [Note: In a diploma of Paschal II from the year 1109, col. 569 of the Bibliotheca, Nantoacum is named first among the priories subject to the abbot of Cluny. Or was it among the Ruthenians, where geographers designate the town of Nayac by its common name?] when a messenger arrived saying that Wilencus had died. This Wilencus had been prior of La Charité. While the pious Father was celebrating Mass for the deceased, according to his customary practice he presented himself as a living sacrifice to the Lord; and thus, holding the Son in his hands, he offered him to the Father and received the one offered with his mouth. Having learned this, he went out to the brothers and disclosed to his companions that at La Charité not Wilencus but Orius had died.

Odo was there, the former prior of Cluny, later bishop of Ostia and afterward supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, Urban II [Note: Odo was made bishop of Ostia around the year 1077 and became pope shortly thereafter; he is written Ottho by the Italians.]. He sent a delegation and discovered, in accordance with the word of the man of God, that it was not Wilencus who had died but Orius.

11. Sabina too, a holy virgin in the monastery of Jouarre [Note: Jouarre, commonly called Jotrum, in the diocese of Meaux, was founded by Ado, brother of Saint Ouen, for nuns who were to live under the rule of Saint Columbanus; later it belonged to the Benedictine order.], a woman of singularly trustworthy testimony, saw the Mother of Mercy with a glorious company of the blessed. She also saw a white bench, suitably adorned, placed among that company, and heard that Hugh, abbot of Cluny, was to depart upon it. Sabina reported the vision, and not long afterward a messenger arrived announcing that the saint had departed—the one whom the vision had indicated would leave.

Thus the saint, approved by miracles and foreshown by the mysteries of revelations, died amid the bodily company of his sons; everlasting in holiness, he departed from the world and lives with the Lord. Worthily buried, he lies at Cluny; yet the holiness of his institutions remains, and the discipline of the order that he taught flourishes everywhere, while in the heavenly places the crown of his merits shines forth. This Hugh became a monk in the fifteenth year of his life, was consecrated abbot in his twenty-fifth year, died in his thirty-fifth year, and rested in the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1109 of the Incarnate Word [Note: The year 1108 was indeed recorded in the printed editions; but since it is certain that Saint Hugh died after Saint Anselm, and indeed during Easter week—and since Easter was celebrated on 5 April in the year 1108—it is evident that there is an error here, which we have therefore corrected.].

## CHAPTER III. From the collection of an anonymous author in the aforementioned library

12. That William [Note: William I, called the Conqueror because he seized the kingdom by force of arms, reigned from 1066 to 1087 and was succeeded by his second-born son, surnamed Rufus, whose death was discussed above in the Life.], prince of the English, greatly loved Saint Hugh. Before he had been able to enjoy his conversation, he heard from his absent friend’s envoy—namely, Lord Warmundus, who later rose from the rank of abbot of Dol [Note: The abbey of Dol, or Burgidol, in Berry, at the river Andria, had been founded in the preceding century; it received this Warmundus as abbot around the year 1074.] to the archbishopric of Vienne [Note: The same man became archbishop of Vienne in 1077 and survived until the year 1083]—the absent man’s blessing, and received from him the gift of his companionship. He removed his royal cap and bowed his head with such humility as though he had been invested by an angel with a gift of divine grace.

When his nobles were astonished because they witnessed something remarkable, saw his otherwise inflexible neck bent so low, and thought they ought to inquire why, receiving nothing visible and being granted nothing by a person who bestowed nothing, he had so emptied his royal majesty, he replied:

“Do not be surprised that I have bowed so devoutly and so humbly, for the reason for so great a blessing [Col. 0923C] and investiture specifically required me to do what I judged ought to be done. Do not think that I have ever received so great a gift, nor that on the day when I obtained the crown of this kingdom I acquired anything so great; for an end will come to all that I possess and must leave, just as there was a beginning when I acquired it. But the glory of heaven, of which I have in some manner received the pledge when I joined myself to the holy Cluniac community, can have no end.”

Thus the prudent William, philosophizing from the treasure of his heart, restrained the astonishment of his men with still greater wonder and directed the eyes of worldly minds toward this, so that they might recognize how highly the saintly Hugh ought to be esteemed who, though absent, had been held in such esteem by so great a man.

That king was considering what weight, benefit, and profit for his soul might come through his envoy, if, by the gracious inclination of the revered head, he could deserve communion with so great a body. Then the king sent to the lord abbot and the holy community an almost wholly golden cope, in which scarcely anything appeared except gold, or electrum, or woven pearl-work and rows of gems; beneath it, bells resounded all around [Note: Bells of this sort may still be seen on the older copes of the church of Aachen, preserved to this day because of their antiquity and for display.], and the golden bells themselves hung down. The queen, however, sent a chasuble, entirely worthy of such senders and recipients, so stiff that it could not be folded.

13. The same William, king of the English, a magnificent man, vigorous in arms, and immensely powerful in wealth and strength, had begun to possess the aforementioned region and had won its royal crown by war. Wishing to organize the bishoprics and abbeys of that land properly, he sent a letter to the illustrious abbot Saint Hugh and begged him to send him six persons from our brothers, by whose counsel he could carry out whatever needed to be done concerning the organization of the churches; once rectors had been appointed, he would be secure concerning the protection and governance of the sheep.

He also added that he would give Cluny one hundred pounds of silver annually for each man, under the title of friendship and favor, lest it perhaps be burdensome for the holy place to be deprived of its own persons and to lose the fruit of their service.

But he who wished to become a buyer could not do so, because he found no seller among the monks. The philosopher of Christ, who judged that nothing was comparable to the souls of his brothers, replied:

“Your request, lord king, proceeds from a good intention, since you wish to organize for salvation the people whom God has entrusted to you. Yet just as what you ask is worthy of your majesty, so what you command is incompatible with our salvation: that I should sell the souls whom I have received at the peril of my own soul and head, out of desire for earthly commerce, and send them into perdition—whether general or particular, that is, to a place where all or some of them might perish and I might have to render an account of them to God. With him gold is worth nothing, silver profits nothing, and no argument of empty excuse has value.

“How, then, could I do for any reward what, even if I did it for the whole world, would be too little for me, when I would perish for one of them who was lost? For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself? (Matthew 16:26.)

“Therefore, most beloved lord, do not ask this of me, since I cannot do it without my own destruction. I do not wish to sell my soul for any price; indeed, I would make it saleable if I sent one of the brothers entrusted to me to a place where I would lose him. I would more gladly give money to obtain monks whom I greatly need for the various places I am to organize than receive money for selling them.

“For what would our chapter fear in those regions where they saw none of our monasteries, at whose harbor they might be able to land or be compelled to take refuge? Command something else, then, and patiently bear this refusal, if what you have asked cannot be done together with the salvation of your friend. Farewell.”

The pious Father sent this reply to that eminent king. At first the king was violently indignant because he had been rejected in his request despite so great a gift. But after his anger subsided, he returned to his senses and recognized that this man of God truly ought to be preferred to all others: no desire for temporal things ruled him, and he considered the salvation of souls incomparable with all gold. For that reason he judged him incomparable with any person possessing any authority, since no greed could bend or alter him from the straight path.

He therefore turned from indignation to admiration, valuing his own rejection more highly than he would have valued acceptance had his request been granted. He restrained the anger that had rushed upon him and yielded to the reason that he considered after the disturbance of his mind had passed.

14. At a certain time [Note: Baronius assigns this to the year 1062 and admits that he does not know the cause of the controversy that arose against the Cluniacs. He conjectures that Count Geoffrey of Anjou was the author of the disturbances, citing the Life of Saint Hugh. But he had nothing whatever to do with the Cluniacs; he was seeking the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours. The whole affair is explained in the Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, col. 309, which recounts the controversy between Drogo of Mâcon and Hugh of Cluny before Peter Damian. The outcome was that Drogo, who had presumed to excommunicate the Cluniacs, was forced to clear himself of ignorance of the apostolic privileges in the year 1063, before the Council of Chalon convened for that purpose.] it became necessary for the holy man, in order to defend his sons, to have recourse to the mother Church and invoke the protection of the Roman see. Therefore, seeking refuge in that city, he obtained—with great labor and difficulty—the lord Peter, bishop of Ostia, surnamed Damian, whom he drew away from the pope’s side so that he might be given to him as a champion for the great Peter and overthrow his adversaries by his remarkable prudence and eloquence [Note: Much could be said here about this legation of Saint Peter, if it had not been treated earlier in his Life, 23 February, §5.].

For that man, through his singular practice of abstinence and the bonds of iron with which he was everywhere worn down, was so weakened that it was scarcely possible to find a way to support the feebleness of his body sufficiently for him to endure the heavy burden of riding [Note: How highly he later regarded the excellence of the Cluniac discipline may be testified by his letters, written after his return to Italy to the community itself and to its abbot Hugh; these are therefore also displayed in the collected library.].

And because he could often be offended by even a slight scandal, he frequently needed to be appeased by some satisfaction. Venerable Hugh inclined himself to this task in such a way as to restore Peter’s mind to tranquility, as though he were another Martin, who considered nothing unworthy if humility advised that it be done.

When that other Gregory had come to Cluny—another Gregory in the abundance of his eloquence, though not in equality of apostolic life—and had seen the hospitality and discipline, and had compared the rod and the staff, he began to hesitate and wonder how men who possessed such abundant goods could be saints or have holy founders, and again how they could fail to be saints or perish when they so devoutly endured so heavy a burden of labor and the observance of monastic discipline.

15. At one time he judged the quantity of their food excessive; at another he wondered that those who fasted lacked the grace that he saw them possess. Nevertheless, as he himself said, if it could be arranged that both virtues—obedience and abstinence—were joined together in them, then certainly nothing would be lacking from apostolic perfection.

For this reason, when he met with the lord abbot, he begged him to abstain from fat for at least two days a week, since in all other respects they were so perfect that they owed nothing to anchorites.

The venerable Hugh, an outstanding guardian of discretion, replied:

“If, dearest Father, you wish to increase the crown of our reward by adding fasting, first try with us the burden of labor for a period of eight days; afterward you will judge what ought to be added. For as long as you have not tasted the stew, you cannot know what seasoning of salt it requires; and if you have not applied at least your little finger, you will by no means be able to judge the burden borne by your brother with discretion and propriety.”

When Peter heard this, he perceived that the weight of such burdens was unbearable to his own strength. He abandoned his request to make the burden heavier and began to strike himself with the very thing by which he had wished to strike others, since he could not direct the arrow against them without wounding himself. He understood that this was a great obligation and that what he himself could not undertake ought to suffice for one who appeared to stand at so great a height of virtues.

Thus the learned prelate returned much more learned than he had come, carrying away with him a great treasure: the avoidance of empty glory and the pursuit of true humility.

16. Venerable Hugh, abbot of this holy Cluniac monastery, diligently devoted the full energy of his mind not only to advancing monastic religion but also, by God’s grace, to improving the divine offices. With the common counsel of the brothers, he decreed that on the holy day of Pentecost the hymn *Veni, Creator Spiritus*—“Come, Creator Spirit”—should be sung at the third hour [Note: The Roman Church later adopted this rite, and it continues among all who use the Roman breviary]. It had not previously been sung, so that we might deserve to be pierced by compunction, inflamed by love, and enlightened by grace through the visitation of that same Paraclete—that is, the Comforter.

And so that the good work of almsgiving might support this most health-giving prayer, he established that on that day an abundant meal should be provided for the poor by the master of the church, the custodian, consisting of bread, wine, and meat, according to this rule: however many brothers there were at the feast, that many poor people should also be fed. If he could not determine the number of brothers himself, he was to learn their number from the refectory servant or from the keeper of the sick.

And so that he might receive from the Lord the reward of so good a work, it was decreed that on that day, at the principal Mass, after the first collect of the familiar Mass, the priest should say silently on his behalf, “Almighty and eternal God.”

Therefore, peace, salvation, and grace from God the Father, and from Jesus Christ his Son, and from the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, be upon those who strengthen and observe this command. But upon those who despise or violate it, unless they quickly repent, may come the anger of that same almighty and eternal Judge, and eternal condemnation in unquenchable fire.

The same Father also decreed, with the consent of the brothers, that a general office should be held each year on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost for all who rest in the cemetery of this place. As is done on the feast of All Saints, all the bells were to be rung at the appointed evening for Vespers, after supper for the office, and on the following day for Mass. At that Mass the tract *De profundis*—“Out of the depths”—was to be sung by two cantors; all priests who sang Mass that day were to sing *Deus, cujus miseratione*—“O God, by whose compassion”—especially for them; the others were to sing seven psalms; twelve poor people were to be fed; and whatever remained from the meal that day was to be distributed as alms.

It was also decreed that the same observance should be carried out throughout all the places subject to this one, for the dead in each place’s cemetery—namely, that it should be performed in the monasteries where there was a community of brothers no less fully. But in cells where no more than five or three men lived, if they could not feed that many poor people, at least as many poor people as there were brothers were to be fed.

## (Year 1078) LETTERS OF SAINT HUGH

### FIRST LETTER. TO WILLIAM I, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He replies to the king, who begged him to send him six monks, at an annual payment of one hundred pounds of silver for each, rejecting the request entirely as commercial and virtually simoniacal.

*[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 453.]

Your request, lord king, proceeds from a good intention, since you wish to organize for salvation the people whom God has entrusted to you. Yet just as what you ask is worthy of your majesty, so what you command is incompatible with our salvation: that I should sell the souls whom I have received at the peril of my own soul and head, out of desire for earthly commerce, and send them into perdition—whether general or particular, that is, to a place where all or some of them might perish and I might have to render an account of them to God. With him gold is worth nothing, silver profits nothing, and no argument of empty excuse has value.

How, then, could I do for any reward what, even if I did it for the whole world, would be too little for me, when I would perish for one of them who was lost? For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?

Therefore, most beloved lord, do not ask this of me, since I cannot do it without my own destruction. I do not wish to sell my soul for any price; indeed, I would make it saleable if I sent one of the brothers entrusted to me to a place where I would lose him. I would more gladly give money to obtain monks whom I greatly need for the various places I am to organize than receive money for selling them.

For what would our chapter fear in those regions where they saw none of our monasteries, at whose harbor they might be able to land or be compelled to take refuge? Command something else, then, and patiently bear this refusal, if what you have asked cannot be done together with the salvation of your friend. Farewell.

### (Year 1078) SECOND LETTER. TO THE BROTHERS OF MOISSAC

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals* V, 130.]

To the sweetest and most beloved brothers and sons living at Moissac under the protection of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to Brother Hunaldo, the abbot: salvation of souls and bodies, and eternal blessing.

Know, dearest sons, how we have always loved you, and with what special affection we have held and honored that place above all the places of our community. We have always granted, and continue to grant, this privilege to you and to your place: that you should be special in the love, honor, and remembrance of our community.

Therefore, sons, we ask you, remembering us, to love, fear, and honor the Lord above all things, and to give him thanks for his benefits. Although many anxieties may have come upon you, his mercy has nevertheless not failed you, granting increase in good things and consolation in your needs.

For this reason, dearest ones, keep him before your eyes in all things and above all things. Do not cease to serve our highest lords, the holy apostles. Guard your order, your sacred religious life, and your holy obedience with the greatest diligence. Consider how worthless everything is that you see in the world. Reflect with how much sweat one must labor to escape that terrible judgment and reach joy that will never end.

The lord abbot whom we appointed over you, a man of good intention and religious character, very dear to us and to our brothers, speaks highly enough of you. Therefore we rejoice, and we wish and admonish you to love him more and more, honor him, and obey him devoutly, as is fitting for so glorious a man.

For the rest, we commend you to almighty God, who may bless, help, and protect you, absolve you from all sins, grant you perseverance in holy religion, and, after this life, through the prayers and merits of the chief apostles whom you serve, lead you to eternal life. Amen.

And because we cannot see you with bodily eyes, let us see one another spiritually. Pray for us and for our brothers.

### THIRD LETTER. TO ANASTASIUS THE HERMIT

He urges him to return to the monastery. (Year 1086.)

*[Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines* IX, p. 491.]

To his dearest son Anastasius, Brother Hugh, a sinner: salvation and a blessed resurrection, and the glorious fellowship of the elect.

I wonder, dearest son, that I have heard nothing about you for so long and have received no knowledge of your life. Therefore I instruct your affection that, if it seems good to you, you should come down to visit the brothers, so that, as I have said, your desirable presence may strengthen and encourage them [Note: Several words are missing here, since they could not be read.].

### (Year 1097) FOURTH LETTER. TO POPE URBAN II

Against Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi.

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IV, p. 999.]

To our most beloved and reverend Father, the supreme pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, the lord Pope Urban: Brother Hugh of Cluny, together with your entire community, sends continuous and most devout prayers of devotion and perpetual peace.

Many people, lord Father, for just and necessary reasons, desire to approach your worthy presence, but they are prevented by various difficulties that stand in their way. Hence some of them come at least to us, as to your household, in the hope that their needs may somehow be advised or assisted.

Among these was Lord Manasses, bishop of Reims, your humble son and also our devoted friend, whom we commended to you in another letter. He complained to us about the Major Monastery, saying that in the church of Blessed Remigius he had appointed a certain monk and that, contrary to what he had hoped, his irreligious conduct had caused the place the greatest harm.

He asked us to intercede with you on this matter. But since, as we have heard, Lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, has informed you of the whole course of events, we respectfully suggest that, if that same monk comes to you, he should not deceive your prudence by any tricks; rather, deal with him according to the wisdom that you have from God.

May the Lord Christ preserve for us and for the universal Church your most reverend and beloved fatherhood, safe and unharmed.

### LETTERS V–VII. TO SAINT ANSELM

They are found among the letters of Saint Anselm, letters 17, 79, and 80 of Book IV of this volume, cols. 210 and 241.

## LETTERS OF VARIOUS PEOPLE TO SAINT HUGH

### I. SAINT PETER DAMIAN

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIV.

### II. SAINT GREGORY THE POPE

See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVIII: *Register*, Book I, letters 14 and 62; Book II, letter 49; Book V, letter 21; Book VII, letters 17 and 33; Book VIII, letter 2.

### III. POPE URBAN II

See *Patrologia*, vol. CLI.

### IV. GEOFFREY, ABBOT OF VENDÔME

See vol. CLVII.

### V. POPE PASCHAL II

See below, under the year 1118.

### VI. HENRY THE EMPEROR, SURNAMED “THE BLACK”

He thanks Hugh for the restoration of his health through Hugh’s prayers. He asks the abbot to receive his son from the sacred font.

*[Spicilegium*, as above, p. 396.]

Henry, by the grace of God Roman emperor and Augustus, to Hugh, venerable abbot of Cluny: grace and salvation.

When we saw the letters of your holiness, we were exceedingly glad. We received yours all the more willingly because we know that you cling to divine contemplation with increasingly fervent devotion. Since you said in them that you had rejoiced greatly over the health restored to us and over the adoption of a son granted from heaven, we offer thanks to your fatherhood and render thanks from the depths of our heart.

We also ask—not so much command as humbly entreat—that your prayer before our most merciful Lord may never cease: for the welfare of the commonwealth, for the honor of the whole kingdom, and for the salvation of ourselves and our people. May the prosperity divinely granted to us become peace and tranquility for the churches and for the whole people.

For what wise person would not desire your prayer and those of your brothers? Who would not hesitate to hold them by an unbreakable bond of charity? Their prayer is purer insofar as it is farther removed from worldly actions, and more worthy insofar as it stands nearer to the divine presence.

As for your statement that, because of the length of the journey, you could not come as we ordered, although we would have received your arrival with gratitude, we forgive you on this condition: that you come to us at Cologne at Easter, if it is possible, so that—you will permit us to say it—you may receive from the sacred font that same boy over whom you rejoiced so greatly and, as his spiritual father, mark him with the gift of your blessing, and thus, cleansed together by the leaven of our sins, deserve to enjoy the Easter solemnity with the unleavened bread of heavenly glory.

### VII. EMPRESS AGNES, WIFE OF HENRY THE BLACK

She asks him to offer prayers to God for the deceased emperor.

*[Spicilegium*, same place, p. 397.]

To our dearest Father and wholly worthy Hugh, abbot … and she who now, by God’s command, is [lacuna]: greeting and devoted service.

Because my lyre has been turned into mourning, I return groaning for joy and lamentable wailing for the exultation that your letters had produced. Yet my heart, wasting away with grief, recoils from recounting everything.

Therefore, since I believe that the swift report of evils has announced my sorrow to you, I beg you to commend to God in prayer, together with your community, my lord, whom you did not wish to preserve longer in the flesh. Obtain also that your son may long be his heir and worthy of God, and strive by your counsel to quiet any disturbances that may arise against him in the neighboring regions of his kingdom. Farewell, Father.

### VIII. HENRY IV, EMPEROR, SON OF THE FOREGOING

He asks the abbot to visit him so that he may be able to make peace with the supreme pontiff.

*[Spicilegium*, as above, p. 397.]

Henry, by the grace of God Roman emperor and Augustus, to Hugh, reverend abbot: what a son owes to a father.

It has been a long time, lord Father, since you visited your sick man as you used to do, and since you cared for your broken man with the encouragement and consolations of your exhortations. Nevertheless, we do not consider this a reproach to your piety; rather, we attribute everything to our iniquities, because perhaps the Spirit of the Lord prevented your holiness from having to weary himself on account of an unfruitful tree.

Yet there is a season for everything under heaven. Just as there is a time for the Lord’s anger, so there is also a time for his mercy. We can often observe this alternation in the Israelite people: when they sinned, they were punished by the Lord; when they repented, they were judged worthy of forgiveness. This plainly occurred when the walls of Jerusalem were destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, the Lord’s temple demolished, and the people led into captivity—when the daughter of Zion sat for seventy years without a king, without a priest, and without sacrifice.

But again, when the heavens distilled God’s mercy, under Cyrus, king of the Persians, the captivity was released, the people returned, Jerusalem was rebuilt, the temple restored, and the rites of the ceremonies were completely reestablished.

Therefore, if, as the Apostle says, all these things happened to them as figures, why should we, who have long endured the Lord’s anger in the destruction of ecclesiastical religion, not hope for a similar mercy in its restoration?

Encouraged by this example, we make known to your serenity that, for the restoration of the churches which in our time and through our sins have, alas, fallen, we wish to labor in every way, as God grants us strength, and from now on to heed the sound counsels of all good men. If in any way we can gather together what has been scattered, join by the bond of unity what has been split apart by the wedge of schism, and compensate through the restoration of peace and justice for the ruin of the Church that has occurred through us, we shall do so.

Furthermore, we inform you that, if God in his favor permits us to reunite the kingdom and the priesthood into one, after peace has been confirmed we intend to go to Jerusalem and see the holy land in which our Lord was seen in the flesh and lived among human beings. With his favor, we greatly desire to worship him there more explicitly, where we know that for our sake he endured slaps, spitting, scourging, the cross, death, and burial. We make all this known to your holiness so that you may pray for us more earnestly and commend us more attentively to God, together with the holy college of your brothers, so that he who in his mercy has anticipated us with good will may deign to direct our work toward a fruitful outcome. [Col. 0933D]

## IX. OF HENRY, THE EMPEROR, SON OF THE AFOREMENTIONED. He complains that his son has risen against him.

Henry, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, Augustus, to the most beloved and dearest Father Hugh, and to all the holy brothers of the monastery of Cluny: the affection of a devoted son and the obedient service of a brother—or rather, of a servant.

[Col. 0934A]

Because we have always kindly experienced your piety and fatherly concern for us, so much so that we believe ourselves to have been freed from many dangers through your holy prayers, therefore, dearest Father, after God we have recourse to you as to the singular refuge of our necessity, and humbly beg that we may at least find with you consolation for our miseries. Would that it might be granted us to see your angelic face bodily, so that, having poured ourselves at your knees, we might familiarly rest in the bosom of your holiness the head that you received from the saving font, and there, while weeping over our sins, recount in order the multitude of our tribulations!

But because not only the great distances of land lying between us [Col. 0934B] but also the astonishing hatred of our raging enemies deprive us of such consolation, we beseech your fatherhood with every devotion not to disdain to receive the letters of our humility—which, with God as witness, contain no falsehood or pretence—and to understand them attentively and mercifully: the unheard-of monstrosity of our betrayal. Indeed, to make it all the more astonishing, it was not so much a domestic or hostile hand—for if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I might perhaps have hidden myself from him—as the hand of the son of our own womb, uniquely beloved by us, that impiously, inhumanely, and unworthily acted against us. Thus, not without grief and immense astonishment, we can cry out to God in the words of the royal Psalmist, resembling in this respect the face of a fleeing son: “Lord, how they have multiplied who trouble me!”

[Col. 0934C]

For we believe that you know—and we do not doubt that you have heard—how, with what affection and intimate love of heart, against the will of many, we raised this same son of ours to the throne of the kingdom. At his very election he swore to us at Mainz that he would preserve our life and personal safety, and that while I was alive he would in no way meddle with the kingdom, with all our honor, or with anything that we possessed or might possess, against our will and command. He likewise swore this to us upon the cross and the Lord’s lance, before all the princes, after he had been enthroned at Aachen.

Yet, setting all these things aside and consigning them to oblivion, by the counsel of traitors, perjurers, mortal men, and our enemies, he separated himself from us in such a way that, desiring by every means to persecute us both in property and in person, from that hour onward he constantly sought to deprive us of kingdom and life. He began to besiege our strongholds and seize as many of our estates as he could; he bound to himself by oath both members of our household and others, against us. Alas! While we awaited from day to day that, touched by inward grief, he might be humbled and come to his senses, he became ever more inflamed by the fury of treachery, making nothing of the fear of God and fatherly reverence. He did not hesitate to pursue us from city to city and to invade everything belonging to us as far as he could.

[Col. 0934D]

Thus we came to Cologne. When he had arranged a meeting at Mainz for the following Nativity of the Lord, we began, after gathering our faithful men, to go there. Hearing this, he came to meet us at a place called Confluentia. Since he could accomplish nothing against us by force there, he began to work by cunning, deceit, and every device. For he sent his messengers to us so that we might speak with him; after taking counsel with our faithful men, we agreed.

When we had met there, he immediately fell at his feet, and we began to beg him most earnestly, for God alone and for the sake of his soul, that he should now cease his inhuman persecution of his father. He, on the contrary, under the appearance and veil of peace and agreement, fell at our feet, weeping, and begged and implored us to entrust ourselves to his faith and his soul, since he was our … and our flesh, and not to hesitate to go with him to the aforesaid meeting … Mainz, where he himself would lead us [Col. 0935B] with every assurance of safety, and would carefully discuss our honor with the princes, as many of them as he could make faithful to us; thereafter, once the business had been completed or left unfinished, he would return us most securely to whatever place we wished. [Note: [Col. 0935D] Here the parchment is worn away.]

After hearing and understanding all this, with our men commending the plan, we entrusted ourselves to his faith and said: “We entrust ourselves to your soul, under the faith by which God willed that a son should love his father.” Then, giving his right hand, he assured us of our safety and honor under that same pledge. Trusting in this, and without any doubt, we sent our men back to the aforesaid meeting, also instructing our other faithful men to meet us there, and so we set out with him.

When we were halfway there, we were privately informed [Col. 0935C] that we were being betrayed. When he learned that this had been reported to us, he began to swear and protest that it was in no way true, again taking us under the aforesaid pledge. Then, on the following day, toward evening, we reached a place called Bingen. At daybreak he surrounded us with the clamor of weapons and every kind of terror, saying that he did not wish to take us to Mainz but to a certain castle.

When we fell at his feet and at those of the others, asking them to take us to Mainz in accordance with the pledge given, or to release us so that we might depart freely and return at whatever time he might determine, with every assurance of safety, we were told that we were permitted to do nothing other than go to the aforesaid castle. What more is there to say? [Col. 0935D] Against our every wish they took us away as prisoners. There, shut up under the strictest guard, we were handed over to our mortal enemies, all our men being excluded except three laymen. Not even a priest was left to us, although we despaired of our life, from whom we might receive the body and blood of the Lord as viaticum, or to whom we might confess our sins.

There too we were afflicted with hunger and thirst and every kind of insult and terror, right up to the very point of death, so that it was absolutely certain to us that we could not live any longer, insofar as it depended on him, unless we satisfied his will. Meanwhile, we were informed [Col. 0936A] that there was no prospect of our liberation unless we immediately surrendered the cross, the lance, and the other royal insignia. When we understood beyond doubt that we could not be freed in any other way, we ordered those who were in the castle where the royal insignia were kept to save our life at least by this means. Understanding the danger to our life, they handed over the aforesaid cross and lance, together with the other insignia, although unwillingly.

After these things had been carried out inhumanely, with God and every right and justice set aside, they led us from the dreadful prison to a place called Ingelheim, near Mainz. Our son came there with our mortal enemies and a great multitude of their men, having left almost all our faithful men at Mainz, in the hope that he would lead us there to them. Having deceived all those men in this hope, we were brought forth again at the aforesaid place for the cruelest interrogations and unjust demands, in the presence of the pope’s messenger. There our enemies brought many improper charges against us, not so much from zeal for rectitude as from a desire for our condemnation—everything, that is, which could be contrary to our safety and honor.

But when we asked that we be permitted to answer and to give a proper account of everything alleged, they peremptorily refused, something even barbarians would not do to a slave. When we saw that violence and prejudice were being inflicted upon us, we then fell at their feet and began humbly to implore them, both for God’s sake and for the sake of their own honor, to defer such interrogations and accusations [Col. 0936C] until the apostolic see, granting us in the meantime the dignity of personal freedom until we reached that see, where, in the presence of the Roman clergy and people, with hatred, envy, and the other things contrary to justice removed, we might either adequately clear ourselves of the charges or humbly offer satisfaction.

But when this too was inhumanely denied us, and thereafter we … [Note: [Col. 0936D] Here too the parchment is worn away.] … whether there was any hope of life or safety, or what … possibility of liberation there might finally be, we were then told that we could be freed from such grievous captivity only if we were willing to carry out what was being proposed to us, even though it was contrary to our right and honor: namely, that we should surrender the imperial crown according to their will. What more is there to say? After they had extorted everything from us according to their will and command, they departed for Mainz and left us in the same place without honor. Then, behold, we were informed that, unless we wished to undergo perpetual captivity, we must depart as quickly as possible. Therefore, cursing that place, we boarded a ship, hastened to Cologne, and thus, by the free mercy of the divine majesty, were scarcely liberated from the cruel hands of our enemies.

But now it is time to bring an end to the tragedy of our long miseries. For this reason we have taken care to lament them before your piety, most loving Father, because in God and in you we have great and singular hope of counsel and assistance, of our safety and liberation. Therefore, what we have delayed doing until now, we now entrust with our whole affection and desire of heart entirely to your faith. Whatever you decide must be done concerning our reconciliation with the apostolic see, and whatever must be done concerning the peace and unity of the holy Roman Church, without prejudice to our honor, we promise before God, without doubt, to do in its entirety everywhere.

Hasten, therefore, dearest Father, to advise us. Do not, we beg you, regret laboring for the salvation of your hired servant, if not for the liberation of your son, because we have sinned against heaven and before you. Moreover, we complain to your piety that our son states everywhere in his letters that we freely surrendered all the royal insignia; let your holiness know that this is entirely untrue. [Col. 0937B]

## X. OF THE SAME. He asks Hugh to be willing to act as arbiter between him and the pope.

[Spicilegium, vol. II, p. 395.]

Henry, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans Augustus, to Hugh, venerable abbot of Cluny: whatever a sinner may offer, yet as a spiritual son, most devotedly and humbly, to his long-desired and beloved Father.

Although, through your familiar monks and brothers, we had resolved to inform and report to you in our own letters the entire sequence of our tribulation and of our unheard-of and horrible betrayal, just as it occurred, [Col. 0937C] nevertheless we did not wish to omit asking through these messengers, with the most ardent devotion, the holiness of your fatherhood—as a publican asks refuge from his sins and a shipwrecked man the harbor of salvation.

We therefore ask, venerable Father, that your holiness’s celebrated goodness, once you have heard and understood the detestable misery of our monstrous betrayal, may be so inflamed by the love of God that is in you, for God alone, to defend our abominable injury, that it may plainly appear that your fatherly holiness is moved solely by divine regard to care for our unheard-of tribulations.

For, before the Roman legate, concerning the case between the pope and us, we wished, with the counsel of religious men, to conduct our entire defense. But because they had determined utterly to destroy us in this life, they were unwilling to receive us in any way.
