Nevertheless, however we may have been treated, we place ourselves under the counsel of you, our Father, and of the other religious men whom you wish to have involved in this matter, so that, without prejudice to our honor, I shall do everything that you decide with regard to the pope.

For the rest, venerable Father, I commend myself to your prayers. We ask that through you we may be presented to your holy congregation and most devoutly commended to their prayers. [Col. 0937D]

[Col. 0938A]

## XI. OF ALPHONSO, KING OF THE HISPANIAS. Having given thanks for Robert, sent to him, he asks that the abbot care for his soul and be willing to receive the annual payment already granted to him by his father.

[Spicilegium, vol. VI, p. 445.]

To Hugh, venerable and most excellent abbot of the Cluniacensians, illustrious with the flowers of virtue, supported by divine grace, and an elder flowing with every sweetness, whom the dignity of his rank glorifies, and to the entire most noble congregation of the apostles Peter and Paul: Alphonso, by the grace of God king of the Hispanias, with all devotion of mind and body, pours out his offering, the guardianship of true charity, the joys of eternal life, perpetual prosperity and health, and whatever is more exalted, from the depth of his heart, with embracing love, in the Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0938B]

How devotedly I love you, most glorious Father, you yourself, as I believe, know better than any teacher could write upon parchment. Robert, whom I regard as superior and dearer than all monks, and your most faithful brother from the depth of his heart, knows how your love has become for me like a fire burning in my heart all day and night. Therefore, even if you had given me everything that you could possess in the world, I think it would be nothing in comparison with that good which, for my sake, led you to send to our regions a portion of your flock, which you have nurtured with spiritual care.

Therefore, with the grace of the Lord enlightening you, [Col. 0938C] I, the servant of the servants of God, entirely subject to your piety, increasingly beg your fatherhood to persevere in the good that you have begun. May you deign to send some members of your most holy religious community, so that they may fill with your sweetness that place of ours and yours, which you began to water with your most holy fountain, while I am being moved about in this fragile existence.

Know also, most holy Father, that the payment [Note: [Col. 0937D] This payment is discussed in the Life of Saint Hugh above.] which my father was accustomed to give to that most holy place of Cluny, I, with God’s approval, shall double during the days of my life. I have drawn up the text of a testament before witnesses, so that whoever after my death receives the rule over what I now possess may pay this payment, which I grant to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to you, and to your most holy congregation, to that most holy place as due. If he should refuse, may he, by the power of God and through the prayers of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, be deprived of that kingdom.

For this reason, distinguished Father, I beg your brotherly affection to ensure that the payment I have added for you is sold for grain, and that what is acquired from it may enable that most holy congregation to sustain its life. Whoever sends this payment elsewhere—which our friend Lord Robert, familiar to you in mind and body, urged me day and night to add—unless he sends it as stated above and as he himself will tell you with his own mouth, may suffer punishments in hell with Judas the betrayer and lack the lamps of his forehead. [Col. 0939A]

Therefore, distinguished Father, I humbly seek your clemency, asking you to favor this petition with a kindly embrace. At present I greatly desire to ask this of you, and I would very much wish, if it pleased you, that Lord Robert be entirely present in our regions. I regard him as supreme and dearest in all matters, and for that reason I would wish him to be with me in life and in death, since I am supported by his … [Note: [Col. 0939D] A word is missing.] and refreshed by his sweetest words. For you know for certain that every counsel given concerning me is for your benefit; therefore I ask you to care for me and not, for any reason of impediment, allow him not to dwell entirely in our regions.

As for the Roman office that we received at your command, know that our land is exceedingly desolate. I therefore beg your fatherhood to arrange for the lord pope to send us his cardinal, namely Lord Gerald, so that he may amend what needs amending and correct what needs correcting. Farewell. [Col. 0939B]

## XII. OF CLEMENTIA, COUNTESS OF FLANDERS. She invites him to reform the monastery of Saint Bertin, which she promises to subject entirely to Cluny.

(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 309.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. To Lord Hugh, abbot of the holy Church of Cluny, Clementia, countess of the Flemings: a blessed portion with the sheep of the right hand. [Col. 0939C]

Because I place very great confidence in the depths of your piety, reverend Father, I now turn confidently to your mercy, sometimes in writing and sometimes through messengers, concerning the religious life to be established through you in our regions. For I do not think that any work could be more pleasing to our Creator than for us here to labor so that this place, which until now has plainly been a church of evildoers, may, through a change brought about by heavenly regard, become a glorious dwelling of those who serve God and live together regularly and piously.

And because your holy prudence wrote to me that, according to the saying of someone mentioned above, I should attend more to the outcome of affairs than to their beginning, and because you feared the disagreements of the nobles [Col. 0939D] and of the brothers of that place, I answer boldly first of all that in this purpose of mine I shall remain altogether firm—indeed, most steadfast—with God as witness. Neither the disagreement of the nobles, which there will be none, since the matter is especially dear to everyone’s heart, nor the disputes or objections of the brothers, which we shall reduce to nothing by every means, will ever cause me, as long as I live, to turn away from so holy a work and so pious an intention.

Therefore I, Clementia, by the grace of God countess of Flanders, with the same authority and stability as my lord, while he was still in his own land, ordering and disposing of whatever belongs to my jurisdiction, with the counsel of my bishops—namely John of Thérouanne and Lambert of Arras [Col. 0940A]—and also at the urging of certain princes whom I summoned to deliberate with me on this matter with especially eager counsel, in accordance with the request of the abbot himself and the will divinely inspired in me, willingly grant to God, to Saint Peter, to you, and to your successors, with the concession of the diocesan bishop, the monastery of Blessed Bertin and everything belonging to it, both externally and internally, as well as everything that has hitherto belonged to us and to our predecessors from that monastery. By the gift of this present document we donate it in perpetual right, for the redemption of my soul and those of my successors, and also for the salvation of my lord Count Robert.

If divine mercy should restore him, and according to the tenor of the lord pope’s letters, we shall certainly subject that place completely to you, with his will and consent in this matter, so that you shall also have the free power to remove an abbot appointed there by you and substitute another if he does not live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the sacred institutions of your Cluniac Church. In particular, no one from elsewhere shall thereafter be permitted to preside there, except one from Cluny. [Col. 0940B]

All these grants have been made and firmly approved under the testimony of the bishops mentioned above—John of Thérouanne and Lambert of Arras—and of my nobles, namely Robert of Bethune, advocate of that abbey, Baldwin, castellan of the same town, and Baldric, a man of great integrity.

It therefore belongs to your prudence and holiness to order that place from among the religious persons and honorable men with whom you abound, for the love of God, in such a way that the wickedness which has long since taken root there may be completely uprooted, and that in the life and moral integrity of those dwelling there the name of the Lord may everywhere be glorified by all. Amen. [Col. 0940C]

## XIII. OF ROGER, COUNT OF FOIX. He grants Hugh the place of Saint Saturninus of Fredelac to be formed according to monastic institutions.

(Martène, *ibid.*, col. 311.)

To Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny: Roger, count of Foix, and his wife Amica, altogether servants of their Savior to the extent of their ability, send greeting and aid. [Col. 0940D]

It is known to us, Father and master and shepherd of souls, as the human race dies everywhere each day before our eyes, that we cannot always live bodily. Therefore, after taking counsel together for the remedy and salvation of our souls and for the remission of the sins we have committed, we have now resolved to give you a portion of the inheritance which we appear at present to possess, so that we may deserve an everlasting reward with the Lord and, after the end of our bodies, may live happily in heavenly rest.

We believe that through the merits and prayers of your order we shall acquire this reward, and more abundantly than we ask, through the overflowing mercy of Christ which, from above, we trust will piously descend upon us. In you we confidently place our trust together with the aforesaid donation.

For example, to the Lord God our Creator and Redeemer Jesus Christ, to his mother, the holy Virgin Mary, and to the holy apostles and patrons of the Cluniac monastery, Peter and Paul, and also to you, Hugh, living in holiness, the most renowned abbot of Cluny throughout the world, I, Roger, and my wife, for the acquisition of eternal life, grant, with everything belonging to it, and with the assent and voluntary consent of the count of Toulouse, the place of Saint Antoninus, commonly called Fredeleiz, so that there, by your appointment, the regular monastic order may be implanted, for the advancement and progress of us all and of all faithful souls. [Col. 0941A]

[Col. 0941B]

## XIV. OF WIGO, COUNT. He writes that the honor of Visilia has been granted to him and asks indulgence for his adversaries.

(Martène, *ibid.*)

To his most beloved lord and master Hugh, most holy abbot of Cluny, and to the most holy convent of my lords, the Cluniac brothers: I, Wigo, called a count, offer faithful service. [Col. 0941C]

I wish your holiness to know that the honor of Visilia, which had long ago been given to you by my predecessors, has now been fully granted to you by me, with the counsel of my nobles and of the wiser canons of Grenoble—namely, with the assent of Rostagnus and Wigo, who labored greatly on your behalf in this matter and endured many adversities from your adversaries—as well as with that of others, namely Ado, Acard, [Col. 0941C] and Adalbert, who steadfastly approved this gift. In the presence also of your brothers, it has been more fully given to you by the lady. Indeed, your adversaries, who had fraudulently seized the aforesaid honor for themselves, have been expelled from it, and your monks have been placed there.

For this reason I earnestly beseech your piety to absolve my father from his offense against you, and, as you know is necessary for him, to hold his memory dear and to have it remembered in your monasteries, just as you perceive that the memory of your monks should be held there.

For me, I earnestly ask you to pray to the Lord, so that I may deserve to please him in the honor of high rank entrusted to me. As for the two knightly brothers, Arnaldus and Wigo, under whose authority the aforesaid honor is held, who once seemed to resist you in this matter but now offer it more fully and promise to offer it to your monks who will dwell there, I ask no less that you forgive them their fault and remember their father and mother. Farewell. [Col. 0941D]

## XV. OF WIDRICUS OF DANOBRIA. He offers him the cell of Saint Christopher of Magno-Vico.

(Martène, *ibid.*, col. 312.)

To the venerable abbot and Father Hugh of Cluny, adorned with the beauty of all religion: the elder Widricus of Danobria, his wife Gepa, and their two sons Baldwin and Rainbald offer devoted service and the gift of eternal happiness.

[Col. 0942A]

Placed between hope and fear, while we live this fleeting life, we wish, with God’s help and with the advice of his faithful, to arrange as far as we can something for the salvation of our soul, so that in the future we may deserve to receive remission of sins and everlasting life.

On our own estate, in a village commonly called Magno-Vico, we have a chapel built in honor of Christ’s martyr Christopher. It is cared for by a certain monk named Walter, who asserts that he is entirely subject to you. There, through the merits of the aforesaid martyr and with God’s cooperation, many miracles already take place.

We have already granted to it as much arable land as can suffice for eight oxen to plow. I have given this church one salt-producing site and one salt pan; my wife has given one salt pan in perpetual right, and we and our successors shall give more. Do not consider it insignificant: every year, on the feast of Saint Andrew, we give the Cluniac church a cartload of salt, and, if God multiplies the property, we too shall improve the gift to you.

We ask your holiness to be willing, for the love of God, to receive the aforesaid place into your care and under your authority, so that through you the name of the Lord may be praised everywhere. Monastic dwellings have already been honorably begun at the aforesaid place, and, with God’s approval, they will be completed through diligent care.

We are sending our letter to your blessedness so that you may inform us what you wish to do about this. We do not wish to make any agreement concerning the matter until we learn whether you are willing to hear our request. Let your piety know that, if you are pleased to accept it, neither I nor my descendants wish to retain any right or advocacy. Otherwise, if you are unwilling, we shall seek counsel in other places; but we would more gladly have our conversion take place among you. Farewell always. [Col. 0942C]

## XVI. OF AMELIUS, ABBOT OF AURILLAC. He entrusts to him the cell of Cariacum for reform.

(Martène, *ibid.*, col. 313.)

To Lord Hugh, by rightful title abbot of the Cluniacensians, most radiant with the splendor of supreme felicity and every prudence, and most learned in the pursuits of venerable discipline: Amelius, though unworthy, abbot of the people of Aurillac, wishing to be the least of his monks, offers the best gift of eternity and divine protection.

[Col. 0942D]

Since we see, dearest Father, monasteries throughout the world rising again for the sake of their restoration, we especially lament the ruin of our monastery, once famous for its holiness. Since, moreover, we cannot fully restore our monastery—which would be the greater undertaking—we at least entrust one of our cells, called Cariacum, to your authority, on the condition that you bring regular brothers from your own community to the aforesaid cell. They are to provide the brothers who have hitherto been living there outrageously with the instruction of regular discipline and carefully establish a proper way of life, so that, through your grace, the souls of the brothers dwelling there may, after the end of this life, immediately deserve to receive future blessings.

But if you fear that either I or any of the present or future brothers of our monasteries might ever attempt to defraud your discipline of anything—which God forbid!—we commit the whole matter to your judgment, by which they may recover from such presumption. If they refuse to do so, just as you have determined … [Col. 0943A] and as we establish perpetually, the brothers of that aforesaid cell, or any priors, shall go to the Roman pontiff, so that whatever they have unwillingly wished to amend through you and your successor, they may not fail to amend according to his judgment. Farewell. Farewell.

## XVII. OF THEOBALD, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE. Count Theobald offers his son so that Blessed Hugh may wash him in the waters of salvation.

(*Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 449.)

[Col. 0943B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul: to Hugh, venerable abbot, to the monastery of Cluny and to that of Cossey, and to Lord Gozechinus, most reverend provost of that place, and to their successors, Theobald, by the grace of God count of the Franks, and his wife Adelaide, with their sons, forever.

Whenever we offer to almighty God, the giver of all good things, something—even if little—that may be useful for the services of his praise, we return to him what is his; we do not give what is ours. Thus, in doing these things, we are not to be elated by our own gifts but to be grateful for gifts received from God. Nothing is more ungrateful, and nothing is more completely alien to Christian piety, than not to minister at least in some small measure to him from whom we have not only been made exalted in the body through present temporal goods, but also hope, through his most abundant mercy, to become heirs of future goods forever. [Col. 0943C]

Knowing, therefore, that great confidence before God belongs to those who give alms, we intend, at his inspiration and gift, to make friends for ourselves in the present, so that after this life we may deserve to be received by them into eternal dwellings.

Therefore I, Theobald, and my wife Adelaide, moved by faith and devotion toward the holiness and religion which, by the generosity of divine grace, is held to be stronger and more celebrated in our times among your holy community—or rather, admonished by divine inspiration—we have sent our son Odo to your fatherhood to be renewed through the mysteries of sacred rebirth. We judge that, by the dispensation of heavenly mercy, it will not be empty for him to have parents more religious than wealthy in Christ.

For the more favorable effect and more effective advancement of his grace and our protection, and for the redemption of our sins, in the service and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we solemnly grant and donate forever to your holy fatherhood and to the monastery of Cluny, by vow and formal conveyance, a certain village in our allod, called Cossiacus, together with that allod, held in every respect under the same right and authority by which we have hitherto possessed it. It is free from the service and dominion of every other person, together with everything rightfully belonging to it: cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses existing on every side by right of that authority; male and female serfs, taxpayers, and persons of other status; all other revenues; and all lawful customs and claims.

No right or customary claim is retained for us, nor any due payment or exaction of servile obligation is to be rendered in any manner, so that every opportunity for oppression or disturbance throughout that entire possession, whether by us or by our officials and servants, may be removed in every way. Those serving God there may enjoy the Lord’s service freely, in complete peace and tranquility. [Col. 0944A–B]

Moreover, wherever and against whomever they need or reason requires our assistance, we promise always to be present with our helping hand, most promptly and most humanely.

## XVIII. OF RAYMUND, COUNT OF GALICIA, AND HENRY, COUNT OF PORTUGAL. They send a copy of the treaty of friendship concluded between them and of the agreements concerning the division of the succession of their father-in-law, Alphonso, king of Castile and León.

(*Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 122.)

To Lord Hugh, most reverend abbot of Cluny, and to the entire congregation of blessed Peter: greetings in Christ from Raymond, count, and his son, and Henry, count and his associate.

[Col. 0944C]

Know, dearest Father, that after we saw your legate, out of fear of almighty God and the blessed apostle Peter and out of reverence for your dignity, we carried out what you commanded us through the hand of Lord Dalmatius Geret.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. A pledge of complete affection, by which Count Raymond and Count Henry are joined in love, together with this oath.

I, Henry, without any falsehood or deceit in this agreement, swear to you, Count Raymond, the health of your limbs, complete devotion to your life, and my unwilling encounter with your imprisonment. I also swear that, after the death of King Ildephonsus, I shall faithfully defend this entire land of King Ildephonsus for you, against every man and woman, and shall come prepared to acquire it for you in every way, as for my sole lord. I also swear that, if I obtain the treasure of Toledo before you do, I shall give you two parts and retain the third for myself. Amen. [Col. 0944D]

And I, Count Raymond, swear to you, Count Henry, by the soundness of your limbs, by my whole affection for your life, and by the unwelcome event to me of your imprisonment. I also swear that, after the death of King Ildephonsus, I shall give you Toledo and all the land subject to it, as well as all the land that you now hold by my grant; you shall possess it on this condition: that you be my man there and hold it from me as your lord. After I have given those lands to you, you shall relinquish to me all the lands of León and Castile. If anyone wishes to resist me or you and does us injury, we shall jointly or each separately wage war against him until he peacefully relinquishes that land to me or to you; thereafter I shall grant it to you. I also swear that, if I obtain the treasure of Toledo before you do, I shall give you one-third and retain the remaining two-thirds for myself.

### The pledge that Count Raymond made into the hand of Lord Dalmatius Geret

[Col. 0946A]

If I, Count Raymond, cannot give you, Count Henry, Toledo as I promised, I shall give you Galicia, on this condition: that you help me acquire all the land of León and Castile. After I have become its peaceful lord, I shall give you Galicia; once I have given it to you, you shall relinquish to me the lands of León and Castile. Therefore, God so commanding, let the holy Church of God likewise intervene with pious prayers. Amen.

[Col. 0945A]

## STATUTES OF SAINT HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY, FOR ALPHONSO, KING OF SPAIN, AS AN EMINENT BENEFACTOR

[Col. 0945B]

To all our brothers and sons serving the Lord in right faith in the monastery of Cluny, both present and future: Brother Hugh, abbot, sends the rewards of the heavenly kingdom and the joys of eternal happiness.

Beloved, it is fitting that, just as we faithfully observe—although not fully, yet insofar as we can—the institutions of our preceding Fathers, so you should both devoutly accept and beneficially preserve what we decree for the common good, so that the merit of obedience may increase for you, and for those on whose behalf such things are prescribed, the everlasting reward of salvation.

Let your fraternity therefore know that we have decreed concerning Lord Alphonso, king of Spain, our faithful friend, who has done and continues unceasingly to do such great and numerous good things for us that we can compare no king or prince, whether of ancient or modern times, with him: namely, that in all the good works performed, by the Lord’s generosity, in our house or in other places subject to our jurisdiction, he shall have a special share, both during life and after death.

Moreover, during his lifetime we have assigned him one psalm—namely, “May the Lord answer you”—to be sung without interruption at the third hour, and at the principal Mass one collect—namely, “We beseech you, almighty God”—likewise for as long as he lives. We have also decreed that on the day of the Lord’s Supper thirty poor people shall be sent to the Mandatum on his behalf. On holy Easter Day, likewise, one hundred poor people shall be fed by the chamberlain on his behalf. In addition to all this, we have determined that he shall have a daily portion in the refectory at the principal table, as though he were seated to dine with us; this portion shall always be given to one of Christ’s poor for the salvation of his soul, both in life and in death.

[Col. 0946B]

Desiring to add an overflowing abundance to this good measure, pressed down and shaken together, we have given him in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—the new church which he himself appears to have built from his own resources—one of the principal altars, so that the divine mysteries celebrated there may avail for his salvation. When he has completed the course of this temporal life with its appointed end, apart from the offices, Masses, and alms that are to be performed for him, a Mass shall be sung for him specially every day for one year at the aforesaid altar.

His anniversary shall be observed in every respect as that of Lord Henry, the emperor Augustus: at Vespers, at the office, and at Mass all the bells shall be rung; the tract shall be sung in copes; the same Mass shall be sung at his altar; twelve poor people shall be fed; alms shall be given for seven days, in addition to the daily portion that is always placed at the principal Mass; and the church’s custodian shall prepare an abundant meal for the brothers.

In all these things that we have decreed should be done concerning him or on his behalf—in all these things, I say—we also wish his most devoted wife, the queen, to be made a participant. In addition, we have granted her twelve poor people on the Lord’s Supper and have decreed that her anniversary be observed as we judged that of the empress Agnes should be observed.

[Col. 0945C]

## STATUTES OF THE SAME

### He receives Lambert, abbot of Saint-Bertin, as a monk of Cluny in the manner of one belonging to the community

[Col. 0945D]

Hugh, by divine grace abbot of the monastery of Cluny, to all our brothers and sons, present and future: after the distinctions of holy conduct, the joys of blessed life.

[Col. 0947A]

Let your charity know, beloved sons, that Lord Lambert, abbot of Saint-Bertin, coming before our humility, among the other gifts of his great devotion did not hesitate to leave the abbey entrusted to him and offer it to us for arrangement, and to become our monk and professed member.

When he saw that our will could in no way be inclined to the things he devoutly requested, he was compelled, at our urging, to return to his own abbey, with the intention that he remain devoutly in our obedience for as long as he lives, and that, as our monk and professed member, he be loved and honored by the entire congregation. When, however, having completed the course of this life, he has paid the debt that all mortals must pay, a thirty-day commemoration shall be celebrated for him in this place, and his anniversary shall be solemnly observed each year.

[Col. 0947A]

## THE EXHORTATION OF SAINT HUGH TO THE NUNS SERVING GOD AT MARCIGNY

*(Cluniac Library, p. 491.)*

[Col. 0947B]

To his sweetest daughters and most beloved sisters, stripped of the pomp of the world and gathered at Marcigny in honor and praise of the holy and indivisible Trinity, under the protection of blessed Mary ever-Virgin and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul: Brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, sends greetings, grace, and blessing, now and forever.

Let your heartfelt charity, O daughters, not be unaware that, ever since we founded that place with divine clemency leading and cooperating, we have most clearly perceived and experienced the presence there of almighty God’s favor and gracious regard. By his grace he has advanced that place in spiritual growth and enlarged it to some extent through temporal benefits.

When at first, as we believe, God ordained it, we had placed there only a few sisters; and when they began to excel in the fervor of charity and religion and in the mortification of vices, the kindly Creator and lover of souls graciously gathered others there, little by little and from every direction, and restored one beautiful sheepfold, as it were a company of white doves. Some of them he has already led out of the temptations of this world by a glorious end and, as we hope, happily raised to the joys of blessed reward. Others—namely, you who remain—he still mercifully awaits, until it please his graciousness to rescue you from the wretched misery of this exile and bring you happily into their fellowship.

To you, therefore, O daughters, this address of ours is directed in particular. With paternal affection we admonish your unity, beseeching you in the Lord and for the Lord’s sake to sigh toward that place and transfer your whole intention there. Regard whatever is seen in the world as nothing and empty, like a passing mist.

Since you do not know the day or hour when the Lord will come to call you, do not be secure, but remain watchful day and night. Concerned for the salvation of your souls, prepare the chambers of your hearts attentively for the embraces of your Bridegroom, that great King to whom you promised faith, taking the greatest care that he find nothing in you displeasing to his majesty.

Consider, therefore, what you have done; reconsider what you have vowed. If any one of you is troubled by her conscience because she has exceeded the proper bounds in thought, speech, or deed, or perhaps in giving or receiving improperly, or in doing anything else contrary to her profession, let her return to her heart and hasten back to the source; let her humbly disclose the matter to her prior in our stead and confess it truthfully, and thereafter, with God’s help, let her avoid such things insofar as human frailty permits.

Whatever good things you have done—whatever charity, humility, patience, obedience, holy compunction, and true confession, or even bodily exercise, whether before the eyes of God alone or toward one another—we enjoin all of it upon you on God’s behalf for the remission of your sins.

And now, since your holy devotion asks that, because advancing age and the weakness of illness prevent our bodily presence and you no longer hope to see us, we give you some memorial in which you may have both consolation and a representation of our memory, we approve your desire and fulfill what you wish through this letter. We want it to be kept among you and read to you in chapter on the five principal feast days.

Therefore, suppliant and prostrate in heart, I invoke almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that through the merits and prayers of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, of Saint Benedict, and of all the saints, he may bless you, absolve you from all the sins you have committed in soul and body, confirm you in your holy purpose, and lead you to a blessed end, where you may receive from his hand what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.

We also ask this of the clemency of the same God: whenever this letter is read to you, may he deign to grant you the fullness of the grace of his blessing and absolution. Amen.

May he also assist all who have loved you in the Lord, helped you, and supported your weakness, and may he make them worthy of his grace. Amen.

Now, I ask you, O daughters, remember me, a sinner, both here and before the Lord. Amen.

[Col. 0949A]

## THE ADMONITION OF SAINT HUGH TO HIS SUCCESSORS ON BEHALF OF THE NUNS OF MARCIGNY

*(The same source.)*

[Col. 0949B]

As long as Christ’s mercy permits his service, religion, and regular discipline to continue in the confession of the holy apostles and in the monastery of Cluny, this admonition of Lord Hugh, abbot, is written for all who shall have deserved to be rulers and governors of that place. Since he strongly suspected that his end was near, he decreed and established that it be made with the approving support of the brothers.

O lords, O Fathers, whom that heavenly Lord and heavenly Father has chosen and promoted so that you might pasture his flock: I mercifully ask you to listen carefully to what is commended to your knowledge and memory in this letter, so that you may be counted with the righteous in eternal remembrance and, on that day, not fear the hearing of evil.

Although I have been a sinner to no small degree and unworthy even that the name of my littleness should be recited in your hearing, I nevertheless presumed upon your reputation for piety and dared to entrust and write to you what, God willing, will not be useless to you, if he grants that the brief and modest speech of my humility may merit your gracious attention.

Although, as has been said, I have been unworthy and deserved nothing other than every extremity, God nevertheless either willed or permitted the name and office of prelate to be placed upon such a man. And he who came into this world more for sinners than for the just has now also made his mercy wondrous, so that in our days his sinners and penitents from so many and such varied regions should flock to the monastery of the holy apostles, and that the Church dedicated in Christ to the apostolic name and honor should advance through the growth both of the number of brothers and of temporal resources.

But if, as has been said, sinners find among us and also in other places somewhere to which they may flee for the salvation of their souls, the weaker sex—and any woman who, having renounced secular life, wishes to serve God—does not easily find a suitable place for this.

It seemed to us not displeasing to God, indeed obedient to his will, if through the work of our mediocrity sinful women also, by his authorship, should obtain the opportunity of serving him that sinful men had previously attained. To them in particular we assigned Marcigny, the place that we founded and built in honor of the holy and indivisible Trinity—not from our own expenses or resources, since we who are Christ’s poor possessed nothing of our own, but solely from what his generosity deigned to bestow.

And now, since in this world all things undergo such change that some people are being born, some living, and some in the tombs, sleeping, as sacred Scripture says, I have, as it appears, already completed the periods of birth and life and have reached the final lot—that lot, I mean, which no mortal, however healthy or powerful, can escape.

Henceforth, if any poor women of Christ have been gathered there in the place under discussion, whatever may happen to them, whatever temporal necessity may weigh upon them, they must not expect the consolation of our visitation or generosity to come to them now. As far as lay within me, paternal concern and paternal benevolence were not lacking to them. But now, in accordance with the prophet Jeremiah’s words, “They have become fatherless,” unless you, my lords whom I address here, are inspired by God, for love of him, to become substitutes for their lost father and procurator.

Therefore, whoever you are who succeed me in name and office, I commend my office to your mercy; in my stead I humbly beg your mercy, that you now do for the aforesaid place what I would do to the best of my ability if I were to survive, and what you are able to do.

May it please your blessedness that what Christ willed to be planted in some manner through his sinner may, through your succession, be watered, so that God may also give the growth and it may benefit you as recompense for eternal salvation.

Let the principal concern first be that which the Lord himself especially commends in the Gospel: the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Those who voluntarily took upon themselves Christ’s yoke should have a religious and ordered life, never without that discipline which is greatly necessary not only for women but also for men.

Let the place always remain under the condition in which we began and maintained it: no child of immature age shall ever be received there into the habit of holiness, nor anyone younger than one whose spirit can be tested to determine whether it is from God—someone who has reached, if not beyond, at least fully, the age of twenty.

If any woman is of a more wanton age, and this is certainly established, we forbid, prohibit, and anathematize, on behalf of almighty God, of the most blessed and undefiled Virgin and Mother of God Mary, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, that she be joined to this community of women.

And so that this decree and command may possess greater authority and stability, we confirm and strengthen it with the authority of our entire Church and with the vow and consent of all our brothers and fellow soldiers in Christ.

Good Jesus, most merciful Jesus, who honored and glorified that sinful Mary after the filth and defilement of the body, so that at your resurrection she deserved to be the apostle of the apostles and the first witness of your resurrection: grant and consent that, on that day, whoever provides consolation and assistance in your name to these sinful women and your voluntary poor may have a share and fellowship with that same Mary.

If anyone in any way opposes them and prevents them from being able to serve you in peace, and does not correct himself through worthy satisfaction, let him experience you as avenger and vindicator, both in this age and in the age to come.

[Col. 0951A]

## THE IMPRECATION OF BLESSED HUGH, ABBOT

To his dearest and most beloved brothers, and to his sons and daughters, present and absent: Brother Hugh, sinful abbot, sends everlasting joy in the Lord Jesus.

Beloved sons and friends, present and future, we have thought it fitting to make known to your charity that the gracious God, who calls into being things that are not as though they were, deigned by his mercy alone to strip me, a certain sinner—guilty and bound by many slippery vices in my youth, which I was wickedly spending—of secular dress, clothe me in the habit of holy religion, and gather me into the flock of this place.

There, while our fathers and brothers were present, they chose me, although unworthy, although living irreligiously and wantonly, and although also protesting sufficiently, as shepherd of this fold, God so arranging it; and at length they laid this exceedingly heavy burden upon my neck.

Nevertheless, as it now appears, almighty God, not because of our merits but because of his immeasurable clemency, has greatly enlarged this place in every direction and enriched it both with brothers and with possessions. He has expanded it not only in our own region but also in Italy, Lorraine, England, Normandy, France, Aquitaine, Gascony, Provence, and Spain.

Therefore, dearest sons, the greater the number of places and brothers, the more grievous the trembling that strikes me, a sinner, on account of their offenses, unless God’s great goodness deigns to have mercy on my soul through your alms and prayers.

For what speech could sufficiently explain how deeply I am bound by guilt, since, constrained by so many and such great sins of my own, I shall have to render an account before the Lord for the negligence concerning so many entrusted to me?

Some, overtaken by death without confession and without receiving the body and blood of the Lord; others, whose negligence I recognized as greatly to be feared but neglected to correct as I should have; some overwhelmed by precipices; others strangled by water or fire, or suddenly seized by many other dangers—these have departed from this wretched life.

And because I did not correct these people, whether those already dead or the others still surviving, as I ought to have done, and because I treated them too leniently in many matters, I fear lest this become an impediment to their eternal reward and perhaps be reckoned against me as an obstacle to eternal glory.

In all these matters may God be present to us as propitious and merciful, and may he graciously hear you when you pray for the remedy of my soul; may he repay both you and all Christians who commemorate me with an unfailing reward on the day of the great judgment.

In this exceedingly grave obedience I have now completed, with your prayers—as I believe sustaining me—a course of sixty years and somewhat more, however inadequately. If at any time I suffered from bodily illness or any other hardship, your prayers and petitions to God were not lacking to me.

Finally, my speech is not sufficient to recount your good and devoted charity toward me and your true obedience. Therefore, insofar as God has enabled me, I have endeavored to love you, treated you moderately, and embraced you as dear sons. If I have sinned in this indulgence, may God forgive me.

And now, sons, since during this passing life I have struggled partly for all of you and for our own needs, and have advanced into my final days without knowing the moment of my departure, I have chosen for myself a certain little obedience called Berziacum, so that when the end of my course arrives, from it, forever and at the proper time, everything necessary in food or drink may be abundantly supplied on the day of my anniversary to the brothers staying in the convent or in the infirmary, who recall the memory of me, a sinner.

We entrusted this obedience, quite poor and almost ruined, to one of our sons, Lord Seguino, to restore. With a certain brother Fulcher, whom we had granted him for this purpose, he rebuilt it to some extent and endeavored, as he could, to acquire vineyards and small plots of land there. Now that it has finally been restored and rebuilt both externally and internally, it shall henceforth answer to the chamber.

We therefore wish and command that whoever holds this obedience shall, on the day of my anniversary, as we have already said, perpetually provide a full meal for the convent.

We have also granted to one of our brothers, namely Lord Peter of Gloucester, who worked very hard for the benefit of this place, that on the day of his anniversary a full provision in every respect be prepared from this obedience for the brothers. We therefore earnestly ask our brother successors not to allow that little place to be devastated by lodging there too frequently or by demanding other customary services from it.

“For what is little,” as the common saying goes, “suffers from a little.” If a brother’s resources in this matter are abundant, however, let him not refuse to provide the services of charity.

Long ago we also ordered that, from the obedience of Saint Hippolytus, a meal for the brothers in the convent be provided annually on the Chair of Saint Peter, the day of our consecration, for as long as I lived, and that afterward it be assigned to our anniversary. Nevertheless, since we have now arranged this otherwise, we wish this provision always to be offered to the brothers on that same day, namely the Chair of blessed Peter.

I earnestly beg the Lord abbot who succeeds me, my Father and lord, whom divine mercy may visit from on high and protect together with the flock entrusted to him; groaning, I humbly beseech him in God, through God, and for God’s sake, to cherish, embrace, and support those servants of God stripped of worldly pomp, gathered at Marcigny for the salvation of their souls and for the praises of God, and to guide that place with every charity.

Although until our time there had been no community of women at all in the fellowship of this place, we nevertheless received these women into the habit of sacred religion—at first few in number, but later greatly increased—and built a place for them in our days. Whoever has shown them mercy, may God show mercy to him, here and in the future.

I also humbly beg and groaningly admonish that same Lord abbot, by the same God and our Lord, to treat and love kindly, paternally, and charitably all of you who survive me.

And you, all my sons and daughters in Christ, present and absent, whoever in our time came to this sacred order, entrusted yourselves, however unworthy I am, to me for the salvation of your souls and submitted your bodies and souls to our direction: may almighty God absolve you and us from all past, present, and future sins.

May almighty Father, almighty Son, and almighty Holy Spirit, the triune and one God, absolve you. I confess—and have confessed—that he is three in person, one in nature, and one in power.

To this almighty God I, guilty and sinful, confess that I have sinned exceedingly and exceedingly in thought, word, and deed. My fault.

I commend you to his mercy, and invoke him on bended knee to bless you and protect you with his right hand. Through the merits and prayers of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, of the blessed apostles, our lords Peter and Paul, to whom he entrusted the power of binding and loosing, and through the intercession of all his saints, may he lead you and us to eternal life.

There may we at last deserve to rejoice forever in you, and you in us, through him who, as God, lives and is glorified in perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

This document is to be read to the future lord abbot before the convent after, God willing, he has peacefully assumed the seat and governance.

[Col. 0953C]

## What Blessed Hugh Relayed in Chapter on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

*(From Peter the Venerable, Book I of the Miracles, chapter 15.)*

[Col. 0953D]

It is the custom of that monastery, Cluny, to celebrate the Savior’s nativity with uniquely devout affection, more devotedly than its other solemnities: with the melodies of chants, the extended length of readings, the lighting of numerous candles, and—far more excellent—with special devotion and a great outpouring of tears, to solemnize it joyfully with the angelic spirits.

When the appointed season returned, the brothers prepared themselves and everything belonging to them in the customary manner. By decorating the churches and arranging the other parts of the monastery more suitably, they strove to appear festive both inside and outside.

That blessed and venerable father Hugh still survived, in the final old age that was near bodily death but also near life after death, eternal life. When the solemnity itself was now imminent, he entered the chapter house where the brothers had gathered and addressed them all in these words:

“Know, brothers, that Jesus, our gracious Savior, has determined to be present at the solemn celebrations of his nativity and your liberation, and to await the service of your devotion with great joy.

“But know also that the wicked enemy, envious of your happiness, is laboring so that, if he can, he may mingle some clouds of his darkness with so great a brightness and diminish, however slightly, the glory of so great a festival.

“For a certain brother”—he said, clearly indicating himself—“saw this very night the mother of mercy, the perpetual Virgin [variant: perpetually Virgin], holding in her sweetest lap the Son whom she had borne that night, while a multitude of holy angels stood beside him with immense light.

“The same divine Child rejoiced and exulted with immense joy, and displayed the gladness of his heart through the gesture of his glorious body and the clapping of his hands. Turning to his Mother, he said to her:

“‘Do you see, Mother, the night that approaches, to be illumined by the joys of my nativity, in which the prophecies of the prophets and the proclamations of the angels will be renewed, and in which all heavenly and earthly things will rejoice together at my birth from you? Where now is the condemned enemy’s treachery? Where is his power, by which before this singular joy he ruled the world?’

“When that shameless one heard this, he came out of his hiding place and presented himself at a distance, shamefully disfigured. With much lamentation and wailing he begged to be admitted. He made this request so that he might somehow obscure, in his customary manner, the joys of such brightness, which he envied.

“‘And if,’ he said, ‘I am admitted into no part of the church, let me at least be received in some place among the remaining offices.’

“‘Go,’ said the Virgin’s Son, ‘gallows-bird. And do not lament that my power has prejudged you; try what you can.’

“Then, released, he went toward the archway of the chapter house, but could not enter. He found both himself so swollen and the entrance to the chapter house so narrow that he was entirely unable to get in. Truly inflated by the ancient plague of pride, he could not pass through the humble entrance, because that entrance does not admit the proud man standing upright but does admit the humble man bending low.

“From there he turned his steps toward the brothers’ dormitory. Trusting that, with his customary fantasies, he could disturb them, he attempted to enter. But because of that same bulk he was repelled from the doorway and withdrew.

“Finally, he placed his hope of doing harm in the refectory, suspecting that, because of the moderate care of their bodies, there would be greater negligence of their minds. There too he encountered so many obstacles made from the divine words read aloud, so many beams made from the devotion of those listening, and so many barriers formed by the charity of those serving the Savior, that, unable to proceed farther in any way, he was forced to turn back.

“Thus rejected from all the monastery’s offices, that pestilential one withdrew from the sight of the most merciful Redeemer and his glorious Virgin Mother, with the confusion he deserved.

“Therefore be watchful, and give immense thanks to the almighty and most merciful Savior, who has both driven the most wicked enemy away from you and himself remained with us [variant: with you] to celebrate his feast.”

These words spoken by the holy man to the brothers reveal the wickedness of the malignant spirits raging against that place and the clemency of the Lord protecting it. Although those wicked enemies generally lay snares for everyone, they pressed more fiercely against recent converts. They grieved while envying the progress of the veterans, but they were angered more sharply by the added conversion of novices, as though by a freshly received wound. And as though postponing the spoils of their former prey in despair after so long a time, they burned far more fiercely against those being snatched from their grasp. Hence they stirred up powerful wars against the novices; hence, armed with various weapons of temptation, they pressed against them with all their strength.

[Col. 0955B]

## PIOUS DONATIONS MADE TO THE CLUNIACS UNDER THE GOVERNANCE OF SAINT HUGH

[Col. 0955C]

### I. Charter of Count Pontius concerning the subjection of the abbey of Moissac to Cluny  
*(Around the year 1060.)*

*(Gallia Christiana nova, Instruments I, p. 37.)*

Although apostolic words declare that there is no authority except from God, divine speech nevertheless indicates through the prophet something concerning the reprobate, saying: “They themselves have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not acknowledge them.”

Therefore I, Pontius, count of the city of Toulouse, lest I be judged by God, the just arbiter, among those who rule wickedly, as one not acknowledged by him, have resolved, with the common and salutary counsel of my wife Adalmodis, countess, and of the princes subject to me—namely, the venerable Bernard, bishop of Cahors, and also Gauzbert, the abovementioned abbot, as well as William and his brother Fulco—that the abbey of Saint Peter of the monastery of Moissac, which until now I and my parents, or my predecessors, the counts of Toulouse, have appeared to hold and possess by legal right from the hands of the kings of the Franks, should henceforth be guarded more correctly and diligently in God’s service.

Therefore I wish it to be known to all my successors that I relinquish the aforesaid abbey of Saint Peter of the monastery of Moissac to almighty God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and also to my most beloved lord, Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and to all his successors who shall be in the place of Cluny, to be governed forever according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. I make this grant before witnesses.

If, however, any of my relatives or successors, or any person whatsoever after my death or after the departure of Gauzbert, the leading man who now appears to be second to me in that abbey and is called its abbot, attempts in any way to violate this cession of mine—which I absolutely forbid under threat of God’s judgment—I leave him to be examined by the power of almighty God and to be restrained by the Roman pope and by the king of the Franks, under whose protection the aforesaid place of Moissac falls.

I, Durannus, abbot and monk of Cluny, confirm and strengthen this instrument of cession, in the hand of the aforesaid abbot, Lord Hugh, in the presence of the entire convent of the monastery over which he presides, by my own choice and through the consecration of the aforesaid Bernard, bishop of Cahors, in whose diocese this place lies, on the day of the solemnity of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, by hand, mouth, and heart.

Bishop Bernard of Cahors confirmed.

Countess Adalmodis confirmed.

Abbot Gauzbert confirmed.

William, surnamed “Mixes-Evil,” confirmed.

His brother Fulco confirmed.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, Tuesday, under Philip, king of the Franks.

*(In the year 1062.)*

### II. Ademarus, vice-count of Limoges, and his wife Humberga give the abbey of Saint Martial to Hugh, abbot of Cluny

*(Baluze, Miscellany, Luc edition, I, 123.)*
### (1062) II. Adhemar, viscount of Limoges, and his wife Humberga give the abbey of Saint Martial to Hugh, abbot of Cluny

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc edition, I, 123.]

Let all the sons and faithful of holy Mother Church, both of the present and of future times, know that I, Adhemar, viscount of Limoges, give and hand over to Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to all his successors who shall regularly govern that same monastery of Cluny, the abbey of Saint Martial of Limoges, with the consent and authority of the lord Iterius, bishop of that city, and of his canons, as well as of my wife Umberga, my sons, and my nobles, for the remission of our sins and those of our parents, and especially of the sins which we have committed against that same abbey [Col. 0957C], since we have consented that the monks living there should not live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and have sold the governance of souls to abbots who bought it simoniacally.

Although blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, extinguished this heresy at its very beginning, at the birth of the Church, nevertheless the holy Pope Leo and all his successors thereafter have condemned it with perpetual anathema. Repenting, therefore, of my past transgressions, and trusting that through the diligence of the aforesaid abbot and his successors the same abbey of Saint Martial can be restored to the regular path, and that the detestable Simoniac heresy can, with God’s help, be utterly expelled, I give and [Col. 0957D] hand over the aforesaid abbey to the aforesaid abbot Hugh and to all his successors, abbots living according to the rule, to possess perpetually thereafter.

As for the abbots whom he or his successors appoint over that place, if, God forbid, they must be removed because of bad conduct, let he and his successors remove them and substitute better men, without contradiction from anyone, retaining nothing in that same abbey, either I or my successors, except these customary dues: two hundred solidi to be paid for gathering the vintage on the feast of Saint Aredius; a pack animal to be supplied for military service together with a servant—which pack animal, once the campaign has ended, is to be returned to the monastery; one received from the count of Poitiers at the viscount’s command; and the bread-and-wine justice when he comes to this village [Col. 0958A].

On the condition that all my successors confirm this donation and handover, and approve and authorize this charter; and that this our handover, so that it may remain stable and unshaken, be confirmed by apostolic authority. If I or any of my successors should wish to violate or oppose this handover, let him incur the wrath of almighty God and perpetual anathema; and let the aforesaid abbot Hugh and his successors have the power to make complaint about it before the bishop of that city, before all Christians, and especially before the Apostolic See.

This handover was made in that same city of Limoges in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1062, in the fifteenth indiction, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, in his second year. The confirmers, signatories, and witnesses of this handover [Col. 0958B] are these:

First, Bishop Iterius signed. Adhemar, the viscount, signed together with his four sons, and his wife Umberga.

### (1064) III. Bishop Eraclius and Count Bernard grant the monastery of Saint Felix and Saint Licerius to the monastery of Cluny

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc edition, III, 48.]

I, Eraclius, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Bigorre, and Bernard, count of Bigorre, desire and ask all the faithful of Christ, both future and present, to be witnesses and supporters of the transaction that we are now about to declare.

[Col. 0958C]

Through the inheritance of our parents, a monastery situated in the territory of Bigorre has devolved into our possession. It was built in honor of blessed Felix the martyr and blessed Licerius, confessor and bishop. For a long time there was a community of monks there. But because of our sins, through our negligence and that of other persons to whose care and administration the same monastery belonged, regular discipline and the monastic order were not maintained there in such a way as either to please God or to benefit us for the salvation of our souls.

We therefore thought it advisable to seek the counsel and assistance of the lord Hugh, reverend abbot and ruler of that venerable college of monks gathered at Cluny, since through the abbots of that place many monasteries have been restored and improved. Moved by that charity which, as the Apostle says, surpasses all things, we too desired to obtain a similar benefit from their holiness.

For this reason, for the salvation of our souls and those of our parents, we make a handover of the aforesaid monastery and of all things belonging to it in any manner whatsoever to the Lord God and his holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the place mentioned above, Cluny, on this condition: that the Cluniac congregation shall hold and possess it by perpetual right; and that the abbot of this congregation, namely the abbot of Cluny, shall, in second place after himself, entrust the care of the monastery to whomever he wishes and in whatever manner he wishes. This shall always be done without contradiction from any mortal.

We also wish it to be free [Col. 0959A] and released from every service owed to our descendants and to any secular or ecclesiastical authority. Let this be clear and beyond doubt: it is our will and our request that this same handover be confirmed by the Roman pontiff, so that whoever attempts to violate or infringe it may know himself, by his authority, to be excommunicated and separated from the holy Church of God.

This charter was written in the castle of Bigorre itself and issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1064, in the fourth year of the reign of Philip, king of the Franks, in the second indiction.

The sign of the lord Eraclius, bishop of Bigorre. [Col. 0959B] The sign of the lord Bernard, count of Bigorre, who gave this charter. The sign of the lord Stephen, bishop of Oloron. The sign of the lord Durand, bishop of Toulouse. The sign of Gregory, bishop of Lectoure. The sign of Peter, bishop of Aire. The sign of the lord Bernard, count of Dormans.

### (1066) IV. Countess Almodis and her son grant the abbey of Saint Giles and its dependencies

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, III, 48.]

To believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all creation, and in his Only-Begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist, and in the Holy Spirit, who gives life and proceeds from both, is a great matter; but to do what he commands is no small thing, while to despise him is dangerous. Therefore it is necessary for everyone to believe in him faithfully, love him perfectly, and obey him humbly.

This is especially fitting for those whom the water of the sacred river has washed, the water of blood has redeemed, and the liquid of chrism has anointed. For this purpose we have been made: faithfully serving God, to sow earthly things so that we may reap heavenly ones, as Scripture says: “Whatever a man sows, that also shall he reap.” How God may be found, he himself says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” These words clearly show that no one is more wretched than the person whom unjust acquisitions oppress, whom frauds and robberies make wealthy.

And since we ought to seek those riches which can adorn and protect us, separate us from the world, and enrich and ennoble our souls, therefore, in the name of God, I, Almodis, countess by God’s will, and my son Raimund, count of Rouergue and Nîmes and most noble of the men of Narbonne, for the repose of the lord Count Pontius, for the remission of our sins and those of our living and dead parents, and for the salvation of our faithful nobles, hand over, give, and grant the abbey of Saint Giles, the place itself, and everything belonging to it, to God and to the lord Hugh, the present abbot of Cluny, and to his successors.

This is on the condition, however, that in the aforesaid [Col. 0960A] abbey, in the demesne which we possess there, we retain the customary services and dues, except that henceforth we shall neither constrain nor dishonor the abbot or the monks. Rather, the power, jurisdiction, and ordering of the abbots and monks of Saint Giles, and of the things which they have customarily held, shall rest with the power of the lord abbot Hugh and his successors, so that he and his successors may, according to their ability and will, regularly order and hold the aforesaid place and all its dependencies according to the Rule of Saint Benedict forever.

But in order that the memory of us and of our parents may be perpetually preserved at Cluny, we retain only this in the gift of the aforesaid abbey: that the successors of the aforesaid abbot shall accept from us or from our successors a gift of the aforesaid abbey without any profit or price. If our successors should not wish to give it freely, as we have said, to the successors of the aforesaid lord abbot, nothing shall hinder the abbots; rather, while they possess the place and all that we have mentioned in the service of God, our gift shall remain complete and inviolate forever.

Let it also be known to everyone that the aforesaid place and abbey are the allod of Saint Peter. Whatever we hold as a gift from the lord Roman pope, we now hand over perpetually to the aforesaid abbot Hugh and his successors, with the rights of the Roman Church and of the lord pope preserved, to be held and regularly ordered, on the condition that the annual census of ten solidi owed to the Roman Church be paid every year.

This donation was made in the year 1066 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, near the city of Nîmes, beside the church of Saint Baudilius, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks. The witnesses and approvers were the bishops: the lord Raimbald, archbishop of Arles and vicar of the Roman Church; the lord Durand of Toulouse; Hugh of Uzès; and Rostagnus of Avignon; Bertran of Maguelone; the abbots Bernard of Marseille, Frotard of Tomières, Bernard of Vabres; Peter, cleric and subdeacon of the Roman Church; the clerics of Nîmes Solomon and Bertran; the knights Pontius Geraldi, viscount of Girona; Tridmund Elisiarni; William and his brother Emenon of Sabran; Peter of Aquinum; Rostagnus of Posquières and his brother Raino; Rainoard of Médenine; Bertran of Capraria and his brother Peter; Hugh of Cassanègues; Segarius son of Solomon; William Bellirot; Umbert son of Gauzbert; and, moreover, the noble Adala, countess of Substantion, consenting to and approving it, together with many other good men known to God.

But if anyone of whatever order or rank should come against this donation to break it, disturb it, or oppose it, let him incur the terrible and dreadful wrath of almighty God, and be tormented in the lowest hell with the most treacherous betrayer Judas and with Dathan and Abiron. Let both he and those who consent with him and wish to resist this [Col. 0961A] donation be punished with all the punishments by which those who depart from God are tormented, unless they repent and come to make amends.

The sign of the lady Almodis, countess, and the sign of the lord Raimund, count, her son, who ordered this charter of donation to be written and asked that it be confirmed by witnesses.

The sign of Rostagnus of Posquières. The sign of Adalbert Guitard of Barcelona. The sign of Berenger of Barbarano. The sign of Elisiarius Dalmatius. The sign of John, cantor of Girona. The sign of Bernard, chaplain of Saint Giles. The sign of Rainard Amatus. The sign of Pontius of Nozeto. The sign of Fredelan Raimund.

[Col. 0961B]

Bernard, monk of Auch, wrote this at their command, on the day and in the year stated above.

Issued by the hand of Henry, monk, in the place of the chancellor.

### (1068) V. Letter of Aimeric, count of Auch, and his brother Bernard, sons of William, by which they give the monastery of Saint Orientius to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, for its administration

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, new documents, 171.]

Let everyone know that I, Aimeric, count of Auch, and my brother Bernard, for our sins and those of our father William, give to God and to Saint Peter of Cluny, into the hands of the lord abbot Hugh [Col. 0961C] and his successors, for administration and arrangement, the monastery of Saint Orientius and whatever it now possesses or shall possess in the future, etc. My maternal uncle Raimund made this gift together with me, etc.

Done in the cloister of Saint Orientius, in the presence of the lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and others. The sign of the lord Hugh, abbot. The sign of the lord Durand, bishop of Toulouse. The sign of the lord William, bishop of Comminges. The sign of the lord Raimund, bishop of Lectoure. The sign of the lord …, abbot of Saint Genesius. The sign of the lord William, abbot of Saint Martin. Brother Malleavus.

Done under Pope Alexander and Philip, king of the Franks, in the year, as I think, 1068, at the synod held at Auch in that year.

### (1069) VI. Charter for the church of Saint Michael of Mont-Alto

[*Chronicle of Auch*, part III, p. 68.]

In the name of the supreme and almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I, William, son of Bernard and archbishop of Auch, and my brothers Raimund, Odo, Otger, Gerald, and Bertran, for our sins and those of our parents, give to God the Lord and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the place of Cluny, over which the lord abbot Hugh appears to preside, the church of Saint Michael of Mont-Alto, with its five dependent churches, vineyards, and fields.

In addition to what our father gave there during his lifetime, we have given one mill on the stream called the Archo, ten denarii of demesne vineyard [Col. 0962A], and half of the forest called Black Valley. Our mother has likewise given half of the church situated in the village called Ulmus, and jurisdiction over the other church in the village called Cazeras. These two are in Lomagne.

Therefore we ask, through almighty God, all those present and those who shall come after us to approve this gift, preserve it whole and inviolate, acquire God’s favor, and become participants in the fellowship of the Cluniac brothers, which we have received in return for this gift. If anyone should presume to bring a claim against or violate this gift, may he fail to accomplish what he seeks; moreover, may he incur the wrath of almighty God and perish, swallowed up with Dathan and Abiron.

This charter was made in the month of December, in the presence of the lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny; Durand, bishop of Toulouse; William, bishop of Comminges; Raimund, abbot of Saint Luperculus of the city of Auch; and many others, while the lord Alexander was supreme pontiff, Philip was king of the Franks, and he governed above; and his kingdom and power endure without end for ever and ever.

The sign of William, archbishop, and of his brothers. The sign of Arnold Lupus and his brothers. The sign of Raimund of Algipoi. The sign of Florian and his brothers. The sign of Arnold of Argano. The sign of Bernard Guermund.

### (1070) VII. Donation of the church of Saint Mary of Arombod to the monastery of Cluny

[*Chronicle of the Church of Auch*, part II, p. 55.]

Let it be known to all, present and future, our friends and household members, that I, Bernard, son of William and of his wife Brachita, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, on the advice of my wife Anselina and of her father Odo, viscount of Lomagne, and of Bernard, count of Armagnac, and of a Cluniac monk surnamed Turnaquelletius, and of our other friends, give to God, to Saint John of Saint-Mont, to the lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and to the monks serving God devoutly there, the church of Saint Mary of Arombod with its dependencies [Col. 0962D], etc.

If anyone should violate it, he shall be accursed by God unless he makes amends, and shall pay the due belonging to Saint Peter. After the death of Sanxio the priest, we also give the other church of Saint Martin of Rican: namely, two parts and the lordship of the land, so that God may be served there day and night by monks and other Catholics. If anyone should bring a claim against or oppose this gift, unless he repents, may he be plunged into the depths of hell with Judas Iscariot and the other condemned.

This charter was made in the month of October, on Thursday, under the thirtieth moon, and publicly written at Saint-Mont, while Philip was reigning as king and William, duke of Aquitaine, was ruling the province of Gascony; and the city of Auch was then under the protection of the lord William, archbishop.

This was done in the presence of the lord Guy, count of Poitiers [Col. 0963A] and of all Gascony, who gave his contribution with his own hand; likewise in the presence of the lord Bernard Tumapellerius, my maternal uncle, and of the lord Arnold, bishop of Agen, and finally of Raimund of Albio, abbot of Condom. The witnesses and inspectors of this affair are these:

Odo, viscount of Lomagne.

Gaillard of Villera.

Bernard of Gailhard.

Odo of Pondenas.

Odo of Pardellano, and many other nobles.

The sign of Fortis, count of Auch [Ausciensis].

The sign of Gerald, count, and of Arnold Bernard, his brother.

### (107…) VIII. Bernard and his wife give the monastery called Saint John the Baptist at Saint-Mont to the Cluniacs

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc edition, III, 44.]

Let it be known to all men that I, Bernard, count, and my wife Ermengard, and our sons Arnold and Gerald, give to the Lord God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the place of Cluny, over which the lord abbot Hugh appears to be more beneficial than authoritative, a certain monastery belonging to us, dedicated to Saint John the Baptist and called Saint-Mont, with everything belonging to it now and whatever shall belong to it forever, so that the rulers of that place may do whatever they wish from now and for ever and ever, without any opposition [Col. 0963C].

If anyone, God forbid, should wish to oppose or invalidate this gift of ours, may he not prevail in what he desires to break; rather, may the wrath of almighty God, of blessed John the Baptist, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul be upon him. May all the curses of the Old and New Testament come upon him, unless he repents and comes to make amends.

But so that this charter may remain firm and stable, I have confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be confirmed by witnesses.

The sign of the lord Bernard, count, who made this donation.

The sign of his sons Arnold and Gerald. The sign of Ermengard, countess.

[Col. 0963D]

### (1073) IX. Notice concerning the monastery of Saint-Mont

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc edition, III, 43.]

Gerald, by the grace of God bishop of Ostia, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, sends perpetual greeting in the Lord to all the sons of the Catholic Church.

When, at the command of the lord Pope Alexander II, we were traveling through Gascony and proceeding toward Spain, we were lodged at the monastery of Saint-Mont. Saint-Mont is a monastery belonging to the Cluniac monastery, built by the venerable Count Bernard, his religious wife Ermengard, and their son Gerald and their other son Arnold [Col. 0964A], who succeeded to their father’s inheritance by right.

The aforesaid count and countess, loving the sweetness of heavenly life, despised transitory riches and, in the Cluniac monastery over which the most reverend abbot Hugh then presided, assumed the habit of holy religion. They built the aforesaid monastery of Saint-Mont in honor of Saint John the Baptist, for the redemption of their sins and for the remedy of the souls of their parents, both those who had departed from the present world and those who were still to come after them.

At first, therefore, the aforesaid place, as one lawfully given and handed over to Cluny, was a new possession of blessed Peter; and we, although unworthy, were exercising the legation of that chief of the apostles. We were asked by Adhemar, prior of that place, and the other brothers [Col. 0964B] to impose the protection and defense of blessed Peter upon all the possessions of the monastery.

Yielding to their prayers, we have decided, by apostolic authority, to fortify under the protection of blessed Peter all places belonging to that same monastery—churches, estates, villages, and everything lawfully acquired or to be acquired—so that henceforth no person, ecclesiastical or secular, may presume to inflict violence or injury upon the property of the aforesaid place or dare to impose unjust customs.

Moreover, we establish and strengthen under the ban of blessed Peter the safeguard which has been set within the appointed boundaries for the security and immunity of those who inhabit them or flee there for refuge. Thus, whoever rashly and boldly presumes to break, violate, or invade those boundaries—that is, the crosses—shall know himself to be liable to the ban of blessed Peter and, by apostolic authority, excommunicated, unless he repents. Furthermore, if he has inflicted any breach of the ban, let him fully restore and make satisfaction within fifteen days; and let him also pay the satisfactions and penalties prescribed by ecclesiastical sanctions, namely nine hundred solidi.

Whoever, moreover, causes himself to be buried in the cemetery of the aforesaid monastery, offers God a pure confession of his sins, and undertakes and performs true penance, we absolve by apostolic authority and declare him worthy to share in the prayers and almsgiving of the brothers.

To make this charter more secure, we have signed it below with our own hand in this book [Col. 0964D], or on the charter: eternal rewards for its guardians, but eternal punishments and the torments of condemned souls for those who despise or violate it.

I, Gerald, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, have reread and subscribed this in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1073, in the eleventh indiction.

### (1073) X. Testament of Unald, abbot of Moissac, concerning tithes redeemed from various secular persons

[*Gallia Christiana*, new documents, I, p. 37.]

God is the origin of peace for all things: he is the God of majesty, the provider of learned thoughts, the propagator of counsels, and the doer of good works. By his will all things are governed; whatever exists and possesses being is governed by God. He provides for human salvation, accommodating himself to human circumstances according to his own law.

Therefore, if the deeds of his faithful are transmitted in some manner to the memory of posterity, what has been done or deliberated upon with honest intention ought not suddenly to be criticized by mockers. For whatever advances the common good is unquestionably useful to keep in everyone’s memory.

Since, then, secular testaments possess great force for investigating matters under deliberation, it is even more fitting to believe that the examples of any religious faithful possess value in comparison with them. Having thus become certain through such arguments, for the benefit of many sons, I, Unald, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Moissac, with the counsel of the brothers who fear the Lord, have acted by every means at my disposal, through gifts given, to bring under our authority every tithe which until now the leading men or provincial knights have appeared to possess, rightly or wrongly.

This was not done to multiply the profit of avarice, but to restore the census which is owed to God by right. Formerly, indeed, by the commandment of the Law, the people brought to God not only tithes but also the first fruits of all things; for whoever dared to pass beyond this was judged unworthy of his sight.

Hence the Savior himself rebukes the Pharisees in the Gospel (Matthew 23:23), who applauded themselves for their justice because, while fulfilling these lesser matters, they abandoned the weightier things of the Law: “You tithe mint and dill and cumin, and every garden herb.” We do not say this because we wish to transfer Christian worship to the observance of the Jewish Law, but so that the enemy may not dare to boast against the faithful people, who are concerned with the greater justice, on the score of the lesser.

Since these things are so, and it is established that they have been promulgated not only by divine but also by human laws, there is no doubt that the person who deliberately attempts, with wicked audacity, to take away things consecrated to God is bound by the guilt of transgression.

Therefore I, the abovementioned abbot Unald, for this acquisition gave to Bertran, the secular abbot, thirty solidi; likewise, to William surnamed “the dry-maker,” two horses, one gold ounce, and sixteen solidi for obtaining this.

He conveyed to us within these boundaries: from Barta itself, as the Tarn River runs; as the parish of Saint Michael is bounded; and, on the other side, below the road leading to Saint Lawrence, as the parish of Saint Lawrence is bounded; and the parish of Saint Ansbert. Thus he gave everything which he himself or others through him appeared to hold within these boundaries. He himself, his wife, and his sons Raimund and Siquerius confirmed it.

In the same manner we gave one horse to Raimund of Puy, and he gave, within these boundaries, at Barta itself, descending along the wall itself, and in this village, whatever he himself or others through him appeared to possess.
