He confirmed it in this way, and he must have his brother likewise confirm it.

That Stephen, namely, when he came to die, with the counsel of his brother, that same Raimund, having become a monk in order to provide assistance in this matter, confirmed that he relinquished all his share of the tithe—namely, from the vineyards of Falquet and Armulf [Col. 0966A].

For this same reason we likewise gave one horse to Stephen of Valleta. He gave within these boundaries, as the public road leading east is determined, and as it is bounded by the lands of William Siccarius, everything which he himself or others through him appeared to hold. He himself confirmed it, and his son did likewise.

We gave ninety solidi to Bernard, to Hugh, and to their brothers of Anazago, who gave to God and to Saint Peter, by perpetual right to possess, all the share of the tithe which they had in the parish of Saint Michael, and whatever others appeared to hold through them.

Likewise, Gaufred of Belpoi gave Saint Peter, for his soul, all the tithe which he himself or others through him held in the parish of Saint Michael; he and his sons gave it.

In the same way, Pontius Faber, lying ill, gave Saint Peter all his tithe, he and his son.

Raimund Gerald and his brother gave Saint Peter and us, in full, all the tithe which he held in the parish of Saint Michael, just as the other persons written above did; and we gave thirty solidi for it.

For this worthy reward of theirs, we judged them worthy to be associates of our brotherhood and participants in all our benefactions—not only them, but also their descendants throughout all time.

We also decreed that after the end of their lives a general commemoration should be made for their souls: namely, an office to be sung and a Mass to be solemnly celebrated every year on the vigil of Saint Michael.

This charter of cession or donation was made in the year of the Incarnation 1073, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, in the hands of the lord Hugh, abbot of the Cluniacs, and of the lord Unald, abbot, by whose foresight and arrangement all these things are known to have been done, and in the presence of many other brothers serving God at Moissac. Their names, those who confirmed this donation, are these:

Bertran, the secular abbot, confirmed it.

Bernard Hugo and his brothers confirmed it.

The wife and sons of William Siccarius confirmed it.

Raimund of Puy, and many others, confirmed it.

[Col. 0966D]

But if anyone, whether an adversary or certainly one of the sons of those who shall succeed them by inheritance, should after their death attempt to violate, distort, or corrupt this charter of legal cession, or to attack or plunder those same places, let him be punished in this manner: may the plague of leprosy, famine, pestilence, the sword, and dreadful death never depart from his house.

### (1076) XI. The abbey of Saint Arnulf of Crépy is given to Hugh, abbot of Cluny

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, 207, from the Cluniac cartulary.]

To the venerable abbot Hugh and to the entire congregation of the monastery of Cluny, Simon, count and servant of your holiness, sends greetings.

[Col. 0967A]

Let it be known to your exalted dignity, most blessed Father, that I love you in God more than all men living in the flesh, and that I seek your advantage and honor insofar as I am able.

Therefore I grant to you and to all your successors the abbey of Saint Arnulf, which has been built in the castle called Crépy, so that it may be wholly subject to you, and so that you may choose there one of your monks who can govern that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

I wish you to know that I have done this with the counsel and consent of my men, namely the leading men, and that I also asked the king to confirm this charter. Philip was present, and Bishop Ivo of Senlis granted his consent.

The witnesses are Simon, Simon the count’s dapifer; Milo; Orphanus.

[Col. 0967B]

Done in the house of Saint Mary of Paris, on the feast of All Saints.

The sign of King Philip.

### (1077) XII. Charter of Fidis, countess of Narbonne, concerning the gift of the church of Saint Peter of Sermur to Hugh of Cluny and Unald, abbot of Moissac

[*Gallia Christiana*, new documents, I, 38.]

Let both those present and those yet to come know that I, Fidis, viscountess of Narbonne, in the name of God and under this written declaration, give to the Lord God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to Unald, abbot of Moissac, to all his successors, to the monastery of Moissac, and to all those serving God there, so long as that place remains in the service of God, the church founded in honor of blessed Peter the apostle, in the place commonly called Sermur, above the Biaur River, in the diocese of Rodez, so that they may have and possess that church with everything belonging to it there in perpetuity.

I, the aforesaid Fidis, viscountess, also give and grant the entire mountain as far as the ridge of another mountain called del Poieth: on the upper side, from the stream Naosa to the Biaur, as both enclose the two mountains; the allod and fief; and the vicaria; the forest adjoining the mountain on every side; vineyards, gardens, houses, mills, fisheries, springs, entrances, and exits.

Likewise I give the head of a holding at Cesairent. [Col. 0967D]

To make this donation firm and stable, I make it with the authority, counsel, and consent of the lord Peter, bishop of Rodez. If anyone of our kin or of any relationship should presume to violate or alienate this donation, which I make for my sins, for the redemption of the soul of my father and mother, and of all my relatives, let him first incur the wrath of God and of all the saints; then, by the authority and power of the lord pope of that time and of all the faithful, let him be condemned until he repents and makes satisfaction.

This donation was made into the hands of the aforesaid abbots and of Bernard the monk, surnamed William, through whose efforts this was accomplished, and of Vitalis the cleric, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, while Philip was reigning as king and the lord Pope Alexander was holding the pontificate of Rome [Note: The error in the numerical dates of this charter is obvious, since Pope Alexander did not preside over the Roman Church in the year 1077; he had left it at his death in 1073, when Gregory VII succeeded him. Therefore, 1067 should perhaps be read instead of 1077.].

The sign of Fidis, viscountess, who ordered this charter to be made and asked that it be confirmed by witnesses.

The sign of Peter, bishop of Rodez; of Pontius of Cassanas; and of Pontius of Panat.

The sign of Hugh Stephen. Amen.

### (1077) XIII. Charter of Hugh Stephen, priest, concerning a donation made to the same recipients

[*History of Languedoc*, II, Documents, p. 295.]

[Col. 0968B]

Let all know, etc., that I, named Hugh Stephen, priest, in the name of God, under this written testimony, give to the monastery of Cluny and to the abbot of that place, the lord Hugh …, and likewise to the monastery of Moissac … the church founded in honor of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, in the place commonly called Sermur, above the Biaur River, in the diocese of Rodez …

To make this donation firm and stable, I make it with the authority of the lord Peter, bishop of Rodez, and likewise with the counsel and consent of Fidis, viscountess, whose allod that place was, and with the consent and presentation of Pontius of Cassanas, Pontius of Panat, his brother, and all my nephews; likewise of Aicfred, Berenger, and his brother, who held that honor as a fief.

I, the aforesaid Hugh, also grant, together with all the knights mentioned above, etc., in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, the lord Alexander [read: Gregory] was Roman pontiff. The sign of Fidis, viscountess, and of Pontius of Cassanas, etc.

### (1078) XIV. Charter by which Bernard, count of Besalú, subjects the abbeys of Camp-Rotund, Arles, and Saint Paul of the Olives to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to be reformed by his cousin Unald, abbot of Moissac

[*Gallia Christiana*, new documents, I, 39.]

Let it be manifest to all for eternity that I, BERNARD, count of Besalú, seeing that certain monasteries which had come to me through kinship with my ancestors had utterly departed from the monastic order and regular life, resolved to restore them to a better condition, for the remission of my sins and the salvation of the souls of my father and mother. Having therefore adopted this salutary counsel, with the authority of my men I give, under the legal instrument written below, to almighty God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the place of Cluny, and to the venerable abbot Lord Hugh and all his successors, for as long as the place of Cluny remains in the order, the right of election and governance [Col. 0969A] of the monastery of Saint Peter of Camp-Rotundus in the territory of Girona, and of the monastery of Blessed Mary called Arles, in the district of Elne; likewise of the monastery of Saint Paul in the valley of Oley, in the county of Narbonne; so that they may hold and govern the aforesaid monasteries forever according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

In order that this cession of mine might remain stable, I redeemed the abbey of Saint Mary of Arles from those who had acquired it as a fief: namely, from Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne, one hundred ounces of gold, and from Arnald Arnald, one hundred ounces of gold. During his lifetime I also left to him from that honor the chaplaincy in the church of Saint Peter of Albania, together with all the knights’ fiefs which Saint Mary possessed in the district of Besalú, except the fief of Bernard Adalbert and that of William Segar. Likewise, I redeemed the abbey [Col. 0969B] of Saint Paul from Peter, viscount of Fenouillèdes, for one hundred ounces of gold, since he had acquired it as a fief; and for as long as he lived I left him from that honor of Saint Paul the village called Maury. Moreover, I entirely renounce all evil customs, market dues, lodging obligations, transport services, and every form of exaction which I, or any of my ancestors, had hitherto seemed to exact in the aforesaid honors of the monasteries.

This donation, as I have already said, I wish to be held by perpetual right; and if anyone—God forbid—should attempt to violate it, I leave the matter to be examined under the judgment of the Roman pontiff. This testament of my concession was made into the hands of my dearest kinsman, Lord Hunaldo, abbot of Moissac, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0969C] 1078, in the era 1116, while Gregory VII held the papacy at Rome and Philip reigned as king of the Franks.

The names of the witnesses who affirmed this are written below.

I, Bertrand, count, affirm this and set my seal to it with my own hands.

+ Sign of Pontius Bledger. Sign of Udalard, viscount. Sign of Adalbert Gausbert. Sign of Arnald Gerald. Sign of Peter Gausbert. Sign of Gausbert Peter.

### XV. Charter of Gaufrid, knight, brother of Saint Hugh, concerning Marciniac in the county of Autun. (Around the year 1080.)

[MARTENE, *Anecdota*, I, 243.]

Human presumption ought not to prejudice divine decrees, for prejudice is indeed done when evil is returned for good. Divine generosity continually presents us with every good in abundance. Even if these gifts are not equal or as worthy as they ought to be, nevertheless, in return for the many things it has bestowed, God does not disdain to receive lesser things from his own creature, to whom he has given everything.

Following this example, though not as is fitting, nevertheless according to the capacity of my understanding, I, Gaufrid, moved in some measure, make a donation to God and to the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose honor and reverence the monastery of Cluny is known to have been built, [Col. 0970A] and over which our brother Lord Hugh appears to preside. I permanently surrender a portion of my possessions situated in the county of Autun, in the village called Marciniac: namely, the church which I desire to build from its foundations for the redemption of my sins, together with my three *condeminae*, my woodland, my meadow, and all the cultivated and uncultivated land which I appear to possess there as lord.

I give this donation to the aforesaid God and place for the salvation of my soul and of my parents, with the assent of Count Theobald, my brothers Andrew and Dalmatius, and all my faithful supporters.

### (Year 1082) XVI. Letter of Guarin, count of the territory of Rosnay, concerning the Church of Saint Margaret, given to the monastery of Cluny.

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. edition, III, 55.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I wish it to be made known to all the sons of the holy Catholic Church, present and future, that I, Guarin, called count of the territory of Rosnay, while I was still a son of this world, reflected—because of the favor of that passing dignity—that I should donate part of my allod and what I possessed in the church of Saint Margaret to the Lord and to Saint Peter of the monastery of Cluny, for the support of the sons of God who are believed to pray to the Lord’s mercy for my sins and those of the whole people. With the Lord’s will, I fulfilled this intention, establishing there brothers who would serve the Lord [Col. 0970C] and the holy virgin under a regular rule.

At that time, however, the altar and one quarter of the church itself were possessed by the brothers of the monastery of Dervy, where the body of the venerable Bercharius rests honorably. Therefore, so that the Cluniac monks might possess the aforesaid church in its entirety, after deliberation with the apostolic lord named Hildebrand, called Gregory in the papacy, so that I might die to the world and live to God, for the remission of all my sins and the salvation of my ancestors, with the apostolic blessing, with the permission of my bishop, Lord Hugh of Troyes, with the support of Theobald, count palatine, and with the praise of my relatives, I gave myself and my allods to the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and also to the venerable Bercharius, in the presence [Col. 0970D] of Lord Abbot Bruno, his monks, and his faithful.

Accordingly, the aforesaid abbot and monks granted to the Cluniacensians the altar and one quarter of the aforementioned church, receiving in exchange the allods which were held in free condition, without the yoke of any advocacy, without any judicial authority or ban, and finally without any payment owed to any person.

These, then, are the allods which I handed over to God, to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the blessed Bercharius, and to his monks, to be held forever: Roserias, Muctium, and Junchereium, with their appurtenances, namely male and female servants, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, meadows, waters, and watercourses.

In order that this gift of mine might remain permanently in the possession of the same church and of the brothers serving God there, and that it might not be rescinded by the unjust invasion of any claimant, I asked Lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See by order of the aforesaid apostolic lord Gregory, to confirm this charter, after pronouncing excommunication, under the testimony and approval of all the bishops, abbots, and other faithful of God assembled at the council of Meaux. He most willingly granted my request and, by the common decree of the entire holy council, confirmed it as I had asked, under the penalty of this anathema.

By the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we excommunicate, separate, and remove from the thresholds of mother Church, and strike and condemn with eternal damnation, all those who commit any fraud or injustice against the church of the monastery of Dervy concerning any of the possessions of the aforesaid allods of Count Guarin, unless, having come to their senses and having satisfied the same church, they perform a worthy fruit of penance.

Sign of Hugh, bishop of Die. Sign of Amatus, vicar of Pope Gregory. Sign of Richard, archbishop of Bourges. Sign of Hugh, bishop of Troyes. Sign of Roger, bishop of Châlons. Sign of Roricius, bishop of Amiens. Sign of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. Sign of Hugh, bishop of Langres. Sign of Haganon, bishop of Autun. [Col. 0971C] Sign of Hugh, bishop of Nevers. Sign of Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. Sign of Landric, bishop of Mâcon.

Count Theobald, his wife named Alaïs, and his son Odo also approved and made their signs.

Sign of Count Theobald. Of Alaïs, his wife. Sign of Odo, his son.

### (Year 1082) XVII. Charter of the foundation of the monastery beneath the castle of Brunechild, in the county of Quercy, subjected to Hunaldo, abbot of Moissac, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

[Gallia Christiana, new edition, I, Instruments, 39.]

[Col. 0971D]

Instructed by divine laws and strengthened by the examples of ecclesiastical sanction, we believe and confess that the impieties and sins committed through human transgressions can, by God’s dispensation, be redeemed and cleansed through the generosity of almsgiving and the continual practice of good works. The very Truth, which is God, bears witness to this when it says: “Give alms, and everything will be clean for you” (Luke 2:41). And again Scripture says: “My son, always do good and offer offerings worthy of God; remember that death does not delay, and the testament of the underworld will be revealed to you” (Ecclesiasticus 14:11–12).

Moved by these and other admonitions of divine speech, we, namely the viscounts called Artmannus and Ademarius, with the Lord’s help provide and arrange [Col. 0972A] to build anew, from our own resources, a monastery for all our sins, in honor of almighty God himself and in memory of the most blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, to whom the power of binding and loosing was granted by the Lord. This is unquestionably for the protection and betterment of both our bodies and souls, and likewise for the remedy of the souls of our parents and of all faithful people, living and dead.

Therefore, prompted by the counsel of many most noble men, we, the aforementioned viscounts, namely Ademarius and Artmannus, grant and donate by perpetual concession to the Lord God, that is, to the holy and indivisible Trinity, and to his most holy apostles Peter and Paul, at their places of Cluny [Col. 0972B] and Moissac, and likewise to the venerable abbots Lord Hugh and Lord Unaldus, and to all their successors, abbots and monks who shall serve the Lord forever in the aforesaid places, the site newly raised and established for this purpose.

The site itself is in the county of Quercy, in the territory beneath the castle of Brunechild, between the rivers Vézère and Aveyron. We give the site with all its appurtenances and adjacent lands; whatever we have designated and donated there or elsewhere for this work, whatever we may yet give, and whatever the inhabitants of the site may be able, with God’s help, to acquire there, so that the inhabitants of the aforesaid Cluniac and Moissac monasteries may hold and possess it as their own allod by perpetual right.

We also give, under the legal instrument and with firm confirmation, our mansus called Mont-Argil, in our own demesne, with all its boundaries, entrances, and exits, to be possessed as an allod in perpetuity. All these things, with all their revenues, both as much as has been shown by us and as much as, with God’s consent, may be acquired there in the future—namely lands, vineyards, waters, woods, meadows, cultivated or uncultivated property—we cede and donate in their entirety, with their entrances and exits, by a firm and stable cession to the inhabitants of the aforesaid monasteries, without any reservation whatsoever.

They are to have, hold, and possess these things faithfully throughout all succeeding ages, on the further condition that neither we nor any man of our generation or of any other generation may ever demand any authority over the aforesaid honors, or justice, or vicariate, or presume to inflict any violence upon the inhabitants of the site within the boundaries designated above. Rather, all these things are to remain free and undisturbed forever for the servants of God.

We also approve and grant that the inhabitants of the same place may forever hold and possess whatever anyone wishes to give from the benefices and fiefs which they hold from us.

We also wish and request that a privilege concerning all these matters be issued by the lord pope of the Roman Church, so that this almsgiving of ours may always remain firm and stable. If anyone should presume to violate or in any way invade it, [Col. 0973A] let him know that he will be condemned both now and forever.

These things were done with the counsel and authority of Lord Gerald, bishop of the Church of Quercy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks and Lord Gregory VII held the papacy of the Roman Church: in the tenth year of his pontificate, in September, on Tuesday, that is, on the Nones of that month, on the nineteenth day of the moon, in the sixth indiction, in the era 1121.

Sign of Artmannus and Ademarius, viscounts. Sign of Raymond Amelius. Sign of Pontius Matfred. Sign of Raterius. Sign of Matfred Amelius. Sign of Amelius Justin. [Col. 0973B] Sign of Bernard, his son, and of Hugh, his brother. Sign of Arnald of Mairac and his sons. Sign of Peter, Stephen, and their brothers. Sign of Bernard Hugh and his brothers.

### (Year 1090) XVIII. Testament of Lord Adefonsus, king of the Spains, to Cluny.

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, III, 44.]

In the name of almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. ADEFONSUS, by the merciful favor of God king of the Spains.

It is fitting for royal majesty to imitate the virtues and good deeds of preceding kings, thereby finding favor with God and men and transmitting to posterity a beloved memory of his name. It therefore came to my mind, King Adefonsus, what distinguished deed my father, King Fredelandus—ever to be recalled with devout remembrance—had performed among his other acts.

Having learned of the renowned, approved, and holy religion of the monastery of Cluny, he was immediately pierced by divine fear and humbly sought association with the brothers serving God and Saint Peter there. He accepted it devoutly, retained it with complete fidelity throughout his life, and rightly believed that he would share in their spiritual benefits if he proved generous from his temporal abundance toward the needs of God’s servants.

Therefore he gave the Cluniac community an annual payment of one thousand gold pieces, commonly called *mancales*, specifically for the clothing treasury; and he established and confirmed that this payment should be rendered annually to the aforesaid place in the same manner by his successors.

Since it has pleased the almighty Creator to strengthen my throne in the kingdom of the Hesperides, I, Adefonsus, king by the grace of God, as heir to my father’s dignity and likewise successor to his good will, entered into a pact of fraternal association with my Cluniac brothers. I established and confirmed it, and doubled my father’s generous payment, paying two thousand *mancales* annually to Cluny.

After consulting with my wife, the queen, and with the first archbishop of Toledo, my other bishops, the leading men of my kingdom, and my faithful, who wished, consented, praised, [Col. 0974A] and approved it, I establish for my most beloved Cluniac brothers, from the aforesaid doubled payment, a royal command which I myself shall uphold most firmly for as long as I live, and which all succeeding kings of the kingdom of Spain shall observe by perpetual law throughout future ages.

I make this constitution for the salvation of my soul, for the souls of my father, mother, and brothers, and for my wife and children, so that it may benefit the living in obtaining eternal life and the dead in attaining everlasting rest.

If any of my royal successors, becoming—God forbid—a violator or transgressor of this command, should attempt either wholly to deny or to diminish the payment established for the Cluniacensians, let him know, as I trust in the Lord [Col. 0974B] God, that he will be alienated from the kingdom of God and disinherited by divine judgment, unless he quickly repents and restores, with worthy satisfaction, the installments of the payment that he denied or diminished.

In order that this command of mine might be held inviolable, I ordered this written charter to be made, and confirmed and strengthened it below with my royal hand and authority. I also subsequently ordered the princes and my faithful to confirm it.

I further obtained from my father, the Cluniac abbot Lord Hugh, who at that time was residing with me in the city of Burgos, that he establish for all his future successors in the abbacy a command concerning the commemoration or service which Lord Abbot Hugh himself appointed and arranged to be continually performed, both for the living and the dead, on our behalf: namely, for my father, my mother, my brothers, myself, my wife the queen, and [Col. 0974C] my children.

These things were enacted in the city of Burgos.

Given at the city of Burgos in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, in the thirteenth indiction, during the days of Easter.

### (Around the year 1095) XIX. Letter of the bishop of Senlis concerning the abbey of Crépy.

[Gallia Christiana, X; Instruments, 207.]

HUGH, by the grace of God bishop of Senlis, to Lord Hugh, his lord and most beloved abbot of the monastery of Cluny: greeting and service.

We wish it to be known to your most benevolent and most beloved holiness that we have willingly assented to the petition of Lord Hugh, count of Crépy, concerning the abbey of Saint Arnulf, with the support of the community of canons of the holy see of Senlis.

We therefore grant that the monastery of Saint Arnulf of Crépy be wholly subjected to the authority of your most holy lordship and most religious holiness. And because we desire an association with your goodness, let it be in your power to appoint and remove whatever person you wish, for as long as you enjoy this life.

Moreover, for your sake we grant that after your death your successor, namely the abbot of Cluny, shall have the power to appoint an abbot in the aforesaid church according to the election of the Cluniac chapter. Nevertheless, the Church of Senlis and its bishop shall not lose what they ought to retain according to God and the authority of the holy Fathers; rather, they shall retain it according to what canonical order requires.

Lest anything in this arrangement seem burdensome to your most benevolent fatherly care, we declare that when, God willing, we have spoken together in person, we shall amend whatever ought to be amended according to your prudent counsel. For the present, however, take counsel concerning the church.

### (Year 1096) XX. Proceedings of the agreement made at the Council of Clermont between Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Pontius, abbot of Casa Dei.

[Col. 0975B] [BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, III, 56.]

Let all the faithful of the Church of God, present and future, know how Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Lord Pontius, abbot of Casa Dei, together with their brothers, through the hand of the lord Pope Urban II and of the venerable archbishops Lord Hugh of Lyon and Lord Aldebert of Bourges, along with many other religious men, after every dispute that had arisen between them on various occasions had been quieted, returned to peace and concord at the Council of Clermont.

It must therefore be known that Lord Abbot Pontius and the brothers of Casa Dei granted to Lord Hugh, abbot, and the Cluniac brothers the monastery of Boort and the church of Ambert, as well as the church of Saint [Col. 0975C] Stephen of the Castle, the church of Digne, the church of Cosantia, the church of Vongey, the church of Prissey, and the church of Seneujac, with all their appurtenances, both lands and possessions and tithes and other revenues, together with a share of the tithe from the church of Cosiac and also a share of the tithe which they held in the Church of the Jews, so that they might henceforth possess all these things forever.

Conversely, the Cluniac abbot and his brothers granted to the abbot of Casa Dei and his brothers the dependency of Châtillon beside the castle of Corziac and the church of Casa Mediana, with everything belonging to them, so that they might possess all these things forever. It was nevertheless stipulated that no more than two or three monks should reside at Casa Mediana. Those living in the castle called Castellutium were to have the right to bury their dead either in the cemetery of the castle chapel or in the church of Auzac, which is parochial.

All other things which, on the day this agreement was made, either the Cluniac brothers or the brothers of Casa Dei held by any investiture were settled between them in perpetual peace, and henceforth neither would bring a claim against the other concerning them.

They also agreed among themselves that whatever lands or possessions might henceforth be given to either community by persons who held them by some investiture, the brothers who received any gift whatsoever from them should possess those lands or possessions without the claim or contest of the others.

In acquiring churches, whoever of them could first obtain a share by the gift of the person invested would hold it in peace. No one from the other congregation could use force or bring a claim against him, nor would he have the right or power to acquire or build a church in that parish.

Any cleric or knight who, when near death, assigned himself for burial to whichever of their places he wished would be buried there without dispute, and whatever he gave, that place would retain in peace, even if he had previously devoted himself or his property to the other party. The exception was that if he had first given anything to another party with an investiture, it could be held only by those who had received that investiture.

No one who wished to enter the monastic order and receive the habit would be prevented by the other party from being received wherever he wished to go, even if he had first devoted himself to that other party. If he had then given anything, the place he entered would possess it in peace, except for those things which he had first transferred to others with an investiture.

Those who had been received into the habit could not transfer from one monastery to the other unless perhaps with the permission of their abbot.

Enacted publicly at Clermont and approved and confirmed by the authority of Lord Pope Urban II, so that it might be held unshakably by both parties, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, on the Kalends of December, in the fourth indiction.

### (Year 1101) XXI. Raymond, viscount of Cahors, embracing the monastic life at the monastery of Moissac and granting two churches to Abbot Ansquitil.

[Col. 0976C] [Gallia Christiana, new edition, Instruments, 40.]

Since it is manifest that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), and Scripture admonishes each person: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus 30:24), I, Raymond, called viscount in the name of God, who had so often received evil things from others, now at last resolve to give good things and choose, through divine inspiration, to have mercy on my wretched soul.

For I have abandoned the life I had lived so wickedly that it is unbearable for all Christians even to hear of it, and, leaving everything behind, I have exchanged it for the monastic religion.

The churches called Calzada, which my parents and ancestors had wickedly alienated through the Simoniac heresy so that their offerings might be distributed not through the hands of the poor but, shamefully, through the hands of concubines, I have, by divine ordering, established and arranged under the governance of those serving God.

These churches, then, which appear to have been built in the county of Quercy—the larger in honor and under the name of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, and the smaller in honor of Saint Audoenus the confessor—with their cemeteries and offerings, lands, vineyards, waters, mills, and every ecclesiastical right, together with everything belonging to them everywhere, I, the aforesaid Raymond, and my sons Pontius and Peter, give and surrender to the Lord God of all and to his most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, at the venerable places of Cluny and Moissac, and to the present abbots, Lord Hugh and Lord Ansquitil, and to all their successors, [Col. 0977A] both abbots and monks serving God in those places, so that they may have, hold, and possess the allod forever, for all time, as long as heaven hangs over the earth.

This I carried out with such devotion through the admonition and diligence of the supreme and illustrious man, our Lord Gerald, bishop of Quercy; through the insistence and long prayers to God of the venerable Abbot Ansquitil and the entire community of Moissac; through the exhortation and, so to speak, partly through the force of my sons Peter and Pontius; and also with the counsel and consent of my friends and of many noble men.

If anyone should attempt to break, violate, or diminish this donation of ours in any way, let him first incur the wrath of the living God and feel himself condemned with Dathan and Abiron [Col. 0977B] to perpetual damnation in hell.

But whichever son or kinsman of mine shall appear better, let him restore the whole of it by his own power to Saint Peter at the aforesaid place of Moissac, so that he may share in this almsgiving of mine and remain the lawful heir of my inheritance. Thus what we are transferring and changing from lay hands, where it has hitherto been, into the support of almighty God and his servants shall remain valid and undisturbed, without disturbance or annoyance, for all time.

This deed of cession was written by the authority and counsel of Lord Gerald, bishop of the holy Church of Quercy, and his clergy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0977C] 1101, in the ninth indiction, while Paschal II presided over the Roman Church as pope, Philip reigned as king of the Franks, and many witnesses were present and confirmed it.

I myself, the aforesaid Raymond, viscount, and my sons Pontius and Peter, viscounts, thus affirm and confirm that it is to be held forever.

I, Ademarius called Ramo, who had held these things badly by succession from my parents and possessed them unjustly, freely and absolutely give and surrender them, together with my son, into the hands and presence of the aforesaid abbot, Lord Ansquitil, and of many other witnesses, both monks and laymen.

Sign of Aimo Elias. [Col. 0977D] Sign of Gaufrid, knight of Calzada. Sign of Peter Amelius. Sign of Sicard. Sign of Hugh, vicar.

### (Year 1103) XXII. The Council of Marseille confirms the settlement made by Norgaud, bishop of Autun, with Lord Abbot Hugh and the Cluniac monks.

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, 125, from the Cluniac cartulary.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

We wish all the sons of the holy universal Church to know what peace and concord Norgaud, bishop of Autun, finally made with Lord Hugh, venerable abbot of the Cluniacensians, and his sons, the Cluniac brothers, after a long controversy, and by what letter he confirmed what had been done.

Complaints had arisen between the Cluniac brothers and the aforesaid bishop of Autun, N., because of injuries inflicted by that bishop. Among the other losses caused by these injuries, the same bishop, together with Lord Berard, prelate of Mâcon, had made certain new privileges which appeared to contain provisions contrary to the privileges of the Church of Cluny.

When Lord Pope Paschal II learned of this, moved by love for Lord Father Hugh and affection for the Cluniac brothers, he took care in his writings to condemn those contrary provisions contained in the privileges of the aforementioned bishops. For this condemnation, and at the same time to conduct and settle the affairs of the Roman Church, he made every effort to send to Gaul the bishop of Palestrina, Lord Milo, charged with the legation of all Gaul.

That legate, coming to Cluny, appointed on a certain day the aforesaid settlement between the bishop and the Cluniac brothers. In that settlement, whatever the privileges of the aforementioned bishops declared contrary against the privileges of the Church of Cluny, he excluded and condemned by order of the lord pope, in the presence of the bishops whom we shall list below and of all who were present; and he confirmed and strengthened the privileges of the Church of Cluny.

In this settlement, the aforementioned bishop of Autun, N., instructed by the decree and letters of Lord Pope Paschal II, and compelled by the justice which the Cluniac brothers possessed in the churches named below, gave, granted, and approved for Lord Father Hugh and the Cluniac brothers the church of Carrelles, the churches of the castle of Lorma—namely the church of Saint Alban and the chapel of the same castle—the church of Molines, and the church of Trevello.

He likewise gave, granted, and approved the church of Monceaux. It was nevertheless established that an annual payment of two solidi should be rendered for this church. The following agreement was also made concerning the same church: if the Cluniac brothers were summoned by the monks of Corbigny to establish their right, and the Cluniacensians were able to produce their witness, they should not delay carrying out the justice of their right in the court of the aforesaid bishop of Autun, N.

He also approved all the churches which they had held either in the time of his predecessor Lord Aganon or concerning which they had received a gift, an investiture, or consent.

By order of Lord Pope Paschal, it was also decreed, fixed, and confirmed through the aforesaid legate of the Roman See, the bishop of Palestrina, Lord Milo, that, as is contained in the privilege granted to Cluny by the aforesaid Pope Paschal II, both the churches and the priests of the churches, together with all the possessions of the Cluniacensians, should remain free and inviolate, without disturbance.

The following provisions were established and fixed concerning the abbey of Vézelay. It was decreed and ordered that the bishop of Autun should not demand profession or obedience from the abbot of Vézelay, nor should the abbot render it to him in any way.

The brothers of Vézelay, however, shall receive the sacred orders from him, provided that the bishop has been canonically ordained. If he refuses to ordain them, they shall be ordained by any other canonically ordained bishop. He shall also provide chrism, without any objection, to the priests serving that abbey.

These things were enacted at Marseille in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1103, through the hand of Lord Milo, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Holy Roman Church, in the presence of the bishops: namely B., bishop of Mâcon, who at that time was exercising the functions of his diocese in place of Lord Hugh, archbishop of Lyon; and the aforementioned bishop of Autun, N.; also in the presence of Lord Gerald, archbishop of Évreux; Lord Herbert, bishop of Titfort; Lord Robert, bishop of Chester; and Lord Pontius, bishop of Béziers.

The aforesaid bishop of Autun, N., had confirmed this settlement and these agreements concerning the donations through the hand of the aforementioned Lord M., cardinal, in the presence of the bishops just named; so likewise he confirmed, approved, and strengthened them at Cluny in the common chapter of the brothers, in the presence of Lord Artald, abbot of Vézelay, Lord Gaufrid, prior of the cloister, and Lord Bernard, chamberlain, and also in the presence of the community.

### (Year 1107) XXIII. Charter of William, count of the Burgundians and of Mâcon, by which he confirms the donations made by his ancestors to Cluny and adds others of his own, recalling his forebears and ancestors.

(Year 1107.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 511.]

Let it be known to all who love truth and peace that I, William, count of the Burgundians and of Mâcon, approve and confirm for Cluny all the donations which my ancestors, the counts of the Burgundians and the counts of Mâcon, have bestowed upon that venerable place up to the present day: namely, Rainald, my father, son of William; William himself, son of another Rainald; Rainald himself, son of another William; and the possessions which Count Stephen, my paternal uncle, gave there.

I also confirm the possession in the county of Lausanne called Aywalla, which my mother Regina, who was the wife of Rainald, count of Mâcon, gave to Marciniac, where she herself has now for many years served God in the habit of a nun under the discipline of Lord Hugh, the venerable abbot.

For my part, I give to the aforesaid place of Cluny whatever came to me by hereditary right from my ancestors at Belmont, which lies in the diocese of Lausanne, and on the neighboring island called the Island of the Counts, insofar as that property pertains to me in people, lands, vineyards, fisheries, and other revenues.

Thus I approve; thus I offer the named possessions for the redemption of my soul, and of Conon, my grandfather and foster-father, [Col. 0980A] and of the rest of my relatives, etc.

Enacted publicly at the village of Berziac (Verzy), into the hands of Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, in the fifteenth indiction, in the eighth year of Lord Pope Paschal II, in the second year of Henry IV, king, and in the fifty-ninth year of the ordination of Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

[Note: In this series of the counts of Mâcon one may observe a custom not rarely used among the ancients: that a grandson bore the name of his grandfather, so that in a certain manner the grandfather seemed to live again in him.]

### XXIV. Charter of a donation for the monastery of Cluny by William and his wife Adeleyda.

[BALUZE, *History of Auvergne*, vol. II, proofs, p. 30.]

Since the authority of divine Scripture testifies to us through Solomon that “a man’s riches are the redemption of his soul” [Col. 0980B], etc., considering these sayings of divine admonition, I, Willelmus, and my wife Adeleyda, for the remedy of our souls and those of our predecessors, have decided to donate from the extent of the estates which God has given us to his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to the Cluniac monastery, over which the venerable Abbot Hugo appears to preside, something in the district of Limagne: namely, the land of Caurossa, with everything contained in it and with its boundaries, on the condition that I transfer and convey perpetually to the aforesaid place and to the monks serving God there the allodial right and whatever property or lordship I possess in it, to be held forever. And so that this charter of conveyance may remain firm and inviolable, we have strengthened it by our authority and caused it to be approved and confirmed by the assent of our faithful [Col. 0980C].

Witness-signature of Willelmus, his son. Witness-signature of Stephanus, his brother.

## XXV. Charter of donation by Willelmus of Thierno to the same Cluniac monastery

*[History of Auvergne, ibid.]*

Since it is most certain to all who judge rightly that all the glory of the present age—or, more truly stated, the entire vain and deceptive falsehood—passes away, etc., I, Willelmus of Thierno, turning these matters over in my mind and at the same time considering with tearful [Col. 0980D] heart the multitude of sins in which I have until now been entangled, resolved, in accordance with Daniel’s counsel, to redeem my sins through almsgiving. And because, alas, to my great sorrow, I have almost withered away from the greenness of good action in the heat of worldly pleasures, I decided at least to support those whose holy life continually offers the fruit of good virtues, since they have been planted by Christ like fruitful trees beside the streams of the holy Scriptures.

For while I feel myself sunk beneath the burdens of my iniquities and stripped of all the feathers of piety, I trust that, through the contemplation of my mind, I shall be lifted on the wings of those who, stripped of the birdlime of all the world’s desires, take on wings like eagles and fly unfailingly toward heavenly things [Col. 0981A]. For this reason, therefore, I give to God, to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to my father and lord Hugo the abbot, and to the other elder Cluniac brothers certain possessions of mine, so that from now on they may possess them by perpetual right and dispose of them as they wish.

These are the following:

First, whatever I possess in lordship in the church or village of Carmis, namely all the revenues, all the customary dues, and all the vicarial rights belonging there, whoever may hold them, so that just as I have held them until now, so from now on the Cluniac elders may hold them.

I also give the village of Siurac, as I held it, together with the customary dues and vicarial rights belonging there.

Likewise, the village of Espentegui, with all its customary dues and vicarial rights [Col. 0981B].

Also half of the enclosed estate of Vensac, with its vicarial right.

Likewise, whatever I possessed at Saint-Pourçain of Borno, with its vicarial rights and customary dues, and as much of the forest of Borno as one league encompasses, in the place which the monks themselves shall choose.

Also forty taxable measures of wine every year in the district of Thierno, ten of beer, and one half-measure of honey; fifty peasants with the customary dues which they owed; and fifty pigs and an equal number of young sheep.

Petrus of Artona, Eldinus of Montalegra, and Petrus of Terzac: these are the witnesses who saw and heard this.

## XXVI. Charter by which Isarnus, bishop of Toulouse, gave the church of Saint Saturninus of Toulouse to the Cluniac monastery [Col. 0981C]

*[Catel, Memoirs of the History of Languedoc, p. 873.]*

In the name of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in whom we are commanded to do whatever we do, in word or deed, and who is the beginning and the end of every good thing.

For the knowledge of those present and those to come, this agreement is written down, which I, Isarnus, by the grace of God bishop of Toulouse, establish and confirm with Hunaldus, abbot of Moissac, concerning the place of Saint Saturninus. I approve and entrust this place to Lord Hugo, abbot of Cluny, and to the aforesaid Abbot Hunaldus, so that God may be served there at all times under the monastic rule [Col. 0981D].

This is the agreement: I retain forever the fourth part of all the offerings of the church of the aforesaid martyr; a personal guardian of the altar; the guardian’s food, to be received from the cloister; and a house for the guardian’s use near the church door, at my pleasure.

I also retain the key of the martyr’s tomb and the key before the altar of Saint Asiclus.

Of everything acquired from the people in the aforesaid church, I retain one third for the church’s works and one third for the bishop, together with one episcopal cubit of candle, another for the provost, another for the dean, another for the sacristan, and another for the works of the same church. I also retain the lighting necessary for my meal, which I customarily receive, and I retain control of all the construction works of the aforesaid church during my lifetime [Col. 0982A].

After my death, it is agreed between us that half of the work of that church shall remain in the power of Saint Stephen and the canons of that see. Once the construction of the aforesaid church has been completed, half of all the offerings of the aforesaid church—namely, those things which are customarily divided among the bishop, the works, and the community of that place—shall belong to Saint Stephen, the bishop, and the canons of that see.

I also retain the meal which I customarily receive on the feast of Saint Saturninus, as it has been established, and one third of everything which shall be offered or given to the aforesaid church for the burial of the dead, beyond five solidi.

Likewise, during my lifetime I retain all the honor of the provostship, deanery, and sacristy [Col. 0982B]. After my death, whatever laymen customarily hold from the aforesaid offices through the hand of the bishop shall remain with Saint Saturninus.

I also retain all the festival stations, as they have been established from ancient times to be held at the see.

I further retain, with the approval and agreement of the aforesaid Abbot Hunaldus and the community of that place, that anyone from the city who wishes to be buried in the cemetery of our see shall be received and buried there without any accusation or contradiction.

All these things written above I, Isarnus, the bishop already named, retain for the benefit of Saint Stephen of our see, for my benefit, and for the benefit of the canons of that see. With regard to the lay fief mentioned above, I have said that it shall belong to Saint Saturninus [Col. 0982C]. And concerning all those things which I retain for myself, my see, and its canons, it is agreed between us that I shall never obstruct anything, transfer anything elsewhere, or create any difficulty against my see or the canons of that see. I make the same agreement concerning all those things which remain the property of Saint Saturninus.

Because of this agreement, and because of the establishment of the aforesaid order, by which the aforementioned Bishop Isarnus consents to and permits the monastic rule to be instituted in the place of Saint Saturninus, I, Guillelmus, count of Toulouse, give, approve, and confirm to that bishop Isarnus that, under penalty of excommunication by the apostolic see or its legate, I shall never oppose him, deprive him of his honor, or inflict any violence upon him.

For the sake of this same agreement, I give and confirm to him that from this day forward I shall exact no judicial dues from any cleric who lives in the suburb or in the city after he has received the tonsure, nor shall I exact judicial dues from his bailiffs or servants who are in the city or the town [Col. 0982D].

All these things, as they are written in this charter, I, the aforesaid count, give, approve, and confirm to God, to Saint Stephen of the aforesaid see, to the aforementioned Bishop Isarnus, and to the canons of that see, present and future. And so that I may never be able to violate them but may always preserve them with firm stability and faithfully observe them, in the name of holy faith I have kissed the aforesaid Bishop Isarnus and the canons of his see.

Furthermore, we establish and determine for perpetual observance that no abbot shall ever be appointed in the aforesaid place of Saint Saturninus. Rather, the aforesaid abbot of Cluny and his successors shall always possess and hold it, together with its prior, through the hand of the bishop and the canons of that see, except for those matters expressly retained above for the benefit of the bishop and the canons of that see, without prejudice to their authority [Col. 0983A].

All this was done in the presence of the aforesaid Abbot Hunaldus; Arnaldu, abbot of Saint Audard; Petrus, prior of Saint Stephen; Ramundus, canon of that same place; Petrus Benedictus; Bernardus Benedictus; Pontius Bernardus of Lavaur; Isarnus Revel; and Pontius Ebrardus.

## XXVII. Charter by which the church of Saint Peter of Céton was given to the Cluniac monastery [Col. 0983B]

*[Bry de la Clergerie, History of the Counties of Alençon and Perche, p. 72.]*

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church, both present and future, that I, Galterius Chesnellus, give to the Lord God almighty, to Saint Peter the apostle of Christ, and to the Cluniac monks who are established at Saint Dionysius in the castle of Nogent in Perche, the church of Saint Peter of Céton, with all its dependencies, everything which I appeared to possess within or outside it: namely, all cultivated and uncultivated land which appeared by right to belong to the church; a cemetery for constructing the monks’ buildings; and also the outer town [Col. 0983C] for building houses for any of their people and for carrying out their entire will.

I also give them the pond for the use of the monks living there to fish, and fishing rights in all my other waters.

I grant them the *voltura* of the mill—the milling of their grain—and the mill-site in the water of Marosaia below Mount Tedbart.

I also add the church of Saint Nicholas, with all its dependencies, cultivated and uncultivated land, and the mill-site below the church.

I likewise remit the *posnadium*—the pannage—of all the pigs of the monks and of their men who serve in that house, throughout all my forests, except only the forest called Corbonum. If my pigs roam in that forest, the monks’ pigs likewise may roam there.

For constructing their buildings and those of all their people, and for heating, I grant them wood throughout all my forests, except the forest of Corbonum.

I also give them all my share of the tithe of the land of Céton and of all my woods, if crops are produced in them.

If any persons hold something of my fief and wish to give it, sell it, or place it in pledge, I most willingly grant permission, on this condition: that they may make no gift or sale to any other place except to the monks of Saint Peter of Cluny [Col. 0984A].

I further add to the aforesaid church of Saint Peter as much of my meadows as can supply grass for one plough throughout the entire year.

I make this gift for the redemption of my soul and those of my father and mother, and for all my relatives, both living and dead, so that the Lord, through the intercession of all the saints, may have mercy on all of us in the present age and in the future.

I make this gift with the consent of my brother Ivo Chesnellus, who later received one horse for his approval, with which he went to Jerusalem.

Lord Count Rogerius also approved and confirmed it, and caused it to be confirmed by his sons, Lord Robert and Lord Hugo.

If anyone should wish to bring a legal claim against this gift, he shall have no share in mercy because of it; and unless he repents and takes refuge in satisfaction, let him perish in eternal damnation with the devil and his angels.

I too shall strive, with God’s help, to resist him until, convicted and reduced to nothing, he is compelled by judicial authority to pay thirty pounds of gold.

And so that this charter may remain firm, these are the witnesses who saw and heard it:

Lord Hoellus, bishop of Le Mans; Guicherius, dean; Gauffridus and another Gauffridus, archdeacons [Col. 0984C]; Fulchradus, archpriest; Guandabertus, archdeacon; Hubertus, archpriest; Oddo and Hesgodres, canons; Hildebertus and Orricus; Rodulfus and Gradulfus, canons; Lord Rogerius, count; Lord Robert and Lord Hugo, his sons; Guillelmus Goiettus; Gulferus of Villeray; Bernardus of La Ferté; Rotrocus of Montfort; Guillelmus Anatomus; Guillelmus Guittardus; Bladinus, provost; Gerogius of Ulmo; Richerius and Girardus Forestarius; Ivo Paganus of Villa-perdita; and Durannus, Gerogius’s man.

Let all Catholics also know that, in all the gifts mentioned above, and in my lordship, and in everything which my men have given or shall give, I have given and conceded, with the consent of my brother Yvo, all the customary dues which I possessed in them: namely, toll, vicarial jurisdiction, theft, arson, abduction, and whatever customary due is usually sought or named in this land [Col. 0984D].

[Col. 0985]

## In the year of the Lord 1110

# Walramus, Bishop of Naumburg

[Col. 0985]

## Historical Notice

*[Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Lower Latin Literature, vol. VI, p. 313.]*

Walramus, also written by others as Waleramus, Gualeramus, or Walrabanus, was bishop of Naumburg from 1090 to 1110. His works are:

1. A letter to Ludwig, landgrave of Thuringia, in which he urges him, after abandoning the pope, to show loyalty to the emperor. Dodechinus published it in the Appendix to Marianus Scotus under the year 1090; Baronius, under that year, no. 8; Goldastus in *Apologia pro Henrico IV*, p. 51; Lunigius in *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, Imperial Archives, part II, appendix, p. 146; and Leuckfeld in *Antiquities of Halberstadt*, p. 693. Ludwig, however, sharply refutes our author in a response said to have been written by Herrandus, bishop of Halberstadt.

2. *On Preserving the Unity of the Church and on the Schism between the Emperor and the Pope.* It was first discovered by Ulrich Hutten and published at Mainz in 1520, in quarto. Simon Schardius later inserted it into his collection *On the Jurisdiction and Authority of the Empire*, giving it first place; Goldastus then included it in the *Apologia pro Henrico IV*, p. 53. See Jacob Burckhard, *On the Life of Hutten*, part II, p. 28, and our work above, book III, p. 420.

3. A short treatise on the investiture of bishops by emperors, in Schardius’s collection *On Imperial Jurisdiction*, no. 14.

4. Martène and Durand published his letter on Saint Leonard the Confessor in *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 635. It was addressed to the most illustrious matron, Lady Gertrude, who, as the editors conjecture, was the daughter of Ecbert, margrave of Saxony—or rather of Meissen—the widow of Count Henry of Northeim, and grandmother of Emperor Lothair.

5. Fabricius mentions another letter to Anselm of Canterbury, which appears in Anselm’s works, p. 137 and following, with notes added on p. 578, above, vol. I, p. 112.

6. His letter to the Church of Bamberg is also found in the Udalrician manuscript, vol. II of Johann Georg Eckard’s *Corpus of Medieval Writers*, p. 263. In it he indicates that an excommunicated person must be avoided.

Add concerning him the *Acts and Deeds of the Bishops of Naumburg* in the *Paullinian Syntagma*, p. 133, and Sagittarius’s *History of the Bishops of Naumburg*, §11.

# Walramus’s Letter to Ludwig, Landgrave of Thuringia, with a Refutation Published under the Name of the Landgrave by Stephanus, Bishop of Halberstadt

*[Baronius, Annals, under the year 1090, no. 8.]*

[Col. 0985A]

## Commentary

In this same year, Bertholdus asserts that the illustrious confessors and champions of the Catholics, Herimannus, bishop of Metz, and Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, departed this life. He likewise asserts that Ecgbert, the margrave, and Berthold, the duke, were also taken from the world—vigorous champions of the Catholics. Thus the way was opened for Emperor Henry to go once more into Italy against Matilda.

With Catholic affairs collapsing in Germany, Bishop Walramus of Magdeburg was given the opportunity to write a letter to Count Ludwig . . . in which he urged him, abandoning the Catholics, to adhere to King Henry. Dodechinus reproduces it in the Appendix to Marianus, together with the reply made against it, in which the same case is argued skillfully and prudently. The first of these, sent by Walramus, bishop of Magdeburg, is as follows:

[Col. 0986A]

## Walramus’s Letter

“Walramus, by the grace of God what he is, to Ludwig, most serene prince, offering himself with the urgency of prayers as wholly devoted to everything.

“Concord is useful to every kingdom, and justice is desirable; for this virtue is the mother of integrity and the preservation of all honor. But whoever, by stirring up internal dissension, provokes others to the shedding of human blood is certainly a man of blood and a participant with him who, thirsting for our blood, always ‘goes about seeking someone to devour’ (1 Peter 5). [Col. 0987A]

“You therefore, most glorious prince, observing that ‘God is the God of peace and not of dissension’ (1 Corinthians 14), should, as far as depends upon you, have peace with everyone. God is love; the devil is hatred. The whole law and the prophets depend upon love (Matthew 12). ‘Whoever hates his brother is a murderer’ (1 John 3), and he has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

“This is proclaimed by Truth itself; this is proclaimed by that disciple of Truth who, having drunk more deeply from the Lord’s breast the truth of the Gospel, makes the city of God rejoice more abundantly with the force of a river. But that chosen vessel, who was caught up even to the third heaven and learned his Gospel not according to man but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, says: ‘Let every soul be subject to higher powers, for there is no power except from God. Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God’ (Romans 13).”

“As our friends dream among little women and the simple crowd that one ought not to be subject to royal power, they therefore say that it is false that every soul ought to be subject to power. But should Truth be accused of falsehood? Or are we seeking to test him through whom Christ spoke in the Apostle? ‘Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?’ (1 Corinthians 10.) The man who resists God’s ordinance considers himself stronger, since there is no power except from God.

“But what does the prophet say? ‘Let all who fight against you, Lord, be put to shame’ (Isaiah 41). And: ‘The men who resist you shall perish’ (ibid.). Rudolf, Hildebrand, Ecbert, and countless princes resisted God’s ordinance in Emperor Henry, and behold, as though they had never existed, they perished, because the beginning of those whose end was so evil must certainly have been evil.

“Now, since those who are on the opposing side fight against us from a distance with their arguments, let us submit the matter to your judgment, or rather bring it before your judgment, using as our courtroom not our own but Christ’s and the testimony of the ancient Fathers. And lest it perhaps be rejected, let this be the law of the contest: either let me pass over to the judgment of the peoples, or let us win you for our Lord the emperor by our triumph.

“Let this also be considered: ‘If anyone preaches another gospel to you besides what was preached to you, let him be accursed’ (Galatians 1). This anathema was not thundered by an instrument of profane vanity, but from the third heaven [Col. 0987D]. Of those who, ignorant of ‘the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, are not subject to God’s justice’ (Romans 10), I may confidently say: ‘Let them curse, but you will bless; let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant shall rejoice’ (Psalm 108), because, as the Lord says, ‘without me you can do nothing’ (John 15), nor do you condemn the just when he is judged. ‘Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master’ (Romans 14).”

[Col. 0987]

## Commentary

Thus far the letter of Walramus, whom the political thinkers of our age may establish as the author and defender of their own doctrine.

“Having received this letter,” Dodechinus continues, “the aforesaid Count Ludwig summoned the venerable Stephanus—also called Herrandus—bishop of Halberstadt, handed it to him to read, and asked him, after he had examined it carefully, to meet it with an appropriate reply in accordance with the rule of truth, and to close the mouth of the blasphemer (Romans 3) and the mouth that uttered iniquity against justice by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the testimony of Scripture, so that he might no longer utter insane barking against the Church of God or rage against it.

“The venerable bishop, having received the letter at the count’s request and examined it carefully, summoned a notary and dictated a letter. In it he first reproached Bishop Walramus as a heretic and a Simoniac; he also proved that King Henry was a heretic and excommunicated, and therefore should not be called king. He declared that Henry sold bishoprics for money, for the sword, for adultery, and for Sodomitic impurity. But let the text of that letter itself be presented, so that the fervor of that venerable man in maintaining justice may be recognized.”

[Col. 0988B]

## Ludwig’s Response

“Count Ludwig to Lord Walramus: whatever is worthy of such a title.

“Just as a good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, so an evil man brings forth evil from an evil treasure. Whence comes such arrogance in you that you provoke me to indignation with such insulting insults? You obliquely call my lords and fathers—men who strengthen me on the path of justice—men of blood like Satan, and you say that the counsels of salvation which they offer are dreams among little women and the simple crowd.

“Does God need your judgment, that you should speak deceitfully on his behalf? Iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers, so that the Prophet rightly says of you: ‘He refused to understand, that he might do good; he devised iniquity upon his bed’ (Psalm 35) [Col. 0988C].

“Although you have spoken as perversely as you are perverse, we nevertheless resolved to keep watch over our mouth, and we kept silent ‘when the sinner stood against us’ (Psalm 38). But divine speech rouses us, saying: ‘Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself’ (Proverbs 26).

“Shall folly resound while wisdom is silent? Shall falsehood speak while truth is silent? Shall darkness cover the earth and the Lord not rise? Rather, ‘the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ (John 1). Through this reflection, ‘our heart grew hot, and in our meditation the fire burned’ (Psalm 38).

“We therefore speak and cry out, and as far as we can restrain ‘the little foxes that destroy the Lord’s vineyards’ (Song of Songs 2) [Col. 0988D], fearing that prophecy which reproves us: ‘You have not gone up to the breach, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord’ (Ezekiel 13).

“Let all sensible people who have ears to hear listen—not you, who have ears and do not hear, who have eyes and do not see (Psalm 113), who have made the light within you darkness. Let them listen, I say, to how profoundly you either do not understand or pretend not to understand, neither what you say nor the matters about which you assert anything (1 Timothy 1).

“You invite us to submit to Lord Henry, whom they call emperor, and—as far as can be understood—you impose the necessity of being subject to him in all things, as though by apostolic argument, saying: ‘Let every soul be subject to higher powers; for there is no power except from God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God’ (Romans 13).

“We say that you understand the Apostle’s sentence badly and interpret it worse. For if every power is from God, as you understand it, what does the Lord mean when he says through the prophet of certain men: ‘They have reigned, but not from me; they have set up princes, and I did not know them’ (Hosea 8)? If every power is from God, as you understand it, what does the Lord mean when he says: ‘If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you’ (Mark 9)? For what is power except an eye?

“Certainly Augustine, in his exposition of the apostolic sentence (Romans 13), ‘Let every soul be subject to higher powers,’ says: ‘If a power commands something which is against God, disregard that power; by fearing [not fearing] the power; otherwise, is there iniquity with the Lord?’ (Romans 9). Is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Far be it! What then shall we say? Is a different prophetic judgment proclaimed by the Apostle? Augustine replies: Certainly not. One Spirit blows different pipes.

“Let us therefore hear the Apostle in agreement with himself, explaining himself and destroying his own enemy and avenger: ‘There is no power,’ he says, ‘except from God.’ What follows? ‘Whoever, you say, resists the power’ (Romans 13), and the rest. Far be it! That does not follow. What does follow? ‘Those powers which exist have been ordained by God’ (ibid.).

“This is precisely what we are asking. O deceitful tongue! O heart plotting evil! O spirit going away and not returning, why have you lied to the Holy Spirit? Let your conscience accuse you. Behold, the wicked flees when no one pursues him. Why did you wish to suppress the truth in order to deceive? Why did you steal the marrow, why the soul, of this sentence?

“For if these words are removed from the middle of the apostolic sentence, it will lie opposite to itself, incoherent and lifeless. The divine word is fulfilled: ‘Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it’ (Proverbs 26). Certainly you will be unable to escape either guilt or punishment by force. Unhappy man, what will you answer to the coming Judge when he demands a place [perhaps: *lucrum*, “profit”] from his merchant servants, since you have brought forth a fraud against the Lord’s money?

“Why did you not fear the judgment and the noose of the betrayer, lest a similar guilt be followed by a similar vengeance? The Apostle, foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that you and others like you—heretics who would arise in the Church—would call good evil and evil good, and would make darkness light and light darkness (Isaiah 5), and would seek opportunities for introducing error from the judgments of truth, first said: ‘There is no power except from God,’ and then, to cut off the interpretation of a reprobate mind, added: ‘Those powers which exist have been ordained by God.’

“Give us, therefore, an ordained power, and we shall not resist; indeed, we shall immediately yield our hands.

“But I wonder whether there is even a drop of blood in you, since you are not ashamed to call Lord Henry king or to say that he possesses an order. Does an order, in your view, grant the right to crime and allow divine and human law, right and wrong, to be confused? Does it seem to you an order to sin against one’s own body—namely, shame upon shame, wickedness upon wickedness—to turn one’s own wife into a brothel through a crime unheard of throughout all the ages of the world? [Col. 0990A]

“Does it seem to you an order, when the Lord says, ‘Defend the widow’ (Isaiah 1), to prostitute widows who demand the justice of judgment through unspeakable contamination?

“Let anyone who calls these things orderly and sound swear that he is of unsound mind; the insane Orestes himself would swear it.

“Until these most miserable times, nature loved secrecy. But your king, handed over to a reprobate mind, has uncovered nature’s veil and exposed every shame openly.

“To say nothing of those innumerable matters—namely, the burning of churches, plundering, murders, arsons, mutilations, and things like them—which he is able to commit but which we cannot enumerate [Col. 0990B], let us speak of the things that weigh most heavily upon the Church of God. Hear the truth, not what is disguised; hear what is grave, not what is witty.

“Everyone who sells spiritual dignities is a heretic. But Lord Henry, whom they call king, sells bishoprics and abbeys. He sold Constance, Bamberg, Mainz, and many others for money; Regensburg, Augsburg, and Strasbourg for the sword; the abbey of Fulda for adultery; and the bishopric of Münster—for it is wicked even to say or hear it—for Sodomitic impurity.

“If you impudently wish to deny these things, with the earth as witness, all the little scholars returning even from the oven will conclude that they are true. Therefore Lord Henry is a heretic. Excommunicated by the apostolic see for these unspeakable evils, he will be able to obtain neither the kingdom nor any power over us, because we are Catholics [Col. 0990C].

“Indeed, since you weary us with hatred of our brothers, understand that we direct hatred against no one from lack of affection but from piety. Far be it from us to say that Henry should be counted among brothers or Christians: because he so often refuses to listen when the Church corrects him, he is regarded as a heathen and a tax collector.

“We offer our hatred of him to God as a great sacrifice, saying with the Psalmist: ‘Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and do I not waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me’ (Psalm 138).

“Commending the dignity of this hatred, Truth says: ‘If anyone does not hate father and mother and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14) [Col. 0990D].

“Therefore those who reproach us for hatred do not do so justly, since, if we stray from the way of God, we are commanded to hate our soul, our father and mother, and every affection that obstructs us on God’s way. Hence, with every diligence and effort, we labor to beware of the enemies of the Church as adversaries ourselves, and to hate them not because they are our enemies but because they are enemies of God.

“As for your urging us to have peace with all human beings, you must remember that the Apostle prefaced this by saying, ‘If it is possible’ (Romans 12).

“It is not possible, however, for us to have peace with those who oppose God. Who does not know that the Lord and Savior not only commends peace when he says, ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’ (John 14), but is himself peace, as the Apostle says: ‘He himself is our peace, who made both one’ (Ephesians 2)?

“What then does our peace say in commending peace? ‘Do not think,’ he says, ‘that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace but a sword’ (Matthew 10).

“What is this? Why does peace bring a sword? Why does peace declare war? Clearly, so that the devil’s peace may be destroyed. For the devil too has his peace, of which the Lord says: ‘When a strong man, fully armed, guards his court, what he possesses is in peace’ (Luke 11).

“O how powerfully the devil now guards his court through you, his satellites! Protected by the shield of falsehood and the helmet of faithlessness, you admit no darts of truth [Col. 0991B] and no arrows of faith. Yet our Lord, coming upon him as the stronger armed man, can overcome your strong man and take away the weapons in which he trusts.

“We are therefore not rightly blamed if we detest that peace, more cruel than any war, which Truth itself condemns while weeping over Jerusalem, saying: ‘If only you had known, even on this day, the things that are for your peace’ (Luke 19). The Psalm also says: ‘I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners’ (Psalm 72).

“As for your condemning Pope Gregory, King Rudolf, and Margrave Ecbert to the worst death, while praising your lord because he has outlived them, it is clear that you remain entirely empty of all spiritual consideration.

“Is it not more blessed to die well than to live badly? ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake’ (Matthew 5) [Col. 0992A].

“By this reasoning you would also consider Nero blessed because he outlived the apostles Peter and Paul, Herod because he outlived the apostle James, and Pilate because he outlived the Lord Jesus Christ. What could be said that is more insane or wretched than such an opinion?

“Therefore restrain your grandiloquent tongue from this blasphemy, unless perhaps you count yourself among those who, at the end, seeing the glory of the righteous and practicing late and fruitless repentance, will groan in anguish of spirit and say:

“‘These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made an object of reproach. We foolishly regarded their life as madness and their end as dishonor. Behold how they have been counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the sun of justice did not shine upon us. What did pride profit us, and what did the boast of riches bring us? All things have passed like a shadow’ (Wisdom 5).

“Writing these words in adamantine memory, we despise every likeness that exalts itself against the truth of God. Though we glory in tribulations, we can be slandered, proscribed, banished, and finally killed; we cannot be bent or conquered.

“And with great rejoicing we celebrate that which you, as a boy growing into manhood, though not yet old in heart, have conceived concerning our fathers: they, despising the commands of princes, deserved eternal rewards.

“Moreover, weighing your statements with careful attention, we wish, as it were, to compare spiritual things with spiritual things. But as …” and much else.

[Col. 0991B]

# Walramus’s Letter to the Church of Bamberg

*[Eccard, Corpus of Medieval History, vol. II, p. 263.]*

[Col. 0991C]

To the most serene lords and most reverend brothers of the holy Church of Bamberg, G. V., bishop of Naumburg, offering servile service with the urgency of prayer and devoting himself entirely to every duty.

It is brotherly to help a brother, and it befits all good men to repel the violence of the wicked. We inform your fraternity that H., together with his satellites, has plundered my provostship. Since we summoned him to make satisfaction under canonical truce, [Col. 0992C] but he does not wish to come, we earnestly beg you—and, in return for this fraternal service, admonish you—that whoever among you possesses this authority should notify him in his prelacy that he has been canonically excommunicated both from the boundaries of the Church and from the fellowship of the faithful. You, too, should regard him as excommunicated and compel him, as a rebel and blasphemer, to make satisfaction.

[Col. 0992C]

## VALRAM’S LETTER ON THE LIFE OF SAINT LEONARD THE CONFESSOR

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 635.)

[Col. 0993A]

Valeramus, by the grace of God bishop of Huenburg, sends devoted service, urgent prayers, and himself wholly devoted in every respect to the most serene matron, Lady Gertrude.

[Note: [Col. 0993C] She is, as we conjecture, Gertrude, daughter of Margrave Ecbert of Saxony, widow of Count Henry of Nordheim, and mother of the noble Otto, of Rixa, wife of Emperor Lothair, and of Gertrude, countess palatine. She deposited the relics of the blessed author, brought from Trier, in the monastery she herself founded at Brunswick in the year of Christ 1115. After a course of two years, as is read in the *History of the Translation* published by Godefrid Libnitius, she happily entered the life of all flesh on 9 December.]

God is wonderful in his saints, and when someone’s mind has been divinely inflamed, the divine miracles ought frequently to be proclaimed. Mary is said to have chosen the better part because, sitting at the Lord’s feet, she listened to his word; whereas Martha is censured for being excessively anxious over the manifold administration of bodily nourishment and for being troubled about many things. Yet, he says, there is one thing necessary, which is divided into parts and tends toward an end; but the one highest good is true eternity and blessedness in itself.

Let fools be carried away by the worthless vanities of this age; but for you, in accordance with the Savior’s admonition, let one thing appear necessary: that you may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of your life, see the Lord’s will, and visit his temple. The daughters of Babylon gather riches for those whom they do not know; but you, storing up treasure in heaven, have surpassed them all.
