Therefore continue what you are doing; perform what you are performing: build a house for Christ and a sanctuary for the Holy Spirit, so that when the house of this earthly dwelling is dissolved, you may find in heaven a house not made by human hands: the city of our strength, Zion the Savior, the heavenly Jerusalem, whose participation is in itself.

Blessed are you who believe, because what you have seen with your eyes you carry out in your works. Thus Saint Leonard first founded a small church in honor of holy Mary. Dwelling there all the days of his life, he was at last transferred from this valley to the mountain of virtues, where all who rejoice have their dwelling.

Blessed be God, because you too, like a turtledove, have found a nest—the altar of the Lord of hosts—where, would that through the intercession of Saint Leonard miracles might be wrought for the salvation of the whole homeland, just as we see them everywhere in the oratories of Saint Leonard, unless the unbelief of all obstructs the miracles.

The perversity of the heretics had grown especially fierce against Christians in the time of Saint Leonard. Therefore, as we have learned from the living voice of the brothers, their malice utterly destroyed the miracles and works of Saint Leonard in this life, or defamed them by adverse interpretation, as it did in the case of our Savior himself.

After his passing, however, their envy added crime to crime, and, so that his memory might be entirely removed from the earth, his Life was burned wherever it could be found. How great, how unusual, and finally how incredible are the miracles performed through him every day—no history of antiquity, in my opinion, reveals anything comparable.

Saint Leonard, as I have truly perceived for myself, is always a helper at the invocation of the desolate, most merciful in times of need and in tribulation. He descends from heaven with a face radiant like the sun, starry eyes, and a garment of dazzling whiteness. At his touch, every hardness of iron is softened like wax before fire; thus captives, released from their bonds, are divinely carried across rivers that block their flight.

He performs many miracles of this kind, surpassing belief, but they are in no way to be denied by the faithful. Just as through Saint Leonard Bohemond recovered his full power from pagan captivity, and the English king recovered his from the tyranny of his brother, so through that same wondrous saint may the Lord also enlarge you toward the east and toward the west, toward the north and toward the south, and may your goodness increase a thousandfold.

May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies, and may all the tribes of Germany be blessed in you. May your excellence increase into thousands upon thousands. Believe faithfully and do not doubt at all, because what I have shared with you of the relics of that wondrous saint I obtained by hearing his very voice, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows.

And lest unbelievers denounce me as an impostor, I trust in his goodness that, because of your devotion, the same thing will happen for you to experience, especially since it has been confirmed by the testimony of many that the most merciful saint speaks with the desolate as one person speaks with a friend.

[Col. 0993B]

## VALRAM’S LETTER TO SAINT ANSELM

He complains about the diversity of ceremonies customarily observed in different ways by different people during the sacrifice of the altar. (It stands among the works of Saint Anselm, prefixed to the treatise *On the Diversity of the Sacraments*. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVIII.)

## Around the Year of the Lord 1110

# GILBERT, BISHOP IN IRELAND OF LIMERICK

[Col. 0993C]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, III, 57)

Gilbert, bishop in Ireland of Lunicensis [also Lumnicensis], today Limerick, around the year 1110 and still living in 1139, wrote a little book *On the State of the Church*, published by Usher in *Irish Letters*, p. 78, and wrongly attributed to Gilbert Crispin by Pitseus, p. 196. Usher prefixed to it a letter of the same Gilbert to the bishops and priests of Ireland, p. 77, followed on p. 88 by another brief letter to Anselm of Canterbury.

[Col. 0995]

## GILBERT OF LIMERICK TO THE BISHOPS OF IRELAND, ON ECCLESIASTICAL USAGE

(USHER, *Irish Letters*, p. 77.)

[Col. 0995A]

To the bishops and priests of all Ireland, Gille of Limerick, the least of the bishops, sends greetings in Christ.

At the request, and also at the command, of many of you, dearest brothers, I have attempted to write down the canonical custom for learning the hours and carrying out the entire office of the ecclesiastical order. I do this not presumptuously, but wishing to obey your most devout command, so that those diverse and schismatic orders by which almost the whole of Ireland has been misled may yield to one Catholic and Roman Office.

For what could be called more indecent or schismatic than for someone most learned in one order to become an ignorant and layman-like person in another Church? Whoever, therefore, professes himself a member of the Catholic Church, just as he is joined to the body by one faith, hope, and charity, so he is commanded to praise God with his mouth and according to one order together with the other members.

Hence the Apostle says: “That with one mind and one mouth you may glorify God” (Romans 15:6). Therefore, just as the dispersion of languages, brought about through pride, was led back to unity through apostolic humility, so the confusion of orders, arising through negligence and presumption, must through your diligence and humility be led back to the consecrated rule of the Roman Church.

Although it is clear from many passages of Sacred Scripture how much unity of conduct ought to be preserved by the faithful, the present painted image of the Church, placed before our eyes, plainly demonstrates it. For it shows that all the members of the Church are subject to one bishop, namely Christ, and to his vicar, the blessed apostle Peter, as well as to the apostolic ruler presiding in Peter’s seat, and that they are governed by them.

For this small work I ask this reward from all of you: that, just as here we ought to praise God with one heart and one mouth, so, aided by your prayers, I may deserve to be able to sing psalms with you in the heavenly places. Amen.

[Note: In the manuscripts used here, the following was appended: the painted image of the Church—mentioned in the preceding prologue and explained in the next little book—surrounded by this περιγραφῇ (*perigraphē*, “outline”). The ark had the figure of the world, for it had three chambers. In the upper part were birds, like angels in heaven. In the middle were human beings—namely Noah and his family—as in this world. At the bottom were animals and reptiles, like souls in hell. But, because of the shortage of engraved type, we were compelled to omit that diagram here.]

[Col. 0997]

## GILBERT OF LIMERICK’S BOOK ON THE STATE OF THE CHURCH

(USHER, ibid., p. 78.)

[Col. 0997A]

The general image of the Church noted above contains the initial letters of the names instead of the names themselves, because the space for writing does not contain all the names in full. The lowest line, however, writes out these three complete words: nuns, canons, and all-encompassing. The entire image presents the form of a pyramid, because below it is broad, where it receives the carnal and married; above it is pointed, where it proposes the narrow way to religious and ordained persons. Nor is only the general form narrowed above; the individual figures contained within it also taper to a point at the top.

The first pyramid, which you see on the left with P written beneath it, is called a parish. At its summit it has a priest, and under him a deacon, a subdeacon, an acolyte, an exorcist, a lector, and a doorkeeper. Amalarius, however, says that there are nine grades of the Church, adding the psalmist and the bishop.

Nevertheless, the bishop, archbishop, patriarchs, and prophets are general grades of the Church. The individual parish is therefore complete only with those upper grades because, by granting forgiveness in baptism and in the Lord’s body, it sends its faithful children to the heavenly homeland. Since anyone in the choir can, simply by the priest’s command, perform the office of psalmist—that is, sing psalms or chant—we do not include psalmists among the grades of the Church.

Thus seven grades have been bestowed on the individual Churches by the sevenfold Spirit. Although individual persons do not serve in all of them, the priest alone, sustaining all seven grades, gratefully ministers to the Almighty.

Those who are contained beneath these grades within the bosom of the parish Church are divided in three ways. Of these, understand those above in the pyramid to be the ones who pray; because some of them are married, we have called them men and women. Those on the left side of the pyramid are the ones who till the soil, both men and women. Those on the right are the ones who fight, men and women alike.

I do not mean that it is the office of women to pray, till, or indeed fight; rather, they are married to and serve those who pray, till, and fight. Nor do we think that those women are separated from the present Church whom Christ places with his mother in the heavenly Church.

From the beginning the Church admits these three legitimate orders of the faithful: one part of it—namely, the clergy—devotes itself to prayer and defends the others from the assault of the deceitful enemy; another, laboring with toil, drives away the others’ lack of food; the third, devoted to the discipline of warfare, keeps the others safe from bodily enemies.

[Col. 0997D]

The second pyramid is labeled “monastery.” At its summit it has an abbot, and beneath him six grades. He himself is a priest, and beneath these are only those who pray, because it is not the monks’ task to baptize, administer Communion, or provide any ecclesiastical service to laypeople, unless perhaps, compelled by necessity, they obey a commanding bishop. Their purpose is to devote themselves to prayer for God alone, having abandoned worldly affairs.

These two pyramids—the parish and the monastery—are possessed as subordinate by the episcopal Church. It too, in the form of a pyramid, is broad at the base because of the two smaller pyramids, and becomes pointed at the top. It is labeled “bishopric,” because it is directed by the bishop in the highest seat.

Because of the limited space, a small pyramid marked with dots is placed beneath it, to indicate that the bishop in the church of his own see has priests and the other six grades, as well as the three orders of the faithful mentioned above; this is clear from the number of dots.

The reason why only two Churches are made subject to the bishop is not that he could be content with two, but that through one he is represented as possessing all the parishes, and through the other all the abbeys that he governs. At a minimum he possesses ten Churches, and at a maximum a thousand.

In the same order, two further pyramids—the parish and the monastery—are shown subordinate to the bishop. Again, two bishops, together with their Churches, are placed under one archbishop. His Church is labeled “diocese”; it has in its own see seven grades and three orders of the faithful.

Thus, outside the parishes and monastery, he governs at most twenty bishops and at least three. In the same manner two other bishops are attached to another archbishop. Two archbishops, together with their Churches and bishops, obey one primate. His Church is labeled “primacy”; it has in its own see seven grades and three orders of the faithful, and outside it the parish and monastery. At most six archbishops obey him, and at least one.

In the same way, on the second page, two archbishops with their four bishops obey another primate.

[Col. 0998D]

Finally, two primates serve one supreme Roman pontiff, the pope, whose Church is labeled “universal” and contains the parish, monastery, bishops, and dioceses. Noah also sits with him at the top of the ark, because just as Noah presided over the ark amid the waves of the Flood, so the Roman pontiff governs the Church amid the waves of the world.

Christ stands above both of them. He is the legislator of both Testaments and made the two one (Ephesians 2:14), the supreme master of the household, who honorably crowns those who keep watch faithfully in this tabernacle in the kingdom.

The emperor is joined to the pope, the king to the primate, the duke to the archbishop, the count to the bishop, and the knight to the priest, because these persons are judged by law to be their equals among secular ranks.

Having completed our common consideration of the figures, members, and head of the Church, let us now explain what is proper to each order.

The married are forbidden to take as wife any woman related to them by blood as far as the sixth or even seventh generation, or a woman whom a close relative has or has had, or a godmother. For the Church says that it is unlawful to contract such a union again with those to whom one has once been joined.

The married are also commanded to attend the house of the Lord and there humbly worship and pray to God; to pay their first fruits, offerings, and tithes faithfully; to avoid evil diligently; to seek good eagerly; and in every respect to obey their pastors.

The office of doorkeepers is to designate the appointed hours by observing them and to guard the church together with what is enclosed in it. They must take care that no Jew, gentile, or catechumen be present at the hour of the sacrifice, and that no dog or any unclean or bloodstained creature enter it; they must expel the excommunicated.

The office of lectors is to read aloud and distinctly everything in the church except the Epistle and the Gospel.

The office of exorcists is to drive demons from possessed bodies by adjuring and commanding them confidently in the Lord’s name, whether those possessed are catechumens or baptized.

The office of acolytes is to light and extinguish the lamps at the appointed hours and to keep ready at the subdeacon’s hand the things necessary for the altar and sacrifice.

These four orders customarily wear in their offices a shoulder garment, an alb, and a girdle; nevertheless, they may enjoy marriage.

The office of subdeacons is to read the Epistle, pour water and wine into the chalice, place the offering on the paten, and thus carry it to the altar for the deacon. For this reason they must be chaste.

Together with the garments mentioned above, they carry in their left hand the *fanon*, something like a broom for wiping the altar, and they bear a certain light burden of the Lord. At solemn celebrations they wear a tunic with tight sleeves.

The office of deacons is to say: “Let those who do not communicate go out”; “Humble yourselves for the blessing”; “Bow your heads before God”; “Go, the dismissal is made”; and “Let us bless the Lord.” It is also their office to read and proclaim the Gospel, to place the sacrifices upon the corporals, to minister to the priest, to bless the paschal candle, and, in the absence of a priest, to baptize and celebrate the hours. They also carry the stole over the left shoulder and wear the dalmatic at solemn celebrations—that is, a tunic with wide sleeves.

On feast days during Lent, however, the deacon and subdeacon wear chasubles throughout the entire Mass, except when they are reading.

The priests’ offices are fourteen: to preside, to be subject, to pray, to offer, to preach, to teach, to baptize, to bless, to excommunicate, to reconcile, to anoint, to administer Communion, to commend souls to God, and to bury bodies. Each of these must be discussed.

To preside is the priest’s office: to judge justly concerning each of his subjects, to impose penance correctly and mercifully, and to command gently.

To be subject is to humble and devote oneself sincerely to the bishop and serve him.

To offer is to sacrifice bread and wine with water every day, and on solemn occasions to sing the *Te Deum*, the *Benedictus*, and the *Magnificat*, and before the sacrifice to burn incense over and around the altar and the sacrifice. The deacon incenses the altar before the Gospel.

It is also his office to pray: humbly to worship God as his creature, to praise him for his wondrous works, to bless him and give thanks for the benefits received, and to plead for those still to be received. All this is carried out especially in the celebration of the hours and of Mass; since it cannot be treated briefly, it will be discussed below.

It is also his office to preach: to call gentiles, Jews, unbelievers, and catechumens to the grace of baptism, and to lead heretics back to the Catholic faith.

To baptize is to immerse in the sacred font, under a threefold immersion, those who have been exorcised, believe, and confess the Holy Trinity. This, like Mass, ought to take place in a church, unless necessity prevents it.

The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood is performed frequently in remembrance of his Passion, as he himself commanded when he said: “This is my body, and this is my blood; do this whenever you receive it in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24–25).

Baptism, however, is not repeated, lest the invocation of the Holy Trinity be thought to have been emptied of meaning, since Christ died once for our sins (1 Peter 3:18).

To teach is to instruct the baptized how they are to be armed against pride with humility, against empty glory with abasement, against envy with benevolence, against anger with moderation, against sadness with cheerfulness, against avarice with generosity, against gluttony with abstinence, and against lust with chastity.

These eight vices, and everything that arises from them, although they are not themselves sins, nevertheless always urge people to sin by consenting to them. For as long as the mind does not consent to them, it does not transgress at all, but rather is crowned.

It is also the priest’s office to preach on each Sunday on which days of the week the faithful ought to fast and abstain from work.

A priest may, in the presence of the bishop, bless water and salt on Sundays, as well as a meal, a bridegroom, a bride, and those about to read lessons other than the Gospel, and the water of judgment, or bread, and other things. [Note: See Juretus’s observations on Ivo’s Letter 74.]

In the bishop’s absence, he may bless a cleric’s tonsure and a widow’s veil, new fruits, candles on the Purification of holy Mary, ashes on the first day of the fast, branches on Palm Sunday, pilgrims, one who is about to read the Gospel, and the people when they are dismissed. He sprinkles blessed water for the blessing of new houses and other new things.

To excommunicate is to exclude from the communion of the faithful those who have fallen into crimes, after they have been recalled once, twice, and three times, if they do not repent, so that no one may share with them either in food or in conversation.

To reconcile is to receive penitents near death, with the bishop’s consent, back into the unity of the faithful after serious offenses.

He may anoint any member of the faithful once during each serious illness, because holy anointing often brings healing not only to the soul but also to the body.

He must administer Communion immediately to the baptized, and to all the faithful three times a year—at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas—and to those near death if they request it by word or sign, or if a faithful witness testifies that they had requested it earlier.

[Col. 1001B]

He must commend to God in prayer the souls of the faithful departing from their bodies, and frequently remember them in the Mass and in prayers.

Although indulgence has been promised to the sinner whenever he repents, punishment nevertheless awaits every sinner: namely, purgatorial fire, which receives for purification those who have immediately departed from the body and have been insufficiently cleansed through the lamentation of repentance.

Therefore, what is done here on their behalf in prayers and almsgiving benefits them for purification, because the sweat of the living is the rest of the dead.

To bury the bodies of the faithful is the priest’s final office. He himself casts earth three times over the body with the gravedigger, saying: “From earth you fashioned me.”

Beside the cemeteries of the saints there are also other places in which the bodies of drowned or slain faithful are buried, because their souls are not forbidden to be commended to God. The bodies of unbelievers and criminals, however, must be cast far from those of the faithful; for those with whom we do not associate while they are alive, neither do we associate with when they are dead.

Having listed and described the priest’s offices, let us now examine the garments in which he must exercise them.

Just as there are seven grades by which the priest is elevated, so there are seven garments by which he is ordained: the daily garment, amice, alb, girdle, *fanon*, stole, and chasuble.

He can perform all the other offices without the chasuble, and sometimes with the stole alone. The daily garments for Mass, as few as possible, are four: shirt, tunic, breeches, and footwear. The Romans nevertheless add leggings. Amalarius also says that the priest ought to be vested in sandals and a dalmatic, but among us bishops use these.

There are therefore eight things by which the priest is supported: the parish, the manor, the courtyard, the cemetery, the church, the altar, the chalice with the paten, and the body with the blood, since each is placed above the preceding one in honor and dignity, as though upon certain steps.

By “parish” I mean the people who pay first fruits, offerings, and tithes. By “manor” I mean the plowland that the priest ought to possess at the least. By “courtyard” I mean the enclosure with its houses.

These are the implements useful to a priest, which suffice without the bishop’s blessing: a sprinkler for blessed water, the text of the holy Gospel, a psalter, a missal, a book of the hours, a manual, and a synodal book; veils; candlesticks with candles; a chest for vestments; a pyx with the offerings and the iron for them; one flask with wine and another with water; a basin for washing the hands with a towel; a hollow trunk or stone into which the water used for washing the sacred vessels is poured; also a hidden container beneath the candle, and a lectern beneath the book.

Each of the higher grades can perform the offices of the lower ones. Thus the bishop performs each office of the priest, although, even in his presence, offering, baptizing, celebrating the hours, anointing, administering Communion, commending the dead, and burying are regarded as belonging in a special way to the priest.

In addition, there are seven offices of a prelate: to confirm, bless, absolve, hold a synod, dedicate, consecrate, and ordain.

To confirm is to anoint the foreheads of baptized members of the faithful with chrism.

By blessing I mean that the bishop blesses things that are not ecclesiastical utensils; by consecrating, that he consecrates the utensils themselves.

The pontiff therefore blesses a queen and a virgin when she is veiled, anyone among the faithful who requests a blessing, and the entire people before the peace. He also blesses the things mentioned above that a priest may not bless in his presence.

The prelate absolves the people from venial sins at the beginning of the fast, and from serious sins on Maundy Thursday.

He also holds a synod twice a year, in summer and autumn. In this way, after all the priests of the entire bishopric have been assembled, the bishop investigates whether any of them lacks anything in the whole order or among the church utensils, and whether any of them has committed an injury against another. This lasts three days. When everything has been settled, those who have been absolved are permitted to depart in peace.

The pontiff also dedicates the courtyard, the church, the altar, and the altar-table. To dedicate is to bring a place to God, bless it, and sanctify it.

The bishop consecrates the church utensils, most of which are shared with priests: namely, priestly and pontifical vestments, altar coverings, the chalice, paten, and corporals, the Eucharistic vessel, chrism, oil and the chrism vessel, incense and the censer, the baptistery, the chest or shrine of relics, the *cymbarium*—that is, the canopy of the altar—the cross, the bell, and the judicial iron. [Note: See the glossary of William Lambard, prefixed to the *Ἀρχαιονομία*, in Henry Spelman’s *Ordeal*, and Francis Pithaeus’s *Capitularia*, etc.]

For he consecrates only those things that are separated from common use for divine worship.

The bishop ordains the abbot, abbess, priest, and the other six grades. For the honor of his dignity, the bishop also uses a staff and ring, gloves and mitre, a belt, dalmatic, and sandals.

He ought to possess Sacred Scripture and the traditions of the Fathers, so that he may judge rightly concerning each matter and respond reasonably to all who inquire.

Everything mentioned above belongs to an archbishop; in addition, he is vested with the pallium of honor, because, with the assistance of all the bishops of his diocese, he ordains a bishop.

If any of them cannot attend the ordination, he confirms his assent to the ordination by excusing himself in a letter and sending representatives.

A primate is also an archbishop, but he does not ordain an archbishop. Both the archbishop and the primate must be ordained at Rome by the apostolic authority, or have the pallium brought to them from Rome by the pope, and be raised by their fellow bishops. This permission is granted only when illness, war, or some other necessary cause intervenes.

The primate presides over an archbishop only in this respect: when there are many archbishops in the same region, he alone among them ordains the king, crowns him on three solemn occasions, and, when councils are held before him for the sake of truth, exercises primacy over them.

The place held by patriarchs among eastern peoples, therefore, primates among us seem in a certain way to hold. Both are subject in the first degree to the Roman pontiff.

But because patriarchs preside over apostolic sees—such as the Jerusalemite, Antiochene, and Alexandrian sees—they ordain archbishops and are in a certain way reckoned as equals of the Roman pontiff.

Yet it was said to Peter alone: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 10:13, as cited). Therefore the pope alone stands above the universal Church. He alone ordains and judges all, and is ordained by all, because the Romans elevate him by the consent of the whole Church, and he is daily clothed in a scarlet cloak so that he may always be shown ready for martyrdom.

[Col. 1003A]

## GILBERT’S LETTER TO SAINT ANSELM

(See above, under Saint Anselm, Book IV, Letter 86.)

## Between the Years 1110 and 1117

# GILBERT CRISPIN, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER

[Col. 1003A]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON GILBERT

(FARRICUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, III, 55)

Gislebertus, called Crispin because of the character of his hair, abbot of Westminster of the Benedictine order from the year of Christ 1084 to 1117, wrote, according to Trithemius, chapter 353, and II, 105 of the *Illustrated Benedictines*, for Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, an altercation between a Christian and a certain Jew—whom Bale and Leland, chapter 152, attest to have been a learned Jew of Mainz—concerning the Christian faith, with Gamaliel and Paul as interlocutors.

Bale and Leland, chapter 152, also attribute this work to Gilbert; it is likewise found in manuscript codices. [Note: Labbe, *Bibliotheca nova MSS.*, p. 26; Pitseus, p. 196.] On the authority of these manuscripts, Gabriel Gerberon published it together with the letter to Anselm prefixed to it. [Note: John Picard had published this letter with notes on Anselm, Book II, Letter 16.] Gerberon included it in his distinguished edition of Anselm, Paris 1675, reprinted in 1721, p. 512.

On this Gilbert, see John Picard’s notes on Book II of Anselm’s Letters, Letter 16. This altercation had appeared without the author’s name at Cologne in 1537, in folio; it was later abridged and interpolated, together with a preface to Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, under the name of William of Campelles, in volume XX of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 1884.

Other writings of Gilbert are cited: a commentary on Isaiah and Jeremiah; homilies on the Song of Songs; *On the Fall of the Devil*; *On the Soul*; *Against the Sins of Thought, Speech, and Deed*; a work on the prologues of Saint Jerome to the Bible; and a book to Cantor of Sées.

Finally, there is the *Life of Herluin, Abbot of Bec*, concerning whom William of Jumièges writes in Book VII, chapter 22, p. 279, of his *History of the Normans*:

> “If anyone,” he says, “desires to know more fully his conversion and manner of life, let him seek out and reread the book written in elegant language concerning the life of that venerable father by the religious man Gislebertus Crispinus, later abbot of Westminster, who was distinguished both by the nobility of his lineage and by secular and divine learning. In it he will sufficiently find what may satisfy his desire.”

This Life was published by D’Achery at the end of the Paris edition of Lanfranc’s works, 1648, folio.

The book *On the State of the Church*, which Pitseus attributes to this Gilbert, has been noted by Oudinus, volume II, pp. 929 and 957, Cave, under the year 1101, and others to belong to Gilbert of Limerick.

Another work, apparently by a different Gilbert, the *Disputation of the Church and the Synagogue*, was published by Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand in volume V of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, pp. 1497–1506.

## DISPUTATION OF A JEW WITH A CHRISTIAN ON THE CHRISTIAN FAITH, WRITTEN BY LORD GISLEBERTUS, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER

(*Works of Saint Anselm of Canterbury*, edited by D. Gerberon, p. 512; in the manuscript of the library of Saint-Remi, B. 10, and from the Victorine manuscript CC. 9 and the Saint-Germain manuscript.)

[Col. 1005]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

Gislebertus sends this disputation to Saint Anselm for examination.

[Col. 1005A]

To the reverend father and lord Anselm, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, his servant and son, Brother Gislebertus, procurator and servant of the monastery of Westminster, wishes lasting prosperity in this life and blessed eternity in the life to come.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint-Remi and Victorinus read *in futuro*, “in the future.”]

I send to Your Paternity and prudence [Note: Ms. Rem. and S. Ger.: “your”] for examination a little book which I recently wrote, committing to writing what a certain Jew once brought forward in disputation with me from his law against our faith, together with the replies I made to his objections on behalf of our faith. I do not know where he came from, but he had been educated in letters at Mainz; he was well versed both in the Law and in our writings, and possessed a practiced mind for disputations against us. He was very familiar to me and often came to me, both on account of his own business [Col. 1005B] and to see me, since in certain matters I was very necessary to him; and whenever we met, we would immediately converse amicably about the Scriptures and about our faith. One day, therefore, God granted both him and me more leisure than usual [Note: Ms. R.: “desire”]; and at once we began, as we commonly did, to raise questions between ourselves. And because he raised his objections quite appropriately and consistently, and explained what he had objected to by pursuing it no less appropriately; while our reply answered his objections with a sufficiently close correspondence [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “the propositions”; Ms. Vict.: “to the matter proposed”], and, relying equally upon the testimony of the Scriptures [Col. 1006A], seemed to him easy to concede and approve [Note: Ms. Vict.: “using”; Ms. R.: “conceding”], certain people who were present asked us to commit this discussion to writing [Note: Ms. Vict. and S. Ger.: “little disputation”]—since it might perhaps benefit some.

I therefore wrote it, and wrote it without revealing either my own name or his, under the persona of a Jew disputing with a Christian about our faith; and I send this written and composed work to Your Excellency for examination and judgment. If the work is worthy of approval, it will please you once it has received the approval of your judgment; but if it is to be rejected, whether wholly or in part, whatever ought to be rejected, receive as spoken privately into a friend’s ear. And since it has become known only to a friend, let it be suppressed in silence, and let no one be given this written page to read, while our mutual affection and complete peace remain intact. Delete whatever you think should be deleted [Col. 1006B], or correct whatever you think can be corrected [Note: Ms. Vict.: “cut out … cut out”]. I confess that whatever judgment you pronounce, I shall receive it with a willing mind and listen with an obedient ear.

Nevertheless, through the assistance of God’s mercy, one of the Jews who were then in London converted to the Christian faith at Westminster. In the presence of everyone he professed faith in Christ, asked for baptism, received it, and, after being baptized, vowed that he would serve God there. He became a monk and remained with us.

Thus that Jewish disputant, after several other matters had been introduced, attacked me by challenging me.

[Col. 1007]

**DISPUTATION OF A JEW WITH A CHRISTIAN CONCERNING THE CHRISTIAN FAITH, WRITTEN BY LORD GISLEBERT, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER**

[Col. 1007A]

**THE JEW** [Note: Vict. does not have these names for the speakers, “Jew” and “Christian.”]

Since Christians say that you are learned in letters and fluent in speech, I would like you to deal with me patiently, explaining by what reasoning and on the testimony of what authority you blame the Jews because we observe the law given by God and obey Moses the legislator. For if the law is good and was given by God, it must be observed; for whose decree should be observed if God’s command is not to be observed? But if the law must be observed [Note: Ms. Vict.: “will be observed”], why do you drive its observers everywhere out like dogs with sticks and persecute them? If, however, you say that it must by no means be observed, Moses must be blamed, since he handed it down to us to be observed with such empty vanity. But if, by making an exception, you say that one part must be observed [Col. 1007B] while another must by no means be observed or must be abolished, advise us how we shall escape the curse pronounced by God: “Cursed is he who does not remain in all the things that are written in the law” (Deut. XXVII, 26). The legislator makes no exception, but commands all those things universally to be observed. You, however, determine the observance of the law and its commandments according to your own judgment. And, so that you may know that in these matters I wish rather to give attention to reason than to contention, let us withdraw from other questions and entirely refuse to seek whose side the favor of the listeners applauds [Note: Ms. Rem.: “and refuse in our minds that it should favor anyone.”].

**THE CHRISTIAN**

You ask all these questions reasonably enough, and it is proper that all of them should be asked; but in equal measure I ask you to deal patiently with me. For if the method of our dispute is to be such that you concede whatever the page of your law testifies, or whatever is established by reasoning so evident that you cannot refute it by anything more evident, I am ready to discuss these matters with you. And I do this wherever you wish [Col. 1008A], more for the sake of truth [Note: MSS. V. and R.: “for the sake of faith”] and out of love for you [Note: Ms. S. Ger. omits the phrase] than from a desire to dispute; nor do I care about the acclamations of men. Let the one prevail to whom reason bears witness and the authority of Scripture gives testimony.

First, therefore, we say, maintain, and affirm that the law is good and was given by God; and consequently we decree that everything written in it, understood in its divine meaning, was to be observed in its own times and is to be observed. We say that the commandments of the law must be understood in a divine sense because, if we take all of them in a human and literal sense, we see many things that contradict and strongly oppose one another.

For when, after the creation of the world had been completed, Moses says, “God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I, 31), how does he later, in distinguishing animals, write that some are clean and others unclean, permitting people to use the former, while commanding them not only not to touch the latter but to punish with death the one who touches them? How can what is very good be unclean? When he named all things and said that they were very good, he excluded neither this animal nor that. How, then, did God create all animals very good, and afterward forbid some or other animals to be eaten, giving as the reason that they are unclean animals? [Note: Ms. Vict. and S. Ger. omit the bracketed passage.] Nor did he prohibit only those that by their nature are harmful to human beings as food; he also prohibited many that are pleasant to taste and equally wholesome in use. These matters therefore contain some sacramental meaning, although they were spoken by God and nevertheless, taken literally, completely disagree with one another. [Col. 1008C] We say that a sacrament is a hidden sign of a sacred reality.]

Likewise, we know that God said to Adam: “Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth [Note: Ms. Vict.: “in the earth”], and all trees that have within themselves the seed of their own kind [Note: Ms. Vict.: “seed”], so that they may be food for you” (Gen. I, 29). By what reasoning, then, did God give the first man all trees for food and immediately afterward forbid him to take for food from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? When he universally commends trees as granted to man, he indicates that no tree was excepted. This therefore must not be understood without a mystery.

In Exodus, among the other commands concerning the making of an altar, the Lord instructed Moses as follows: “You shall make an altar of earth for me, and upon it you shall offer your burnt offerings and your peace offerings” (Exod. XX, 24). He then added what material the altar might be made from and how it was to be made: “But if you wish to build it from stones, you shall build it from uncut stones” (ibid., 25).

In the completion of the tabernacle, its vessels, and its utensils, we read: “Moses made the altar of incense from acacia wood, having a square of one cubit on each side and a height of two cubits” (Exod. XXXVII, 25). Shortly afterward: “He also made the altar of burnt offering from acacia wood, five cubits square and three cubits high” (Exod. XVIII, 1). It was certainly not made rashly or presumptuously that it was made with such precise dimensions of height and squareness. Again, a little later: “He cast bronze bases at the entrance of the tabernacle, and the bronze altar with its grating” (ibid., 30). Finally: “The lampstand shall stand with its lamps, and the golden altar on which incense is burned before the ark of the testimony” (Exod. XL, 5).

How, then, does God command that you make an altar of earth and offer your burnt offerings upon it, while Moses, on the contrary, made a wooden altar of incense, also made a wooden altar of burnt offering, made a bronze altar, made a golden one, and at times even made one of stone? It therefore seems very contradictory that Moses himself should act in a manner different from and other than what the Lord commands through Moses. This must accordingly be understood otherwise than the literal wording suggests.

Again, since Moses says that God created all these things for human use and recalls that he subjected them all to man—“so that he may rule,” he says, “over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the animals of the earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth” (Gen. I, 26)—why does he later forbid a man to plow with an ox and a donkey? You may place any load you please upon a donkey; and why is it not permitted to put a yoke upon an ox together with a donkey? It is permitted to lead an ox and a donkey to pasture, and the law permits them to be together and feed together in the pasture, yet it prohibits and forbids them to plow together.

But if this is because the law calls the donkey an unclean animal, why does it permit all the other things mentioned concerning it and single out only plowing? The horse is declared in the law to be an unclean animal, as are many others; yet the law does not prohibit plowing with an ox and a horse or with an ox and another unclean animal.

We see this contradiction not only in the commandments just mentioned, but also in very many other legal ceremonies [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “institutions”], unless we understand them in an appropriate sense [Col. 1010A]. These things must therefore be understood and examined in a discerning and divine sense, because it is impossible for all of them to be fulfilled when taken literally.

If, however, we take the law in its proper sense, we shall be able to observe all the commandments of the law with the proper observance. I understand some to be literal, without any deep symbolism, and others to be veiled under figures. Some were commanded to be observed for a time; others are to be observed without any determination of time.

For those things that were anticipatory signs of some sacrament and figures of a future truth ought not to retain their anticipation and figure once the reality and truth they signified has been revealed in its own time. Just as, in ordinary speech, we use changes in the forms of verbs, saying “it will be” so long as something is future, then omitting “it will be” and taking up “it is” in the present, and, when indicating that it has already passed, using “it was,” so too, when the present sacrament of some mystery is revealed, would its figure or sign still be needlessly retained?

Those things, however, that were not signs of some mystery, but openly signify the truth of faith or commend the upbuilding of charity [Note: Ms. Rem.: “truth”], are to be observed by both us and you not temporarily but perpetually; and their transgression can in no way go unpunished.

The truth of these figures that existed in the law and had been awaited for so many ages finally had to be manifested. Was it to be promised forever: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak of things declared from the beginning” (Ps. LXXVII, 2)? Was it to remain forever in the future: “Until he comes to whom it is appointed to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10)? At last, therefore, at the times predestined by God, there came the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, opening our understanding so that we might understand the Scriptures and dissolving the profound mysteries written about him in the Law and the Prophets—the one in whom you must believe.

**THE JEW**

If this or that word of God is to be observed for a time, and then, having been annulled, another is to be observed for another time, so that by successive periods the divine ordinances are changed, how will “God has spoken once” stand firm (Ps. LXI, 12)? How will “Your word, O Lord, remains forever in heaven” be valid (Ps. CXVIII, 89)?

What difference does it make to me, I ask, why God judges this animal clean and that one unclean, permits the use of this one and forbids the use of that one? For who has assisted the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, so that he should permit this to be done and forbid that? He commanded it. It must therefore be obeyed [Note: Ms. Rem.: “observed”], and obedience to him is the highest virtue [Col. 1011A]. He forbade it. It is therefore no longer permitted to be done; and if it is done afterward, we call it sin and say that it must be punished with the due penalty.

To preserve the figure of the letter, shall we disregard the letter? To preserve one, what reason is there to condemn the other [Note: Ms. Vict.: “so that we condemn the other”]? Let us preserve the letter, and let us preserve the figure of the letter as well. Let the letter remain for our small understanding, let it remain for yours too, and let there be added the spiritual understanding of the hidden mystery granted to us [Note: MSS. Rem. and S. Ger.: “to you”] by God.

Let us abstain from pork because the law commands it; and let us also abstain from whatever is signified by the pig—sin [Note: Ms. R.: “if there is anything that is signified by the pig, namely sin”]. We must not plow with an ox and a donkey because the legislator forbade it; and if you understand anything that ought to be avoided through this coupling of donkey and ox, it is right to avoid it—indeed, it is a sin not to avoid it [Note: Ms. Rem.: “if we understand”]. And so with the rest. For thus the law is fulfilled, and it is judged that it must be fulfilled.

But, having given this preliminary account, let us come to Christ, in whom the whole cause of the question and controversy consists. For you say that he is the author of a new worship, new institutions, and a law wholly changed, and you say that I must believe in him.

I believe that Christ was indeed a prophet, outstanding above all in every excellence of virtue, and I shall believe Christ; but I neither believe nor shall believe in Christ, because I believe only in God, and in one God. “Hear, Israel,” he says, “your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4): one, not threefold, as you Christians both affirm by denying and deny by affirming. For you say: God is the Father, God is the Son, God is the Holy Spirit; the Father is one, the Son another [Col. 1011C], and the Holy Spirit another; and yet there are not three Gods, but one God. You say both things; let whoever wishes believe either one or both.

But Israel, our people, hears and believes: “Your God is one God”—not created in time, not made from a woman. For, properly speaking, before time existed, he himself was; he himself created time, and under time he himself created heaven, earth, and all that is in them.

Another command follows in the Decalogue: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. XX, 7). The one who attributes the name and worship of divinity to a human being takes the name of God in vain. For if every living human being is vanity, the one who believes a human being to be God and calls him God attributes to a human being the name and worship of divinity.

I therefore do not believe in Christ, nor is my hope in Christ, because: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIX, 5). But I believe Christ, and I shall believe Christ when he comes, because Moses bears witness and says concerning him: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me” (Deut. XVIII, 15).

And since it was to be desired with every prayer that he should come, and since one might recognize his coming by a sign, hear what the prophet Isaiah proclaims concerning this: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains, and all nations shall flow to it, and they shall say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. II, 2–3).

If Christ has already come, where throughout the whole world, apart from the small Jewish people, is it said, “Let us go up to the house of the God of Jacob”? Some of you say, “Let us go to the house of Peter”; others, “to the house of Martin.” But no one says, “Let us go to the house of the God of Jacob.”

Hear further about the coming of Christ: “And they shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for battle” (ibid., 4). Is the military order in our time beating its swords into plowshares and its spears into pruning hooks? The smiths scarcely suffice; iron scarcely suffices for the manufacture of military weapons. Where on earth can it be found that “nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they train any longer for battle”? Everywhere in the world a neighbor lies in wait for his neighbor, oppresses and kills him; nation fights against nation with all its strength, kingdom rises against kingdom, and from earliest childhood each person is trained for battle.

It is therefore clear that you Christians are greatly mistaken about Christ and about his coming.

**THE CHRISTIAN**

Indeed, God spoke once, and it is impious that any word of God should ever be annulled. The divine ordinances are not changed by any succession of times [Col. 1012C], because Christ did not come “to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.” “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things have been accomplished” (Matt. V, 18). Does Christ wish to condemn the law when he threatens, saying, “Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things have been accomplished”? He therefore does not wish to abolish it, but to fulfill it.

The law forbids murder; Christ forbids anger and hatred. The law forbids adultery of the flesh; Christ forbids even the desire of the heart [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “of the flesh”].

The law forbids you to eat pork; at that time abstinence from the flesh of that animal was necessary for you [Note: Ms. Vict.: “from its flesh, and abstinence from it was then necessary for you”], because it was a figure of the future truth, and the figure had to be observed until the Truth itself should be present. Now, however, it is not necessary for us—or for you—because the truth of the figure itself is already present [Col. 1012D]. Nevertheless, it is permitted to abstain, and many of us abstain not only from it but from every other kind of meat as well; each of us remains accountable to one and the same great Judge.

Moses calls swine’s flesh unclean when he forbids it, and for this reason you say that it is not permitted to eat it. Yet Moses himself—not another Moses—calls swine’s flesh clean and very good, and writes that God made it good for eating, just as the other creatures; therefore we say that it is permitted to eat it.

After he had declared that God created all things—the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and all the animals of the earth in which there is a living soul—he added shortly afterward: “God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I, 31) [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “enumerated”]. What is very good is in no respect evil. But what is in no respect evil—how can it be evil and unclean? Whatever of the nature made by God is considered in swine’s flesh is clean and very good, and it is permitted to eat it.

Because, however, pleasure and uncleanness are signified by this animal, it is designated as unclean for this reason [Note: MSS. S. Ger. and V. omit the bracketed passage: “so that this vice may be avoided more diligently; the animal by which it is signified is also forbidden as food”], and it is not permitted to indulge that uncleanness.

If, then, this animal is understood to be both clean and unclean, and God permits us both to use it and not to use it, sacred authority also testifies: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the heart: fornications and the other vices that he enumerates defile a person” (Matt. XV, 11) [Note: Ms. Vict. omits “which”]. It is therefore not swine’s flesh, which enters the mouth, that defiles a person, but pleasure and the desire for any unclean pleasure that proceeds from the heart; that is what defiles a person [Note: MSS. R. and S. Ger.: “and the uncleanness”].

For this reason the apostle Paul also says: “Take whatever is set before you to eat with thanksgiving, asking no questions for the sake of conscience” (I Cor. X, 27) [Note: Vulgate: “Eat everything that is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience”].

By the same reasoning, it is permitted to plow with an ox and a donkey, and it is forbidden that we plow with an ox and a donkey [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “we are forbidden”]. “Is God concerned with oxen?” as the apostle Paul says (I Cor. IX, 9). Or does the law say this on our account? Therefore, whoever cultivates the earth should plow with an ox and a donkey if he cannot do better, because God permits it, since he created all these things for human use.

But because the ox divides its hoof and chews the cud, and is entirely suitable for cultivating the earth, it signifies a discerning ruler in the Church, one who has understanding in what he does, who distinguishes right from wrong, and who meditates upon the commandments of God that he hears and reads, chewing them over within himself day and night. He is not useful only to himself, but builds up others and instructs them by teaching.

Such a suitable preacher ought not to be joined in preaching the word of God to another who is morally undiscerning, or an ignorant and unlearned man, because the latter is not only useless to himself through evil living, but by his bad example and unclean manner of life [Col. 1013D] is harmful to others. These vices are signified by the donkey, which neither divides its hoof nor chews the cud and is altogether a very sluggish animal.

The matters stated concerning the making of the altar, and why the Lord forbade man to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, contain a profound mystery within themselves; but their examination belongs elsewhere and to another discussion.

“These things happened figuratively,” and were spoken to you; “but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come,” as Paul, our apostle from your people, says (I Cor. X, 11).

The ends of the ages are the last days, concerning which Isaiah foretells, saying: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Isa. II, 2). To it all nations will truly flow together, as the Psalmist also foretold: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. XXI, 28).

All the ends of the earth already believe in God [Note: Ms. Vict.: “Christ”]; already all the families of the nations worship Christ and say with one united voice: “Let us go to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isa. II, 3)—not to the house of Jacob, but “to the house of the God of Jacob,” that is, to the house of the God whom Abraham worshiped, whom Isaac worshiped, whom Jacob worshiped, and whom Moses and Aaron also worshiped, so that they may show that there is one God of those who were faithful before the law, of those who existed under the law, and of those who now exist as believers in God among the whole multitude of the nations.

As for your accusation that we say, “Let us go to the house of Peter, let us go to the house of Paul, and to the house of Martin,” no one who understands properly takes this as literally stated. We do not make a house for Peter or Paul; rather, we build it for God in honor and memory of Peter or Paul. Nor is it permitted for any bishop to say at the consecration of churches: “To you, Peter,” or “to you, Paul, we consecrate this house or this altar” [Col. 1014C]. [Note: Ms. Vict. omits the bracketed passage: “Rather, to you, God, in honor of Peter or Paul, we consecrate this house or this altar.”]

This house is called above all “the house of the God of Jacob,” and is specifically named “Jacob,” because Jacob is the first of all who is read to have established this house for God. “Jacob,” it says, “raised up a stone as a pillar, pouring oil over it, and said: Truly this place is holy” (Gen. XXVIII, 18). After listing the heavenly mysteries he had seen and adding that he was astonished, he said: “How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (ibid., 17).

The house of our God is therefore the house of the God of Jacob, because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob worshiped the God whom we worship. In this house of God the divine word is read daily; the faithful people are taught what good things they should seek and what evils they should avoid, and at the same time what rewards accompany the things that should be sought and what punishment follows the evils they commit.

There too civil cases are conducted by Christians, accusations by neighbors against neighbors are heard, and the proper punishment is inflicted for each person’s offense. “You shall not kill,” says the law (Exod. XX, 13); “but whoever kills”—or rather, as Christ himself added, “whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22) [Note: Ms. Rem.: “also”].

For the one whose anger and hatred are removed is not permitted to use sword and spear. Whoever renounces anger and hatred can very easily renounce spear and sword. It is much easier to beat one’s sword into a plowshare and one’s spear into a pruning hook than, after suppressing the swelling of the heart, to become humble from being proud, a servant from being free; to renounce wife, children, house, weapons, fields, horses, and everything one possesses, and, beyond that, to renounce oneself.

Yet we often see this happening—and you see it too—because many who once lived amid worldly affairs, proud and powerful, fully equipped for war and eager for battle, coveting the property of others, renounce for God all worldly pomp, travel voluntarily as the poorest of people through various places [Col. 1015B], seek the intercession of the saints, or, enclosed in some cave, live under the authority of a superior [Note: Ms. Vict.: “living in submission under some superior”].

In the dwelling together of such servants of God, that other miracle announced through the prophet Isaiah is also fulfilled: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together, and a little child shall lead them” (Isa. XI, 6). The little child leads the lion and the bear with the lamb when, in the house of God, a shepherd commands those who were once noble and ignoble alike, powerful and powerless, strong and weak alike.

The child is a child not in understanding but in malice; little not in the proper strength of governance, but because he is free from all worldly arrogance and from contempt for his lineage.

To put it briefly, this is the institution of Christian life [Note: Ms. S. Ger. omits “of life”]: that each person should love his neighbor as himself, and should not do to others what he does not wish done to himself. This is the word of which the apostle Paul says: “The Lord has accomplished and abbreviated his word in justice upon the earth” (Rom. IX, 28).

Concerning this accomplishment of the word, the prophet Isaiah says: “The completed and abbreviated work shall overflow with righteousness” (Isa. X, 22); for the Lord God of hosts will accomplish and abbreviate it in the midst of the earth.

The same prophet Isaiah had also foretold concerning this Word: “Come,” he says, “let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and the Lord will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths, because the law shall go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3).

What other law, I ask, is foretold as going forth from Zion? What word of the Lord, I ask, is foretold as going forth from Jerusalem? The law given through Moses did not go forth from Mount Zion, because it was not given on Mount Zion, but on Mount Sinai.

What law, then, went forth from Zion except the law of the New Testament given through Christ? It went forth from Mount Zion because, from Mount Zion, as Christ was about to ascend into heaven, he entrusted his disciples with the law to be preached throughout the world: “Go,” he said, “into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Marc. XXIV, 49) [Note: MSS. Rem. and S. Germ. add: “the law that is announced and spread from those places throughout the whole world? ‘Remain,’ he says, ‘in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke XXIV, 49); and, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said, ‘Go,’ and so forth.”].

This is that good word—that is, the Gospel—which went forth from Jerusalem: “Preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (ibid., 16).

In this Gospel the Lord taught his ways, new ways. The old ways were: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. XXI, 24). The new ways are: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also; and from the one who takes your tunic, do not withhold your cloak” (Matt. V, 39).

The old ways were: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (ibid., 43). The new ways are: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. XII, 20).

These are the ways of the Lord; these are the paths of the Lord, along which perfect Christians walk [Note: Ms. Ger. omits the bracketed passage: “although now few Christians preserve this way of Christian life”]. Once kings walked in them, together with the nations subject to those kings [Col. 1016B].

But what if some powerful or violent person acts wickedly and refuses to be corrected? “Vengeance is mine, says the Lord, and I will repay” (Hebr. X, 30).

And how great will be the severity of that divine punishment? Hear the Psalmist: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. XLIX, 3–4).

Nevertheless, concerning the last days of those times, around the consummation of the age, these evils and much worse were foretold by Christ and by the prophets before Christ. “Nation will rise against nation,” he says in the Gospel, “and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences and famines, and there will be great signs” (Luke XXI, 10); “and unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 22).

Accordingly, in Daniel’s final vision, concerning the end of times and that intolerable tribulation near the end of the age, we read: “And the king shall act according to his will, and he shall be exalted and magnified against every god [Note: Ms. Rem.: “the name of the Lord”], and against the God of gods; he shall speak magnificent things, and he shall prosper until the wrath is completed” (Dan. XI, 36). A little later: “There shall come a time such as there has not been from the beginning until that time” (Dan. XII, 1).

Concerning the shortening of the tribulation he added: “How long until the end of these wonders?” And I heard the man clothed in linen swear by the One who lives forever: “For a time, times, and half a time” (ibid., 6–7).

In the last days, therefore—that is, as the evening of the world approached—when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son into the world, that peace mentioned above existed in the primitive Church of God and continued for a long time, far and wide. But near the end of the age—that is, near the end of the last days—the dissension throughout the world and the tribulation mentioned above [Note: MSS. Vict. and S. Ger.: “below”] will boil over and become extremely savage; indeed, it has already begun to boil over.

We have now answered briefly and concisely what you proposed concerning the coming of Christ; we shall answer more fully when both time and reason have brought us to that subject. Let us return to Christ, in whom I said and say that you must believe.

Although I willingly concede that the statement has been made, and, without compromising the assertion of faith, acknowledge that it is to be approved [Note: MSS. Vict. and S. Ger.: “approved”], namely, that we must believe in none but God, and in one God, nevertheless I said and say that you must believe in Christ.

We by no means take the name of God in vain, because we attribute neither the name nor the worship of divinity to any creature; and if anyone says that it ought to be attributed, we utterly refute him. Nevertheless, I said and I say that you must believe in Christ, because it is established that Christ is God and man. [Col. 1017B] For although we believe that God assumed man into the unity of his person, and believe Christ to be God and man, nevertheless we believe that there are two natures in him, and we assert that the properties of both natures are entirely distinct. For, while remaining unchangeably God in what he was, he assumed what he was not. The Word, which was in the beginning with God, through which all things were made and without which nothing was made, became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14). Since, therefore, Christ is God, he is the Son of God by power, not by grace; consubstantial with the Father, equal and coeternal, existing before all times—and in him we believe. [Note: MSS. Rem. and S. Ger. omit the words enclosed in brackets.]

Since, however, he was made in time, he is man; he is the Son of God, not by power but by grace, inferior to God, made a little lower than the angels, made subject to time, born of a woman [Note: MSS. V. and S. Ger.: “female.”]—and it is in this assumed man, of course, that we do not believe.

[Col. 1017C] Likewise, because he is God, he could neither die, suffer, nor be born; because he is man, he could and willed to die, suffer, and be born, and through the mystery of his passion he redeemed us from death. The prophet Isaiah himself, foretelling that Christ would be God and man, says: “Behold,” says the Lord, “I will lay in Zion a tested stone, a cornerstone, precious; whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16). He calls him a stone and plainly follows with: “Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.” [Note: Ms. Rem. omits “equal.”]

Through this tested, cornerstone, precious stone, therefore, he clearly designates Christ as man. But if he were man alone, surely the prophet would be urging idolatry and sacrilege by admonishing us that we ought to believe in a man. [Col. 1017D] Since, however, he is not man alone but also God, of whom it is said in the psalm, “Those who wait for him shall not be put to shame” (Psalm 25:3; supplied: Psalm XXIV, 3), therefore he added: “Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.”

Thus Christ, because he is man, was placed in Zion as a tested, cornerstone, precious stone: a tested stone because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth; [Col. 1018A] a cornerstone because he justifies circumcision by faith and the uncircumcised through faith, gathering both walls into himself and making both peoples one in himself; a precious stone because his death was of such value before God that it removed the sins of the whole world.

Yet although he was a tested, cornerstone, precious stone, we believe not in him but in accordance with the worship due to him. Since he is also God—and hence it follows, “Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame”—we believe both in him and in accordance with the worship of divinity due to him.

[Note: MSS. Rem. and S. Ger. read: “Although, therefore, he was a man—a tested, cornerstone, precious stone—and we believe in him; because, as I said, we believe Christ to be God and man. Since he is also God—and hence it follows, ‘Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame’—those who believe in him shall not be put to shame through the worship of divinity due to him.”]

As for your assertion that we, by denying, say and, by saying, deny that God is one and three, we reject in every way the statement that God is “one and triple,” because we affirm no triplicity in God; rather, we affirm one Triune God, because in the unity of the Godhead we believe in a Trinity of persons. Why it ought not to be called “triplicity,” and why it may be called “Trinity,” [Col. 1018B] we shall explain in its proper place, and what we say we shall establish by reason and authority.

**JEW.**

What reason [Note: Ms. Rem.: “dispute.”], what authority of the Scriptures compels me to believe that God can become man, or that God, having become man, already exists? If there is no change in God, nor any shadow caused by alteration (James 1:17), how can such a great alteration of things occur with him that God becomes man, the Creator becomes a creature, and the incorruptible is believed to have become corruption? How, I ask, are we to understand: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain. You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are always the same” (Psalm 102:25–27; supplied: Psalm CI, 26–27)? [Col. 1018C] How is God “always the same” if he can be altered into man?

If God is immeasurable, how could he be measured and confined within the lowly and small dimensions of human limbs? If God is uncircumscribed, by what argument will it be said that he was bodily circumscribed and could be wholly contained within the narrow womb of a mother?

Furthermore, if God is that than which nothing greater or more sufficient can be conceived, by what necessity was he compelled to share in human misery and made a participant in and sufferer of such great evils? Finally, if God became man, how will what he himself spoke to Moses stand: “For man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20)? It seems highly contradictory that God should have become man [Col. 1018D] and yet could not be seen by man or by his very mother. [Note: Ms. S. Germ.: “that God should be man,” etc.]

Heaven forbid that you should say that anything illusory existed concerning God! Therefore we confess that it is in no way permissible to devise such things about God, much less to say or proclaim them, since neither reason allows that this can happen nor does any authority of Scripture present itself that agrees with or even approaches this error of yours.

For as to that prophecy of Isaiah, which you utterly distort by interpreting it according to your own understanding: [Col. 1019A] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, that is, ‘God with us’” (Isaiah 7:14)—what bearing does this have on the matter under discussion? Will a virgin who has never been violated but has been married to a man, while still remaining a virgin, conceive and bear a son?

We readily accept that “God with us,” that is, “his name shall be called Emmanuel,” was said about Christ; he would be of such dignity and grace with God that in him and through him the Lord—that is, the power of the Lord—would be with us. But whenever, at the solemnities of your Masses, you say, “The Lord be with you,” does it immediately follow that God becomes man, or that a man made God stands among the crowd? [Note: Ms. Rem.: “exists.”]

Thus the prophet, recalling a sacred matter [Note: MSS. Vict. and S. Germ. read “sacredly.”] and foretelling the preeminence of the Christ who was to be born, said nothing absurd about him, nothing contrary to nature, and left no room for wicked suspicion: [Col. 1019B] “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive.”

With what presumptuous rashness, then, does any human being dare to write what the prophet in no way dared to say—that a woman would conceive from God and bear a son conceived from him? [Note: Ms. San. Ger. reads “him.”] The prophet said, “She conceived and bore a son” (Isaiah 8:3); you infer from your own interpretation and disseminate as an invention everywhere: “And she remained a virgin after childbirth,” although you accept that this was nowhere said by the prophet. [Note: Ms. Vict.: “you accept that this was nowhere said by the prophet.” Ms. S. Ger.: “whether this was said by the prophet,” etc.] It is therefore an insult that, with such shameless boldness, you interpret the sacred utterances of the prophets by inventing meanings according to human will.

**CHRISTIAN.**

[Col. 1019C] We fear no contradiction of realities in this mystery, and we dread no disharmony with the Scriptures. But for the moment let us set aside the authorities of Scripture [Note: Ms. Vict. reads “again.”], by which, with God’s help [Note: Ms. Rem.: “with God’s assent.”], we shall establish in every way that God became man and was seen by human beings.

For the prophet Jeremiah plainly proclaims this, excluding every ambiguity of equivocation [Note: MSS. Vict. and S. Ger. read “invocation.”]: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He discovered the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen” [Note: Vulgate: “his beloved.”] [“Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).] [Note: Ms. Rem. omits the words enclosed in brackets.]

“Afterward”—he says—after the law had been given, after the way of discipline had been given to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen—God became man and lived among human beings, born of a virgin, [Col. 1019D] with the womb of his mother closed, while the whole integrity of his dignity remained intact. [Note: Ms. S. Germ.: “divinity.”]

Hence the prophet Ezekiel says: “And the Lord said to me: [Col. 1024C] This gate shall be closed, and it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it [because the Lord God of Israel entered through it, and it shall be closed for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat his bread before the Lord] (Ezekiel 44:2–3).” [Note: Ms. Vict. omits the words enclosed in brackets.] “The virgin therefore conceived, because the gate shall be closed and no man shall pass through it.” [Note: The bracketed clause is absent in Ms. Vict.]

[Col. 1020A] The virgin remained a virgin after childbirth because “the Lord God of Israel entered through it, and it shall be closed.” The Lord God of Israel himself entered through her, becoming man, as the psalm says: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 19:6). And although he was man, he was nevertheless the prince. As another psalm says: “Free among the dead” (Psalm 88:6), he shall sit “to eat bread before the Lord” (Ezekiel 46:3). What bread? “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34).

“God with us”—not as we say at the solemnities of the Mass, “The Lord be with you,” but as Isaiah says more explicitly elsewhere: “A child is born to us and a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, [Col. 1020B] Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). [Note: Ms. Vict. omits the words enclosed in brackets.]

Since that conception was new and unprecedented and was the mystery of a great matter, the prophet therefore prefaced it: “For this reason the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14).

As for that absurdity conceived and invented by your understanding—that she conceived from the substance of God—no believer is permitted to say or think it [because she conceived from God, that is, from the power [Note: Ms. Rem.: “this is the power.”] and might of God, since she conceived neither according to human usage [Note: Ms. Rem.: “understanding.”] nor from any seed of a man]. [Note: Ms. Vict. omits the words enclosed in brackets.]

For he who first created man without the seed of a man, from nothing, was able to create Christ as man without the seed of a man, from something—that is, from his mother’s flesh. [Col. 1020C] And because, had he been conceived according to ordinary human usage, he would not have been free from original sin, nor would he have been “free among the dead,” so that among the dead he alone would be free, as the Psalmist says, and free from sin, therefore he had to be born without sin—that is, from a virgin, without intercourse with a man.

So that these statements may be made without prejudice—for we reserve the testimonies of Scripture to be set forth in their proper place—supreme necessity and reason also demanded that God become man and restore us to life through the mystery of his humanity. He therefore became man, not ceasing to be what he was, but assuming what he was not. We say that God became man not through the conversion of divinity into flesh, but through the assumption of humanity into God.

Just as rational soul and flesh, because of the unity of person, are one man [Note: Ms. Vict. is defective here.], [Col. 1020D] although soul and flesh are entirely of different natures, and the soul is not converted into flesh, nor flesh into soul, but, while both natures remain, the unity of the person is preserved, so God and man, because of the unity of person, are one Christ. Yet God was not converted into man, nor man into God; rather, while the nature of God and the nature of man remain distinct [Note: Ms. Rem.: “different.”], the indivisible unity of the person of God and man is preserved and worshipped. [Note: Ms. Rem.: “is preserved.”]

[Col. 1021A] For not everything that in some way comes to be something other than it was ceases to be what it was. In the alteration of certain accidental qualities, for example, when a black man becomes white or a white man black, the one quality is entirely replaced by another when the latter supervenes. But when a man becomes armed or unarmed, or from naked becomes clothed, or from clothed naked, the man himself neither receives nor loses anything through such an alteration.

God therefore assumed man into the unity of his person through his innate goodness, not through anything of ours, and because of a great necessity—not his, but ours—and for a reason that is great and ought to be approved by you, if you wish either rationally to admit what you hear or reasonably to reject it.

As for the authority of Scripture, interpreted with exact understanding [Note: Ms. Rem.: “not with exact understanding.”], it will be put before you so clearly [Note: Ms. Rem. reads *opponentur*, “will be set against you.”] that you will be unable to devise anything that can be brought against it. [Note: Ms. S. Ger. reads *apponatur*, “be put before it.”]

[Col. 1021B] You know how explicitly Genesis commends the manner in which the first man was created, how superior he was in the dignity of his nature, and with what eminence he was placed above the other animals of the earth. “Rule,” it says, “over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the beasts of the earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth” (Genesis 1:28).

Hence he received from God the command concerning what was forbidden: “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. On whatever day you eat from it [Note: Ms. S. Ger. omits “from it.”], you shall die the death” (Genesis 2:16–17).

What was forbidden under so severe a threat of condemnation was not to be taken lightly. Yet, compelled by no necessity but overcome by his own will, and yielding to his wife, he preferred to obey his wife rather than God’s command. She touched it and ate; she gave it to her husband, and he ate. [Col. 1021C] By biting the forbidden thing, both incurred the curse of death and condemnation.
