Adam, having become disobedient to God, immediately lost every right that had been granted to him. He felt the yoke of his dominion shaken off by the other animals; and, now losing his dignity, he was ashamed of his nakedness. Running to the leaves of the fig tree, he covered the shameful indecency of his limbs.

Thus deceived by the enemy and shamefully subjected to the enemy, they were soon expelled from the paradise of delight in which they had been. The entrance to paradise was closed, and that turning, flaming sword was placed to guard the way to the tree of life.

Thanks be to God: although that sword was flaming [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “although the sword was flaming.”], it was not fixed forever but was turning, because at some time it was to be removed by God’s mercy.

[Col. 1021D] Thus the unhappy and wretched parents begot children born under the same condition of death and misery. Man was born for labor; man died for labor. He was conceived in sins and brought forth in sorrows; wretched, he was born for hardships and toil.

“In the sweat of your face,” the Lord said to Adam, “you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

Hence blessed Job also says: “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, [Col. 1022A] is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14:1–2).

After such a life, however it may have been, where did the dead then go? No one went to heaven; all went to hell. Yet the righteous had good hope that they would be rescued from the underworld through Christ and would deserve, through Christ, to be carried upward to the heavenly realms.

Hear the most eminent Fathers openly bearing witness to this. “I shall descend,” says the patriarch Jacob, “mourning for my son into hell” (Genesis 37:35). And elsewhere he says to his sons: “You will bring my gray hairs down with sorrow to the underworld” (Genesis 42:38).

Hence blessed Job, concerning whom the Lord testified that no man on earth was like him (Job 1:8) [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “with God as witness.”], says: [Col. 1022B] “Hell is my house, and in darkness I have made my bed” (Job 17:13). Nevertheless, seized by the hope of deliverance, he added shortly afterward: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth” (Job 19:25).

In bearing witness to a Redeemer, he does not deny that he had been sold or taken captive [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “that he had fled as a captive.”], and that he had been redeemed.

Hear also blessed David: “God will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld when he receives me” (Psalm 49:15; supplied: Psalm XLVIII, 16). He says that his soul was received from the underworld and was to be redeemed from the underworld. Hence elsewhere, rejoicing, he says: “Lord, you brought my soul out of hell; you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Psalm 30:4; supplied: Psalm XXIX, 5).

To whom does he say, “You brought out” and “you saved,” except to the one of whom he says in another psalm: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 68:5; supplied: Psalm LXVII, 5)? [Col. 1022C] And because he did not wish to ascend above the setting alone, hear what the Psalmist added [Note: MSS. Germ. read “subjoined”]: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Psalm 68:19; Ephesians 4:8; supplied: Psalm LXVII, 19; Ephesians IV, 8).

Hezekiah too, about to die, said: “I said in the middle of my days: I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isaiah 38:10). And afterward he added: “But you have rescued my soul so that it would not perish” (ibid., 17).

This, I say, was the hope of the righteous who were dying at that time. No one therefore went to heaven; all who died then descended into hell.

It was therefore necessary that the expiation of original sin and the removal of such great evils should take place—not through any merit of created man, but through the innate goodness and grace of the excellent Creator.

[Col. 1022D] So that man would not perish forever, man had to be restored. But he could not be restored unless God assumed man, underwent our necessity, himself became our advocate against the adversary, and, conducting the case of our cause, brought it to an end—not by persuasion [Note: Ms. Rem.: “not by giving what was his.”], but by excluding the adversary through a just judgment of reason.

Man therefore had to be restored to God through the man who had taken himself away from God. But what man, born from the common mass of perdition, could accomplish this, [Col. 1023A] so as to restore the remainder of the human race? For scarcely is the justice of each person sufficient for himself; not even an infant is free from sin, whose life upon earth is but a single day.

And if a new man, or a man born from elsewhere [or an angel made man] [Note: Ms. Rem. omits the words enclosed in brackets.] were to liberate man, he could not in this way restore him to the original state of innate dignity.

For since man was created equal to the angels—not by nature, but by the grace of reason and granted freedom—he was subject to serve God alone, the Creator. He could not be restored to that same state of freedom either through a man or through an angel. For whoever is redeemed from servitude by another is judged to be subject to the one by whom he is redeemed, in order to serve him.

Since, therefore, complete restoration of man could not be accomplished through another, it was necessary that the Creator should help the creature, that the Creator should assume the creature, [Col. 1023B] so that, restored through the Creator himself, man would remain subject to serve the Creator alone, and the enemy would justly lose the dominion he had held over the human race.

For the enemy had found nothing belonging to him in Christ: Christ had been neither conceived in iniquities nor born in sins, nor had he contracted any stain of sin at all through living. By what unjust presumption, then, did death sin by striking him in whom it had found nothing belonging to it and over whom it had no right whatsoever? Justly it lost the jurisdiction that it had obtained over the first man and his descendants through the sin of the first man.

The death of Christ was therefore a sacrifice and propitiation for original sin before the Father, and it became the full and complete restoration of the human race. [Col. 1023C] At his death the entrance to paradise was opened, and that turning, flaming sword was removed.

Now, fastened to the cross and dying, he said to the Thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Then also was fulfilled what was said through the prophet Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, I shall be your bite” (Hosea 13:14).

The mystery of this restoration of ours was therefore promised in the prophets—sometimes through figures of things, sometimes through riddles of words, sometimes through an explicit and open promise.

In those earliest times, when God spoke to Abraham concerning this mystery, he said: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 26:4). [Note: Ms. Rem. omits the words enclosed in brackets.] [For in Christ, who was descended from his seed, all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.]

[Col. 1023D] For the whole human race, oppressed under the curse of its first parent, is released through him from that curse and restored to the former blessing and grace. For no nation is blessed in Isaac, nor is any nation recorded as having been subjected to his dominion.

As for David and Solomon, who were stronger and more powerful than the other kings of that land, how are all nations blessed in them, when all the surrounding nations except the Jewish nation were hostile to them and were always fighting against them? [Col. 1024A] Any mention of their successors, kings driven from their kingdom, taken captive, and disinherited, would be futile.

In Christ, therefore, it remains for these things to be understood, and, once understood, to be fulfilled in every way.

**JEW.**

You do violence to Scripture and twist the Scriptures in support of your faith. For the prophet Ezekiel plainly calls it a gate and speaks of a gate; you call it a woman and argue about a woman according to your will. These things are wholly remote from one another and bear no resemblance to each other.

Finally, this last example plainly refutes your entire argument concerning the birth of Christ. For God said to Abraham: [Col. 1024B] “In your seed”—that is, in Christ, who was descended from his seed—“all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:8; supplied: Genesis XXII, 8). God said that Christ would be descended from Abraham’s seed; you say that he was born without any seed of a man.

But proceed to the remaining examples from Scripture, to see whether any have been stated more explicitly and are more consonant with your position and faith. [Note: Ms. S. Ger. omits “and.”]

**CHRISTIAN.**

Whoever follows and answers the opposing arguments step by step responds appropriately to what is put forward. We say that the prophet Ezekiel spoke figuratively about that gate, since what he said about it cannot in any way be taken literally:

“And the Lord,” he says, “said to me: This gate shall be closed, and it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel entered through it, and it shall be closed for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate and shall go out by its way” (Ezekiel 44:1–3).

No one can fulfill these words literally. For if the Lord God of Israel, who speaks through the prophet, says, “Heaven is my throne and earth is the footstool of my feet” (Acts 7:49), and elsewhere, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24)—if, I say, the Lord God of Israel is wholly everywhere, from where did he enter through the gate, and by what route did he depart through that gate?

If God is uncircumscribed, how can it literally be understood that he sits in the gate? [Col. 1024D] How will it be closed for the prince if the prince himself, the Lord God of Israel, enters through it and sits in it to eat bread before the Lord?

What bread, or what sort of bread, made from what source or brought from where, does the Lord God of Israel eat before the Lord? Who is this other Lord before whom the Lord God of Israel eats bread?

Since these things cannot be taken literally, that gate must be understood in such a way that all these statements may be considered and, once considered, understood as capable of being fulfilled consistently.

[Col. 1025A] The Lord God of Israel therefore entered through that gate and came forth to us, because God became man in the womb of a virgin, from the flesh of a virgin. Otherwise he would not have been free from original sin, as it is read in the psalm: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 19:6).

He came forth to us as man and, as Jeremiah testifies, “was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38).

The gate shall be closed because it shall be closed to a man [Note: Ms. Rem.: “because the virgin shall be closed.”], and no man shall pass through it. It shall be kept closed for the prince, so that he may enter through it, because the Lord God of Israel entered through it.

For before Christ’s conception and birth, his mother was not known by a man [Note: Ms. Rem.: “the virgin was not known.”], since the gate shall be closed and shall be kept closed for the prince.

And because this entire mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation was accomplished solely by divine power, without human contamination, [Col. 1025B] the prophet Isaiah says elsewhere: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth a Savior” (Isaiah 45:8).

“By dew,” he says, “and by a heavenly cloud”—that is, solely by God’s creation and operation, as he added shortly afterward, “I, the Lord, created him”—the earth was opened, namely, the virgin’s womb, and brought forth the Savior (ibid.).

The prince himself shall sit in it, because in that humanity also which Christ assumed for us he received all things subjected to him. Hence it is said in the psalm: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands” (Psalm 8:6).

He eats bread before the Lord, doing the will of his Father, who sent him to us.

[Col. 1025C] Concerning this Lord and the Lord, it is said in the psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 110:1). Which Lord says this, and to which Lord does he say it? Hear it more explicitly in another psalm:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:7–8).

The Lord, therefore, is the Father, and the Lord is the Son. But since nothing external is taken into God, and with God there is no succession or mutability of times, and no diversity of essence can be conceived in God—for who could unite diverse things in God?—since, I say, none of these things exists in God, but whatever is in him is wholly one and the same in substance, existing before all things and subsisting after all things, it follows that just as the Father is God, [Col. 1025D] so the Son is God, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial.

Yet they are not two gods, but one God, because the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance in every respect. [Note: Ms. S. Ger. omits “is.”] The same must necessarily be understood of the Holy Spirit.

That the Holy Spirit exists is plainly read in many passages of Scripture: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:2). And elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 33:6). And elsewhere: “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5); [Col. 1026A] and in very many other places of the Old Testament there is mention and discourse concerning the Holy Spirit.

Since the Spirit of God is not of another substance than God, but God and his Spirit are wholly of one and the same substance, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial—for whatever is substantial in God is wholly one and the same, since from whom would God receive anything different from himself?—since, I say, this is so, it follows that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and yet they are not three gods but one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

We admit no triplicity in the unity of the Godhead, since triplicity removes the simplicity of essence; yet we admit a Trinity of persons, since the Trinity of persons does not take away the unity of essence. [Col. 1026B] It is more appropriate to say “a Trinity of persons” than “a triplicity of persons,” lest each person be understood as existing in a threefold manner.

But since discourse concerning the unity of the Godhead and the Trinity of persons within the unity of the Godhead ought to take place among the faithful alone—for whatever is examined through discussion and directed by the testimony of authority may be said without danger—if you wish, let us proceed to the remaining testimonies of Scripture concerning Christ. Later we shall return to examine these matters as we are able.

Although no human reason can comprehend this mystery, nevertheless “we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13:12); and “the invisible things of God are understood and seen through the things that have been made, and his eternal power and divinity likewise” (Romans 1:20).

[Col. 1026C] That other example which you introduced in refutation presents no obstacle to us. For if the mother of Christ, from whose flesh Christ received flesh in her womb, arose from the seed of Abraham, Christ derived his origin from the seed of Abraham, even though he was born from a virgin mother without any seed of a man.

**JEW.**

If it is permissible for Christians to read and interpret the Scriptures concerning Christ in this manner, you will find many more passages that you will be able to interpret in one way or another. We are not ignorant of your writings, and perhaps you say that many things are written among you which we do not believe to be written among us.

But if God grants life to you and me, I shall return to you at greater leisure; we shall compare copies of the books among us and among you, and investigate these examples. [Col. 1026D] I myself admit that it would be the height of foolishness, indeed madness, for either you or me to resist evident examples and authorities of Scripture. Therefore there is no need for you to continue disputing further at present.

For in truth, you Christians produce many statements from the law and the prophets that are not written in the law and the prophets. The passage you cited from Jeremiah—“Afterward God was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38)—and many other passages attached to this argument above, Jeremiah did not say or write.

If you find that this is written in Jeremiah, I concede that the other statements have been made with complete truth [Note: Ms. Rem.: “are completely true.”] [Col. 1027A] But if you do not find it in Jeremiah, lay aside such hostility toward us. Be ashamed of the falsehood invented against us, and acknowledge that the truth first preserved among us remains in the law and the prophets.

And as for what all you Christians utter against us with such stern expression: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14)—Isaiah did not say or write this, but only: “Behold,” he says, “the hidden woman shall conceive and bear a son.”

Even if Isaiah had said precisely what you say, he nevertheless did not add what you add on your side: that the virgin remained a virgin at conception and that she remained a virgin after childbirth. Neither Isaiah nor any other prophet said this.

**CHRISTIAN.**

[Col. 1027B] Because Christ is the truth, the faith of Christ has no need of falsehood, nor is there any place for falsehood in the Church of Christ. What we produce as written in the law and the prophets, we received from you as written in the law and the prophets. For the Church of Christ received the law and the prophets from you, and what it received from you it will preserve unchanged through so many ages, even to the present time.

In the time of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, seventy interpreters, the most learned teachers of your people at that time, translated the law and the prophets from Hebrew into Greek. Later, our translators translated them from Greek into Latin, either word for word or sense for sense. From those earliest copies we received everything that we have written in the law and the prophets.

[Col. 1027C] Read the new books; read the ancient books of the Old Instrument [Note: Ms. Rem.: “the codices of the Old Testament.”]; read among the Greeks; read among the Latins. You will never find among us any variation in the law or the prophets, but everywhere throughout the whole world you will find among us the same truth and the unity of truth in the law and the prophets.

What I cited from Jeremiah, Jeremiah wrote and said. The whole Church of Christ throughout the world bears witness that Jeremiah said this, and from the earliest times it received this from your earliest interpreters and has held it without any dispute over alteration.

Although it is not contained in the book entitled under Jeremiah’s name, Jeremiah nevertheless said it, because the one who wrote this wrote it from Jeremiah’s mouth: Baruch, who served as Jeremiah’s secretary. Hence it is read in Jeremiah as follows:

[Col. 1027D] “Jeremiah therefore called Baruch, son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the Lord that he had spoken to him in the scroll of the book” (Jeremiah 36:4). [Note: Ms. S. Ger.: “that the Lord spoke to him.”]

**JEW.**

From these seventy doctors, we have no other information than that, in the time of Moses, Moses himself selected seventy elders of the people, whom he appointed as his assistants and as judges of the disputes that arose among the people. These men neither taught the Scriptures, since they did not yet exist, nor interpreted the Scriptures. As the succession of times and events progressed, David and the prophets later appeared among us, who said many things and wrote many things; but what they said, they said in the Hebrew language, and what they wrote, they wrote in Hebrew style, and among us. Therefore, whatever else anyone has interpreted from the Law and the Prophets differently from what is preserved among us and differently from what the first exemplar contains, he has interpreted falsely, and it can have no authority. Consider, then, where you obtained it, since you did not obtain these things from us.

**CHRISTIAN.**

We do not say that those seventy men under Moses were interpreters, but only elders of the people and judges. We say, however, that those were the seventy interpreters whom the Jewish people sent for that office to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, after the kingdom of the Jews had already been subdued by Antiochus, king of Egypt [Ms. Rem.: “under”]. These men were sent by you to Alexandria, and at Alexandria they translated from Hebrew into Greek all the Scriptures that you then possessed. But whether it is now thus among you, or has been altered in some way, or has been completely removed, I do not know. Nevertheless, since the Law decreed that “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19:15), it must plainly be conceded that among you that word should stand which the seventy interpreters, approved witnesses of your nation, jointly attest [Ms. S. Ger.: “attest by agreement”] to have been spoken and written in Jeremiah—for they were not yet Christians.

Indeed, at the beginning of our faith your nation, a rival of our faith, still possessed great prominence and had many men of the highest eloquence and intellect, thoroughly trained in both languages, Hebrew and Latin. Many gentile philosophers at that time were likewise equally trained in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin literature. All of them rose up against our faith and stirred up questions, conflicts, and seditions; I say, they raised questions at home and, for the most part, abroad as well, even when universal councils had been announced throughout the provinces. The Law and the Prophets were in their hands [Ms. S. Ger.: “in their hand”]; the cited testimonies were examined and discussed in both languages. Yet none of you presumed to make this accusation, namely, to charge them with a false translation by which you could easily deprive us of our faith.

The gentile philosophers, therefore, entirely omitting this accusation, treated the prophets with contempt and rejected their sayings, but attempted by clever verbal sophistry to injure our faith. The philosophers of your nation neither wished nor were able to refute the prophets; instead, likewise omitting this accusation, they said that the Scriptures ought to be understood in a very different way, expounded them according to their own interpretation, and attempted to make the prophets’ words conform to the circumstances and times of their own case. But although “the kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ,” in vain did “the nations rage and the peoples devise vain things” (Ps. 2:1–2).

But concerning these matters Isaiah, inspired by the same Spirit by which Jeremiah was inspired, foretells the same thing, although in other words:

> “Thus says the Lord: Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am the very one who was speaking; behold, I am present” (Isa. 52:6);

that is, I myself [Ms. S. Ger.: “I myself”] who spoke through Moses, who spoke through the other prophets, have spoken through my own person: “behold, I am present.”

To meet him, that same prophet exhorts you elsewhere:

> “Prepare yourself, Israel, to meet your Lord, for he is coming” (Amos 4:12);

and concerning his coming to us he speaks even more clearly:

> “Upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen” (Isa. 9:2).

What light, I ask? Hear it without any ambiguity:

> “For a child is born to us, a son is given to us” (ibid., 9:6).

Who, I ask, is this child who is born to us, this son who is given to us? Hear further:

> “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (ibid., 9:2).

And what kind of peace?

> “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (ibid., 9:7),

because, as it continues,

> “from now and forever it shall be” (ibid.).

> “I myself who was speaking” (Isa. 52:6), who “discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob my servant and to Israel my chosen one” (Baruch 3:37); “behold, I am present” (Isa. 52:6), made human, “living among human beings on earth” (Baruch 3:38).

Christ, therefore, because he is human, is “the child born to us, and the son given to us”; and because he is also God, “his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace, and there shall be no end of peace, because from now and forever it shall be.”

If that child, like any other, had been conceived in iniquities and his mother had borne him in sins, how would that child differ from another? How would he alone “be free among the dead”? (Ps. 87:6.) How would that same prophet call his generation ineffable?

> “Who,” he says, “shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:7–8.)

But he was astonished at his generation and called it ineffable because his mother neither conceived him in iniquity nor bore him in sins: a virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, and therefore he alone was “free among the dead.”

Finally, concerning what you deny to have been written in Isaiah—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14)—your seventy interpreters, approved witnesses by faith and knowledge, translated it in this way, and the prophet himself wished it to be interpreted in this way when he said and wrote:

> “Behold, the hidden woman, as you say, shall conceive and bear a son.”

For if he understood “hidden” in the ordinary sense, that is, shut up at home, and nothing more, what is remarkable or new in such a conception? What sign of a mystery did he intend that conception to be?

> “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold,” he says, “the hidden woman shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (ibid., 7:14–15).

[The enclosed passage is omitted by Ms. S. Ger.]

If these words are understood literally and in the ordinary sense, how will that child, by eating butter and honey, know how to reject evil and choose good? What discernment between good and evil does the eating of honey and butter provide? Why write that the child would eat butter and honey if he intended these words to be understood literally? What sign, or sign of what, would it be that some girl, “hidden”—that is, shut up at home—should conceive?

All these things, therefore, unless they are understood as figurative and spoken in a spiritual and mystical sense, are judged to have been spoken by the prophet in an entirely childish and empty manner. Since it is absurd to believe and say this, the hidden woman—that is, one preserved from the love of a man and from every contagion of sin—conceives, just as the angel answered the Virgin:

> “How,” she said, “shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:34–35).

“I shall overshadow you,” he says, by hiding you from every heat of lust. Therefore,

> “the holy one who shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid., 1:35).

To him God the Father says in the Psalm:

> “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7).

And because by this “today” he wished to be understood not a present and passing time but the perpetuity of eternity, therefore in another psalm he says:

> “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

What, then, is “Today I have begotten you, and before the morning star I begot you,” except: Before time and times, I, God the Father, begot you, God the Son, coeternal with me, although under time and the condition of time I created you as a human being made from a woman?

David briefly commends these two natures in Christ in another psalm:

> “Truth,” he says, “has arisen from the earth” (Ps. 84:12),

because, born from a woman, he arose from the earth as a human being [Ms. S. Ger.: “has arisen,” that is, “born from a woman”]. But because “every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11), he who is not a liar is more than human—indeed, he is truth itself and God.

Therefore this child, human and God, ate butter and honey, because, as the same psalm says shortly before:

> “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84:11).

Butter signifies the grace of anointing and mercy; honey, which, when applied for the treatment of wounds, heals by being eaten, announces the severity of judgment and truth [Ms. S. Ger.: “signifies”]. Although Scripture says, “He has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes” (Rom. 9:18), neither his showing mercy nor his hardening ever in any respect departs from justice or truth. The truth everywhere accompanies God’s mercy and judgment, and in Scripture truth is often used for either of them:

> “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

And in another psalm:

> “The works of his hands are truth and judgment” (Ps. 110:7),

because whether he shows mercy to whom he wishes or judges and punishes whom he wishes, he is truthful and just—truthful and just in showing mercy, truthful and just in imposing the sentence due to judgment.

[Ms. Rem. omits the enclosed words.]

Christ, therefore, will eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good—that is, so that he may make it known that he rejects evil and chooses good, rewarding each according to his works, rewarding the good and condemning the evil with the punishment due to their wrongdoing.

Concerning this mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, let us see what the same prophet says elsewhere, and let us review the prophecy briefly:

> “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he arose like a young shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground; and there was in him neither appearance nor beauty, and his face was as though hidden and despised, so that we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our weaknesses and carried our sorrows. For he was wounded because of our transgressions; he was crushed because of our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep; each of us turned to his own way, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away; who shall declare his generation? Therefore he shall give the ungodly for his burial and the rich man for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand” (Isa. 53:1–10).

The prophet saw your minds obstinately set against believing [Ms. Rem.: “destined”], and said:

> “Lord, who has believed our report?”

And he indicates what he had heard:

> “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

Concerning this arm he himself says elsewhere:

> “The Lord has prepared his arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10).

This is the arm of the Lord, this the salvation of God, concerning which the Psalm says:

> “I shall place him in salvation; I shall act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6).

To whom has it been revealed? For you rejected him who had come, sent to you, just as he himself complains through the same prophet Isaiah:

> “The ox knows his owner, and the ass his master’s manger; Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood me” (Isa. 1:3).

Therefore it is said more clearly in the Psalm:

> “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:45).

You rejected him because he was human, because he was a child born. Hence it follows:

> “And he arose as a young shoot before him” (Isa. 53:2).

For from the root of Jesse a branch came forth; from the branch the young shoot arose. The young shoot grew because “Jesus advanced in age and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2:52). And because the appearance of his divinity was hidden and despised beneath the cloud of the humanity he had assumed, “we did not esteem him.”

> “Truly he himself bore our weaknesses,”

that is, he took them away,

> “and he himself carried our sorrows,”

that is, he bore them away.

> “For he himself was wounded because of our transgressions; he was crushed because of our crimes” (Isa. 53:4–5).

Therefore the apostle Paul says:

> “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

> “The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:5).

For he is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Existing as mediator between God and human beings, by his death he reconciled us to God, because his death was before God a sacrifice for original sin and an expiation.

> “We all went astray like sheep” (ibid., 53:6),

by failing to recognize the arm of the Lord that the Lord prepared in the sight of all the nations, and by failing to regard him as God in a human being.

> “Each of us turned to his own way” (ibid.),

because he strayed from him who is the way, the truth, and the life.

> “And the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all” (ibid.),

because he endured death for the iniquity and sin of the whole world.

For, as the Apostle says, “he was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13)—that is, he shared the death that the curse pronounced by God brought upon the first human being:

> “On whatever day you eat, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2:17).

He endured death for us, and by his death he annulled that curse and death.

And because he endured all these things by his own will, not under compulsion, he adds:

> “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

These things seem to belong to the humanity he assumed. The other things that follow surpass humanity and belong to God alone.

Hence he himself says in the Gospel:

> “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

But whence came this freedom in him? Because the prince of this world found nothing of his own in him, because

> “from distress and judgment he was taken away” (Isa. 53:8),

because once dead he could not be held by death itself.

For he rose from the dead, as the Psalm says:

> “My flesh shall rest in hope, because you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your seed to see corruption” (Ps. 15:9–10).

Whence, then, came such great power in a human being? Because he was more than human:

> “For God was in Christ,”

as the apostle Paul says,

> “reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19),

whose generation is ineffable (Isa. 53:8).

For who shall declare how God, from himself, begot a Son consubstantial with himself before times and forever? [Ms. Rem. omits the enclosed words: “How he was created as a human being at the appointed times from a mother without the seed of a man, and God himself assumed him in the unity of person, who shall declare?”]

No one, therefore, shall declare either the one or the other generation of Christ.

> “Because of the crime”—not indeed his own, but that of my people—“I struck him” (Isa. 53:8).

For what crime did he commit, who did not sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found? (ibid., 53:9.)

If it is true what blessed Job testifies—“Every human being is a liar”—and elsewhere, [Ms. S. Ger. omits the enclosed words: “There is no human being who does not sin, nor even an infant whose life is one day upon the earth”]; if it is true what blessed David also testifies:

> “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11),

and elsewhere:

> “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2),

then he who commits no sin is more than human. The excellence of his prerogative was above that of humanity, since he “did not offend in word” (James 3:2), and “no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22).

Concerning the same mystery the Psalm says:

> “You are beautiful beyond the sons of human beings; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever” (Ps. 44:3).

And immediately addressing the same person, it continues:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (ibid., 44:7).

[Ms. Rem. omits the enclosed words: “Go through the psalm and see that up to this point the psalm continues with one and the same person.”]

He is therefore God, to whom it is said:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.”

To whom, indeed, is it said, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever,” except to him of whom he had said above:

> “You are beautiful beyond the sons of human beings; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever”?

In calling him beautiful beyond the sons of human beings, he does not separate him from human nature, and it is clear that he is human. The same one whom he calls beautiful beyond the sons of human beings he openly names God in the following verse, saying:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”

From these and other examples in Scripture we have believed, and we assert that it must be believed, that Christ is God and human being, with the essence of each nature entirely distinct [Ms. S. Ger.: “indeed distinct”].

We say that he has already come [Ms. S. Ger.: “we believe that he has come”], because we see that the signs which the prophets foretold concerning his coming have already followed.

To take one example from many, Jacob, blessing his son Judah, said:

> “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

Therefore, since for thousands of years a ruler has failed from Judah, and a leader from his loins, and even the name of the Jews has now almost vanished, we say that Christ, the expectation of the nations, has already come.

And in the Psalm it is said:

> “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and bend their backs forever” (Ps. 68:24).

Since, therefore, your back has now been bent to other nations throughout the entire world, the ruler has failed from Judah, and the leader from his loins; and therefore we say that Christ, the expectation of the nations, has already come.

Likewise, since this has been fulfilled:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight” (Ps. 21:28),

we say that Christ, the expectation of the nations, has already come; to him belong honor and dominion throughout eternal ages of ages.

Those, therefore, who have believed in him shall not be confounded, as the prophet Isaiah testifies. Those, however, who have not believed, hear concerning the nations:

> “Let all those who worship carved images and glory in their idols be confounded” (Ps. 96:7).

Hear also concerning the Jews:

> “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written among the righteous” (Ps. 68:29).

**JEW.**

From this inference of yours, therefore, it can be concluded that Christians too should be confounded, because Christians worship carved images and glory in their idols. For you sometimes depict God himself as a wretched man hanging on a gallows, fastened to a cross with nails—a sight horrible even to behold—and you worship it. Around the cross you depict a half-formed boy, the sun, frightened I know not from where, and a sorrowful half-formed maiden, the moon, fleeing and concealing part of the horn of her light. At other times you depict God seated on a lofty throne and making a sign with an outstretched hand; around him, as though to display great dignity, you place an eagle, a human being, a calf, and a lion.

Christians carve, make, and paint these images wherever they can; and wherever they can, they worship and venerate them. Yet the Law given by God altogether forbids this. For in Exodus it is written:

> “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters; you shall not worship them or venerate them” (Exod. 20:4).

The Law therefore eradicates every carved image, and it condemns with a dreadful judgment the one who makes one.

[Col. 1034C]

**CHRISTIAN.**

If the Law condemns every carved image in this way, and if it is in no way permitted to make the likeness of anything, then Moses sinned, since he fashioned and carved likenesses of things; indeed, the Lord sinned, since he commanded them to be fashioned and carved.

For in Exodus the Lord commanded as follows:

> “You shall make me a sanctuary, according to the complete likeness of the tabernacle that I shall show you, and of all its vessels, for its worship” (Exod. 25:8–9).

A little later:

> “You shall also make a plate of purest gold, on which you shall engrave, by the work of an engraver, ‘Holy to the Lord’” (Exod. 28:36).

Again:

> “You shall take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel, by the work of a sculptor and the engraving of a jeweler” (ibid., 28:9–11).

Behold, likenesses of things are fashioned, and the Lord commands them to be fashioned. Behold, sculptures are made for the Lord in onyx stones and gold.

In the Book of Kings, where the temple is built for the Lord, we read:

> “He carved all the walls of the temple round about with various engravings and with the lathe, and he made in them cherubim, palm trees, and various figures, as though projecting from and emerging out of the wall” (3 Kings 6:29).

He also made a molten sea, ten cubits in size, and it stood upon twelve oxen (3 Kings 7:23–25).

A little later:

> “In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high” (3 Kings 6:23).

Again:

> “The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, into the inner sanctuary of the temple, beneath the wings of the cherubim” (3 Kings 8:6).

Clearly he names paintings and sculptures, not condemning but approving the sculptures made in the temple of the Lord. For God himself indicated that he had accepted all these things by approving what had been made:

> “The priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord” (ibid., 8:11).

The prophet Isaiah said:

> “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a high and lofty throne. Seraphim stood above it; six wings belonged to one and six wings to the other” (Isa. 6:2).

Concerning those four kinds of living creatures which you unjustly mocked, the prophet Ezekiel speaks as follows:

> “The likeness of the faces of the four living creatures: the face of a human being, and the face of a lion on the right side of all four; the face of a calf on the left side of all four; and the face of an eagle above all four” (Ezek. 1:10).

[Ms. Rem. omits the enclosed words.]

What Isaiah saw, he said and wrote; what Ezekiel saw, he said and wrote, even though after them it was written, spoken, and marked by some sign in a picture. For just as letters in a certain manner become figures and signs of words, so paintings are likenesses and signs of the things contained in Scripture.

What more is there to say? Let us gather the argument and approach the end of the question under discussion. God prohibited the making of carved images, and yet, as we read, carved images were commanded by God to be made. Therefore the commandment of the Law must be understood appropriately—or rather, it must be understood as the Lawgiver himself declares:

> “You shall not make a carved image” (Exod. 20:4),

and he demonstrates the reason:

> “You shall not worship them or venerate them” (ibid., 20:5).

Once the idolatry of faithless worship has been excluded, carved images were made by them and may be made by us. We make paintings for God, engravings for God, and sculptures for God; but we neither venerate nor worship them with divine worship.

For even of the cross itself, which we call the holy cross, we certainly say that it is wood, not God, and we say that it possesses no power either in itself or from itself. After it has been sanctified by episcopal blessing in memory of the Lord’s Passion, we raise, worship, and venerate the cross—not with divine worship, but with the worship of due reverence, just as the Psalm says:

> “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98:5).

We call this the worship of due reverence because we use the word in another sense. We say, “A Christian worships God,” and in another sense, “A farmer cultivates his field.” Likewise, we say in one sense, “A person worships God,” and in another, “A person worships a man of some dignity or some symbol of a person of dignity.”

For in the Book of Kings we read that Bathsheba worshiped King David, and in many places in your Scriptures we read that one human being worshiped another, although it is written in the Law:

> “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:13, 10, 20; Matt. 4:10; Luke 4:8).

Therefore, when a Christian worships the cross, he worships in the religious worship due to God the Passion of Christ in the cross, because of the Passion of the human being assumed by God into the unity of person; and with the worship of due reverence he worships the image of the cross, the carved likeness of the Lord’s own Passion.

To conclude briefly and in a few words [Ms. Rem.: “to exclude”]: a Christian does not worship any image of anything whatsoever with divine worship. Nevertheless, with the worship of due honor, he venerates and honors consecrated images and paintings of sacred things.

Read the Scriptures, therefore—the Law and the Prophets—and you will see that all the things I have said are written in the Law or the Prophets, either in the same words or with precisely the same meaning. Consider, I say, and reconsider what you are awaiting, how long you are awaiting it, and by what sign you will recognize the thing awaited when it arrives [Ms. S. Germ.: “when it has arrived”]. For the one who was promised as the one to be sent has already come, as the signs by which Jesus Christ, the expectation of the nations, was foretold testify. To him belong honor and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: As is clear, this letter is by Gislebertus and ought to have been placed before this disputation; in the Victor manuscript it is prefixed to it under the following title: “Here begins the dispute of a certain Christian and Jew concerning the Catholic faith.”]

To the most reverend Alexander, bishop of Lincoln by the grace of God, a certain defender and servant of the Christian faith wishes, in the Spirit of God, to think rightly and always to rejoice in his consolation.

Having been instructed to a very considerable degree by these writings, he says, and educated not only in human but also in divine laws, and endowed with the honor of personal grace, I send you a brief disputation for examination by your judgment, which I recently composed after engaging in debate with a certain Jew.

Since I had come to know a certain Jew on account of a particular matter, at length, compelled by love, I frequently urged him to abandon Judaism and become a Christian. I had also shown him, by the light of truth, the many paths of his error, and I supported what I said by testimonies from both his Law and ours. But when he persisted with hardened heart in his unbelief and defended his error with foolish questions and arguments, we finally came together by friendly agreement and sat down for the sake of debate.

The listeners then asked me to commit this to writing for the benefit of the faith. Gladly obeying them, and according to the capacity of my small intellect, I set down in writing a debate between a Jew and a Christian. If anything has been well said in it, let it be attributed to the grace of God; if anything is idle or useless, let your prudence know how to cut it out. Whether you remove the whole or only part, I shall most willingly accept whatever you decide to do.

That Jew, therefore, being highly learned in his own Law and not ignorant of our writings, began as follows.
