# INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS FOUND IN THE WORKS OF SAINT ANSELM

[Note: This index refers to the works of Anselm of Canterbury in PL 158 and 159. In this index, Arabic numerals refer to the column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

The reader is referred back to the bold numbers inserted in the text.

## A
Abbatial election, 430, 431, 432. Election of an abbot by agreement with the ruler, 367. A monk must not be appointed or blessed as abbot without the permission of his own abbot, 357, 358. One elected abbot must not flee the burden in order to indulge his own repose, 406. Blessing or consecration of an abbot by a bishop, 361, 431, 432. In it, a new profession of obedience must not be demanded, 361. It is the bishop’s duty to resist an election by which someone living irreligiously has been appointed abbot, 392. What an abbot should be like, 338. An abbot should strive to be loved rather than feared, 338. Let him be a father and shepherd, not a tyrant and exactor, 338. By his own authority he cannot absolve Simoniacs converted to the monastic order, 425. He can dispense from or alter vows made without an oath before profession, 421. Abbots should receive churches only through the hands of bishops, and not from laymen, 383. Through the presence of a regular abbot, monastic religion is to be restored, 345. An abbot may be elected bishop, 366. With the consent of the monks, 363, 364. Nor should he lay down the burden except with the consent of the brothers, 417. Excessive concern of abbots with the affairs of the monastery is censured as deceit and avarice, 338. Deposition of an abbot, 406. An abbess should not entrust an abbey to another except with the authority of the ruler, the archbishop, and the bishop, and with the consent of the nuns, 397.

One procuring an abortion is barred from sacred functions, 374. Abortives. See Infants.

Absolution from sins granted by Anselm in letters, 372, 389, 399, 410, 415, 420, 445, 450. Also with the imposition of penance, 389. Whoever adds sins to sins in hope of forgiveness does not deserve absolution from sins, 346.

Abstinence from food, 191. The abstinence of monks, 327. See Fasting.

Accident. Something happens to someone when something occurs in relation to that person which was not there previously and which can be absent, 52. Some accidents produce change, such as colors, etc., 14. Others produce no change either by approaching or withdrawing, such as certain relations, 14. Accidents that do not change a thing are improperly called accidents, 14. See Color.

Action. See Intention, Works. [Col. 1044]

ADA, countess. Her affection for Anselm, 448. Anselm urges her to renounce the world, 448.

ADALA, countess. Anselm earnestly begs her to obtain from her son permission for Engelhard of Castro-leonis to leave military service, 340.

ADAM. Adam, son of God, 174. Because he was made by God, 174. And by grace, 174. By the name “Adam,” both Eve and Adam are understood, 100. Adam was made from clay, 57. God made human nature in Adam alone, 88. Human nature was wholly in Adam, 98, 101, 142. God made nature in Adam so that human beings might be propagated from it, 100. Every human being is either Adam or from Adam, 101. Eve alone is from Adam alone, 101. All the others are from Adam and Eve, 101. God subjected the power of propagating nature to Adam’s authority, so that he might use it according to his will, 100, 104. Adam received the power to will nothing without reason, 100. And he was able to preserve this power, 100. God ought to have made Adam only just, 102. God made Adam rational and just at the same time, 101.

Adam’s blessedness. Adam’s blessedness in paradise, 134. God gave him blessedness for his benefit, but justice for His own honor, 134. Adam was made blessed, 101.

Adam’s sin. He could preserve all his goods without any difficulty, 30, 101, 241. But he did not preserve them, 241. Rather, he deprived himself of them and subjected himself to their opposites, 101. By sinning, Adam became a slave of sin and misery, 101. He cannot repay what he owes, 101. He is powerless to recover the goods he lost, 101. He could not preserve his goods except those whose power of generation he had received subject to his will, 101. It was in Adam’s power that what he was naturally, the others should be through him, 104. Thus it lay within the freedom of his choice to propagate them such as he himself was in justice and happiness, 104. Adam received goods to preserve for himself and his descendants, 104. He voluntarily lost them for himself and his descendants, 104. He lost grace by sinning, 174. He lost original uprightness when he turned away from what he ought to have done and turned toward what he ought not to have done, 65. Adam’s person sinned by his own will, not because nature required it, 104, 134. On the very day on which he ate, he is said to be destined to die, because on that day he received the necessity of dying at some time, 100. In Adam, nature was stripped of justice, 104. The person deprived nature, in Adam, of the good of justice, 104. The human race was condemned through Adam’s sin, 100. Why Adam’s sin is charged to him more than to Eve, 100. If Adam had not sinned, his descendants would necessarily have had justice together with rationality, 101. Because Adam and Eve sinned, everything they were became weakened and corrupted—namely, body and soul, 97, 98. See Human Being, Sin.

Adam’s restoration. God was merciful toward Adam and helped him return to His grace, 212. He is believed to have received remission of his faults through Christ, 92, 174, 175. He was counted among the children of adoption, 174. Adam and Eve belonged to Christ’s redemption, 92. Although Scripture does not say this, 92. See Christ, Satisfaction.

God did not will to make anything from Adam other than what He was going to make from human nature, 88. Christ is from Adam, 56, 57. See Human Being.

Adoption. Among the Jews there was a frequent custom of adopting, 174. Someone is rightly said to have begotten the person whom he adopted, 174. For he begot him by benefaction, 174.

Adoration. See Cross.

ADRIAN, a monk of Canterbury, 417. He left the cloister with Ainertus, 417.

Flattery. The sinner’s oil attacks the head when the flatterer’s favor caresses the mind, 182. The favor and praise of vices is especially condemnable, 182. See Praise.

ADULTERER, ADULTERY. Fortunate is this adulterous woman, who is absolved from the past and made secure concerning the future, 231. Adultery is prohibited by the natural law, 151.

Adversity. Concerning adversity, 191. We expect a judge to be so much more lenient as we now endure him patiently in his severity, 318. Adversities compel us toward God, 181, and separate the mind from earthly things, 181. If God has pressed down His hand, we promise to do what must be done; if He has held back His sword, we do not fulfill our promises, 251. If He strikes, we cry out that He spare us; if He spares us, we provoke Him again to strike, 251. If distress comes, we ask for time to repent; if mercy has looked upon us, we abuse the patience that spared us, 251. God permits His own to be afflicted, 184. See Affliction, Evil, Patience, Tribulation.

Sickness. See Disease, Punishment of sin.

Enigma. When we speak through enigmas, we signify by one thing what we either do not wish or are unable to express literally, 24. We often see something not literally as the thing itself is, but through some likeness, 24. When we say or see one thing not literally but through a likeness, we both say and do not say, see and do not see, one and the same thing, 24. For we say and see it through another thing; we do not say and do not see it according to its proper meaning, 24.

Equanimity. Concerning equanimity, 191 and 192. See Patience.

Eternity. To exist or live eternally is to possess an interminable life, wholly and perfectly, all at once, 13. In eternity all things exist together without movement, 125. Eternity is never unlike itself, 13. Eternity is compared with a point, 48, 61; it is one, simple, and indivisible, 48. Eternity within eternity, or point within point, is nothing other than one eternity and one point, 48, 61. Through something temporal and local, something eternal can be understood, 57. There cannot be or be conceived several eternities, 48, 61. The immutable presence of eternity, 125. The eternal present contains all times and the things that exist in each time, 125. Our intellect cannot pass beyond eternity, as though it could reach back to its beginning, 60. See Creature, Time.

Affability. Concerning affability, 192.

Affirmation. Affirmation signifies that what is, is, 110. When affirmation signifies that what is, is, it signifies what it ought to signify, 110. See Proposition, Truth.

Affliction. See Adversity, Evil, Patience, Tribulation.

AINERTUS, brother of Gerard the moneyer of Arras, 316.

AIRARD, a Canterbury monk, departed from the cloister with Adrian, 418.

The monastery of St. Albans, 387, 451. Its prior was Bernard, 451. In it disagreement arose concerning the two natures in Christ, 451.

ALBERIC, cardinal, 448. What had been asked of Anselm concerning him, Anselm gladly did, 448.

ALBERT, physician and friend of St. Anselm, 320, 321. Anselm urges him to convert from the world, 321, 325. Anselm entrusts to him the care of Maurice in his illness, 321. His advice is sought concerning the headache of Lanfranc’s nephew, 323. Anselm thanks him for his care of Maurice, 325.

ALBRITUS, 434.

What “white” signifies, 149, 150.

ALEXANDER, king of the Scots, 414. He succeeded his brother by hereditary right, 414.

ALEXANDER, a monk; he carried Anselm’s letters, 436. [Col. 1046] He was sent by Anselm as a messenger to Paschal II, 383.

ALFERUS, prior of the monastery of St. Edmund, 410.

Nourishment. What bodily nourishment is, 238.

Other. It is impossible for anyone to be other before being what he is, 52. Someone becomes other after he exists; someone becomes other in existing, 52.

Altar. Whether an altar that has been moved ought to be consecrated again, 423. When the principal altar has been violated, the entire church, together with the altar, must be consecrated, 423. The altar does not exist for the church, but the church for the altar, 423. When the principal altar has been violated, it no longer seems to be a church, 423. An altar moved from its foundation is no longer an altar, 423. A portable altar must not be consecrated without a foundation, 423. Nevertheless, in Anselm’s time, bare stones not fixed anywhere were consecrated, 423. The altar stands in the place of the Christian faith, 423. We offer our sacrifice only on an altar, 423. See Church.

Ambition. The ambition of worldly vanity is iniquity, 347.

AMBROSE. See AUGUSTINE.

Friend. See Love of Neighbor.

Love. Nothing is loved except what is known, 21, 91. The memory and understanding of anything are idle and useless unless the thing itself is loved or rejected as the thing requires, 20. A person loves those things whose loss he cannot bear without sadness, 337. Nothing can better repay what was given through love than love, 259. There are two loves, one good and one evil; one sweet and one bitter: they cannot both be contained at once in a single heart, 259.

Love of God. Concerning the love of God, 227, 228. Whoever loves something other than God does not have the love of God in him, 259. The pleasure and desire for God by which God is loved are holy, good, chaste, pure, and secure, 259. To love God above all things is just and reasonable, 191, 267. God must be loved with the whole heart, etc., 26, 220. No one can love God except through God, 220, 223. The love of the highest good, 87. Every person must strive toward the highest good with his whole heart, 26. Nature can love the highest good above all things only if it is just, 87. It is the greatest fault and the greatest evil not to love the highest good, 26. See Highest Good, God.

Love toward God is not transitory but eternal, 253. It is not idle, 252. The love of God is chaste, sober, and sweet, 227. God alone and without end is to be loved, 25. Everything is vanity except loving God, 201. No one can ever love God as much as he ought, 224. The enemies of God hate nothing in a person except what loves God, 216. Whoever loves supreme justice is incapable of despising anything just or admitting anything unjust, 27. Two things belong to the love of God: affection and work, 230. Affection is nourished by meditation, 230. The love of God grows through remembrance of past benefits, experience of present benefits, and consideration of future benefits, 230. Whoever loves God more than himself already begins to possess what he wishes perfectly to have in the kingdom of heaven, 349. If you wish to be a king in heaven, love God and human beings for His sake, 341. The love of God excludes every other love, 349. Whoever wishes to possess perfect love of God should love contempt, poverty, etc., 349. The kingdom of heaven is purchased by the love of God, 349. Whoever does not love God loses what he lives by, 228. Whoever accuses another of living for God is dead, 228. A rational soul is useless to itself without love of the highest good, 26. Whoever loves God walks upon the sea, 161. How great a good it is to love God, 201. Whoever loves God becomes God himself, 201. The love of God is sought from God Himself, 257, 291, 262. The reward of love for God is blessed life, 25.

If what serves love is so great, how great is what is repaid to love? 26. If the support of love is such, what is the profit of love? 26. It is inconsistent with the character of the most just One not to distinguish between the person who loves and the person who despises what ought to be loved supremely, 26. Either not to love one who loves Him, or not to benefit from being loved by him, 26. Nothing can be the reward of this love except what surpasses all created natures, 26. If He gave a rational essence so that it might be loving, what will He give to the lover if he does not cease to love? What will supreme goodness repay to the person who loves and desires it, except itself? 26. Whatever else it gives, it does not repay him, 26. Nor does that other thing console the lover or satisfy the one who desires, 26. If supreme goodness wishes to be loved and desired in order to give something else in return, it does not wish to be loved and desired for its own sake but for the sake of something else, 26. And thus it does not wish itself to be loved, but something else, 26. It is impious to think this, 26. The punishment of the soul that does not love God, 26. The soul that despises love of the highest good will be eternally wretched, 26. It is not reasonable that the soul which despises the highest good should lose existence or life itself, 26. It is not just that, after guilt, it should receive as punishment the existence it had before every guilt, 26. See Soul and Rational Creature.

Love of parents for children and of children for parents. Concerning the love of parents for their children, 210. Love toward father and mother is commanded by God, 255. [Col. 1047]

Love of neighbor. Nature teaches that a person should do for another what he wishes done for himself by that other, 84. God commands that one love one’s neighbor as oneself, 267. Whoever does not love his neighbor and help him as much as he is able, so that he may advance in the good, is not loved by God, nor does God regard his works, 248. Let no one be your enemy except the devil, 191. It is more pleasing to God to love one’s neighbor than to be loved by one’s neighbor, 418. We ought to strive more to love than to be loved, 418. The reward is owed to the lover, not to the loved one, 418. Concerning love of enemies, 192. So that they may acquire friends from every quarter, monks should show kindness or at least offer the grace of conversation, 372. They should never think that they have enough friends, 372. But whether rich or poor, they should all be joined together in the love of brotherhood, insofar as this benefits their church and their salvation, 372. The absence of friends must be endured through obedience, 313, 316, 335, 337.

AMOS—that is, “honoring,” “strong,” or “tearing away the people,” 176.

ANASTASIUS, a monk. St. Anselm seeks his friendship, 314.

ANESGOTUS. He excuses himself, 318.

Angel. The name “angel” is taken from his office, 43. An angel—that is, a messenger of God, 43, 176. An angel is a substance, 43. The number of the elect was not complete among the angels, 81, 82, 83. It can be said to the angel himself that he has only what he received, 62 and following, 67. And he did not have what he did not receive, nor what was not given to him, 70. Whether an angel who is capable of willing, but does not yet will anything, can by himself will something, 67. An angel could will nothing except justice or advantage, 64. Without any preceding sin, an angel had not deserved to suffer any evil, 71.

Grace, knowledge, and freedom of the angels. All angels were made in justice, 64. See Justice, Rational Nature. As long as an angel possessed a right will, he wished to persevere in that same will, 64. He knew that he could change the will he held, 71. He knew that he ought not to will what he willed by transgressing, 71. He knew what he ought or ought not to will, 71. If he had not known this, he would have been neither just in retaining justice nor unjust in abandoning it, 71. He could not have been ignorant that he would be justly punished if he sinned, 71, 72. But he could not comprehend whether God would do something that He could justly do, 72. An angel is rational, 71. He could not believe that God would damn His creature because of its fault, 72. No example of avenging justice had preceded, 72. He was certain that the number in which those who were to enjoy God had been made could not be diminished and remain incomplete, 72. He could not know whether God, if he fell, would substitute human nature for angelic nature or angelic nature for human nature, 72. Foreknowledge of punishment was not advantageous to the angel, 72. The good angels could have sinned before the evil angels fell, 64. The good angels preserved justice by their power, not by necessity, 64. See Free Choice. Therefore they deserved grace from God, because they stood while others fell, 64. The angels owe God equal gratitude, 70. The angel who stood and the one who did not stand were endowed with equal knowledge, 72. An angel could not be forced to fall, 71. The angels received from God both the ability to retain and the ability to abandon justice, 70. God gave the angels the ability to abandon justice so that they might in some way give it to themselves, 70. If they could not in any way take justice away from themselves, they could not in any way give it to themselves, 70. The affection or will for uprightness was separable in the angels, 133. See Sin of the Angels, Free Choice.

The perseverance and blessedness of the angels. The angel who stood persevered because he had perseverance, 62. He had perseverance because he received it, 62; he received it because God gave it, 62. The good angels preferred the justice they possessed to the greater thing they did not possess, 61. Therefore they received that greater thing which they did not possess, 64, and remained in true security in the good they possessed, 64. They were not confirmed by the fall of the wicked but by their own merit, 81. All would have been confirmed if each had stood, 81. The good angels never sinned, 83. The good angel made himself just by not taking justice away from himself when he could have done so, 70. He gave himself blessedness, 70. The good angels advanced after the ruin of the wicked, 81. God preserved the blessed angels from sin through His Son, 281. There is no injustice in the good angel, 77. The holy angels neither wish nor are able to sin because of the grace of confirmation, 64, 72, 108. This one cannot depart because he remained by good will alone, 72. For these angels, the inability to abandon what they have retained is the reward of justice, 72. The angel now has knowledge that he will not fall, 72. Therefore he cannot sin, 72. This inability is glory for the angel, 72. For this reason he is to be praised, because he cannot depart from justice, 72. The good angel did not advance to this knowledge because the evil angel sinned, 72, but possessed this knowledge through the example of the fallen angel, 72. If neither had sinned, God would have given both the same knowledge through the merit of perseverance, 70.

The blessedness of the angels is greater than the blessedness that belonged to humanity in paradise, 134. The good angels obtained whatever they could wish for, 64, and do not see what more they could wish for, 64 and 72; therefore they cannot sin, 64 and 72. They can wish for no good thing in which they would not rejoice, 64. The good angel must always give thanks to God for blessedness, 70. There is no injustice in the good angel, 77, and no justice in the evil angel, 77. The choirs of angels sing to God without end, 34, 242.

Sins of the angels. There is no doubt that the devil sinned, 64. How the angel sinned, 64. He could not even have anticipated his fall by any suspicion, 71, 72. An angel could not be unjustly condemned by the just God, 64. Justice did not depart from the angel; rather, he abandoned it, 73. He abandoned it because he willed what he ought not to have willed, 73. No cause preceded his will except that he was able to will, 73. He sinned by willing something which at that time he ought not to have willed, 64. He sinned by willing an advantage which he ought not to have willed, 64. He wished to be greater than God by willing what God did not want him to will, 64. Anselm does not know what good the evil angels desired to have in greater measure, 65. The angels could by their own merit advance toward some good that they had not received at creation, 65. Whence did the angel’s disordered will arise—from the angel himself, from God, or from the devil? 65. The angel willed what he ought not to have willed only because he willed it, 73. And this will had no other cause, 73. This will was its own efficient cause and effect, 73. He did not fail to will what he ought because the will failed while God failed to give it, 64. Rather, by willing what he ought not to have willed, he expelled the good will with an evil will, 64.

He received the possession of a good will for as long as he possessed it, 63. He could have received the ability always to retain what he abandoned, 63. God had given him only the will and ability to receive perseverance, 63. But He had not given him the reception of perseverance itself, 63. He willed and was able to receive perseverance, 63. Yet he did not receive perseverance, since his will was changed, 63. He did not lack or fail to receive perseverance because God did not give it, 63. Rather, God did not give it because he did not receive it, 64. And he did not receive it because he did not wish to receive it, 64. He did not wish to receive it, and did not receive perseverance, because he did not desire it completely, 63. But after his will was changed, he willed what he ought not to have willed, 64. Thus he did not receive it because he abandoned it, 63. He wished to abandon what he had because he did not wish to retain it, 64. He voluntarily relinquished the will he had, 63.

He sinned by disorderedly willing more than he had received, 64, 71. He sinned both by willing what he ought not to have willed and by not willing what he ought to have willed, 64. He did not will more than he ought because he did not wish to retain justice, 64. Rather, he did not retain justice because he willed something else, by willing which he abandoned justice, 64. By this very act the angel willed in a disordered way to be like God, because by his own will he willed something, 61. The evil angel now knows through his own experience what the good angel now knows only through the example of another, 72. For the evil angel his knowledge is to his disgrace; for the good angel his knowledge is to his glory, 72.

The evil angel could have given justice to himself, 70, because he could have taken it away from himself, and could have not taken it away, 70. The evil angel is blameworthy because he cannot return to justice, 72. He cannot return because he departed by evil will alone, 72. He must none the less render to God what belongs to God, 70. He took away from himself what God gave and refused to receive what God offered, 70. The inability to recover what he abandoned is the punishment of sin, 72. The angels did not fall by necessity, 81. Other angels cannot be substituted for the angels who fell, 81. If an angel had perseveringly preserved justice, he would never have sinned and would not have been miserable, 64. God makes the evil angel unjust by not restoring justice to him, although He could do so, 70. The evil angels can will no good thing without lacking it, 65. There is no justice in the evil angel, 77. See Devil.

Angelic guardianship. The angels have with us a kind of kinship of spiritual relationship, 171. They call us their brothers, 171. The angels offer and present to God, for the elect, the chastity and patience of Christ, 170. They will stand before the Lord with all the elect, bearing the offerings of good works, 170, 171. They drive sinners toward death, 168. They present human beings to God after death, 182. God sent His angels to Adam and to other human beings, warning them to repent, 212, 213. Temporal causes are referred by the angels to eternal truth, 182. The angels report all our works and prayers to God, 168, 182, 226. This is not so that He may learn what He did not know, 182, but by asking what is being done concerning them and concerning us, or by advising what they should do, 182 and 168. Angels are assigned to our guardianship, 168, 226. Through the angels, by Christ’s command, the affairs of our salvation are administered, 225. They bring us the secrets of the supreme counsel, 226. Healings are accomplished through them, 226. Among them Michael is preeminent, 226, a noble standard-bearer, 226. The angels are the work of divine wisdom, 226. He created them for the work of His ministry, 226. The protection and guardianship of the angels, 226. They intercede with God for us, 226. They are grieved by evils, 168. Their displeasure at our evils is called their sadness, 168. See Rational Nature, Spirit.

England. England is shaken by wars, 379, 380, 432. England’s evils, 381. The bishops of England declare that they will give their primate no advice except according to the king’s pleasure, 381. The morals of the English are utterly corrupt, 319.

ANHELITS, abbess, 430. She venerated a certain dead man as a saint, 430. Anselm forbade her to do this, 430. To her disobedience Anselm threatened suspension, 430. See Cult of the Saints.

Soul, mind. The soul is spiritual, 238. By nature it tends toward higher things, 238. The soul possesses certain powers within itself, which it uses as instruments for appropriate purposes, 132. There is reason in the soul, 132. It uses reason for reasoning, 132. Through the soul a human being is called rational, and without it there is no human being, 98. St. Augustine neither accepts nor rejects St. Jerome’s opinion that God creates new souls every day, 170. St. Augustine put forward no certain opinion concerning the origin of the soul, 170. The soul is a substance, 43.

The rational soul surpasses all creatures, 26. It was made so that, if it preserves what it exists for, it may at some time live happily, truly secure from death itself and every other trouble, 25. The human soul was made so that it may always live if it always wishes to do what it was made for, 25. The life of the human soul will never be taken away if it always strives to love the highest life, 25. The human soul is a rational creature, 25. It was made to love the highest essence, 25, 26, and to love it without end, 25. Supreme Wisdom did not make the rational soul so that it might at some time despise the highest good, which is the highest essence, or lose it through some violence while wishing to retain it, 25.

The soul contains nothing by local circumscription, 13. Intellect, or rationality, is not contained circumscriptively in the soul. The soul is wholly present in each of the limbs, 32, 203. Otherwise it would not wholly perceive in each of them, 32. The rational mind is not perceived by any bodily sense as to what it is, what kind it is, or how great it is, 9. It is greater than the body and than every sensible thing, 9. All human souls are of the same nature, 26. Every human soul is immortal, 26. Every human soul will either always be miserable or at some time be truly blessed, 26. Before it existed, the soul could possess neither guilt nor experience punishment, 26.

The more precious part of a human being, namely the mind, is sick, 186. A human being neither perceives in the limbs nor acts except through the soul, in which the will exists, 99. As long as the soul remains in the body, the human being lives, 211. When the soul abandons the flesh, the human being dies, 211. The soul gives life to the flesh while it remains in the flesh, 211. The flesh gives life to the soul while the flesh itself performs works, 211. Let the soul rule the flesh, reason the soul, and grace reason, 228. Without a rational soul, a human being does not possess rational will, 99, 102. Immediately after conception, the fetus does not possess a rational soul, 99, 102. A human being lives according to the soul while he guards the will and commandments of his Creator, 238. He dies according to the soul when he does not obey the divine commandments, 238. The nourishment of the soul is the will of God, 238. From what the soul lives, 29.

As soon as the soul of a just person departs from the body, it sees all its works, 211. It sees all its good deeds, 211. Therefore it rejoices, 211. The angel who guarded it immediately receives it, 211. He places it before the throne of God, 211. Other angels and saints meet it and joyfully welcome it, 211. The soul of a sinner is forced to leave the body, 211. The angels of Satan immediately receive it, bind it with fiery chains, and drag it away to the torments of hell, 211. The souls of the righteous, released from their bodies, already stand before the sight of the Creator’s glory, 158. Concerning the misery of the unjust soul when it is separated from the body, 207, 211. The mind is the more precious part of a human being, 186. See Human Being, Mind, Reason, Life, Will.

Animal. The definition of animal is the same in all animals, 117. Every animal is rational or irrational, 149.

ANSELM (St.). Anselm’s modesty, 3, 41, 42, 49, 61, 75, 97, 103, 318, 334, 335, 389, 391. Anselm rejected praise, but not affection, 139, 389, 391. He professed conversion of conduct and obedience according to the Rule of St. Benedict, 361. He vowed to live according to the same Rule, 297. His daily fasting, 387. He lacked nothing for the fullness of justice and the integrity of teaching, 387. His breast was a sanctuary of virtues, 387. He was an interpreter of heavenly truth, 387. A victor over human nature, 387. His zeal in defending the dignity of his church, 440. For the freedom of the Church he fears neither exile, nor poverty, nor torments, nor death, 394, 398, 400, 407.

His reverence and obedience toward the apostolic see, 384, 385, 428, 429, 431, 440. Because of this he suffered tribulations, 428. He suffered in England for four years and in exile for two years, 429. He was an exile for three years under King William, 382, 427. His gentleness, 343, 346, 351, 359, 360. His almsgiving and care for the poor, 434, 435, 444. His humility, 318, 334, 335, 369. It is asked why Archbishop Lanfranc greeted him, then abbot, as lord and father, 329. He grieves that he has no leisure for reading or prayer, 327. He excuses himself from responsibility for the studies of a young man entrusted to him, 318. His opinion concerning almsgiving and the abstinence of monks, 327. With God revealing it, he came to understand what he had written about presence, predestination, grace, and free choice, 134.

He yields to the authority of his elders. His statements accord with the writings of the holy Fathers, especially blessed Augustine, 3, 45. He sends the Monologion to Archbishop Lanfranc for correction, 335, 451. Anselm’s reputation was greater than that of Lanfranc and Guitmund, 318. He was closely joined in friendship with the noblest of the Northmen, 318. He taught declensions, 331. Anselm was prior of Bec, 319, 320. He asks Lanfranc for the Life and Rule of St. Dunstan, 323, 324. He also asks for Bede’s treatise On Times, 324. He asks for the Aphorisms with glosses, 325 and 330. He freely grants to Durand, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, a union of fellowship, 334. He asks that his name be inscribed last, after the names of the brothers of that monastery, 335. Anselm confirms by the authority of St. Augustine certain points noted by Lanfranc in that book, 337.

Anselm is wrongly criticized for having said, following the Greeks and Augustine, that in God there are three substances and one person, 337, 339. He does not wish the Monologion to be disseminated indiscriminately among the unlearned, 339. Abbot of Bec, 341, 343, etc. He exhorts the monks of Bec whom he sent to England to exhibit in their conduct what they profess in the habit of religion, 343. He rebukes a drunken chamberlain, 343. He sets out for England, 344. He boards the ship at the first hour, arrives at the ninth hour, reaches Lanfranc in the evening, and is received at his estate called Liming, 344. In certain little works he added the title “abbot” to his name, not to display a more honored person, but to exclude ambiguity in the name, 345. He has no leisure for dictation, 345. He recovered from illness, 346. His life had once been worn down by secular conduct, 347. He sends the Monologion and Proslogion to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, 345, 346. He corrects the titles of the Monologion and Proslogion, 347. He crosses again to England, 347. He sets out for England a third time, 351, 360.

In response to Anselm’s prayers, Pope Gregory VII commends himself, the Church, and the conversion of heretics, 353. His religious life and learning, 353. Pope Urban II commands him to assist and advise the less experienced bishop of Beauvais, 353. He made John, a cleric of the Roman Church, a monk, 353. A complaint against Anselm was made concerning this, 353. He defended the bishop of Beauvais against the unjust persecution of canons and priests, 354, 380. By a privilege of the apostolic see he freed the monastery of Bec from episcopal authority, 354. At his judgment Urban II decides whether the bishop of Beauvais ought to resign the episcopate, 354, 380.

He proposes to write against the man who said that there are three things in God, 355. He responds to a question from Robert, abbot, concerning one who determines to sin, is divinely prevented, and rejoices that he has been prevented, 355, 356. He defends Lanfranc and himself against the errors of Roscelin, 337. He pronounces anathema on anyone who asserts that the three persons in God are three things, as there are three angels, 357. He rejects the election of Lanfranc’s nephew as abbot of Saint-Wandrille, made without his permission, 357, 358. He is seized by fever, 358, 359. When he proposes to send for the prayers of the monks of Caen, the fever departs, 359.

Anselm was elected archbishop of Canterbury against his will, 362, 366, 368, 374. He was carried to the church almost lifeless, 374. He was compelled to consent lest he resist God’s will, 374. He urges the monks of Bec to consent to this election, 363, 364. He is accused of having pretended to resist this election while truly desiring it, 363, 365, 368, 369. He was advanced by the ailing king, and the pastoral staff was forcibly pressed into Anselm’s hand by the king himself, 363. When he was elected, many thought that they themselves would rule above all, saying that Anselm would always be dealing with God and would not concern himself with the affairs of the Church, 364.

The king of the English, by the counsel and request of the nobles and by the petition and election of clergy and people, gave Abbot Anselm the governance of the Church of Canterbury, 364. Anselm clears himself of the charge of ambition and greed, 365, 366, 367, 368, 369. He professed himself a monk, 366. He writes concerning the election of an abbot in the church of Bec, 367, 371. His sight was weakened by tears, 371. His consecration took place on the first Sunday after the feast of St. Andrew, namely on the day before the Nones of December, 371. He continually acquired friends for the church of Bec, 372. His dispute with the bishop of London, 372. His concern for the conduct of the people of Bec, 373, etc. [Col. 1051]

He supports Pope Urban II and opposes Guibert, 374, 380. For six months after the election he left nothing undone to secure his release, 380. He was consecrated, 374. He promised a considerable sum of money to the king of the English when the king was going to Normandy, 374. So that he would give more, the king…

He demands it; and he himself absolutely refuses to give it, 374. Hence the king becomes hostile toward Anselm, 374. The king prevents him from requesting the pallium, 374. He asks the king to convene a council, 374. He warns him to correct certain things that he was not conducting properly, 374. He himself is prepared to make satisfaction, 374. The king rejects it, 374. For this reason Anselm refuses to give the king money, lest he appear to have purchased the archbishopric, 374, 375. He opposes the king when the latter gives the lands of the Church of Canterbury to soldiers, 375. He wishes either to resign the archbishopric or to request the pallium from Urban II, 375. He cannot leave Canterbury because of fear of enemies, 379. The king orders him, by word and letter, to guard Canterbury and to command the knights and foot soldiers to be summoned from every direction, 379. Therefore at that time he cannot convene a council, although Cardinal Legate Walter advised him to do so and he himself had it in mind, 379. He clears himself of the charge of schism, 379, 380. He is consecrated by the bishops under a profession of obedience to the Roman pontiff, 380. The Roman pontiff sent him the pallium, 380. He sends a small gift to Urban II, 380. He groans under the burden of the archbishopric, 380. He takes care that his debts be paid, 434. The discord between the king and Anselm and the evils it produced, 400. After requesting but not obtaining permission from the king to go to Rome, Anselm leaves England and goes to Rome, 381. At Rome he repeatedly laid his case before Urban II. In the third year after he left England, he writes to Paschal II about his own troubles and those of all England, 382. Having nothing, he is received and supported by Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, 382. He does not wish to return to England unless he is free to prefer God’s law and the apostolic decrees to the king’s will, 382. Nor unless the king restores the lands of the Church and returns whatever he has usurped from the archbishopric, 382. Why Anselm does not excommunicate the king, 382. King Henry I recalls him, 382, 383. He congratulates Paschal II on his return, 382. He consoles Burgundius and his wife, his sister, because God has taken their young children to eternal life, 383. He urges them now to serve God with their mouths, 383. The case of Bishop Ralph is entrusted to Saint Anselm, 384. He consults Paschal II about several matters, 384. He took part in the Roman council, 384. He sends his legates to Rome concerning the matter between himself and the king, 384. He suffers persecution for nine years, 384. He founded the monastery of Saint Werburga, 385. He sends to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, a book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, 386. Through his vigor the peace of the kingdom and the dignity of the priesthood were strengthened and defended, 387. He blessed Matilda as the king’s wife and consecrated her for the coronation, 387, 388. He suffers insult because letters copied by him were falsely circulated, 389. He restored to the monks of the Church of Canterbury a portion of the altar and a manor, 393. He reproves Samuel, bishop of Dublin, on three matters, 393. He consults Paschal II about investitures, 393, 394. He leaves England in midsummer and reaches Chartres, where he is received by the countess, the king of England’s sister, and by the bishop, 395. Because of the excessive heat he returns to Normandy, 395. He stays at Bec, 396, 398. From there, before the Assumption of Blessed Mary, he sets out for Rome, 398. He was present at the festival at Chartres, 398. He is criticized for the intimacy he maintained with those whom the king did not love, 398. He comes to Rome, 398. He returns from Rome but does not come to England, and why, 399, 439. So that he might not communicate with excommunicated bishops, 439. He is accused of having defamed the king and Robert, bishop of Lincoln, through his monks, 400. He clears himself of that charge, 400. He swore that he would observe not Lanfranc’s example but God’s law, 400. He is accused that, while prohibiting the king from granting investitures, he himself gave churches to laymen, 404, 439. He clears himself of that charge, 439. The kings of France invite him to come to Gaul, 440. The case of the archbishop of Rouen is entrusted to Anselm, 416. He says that he swore to observe not the custom of the king or of his predecessors but God’s law, 438, 439. Hence the king becomes angry, 439. He reproves the king for exacting money from priests as a penalty for violating the council of London, 407. An agreement is made between him and the king at the castle of Eagle, on the eve of the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, concerning his reinstatement and the restoration of everything to him, 407. Nevertheless, he does not wish to return to England until the king’s envoy has returned from Rome, 407 and 408. He condemns the marriages of priests, 408. He deprives priests who keep women of every ecclesiastical benefice, 408. He excommunicates them, 408. He sends Baldwin and William, his legates, to Rome, 410, 411, 416. His charity toward converts to the faith, 409. The bishops of England entreat him to return quickly to England and promise their assistance, 410, 411. He refuses, although asked by the queen, to give testimony about an unknown man, 413. Recalled by the king, he returns to England and is received by everyone with joy, 413, 418, 427. He sent monks to Scotland, 414. He places Thomas, the elected bishop of York, under interdict, [Col. 1052] 422. He prevents the pallium from being sent to him, 421. He prevents the pallium from being granted to the bishop of London, 421. He opposes the legation that Paschal II had given to the archbishop of Vienne, 427. Anselm’s grave complaint concerning Roger, abbot of Saint-Evroul, before the archbishop of Rouen and all the bishops and abbots of Normandy, 432. He wishes to send the books *Why God Became Man* and *On the Virgin’s Conception* to the pope, 441.

**ANSELM, SAINT, nephew of Anselm.** Concerning Anselm the nephew, 391, 392, 395, 434, 441. Anselm, nephew of Archbishop Anselm, son of Burgundius and Riceza, 382. He was offered to God by his parents, 383. His love for God, 383. Archbishop Anselm commends him to Ernulf, prior of Canterbury, 383. Archbishop Anselm orders him to study grammar and to exercise himself more in prose than in verse, 383. He recovered from a prolonged illness, 392. He stays with Archbishop Anselm in exile at Lyon, 382.

**ANSFRED**, Anselm’s servant and messenger, 373, 414. He comes from England to Bec, 373.

**Antichrist.** During the persecution of Antichrist, no one, even among the perfect, will be without fear, 161. The deceptive signs or miracles of Antichrist, 161. Then there will be great temptation, 161. See *Judgment*.

**Antiphonary.** An antiphonary is to be written out with musical notation, 319.

**ANTONY**, subprior of Canterbury, 376, 400. He is reproved for being suspicious, 400.

**Aphorisms.** Anselm arranges for the aphorisms, with glosses, to be copied by the monk Maurice and brought to him, 325, 330.

**Apostate.** See *Monk*.

**Apostles.** The apostles were the first among the Jews to believe, 180. Christ entrusted the governance of the Church to the apostles, 160. The apostle Thomas went to India, 158. Bartholomew was sent to India, 158. Matthew went to Ethiopia, 158. The apostle John went to Asia, 158. Andrew went to Scythia, 158. The apostle Philip went to Scythia, 158. Peter went to Italy, 158. Paul went to Spain, 158. Through the wickedness of malicious people, the apostles were an odor of death, 133. Through their uprightness, the apostles were a good odor, 133.

**Appetite.** The natural will to avoid harm or to possess an advantage, 68. Without this, no one is moved by love or fear, 68. Appetites are not in themselves just or unjust, 98, 134. When brute animals assent to their appetites, they are not called unjust, 98, 134. To desire any of the lowest pleasures is not evil, 70. Appetites are not removed in baptism, 98. See *Baptism*, *Good*, *Concupiscence*, *Will*.

**Water.** A new church is sprinkled with blessed water, 423. See *Church*. Water is added to wine in the Mass so that the water which flowed with the blood from Christ’s side may be represented, 453. See *Mass*.

**Aquicinum.** The monastery of Aquicinum, 424. Its abbot was Gelduin, 424.

**Eagle**, castle: the king of England and Anselm reached an agreement there, 408.

**Archdeacon.** The revenues of the archdeaconry of Canterbury, 409. They are spent on almsgiving, 409.

**ARISTOTLE** asserted concerning singular things that everything exists necessarily, 94. In what sense Aristotle said that grammar is among the things that are “in a subject,” 145, 146. Aristotle’s *Categories*, 147.

**ARNULF (SAINT)**, abbot: he extinguished the accusation that was troubling Abbot Walter, 330.

**ARNULF**, monk: Anselm advises him not to choose where he may teach, but where he may be taught, 323. He is the teacher of the monk Maurice, 331. Learned in declensions, 331. Anselm greets him as a man of Beauvais, 336.

**ARNULPH**, abbot of Troarn. Suffering from a serious illness, he wishes to lay down his burden, 416. He must not do this except with the consent of the archbishop and the brothers, 417.

**ARPHAXAD.** See *Cain*.

**Art.** A painting or any work exists in the mind of the craftsman before it exists in reality, 35 and 36. A work in the mind of the craftsman is life, 36. And it is nothing other than the craftsman’s own knowledge, 36.

The donkey signifies the gentile people, 180.

**ATHELIZ**, abbess of Winchester, 393. See *Winchester*.

**Arras.** A moneyer from Arras becomes a monk, 316.

**Avarice, avaricious person.** Concerning avarice, 198. Iniquity is an insatiable greed for riches, 347. Some accumulate riches through honorable labor but with an unlawful desire, 184. The sins of avarice, 196. See *Riches*. The more an avaricious person increases his money, the more he burns with thirst for money, 188.

To listen to the Holy Spirit is, as it were, to learn, 55. What our hearing is, 172. What God’s hearing is, 172.

**AUDOENUS (SAINT).** The monastery of Saint Audoenus, 413. Its abbot was Helgotus, 413.

[Col. 1053]

**AUGUSTINE (SAINT)**, son of truth, 108. His books *On Genesis Literally*, 451. His view concerning the persons and substance of God, 337, 339. His view concerning the origin of the soul, 107. And concerning semen—whether guilt exists in it, 107. The authority of Saint Ambrose is set against that of Saint Augustine, as though Augustine were saying that guilt exists in semen, 107.

**AUGUSTINE (BLESSED)**, apostle of the English, 421.

**Unleavened bread.** Bread, whether unleavened or leavened, is bread, 135. There is no substantial difference, 135. The objections of the Greeks in favor of leavened bread and against unleavened bread are answered, 136. Unleavened bread is more suitable for effecting the reality of the Lord’s body, 136. And sacrifice is better offered with unleavened than with leavened bread, 135, 136. In both the Old and the New Scriptures, leaven signifies sin, 136. The Greeks favor the pagans by sacrificing with leavened bread, 136. The Greeks anathematize those who use unleavened bread, 135—and consequently Christ, 135. Christ did not make his body from unleavened bread in order to observe the legal command concerning unleavened bread, 135, but in order to approve the use of unleavened bread, 135. Those who sacrifice with unleavened bread are not Judaizing, 135, 136. For they do not sacrifice with unleavened bread in order to observe the old law, 135, nor in order to signify the future Christ, 135 and 136, but in order to imitate the Lord, 135. The ancient Passover was celebrated with unleavened bread, 135, 136. It was a figure of our Passover, 136. Unleavened bread signified that Christ, sincere and pure, would come, 135. It also signified that we, who were going to eat Christ’s body, ought to be cleansed from every leaven of wickedness, 135. Indeed, it now signifies that Christ came without sin and that we ought to be without sin, 136. Christ did not forbid us to sacrifice with unleavened bread, 136. Rather, by his own deed he commanded it, 136. Whether someone sacrifices with unleavened or leavened bread, he is sacrificing, 155. Christ blessed unleavened bread, 135. The meal at which this took place required it, 135. See *Waleran*.

Monks of Bayeux, 318.

Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, 429, 436. He succeeded his brother, 429. Anselm congratulates him on his advancement to the kingdom, 429.

Baldwin, abbot: Anselm entrusts to his governance the monks whom he sends to England, 342.

Baldwin, monk of Bec: Anselm sends him to England, 361. Through him the monks of Bec ask Anselm to return to them, after declining the bishopric, 364.

Baldwin of Tournai, monk, 381. (Where “Baldemus” is wrongly read), 400, 444, 449. Anselm sends him to the pope, 383, 440. He returned from Rome, 441, 444.

The most precious balsam, 157. See Chrism.

## Baptism

Baptism is the beginning of salvation, 176. In baptism the first door of the Church is opened through Christ, 383. Baptism is a figure of death and burial, 136. It takes place in water, 136.

The baptism of John, 136, 173. It took place in water, 136. It was a figure of our baptism, 136. It is not better than Christ’s baptism, 173.

The water flowing from Christ’s side signified the water of baptism, 453. Through baptism the people are renewed by the outpouring of Christ’s blood, 453. In baptism faith is promised to God, 213.

The age of thirty years indicates the mystery of baptism—namely, faith in the Trinity and observance of the Decalogue, 174. Christ is the one who baptizes, 454.

The Christian soul is a candidate for the heavenly washing, endowed with the Holy Spirit, sworn by the Christian profession, and betrothed as a virgin to Christ, 208.

In baptism original injustice is remitted, 131, 170. In it every fault of weakness and corruption that people incur on account of the sin of their first parent is remitted, 131. No offense is imputed to them after baptism except what they commit by their own will, 131. Every sin is removed in baptism, 98, 131. In baptism all sins are washed away by Christ’s blood, 131. In baptism faults are erased without delay, 180.

The corruption itself and the desire of the flesh are not immediately erased in baptism, 131. Through baptism and the Christian faith, the blessedness that Adam possessed before the sin is not promised to us, 131.

Why those who have been baptized and martyrs do not immediately become incorruptible, 131, 132. If human beings passed into incorruption through baptism, there would be no one who would not hasten toward this blessedness, 131.

Through the sacrament of baptism grace is given, 288. Rising from the washing, one becomes a participant in Christ’s resurrection, 170. Through the cleansing of baptism we are enrolled among the children of adoption, 254. A person is first a child of God when he rises from baptism, 173.

The baptized person, if he is not to lose the grace he has received, ought to grow through the labor of holy action, 176. [Col. 1054] Whoever has been baptized in Christ has heaven opened to him, and God above is ready to receive him, 176. Whoever has been baptized ought to ascend by the steps of the ladder stretched from baptism to God, 176. The steps of this ladder are the virtues, 176. Whoever has been baptized should not be lazy, but should proceed by the way of God’s commandments toward the heavenly homeland, 176.

He sins worse than the devil who sins after the grace of regeneration, 288. See Sin; Penance.

## Beard

It is unbecoming for a man who ought to have a beard not to have one, 69. It is not disgraceful for a man who is not yet supposed to have one not to have a beard, 69.

At it Anselm defended the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, 424.

A most devout woman, 415. Wife of Hugh, count of Flanders, 333. Anselm greets her from England, 351, 361.

The monks of Battle in the city of Exeter suffer numerous grievances from the clergy of that city, 373. Archbishop Anselm complains about these matters to the bishop of Exeter, 373.

Prior of Bath, 420.

## Blessed; Blessedness

Those who have whatever they desire are called blessed, 160. It is necessary that some human beings attain blessedness, 86. No one can be blessed if he has what he does not want or does not have what he wants, 68.

No one ought to be, nor can be, blessed who does not have a just will, 62, 69. Someone who wants what neither can nor ought to be cannot be perfectly or commendably blessed, 68.

Those who enjoy God will be called children of God and gods, 242, 244. They will be certain that they will never lose their good, 244. They will be omnipotent with respect to their own will, just as God is with respect to his, 34, 242. And just as they will want nothing other than what he wants, so he will want whatever they want, 242 and 349. Whoever enjoys God, whatever he wills, will be; and what he does not will, will not be, 34, 234, 242, 349.

There will be bodily and spiritual goods there, 349. What and how great are the goods belonging to those who enjoy God, 34, 242, 243. The goods of the blessed, 200, 234, 235, 253, 259.

God is seen by the blessed in himself and in creatures, 182, 235. The present face of God is the food of the righteous, 182. God’s face is seen without deficiency by the saints, 182. While God’s face is seen without deficiency, the mind is fed without end with the food of life, 182.

God loves the blessed more than they love themselves, 34, 242. The blessed love God, themselves, and one another through him, 242. He, however, loves himself and them through himself, 242.

All the blessed will have one will, 34, 242, 349, because they will have no will except God’s will alone, 349. The joys of the blessed city, 229.

The joy of the blessed is multiplied by the blessedness and joy of others, 35, 243. The blessed rejoice over the blessedness of others as much as over their own, 243, because they love others as themselves, 243 and 349. They rejoice more in God’s happiness than in their own and that of others, 549, because they love God more than themselves and others, 349.

They will rejoice as much as they love, and love as much as they know, 35, 243. That joy will not enter into those who rejoice; rather, those who rejoice will enter into that joy, 243. That joy will be full, 243.

People in heaven will be such as the good angels now are, 85. In blessedness there will be one love of God and humanity and one will, 239. In heaven the truth of the Scriptures will be revealed, 163. In the elect angels and in the saints the affection of willing justice is inseparably present, 116.

The will, like the essence, will in some manner be immutable in the blessed, 238. In the blessed, free choice will be liberated from every evil, 238. See Free choice.

Blessedness consists of the advantages that every rational creature desires, 64. Blessedness is sufficiency in which there is no want, 85. Or, sufficiency of appropriate advantages without any want, 134. Blessedness is the most perfect state formed by the gathering together of all goods, 160.

For a human being, nothing is sufficient except God, 228. God is blessed life itself, 203. Rational nature is—or will be—blessed through the contemplation of God, 81. See Rational creature.

The blessedness for which human beings were made cannot be possessed in this life, 79. It cannot be attained unless sins are forgiven, 79, 85. Faith in these matters is necessary for salvation, 79.

The will for blessedness is not blessedness, 133. The desire for blessedness, 84, 177, 319. Those things that more powerfully arouse the desire for heavenly blessedness, 349. Sorrow because one is not yet there; fear of not arriving, 84. No joy ought to be felt except over those things that give assistance or hope of attaining it, 84.

No one can be blessed who does not want blessedness, 68. This is to be an advantage, 68. Everyone wants blessedness, even the unjust, 68. Everyone wants things to go well for himself, 68, and does not want things to go badly for himself, 68.

Once this sole will is granted, a rational creature cannot fail to want blessedness, 68. Once this sole will is granted, it can want what it thinks will be useful for blessedness, 68. Whoever wants something for the sake of blessedness wants nothing other than blessedness, 68. [Col. 1055]

Whoever received only the will for blessedness could not want anything else, 68, 69. Nor can he fail to want the blessedness that he understands to be greater, 68. Rather, he wants to be blessed to the degree that he recognizes this to be possible at a higher level, 68. And thus he wants to be like God, 68.

Whoever wants blessedness alone (in general) wants only advantages, 68. Through the affection for advantage, all the righteous want to be blessed, 68, 116. Not everyone who possesses the will for blessedness possesses blessedness, 133.

A good life is followed by blessed life, 201. The fullness of blessedness, 349. The eternity of blessedness, 211.

The only good of a human being is to enter into the joy of the Lord and to attend contemplatively upon it, 164. The body will be spiritual, not by nature but by power, 34, 242. The elect will be changed into the immortality of immortal bodies, 82.

To be released from the body and to be with Christ is blessedness, 240. To be bound to the body and absent from Christ is misery, 240. This misery is feared as something to be lost, while this blessedness is not desired as something to be possessed, 240.

Every rational soul, if it diligently strives—as it ought—to desire the highest blessedness through love, will at some time receive it, 26. In blessedness, what is now seen as though through a mirror and in an enigma will then be seen face to face, 26. It will enjoy it without end and will be eternally blessed, 26.

Enjoying it, the soul will be unable to be tormented by fear or deceived by deceptive security; having already experienced God’s indulgence, it will be unable not to love it, 26. Nor will that highest goodness abandon the one who loves it; nor will there be anything more powerful that could separate them against their will, 26. In blessedness there is immutable sufficiency, 26.

There is no blessedness if there is no justice, 68, 69. No one can attain blessedness while in sin, 84. No unjust person will be admitted to blessedness, 85. No one is admitted to it unless there is absolutely no injustice in him, 85, 86, 129.

Eternal life has not been promised to all the just, 129, but only to those who are just without any injustice, 129. The blessedness promised to the just will be likeness to the angels of God, 129. Blessedness is given only to one whose sins have been entirely forgiven, 86. Whoever does not pay God what he owes will not be able to be blessed, 85, 86.

Which things will at some time be blessed, or which will at some time be miserable, cannot be comprehended by a human being, 26. See Good; Rational creature.

The entrance to paradise is open to the good, 211.

## Bec; the monks of Bec

The Church of Bec: Anselm calls it his mother and his nest, 422. In the time of St. Anselm the monks of Bec professed obedience according to the Rule of Benedict, 367. The poverty of the monastery of Bec after the death of Herluin, its abbot, 341. After his death, a great sign was made from one broken thing and one thing in discord, 349.

Anselm obtains from Urban II, Roman pontiff, the exemption of the monastery of Bec from episcopal jurisdiction, 354. The monks of Bec, 351. They are compelled to plead before the king on Sunday, 341.

Anselm writes to them about his prosperous voyage to England and urges them to live in peace and in monastic religion, 344. He writes to them about his second voyage to England, 347. They do not wish to consent to his election as bishop of Canterbury, 363.

Bishop Gundulf of Rochester consoles them for the loss of Anselm, 364, and advises them not to resist his election, 364. They consent to his election, 364. Anselm commands them to declare this consent in letters to the king and to Anselm, 364.

One smaller part of them consented in chapter, while the larger part did not consent, 365. Anselm advises them to elect William as abbot, 367. If they had not consented to Anselm’s election as archbishop, the destruction of the Church of Bec was imminent, 368.

Anselm sends them the greetings and assistance of the king of the English, 271. Anselm informs them that his consecration is to take place on the day before the Nones of December and asks them to communicate this to the other monks and friends in France, 37. In a letter Anselm gives them absolution and prays that God may absolve them from all their sins, 372.

Anselm urges them to live according to his admonitions, 373; to persevere in goodness and not wander outside the cloister; and to submit to and obey their prelates, especially the abbot, 376. He urges them not to judge the actions of their prelates, 376 and 381.

The abbot of Bec is elected with the favor of the prince of Normandy, 367. The prior of Bec was Baldric. See Baldric.

In the calendar of Bec, those who died in the monastery of Ralph were noted, 319. The monks of Bec at Conflans, 346.

Bede’s treatise *On Times*, 324.

Iniquity is the bloody confusion of wars, 347. At that time wars were raging so fiercely in France that there was no freedom or safety of travel, 328. Wars in England, 379, 380.

The bishop of Beauvais. See Fulk.

The tribulations of the Church of Beauvais, 393. The corrupt morals of the canons and priests of Beauvais, 354. They could not be corrected by their bishop, 354. Their hatred and persecution of the bishop, 354.

The canons and priests of Beauvais keep concubines, 354. They want their sons to be promoted to holy orders, 354. They grant them their prebends as though by hereditary succession, 354.

The Rule of Benedict, 431, 432. In profession according to the Rule of St. Benedict, conversion of conduct and obedience according to that Rule are promised, 361. The Rule of St. Benedict commands obedience to be shown not only to abbots but to every superior, 361.

## Benefits

The benefits of God: their remembrance and the giving of thanks for them, 214, 215, 233, 254, 235, 236. By considering his own dignity and God’s benefits, a person is kindled to love God, 202.

It is a benefit of God that we were not cast out as miscarried abortions; that he gave us sound limbs, 333, etc.; that he willed us to be born among people through whom we might come to faith and the sacraments, 333; that we were raised by Christian parents, 333; and that, harmed by no one, we were nourished in his faith and good will until a suitable age, 233.

Whoever is not forgetful of himself—how does he forget the one from whom he received everything? 237.

The sinner fights against God with God’s benefits and serves in the devil’s army against God with God’s pay, 214, 215. See Thanksgiving; Gratitude.

The monastery of St. Bertin, 416. Its abbot was Lambert, 416. It was subject to the abbot of Cluny, 416. See Lambert.

## Good

We discern that there are very many goods through the senses of the body and through the reason of the mind, 4. We desire only those things that we think are good, 4.

Every good is an essence, 61. And every essence is good, 62. Nothing is usually thought good except either what is useful, such as health, and so forth, or what is honorable, such as beauty, and so forth, 4.

If the useful and the honorable are goods, they are goods by the very fact that all goods are goods, 4. All other goods, apart from that through which all things are good, are good through something other than what they themselves are, 4.

“What is itself” is simply better than “what is not itself,” 9. “What is not itself” is in some respect better than “what is itself,” 9. Many things are relative, and for these “what is itself” is not simply better than “what is not itself,” 9.

We want nothing except what we think just or advantageous, 64. There is a twofold good: one good that is justice; the other, which is called advantage, 64, 68, 125.

In no way is that good by which the highest good is changed or corrupted. That is not a simple good whose will will be the highest good, 10.

### The highest good

Whatever is not the highest good is less than something, 45. The highest good is the highest essence, 62. See Blessedness; Good; Rational creature.

All things are good through one thing that is the same in different goods, 4. That through which all things are good is a great good, and it alone is good through itself, 4, 25.

No good that is good through another is equal to or greater than that which is good through itself, 25. Therefore that is supremely good which alone is good through itself, 25. What is supremely good is supremely great, 25.

There is therefore one thing supremely great and supremely good—that is, the highest of all things that exist, 25. All goods are good through one thing that is good through itself, 4, 5, 25. See Good God; God, cause of things.

There is one and only one nature that is the highest good, 25. The highest being, 25. Whoever possesses that good possesses all other goods, 212.

He is lovable and praiseworthy who strives to be good, 378. He who is good to the good and the evil is better than he who is good only to the good, 31, 2, 32. He who is good to the evil both by punishing and by sparing is better than he who is good only by sparing, 32.

In creatures the essence that is goodness is not the same as the essence that is power, 238. See Good God; End.

The ox signifies the Jewish people, 180.

Boso, a monk of Bec, and Anselm’s love for him, 374, 375.

## Irrational creatures

The will of the blessed, desiring pleasures, is not evil, 70, because it is irrational, 70. The appetite of irrational creatures, [Col. 1057] 70. See Appetite; Concupiscence; Will.

## BURGUNDIUS

Burgundius, husband of Riceza, Anselm’s sister, 382. His son Anselm: he offers him to God, 382. See Anselm, nephew.

His other children died while still little, 383. He ought to reckon this as God’s grace, 383.

Burgundius and his wife Richera, Anselm’s sister, 390, 391. Anselm urges them to keep their end daily before their eyes, 391, and not to come to it, 391 and 392.

Burgundius, Richera’s husband, proposes to go to Jerusalem, 391. Anselm prescribes that he prepare himself by a general confession, 391.

# C
Cadomene monks, among whom was Ernulfus, professed the Rule of St. Benedict, 361. See Ernulfus.

Blindness. A person is called blind not only when he has lost sight, but also when he does not have what he ought to have, 27. Blindness is nothing other than lack of sight, or the absence of sight where sight ought to be present, 344, 99. See Privation.

CAINAN. Of Cainan and Arphaxad Moses says nothing in Genesis, 174, 175.

Chalice. See Mass.

Great heat exists without any cold at all, 134.

Calumnies are to be endured patiently, 330, 331. See Injuries, Anger, Vengeance.

Canon. See Mass.

A canon lawfully absent may receive the full revenues of his prebend, 388.

Concerning the religious life of the regular canons, Anselm earned nothing except their love, 429.

The regular canons of Mount Saint-Éloi, 429.

To sing a new song and a hymn to God is to walk in the ways of the new man and to recall the joys of the heavenly homeland, 206.

The Church of Canterbury is called Dorobernensis, 393.

The Church of Canterbury was sanctified from the beginning through the favor of the Apostle Peter, 363; nobly founded through Gregory’s zeal, 363; and endowed with a special privilege by Saints Boniface, Honoratus, Agatho, and others, 363.

The primacy of the Church of Canterbury and its rights, 373, 421, 449.

The archbishop of Canterbury is the legate of the apostolic see in England, 427.

He is abbot of the Canterbury monastery, 377.

The bishops of England cannot establish a decree without the archbishop of Canterbury, 437.

The bishops of York render obedience to the archbishop of Canterbury, 422.

The archbishop of Canterbury, as primate, ought to crown the king of England, 298.

The archbishop of Canterbury has the right to dedicate the churches of his villages, even when they are situated in another diocese, 373, 428.

The archbishop and the monks of Canterbury are not two bodies but one, 396.

Anselm restored an oratory and a manor to the monks of that Church, 393.

The monks of Canterbury promised stability in their profession, 418.

Many of them were learned in the sacred Scriptures, 404.

The king of England exacts money from them, 441.

They suffer many things on Anselm’s behalf, 404.

He himself exhorts them to patience and the other virtues.

Anselm rebukes the disobedient monks of Canterbury, 377.

Claricus of Beauvais becomes a monk in the Church of Canterbury, 437.

The revenues of the archdeaconry of Canterbury are to be spent on alms, 409.

The king gives the lands of the Church of Canterbury to soldiers, 375.

Head. A severe headache is described, 323.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, 406.

The monastery of Chartres, 398.

The countess of Chartres, sister of Henry, king of the English, 445. Through her the king and Anselm were reconciled, and the king restored Anselm to his position, 445. Her respect toward the pope’s legates, 440. A dispute between her and the Church of Chartres, 440.

Anselm went to Chartres on his way to Rome, 434. There he was received by the bishop and the countess, 434. On their advice, because of the excessive heat, he returned to Bec, 434. See Anselm.

Flesh. Whence the flesh lives, 211, etc.

The flesh is, as it were, naturally inclined toward weakness, 238.

The Apostle calls every vicious movement “flesh,” 415.

Whoever lives according to the desires of the flesh has not the image of God but the likeness of an animal, 238.

To walk according to the flesh is to agree with the flesh by one’s will, 415. See Concupiscence.

Durand, abbot of the House of God, 334, 335.

“Castle” has a twofold meaning, 178.

The castle signifies Mary, 178.

Chastity. Concerning chastity, 191. See Concupiscence, Fornication, Modesty, Virginity, Pleasure.

Categories. One and the same thing cannot be placed under different categories, 149. See Aristotle; God, Substance.

Cause. Whatever produces something is the cause of what is produced from it, 7.

How something can be made from nothing, 7.

Every cause contributes something toward the essence of its effect, 7.

It cannot be understood that something should come from what is utterly nonexistent, 7.

But everyone says: “Nothing comes from nothing,” 7. [Col. 1058]

Substance can be said to be made from nothing in three ways, 7.

We are said to make a thing:

1. When we make the thing;
2. When we are able to make it not exist and do not do so, 70.

That which is said to exist through something seems to exist either through an efficient cause, through matter, or through some instrument, 6.

Whatever exists either through an efficient cause, through matter, or through some instrument exists through another, 6; and it is posterior to, and in some way less than, that through which it has existence, 6 and 15.

The formless or confused nature of the elements appears to be the matter of all bodies distinguished by their forms, 6.

Whence the formless matter of the elements comes, 6.

The matter of the corporeal universe cannot come from any matter other than either the highest nature, itself, or some third essence, 6.

There is no third essence apart from the highest nature, which exists through itself, and the whole of what exists through it, 6.

Therefore the universe of things cannot come from some third essence, 6.

The universe of things cannot come from itself, 6.

Otherwise it would not exist through that through which all things exist, 6.

And it would be both prior and posterior to itself, 6. See Element.

Everything that is matter comes from another and is posterior to it, 6.

Nothing is other than itself or posterior to itself, 6, 15.

Nothing exists materially from itself, 6.

Nothing is rationally made by anything unless, in the maker’s understanding, there first exists some exemplar of the thing to be made—its form, likeness, or rule, 7. See Ideas.

A craftsman who is about to make something belonging to his art first expresses it within himself through a conception of the mind, 81, 17.

“To exist through something” and “to exist from something” do not always have the same meaning, 6.

Whatever is from something is also through it; and whatever is through something is also from it, 5.

What is from matter and through an artisan may be said to exist through matter and from the artisan, 5.

Yet it is from matter in one way and through the artisan in another, 5.

It cannot in any way be understood that something which exists should exist through nothing, 6.

Whatever exists exists through one thing, 5; everything that exists either exists through something or through nothing, 5.

Nothing can come to be through itself, 15.

Whatever comes to be is posterior to that through which it comes to be, 15.

The one from whom someone derives his being cannot be the one who exists from himself; nor can one who is from another be the one from whom he derives his being, 50, 51, 61.

Whatever begins to exist from something or through something is not identical with that from which and through which it begins to exist, 10.

No thing exists through that to which it gives existence, 5.

That from which something exists is more primary and more worthy than it, 60; this is not so in divine things, 60.

Someone can be understood to be other than another before he belongs to that other, 51.

Nor can someone belong to another unless he is other than that other, 51.

What comes to be through or after something that must first come to be is said to come to be on account of that thing, 78.

If that through which several natures are equal is other than what they themselves are, they are less than that through which they are equally great, 5.

The cedar surpasses all trees in height, 156.

The cellarer, because of advancing age, ought not to relinquish the office entrusted to him, 419.

Le Mans. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. See Hildebertus.

Ceremonies. See Mass.

The candle signifies Christ, 171. See Purification of Mary.

Charity. Christ brings forth love that is not shameful but beautiful, not lustful but chaste, 158.

Wisdom, which is Christ, is the mother of beautiful love, 158.

It is the mother of filial fear, 158.

[Col. 1064]

**Concubine, one who keeps a concubine.** See Presbyters, Viaticum.

**Desire, covetousness.** Desire is an act of will, 65. There is good and bad desire, just as there is good and bad will, 65. Holy and chaste desire is love of God, 259. Vicious appetites are one thing, and a vicious will another, 133. The Apostle calls appetites “flesh” and “desire,” 134. The pleasure or desire of the flesh is the greatest of all evils, 249. It is born with a person, grows, and does not leave him except in death, 249. The very movements, or appetites, of desire to which, because of Adam’s sin, we are unwillingly subject: Sacred Authority shows that these are imputed as sin to those who are not in Christ, 131. The appetites of the flesh are called unjust because they are in a rational creature, where they ought not to be, 134. It is not sin to feel appetites, but to consent to them, 98. Corruption and the appetites of the flesh are the punishment of sin, 131. After baptism they are not sins in themselves, 131. Appetites are not taken away in baptism, 98. After baptism corruption remains for the merit of faith and hope, 131. Desires of the flesh hinder contemplation of heavenly things and drag one into the depths of vices, 206. The movements of the flesh and of the passions are to be calmed by disdaining them, 414. They are not imputed as sin if the will in no way associates itself with them, 414. For each person, his own covetousness is a storm, 161. The “lake of misery” is the depth of human covetousness, 205–206. To overcome your covetousness, invoke the divinity of Christ, 161. See Appetite, Flesh, Mortification.

**The Sacrament of Confession**, 212. Christ instituted it, 212. Through confession every burden of sin is lightened, 212. In true confession every stain of wrongdoing is cleansed, 168, 212. General confession of sins, 391. Secret confession of sin made to a priest, 332. Confession of sins made to God, 248, 249, 252, 253. Many would rather choose to remain hidden until death than, on the occasion of confession, be brought to certainty or suspicion concerning some crime, 140, 332. Confession of sins, 250, 251, 255, 256, 270, 297, 285, 390, 391, 410. It is a sacrifice, 250. Through confession and penance every debt of guilt is remitted, 168. The way of confession must not be obstructed, 140, 332. The vices of the heart are to be revealed, 193. Confession of all sins is to be made to priests, 185. The measures and degrees of vices are to be explained to the ecclesiastical pastor, 182. The person to whom one confesses is not made responsible for the sin if he does not compel the penitent, without the latter’s consent, to cease from the duties of his order, 140, 332. But he appears to be guilty of a grave crime if he compels him, 332. See Absolution, Penance.

**Confidence.** The error of those who do not begin to follow Christ because they fear that they may fail through their weakness is to be mourned, 348. Commit yourself wholly to God’s help, and you will not feel any failure in God’s service, 248. They rejoice in failing so that they may fail, and fear to advance lest they fail, 348. See Hope.

**Marriage.** See Matrimony.

**CONNIUS**, a friend of Anselm, 394.

**Marriage bond.** See Matrimony.

**Blood relatives.** Those who are near by blood owe one another, by that very right, the reverence of charity, 142. See Matrimony.

**Consent.** See Desire, Will.

**Counsel.** It is fitting for a wise person to make use of wise counsel, 335. Everything is to be done with counsel, 335. One should deliberate at length, 193.

**Companionship.** Good companionship, 192.
