**Custom.** If the unity of charity is preserved in the Catholic faith, differing custom does no harm, 139. Variations of customs are nothing other than variations of human sensibilities, 139.

**Contemplation.** Contemplation of God, 260. The soul is not brought to contemplate inward things unless it diligently withdraws from those things that entangle it outwardly, 166. Consideration of weakness is the way to contemplation, 165. Whoever advances in contemplation of God so as to see him does so with great fear and reverence, 164. The reward of contemplation is to see God, 159.

**Contempt.** See World.

Continence between spouses is praised, 356.

**Conversion.** It is not words perceptible to the senses but the Holy Spirit who converts the heart, 54. This is to kill the wicked person, 54. When the Holy Spirit visits the sinner’s heart through grace, he immediately cleanses it from every stain of vice, 250. Conversion must not be delayed, 210 and following; through these passages the soul is roused to conversion, 210. If we do not correct ourselves now, God, who is most just, will condemn us, 211. No one can correct himself without God, 263. Those who say, “Convert us, O God,” have already been converted to some extent, 130. Whoever postpones correcting his life abandons certainty for uncertainty and deserves not to receive what he awaits, 346. Conversion of morals, 195. Conversion is a greater miracle than resurrection, 121. See Grace.

[Col. 1065]

**To believe with the heart**, 128. A person does not have a right heart who believes rightly and understands rightly but does not will rightly, 128.

**Guarding the heart**, 312, 327, 355, 377. The most effective means is always to keep the heart occupied with reading, prayer, or useful thought, 377. Those guard their heart with every care who guard their actions at every hour, 184.

**Purity of heart**, 159. It restores the image of God, 159. It is the beauty of the mind, 377. The vision of God is especially promised to it, 377. It is reached only through guarding the heart, 377. A pure heart ought to think only about the things that belong to God and apply itself to the divine commandments, 159. The hearts of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists are fertile with saving seeds, 130. Understanding belongs to the pure in heart, 159. And it is given, 159.

**CORNELIUS**, 419. The king of Ireland asks that he be sent to him, 419.

**CORNELIUS**, a monk of Canterbury, 438. His father becomes a monk in the Church of Canterbury, 438.

**Body.** Only corporeal things are perceptible, 31. The senses are concerned with the body and are in the body, 31. In the body, the limbs and senses are each suited to their own functions, 132. Only corporeal things are circumscribed, 32. See Place, Spirit.

**Correction.** Everyone is bound to correct the evils that he can correct, 417. It is better to maintain peace with everyone than, by speaking uselessly about good things, to give the wicked an opportunity, 314. There should be moderation in correcting faults, 400. Even the public accusation of lesser faults is customary among monks, 400.

**Creature.** No creature possesses anything from itself, 62. Creatures are nothing but some imitation of the supreme essence, 16. Creatures do not possess a simple and absolute essence, 16, but have scarcely any imitation of true essence, 16. Among created things, that exists more and is more excellent by nature which is more like the supreme nature, 16–17, 24. Creatures are said to exist not simply and absolutely, but scarcely to exist at all, 15. Yet they are not altogether nonexistent, 15, 30. Whatever is other than the supreme nature exists not through itself but through another, 15. Whatever receives being from another returns from being to non-being, so far as it is concerned, unless it is sustained by another, 15. Truth is not in a creature, 161. Creatures exist mutably, 15. At some time they were, or will be, what they are not, 15. They are what at some time they were not, or will not be, 15. Whatever has been made is other than God, 56. Everything is said to have been made from nothing—that is, what previously was nothing is now something, 7. What does not exist and never existed can be said to have been made from nothing in the sense that it was not made at all, 7. Everything that exists, apart from the supreme essence, was made from nothing—that is, not from something, 7, 14. There are three courses of things: the miraculous, the natural, and the voluntary, 101. The miraculous course is subject to no law, 101. Creatures possess nothing except what they have received from God, 101. Nor did God give them anything except beneath himself, 101. What exists through itself and what exists through another do not receive the same mode of existence, 6, 14. See Cause, Existence.

The more excellent a created essence is, the more it teaches what the mind itself ought to judge concerning the Creator, 24. Many think that all things were created simultaneously, 81. Created things can at least be conceived as having an end, 34. Created things, even those that will not have an end, do not yet possess, from their eternity, what is going to be, 34. Nor do they now possess what is past, 34. The perfection of the world’s creation lies not so much in the number of individuals as in the number of natures, 81. The rational creature was made to avoid evil, 65. See God, Cause of Things.

**Cross.** The Holy Cross: its powers and effects, 274–276. It is worshiped, 274–275. Prayer to the Holy Cross, 274–276. The standard of the cross is worshiped in the name of Christ, 220. The crown of thorns, the nails, and the lance are also worshiped, 220. The breadth of the cross signifies charity; its length, eternity; its height, omnipotence; its depth, inscrutable wisdom, 220. It was necessary that the devil should be conquered through the wood of the cross, 75. Blessings are given with the sign of the cross, 139. A cross is not to be carried before a bishop, 434. A cross is to be carried only before an archbishop confirmed with the pallium, 393.

**Worship of the saints**, 430. Worship due to the saints is forbidden to be offered to a particular dead person, under penalty of interdict, 386. See Anhelis.

**Fault.** See Correction.

**Covetousness.** See Desire.

**Care.** See World.

**Cypress.** It is evergreen, 1, 7. It bears fruit, 7. It smells good, 7.

# D
## Daemon

See Devil.

## Damnation

Damnation and eternal death, 248. God condemns only on account of injustice, 98. For one who lives wickedly, condemnation is open, 248. Eternal destruction is open to the wicked, 211. For one who boasts of a good life, certain death and eternal damnation await, [Col. 1066] 248. The punishment of damnation is eternal, 168, 169. The howling of condemned souls, 211. It would be better for the condemned if they had never been conceived, 274. One who has been condemned in hell is wholly dead, 186. Death is eternal damnation, 186. After death no remedy can be found, 186. Whoever has once been handed over to eternal damnation can never afterward attain redemption, 186. After death the sinner is handed over to the demons to be possessed by them forever, so that, enduring everlasting punishments, he may satisfy divine justice, 186. The condemned person is never able to repay the debt, 169. Nor can he amend through repentance and good works what he has done badly, 169. And therefore he is compelled always to endure punishments, 169. Not all deserve to be tortured equally in hell, 104. After the day of judgment there will be no angel or human being except either in the kingdom of God or in hell, 104. In eternal misery there is inconsolable need, 26. The condemned grieve over their sins uselessly, 191. Damnation is not imposed for a light fault, 131.

See Hell, Death, Sin.

## To give

Not giving is not always the cause of not receiving, 63. But giving is always the cause of receiving, 63. Both the person who freely grants and the person who permits without approving are said to give, 70, 73.

## David

David began to reign at the age of thirty, 173.

## Debtor

Every human being is God’s debtor, 182. One who is bound by debt cannot profess the monastic life, 316, 319. Every righteous person is God’s debtor, 183. Whoever has received every good thing from him, 183. Tithes may be redeemed from laymen, 424. Tithes donated by bishops to monasteries, 424.

See Church property.

## Definition

A legitimate definition is one that contains neither more nor less, 116, 117.

## Delight

These lowest things have their delights and their loves; but they do not delight in the way God does, 258.

See Advantage, Pleasure.

## Delights

Spiritual delights, 180. When spiritual delights are possessed, they are still present in desire, 158.

## Tooth

“To gnaw with a Theonine tooth,” 320.

## Desire

Good desire is from God, 223.

See Blessedness, Good, Concupiscence, Intention, Will.

## Detraction

Detraction or slander, 192. It is a serious crime, 192. He condemns both those who slander and those who listen, 192.

## Despair

See Confidence, Hope, Mercy of God.

## Devotion

A “great voice” is understood to be one that is more devout than loud, 185.

# God

“God” is the name of a substance, 45. Every human being ought to believe in the one supreme essence alone, 27.

## The existence of God

That one supreme nature exists, and many other things that we believe about God, reason can persuade us of to a considerable extent, 4. It is readily apparent to the rational mind that God exists more than all things, 30. The discussion of God is undertaken not on the authority of Scripture but on the force of arguments, 3. Reason persuades us that some nature so surpasses all others that it has no superior, 5. It is demonstrated that that than which nothing greater can be conceived necessarily exists in reality, 37–40. That than which nothing greater can be conceived is truly understood, and therefore exists in the understanding and in thought, 37. If that than which nothing greater can be conceived can be conceived to exist, it necessarily exists, 37, 38. It is proper to God that he cannot be conceived not to exist, 28. That one being through which all things that are exist must exist, 5, 14. That one being exists through itself, 14 and 8. Something exists than which nothing greater can be conceived, both in the understanding and in reality, 30. That than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot be conceived not to exist, 30, 31, 38. Something can be conceived that cannot be conceived not to exist, 30. That which cannot be conceived not to exist is greater than that which can be conceived not to exist, 30. That than which nothing greater can be conceived is not that than which nothing greater can be conceived if that than which nothing greater can be conceived can be conceived not to exist, 30. God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived, 30–32, 36, 40. And he is that which cannot be conceived not to exist, 30. Whoever conceives that than which nothing greater can be conceived conceives something that cannot not exist, 40. Everything can be conceived not to exist except that which exists supremely, 28. Even the fool is compelled to admit that there is at least in the understanding something than which nothing greater can be conceived, 30. God can be conceived not to exist according to the spoken word; according to reality, he cannot, 31. No one who understands what God is can conceive that he does not exist, 31. God cannot not exist even in thought, 31. No one can understand that God does not exist, 30. If that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists, it can neither in actuality nor in the understanding not exist, 37. Whatever can be conceived and does not exist, if it existed, would not be that than which nothing greater can be conceived, 37, 38. Whatever can be conceived not to exist, if it exists, is not that than which nothing greater can be conceived, 38. It can neither not exist nor be conceived not to exist, 38. That which is greater than everything is not for that reason that than which nothing greater can be conceived, 38, 39. Nor is it thereby proved to exist in reality merely because it exists in the understanding, 39. That than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot exist only in the understanding, 30. And even if that than which nothing greater can be conceived were not known to be understood, nevertheless that than which nothing greater can be conceived could be conceived, 39. That than which nothing greater can be conceived is thereby proved to exist because it is conceived and understood, 30, 38–40. Whatever can absolutely be conceived to be better if it exists than if it does not exist, this we believe of the divine substance, 40. That God truly [is], 30.

It is not for that reason the case that there is no nature than which nothing greater can be conceived because the fool has said in his heart, “There is no God,” 30. There is something best, greatest, and supreme among all things that exist, 4. Something supremely great exists, 4. There is something—whether it is called substance, essence, or nature—that is best, greatest, and supreme among all things that exist, 5. Whatever exists through itself is greatest of all, 5. There is one nature alone that is good and great through itself; it is through itself what it is, and through it whatever truly is good, great, or anything at all exists, 5, 14, 21, 22, 46. The creative essence exists more truly than the created essence, 17. God alone truly is, 15, 30, 203, 238. For he is always what he is, 238. God alone is what is, and he alone is the one who is, 34. No thing preceded the supreme nature, even in thought, through which the supreme nature came from nothing, 6. The supreme essence is not from nothing through itself, 6. Nor is it from nothing through another, 6. The supreme nature in no way exists through another, nor is it posterior or inferior to itself or to anything else, 6. Nor consequently is it from itself as from an efficient cause, or as from matter, or as from an instrument, 6. Nevertheless it is not through nothing or from nothing, 6. When God is being treated accurately, no form of love is to be neglected, 35. Arguments against God’s existence arising from the fiction of an island, 36–39. The supreme nature is said to be from itself and through itself, 6. It is understood to shine and to be shining from itself and through itself in the way that light does, 6. There is and was nothing other than the supreme essence and the things made by it, 7, 15.

## The essence of God

God is one undivided and simple nature, and three persons, 45. This has been proved by the arguments of the Fathers, especially Saint Augustine, 45. It is also proved throughout Saint Anselm’s *Monologion* and *Proslogion*, 45. According to its essence, the supreme nature is whatever is simply better to be than not to be, 9, 31. It alone is that than which nothing is wholly better, and it is better than all things that are not what it is, 31. To one asking where the supreme essence comes from, it can rightly be answered: “from nothing”—that is, it was not made at all, 7. It did not begin through itself or from itself, through another or from another, through nothing or from nothing, 10. It is from itself, while other things are from it, 5, 6, 22. There is not one essence that is through itself and from itself, and another through which and from which it itself exists, 10. How the supreme nature is through itself, 6. It is always through itself, 19. It is through itself whatever it is, 6, 12, 14, 15, 22, 31, 32. All other things are through it whatever they are, 32. God is something greater than can be conceived, 33. Neither is God without a person nor a person without God, 61. The supreme essence is called “substance” only by taking “substance” as equivalent to “essence,” 14. It is itself beyond and above every substance, 14, 27. It shares with creatures only a common name, whose signification is very different, 14. The supreme nature is not included in the common treatment of other natures, 14. It neither divides itself into several substances as a common nature does, 14. Nor does it join itself to another through a sharing of essence as an individual nature does, 14. It is free from the nature and law of all things that it made from nothing, 13. How different the essence of God is from created essence, 60. God has nothing other than God in himself, 58. Nor is God outside God, 58. Nor is God unlike God, 58. God needs nothing, 45, 84, 248. No nature is superior to God, 44. God is not greater than God, 58. God is the supreme spirit, 31.

## The supreme God

Whatever is not supreme among all things is less than that which can be conceived, 31. The supreme essence is not one of those things above which there is something else, 9. Rather, it is that to which everything else is inferior, 9. God exists supremely and is supreme over all things, 5, 9, 31, 32.

See below, Attributes of God.

He is the supreme essence, supreme life, and so forth—that is, supremely existing, supremely living, and similarly in other respects, 10. God is greater than all, better than all, more beautiful than all, and more powerful than all, 201. All great things are great through one thing that is great through itself, 4, 5. Whatever is less than something else is in no way God, 45. Everything other than the supreme nature is less than it, 6. Nothing can be equal to the supreme Spirit except the supreme Spirit, 21. It is impossible for the supreme good to contain anything imperfect, 48.

## God incomprehensible

What is so incomprehensible and ineffable as that which is above all things? 24. No knowledge comprehends the height of God’s majesty, 164. God is not known by a creature except insofar as he wishes to reveal himself, 161. Nothing about God can be understood except through God’s light and truth, 32. God cannot be conceived through himself or through a similar form, 36. Human reason cannot aspire to the incomprehensible property of the Godhead, 151. The eye of the soul seeking God is darkened by its own weakness and beaten back by God’s brilliance, 53, 242. It is obscured by its own shortness and overwhelmed by God’s immensity, 242. A creature cannot understand what purity, simplicity, certainty, and splendor there are in God, 242. Nothing can be perceived of the supreme nature through its own property, but only through something else, 24.

See Knowledge of God; Mind; Rational creature.

How that supreme nature is incomprehensible and ineffable, and yet what has been discussed and made explicit about it is true, 24.

## God ineffable

When something is said in words about the supreme nature, the words are common to other natures, but the meaning is in no way common, 24. It can be said to be ineffable, and it can be conceived as inconceivable, 29. Yet what is ineffable cannot be said, nor can what is inconceivable be conceived, 29. The supreme nature is ineffable because words cannot in any way express it as it is, 24. Nevertheless it is not false if something about it is estimated through something else, as in a riddle, 24. It would be astonishing if words or names that we adapt to things made from nothing could be found that were worthy to be said of the creative substance, 9. We do not possess names by which we may properly speak about God, 151.

## Knowledge of God

The human mind can understand itself and the supreme essence, 16. Otherwise it would in no way distinguish itself and that essence from irrational creatures, 16. The readiest method of investigating the supreme nature, 40. God is supremely perceptible, 31. From a lesser good the greater good is known, 39. From created goods that than which nothing greater can be conceived is known, 39. One approaches knowledge of the supreme nature more closely through what more nearly resembles it, 24. It is clear what belongs to all things and what does not belong to all things as the supreme nature, 9.

## Names of God

Whatever names are said of the supreme nature express it not so much according to its proper character as through likeness, 24. They establish in the mind something much lesser, indeed something far different, from what the mind tries to understand, 24.

See Riddle.

Even the name “wisdom” is insufficient to display that through which all things were made from nothing and are preserved from nothing, 24. The name “essence” cannot express that which is far above everything and very far outside everything, 24. The name “God” is properly assigned only to the supreme essence, 28. By the name “God” nothing is understood except a substance regarded as above every nature, 28. The name “God” signifies the essence itself, 57.

## Attributes of God

Whatever is said of the supreme nature essentially is the same as everything else, whether taken together or singly, 10, 33, 34. When “justice” or “essence” is said, it signifies the same as the other attributes, or as all of them, or as each individually, 34. Whatever is said essentially of the supreme substance is one, 10. The supreme nature is, in one manner and under one consideration, whatever it is essentially, 10, 33. Whatever is essentially in any way is the whole of what it is, 10. Whatever is said relatively of the supreme nature does not signify its substance or designate its natural essence, 91. If none of these relative attributes existed, it would not be supreme or greater, 91. Yet it would not thereby be understood less, nor would it be anything other than the whole of what it is, 91. The supreme nature can fail to be understood as supreme, or as greater and greatest, 91.

The supreme is not simply better than the non-supreme, and the non-supreme is not in any respect better than the supreme.

See The supreme God.

In the supreme nature, whatever exists apart from relatives is either itself better than not-itself, or not-itself is in some respect better than itself, 91. God is whatever is simply better than not-itself, 9, 31, 32. When it is said that he is just, great, or something similar, this does not show what kind or how great he is, but what he is, 10. He is whatever he is not through something else but through himself, 6, 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 31, 32. The supreme nature is just not because it possesses justice but because it is justice itself; and the same applies to the other things said of God, 11, 32. God is life itself, light, wisdom, goodness, eternal blessedness, blessed eternity, and every good, 32, 242. This is everywhere and always, 32. He is living, wise, powerful and almighty, truthful, just, blessed, and eternal, 9, 31, 32. Life, wisdom, and the other attributes are not his parts, but all are one, 33. Each of these is the whole of what God is, and what all the others are, 32. Yet the supreme nature, which is so many goods, is not composed of them, 10, 14, 15, 33, 34. These are not several goods but one good signified by several names, 34.

See Simplicity of God.

The properties of the supreme substance are investigated, 8. The supreme nature exists, lives, perceives, and is rational in its own singular manner, 16. It is perceptive, omnipotent, merciful, and impassible, 31, 32. How is God perceptive if he is not a body, omnipotent if he cannot do everything, or merciful if he is impassible? 31.

## God is not a body but a spirit

The supreme essence is spirit, not body or anything perceptible, 9, 14, 31. It has no limb or any part, 58. It does not know through bodily sensation, 31. For the supreme nature, to be and to live are the same, 13.

## God immortal and incorruptible

If the supreme essence is going to have an end, it is not supremely immortal and supremely incorruptible, 10. It will have an end neither willingly nor unwillingly, 10. If it is to perish unwillingly, it is not supremely powerful, 10. If the supreme nature had either a beginning or an end, it would not be true eternity, 11. The good whose will brings the supreme good to an end is not a simple good, 10.

See Eternal God.

## The one God

There is one God, 15, 43, 45, 46, 59, 228. The supreme essence is entirely an individual Spirit, 14. Nor can it be divided, 228. There cannot be several supreme essences, 14, 21. God is one not only in nature but also in number, 43. There are not several supreme goods but one supreme good alone, 45, 46. Truth entirely excludes the existence of several beings through which all things exist, 5. Reason permits no plurality to exist through one another, 5. That through which all things exist is either one or many, 5. If there are many, either they are themselves related to one thing through which they exist, or the several things individually exist through one, or they exist through themselves, or they exist through one another, 5. If several things exist through one, then all things do not exist through several but through that one through which the several exist, 5. If several things individually exist through themselves, there is one power or nature of existing through itself by which they have the ability to exist through themselves, 5. For through that same one they exist through which they possess the ability to exist through themselves rather than through several things that cannot exist without that one, 5. A nature that comes together into perfect unity is more worthy than one that admits plurality within itself, 48. Where there is plurality, there is difference, 48. Where there is difference, there is not perfect concord, 48. Perfect concord is that which comes together into one identity, 48. “God in God” does not add a number to God; there is only one God, 48, 61. There is no other God besides him, 245. The unity and simplicity shared by the supreme nature are commended, 19.

## God simple

God’s nature is simple and in no way composite, 10, 44. God is wholly whatever he is, 10, 33, 61. The supreme essence is a true and simple good, 10. It is impious to say that it is composed of several goods, or that what belongs to every composite enters into it, 10, 12, 33, 44, 45.

See Composite.

If God is composite, something greater than God can be understood, 44. There are no parts in God, 33, 34, 51, 61. God is unity itself, not divisible by any understanding, 14, 33. He is free from every law of place and time and from composition of parts, 47, 48.

## God immutable

The supreme essence is in no way changeable, 14, 155. A good that is not changed or moved is better, 39. The supreme essence is subject to no accidents, 27. It is not changeable by any accidents, 14, 27. Accidents that do not alter a thing may be said of the supreme nature, 14. Truth is always immutable, 93.

## The true God

God is truth itself, 93. He is supreme truth, 10, 11. God cannot lie, 91. Supreme truth subsisting through itself belongs to no thing, 115. But when something conforms to it, it is called the truth or rectitude of that thing, 115.

## God immeasurable

On the immensity of God, 228. God is everywhere, 9, 11, 168. He is in all things and in everything, 168. God is wholly everywhere, 35, 203, 228. He is present everywhere and sees all things, 195. God fills heaven and earth and all things, 227, 228. Where the creative essence is not, there is nothing, 9. It is not determinately in any place or time, 11, 12. It is not determinately in any place or time through itself, but through its power it is wherever and whenever anything exists, 11. As God’s power is, so God’s substance is always and everywhere, 45.

The supreme nature is not wholly in each place at one time, 12. Nor is it wholly in each place at different times, 12. Nor in any way wholly in all individual places, 12. It is in no place or time—that is, it is nowhere and never—in the ordinary sense, 12, 13, 33. It is in every place and time, that is, everywhere and always, 11–13, 32, 45. In what sense the supreme essence is in every place and time and in no place and time, 12, 13. It is not wholly in all places and times as though it were distributed by parts among them, 12. It is impossible for the creative essence to be everywhere and always, that is, in every time and place, 12. When it is said to be in a place or time, this means that it is present, not that it is contained there, 13. It would be more fitting to say that it is with a place or time rather than in a place or time, 13. It is in all things that exist and is wholly present in each individually, 13. It is more suitably said to be everywhere, or in all things that exist, than in all places, 13.

God is above all things, sustains all things, surpasses all things, and contains all things, 203. Nothing contains God; rather, he contains all things, 33. All things are in God, 33. He carries and surpasses, encloses and penetrates all other things, 9, 13. A creature can in no way escape the immensity of the Creator and Preserver, 9. The creating and preserving essence cannot in any way surpass the totality of created things, 9. No good, indeed nothing at all, exists without it or where it is not, 11, 12. Supreme truth admits neither the magnitude nor the smallness of local or temporal extension, 13. God alone is uncircumscribed, 32. God is in all places without a place, without movement, and remains, 228. God is great without spatial extent, 34.

## Eternal God

God’s eternity is an interminable life existing wholly and perfectly all at once, 14, 15. The supreme nature is without beginning and end, 10–15.

See Truth.

The supreme nature cannot in any way be conceived to have an end or to be nonexistent for any length of time, 34. God’s eternity is wholly present to him, 33, 34. A good without an end is better, 39; better still is one without both beginning and end, 39. That than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot be conceived except without a beginning, 37, 38. That than which nothing greater can be conceived is always and everywhere wholly present, 37. God is before and beyond all things, including those that will not have an end, 33. For those things cannot exist without God, whereas God would exist even if they did not, 34. Whatever exists at any time or in any manner, God is wholly and always that, 34.

Eternity belongs only to the creative essence and not to created things, 14, 15, 32; it alone lacks both beginning and end, 32. God’s eternity is not a part of God, 33. The eternity of the supreme nature is nothing other than the nature itself, 12–15, 33, 48. God is eternity, 61; outside eternity there is nothing, 61. And outside God there is nothing, 61. His age is nothing other than his eternity, 12, 13. Nothing preceded God or will follow him: that is, nothing was before him, and after him nothing will be, 11. God always was, is, and will be, 11. In God, “was” and “will be” cannot exist, 161. The statement “nothing was before the supreme essence” has a twofold meaning, 11. God always was—that is, there was never a time when he was not, 328. The word “always,” when said of God, signifies eternity rather than the whole of time, 13.

The supreme nature is not distinctly and separately wholly present in each individual time, 12. The supreme nature is not extended in parts through the parts of time, 12, 13, 15, 33. It has neither past nor future nor a passing present, 33, 161, but only present being, 31. God’s eternity is “the age” because of its indivisible unity, and “the ages” because of its interminable immensity, 34.

## God omnipotent

The omnipotence of God, 228, 250. The supreme nature is omnipotent, 10. The power of the supreme essence is nothing other than the supreme essence itself, 11, 13, 45. God is omnipotent because he can do whatever he wishes to do, 250. God can do through himself whatever he wills, 34, 242. By his power he encloses all things made by him by containing them beneath himself, 13, 47. Power is not accidental to God, 45. God cannot exist or be understood without power, 45. Power is substantial to God, 45. It is not a part of God’s substance, 45. God’s being and his power are the same, 45. God’s power is always and everywhere, 45. If all things were to perish, he could restore them just as he made them, 84. It is not impotence but power in God that he cannot be better or richer, 248.

God cannot lie or be corrupted, nor remain silent so that what is true becomes false, and so forth, 31, 67. This is not because he is impotent but because he is omnipotent, 67. When we say that God must always speak truth and must never lie, this means that nothing can cause him not to speak truth or to lie, 94. Since even a small incongruity is impossible in God, 46, 79, 84. When God is said not to be able to do something, no power is denied to him; rather, unconquerable power and strength are signified, 93. When God is said not to be able, this means that no thing can bring it about that God does that thing, 93. Once something has happened, it cannot now be unhappened; it is always true that it has happened, 93. It is not rightly said that it is impossible for God to make what is past not past, 93. God is said not to be able to do anything opposed or perverse to himself, 67. God is so powerful in blessedness and justice that no thing can harm him, 67. God is subject to no law and no judgment, 79. God is more truly omnipotent because he can do nothing through impotence and nothing can act against him, 312. God’s omnipotence is explained through its effects, 151. God is improperly said not to be able to do something, 63.

## God impassible

The divine nature is impassible, 77. Nor can it be humiliated, 77. Nor does it labor in what it does, 77. The divine nature neither needed nor could be humbled, 222. It is impossible for God to lose his honor, 80. Nor can his honor be diminished or increased, 80. He himself is an incorruptible honor to himself and in no way changeable, 80. Nothing can harm the supreme good, 67.

See God immortal.

As far as lies in him, God cannot honor or dishonor anyone, 81. One honors God as far as lies in oneself when one subjects one’s will to his will, 81. One dishonors God when one withdraws one’s will from his will, 81. The divine nature was not humbled in Christ’s death; the human nature was exalted, 222.

## God wise

Supreme wisdom is nothing other than the supreme Spirit, 16. Supreme wisdom always knows through itself, 19. The supremely simple nature is nothing other than its own understanding, and is the same as its own wisdom, 15. The supremely great is not called great by spatial extent, as a body is, but by wisdom, 4. It is better and more worthy to be great in wisdom than in spatial extent, 4.

It is not fitting for God to do anything unjustly or disorderly, 80. It is not fitting for God to leave anything disordered in his kingdom, 72, 79, 84. In God, every small incongruity entails impossibility, 46, 79, 84. In God, every slight reason, unless overcome by a greater one, is accompanied by necessity, 79. The very thing that someone perversely wills and does, God’s wisdom converts into the order of the universe, 80. God’s wisdom converts sins themselves into the good of the universe, 80. God’s wisdom orders even evils well, 76. It is impossible for there to be deformity in the order of the universe, 80. It is impossible for God to fail in his disposition, 80, 86.

## God omniscient

Knowledge and understanding belong to supreme wisdom, 23. Knowledge and understanding pertain to the essence of the supreme nature, 23. The supreme Spirit, just as he is eternal, so eternally remembers himself and understands himself, 26, 20. It cannot be denied that supreme wisdom remembers itself, 20. Even if nothing existed apart from the supreme essence, it would understand itself, 16. The supreme Spirit remembers himself and understands himself to the extent of his essence, 21. It is natural to eternal and unchangeable knowledge and understanding always to behold as present what it knows and understands, 23. The speech and knowledge of the Creator are far superior and truer than those of created substances, 17.

Every truth, and nothing but truth, is present in eternity, 125. God’s immense truth sees in a single act of vision whatever has been made, and by whom, through whom, and how it was made from nothing, 33. God knows every truth, 124, and knows nothing except truth, 124, 125, 127. God is ignorant of nothing, 182. It cannot be denied that God knows what he wills and does, and foreknows what he will will and do, 125. God sees things as they are, whether spontaneous or necessary, 124, 125, 127; and as he sees them, so they are, 124. To know God is to know perfectly, 245. He knows all things supremely, 31. God foreknows all things, 126.

See Predestination; Foreknowledge.

If God receives knowledge from things, those things exist before his knowledge and therefore are not from God, 126. Things cannot exist from God except through his knowledge, 126. The supreme Spirit knows all the things he knows in the same way in which he speaks them, 17. Human beings cannot comprehend how the supreme Spirit speaks or knows the things that have been made, 17, 24, 228. God’s knowledge is indescribable, 228. God does not know through bodily sensation, 31.

## God loving himself

The supreme Spirit, just as he remembers and understands himself, so he loves himself, 20. God always remembers, understands, and loves himself, 203. The supreme Spirit does not remember and understand himself because he loves himself, 21. Rather, he loves himself because he remembers and understands himself, 21. The supreme Spirit loves himself to the extent that he remembers and understands himself, 21. It is wholly the same thing that loves or is loved in the Father and in the Son, 21. It is necessary that the two—the Father and the Son—love each other and each himself with equal love, 21. The love of the supreme Spirit is as great as he himself is, 21.

## God good

There is one supremely good thing, 4; all good things are good through one thing that is good through itself, 4. God is that very good in which every good exists, 34, 242. Whatever the supreme nature is as a good, it is supremely so, 10. Therefore it cannot fail, 10. How delightful that good is, 10. It is more pleasing than all created goods, 10. The supreme nature is good through itself, and nothing else is good except through it, 25. God’s essence is nothing other than goodness, 238. God is good from himself, eternally and essentially, 238, 248. No good can be understood before that good without which nothing is good, 6. The supreme nature is the good without which there is no good, 6. God can neither be nor will anything other than being good, 238. God is the good to which no evil can draw near, 212. God is never anything except good, 212. Nothing is greater or better than God, 80, 196. God cannot be or be understood to be better, 32, 248. If any mind could think of something greater than God, the creature would rise above the Creator, 30. No good is absent from the supreme good through which every good exists, 31. God’s goodness is incomprehensible, 31. God is a good wholly sufficient to himself, 34. No one is good except God alone, 228. God needs no one, 87. God is great without quantity, good without quality, and therefore truly and supremely good, 228. God is all good things, 240. In himself he possesses harmony, fragrance, taste, smoothness, and beauty, 33, 242. Why the soul does not perceive these things in God, 242. The Creator’s goodness toward humanity is beyond estimation, 237. God would be less good if he were kind to no evil, 31.

See Merciful God.

He spares the wicked because he is wholly supremely good, 31. God is our ultimate end, 177. God is the supreme good, 31, 45, 196. God is the unchangeable good through which the rational creature becomes blessed, 182.

See Blessedness; Good; Rational creature.

## God just

God’s justice is nothing other than God himself, 80. The supreme nature is not just except through justice, 10. Nor can it be just except through itself, 10. The supreme nature is justice itself, 10. When it is said to be just through justice, this is the same as saying that it is just through itself, 10. It is the same to say of it that it is just and that it is justice, 10. If one asks what the supreme nature is, nothing truer can be answered than “justice,” 10. Blessedness and justice are not different in God but one good, 67. The supreme nature is not properly said to possess justice but to be justice, 10. It is just that God should be so just that no one more just can be conceived, 32.

God is supremely just and wholly just, 31. Nothing is more just than God’s justice, 80. The supremely just does nothing unjust, 31. Nothing is more unjust than for a creature not to pay its Creator what it takes away, 80. God preserves nothing more justly than his honor, 80. It is necessary that honor taken from God be restored or punishment follow, 80. Nothing is more just than for the good to receive good and the wicked to receive evil, 32. The supremely just Creator does not unjustly deprive anyone of the good for which that person was made, 26. It is not fitting for God to leave a sinner unpunished, 80. If sin is left unpunished, the sinner and the non-sinner will be alike before God, 79. It is not fitting for God that the sinner and the non-sinner be alike before him, 79. Justice permits punishment to be imposed only on account of sin, 86. If sin is neither paid for nor punished, it is subject to no law, 79. And injustice is freer than justice, 79. And injustice makes one like God, 79.

God punishes sinners so that he may exact from the unwilling the honor they refused to render willingly, and so that nothing may be disordered in his kingdom, 99. God shows himself to be the sinner’s lord when he subjects the sinner to himself by finding and torturing him, 80. And he takes away from him what belongs to the human being, 80. What justice is it to give eternal life to one deserving eternal death? 31. It is not contradictory for God both justly to punish and justly to spare, 32. “The Lord is just in all his ways,” even though the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, 32. It is just that God punish the wicked, 32. And it is just that he spare the wicked, 32. When he punishes, it is just because punishment accords with the sinner’s merits, 32. When he spares, it is just because sparing accords with his goodness, 32. In sparing the wicked, God is just according to himself but not according to us, 32. God is just according to himself both when he punishes and when he spares, 32. For those whom he wills to punish, it is not just that they be saved; and for those whom he wills to spare, it is not just that they be condemned, 32.

Whatever is not done justly ought not to be done; and whatever ought not to be done is done unjustly, 32. God, the just judge, inflicts torments for evil deeds, 210. Those who turn back from evil and do good he rewards with an eternal recompense, 210. God repays good things to the good and evil things to the wicked out of goodness and yet also out of justice, 31. God saves the just with justice accompanying them; he frees sinners with justice ruling over them, 32. The former with their merits assisting, the latter with their merits resisting, 32. The former by recognizing the good things he has given; the latter by forgiving the evil things he hates, 32.

See Damnation; Merciful God; Hell; Punishment of sin.

## Merciful God

The mercy of God, 212 and following. It is wondrous how God, who is supremely just, spares the wicked, does not punish them, and even grants them good things, 31, 32. How God not only spares the wicked but also grants them good things, 32. It appears from where God is merciful, and not—
It is perceived: it is discerned from where the river of mercy flows, but the source from which this river arises is not seen, 31. In the most secret place of God’s goodness lies the reason why he is merciful, 34. God’s mercy does not oppose justice; indeed, there is no mercy without justice, 32. God is merciful precisely because he is supremely just, 32. He is merciful for this very reason: because he is supremely just, 32. Nor is he supremely good except because he is supremely just, 32. God’s mercy arises from his justice, 32. God is merciful in relation to us, who experience the effect of his mercy, 31, 32. He is not merciful in himself, since he does not experience the feeling of compassion, 32. God is merciful because he saves the wretched and spares sinners, 31. Yet he is not merciful, because he is moved by no compassion for misery, 31. If God ought not to show mercy, then he shows mercy unjustly, 32. It is impious to say this, 32. Therefore God shows mercy justly, 32. Nothing is more benevolent than God, 79. God’s mercy made us when we did not exist, 213. Mercy and pity are not necessary where there is neither misery nor need, 190. God is more wondrous in the depths of his compassion, 252. The Redeemer’s compassion surpasses the sinner’s wickedness, 209, 247. The greater the sinner’s unhappiness, the more wondrous is the compassion of the one who grants pardon, 293. It is improper to attribute to God such mercy as would forgive a person merely because that person cannot repay, 86. Such mercy would make a person blessed on account of sin, 86. And it would be excessively opposed to justice, 86. It is impossible for God to be merciful in this way, 86. Benevolence should not be called benevolence if it does something unfitting for God, 80. God does not desire death, but desires the sinner’s conversion, 209, 212. God begins a good work in us for our sake, not for his own, 87. God alone makes the unclean clean and sinners just, 268. See Good God.

## God’s love for us

Unless God loved one who did not love him, he would not make that person loving, 224. God loves us first, 221. [Col. 1073] The good that demands to be loved above all things compels itself no less to be desired by the one who loves it, 26. The supremely good Creator loves every nature that truly loves him, 25. God’s love and compassion toward us, 75. God’s love toward sinners, 210. See Good God. Merciful God.

## God’s will

The divine nature cannot be understood without will and power, 45. God’s will is understood in four ways: as God’s knowledge and as his ordering of all things through wise arrangement; as the will of the saints; as human reason; and as the divine commandments, 151. In what sense does God will sin—for example, adultery? In the sense that he foreknows and foresees it, 151. God does not will sin—for example, adultery—in the sense that he does not command or inspire it, 151. Whatever God ordained from eternity that he would do, he left nothing unfulfilled, 151. God’s will is understood according to a certain affect of divine mercy, 151. In what sense does God will all people to be saved? 116, 151, 152. God wills all people to be saved; that is, he causes the saints to will that all be saved, 151. And he himself wills this because he has ordained it, 151. God’s effective will accomplishes whatever he wills, 116, 152. In accordance with this will it is said: “He has done whatever he willed,” and “He has mercy on whomever he wills,” 116. According to the approving will, it is said that God wills every human being to be saved; that is, it pleases him that, if all human beings were just, each one would be saved, 116. According to the permitting will, it is said that he hardens whom he wills, 116.

God’s will is of several kinds. One is effective: it accomplishes whatever he wills. Another is approving: it approves something, and by it God wills all people to be saved. Another is granting: it grants that something happen; by this will God wills that a person who has not resolved to do better should marry. Another is permitting: it permits something to happen which is sometimes evil; by this will God is said to will evils, 152. God’s will is called that which he himself produces in hearts, 152. God sometimes makes his saints will what he himself does not will, 152. The saints, sometimes piously and holily inspired, will and pray for what God does not will, 152. God sometimes does not do what the saints, inspired by him, pray for, 152. God made all things, including future things, which he willed by a will that is foreknowledge, 152. God wills all people to be saved; that is, no one is saved except those whom he wills to save; or, some are saved from every kind of human being; or, he compels no one to be damned, 152.

Just as it is evil to use a good thing badly, so it is good to use an evil thing well, 152. God’s will is always good, 222. Only that is just which God wills; what he does not will is not just, 32. Nothing is right or fitting except what God wills, 79. Whatever he wills is just; whatever he does not will is not just, 80. When it is said, “If God wished to lie, lying would be just,” two impossibilities are being asserted, 80. If God were to will something unfitting, it would not thereby be just because he willed it, 80. It does not follow that, if God wished to lie, lying would be just; rather, it would follow that he was not God, 80. It is true only of those things whose being willed by God is not unfitting to say, “If God wills this, it is just,” 80.

God’s will ought to suffice as a reason when he does something, even though we do not see why he wills it, 77. God’s will is never irrational, 77. In God, will is not one thing and rectitude another, 114. In God, power is not something other than divinity, 114. It is rightly said of God that he possesses rectitude of will, voluntary rectitude, or right will, 114. Likewise, one may speak of the power of divinity or of powerful divinity, 114. God’s will is his work, and his willing is his ability, 228, 236. Whatever God wills must exist; what God wills cannot fail to exist, 34, 124, 242. God alone is governed by his own will, 64.

Sometimes it is praiseworthy, and sometimes blameworthy, to conform oneself to God’s will, or to will what God wills, 151, 152. Human will is good only when it wills what God wills it to will, 152. God’s will is the teacher of the human will, 152. It is incomprehensible, 152. What happens against God’s will does not happen apart from his will, 152. God permits nothing except willingly, nor would he permit good to be done badly unless he could also bring good out of evil, 152. Divine ordinance is not improperly called God’s will, 152. We call whatever God mercifully works in us his will, 152. Punishment and the rejection of certain persons, brought about by God’s hidden severity as an act of justice, are also called his will, 152. God’s will is whatever happens, insofar as it is found to happen in creatures, 152.

## God’s freedom

God’s will is compelled by no necessity and is subject to no necessity, 93, 12, 94. Every necessity is subject to God’s will, 94. It is not necessary for God to will what he wills, 93, 124. Nothing is necessary except because he wills it so, 93. No necessity precedes God’s willing or not willing, 93, 94. God is just by necessity, but not by compulsion, 123. This is not because he is compelled, but because nothing can make him unjust, 123. God does everything he wills, and does only what he wills, 93, 94. God does nothing by necessity, 87, 93. For he is in no way compelled or prevented from doing anything, 93. See God, the cause of things. [Col. 1074]

God is improperly said to do something by necessity, 93. In God, the necessity of doing something is nothing other than his spontaneous immutability, 93, 94. What God immutably proposes to do, before it occurs, cannot fail to happen, 93, 94. Nevertheless, there is in him no necessity of doing or impossibility of not doing, 94. For only will operates in him, 94. God does something by the necessity of avoiding dishonor—that is, by the necessity of preserving honor, 87. This necessity is nothing other than the immutability of honor which he possesses from himself, 87. This immutability is improperly called necessity, 87. God immutably wills and does many things, 93, 94. God’s purpose is immutable in eternity, 125. But in human beings it is sometimes changeable through freedom of choice, 125. What cannot be changed in eternity may sometimes, before it occurs in time, be changed through free will, 125, 127. What God has ordained to be done is already accomplished in his sight, 156. God changes his works, but does not change his plan, 227. God does not repent of the good he has done, 83. In creating the human being, God freely bound himself to complete the good he had begun, 87.

## God, the cause of things

Whatever exists exists through the supreme essence, 7. Apart from the supreme essence nothing exists unless it brings it about, 7. Everything that exists is either Creator or creature, 62. Whether Creator or creature, it can be possessed only from the Creator himself, 62. He alone has from himself whatever he has, 62. All other things have anything at all only from him, 62. And from him they have only something, 62.

In what sense not-being, or ceasing to be, or nothingness is from God, 61. Whoever can make something not exist, and does not do so, is said to make it exist, 62. Whoever can make something exist, and does not do so, is said to make it not exist, 62. In this sense God is said to do many things which he does not do, 62. Therefore what existed returns to non-being because God ceases to make it exist, 62. A creature has its non-being not from God but from itself, 62. And when it returns to non-being, it does not return to something belonging to God, but to what belongs to it, 62.

From the highest good there is nothing but good, 62. And every good is from the highest good, 62. From the supreme essence there is nothing but essence, 62. And every essence is from the supreme essence, 62 and 99, 126, 127. Whatever flourishes does so through one thing, 8. That one thing alone flourishes through itself, while other things flourish through something else, 8. Nothing has been made except through the creative presence of the essence, 8, 9, 28, 62. Nothing flourishes and continues to exist except through the power of that same essence, which preserves it, 62.

God made the whole substance from nothing, 7, 120. And he can reduce it to nothing, 120. God made all that exists from nothing, 238. The supreme essence could not make anything at all through anything else—whether instrument or aid—but only through itself, 7. Whatever the supreme nature made, it undoubtedly made either from something, as from matter, or from nothing, 7. The essence of everything that exists was made by the supreme essence, and indeed from no matter, 7. Whatever exists may be said to be from the supreme nature and through it, 5. No lesser nature is materially from the supreme nature, 6, 7. If something lesser than the supreme nature could arise from its matter, the highest good could be changed and corrupted, 6. The universe of things cannot arise from the matter of the supreme nature, 6. It cannot arise either from itself or from something else, 7. Therefore it arises from no matter, 7.

The supreme substance made all things through nothing other than itself, 8, 15, 17. God made all things from nothing by his will alone, 28, 101, 228. He himself is the one from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist, 91, 28. Things do not come from the supreme nature as from an assistant or instrument, 6. Whatever the supreme Spirit does, his Word also does, 17. And whatever the Word of the supreme Spirit does, the supreme Spirit himself also does, 17. Whatever exists through something else is less than that through which all other things exist and which alone exists through itself, 5, 14. All good things are from God and in God, 240.

God makes good works by his goodness alone, 134. For he creates the will with free choice and gives it justice, through which it acts, 134. God made evils solely through human fault, 134. For he would not make them if the human being did not wish to make them, 134. God makes in evil things what they are, 134. For he established in the human being a will with freedom of choice, 134. In good things God possesses both the fact that they are good by essence and the fact that they are good by justice, 134. In evil things God possesses only the fact that they are good by essence, not the fact that they are evil through the absence of the justice that ought to be present, 134.

God alone is the one through whom everything is good for each person and without whom nothing is good for anyone, 28. All things need God in order to exist and in order to exist well, 34. Without God, things are bad for us, 30, 242. Some things are done solely by God’s power and will, some by created nature, and some by the will of a creature, 101. Created nature cannot do anything by itself except what it has received from God’s will, 101. The will of a creature cannot act by itself except insofar as nature assists or permits it, 101.

Nothing unjust is from God, 99, 126. God makes a creature unjust only when he does not make it just, 70, 127. He gives an evil will by not preventing it, although he can, 70, 73. Nothing is from God except good, 99. God made every creature good, 38. God makes all works, both good and evil, 126. In good things he makes both what they are and what makes them good, 126, 127. In evil things he makes what they are, but not what makes them evil, 126, 127.

God did not make the will vicious and inclined toward evil, 133. The will does nothing which God does not do: in good things, by his grace; in evil things, not by his own fault but by the fault of the will, 127. He is more truly said to do everything that nature or will does who makes nature, together with the instrument of willing and its affections, 133. God makes each individual action, including those performed by an evil will, 70. God made all substantial and accidental natures, universal and individual, 70. This includes things brought about by an unjust will and a dishonorable action, 70. Whatever is something is from God and belongs to God, 70, 73. Whatever is evil, or nothingness, is made by the unjust one and belongs to him, 70.

God is not the author of evil, nor can he make it, 228. He did not make sins, 215. He makes the evil that is harm or something, 116. He does not make the evil that arises from injustice, or nothingness, 116. God makes all actions and all movements because he makes the things from which, out of which, through which, and in which they occur, 116. And no thing has ultimate power to will or do anything except by his giving it, 116. God is said to make the evils which he does not make because he permits them, 116. God is said to harden a person when he does not soften that person, 127. God is said to lead into temptation when he does not deliver from it, 62, 70, 167. God gives when he permits something to be seized, 73. When the devil willed what he ought not to will, he received this from God because God permitted it, 70, 73. Yet he did not receive it because God consented, 70.

God is wondrous in his works, 252. God created all, 155. He has right over all, 155. He rules over all, 28. God must complete what he began, 83, 86, 87, 88. “Because of his own immutable [reading incomplete],” 87. He who created the first human being also creates those who come into being through the created nature established by him for propagation, 101. God’s command is an effective power, 161.

It is incomprehensible how supreme wisdom knows the things it has made, 24. The wisdom of the craftsman is praised and proclaimed according to the excellence of the work, 131. No evil remains disordered in the kingdom of omnipotent wisdom, 72, 79, 84. In God we live, move, and exist, 203. The human being owes God everything he is, everything he understands, and everything he moves, 216. The devil and the human being belong only to God and are within his power, 72. God owes nothing to anyone, 84. But every creature is in debt, 84. It is not fitting for a human being to deal with God as an equal with an equal, 84. See Creature.

## The vision of God

The vision of God, 30, 241. In this land of the dying, God cannot be seen by mortal eyes, 260. No human being has seen or can see God, 228. The soul does not see God, who is light, completely because of its own darkness, 33, 242. The light in which God dwells is inaccessible to our powers, but one approaches it through divine gifts, 164. The light in which God dwells is inaccessible, 32, 33, 242. Why do we neither see nor perceive it, although it is everywhere? 242. God is light and darkness, 242, 116. Whoever sees the Son or the Father sees the Holy Spirit also, 58. Whoever sees God’s essence cannot see one of the three persons without the other two, 58. The teaching of the Law and the Prophets will withdraw when the manifestation of the divine vision has appeared to the saints, 164.

## Worship of God

See Praise.

Nothing is so worthy of veneration according to its dignity, and nothing should be petitioned for in every matter, as the supremely good and supremely powerful Spirit, 28. How desirable it is to be continually in God, 203. To possess God is eternal life, 253. To be separated from God is eternal death, 253. How blessed it is to remain in God and for God to remain in us, 203. It is sweet to possess life in God, 203. God’s absence from the soul is a grave evil, 239, 240. The soul’s grief over God’s absence, 239, 240, 241. Everything except God must be excluded by the one who seeks God, 29, 241.

No human being could knowingly wish to kill God, 91. The devil was not in the truth, nor did he abandon the truth except by his will, 110. He sinned in heaven without anyone persuading him, 85. He remained in truth and rectitude as long as he willed what he ought to will, 110. When he willed what he ought not to will, he abandoned rectitude and truth, 110. He freely abandoned willing what he ought to will, 64. He justly lost what he possessed, 64.

The devil is the enemy of the human being, 210. His deceptions, 210. Inflamed by envy, he persuaded the human being to sin, 83, 85. The human being and the devil seem to have sinned more particularly against the Son of God, 47. The human being ought to have been punished by the one to whom he had consented in order to sin, 76. After sin, the human being is justly tormented by the devil, 76, 77. Nevertheless, the devil torments the human being unjustly, 77. The devil had no merit by which he could punish, 76.

The human being did not sin against the devil but against God, 222. Nor did the human being belong to the devil; rather, both the human being and the devil belonged to God, 222. After sin, the human being owed nothing to the devil, 222. The devil harassed the human being not out of zeal for justice but out of wickedness; not at God’s command but by his permission; and not because the devil’s justice demanded it, but because God’s justice demanded it, 76, 222. There was nothing in the devil on account of which God ought to conceal or delay his power in order to save the human being from him, 222. God owed the devil nothing except punishment, and owed the human being only a return—that is, that the human being should overcome the devil, 222.

There are more demons than there were human beings living on the day Christ died, from whom their number is to be restored, 92. Whoever conquers the devil honors God, 85. Whoever is conquered by the devil dishonors God, 85. Satan will be released in his full strength against the just at the end of time, 161. It is the duty of demons to torment the reprobate, 169. An evil human being is called a devil, 83. See Angel.

## DIDACUS

Bishop of Santiago, 342. He asks Anselm for soldiers against the Saracens, 342.

The reasoning of the dialecticians is wrapped up in bodily imaginings, 43, 44. Dialecticians must be completely driven away from disputation about spiritual matters, 42. The errors of the dialecticians, 42, 43, 44.

## Dialogue

Things investigated through question and answer please many people, especially those who are slow, and are more readily understood by them, 75.

## To defer

It is good to defer something so that it may be done better, if the matter is certain, 346. See Conversion.

## DIONYSIUS (Saint)

On light and divine darkness, 164.

## To learn

What is learning except receiving knowledge? 55.

## Discord

See Concord, Peace.

## Discernment

On discernment, 177, 193. See Rational creature.

## Legitimate dispensation

The holy Fathers and the apostles made use of dispensations, 384.

## Disputation

On disputation, 183.

## To dispossess

To dispossess, 435, 436.

## The rich; riches

The rich are always miserable, 196. The death of the rich, 196. The vices of the rich, 196. God often gives riches in anger, 198. Even the impious possess these goods, 198. They are not therefore good, 198. The vanity of riches, 196. It is unjust that one person should abound in riches while another is in need, 184. See Greed.

## To teach

One should desire to be taught before teaching, 323.

## Pain

Pain is something, 73.

## Gifts

See Benefits.

The gifts, or operations, of the Holy Spirit, 159, etc. They correspond to the seven virtues or beatitudes, 159.

## DONATUS

Bishop of the Church of Dublin, 393. Archbishop Lanfranc gave him books and ornaments, 393. He was succeeded by Samuel, his nephew, 393. See Samuel of Dublin.

## The Church of Dorobernia

See the Church of Canterbury.

## The bishop of Dublin

Donatus, 393. He was succeeded by Samuel, his nephew, 393, 434. Anselm rebuked him because he spent the Church’s goods improperly and harassed the monks serving God in that church, 393. Also because he had a cross carried before him, 393. There were monks in the Church of Dublin, 393, 434. Archbishop Lanfranc gave him goods, 434.

## DUNSTANUS (Saint)

His miracles, 298. His conversations with angels, 298. He was refreshed by their songs, 298. He was led by them into heaven, 298. He foretold the day of his death, 298. He obtained a postponement of death so that his people would not lack a shepherd on the feast of the Ascension, 298. Saint Peter appeared to Saint Dunstan and gave him a sword inscribed with the word of God, 364. This prefigured that Dunstan himself would become archbishop of Canterbury, 364. Saint Dunstan established a rule of monastic life, 323. Anselm sought a written account of his life and institutions, 323, 324.

## DURANDUS

Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, he praised Anselm’s meditations, 334. He requested unity of fellowship with Anselm’s congregation, 334. He asked him for the Epistles of Saint Paul, 334.

## E

EADMER and Alexander, Canterbury monks, are accused of having defamed the king, 400. EADMER, or Edmetus, or Ermerna, or Elmerus, or Almerus, 318, 334. Monk of Bec, Anselm’s staff of old age, 375. He transcribes the books *Cur Deus homo*, 375.

Monastery of St. Edmund, 389, 392, 410, 431, 432, 433. Its monks are subjected to force concerning the election by Abbot Roger and by Robert, a monk of St. Évroul, 431, 432, 433. It is in the archbishopric of Canterbury, 433. Its abbot ought to be consecrated by the archbishop of Canterbury, 433. Roger, abbot of St. Évroul, attempts to intrude Robert, a young monk of his own monastery who was living disorderly, as abbot of this monastery, 433. From this the monks suffered persecution, 433. See Elpherus.

The bishop of York ought to make a profession of obedience to the archbishop of Canterbury, 421, 422. He ought to be consecrated by him, 422 and 420. He is accustomed to be honored with the pallium, 428. The archbishop of York and two other bishops, the king’s legates, are liars and perjurers, 393, 394. They are excommunicated, 394. They lie that the Roman pontiff does not prohibit investitures and would not excommunicate the king if he carried them out, 394. They attempt by a lie to induce St. Anselm to grant investitures to the king, 393, 394. See Thomas.

[Col. 1077]

**Drunkenness.** Whoever desires an immoderate pleasure in drinking loses grace, 129.

**EBRULPHUS (St.), abbot and monks**, 431, 432. The abbot of St. Évroul gave a disorderly-living young monk as abbot to the church of St. Edmund, 392. Anselm bitterly complains about him, 392. See Edmund. The monks of St. Évroul profess the Rule of St. Benedict, 431.

The Church is the city of God, 156. In heaven and on earth—that is, in angels and human beings—156. The Church is the seat of Christ’s majesty, 161. The Lord is always in the Church, 184. The Lord promises that he will be with the Church until the consummation of the age, 41. The faithful are members and the body of Christ, 169, 170, 171, 184. What is done to them is rightly said to be done to him, 169, 170, 171. The body of Christ, which is the Church, is called Christ, 169. All the faithful together with their head are Christ, 169. Christ’s body requires purification, but Christ himself does not, 169. See Church.

God cannot be found outside the Church, 172. The Church is represented by a little ship, 160. The Church can be disturbed by waves but cannot be sunk, 160, because Christ prays, 160. To wish to overthrow the customs of the Church is a form of heresy, 141. Any church, even one enlarged through a kingdom, may establish something according to the true faith that can profitably be read or sung at a gathering of the people, 59.

The liberty of the Church, 384, 429, 430, 440. God loves nothing more in this world than the liberty of the Church, 440. Divine things belong to no one’s possessions, 384. The Church was commended to kings and princes for protection, not given to them for hereditary domination, 389, 391, 429, 430.

**Church property.** Princes or laypeople ought not to retain tithes and church property, 433. Rather, they are bound to restore them if they do not wish to be excluded from God’s kingdom, 433. A bishop ought not to tolerate a king’s taking church property and giving it to soldiers, 375. It is permitted to lease church property, 404. It is permitted to redeem tithes and other church property from laypeople, 424.

**Defense of the Church**, 388, 389, 391.

**Consecration of a church.** The consecration of a church and altar, 423. If some part of a church is destroyed and rebuilt, or a new part is constructed, while the altar remains unmoved, the church need not be consecrated; it is only to be sprinkled with blessed water, 423.

EDIT, a virgin, 414.

**EDMERUS.** See EADMERUS.

EDULPHUS, a Winchester monk, is nominated by Queen Matilda as her candidate for abbot of Malmesbury, 410. He sends Anselm a cup together with letters requesting Anselm’s confirmation, 410. For this reason Anselm refuses to confirm him, 410.

**Need.** See Indigence, Poverty.

**The elect.** The number of the elect was not complete among the angels, 81, 82, 83. Whether more human beings are to be elected than the number of angels who fell, or not: whatever opinion is held about this, there is no danger to the soul, 83. The elect do not rejoice at the fall of the angels, 82. So many human beings will be taken up into glory as there remained angels there, 83. There was never any time without Christ’s elect, who were liberated by him from original guilt, 175. There are more elect human beings than there were at the time of Christ’s death, 92. The elect portions of the Church are God’s, 156. The multitude of the elect is God’s inheritance, 155. The elect are members of Christ, 157, 158. In finishing they accomplish more than they propose in beginning, 158. All the elect may rightly be called not only one but also a single person, 158. There is no one among the elect who is not counted either in the order of confessors or in the order of martyrs, 170. The world will be renewed immediately after the number of the elect has been completed, 83. God does not dwell and rest continually in everyone, but in those who are foreknown, 155. The wisdom of God does not dwell in those who believe for a time, 155. See Predestination.

**Election.** Princes and laypeople ought not to interfere in the election of bishops, 394. Councils have decreed that secular princes are to be barred from ecclesiastical elections, 383. See Abbot, Bishop, Prelate.

**Almsgiving**, 193. Anselm’s opinion concerning almsgiving, 327. Through almsgiving one reaches eternal life, 237. Whoever does not distribute wealth to the needy poor takes it away from them, 184. Wealth is unrighteousness, 184. The alms of the poor are not to be diminished, 376. Alms from the wealth of unrighteousness, 183, 184. We ought not to acquire what we give as alms through robberies, usury, and fraud, 183. Alms are not to be given through servants, 409. See Greed, Wealth, Poverty.

**Elements.** The entire mass of this world consists of earth, water, air, and fire, 6. The four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—can be understood apart from the forms that we see, 6. See Cause.

ELIAS, a count, asks Anselm for counsel concerning salvation and for absolution, 450. The abbot of Ely is not absolved from excommunication on account of repeated investiture, 416.

[Col. 1078]

The regular canons of St. Eligius of Mende, 429.

ELINANDUS, a Bec novice, 345. Anselm exhorts him to beware of the devil’s temptations, 345.

**Eloquence.** Whoever says beautiful things without solid reasoning paints above the cloud, 75. See Preaching.

ELPHERUS, prior of the monastery of St. Edmund, 432. He and his monks suffer harsh treatment because he does not accept the abbot who was forcibly intruded, 432. See Monastery of St. Edmund. Anselm instructs him to communicate with Count Robert, 446.

ELVREDUS, servant of Hugh of Lyons, 391. He came from Apulia to Lyons, 391. Through him Hugh writes to Anselm, 391.

ENGELHARDUS, 317.

ENGELHARDUS of Lenis Castle, Anselm’s friend, 340. Though very old, he wishes to abandon military service, 340.

**ENOCH.** He was transferred to paradise after his death had been postponed, 175. Whom he signifies, 175.

**Proposition.** A proposition is true and correct when it signifies that what is is, 109, 110. It is the same for a statement to be correct and true, 110. A negative proposition is one that signifies that what is not is not, 110. A statement that signifies that what is not is has truth and correctness, 110. A statement has two kinds of correctness: 1. when it signifies what it received the power to signify; 2. when it signifies that for which it was made to signify, 2. The latter is immutable and is always present in a statement naturally; the former is changeable and is present neither always nor naturally, but accidentally and according to usage, 2. Some propositions possess these two truths or forms of correctness inseparably, 2. Many things are said according to the form of speech that are not so according to reality, 344. See Truth.

**Bishopric, Bishop.** A bishopric is to be accepted only through obedience, 416. A bishopric ought not to remain without a pastor for more than three months, 420. An abbot may be elected bishop, 366. An elected but unconsecrated bishop does not have the governance of souls, 420. Nor can he confer it, 420. Nor is he able to consecrate a bishop, 420. The consecration of bishops is not to be performed by one bishop alone; it is to be performed in the places where they are to be ordained, 417, 419. If a bishop is established without a definite place and consecrated by one bishop alone, both the one ordained and the one ordaining are to be deposed, 419. Unless a bishop has a definite parish and people, he is not to be ordained, 439. He ought not to be ordained by fewer than three bishops, 439.

A bishop is the guardian of his church, 375. Bishops swear that they will preserve not the customs of kings or predecessors but the law of God, 438. Bishops retain their authority as long as they agree with Christ, 370. They deprive themselves of it when they disagree with Christ, 370. Every bishop who has the voice of Christ is Christ, 370. A bishop who does not have the character of a bishop declares that he is not a bishop, 302.

An accused bishop must clear himself by the seventh person of his order, 384. Unless he clears himself by the judgment of bishops, he is to be sent to the Roman pontiff, 384. If he refuses to appear before him, he is to be removed and another substituted in his place, 384. What the pope absolves, a bishop cannot bind, 385.

A bishop cannot be transferred without the consent of the archbishop, the bishops of the province, and apostolic authority, and without serious deliberation, 412. It does not belong to princes but to bishops to punish guilt for violations of the canons, 407. All churches ought to be under the authority of bishops, 383. A bishop ought not to distribute church property as if it were his own, 434. It is better for a bishop not to possess the lands of his church than to possess them diminished, 375. A bishop ought not to tolerate a king’s taking church property and giving it to soldiers, 375. It is glorious for a bishop to be stripped and expelled for justice, 393. Whoever has stripped a bishop of his possessions cannot be reconciled to God unless he restores everything to him, 402.

The bishops of England declare that they will not give counsel to the primate except according to the king’s will, 381. Several bishops burden monasteries with a certain harsh domination and according to their own will, 354. A bishop cannot keep a monk with him against the abbot’s will, 352. A bishop ought to strengthen the monks whom he can by advising and assisting them, 373. Obedience is owed to bishops, 433. A bishop’s ring, the seal of faith, 394. See Election, Prelate.

ERMENGARD, a noble woman, 356. With her husband’s consent she had vowed continence. For this Anselm praises them, 356. Yet she prevents her husband from becoming a monk. For this Anselm rebukes her, 356. He begs her to permit it when her husband requests it, 356. He does not dare advise her, but Anselm begs her that she too should renounce the world, 357.

ERNULPHUS, a Canterbury monk, 376. Prior of the same church, 395, 396, 397, 399, 409. A man learned in sacred letters, 404, 405. A spiritual man, with another Anselm in him, 405. Anselm sends him a privilege granted by the pope, 437. Anselm instructs him to have the books *Cur Deus homo* and *De conceptu Virginis* carefully transcribed, 441. He is required to pay the money given for chrism, 434. See Anselm, Canterbury.

ERNULPHUS, elected abbot of the diocese of Bayeux, 361. The bishop of Bayeux invites him to receive the blessing, 361, and demands from him a new profession of obedience, 361. Anselm writes to him that this ought not to be done, 361. He had professed obedience according to the Rule of St. Benedict, 361. His brother was Lord Nicholas, 361.

ERNULPHUS, chaplain of Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, 439.

ERNULPHUS, son-in-law of King Muriardach, 447. Anselm intercedes for him, 447.

**EUCHARIST.** Concerning the body and blood of the Lord in the sacrament of the altar, 452, 453. The truth of Christ’s flesh and blood on the altar is proved, 453. Testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning this truth, 453. Christ gave us for eating the flesh that he assumed for us, and he does not cease to minister it in the sacrifice of the altar, 211.

We eat and drink the true body and blood of Christ on the altar, 264, 265, 266, 268, 270. The same flesh is eaten that was taken from the Virgin and cooked on the cross, and the same blood is drunk that was poured out on the cross, 265, 267, 452. It is not figuratively but truly Christ’s body, 452; nevertheless, it may be called a figure and sacrament, 452.
