It is a figure if something other than what is perceived by bodily sight and taste is understood, 452 and 453. What the sacrament of the body and blood signifies, 453.

The priest holds in his hands Christ’s body, which was born from the Virgin, and so forth, 266, 268. Through divine power, with the bread being changed into Christ’s body, we offer sacrifice, 135. The Holy Spirit makes our offerings Christ’s body and blood, 268. Christ is the one who, through the Holy Spirit, makes the bread pass into his flesh and the wine into his blood, 454. It is effected not by the merit of the consecrator but by the Creator’s word and by the power of the Holy Spirit, 454.

From bread we make Christ’s flesh, 135. Through the words of consecration the bread is changed into Christ’s body, 453. The substance of the bread and wine does not remain, 453. Their appearances nevertheless remain, 453. After consecration it is not bread, 452. Yet it may be called bread, 452. Christ calls himself and his flesh bread, 135, because just as a person lives temporarily by this bread, so by that bread he lives eternally, 135.

Christ’s flesh is eaten daily and his blood drunk daily by the priest, 265. Christ’s incorruptible body is crushed by teeth and, according to its appearances, even gnawed by mice, 453. It is not to be asked what becomes of Christ’s body when it has been eaten, 453. Through eating his flesh and through right faith Christ restores a person completely, 266. See Communion.

EUDO, dapifer of King Henry, 443.

EULALIA, abbess in England, 412.

EUSTACHIUS, father of the monk Gaufredus, 397. After his wife, with her consent, had become an anchoress, he took another wife, 397. Brother of Lord Robert, 397.

EWERARDUS, 437, 438, 439.

EVA was from one man alone, 101. Eve sinned first; Adam sinned afterward and through her, 100. If Eve alone had sinned, it would not have been necessary for the whole human race to perish, but only Eve, 100. See Adam, Human Being.

Anselm calls Eve his lady and calls himself her firstborn son, 344. He also sends her greetings from England, 351, 361.

**GOSPEL.** The Gospel ought to be preferred to the law, 165. There is nothing in the Gospel except what is wholly true, 175, and except what is from the Holy Spirit, 175.

**Exaltation.** We are accustomed to rejoice together at the exaltation of our ancestors, 82.

**Examination.** We must reconsider not only the good things we have received but also the evils we have done, 204, 205.

**Excommunication.** Concerning excommunication, 332, 390, 394, 436, 437. A bishop ought not to pronounce a sentence of excommunication in his own case, nor when it is foreseen that excommunication will be despised and mocked, 382. Excommunication applies to those who accept investitures from laypeople, to laypeople who grant them, and to bishops who consecrate those so invested, 394, 404.

If an excommunicated person wishes to attend divine services, he is to be admonished, 332. If he rejects the admonition, action is to be taken according to the sentence of excommunication, or the apostolic authority is to be consulted on the matter, 332. How excommunicated persons are to be avoided, 400. Excommunicated persons are not to be admitted to monastic profession unless their bishop’s absolution has first been granted, 425.

**Example.** What is good is persuaded more effectively by example than by words, 338.

**Existence.** Whoever certainly knows that he exists cannot think that he does not exist, 36. No person can exist from himself, 52, 56. What exists in time and subsists through another is not properly and absolutely, 34. What begins to be progresses from non-being to being, 57. What is not somewhere or at some time can be thought not to be anywhere or ever, 37. See Thinking.

The existence of God. [Col. 1080]

OSBERN, bishop of Exeter. See Osbern. The clerics of Exeter unjustly harass the monks, 373.

EZECHIEL was thirty years old when he began to prophesy, 174.

## F

**To do and to will** are spoken of in six ways, 116. “To do” is used broadly for non-action, 116. See Cause.

**Crime.** A person is to be marked by the name of “crime” when he falls into an act or is abandoned in an evil will, 356; not the person who is neither precipitated into an evil deed nor rescued from a perverse will, 356. See Intention.

Christ is said to deceive when he permits someone to deceive, 221. See Christ, Truth.

**Falsehood.** How it is contrary to understand false things, 39. False things are understood in some manner, 39. False things can be thought but cannot be understood, 36, 28. False things are in the intellect when they are thought, yet they are not in reality, 35, 39.

FARMANNUS, a Canterbury monk, is sent from England to Bec by Anselm, 373. He asks Anselm for permission to visit him, 406. He also asks permission to live elsewhere, 406. Both requests are refused, 406.

**February**, that is, “the purifying month,” 171. In February the Romans held a procession, purifying the city every fifth year—that is, going around it and cleansing it, 171.

**Woman.** God made woman so that human beings might multiply from both sexes, 88. He made her from Adam alone, 88. The beginning of damnation is from a woman; the cause of salvation is born from a woman, 88. Women should not despair that they belong to the lot of the blessed, 88. It was fitting that the author of salvation should be from a woman, 75.

Woman is a sweet evil, 197. Satan’s torch, 197. Rarely chaste, 197. To be fled, 197, 198. She has cast down stronger men, 198. The origin of death, 198. The death of the soul, 198. Women’s luxury, 197, and so forth. She approaches monks while pretending piety, 198.

**Feasts.** At the birthdays of the saints we rejoice in their glory, 82. A fine is demanded for a broken feast, 450.

**Faith.** The will cannot will to believe unless it has received correctness, 130. To will to believe what ought to be believed is to will rightly, 130. No one can will this if he does not know what ought to be believed, 130. Mental conception alone does not produce faith, 130. When the correctness that comes through grace is added to the one willing, faith is produced, 130.

The necessity of faith, 27. The soul cannot love or hope for what it does not believe, 27. Faith is necessary so that the soul, by believing, may tend toward the supreme essence, 27. To believe in the supreme essence is, by believing, to tend toward it, 27. Whoever believes in the supreme essence believes all those things that pertain to tending toward it, 27. He does not believe in it either if he believes what does not pertain to tending toward it or if, through what he believes, he does not tend toward it, 27. To believe in it, or to tend toward it, is the same as to believe in it, or to tend toward it, 27. Nevertheless, it is more fittingly said “to believe in it” or “to tend toward it,” 27. No one can tend toward the supreme essence unless he believes, 27. Believing in it benefits no one unless he tends toward it, 27. Faith will be useless unless it can act and live through love, 27. Faith accompanied by love is not idle, 27. Faith that lacks love does not act, 27.

Whose faith is necessary for salvation, 79. We believe those things that clearly follow from what we read in Scripture and in councils. In matters concerning God that he cannot grasp, the intellect must submit to Christ’s authority, 47. See Sacred Scripture.

A faithful person does not seek to understand in order to believe; rather, he believes in order to understand, 30, 242, 74, 75, 357. The depths of faith must first be believed before they are examined by reason, 75. The unspeakable rashness of those who argue against what faith believes because they cannot grasp it intellectually, 42, 43, 357. They are compared to owls, 42.

One ought not to doubt that something is what is certainly known to be, even if one cannot comprehend or explain how it is, 24. It is not reasonable for anyone to deny something merely because he does not understand it, 39. Through obedience to faith we are advanced toward understanding, 42. Understanding is between faith and vision, 41. The more someone advances toward understanding faith, the nearer he approaches vision, 41.

God is the one who gives understanding of faith, 30. Sometimes the understanding that was given is withdrawn, and faith itself is overturned when a good conscience is neglected, 42. Whoever does not seek God’s commandments does not find understanding of faith, 42. Whoever does not believe will not understand, 42. We must see not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, so that by judging we may examine the depths of faith, 42. The person who does not take care to understand what he believes is accused of negligence, 75.

We believe and understand with the heart, just as we will with the heart, 128. It was given to rational creatures rightly to believe and understand in order to will rightly, 128. Faith is spoken of and given for the purpose of right action, 128. A person who does not rightly will to act according to faith is said to have faith only in the sense of dead faith, 128. Faith without works is dead; but dead faith is not faith, 299. Whoever has dead faith does not have faith, 299. It is impossible to please God without faith, which is nothing without good works, 299. Whoever does not have faith is dead, 299, because the just person lives by faith, 299.

Faith without love may be called dead, 27—not because it has lost its own life, that is, love, 27, but because it does not possess the love that it ought always to have, 27. Living faith is faith that believes what ought to be believed, 27. Dead faith is faith that merely believes what ought to be believed, 27.

Without faith and hope no human being possessing understanding can merit the kingdom of God, 131. Faith and hope concern things that are not seen, 131. Faith alone without works is not sufficient, 185. Once established in faith, a person may seek the reasoning of faith, 41. Our faith is to be defended by reason against the impious, not against Christians, 357.

A Christian ought not to argue about how something that the Church believes in its heart and confesses with its mouth can not exist, 42. Rather, while always holding to the faith, he should seek the reason why it exists, 42. If he can understand, let him give thanks to God; if he cannot, let him not put out horns for goring, but bow his head in reverence, 42, 357. Whoever wishes to understand in order to believe falls into error, 42. Faith is treated one way with Christians and another way with unbelievers, 357. A Christian ought to advance to understanding through faith, not approach faith through understanding, 357. If he is unable to understand, he ought not to depart from the faith, but to revere what he cannot grasp, 357.

**The faithful.** There are three orders of the faithful in the Church: superiors, continent persons, and married persons, 162. They are represented by the apostles who were present at Christ’s Transfiguration, 162. The multitude of the faithful is the honored people, 156. The entire Christian people is divided into two parts: sinners and the just, 182. See Christians.

**Figure.** Something is a figure when something other than what is perceived by bodily sense is understood, 452. Under the Law nearly everything was done in figure, 135. Christians use certain future things that represent past things, 136.

**End.** In all his thought and action a person ought through love to direct himself toward the supreme nature as his sole end, 27. See Good, Crime, Intention, Rational Creature, Will.

A son is always more like his father than a daughter is, 19. In created generations no single individual is sufficient by himself to beget offspring, nor does any one exhibit the complete likeness of a parent, 18.

**SON OF GOD.** Knowledge of the generation of the Son of God, 164. “The Son is the essence of the Father” is the same as “the Son is an undifferentiated essence from the Father’s essence,” indeed, “an essence from the Father,” 20, 22. The Son is the Father’s power, wisdom, truth, justice, and whatever belongs to the essence of the supreme Spirit, 22, because he has it from the Father, 22.

The Son is the understanding, or wisdom, of the Father’s memory, 20. Whatever the Son knows or understands, he also remembers, 20. The Son is the memory of the Father, and the memory of memory—that is, the memory of the Father who is memory, 20. Just as he is the wisdom that knows the Father and the wisdom of the Father—that is, wisdom knowing the Father through wisdom, 20. The Son is memory born from memory, just as wisdom is born from wisdom, 20. The Son may be called the understanding, wisdom, and knowledge of the Father, 20, because he understands, knows, and recognizes the Father’s essence, 20.

The Son may aptly be called the Father’s truth, 20, because he is not an imperfect imitation but the complete truth of the Father’s substance, 20. The offspring born from the supreme Spirit alone is the offspring of that Spirit’s memory, 20. The Son is the understanding of understanding, the knowledge of knowledge, the wisdom of wisdom, and the truth of truth, 20.

Although the Son is mindful of himself and loves himself, he is not the Father or the Spirit of anyone, 23, 24, because he is not generating memory or love proceeding from another, 24. Rather, he is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds from him, 24.

The Son is God from God by being born, 49, 50. The Son is born eternity, 48. Through this the Son is another than the Father: because he exists from him by being born, 52, 60. The Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit according to his humanity, 46. The Son is not another from the Father for any reason other than that he exists from him, 53. What the Son has from the Father, he has from no one other than himself, 60. For one God is not another God from another God, 60. Yet he is another from another, 60.

It is not contradictory for the Son to subsist through himself, 19, and to have being from the Father, 19. The Son is an essence born from the Father’s essence, 19. Yet he is not thereby another, less perfect essence or wisdom, 19. In being born from the Father the Son does not leave the Father, 57, 61. He is divided from the Father neither in place, nor in time, nor in essence, 61.

It is more fitting for the Son to be called the Father’s essence than for the Father to be called the Son’s essence, 20. The Son has his essence from the Father, while the Father has it from no one, 20. He has the Holy Spirit from the Father, 54, and the Holy Spirit is from him, 59, 60. The being of the Father and of the Son is the same, 54. He is another person than the Father, 46. He is equal to the Father in all things, 161. He is altogether the same as the Father and one and the same God, 59. He is neither greater nor lesser, earlier nor later, than the Father, 60, 164. Nor does he have anything different from the Father, 164.

Nothing is more like another than the offspring is like the supreme Father, 19. The offspring of the supreme parent is not a daughter but a son, 19, 49. He is the radiance of eternal light, the true image of the Father, and he did not regard equality with God as plunder, 47. He is perfectly the supreme essence, 19. He is perfect through himself, 19. The Son, considered singly, is perfectly the supreme Spirit, 19. Uncreated and creator, 22. He is the one who is supreme and is promised to be called Son, 160.

The name “Son” signifies only God who is the Son, or the relation by which he is related to the Father, 58. From that relation he is called Son, 58. The Son’s birth may be called procession, 57. The Son is neither born nor proceeds from the Holy Spirit, 51, 52. See God, Father, Holy Spirit, Trinity, Word of God.

It is more fitting for the Son to make supplication to the Father than for one person to supplicate another, 46. See Incarnation.

The Son of God is said to have been created, 155, and to have been begotten by the Father before the ages, 155. The Son of God assumed a most pure flesh and a most holy soul, 170. See Christ, Incarnation.

Through adoption we become sons of God by believing in the Son of God, 174.

**Scourging.** See Beating.

FLAMBARDUS. See Ranulphus.

FOLCERARDUS, a monk, 328. Anselm’s kinsman and cousin, 348, 375. He remained at Bec for some time, 375. Anselm had the prayers transcribed for him, 328. Abbot Henry intended to send him to Bec, 348. He is an exile for God’s sake, 375. Archbishop Anselm sends him greetings, 375.

FOLCERALDUS, Saint Anselm’s uncle. See Lambertus.

Fordwick, 442.

**Fornication.** Whoever commits fornication offends God, contaminates the soul, and defiles the entire beauty of the body, 142. Repentance for fornication should be continual, 209. Torments of hell are prepared for fornicators, 209. See Virginity.

**Fortitude.** The spirit of fortitude is appropriate to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, 159. The vanity of strength, 197.

Cold exists without any heat, 134. One cold is greater than another, 134.

FRODELINA. Anselm seeks knowledge of her, and she seeks knowledge of Anselm, 325.

**Fucus.** Against *Fucus*, 197.

FULCO. Anselm advises Fulco to refuse the dignity offered to him insofar as he can do so without sin, but in such a way that he finally accepts it out of obedience, 330. Anselm begs him, as abbot, to deal more mildly with a penitent apostate monk, 346.

FULCO, bishop of Beauvais, although inexperienced, is confirmed by Pope Urban II on Anselm’s recommendation, 353. Urban II orders that Anselm, either personally or through one of his monks, should assist and advise him, 353. At the insistence of the king of the Franks and the clergy of Beauvais, with the consent of the archbishop of Reims, Anselm compels him to accept the episcopal burden, 354. A severe persecution is stirred up against him by canons, priests, and certain laypeople, 354, because he wishes to prohibit their evil customs, 354. He visits the Roman pontiff, 354. Anselm begs that he be sent back strengthened by apostolic letters, 354. Anselm instructs him concerning what he was to answer at the Council of Reims on behalf of Lanfranc and of Anselm himself against Roscelin, 357. His love for Anselm, 369. See Anselm.

For his sake Anselm asks Urban II to judge him according to his prudence, 380.

**Thief.** Man and the devil were thieves, 76. One, persuaded by the other, was stealing himself from God, 76.

**Future.** A statement that says that something will be is not true unless something will in reality be; nor will anything be future unless it is in supreme truth, 113. See Free Choice, Necessity, Foreknowledge.

## G

**GABRIEL**, interpreter of God, 273, 284.

**GALO**, bishop of Paris, 406.

**GALO**, abbot of Saint-Quentin, 392. He is elected bishop of Beauvais, 392. Anselm commends him highly, 393.

**Joy of eternity**, 182. See *Beatitude*.

**GAUFRIDUS.** See *Godefridus*, *Goffridus*.

**GAUFRIDUS**, monk of Bec, 397. Son of Eustace, 397.

**GAUNILO**, monk of Marmoutier, author of the book *On Behalf of the Fool*, 35. He refutes Anselm’s reasoning, 35, 36. His own reasoning is itself refuted, 37, 38, 39, 40. He refutes Anselm without malice, 40.

**GELDUINUS**, abbot of Aquicinctum, 424. He consults Anselm about redeeming tithes and about simoniacs, 424, 425.

**Genealogy.** Scripture does not construct genealogies through women, 174. The genealogy of Christ: see *Christ*. The genealogy of Mary: see *Mary*. Among the Hebrews, the names of generations are reckoned sometimes according to nature, sometimes according to law, 174.

**Generation.** To give life is to receive death, 91. The propagation of a man from a woman alone, of a woman from a man alone, and the creation of a human being from clay is not natural or voluntary, but miraculous, 101. Adam did not receive the nature of procreating except through a man and woman together, 101. In the heavenly city human beings will not procreate, 131. Human beings would have procreated in paradise, 131. The procreation of human beings will continue until the number of the elect is complete, 83. When that number is complete, the generation of human beings will cease, 83.

**Gentiles**, what they are like, 181. They are called to Christ’s banquet, 181.

**GERARDUS**, elected bishop of York, 385, 386, 389, 410, 413. He approaches the Roman pontiff for the pallium, 385; Anselm commends him to the Roman pontiff, 385. He succeeded Thomas, 422. Another Thomas succeeded him, 421, 422. The pope ordered him to make his profession to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, 413. His zeal against the evils of the Church, 443; he suffers serious difficulties on this account, 443. His concern for the integrity of his clergy, 431. He favors royal injustice, 436. Anselm, though absent, does not wish to judge him while he is absent, 398. He himself denies the charge brought against him, 398. He died, 421.

**GERBERTUS.** He is able to answer the learned questions of Walter, who lived under his authority, 339.

**GERONTO**, or **GERONTINUS**, abbot, 398.

**GERVINUS**, bishop of Amiens, 378. He asks Anselm, archbishop, to consent to the election of Northmannus, a monk of Canterbury, as abbot, 378. Anselm replies that he cannot grant this request, 378.

**GILDA**, 343.

**GIRARDUS**, 436. He declares himself Anselm’s helper even unto exile, 437.

**GIRARDUS**, bishop of the Morini. Anselm asks him to excuse a certain monk of Bec from governing the church of Saint Vulmar, lest the wolves tear apart the sheep, 360.

**GIRARDUS**, bishop. He is a witness in the letter by which King Henry recalls Anselm, 382.

**GIRARDUS of Arras**, brother of Ainertus. He is recalled from the monastery of Bec because of debts, 316. Anselm commends him to Lanfranc’s charity, 316. Anselm excuses his delay to Lanfranc, 319. He escorted Anselm to the sea when Anselm was going to England, 344. Through him Anselm writes to the monks of Bec about appointing an abbot, 371.

**GISLEBERTUS**, a monk of Bec, 409. Anselm sends him to the king of England, 409. Anselm’s affection for him, 339, 355.

**Gislebertus of Bec.** Anselm sends him to Lanfranc, asking Lanfranc to send him back soon, 346. When he is elected abbot of Westminster, Anselm congratulates him, 347. He was brought up in a holy way of life, 347. Anselm intercedes for him with Walchelin, bishop of Winchester, 352. Anselm informs him, as abbot, that he has been seized by a fever, 359. He also commends to him Richard, his servant, after clearing him of slander, 359. Gislebertus, bishop of Évreux, had suspected that Anselm had been drawn to the archbishopric by ambition, 368. Anselm clears himself before him of this slander, 368. He commends to him the church of Bec, left without a pastor, 368. Anselm commends one of his monks to the prior of Bec, 360.

**GISLEBERTUS**, bishop of Limerick in Ireland, 417, 447. Through his efforts, the canonical election and consecration of abbots and bishops took place in Normandy, 447. Anselm sends him twenty-five small pearls, 447.

**GISLEBERTUS**, abbot of Caen. While Anselm was meditating on the assistance of his prayers and those of the monks of Caen, he was freed from a fever, 358.

**GISLEBERTUS**, another monk of Bec, 409, 372. Through him William, the elected abbot of Bec, wrote to Anselm, the elected archbishop of Canterbury, 372. Anselm sends him to the king of England, 409.

**Glory.** The glory of the Lord and of the saints is compared only with the sun, 163. What those who desire to see the glory of the Lord ought to be like, 162, 163. See *Beatitude*.

**GODEFRIDUS.** See *Gaufridus*.

**GODEFRIDUS DE MELLINGES**, 434.

**GODIT**, a virgin, 414.

**GOFFRIDUS.** See *Gaufridus*, *Godefridus*.

**GOFFRIDUS**, bishop of Paris. He violently removed Walerannus, a cantor of the church of Paris who had put on the monastic habit, from the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, 369. For this Anselm rebuked him severely, 370.

**GOFFRIDUS**, sacristan of Cluny, 431. Abbot Hugh sends him to England, 431.

**GOFFRIDUS**, uncle of Juhel, 420. His virtues, prayers, and abstinences, 420.

**GONDULPHUS**, a monk, 315. Among Saint Anselm’s closest friends, 313, 314, 317, 321, 324, 329, 342. His services to the monks of Bec, 314, 317, 321. Anselm sends him three prayers to Saint Mary which he had composed, 319. Anselm commends the monk Maurice to him, 321. He asks him for a copy of the *Aphorisms* with glosses, 325, 331, 334. He thanks him for gifts, 333. He himself sent gifts to Hugh and to Basilia, his wife, 333. He is promoted to the bishopric of Rochester; Anselm congratulates him on this, 337. Anselm commends to him the monks of Bec whom he is sending to England, 342. See *Anselm*. Anselm asks that the drunken chamberlain do penance according to Gondulphus’s judgment, 343. Anselm entreats him on behalf of Moses, a repentant Canterbury monk who had fled, 359. He consoles the monks of Bec over the loss of Anselm, 364. He also urges them to consent to Anselm’s election, 364. He assists Anselm in exile, 435, 439. He takes care of Anselm’s affairs while Anselm is in exile, 435.

**GONDULDHUS**, father of Saint Anselm, 513.

**Greeks.** The Greeks say that there are three substances in God, 49, 452. The Latins say that there are three persons in God, 452. By “substances” the Greeks understand what the Latins understand by “persons,” 452. See *Trinity*. The Greeks anathematize the use of unleavened bread, 135. They favor the pagans, 136. See *Unleavened bread*. They do not hold the same opinion as the Latins, 135, yet they do nothing contrary to the faith, 135. The Greeks deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, 49, 50. Nor do they accept Latin teachers, 50. Nevertheless, they venerate the Gospels, 50. In other matters concerning the one and triune God, they believe the same things as the Latins, 49, 50. See *Holy Spirit*.

**Grammar; grammarian.** Grammar is a quality and exists in a subject, 146. The study of grammar, 434. Whether a grammarian is a substance or a quality, 143. The dialecticians disputed this question vigorously in Saint Anselm’s time, 150.

**Grace.** There is one kind of grace that does not concern salvation, 128, and another without which no human being is saved, 128. Every creature exists by grace, 128, because it was made freely. There are many gifts of grace without which a human being can be saved, 128. Whatever assists free choice in accepting or preserving uprightness must all be attributed to grace, 124.

Being sent is grace; preaching is grace; hearing preaching is grace; understanding through hearing is of grace; and uprightness of will is grace. All these things are necessary for faith, 130. The law does not justify, 171, but the hidden grace of the Holy Spirit through faith in Christ does, 171. The letter commanding one to turn away from sin reveals sin, 136. But unless grace assists so that what is commanded may be done, it makes the disobedient person a transgressor, 136, and it is a killing letter, 136.

What a person does not have from himself but from God, he ought to call not so much his own as God’s, 78. To everyone except God alone it is said: “What do you have that you did not receive?” 62, 129. Whatever we receive from God, let us ascribe to God’s grace, not to our merits, 193, 205. What a human being gives back to God comes from God’s gift, 220. A sinner cannot return to God by his own merits, 215. Grace precedes our merits, 215. Nothing is pleasing to God unless it has been received from him, 215, 216. We cannot serve or please God except by God’s gift, 215, 236, 249.

Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more; so that where misery abounds, mercy may abound still more, 315. Through holy devotion and the grace of God, it is possible for a Christian to become free from every injustice, 129. From God the creature has both the fact that it is good and the ability to do good, 238. Whoever is good is good from God, 248. When we are good, God makes us so; we do not make ourselves, 263. Without God we are powerless, 30, 242. A human being cannot seek God unless God himself teaches him, nor find him unless God himself reveals himself, 30, 242. A human being cannot begin anything good without God, just as he cannot preserve or complete it without him, 263.

It belongs to God, by his grace, to precede us; it belongs to us to preserve diligently, with his help, what we receive, 385. No one receives uprightness except by preceding grace, 129. No one preserves it except by the same grace following after, 129. All our goods are God’s gifts, 236. God alone is the reformer of the creature, which he alone formed, 215. No one can be freed by his own righteousness without God’s mercy, 249. All our salvation is the great mercy of God, 249. No one can attain eternal life except through grace, 158. The whole power of the soul comes from God, 220.

It is the work of God’s will alone when human hearts are taught by the Holy Spirit those things which they know neither through themselves nor through a creature, 101. No human being has from himself the truth he teaches or a just will; these come from God, 78. Human thought cannot change by itself unless divine grace comes to its aid, 107. Without divine grace assisting them, human beings are nothing but mute animals, naturally begotten for captivity and destruction, 107. If the soul wills anything good, it is God’s gift, 261. To turn away from evil comes from the help of grace, 213, 250. No one can overcome vices without divine assistance, 195, nor do good, 213. That we love God or anything good—we have this not from ourselves but from God, 267. Love and fear of God, and shame for sin, by which mercy is obtained, are possessed only through God’s grace, 216.

The will to obey exists only through grace, 130. What a human being wills and pursues is to be attributed to God’s grace, not to free choice, 129. When a person does not accept grace, or rejects grace once accepted, this is attributable not to God but to the human being, 129. Comparison of grace and clothing, 129.

No creature can attain uprightness except through grace, 70, 121, 128, 129, 130. Nor, after abandoning it, can a creature recover it unless God restores it, 70, 121, 134. A will that has abandoned uprightness is enslaved to sin through its inability to recover uprightness by itself, 121, 134. No one returns from sin unless he is drawn back by grace, 296. A human being can return from sin and its slavery only through another, 121. From uprightness he can turn away only by himself, 121. Once its affection for justice has been lost, the will cannot will justice unless it is restored by grace, 134. A human being who fell voluntarily cannot rise again in any way unless grace lifts him up, 131. Yet by his own desert he sinks from sin into sin unless mercy restrains him, 131. It is a greater miracle when God restores uprightness to a will that had abandoned it than when he restores life to a dead person, 121. For by abandoning uprightness, the will deserves always to need it, 121. See *Conversion*.

The works that Christ begins honorably in the saints by setting them before them, he completes honorably, 158. When God brings to completion in a human being the good that he began, we must attribute the whole thing to grace, 87. The Lord never ceases to bestow the gifts of his grace, 41. From the time human beings were created, there has never been a period without someone belonging to Christ’s reconciliation, 92. To Christ’s reconciling grace belong not only those who are baptized in the New Testament, but also those who, from the beginning of the world, believed in him who was to come, 175. Redemption through Christ benefited not only those who lived at that time, but also others, 92. This is explained by comparison with a king, 92.

We have been called by grace; the rest have been abandoned by justice, 233. What has been denied to innumerable others has been granted to us by grace, 233. Grace does not come from merits, 129; it is not given to everyone, 129 and 233. By preserving justice, a human being merits an increase of the justice received, 129. The increase of justice and the power to act according to a good will are fruits of the first grace, 129. And grace is given for grace, 129. God does not show equal mercy to all those on whom he has mercy, 131. Nor does he harden all those whom he hardens equally, 131. See *Hardening*, *Sin*.

One person ascends the way to heaven more vigorously than another, according as it has been divinely given to each, 176. God gives grace to the saints according to measure, 178, but to Christ without measure, 178. See *Christ*. Confirming grace gives the inability to will to sin and the inability to sin, 128. The final mercy is that which makes a person blessed after this life, 86. God has mercy on whomever he wishes, 129, 231. Let us weep and pray that he may wish to do so, 231. Petition for grace and virtues, 193, 235, 236, 237. The effects of grace, 157. Increase of grace, 129, 176. Where God is not present through grace, he is present there through vengeance, 228. It is almost always unknown whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose have not, 140, 332. The grace of regeneration lost, 287. See *Baptism*, *Penance*.

No one can take the goods of grace away from a human being unless that person voluntarily abandons them, 237. Thus grace follows its gift: it never abandons a human being unless, through free choice, that person wills something else, 119. It is unfitting for God to take away, or permit to be taken away from, one who loves it what he freely gave to one who did not love it, so that the former may not love it by necessity, 25. It is evil to be abandoned to the hand of one’s own counsel and ruled by one’s own choice, 236, 237. God is asked not to entrust a human being to weakness, or to will, or to anything else, but only to God’s disposition, 251, 254.

At times we are illuminated through Christ’s grace, but because our merits demand it, we are not assisted, 165. Christ approaches and touches when he illuminates in order to assist; he approaches but does not touch when he illuminates but does not assist, 165. Very often we see what ought to be done, but are unable to carry it out; we strive and grow weak, 165.

The Father is said to draw and impel by giving the will, 78. In this drawing or impulse no necessity of violence is understood, 78, but rather the spontaneous and beloved perseverance of the good will received, 78.

**Harmony of grace and free choice.** Free choice with respect to the things that concern salvation, 128. See *Free choice*. When Sacred Scripture says something on behalf of grace, it does not remove free choice, 129 and 130. Nor, when it speaks on behalf of free choice, does it exclude grace, 130. Neither grace alone nor free choice alone works human salvation, 129, 130. The Lord does not say, “Your free choice is of no value to you,” but, “It can do nothing without my grace,” 129. Free choice needs to be sustained by God’s grace, 139. Free choice exists together with grace, 128, 129, 130, 131, and works together with it, 128, 132. In adults, grace assists natural free choice, 129. Free choice without grace is of no value for salvation, 129. In many ways grace assists free choice so that it may preserve the uprightness it has received, 129. Grace assists free choice by moderating or completely removing the force of temptation, 129, or by increasing the affection for uprightness, 129. When uprightness is preserved, not as much should be attributed to free choice as to grace, 129. Grace is compared to oil, 157.

**Thanksgiving; gratitude.** The love and service—or gratitude—of one human being toward another who has benefited him, 257. See *Benefits*.

**GREGORY I (Saint)**, 388.

**GREGORY VII** commends himself and the Church to the prayers of Anselm, the abbot, 353. He also orders Anselm to do justice to one of his converts before Hubert, 353. He sent Hubert, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, to England, 353. See *Hubert*.

**GUALTERUS**, a monk, 418, 441. Anselm asks the prior about him, 441. He is the teacher of Anselm’s nephew, 441. Anselm asks him to instruct and correct Robert of Briodna, recently converted, in a spirit of gentleness, 359, 360.

**Gualterius**, an abbot, suffers slander, 330. Anselm writes to him that he should return to the monastery and that the sheep ought not to be abandoned because of slander, 330.

**GUALTERUS**, under Abbot Gerbertus, consults Anselm about certain questions, 339. Anselm does not wish to answer him about them in writing, 339.

**GUALTERUS**, prior of the monastery of Saint-Wandrille, 358.

**GUALTERUS**, bishop of Albano and cardinal legate of the Roman Church, 379, 380. He wishes to discuss with Anselm the convocation of a council in England, but in vain because of the wars, 379. He himself brought the pallium to Anselm, 379, 380. He asks Anselm to allow the monks of the Church of Canterbury to possess their property peacefully, 380.

**GUARNERIUS**, a learned man, proposes to become a monk while his life is in danger, 405. He becomes a Canterbury novice, 408.

**GUIBERTUS**, antipope, 374. Anselm opposes him, 374.

**GUIDO**, a novice of Bec, 320. He is assigned to teach the boys, 323. His virtues—obedience and humility—323. While he is staying in England, Anselm greets him, 334 and 336, and urges him to make progress, 336. He returns from England to Normandy, 434. Anselm commends him as a familiar associate to the archbishop of Rouen, 434. In a letter he asks Anselm for absolution, 445.

**GUILLELMUS**, archbishop of Rouen, 392, 432, 434. Anselm’s friend, 354. He did not seek to dominate monks, 354. He orders Anselm to undertake the burden of the archbishopric of Canterbury, 367, 368, 374. Anselm complains bitterly to him about the abbot of Saint-Evroul, 432, 433. He promised to recall the monk whom that abbot had intruded, 433. He has not yet fulfilled his promise, 433. Anselm writes to the pope about his case, 454. The pope entrusts his case to Anselm, 416. See *Anselm*.

**GUILLELMUS**, canon and dean of the Church of Rouen, 433. Elected bishop of Winchester, 382, 393, 403, 410, 429. He refuses to be consecrated by bishops excommunicated on account of investitures, 433. His steadfastness on behalf of the truth is praised, 403, 405. He is stripped of his possessions and expelled, 393, 433.

**GUILLELMUS**, king of the English, consents to Anselm’s election as archbishop of Canterbury, 363, 364. While ill and lying in bed, he gives Anselm the pastoral staff, although Anselm resists, 363, thereby giving him governance of the Church of Canterbury, 364. Once Anselm had been advanced to the archbishopric, the king recovered and, from being savage, became gentle, 363. He asks Robert, count of the Normans, and William, archbishop of Rouen, to consent to Anselm’s election, 365.

After Anselm’s consecration, he demands a large sum of money from him, 374. He becomes angry when Anselm refuses to give it, 374. He does not want Anselm to request the pallium, 374, nor to convene a council, 374. He speaks threateningly against Anselm, 375. He gives certain lands of the archbishopric of Canterbury to soldiers, 375 and 381. He wishes to compel Anselm to litigate concerning them, 381. He maintains that soldiers of England formerly held such lands from the Church of Canterbury, 381. Since these soldiers died without heirs, he says that he can appoint whomever he wishes as their heirs, 381. His hatred of Anselm, 375.

By voice and by letter he entrusted Canterbury to Anselm’s custody against its enemies, 379. He sends a messenger to the archbishop of Lyon concerning his case against Anselm, 381. Without his command he did not want a papal legate to be received or called in England, 381. Nor did he want Anselm to write to the pope, receive letters from the pope, or obey the pope’s decrees, 381. For thirteen years the king allowed no council to be held, 381. He was angered at Anselm for requesting permission to go to Rome, 381. He denied this permission and forbade Anselm thereafter to request it, 381.

As soon as Anselm left England, the king taxed the food and clothing of the monks of the Church of Canterbury, 381, and converted the entire archbishopric to his own uses, 381. The pope admonished him, but he did not repent, 382. King William died, 382, 427. Henry succeeded him, 427. See *Henry*. At King William’s death the whole world was shaken concerning the kingdom of England, 427. Because of his violence, Anselm was exiled from England for three years, 427. He promoted Flambard, a simoniac, to a bishopric, 427.

**GUILLELMUS de Warenne**, kinsman of Henry, king of the English, 427. The king had promised him his daughter in marriage, 427.

**GUILLELMUS**, a monk of Bec and prior at Pexeium. Anselm judged him more worthy to be elected abbot of Bec in place of the prior there, 367, 371. By holy obedience Anselm ordered him that, if he were elected, he should undertake this burden, 367. He was elected abbot of Bec, 371. Anselm therefore congratulates him, 371. Anselm warns him not to allow the monks to wander outside the cloister and not to diminish anything from the alms of the poor, 376. Other matters concerning him, 421, 422, 423.

**GUILLELMUS**, a monk under Abbot Robert. The abbot consults Anselm about him, 355.

**GUILLELMUS**, a monk, abandoned the cloister, 404. His penance, 404.

**GUILLELMUS Calvellus** took away a market belonging to the Church of Canterbury, 442, 443. Anselm threatens him with excommunication unless he restores it, 443.

**GUILLELMUS de Wareswalt**, envoy of Henry I, king of the English, to the Roman pontiff, 385, 428, 435, 439, 440, 443, 446. See *Warelwast*.

**GUILLELMUS**, archdeacon of the Church of Canterbury, 340, 393. He excommunicates contumacious priests who kept women, 408. Anselm confirms his sentence, 408. Anselm reproves him for receiving Peter and Solomon, enemies of the Church, in his house, 443.

**GUILLELMUS**, brother of Gaufridus, 444. He commends himself and his brother to Anselm’s prayers, 444.

**GUILLELMUS**, son of Godefridus of Mellinges, 454. See *Godefridus*.

**GUILLELMUS de Metestante**, 398.

**GUILLELMUS**, son of Hion, 434.

Anselm urges **William**, a soldier, to renounce the warfare of the world and enlist in the warfare of Christ, 347, 348, 350.

**GUILLELMUS**, chamberlain, 448. He married a kinswoman, 448.

**GUILLELMUS**, son of Rodulphus. He demands from Ernulphus, prior of Canterbury, money that had been given for chrism, 443. See *Ernulphus*, *Rodulphus*.

**GUIMUNDUS**, a man of Haimo the viscount, 393.

**GUITMUNDUS (D.)**, 318.

**GUNFRIDUS of Caen**, brother of Abbot Roger, 326. He is commended to Prior Helgotus, 326. See *Helgotus*.

**GUNTERIUS**, canon of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, 406. He is substituted by the canons of that church in place of the abbot of the order, 406. See *Church of Saint-Quentin*.

HACO, earl of the Orkneys, 448. Anselm urges him to draw his people toward the Christian religion by his admonitions, 448.

HAEDUS, “kid,” in two senses, 178.

HAERETICUS, “heretic.” One should not write against a heretic who has returned to the truth, 42. A prayer for heretics and schismatics, 151.

HAIMO and RAYNALDUS, Anselm’s kinsmen, 351–352. They go to Bec to visit Anselm, 352. From England, Anselm urges them to assume the monastic habit at Bec, 352.

HAIMO, sheriff, 393. He had usurped certain goods of the Church of Canterbury, and his men devastated Anselm’s house at Sandwich, 442–443.

HAIMO, father of Robert, 382.

HAIMO, son of Vitalis, 393.

HAIMO, steward of Henry, king of England, is witness to the letter in which the king recalls Anselm, 382.

HARDUS, friend and close associate of Count Elias, 450. See Elias.

HELGOTUS, prior, 319. Anselm commends to him Geoffrey, who was staying at Caen, the brother of Roger, the abbot, 326.

HELGOTUS, abbot of Saint-Ouen, 413. Anselm’s friend, 413.

HENRY, the emperor, adhered to Pope Paschal II, 138.

HENRY, brother of William, king of the English, is elected king by the clergy and people of England after William’s death, 382. He is consecrated by the suffragans of the exiled Anselm, 382. Thereafter he excuses himself to Anselm, 382. He orders him to return to England and promises that he will go to meet him, 382. Anselm is received by him with great honor, 427. He entrusts himself and his kingdom to Anselm’s counsels, 427. He invaded the kingdom after breaking his oath, 382. Through his legate William he writes to Paschal II about the dispute between himself and Anselm, and receives a reply from him, 384–385. He troubles Anselm, 391. He grants bishoprics and abbeys, 394. In Anselm’s absence he demands money from the monks of Canterbury, 396. Concerned about Anselm’s journey to Rome, he writes to him, 398. He had not yet been crowned when Anselm returned from Rome, 399. He agrees that, while Anselm is unwilling to return to England, he should meanwhile have sufficient resources from the goods of the Church of Canterbury, 401–402. His brother Robert, the count, 403; hostility between him and his brother Robert, 403. He demands money from the priests of England as a penalty for violating the council, 407. At last he reinstates Anselm in the archbishopric and restores everything to him, 407. He approves the marriages of priests, 407. He wishes to abandon investitures, but not homage, 411. After Anselm’s return to England, he entrusts all his affairs to him, 413. He threatens to resume his investitures because permission was being granted to give them to the Teutonic king [Col. 1088], 421. He is distressed by Anselm’s illness, 445. He instructs him to await him in Normandy and announces that he will soon travel there, 445–446. He holds Count Robert captive, 447. He had promised his daughter to William of Warenne, his kinsman; he consults Anselm about this matter, 447. A conference takes place between him and Louis, king of France, 449. He entrusts his son, his daughter, and his kingdom to Anselm, 449.

HENRY, the monk: Saint Anselm comforts him concerning his absence, 313. He commends Herluin to him, 314. He wishes Henry to have what Saint Anselm writes to Gondulf written out for him, 315. Anselm writes that it is not expedient for him to travel from England to Italy to his sister in order to free her from servitude, 317. Anselm commends the monk Maurice to him, 320. Anselm thanks him for taking careful care of Maurice, 323. Prior of the monastery of Canterbury, 329, 358, 376. Anselm thanks him for the gold he had sent him, 329, and for his affection toward the monk Maurice, 329. Anselm asks him to pardon Osbern, 319. He is attacked by the slanders of the envious, 331. Anselm urges him to bear these equally patiently, 331. He was on bad terms with his archbishop Lanfranc, 331, 335. Anselm greets him, 331. He commends Osbern to him, whom he is sending back, 333; Anselm urges him to obedience and patience, 335. He commends to him the monks whom he is sending to England, 342. This man, the abbot, proposed sending Folcerald to Bec, 348. Anselm begs him on behalf of a fugitive monk, 358. The archbishop Anselm himself commands that all the brothers of this monastery obey him as they obey Anselm, 377.

HENRY, chamberlain at Bec, a drunkard, 343. He is rebuked by Abbot Anselm, 343.

HENRY OF GORNAY: Anselm asks him to await patiently what he has requested, 343. He greets him from England, 351.

HENRY, count: he is a witness to the letter of King Henry to Anselm, 382.

Anselm urges HENRY, his most beloved friend, to despise the world, 352.

HEREBERTUS of Norwich, 410.

HERENGODUS, 435.

Herb. The earth produces useless and harmful herbs without human care; necessary things only with labor, 130.

Hergas. The church of Hergas, 398.

HERLUINUS. Saint Anselm commends him to Henry, 314. Through him he wrote to Gondulf, 314. He urges him to hate the world, 315. Anselm greets him, 318, 325, 330, 334. Anselm prays to God for him and commends the monk Maurice to him, 321. He urges him to make progress, 327, 336. See Maurice.

HERNOSTUS, 311. Bishop of Rochester, 327. Overwhelmed by pains, 328. Anselm urges him to patience, 328.

HEREWARDUS, bishop of Wales, 374. Anselm places him under interdict, 374.

The brutality of HEROD, who killed many thousands of infants, 217.

HERVAEUS, bishop of Bangor, 412.

The opinion of Saint Jerome concerning the origin of souls, 107. See Soul; Augustine.

HILDEBERTUS, bishop of Le Mans, 386, 424, 430. His affection for Anselm, 424. From him he requests and receives the disputation *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks*, 386, 424. He sends Anselm a fan, 424. Anselm promises him that he will send other works of his as well, 430.

HIO, father of William, 434.

Today. The noun *hodiernus* is not a verb, although it signifies time, 147–148.

HOLWARDUS. Anselm cares for him, 320. An Englishman and Osbern’s cousin, 334, 336. Anselm greets him, 336.

Homicide. Someone can at times kill a human being without injustice, as Phinehas did, 98. A public or secret murderer must be excluded from the priesthood, 425.

Homage. Those who have rendered homage to the king concerning churches are not excommunicated and must not be excluded from ecclesiastical blessing, 416. It is not lawful to render homage to another concerning land held from one lord, even if he unjustly harasses his sons, 403. A cleric must not render homage to a layman, 374.

Human being. Definition of a human being: a mortal rational animal, 81, 145. A human being consists of two natures, soul and flesh, 238. In every human being nature and person exist together, 97. A human being is not called body, rational, and human being in one way or under one consideration, 10. Rather, under one aspect he is body and under another rational, 10. None of these individual aspects is the whole of what a human being is, 10. When “human being” is uttered, common nature is signified, 47. When this or that human being is mentioned, or someone is designated by a proper name, such as Jesus, a person is signified, 47. Human nature belongs to God, 171.

God can make a human being in four ways, 88: neither from a man nor from a woman, as Adam; from a man without a woman, as Eve; from a man and a woman, as human beings; and from a woman without a man, as Christ, 171.

God made Adam from clay, 101. The human being was created on the sixth day, 159. Each descendant of Adam is a human being by creation, Adam by propagation, and a person by individuality, 100. A human being does not have being from Adam but through Adam, 100.

The dignity and misery of the human condition, 202. The human being was made more honorable than the other creatures so that he might live honorably among them according to God’s good pleasure, 237. All things were created for human use, 200. There would be no human being unless God were in him; and unless the human being were in God, God would not be in the human being, 227. A human being owes his whole self to God, 223. From earth he returns to earth, 201.

Our first parents originally had strength and incorruption, and the power always to preserve justice without difficulty, 97. See Adam.

The human being is the image of God, 198, 200, 202–203, 241, 250, because he is rational, 238, and because he was made to think about and love God, 30, 242, 247. See Image; Rational nature.

Just as God is good by his will, so the human being, in God’s likeness, is good by his will, 238. He was created by God to live according to the will of his Creator, 237. The human being is good because he imitates the one who is good from himself, 238.

The human being was made for blessedness, which cannot be possessed in this life, 79–80. This faith is necessary for salvation, 80. The human being was made for the kingdom of God, 104, 132; to see God, 30, 241; and to enjoy blessed immortality in body and soul, 74.

Human nature was made for its own sake, and not only to restore individuals of another nature, 81. Even if no angel had perished, human beings would have had their place in the heavenly city, 82. Whether human beings were made only for the restoration of the fallen angels, 81–83. Whether human beings were made to complete with the angels the number of the elect before an angel fell, 83. God determined to restore from human nature the number of angels who had fallen, 81, 83. The heavenly city was to be completed from human beings, 91. There will be more blessed human beings than there are miserable angels, 83, 83.

The human being before sin. The human being was created just, 85, 97–98, 102, without any sin, 102. The human being was created in justice, 81, 85, 97–98, 102, without any sin, 102, and without any need, 134. At the same time he received both the will for blessedness and blessedness itself, 134, as well as the will for justice—that is, rectitude, which is justice itself—and free choice, without which he could not preserve justice, 134.

He was placed in God’s stead between God and the devil, 85, for God’s vindication and honor and for the devil’s confusion, 85. In paradise he possessed a certain immortality, that is, the power not to die, 82, and he was immortal in power, 85. But this power was not immortality itself, 82. By sinning he justly incurred the punishment of mortality, 85.

He was a king, 185. His kingdom was paradise, 185. Through disobedience he was expelled from that kingdom, 185. God gave the human being justice in such a way that he could abandon it, 134, and so that, if he persevered in it, he might deservedly be advanced to fellowship with the angels, 134. But if he abandoned it, he could not recover it by himself, 134; he would be deprived of the blessedness he possessed, 134, and would not attain the blessedness of the angels, 134. Instead, in the likeness of brute animals, he would be subject to carnal appetites, 134.

He could, and indeed easily could, avoid sin, 85. If sin had not preceded, every human being would have been born simultaneously just and rational, like Adam, 97–98, 101. If the first human being had not sinned, he and his entire race would have been so firmly established in the good that they could not have sinned, 82, 88. He would have been only God’s servant and equal to the good angels, 76, and he was to be transformed in body into incorruptibility, 87. Whole—that is, in soul and body—he would have been eternally blessed, 87. The human being ought always to have possessed justice, 134. The will or inclination toward rectitude was separable in the first human being, 133.

The devil and the human being sought through robbery and falsehood to make themselves like God, 46.

The human being after sin. We all sinned in Adam, although we did not yet exist, because the necessity arose that, once we existed, we would sin, 100. In him we all fell, in whom we all sinned, 33. In him we all lost the good, 33. The first human being easily held the good, 33. Through his wrongdoing he lost for himself and for us what, when we wish to seek it, we do not know, and when we seek it, we do not find, 33.

The whole of human nature sinned in our first parents, 82, because the whole of human nature was in our first parents, 82. The whole of it would have conquered in them if they had not sinned, 82. The will freely became unjust, 134. After abandoning justice, it remains unjust by necessity and a slave to injustice, 134. By itself it cannot return to justice, 100, 134. It freely allowed itself to be conquered by the devil’s will, against the will of God, 85. It lost the power to avoid sin, 85, and human beings cannot be without sin, 82.

The fall of the human being, 184. The human being lost that for which he was made, 30, 241. He lost the blessedness for which he was made, 241, 134, and found the misery for which he was not made [Col. 1090], 30. The good things he lost and the evils he incurred, 30, 103, 237, 241–242.

The human being, in abandoning justice, lost blessedness without losing the will for blessedness, 134. This will is now turned toward false goods and the advantages of brute animals, 134, because it cannot now possess the true advantages suited to rational nature that it lost, 134.

The human being made himself weak and mortal, 85. The human race had been utterly ruined, 76. Having become needy, nature makes all the persons of its descendants sinful and unjust, 104. The whole mass of human nature was expelled from paradise in our first parents, 173, and from that time heaven’s door was closed to it, 173.

By that very rectitude the human being is both slave and free, 121. He is a slave of sin, 121–122, and cannot avoid sinning, 121. He cannot always do the good he wishes, 249.

The soul has been infected by carnal appetites through the corruption of the body and through need of the goods it lost, 98. The human body is subject to corruption and carnal appetites, like the bodies of brute animals, 98. Because Adam refused to be subject to God’s will, the nature of propagation was not subject to his will, 101. And it lost the grace that he could have preserved for his descendants, 101.

Although rectitude of will may be present, rational nature nevertheless retains what belongs to it, 118. Through sin the human being did not lose free choice, 185, but possesses the capacity for understanding and willing by which, when he possesses rectitude, he can preserve it for its own sake, 122. In what he lost through sin, the human being ceased to be a king; in what remained, he became a petty king, 185.

The devil is called an evil human being, 85. The human being always, or almost always, resists God’s will, 237. All creatures, because of the human being, are concordant with the will of their Creator, 237, and inviolably preserve the order established for them, 240.

The restored human being. Human nature is weaker than angelic nature, 81. The weakness of human nature excuses God and confounds the devil, 81. The human being was to be restored to the likeness of the angels, 222. This cannot happen except through the remission of all sins, 222. See Satisfaction.

The image of God cannot do that for which it was made unless God renews and reforms it, 30. God reformed the human being with the same ease with which he formed all things by a single word, 216. God restored human nature more wonderfully than he established it, 92. The former he did concerning a sinner and against merit; the latter he did neither concerning a sinner nor against merit, 92. See Christ; Redemption.

Scourging remains after reconciliation, 132. The human being is redeemed from sins through Christ, 132, and given the kingdom of God, 132. provided he perseveres to the end in the faith which they promise at baptism, 132.

Honesty. Where piety increased, honesty abounded, 142.

HONFRIDUS, 338. His teaching, 338. Anselm commends someone to him for instruction, 338. He urges him to despise the world, 338.

Honor. See Impassibility; Glory; Vanity. The loftiness of honors is the greatness of crimes, 193.

The reception of guests in monasteries, 376.

Offering. See Mass.

HUBERTUS, subdeacon and legate of the Apostolic See in England, 353. Anselm is to obtain justice before him for one of his converts, 353. He died at Bec, 353. He had collected much from the revenue of Saint Peter in England, 353.

HUGO, archbishop of Lyon, 345, 347. Anselm sent him the *Monologion* and *Proslogion*, 347. Anselm commends to his care certain monks whose monastery’s monastic discipline had been destroyed, 345. He wishes Anselm to write about certain matters, 345, 347. Anselm consults him about lands that the king, angered against him, was taking from the Church of Canterbury, and about requesting the pallium from Urban while the king resisted, 374–375. The king of England sends a messenger to him on behalf of his cause against Anselm, 281. Anselm, having more debts than possessions, is received and supported by him, 382. Returning from Jerusalem, he offers his house to Anselm, who was contemplating flight, 391. Anselm consults him about the liberty of the Church, 411. He advises Anselm to return to England and not resist the ordinance of the supreme pontiff, 391. Anselm congratulates him on his successful return from Palestine, 432. His friendship toward Anselm, 446. His death on the Nones of October at Scusium, while going to a council, 446. He was buried in the abbey of Saint Just, 446.

HUGO, abbot of Cluny, 431. Anselm’s friend, 431. He commends Geoffrey, the sacristan of Cluny, to Anselm, 431. Anselm writes to him about the death of Hugh of Lyon, 446. He sends monks to England, 446, and commends them to Anselm, 446.

HUGO, the monk: he is to bear through obedience the burden of his prelate, even if undisciplined, unless that prelate himself grants him permission to depart, 314.

HUGO, a recluse of Caen, 325, 348. He informs Anselm that the most devout Frodelina desired his acquaintance, 325. He sends two laymen to Anselm so that they might be stimulated by exhortations to love of the heavenly homeland, 348. Through them he asks Anselm for admonitions concerning salvation, by which he might be able to answer the laypeople who visit him [Col. 1091], 348.

HUGO, count, holds a Cluniac monk in prison, 446. Anselm orders him to release him and make satisfaction for the crime, 446.

HUGO, count of Chester, 431–432. His son Robert, a monk of Saint-Evroul, 432. See Robert.

HUGO and BASILIA, husband and wife: Anselm presents them with gifts from the monk Gondulf and reads Gondulf’s letter to them, 335. See Basilia.

HUGO, son of Mabilia, 435. He wishes to sell land that is not his, 435. See Mabilia.

HUGO, deceased, 351.

Humility. The three kinds or degrees of humility, 395. The more someone advances in humility, the more he excels in the other virtues, 378. The more the saints advance in the vision of God, the more they recognize themselves to be nothing, 165. One who sees himself to be dust before God’s eyes has no fixed status, 163. Whoever thinks of God’s excellence considers himself worthless, 165. The saints who concentrate attentively on heavenly things humble their virtues, 165, because in God’s innocence and holiness they see how greatly they themselves sin every day and how little of the perfection of holiness they possess; and they lay aside all presumption concerning their own strength, 165.

Whoever wishes to serve God should be content with every kind of lowliness, 191. Let him regard himself from the heart as lower than others and declare with his tongue that he is lower than everyone, 191. See Pride.

HYDIT, a virgin, 414.

The dropsical person thirsts the more, the more he drinks, 180.

I

IDA, countess, 338, 372, 388–389. Her charity toward the monks of Bec and toward everyone, 338, 350. Anselm greets her husband, 350. Anselm urges her to make progress, 355. Her monastery, 355. What she herself requested, Anselm presented to the king of the English, who did not approve it, 355. Anselm calls her his sister and daughter, 372, and grants absolution to them by letter, 372. He greets her, Robert’s wife, 376. Her cleric and chaplain Lambert, 372. See Lambert.

Anselm grants Ida absolution from sins by letter, imposing penance, 389.

Idea; divine ideas. The supreme Spirit is the supreme reason in which are all things that have been made, 17. Things made from nothing were not nothing before they were made, insofar as they existed in the reason of their maker, 7. Before all things were made, there was in the reason of supreme nature what they would be, or of what kind, or in what manner they would exist, 7, 17. Creatures in themselves are a mutable essence, created according to an immutable reason; in the creating Spirit they are the first essence and the first truth of existence, 17. All things are life and truth in God’s knowledge, 17. Creatures are always in the supreme Spirit; they are not what they are in themselves but what that same Spirit is, 17. See God, cause of things; Creature.

Fire, in two senses, 178.

Human ignorance and the difficulty of acting well, 206. At times a human being does not understand what is useful, 84. Error does not excuse one who ought to have known, 394. Ignorance diminishes sin, 395. See Inability; Punishment of sin.

An image is more or less true according as it more or less imitates the thing of which it is the likeness, 15. The difference between image and likeness, 203. Image is more worthy than likeness, 203. Always to remember, understand, and love God is to be in his image, 203. What it means to be created in image and likeness, 202. If a human being agrees with God’s will and wills the same thing as God, he expresses the image of God, 238. A rational creature ought to strive for nothing so much as to express by a voluntary act this image naturally impressed upon it, 25. The image of God in the human being has been effaced by the attrition of vices, 30, 242. See Human being; Mind; Rational creature.

Impossible; inability. “Impossible” is that from which, once posited, another impossibility follows, 123. Something cannot simultaneously be and not be, 124. See Existence.

That which we cannot accomplish without difficulty is called impossible, 132. It is impossible for God to be contrary to himself, 86. See God omnipotent.

Power. The inability to render to God what one owes does not excuse a human being, 85, because the effect of sin does not excuse the sin he commits, 85. See Sin.

The inability of the will to preserve rectitude arises not from impossibility but from difficulty, 120.

Incarnation. Why God became human, 74 and following. Many ask about this question, 74–75. This question is difficult in its investigation but intelligible and lovable to everyone in its solution, 74. The holy Fathers have said enough about it, 74. To understand the necessity of the Incarnation, knowledge of power, necessity, and will is required, 75.

No human intellect can penetrate the Incarnation, 92. It is established that God had to become human, 92. It was not fitting that what God had purposed concerning the human being should be utterly annihilated [Col. 1092], 76. That purpose could not be brought to fulfillment unless the human race were liberated by its own Creator, 76. This is the necessary reason why God had to become human, 76.

It was necessary that God assume a human being into the unity of person, 94, so that the one who, in nature, had to make satisfaction but could not, might be in a person who could do so, 94. Before the ages God predestined that the Word should become flesh, 156. To the Gentiles, the claim that God became incarnate for human beings is either impotence or folly, 76. The humility of the Incarnation does not conflict with reason, 77.

The divine nature cannot be changed into human nature, nor human nature into divine nature, 88. Nor can those natures be so mixed that one third nature arises from two corrupted natures, 88. One divine person was incarnate; the other two were not incarnate at the same time, 45–46. It is impossible for several divine persons to be incarnate in the same human being, 46. For it is not possible for several persons who are distinct from one another to be one person, 46.

The one who was to become incarnate was to pray for the human race, 46, and to fight against the devil, 46. When the Son became incarnate, no contradiction followed, 46. No other person of God ought to have become incarnate except the Son, 46. Only the person of the Son became incarnate, with the cooperation of the other two, 44. Why the Son became incarnate rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, 46–47.

Whence and how God assumed human nature, 88. It is necessary that these two complete natures come together in one person, 88. Two natures come together in one person, just as body and soul come together in one human being, 88. The person was to be the human God, possessing that by which he would surpass every essence that is not God, and every debt that sinners ought to pay, while owing nothing on his own account, 222.

Another nature, not another person, was assumed by the Word, 43, 47. The human being assumed by the Word was not a person [in his own right], 43, but was assumed not into unity of nature but into unity of person, 46–47. In Christ one person is several natures, and several natures are one person, 47. In Christ God is a person and the human being is a person, yet they are not two persons but one person, 47. For in Christ God and the human being are the same person, 47. There is not one God and another human being in Christ, 47. Nevertheless, God is one thing and the human being another, 47. The very same one is God and human being, 47.

The human being is not the same as the human being assumed by the Word, 47. The Word and a human being simply considered are not the same person, 47. The human being assumed is the same person as the Word, 47. Nevertheless, the Son of God makes this so, 46. Through the unity of person, the human being is the Son of God, 46. Therefore what the human being does is said to be done by God, or by the Son of God, 46. The Son of God is called Creator because he became human, 155.

In the Incarnation the divine nature is not humbled; rather, human nature is exalted, 77. The Son’s supplication does not arise from the Divinity but from the humanity directed toward the Divinity, 46. The Incarnation of the Word restores the good lost through sin, 205, etc. The Word did not assume what was harmful to his work, 91; therefore he did not assume ignorance, 91. The body assumed is the tabernacle of incarnate wisdom, 155. See Christ; Redemption; Satisfaction.

To need. To have something less than another thing does not always mean to be in need, 134. To need is to lack something when it ought to be possessed, 134. Where there is need, there is misery, 134. No one needs a thing he does not want, 116. See Poverty.

Individuals chiefly subsist—that is, underlie accidents, 27. See Accident; Substance; Universal.

Hardening. See Obduracy.

Infants were in Adam causally or materially, as in a seed, when he sinned, 104. In themselves they already exist personally, 104. In him they were not other than him; in themselves they were other than he, 104. Therefore they were in him, but were not themselves [present] in him, because they did not yet exist as themselves, 104. To exist in this way is not to be nothing or a kind of emptiness, 104. See Original sin.

The souls of infants are neither lovers of the highest good nor despisers of it, 26. How and by what merit the souls of infants are distributed to eternal blessedness or misery cannot be comprehended, 26. An infant has no sin except original sin, 98. If there were no original contagion in little children, they would suffer nothing evil either in body or soul under the great power of the just God, 108. Those who are suffocated within the mother’s womb seem to be conceived for punishment rather than for life, 233.

An infant does not bear the sin of its father but its own, 105. How the sins of parents harm infants, 105. An infant who dies without baptism is condemned, 98. In infants, grace alone works salvation, without their free choice, 128–129. It is grace because the will is given to others, so that they may assist infants by their faith, 128. Christians assist infants by their faith, 128. The Catholic Church holds that baptized infants are admitted to the kingdom, 106. They are saved as just through Christ’s justice, since he gave himself for them, and through the justice of the faith of Mother Church, which believed for them, 108. The inability to possess justice after baptism is not counted against them as guilt, 106. It is not God’s anger but grace when God snatches innocent little children from this life, 383. See Baptism; Grace; Inability; Sin.

Hell. On hell, 452. The torments of hell, 211. These will never wipe out sins; rather, sins will always retain the torments, 296. See Damnation; Devil.

It should be shown to unbelievers and ungodly people how irrationally they despise us, 357. See Faith; The faithful.

Infinite. The distinction of degrees within natures and the infinite multitude of natures are absurd, 5.

Beginning. What can be thought to exist but does not exist can be thought to exist through a beginning, 37. See To think.

Wrong. A brother’s sin must be forgiven, 191. God commands us to forgive completely those who sin against us, 79. It belongs to God alone to take vengeance, 79, 84. See Vengeance.

We must forgive those who sin against us if we wish to have forgiven what we have sinned against God, 167. Whoever knows that greater things have been forgiven him by the Lord readily forgives lesser things to a convert, 167. God will demand back what he had forgiven from the person who demands a debt from a convert, 167, 169. Sins forgiven through penance return when forgiveness is denied to a brother, 169. A brother’s sin must be forgiven from the heart—that is, not hypocritically but sincerely, 169. The sins we commit against God are great and many, 168. The sins people commit against us are slight and small, 168. Some are so offended by a brother’s fault that they wish their brother to perish beforehand in eternal punishments rather than forgive him, 168. See Love of neighbor.

Injustice. See Justice.

Unjust. See Injustice.

Innocence. He is happier who has always preserved innocence than one who, having suffered shipwreck through sin, escaped death, 233. Insensible things can possess neither guilt nor grace, 117. See Justice; Rational nature.

Intellect. Intelligence, 20–21. Whatever is understood is in the intellect, 30, 38. It is one thing for a thing to be in the intellect and another to understand that the thing exists, 30. See To think; Existence; Mind.

What is understood in some way is more easily proved, 39. The intellect cannot pass beyond eternity, 60. See Eternity.

Such as the intention is, such is the work, 193. To remember, understand, and love the highest good, a human being ought to direct everything he lives toward it, 203. To move in God is to direct every movement of one’s will and action into him and toward him, 203.

One who wishes to do a good work but is prevented, and rejoices that he has been prevented, is not to be praised, 356. One who plans to perform a small deed but is not permitted to do so, and rejoices that he has not been handed over to his desire, must be judged to have committed the crime he intended, 356. As long as someone remains in the will to commit a crime, he is to be judged for the crime, 356. There is a great difference between the one whom God’s anger abandons even to a reprobate action and the one whom grace, rescuing him from the precipice, restores to a good intention for action, 356. The one who slips into the act or is abandoned to an evil will is to be marked with the name of criminal, 356—not the one who is not plunged into an evil deed and is rescued from a perverse intention, 356. See Highest good; Crime; Rational nature; Will.

To question. God questions us in three ways, 10: by the severity of the scourge, 20; by commanding what we wish, 30; and by concealing some things and revealing others, 172.

Investiture. Against investitures, 389, 393, 399, 404, 421, 394, 427–428. Laymen ought not to give investitures, 389. The Teutonic king gave investitures, 421. The pope did not approve this but tolerated it because of the fierceness of that people, 421. All who advised King Henry concerning investitures, and those who accepted them, are excommunicated, 436.

Envy. It devours all good things, 192. It gnaws at its own author, 192. The envy of human beings burns them and, by burning, makes them sad and causes them to walk in weakness, 428. It always envies the virtuous man, 331. Whoever fears the persecution of envy must either find a place where the vicious lie hidden or renounce the virtues, 331.

Unwilling. See Free choice; Necessity; Will.

Invocation of the saints, 211.

Anger. God cannot become angry in his nature, 169. God’s anger is his vengeance, 169. God is provoked by our evils, 169. Whoever does not have God appeased will by no means escape him when angry, 228. God’s great anger is not to call sinners to repentance but to leave them in their sins until death, 181. To be angry with one’s brother is a serious fault, 131. Anger must be restrained, 192. See Wrong; Patience; Vengeance.

IVO, bishop of Chartres, 406.

J
## J

**JACOB**, interpreted as “supplanter,” 155, 166. He signifies wrestlers who, with labor, supplant vices, 155.

[Col. 1094] **JANNE**, that is, “prepared,” 176.

**Fasting**, 388. Unless you are disciplined by fasts, you cannot overcome temptations, 191.

**Jericho** is called “moon,” 157.

**Jerusalem**, the city chosen by the Lord, 436. Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” 156, 17. It signifies the Church, 156. The Jerusalem above, 156. The king of Jerusalem, 429, 436. See **Baldwin**.

**JESUS**, that is, “salutary” or “savior,” 171, 176, 208. Sent by God to save the world, 171. Jesus, redeemer of captives, savior of sinners, hope of exiles, and so forth, 220. See **Christ**.

**JOHN** means “in whom there is grace,” 166.

**JOHN THE BAPTIST (St.)**, 287. Praised by the archangel before he was begotten by his father, 287. Filled with God before he was born of his mother, 287. Knowing God before he was born into the world, 287. He was conceived through a miracle, 102. Yet not without sin, 102, because he was conceived through natural propagation, 102.

**JOHN (St.), the Apostle**, is said to have remained a virgin, 162. Reclining on the Lord’s breast because of the privilege of virginity, 231.

**JOHN (St.) DAMASCENE**, 108.

**JOHN, bishop of Tusculum**, 440.

**JOHN, cardinal**, 440.

**JOHN, formerly a bishop and a monk of Bec**, is sent as a legate of the Apostolic See to England, 382.

**JOHN.** He writes to Anselm about the man who said that the three persons in God were three things, 355. He was soon to depart for Rome, 355.

**JOHN, prior of Bath**, 420.

**JOHN, prior of the canons of Mont-Saint-Éloi**, 429. Anselm sends to him one of his household to be instructed, 429.

**JOHN and BOSO**, monks under Abbot Ralph, 360. They lose Anselm’s notebooks; when they make excuses for this, Anselm gently consoles them, 360. He promises that he will send them mercy [the supplied reading *miseriam* is perhaps corrupt], 360.

**JOFFRIDUS.** Through him William, the elected abbot of Bec, wrote to Anselm, 372. See **Goffridus**.

**JOSEPH**, that is, “increase,” 176. Joseph, thirty years old, assumed the administration of the kingdom, 173. Joseph was by nature the son of Jacob, and by law the son of Heli, 174. Thus he appears to have had two fathers, Heli and Jacob, 174. Joseph was a relative of the Virgin Mary, 174. Mary’s genealogy is to be described through Joseph, 174. See **Mary**.

**JOTTERANNUS, archbishop of Lyon**, 447. His tribulation, 447.

**The jubilee** is, in the Law, the fiftieth year, 183.

**Jew.** The Jewish people thirsted only for the goods of the present life, 180. They did not know how to possess their own heart, but clung to earthly things, 141. It is a great glory for believing Hebrews that God assumed flesh from their race, 171. God rejects the Jews, 18. A Jew converted to Christ, 409. Whoever does in another manner what the Jews do does not thereby Judaize, 135.

**JUDAS** is called “the devil” by the Lord, 83.

**Judge.** It does not belong to him to do both things, namely, to make a complaint and to carry out vengeance, 382.
