He himself will judge the sinner, for whatever the transgressor does is directed against his dishonor, 208. He will judge who repaid good for evil, whereas the sinner repaid evil for good, 208. What sort of judge he will be at the end, 208.

**Judgment.** The condition of souls separated from the body, 207. The soul is accused by demons even for the slightest negligence, 207. A fearful hour: a dreadful examination; a stern judge; insolent adversaries, 207. A just soul will not fear that fearful hour, 207. See **Soul**.

The terror of God’s judgment, 191, 207, 234. The horror of those condemned, 234. The beauty and joy of those glorified, 234. The time of the universal judgment is uncertain for everyone, 162. The hour of each person’s departure is uncertain, 162. The saints are to receive the kingdom on the day of judgment, 162.

In the sight of angels and human beings all our sins, even those of our thoughts, will be revealed, 191, 253. We shall give an account of each act, 167, 168. Whatever we do is, as it were, written in a book, 183, so that it may be recited before Christ on the day of judgment, 183.

On the day of judgment, not everything that has not been directed toward God’s will will be condemned, 208. On the day of judgment many things that now appear either good or not sinful will be seen to be sins, and more terrifying than those that now appear so, 208. Then there will be no time for mercy, nor will repentance be accepted, 208.

The sinner’s judges and accusers, 299. The sinner will be accused by as many persons as provided him examples and admonitions for living well, 253. At the end, on one side there will be accusing sins, on the other terrifying justice; beneath, the dreadful abyss of hell lying open; above, the angry judge; within, a burning conscience; outside, a world on fire; and so forth, 208. The soul’s distress on the last day, 208.

It must be considered how you are to be placed before the judge, 191. Whoever does not awaken and tremble at the voice of the day of judgment is not asleep but dead, 207. The joy of the righteous when they hear, “Come, blessed ones,” 207. At the end of the age Christ will hand over the reprobate so that they may be carried off by the devil into eternal damnation, 207. See **The condition of separated souls**.

**JUSTI (St.), monastery.** Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, was buried there, 446.

**To justify.** A sinner cannot justify a sinner, 85. See **Redemption; Satisfaction**.

**Justice, Just, Injustice, Unjust.** God’s justice leaves nothing disordered in his kingdom, not even sin, 222. To order rightly a sin for which satisfaction has not been made is to punish it, 79. If sin is not punished, it is left disordered, 79 and 84.

Justice gives each person what is his or her own, 171. Justice is rectitude of will preserved for its own sake, 98, 99, 114, 115, 126, 128, 129, 133. This definition is perfect, 114, 115, 126. Justice, truth, and rectitude of will are the same, 65. As soon as we possess and will the rectitude of the will, it must be called justice, 114.

To preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude is to will what God wills that person to will, 121, 126. This is justice, or rectitude of will: the will of a rational creature subject to the will of God, 79. That will is to be called just which preserves its rectitude for the sake of rectitude itself, 114. The will, or affection, that is directed toward willing rectitude is itself rectitude, 133. No one can will rectitude except through rectitude and while possessing rectitude, 133. The will of justice is justice itself, 133.

There is no justice that is not rectitude, 114. Nor is any rectitude other than that of the will called justice in itself, 114. We have justice only by willing, 114. If we will it, by that very fact we have it, 114. We preserve it only when we will it, 114. As long as we will it, we preserve it; and as long as we preserve it, we will it, 114. As soon as it is received, it is possessed, and we will it, 114.

By nature, receiving justice is prior to willing and possessing it, but in time these occur together, 114. Likewise, by nature, willing and possessing justice are prior to preserving it; but in time these occur together, 114. The will is one thing, and rectitude—which is right—is another, 126.

The affection of willing justice is better than the affection directed toward advantage, 116. Through the former every just person is just, 116. No one can be blessed except through it, 116. The soul would be blessed through the love of justice alone, even in the absence of any other advantage, 116. See **Blessedness; Good**.

Rectitude of will is justice in no way unless it is preserved for its own sake, 114, 128. Whoever preserves rectitude only for the sake of something else does not love justice, but that for the sake of which he preserves it, 128. Therefore he is not to be called just, 128.

There is original justice and personal justice, 97. Personal justice is what an unjust person receives—justice that he did not possess from the beginning, 97. Original justice is what Adam and Eve possessed at the very beginning of their existence, 97. See **Adam; Man before sin**.

Justice is determined in three ways: first, when we preserve for our nature what belongs to it; second, when we do for our neighbor what we want done for us; third, when we repay to God what belongs to God, 159. Justice is not fully accomplished in us until God is all in all, 159.

Justice is not one thing in one person and another in another, 4. Praiseworthy justice, or rectitude, is found only in a rational nature that knows and wills it, 114. Justice is rectitude of will, not of knowledge or action, 114. Whoever wills what he ought, even if he wills what he ought unknowingly, does not possess praiseworthy justice, 114. See **Rational nature**.

From the one by whom we simultaneously receive the possession, willing, and preservation of rectitude of will, we receive justice, 114. Justice alone is the very good by which angels and human beings become good, 65. Justice is not natural to a human being or an angel, 126, but it can be separated from them, 126. There is no injustice in the good angels, 129. No one will be joined to them with any injustice, 129. See **Angel; Blessedness**.

Justice is that truth of the will in which the devil did not remain, 133. The obligation to possess justice was made by the one who gave it; the failure to possess it was caused by the one who abandoned it, 69. The will is not reproached for being obliged to possess justice, but for not possessing it, 69. The obligation to possess justice adorns nature; not possessing it disfigures it, 69. A nature that is not obliged to possess justice is not deformed by not possessing it, 69.

The will must always possess justice, 127, 134. What once received justice must always possess it, 69. Received justice made the will a debtor, 69. God requires from every rational creature—and the creature owes this to him through obedience—that it hold justice unwaveringly in living and speaking, 77. Justice is something good, 69.

Rectitude is the cause of no evil, 133; rather, it is the mother of every good merit, 133. It favors the spirit that desires against the flesh, 133. If evil sometimes appears to follow from it, it does not arise from rectitude itself but from something else, 133. When a human being possesses rectitude, he is not a slave of sin, 121, nor does he possess the inability not to sin, 121.

Rectitude is an increase given by God, 130. An essence is not right except from God, 127. Justice or injustice exists through the will, 64. In adults salvation is through justice, 128. Justice governs the human will, 73. Human justice is under the law, 79. God repays according to the measure of justice, 79. Whoever does not preserve justice by free will does not possess it, 127. Whoever does not will justice ought not to be blessed, 68. See **Blessedness**.

Not everyone wills justice, 68. The rectitude of willing something is given to no one who does not understand rightly what he ought to will, 130. Because of rectitude, a person wants to learn so that he may know how to live rightly, that is, justly, 133. Every perception or understanding of rectitude is a seed of right willing, 130.

No one can possess rectitude from himself except by willing, 129. No one can will it except by possessing it, 129. No creature can in any way possess rectitude from itself, 129, nor can it possess it from another creature, 129. No one preserves justice except by willing what he ought, 64. Nor does anyone abandon it except by willing what he ought not, 64. Two things are necessary to the will for justice: to will what it ought, and therefore to will it because it ought, 64.

No one sins by willing justice, 64. The will cannot, through free choice, will justice when it does not possess it in the same way that it can preserve it when it does possess it, 134. God cannot take rectitude away from a will that possesses it, 120, 121, 126. God is said to take rectitude away when he does not cause it not to be abandoned, 121.

Every rational creature is bound to preserve justice perseveringly, 77, 90, and ought rather to die than abandon it, 77. Christ died for this, 77. The Apostle calls justice the law of God because it is from God, and the law of the mind because it is understood through the mind, 98.

By abandoning justice, the will lost something great, 5, 6. A human being cannot acquire justice by himself, 70, nor recover by himself what he has lost, 70, 134. Whatever things are called just in relation to one another cannot be understood as just except through justice, 4. Nothing is just in itself except justice, and nothing unjust or sinful except injustice, 98.

Before receiving justice no one is just or unjust, 70. After receiving justice no one becomes unjust except by voluntarily abandoning justice, 70. Injustice is nothing other than the deprivation or absence of the justice that ought to be present, 65, 69, 73, 98, 99, 126. The absence of justice has no essence, 69, 126. Before justice was given, its absence was not injustice; but after justice has been abandoned, that absence is rightly called injustice, 69.

Injustice alone is the evil that makes people evil, 65, 73. Injustice exists only in a nature that ought to possess justice but does not, 98. Injustice is simply evil, which is nothing, 70, 73. A nature in which injustice exists is not simply evil, but something evil, 70.

Injustice is not some thing that infects the soul as poison infects the body, 99. Injustice is said to do evil works because the will does them in the absence of justice; if justice were present, it would prevent them from being done, 99. When justice remains, there is much tranquility, 66. In many cases justice appears to be nothing other than resting from evil, as in chastity and patience, 66.

Something may be just and unjust under different considerations, 76. The very willing of what is unjust, insofar as it exists, is good, 126, and is from God, 127. Only what God wills is just; what he does not will is not just, 32.

The just are called upright in heart, that is, in will, 115, 128. No one is understood to be upright except one who has an upright will, 115. Those who are properly and absolutely called just and upright in heart, 129. Someone may be just in one respect and unjust in another, as one who is chaste but envious, 129. Such people are not promised the blessedness of the just, 129.

The children of light are called just, 183. There are just people who never perform great good works, 183. Holy people are called children of Israel, as well as children of Abraham, 83. All who live justly are angels of God, 83. They imitate the angelic life, and equality with the angels is promised to them, 83. Confessors and martyrs are also called so, 83.

A just man is possessed by the virtues, and no vice has any dominion over him, 177. A just man has God dwelling in him, 203. A just man does not fix his mind on love of the present age, 177, but continually strives toward the future age through desires and progress, 177. See **World**. By advancing daily through the degrees of the virtues, the just man becomes nearer to heaven, 177. The just man prays for the last things, 177. The just man bears with difficulty the delays of the present life, 177. The just man carefully distinguishes between virtues and vices, 177.

Concerning the glory and goods of the just soul when it leaves the body, 211, and following. See **Soul**. Eternal life is promised to the just, 128. See **Blessedness**.

He is not just who does what he ought if he does not will what he does, 113. Whoever wills what he ought under compulsion or because he has been hired is not to be called just, 114. Whoever does not will what he ought is not just, 114. Whoever does not render what he owes is unjust, 85.

**Oath.** Concerning an oath, 193. He does not swear who says that he will do something in the name of the Lord, 366.

[Col. 1097]

## L

**Labor.** The Savior has determined to lead his elect through the labors of this life into the life of future blessedness, 162. See **Rest**.

**Tears.** Concerning tears, 191. The gift of tears is sought from God, 257, 260. One must mourn for sins and for desire of the heavenly homeland, 159. The former washes away filth; the latter inflames lovers of the future life, 159. Jesus’ tears bear witness to his special friendship toward Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, 231.

**Joy.** No joy ought to be felt except over those things that give help or hope of attaining blessedness, 84.

**Layman.** A bishop who has already been consecrated ought not to receive churches that are not in his parish from the hand of a layman, 383. But if they are in his parish, he may receive them, 383. For they are returned rather than given, 383. See **Bishop; Excommunication; Investiture; Council of Lateran**.

**LAMBERT**, chaplain of Countess Ida, 388. He attended the election of St. Anselm, 372. He remains in England on Ida’s business, 388. He asks Anselm that he lose nothing from his prebend, 388.

**LAMBERT**, abbot of the monastery of St. Bertin, 416. He is elected archbishop of Reims, 416. Anselm advises him to undertake the burden solely through obedience and not to refuse it contrary to obedience, 416. The abbot of St. Bertin was subject to the abbot of Cluny, 416. See **Monastery of St. Bertin**.

**LAMBERT**, abbot, 381. Anselm pleads with him on behalf of a monk who had fled but repented, 381.

**LAMBERT and FOLCERALD**, Anselm’s uncles, 318, 328. Anselm frightens them away from love of the world, 328.

**LAMBERT**, teacher of the monks William and Roger, 318.

**LAMBERT**, a nobleman. Anselm exhorts him to despise the world, 356.

**LANFRANC**, elected archbishop of Canterbury, 311. He had been abbot of Caen, 316. He had also been prior of Bec, 316, 341. His gifts to the people of Bec, 316, 341. His moderation in gifts, 326. His mercy in providing assistance, 317. His prudence, 325.

Lanfranc sent his nephew to Bec, 319, 320. He departed for Rome, 319. He exhorts his nephew and the novice Guido to humility, 320. He rebukes his nephew because he had transgressed his command not to read for a year, 320. He asks Anselm’s opinion concerning certain assertions, 326. His work on the Epistles of St. Paul, 333.

Anselm sent him his **Monologion** for examination, 335 and following, 336, 337. Lanfranc advised Anselm to confirm his statements by divine authority and to consult learned men in Sacred Scripture, 337. He noted certain things in Anselm’s **Monologion**, 337.

He sent twenty pounds to the people of Bec through Abbot Herbert, 341. To the same people he sent gold for making a chalice, 341. In his judgment, a drunken chamberlain ought to be punished, 343. When he was ill, Anselm sympathized with him and commended the needs of his monastery, 361. The people of Bec always mourned him after his death, 365.

Lanfranc had dedicated the churches of his villages within whatever diocese they lay, 373. He had given goods to the Church of Durtal, 434. After his death, Anselm defends him against Roscelin’s error, 357. See **Anselm; Roscelin**.

**LANFRANC THE YOUNGER**, nephew of Archbishop Lanfranc. St. Anselm greets him on account of his praiseworthy character, 313, 314. He is sent to Bec by Archbishop Lanfranc, for which Anselm greatly rejoices, 319, 320. Archbishop Lanfranc ordered him not to read for a year in the refectory, the chapter house, or the monastery, 320. He transgressed this command, 320. His virtues, 323. He suffers from a severe headache, 323. Anselm’s love for him, 333. Anselm asks that he be sent to him, 335. Anselm asks him to return as soon as he can without inconvenience, 336.

He is made abbot of Saint-Wandrille against the will of Anselm, his abbot, 357, 358. Anselm therefore rebukes him more severely, 358. He becomes cruel toward the monks of Saint-Wandrille, 358. He was present when the monks of Bec were summoned in their congregation to give their consent to Anselm’s election as archbishop of Canterbury, 365. See **Anselm; Lanfranc; Monks of Saint-Wandrille**.

**LANFRID**, abbot of Saint-Wimari, 377. Anselm urges him not to abandon the flock that wishes to live under his obedience, even if another wishes to act disorderly, 377.

**LANZONI.** St. Anselm prescribes for him the standard of a holier life, 312. He warns him to beware of the devil’s temptations, 321, and to maintain stability in the monastery, 321, 322.

**Falling.** Those who have fallen must abstain for a time, 332. See **Communion; Penance**. A carnal fall prevents access to and return to sacred orders for two reasons: first, because of guilt; second, because of the disfigurement of the sacred order, 140, 332. See **Order**.

The Lateran Council under Paschal II forbids a cleric to perform homage to a layman or to receive a church or ecclesiastical gifts from the hand of a layman, 383.

[Col. 1098]

**Thief.** The thief remained in sins until the departure of his soul, 213. At the point of death he confessed his evils and found mercy, 213. On that same day he was in paradise, 211. The thief sanctified on the cross, 274; he recognized Christ hanging on the cross more truly than Christ teaching in the Temple or performing miracles, 274. The thief on Christ’s cross was a confessor and martyr, 274.

Some thought that this thief had been the son of the chief of thieves and that Christ, as a child, had been returned by him to his mother—the child whom they themselves had stolen, 230. A strong and swift thief is evil because he is harmful, 4.

**Praise.** Praises are to be despised, 320. The praise of God, 254. Human beings were created to praise God without end, 203. The rule set before the saints is to praise and love God, 103. God is to be praised with the whole heart, 103, 206. See **God; Honor**.

For God to be praised by a creature that does not understand him means that God is understood by a rational creature to have made it good and beautifully ordered it, 238.

**LAURENCE**, archbishop of Canterbury. When he was fleeing through fear of the pagans, the Apostle Peter scourged him, 364.

**Lepers** signify sinners, 184.

**LERMENDESIS**, countess. Anselm commends her to the people of Bec, 364.

**Law.** The Old Law is called the law of God because it is from God, and the law of Moses because it was administered through Moses, 98. Evangelical truth is to be preferred to the Law, 165. Those who do not wish to be subject to God’s law are reckoned enemies of God, 389, 391. See **Will of God**.

God’s institution can be divided into two parts: the precepts of the divine Scriptures and the natural law, 151. The natural law is God’s institution, 151. The natural law is what has been implanted in human beings, 151. The natural law is this: “What you would not want done to you, do not do to another,” 151. Whoever opposes this law of God does not preserve God’s will, 151.

The precepts of the Scriptures are called the will of God, 151. In apostolic and ecclesiastical constitutions the law of God is understood, 438. See **Church**. The proper observances of the Churches are rightly called the will of God, 151. Whoever does not comply with them deviates from the will of God, 151. The Law does not justify. See **Grace**.

**Church of Lisieux in England**, 412.

**Free choice.** What the freedom of choice is, 117 and following, and whether we always possess it, 117. Every freedom is a power, 118. Freedom of choice is the power to preserve rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself, 118, 122, 126, 129, 132. This definition is perfect in genus and differences, 122, 126.

Freedom of choice consists of reason, which is able to recognize rectitude, and of will, by which we can hold to it, 119. Freedom of choice is not the power to sin and not to sin, 117. Some thought that freedom of choice meant being able to sin and not to sin, 117. Neither freedom nor any part of freedom is the power to sin, 117.

Freedom exists only for what is expedient, 80. The will that cannot deviate from the rectitude of not sinning is freer than one that can abandon it, 117. The power to sin, when added to the will, diminishes its freedom; when removed, it increases it, 117. Rectitude is preserved through free choice, 129. One sins through free choice, but not through that by which it is free, 118, rather through the power to sin, 118. See **Sin; Will**.

One sins through free choice when one sins voluntarily, without anything compelling and without any necessity, 117, 118. The freedom of God is one kind of free choice, belonging to God alone; another kind is made and received from God, belonging to angels and human beings, 122, 126. Of the latter, one kind holds rectitude and another lacks it, 126.

That which holds rectitude does so either separably or inseparably. The separable kind belongs to all angels before the fall and to all human beings before death, 126. The inseparable kind belongs to the elect angels after the fall of the others and to the elect human beings after death, 126. That which lacks rectitude lacks it either recoverably, as in human beings during this life, or irrecoverably, as in the reprobate angels after their fall and the reprobate human beings after this life, 122.

God and the angels, although they cannot sin, possess free choice, 117. Human free choice differs from the free choice of God and the good angels, 117. Nevertheless, the definition of free choice is the same in both, 117. See **Angel; Will of God; Human being; Rational nature; Will**.

The free choice of God and the good angels cannot sin, 117. God gave rational creatures free choice, 129. Through the power to sin, voluntarily, through free choice, and not from necessity, our nature and the angelic nature first sinned, 117. Sin could dominate it, and yet it was free, 117, 118.

The angel and the human being possess free choice even after they have sinned, 118, 119, 121. They received freedom of choice in order to preserve the rectitude of will for its own sake, 118—not in order to possess it from themselves or to recover by themselves what they had lost, 118. See **Adam; Angel; Human being**.

We possess the power to preserve rectitude of will as long as reason and will are in us, 119, just as we possess the power to live even if we are placed in darkness, have our eyes bound, or no visible object is present, 119.

Rational nature always possesses free choice, 121, 122, 126, because it always possesses the power to preserve the rectitude of will for the sake of rectitude itself, 126, even when it does not possess that rectitude, 121. Things done through free choice occur through no necessity, 123. Many things occur through no necessity but through free will, 125. See **Necessity**.

We do not possess free choice in every respect, 126. Choice is not identical with the freedom by which it is called free, 126. Many things occur through free will which, before they occur, may never occur, 124. Yet in a certain sense they occur necessarily, 124. Some necessity and freedom of choice are not contradictory, 123. See **Necessity**.

The agreement of free choice and foreknowledge, 71, 72. See **Foreknowledge**. Many think that free choice contributes nothing to salvation or damnation, but only necessity does so because of foreknowledge, 126. Concerning freedom of choice in matters relating to salvation, 126, 127.

The force of necessity does not act where choice of the will alone operates, 126. The power to preserve rectitude is always free, 126. By this freedom, choice and will are called free, 126. Freedom exists where there is no necessity of abandoning rectitude, 126.

The will cannot be deprived of its freedom either by itself or through another, 121. The will does not act by necessity: if it did not will spontaneously, it would not act, 124, even though what it does may necessarily come to be, 124. The will is neither compelled nor prevented by anything else, 123. What occurs from the will occurs through freedom, 123. See **Will**.

Whatever happens through the operation of a spontaneous will does not happen by necessity, 128. In the time of St. Anselm there were many who utterly despaired of free choice being something real, 128. There were also those who thought that the entire effectiveness of the virtues consisted in free choice alone, 128.

Whoever wills from necessity, so that he cannot will otherwise, can be called neither just nor unjust, 69. God gave justice to the will in such a way that he did not remove the power of exceeding it, 69, so that it might merit never being able to will what it ought not to will, 69.

The work of sin occurs by necessity when a person wills it, although he does not will by necessity, 124. A human being does not will by necessity, 124. The sin of the will does not occur by necessity, just as willing is not necessary, 124. See **Sin**.

No one sins unwillingly, that is, without willing, 119. No one abandons rectitude except by willing, 119, 129. A human being cannot will unwillingly, 129, because he cannot will while unwilling to will, 129.

In what sense someone is said to do something unwillingly, 119. One kind of will is that by which we will something for its own sake; another is that by which we will something for the sake of something else, 119. Someone is said to act unwillingly when he does not will an act for its own sake and wills it only for the sake of something else, 119; or when, unwillingly, he is in distress about which of two alternatives to do, 119; or when he can refrain from doing something only with difficulty and reluctance, 119. In all these cases the will is free, 119.

The will is free because it wills only while willing, 119. The will is free when an external power cannot subject it without its consent, 119. The appetite of a horse, however, is not free, 119, because the will itself does not subject itself in the horse, 119.

The will possesses consent neither naturally nor by necessity, but from itself, 119. Everything is free that cannot be compelled or prevented unless it wills, 119. That which cannot overcome an unwilling will does not infringe freedom, 120. There is no free choice in irrational animals, 119. This difficulty does not permit freedom of the will, 119.

Human beings are left to free choice, 168. Free choice is of some benefit in one who wills and acts, 129. Natural freedom of choice without justice is idle, 134. The will has become the servant of its affection directed toward advantage, 134. Once justice is removed, it can will nothing except what that affection wills, namely, advantage, 134.

If free will joins itself to the soul through free choice, then, with the help of grace, it raises the flesh upward, 239. If it joins itself to the flesh through free choice, the will and the flesh drag the soul downward, 239. See **Angel; Will of God; Grace; Human being; Necessity; Sin; Predestination; Foreknowledge; Power; Temptation; Will**.

**Lust.** It is better to die than to be stained by lust, 191. The remedy for lust is remembrance of death, judgment, and hell, 191. See **Pleasure**.

**ROBERT, bishop of Lincoln**, 444. See **Robert**.

**Tongue.** The perfect athlete of God restrains the tongue, and so forth, 191. Sins of the tongue: lying, detraction, and flattery, 214. See **Flattery; Detraction; Lying; Idle words**.

**Place** is something, 11, 12. One whole thing cannot be wholly in several different places at the same time, 12, 13. Of what is wholly in a place, none of it is outside that place, 12. Of what is wholly in any place, none of it is simultaneously in another place, 12. How something wholly in one place may also be wholly in another place at the same time, 12.

The impossibility of being wholly in each of several places at the same time is said only of things that do not exceed the space of a place, 12, 13. A place exists only for a thing whose quantity it contains by circumscribing it and circumscribes by containing it, 13. See **Angel; Soul; Body; Spirit**.

One place is distinguished from another in such a way that each place exists, 12. What is wholly in one place is distinguished from what is wholly in another place at the same time in such a way that each is a whole, 12.

That which is wholly everywhere at once is uncircumscribed, 32. That which is simultaneously circumscribed and uncircumscribed is wholly somewhere in such a way that it can simultaneously be wholly elsewhere, but not everywhere, 32. That which is circumscribed is wholly somewhere but cannot simultaneously be elsewhere, 32.

What is enclosed by place or time is less than what no law of place or time restrains, 32. Local expressions—“where,” “there,” and so forth—are often attributed to things that are neither places nor contained by local circumscription, 32.

**London.** The Council of London under Anselm, 407. It is violated by priests, 407. The Second Council of London under Anselm, 431. Nothing is to be relaxed from its decrees, 431. The Third Council of London under Anselm, 437. Anselm does not want it made public until the matter of the bishopric has been reconsidered by the council, 437.

The bishop of London wants to dedicate the churches of villages situated within his diocese but belonging by their own right to the bishop of Canterbury, 372. Anselm opposes him, 372. The bishop of London had never had the pallium, 421. A London cleric becomes a monk of the Church of Canterbury, 437.

We speak to God when through desire we ask for his face, 172.

**LOUIS**, king of the Franks, 440. He sympathizes with Anselm and invites him to come to Gaul, 440. His conference with Henry, king of the English, 449. He gave hostages to the king of the English, 449.

Light in light: there is only one light, 61.

The archbishop of the Church of Lund in Denmark, a friend of Cardinal Alberic, 448. Anselm asks him not to admit foreigners to ecclesiastical orders, 448.

The monastery of Saint Maglorius in Paris, 346. Monks were there on account of the schools, 346.

**Evil** is either that which is not good, or the absence of a good that ought to be present, 67, 99. It is nothing, 65, 66, 73, 99, 126, 343, 344. If evil is nothing, how does its name signify something? 343, 344. It is not contradictory that evil is nothing while the name of evil signifies something, 66, 343, 344. “Evil” and “nothing” signify something, but what is signified is neither evil nor nothing, 66. By the name “evil” and “nothing,” something is signified not according to the thing itself but according to the form of speech, 66.

There are two kinds of evil: one is injustice; the other is called misfortune or affliction, 68, 73, 126. See *Good*. Evil that is affliction is sometimes nothing, as in blindness; sometimes it is something, as in sadness, 73, 99. Evil is nothing other than the absence of abandoned justice in the will, or in some thing because of an evil will, 70. Evil that is affliction we always hate, 73. This is what we shudder at when we hear the name “evil,” 73. To be able to do evil is not power but impotence, which drags downward, 248. A person does evil by his own fault because he does it by his own will, 129. What is simply evil does not belong to God, but to one who wills or moves the will, 70, 73.

In good things, a human being possesses what is not evil, 134, because, although able to abandon justice, he did not abandon it, 134. In evil things, a human being possesses only what is evil, 134, because he does those things alone by his own—that is, unjust—will, 134.

In every nation there are many who live perversely and few who act well, 155. We must not do evil so that good may come, 400.

**Mammon.** To seize another’s property is “the mammon of iniquity,” 183. See *Greed*, *Riches*, *Meekness*.

On meekness, 159. Meekness is to be loved, 191. Christ is its teacher, 159. It possesses the true land, 159. See *Injury*, *Anger*, *Patience*.

### Mary the Virgin (Blessed)

The Virgin herself was brought forth from Adam like all others, 104. Anselm presents her as conceived in iniquities and born with original sin, 91, and as having sinned in Adam, 91. If the Virgin had not been clean, Christ could not have been from her, 92, 93. The Blessed Virgin belonged to those who, before Christ’s birth, were cleansed from sins through him, 92. Her purity was from Christ alone, 92. She was pure through his future death, 92. If Christ were not going to die, the Virgin would not have been pure, 92. She could in no way have been pure except by believing in Christ’s true death, 92, 94. Through this faith in Christ’s certainly future death, the Blessed Virgin was cleansed, 93, 94. The Virgin did not believe that Christ would die except because he himself willed it, 94. The Virgin’s faith concerning Christ’s future death was true, 94. Yet the truth of this faith was not the cause of his dying willingly, 94. Rather, because this was going to happen, her faith was true, 94.

God the Father gave his only Son to the Virgin so that he might naturally be one and the same Son, common to God the Father and the Virgin, 103. The Son himself chose to make Mary his mother substantially, 103. The Holy Spirit willed that he from whom the Spirit proceeded should be conceived and born from the Virgin Mary, 103. Before she conceived Christ, the Virgin was cleansed through faith, 103. Even if there were sin in the whole essence of the Virgin, she could have been made clean through faith so that she might conceive Christ, 103. It was fitting that the conception of the God-man should take place from a most pure mother, 103.

The Blessed Virgin was worthy to conceive from the Holy Spirit, 169. She had no need of purification, 169, 170. In the Blessed Virgin neither the will of a creature sowed offspring nor nature brought it forth, 104. Rather, the Holy Spirit miraculously created a man from the Virgin, 104. See *Incarnation*.

No one ever approached her with the sense of lust, 178. It was fitting that the Virgin should shine with that purity than which none greater under God can be conceived, 103.

The humility of the Blessed Virgin, 178, 179. In her there was neither proud virginity nor defiled humility, 178. Humble virginity and Virgin humility, 178. Mary’s sublimity, 179.

Panegyrics on the Virgin Mary, 273, 276, 277, 278, 279, 281, 282, 283, 284, 286. Prayers to the Blessed Virgin Mary, 276, 277, 278, 279, 280, 282, 283, 284, 285, 286. A certain apparition to a servant of his who was dying said that she was the mother of mercy, 278. The Mother of God is our mother, 281. Mary is our mediatrix, 283.

Mary alone was at once mother and virgin, 179. It is impossible for another woman to be both mother and virgin at once, 179. Through faith Christ entered Mary, 179. Jesus did not violate the Virgin’s enclosure, 179.

The virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 178, 179, 276, 277, 278, 279. Blessed Mary as virgin and mother, 276, 277, 278, 283. The new and undefiled virgin expiated the deed of the ancient woman, 276. While Mary is silent, none of the saints will pray and none will help; when she prays, all will pray and all will help, 277. Without her there is neither piety nor goodness, because she is the mother of all virtues, 277. God created everything, and Mary gave birth to God, 281. God, who made everything, made himself from Mary, 281. God is the Father of created things, and Mary the mother of recreated things, 281. Just as it is necessary that everyone turned away from and despised by Mary should perish, so it is impossible that anyone turned toward Mary and regarded by her should perish, 281.

The Virgin Mary was singular in both the contemplative and active life, 179. Her duties toward Christ, 179. How she was troubled, 179. Mary’s contemplation, 179. Her wisdom, 179. The wisdom and power of God in her, 179. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Mary, 179. She knew that divinity was present in her Son, 179. She was exalted above the choirs of angels, 179.

Through Mary’s fertility, the sinful world was justified; the condemned was saved; the exile was brought back, 281. Nothing is equal to Mary; nothing except God is greater than Mary, 281. Just as defilement came through Eve, so cleansing returns through Mary, 170. Mary is unique, 178, 170. She is the mother of Jesus, 170.

**The Nativity of Mary.** The feast of the Nativity of the holy Virgin, with an octave, 386. The octave of the Nativity of Blessed Mary was already being celebrated in several churches, 438. Many petitioned that it should be celebrated in the Church of Canterbury, 438.

**The Presentation of Mary in the Temple.** The Blessed Virgin, sealed by a vow of virginity, 217. This was the first vow of virginity, 217.

**The Annunciation of Mary.** Having entered her chamber, Blessed Mary was turning over books in which the birth of the Virgin and the coming of Christ had been prophesied, 230. She is greeted by the angel, 230. She conceives God. She visits Elizabeth. She gives birth to Christ. These and her other mysteries are piously contemplated, 230. The announcement of the Incarnation, 284.

Jesus is from Adam and Eve through Mary, 101. Jesus is from Mary alone; Mary is from Adam and Eve, 101. In the Blessed Virgin neither the will of a creature sowed offspring nor nature brought it forth, 104. Rather, the Holy Spirit miraculously created a man from the Virgin, 104. She conceived Christ from the Holy Spirit, 174. The Holy Spirit had purified her from the beginning, 170. She was full of grace before the Holy Spirit came upon her, 108. There was neither sin nor the inclination to sin in her when the Holy Spirit came upon her, 108. Abundant grace came upon the Blessed Virgin through the coming of the Holy Spirit, 108. The Virgin was overshadowed because the event was sacramental, 108. The Trinity alone, by itself and with the Virgin alone, willed to accomplish the Incarnation, 108. See *Incarnation*. To the Virgin alone was given knowledge of the mystery of the Incarnation, since to her alone it was given to experience it, 108.

The seed taken from the Virgin was clean, although it came from a sinful stock, 102. There could be no stain of sin in that which the Son of God assumed into his own person from the Virgin, 100, 101. The seed assumed from the Virgin did not acquire any necessity of having sin, 100, 101, 102. The Son of the Father and the Son of the Virgin are the same, 452. The Blessed Virgin is believed to be *θεοτόκος* (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), 267.

**The Purification of Mary.** The feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, 169. The Purification of Blessed Mary, 285. It is the custom of the Church for the faithful to carry candles at the feast of the Purification, 171. The procession customarily held on the feast of the Purification, 171.

**The Assumption of Mary.** The glory and happiness of her Assumption, 285.

### Marriage

The union of the two sexes is not unjust when it occurs in marriage, and likewise among animals, 98. Holy weddings and an undefiled marriage-bed, when lawfully and with fear of God they are celebrated, 142, 198. They absorb punitive shame, 142. Those who marry become one spirit, 142, and become one flesh, 142.

Among the Jews, the natural law of affection concerning the concealment of shame scarcely passed beyond the third degree of consanguinity, 142. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Othniel, for honorable reasons, married women of their near blood relation, 142. Marriages between relatives are prohibited, 141, 142, 447. To what degree, 447, 448. Anselm nowhere reads the reason for this command, 141. In this matter the simple and pure reason is to obey authority and follow the custom of the Church, 141. The command is common to Jews and Christians: not to approach close blood relations, 141. Which women, and whose nakedness, must not be uncovered, 142.

Marriages within the blood relationship, if contracted, must be dissolved, 141. Among the Jewish people, it was not permitted to mix marriages from tribe to tribe, 141, so that possessions might not be divided, 141. For another reason—namely, charity—Christian piety prohibits marriages between relatives within several degrees, 141. The Christian religion prohibits marriages between relatives up to the sixth degree of consanguinity, 141, 142. Even among barbarians it is considered a sacrilege to violate this degree, 142.

In Ireland, marriages openly and with impunity took place between relatives, 417. Free men also exchanged wives, 417, 419. William the Chamberlain married a relative, 448. It is a condemnable crime for a man, after his wife has been enclosed by mutual consent, to marry another, 397.

The burdens of marriage, 198. What a husband should fear from a bad wife, 198.

### Mauritius

Mauritius, a monk of Bec, 320. He suffers from a head ailment, 320, 321. He is sent to Lanfranc, archbishop, 320, 321, to whom Anselm commends him, 321. Anselm instructs him, upon returning, to bring whatever he may have been able to write about the *Aphorisms* and the glosses, 325, 330. Anselm thanks him for the gifts he sent, 326. He proposes to copy a small work on the pulses, 330. Anselm taught him the science of declension, 331. He possessed Anselm’s letters, 361. Anselm’s affection for him, 329, 330, 331, 334, 337. He is expected to return to Bec shortly, 330. When he wishes to leave, Lanfranc does not want to release him, 337. He wrote to Anselm about a monk who was staying at the king’s court, 343. Anselm sent him his writing on evil, 343.

Through constant meditation a person is enlightened toward knowledge of himself, 214. Meditation produces knowledge, knowledge compunction, and compunction devotion, 214. Meditation on God is a sweet food, 253. Prayers or meditations written for the love and fear of God and for self-examination, 202. They should not be read amid tumult or hastily, 202. Robert, count of Meulan, 443, 444, 445. Opposed to the liberty of the Church, 408. Supporting royal wickedness, he is excommunicated by apostolic authority, 332, 408, 436. ### Lying

Every lie is a sin, 193. In lying there are two powers: one of willing to lie, the other of lying, 93. A will can in no way wish to lie unless it is corrupt, 80. Sometimes more is said by an action than by a word, 113. Sometimes a person lies more by an action than by a word, 113.

### Mind

The rational mind is closest to the supreme nature, 25. The rational mind, and it alone, can investigate the supreme nature, 16, 24. The rational mind is especially able through itself to know and discover the supreme nature, 24, 25. The more diligently a person applies himself to learning about himself, the more effectively he rises toward knowledge of the supreme nature, 25. The more he neglects to look upon himself, the farther he withdraws from knowledge of it, 25. The mind is like a mirror for itself, in which it may contemplate the image of God, 26. It, and it alone, can remember, understand, and love God and itself, 20, 25. Therefore it is the true image of the Trinity, 25, 30. See *Soul*, *Incomprehensible God*, *Knowledge of God*, *Rational Nature*.

The instability of the human mind, 239.

The feast of Saint Michael, 434, 437. Saint Michael is the ruler of paradise, 270. See *Angel*.

### Miracles

Those things that God alone does are always wondrous, 101. God performs many works through creatures that they would in no way perform according to their own use and purpose, 101. When water is suddenly changed into wine, it is the work of God’s will alone, 101. When the sea provides a dry path for the people, it is the work of God’s will alone, 101. Miracles calm the storms of persecutions, 160.

### Mercy

Mercy, or compassion for the wretched, 159. It arises from other virtues, 159. The light of justice is mercy; the virtue of mercy is justice, 159. To be merciful is to have a wretched heart through compassion for the wretched, 31. The spirit of counsel belongs to the merciful, 159. No one shows mercy unless he is prompted by the spirit of counsel, so that he may see to whom mercy should be shown, 159.

The fountain of mercy is drained by no iniquities and polluted by no crimes, 213. Sins cannot overcome God’s goodness, 212, 213. It is not fitting for God to forgive sins through mercy alone, 79. See *God’s Justice*. To forgive sin through mercy alone is nothing other than not punishing it, 79. God does not will the death of the sinner but life, 250. The Holy Spirit inspired this prayer: “Have mercy on me, O God,” etc., 249. See *Merciful God*, *Hope*.

### Mass

The solemn rites of the Mass, 268. Christ is the sacrifice and the priest on the altar, 268. The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood is the remission of all sins for the living and the dead, 267, 260. Christ is sacrificed every day because we sin every day, 454.

At the very hour of the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, do not doubt that the angels are present and, with great reverence, render ineffable service to the flesh and blood of their Creator, 267, 268. All the saints see the price of their redemption being celebrated on earth, 267. Food should not be taken before Mass has been heard, 78.

The variety of the manner in which the mysteries are celebrated is consistent with the faith, 139. If the sacraments were celebrated in one way throughout the whole Church, that would be good and praiseworthy, 139. These differences in celebration do not differ in the substance of the sacrament, its power, or the faith, 139. Nor can they all be brought together into one custom, 139. Therefore these differences should rather be tolerated peacefully and concordantly than condemned discordantly with scandal, 139.

Some, when sacrificing the body and blood of the Lord, make individual crosses for each item from the beginning in the Canon, 139. Others make them only where the bread or body is named separately, and where the chalice or blood is named separately, 139. In the Mass the body and blood of the Lord are sacrificed, 139. The Canon of the sacrifice, 139. There is one offering and one victim in the bread and wine that we offer, 139. Those who make one cross over both differ from Christ, 139, but without offense, 139. Those who do not sacrifice the chalice after the supper, nor always at vespers, differ from Christ, 139.

In the celebration, provided the truth of the matter is preserved, we may differ without blame, 139. Christ is the author of the sacrifice that we celebrate, 139. It is more fitting for the bread and wine to be marked with one cross at the words “these gifts,” etc., 139. When several things are blessed together, individual crosses are not assigned to individual things, 139.

There is a variety in covering the chalice during the sacrifice, 139. Some cover the chalice with a cloth, others with a corporal, from the beginning, 139. Christ’s nakedness in death does not require that the chalice be uncovered from the beginning in the sacrifice, 139, 140. There is variety in marking crosses over the bread and wine in the Mass, 139. See *Unleavened Bread*.

### Sending

The Holy Spirit sends the Son as the Father does, according to his humanity, 54. This is because the Son appeared in the world through the one will of the Father and the Holy Spirit, 54. In the sending of the Father, the sending of the Son is to be understood, 54. The sending of the Father and the Son is one and the same, 54. What does it mean for the Father to send the Holy Spirit in the name of the Son? 53, 54. The Father sends the same Holy Spirit whom the Son sends, 54. The Father does not send unless the Son sends, nor does the Son send unless the Father sends, 54. The Son does not send the Son, 53. See *Holy Spirit*, *Trinity*.

Softness is to be avoided, 191. The humility and poverty of Christ’s Nativity condemn the luxuries of those who live in softness, 217. See *Pleasure*.

### Monastic Life

What monastic life should be, 420. The cloistered life of the monastic vocation is, in a certain sense, the paradise of this life, 415. A monk ought not to recall worldly things in his mind, 415. Monks and nuns must avoid association with secular people, 412.

The true conduct of a monk, 195. What a monk should be like, 194, etc. See *Observance*. It is not the tonsure but virtue that makes a monk, 194. Harmony among monks, 420.

### Monk

It is an error to prefer the clerical life to the monastic life, 346. The purpose of the monastic life is superior to clerical conduct, 346. A cleric may become a monk, 370. Many things oppose one who is considering converting to the religious life, 158. The holy Fathers understood that evangelical perfection is more fully accomplished in the monastic vocation, 370. The goods of the monastic vocation, 370.

Blessed Gregory instructs Bishop Desiderius not to prevent a cleric from undertaking the monastic way of life, 370. It is horrifying even to hear that those whom Christ chose from the world should be confined by a bishop in the world; that those whom Christ draws to the harbor from the storms of the world should be dragged back by a bishop from the harbor into the storms of the world, etc., 370. To prevent a soul from following Christ’s counsel—that is, the monastic institution—is a persecution that the soul must avoid, 370. To recall anyone from the monastic institution is a grave sin, 370.

The burden of monastic life is not unbearable, 346. Parents hand over their son to the fellowship of monks through God’s inspiration, 272. One who is held by debt cannot make monastic profession, 316, 319. The excommunicated are not to be admitted to monastic profession, 425.

Not monks alone attain salvation, 352. But those who try to love God alone attain salvation more certainly and more fully, 352. There is also danger within the monastic order, 352. We should have greater hope for those nurtured in holy conduct than for those whose life has been worn down by secular conduct, 347.

The virtues of monks are obedience, humility, and observance of the Rule, 200. The exercises of monks are reading, labor, and prayer, 195. A monk ought not to devote his life to the study of the schools, 323. A monk may not live outside his own monastery, even for study or in another monastery, except with his abbot’s permission, 346. A monk is forbidden to remain at the king’s court, 343.

Through monastic profession all other lesser vows previously made are dissolved, 378. Vows to go to Rome and Jerusalem are fulfilled in monastic profession, 409. Monks are forbidden to go to Jerusalem, 413. A monk should not judge the conduct of others or the customs of a place if they are not contrary to divine commands, 322. Monks should confess their sins to their prior or to one whom he has authorized, 410.

God is more angry with a sinning monk who does not repent, 352. God more kindly receives a repentant monk who returns to his vocation than a non-monk who does not come to that same vocation, 352. It is better for both the innocent and the penitent to come to and return to monastic life than to withdraw from it, 352.

Monks must not be forbidden to sound their signals according to their order, 373. Monks must not be forbidden to seek the people’s help in constructing their church, 373. Monks who willingly leave the monastery cloister harm themselves and others, 376. An abbot ought not to grant monks permission to leave the cloister, 376.

A monk must remain in the monastery in which he made his first profession, 398. Whoever freely made a monk’s vow in one monastery and afterward did so in another is bound to remain in the first, 349. Stability in a monastery is required unless it is such that the monk is forced unwillingly to do evil there, 322. One should not leave a monastery unless forced there to do evil, 322.

Because of lack of bodily or spiritual goods, monks may leave the monastery with the bishop’s permission, 345. A monk who disagrees with an undisciplined prelate is advised to leave him with the prelate’s permission, 314. If he does not grant permission, the monk must bear his burden through obedience, 314.

A monk ought not to leave the monastery, even with a good purpose, except with his abbot’s permission, 322, and only in order to live regularly under the obedience of some abbot, 323. Whoever has publicly worn the monastic habit, even if he has not read the profession, is bound before God always to live in the holy vocation and habit, 423. If he abandons them, he is judged an apostate, 423. See *Novice*.

A cleric who has adopted the monastic institution sins damnably if he returns to the clerical state, even with the authority of his own bishop, 370. Fugitive monks, 437. An incorrigible monk is excommunicated, 437. An apostate monk is excommunicated, 418. No one can absolve him from that excommunication unless he returns to the monastery, 418.

A monastic habit is put on a dying person, 319. The dead person’s name and day of death are entered in the monks’ calendar if he received the blessing, 319. Temptations must especially be avoided by monks, particularly novices, 321, 322, 344, 345. See *Novice*. The devil casts repentant apostate monks down through shame, 404.

### Illness

The will is never so affected that it would at some time desire illness, 132. Illnesses, 199, 200. Sickness wounds the flesh and chastises the mind, 191. Through illnesses the saints always made progress, 417. In illnesses grace is always increased if the good will does not diminish, 417.

The valley of Morianna, 398.

### Death

It is contrary to God’s wisdom and justice for a human being to die if he is without fault, 87. If a human being had never sinned, he would never die, 77, 87. Death comes from sin, 30, 241. Through Adam’s fault death rules over all, 217. Nothing is more uncertain than death, 214. Nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death, 214, 183.

For one whose life is a burden, the world a weariness, and the flesh a pain, death is a desire, 234. Not to fear death because of a clear conscience is preferable to all the goods of this life, 234. Three things remove fear of death: serenity of conscience, firmness of faith, and certainty of hope, 233. Death is the beginning of rest, the goal of labors, and the destruction of vices, 234.

The death of the elect is precious, 234. Angels attend the death of the elect, oppose their enemies, and place their souls in a place of peace, 231. At the death of the wicked, the worst spirits draw their souls from their bodies and hand them over to punishments, 234. See *Soul*, *Damnation*, *Judgment*.

That is why dissolution from the body is feared: because it is uncertain whether one will come to be with Christ, 240. It is wretched for a person to die unwillingly, 77. Death spares no one, 199. Why the one who dies the death of the soul dies more greatly and more terribly than the one who dies the death of the flesh, 299, 300. See *Soul*.

With how great a peace those sleep who sleep in the Lord, 294. No force can drive anyone from this life until it pleases God, 264. The end of the world for each person is the hour of his death, 169. Admonition to one who is dying, 194. Prayers for a sick person near death, 194. Calendar of the dead, 319. In it the name and day of death are recorded, 319. The condition of the body after death is described, 206. Prayer for the dead, 245, 255. A sinner who dies deserves only the punishment of eternal death, 215. See *Damnation*.

### Mortification

Whoever lives according to the flesh is carnal and animal, and does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, 42. Whoever puts the deeds of the flesh to death through the spirit becomes spiritual, 42. He judges all things and is himself judged by no one, 42.

Bodily afflictions must be moderated if they turn into illness, 420. Bodily exercise is good, 420. But God loves more a heart full of piety, love, etc., 420.

### Moses

Moses is truthful, 175. The five books of Moses, 181. Moses is praised for meekness, 159.

Moses, a monk of Canterbury, abandoned the cloister, 358, 359. Later, repentant, he fled to the monastery of Bec, 358, 359. On his behalf Anselm entreats Gondulf, abbot of the monastery of Westminister, and Henry, the prior, together with the whole community, prepared to make satisfaction for him, 359.

Dead to the world, a person has no hope in it, 178. Whoever loves the world is swallowed up by the world, 161. The world knows how to devour its lovers, not to carry them, 161. Love of the world and of the flesh is anxious, 258. When the world smiles at you, do not smile at it: it does not smile so that you may laugh at the end, but so that, while its ruler laughs, you may mourn with the world as it mourns, etc., 312, 315.

The world is not to be loved, 312. The world has gold in its horn but hay in its tail, 312. One must not become entangled in secular affairs, 236. The cares of the world must be cast aside, 193. Temporal and perishable things must be despised, 191. Heavenly things must be desired, 191. The more someone tastes the sweetness of heavenly life, the more he grows weary of everything that pleased him in the lower things, 164. When the glory of God and the saints is seen, the mind suddenly forgets all earthly things, 164. Dead to the world, 193.

This mass of the world is to be renewed for the better, 52. In the renewal of the world, both natures—the rational and the non-rational—will be perfected together, 82. And it will rejoice eternally in God, 82. See *Judgment*.

### Purity

See *Heart*.

### World

Before it was made, the world was nothing, 67. Before it existed, the world could do nothing, 67. And therefore it could not exist before it existed, 67. It was both possible and impossible for the world to exist before it existed, 67. It was possible for God, in whose power it lay that it should be made, 67. It was impossible for that in whose power it did not lie that it should exist, 67. Therefore the world exists because God could make the world before it came to be, 67—not because the world itself could exist beforehand, 67. See *Power*.

The world is not wholly everywhere but exists in parts, 37. One must renounce the world, 193. Hatred of the world, 315, 338. Those whom the sweetness of the world attracts are seized by eternal bitterness, 315. The world does not favor people in order to nurture them but in order to suffocate them, 338. Whoever loves secular pleasure is a friend of this world, 315. The world should be mocked when it laughs, 312, 315. The glory of the world is not glory but a devouring fire, 338. After it caresses someone with its brightness, it torments him with burning, 338.

Contempt for the world, 159. To those who show such contempt, eternal things are rightly promised, 159. Contempt for the world is recognized through fear of the Lord, 159. The vanity of the world, of honor and riches, 195, 196, 197, 198, 199, 200, 201. This world is an empty sponge, and all its desire is more bitter than vinegar, 220. Whoever has cast away the glory of the world has shown himself to be dead to the world, 178.

### Muriardarchus

Muriardarchus, king of Ireland, 417, 419. Anselm praises him for the peace of his kingdom, 417, 419. Anselm exhorts him to correct the evils of his kingdom, 417, 419. He thanks Anselm, 447. His son-in-law is Ernulf, 447.

Anselm supplied a book of music to the prior of Caen, 360.

### Changeable

Any law, if it is changeable, does not truly exist, 161. For it is not true being where there is both being and non-being, 161. See *Immutable God*.

### Existence
## Birth

Many things are said to be born from something with which they have no likeness, such as apples from a tree, 18. See **Generation**.

## Nature

Nature is the same as essence, 5. A nature superior to the others, or inferior to none, is either alone or several natures equal only to it, 5, 46. Several natures cannot be equal through being different, but only through one and the same thing, [Col. 1107] 5. Some natures are more or less than others, 16. See **Existence of God**. Not all natures are equal in dignity; some are better than others, 5.

That one and the same thing through which several natures are equally great is either identical with what they themselves are—that is, their very essence—or it is different from what they themselves are, 5. See **One God**. If that one thing through which several natures are equal is their very essence, there are not several essences, but one essence, or one nature, in several things, 5.

Living natures excel nonliving ones, sentient natures those without sensation, and rational natures irrational ones, 16.

## Necessity

Every necessity is either compulsion or prohibition, 93. These two necessities are contraries that correspond to one another, just as “necessary” and “impossible” do, 93. Whatever is compelled to exist is prohibited from not existing, 93. And whatever is compelled not to exist is prohibited from existing, 93. Whatever must exist cannot not exist, 93. Whatever must not exist cannot exist, 93.

Not every necessity is compulsion or prohibition, 123. There is antecedent necessity, which is the cause that a thing exists, and consequent necessity, which the thing itself produces, 94. Wherever there is antecedent necessity, there is also consequent necessity; but wherever there is consequent necessity, antecedent necessity does not immediately follow, 94.

There is a necessity to which a person submits unwillingly, and which takes away or diminishes the gratitude owed to one who does good, 87. There is also a necessity which someone endures not unwillingly but willingly, and through which greater gratitude would be owed to the one doing good, 87. This should not be called necessity, but grace, 87, because he preserves it when no one compels him, 87. A promise, and the necessity of keeping it, does not diminish the benefit, 87. See **Vow**.

When something is said to be future, it does not thereby exist by necessity, although it is future, 124. For it can happen that it does not exist, even though it is future, 124. What is asserted to be future only by consequent necessity does not exist by necessity, 124. Antecedent necessity; consequent necessity, 127. Antecedent necessity makes a thing exist, 124. Not every future thing is future by necessity, 127. Every future thing is future by necessity, 124. See **Free Will**.

Every necessity and impossibility is subject to God’s will, 222.

## Negation

Negation is the same as the removal of something, 66. The negation of something cannot be signified except together with the signification of that very thing whose removal is signified, 66. Many things are said according to the form of speech which are not so according to reality, 66. Whoever denies something understands the negation that he makes and all its parts, 40. The expression “not something” removes from the intellect everything that is something, 66.

## Nothing

The expression “not something,” or “nothing,” signifies something by removing or denying it; and it signifies nothing by establishing it as nothing, 66. “Not something” and “nothing” do not differ, 66. It cannot be said what that is which is not something, 66. It is not contradictory for “nothing” to signify nothing and something, 66. By considering the difference in signification, the name “nothing,” or “not something,” signifies both nothing and something, 66. Thus the word “nothing,” or “not something,” signifies that everything which is something is to be removed by the intellect, 344.

The name “nothing” does not prove that nothing is something, 66. The name “evil” does not prove that evil is something, 344. Nothing neither exists, nor is an essence, nor is good, 62. Nothing exists through nothing, 5. Nothing neither comes nor departs, 73. Whence does nothing come into something? 73. What is nothing has nothing, 67. Nothing has any power, 67.

## Nobility

Whoever devotes himself to virtues possesses a distinguished and celebrated name, 177. The vanity of nobility, 197, 200. True nobility is that which shines through virtue, 197.

## Name

A common noun is the name of a thing by which the thing itself is called in ordinary speech, 146. Often one man was called by two names, 174.

**NORMANNUS**, a monk of Canterbury, asked Anselm to write a consolatory letter to Walter, prior of Saint-Wandrille, 358. He went overseas without the knowledge of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and the monks of Canterbury, 378. He was elected abbot in the diocese of Amiens, 378. Anselm neither wishes nor ought to consent to his election, 378.

## Last Things

Whoever thinks about the last things does not easily sin, 211, 212. See **Damnation**, **Hell**, **Judgment**, **Death**.

A novice ought to conduct himself in the monastery according to the Rule before profession, as a test of stability, 349. During the period of probation, a novice cannot be compelled to remain; rather, free permission is granted him to learn, 349. Nevertheless, he sins if he abandons the good intention he has accepted; and before God he is convicted of falsehood if he recoils from what he has often promised well with his mouth, 349. See **Monk**, **Vow**.

## Number

The number three, 175. The number four, 175. Ten, 168. The number eleven signifies the transgression of ten, 175. Ten is the number of justice, 175. It signifies blessedness, 175. The number thirty-three, 170. It signifies the time of faith, 170. The number forty, 169. The number fifty signifies repentance and remission, 183. What the number seventy-seven signifies, [Col. 1108] 175. Why an offense is to be forgiven seventy times seven, 175. The number one hundred signifies perfection, 182. The number one thousand, 168.

## Marriage

See **Matrimony**.

# O

The hardening and blinding of the sinner, 296. See **Grace**, **Punishment of Sin**.

## Obedience; Disobedience

On obedience, 395, 412. To will to obey is to will rightly, 130. To obey God is to preserve the order commanded for oneself, 80. When a rational creature wills what it ought, it honors God, 80. When it does not will what it ought, it dishonors God, 80. Every created will ought to be subject to the will of God, 79. This is the debt whose payment causes no one to sin, 79, and which everyone who fails to pay incurs sin by failing to pay, 79. This is the honor we owe God, 79.

To God who commands, a person owes everything that he is, everything that he has, and everything that he can do, 84. In obedience, a person gives God nothing that he does not owe him, 84. Whoever does not render this honor to God takes from God what belongs to him and dishonors God, 84. A will subject to God produces works pleasing to God, if it is able to act, 79. If it is unable, it alone, by itself, is pleasing, 79. Without it no work is pleasing to God, 79.

Everyone who obeys God acts justly, 171. Obedience is true and simple when a rational nature preserves the will received from God not by necessity but voluntarily, 78. Human nature’s obedience is perfect and most free when it voluntarily subjects its free will to the will of God, 222, and when it completes the good will it has received through spontaneous freedom, without any compulsion, in action, 222.

One must yield to greater authority, 83. One must yield to authority in good things, 193, but not in evil things, 193. Obedience is involved when it alone drives a person into dangers or protects a person from sin; or, if he sins, the sin is very venial if repentance always accompanies it, 416. Whoever lives in disobedience does nothing without blemish, 416. Do not comply when you are commanded to do evil, 416.

Obedience does not consider what it is doing, 385, 412. Without obedience one does not attain the kingdom of heaven, 385. Disobedience expelled humanity from paradise, 383, 412. According to the Rule of Saint Benedict, obedience is owed not only to abbots but to all superiors, 361, 366.

One who is going to serve the eternal King must renounce his own will, 191. An action performed out of obedience is of greater merit than one performed out of one’s own will, 386. The reward of obedience is eternal life, 205. The soul that has not obeyed is not heard worthily, 289.

## Offering

What has once been offered to God should not suitably be appropriated for the uses of others, 384. See **Mass**.

## Observance

The vigor of monastic observance, 395, 412. Observance in small matters, 377, 385, 387, 412, 420, 452. It is a deception to think that there is no fault in small excesses, 377. The vigor of monastic discipline is preserved through observance in small matters, 385, 387. Whoever does not despise small things makes progress—not, I say, little by little, but effectively, 420.

The eyes of Christians are the eyes of Christ, 204. They ought not to look upon vanities, 204.

Hatred of one’s neighbor, 192. Hatred is not expiated even by martyrdom, 192. See **Love of Neighbor**, **Injury**, **Anger**, **Vengeance**.

**ODO**, bishop, 444.

**ODO**, abbot of Saint-Quentin, is deservedly deposed, 406. See **Monastery of Saint-Quentin**.

**ODO**, 312, 409. Anselm urges him not to delay his conversion, 409. Anselm sends greetings from England to him as an old friend and a new fellow soldier, 351.

**ODO**, monk and cellarer, 419. He wishes to relinquish his office on account of his age, 419.

**ODO OF LONDON**, 442, 443. See **London**.

## Offense

See **Injury**, **Anger**, **Sin**.

## Divine Offices

We ought to perform the divine offices through those things which we recognize as more worthy, 136.

The olive is a messenger of peace, 157. Through it mercy is signified, 157.

## Works

The letters that we write are our actions, which we consign to divine remembrance, whether good or bad, 383. The whole of life is either sinful and damnable, or fruitless and contemptible, 207. If life is fruitless, it is also damnable, 207. If it is barren of good works, it is dead; and the more fruitful it is in evil, the more dead it is, 299. It is necessary to displease God through evil works, 299. See **Sin**.

Whoever has more good merits than bad may rejoice; whoever has more bad merits than good ought to fear, 390. Every work performed according to Christ is free from sin, 158. Good works raise one upward and lead one into heaven, 211. Evil works plunge one downward, 211, and drag one into hell, 211. Without good works no one is able to attain the contemplation of the majesty of his Creator, 162. Those who, after repentance, do not confidently exercise themselves in good works, 185. See **Faith**, **Intention**, **Will**.

## Opinion

Different opinions may be held concerning certain matters without danger to the soul, 83.

## Prayer

Prayer is a gift of God, 216. God does not give it without purpose, 216. God is to be entreated and worshiped, 28. Prosperity is to be hoped for from God alone, and from adversities one must flee to him alone, 28. For a serious matter one must petition God alone, 28.

God is near to all who call upon him in truth, 245. To call upon God in truth is to call upon the Father in the Son, 245. What is sweeter than to entreat the Begetter in the name of the Only-Begotten, and to move the Father to mercy by recalling the Son? 245, 12. This very thing contributes to the remedy for sin: that the sinner should petition, 84.

The devotion of prayer that is not feigned is kindled more intensely the more one applies oneself to prayer, 295. Prayer is not to be abandoned because of vain or evil thoughts, 414. Without hope of God’s forgiveness, no petition is made, 215. The soul that has not obeyed is not heard worthily, 289.

Frequent prayer, 191. Rising during the night for prayers, 191. It is not inappropriate for prayers to be offered in the Church by the saints for schismatics and heretics, Jews and Gentiles, 151. In the Lord’s Prayer we ask for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, 159. See **Contemplation**, **Praise**, **Meditation**.

The people of the Orkneys are insufficiently instructed in the Christian religion because of the lack of a bishop, 448.

## Sacred Order

Sacred order, 140, 332. The exercise of sacred order requires a person pleasing to God, 149, 332. The age for receiving the priesthood, 174. The age of thirty years is the age for assuming the office of the dignity of teacher and priest, 174.

A person conscious of a crime may always abstain from sacred things, without God disapproving, 140, 332; he cannot presume to exercise them unless God approves, 332. See **The Fallen**.

The judgment of the holy Fathers concerning the fallen is to be understood in this way: they openly prohibit those who have fallen from sacred functions, but allow those who have fallen secretly, after worthy repentance, to approach sacred functions, 140, 332. In such a matter it is safer for each person before God to fear more than to trust, 332.

Secretly fallen men who hold sacred orders may use their orders if they have voluntarily and secretly confessed with contrition of heart, 140, 332, according to the letter of Pope Callixtus and the letter of Saint Gregory to Secundinus, 332. The dignity of sacred order is not discolored among human beings on account of a person whose sin they do not know, 140, 332.

A man ordained by an interdicted bishop ought not to exercise the orders he has received, nor should he be ordained again by any bishop, 374. Whoever gave a woman herbs to kill her husband must not be promoted to sacred orders if that man was killed by those herbs, 374. See **Abortion**, **Homicide**.

**ORDUVINUS**, a monk, asks what he should reply to Anselm’s detractors, 404. He asks permission to visit Anselm, 406.

## Original Justice

See **Adam**, **Angel**, **Human Being**, **Justice**.

## Original Sin

See **Infants**, **Original**.

The Christian’s mouth is Christ’s mouth, 204. It ought to be opened not for detraction, not for lies, and not for idle speech, but for the praises of God and for the edification of one’s neighbor, 204.

**OSBERNUS**, deceased: Anselm commends his soul, 313, 314, 444.

**OSBERNUS**, bishop of Exeter, wrongly prohibits the monks from ringing their bells according to their custom, 373. Therefore Anselm, archbishop, complains and admonishes him to protect the monks against the burdens imposed by his clerics, and not to prohibit them from ringing their bells according to their custom and seeking help from the assembly of the people for the construction of their church, 373.

**OSBERNUS**, another Canterbury monk, 376, living with Gondulf, is greeted by Saint Anselm, 314, 318. While living at Bec, he increases in virtue and knowledge, 323. He is severely afflicted by vertigo, 323. His illness is described, 323. While he remains at Bec, Anselm asks Prior Henry to pardon him for a certain fault, 329. Anselm sends him back at the command of Archbishop Lanfranc, 333. His amendment of character, 333.

He invites Anselm, elected archbishop of Canterbury, and persuades him to undertake the burden, 363. He urges him to hasten his inauguration, 365. He had already praised Anselm for thirteen years, 365. He will always grieve Lanfranc’s death, 365.

**OSMUNDUS**, bishop of Winchester, 377. Archbishop Anselm commands that Abbess Matilda obey him, 377. See **Matilda**, **Winchester**.

Idleness is to be avoided, 195, 385. Idleness is the enemy of the soul; works, 388. See **Faith**, **Works**.

PALLADIUS, *Book on Agriculture*, 107. No one ought to possess the pallium before consecration, 448. A metropolitan bishop ought to request the pallium within a year, 375. Money for the pallium is to be sent to Rome, 448. The archbishop of York possesses the pallium, 428.

**Bread.** See *Unleavened Bread*, *Eucharist*.

**Pope.** The pope is distinguished by the title “Majesty,” 354, 439. The Christian faith [Col. 1110] is to be guarded, and the governance of the Church has been entrusted by God to the supreme pontiff, 41. If anything contrary to the catholic faith arises in the Church, it must be referred to him, so that it may be corrected by his authority, 41. The direction and counsels of the children of the Church depend upon the authority of the Apostolic See, 427. Obedience is owed to the Roman pontiff, 430. It is not for a bishop to bind what the Roman pontiff has absolved, 385. Apostolic decrees are to be preferred to the will of the king, 382. In England the “Apostolic”—that is, the pope—is neither received nor named without the king’s command, 381.

**Parable.** In the parables of Scripture, not everything is similar, 55.

**Paradise.** Before Christ’s death, no soul could enter the heavenly paradise, 92. He promises paradise who hangs upon the tree, 24, 274. See *Thief*. Paradise is where Christ is; and to be with Christ is to be in paradise, 274. Paradise is open to the good, 211. See *Blessedness*.

**Paralytic.** He received remission of sins, although confession had not preceded it, satisfaction had not merited it, and contrition had not required it, 231. He was seeking the health of his body, not of his soul, and he received the health of both body and soul, 231.

**Parisian.** See *Galo*, *Goffridus*.

**Passover.** See *Unleavened Bread*.

**PASCHAL II**, Roman pontiff, 381. Anselm writes to him about England’s troubles, 381. He congratulates Anselm on his return to England, 382. He writes to Anselm about restoring the tribute of Saint Peter, 382, and that he should make peace between the king of England and the count of Normandy, 382. He confirms the primacy of the Church of Canterbury, 383. He grants that the kingdom of England should be subject to the judgment not of any legate but of the Apostolic See, 383. He replies to Anselm’s consultation, 383, 384. He entrusts the case of Bishop Ralph to Anselm, 384. Anselm consults him about investitures, 393. He replies to Anselm concerning these matters, 394. He orders Anselm to have no communion with those who have received investitures from the king’s hand, 399, 400, 408. His canonical election is defended, 409; his adversary had no election but was an invader, 409. He excommunicates the Count of Meulan and others who support the king in the matter of investitures, 445. He absolves those who in England had received investitures, or had blessed those invested, or had performed homage, 416. He makes concessions to Henry, king of the English, 416. He absolves those who had supported the king and afterward labored for the liberty of the Church, 416. He commits the case of the archbishop of Rouen to Anselm, 416. While Anselm was in exile, he had entrusted the legation in England to the archbishop of Vienne, 427. He severely rebukes Gerard of York because he supported the king against Anselm, 436.
