Anselm writes to him concerning the case of William, archbishop of Rouen, 445. Under the rule of Paschal II, peace was restored to the Church, 139.

**Passion.** Recollection of the mysteries and passion of Christ, 255, 256, 271. See *Christ*. The reproaches, sufferings, and death of the Son are explained to the Father, 246.

**Father.**

**The eternal Father.** The name “Father” signifies God, who is Father, and his relation to the Son, 50. He receives the name “Father” from this relation, 58. It is more fitting for the supreme Spirit to be called “Father” than “Mother,” 19, because the first and principal cause of offspring is always in the father, 19. No relation of parent and offspring seems so appropriately applicable to anything as to the supreme Spirit and his Word, 18, 19. It is proper to the one to be the truest parent and to the other to be the truest offspring, 19; the one is most truly Father, and the other most truly Son, 19. The one should not be called “mother,” nor the other “daughter,” 19, 49, although the one is Truth and the other Wisdom, 49.

Nothing is more fitting than that the Father should be understood as memory, just as the Son is understood as Word, 20. Memory most suitably receives the name of parent, 20. The Father is memory or wisdom born from no one; thus he remembers himself, so that he himself is his own memory, 20. He is perfectly the supreme essence, 19. He is perfect through himself; he exists through his essence, is wise through his wisdom, and lives through his life, 19. The substance itself of the Father is understanding, knowledge, wisdom, and truth, 20.

Although the Father is understanding and love, he is not the Son or the Spirit of anyone, 23, 24, because he is neither begotten understanding nor love proceeding from anyone, 24. Rather, he is only the one who begets and the one from whom another proceeds, 24. The Father alone is perfectly the supreme Spirit, 19. He is uncreated and creator, 22. No one makes, creates, or begets the Father, 22. Either the Father is from the Son, or the Son is from the Father, 51. The Father alone begets the Son, but does not make him, 22. God the Father begot his only Son from his own heart, equal to himself, 103.

The mouth of the Father is nothing other than his essence, 54. In saying himself, the supreme essence, the Father generates and the Son is generated, 24. The Son has being from the Father, 60. The Father gives the Son to have essence, wisdom, and life in himself, 19, so that through his essence, wisdom, and life he may subsist, be wise, and live, 19.

There is not one God the Father and another God the Son, 60. Rather, the Father is one and the Son another, 19, 60. The Father is not more God than the Son, 60. The things that belong to the Father [Col. 1111] also belong to the Son, 60. It is impossible for the begetter to be other than what the begotten is, or for the father to be other than that which is his, 19. The being of the Father and the Son is the same, 19, 20. The Father may rightly be called the essence of the Son, and the Son the essence of the Father, 19; and each may be said to possess the essence of the other, 19, 20—not as though either existed not through himself but through the other, 19. Each exists through himself and is wise through himself, 19. For the Father and the Son, to have essence is nothing other than to be essence, 19, 20.

The Father and the Son are essentially spirits, but they are not the spirit of anyone, 22, 49. The more truly one is parent and the Word offspring, the more sufficiently the one provides for the perfection of the other’s birth, and the more fully what is born expresses the likeness of the one from whom it is born, 18. Only he whose Word it is should be called begetter and unbegotten, 22, because he alone is Father and in no way is from another, 22.

The Father and the Son are opposed in their relations, so that neither ever receives what is proper to the other, 19. They are nevertheless in agreement by nature, so that each always possesses the essence of the other, 19. The essence of the Father and the Son is one, 19. Paternity and filiation are distinct from one another, 43. The relations of the Father and the Son are multiple, 21, and the relation of the Father is one thing, that of the Son another, 21. According to paternity and filiation, there is no will or power belonging to the Father or the Son, 44.

He whose Word or image it is is neither image nor Word, 18. According to their proper characteristics, the Father and the Son are not one thing but two, 43—not in substance but in relations, 43. The Father and the Son are not one but two, 19, 43. Yet what the two are remains hidden, 19. In the Father and the Son there is one common reality, namely God, and two proper realities, namely Father and Son, 43. There is no distinction of sex between them, 19, 49.

How is it that no person whatever, even an uncreated one, knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, or anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him? 55. The Father loves himself, the Son loves himself, and each loves the other, 21. The Father and the Son remember themselves, understand themselves, and each remembers and understands the other, 21.

The holy Fathers did not say everything that could have been said, 41. Anselm said nothing that does not cohere with the sayings of the holy Fathers. See *Anselm*.

**Patience; impatience.** On patience, 192. Patience exists only in tribulation, 331. Patience is to bear evil rather than return it, 192. When a guilty person is punished, impatience is to be condemned, lest the guilty person be condemned more unhappily, 335. When an innocent person is afflicted, patience must be preserved, so that the innocent person may be crowned more happily, 335. Let each person attribute to his own sins the evils he suffers, 390. Through the experience of afflictions, grace works incorruptibility in us, 71. The spirit of patience belongs to the peaceful, 159. In them there is no rebellious movement, 159. They shall be called children of God, 160. See *Adversity*, *Injury*, *Anger*, *Gentleness*, *Vengeance*.

**PAUL (Saint).** Moistened by the tears of the people of Miletus and Ephesus, 364, he nevertheless left them in order to go among foreign nations, 364. Although he followed all the other apostles in time, he surpassed them in labor and effectiveness, 298. Saint Paul is the mother and nurse of Christians, 300. What Christian was not born and strengthened in the faith through Paul’s teaching? 300.

**PAUL**, elected abbot of Saint Alban’s. Anselm congratulates him on his election and prescribes how he ought to conduct himself, 337, 338. He is to teach by example those whom, because of the diversity of languages, he could not teach by word, 338.

**Poverty.** Blessed are the poor in spirit, who live for God by despising everything—not from necessity but by devoted will, 159. Evangelical poverty has two parts: renunciation of possessions, even for works of piety, and contrition of spirit, by which one renounces oneself, 159. Poverty is rightly placed first among the virtues, 159. Without it preceding them, the things that follow are of no value, 159. Poverty itself earns blessedness through the help of divine grace, 159. The benefits of poverty, 196.

**Peace.** Peace is to be loved, 192.

**Sinner.** A sinner does not cease to be a son of the Church, 240. Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin, 240. See *Humanity after Sin*. God cannot dismiss a sinful human being unpunished, 240. See *God, the Just*. A sinful human being is compared to a pearl polluted in mud, 83. A rotten dog is less offensive to human beings by its stench than a sinful soul is to God, 207. Nothing remains for the sinner except to weep throughout his whole life over his whole life, 207.

Whoever does not submit to God’s commandments deviates from God’s will, but does not depart from the order of his foreknowledge, 151. Although the sinner does not wish to be subject to the divine will, he cannot escape it, 80. If he wishes to flee from the commanding will, he runs beneath the punishing will, 80—just as one who cannot flee from the sky while beneath the sky except by approaching the sky, 80.

Every sinner is a thief, 72. There is a great difference between sinner and sinner—that is, between one who sins more and one who sins less, 213. There are sinners who, once corrected and repentant, perform wonderful deeds, 183. The notorious sinful woman was the first to see the glory of the resurrection and announced it to the apostles, 224.

**Sin.**

**Definition of sin.** Sin is transgression of the law, 175. To sin is nothing other than not rendering to God what is owed, 79. To sin is to dishonor God, or to take away from him what is his, 79, 222. Sins are commonly called debts, 182. Sin is a dreadful name and a detestable reality, 296. The foulness of sin is to be avoided more than any enormity of torments, 196. In sin there is injustice; in torments, justice, 196. To sin is an evil and bitter thing, 288. Sins have easy entrances and difficult exits, 288, 299.

Every sin is injustice, 98; injustice is altogether nothing, or has no essence, 98, 126. We wish God to preserve what he promised, and we do not fear failing to observe what he commanded, 251. See *Justice*. Sin may be called a kind of corruption of virtue, 107.

**Division of sin.** Each person’s sin is found in nature and in person, 97. The sin that each person draws along with nature at its very origin is called original sin, 97. It may also be called natural sin, 97. The sin that each person commits may be called personal sin, because it is committed through the defect of the person, 97.

Sin of thought, 170. Because of it the soul is judged unworthy of the fellowship of angels, 170. To sin in the will is nothing other than to will what one ought not to will, 124. Actions performed by an unjust will are called sins because sin is in the will by which they are performed, 99. One thing is understood when the action itself is considered, and another when it is considered whether the action is just or unjust, 99.

There is a difference between sin committed knowingly and sin committed through ignorance, 91. Sin committed through ignorance is venial, 91. Some things cannot be done except unjustly, 98. Injustice alone is sin in itself, 131. The things that follow injustice are designated sins until injustice itself is remitted, 131.

**Gravity of sin.** Every sin dishonors God, 208. A human being ought not to dishonor God, even if it were necessary that everything that exists, while God did not exist, should perish, 222. No sin should be considered small, 208, 412. One sin is greater than another, 412. We sin gravely whenever we knowingly do anything, however small, against God’s will, 84. He always commands us not to sin, 84. It is preferable that everything that is not God should perish than that a light sin should be committed, 84, 222.

A perverse will is a horrifying marvel; voluntary perversity is a wondrous miracle, 209. Sins appear more horrifying the more carefully they are considered, 290. Sins are hateful to the degree that they are evil, 91.

**Cause of sin.** Whoever can do evil and does it, can and does it through his own evil, 248. For a human being it is guilt not to possess what he ought to possess, 248. It is guilt to possess what he ought not to possess, 248. It is guilt for a human being not to have the power he received in order to be able to avoid sin, 85.

Nowhere in human nature, apart from the will, is there sin, 103. No one abandons the rectitude of the will received by grace because the power to preserve it fails, 132, but because the will to preserve it fails, 132. Adam’s descendants sin by natural necessity, 104. This necessity was merited by Adam’s own personal will, 104.

No one can live upon earth without touching some sin, 79, 85, 163, 169, 170, 454. This is a necessary belief for salvation, 79. What kind of inability excuses sin? 85. See *Inability*, *Infants*.

A human being has from himself what makes him fall into guilt, but from himself he does not have what enables him to rise again into forgiveness, 168. Worldly service is sin, 225. The tribute of sin is threefold: pleasure, consent, and habit, 225. It is paid by heart, mouth, and deed, 225.

**Effects of sin.** All sins injure the soul, 142, but they do not disfigure the body, 122. Justice is abolished when the just person falls, 252. The repentance of one who returns to the same thing collapses, 252. The more freely a person sins, the more he is sick, 186. Whoever sins willingly falls without end, unless he is held back by mercy, 296.

Sins promise sweetness while they attract; when they drag a person along, they drench him in bitterness. While they persuade, they anoint; after they have persuaded, they pierce the soul until death, 299. Sins tear the conscience apart, 279. When justice departs, a cruel affection takes possession of the soul, 66. It makes a person anxious through concern over shameful and laborious works, 66.

Sins are often not erased when an act has been erased, and are often erased when the deed has not been erased, 991.

**Punishment of sin.** Through sin a human being dies, even if he lives to some extent, 250. The abyss of sins calls upon the abyss of judgments and punishments, 296. Whoever sins despite foreseeing the punishment is to be punished all the more, 72. If sin is nothing, why does God punish a human being for sin? 99. God punishes sinners only for sin; yet not for nothing, but on account of something, 99.

A person who sinned willingly cannot, by himself, avoid either sin or the punishment of sin, 77. Whoever sins ought not to be dismissed unpunished unless mercy spares him, 77. See *God, Merciful*. By sinning, a human being seizes what belongs to God; by punishing, God takes away what belongs to the human being, 80—and by this he proves himself that person’s lord, 80.

When human nature first sinned, it was scourged by this punishment: that it should never naturally generate offspring except such as we see infants being born, 132; and that after this life it should remain forever exiled in hell from the kingdom of God, for which it was made, 132.

After Adam’s sin, there remained in nature the debt of the complete justice that it had received, 98; the debt of making satisfaction, because it had abandoned that justice, 99; and the corruption it incurred on account of sin, 99. If human nature had not sinned, it would have been propagated as God made it; after sin, it is propagated as it made itself by sinning, 98. See *Adam*, *Humanity*.

Human nature was also made weak for willing the justice it had abandoned, 134. Because of the sin of the first parent, humanity suffers countless afflictions, 71. The fact that human nature has been diminished from the dignity, strength, and beauty of its first condition is charged to it as guilt, 131, because through this it diminished God’s honor and praise, 131. The corruption of our nature is sometimes the punishment of sin, not sin itself—for example, illnesses and other afflictions, and death itself, which occur without sin in holy persons, 107. In proportion as human nature, a precious work of God, diminished and defiled itself, so greatly did it dishonor God by its guilt, 131. This is counted as such great sin against it that it is erased only through the death of God, 131.

The faculties of our soul have been obstructed by the ancient sickness of sin, 33. It is part of the punishment of sin that one cannot do the good that one has been given to know, 165. The punishment of sin is the necessity of sinning, 107. Diseases, death, and so forth are punishments of sin, 107. See *Disease*. Death is from sin and is the punishment of sin, 30, 85, 241. See *Death*.

Because of sin, human nature incurred corruption and the appetites of animals, 133. By sinning, the human being did not altogether lose what he had been made to be, 133, so that there might remain one who could be punished and toward whom God could show mercy, 133. The misery of humanity in sin, 223. Torments owed to sins, 293, 296. The guilt is not light when condemnation to death follows it, 131. Equal punishment does not follow unequal sins, 104. The vengeance will be harsher in proportion as a longer life has been granted for repentance, 240.

From whomever the punishment of sin is removed, sin itself is also removed; but the reverse does not follow, 108. Why does the punishment of sin remain in us after sin has been erased? 131. See *Baptism*. *Concupiscence*. A crime that God does not impute, and that not everyone considers to be a crime, neither condemns nor disfigures, 140, 332. In God’s sight, a person’s office is not condemned on account of guilt that God himself forgives, 140, 332.

Petition for forgiveness of sins, 236. Sins forgiven through repentance return when forgiveness is denied to a brother, 169. See *Injury*. See also *Concupiscence*, *Humanity after Sin*, *Ignorance*, *Inability*, *Justice*, *Free Will*, *Repentance*, *Will*.

**Original sin.** On original sin, 94, 97, etc., 223. It is sin from nature—that is, natural or original sin, 104. It is sin from the person—that is, personal sin, 104. “Original” derives its name from origin, 97. Original sin is so called either because it descends to individuals from those from whom they have their natural origin, or because it is from an origin—that is, from the beginning of each person—since it is drawn in at the very origin of that person, 97.

A righteous offspring can be born from a sinful parent, 103. Adam and Eve’s sin was propagated to all human beings, 88. Adam’s personal sin passes into all his descendants and is in them original or natural sin, 104. Just as personal sin passes into nature, so natural sin passes into the person, 104.

Whoever is propagated through nature draws sin along with him, 101. Adam could not transmit evil to any person propagated from himself, because in that generation neither the nature given to him for propagation nor his will was able to accomplish anything, 101. No one was free from Adam’s sin except the man who was made without the seed of a man, 82. Among human beings, the Son of the Virgin alone was conceived in his mother’s womb and born from his mother without sin, 98. See *Christ*, *Infants*, *Mary*.

All Adam’s sons except Christ possess original injustice, 103. All are sinners and children of wrath, 103. Each person is burdened by Adam’s sin and is guilty of debt, 100, 101—not because he is a human being or because he is a person, but because Adam is a sinner and the person is propagated from that sinner, 101.

Adam’s sin descends upon infants, 103, 104. Nevertheless, they ought not to be punished for this as though they had personally committed it, 104. Yet none of them is born without sin, which is followed by condemnation, 104. A human being is already conceived and born in darkness and sin, 33, 85, 98, 100, 103. The corruption of nature passes into all who are begotten from paternal seed, 107. It is itself the punishment of sin and has its cause in the sin of the first parent, 107.

Seed is drawn from parents together with the necessity of future sin once it has been animated by a rational soul, 100. How the seed is unclean, 100; and how an infant is said to be conceived in sins, 100. There is no uncleanness of sin—or sin itself—in the seed before the rational soul, 100, 101, 102. [Col. 1114] Rather, from the seed itself and from the conception through which the human being begins to exist, the person receives the necessity of possessing the uncleanness of sin once he has a rational soul, 102.

There is no more guilt in seed than in spittle or blood when it is emitted, 100, 107, 108, because there is no will in them, 108. Sin is not immediately present in infants from the moment of conception, 100. It is not in the infant before the infant has a rational soul, 98.

When the infant becomes rational, human nature does not possess in him the justice it received in Adam and ought always to possess, 103. Therefore he has original sin, 103. Human nature in infants is born with the debt of making satisfaction for Adam’s sin, 98, 100, and with the debt of possessing original justice, 98. Therefore it is born in sin, 98, 100. In all naturally begotten infants, human nature is born with sin and under the scourge, 132.

Original sin appears to be the debt of making satisfaction for the first sin and recovering justice, 98. It exists only in the soul and rational nature, 98. Infants draw sin not from their person but from their nature, 104; it is caused not by their will but by natural need, 104. It makes the persons of infants sinful, 104.

Although the whole mass of the human race is called sinful, sin exists only in the will, 102. Original sin is absolutely sin, 98. It is injustice, 98. Inability does not excuse human nature, even in infants, from the debt of making satisfaction for the first sin and from the debt of possessing justice, 98, 103, 131, because human nature itself made this condition for itself, 131.

God owes a human being conceived and born in sin nothing except punishment, 129. Personal and original sin have a similar condemnation, 104. They exclude from the kingdom of God, 104. God condemns on account of original sin, 98. Original sin is not so grave, 103, 104. It blinded humanity, 205. Whether the sins of near parents are reckoned as part of original sin, 98. See *Adam*, *Baptism*, *Humanity*, *Infants*.

**Pilgrimage.** On pilgrimage, 409. The vow of pilgrimage, 376.

**Danger.** It is not reasonable counsel that, because there is danger everywhere, you should choose to remain where the danger is greater, 352. Perjury and certain other things that must not be named can never be done except unjustly, 98. Persecution is to be endured bravely for the sake of justice, 400. If persecution of the body is to be fled, how much more the persecution of the soul? 370.

**Perseverance; to persevere.** To persevere is to complete; hence when we say “to persevere in leading,” we mean “to lead through to the end,” 63. To persevere in willing is to will resolutely, 63. The perseverance of the angels. See *Angel*.

It is not always the case that not-wishing-to-hold comes before not-wishing-to-abandon, 63, 64. Sometimes the wish to abandon comes before the refusal to hold, 64. When we do not wish to hold something for its own sake, the refusal to hold comes before the wish to abandon, 63, because we abandon it for this reason: that we do not wish to hold it, 63. When you desire something else more, which you cannot have unless you abandon what you hold, then the wish to abandon comes before the refusal to hold, 63, 64.

The virtue of a good work is perseverance, 257. No one perseveres in goodness unless he is among the children of the heavenly Jerusalem, 185. Salvation is granted only to those who persevere, 253. Salvation is certain for the person who, while striving to love God alone, preserves his purpose to the end, 352. If he perseveres in injustice, he will be wholly and equally miserable forever, 87.

**Person.** Every individual human being is a person, 431. A person is a nature possessing a collection of properties by which a human being becomes an individual and is distinguished from others, 47. “Person” is said only of an individual rational nature, 27. “Substance” is said principally and most properly of individuals, 27. In human beings there are as many substances as persons, 27. If there are several persons among human beings, there are also several human beings, 61. Human persons are diverse because the collection of properties is not the same, 61. There cannot be one and the same collection of properties belonging to different persons, 47. Nature subsists in persons, and persons do not exist without nature, 104.

**PETER**, that is, “the one who recognizes,” 166. Peter, 161. He signifies the order of preachers, 161. He signifies the elect, 163; those set over others, 162. Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, 270, 288, 289. First in order, 273. The apostle Peter sat at Antioch, then at Rome, 364, 366. He did not sin by leaving the see of Antioch in pursuit of greater progress, 366. The primacy of Peter, 162.

**PETER**, chamberlain of the supreme pontiff, 421. Nuns of Saint Peter above the Div, 346. The monastery of Saint Peter at Carbot, 398.

**PETER**, Anselm’s cousin, 328.

**PHILIP**, king of the Franks, 44. He promises Anselm every assistance and invites him to come to Gaul, 440. [Col. 1115]

**PHILIP of Prajosa**, 433.

**PHILIP**, a monk, left the cloister, 404. His repentance, 404.

**Piety.** Christian piety does not wish to judge honorable anything that acts contrary to the propriety of nature, 142. The spirit of piety belongs to the gentle, 159.

**Punishment.** See *Condemnation*, *Hell*, *Punishment of Sin*, *Satisfaction*, *Repentance*, *Will*.

**Repentance.** True repentance and true confession consist in mourning the evils committed and not committing again what ought to be mourned, 250. To mourn sins, 191. Through repentance and confession sins are cleansed, 209, 211. Without labor, contrition, confession, and even prayer, sins are never forgiven, 331. No sin is so grave that it cannot be erased through repentance, 212.

God shows mercy to all who cleanse their wickedness through repentance and good works, 250. Sinners ought to be certain that they will obtain forgiveness if they take care to abandon their sins and practice repentance, 213. Whenever a sinner returns with worthy repentance, he is received, 222. Yet this repentance is not promised to the sinner, 222.

Deep grief over the loss of the grace of the first justification, 287, 288. It is the work of the Holy Spirit that the sinner is displeased with his crimes and strives to do what pleases God, 250. This cannot be accomplished by his own powers unless he is enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, 250.

Repentance is to be administered according to what discretion, 390. Public punishment for hidden sins is not to be imposed upon an unwilling person, 140, lest the way of confession be blocked, 140. A person who voluntarily and secretly reveals a hidden crime through humble confession ought not to be prohibited against his will, 140, 332. See *Fallen Person*.

For this reason God sent the patriarchs and prophets, so that they might preach repentance, 212. The repentance of one who returns to the same thing collapses, 252. See *Absolution*, *Confession*, *Conversion*, *Falling*, *Order*, *Satisfaction*.

The habit of the penitent, 191. The prayer of the penitent, 214 and following; 115 and following. In confession sins are purged on account of the repentance that the penitents are going to undertake, 185. Once those proceeding toward confession and repentance condemn and abandon their sins with the full deliberation of the mind, they are freed from them in the sight of the inward examiner, 185. Nevertheless, they must come to the priests and seek absolution from them, 185. Thus those who have already been cleansed before God may also be shown clean to human beings by the judgment of the priests, 185.

This itself belongs to the resolution of sin: that the sinner should beseech, 84. To receive penance for sins from a priest, 250. To promise amendment and even swear to it, 250. Satisfaction for sins, 390.

**Possible.** See *God, Powerful*, *Inability*, *Impossible*, *World*, *Power*.

**To possess.** The possessor is greater than what is possessed, 58.

**Power; ability.** Sometimes a person is said to be able, not because the power is in him but because the power is in another, 93. Thus a person is said to be able to be defeated when another can defeat him, 93. Sometimes a person is said to be unable when the power is in him and not in another, 93. Thus a person is said to be unable to be defeated when he possesses such strength that another cannot defeat him, 93. The ability to be defeated is not power but inability, 93. The inability to be defeated is not inability but power, 93.

Everything that exists, by the very fact that it exists, can exist, 67. Not everything that exists could have existed before it existed, 67. If the will wills, it is necessary that it be able to will, 67. To be able to will or act through oneself is to possess everything sufficient for willing or acting, 67. Whoever has nothing that he did not receive can do nothing through himself, 67.

There are two kinds of power: one that precedes the thing, and another that comes to be with the thing, 67. Power is an aptitude for doing, 116, and every aptitude for doing is power, 116. An aptitude *ad faciendum* (“for doing”) is one thing, and an aptitude *faciendi* (“of doing”) another, 116. The definition of power is legitimate, 116.

We have no power that by itself is sufficient for action, 118. When the things without which our powers cannot be brought to action are absent, we are nevertheless said to possess those powers, 118. Thus a person who possesses sight has the power to see a mountain; yet if the mountain is absent or there is no light, it cannot be seen, 118.

Four powers must concur for an action: first, in the agent; second, in the object; third, in the assisting medium; fourth, in the non-obstructing medium, 118. Many things are said to be possible not through their own power but through another’s, 67. Many things are said to be impossible not through their own inability but through another’s, 67. Power or inability may be divided in several ways, 67.

We often say that a thing can be, not because it can be through itself but because another thing can make it be; and that a thing which can be cannot be because another thing cannot, 67. Whatever does not yet exist cannot exist through its own power before it exists, 67. But if another thing can bring it into existence, it can exist through another’s power, 67. See *Impossible*.

In preserving life there are two powers: one, the will to preserve life; the other, the power of preserving life, 93. A thing is said to belong to someone when it lies within that person’s power to possess it, [Col. 1116] 80.

Sometimes “power” is improperly used for “inability,” 31; “to do” for “not to do,” 31. Inability that does not arise from guilt excuses to some extent, 85. Inability that involves guilt neither diminishes nor excuses sin, 85. A person who through his own guilt has cast himself into the inability not to sin and not to make satisfaction for what he has sinned is inexcusable, 85. This inability is guilt, 85. Inability that descends from guilt does not excuse the person who is unable while the guilt remains, 131.

Not only the inability to possess justice but also the inability to understand it is charged as sin against the unbaptized, 131, because it descends from sin, 131. See *Inability*. As long as a person possesses this inability without satisfaction, it is sin for him, 86. See *Sin*.

Those who are unable to receive the word of God because of their own guilt are rightly rebuked, 131. If some who strive do not progress or fall away, this happens not through impossibility but through difficulty, 132. Nor does this deny the efficacy of free will, 132.

The ability to be corrupted or to lie, or the ability to make what is true false, or to make what has happened not have happened, is not power but inability, 31. Inability is the ability to will to lie, deceive, or change one’s will, 94.

Earthly powers have been ordained by God to exact vengeance, 79. When they exact it, it is God who exacts it, 79.

**Teacher.** See *Prudence*.

**Commandment.** See *Church*, *Law*.

**Predestination.** Predestination is not properly said of God, 127. For God there is nothing before or after, 127, but everything is simultaneously present to him, 127. In God, foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification are simultaneous in the eternal present, 125. None of these is earlier or later with God, 125.

Predestination and foreknowledge do not disagree, 127. As God foreknows, so he predestines, 127. Some future things are predestined through free will, 127. God does not foreknow or predestine anyone as necessarily destined to become just, 127. Predestination does not change, 127. God predestines only as something exists in his foreknowledge, 127. Predestination does not exclude free will, nor does free will oppose predestination, 127.

Predestination is the same as preordination or predetermination, 127. To predestine is to preordain and establish that something will be future, 127. Predestination may be spoken of not only with respect to the good but also with respect to the wicked, 127. Nor is it incongruous to say that God predestines the wicked and their evil works when he does not correct either them or their evil works, 127. God is said to foreknow and predestine good things in a more special way, 127.

It is necessary that the things foreknown and predestined come to pass, 127. Yet some things foreknown and predestined do not occur through a necessity that precedes the thing, but through one that follows it, 127. In predestining, God does not compel the will or resist the will; rather, he leaves it in its own power, 127.

God is to be loved, who by predestining distinguished us from the condemned community, by calling separated us, and by justifying purified us, 234. Rational nature has been foreknown by God within a certain rational and perfect number, 811. That number can be neither greater nor smaller, 811.

We are certain, because Truth says so, that the elect are few; but how few they are, we are uncertain, because Truth is silent, 312, 327, 372. Whoever does not live as one of the few should fear rejection, 372. No one knows or ought to be certain that he belongs to the number of the elect, 372. It cannot be understood why God saves some of the wicked rather than others, or condemns some rather than others, 32.

**Preaching; preacher.** He leads Christ to sinners who preaches Christ to sinners, 182. Rare is the person who preaches Christ, 181. The wisdom of preachers is subject to those who preach, 173. The wisdom of preachers or teachers is Christ, 173. Those who speak of Christ are called angels—that is, messengers of God, 176. The order of preachers is that servant who tells those invited to come, 181. Lesser things are to be preached to lesser people, and greater things to greater people, 167.

Everyone is to be taught according to the measure of his capacity, 167. The preaching of the faith is compared with agriculture, 130. The faithful are God’s cultivated field, 130. God does not give growth to every seed, 130. Nevertheless, he commands his farmers to sow his word most earnestly and persistently in hope, 130. It is not superfluous to invite people to the faith of Christ and to the things that this faith requires, 130. Even though not all accept this invitation, 130. Why those who do not receive God’s word are reproved, 130, 131. Since they cannot do this unless grace directs their wills, 131. Good morals are valued in one who is silent, and eloquence is despised in one who is sluggish, 338. Preachers received the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter, 171. They absolve and bless the faithful person who is dying, 171. And they pray that, when he departs from here, he may be received in heaven, 171.

**Prelate.** One elected bishop ought to flee so great a burden, 409. The one who flees ought rather to be compelled to accept the burden, 409. The office of prelate is to be avoided insofar as this can be done without sin, 330. Nevertheless, if obedience compels it, it is to be accepted, 330. The shepherd of the Church must be appointed through Christ alone, [Col. 1117] 383. Whoever does not enter through truth does not enter through Christ, 358. Whoever does not enter through uprightness does not enter through truth, 358. Whoever does not enter through regular election does not enter through uprightness, 358. Such a person is made prelate not by Christ, but by his own greed and by the rashness of those who do not perceive the things that belong to God, 358. A prelate should conduct himself so that he never excludes either justice by favor or favor by justice through any private underhanded encroachment, 371. The reputation of any vice, whether true or false, has greatly harmed the weak in the Church of God, especially when it concerns prelates, 369. A prelate ought not to abandon the flock entrusted to him, even if not all those under him advance in the Lord, 377. An abbot cannot lay down the burden imposed upon him except with the permission of the archbishop and bishop, 377, 378. A shepherd ought not to abandon the flock entrusted to him because of slander, 330. See **Shepherd**. A provost is removed from his office by death, 182. A shepherd is to be recalled from a Church in which he cannot remain peacefully or prevail against evils, 360. A shepherd anxious about the burden imposed upon him, 236. He asks for the graces and virtues necessary to him, 236. The anxiety of prelates concerning their sins, 302. God often works more through the life of unlearned people (prelates) who seek the things of God than through the cleverness of the learned who seek what belongs to themselves, 354. Prelates are to be obeyed sincerely, 376. Subjects must not judge the deeds of prelates, 376, 381. The ordinances of prelates are to be received as though inspired by God, 381. As long as a prelate does not compel someone to turn from good toward evil, submission to him must not be abandoned, 314. One must not withdraw from an undisciplined prelate, even if he obstructs greater goods, 314. The wickedness and correction of the ruler of the Church, 181, 183. Prelates who, concerning God’s goods, seek not his profit but their own, and harm those whom they ought to have benefited, 182. Many prelates, as though concerned lest God’s property be destroyed in their hands, act so that God’s law may be scattered in their hearts, 338. A prelate who dissipates the goods of the Church, 182. The evil examples of prelates, 182. Angels report to God the evil works of prelates, 182. At the end, the Lord himself examines the deeds of rulers, 182. He who daily judges the actions of subjects through their rulers, 182. Benedict writes against the pride of priests and prelates, 384. See **Benedict**. The steward designates the ruler of the Church, 182. The bishop’s staff as a sign of pastoral office, 394.

**Foreknowledge.** To foreknow is nothing other than to know what is future, 124. God foreknows certain things as future through the free will of rational creatures, 124, 127. Foreknowledge exists when something is understood by a certain rational account, 71. Necessity of the thing follows from it, 71. God’s knowledge is not properly called foreknowledge, 71, 127. Rather, it is knowledge of what is present, 127. God foreknows only what is true, 127. God’s foreknowledge does not err, 127. Only what is future is foreknown, 123. God foreknows all future things, 123, 124. The things God foreknows must be future, 124, 125. Not everything he foreknows exists by necessity, 124. He foreknows certain things that come about through freedom of the will, 124, 127. He does not foreknow all future things as necessary, 124. Whatever God foreknows must be future in the manner in which it is foreknown, 124. If something is future without necessity, something must be future without any necessity whatsoever, 124. God does not simply foreknow that someone will sin or will not sin, 124. Rather, he foreknows that the person will sin or will not sin without necessity and by will alone, 124. God’s foreknowledge and freedom of choice stand together, 711, 123, 124, 125, 126, 127. Those who defend one side and deny the other are lost, 71. The necessity by which free things that are foreknown will be future descends from free will, 124, 125. If God foreknows something, it must be future; it is the same as saying, “If it will be, it will necessarily be,” 124. This necessity follows from the thing’s positing, 124. Consequent necessity neither compels nor prevents a thing from being or not being, 124. It signifies nothing other than that what will be cannot at the same time not be, 124. What is future cannot at the same time not be future, 124. A future thing must be future, 124. Before an action exists, it is not necessarily future, 124. For it can happen that it will not be future, 124. See **Future**. Whatever Scripture declares to be necessary concerning things that occur through free choice, it speaks of according to eternity, not according to time, 125. The force of eternity makes God’s foreknowledge and free choice not conflict, 125. It was not hidden from God what a human being was going to do when he created him, 87. No one can deviate from the order of divine foreknowledge, 151.

**Presence of God.** We are always in God’s sight, 84. God’s presence restrains sins, 193.

**Presumption.** See **Confidence**, **Mercy**, **Hope**.

**Pratellis**, abbot of, 451.

**Priests.** Concerning priests who had wives in England, 190. The marriages of priests condemned by the council under Lanfranc, 407. Anselm rejects them, 407, 408. King Henry approves them, 407. Priests keeping women are deprived of their benefices, [Col. 1118] 408. They are excommunicated, 408. Against priests who keep concubines, 140, 332, 438. Baptism is not to be received from them if others—whether clerics or laymen—are present, 438. The faithful ought not to attend priests celebrating who stink with manifest lust, 140, 332. This is so that, driven away even by human disgust, they may not dare to pollute sacred things, 332. What such men administer is therefore not to be despised, 332. But the men themselves are to be accursed, 332. Insofar as it concerns them, they themselves defile the sacred altars, 332. Concerning the sons of priests and concubines, 383. The sons of priests are to be excluded from their fathers’ prebends and from sacred orders, 354.

Princes ought to love justice, 376. See **King**. Princes are not lords of the Church but its advocates, 389, 391. See **Church**, **King**. Princes are especially bound to correct the evils of their subjects, 417. See **Correction**.

A beginning seems to belong only to a thing that is beginning, 57. A cause seems to belong only to some effect, 57. The name “effect” suits a thing that comes into being, 57. See **Cause**.

**Prior.** **Earlier.** A prior ought to agree with the abbot, 376. Some things are prior by nature although they are simultaneous in time, 114.

**Privation.** The absence of that which is something is not itself something, 67. Blindness is called something according to the form of speech, 67. In reality it is not something, 67. To have it is not to have something but to lack something, 67. Blindness is nothing other than lack of sight where sight ought to be, 67. The absence of sight is no more something where sight ought to be than where it ought not to be, 67. In what sense injustice or blindness is said to do something, 73.

**Privilege**, 437. See **Beccensis Prodigy**.

**Prodigy.** Signs signify something present; prodigies portend something future, 186. *Prodigia*, as though “things said beforehand” (*porro dicta*), 186. See **Miracles**.

**Progress.** As long as a person lives, he does nothing but go onward, 415. He is always either ascending or descending: ascending into heaven by living well, or descending into hell by living badly, 415, 452. This ascent or descent is recognized by the soul when it leaves the body, 415. Whoever ascends through good morals will be placed in heaven; whoever descends through evil morals will be buried in hell, 415. The Christian soul should attend carefully to whether it is ascending or descending, 415. Those who make progress ascend; those who fail descend, 175. The pursuit of progress, 312, 321, 327, 355, 372, 378. Careful examination of one’s progress, 312, 327, 452. The just person always strives to gain new increase, 176.

**Monastic profession**, 423. Formerly it was made by habit alone and by monastic conversion, 423. A monk’s surrender or obligation was made through the voluntary reception of the cowl, 350. See **Monk**, **Vow**.

The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets, so that it might not conflict with their judgment, 173.

**Prosperity**, 191, 192. The contrary wind is not adversity in the world but prosperity, 161. And then especially God is to be invoked, 161. It is a mark of great virtue to struggle with good fortune, 161. See **Adversity**, **Affliction**, **Tribulation**.

**Providence.** Everything is governed by none other than God, 28. Everything is governed not by chance but according to many considerations, 28. God cares for everything, 245. For he is Lord of all, 245. Everything is subject to God’s ordering, 129. We ought to pay more attention to what the Lord, whose we are, does with us than to what we ourselves want, since we do not belong to ourselves, 313. Whether we live or die, we belong not to ourselves but to the Lord, 313. See **God the Wise**, **God’s Will**, **God as the Cause of Things**.

**Prudence.** The first part of prudence is to assess the character of the person whom one is going to instruct, 107.

**Chastity; unchastity.** Impure thoughts and unchaste impulses, 249, 256. See **Concupiscence**, **Virginity**.

**Beauty.** The vanity of beauty, 197, 198. See **Cosmetics**, **Woman**.

**Pulse.** A book on the pulse: knowledge of it is not especially useful, 330. Mauritius had decided to transcribe it, 330. See **Mauritius**.

A point added to a point is only one point, 61.

**Purity.** See **Purity of Heart**, **Chastity**.

**Pusillanimity.** See **Confidence**, **Merciful God**, **Hope**.

## Q

**To seek.** What is sought is what is hidden and not possessed, 155.

**Quintinus (Saint).** The church of Beauvais, 406. Its canon Gunterius, 406. Odo, abbot of this church, 406. He is deposed, 406. See **Gunterius**, **Odo**.

## R

**Radulphus**, nephew of Bishop Gundulphus, 393.

**Radulphus of Chichester**, 410.

**Rainaldus**, kinsman of Anselm, 351, 352.

**Rainaldus**, archbishop of Reims; he convenes a council [Col. 1119] against the blasphemies of the cleric Roscelin, 357. See **Roscelin**.

**Rainaldus**, abbot, 339. At his request Anselm sends him the *Monologion*, 339.

**Rainaldus**, monk of Bec; Anselm sends him greetings, 374.

**Rainaldus** rejected the bishopric into which he had been unwillingly and improperly intruded, for the sake of truth, 405.

**Rainerus**, abbot of Mont-Sainte-Trinité, 352.

**Rainerus**, cleric of Countess Ida, was present at Anselm’s election as archbishop, 372.

**Ranulphus**, bishop, restored by the king to his bishopric at the command of Paschal II, 384. He is accused before the Roman pontiff of very grave crimes, 384. Paschal II entrusts Anselm with the examination of his case, 384.

**Ranulphus Flambardus**, a most infamous priest and chief of the tax collectors, 427. This simoniac was raised to the episcopate by William, king of the English, 427. He was captured by King Henry for money, 428. Anselm sent four bishops to him, 428. Later he secretly fled to Normandy, 428. He made himself lord of the pirates, 428.

**Reason** must be the chief ruler and judge of all that exists in a human being, 43.

**Reason**, which is the instrument of reasoning, is one in a human being, 133.

Just as it belongs to beasts to want nothing with reason, so it belongs to human beings to want nothing without reason, 100.

Human beings ought always to want nothing without reason, 100.

There may be several reasons for the same thing, any one of which by itself may be sufficient, 97.

God begins to call a person to account when, through weakness, he draws him to bed and to death, 167, 168.

Rational nature is nothing other than God, an angel, and the human soul, 98.

God made nothing more precious than rational nature, 87.

God made rational nature so that it might rejoice in him, 87.

The rational creature was made just, 77, 86, 87, and so that, by enjoying God, it might be blessed, 87.

A rational creature cannot have its first will from itself, 68.

Rational nature could be neither just nor blessed without the will for justice and blessedness, 133.

God willed to make rational nature just and blessed, so that it might enjoy him, 133.

God created it to understand and love him, 134.

Only the rational mind is capable of investigating the supreme nature, 24.

Rational nature was made for this purpose: to distinguish between good and evil, and between the greater and lesser good, 25, 86.

It receives the power of distinguishing so that it may hate and avoid evil, and love and choose good, 86.

And so that it may love and choose the greater good more strongly, 86, 27.

It distinguishes in vain if it does not love and avoid things according to its discernment, 25, 87.

It was made to love and choose the highest good above all things, 87.

Indeed, it was made to love nothing except that good or for the sake of it, 87.

Whoever loves the highest good for the sake of something else loves not the highest good itself but something else, 87. See **Love**, **Good**, **End**, **Human Being**, **Will**.

Nothing was naturally given to a rational creature so pre-eminent and so like the supreme wisdom as the capacity to remember, understand, and love what is best and greatest of all, 25.

Nothing else was implanted in any creature that so clearly bears the image of the Creator, 25. See **Image**.

A creature cannot understand God unless it is rational, 238.

Why God made rational nature capable of doing evil, although it was made in order to avoid evil, 65.

No nature is indebted to justice except the rational, 98.

No nature other than the rational is receptive of justice, 98.

It is not itself the good by which it is to become blessed, 182.

Rational nature was created in justice, 101.

Nor can God create it unjust, 103.

It is not fitting for God to compel it to be miserable without guilt, or to be subject to any evil, 77, 102, 103.

Whoever does not understand this does not understand what is unfitting for God, 102.

Therefore God did not make it miserable without a preceding fault, 134.

God will not allow it to perish utterly, 87.

A rational creature ought to dispose a non-rational nature in accordance with God’s will, 238.

Nothing lacking reason can incite either to sin or to virtue, 107.

Whatever is more fitting and more rational must exist, 92.

**Rectitude.** See **Justice**.

**Redemption.** The restoration of human nature ought not to have been left undone, 94.

The redemption of humanity could be accomplished by no other than a person of God, 76.

Humanity is the servant of the one by whom it is redeemed, 76.

Humanity ought to have been restored to the dignity it would have possessed had it not sinned, 76.

A human being whom God might have generated from the sinful mass of the human race, while himself having no sin, could not redeem sinners, 102.

A human being who is not God is not sufficient to redeem others, 102.

It was impossible for the world to be saved in any other way than through the death of the God-human, 74, 79.

No one other than the Son of God could save the world, 78.

The world could not be saved except by Christ’s death, 164.

God did not need to redeem the world by his death, 222.

But human nature needed the human being to satisfy God in this way [Col. 1120], 222.

The redemption of human nature through Christ, 221, 222, 223.

A sinner cannot return to life in any other way than by being redeemed through Christ’s blood, 213.

The power of sinners’ salvation is Christ’s power, 221.

The power of Christ redeeming the world is a hidden strength, a concealed power, an unseen virtue, 222.

What can a human being commit that the Son of God, having become human, would not have redeemed? 247.

A human being is not redeemed by Christ’s death only once, but whenever he returns with worthy repentance, 222. See **Christ**, **Grace**, **Incarnation**, **Salvation**, **Satisfaction**.

**The bishop of Hereford**, a man very well educated in ecclesiastical disciplines, 428. He was elected in place of the archbishop of York, 428. The king forbids the pallium to be given to him, 428. Anselm asks that it be given to him, 428.

The kingdom of God is within us, 203.

God proclaims that he has the kingdom of heaven for sale, 349.

He asks nothing for it except love, without which it ought not to be given, 349.

“Give love, then, and receive the kingdom; love, and possess it,” 349.

To reign in heaven is to have one will with God, the angels, and holy human beings through love, and to exercise all power as one, 349.

The kingdom of heaven is seized by the violence of extraordinary virtue, 177.

Kingdoms are granted to evil men; power to crime, 198. See **King**.

**Rule.** See **Saint Benedict**, **Saint Dunstan**.

**Relation, relative.** No relative is substantial to that of which it is predicated relatively, 91.

Not even relatives themselves, or relations themselves, exist through one another, but through their subjects, 5.

There is no relation of father without the relation of son, just as there is no relation of son without the relation of father, 53. See **Son**, **Father**.

There are several relations in God, 43.

Relations in the divine persons do not introduce plurality into unity, nor does unity introduce singularity into the relations, 61.

When substance has being from substance, two relations incapable of being joined arise there, 50. See **Accident**, **Son**, **Father**, **Trinity**.

**Religious.** See **Monk**.

**Of Reims.** The Council of Reims under Archbishop Rainaldus against Roscelin’s errors, 357.

**Remission.** See **Injury**, **Redemption**, **Satisfaction**, **Vengeance**.

**Renerius**, 430. Anselm commends him to King Baldwin, 430. He belonged to King Baldwin’s household, 430.

**Renewal.** See **Christ**, **Grace**, **Redemption**.

**Rest.** Whoever does not cease from evil denies God rest, 155.

What it means to seek rest for God, 155.

God says that he labors when he endures the harsh perversities of human beings, 155.

God labored in mortal flesh because of our weakness, 155.

God finds rest in those who have ceased to sin and live holily and justly, 155.

After labor, rest is usually sought, 155.

In this life rest should not be requested, 162. See **Labor**, **Way**.

**Thing.** We call anything a “thing” that we in some way say is something, 43.

Whether there are three things in God. See **Roscelin**, **Trinity**.

**To answer.** It is not always easy to answer a foolish person wisely, 73.

An appropriate question often facilitates an answer, while an inappropriate one makes it more difficult, 73.

God’s answering consists in teaching through hidden inspirations the person who has humbly acknowledged that he does not know, 172.

God answers those who speak when he appears to us who love him, 172.

**Resurrection.** The future resurrection of the dead, 87.

Humanity will be restored together with its body, 87.

A human being ought to be restored in the condition he would have had if he had not sinned, 87.

The resurrection of bodies, 134.

The blessed souls await it, 134.

The body will rise again at the end, 178.

When the dead rise, this is the work of God’s will alone, 101.

A king is not the lord but the guardian of the Church, 429.

The king is the advocate of the Church, 429, 375.

Many wicked kings think that the Church has been given to them as though they were its lord, 429. See **Church**.

Let the king consider whom he appoints to ecclesiastical dignities, 428.

In these matters he should not listen to unfaithful counselors, 428.

It is more beneficial for no human being than for a king to submit himself to the law of God, 402.

No one withdraws from that law more dangerously than a king, 402.

It is no slight sin for a king to strip a bishop of his possessions, 402, 408.

What sort of men kings ought to show themselves to be, 414.

Kings rule well when they rule over themselves, 414.

They do not subject themselves to vices but overcome them through steadfast courage, 414.

We are truly kings if we rule our disordered impulses and recall them to the will of the Creator, 211.

Our soul becomes queen when it is joined to Christ in mind, 211.

Kings and powerful men waste away under cares and fear, 196.

After sin, the human being is a petty king, 185.

The coronation of kings, 298.

The kings of the Franks favor Saint Anselm and write to him. See **Louis**, **Philip**.

**Richard**, monk: the bishop-elect Gundulphus takes him into his service, 337. Anselm commends him to Gundulphus, 337. He is coming to Bec, 343.

**Richard**, monk of Bec, 342, 343, 378. Before becoming a monk, during an illness he vowed that he would go to Saint Giles, 378. Anselm writes to him that this vow did not bind him after his monastic profession [Col. 1121], 378. He releases him from this vow, 378. He is appointed the first abbot of the monastery of Saint Werburga, 383. See **the monastery of Saint Werburga**.

**Richard**, servant of Gilbert, abbot of Westminster, 359. God himself excused him from the crime laid to his charge, 359.

**Richard**, abbot of Pratellis: his commentaries on the Book of Genesis, 451.

**Richeza**, or **Richera**, Anselm’s sister and the wife of Burgundius, 382, 392. Anselm urges her, since she is without children, to serve God alone with her husband, 383.

**Robert**, bishop of Lincoln, 401, 444.

**Robert**, bishop of Chester, 410.

**Robert**, abbot, consults Anselm about a man who intends to sin but is divinely prevented, 355.

**Robert**, cleric of the king’s chancellor, 444.

Robert the cleric was with Anselm during his exile, 438, 439.

**Robert**, monk: Anselm commends himself to his prayers, 312. He insists that Anselm give thanks to Gundulphus for his benefactions, 314. Through him Anselm commends Girard to Lanfranc, 316. Through him Anselm writes to Lanfranc, 320. Through him Anselm sends his *Monologion* to Lanfranc, 336. Anselm entrusted him with conducting legal proceedings, 351. He leaves the monastery of Bec and is recalled by Anselm, 351. At his insistence Anselm intercedes for Gilbert with Walchelin, bishop of Salisbury, 352.

**Robert**, monk of Canterbury, 395, 438. He guards the archbishop’s house while Anselm is traveling to Rome, 395.

**Robert of Briodna**, monk, 359. His character, 360. Anselm commends him to Walter’s gentleness, 359.

**Robert**, son of Count Hugh, monk of Saint-Evroul, 451, 432. He was intruded by force as abbot of Saint Edmund’s, 432.

**Robert**, count of Normandy, 367, 368, 403, 446. Prince of all Normandy, 413. Brother of Henry, king of the English, 403, 446. He labored for the liberation of the Church in Asia, 382. He complains that the king of the English invaded the kingdom after breaking his oath, 382. He excuses himself for not having rightly thought or spoken about the election Anselm had accepted as archbishop of Canterbury, 371. He asks Anselm’s advice about appointing an abbot of Bec, 371. Anselm writes to him that William the prior of Pexio should be elected abbot of Bec, 371. With his favor the abbot of Bec is elected, 367. He unjustly harasses William, bishop of Winchester, 403. The king demanded that William perform homage to him for the castle that he held from Count Robert, 403. He is held captive by the king, 447. He had married a kinswoman, 447.

**Robert**, count and prince of Flanders, 376, 430. Anselm urges him to love justice more and more, 376. He commends to him the brothers whom Anselm sends to Flanders, 376. He granted the regular election of abbots, 430.

**Robert**, count, brother of Count Ernulphus, 433.

To Robert, count of Meulan, because he favors the king in the matter of investitures, the pope threatens the wrath of God, 443. He had promised to act with the king so that he would abandon the investitures, 443. See **Meulan**.

**Robert of Leminges**, 437. If he becomes a monk, Anselm grants his wife the lands that she held from the Church of Canterbury, 437.

**Robert of Montfort**, 398.

**Lord Robert**, brother of Eustace, 397. Through him the abbess of Caen consults Anselm, 397. He accompanied Anselm on his journey to Rome, 398.

**Robert**, son of Haimo: he is a witness in the letter by which Henry, king of England, recalls Anselm, 382.

**Robert**, son of Warson, 393.

**Robert**, a Christian converted from Judaism, 409. Anselm commends him to the alms of Prior Ernulphus and Archdeacon William, 409. Anselm commends him to Bishop Gundulphus and Prior Ernulphus, 444.

**Robert**, servant of the poor, 437.

**Robert** cares for the servants of God, 414, 415.

**Rodulphus**, bishop of Chichester: Anselm complains to him about his archdeacon, 450.

**Rodulphus**, abbot, 360. Anselm sends him greetings, 360.

**Rodulphus**, abbot of Sées, consults Anselm about a monk ordained by a bishop while under an interdict, and about a monk who sought herbs for a woman with which to kill her husband, 374.

**Rodulphus**, monk: the congregation of Bec never said that it would not provide him with books, 315, etc. Anselm excuses himself for having called him “lord” and consoles him concerning his absence, 316. He urges him to undertake the duties of his office, 316. Anselm implores him to copy an antiphonary with musical notation, 319. A book to be lent out of charity, 315, etc. Rodulphus the monk was captured with his servants, after the soldiers had taken away the horses, 328. Anselm writes that what he had ordered concerning his horse and the monk of Saint-Germain should be done, 346.

**Rodulphus**, novice of Bec, 344. Anselm congratulates him on his conversion [Col. 1122], 344. Anselm warns him to guard against the temptations of the devil, 344 and 335. He was from Beauvais, 356. Formerly the companion of Lambert, a nobleman, 356.

**Rogerius**, monk of Bayeux, 318.

**Rogerius**, a monk, sent some monks ahead to Bec, 336. Anselm awaits his arrival, as he had promised, 336.

Anselm commends to Roger, abbot, the people of Bec, distressed by his separation from them, 367. He protests to him that he undertook the burden of the archbishopric not from any desire but from charity and obedience, 368.

**Roger**, monk of Caen, 336. Anselm sends him greetings, 336.

**Roger**, abbot of Saint-Evroul in Normandy, 326, 431, 432. He uses force against the election of the abbot of Saint Edmund’s in England, 432. See **the monastery of Saint Edmund**. He asked Anselm to commend his brother to the charity of Helgot, the prior, 326.

**Roger**, friend of Anselm and of William, bishop of Winchester, 433.

**Roger Puntel**, 438.

**Rohaidis**, a lady: her benefactions to the people of Bec, 342. She asks Anselm to send monks to England; he sends them and commends them to her charity, 342.

**The Roman Church.** Whoever takes away the property of the Roman Church is guilty of sacrilege against all the churches, 382.

**Roman.** The Roman Council under Urban II against investitures, 394, 427, 428, 429. It excommunicates the king and all laymen who grant investitures, as well as those who receive them and become their men, 394, 428, 429. Anselm attended it, 429. Its decrees against investitures, 429. The king of England and the bishops refuse to accept them, 429.

The Roman Council under Paschal II, 436, 441. It excommunicated those who advised investitures as well as those who received them, 436. It was held during Lent, 436.

**Romescot**, or Saint Peter’s tax in England, 353, 382, 398, 434.

**Roscelin’s erroneous reasoning**, 412, 43 and following, 353, 357. It is refuted, 43 and following, 357.

He taught that there was in God a plurality of substance like that possessed by several angels or several souls, 41, 42, 43, 357.

He said that either there are three things in God, or the Father and the Holy Spirit are incarnate equally with the Son, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, etc., 357.

Rainaldus, archbishop of Reims, convenes a council against Roscelin, 41, 357.

At the council he falsely renounced this error solely from fear of death, 41, 42.

He himself persists in his error, 42.

At that time many people were laboring over Roscelin’s question, 42.

The comparison “just as there are three angels,” etc., does not belong to Roscelin but to the person who entrusted his question to Anselm, 44.

Roscelin’s reasoning either denies, with Sabellius, that there are three persons in God, or introduces three gods, 44.

It destroys our faith, 44.

On Roscelin’s behalf it is answered that these three things are not three gods, 44.

It is shown that if there are three things, there are three gods, 44.

Roscelin limps on both feet in the matter of the Incarnation of the Word, 46.

He dreams that a human being was assumed by the Word more into unity of nature than into unity of person, 46.

He did not deny that there are three persons in God, nor that the Son is incarnate, 45, 46.

He said that Lanfranc and Anselm held his view, 357.

Anselm’s letter against Roscelin’s statements was begun before Anselm sailed to England for the second time, 360.

**Rumsey**, a monastery of nuns, 386. There a certain dead man was venerated as a saint, 386. Anselm forbids this, 306.

## S
## Priest, priesthood

A priest is a mediator between God and the people, 298. Whoever is called a priest but does not fulfill the priest’s office by worthy works ought above all to fear concerning the dignity of this office, 265. The dignity of the priesthood is worthy of more than can be estimated, 261. With what reverence and purity of conscience the ministry of the priesthood—that is, the mystery of Christ’s body and blood—must be performed, 264–269. Service at the altar is a very salutary thing for a good priest, 264. But it is very dangerous for one who handles it unworthily, 264. It is salutary counsel to cease from sins and render service at the altar to God, 264. It is better to serve God at the altar than, through fear of sin, to abandon his service and lie more securely in the condemnation of sins, 264, 269. It is better that God should strike us for some offense in his service, while we nevertheless perform his service, than that he should condemn us because, through fear of sin, we refuse to perform his service, 264. If a priest’s sins are criminal, it is more useful for him humbly to abstain from offering the sacrifice than, through presumption, to incur greater condemnation by offering it; he should do so until, after beginning or completing his penance, he can approach the service of the altar more securely, 264. Those who are to be barred from the priesthood, 425.

## Sacrifice

The offering of the sacrifice is performed by a priest, 264. The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood on the altar, 266–269. The sacrifice must be made from bread, whether unleavened or leavened, 136. Our sacrifice is offered only on the altar, 423. Whether it is more useful to abandon the office of the altar or to perform it, 264, etc. See Unleavened bread, Eucharist, Mass, Priest.

## World, worldly matters

See Eternity, World.

The monastery of Séez, 413.

**SALATHIEL** appears to have had two fathers, 174.

## Salvation

A creature cannot save a creature, 129, nor give it that by which it may be saved, 129. Our salvation is from God, 231. There is no salvation in anyone other than Christ, 176. Whoever wishes to be saved must have many more good merits than bad ones, 390. Of adults, whoever is saved is saved through justice, 128. See Incarnation, Redemption, Satisfaction.

**SALVINUS**, a monk and friend of Gondulf, resides at Bec and obtains pardon for a certain fault from Prior Henry, 329.

**SAMSON**, bishop of Worcester, 410, 449. Anselm implores his assistance against the arrogance of Thomas, the elected bishop of York, 449. He promises Anselm all his help, 450.

**SAMUEL**, bishop of Dublin, 393, 434. He succeeded his uncle Donatus, 393. He unjustly expels the monks of his church, 393. He has the cross carried before him, 393. He distributes church property as though it were his own, 393.

**SAMUEL**, a monk of Caen, 336. Anselm greets him, 336.

A nun has cast off the holy habit, 422–423. She cannot be saved unless she returns to the habit and religious profession she abandoned, 423.

The cult of the saints, 430. See Anhelitz.

Sandowik, the house of Sandowik, 442.

## Wisdom

On wisdom, 193.

The wisdom of God. See God.

A rational creature becomes wise through participation in God, 182. To be wise without God is to be foolish, 245. In order that we may learn wisdom, the heart must be cleansed by faith, 42. The eyes must be enlightened through obedience to the commandments, 42. Through obedience to God’s testimonies we must become little ones, 42. The spirit of wisdom is sweeter than honey, 158. Dialecticians cannot understand human wisdom as anything other than the soul, 42.

## Satisfaction

As long as someone does not repay what he has stolen, he remains in guilt, 79. Human nature sins as long as it does not make satisfaction for Adam’s sin, 100. No one can be released from sin unless he repays what he took by sinning, 84. The one who makes satisfaction must be of the same kind as the one who sinned, 88. The remission of sin does not take place unless the debt has been repaid and complete satisfaction has been made according to the magnitude of the sin, 86, 222. God’s justice requires that a human being return to God what he took away, 85. Either the sinner pays what he owes, or God takes it from one unwilling to pay, 80. Every sin must necessarily be followed by satisfaction or punishment, 81. After sin, a human being cannot be saved without satisfaction for sin, 83, 86; nor raised to equality with the angels, 83; nor restored to the good for which he was made, 103; nor rescued from the evils into which he fell, 103.

God will perfect in human nature what he began—that is, he will bring it to blessedness, 87–91. This cannot happen except through satisfaction for sin, 87–91, and unless there is someone who pays God something greater than everything that is not God, 87. No sinner can make this satisfaction, 87. No one can make it except God, 88. And no one ought to make it except a human being, 88. Nothing is above everything that is not God except God, 88. Therefore God must make this satisfaction as a human being, 88, 91.

Human nature by itself is unable either to make satisfaction for sin or to recover the justice it abandoned, especially in infants, 98. Whatever is not God could not suffice to make satisfaction to God, 222. Nothing created can satisfy God for even the smallest sin, 84. A human being cannot return to God what he owes him for sin, 86. Satisfaction for sin cannot be found outside the Christian faith, 86. God does not demand from any sinner more than he owes, 104. No sinner can repay as much as he owes, 104.

The satisfaction that every sinner ought to make, 79, 84. For complete satisfaction, the sinner must give something of his own which is not owed to God and cannot be demanded from him, 79; and something that surpasses everything that is not God, 85, 222; and something greater than that for which he ought not to have sinned, 222. It is not enough to return what was taken away; for the insult inflicted, the sinner must return more than he took, 79. One gives from debt who gives what he does not have from himself, 84. He must not count as payment of the debt what he owes because of sin, 84. Satisfaction must correspond to the measure of the sin, 84.

The satisfactions that a human being pays to God are penance, a contrite heart, abstinence, bodily labor, the mercy of giving and forgiving, [Col. 1124] and obedience, 84. A human being owes all these things to God even if he has not sinned, 84. A human being cannot satisfy God except by conquering the devil, 85. This itself belongs to the payment of sin: that the sinner should supplicate, 84. Whoever corrects everything he has done wrongly and thereafter lives religiously returns everything he owed the Lord, 169. See Christ, Injury, Penance, Redemption.

**SAUL.** How he is said to have been one year old and to have reigned only two years, 175.

## Schism

Two men contend for the papacy, 444. The schism between Urban and Guibert, 374. See Heretics.

## Knowledge

On knowledge, 193. The spirit of knowledge is fitting for those who mourn, 159. From God’s light shines every truth that gives light to a rational being, 33. He is insane who asserts that something is impossible because he does not know how it exists, 86. Whatever is truly inferred by necessary reasoning to exist must not be reduced to doubt, even if reason does not perceive how it exists, 86, 91. What cannot exist cannot be inferred with certainty to exist, 71. Knowledge is nothing other than truth, 123.

Creatures exist in themselves otherwise than in our knowledge, 17. In themselves they exist through their essence, 17. In our knowledge their essences are not present, but likenesses of them are, 17. They exist more truly in themselves than in our knowledge, 17. See Existence, Idea, Intellect.

No one knows the good perfectly except one who knows how to distinguish it from evil, 81. No one can distinguish good from evil who is ignorant of evil, 91. Many things are retained in memory and understood that are not loved, 21. See Love. Memory and understanding of a thing are useless unless the thing itself is loved or rejected, 20. One should not be said to have a correct understanding who does not will correctly according to it, 128. Whoever adds to knowledge adds also to sorrow, 314. Your knowledge is nothing if another knows what this is like, 218. The vanity of knowledge, 199.

## Holy Scripture

We preach nothing usefully that holy Scripture has not brought forth or does not contain within itself, 130. Just as Scripture opposes no truth, so it favors no falsehood, 130. Whatever openly contradicts holy Scripture is false, 83. Divine Scripture often asserts that something is what it is not now, because it is certainly going to be, 100. Certain things in Scripture are spoken not historically but spiritually, 186. In holy Scripture one thing often signifies different things, 178. In Scripture part of the years is sometimes omitted, 175. Thus Saul is said to be one year old and to have reigned only two years, 175.

One must not answer with the authority of holy Scripture someone who interprets it with a perverse meaning or does not believe it, 432. Rather, error must be demonstrated by reasoning to someone who does not heed holy Scripture, 432. How things omitted in Scripture are to be understood, 58. By the very fact that holy Scripture does not deny what is said by reason, it is accepted on its authority, 130. Whatever is clearly inferred from it by reason is accepted on its authority, 130. If Scripture unmistakably conflicts with our understanding, we must believe that our reasoning is supported by no truth, 130. Holy Scripture contains the authority of every truth that reason infers, since it either openly affirms it or in no way denies it, 130.

Study of holy Scripture is enjoined above all, 312. Everyone must approach questions concerning the sacred page with the greatest caution, 42. Whoever seeks to live piously meditates on holy Scripture, 159. He does not criticize what he does not yet understand. The more we are nourished in holy Scripture by those things that feed obedience, the more sublimely we are raised to those things that satisfy through understanding, 42. Whoever does not meditate on God’s testimonies does not obtain understanding of the faith, 42. See Faith.

## Secret

A good intention must not be publicized, 346.

**SEIT**, a virgin, 414.

## Seed

“Seed” is said equivocally: of what is sperm and of those who derive from seed, 107. When seed is called accursed and wicked, the term is taken for those who derive from seed, that is, for a race or lineage, 107. To exist and to be reckoned in the seed is not something vain and empty, 104. Things truly exist in seeds before they exist in themselves, 104. That guilt is not in the seed, 107. Human seed is not capable of justice before it becomes a human being, 98. In the seed there is neither the tinder of sin nor corruption of nature, 107. What cannot have either blame or praise cannot be the tinder of sin or virtue. See Original sin, Predication.

The disadvantages of old age, 197.

## Sense, sensible, to perceive

The senses are about the body and in the body, 31. Only corporeal things are sensible, 31. Someone may be said to perceive who in some way knows, 31. To perceive is nothing other than to know or to be directed toward knowing, 31.

## The Seventy Interpreters

The seventy elders held the teaching office in the synagogue from the time of Moses, 175. They received it from the spirit of Moses, 175. They learned the Law from Moses’s own testing, 175. If something had been omitted and could be supplied, or if it could be interpreted differently, they knew how to do so, 175. The Seventy Interpreters do not err even when they say what the Hebrews leave unsaid, 175.

## Speech

What speech ought to be like, 192. To speak about God is complete refreshment, 253. See Conversation.

## Severity

On severity, 193.

**SEVERUS (St.).** The monastery of Saint Severus, 392.

## Sex

In natures that have a distinction of sex, being a father or son belongs to the better sex, 19, while being a mother or daughter belongs to the lesser, 19. In some beings the female sex is always greater and stronger, while the male is lesser and weaker, 19.

**SIMEON**, that is, “hearing” or “one who hears sorrow,” 170.

## Likeness

To wish to be like God is not evil, 70. The Son of God wishes to be like the Father, 70. Would that desire be unjust which wished to be like God? 68. See Image.

Simony, or even suspicion of it, must be avoided, 403, 410. The root of simony is pleasing secular persons in order to obtain ecclesiastical honors, 383. It is not permitted to accept a church from a king in exchange for the lands of another church which the king has seized, 384. Simoniacs, even if they pass into the monastic order, cannot be restored by an abbot, 425.

## Simple

It is false that no nature is simple, 45. See Composite.

## Zion

Zion means watchtower or contemplation, 156. Mount Zion is the Church of the saints, 156.

## Thirst

Those who love the true good are always thirsty, 159.

## Sodom

The Sodomitic sin was public in England, 390.

The sun in two senses, 178. Nothing is clearer than the sun, 163.

## Sleep

The will has never been so constituted that it would at some time wish never to sleep, 132. The sleep and vigils of the saints, 166. Those who fall asleep with respect to outward things and keep watch in inward things penetrate the inner mysteries, 166.

## Hope

Besides the love of God, hope is necessary, 26. Holy hope is the hope of attaining the kingdom of God and his justice, 158. No one but Christ engenders hope concerning holy things, 158. All hope rests on Christ’s passion and merits, 247. God does not abandon those who hope in him, 236. One must never despair of God’s mercy, 212 and following, 250. Whoever despairs of God is separated from him, 300. Hope in mercy in such a way that you fear justice, 191. Whoever sins in hope of remission does not deserve remission, 346. See Merciful God.

## Spirit

No essence is known to be more worthy than spirit and body, 14. Spirit is an essence more worthy than body, 14, 31. See Soul, Body, Mind.
