Created spirits are both circumscribed and uncircumscribed, 32. See Soul, Place. Created spirits are in some respect uncircumscribed and eternal, 32. See Eternity, Place.

## The Holy Spirit

If there were never anything other than the supreme Spirit, the Father and the Son would nevertheless love themselves and each other, 211. The love of the supreme Spirit is the supreme Spirit, 21–22; this love is one and common to the Father and the Son, 34. The love of the Father and the Son is not unequal to the Father and the Son, 34, because the Father and the Son love one another as much as they are good, 34.

The Holy Spirit is not something other than the Father and the Son, 34, because from supreme simplicity nothing can proceed other than what the thing from which it proceeds is, 34. He is the love of the Father and the Son, and proceeds from both through a certain ineffable breathing of their own, 22. He is the communion of the Father and the Son, 22. Therefore he assumes as a proper name a name common to them, 22. By the name “Spirit” it is indicated that love knows the very thing that the Father and the Son know, 22. The love of the Father and the Son is supreme wisdom, supreme truth, supreme goodness, and whatever may be said of the substance of the supreme Spirit, 22. The love of the supreme Spirit is not something other, but the very same thing that the Father and the Son are, namely, the supreme essence, 21–22, 56. The love of the supreme Spirit proceeds from the fact that he remembers himself and understands himself, 211. Love proceeds ineffably from the unchangeable essence, not by departing from it but by existing from it, 22.

The love of the Father and the Son alone is neither begotten nor unbegotten, 22, because it is neither the Son nor wholly unrelated to another, 22. The supreme essence cannot more suitably be said to emit love than by breathing, 22. The love of the supreme essence may fittingly be called its spirit, 22. The name “Holy Spirit” is not alien to the Father and the Son, 43, because each is spirit and holy, 43. Each love is uncreated and creator, 22. The Spirit of the Father and the Son is the essence, wisdom, and power of the Father and the Son, 22, because the Spirit has exactly the same essence, wisdom, and power as the Father and the Son, 22. God is not greater than the Holy Spirit, 58.

The Holy Spirit is the spirit of someone, 49. The name “Holy Spirit” is used as a relative name, 49, and signifies someone’s spirit, 49. By the name “Holy Spirit,” spirit is not understood absolutely, but the Spirit of God, 49. The Holy Spirit is God from God by proceeding, 49–50, 53. Two processions of the Holy Spirit may be distinguished: first, by which he exists from the Father; second, by which he is given or sent, 53.

The Spirit of God is of the essence of God and proceeds from the divine essence, 54, 57, 55. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth and lips, 54–55, and proceeds from the one whose mouth or lips he is the Spirit, 55. The Holy Spirit is not given by the Father to the Son as to one in need or less perfect, 54. The Father and the Son emit love not from their relations but from their very essence, 21, 57–58. The Holy Spirit is not from relation, 53, 56. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the deity of the Father, not from fatherhood, 56. He is not from that by which the Father and the Son are distinct from each other, but from the divine essence in which they are one, 57.

A certain bishop who favored the Greeks held that the Holy Spirit is constituted by not having being from the Father, 52. He was a person of no small authority among his own people, 52. Why Anselm did not answer him immediately, 52. The Holy Spirit is one and the same God as the Father, 52, 60. The Holy Spirit did not exist before he was distinct from the Father, 52. If the Holy Spirit is from no one, he is not distinct from the Father, and there are only two persons in God, 52. The Holy Spirit is not distinct from the Father because the Father has a Son while he does not, 52, nor because he proceeds from someone while the Father proceeds from no one, 52. Nor is he distinct because he is the Spirit of the Father, if he does not have his being from him, 52. Nevertheless, by this it can be proved that they are distinct from one another, 52.

If the Holy Spirit is not from the Father, it cannot be discovered from where he is distinct from the Father, 52, 60. Through procession he has his being from the Father, and by this he is distinct from the Father, 53. The Holy Spirit is not something other than the Father except because he has from him the being that he has, 52, 61. The Son and the Holy Spirit have their being from the Father, 51, but in different ways: the one by being born, the other by proceeding, 51, 60. The Son is from God by being born; the Holy Spirit by proceeding, 57. If the Son and the Holy Spirit were not many through some other distinction, they would be distinct solely because the one exists by proceeding and the other by being born, 51, 60.

The Son and the Holy Spirit are related to one another by the very difference between birth and procession, as distinct and other from one another, 50. The Son is understood to be from the Father in one way, and the Holy Spirit in another, 50. The Son is from God who is his Father, 50. The Holy Spirit is not from God as his Father, but from God who is the Father, 50.

The Holy Spirit, or the love of the supreme Spirit, proceeds from the Father and the Son, 21, 34, 49. The Holy Spirit is proceeding eternity, 48. When love is understood to proceed from the Father and the Son, it does not immediately display the image of the one from whom it is, 21. Therefore it is not their son, 21. If the love of the Father and the Son were their offspring, either one would be father and the other mother, or both would be father or both mother, 21. It is contradictory to call the Father and the Son two fathers, or to make one the father and the other the mother of love, 21.

Although the Spirit is memory and understanding, he is not the Father or the Son, 23–24, because he is neither begetting memory nor begotten understanding, 24, but whatever he is, he proceeds, 24. The Father and the Son do not make or beget, but breathe their love, 22. The name “birth” does not apply to the procession of the Holy Spirit, 57, 61. Love proceeding from the supreme Spirit is not wholly unbegotten, nor is it properly begotten like the Word, 22. Love proceeding from the Father and the Son is not the Son of the Father or of the Son, 21–22.

The Holy Spirit cannot be the Son, 50–51, 60: first, because the Holy Spirit is from the Father by proceeding, while the Son is from him by being born, 60; and second, because the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from the Son, 51, 60. We altogether deny that the Spirit is the Son, 53. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and yet is not the Son, 49–50. Nor is the one from whom he is his father, 50.

The Spirit is called the Spirit of God, 49, 58–59, because he proceeds from God, 59. He is the Spirit of the Father because he proceeds from the Father, 49, 58–59. He is also called and believed to be the Spirit of the Son, 49, 51, 54, 58–60. The Greeks say that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son because he is given by the Son, 59. But this is read in no Scripture and does not follow from any Scripture, 59.

The Holy Spirit is not called the Spirit of God as a possession or as a member, 38. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is expressed when the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son, 58. If he is not from the Son, the Holy Spirit is no more the Son’s than the Son is the Holy Spirit’s, 56, 60. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son because he is from him, 54.

The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is proved, 51 and following. Either the Father is from the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit is from the Father, 51. Either the Son is from the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit is from the Son, 51, etc., 52. Either the Son is from the Holy Spirit as he is from the Father, or the Holy Spirit is from the Son as he is from the Father, 51, 60. By the fact that the Holy Spirit is God from God, it is proved that he is from the Son, 52–53. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father entails his procession from the Son, 53, 55. What proceeds from the deity of the Father also proceeds from the deity of the Son, 59.

The Holy Spirit is from the essence of the Father and the Son, 56–57. This essence is the very essence of the Holy Spirit, 57. Yet he is not from himself, 57, but only from the Father and the Son, 57. That from which the Holy Spirit is does not belong more to the Father than to the Son, 57–58. Therefore it cannot be understood why he should be more from the Father than from the Son, 57.

It is not stated in the Creed that the Holy Spirit is God from God, 53. The love of the supreme Spirit proceeds not from that in which the Father and the Son are many, but from that in which they are one, 21, 57–59. The essence of the Holy Spirit is from the essence of the Father, 58. Hence it is necessary that the Holy Spirit be from the Son, 58. Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because he proceeds from the one true God who is Father and Son, 53, etc.

For the sole reason that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, the Son cannot be from the Holy Spirit, 60. The Son does not more properly proceed from the Father than the Holy Spirit from the Son, 57. Therefore the Son is not from the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is from the Son, 61. And therefore the Holy Spirit is from the Son because the Son is not from him, 61.

The Holy Spirit does not relate differently to the Father and to the Son, 54. Nor is he more one’s than the other’s, 54. It is impossible to show how the Holy Spirit does not proceed from both, 54. If the Holy Spirit is not from both, both do not send him, 54, and he is not of both, 54. Nor does the Son give him more than he gives the Son, 54. The Holy Spirit is no more the Son’s than the Son is the Holy Spirit’s, 54.

When the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, he also proceeds from the Son, 56–57. The Holy Spirit is not among those things that exist through the Son, 56. By receiving wisdom from the Son, the Holy Spirit receives essence from him, 55; that is, he has essence from the essence of the Son, 55. The Lord’s breathing upon the disciples signifies nothing more suitably than that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, 54, 53. Just as a lake is from a stream and a spring, so the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, 57.

When the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, the Son is not excluded, 58. If it is not true that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, the Christian faith and God’s authority are destroyed, 60. If it is true, it brings about many truths, 60. Among the things the Church believes, and as a consequence of them, is contained the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, 58–60. Divine authority sufficiently affirms this procession when it asserts the basis from which it is proved and teaches nothing by which it is denied, 60.

All peoples and kingdoms that use Latin letters agree alike that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, 59. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is proved by the Greeks’ own arguments, 49. The Greeks do not deny that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, 49, 58. The faith of the Greeks concerning the Holy Spirit, 49–50, 52, 57–59. The Greeks confess that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father, and the Spirit of the Son, 58. The Greeks assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, 56, but they do not prove it, 56. The Greeks grant that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and from the Son, as a lake is from a spring and a stream, 57. They dispute only about the name “procession,” 57.

The Greeks criticize the Latins because *Filioque* (“and from the Son”) was added to the Creed, 52, 59. Other additions to the Creed, 32, 53, 59. The Father and the Son are not two causes but one cause of the Holy Spirit, 57. Nor are they two principles of him but one, 57, 59. He proceeds not from them as from two springs but from one spring, 59. The Holy Spirit is not more, or more principally, from the Father than from the Son, 59–60. The Holy Spirit is principally from the Father in the sense that the Son has from the Father that the Holy Spirit should be from him, 60.

He is not first from the Father rather than from the Son, 57, 59, nor from the Son rather than from the Father, 59. Nor is he greater or lesser by existing from the Father than by existing from the Son, 59. He is neither more nor less from one than from the other, 59, but once and wholly from the whole and simple one God, 59.

Love does not proceed differently from the Father than from the Son, 21. The Father and the Son have exactly the same relation to love, 21. From the Father alone proceeds the whole love of the supreme Spirit, 21; from the Son alone, the whole, 21. From the Father and the Son there do not proceed two wholes, but one and the same whole love, 21. Whether there are two loves, one proceeding from the Father and another from the Son; or one love, not whole but partly proceeding from the Father and partly from the Son; or one whole and identical love from each individually, 21.

Receiving essence from the Father, from which the Holy Spirit proceeds, is not the same as receiving the Holy Spirit from the Father, 54. The Holy Spirit does not leave God when he proceeds from God, 61. He is not outside the Father and the Son, nor are the Father and the Son outside the Holy Spirit, 58. He is not distinct from the Father precisely because he is sent, 52–53. He is from the Father before creation, 53. He is sent and given by the Son just as by the Father, 52–53, 60. He is given or sent only to a creature, 52. It does not follow from this that the Holy Spirit is given or sent, 52. He is everywhere and unchangeable, 52. With respect to the Holy Spirit there is nothing that previously was not, 52.

The sending of the Spirit in the name of the Son and by the Son confirms his procession from the Son, 53–54. The knowledge of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than his essence, 56. He has essence from the one from whom he hears what he speaks and teaches, 55. The Holy Spirit has from another the knowledge of what he speaks, 55. For the Holy Spirit, hearing is something like learning, 55. It is impious to suppose that the Holy Spirit does not know the Father and the Son, 55.

The Holy Spirit never begins to exist and is not the effect of anything, 57. Whatever is not the divine essence is beneath the Holy Spirit, 55. The Holy Spirit does not receive anything from what is beneath him, 55. The names of the Holy Spirit, 255. The Holy Spirit is signified by waters, 259. Nothing more delightful is found for contemplation in the Father and the Son than the affection of mutual love, 20. For the Holy Spirit to speak is to teach, 55. The Holy Spirit teaches all truth, 58. The Holy Spirit does not teach without the Father and the Son, 68, because he teaches by virtue of being one with the Father and the Son, 68. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are requested in the Lord’s Prayer, 159. The Holy Spirit goes and withdraws, 53. See God, Son of God, Father, Trinity.

## Word

Stability in the monastery is promised by monks in their profession, 513.

**STEPHEN (St.)** was the first to lay down his life for Christ, 161.

**STEPHEN**, a monk of Mount of the Holy Trinity, is recalled by the abbot after having been granted for a time to Walchelin, bishop of Winchester, 352.

**STEPHEN**, Anselm’s archdeacon, 386.

**STIGAND**, archbishop of Canterbury, 428. He gave estates to the Church of Canterbury, 428.

## Substance

Every substance is either primary or secondary, 146. Every substance is either universal—that is, essentially common to many—or individual, which shares a universal essence with others, 14. There are many essences besides the one properly called substance, 65. Not every essence is substance, 65. Every substance is susceptible to differences and to change in accidents, 14. What the Greeks signify in God by “substance,” we signify by “person,” 3.

Every essence, insofar as it exists, is to that extent like the supreme essence, 24. Things which, taken individually, diminish any essence by removing what makes it be more and more, when taken in an ordered way constitute it by leading it to be more and more, 16. If from a sensible and rational substance one removes, even in thought, its rationality, then its sensibility, then its life, and finally its existence, that substance is reduced to non-being, 16.

## Supreme

The supreme is that which so rises above other things that it has neither an equal nor anything more excellent, 14, 46. The supreme good cannot be changed or corrupted, 62. Whoever loves the supreme good for the sake of something else loves not it but something else, 87. See Good, End, Intention, Rational nature, Will.

## Pride

There are three kinds of pride: first, in estimation; second, in the will; third, in action, 394–395. Pride found only in action is lighter, 395. Pride found only in the will is more damnable, 395. Pride found in estimation is more incurable, 395.

On pride, 191, 248–249. It seeks praise, 248. Or, when it avoids praise, it takes glory from that very avoidance, 248. It despises those who do not praise its works as though they knew nothing, 248. God curses pride, 248. The daughters of pride are anger, impatience, discord, indignation, resentment, weariness of spirit, greed of the belly, grumbling, avarice, and rapacity, 249.

It often happens that someone who has long labored in works of virtue is moved by the vice of vainglory, 178. Vainglory not only stains a person with evil works but also destroys him through good works, 247–248. It is begotten by pride, which overthrew the first human being, 248. It rises to the virtue of loving God and neighbor. Pride overthrew and wounded the first human being and expelled him from happiness, 247. Against vainglory, envy, and pride, 247.

Except for pride, it makes no difference whether someone is called a servant or free, 317. Nothing is more wretched than a person who exalts himself over a good work, 248. Pride lies in hell, 248. Humility remains in heaven, 248. Certain condemnation awaits the proud, 248. See Humility.

## Suspension from divine offices

It compels one to repent of confession and causes many to dread confession: namely, when someone is forced to cease unwillingly from the office of his order because of hidden sins, 140, 332.

The Nicene Creed is accepted by Greeks and Latins, 59. Not everything that the faith believes is placed in it, 59. In it the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is not stated, 58. Nor are the names “person” or “Trinity,” 59. Why the Latins added *Filioque* to the Nicene Creed, 59. See Holy Spirit. Why this addition was made without the consent of the Greeks, 59. This addition is not a corruption, 59.

The Creed: “Whoever wishes to be saved,” etc., 357.

- Talentum: The talent is the greatest among all kinds of weights, 168. The talents given by God are to be used, 355.
- *Te Deum*: This hymn is sung at the election of an archbishop, 363.
- [Col. 1129] Bishop of Tedford, 449.
- Tempest: Each person’s desire is his own storm, 161. See *Desire*.
- Time: Time itself is something, 11, 12. Time exists only for a thing whose duration it both delimits by measuring it and measures by delimiting it, 13. Even if this or that thing did not exist, the same time would nevertheless exist, 115. Time is not called the time of this or that thing because time is in the things themselves, 115, but because the things themselves are in time, 115. There is no time when nothing exists, 11. Time is not always a whole, but exists in parts, 37. Something that is a whole cannot exist simultaneously in each individual time, 12, since the times themselves do not exist simultaneously, 12. Time is in some respect unlike itself, 13. Temporal present, 125. The time of the world consists of six ages, 162. Three divisions of time: (1) before the Law; (2) under the Law; (3) under Grace, 181.
- Temptation: Temptation compels only the will, 119, 121, 126. Therefore no temptation can properly be said to conquer a right will, 120. The force of temptation does not turn the will away from uprightness if the will itself does not desire what temptation suggests, 120, 129. Temptations must be avoided, 345, etc. Temptations and the suggestions of the devil, which intrude unexpectedly, must be driven away diligently, 424. The devil cannot tempt a person unless God permits it, 83. Whoever conquers the devil honors God; whoever is conquered by the devil dishonors God, 85. See *Conquer*. Christ will not allow the elect to be tempted beyond what they can do, 161. In temptation, let us cry out to Christ, 161. No temptation, even an inward one, will be able to overcome a soul whom God defends, 256. The will is conquered by temptation not because it is less strong, but because it wills uprightness less strongly, 120, 121.
- Earth, earthly: It is a great labor to burn with earthly desires, and a great rest not to desire earthly things, 157. See *World*.
- Teso, monk: Through him the monks of Bec ask Anselm not to accept the bishopric but to return to them, 364. Through the same man they signify by voice that they consent to his election, 364.
- Testament: The Law and the Prophets agree with the Gospel and are one, 166, 167. The Old Testament is contained in the New, 167.
- Theardus: A former cleric, later a Cluniac monk, 446. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, commends his case to Anselm, 446.
- Theodoricus, monk, 438, 444. He writes books, 444. Anselm instructs him to place the Apostle’s complete statement at the beginning of the fourth chapter of his book *On the Conception of the Virgin*, 438.
- Theodorus, monk, 441.
- Theophilus: Delivered over to the devil by a written pact, he is freed through Mary, 286.
- To gnaw with a Theonine tooth, 320.
- Thomas, bishop of York, 413, 422. He made his profession to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, by command of Alexander II, 422. Gerard succeeded him, 422. See *Gerard*.
- Thomas, another bishop of York, successor of Gerard, 420, 421, 422. He was to be consecrated by the archbishop of Canterbury, 422. He was elected archbishop through Anselm’s favor, 449. By Anselm’s order he received the major orders, 449. Twice by clerics, and a third time by two bishops, Anselm admonished him to receive consecration from him, 449. He neglected this, 449. Before being consecrated, he wished to consecrate the bishop of St Andrews in Scotland, 420. Anselm appointed Sunday, the fifth day before the Kalends of October, for his consecration, 448. Anselm prevented the pallium from being sent to him while he was still unconsecrated, 421, and placed him under interdict, 422.
- Tiberius: A familiar of Paschal II. He was sent by him to England, 382. Through him the pope wrote to Anselm, 398.
- Fear of God, 249, 252. The root of wisdom is fearing God, 156. Filial fear, 159. Of this it is said, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” 159. Chaste fear arises from charity, 158. Beautiful love produces chaste fear of God, 158. God is to be feared as Lord and loved as Father, 253. Holy fear remains, 253, because it makes the saints remain, 253. Nothing is lacking to those who fear God, 253. The fear of God is exceedingly strong, 216. The fear of the Lord drives out sin, 156. It is not honorable to refrain from sin solely through hatred of punishment, 72. Whoever avoids sin out of fear of punishment is not just, 72. Hatred of punishment is useless for avoiding sin when love of justice alone is sufficient, 72. More praiseworthy is the person who stands firm while seeing no punishment than the one who stands firm while looking at punishment, 81. Through fear one reaches love, 240, 253.
- Tribulation: God’s servant should not regard as tribulation what is not tribulation, 337. That is not tribulation which harms neither body nor soul, 337. Even there Christians are sometimes troubled by the destruction of human things, 160. They think that this is not done by God but by the enemy, 160. Waters signify tribulations and peoples, 161. See *Adversity*, *Evil*, *Patience*, *Prosperity*.
- Trinity: Faith in the Holy Trinity, 27. In Scripture we do not read that there is one God who is three persons, or that one God is a Trinity, or “God from God,” 58; but these propositions follow most clearly from Scripture, 58, and therefore we believe them, 58. One cannot err without danger in matters concerning the Trinity, 45. The three divine persons are not three things but one, 45. The Trinity is both threefold and simple divinity, 225. How God is indivisible unity and an unassociated plurality, 30, 51. It is advantageous for every person to believe in a threefold Unity and a single Trinity, 27. In God, three are said of one and one of three, 47, 48. The intellect does not grasp this, 48. We must believe in the Father, the Son, and their Spirit—in each individually and in all three together, 27. There is one God, and he himself is three persons, 44. Nor is anything God except the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 50. God is not the Father, Son, or Spirit of anyone except God, 50. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; nevertheless they are not three Gods but one God, 47. It is impious to say that any individual person is not God, 44. The three divine persons are not called God accidentally, 45. The three persons in God do not have the name “God” by power or will, 45. Only the supreme Spirit is ineffably threefold and one. One Trinity, or threefold Unity, may be called one essence and three persons, or three substances, 27. In God there is one nature and several persons, and several persons are one nature, 47. The individual Father, the individual Son, and the individual Spirit are the supreme essence, 27. The Father, Son, and their Spirit together are one and the same supreme essence, 27, 21, 22, 51, 57. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, 50, 45. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, 45, 50, 177, 452. These three are one uncreated being and one creator, 22. There is not one God the Father, another God the Son, and another Holy Spirit, 58.

  The supreme Trinity may be called three substances, according to the Greeks, 3. The Greeks confess three substances in one essence, just as we confess three persons in one substance, 3, 339. What exists as three in God the Latins call persons and the Greeks substances, 49. They signify by “substance” the same thing that we signify by “person,” 49, and do not differ from us in faith in any respect, 49. Scripture nowhere says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons or three substances, 452. Properly speaking, three persons, like three substances, are not said of God, 339. The Father, Son, and their Spirit are not three persons—that is, three individual substances, 17. Only because a name is lacking by which plurality in one essence may be signified do we say that there are three persons, or substances, in the supreme nature, 17. If the three persons in God were three separate things, it would follow that there are three Gods, 45. The three persons are not said to be in God because they are three separate things, 47, but because they bear a certain likeness to three separate persons, 47. If there are three things in God, God is composed of three things, 44. No one denies that the three persons in God are three things if by “things” one understands three relations, 355. A Christian is not one who asserts that the three persons in God are three things, as three angels are, 357.

  The Father and the Son have the same divinity and essence, 56, 57. The Father is not one thing and the Son another, 241. Love is not something other than what the Father and Son are, 240. There is not another God the Father from whom the Son is, 57, nor another God the Father and Son from whom the Holy Spirit is, 57. God is wholly Father, wholly Son, and wholly Holy Spirit, 61. What each one individually is, the whole Trinity together—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is, 34. Each individually is nothing other than supremely simple unity and supreme onefold simplicity, 34. The Father, Son, and their Spirit are not three speakers, although each individually is a speaker, 23. Nor are there several things that are spoken when each one speaks of himself and the other two, 23. For there only their essence is spoken, and that essence is one, 23. The Father, Son, and their Spirit each speak of himself and of the other two, just as each understands himself and the others, 23. What is said singularly of one divine person is understood of all three, 57, 58, 61, except when it is attributed to that person by which he is not one with the others, 61. Whatever belongs essentially to the supreme nature, although it is said of each of the three persons, does not admit plurality, 23, 43, 44; it is what they are, just as it is one, so that it cannot be said plurally either of each individually or of all three together, 24, 43, 44. Whatever is said of one God is said of the whole God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 50.

  The will and power of the three persons in God are one, 43, 44, 45. In God, proper things are always understood distinctly from common things, and common things from distinct things, 45. Each person in God is what is common to the others and what is proper to himself, 43. The Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, and the Holy Spirit is eternal, 50. Whether taken together or individually, they are only one eternal being, 50. The same conclusion applies to everything said of God wherever the relation of origin does not intervene, 50. What is common to the divine persons—such as omnipotence and eternity—is understood in the name “God,” 43. What is proper to each—such as begetter and Word—is signified by the names “Father” and “Son,” 43. Being God is not the same as being Father or Son, 49. Nor does the name “Father” or “Son” signify the same thing as the name “God,” 49. The Father is no more God than the Son is, 53.

  God is “from God” either by being born, as the Son, or by proceeding, as the Holy Spirit, 51, 61. The God who is born is not other than the God from whom he is born, nor is the one who proceeds other than the one from whom he proceeds, 49. Nevertheless there are several, insofar as the one from whom someone is born or proceeds is distinct from the one who is born and the one who proceeds, 49, 50. What is born and what proceeds in God is the very same as that from which the one born and the one proceeding exist, 60. In the supreme essence there is only one Father, one Son, and one Spirit—not three Fathers, Sons, or Spirits, 23, 24. The Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; the Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son, 50. Yet the Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct from one another and are several, 50. The Father is understood as memory, the Son as understanding, and the Spirit of both as love, 22.

  The sole cause of plurality in God is the relation of origin, 50. This alone prevents the persons from being said of one another and prevents what is proper to one from being attributed to another, 50. In the divine persons, distinction exists because the collection of properties is not the same, 61. The relation of origin limits the consequence of God’s unity, 50, 51. What is born or proceeds from God is not outside that from which it is born or proceeds, 48, but is offspring in the parent and parent in the offspring, 48; and what proceeds remains in those from whom it proceeds, 48.

  It cannot be stated why the Father, Son, and their Spirit are three, 27. The Father is the Father of someone, and the Son is the Son of someone, 44. It is impossible for the Father to be the one whose Father he is, or for the Son to be the Father whose Son he is, 44, 50. The Father is one, and the one whose Father he is another; likewise the Son is one, and the one whose Son he is another, 44. Otherwise there would be neither Father nor Son in God, 44. The persons in God are several because they are distinct from one another, 46. They are not other substances or several things according to substance, but one substance, 46. The three persons in the Godhead are not like persons among human beings, 61. Insofar as God exists relatively, he admits plurality of persons; insofar as he exists in himself, he preserves singularity, 61. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are several, or three persons, because they are distinct from one another and cannot be said of one another, 46, 47, 48. They are not other substances or several according to substance, but one, one substance, 48. They have plurality according to their relations, 48.

  When “God, the Father” is named, he is signified as the one from whom someone is born, 49. When “Son” is named, he is understood as the one who is born from someone, 49. When “Holy Spirit” is named, he is shown to be the one who proceeds from someone, 49. The Father is the principle of the Son, 57. The Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit, 57, because the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, and the Son is from the Father, 57. The Son is from the Father because the Father is not from him, 60; and the Father is not from the Son because the Son is from the Father, 60. The Holy Spirit is from the Father because the Father is not from him, 61; and the Father is not from the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is from him, 61. The Trinity is explained by comparison with a stream, a spring, and a lake, 48, 56, 57.

  Birth or procession in the Godhead must be understood very differently from birth or procession among created things, 60, 61. In the divine processions there is nothing earlier or later by nature, time, or in any other respect, 60. Rather, everything that exists is identical with itself and wholly sufficient to itself through itself, 60. Nothing there is born or proceeds as though advancing from non-being into being, 60. Our intellect cannot judge this birth and procession, 60. The birth of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit are without beginning, 48. The Son and the Holy Spirit are from the essence of the Father, 51. It is impossible for God from God to be as a whole from a part, a part from a whole, or a part from a part, 51. The God who is from God is wholly from the whole, 51.

  There are six distinctions between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 61. Each individually has one property of its own, which distinguishes it from the others, and two properties both common and proper, such that by the one it shares with one person it differs from the other, 61. The Father alone has the Son, by which he differs from the other two, 61. He has the Holy Spirit, which he shares with the Son and by which he differs from the Holy Spirit, 61. But he does not have a Father, as neither does the Holy Spirit, and in this he differs from the Son, 61. The Son alone has the Father, by which he differs from the Father and the Holy Spirit, 61. He has the Holy Spirit, as does the Father, and in this he is distinct from the Holy Spirit, 61. But he lacks a Son, as does the Holy Spirit, and in this he differs from the Father, 61. The Holy Spirit alone is one from whom another does not proceed, 61. He does not have a Father, which he shares with the Father and by which he differs from the Son, 61. He does not have a Son, which he shares with the Son and by which he does not agree with the Father, 61. The Father alone is from no one, and from him the other two are, 61. The Holy Spirit alone is from two and from him no one is; the Son alone is from one and from him one is, 61. It is common to all three to have a relation to two, 61. Sometimes we attribute to each person what is proper to one, 61; sometimes to one what is common to all three, 61.

  In God each person is either God from whom God is, or God from God, 60. The Father is the God from whom God is, but not God from God, 60. The Son is God from God and the God from whom God is, 60. The Holy Spirit is God from God, but is not the God from whom God is, 60. The God from whom God is and the God who is from God are not two Gods but one and the same God, 60. The Father alone is unbegotten, the Son alone begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, 49. The Father is God begetting, the Son is God begotten, and the Holy Spirit is God proceeding in an ineffable manner, 57. The Father is Father only of the Son, 50. The Son is Son only of the Father, 50. The Holy Spirit is Spirit only of the Father and the Son, 50.

  There are no degrees of rank in God, 55, nor intervals among the persons, 55. The Father is neither earlier nor later, greater nor lesser, than the Son; nor is one more or less God than another, 59. The Son is neither lesser nor later than the Father, although he is from him, 55. The Holy Spirit is neither lesser nor later than the Son, although he proceeds from him, 55, 56. The Trinity is compared with the sun, its radiance, and its heat, 55, 56. The Father, Son, and Spirit of both exist in one another with such equality that none surpasses another, 22, and none exists without another, 22. Each of them is the supreme essence, and all three together are nothing other than one supreme essence, which cannot exist without itself or outside itself, nor be greater or lesser than itself, 22, 27. Each is no less in the others than in himself, 23. The whole Father is in the Son and the common Spirit, 22. The whole Son is in the Father and the same Spirit, 22. The same Spirit is wholly in the Father and the Son, 22.

  This is because the memory of the supreme essence is wholly in its understanding and in its love, 22; its understanding is wholly in its memory and love, 22; and its love is wholly in its memory and understanding, 22. The supreme Spirit understands and loves his entire memory, 22; remembers his entire understanding and loves it wholly, 22; and remembers his entire love and understands it wholly, 22. Thus the Father is understood as memory, the Son as understanding, and the Spirit as love, so that neither requires the other in order to remember, understand, or love himself, 22, 24. Each individually is the supreme essence, which through itself remembers, understands, and loves, 24. Thus each individually is essentially memory, understanding, and love, and whatever belongs to the supreme essence, 22, 23.

  The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle of creation, or one creator—not three principles or three creators, 57. They are the principle of creation not by that in which they are three, but by that in which they are one, 57. Nevertheless the Father is a principle, the Son is a principle, and the Holy Spirit is a principle, 57. What the Father reveals, the Son and the Holy Spirit also reveal, 58. What the Father knows, the Son and the Holy Spirit also know, 58, 61. To reveal and to know is common to the three persons, 61, because they reveal and know by that in which they are one, 61. The Trinity is declared in Christ’s baptism, 173. See *God*, *Son of God*, *Eternal Father*, *Relation*, *Holy Spirit*, *Word of God*.
- Wheat signifies virtues and spiritual gifts, 183.
- Arnulf, abbot of Troarn, 416. See *Arnulf*.
- Tudo: Anselm commends to him the church of Bec, deprived of its pastor, 371.
- Turoldus, monk of Bec, 415. Anselm congratulates him on his conversion from the world, 415.

- *Turpe*, *turpitudo*—Shameful, shamefulness: It is shameful when one part does not fit another, 142. In the human body before sin there was nothing shameful and nothing discordant, 142. The body was entirely subject to the soul, and the soul to God, 142. But the body ceased to be obedient to the soul rebelling against God, 142. When that harmony was dissolved in the first human beings, shamefulness became a no small original punishment, 142. This shamefulness passes to posterity together with original sin, 142. See *Original Sin*, *Punishment of Sin*. The bodily members that are shameful and require covering, 142.
- Turtle dove: A most chaste bird and most faithful to its mate, 170.
- Bishop of Tusculum, 440.
- Safe, safety: One must do what is safer, 140, 332. See *Danger*.

## U

- Umbertus: Count and margrave, 391. A kinsman of Anselm, 391. He received Anselm as he was traveling to Rome and supplied him with what he needed, 391. Anselm urged him to defend the Church, 391.
- Universal: Whoever does not understand how several human beings in one species are one human being does not understand how several persons, each of whom is God, are one God, 43. Dialecticians—or rather, dialectical heretics—think that universals are nothing but a breath of the voice, 42. See *Dialecticians*, *Substance*.
- Urban: Under Urban II and Guibert there was a schism, 374. Anselm supported Urban II’s side, 374, 380.
- Urban II, pope, successor and vicar of the apostle Peter, 135. Reluctantly, in response to the prayers of Anselm and others, he granted the bishopric of Beauvais to an inexperienced man, 353, 354. He ordered Anselm to assist the inexperienced bishop of Beauvais as helper, admonisher, corrector, and adviser, either personally or through one of his monks, 353. He ordered him to visit the Roman see within a year, 353. He ordered that what Hubert, when dying, had left at Bec be sent promptly to the Roman see by Anselm, 353. He declared the innocence of the bishop of Beauvais, 354, but judged him unequal to the persecution of the canons, 354, and advised him to resign the bishopric, 354. Nevertheless, he left judgment of the matter to Anselm’s discretion, 354. Anselm asked him, in his wisdom, to judge concerning this Fulk, the bishop, 380, and sent him a small gift, 380. Urban sent a legate to England and through him sent Anselm the pallium, 380.
- Urso, or Ursus or Ursio: A friend of Anselm, 322. He compelled Anselm to write an admonition to Lanzon, a monk, 322. Anselm wished him to be told that he had recovered his health, 346. At Bec he made the petition and vow of a monk, 349, 350. Later, elsewhere under Abbot Peter, overcome by the importunity of those entreating him, he made the petition and vow of a monk, 350. He ought to remain faithful to his first promise, 350. For this reason Anselm retained him when he was willing, 350.
- Ursio: Prior of the monastery of St Martin in the Fields, 370. A friend of Anselm, 370. During his priorship, Walerannus, canon and cantor of the church of Paris, entered the monastic institute there, 370. See *Walerannus*.

## V
Vanity. Whatever the love of this world produces is deceitful, 214. Other goods without the highest good are nothing but vanity, 212. The vanity of this world’s glory, 212. The vanity of life, 197, 199. The punishment of monks: what merit it has, 386.

Word. Every word is the word or image of something, 18. Every word is the word of something, 16, 17. If no creature ever existed, there would be no word of it, 16. This word itself, insofar as it is a word or image, is directed toward another, 18. One must cling not so much to words as to truth, 62. A word is a significant sound expressing time, 147, 148. A word is seed, 130. Without it no one can be converted, 130. Whoever hears and does not obey is said not to hear, 130. See Preaching. The word that is seed does not produce fruit by itself, 130. But it remains without germination until God turns the human will toward willing conversion, 130. Idle words, 19, 251. To know and to understand is nothing other than to speak, 23.

The Word of God. To speak is, for the highest Spirit, the same as to behold by something like thought, 23. The speech, or Word, of the highest Spirit is nothing other than the understanding of that same Spirit, 15, 17. It is nothing other than the highest essence, 8, 15. The Word is existence itself in its truth, 16. When the highest Wisdom understands itself by speaking, it begets its consubstantial likeness, that is, its Word, 17. The Word of the highest truth is itself the highest truth, 16. The speech of the highest Spirit cannot be a creature, 15. The speech of the highest Spirit is consubstantial with it, 15, 16, 17. Even if no other essence existed, the Word of the highest Spirit would necessarily exist, 16. And it would be coeternal with it, 16, 17. If the highest Spirit eternally understands itself, it eternally speaks itself, 16, 20. If the highest Spirit eternally speaks itself, its Word is eternally with it, 20.

The speech of the highest Spirit could not come about by itself, 15. That whose word it is cannot be its own word, 18. The Word cannot be that whose word it is, 18. There is an ineffable plurality of the Word and of that whose Word it is, 18. Necessity compels there to be two, but what these two are cannot be expressed, 18. It is proper to the Word to be, or to be born, from another; it is proper to that whose Word it is that another be, or be born, from it, 18. The Word and that whose Word it is, insofar as they exist substantially or in relation to the creature, hold an indivisible unity, 18. Insofar as the latter is not from the former, while the former is from the latter, they admit an ineffable plurality, 18.

The Word of the highest Spirit is not from it in the manner of the things made by it, 18. Rather, it is as creator from Creator, the highest from the Highest, 18. It is not from it in such a way as to be made by it, 18. It is from the highest Spirit as the same thing from the same thing, 18. It is from the highest Spirit in such a way that it possesses its perfect likeness, as offspring possesses the likeness of its parent, 18. It could not be from it in a more fitting way than by being born, 18. The Word appears to be born from memory, 20.

In the highest essence [Col. 1134] there cannot be any word other than that which can truly be called its image, 23. The Word is the image and Son of that whose Word it is, 23. It cannot be called the image or Son of itself, or of the Spirit proceeding from itself, 23. For it does not imitate itself or that proceeding from it in existence, 23. The Word belongs only to that from which it has being by being born, and in whose likeness it exists in every respect, 24. That it is Word or image is so proper to the Word that it can in no way belong to another, 18. The Word of the highest Spirit is its perfect likeness, image, figure, and character, 17, 21. Therefore it is most fittingly its Word, 17. And its offspring, or Son, 21. Only the Word should be called begotten, 22, 49. Because he alone is Son, 49.

There is nothing in the Father who speaks that is not in the Word by which he speaks himself, 34. For the Word of the Father is truthful, just as the Father himself is truthful, 34. God is so simple that nothing other than what he is can be born from him, 34. All things that are in the highest Spirit are in the same way in his Word, 17. There is one Wisdom who speaks in those three, and one substance that is spoken, 23. How is it that in the highest essence there are not as many words as there are speakers and as there are those who are spoken, 23? Yet there are not several words, but one Word, 23, 15, 12. Nor is that Word the Word of three, but of one of them, 23, 24. The speech of God is supremely simple, 15.

The secret of the generation of the Word surpasses every power of human understanding, 24. The effort to explain how this occurs must be restrained, 24. It cannot at all be explained how the highest Wisdom knows or speaks itself, 24. Of this it is possible for a human being to know nothing, or scarcely anything, 24.

The form of things which, in the reason of the highest nature, precedes the things to be created is nothing other than a certain speech of things in that reason itself, 8. The Word, or speech, of things was in the highest substance before they existed, so that through it they might come to be, 8. And it is present when they have been made, so that through it they may be known, 8. Creatures are more truly in the Word, or understanding, of the Creator than in themselves, 17. Whatever has been made, whether it lives or does not live, whatever its mode of being, is in the Word itself life and truth, 17. See Idea.

Through natural and intimate speech he made all things, saying them by one Word, 8, 15, 17. Whether the highest Spirit says both itself and creatures by one and the same Word, 16, 17. God speaks himself and the things he makes through his consubstantial Word, 16. There is one substance of the Word by which the highest Spirit speaks itself, and of the Word by which it speaks the things it makes, 16. There are not two Words, one by which the highest Spirit speaks itself and another by which it speaks the creature, 16. Rather, by one and the same Word he speaks both himself and it, 17. The highest Spirit does not speak the creature by the word of the creature, 17. Whatever the highest Spirit speaks, it speaks by its own Word, 17.

Whether the Word through which all things were made is the word of creatures, 16, 17. Whether the Word by which all things are spoken and made is the likeness of those things made through it, 15, 16. The Word is not the likeness of creatures, but a true and simple essence, 16. The Word is not more or less true according as it is more or less like creatures, 16. Whatever the highest Spirit is in relation to the creature, its Word also is; and likewise, 18. The highest Spirit and its Word are not two creative highest essences, 18. Nor are they two creators or two principles of things, but one Creator and one principle, 18, 19. Nor are there two Words or two images; nor two Fathers or two Sons, 19.

Comparison of the speech of the highest Artificer with the speech of a craftsman, 8. Threefold difference between the speech of the highest Artificer and that of a craftsman, 8. The speech of the creative substance is neither taken up nor joined from elsewhere, but is alone and first sufficient to complete the work; the speech of a craftsman is not so, 8. The things made by the Father through the Word were made by the Word itself, 56. See God; Cause of things.

The Word made flesh leads us who have fallen back to God, 184. See Christ; God; Son of God; Father; Trinity. God speaks to his people either through inward inspiration, or through the Scriptures, or through preachers, 161.

Word of the mind. There is no speech of mind or reason when significant vocal words for things are conceived in thought, 8. Rather, it occurs when the things themselves, already existing, are contemplated by the mind, 8. We can speak one thing in three ways, 8. Corresponding words belong to these three kinds of speech, 8. The speech of our mind is nothing other than the inspection of one who is thinking, 23. Whatever the mind thinks, it expresses its likeness, 17. That likeness which is expressed in the mind’s act of contemplating the thing itself is the word of the mind, 8. The more truly the mind expresses the likeness, the more truly it thinks, 17. The Word is the image of a thing formed from thought, 17. Or thought itself, formed according to its likeness from memory, 20. That is the most proper and principal word of the thing, 8.

All the words by which we speak things in the mind—that is, think them—are likenesses and images of the things whose words they are, 15. Words of the mind are truer because they are more like the things, 8. When the rational mind understands itself by thinking, it produces from itself the image, or [Col. 1135] word, of itself, 17. The thought of itself is its own image, 17. The word of the rational mind can be separated from it only by reason, 17.

When something external to the mind is thought, the word of the thing thought does not arise from the thing itself, 23. Rather, it arises from the image of the thing that is in the thinker’s memory, or that is drawn through bodily sense from the thing present, 23. The natural words of the mind are the same among all peoples, 8. Where these words are present, nothing else is necessary for knowing the thing, 8. And where they cannot be present, everything else is useless for demonstrating the thing, 8. There are as many words of one thing as there are people thinking about it, 23. Because in the thoughts of each person there is the word of that thing, 23. There are as many words in the mind of the thinker as there are things thought, 23.

Truth is rectitude perceptible by the mind alone, 113. This definition is adequate, 113. Truth, rectitude, and justice are the same and define one another, 113. Whoever knows one of them cannot be ignorant of the others, 113. By the two names “rectitude” and “truth,” one thing is signified, and it is the genus of justice, 115. The devil did not stand in truth—that is, in justice or rectitude, 133. In whatever thing truth exists, it is nothing other than rectitude, 115. Although there are many truths according to the many things, there are nevertheless not many rectitudes, 115. Although the things themselves in which they exist vary, it is not therefore necessary that the rectitudes vary, 115. The truth of what is true is in the true itself, 110. There is one and the same immutable rectitude and truth in all true things, 115.

Things exist more truly somewhere through their essence than through their likeness, 17. It cannot be conceived that truth has a beginning or an end, 11, 109, 113. If truth has a beginning, then before it began it was true that there was no truth, 113. Thus truth existed before there was truth, 113. If truth will have an end, then after it has ended it will be true that there is no truth, 113. Thus truth will exist after truth has ended, 113.

Truth deceives no one, 221. Yet truth does not reveal itself to everyone, 222. Nevertheless, it denies itself to no one, 222. The highest truth is rectitude, 113. In the truth of God is everything that is true; outside him there is nothing but nothingness and falsehood, 33. Whoever has seen light and truth has seen God, 32. And whoever has not seen God has not seen light and truth, 32.

The highest truth is not rectitude because it owes something, 113. Everything owes something to it; it owes nothing to anyone, 113. The highest truth, or rectitude, is the cause of all other truths and rectitudes, and nothing is its cause, 113. See Justice; Rectitude.

In truth, which remains, there is no change, neither past nor future, but only the present, 161. Truth is not in a creature, 161. Nothing is true except by participating in truth, 110. Among created truths, some are merely effects; some are effects of one truth and causes of another, 113. Rectitude found in bodily things is not truth and differs from the rectitudes mentioned above, 113. The rectitude of bodies is perceived by bodily sense, whereas these are perceived by reason alone, 113.

Of one and the same thing there cannot simultaneously be a true affirmation and its negation, 44. The truth of speech, thought, will, or action is rectitude because they signify, think, will, or do what they ought, 113. Rectitude by which a signification is called right does not have being or non-being through the signification, 115. Truth is improperly said to belong to this or that thing, 115. For truth is not in things, or from them, or through them, 115. Rather, things exist through it and according to it, 115. Whether truth is shown invincibly by one argument or by several, it is equally defended against every doubt, 86. There is truth of action, 110. Every truth is taught by God, 58. See Justice.

Clothing. God clothes and adorns the faithful soul with himself, 203, 204. Eternal punishments for expensive clothing, 191.

Viaticum. Let priests who have denied viaticum to those placed at the point of death be punished as murderers of souls, 384. See Communion.

Vigil. Those who are watchful in mind are raised toward the light of heavenly vision, 163. The night has twelve hours, 160. And four military watches, 162. Three hours are assigned to each watch, 162.

To conquer. To will rectitude perseveringly is for the will to conquer, 119. To will what one ought not is for it to be conquered, 119. See To honor. A human being does not satisfy God unless he conquers the devil, 85.

Vengeance. The act of one who strikes back is unjust, 76. The person struck ought not to avenge himself, 76. Vengeance does not belong to a human being, 84. For neither does the one who takes vengeance belong to himself, nor does the one from whom he takes vengeance belong to him; both are servants of the Lord, 84. If he avenges himself on a fellow servant, he arrogantly presumes the judgment that belongs properly to the Lord and Judge of all, 84. Vengeance belongs to God alone, 84. Some are so offended by their brother’s fault that they wish their brother to perish first in eternal punishments rather than forgive him, 168. See Injury.

Wine. A vow never to drink wine, 421.

Virginity is lost irrecoverably, although it ought to be preserved perpetually, 208. She who has lost virginity through fornication is faithless toward God, perjured before God, and an adulteress against Christ, 209. Rejected by God, cast to the devil—or rather, rejecting God and embracing the devil, 209. Lament for virginity wrongly lost, or repentance for fornication, 208, etc. After losing virginity, more women have pleased God through repentance in chastity than many others, although holy, have pleased him in virginity, 423. When lust cannot attack virginity, pride usually attacks it, 178. VIRGIT, virgin, 414. Virgin (Blessed). See Mary. Virgins to be consecrated to God by the bishop, 423. A fallen virgin is aroused to repentance, 422, 423.

Virtue. No one can possess any virtue except through Christ, 158. Virtues are requested from God, 251, 252, 253, 254. Whoever thinks it excessively harsh and impossible to abstain from worldly pleasure and persevere in the practice of the virtues has not tasted how praiseworthy and delightful it is not to serve vices but to rule them through love of the heavenly kingdom, 345. One perfected in the virtues is dedicated to the happiness of the future age, 177. The stages of the virtues, 159. They are designated by the names of the Fathers, 176, 177, 178.

Sight is the instrument of seeing, 132. It has several capacities, 133. Both the person who sees and the sight by which he sees are said to see, 134. The feet are directed by sight, 73.

Life. Whatever lives, or senses, or possesses reason, is more like the highest nature than what in no way lives, senses, or is capable of reason, 16. Whatever acts shows that life is present in it, 27. Neither place nor time excuses anyone from being able to live well, 343. The longer someone has lived, the shorter the time he will live, 312, 321. The span granted to each person for living well decreases daily, 312, 321. Hope of continuing to live extinguishes the purpose of a holy life, 312, 321. Love of the present life—or rather, of misery, 240. To give life is to receive death, 912. The present life is a way, 415. Life is temptation and warfare, 195. What greatness is there in a long life unless it is truly secure from the assaults of troubles? Whoever, while living, is subject to troubles either by fearing or by suffering them, or is deceived by false security—what is he doing except living miserably? 25. Whoever lives free from these things lives happily, 25.

The evils of this life, 220. Life [quot cutis: reading uncertain], subject to vices and illnesses, 199. The vanity of life, 197, 199, 200, 201. Martha signifies the active life, 179. Mary signifies the contemplative life, 179. The duties of the contemplative life, 179. The duties of the active life, 179.

VITALIS, a monk of Caen, 336. Anselm greets him, 336. VITALIS, duke, 352. His goodwill toward Henry, a friend of Anselm, 352.

Vice. Even after much practice of the virtues, the stains of some vices often assail the mind, 177. A single kind of vice makes someone vicious, whereas no single kind of virtue makes someone virtuous, 395. The extinction of individual vices is requested from God, 252, 253. See Virtue. The image of God is erased by vices, 30, 242. See Image.

Calling. God’s calling is to look upon us by loving and choosing us, 172. Our response is to obey his love through good works, 172. God calls when, through the distress of illness, he presses someone toward death, 182. Even if all Jews had believed, the Gentiles would nevertheless be called, 82. Yet the contempt of the Jews was the occasion for the apostles to turn to the Gentiles, 82. See Grace; Predestination.

Will. The will is in the soul, 132. The soul uses it for willing, 132. Rational will is not the whole soul, 132. Reason, or will, is something in the soul, 132. See Soul.

“Will” is used equivocally, 116, 120, 132, 133, 134. There is the will that is the instrument of willing; the will that is the affection or aptitude of that instrument by which it is ready to will; and the will that is the act or use of the instrument, 134. The will is the soul’s natural instrument, 134. The principal affections of the will are two: the affection of willing advantage and the affection of willing justice, 134. The affection of willing advantage is always and inseparably present in the will as instrument, 116, 133. One will is the instrument, another the affection, and another the use, 132, 133. We always possess the will that is the instrument of willing, 132. We possess the will that is the affection or aptitude for willing even when we sleep, 132. We possess the will that is use only when we will, 132, 133. In a just person there is the will, or affection, of justice even when he sleeps, 132. The will that is the instrument is one in a human being, 133. Whatever we will, we will either from the affection of advantage or from the affection of justice, 116, 133.

The various division of the will, 116. One will is effective, another approving, another permitting, 116. The effective will effects what it wills, and would effect it if it could, 116. The approving will approves what exists, and would approve it if it existed, 116. The permitting will permits what is said to be willed if it exists, and would permit it if it existed, 116. The effective will is also approving and permitting, 116. The approving will is also permitting, 116. The merely permitting will is neither effective nor approving, 116. See Will of God.

The will wills nothing except either advantage or rectitude, 133. Whatever else it wills, it wills either for the sake of advantage or for the sake of rectitude, 133. Even when deceived, it thinks that what it wills is related to these, 133. Through the affection for willing advantage, it always wills both happiness and to be happy, 133. Through the affection for willing rectitude, it wills rectitude and to be upright—that is, just, 133.

God ordered the human will so that the will as instrument would use the will, or affection, which is justice, for command and governance, 134. And would use the will directed toward advantage for obeying without any inconvenience, 134. The will as instrument, what it wills, and the affection by which it wills are all said to will, 134. To will is nothing other than to use the power of willing, 73. The will as instrument moves all the other instruments that we use voluntarily, 133. And it produces all voluntary movements, 133. It moves itself by its own affections, 133. It may be called an instrument moving itself, 133. The will as instrument does nothing without its affections, 133, 134. The will that is the power of the soul by which the soul wills is one thing; justice is another; and the affections or uses of the will are another, 98.

The affection of willing justice is not always and inseparably present in the will, 116, 133. The will was made right, 65. A right will is one turned toward what it ought to will, 65. The will and its conversion are something, or certain essences, but they are not substances, 65. The will is, as it were, midway between soul and flesh, 238. The better things that lie within one’s power ought more to lie within one’s will, 25. Each person is drawn by the will toward what he unchangeably wills, 78.

The will cannot move or will anything unless God permits it, 70. Whatever moves itself toward willing first wills to move itself in that way, 68. Whoever wills moves himself by his will toward other acts of willing, 68. Whoever wills nothing can in no way move himself toward willing, 68. No one wills what he can will merely because he can, without another cause, 73. Although he never wills what he cannot will, 73. Every will wills for some reason, 114. The will ought to be no more right in willing what it ought than in willing for the reason for which it ought, 114.

The will does not will rightly, nor does it will rectitude, unless it is right, 128. The will is not right because it wills rightly; rather, it wills rightly because it is right, 128. When it wills rectitude, it wills rightly, 128. Nor does it will rectitude unless it possesses rectitude, 129. It wills rightly when it wills what it ought, 130. A right will wills the rectitude it does not yet possess when it wills more rectitude than it has, 129. No one can will rightly unless he possesses rectitude of will, 130. The truth of the will is nothing other than its rectitude, by which a person wills what he ought, 110.

No will is evil, even when it abandons justice; rather, insofar as it exists, it is good and a work of God, 70, 73. The will is not evil except insofar as it is unjust, 70. The power to will anything whatsoever comes from God, 70, 73. A good will is no more a thing than an evil will, 65. Nor is the latter more evil than the former is good, 65. A good will is not the good itself that makes good people good, 65. An evil will is not the evil itself that makes evil people evil, 65. See Justice and Injustice.

Even the will in which justice or injustice exists is not called just or unjust in itself, 98. The will ought to will nothing except justly, 134. Whatever the will wills without rectitude, it wills unjustly, 134. An unjust will is one that does not possess the justice it ought to possess, 69. Only injustice is censured in the will, 69. The will for happiness, whatever it wills, is not evil before it receives justice, 70. Justice, like injustice, can exist only in the will, 98, 99. Nothing is called just or unjust except the will, or because of a just or unjust will, 98, 99, 126. Nothing is called evil except an evil will or because of an evil will, 70.

The will as instrument was made good, just, and strong for preserving justice, 134. It was made evil through free choice, 134. The will for advantage was created good, 134. It became unjust because it was not subject to justice, 134. The will for advantage ought to will nothing without justice, 134. See Advantage; Justice.

Every action derives praise or blame from the will, 414. No action is called unjust in itself, but because of an unjust will, 98, 126, 127. Every action performed with a right will is right, and every action performed with a will that is not right is not right, [Col. 1138] 44. A person is called just by a just will and unjust by an unjust will, 44. That will is certainly right which is subject to the will of God, 44. No will is just except one that wills what God wills it to will, 120. Whatever does not will this is plainly unjust, 121. See Justice.

Whether a will that could will only intimate and unclean advantages would be unjust and blameworthy, 68. When the will resists the appetites, it is a just will, 68. The will is good when it wills what God wills it to will, 152. In what sense it is not always good to will what God wills, 151. The will is corrupted by abandoning truth, 80.

For actions of the will that are unjustly performed, the members and senses through which they are performed ought not to be blamed, 99. God subjected the members and senses to the will, 99. At the command of the will, the members and senses cannot refrain from moving and from doing what it wills, 99. The will itself moves the members and senses as its instruments and produces the works they appear to perform, 99. Whatever they do must be attributed entirely to the will, 99. Only the will is punished, even when the members and senses are punished, 99. Nothing is punishment except what is against the will, 99. No thing feels punishment unless it possesses a will, 99. Just as the will operates in the members and senses, so in them it is itself tortured and delighted, 99. A human being is not just or unjust because he senses, but is unjust because he consents to the will when he ought not, 98.

No one can will what he has not first conceived in his heart, 130. The will turns toward what it wills more strongly, 121. A right will does not fail by itself, but because another will expels it, 132. The will often and greatly hinders the mind from understanding rectitude, 104. God does not demand works beyond one’s ability where he sees integrity of good will and good conduct, 345.

Freedom of the will. Temptation can compel the will only when it wills, 119, 121, 126. Therefore the will is free to preserve rectitude and free to resist sin and temptation, 119, 126. The will is overcome not by another power, but by its own, 119. If a person wills to sin, he must sin, 124. But by a consequent necessity, 124. Free will can refrain from willing before it wills, 124. Because it is free, 124. Once it wills, it cannot refrain from willing; it must will, 124. For it is impossible for the will simultaneously to will and not will the same thing, 124. The will has been given this: that what it wills should be, and what it does not will should not be, 124. The work of the will is voluntary or spontaneous, 124. Because it is performed by spontaneous willing, 124. It is also necessary in two ways, 124. The necessities by which an action is called necessary are produced by freedom, 124. What the good will wills must exist in those things that occur if it wills and do not occur if it does not will, 124. See Free choice.

Proper will. A proper will is one subject to no other will, 46. It belongs to God alone to have a proper will, 46. And to will something by a proper will, 46. For if there were another will subject to no one else, the will of God would not be preferred to all, 46. Nor would it be the only will subject to no other, or to which no other is superior, 46. Whoever uses a proper will makes himself like God by robbery, 46. And, insofar as he can, deprives God of his proper dignity and singular excellence, 46, 147. A proper will is one that is against the will of God, 46. When someone wills what God forbids him to will, he has no author of this will except himself, 46. Whoever subjects his will to the will of another human being nevertheless has a proper will if it is against God, 46. For he himself is the author of subjecting it in that way, 46. Each person is judged before God concerning his own will, 414. See Angel; Soul; Appetite; Concupiscence; Will of God; Free choice; Sin.

Carnal pleasure, 422. The mud of excrement is the stench of carnal pleasure, 205, 206. See Flesh; Concupiscence; Modesty; Virginity.

Vow. Nothing should be vowed without consideration of one’s strength, 193. To bind oneself by a vow to do good is praiseworthy, 346. Whoever makes a good vow pleases God by the vow itself, 346. Whoever has vowed something good should hasten to fulfill what he vowed, so as to please God more, 346. A vow, or purpose of holy conduct, does not diminish the grace of a good work, 87. Whoever keeps what he vowed without reluctance is no less, but more, pleasing to God than if he had made no vow, 87. Nor should he be said to live holily by necessity, but by the same freedom with which he vowed, 87. He has denied himself for God not only the common life but also its license, 87.

Monastic vows, 346, 349, 350. Monastic vows are made before witnesses, 349. Vows must be fulfilled, 195. It is a grave sin to vow to God what one does not wish to fulfill, 195. The members of Christ fulfill what they vow and do what they promise, 158. Those who do not fulfill what they have vowed are faithless, 193. “For a shameful vow, change your decision,” 193. The vow of chastity, 397. In monastic profession all other vows made without an oath are fulfilled, [Col. 1139] 409, 421. Especially in the Cluniac order, 421. And the superior can alter them, 421. The vow of pilgrimage to Saint Giles, 378. A vow never to drink wine, 421.

Voice. Voices signify nothing except things, 148.

W

WAILFRIDUS, bishop of Saint David’s, 433.

WALCHELINUS, bishop of Winchester, 352. He cannot retain for a time, against the unwilling and protesting abbot, Stephen, a monk of Monte Sanctae Trinitatis, who had been entrusted to him by Abbot Rainer, 352. Anselm intercedes with him, at the request of the monk Robert, on behalf of Gislebert, 352.

WALDRICUS, chancellor of King Henry, 443, 445, 446.

To the questions of Walerannus, bishop of Neuburg, Saint Anselm responds, 135, etc. He does not greet him, 135. Because he thought that Walerannus favored Emperor Henry against Pope Urban II, 135. Anselm sent him the treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks*, 135. He wrote to him a letter *On Leavened Bread*, 140. Walerannus was at peace with Pope Paschal II, 138, 139. For this reason Anselm greets him, 137. Walerannus, canon and cantor of the church of Paris, becomes a monk in the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, 369, 370. The bishop of Paris forcibly withdrew him from there, 370. Anselm warns that he can no longer remain in the clerical state without grave guilt and certain danger to his soul, even if he does so by the authority of his bishop, 370.

WALTERUS. See GUALTERUS.

The prior and monks of the monastery of Saint Wandrille, 358. Lanfrancus’s nephew is elected abbot over them against the will of Anselm, their abbot, 357, 358. They suffer harsh treatment from him, 358. Anselm consoles them, 358.

WARELWAST (Willelmus de), 382, 398, 435. At Rome he was on the king’s behalf, together with Anselm, 399 and 435, 443, 446. He advises Anselm that, if he wishes to return to England, he should agree with the king, 399. [Col. 1140]

WARNERIUS. See GUARNERIUS.

The monastery of Saint Werburga, 385, 386. Saint Anselm founded it, 385.

The bishops of Worcester, 373. See Wlstanus.

The bishop of Worcester, 428.

WILLELMUS, abbot, consults Anselm about an excommunicated count, about priests living with concubines, and about reconciling those who have fallen while holding sacred orders, 332.

WILLELMUS and ROGERIUS, monks, 318. Anselm urges Willelmus not to let the seed of good will that has begun to germinate in him wither through love of the world, 326. Those two men were from Bayeux and were educated, 334. They reported much to Abbot Durandus of the House of God concerning Anselm’s religious life and piety, 334.

WILLELMUS, a monk: he came from England to Bec, 373. He fosters murmuring among the Canterbury monks, 377. He is shown indulgence because of his illness and in memory of Lanfranc, 377.

WILLELMUS, a monk of Chester: while Anselm was alive, he composed a poem in his praise, 378. Anselm urges him always to make greater progress, 378. See Guillelmus.

WIMUNDUS. See GUIMUNDUS.

Guillelmus, bishop of Winchester, 393. See Guillelmus.

The bishop of Winchester is to be consecrated by the archbishop of Canterbury, 429.

Attelis, abbess of Winchester, 393.

Wlfricus, a monk, abandoned the cloister, 404. His penance, 404.

WLGARUS DE LIMINGES, Anselm’s servant, 438, 439.

WLSTANUS, bishop of Worcester, 428. Anselm, archbishop, seeks counsel and assistance from him against the bishop of London, 373.

Z

ZACHARIAS. The silence of Zacharias, who did not believe, 180.

ZOROBABEL. By natural descent he was born from Phadaia, and by the law he was the son of Salathiel, 174. [Col. 1139]

ORDER OF THE MATERIAL CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

Continuation of the third part of the works of Saint Anselm.

Third book of the letters containing those written by the archbishop of Canterbury.

**LETTER I.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — That, however reluctant he was, he has been elected archbishop of Canterbury. He urges them to consent to this election. 1

**LETTER II.** — Osbern to Anselm. — He advises him humbly to undertake the burden of the archbishopric of Canterbury. 11

**LETTER III.** — Bishop Gundulf to the monks of Bec. — That they should not grieve over Anselm, their abbot, having been taken from them. 17

**LETTER IV.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — That they should write to Anselm himself and to the king that they willingly consent to his election as archbishop of Canterbury. 18

**LETTER V.** — Osbern to Anselm. — That he should hasten his inauguration. 18

**LETTER VI.** — The monks of Bec to Anselm. — The men of Bec yield Anselm to the Church of Canterbury. 19

**LETTER VII.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — He bears most grievously that he has been taken away from the men of Bec, and that, contrary to the accusations of certain ill-wishers, he did not refuse the archbishopric out of feigned humility. 20

**LETTER VIII.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — That they should elect William, formerly prior at Pexeium, as abbot; and he commands William to undertake this responsibility. But he forbids Baldwin to resign the priory. 26

**LETTER IX.** — Anselm to Roger, abbot. — Commendation of the men of Bec. 27

**LETTER X.** — Anselm to Gislebert, bishop of York. — That he undertook the burden of the archbishopric not out of desire for honor or for any earthly thing. 29

**LETTER XI.** — Anselm to Fulk, bishop of Beauvais. — It has the same subject as the preceding letter. 32

**LETTER XII.** — Anselm to Geoffrey, bishop of Paris. — That he should release the cantor of the Church of Paris who, intending to receive the monastic habit at the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, had been forcibly taken away from there by him; and that he should not bind again to the world one who had chosen Christ. 35

**LETTER XIII.** — Anselm to Walerannus, cantor of the Church of Paris [Col. 1140]. — That he should vigorously pursue the way of life he has undertaken. 37

**LETTER XIV.** — Anselm to Frido. — He indicates that he has already replied that Lord William should be placed over the Church of Bec, and he commends the Church of Bec to Frido’s charity. 38

**LETTER XV.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — Concerning the most gracious letter sent to him by Robert, duke of the Normans; and that his consecration would take place on the day before the Nones of December. 39

**LETTER XVI.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — He congratulates the abbot whom the men of Bec have substituted in his place, instructing him to be a father to the monks and the monks themselves to obey him as sons. 40

**LETTER XVII.** — Anselm to the monks of Bec. — Replying to their letter, he consoles them concerning his absence and absolves them from their sins, as they had requested. 41

**LETTER XVIII.** — Anselm to Countess Ida. — He exhorts the countess to persevere in holiness. 42

**LETTER XIX.** — Anselm to Wulstan, bishop of Worcester. — He asks his advice against the bishop of London, who wished to dedicate the churches of villages belonging to the archbishop of Canterbury within his own diocese. 44
