**LETTER XX.** — Anselm to Osbern, bishop of Exeter. — That the clergy of Exeter should not be burdensome to the monks, and that the bishop should allow them to distinguish the divine offices by the sound of the bells. 47

**LETTER XXI.** — Anselm to William, abbot, and to the monks of Bec. — What he is like must be learned from the mouths of the messengers. 48

**LETTER XXII.** — Anselm to Boson. — That it should not be attributed to laziness that he has not written to him. 48

**LETTER XXIII.** — Anselm to Abbot Ralph and his monks. — A monk who had been ordained by a bishop while under interdict is subjected to perpetual interdict. And the man who sought from a woman herbs with which to kill her husband, if the husband was killed by them, must never be ordained. 51

**LETTER XXIV.** — Anselm to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. — He consults the primate of Lyon about what ought to be done amid his many adversities. Concerning the schism between Urban, whom he supported, and Guibert. He promises the king a large sum of money which, by God’s mercy, he does not pay; hence the king becomes angry. 53

**LETTER XXV.** — Anselm to Boson. — Why he does not write more frequently, because of the king’s anger and hostility. And concerning the book *Why God Became Man*, which Eadmer was copying. 56

**LETTER XXVI.** — To William, abbot, and the brothers of Bec. — That they should pray for him without ceasing and persevere steadfastly in their holy purpose, but especially that they should not wander outside the cloister. That he should not allow almsgiving to be diminished. 56

**LETTER XXVII.** — To Prior Baldwin. — He praises him for his good reputation and seriously forbids subjects to judge the deeds of prelates. 58

**LETTER XXVIII.** — To Robert, count of Flanders. — He exhorts him to pursue justice more and more earnestly. 58

**LETTER XXIX.** — To Prior Henry, Subprior Anthony, Ernulf, Osbern, and the other monks of Canterbury. — That the monks of Canterbury should obey the prior and subprior, and him, in such a way. 59

**LETTER XXX.** — To Matilda, abbess, and the nuns of Winchester. — He earnestly begs that the prayers begun in his name may be continued perpetually and that the nuns devote themselves continually to piety. 60

**LETTER XXXI.** — To Lanfrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Walaricus. — That he should not abandon his flock because of various troubles. 62

**LETTER XXXII.** — To Gervin, bishop of Amiens. — A monk who secretly departed without the knowledge of his prelate cannot be ordained abbot. 64

**LETTER XXXIII.** — To Richard, a monk. — A professed monk is not bound by a vow of pilgrimage that he made while in the world. 64

**LETTER XXXIV.** — He declares that he is not as virtuous as the monk had portrayed him in his poems. 65

**LETTER XXXV.** — To Walter, a cardinal. — He cannot act or provide for the needs of the Church with Walter without his consent and the counsel of the other bishops, especially at a time when enemies were invading England. 66

**LETTER XXXVI.** — To the same. — He refutes the calumnies brought against him and indicates that he neither supports the schism nor is then able to provide for the affairs of the Church. 67

**LETTER XXXVII.** — To Pope Urban. — He begs to be advised why he has not yet approached the pope and what ought to be done. 71

**LETTER XXXVIII.** — To Abbot Lambert. — That he should receive a fugitive monk who is penitent. 72

**LETTER XXXIX.** — To the monks of Bec. — He praises the men of Bec highly for their steadfastness in observing the order. He also exhorts them above all not to judge the deeds of prelates. 73

**LETTER XL.** — To Pope Paschal. — He excuses himself for not yet having greeted him by letter; after explaining his calamities, he gives the reasons why he left England and earnestly begs not to return to England until all the Church’s possessions have been restored. Meanwhile, he declares that he is being supported at Lyon by the archbishop. 74

**LETTER XLI.** — From Henry, king of the English, to Anselm. — He excuses himself for having been inaugurated by other bishops because of the imminent enemy attacks and begs Anselm to return to England as quickly as possible. 75

**LETTER XLII.** — From Pope Paschal to Anselm. — That, now restored to the Church of Canterbury, he should devote himself to restoring the English Church and reconcile the king of the English with the count of Normandy. 76

**LETTER XLIII.** — Anselm to Burgundy and his wife, Richeza. — He congratulates them that his nephew has been dedicated to God’s service, and that God has taken their younger children so that they might now serve God more freely with their whole minds. 76

**LETTER XLIV.** — From Pope Paschal to Anselm. — That he should act steadfastly in defending the liberty of the English Church. 77

**LETTER XLV.** — From the same to the same. — He replies to Anselm, who had consulted him about several doubts. 77

**LETTER XLVI.** — From Benedict to Anselm. — A consolatory letter, composed with affection for his friends. 77

**LETTER XLVII.** — Anselm to Pope Paschal. — After hearing the decrees of the Roman council, which Anselm had attended, the king asks the supreme pontiff about them; Anselm asks that the pope’s judgment be communicated to him. 78

**LETTER XLVIII.** — Anselm to the same. — He awaits counsel in the adversities he has now suffered for nine years. He also asks him to grant the pallium to the elected bishop of York. 79

**LETTER XLIX.** — Anselm to the monks of Chester. — He rejoices in the progress of his monks and exhorts them to careful observance even in the smallest matters. 79

**LETTER L.** — Anselm to Bernard, a monk. — One scourging received out of obedience is worth more than countless scourgings arising from one’s own judgment. 81 [Col. 1142]

**LETTER LI.** — Anselm to Stephen, archdeacon. — That he should prohibit the abbess and nuns of Romsey from the superstitious worship of a dead man whom they regarded as a saint. 82

**LETTER LII.** — Anselm to Gerard, archbishop of York. — He explains that truces were granted with his consent to the sacrilegious man who had taken a veiled woman as his wife. 83

**LETTER LIII.** — From Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to Anselm. — He gives thanks for the treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit against the Greeks*, written and sent to him. 84

**LETTER LIV.** — To the monks of St Albans. — He exhorts the monks to continual observance of their rule. 87

**LETTER LV.** — From Matilda, queen of the English, to Anselm. — That he should moderately relax his daily fast. 88

**LETTER LVI.** — Anselm to Countess Ida. — Concerning her son, whom he admonished, and concerning the benefice of his chaplain Lambert. 90

**LETTER LVII.** — Anselm to Matilda, queen of the English. — He gives thanks for her gifts and friendly admonition. 90

**LETTER LVIII.** — Anselm to Countess Ida. — He gives thanks for the generosity shown to his envoys; praises her concern in matters concerning salvation and absolves her from her sins, imposing a penance. 92

**LETTER LIX.** — Anselm to Countess Clementia. — He praises the count because he granted no investiture, and celebrates this as having been done through the countess’s counsel and prudence. Anselm also exhorts her always to advise her husband. 92

**LETTER LX.** — Anselm to Gerard, archbishop of York. — He says that he did not write the letters for which the bishops of England accused him. 93

**LETTER LXI.** — Anselm to the monks of Saint Edmund. — He proclaims the monks’ unbroken steadfastness amid adversities. 93

**LETTER LXII.** — Anselm to William, archdeacon. — Concerning the acts of the Council of London: they are not to be published until he has communicated them to the bishops, first and again. Meanwhile he offers several of the chapters’ judgments. 94

**LETTER LXIII.** — Anselm to Burgundy and his wife, Richeza. — That they should remember the future life and kindle one another’s love for it. 98

**LETTER LXIV.** — From Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Anselm. — Concerning his safe return from Jerusalem. 101

**LETTER LXV.** — Anselm to Humbert, count and marquis. — He rejoices at receiving his letter and at the same time briefly reviews the benefits Humbert has conferred upon him. He admonishes him to protect the Church, not to dominate it. 102

**LETTER LXVI.** — Anselm to Burgundy and his wife, Richeza. — He informs them that he is going to Jerusalem and what he intends to do. He tells Burgundy to make a general confession of all his sins from childhood and to arrange his affairs so that he does not leave his wife without help and counsel. 104

**LETTER LXVII.** — Anselm to Richeza. — He cannot return to England with a clear conscience, nor live there peacefully. He also says that her son, his nephew, has been consecrated. 105

**LETTER LXVIII.** — Anselm to William, archbishop of Rouen. — That he should recall the abbot of Saint Edmund, who had been intruded by the abbot of Saint-Evroul, and that the property and people of that Church, from which it had been unjustly stripped, should be restored to it. 106

**LETTER LXIX.** — Anselm to Pope Paschal. 106

**LETTER LXX.** — Anselm to Atheliz, abbess of Winchester. — That there should be no grief over the bishop of Winchester, who was expelled for the sake of justice. 108

**LETTER LXXI.** — A charter by which Anselm restored the Oratory and the suburban estate to the monks of Canterbury. 108

**LETTER LXXII.** — Anselm to Samuel, bishop of Dublin. — He reproves him for giving the property of his Church indiscriminately to outsiders and advises him to restore it. 109

**LETTER LXXIII.** — He earnestly begs to be informed of the proper procedure concerning ecclesiastical investitures. 110

**LETTER LXXIV.** — From Pope Paschal to Anselm. — A reply to the preceding letter. 111

**LETTER LXXV.** — Anselm to his friend Connius. — He explains and subdivides three forms of pride. 112

**LETTER LXXVI.** — Anselm to Prior Ernulf and the monks of Canterbury. — From Chartres, where he was received by the countess and the bishop, he writes about the success of his journey and exhorts the men of Canterbury to cling firmly to their religious discipline. 113

**LETTER LXXVII.** — Anselm to the same. — On the same subject as the preceding letter. 114

**LETTER LXXVIII.** — Anselm to Archbishop Gundulf [Col. 1143]. — The king ought not to demand money from monks or from the Church. 115

**LETTER LXXIX.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — He exhorts the king to obey the heavenly King. 116

**LETTER LXXX.** — Anselm to Ernulf and the monks of Canterbury. — Concerning the admission of clerics as monks. 116

**LETTER LXXXI.** — Anselm to Queen Matilda. — Concerning his safety and the appointed time of his journey to Rome. 117

**LETTER LXXXII.** — Anselm to Arnulf and the monks of Canterbury. — That the monks of Canterbury should not be disturbed but serve God in peace, whatever the king may do. 118

**LETTER LXXXIII.** — Anselm to Eustace. — After, with Anselm’s consent, his wife had been enclosed, he had taken another woman to himself; Anselm reproves him for this sin. 118

**LETTER LXXXIV.** — Anselm to Matilda, abbess of Caen. — Feeling herself weakened, she consults Anselm about whether she ought to lay down her burden. He replies that she may laudably do so with the consent of the count, the archbishop of Rouen, and the nuns; otherwise, she should divide her burdens and entrust to wiser sisters those tasks that she herself is unable to fulfill. 119

**LETTER LXXXV.** — Anselm to Gundulf, bishop of Rochester. — He praises him for his concern for the affairs of the Church of Canterbury. He does not wish the bishop of York to be condemned unheard and in his absence. 120

**LETTER LXXXVI.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — He congratulates the king on being concerned for him. 123

**LETTER LXXXVII.** — Anselm to Abbot Geronton. — A cleric bound by an oath of religious profession to two Churches: in which one ought he to remain? For several reasons, it is better for him to remain at Chartres than to return to Geronton. 123

**LETTER LXXXVIII.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — What the pope replied to the consultation concerning the granting of benefices; and that Anselm will obey the pope. 124

**LETTER LXXXIX.** — Anselm to the brothers of Canterbury. — Concerning his return to England, which the monks of Canterbury greatly desire. 125

**LETTER XC.** — Anselm to Ernulf. — On the same subject. 127

**LETTER XCI.** — Anselm to Anthony, the subprior. — He praises and admonishes him. 130

**LETTER XCII.** — Anselm to Gundulf. — He gives thanks to the bishop, who has deserved well of him. 130

**LETTER XCIII.** — From Matilda, queen of the English, to Anselm. — Worthy of a queen’s heart and full of holy affections. 131

**LETTER XCIV.** — From Henry, king of the English, to Anselm. — He grieves that Anselm stubbornly resists him. He indicates that he has sent to the apostolic authority and, meanwhile, agrees that Anselm should duly hold the benefice of the Church of Canterbury. 133

**LETTER XCV.** — Anselm to Henry. — A reply to the preceding letter. 133

**LETTER XCVI.** — From Matilda, queen of the English, to Anselm. — She explains how greatly Anselm’s letter has gladdened her. 134

**LETTER XCVII.** — Anselm to Queen Matilda. — He replies to the preceding letter. 136

**LETTER XCVIII.** — Anselm to William, bishop of Winchester. — That he cannot harm the opposing count because of the injuries inflicted upon him by that man. 137

**LETTER XCIX.** — From Matilda, queen of the English, to Pope Paschal II. — She gives thanks for the exhortatory letter sent to her husband. 138

**LETTER C.** — Anselm to Orduvin. — He congratulates the monk on his steadfast devotion and suggests what he should answer to his detractors. 138

**LETTER CI.** — Anselm to the brothers of Canterbury. — What attitude the monks of Canterbury should adopt amid the calamities they are enduring in his absence. 139

**LETTER CII.** — Anselm to certain apostate monks. — He advises monks who have returned to the cloister not to abandon their penance out of shame. 140

**LETTER CIII.** — Anselm to Warner. — That he should not despise the holy purpose which he began out of fear of death, but should advance in it through holy love. He entrusts him to the care and counsel of Prior Ernulf and advises him to read his letter to Lanzon. 141

**LETTER CIV.** — Anselm to Raynald. — He consoles the devout man who, for the sake of truth, rejects the bishopric into which he had been unwillingly intruded. 141

**LETTER CV.** — To William, bishop of Winchester. — He exhorts him to persevere, with the firmness of spirit with which he began, in observing ecclesiastical ordinances. 142 [Col. 1144]

**LETTER CVI.** — Anselm to Gunter, canon of Saint-Quentin. — Although he is exceedingly fond of quiet, if he has been elected he nevertheless ought, through obedience, to serve his brothers and undertake the burden of the abbacy. 144

**LETTER CVII.** — Anselm to Matilda, queen of the English. — Concerning the queen’s goodwill toward him. 144

**LETTER CVIII.** — Anselm to Farmannus, Orduvin, and Benjamin. — Why he cannot grant their request that they come to him. He replies to each of their difficulties. 144

**LETTER CIX.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — He reproves the king for unjustly exacting money from the priests of England who had violated the Council of London held by Anselm, since the punishment of this fault belongs only to the bishops. 146

**LETTER CX.** — Anselm to Prior Ernulf and the brothers of Canterbury. — He excuses himself for having informed them late about the agreement between himself and the king, in which the king reinvested him with the archbishopric after restoring all the property of the Church of Canterbury. Nevertheless, Anselm does not wish to enter England until the king’s legate has returned from Rome. Meanwhile, having recovered the use of his authority, he deprives every priest who kept women of every ecclesiastical benefice. He permits the count of Meulan, who had promised his support to the Church, to enter the Church. 148

**LETTER CXI.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — He says that he is not displeased by the king’s legate remaining in Rome beyond the appointed time, but by his own prolonged absence from his flock, especially since the king sets no deadline. 149

**LETTER CXII.** — Anselm to Bishop Gundulf, Prior Ernulf, and others. — He confirms the anathema justly pronounced by his archdeacon against priests who keep women. 150

**LETTER CXIII.** — Anselm to Warner. — He praises him for his holy desire to return to his father and at the same time advises him to be most observant of the order. 151

**LETTER CXIV.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — He sends Gislebert of Bec to the king, someone whom the king may safely trust with messages to Anselm. He declares Paschal canonically elected and the other man an invader of the apostolic see. 151

**LETTER CXV.** — Anselm to G——, abbot. — He advises the man elected bishop that, while preserving obedience, his spirit should flee so great a burden. But he advises those who elected him to compel him to undertake the burden because he is the more worthy. 152

**LETTER CXVI.** — Anselm to Odo. — He further inflames the man already burning with zeal to pursue a purer kind of life. Vows to go to Rome or Jerusalem are fulfilled in monastic profession. 152

**LETTER CXVII.** — Anselm to Prior Ernulf and Archdeacon William. — That they should receive and assist Robert most kindly as he abandons Judaism and embraces Christianity. 153

**LETTER CXVIII.** — Anselm to Prior Alfer and the monks of Saint Edmund. — He praises their unconquered spirit amid adversities. He exhorts them to confess their sins to the prior and to guard their hearts with every vigilance. 155

**LETTER CXIX.** — From Matilda, queen of the English, to Anselm. — How highly she values Anselm’s letters. And that she granted the abbacy of Malmesbury to Edulf, saving all the rights of the archbishop. 156

**LETTER CXX.** — Anselm to Matilda. — He refused to confirm Edulf as abbot because she had sent him a cup with letters through messengers. 156

**LETTER CXXI.** — From Gerard, archbishop of York; Robert, bishop of Chester; Herbert, bishop of Norwich; Ralph, bishop of Chichester; Samson, bishop of Worcester; and William, elected bishop of Winchester, to Anselm. — They invite Anselm to England, promising him their assistance. 157

**LETTER CXXII.** — Anselm to his bishops. — He grieves over the misery of the English Church and of the bishops, and rejoices in the assistance they have promised him. 158

**LETTER CXXIII.** — To Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. — He asks to be strengthened by the archbishop’s prudent replies. 159

**LETTER CXXIV.** — From Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, to Anselm. — He replies to the preceding letter. 160

**LETTER CXXV.** — Anselm to Eulalia, abbess. — He is most grateful for the prayers of the prelate and her daughters. He exhorts them to be obedient and faithful even in the smallest matters. 161

**LETTER CXXVI.** — Anselm to Henry, king of the English. — The transfer of a bishop ought not to take place without the consent of the archbishop and the bishops of the province, and without great deliberation and apostolic authority. 162

**LETTER CXXVII.** — Anselm to Mabilia, a nun. — That one consecrated to God should abstain from the society of secular people. 163 [Col. 1145]

**LETTER CXXVIII.** — Anselm to Matilda, queen of the English. — He refuses, although asked by the queen, to give testimony concerning a man unknown to him. 164

**LETTER CXXIX.** — Anselm to Helgot, abbot of Saint-Ouen. — He explains to his friend, who is most eager to know, how matters stand after his return to England. 164

**LETTER CXXX.** — Anselm to P——, a monk of Saint-Martin of Sées. — He disapproves of the desire of a monk planning to go to Jerusalem, in accordance with the judgment of the apostolic authority which he himself had heard from him. 165

**LETTER CXXXI.** — From Pope Paschal II to Gerard, bishop of York. — That he should show Anselm fidelity according to ancient custom. 166

**LETTER CXXXII.** — Anselm to Alexander, king of the Scots. — He congratulates the king on being raised to his father’s throne. 166

**LETTER CXXXIII.** — Anselm to Robert and his sisters and daughters. — He sends the exhortation they requested, to kindle them to live well: that they should have a good will in all things; that they should strive to conquer troublesome thoughts and involuntary impulses by despising them, lest they be disturbed by them. 167

**LETTER CXXXIV.** — Anselm to Walerannus. 169

**LETTER CXXXV.** — Walerannus to Anselm. 169

**LETTER CXXXVI.** — Anselm to Walerannus. 169

**LETTER CXXXVII.** — Anselm to Turold, a monk of Bec. — He rejoices greatly that Turold has renounced the world. 169

**LETTER CXXXVIII.** — Anselm to Basilia. — He writes a very devout letter to this most devout woman. That a person is always either ascending into heaven or descending into hell, and that one ought to pay especially close attention to this. 170

**LETTER CXXXIX.** — To Lambert, abbot of Saint Bertin. — He advises him to accept the governance offered to him. 171

**LETTER CXL.** — From Pope Paschal to Anselm. — He rejoices greatly that Henry has obeyed the ecclesiastical commands. He absolves Anselm from the excommunication which Anselm feared he had incurred because of the king’s investitures. He gives him authority to absolve others who had received investiture from the king, and the king himself, except the abbot of Ely. 172

**LETTER CXLI.** — Anselm to Arnulf, abbot of Troarn. — He shares in the suffering of the man afflicted by illness and gives the requested advice concerning relinquishing the provostship: he should give it up if the archbishop and the brothers consent. 172

**LETTER CXLII.** — Anselm to Muriardach, king of Ireland. — He praises this king for the prosperity of his peaceful reign. He admonishes him to correct what needs correcting, especially the marriages of relatives and the ordinations of irregular bishops. 173

**LETTER CXLIII.** — Anselm to Gislebert, bishop of Lunice. — He gives thanks to the prelate, who rejoices that the affairs of the Church were prospering under his auspices. 174

**LETTER CXLIV.** — To an apostate monk. — Through commands, counsels, and threats, he recalls two wandering sheep to the flock. 175

**LETTER CXLV.** — Walter to Anselm. — He exults in Anselm’s happy return to England and at the same time asks him for some pious consolation. 176

**LETTER CXLVI.** — Anselm to Walter. — A reply to the preceding letter. 177

**LETTER CXLVII.** — Anselm to Muriardach, king of Ireland. — He repeatedly begs him to remedy, or arrange to have remedied, the pestilential customs of his kingdom. He asks that men no longer exchange their wives for the wives of others, and that a bishop be established in one fixed place and ordained only by several bishops. 178

**LETTER CXLVIII.** — Anselm to Odo, a monk. — That he should not abandon the office entrusted to him because of advancing age. 180

**LETTER CXLIX.** — Anselm to Thomas, archbishop of York. — A Church ought not to be without a pastor for more than three months; therefore he orders Thomas to present himself at Canterbury on the eighth day before the Ides of September, to be consecrated by Anselm. He also warns him not to presume to consecrate the elected bishop of Saint Andrews in Scotland before he himself has been consecrated. 181

**LETTER CL.** — Anselm to Geoffrey. — He praises the good man for the integrity of his life and warns him against whom he should beware, especially lest, in discerning the deeds of others, he despise them. 182

**LETTER CLI.** — Anselm to Prior John and the congregation of Bath. — They will become God’s house and temple if they preserve mutual harmony and maintain observance even in the smallest matters. 183

**LETTER CLII.** — Anselm to Pope Paschal II. — That he should not send the pallium to the archbishop of York before his consecration, nor to the bishop of London, who had never possessed it, lest the primacy of the Church of Canterbury fall from its dignity, something Anselm absolutely cannot tolerate. He also asks whether the pope permits the king of the Germans to grant investitures, as the king of England had heard. 184

**LETTER CLIII.** — From Pope Paschal to Anselm. — He replies to the preceding letter that he will in no way diminish the dignity of Anselm’s Church, nor has he ever tolerated investitures being granted by the king of the Germans. 186

**LETTER CLIV.** — Anselm to William, abbot of Bec. — Vows pronounced before monastic profession remain at the disposition of the prelate. 186

**LETTER CLV.** — Anselm to Thomas, archbishop of York. — He forbids him all the duties of the archbishopric until he has given Anselm the fidelity promised according to ancient custom. 187

**LETTER CLVI.** — Anselm to William, abbot, and the congregation of Bec. — He has nothing more important than them and will not forget them unless he ceases to exist. 188

**LETTER CLVII.** — Anselm to a certain lady. 189

**LETTER CLVIII.** — Concerning the marriages of relatives. 194

**LETTER CLIX.** — Anselm to William, abbot. 194

**LETTER CLX.** — From Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to Anselm. 195

**LETTER CLXI.** — From the same to Anselm. 196

**LETTER CLXII.** — From the same to Anselm. 197

**LETTER CLXIII.** — Anselm to Gelduin, abbot of Auchy-les-Mines. 198

**LETTERS CLXIV–CLXXXVIII.** — They are found in Eadmer’s *History of Recent Events*. 198

EPISTLE XCV.—Anselm to Pope Paschal. 248

EPISTLE XCVII.—Samson, priest of the Church of Worcester, to Anselm. 249  
EPISTLE XCVIII.—Anselm to Count Elias. 249  
EPISTLE XCIX.—Anselm to Count Robert. 250  
EPISTLE C.—Anselm to Ralph, bishop of Chichester. 250  
EPISTLE CI.—Anselm to R., bishop. 250  
EPISTLE CII.—A certain person to Anselm. 251  
EPISTLE CIII.—Anselm to Lanfranc.—He sends him his work entitled *Monologion* for correction or approval. 252  
EPISTLE CIV.—Anselm to Bernard and his monks. 252  
EPISTLE CV.—Anselm to Abbess F. and her community. 254  
EPISTLE CVI.—To Gilbert.—On the sacrament of the altar. 254  
EPISTLE CVII.—Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, on the body and blood of the Lord. 255  
EPISTLE CVIII.—Gilbert, abbot, to Anselm. 258  
EPISTLE CIX.—Anselm to Richard the monk.—He urges Richard, a monk of Bec, to put obedience before indiscreet afflictions of his body. 257  
EPISTLE CX.—Anselm to Robert, *Seyt*, editor.—He urges observance in the smallest matters, and that they should always imagine the angels standing beside them and imitate their way of life. 257  
EPISTLE CXI.—Anselm to Hugh.—He urges Hugh the monk, from whom he had heard that he was greatly loved, neither to conceal nor defend his faults, always to wish his heart to be open to his abbot, and to subordinate his own opinions to obedience. 259  
EPISTLE CXII.—Anselm to William.—He admonishes his friend William always to be present to God and to preserve his love in such a way that he strives with every effort to avoid offending God. 260  
EPISTLE CXIII.—Anselm to Herbert, bishop of Thetford.—He urges Herbert, bishop of Thetford, to prohibit from sacred functions priests disobedient to the council and unwilling to dismiss women, and to substitute others—whether clerics or monks—for them in ecclesiastical duties. 260  
EPISTLE CXIV.—Anselm to his nephew.—He commends good morals, diligence, and continual use of the Latin language to his nephew Anselm. Concerning his sister, the nephew’s mother, he reports that the nuns admitted her at Marcigny, but when he asked for her back, they refused her to him. 261  
EPISTLE CXV.—Anselm to Cardinal Walter.—He asks Walter, cardinal-bishop of Albano and papal legate in England, to obtain aid and support for him from the Roman pontiff to sustain the burden of his archbishopric. 262  
EPISTLE CXVI.—Anselm to Donnald, Donatus, and the other bishops.—He asks the bishops of Ireland to pray to God for him, oppressed by many hardships, while also admonishing each of them to fulfill the duties of his office and, if any controversy should arise among them, to refer the entire matter to him. 262  
EPISTLE CXVII.—Anselm to Hugh the archdeacon.—He states with how much honor and generosity he was received by everyone during his exile. 263  
EPISTLE CXVIII.—Anselm to Lambert, bishop of Arras. 264  
EPISTLE CXIX.—Anselm to the same. 265  
EPISTLE CXX.—Anselm to Hernostus. 265
